# Patrologia Latina, volume 132 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Volume 132

## Volume Front Matter

## Series Title Page

*The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all monuments of Catholic tradition surviving from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with certain manuscripts, and most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating their subject matter; expanded with doubtful and apocryphal works, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual biblical books, and in which places of their works they have done so.*

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete series in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The *Patrologia* has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition sell for one thousand francs; three hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are supplied in this edition only in Latin translation.

# Tenth Century

## The Complete Works of Regino, Abbot of Prüm, and Hucbald, Monk of Elnone

Revised according to editions of better authority and illustrated with various monuments, namely, minor works on the art of music supplied by Dom Martin Gerbert, abbot of Saint Blasien in the Black Forest, *Collection of Ecclesiastical Writers on Music*.

Also included are the letters and privileges of John X, Leo VI, Stephen VII, Leo VII, and Stephen VIII, Roman pontiffs.

Interspersed are surviving writings or fragments of the writings of Robert of Metz; Radbod of Utrecht; Waldrammus of Strasbourg; Salomo of Constance; Stephen of Liège; Walter of Sens; Dado, bishop of Verdun; Hervaeus of Reims; Agio of Narbonne; Seulfus of Reims, archbishop; Odilo, monk of Saint Medard of Soissons; Radbod of Dol; Abbo, monk of Saint-Germain; and Cyprian of Córdoba.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete series in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, on the street called d’Amboise, near the gate of Paris commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1853.

# In the Year of Our Lord 915: Regino, Abbot of Prüm

## Regino’s Chronicle

[Col. 0009]

## Pertz’s Preface to Regino’s Chronicle

(*Monumenta Germaniae historica*, vol. 1, p. 537.)

[Col. 009]

[Col. 0009A]

Regino, if the sixteenth-century *Annals of Prüm* are to be trusted, was born of noble parents at Altrip on the Rhine. From the year 892 onward he governed the monastery of Prüm in the Ardennes. Having been deprived of this office through the actions of rivals, as he himself complains, in 899 he “endured Richarius, brother of Gerhard and Mathfrid, the most powerful counts in Lotharingia, as the envious successor to his office.” He spent the remainder of his life in the monastery of Saint Maximin near the walls of the city of Trier, where he also died. His gravestone, together with a broken crozier, was discovered in 1581. Its inscribed elegies, although badly mutilated, seem to indicate the year of his death, 915:

“[lacuna] *fessa* [‘weary,’ with the antecedent lost] contains Regino’s bones. He himself, a distinguished and pious abbot, once presided over the monastery of Prüm with beneficent ways, after [lacuna].”

[Col. 0009B]

“... 915.”

The leisure that he enjoyed during the final years of his life he devoted to composing both chronicles and, at the command of Ratbod, archbishop of Trier, two books *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines and the Christian Religion*, as well as a letter *On Harmonic Instruction* addressed to the same Ratbod and prefixed to a lectionary for the whole year. The latter work has not yet been published. Stephen Baluze published the books on ecclesiastical discipline at Paris in 1671, after Joachim Hildebrand. The first book deals with ecclesiastical matters and persons, the second with the life and conduct of laypeople. The books of the *Chronicle*, together with the continuation by an anonymous author down to the year 967, have often been printed, since everyone had long been convinced that they contributed greatly to the elucidation of history.

Nevertheless, after examining them somewhat more carefully, we must admit that most of them offer readers no usefulness at all. For the first book, constructed upon Bede’s *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World* as upon its foundation [Col. 0009C], contributes almost nothing of its own in recounting events, but merely reproduces the very words and statements of its sources. Besides Bede, it copies an ancient martyrology [Col. 0010A] or lives of the saints; the deeds of the Frankish kings; Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*; the deeds of the Roman pontiffs; the deeds of Dagobert; and the lives of Saints Goar and Lambert. Toward the end of the book, when Bede’s *Chronicle* was no longer sufficient for arranging events in chronological order, it also used the *Annals of Petau* for the years 4, 5, 10, 15, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, and 26 of Charles the Mayor of the Palace.

In the second book one may distinguish three different styles of composition. For the years 741–814, the author relies on the *Annals of Lorsch*. Apart from what he took from them and quite often corrupted [Note: For example, in 796, Iring, prince of the Avar people; in 799, the city called Oscaclavis; in 803, Calistus and Candidatus; in 806, Geta the patrician; in 808, the king of the North Danes; in 810, “having crossed the Rhine at the place called Lippa”; and many similar examples.], he incorporated a closing passage concerning King Pippin’s consecration [Note: Bouquet, vol. 5, pp. 9–10.], and in the years 746 and 753 made use of certain things heard from the narration of elders. Although these accounts were of doubtful reliability, later writers nevertheless found them pleasing.

For the years 814–870 he so greatly distorted the order of events that it is clear that all these matters must be attributed not to written monuments but to the reports and memory of the Fathers—sources which, as he himself admits, were not sufficiently reliable. Only for the years 829, 847, 851, and 860 does he seem to have consulted the necrology of his monastery; and, in recounting [Col. 0010B] the dispute between Lothair and Theutberga, some collection of letters, such as the distinguished Wyttenbach reports still to exist at Trier [Note: *Archiv*, etc., vol. 3, pp. 377–380].

Finally, after the year 870, he himself, an attentive observer of his own age, preserved many things otherwise unknown to memory. Yet even in these passages it could not happen that everything he assigned to its own year had actually occurred then, since he did not begin the entire work until after the year 900 [Note: After the death of Zwentibold, king of Lotharingia. Cf. the account of King Rudolf under the year 888; perhaps also after the year 901, to which is assigned the invasion of Italy by the Hungarians, although it had already occurred in 900.]. [Col. 0010C] He completed it in 907, before news of the death of Alan, king of the Britons, could reach Germany [Note: Compare the Chronicle under the year 874: “Alan, who until now has vigorously governed this land—Britain.”]. He appears to have added the preface to Adalbero, bishop of Augsburg, at the beginning of 908, while Burchard, duke of the Thuringians, was still alive [Note: Compare the Chronicle under the year 892: “The duchy is entrusted to Count Burchard, who has vigorously governed it until now,” and the preface.].

[Col. 0011A]

The question of what sort of authority should be attributed to Regino, and in which matters, can now be judged. Whatever he drew from other sources should be sought not in him but in the sources themselves. The closer the remaining material comes to the year 900, the greater the confidence it deserves. The entire structure of the work, together with what he says about himself under the years 892 and 899, persuades us that the author never deliberately falsified the truth.

He counts the years from the incarnation of the Lord. From a comparison of the years 34, 888, and 892, it is beyond doubt that by this expression he means the day of the Nativity and that he begins the year on 25 December.

The work became so well received by people of later ages that it not only acquired a continuator in the same century and was almost entirely copied by the annalist of Metz, but was later also adapted for their own purposes by leading historians such as Hermannus Contractus, Sigebert of Gembloux, and Otto of Freising. In addition, the account of the destruction of Trier in 882 in the *Deeds of the Treveri*, several passages in the *Saxon Chronographer* and Hugh of Flavigny, and many more in the *Saxon Annalist* were derived from it. No one will fail to see how useful all these works are for restoring Regino’s text.

I had still greater assistance for this purpose when I was able to consult ancient manuscripts of Regino, either discovered through the efforts of our associates or collated with printed editions at the expense of the Society. The following manuscripts therefore served the new edition:

[Col. 0011B]

1. A codex of the public library of the city of Schaffhausen, written on parchment in quarto, from the tenth or eleventh century. It was discovered by the late Ittner, intimate counsellor of His Serene Highness the Grand Duke of Baden, whom, while he lived, we counted among the most ardent promoters of our work. In 1821 it was most diligently collated with the printed editions by the distinguished Carl Dumge, archivist to that prince. He reports that it is the work of more than forty scribes, some of whom excelled in the beauty of their handwriting. I found it the best of all those available to me. Next in quality is:

2. A codex of the court library at Karlsruhe, written on parchment in large octavo, consisting of eighty-eight folios and copied in the eleventh century. It was discovered by the distinguished Molter, one of the counsellors of His Serene Highness the Grand Duke of Baden and director of the Karlsruhe library, who voluntarily presented his very careful collation to the Society. From an inscription at the end, the codex seems formerly to have belonged to a certain Albert, if I am not mistaken, of Kneringen. [Col. 0011C] The first lines before the words “and the study of all philosophy” have been erased, and no continuation has been added.

One folio containing the history of the years 901 and 902 is missing. The entire account of the years 773–794, beginning with the words “Then the king set up camp at the same enclosures” and ending with “But when they had heard,” is missing from its proper place. Nevertheless, everything that is read in Regino from the words “In the year 783, after these things, Bertrada died” through the end of the year 795 has been inserted between the words “The leaders of this faction were” in the year 801 and the beginning of the following year.

3. A codex formerly belonging to the monastery of Prüm and now to the public library at Trier, written on parchment in small quarto. After Regino it contains the first eight chapters of Thegan, Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* and *Annals*, and finally the remaining chapters of Thegan. At the end it bears an old inscription:

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1084, this volume was written by [Col. 0011D] Arnold the scholar, at the command of Lord Wolfram, the pious and venerable abbot of the monastery of Prüm.”

The collation of the entire codex is due to the distinguished Wyttenbach, whose observations on the book’s various fortunes will be worth reading:

“The manuscript codex which I collated was written in 1084 by a monk of the monastery of Prüm. By some accident, however, it came into the hands of a prior of the monastery of Echternach in the sixteenth century. This prior, Father Henry, at the urgent and diligent request of Peter Uren, pastor at Seffern, made at the monastery of Saint Maximin in Trier, sent it back to Prüm in 1582.

“Afterward, in the course of time, it again passed through the hands of many people. It was also granted by Archbishop John to the college of the Society of Jesus, which at that time was engaged in the study of the history of Trier, in 1589. Finally, it was returned to the library of Prüm, its true and proper owner, in 1604. In our own time it was kept by a certain monk [Col. 0012A] of the abbey of Prüm; after his death it passed into my possession in 1820.”

The codex was regarded by the inexperienced as an autograph. Although certainly of good quality, it was not copied directly from the autograph, but, together with the Schaffhausen and Karlsruhe codices, descended from a manuscript already corrupted in several places. Arnold the monk also attempted to fill its lacunae.

These three codices agree with one another, as in many other matters, especially in this: none of them contains any continuation after the year 906, nor does any of them contain the sentence under the year 892—although it does not linger over it—“through the actions of rivals I endured Richarius, brother of Gerhard and Mathfrid, as the envious successor to my office.” I therefore suppose that this sentence is likewise absent from all the other codices that extend only to the year 906. Conversely, all the codices known to me that extend beyond the year 906 preserve that sentence, but omit the immediately following passage:

“the slanderous complaint [Col. 0012B] of the opponents concerning past causes and elapsed times ...”

3b. Besides these, I learned from Gatterer’s book *Historical Library*, vol. 10, p. 251, that a codex lacking a continuation is preserved at Cambridge in Clare Hall. I was unable, however, to gain possession of it.

4. The *Annals of Metz*, compiled in the tenth or eleventh century, omit all the Prüm material and therefore omit both of these sentences. Since, however, in those places where the three codices mentioned above differ from the others they come closer to the readings of those three codices, they should be regarded as having descended from a codex to which no continuation had been added.

5. All the printed editions of Regino depend on the first edition, printed in 1521. That edition contains both the continuation and the two sentences, one of which, as I have noted, is always absent from the manuscripts. I therefore suppose that the first editor had two codices in hand: one without the continuation, the other supplied with it.

a) The first edition of Regino’s work, prepared by Sebastian von Rotenhan, “casually revised with the assistance of Johannes Huttich,” appeared at Mainz in August 1521 under the following title:

[Col. 0012C]

“Annals of Regino, monk of Prüm, discussing not so much the lives of the emperors as the deeds of other Germans, learnedly and concisely, published nearly six hundred years ago.”

It contains an image of Regino and heraldic arms, owed to Rotenhan’s ingenuity, which today no reader would regret lacking. The editors had either obtained more defective manuscripts or were less skilled at reading them; yet they said not a word about their sources.

b) Nor did Simon Schardius, when he inserted Rotenhan’s book into his four *Chronographs* in 1566, give it any new attention. He even left the word “six hundred” untouched in Rotenhan’s title.

c) The first edition was received with almost the same carelessness into volume 1 of Pistorius’s *German Writers*, published at Frankfurt in 1584 and again in 1669.

d) The Strasbourg edition, undertaken in 1609 at the expense of the bookseller Lazarus Zetzner, was corrected in several places with the help of a certain Karlsruhe [Col. 0012D] manuscript or one closely related to it.

e) The third Pistorius edition, published at Regensburg in 1726 by Burkhard Gotthelf Struve, was furnished with annotations and occasionally corrected with the aid of Paul the Deacon and the annalists of Metz and Saxony. Nevertheless, it is full of defects and contributed little either to correcting or illuminating the text. Bouquet certainly supplied better observations to the annalist of Metz, whom he had intended to insert in place of Regino into his collection.

6. All of Regino’s codices in which some continuation is found agree so unmistakably with one another, both in certain sentences and in the order of words, that there can be no doubt that they have a common origin. Among them, the codex of the Royal Library of Paris, numbered 5016, holds almost the chief place because of its closer affinity with the preceding manuscripts.

It is written on parchment in folio and dates from the eleventh century. It seems formerly to have belonged to the monastery of Saint Mary of Ottenburg in the diocese of Mainz [Col. 0013A] [Note: Compare Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. 3, p. 328.]. It carries the continuation down to the words under the year 959, “the siege of Caprimont,” without completing the sentence.

Since the *Chronicle* of Hermannus Contractus is appended to it in the Regino codex of Muri and in the three manuscripts descended from that codex—the Engelberg manuscript, the fourteenth-century Einsiedeln manuscript, and the Augsburg manuscript [Note: Compare *Prodromus of Sacred Germany*, pp. 8, 9, 14; *Archive of the Society*, etc., vols. 3 and 5, p. 762; Placidus Braun, *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra*, p. 110]—I believe that all of them derive from the Paris manuscript.

The Paris codex was collated with the printed editions at the Society’s expense, but not with the diligence that should have given attention even to minor details.

7. In contrast, the five codices preserved in Austria were carefully placed at our disposal by Mr. Joseph Pirsner, a Carniolan jurist. First among them must be mentioned the codex kept in the Imperial Library at Vienna among the secular historians, numbered 332. It is written on parchment in folio and was copied at the end of the eleventh century. It formerly belonged to the monastery of Admont in Styria, and therefore may perhaps have descended from a Salzburg codex.

[Col. 0013B]

Besides Regino, it contains Thegan and Victor’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*. Almost everywhere the scribe uses *ci* before a vowel in place of *ti*: *ocium*, *accio*, *licium*, *succedencium*. He also writes *Arnulfus*, *Haistulfus*, and *Ruodolfus* rather than *Arnulphus*, *Aistulphus*, and *Rudolphus*; *adhulterium* and *adulterium*; *adhulescens*, *adulescens*, and *adolescens*; *iohannes*; *habundare*; *actenus*—rarely *hactenus*; *hac* and *hubi*—rarely *ac* for *et*, and *ubi*; *Ugo*—rarely *Hugo*; *hlotharius*; *hludowicus*; *michahel*; *ostis*; and *lotharius*, *ludowicus*, *michael*, *ostis*.

It writes *exortari*; *pascha* and *pasca*; *nichil* and *nihil*; *aetiam*, *aeciam*, *etiam*, and *eciam*; *poene* and *pene*; *equus* and *aequus*; *coepit* and *cepit* with the same meaning; *aecclesia* and *ecclesia*; *fresia*; *fresones*; *sterelitas*; *longobardi*—rarely *langobardi*; *nicoforus*; *eclypsis*; *paralisis*; *dionisius*; *hierosolima*; *scithia*; *stilus*; *elemosina*; *silva* and *sylva*; *radisbona* and *radasbona*; *traicere*; *proicere*; *belua*; *milia*; *litus*; *litterae* and *literae*; *pellex* and *pelex*; *quattuor*; *brittones*; *affrica* and *africa*; [Col. 0013C] *cincxi*; *extincxi*; *ascensus* in place of *assensus*; *obtimates* and *optimates*; and *abba* and *abbas*. It offers some distinctive readings under the years 775 and 944.

8. The Saxon Annalist copies out Regino and his continuation in such a way that he often abbreviates and adapts them for his own purposes; he must therefore also be taken into account. I have also noted certain readings from a codex formerly seen in the monastery of Saint Godehard at Hildesheim, whether of Regino or, as Eckard maintains, of the Saxon Annalist, written in the margin of the Pistorius edition by the elder Meibom and preserved in the Royal Library at Hanover.

9–10. The codices of the Imperial Library at Vienna among the secular historians, nos. 669 and 1068, written on parchment in folio and dating from the twelfth century.

[Col. 0014A]

11. A parchment codex in folio from the twelfth century, belonging to the library of the monastery of Klosterneuburg in Austria.

12. The Vienna codex of secular history, no. 1080, written on paper in folio in the fifteenth century: all recognize one and the same source. This is shown, among many other things, by the fact that they report that Emperor Arnulf was buried not at Ötting but at Regensburg, in the monastery of Saint Emmeram, and share the same closing clause:

“Thus far Regino. We have added what follows, attaching Regino’s continuation to Regino.”

Since Austria received its writings from Bavaria, and the same clause is read in a parchment codex of the tenth century, formerly from Freising and now preserved in the Royal Library at Munich [Note: Compare Docen in V. Aretin, *Contributions*, vol. 7, pp. 239, 242], I supposed that it was the source of the Austrian manuscripts and consulted our Docen about several of its readings.

The distinguished scholar replied that the remaining readings agreed with those in the Austrian codices, but that the passage concerning Arnulf’s burial—now reading as in the printed editions—had formerly been erased by scraping, and that the following had been written in the margin [Col. 0014B]:

“*Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendatium*”—“You will destroy all who speak falsehood.”

It may therefore now be confidently asserted that the Freising codex is the source of the Austrian manuscripts. Nevertheless, although the Austrian manuscripts agree with it in a remarkable way, it was by no means necessary to collate the entire Freising manuscript with the printed editions.

These are the resources with whose help I undertook the new edition of Regino. In addition, at Modena I examined a Regino codex written in 1093 in the ducal library. It contained only the first book and could therefore be of no use to us.

According to Mabillon, the Gembloux codex burned together with the monastery. At Paris there are royal codices nos. 5017, from the twelfth century; 5018, from the twelfth century and containing a continuation; and 5922, from the twelfth century, defective at the end. At London there are the Harley manuscript no. 3676 and the Cotton manuscript *Tiberius* C. XI.1. At Cambridge, in the library of Saint Benedict, there is a *Chronicle of the Abbot of the Monastery of Prüm from the Birth of Christ to the Year 1002*. According to Gatterer, others exist in Holland, and it is reported that a tenth-century codex was formerly at the monastery of Muri [Col. 0014C] [Note: Compare *Archive*, etc., vol. 5, p. 767]. May their absence not awaken regret among the readers of this edition.

For the rest, I revised the first book and part of the second, up to the year 814, only cursorily with the aid of the Schaffhausen codex, adding whatever seemed more important among the material found elsewhere. For the years 814–906 I corrected the Schaffhausen codex with the assistance of the others.

Regino dedicated his work to Bishop Adalbero. At that time there were two men of that name, one presiding over the church of Basel, the other over the church of Augsburg. Regino mentions the Augsburg bishop in his Chronicle under the year 887, and with great praise; it is reasonable to suppose that the work was dedicated to him.

[Col. 0013]

# Chronicle

[Col. 0013]

## Here Begins the Preface to the Following Work

[Note: The preface together with the first book is absent from manuscript 10.]

To the most excellent in intellect and richly distinguished in every branch of philosophical study, Lord Adalbero [Note: *Adhalbaroni*, manuscript 1; *adalperoni*, manuscript 7], bishop [Note: *bishop of Trier*, manuscript 5], Regino, although the least of all Christians, yet in every respect most devoted to your [Col. 0014] eminence, sends the faithful service of his prayers.

I have sent to your singular wisdom for examination the chronicle [Note: *The chronicle which...*, manuscript 5] that I have committed to writing concerning our own times and those of our predecessors [Col. 0015A], so that by your discerning judgment it may either be approved or condemned.

I have divided it into two little books, beginning with the first year of the Lord’s incarnation and bringing the work undertaken to completion down to the present year, which is reckoned as the nine hundred and eighth from the aforesaid incarnation of the Lord.

For it seemed unworthy to me that, although the historians of the Hebrews, Greeks, Romans, and other peoples have transmitted in writing to our knowledge the events accomplished in their own days, there should be such perpetual silence concerning our own times, although they are far less important, that it might seem either that human activity had ceased in our days, or perhaps that people had done nothing worthy of being committed to memory [Col. 0015B], or, if events worthy of remembrance had taken place, that no one qualified to record them in writing [Col. 0016A] had been found [Note: “that a notary had been found,” manuscript 6], while the notaries through negligence languished in idleness [Note: “the notary ... languishing,” manuscript 7].

For this reason I did not permit the times of our fathers and our own times to pass wholly untouched. Rather, I took care to record a few things from among many, and, once I had reached the present age, I restrained my pen on account of certain people who are still alive, leaving it to posterity to set these matters forth more fully.

Receive, then, this small gift with the same kindness with which it has been sent from my own lowliness. At the end I ask the reader that, if these statements of ours, whatever their character, should please him and he should wish to have them copied for himself, he should in no way omit this little preface [Note: “but have it written at the very beginning of the booklet,” absent from manuscripts 1, 2, and 3].

[Col. 0016B]

May divine providence deign to preserve the glory of your eminence for a long time in safety, for the benefit of many.

## The Preface Ends

[Note: “The preface ends. Many dispute, and the matter is still undecided, whether *chronica* is feminine or neuter; but to us it seems preferable to use it as neuter.” Thus manuscript 2.]

# Here Begins the Little Book on the Times of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Col. 0015]

[Col. 0015C]

In the forty-second year of the reign of Octavian Caesar, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born. On that same night he was announced by angels and visited by shepherds. On the eighth day he was circumcised. On the thirteenth day, with the star as guide, he was adored by the Magi and proclaimed through mystical gifts. On the fortieth day he was brought by his parents into the temple with an offering, received by Simeon, and recognized by Anna. After this he was carried into Egypt, where he remained until the death of Herod.

In the second year of the Lord’s incarnation, Herod sent men into Bethlehem and all its territory and ordered the slaughter of the innocent children. Then, turning his weapons against members of his own household, he killed many. He murdered his beloved wife Mariamne; ordered the sons [Col. 0015D] whom he had fathered by her, Aristobulus and Alexander, to be strangled in Samaria; and finally struck down with the sword Antipater, born of Doris, the instigator and accuser of all evils. After this he perished by a miserable death in the sixth year of the Lord’s incarnation, but in the thirty-sixth year of his reign.

In the seventh year of the Lord’s incarnation, Archelaus, Herod’s son, reigned in Judea. The Lord Jesus was brought back from Egypt and, because of fear of the aforementioned king, withdrew to Nazareth, a city of Galilee, where he lived until the time of his baptism.

[Col. 0016C]

In the twelfth year of his age, the Lord Jesus went up to Jerusalem. There, sitting in the temple among the teachers, he was found by his parents after three days.

In the fifteenth year of the Lord’s incarnation, Archelaus was accused by the Jews before Caesar and sent into exile in the city of Vienne in Gaul. The Jewish kingdom was divided among his four brothers, Herod, Antipater, Lysanias, and Philip. After ruling the Roman empire for fifty-six years and six months, Caesar Augustus died.

In the sixteenth year of the Lord’s incarnation, Tiberius began to reign, and he reigned for twenty-six years.

In the twenty-seventh year of the Lord’s incarnation, Pilate was sent by Tiberius as procurator of Judea.

[Col. 0016D]

In the thirtieth year of the Lord’s incarnation, and the fifteenth year of Tiberius, John preached the baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins throughout the region of the Jordan and baptized many. Among them he immersed in the waters of the Jordan the Redeemer of the world himself, who washes away the sins of all. After his baptism the Lord withdrew into the desert and fasted for forty days. After the fast, having overcome the tempter, he entered Galilee in the power of the Spirit, called the apostles, proclaimed the kingdom of God, and performed many signs and miracles.

In the thirty-second year of the Lord’s incarnation, John the Baptist, [Col. 0017A] through the plotting of Herodias and by order of King Herod, was beheaded in prison.

In the thirty-third year of the Lord’s incarnation, but the eighteenth of Tiberius, the Lord redeemed the world through his Passion. Forty days after the resurrection he ascended into heaven; on the fifty-eighth day he sent the Paraclete Spirit. Matthias was appointed an apostle in the place of Judas. James, the Lord’s brother, was appointed bishop of Jerusalem. Seven deacons were ordained. Stephen was stoned.

In the thirty-fourth year of the Lord’s incarnation, according to the Latins, who reckon the year as beginning in January, Paul, while traveling to Damascus, was called from heaven by Christ. According to the Hebrews, who begin the year in March, this occurred in the same year in which the Lord suffered, in the eleventh month, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 0017B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 39, Gaius reigns for 4 years, 10 months, and 8 days. If, therefore, to these 10 months we add the 6 that remained from Octavian’s 56 years, there will be 17 months; subtracting 4 of them leaves a complete year, which seems to be inserted at this point. Herod Agrippa is placed over the Jewish people.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 43, Herod the tetrarch perishes in Spain, together with Herodias, in grief. Pilate, who pronounced the sentence of death at the Lord’s Passion, takes his own life.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 45, Claudius reigns for 13 years, 7 months, and 28 days. Let us therefore add to these 7 months the 4 that remained above: they make 11 months; and to these 28 days let us add the 8 days, making 36 days—that is, a year and 6 days—which seems to be counted into the chronology at this point.

[Col. 0017C] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 47, James, the brother of John, is beheaded by Herod, and Peter is sent to prison. That same Herod is struck by an angel. At Antioch the Holy Spirit addresses the disciples: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas.” Agrippa, the son of Herod, reigns in Judaea until the destruction of the Jews.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 48, but the fourteenth year after the Passion, and the fourth year of Claudius, Paul and Barnabas went up to Jerusalem. Concerning this ascent, Paul himself writes to the Galatians: “Then, after thirteen years, I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also, and I conferred with them—that is, with the apostles—the gospel that I preach among the nations.” Thus, in the thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion, in accordance with the agreement of James, Cephas, and John, Paul departed for the teaching and apostleship of the Gentiles; here the very number he gives must be reckoned as years.

[Col. 0017D] For we know that the apostles Peter and Paul suffered after the Lord’s Passion in the thirty-eighth year, that is, in the final year of Nero, and that blessed Peter occupied the episcopal chair at Rome for twenty-five years. But twenty-five years plus fourteen make not thirty-eight, but thirty-nine. It follows, therefore, that we should believe that blessed Peter came to Rome in the same thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion in which Paul addressed him at Jerusalem—that is, in the fourth year of Claudius—and at the same time, if I am not mistaken, this calculation proves that Paul came to the faith in the same year in which the Lord suffered.

[Col. 0018A] In that same year there was a most severe famine, of which Luke makes mention, and Claudius entered Britain.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 53, Claudius expelled the Jews who were rioting from Rome.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 59, Nero reigns for 13 years, 7 months, and 28 days.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 61, Festus succeeds Felix as procurator. Paul is sent to Rome in chains, in Nero’s second year.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 63, James, the brother of the Lord, is stoned by the Jews. Albinus succeeds Festus in the governorship of Judaea, and Florus succeeds Albinus.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 70, Vespasian, commander-in-chief, is sent with an army into Judaea.

[Col. 0018B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 72, Peter is crucified at Rome and Paul is beheaded. During Nero’s persecution, Processus and Martinianus [47; significance unclear in the printed text] are crowned at Rome; they had been baptized by blessed Peter and confined in the Mamertine prison. Torpes, Marcellus, and Apuleius; at Alexandria, the evangelist Mark suffers martyrdom in Nero’s eighth year. At Milan, Nazarius and Celsus; at Miceria near Aquileia, Bishop Hermagoras and the deacon Fortunatus; Felix together with Constantia.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 73, Vespasian reigns for 9 years, 11 months, and 22 days. To these 11 months are added Nero’s 7, making 18 months; and to those 22 days are added his 28 days, making 50 days—that is, a year, 7 months, and 20 days—which is the year inserted at this point.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 74, the kingdom of Judaea [Col. 0018C] is overthrown by Titus, and the Temple is destroyed. In his time, Bishop Apollinaris, sent by blessed Peter to Ravenna, is crowned.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 83, Titus reigned for 2 years and 2 months.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 85, Domitian reigned for 15 years and 5 months. To these 5 months let us add Vespasian’s 7; the complete year inserted here is obtained. In his time, the apostle John is cast into a vessel of boiling oil at Rome, before the Latin Gate, and is exiled to the island of Patmos, where he writes the Apocalypse. Flavia Domitilla is exiled to the island of Pontia. Anacletus, the third pope after Peter, is crowned with martyrdom.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 90, Nerva reigned for 1 year, 4 months, and 8 days. The apostle John is recalled from exile and writes the Gospel at Ephesus. In his time Eutices, Victorinus, and Maro suffer martyrdom at Rome; at the city of Amiternum, Victorinus, bishop and brother of Severinus.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 91, Trajan reigned for 19 years, 6 months, and 15 days. If we add to these 5 months Titus’s second year and Nerva’s 4 months, a year is formed, which is fitted in here; the 28 days noted above remain.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 101, the apostle John rested at Ephesus. In Trajan’s time the following are crowned with martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Clement; Alexander, the fourth pope after Peter; Quirinus and his daughter Balbina; Sulpitius and Servilianus; the virgins Domitilla and Seraphia; Nereus and Achilleus; Ignatius of Antioch, bishop; at Jerusalem, Symeon, bishop and son of Clopas; and in Pontus, Phocas, bishop.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 111, Hadrian reigned for 11 years. In his time the following suffer martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Sixtus, Getulius, Sabina, and the virgin Seraphia; at the city of Mesena in Apulia, Bishop Eleutherius together with his mother Anthia. At Athens, Quadratus and Aristides are renowned, as is Dionysius, bishop of the Areopagus; at Tibur in Italy, Symphorosa together with her seven sons.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 123, Antoninus, surnamed Pius, reigned with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for 22 years and 3 months. The philosopher Justin is renowned. Hermes writes a book to Bishop Suppius, which is called *The Shepherd*.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 125, Marcus Antoninus Verus reigned with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus for 19 years and 1 month. In the time of these rulers and those mentioned above, the following were crowned with martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Anicetus, Pope Victor, the presbyter Symetrius, Felicitas with her seven sons, Julius and Antoninus, Eusebius and Pontianus, Peregrinus and Vincentius; at Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, forty martyrs under the judge Agricola. At Spoleto, Concordius. At Smyrna, Polycarp, bishop and disciple of Saint John. Also Germanicus and Pionius; at Apamea, Alexander and Gaius; at the city of Cortina in Crete, Philip, bishop; at Pergamum, a city of Asia, Carpus, bishop, Papirius the deacon, and Justin the philosopher; at Lyon in Gaul, Bishop Irenaeus with many others, Photinus, bishop of that same city, and Blandina with forty-eight others, Epipodius and Alexander; in Syria, Victor and Corona; at Milan, Faustus; at Chalon, Marcellus; likewise in the territory of Chalon, at the fortress of Trenortus, Valerianus; at Alexandria, Ptolemy and Lucius.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 144, Lucius Antoninus Commodus, after the death of his father Antoninus Verus, reigned for 13 years. In his time several people suffered martyrdom, whom we have listed above. We have not been able to set these events out in the exact order of the emperors’ reigns, because in some accounts of the passions of the saints named above the emperors’ names are placed so confusedly that, when an event is said to have occurred under Antoninus, it is unknown whether it was under Pius or under Commodus; and when it is said to have occurred under Lucius, it is uncertain whether it took place under Aurelius, Commodus, or Antoninus. It is nevertheless reported that in this period Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, suffered martyrdom.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 157, Helius Pertinax reigns for 6 months.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 158, Severus Pertinax reigned for 17 years. Clement, Father of the Alexandrian Church, and the philosopher Pantaenus become renowned. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, are held in distinction. Leonides, the father of Origen, is crowned at Carthage; Perpetua and Felicitas are handed over to the beasts.

[Col. 0020A] In the one hundred and seventieth year of the Lord’s incarnation, Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, son of Severus, reigns for 7 years.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 171, Macrinus reigns for 1 year.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 172, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus reigned for 4 years.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 176, Aurelius Alexander reigned for 13 years. Origen is regarded as renowned throughout the whole world. In his time the following are crowned with martyrdom at Rome: Pope Callistus, Pope Urban, the virgin Cecilia, Tiburtius and Valerianus, the presbyter Calepodius, the presbyter Asterius, the consul Palmatius with his wife and children, and the senator Simplicius.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 189, Maximinus reigns for 3 years. In his time Pope Anteros and Pope Pontianus are crowned at Rome; at Caesarea in Palestine, the presbyters Pamphilus and Maximus.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 192, Gordian reigned for 6 years. Origen, at Caesarea in Palestine, instructed Theodore, surnamed Gregory, and his brother Athenodorus in divine philosophy.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 198, Philip reigned with his son Philip for 6 years; he was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 204, Decius reigned for 1 year and 3 months. To these months add the 3 months of Antoninus Pius, 1 of Marcus Antoninus, and 6 of Helius Pertinax; a year is formed, which is placed here. One month and 28 days remain, noted above.

[Col. 0020C] In his time the following are crowned with martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Fabian, Pope Xistus, Laurentius, the deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus, Abdo and Sennes, Hippolytus and Concordia, Irenaeus and Abundius, Pope Cornelius, the virgin Victoria, and Miniates; at Antioch, Bishop Babylas; at the city of Apollonia, Leacus, Tirsus, and Gallinecus; at Jerusalem, Bishop Alexander; at Nazianzus, Trypho; in Egypt, at the city called Thinis, Bishop Phileas and the tribune Philoromus with many others; in Sicily, at the city of Catania, the virgin Agatha; in Persia, Polochronius, bishop of Babylon and Ctesiphon; Egen of Pamphylia; Bishop Nestor at the city of Corduba; the presbyter Parmenius with his companions at the Circensian Colony; Marianus and James at Tyre; Anatholia and Audax in Africa; Nemesianus and Felix; the presbyter Rogatianus and Felicissimus with many others; at Antioch, Bishop Asclepiades; at Alexandria, Agatho and Serapion, Arsenius and Dioscorus with their companions.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 206, Gallus reigned with his son Volusianus for 2 years and 4 months. The teacher Origen dies and is buried at Tyre.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 209, Valerian reigned with Gallienus for 15 years. In their time the following are crowned with martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Stephen, the virgin Eugenia, Jovinus and Basilus, Pope Lucius, Basilla, and the virgins Rufina and Secunda, Tertullianus, Protus and Hyacinthus, Pope Xistus, Valerianus, Nemesius; at the Spanish city of Tarragona, Symphronius and Olympius; at Verona, Bishop Zeno and Fructuosus, bishop and confessor, together with the deacons Augurius and Eulogius. At Caesarea in Palestine, Marinus and Artemius; in Africa, at the city of Tuburnum, Lucernaria, Maxia, Donatilla, and the virgin Secunda. In the territory of Cavaillon, at the village of Mitanum, Bishop Privatus. Theodore, surnamed Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, shines forth in the glory of his miracles.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 224, Claudius reigned for 1 year and 9 months. To these add Volusianus’s 4 months; a year is formed, which is counted here, and 1 month remains. In his time the following suffer martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Felix, Marius and his wife Martha with their sons, and forty-seven soldiers who were baptized by Pope Dionysius; the virgin Cyrilla; at Terracina, a city of Campania, the presbyter Felix and Eusebius.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 226, Aurelian [Col. 0021B] reigned for 5 years and 6 months. In his time the following suffer martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Eutychianus, Theodora, Basilides, Tripos, and Mandalia; at Linguires, the holy Gemini; at the city of Loonium, Conon; at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Mamas; near the city of Praeneste, Agapitus; at the city of Salona, Anastasius; at Augustodunum, Symphorianus; in the territory of Viviers, at a place called Gentibus, the subdeacon Andeolus, the presbyter Andochius, the deacon Thyrsus, and Felix; at the fortress of Dijon, the presbyter Benignus.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 232, Tacitus reigned for 6 months. Add Aurelian’s 6 months, and a year is formed. Florian’s 88 days remain; join to these the 28 days that remained above, making 108 days—that is, 3 months and 18 days. Add the 2 surplus months, making 5 months and 18 days. Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, is held in distinction.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 233, Probus reigns for 6 years and 4 months. Add Tacitus’s 6 months and the 5 months written above; a year is formed, and 3 months remain.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 240, Carus reigned with his sons Carinus and Numerianus for 2 years. In their time the following are crowned with martyrdom at Rome: Chrysanthus and Daria; Claudius and his wife Hilaria, with their sons Jason and Maurus; and seventy soldiers.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 242, Diocletian reigned with Maximian and Constantius; and, after Diocletian’s death, Maximian with Severus, Galerius, and Maximian, for 20 years. In their time the following are crowned with martyrdom: at Rome, Pope Gaius, the deacon Cyriacus, Largus and Smaragdus, Apronianus, Papias and Maurus, Claudius and Propedigna with their sons, the presbyter Gabinius, Castulus, Pancratius, Arthemius with his wife and daughter, Sebastian, Marcus and Marcellianus, the presbyter Marcellinus, Peter the exorcist, Tranquillinus, Nicostratus and his wife Zoe, Primus and Felicianus, Claudius, Castorius, Victorinus, Symphorianus, Basiliscus, Faustinus, Simplicius and Beatrix, Tiburtius the son of Chromatius, the virgin Susanna, John, Crispus, Genesius, Felix and Adauctus, Lucia [Col. 0022A] and Geminianus, Sergius and Bacchus, Chrysogonus, Saturninus and Sisinnius, the Four Crowned Ones, Theodorus, Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thraso; at Spoleto, the presbyter Gregory, Bishop Sabinus, and the deacons Exsuperantius and Marcellus; in the Parmarian Islands, Anastasia; at Antioch, Julianus and Basilissa.

In Spain, at the city of Zaragoza, the deacon Vincentius. At Barcelona, the virgin Eulalia and Cucufas. At Girona, Felix. At Cucumis, the virgin Juliana. At Tyre, Tyrannio, Silvanus, Peneleus, and bishops with an innumerable multitude. At Sirmium, Serenus. At Nicomedia, Peter and Lucianus, the presbyter of Antioch; Bishop Anthimus; Pantaleon; John; Hadrian; Dorotheus; Gorgonius; and Eleutherius. At Smyrna, Bishop Irenaeus. In Palestine, at the city of Gaza, Silvanus. At Milan, Victor. In Illyricum, at the city of Siscia, Bishop Quirinus; at Tarsus, Boniface; at Aquileia, Felix and Fortunatus; in Cilicia, Vitus and Modestus with Crescentia; the virgin Lucia; in Britain, Albanus; at Massilia, Victor; at Augusta, Afra; in the province of Raetia, Theodora of Nicaea in Bithynia with her sons; in Spain, at the city of Complutum, Justinus and Pastor, brothers; in Sicily, at the city of Catania, the deacon Euplius; at the Italian city of Pergami, Alexander; at Chalcedon, Euphemia. At Naples in Campania, Bishop Januarius, and Beneventanus and Sosius, deacons; at the city of Mesena, Faustus and Desiderius. In Palestine, Bishops Peleus and Nilus; at Cyzicus, Fausta and Evilasius; at Agaunum, Mauritius with his companions; at Antioch, Bishop Cyprian [Col. 0022C] with Justina; at the city of Aegea, Cosmas and Damian; in Gaul, at the fortress of Solodorum, which lies on the river Arola, Victor; at Cologne Agrippina, Gereon with his companions; at Tarsus, Taracus, Probus, and Andronicus; at Venusia in Apulia, Bishop Felix and the presbyters Audax and Januarius; at the city of Soissons, Crispinus and Crispinianus; at Sidon, the presbyter Zenobius; in the territory of Agaunum, Tiberius, Modestus, and Florentina; in Scythia, at the metropolis of Phrygian Salaria, Mennas; at Antioch, Romanus; at Alexandria, Bishop Peter; in Africa, at the city of Colonia, a virgin. In Tuscia, the virgin Barbara. In Spain, Leocadia; at the city of Mérida, the virgins Eulalia and Julia.

[Year of the Lord’s incarnation 243. In the time of this Constantius, peace having been restored to the churches, the bishops are returned to their private sees, and several other things beneficial to the Christian religion are granted. Among these, the monastery of the servants of God at Trier is also begun. With the assent of the aforesaid ruler, John, an abbot and a man of remarkable holiness, laid its foundations between the walls adjoining the city. Blessed Augustine mentioned this monastery in his book *The Confessions*.]

[Note: [Col. 0021D] This is absent from Codices 1, 2, 3, and 6, and perhaps from the others as well.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 263 [Note: [Col. 0021D] Everything from the year 263 through the year 746—that is, three gatherings of four leaves—is missing from the formerly Brisingian manuscript.]

Constantine, the son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, reigns for 30 years and 10 months. Add to these the 3 months that remained above: a year is formed, and 1 month remains. Pope Sylvester is held in distinction. Through his efforts, the most illustrious synod of 318 Fathers from the whole world is celebrated at the city of Nicaea. The Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ is discovered by Judas. But, as we read in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, the same Cross of the Lord was discovered under Constantius, Constantine’s father, and Eusebius, the Roman pontiff. For it is written there as follows: “In his time, that is, in the time of Eusebius, the Cross of Christ was found on the fifth day before the Nones of May”; and Judas, who is also called Quiriacus, was baptized.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 295, Constantius reigned with Constantine and Constans, brothers, for 27 years, 5 months, and 13 days. In their time Maximinus, bishop of Trier, is held in distinction; James, bishop of Nisibis, is recognized; Antony the monk dies in the desert; and Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, is recalled from exile. Pope Julius is sent into exile; Pope Liberius is deported into exile, and, after his recall, favors the heretics. Pope Felix is deposed and killed by the heretics. The presbyter Eusebius is confined in a certain room on account of the Catholic faith and dies there after 7 months. Dionysius, bishop of Milan, is condemned to exile in Cappadocia. Paul, bishop of Constantinople, is strangled by the Arians. Paulinus, bishop of Trier and successor of Saint Maximinus, is banished into exile by Constantius on account of the Catholic faith and, even beyond death, is worn down in exile by changing the Christian name. At last he dies in Phrygia; from there he is brought back to Trier.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 310, Julius reigned for 2 years and 8 months. Add the 6 months that remained, and a year is formed; 2 months and 18 days remain. In his time the following are crowned with martyrdom: at Rome, the presbyter Priscus, Priscillianus the cleric, Benedicta the woman, the presbyter Pigmus [Pimenius], Gordianus, the virgin Demetria, the presbyter John, and likewise John and Paul, Faustus and Dafrosa; at Ostia, Hilarianus, bishop of Jerusalem, Quiriacus and Judas; at Alexandria, Gallicanus; at Vercellae, Bishop Eusebius; at the city of Aricia, Bishop Donatus; at Antioch, the presbyter Theodoricus.

[Col. 0023D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 314, Jovinianus reigns for 8 months. This ruler summons Bishop Athanasius by official letter.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 315, Valentinian reigned with his brother Valens for 11 years. At Rome, Pope Damasus is held in distinction; at Milan, Bishop Ambrose is held in distinction. Bishop Hilary of Poitiers dies; Athanasius dies at Alexandria.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 327, Valens reigns with Gratian and Valentinian, the sons of his brother Valentinian, for 4 years. The Huns drive the Goths from their own settlements. The Goths ravage Thrace.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 332, Gratian reigned with his brother Valentinian for 6 years. Theodosius is created emperor by Gratian. A synod of 150 Fathers is convened at the city of Augusta under Pope Damasus. Theodosius makes his son Arcadius a partner in the empire. Maximus is made emperor in Britain; at Lyon in Gaul he kills Gratian Augustus and expels his brother Valentinian from Italy. Martin, bishop of Tours, shines forth in the glory of his miracles. Jerome, interpreter of Sacred Scripture, is held in distinction at Bethlehem.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 339, Theodosius, who while Gratian was alive had already ruled the East for 5 years, reigned for 11 years after Gratian’s death and killed the tyrant Maximus four miles from Aquileia. Pope Siricius governs the Roman Church. Jerome writes the book *On Illustrious Men*. In Egypt, John the hermit is celebrated; he foretold Theodosius’s victory over the tyrants.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 350, Arcadius, the son of Theodosius, reigned with his brother Honorius for 15 years. The Goths attacked Italy, while the Vandals and Alans attacked Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0023] “Vandals and Anani” in 1, 2, and 3; see “Alani” in 6.]

The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah are revealed. Pope Innocent governed the Roman Church. Saint Martin, bishop, passed to the heavenly realm. Severinus, bishop of Cologne Agrippina, is held in distinction. Augustine, an outstanding bishop and teacher, expounds divine philosophy in the church of Hippo. Pelagius the Briton attacks the grace of God.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 364, Honorius reigned with Theodosius the Younger, the son of his brother, for 15 years. Alaric, king of the Goths, invades Rome in the seventh year of Honorius. The bodies of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Gamaliel, and Nicodemus are revealed to the presbyter Lucianus. Popes Boniface and Celestine govern the Roman Church. Jerome the presbyter died in the twelfth year of Honorius, at the age of 97; he completed his books over 50 years.

[Note: [Col. 0023] “He completed his books in one year” in 1, 2, and 3; “as above” in 6.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 370, Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, reigned for 26 years. Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius, is appointed emperor at Ravenna. The people of the Vandals, Alans, and Goths devastate Africa. Bishop Augustine passed to the Lord amid the very hardships of the sieges. After capturing Carthage, the Vandals crossed into Sicily. Xistus governs the Roman Church. In his time Leo the Great obtained the apostolic chair; to him and to Pulcheria Augusta, Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, writes at length concerning the error of Eutyches and condemns Eutyches.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 397, Marcian and Valentinian reigned for 7 years. John the Baptist reveals his head to two monks.

[Col. 0025A] Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, and Lupus, bishop of Troyes, are sent into Britain. After this Germanus dies at Ravenna.

[Severus, bishop of Trier; Polychronius of Verdun; and Albinus of Châlons, disciples of Saint Lupus, are held in distinction. At Orléans, Bishop Timavus shines forth. 6.]

Bishop Leo writes many statements of faith to Marcian. Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, condemns the error of Eutyches and is rebuked by Pope Leo because he had wished to subject to himself, contrary to the Council of Nicaea, the churches of Antioch and Alexandria. The patrician Aetius is killed by Valentinian at Arles. Bishop Hilary, a most learned and distinguished man, who composed the *Life of his predecessor, Saint Honoratus*, dies.

[Col. 0025B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 405 [Note: [Col. 0025D] “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 415” in 1.]

Leo reigns for 17 years. Pope Leo writes very extensively to this Leo. Theodore, bishop of a city in Syria, writes an ecclesiastical history from the end of Eusebius’s books. Pope Hilary governs the Roman Church. Victorinus, at the command of Pope Hilary, describes the cycle of the Great Year.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 414, Zeno reigned for 17 years. Odoacer, king of the Goths, took possession of Rome. Theoderic, surnamed Walager, ravages both Macedonias. Huneric, the Arian king of the Vandals, after driving more than 334 bishops into exile in Africa, closed their churches and afflicted their congregations with various punishments. Pope Felix condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter of Alexandria. Gelasius, a prudent man, succeeds Pope Felix in the pontificate. He too condemned Acacius and Peter. After him Anastasius becomes pontiff; he wished secretly to recall Acacius but was unable to do so, and he too was struck down by divine will.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 421, Anastasius reigned for 29 years. Trasamundus, king of the Vandals, sent 220 bishops into exile in Sardinia. In his time and in Zeno’s, during the Vandal persecution, the following are crowned with martyrdom: in Africa, Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, and more than 500 with him; likewise Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servius and Rusticus the subdeacons, Rogatus and Septimus the monks, and Maximus the boy, who were first thrown into a fire and then killed with oar shafts.

[Col. 0025D] Likewise Marcianus and Satyrianus, and the virgin Maxima, were cruelly killed with 370 others. Likewise Papias and Mansuetus. The bishops Vulteius, Valerianus, Urbanus, and Crescens, Felix and Hortolanus, completed the course of their lives in confession. Likewise Dativa, Dionisia, and Emilianus the physician with many others, and Bishop Valerianus.

Pope Symmachus governs the Roman Church and supplies money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to the bishops sent into exile. After him Pope Hormisdas is appointed.

Clovis, king of the Franks, who reigns in Gaul for 30 years, kills the patrician Syagrius. He expels Gundobad, king of Burgundy. He makes the Alamanni tributary. In the twelfth year of his reign, he is baptized together with the Franks by Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims.

[At Arras, Vedastus is ordained bishop. 6.]

Mamercus, bishop of the church of Vienne, institutes three-day litanies before the Lord’s Ascension. Clovis engages Alaric, king of the Goths, in battle near Poitiers, depriving him of both kingdom and life. Amalric, the son of Alaric, obtains his father’s kingdom in Spain. The emperor Anastasius sends royal gifts to Clovis. Clovis kills his kinsman and partner in the kingdom, Ragnachar. From Saint Martin’s passing until Clovis’s death there are 112 years. His four sons—Theodoric, Clodomer, Childebert, and Clothar—divide their father’s kingdom among themselves. The emperor Anastasius perishes by a thunderbolt.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 450, Justin the Elder reigned for 8 years. Pope John is sent by Theoderic, king of the Goths, to Ravenna under guard on account of the Catholic faith, and dies there. The same tyrant kills the patrician Symmachus. He thrusts Boethius, second to none in the liberal disciplines, into prison; there, together with Philosophy herself, Boethius laments through remarkable arguments of disputation. The aforesaid Theoderic dies a sudden death. Athalaric succeeds to the kingdom.

Benedict the father, first at the place called Subiaco and later at the fortress of Cassino, shone forth as a man of great virtue through apostolic virtues. Felix and Boniface govern the Roman Church. Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, builds the monastery of Agaunum dedicated to the saints. He is killed by the aforesaid sons of Clovis. Theodoric, together with his son Theodebert and his brother Clothar, ravages Thuringia. He destroys Ermenfrid, duke of the Thuringians, at Tolbiac.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 459, Justinian, the grandson of Justin through his sister, reigned for 38 years. Through the patrician Belisarius he decisively defeated the Persians. Through that same Belisarius, after capturing their king Gelimer, he destroyed the nation of the Vandals to the point of annihilation and restored all Africa to the Roman Empire after 96 years. Again, through the strength of Belisarius, he defeated the Gothic nation in Italy after capturing their king Witigis. He also defeated the Moors, who afterward were harassing Africa, and through the consul John brought down their king Athalas by extraordinary valor.

He also reduced the Roman laws, whose excessive length was burdensome, and corrected their useless inconsistencies with remarkable brevity. He also built in Constantinople a temple which he named, in Greek, Ἄγιαν Σοφίαν, “Holy Wisdom.” Its construction surpasses all other buildings so greatly that no similar one can be found anywhere throughout the breadth of the earth.

In his time Cassiodorus was renowned at Rome for both secular and divine learning. First he became consul, then senator, and finally a monk. At Rome Dionysius the abbot writes the paschal cycles. At Constantinople Priscian of Caesarea explored the depths of the grammatical art, so to speak; and likewise Arator, a subdeacon of the Roman Church and a remarkable poet, adorned the deeds of the apostles in hexameter verse.

[Col. 0027A] In his time John, Agapitus, Sylverius, and Vigilius governed the Roman Church. Sylverius is sent into exile by Belisarius at the command of the empress Theodora, and dies there. Vigilius too, because he refused to recall Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, is thrust into exile by Justinian. Recalled from exile, while returning to Rome, he dies at Syracuse in Sicily from the pain of a stone. Pelagius succeeds him in the pontificate.

At the same time Alboin, son of Audoin, already the tenth ruler of the Lombards, reigns; he had taken Clothsuinda, daughter of Clothar, king of the Franks, in marriage. Childebert, king of the Franks, enters Spain with an army and kills Amalric, son of Alaric, in battle, carrying away much gold and silver from there. Clothar stabs the sons of his brother Clodomer with a sword. King Theoderic dies, and his son Theodebert reigns after him.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 498, Justinian the Younger reigned for 11 years. The patrician Narses kills Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy. He fought against Bucellinus and Emingo, commanders of Theodebert, king of the Franks, who were plundering Italy, and killed them. Narses is accused by the Romans before Justin and his wife Sophia of oppressing Italy with servitude, and immediately the prefect Longinus is sent to take Narses’s place.

Among other things, Sophia is said to have ordered him, because he was a eunuch, to go and divide portions of wool with the girls in the women’s quarters. To this he replied that he would weave for her such a web as she could not lay aside while she lived. He immediately sends a message to the Lombard people to come and take possession of Italy.

Pope John governs the Roman Church. The kings Childebert and Clothar enter Spain with an army and besiege the city of Zaragoza. The citizens, clothed in hair shirts, carry the tunic of Saint Vincent around upon the wall and beseech God with contrite hearts. The kings, moved by divine inspiration and compassion, lift the siege. The bishop of that city gives King Childebert Saint Vincent’s stole as a gift. From there the king built at Paris a basilica in honor of blessed Vincent.

Alboin entered Italy with the Lombards and placed his nephew Gisulf in charge of the Forum of Julius. King Theodebert entered Italy, engaged the Lombards in battle, and defeated them; returning to Francia, he died. Not long afterward King Childebert died at Paris and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent. The kingdoms held by the brothers and nephews were brought under the authority of Clothar.

In these times Bishop Medard departed to the Lord, and King Clothar buried him at Soissons with due honor. After this King Clothar died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Medard. His four sons divided his kingdoms among themselves. Heribert received Childebert’s kingdom and established his seat at Paris; Guntran held the kingdom of Chlodomer and established his seat at Orléans. Hilperic held the kingdom of his father Clothar and had his seat at Soissons. Sigibert established his seat at Reims or Metz, in the kingdom of Theodoric. When the Huns, who are also called Avars, learned of Clothar’s death, they attacked Sigibert. He met them in Thuringia and powerfully defeated them beside the River Elbe.

This Sigibert sent an embassy to Spain to seek Brunichild, daughter of King Athanagild, and took her in marriage. By her he had a son whom he named Childebert. Heresbert, having abandoned his lawful wife, whose name was Ingoberga, joined her two sisters, Marcovefa and Merofilda, to himself in marriage. For this crime he was excommunicated by Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris; then, struck down by the just judgment of God, he died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Romanus. His kingdom was seized by Sigebert.

Heilperic took Geilsuinda, Brunichild’s sister, in marriage, but after a short time, at Fredegund’s instigation, he strangled her in bed. Then he repudiated Queen Audovera because, at Fredegund’s urging, she had taken her own daughter from the sacred font, and he joined that same Fredegund to himself in marriage. By the aforesaid Audovera he had three sons, Theodebert, Meroveus, and Clovis.

Theodebert, by order of his father, seized the region beyond the Loire that had been held by his uncle Herebert. At Poitiers he fought with Guldald, the duke of Sigibert, and defeated him. Sigibert came to Paris with an army and attacked his brother Helperic in battle; in that engagement the aforementioned Theodebert fell. Helperic, fleeing with his wife and sons, entered Tournai [Note: “[Col. 0027] Helperic, fleeing with his wife and sons; Albinus, Bishop of Angers, is distinguished; he entered Tournai” (1).] and fortified himself there. While Sigibert was pursuing Helperic there, Sigibert was killed through the treachery of Queen Fredegund by two of her boys. His brothers buried him in the basilica of Saint Medard.

At that time Brunichild was staying in Paris with her son, still a small child. The duke Gundald secretly seized the boy by night and carried him away, taking him back to his father’s kingdom. Brunichild herself was sent into exile at Rouen. Meroveus, the son of Helpric, came there and joined her to himself in marriage. For this reason he was later tonsured by his father, became a monk, and was ordained a priest.

At the same time Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris, passed to the Lord and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent. Childebert sought his mother Brunichild, whom Helperic ordered to be returned. Narses the patrician came from Campania to Rome and died there; his body was taken to Constantinople in a leaden chest, together with all his riches. Pope Benedict governed the Roman Church.

The poet Fortunatus was renowned in Gaul. He was born in a place called Duplalis, not far from the fortress of Ceneta or the city of Tarvisium, but was nevertheless brought up and educated at Ravenna. He became most distinguished in grammar, rhetoric, and meter. Out of love for Saint Martin he crossed into Gaul, living first at Tours and then at Poitiers, in which city he was ordained bishop.

King Albuin, with the Lombards, captured Tarvisium, Vicentia, Verona, and the other cities of Venetia. Then, entering Liguria, he captured Milan and all the cities of Liguria. The city of Ticinum, after enduring a siege for more than three years, surrendered to the Lombards. They captured all the cities by force of arms, except Rome and Ravenna, or certain fortresses situated on the seacoast. After Albuin had reigned in Italy for three years and six months, he was killed by the treachery of his wife.

Elmigis, who had killed Albuin, fled with Queen Rosimund to Ravenna, to the prefect Longinus, taking with them Albisinda, the king’s daughter, and the entire Lombard treasury. There both of them died by poison. Longinus sent Albisinda, Albuin’s daughter, with the Lombard treasures to Constantinople.

The Lombards entered Gaul. The man of God Hospicius, who was confined at Nice, foresaw their arrival long beforehand, the Holy Spirit revealing it to him. Amatus, Duke of King Guntran, met them, but when battle was joined he was destroyed by the Lombards. Mummulus was appointed in his place; he killed many of the Lombards and compelled them to return to Italy.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 510, Tiberius Constantine reigned for seven years. While he was still Caesar under Justin, and was governing the palace and giving alms daily, the Lord supplied him with a great abundance of gold. For as he was walking through the palace, he saw on the pavement a marble slab on which the Lord’s cross had been carved. Ordering it to be lifted, he found buried beneath it a great treasure containing more than a thousand hundredweights of gold.

The treasure of Narses was also revealed to him by an old man who had buried it in the ground with others. It was so great that the cistern in which it had lain could scarcely be emptied by those carrying it away, even after many days. The Empress Sophia attempted to lay a plot against him. For while he was proceeding to a villa to enjoy the thirty days of the grape harvest according to imperial custom, she summoned Justinian, the nephew of her husband Justin, wishing to raise him to the throne. When Tiberius learned of this, he seized the empress, stripped her of all her treasures, and left her only food.

His army defeated the Persians and brought back such spoils, together with twenty elephants, that they were thought capable of satisfying human greed. King Helperic of the Franks also sent envoys to him and received from him many ornaments, including gold pieces weighing one pound each. On one side they bore the emperor’s image, with the inscription around it, “Tiberius Constantine, perpetual Augustus”; on the other they bore a chariot and a charioteer, with the inscription around it, “The Glory of the Romans.”

In his days, when Gregory the deacon was serving as apocrisiarius in Constantinople, he composed the books of the *Moralia*. He also defeated Eutychius, bishop of that city, in the presence of the Augustus, because Eutychius was mistaken concerning the resurrection.

Pope Pelagius governed the Roman Church. He was ordained without the ruler’s authorization because the Lombards were besieging Rome and no one could get through. King Helperic, on Fredegund’s advice, made new assessments throughout his entire kingdom, so that every landholder was to give the king one amphora of wine from each arpent of land and one modius from each jugerum. The people, severely oppressed by this, cried out to the Lord.

The Lord sent a plague upon the king’s household, and the king himself began to fall ill; two of his sons also died. Terrified, the king burned the assessments and remitted the tribute. After this he had intercourse with his wife, who bore a son whom he named Clothar. This son later became a great king and fathered Dagobert.

[Col. 0030B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 517, Maurice reigned for twenty years. As Tiberius perceived that the day of his death was approaching, he chose Maurice for the imperial office with the agreement of the Empress Sophia. He adorned his own daughter with royal ornaments, gave her to Maurice, and with her transferred the whole empire.

After the Lombards had been ruled by dukes for ten years, they set over themselves as king Otharis, son of Cleph. Because of his rank they also called him Flavius, and the Lombard kings used this title. The dukes who were then in office, in order to restore the kingdom, contributed half of all their possessions for royal purposes, so that the king himself and those who attended him might be supported through their various offices.

The Emperor Maurice sent fifty thousand solidi through his envoys to Childebert, King of the Franks, asking him to expel the Lombards from Italy. Childebert entered Italy with the Franks. The Lombards offered gifts and made peace with him. The emperor demanded the solidi, but Childebert, trusting in the strength of his own forces, gave no answer concerning this matter.

The same Childebert, waging war against the Spaniards, defeated their battle line. The cause of this conflict was as follows. Childebert had given his sister Ingund in marriage to Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, King of the Spaniards. Hermenegild had been converted to the Catholic faith through the preaching of Leander, Bishop of Seville, and the encouragement of his wife. His impious father struck him with an axe on the very sacred day of Easter.

After her husband’s death, Ingund wished to return to Gaul, but she was captured by pirates and taken to Sicily, where she died. Her son was sent to the emperor.

At that time there was a flood of waters in the cities of Venetia and Liguria, and likewise in the other regions of Italy, such as is believed not to have occurred since the time of Noah. Immediately afterward there followed a groin-plague, which devastated the people with such slaughter that, from an incalculable multitude, only a few remained.

During this tribulation Gregory was unanimously elected pope by all and raised to the papal throne.

At the same time this same Pope Gregory sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with several other God-fearing monks, to Britain. Through their preaching they converted the English to Christ.

King Reccared, brother of the martyr Hermenegild, was converted to the Catholic faith through the preaching of Bishop Leander.

The English nation was converted to Christ, and their king Ethelbert was baptized.

Pope Gregory sent to Bishop Leander the books of the *Pastoral Rule*, which he had written at the beginning of his episcopate, and also the books that he had composed long before at Constantinople in his *Exposition of Blessed Job*. He likewise sent him the pallium, received through the blessing of Saint Peter.

The Emperor Maurice sent an embassy to King Childebert, instructing him to complete now what he had not done before: to remove the Lombards from Italy. Childebert sent an army into Italy, but when battle was joined with the Lombards, the Frankish lines were severely worn down. Paternus, Bishop of Avranches and a citizen of Poitiers, was distinguished.

King Flavius Otharis took Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, Duke of the Bavarians, in marriage.

Childebert, once again sending a Frankish army into Italy, directed it against the Lombard battle line with twenty dukes. They traversed Italy for three months, captured very many fortresses, and brought back from there an innumerable multitude of captives. They could not harm King Otharis, however, for he had fortified himself within the city of Ticinum.

Because it was summer, the army was severely afflicted by dysentery on account of the unaccustomed climate, and for that reason was compelled to return to its homeland. Tassilo was appointed duke over Bavaria by Childebert.

King Otharis sent envoys to Guntran, King Childebert’s uncle, so that through his influence peace might be established between Childebert and Otharis himself.

Concerning the vision of King Guntran.

King Guntran was a peaceful man, adorned with every virtue. One day he had gone hunting in a forest. While his companions ran here and there, as usually happens, he remained alone with one faithful servant. Overcome by deep sleep, he fell asleep with his head resting on the servant’s knees.

A small animal came out of his mouth and attempted to cross a little stream that ran nearby. Then the man in whose lap Guntran was resting drew his sword and made a bridge for it with the sword. The animal crossed to the other side and entered a certain opening in the mountain. After a short while it returned, crossed the stream by the same sword, and entered Guntran’s mouth.

Immediately awakened from sleep, Guntran declared that he had seen a wondrous vision. He said that he had crossed a certain river by an iron bridge and had seen a great quantity of gold in a cave. When the man in whose lap he had slept had related the event in order, the place was excavated and immeasurable treasures were found. From this gold he made a solid ciborium of extraordinary size and weight and had it placed over the body of Saint Marcellus the martyr in the city of Chalon. No work made of gold anywhere can be compared with it.

Not long afterward the same king, having distributed his treasures to churches and the poor, died and was buried in that same basilica.

[Col. 0032A] Childebert and his sons obtained his kingdom. At the same time Saint Goar, a priest, came from Aquitaine. In the territory of Trier, in the district of the Trigorii, above the bank of the Rhine and the stream called the Wochara, he built an oratory in honor of the holy Mother of God. Devoting himself to prayer, almsgiving, and preaching the word, he rested full of virtues in that same place.

Around this time King Helpric was killed through the treachery of his wife Fredegund as he returned from hunting, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent at Paris. Clothar, still a boy, was raised to the kingship by his mother and Landric, who was then mayor of the palace.

[Col. 0032B] When Childebert heard that his uncle was dead, he attempted to seize his kingdom. He came with an immense army of Franks and Burgundians to the vicinity of Soissons, where Fredegund and the duke Landric met him. Battle was joined, and Childebert’s army was severely slaughtered and fled.

After this, Childebert died. He had two sons: one by a concubine, named Theodebert, who was the elder, and the other by the queen, named Theodoric. Arnulf was mayor of the palace under this king. Theodebert obtained his father’s kingdom; Theodoric obtained the kingdom of Guntran—that is, Burgundy—with his grandmother Brunichild.

After this a war arose between Clothar and Theodoric beside the River Aroana. Such slaughter was inflicted on both peoples that the riverbed itself, filled with human corpses, seemed to pour out blood rather than water. In the aforementioned battle, as they say, an angel of the Lord was seen holding a drawn sword over the people.

At this time Saint Columbanus, a holy father from Ireland, came to Burgundy with Saint Gall and other outstanding disciples.
