There, with the permission of King Theodoric, he built the monastery called Luxeuil. Later driven out by Brunichild, he entered Alamannia and left his disciple Saint Gall there. He himself crossed into Italy and built the monastery called Bobbio, where he became the father of many monks.

[Col. 0032D] At the same time King Otharis died, and Agilulf, Duke of Turin, having taken Queen Theodelinda in marriage, was raised as king over the Lombards. Pope Gregory wrote many things to them concerning the preservation of peace between the Lombards and the Romans. He also sent the aforementioned queen the four books that he had composed concerning the lives of the saints. He called this work a *codex of dialogues*, that is, of two conversations, because he had produced it in conversation with his deacon Peter. Through this queen the Church obtained much benefit.

Agilulf made perpetual peace with Theodoric, King of the Franks. The monastery of Saint Benedict the abbot was invaded by the Lombards at night. The monks made for Rome, taking with them the book of the holy Rule, as well as a weight of bread and a measure of wine.

The Emperor Maurice was killed with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 538, Phocas reigned for eight years. In the second year of his reign Pope Gregory departed to the Lord, and Sabinian succeeded him in the pontificate. When Sabinian died, Pope Boniface was appointed. He obtained from the ruler Phocas that the Apostolic See should be the head of all the churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was first among all the churches.

After sitting in the papal chair for eight months and twenty days, he went to the Lord. In his place Boniface was again consecrated. He asked Phocas that, in the ancient shrine called the Pantheon, which had been built by Caesar Domitian, he might be permitted to consecrate a church for himself. The emperor granted this. After him Deusdedit was raised to the pontificate.

Eleutherius, the emperor’s patrician and chamberlain, killed the tyrant John in the city of Naples.

The Persians waged extremely serious wars against the Roman state. Entering Jerusalem, they carried away the standard of the Lord’s cross. The monk Anastasius suffered a glorious martyrdom. After enduring much for Christ at the hands of the Persians, he was finally beheaded by Khosrow, their king, together with seventy others.

In Francia a most grievous war arose between the brothers Theodoric and Theodebert, at the instigation of their grandmother Brunichild. The cause was that Theodebert was said not to be the legitimate heir to the kingdom, because he had been born of a concubine. The two sides fought with all their strength at the fortress of Tolbiac.

Theodebert turned his back and fled to Cologne. He was dragged from there, tonsured by his brother, and made a cleric; shortly afterward he was slaughtered by that same brother, and his two sons were killed.

After this the aforementioned Theodoric perished through Brunichild’s treachery by poison, and his two sons were killed by Brunichild. The kingdoms held by the aforementioned kings passed into the power of Clothar.

Because of the many crimes she committed, Brunichild was tied by order of Clothar to the tails of untamed horses and torn apart. Agilulf, King of the Lombards, died, and his son Rodoald was established in the kingdom.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 546, Heraclius reigned for twenty-six years. He undertook war against the Persians and, after killing their king Khosrow, received the Persians into submission. He restored the wood of the holy cross to Jerusalem, from which it had been taken, with great reverence.

Boniface V, Honorius, Severinus, and John governed the Roman Church.

King Edwin of the English, through the preaching of Bishop Paulinus, was converted to the faith of Christ together with his people. Pope Honorius rebuked the Scots by letter because they were mistaken in their observance of Easter; John, the successor of Severinus, did likewise.

At this time Arnulf was mayor of the palace of King Clothar. He was a man who, as later became clear, was beloved by God. After the glory of the world, he submitted himself to the service of Christ and proved remarkable in his episcopate.

Dagobert, Clothar’s son, while still a boy, was entrusted by his father to Arnulf so that Arnulf might raise him according to his wisdom and show him the path of the Christian religion. When Dagobert reached manhood, he beat Sandragisil, Duke of Aquitaine and his father’s dear counselor, because Sandragisil had treated him with a certain insolence, and he disfigured him by shaving his beard.

When his father learned of this, he sought to punish him. Fearing his father’s anger, Dagobert fled to the basilica of Saints Denis and his companions and humbly sought their protection. Through the merits of the saints interceding for him, no one could remove him from there until his father forgave the offense. For this reason he came to love that place above all others, later bestowing great gifts upon it and granting it numerous estates.

After this Dagobert was sent by his father to reign in Austrasia with Duke Pippin and was commended to the counsel of Saint Arnulf, Bishop of Metz. When Rodoald, King of the Lombards, died, Rothari was placed over the same kingdom.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 572, Heraclon, son of Heraclius, reigned with his mother Martina for two years. Cyrus of Alexandria, and Sergius and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, taught as doctrine that there was one operation and one will in Christ, of divinity and humanity. For this they were condemned by Pope Theodore and the other bishops.

Dagobert, son of Clothar, fought with the Saxons and was severely wounded by them. He summoned his father for help through an envoy. Clothar came quickly with an army, killed their duke Berthold, and so thoroughly subdued the Saxons by force of arms that he killed every male inhabitant of that land who exceeded the length of the sword that he happened at that time to be carrying.

Around this time Sisenand and, after him, Chintila reigned in Spain. During their reigns a synod was held twice in the city of Toledo, where many decrees concerning the Catholic faith and Christian religion were promulgated and confirmed in writing. Under these kings Isidore, Bishop of the Church of Seville, flourished. He was inferior to none of the teachers of his own time and discussed many matters concerning the rules of faith and ecclesiastical discipline.

After this period the wife of the Persian king, named Caesara, came to Constantinople in private clothing for the love of Christ. After several days she was baptized and lifted from the sacred font by the Augustus. Her husband, seeking her, came peacefully to Constantinople with forty soldiers. He was received with fitting honor, baptized together with all whom he had brought with him, lifted from the font by the Augustus, and honored with many gifts. Having received his wife, he returned to his homeland.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 575, Constantius, son of Heraclius and brother of Heraclon, reigned for six months. Paul, the successor of Pyrrhus, tormented the Catholics not only with the mad doctrine of his predecessors but also through open persecution. For this reason he too, like his predecessors, was condemned by the Apostolic See.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 576, Constantine, son of Constantius, son of Heraclius, reigned for twenty-eight years. Deceived by the aforementioned Paul, he became a heretic and promulgated a *Typos* against the Catholic faith. It declared that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ should be confessed, as though Christ were to be believed to have no will or operation.

Therefore the bishops named above were condemned under anathema by Pope Martin and 105 bishops. For this reason Pope Martin was sent into exile at Cherson, where he died and where he also shines with the glory of miracles. Pope Eugenius was appointed; when he died, Vitalian was installed in his place.

When Rothari, King of the Lombards, died, the vigorous man Grimoald obtained the kingdom. At this time King Clothar of the Franks died and was buried in the suburban basilica of Saint Vincent at Paris.

Dagobert obtained the monarchy of the entire empire, except that he granted to his brother Heribert the territory beyond the Loire and the boundary extending toward the regions of Gascony—namely, the districts of Toulouse, Cahors, Agen, Périgueux, and Saintes, as well as the land excluded from these districts toward the Pyrenean mountains.

King Grimoald persecuted Bertarit, a powerful man. Although the king had received him into his allegiance, he was, provoked by the tongues of flatterers and slanderers, plotting to kill him treacherously. But through the resourcefulness of Hunold, his most faithful retainer, Bertarit was lowered by a rope over the wall of Ticinum and fled to Francia, to Dagobert, thus escaping the danger of death.

At the same time Archbishop Theodore and the most learned abbot Adrian were sent to Britain by Pope Vitalian. They enriched many of the churches of the English with the fruit of apostolic teaching. Among other things, Archbishop Theodore described, with wondrous and discerning judgment, the judgments of penitents—namely, for how many years a person ought to repent for each individual sin.

[Col. 0035C] In those days the Augustus Constantine, wishing to wrest Italy from the hands of the Lombards, departed from Constantinople and came to Athens. Crossing the sea from there, he landed at Tarentum, then entered Beneventum and captured nearly all the Lombard cities through which he passed. He razed Luceria to the ground.

Then he surrounded Beneventum with his entire army, where Rumald, son of King Grimoald, had shut himself in. The emperor took Rumald’s sister hostage, lifted the siege, and departed for Naples. From there he proceeded to Rome. At the sixth mile from the city, Pope Vitalian met him with the priests and the Roman people. The pope offered Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold.

The emperor remained at Rome for twelve days and removed all the ancient bronze fittings that had been installed as ornaments of the city, to such an extent that he even stripped the basilica of Saint Mary, which had once been called the Pantheon, and carried away its bronze tiles.

After this he returned to Naples and by land proceeded to the city of Rhegium. Entering Sicily, he settled at Syracuse. He remained in Sicily for six years. After numerous and unheard-of depredations, he was killed by his own men in a bath.

After his death Mezentios seized the kingdom in Sicily. But without the consent of the eastern army, against him the soldiers of Italy came to Syracuse—some through Istria, some through Campania, and others from the regions of Africa and Sardinia—and deprived him of life. The head of the false emperor was carried to Constantinople.

When the Saracen people heard this—they had already overrun Egypt and Alexandria—they suddenly came with many ships and invaded Sicily. They entered Syracuse and inflicted a great slaughter on the people. They also carried off immense booty and all the bronze and other kinds of ornament that Constantine had removed from Rome, and returned to Alexandria.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 605, Constantine, son of the earlier Augustus Constantine, reigned for seventeen years. Pope Donus held the Apostolic See. When he died, Pope Agatho was ordained.

The Augustus Constantine caused 150 bishops to assemble in the imperial city. Among them were envoys of the holy Roman Church, sent by Pope Agatho: John the deacon and John, Bishop of Porto. They all condemned the heresy that asserted one operation and one will in the Lord Jesus Christ.

At that moment such a quantity of spiders’ webs fell among the people that everyone marveled. By this it was signified that the filth of heretical depravity had been driven away. George, the patriarch of Constantinople, was corrected; the others, however, persisting in their defense, were struck by the punishment of anathema.

The correct and true faith is this: in our Lord Jesus Christ, just as there are two natures—that is, of God and of man—so also there are believed to be two wills or operations.

At this time there was an eclipse of the sun on the fifth day before the Nones of May, [Col. 0036C] and immediately afterward an extremely severe plague followed for three months: July, August, and September. Then it visibly appeared to many that a good angel and an evil angel were passing through the city by night. At the command of the good angel, the evil angel, who seemed to carry a hunting-spear in his hand, struck the door of each house with the spear. Whenever he struck the door of any house with the spear, that many people from that house died on the following day.

At this time King Dagobert ordered Brunulf, the uncle of his brother Heribert, to be killed because of his disloyalty. He was killed by the dukes Amalgarius and Arnebert and by the patrician Willibald.

After the departure of Saint Arnulf, Dagobert continued to act on the advice of Pippin, who was called mayor of the palace, and of Cunibert, bishop of the city of Cologne. Strongly admonished by them and embracing the love of prosperity and justice, he was exalted by the favor of all the nations subject to him.

He had a son by a certain girl named Regindruda, whom his brother Heribert of Orléans lifted from the sacred font. For while Bishop Amandus was blessing the child and making him a catechumen, when the prayer had ended and no one had answered “Amen,” the Lord opened the child’s mouth. Although he was no more than forty days old, he answered “Amen” in the hearing of everyone. The child was named Sigibert.

Bishop Arnulf and Abbot Romaric were distinguished.

That year King Dagobert’s envoys, Servatus and Paternus, returned from Constantinople. The emperor had asked Dagobert to order all the Jews in his kingdom to be baptized according to the Catholic faith, or else to expel them from the kingdom, since he had learned from the signs of the stars that, by divine will, his empire was to be devastated by circumcised peoples.

The king carried this out with the greatest zeal, but the sign had been given to the emperor not concerning the Jews, but concerning the Saracens.

After this Heribert died, leaving a small son named Helpric, who also died shortly afterward. The kingdom he had held passed to Dagobert.

King Grimoald of the Lombards entered into a firm treaty of peace with Dagobert. When the exile Bertarit learned of this, he feared Grimoald and decided to leave Gaul and hasten to the island of Britain.

Meanwhile Grimoald died. Bertarit had already boarded a ship and sailed some distance across the open sea when a voice was heard from the shore: “Let Bertarit return to his homeland, for today is the third day since King Grimoald died.” He immediately returned, obtained the kingdom of the Lombards, and made his son Cunibert his partner in the kingship.

When Pope Agatho died, Leo the Younger succeeded him. After him Benedict was ordained.

King Dagobert fought with the Slavs and defeated them. At that time they were ruled by a duke named Samo. He also restrained the rebellious Gascons by the sword.

The Huns and Bulgars fought one another. The Huns defeated the Bulgars, who, after being conquered and expelled from Pannonia, came to King Dagobert—nine thousand of them with their wives and children—and asked for land in which to settle. The king ordered them to be received into Bavaria for the winter, but had them scattered among all the households and killed in a single night, together with their women and children.

Around this time, after Sisebut, King of Spain, had died, a certain Sisenand, one of the nobles, sought King Dagobert’s aid so that he might obtain the kingdom of Spain. In return for this favor he promised the king a golden dish weighing fifty pounds of gold.

The king sent an army with the dukes Abundantius and Venerandus, and Sisenand obtained the kingdom through the strength of the Franks. Because the Goths opposed it, he did not send the dish; instead he paid King Dagobert two hundred thousand solidi for it. The king gave this silver to Saint Denis.

Queen and virgin Edildrud was renowned among the English.

The Saracen people proceeded from Egypt into Africa with a huge multitude, besieged Carthage, and, after cruelly ravaging it, leveled it to the ground.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 612, Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine, reigned for ten years. John, Conon, and Sergius governed the Roman Church. Kilian, Bishop of Würzburg, and his disciple Arnual [Note: “Arnual” (2). “There is no mention of Saint Kilian and his disciple in manuscript 6.”] became distinguished.

Justinian took Africa away from the Saracens and made peace with them by land and sea. Because Sergius the pontiff was unwilling to favor or subscribe to the error of the synod that Justinian had held at Constantinople, Justinian sent his protospatharius Zacharias and ordered Sergius to be carried to Constantinople. But because the soldiers resisted, Zacharias could not fulfill the emperor’s command.

The tyrant Adalgis, Duke of Trent, with the support of Aldo and Grauso, citizens of Brescia, and many other Lombards, fought against King Cunibert and expelled him from the kingdom. But when Cunibert had recovered his strength, he killed the aforementioned tyrant in battle.

King Dagobert came from Metz and, with the counsel of the bishops and nobles, raised his son Sigibert to the kingship of Austrasia. He commended him to Cunibert, Bishop of the Church of Cologne, and to Duke Pippin.

The following year a son was born to him by Queen Nandhilda, whom he named Louis. He designated that, after his departure, the kingdom of Neustria and Burgundy should be given to him.

After this Dagobert himself died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis. He was prudent in counsel, cautious in judgment, vigorous in military discipline, generous in almsgiving, diligent in arranging peace among the churches, and especially devoted to enriching the monasteries of the saints. Although he cultivated all holy places, he cultivated above all the monasteries of Saints Denis, Martin, and Maurice, and ennobled them with every ecclesiastical dignity.

His sons held his kingdom as he himself had divided it during his lifetime. Ega, the mayor of the palace, administered the kingdom of Clovis together with Queen Nantilda.

Around this time, when the fortress of Monte Cassino was a desolate wilderness, Franks from the region of the Celmanici or Orléanais came and carried away the bodies of the venerable father Benedict and his sister Scholastica, taking them back to their own country.

The body of Saint Benedict was buried in the territory of Orléans, in the monastery called Fleury. The body of Saint Scholastica was buried in the region of Le Mans through the devotion of religious people.

After King Cunibert died, a great dispute arose among the nobles over the Lombard kingdom. Many were killed, and some were blinded. The women who had boasted that they would become queens were also disfigured, their noses and ears being cut off. At last Heribert, Duke of Turin, obtained the kingdom.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 632, Leo, seizing the imperial dignity [Col. 0038D], deprived Justinian of the kingdom and kept him in exile in Pontus; he ruled the Roman Empire for three years. Pope Sergius found in the sacristy of the blessed apostle Peter a large portion of the wood of the Lord’s cross, which from that time onward was kissed and adored by all the people in the Constantinian basilica on the feast of its Exaltation [the Latin is corrupt].

In Britain, Cuthbert, bishop of the church of Lindisfarne, was held in renown; in Gaul, Audoin, bishop of Rouen, Eligius, bishop of Noyon, and Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, were held in renown. At this time also the venerable man Willibrord, surnamed Clement, of the English nation in Britain [Col. 0039A], crossed into Gaul for the sake of the grace of the Gospel. He was consecrated bishop of the Frisians by Pope Sergius and sent back to that same people to preach.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 635, Tiberius reigned for seven years. Rising up against Leo, he invaded his kingdom and kept him under guard in the same city for the entire time that he himself reigned. Gisulf, duke of Benevento, devastated Benevento and Campania by fire, sword, and captivity. John governed the Roman Church. He redeemed all the captives whom Gisulf had taken and made the Lombards return home. Another John succeeded him.

King Louis, uncovering the body of the blessed Dionysius with insufficient reverence, though eagerly, broke off and seized a bone of the arm. Immediately, struck with stupor, he fell into madness [Col. 0039B], and after two years ended his life together with his kingdom.

At this time a synod was held at Aquileia which, through ignorance of the faith, hesitated to accept the fifth universal council, which had been held in the time of Pope Vigilius against the heretics who asserted that blessed Mary had given birth to a mere human being, not to God and man. At that synod it was authoritatively established in accordance with Catholic teaching that Mary should always be called θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), because she gave birth not merely to a human being, but truly to God and man.

In that age Lambert, bishop of the church of Tongeren, became renowned. After he had rebuked the royal household, inflamed by religious zeal, he was unexpectedly confined within a church house at Liège by the most wicked Dodo and other men sent from the palace, and was killed.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 642, Justinian [Col. 0039C] reigned a second time together with his son Tiberius for six years. Recovering the kingdom, he killed the patricians who had expelled him. He also seized Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and ordered their throats to be cut in the middle of the circus before all the people. He sent the patriarch of Constantinople, Gallicinus, to Rome with his eyes torn out, and appointed Cyrus, the abbot who had cared for him in exile in Pontus, bishop in Gallicinus’s place.

Sisinnius and Constantine governed the Roman Church. Justinian ordered this Constantine to come to him; he received him honorably and sent him back. When Constantine prostrated himself on the ground and asked to intercede for Justinian’s sins, Justinian renewed all the privileges of the Church. When Justinian sent an army into Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had confined there, the same pope strongly opposed him, but nevertheless could not prevent it. The army sent against Philippicus went over to his side and made him emperor. Coming against Justinian at Constantinople, he fought him at the twelfth milestone from the city, killed him, and obtained the kingdom.

As we stated above, Philippicus ruled for six years on this second occasion. Leo mutilated his nostrils when Philippicus was expelled; after Philippicus had again been restored to the imperial power, whenever he wiped away a running drop of rheum with his hand, he almost invariably ordered one of those who had opposed him to have his throat cut.

While these things were happening in the East, Ansprand, who had spent nine years in exile in Bavaria, came with the Bavarians into Italy [Col. 0040A] and fought King Heribert, defeating him. When Heribert wished to flee to Francia, he entered the river Ticino and attempted to swim across it with his horse; but because he was weighed down by gold, he was suffocated and drowned. Ansprand obtained the kingdom for only three months. After his death, his son Liutprand was established on the royal throne.

Among the Frankish people also, after Pippin had been removed by death, his son Charles succeeded him in the principate, although he wrested that principate from the hands of Reginfrid through many wars and battles. For while he was being held in custody, he escaped by divine providence. At first he engaged Reginfrid in combat two or three times with a small force; finally, after a great battle, he defeated him at Vincy. To Reginfrid, however, he granted, as they say, one city in which to dwell—namely Angers [Col. 0040B]—while he himself undertook the government of the entire Frankish people.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 648, Philippicus reigned for one year and six months. After he had been confirmed in the imperial dignity, he removed Cyrus from the episcopate and ordered him to return to Pontus to govern his monastery. Philippicus sent Pope Constantine letters containing an erroneous doctrine, but Constantine rejected them. The Roman people decreed that they would accept neither the name, nor letters, nor image on coins of a heretical emperor. Against Philippicus, Anastasius—also called Artemius—rose up, expelled him from the kingdom, and deprived him of his eyes.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 650, Anastasius reigned for three years. He sent letters to Pope Constantine through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy [Col. 0040C], in which he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the sixth council. After Gisulf, duke of Benevento, died, his son Romuald succeeded him.

About this time Petronax, a citizen of the city of Brescia, moved by divine love, sought the fortress of Cassino and rebuilt the monastery of Saint Benedict, which had by then remained destroyed for one hundred and ten years. There he became the father of many monks. Pope Gregory was appointed; he ordained Boniface, born in Britain, as bishop, and through him preached the word of salvation in Germany, illuminating that people, who sat in darkness, with the light of the Gospel.

[Col. 0040D] Prince Charles engaged in many battles against Ratbod, king of the Frisians. This tyrant was struck down by divine providence in the fourth year of the aforesaid prince. In the fifth year of his reign, that same Charles fought against the Saxons and defeated them.

The emperor Anastasius sent a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens. The army, turning back halfway, elected Theodosius emperor and compelled him to assume and retain the imperial throne. Theodosius defeated Anastasius in a serious battle near the city of Mycenae; seven thousand of the army fell. After Anastasius had given him an oath, Theodosius made him a cleric and had him ordained priest.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 654, Theodosius reigned [Col. 0041A] for one year. After receiving the kingdom, he immediately set up again in the imperial city, in its former place, the image depicting the holy synod, which Philippicus had thrown down.

In those days the river Tiber flooded so greatly that, overflowing its bed, it inflicted much destruction on the city of Rome. It rose in the Via Lata to a height of one and a half men, and the waters descending from the gate of Saint Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge joined together.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 655, Leo reigned for nine years. At this time the Saracen nation came with an immense army, surrounded Constantinople, and besieged it continuously for three years, until, while the citizens cried out to God with great persistence, very many of the Saracens perished from hunger, cold, war, and pestilence [Col. 0041B], and, worn out by the siege, withdrew. A very great multitude of them perished in a storm at sea; within Constantinople itself, three hundred thousand people died of pestilence during the siege.

King Liutprand transferred the bones of Saint Augustine, bishop, from Sardinia and buried them with due honor in the city of Pavia. The same king besieged Ravenna, attacked its fleet, and destroyed it.

In the tenth year of his reign, Prince Charles fought with the Bavarians and defeated them. In the fifteenth year of his reign, the same king entered Alamannia, fought against Lantfrid, and subjected that people to himself. In the sixteenth year of his reign, he entered Gascony and terrified Duke Eudo of Aquitaine by war.

In the seventeenth year, the Saracens came from Spain with their wives and [Col. 0041C] children and entered the province of Aquitaine in Gaul as though intending to settle there. Charles, as has been said, was then at odds with Eudo, prince of Aquitaine; nevertheless, joining forces, they fought against those same Saracens with a common purpose. For when the Franks rushed upon them, they killed 375,000 of them. Eudo also attacked their camp, killing many in the same way, and devastated everything. Only 1,500 of the Franks fell, as is contained in the letter sent by Eudo to Pope Gregory concerning that victory.

At that time the emperor Leo burned the images of the saints that had been taken down, and ordered the Roman pontiff Gregory to do the same if he wished to retain his favor. But the pontiff refused to do this. The entire army of Ravenna and of Venice likewise resisted such commands with one accord [Col. 0041D]; and unless the pontiff had restrained them, they would have appointed another emperor over themselves.

At the same time King Liutprand invaded the forts of Emilia—Feronianum and Montembellum, Buxeta and Perticeta, Bononia and the Pentapolis, and Auximum—but after some days they were returned to the Romans through the efforts of the Roman pontiff.

Leo Augustus proceeded to worse measures, compelling all who lived in Constantinople, by force as well as by persuasion, to take down the images of the saints, and burning every one that he could find. Since many of the people tried to prevent such a crime, some of them were beheaded and others mutilated in part of their bodies [Col. 0042A]. Because Patriarch Germanus did not consent to this error, he was expelled from his own see, and the presbyter Anastasius was ordained in his place.

About this time Prince Charles sent his son Pippin to King Liutprand so that, according to custom, he might cut his hair. After cutting his hair, Liutprand became his father and, having enriched him with many royal gifts, sent him back to his father.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, Charles came with an army into the Wistrachia and subjected it to his rule. In the twentieth year of his reign, he again entered Gascony with a strong force and deprived Eudo of both kingdom and life; in the following year he fought against Eudo’s sons.

In the twenty-second year of his reign, an army of Saracens again entered Gaul [Col. 0042B] and caused great devastation. Charles engaged them in battle not far from Narbonne and overthrew them with a very great slaughter, as before.

In the twenty-fourth year of his reign, the Saracens again entered the territories of Gaul, came as far as Provence, captured Arles, and demolished everything around it. Then Charles sent to King Liutprand and requested assistance against the Saracens. Without delay, Liutprand hastened to his aid with the entire Lombard army. When the Saracen people learned this, they immediately fled from those regions.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, Charles, the most warlike and victorious prince of the Franks, died.

Thus, if I am not mistaken, the years reckoned from the incarnation of the Lord [Col. 0042C], beginning with the forty-second year of Octavian’s empire and extending to the final year of Leo Augustus, who is known to have reigned in the time of Prince Charles, amount to 718 years, 3 months, and 2 days.

Let us also distinguish, if it pleases, these same years of the Lord according to the periods of the Roman pontiffs, and let us see how the periods of the princes and bishops correspond to one another.

The blessed apostle Peter sat in the episcopal chair at Rome for 25 years, 2 months, and 2 days.

It follows, as we suppose, that the total from the time of the blessed apostle Peter to Pope Zacharias [Col. 0044B], who at the beginning of Pippin’s reign governed the Roman Church, is 703 years, 8 months, and 26 days. If to these we add the 15 years of Octavian, 23 of Tiberius, 3 of Gaius, and likewise 3 of Claudius—for the apostle Peter came to Rome in the fourth year of Claudius, and that year itself is counted in his pontificate—the total is 747 years. Thus the years of the pontiffs exceed the years of the Roman princes by 29 years. Let the prudent reader judge which of these reckonings ought rather to be followed.

This much, however, we know for certain: neither the number of years of the emperors nor that of the bishops agrees with the cycles of Dionysius, since in one reckoning more and in the other fewer years are found. For according to Dionysius, Prince Charles died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 741, and Pippin assumed the principate. It may be that, through the fault of the copyist [Col. 0044C], the number of years has been corrupted.

We have carried this account forward from the very year of the Lord’s incarnation to this point for the following reason: since the book that follows, composed by our littleness, declares through the years of the same incarnation of the Lord the periods of the princes and their deeds, this book likewise briefly demonstrates when, where, and what was done under each prince. It also names the triumphs of the holy martyrs and confessors, and states in which places and under which kings they received the crown of glory. Therefore, where this book ends, let the other begin in succession; and where the other begins, let this one come to its end.

**THE FIRST BOOK ENDS.**

**HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE DEEDS OF THE FRANKISH KINGS.**

[Col. 0044D]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 741, Charles, son of Pippin, mayor of the palace and the most warlike duke of the Franks, died.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 742, his sons Carolomannus and Pippin led an army against Hunold, duke of the Aquitanians. They captured the fortress called Lucas, and on that same journey divided the Frankish kingdom between themselves at a place called Old Poitiers. Afterward, in that same year, Carolomannus ravaged Alamannia with an army.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 743, Carolomannus and Pippin led an army against Odilo, duke of the Bavarians, entered battle, and emerged victorious [Col. 0045A]. Carolomannus went into Saxony without his brother and captured the fortress called Hochseoburg through an agreement and terms of peace. He took the Saxon Theoderic as a hostage; after giving oaths, Theoderic was released to return to his homeland, but, disregarding his oath, he broke faith [Note: [Col. 0045] “He broke faith.” At this time the monastery of Fulda began to be founded by Saint Boniface, archbishop, in the wilderness of Bochenia 3.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 744, Carolomannus and Pippin again entered Saxony with an army, and the aforementioned Theoderic was captured once more.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 745, Carolomannus confessed to his brother Pippin that he had resolved in his mind to leave the world and, for the love of God, abandon his earthly kingdom, so that in the life to come he might receive a hundredfold possession. In that year they undertook no expedition; instead, each prepared himself: Carolomannus for the journey he had decided upon, and Pippin to accompany his brother honorably to the place, with gifts and fitting generosity.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 746, Carolomannus went to Rome, where he was tonsured. On Mount Soracte he built a monastery in honor of Saint Sylvester. After staying there for some time, he proceeded as far as Saint Benedict’s monastery at Cassino, where he became a monk.

A memorable story is told about this holy man. While he was still at Rome, in the monastery he had built, everyone revered him and raised him up with praises because of his royal nobility and, more importantly, because he had despised an earthly kingdom and the glory of the present world. Fearing the favor of human praise, this man full of God—who had abandoned so much for Christ—resolved to flee rather than become subject to vainglory. Confiding this plan to one faithful companion alone, whom he had found faithful in all things from childhood, he fled with him by night, without anyone knowing, and reached Mount Cassino. Carrying nothing of all the goods necessary for the body, he followed Christ naked.

According to the custom, he knocked at the monastery gate and asked for an interview with the father of the monastery. When he had come into his presence, he immediately fell to the ground, declared himself a murderer and guilty of every crime, begged for mercy, and sought a place of penance. When the father learned that the man was a foreigner, he asked what his homeland or nation was. The man confessed that he was a Frank and had left Francia for such a crime, ready to bear exile gladly, provided only that he did not lose his heavenly homeland.

The spiritual father granted his requests and ordered that he and his companion be received into the novices’ cell and tested there according to what the Rule commands—tested all the more strictly because he was a man of a barbarian and unknown nation—fulfilling the apostolic saying: “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God.” Thus, after being tested in all patience, he was joined to the community together with his companion. When the year had been completed, he professed stability, conversion of conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0046A].

He began to conduct himself irreproachably among the brothers, excelling in every virtue. It happened that, as is customary, he was appointed weekly server in the kitchen. Although he performed this duty willingly, he offended through ignorance in many matters. The cook, boiling with anger, slapped him and said: “Is this how you ought to serve the brothers?” Moved by this, he answered with a calm expression: “May the Lord forgive you, brother, and may Carolomannus forgive you.” For he had not revealed his name to anyone, lest he be recognized by it.

Again, when he had made mistakes in preparing certain foods, he was struck once more by the cook, to whom he uttered the same imprecation as above. When the cook was beating him cruelly for a third time, his inseparable companion in exile became indignant that so great a man should be treated so insultingly by so contemptible a person. No longer able to bear it, he seized the pestle with which bread was crushed to be put into the brothers’ vegetables and struck the cook with all his strength, saying: “May God not spare you either, worthless servant, nor may Carolomannus forgive you.”

When the brothers heard this, they were greatly disturbed that a foreigner, received out of mercy, had dared to do such a thing. He was therefore immediately committed to custody, so that on the following day such presumption might be punished more severely.

On the next day he was brought out of custody and placed in the middle of the assembly. Asked why he had dared to lay hands on the serving brother, he replied: “Because,” he said, “I saw a worthless servant dishonoring with words—and even striking with blows—the better and nobler man than all those whom I know to live on earth” [Col. 0046C].

They were greatly enraged that he had preferred the man who had come as a foreigner to all the others. They asked who this man was who surpassed everyone in goodness and nobility, and why he had not at least spared the father of the monastery. Compelled by necessity and unable to conceal what God now wished to be revealed, he said: “This is Carolomannus, formerly king of the Franks, who for the love of Christ abandoned his kingdom and the glory of the world; he humbled himself from such greatness so completely that now he is not only insulted by the basest persons but even abused with blows.”

On hearing this, they rose trembling from their seats, prostrated themselves at his feet, asked forgiveness for their contempt, and confessed their ignorance. He, however, threw himself on the ground and began with tears [Col. 0046D] to deny that this was true, saying that he was not Carolomannus but a sinful man and a murderer, and that his companion had invented the story out of terror at the offense he had committed.

What more is there to say? Once recognized by everyone, he was treated with great reverence. We have not allowed this story to pass over in silence; now let us return to the chronicle.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 747, Gripho fled into Saxony. Pippin, traveling through Thuringia, entered Saxony as far as the river Missaha, at a place called Scahaningi [Col. 0047A]. Gripho, having gathered a force, took up a position with the Saxons beside the river Obacrus, at a place called Orhemum.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 748, Gripho left Saxony, reached Bavaria, and subjected the duchy itself to his authority. He captured Hiltrude and Thassilo and subjected them to his rule. Suideger came to aid the aforementioned Gripho. When Pippin heard this, he came there with an army and subjected all those named above to himself. He took Gripho and Lantfrid with him to Francia and established Thassilo as duke of the Bavarians. He sent Gripho into the regions of Neustria and gave him twelve counties. From there Gripho fled again, sought Gascony, and reached Waifarius, duke of the Aquitanians.

[Col. 0047B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 749, Burchard, bishop of the church of Würzburg, and Folrad, chaplain, were sent to Rome to Pope Zacharias to ask about the kings in Francia who, although they did not possess royal power in those times, were nevertheless called kings—whether this was right or not. The aforesaid pope sent word to Pippin that it seemed better to him that the one who possessed power should be called king than the one who remained without royal power. To prevent the order of Christianity from being disturbed, he ordered by apostolic authority that Pippin be created king and anointed with the oil of holy unction.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 750, Pippin was elected king according to the custom of the Franks and anointed by the hand of Boniface, of blessed memory, archbishop of the city of Mainz [Col. 0047C]. He was raised up by the Franks to the kingship in the city of Soissons. Hilderic, who was falsely called king, was tonsured and sent to a monastery.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 751, King Pippin traveled into Saxony. Bishop Hildegarius was killed by the Saxons at the fortress called Wigberc, yet King Pippin emerged victorious and reached as far as a place called Rimiae. He returned to Francia, where he was informed that Gripho, his brother, who had fled into Gascony, had been killed.

Pope Stephen came to Francia seeking comfort and assistance on behalf of the rights of Saint Peter. Carolomannus also came, the monk and brother of the aforementioned king, at the command of his abbot, as though to obstruct the apostolic petition. In this year the lord king celebrated Christmas at Theodon’s estate and Easter at Carisiacum.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 752, the aforementioned Pope Stephen confirmed Pippin as king by holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Charles and Carolomannus, to royal dignity. In that same year Saint Boniface, archbishop, while announcing the word of God, was killed by pagans in Frisia and fell as a martyr of Christ [Col. 0048A]. Abbot Walfrid became renowned in Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0047] *waltfridus* 7; *walfredus* and *walifredus* 8–12; *wolfridus* 5. He seems to be referring to Paul the Deacon or Strabo.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 753 [Note: [Col. 0047] A.D. 752, Pippin king, 2], King Pippin entered Italy at the apostolic invitation, seeking the rights of the apostle Peter. Haistulf, king of the Lombards, opposed those rights and went to the Lombard Thermopylae—that is, the mountain passes. He came to meet King Pippin and the Franks, and when battle was joined, Pippin emerged victorious with the Lord’s help and through the intercession of blessed Peter.

In that same year Pope Stephen was restored to his see by the envoys of King Pippin, Folrad and many others. When King Haistulf had been enclosed in the city of Pavia, necessity compelled him to promise that he would fulfill the rights of Saint Peter. On the basis of this promise, King Pippin received forty hostages and returned to Francia after the oaths had been confirmed.

Nor have we judged it superfluous to insert into this work the letter of that same Pope Stephen, written for this reason. It runs as follows:

“Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God. Just as no one ought to boast of his own merits, so the works of God that are performed in him through his saints, without his merits, ought not to be kept silent but proclaimed, as the angel admonishes Tobias. Therefore, because of the oppression of the holy Church by the most savage and blasphemous king—Haistulf, whose name ought not even to be spoken—I came to the excellent and most faithful lord of Saint Peter, the most Christian King Pippin, in Francia. There I fell ill almost unto death and remained for some time in the Parisian district, in the venerable monastery of the holy martyr Dionysius.

“When the physicians had already despaired of me, I was praying in the church of that same blessed martyr beneath the bells. I saw before the altar the lord Peter and the teacher of the nations, the lord Paul, and with my whole mind I recognized them by their *surcaria* [the printed word is uncertain]. Then I saw the blessed lord Dionysius at the right hand of the lord Peter, slender and taller.

“The good shepherd, the lord Peter, said: ‘This brother of ours is asking for health.’ And blessed Paul said: ‘He will be healed now.’ Approaching, he amicably placed his hand upon the breast of the lord Dionysius, looked toward the lord Peter, and the lord Peter said cheerfully to the lord Dionysius: ‘His healing is granted through your favor.’

“Immediately blessed Dionysius, holding a censer of incense and a palm in his hand, came to me with a presbyter and deacon who were standing to one side, and said to me: ‘Peace be with you, brother. Do not be afraid; you will not die until you have safely returned to your see. Rise up healed, and dedicate this altar in honor of God and of the apostles Peter and Paul, whom you see, celebrating masses of thanksgiving.’

“Immediately I was made well, and I wished to fulfill what had been commanded me. Those who were present, however, said that I was delirious. Therefore I reported to them, and to the king and all his people, in due order what I had seen and how I had been healed, and I fulfilled everything that had been commanded me. These things took place in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0049A] 753, on the fifth day before the Ides of August.”

Strengthened by Christ’s power, during the celebration of the consecration of the aforesaid altar and the offering of the sacrifice, he anointed Pippin, king of the Franks, and his two sons, Charles and Carolomannus, as kings [Note: [Col. 0049] “He anointed them as kings,” etc. … “and intended to consecrate them”; cf. the clause concerning the consecration in Bouq., vol. V, pp. 9, 10.]. He also marked Bertrada, the wife of that king, clothed in royal robes, with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit in the name of God. Blessing the Frankish nobles with apostolic benediction, he bound them by the authority of Saint Peter entrusted to him by Christ. He adjured them never, throughout succeeding generations, to presume in any way to establish over themselves a king from another lineage, but only from the lineage of those whom divine providence had chosen to guard the apostolic see and whom, through him—namely, the vicar of Saint Peter, indeed of the Lord Jesus Christ—it had deigned to raise to royal power and consecrate with the most sacred anointing.

With these matters inserted, let us return to the chronicle. When King Pippin, as stated above, had entered Italy, Carolomannus the monk remained in the city of Vienne together with Queen Bertrada. There he was seized by illness and ended his final day.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 755, when King Pippin learned that the promises made by Haistulf concerning the rights of Saint Peter were not being fulfilled, he entered Italy again, besieged Pavia, and surrounded Haistulf with a siege. Haistulf again gave a firm promise concerning the rights of Saint Peter, that they would remain secure; moreover, Pippin conquered Ravenna together with the Pentapolis and the entire Exarchate and handed it over to Saint [Col. 0049C] Peter.

When King Pippin had returned to Francia, the aforementioned Haistulf was planning to break the promises he had made. One day, while he was engaged in hunting, he was struck by God’s judgment and ended his life together with his kingdom. How Desiderius was placed in the kingdom, we shall say later.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 756, the emperor Constantine sent King Pippin, among other gifts, an organ. King Pippin held his assembly at Compiègne. There Thassilo, duke of the Bavarians, came and became his man; by hand-pledges and many oaths, he swore allegiance to Pippin and his sons over the bodies of Saint Dionysius, Saint Germanus, and Saint Martin. His leading men likewise did the same.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 757, King Pippin traveled into Saxony and entered the Saxon fortifications by force. At a place called Sitnia, many of the Saxon people were slaughtered. They then promised to do the king’s entire will and also to provide tribute, namely 300 horses each year.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 758, a son was born to King Pippin, and the aforementioned king gave him his own name. The child lived for two years and died in the third [Col. 0050A]. In that same year Pippin celebrated Christmas at Lengolare and Easter at Iopila.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 760, King Pippin saw that Waifarius, duke of the Aquitanians, was entirely unwilling to render to the churches in Francia the rights due to them from the possessions and estates belonging to those churches that lay within his duchy. He therefore took counsel with the Franks to travel into Aquitaine and seek the aforesaid rights. He reached as far as a place called Thedoad.

When Waifarius learned this, he was terrified by fear and sent envoys, Otbert and Dawin. He gave as a hostage his kinsman Adalgarius and sent word to Pippin that he would restore everything the aforesaid king was seeking in ecclesiastical matters. Pippin celebrated Christmas at Carisiacum and Easter likewise [Col. 0050B].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 761, Waifarius, giving no thought to the hostages and oaths he had given, sent an army to avenge the injury he had suffered from the Franks in the preceding year. They came as far as the city of Chalon, devastating everything. While the aforesaid king was holding an assembly at an estate called Duria, news was brought to him of what Waifarius had done. He immediately moved the army, entered Aquitaine, captured many forts—namely Bordeaux, Clarus Mons, Cantela, and Auvergne—and reached as far as Limoges, devastating everything. He celebrated Christmas at Carisiacum and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 762, King Pippin [Col. 0050C] ravaged Aquitaine with an army and captured the city of Bourges and the fortress called Thouars. He celebrated Christmas at the estate of Gentilly and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 763, King Pippin held his assembly at Nevers and entered Aquitaine for the fourth time. There Thassilo, duke of the Bavarians, disregarding his oaths, fraudulently withdrew from the campaign, forgetting all the benefits that the king, his uncle, had bestowed upon him. Returning to Bavaria, he no longer wished to see the face of the aforementioned king.

The king, however, traversing Aquitaine, reached as far as Cahors. Returning by way of Limoges, he came into Francia. A severe winter followed. The king celebrated Christmas at the estate called Longolare and Easter likewise [Col. 0050D].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 764, King Pippin held his assembly at Worms and carefully dealt with the dispute between Waifarius and Thassilo. He celebrated Christmas at Carisiacum and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 765, the king held his assembly at Attigny, and in that year, as in the preceding one, he went nowhere. He celebrated Christmas at the estate of Aix and Easter likewise.

[Col. 0051A] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 766, King Pippin went into Aquitaine and held his assembly in the city of Orléans. He restored the fortress of Argenton, which Waifarius had previously destroyed, and left Franks there to hold Aquitaine. He did the same at Bourges. He celebrated Christmas at Salmoniacum and Easter at Gentilly.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 767, the king held a great synod at the aforesaid estate between Romans and Greeks concerning the Holy Trinity and the images of the saints. Afterward he entered Aquitaine by way of Narbonne. He captured Toulouse and Gévaudan and celebrated Easter in the city of Vienne.

In the same year, in the month of August, he entered Aquitaine again [Col. 0051B], came as far as Bourges, and held a synod there. From there he proceeded as far as the Garonne, captured many cliffs and caves, as well as the forts of Scoralia, Torinna, and Petrocia, and returned to Bourges. There he was informed of the death of Pope Paul; there also he celebrated Christmas.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 768, King Pippin, while traveling, captured Remistagnum and reached as far as the city of Saintes. There he captured Waifarius’s mother, his sister, and his nieces. From there he went to a place called Montes. Heriwicus came to him there; he had another sister of Waifarius with him. Returning from there, Pippin celebrated Easter at the fortress called Sels.

After this, taking Queen Bertrada with him, he reached the city of Saintes. There he left the queen with the servants and proceeded to Périgord. After Waifarius was killed, he returned in triumph to Saintes. Remaining there for several days, he began to fall ill. From there he departed and came to Tours, where he went to pray at Saint Martin’s. Leaving there, he scarcely reached Paris and Saint Dionysius. There he ended his final day, on the eighth day before the Ides of October.

The lords Charles and Carolomannus were raised to the kingship: Charles at the city of Noyon, Carolomannus at Soissons, on the seventh day before the Ides of October. Charles celebrated Christmas at Aix and Easter in the city of Rouen.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 769, King Charles entered Aquitaine with an army, because Hunald had planned to rebel; and, with God’s help, he received all Aquitaine and [Col. 0051D] Vasconia into submission and destroyed Hunald’s wicked plans. From there he departed and came to the city of Cologne; there he took with him a number of Franks, with their weapons and all their equipment, and went to the river Dordogne. There he built a fortress called Fronticis and stationed Franks in that garrison. Then he sent envoys to Lupus the Vasconian, ordering him to bring Hunald and his wife before him, since they had fled to him. The aforementioned Hunald and his wife were brought to the named fortress. After receiving them, he returned to Francia [Col. 0052A] and celebrated Christmas at Düren and Easter at the public settlement of Liège.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 770, Charles held a synod in the city of Worms. Queen Berta went to Bavaria, and from there entered Italy. The king celebrated Christmas at Mainz and Easter at Heristal.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 771, King Charles held a synod at Valenciennes. In the same year King Carloman died at the estate of Salmontiacum, on 4 December. Charles came to the estate of Carboniacum, where Folcarius and Folradus, chaplains, came to him with other bishops and priests, and the counts Werinus and Adalhartus, with the other leading men who had belonged to Carloman. Carloman’s wife, however, [Col. 0052B] went with very few Franks to the region of Italy. The king celebrated Christmas at Attigny and Easter at Heristal.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 772, King Charles held a synod at Worms. From there he proceeded into Saxony, captured the fortress of Heresburg at the first assault, and reached Ormensul. He destroyed that sanctuary and carried away the gold and silver that he found there. At that time there was a great drought, so that water failed at the place mentioned above. The king wished to remain there for two or three days in order to destroy the sanctuary completely, but water was lacking for the army. Suddenly, by the generosity of divine grace, without anyone’s foreknowledge, an extremely abundant stream of water poured forth in a certain torrent, so that the entire army had sufficient water. [Col. 0052C] After the sanctuary had been destroyed, the king came to the river Weser, where he held an assembly with the Saxons, received twelve hostages, and returned to Francia. He celebrated Christmas at Heristal and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 773, the king came to spend the winter at the estate of Düren. There Peter, an envoy in the name of Pope Hadrian, approached him, inviting him, together with the Franks, to come for the love of God and to obtain justice for Saint Peter against Desiderius and the Lombards. The aforesaid envoy had come by sea as far as Marseille and from there by land to the king; he came by sea because the roads had been closed by the Lombards against the Romans. Then the king consulted his faithful men about whether he should grant the apostolic’s requests. Since all approved this, he departed for those regions. Coming to the city of Geneva, he held a synod there and divided the army into two parts. He himself proceeded with one part over Mount Cenis and sent his uncle Bernard with the other part over Mount Joux. The two armies joined at the passes. When Desiderius learned of this, he came to meet the king and the Franks with armed forces [Note: [Col. 0051] “he came to meet them with armed forces.” From this point, omitting the intervening material, the year 794 follows: “When they heard that they were coming from two directions,” etc.; the remainder follows after the words of the year 801. “The leaders of this faction” has been inserted.]. Then the king set up camp at those same passes and secretly sent one troop of picked men through the mountains. When Desiderius learned this, he immediately abandoned the passes [Col. 0053A] and entered Pavia as quickly as he could. The king, with everyone, entered Italy without injury, with the Lord’s help and through the intercession of blessed Peter. When he reached Pavia, he besieged Desiderius, who was hiding inside, and there, in his own camp, celebrated Christmas; he celebrated Easter at Rome.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 774, while the king was delayed in those regions on this business, the Saxons, seizing the opportunity and setting aside their oaths, attacked the borders of Francia and came as far as the fortress called Buriaburg. The inhabitants of the place, anticipating their arrival, withdrew into the aforesaid stronghold. When this savage people began to burn the buildings outside the villages, they came to a certain basilica at a place called Friedeslar, which the holy martyr Boniface had consecrated and had foretold through the spirit of prophecy would never be destroyed by fire. The Saxons began with every effort to attack that basilica, seeking by any means to burn it with fire. While they were doing this, two young men in white garments appeared to certain Christians who were in the fortress and also to certain pagans who were in the same army. They protected the basilica from the fire, and for this reason the Saxons could ignite the fire neither inside nor outside it. Meanwhile, terrified by divine majesty, they were overcome by fear and fled, with no one pursuing them. [Col. 0053C] Later one of those Saxons was found dead beside the basilica, kneeling and leaning forward upon his feet, holding fire and wood in his hands, as though he were blowing with his mouth in order to burn the basilica.

While this was happening, Charles returned from Rome and came to Pavia. He captured the city by force, and moreover took King Desiderius with his wife and daughter and all the palace treasury. There all the Lombards who came from every city of Italy submitted themselves to his rule. Adalgisus, son of King Desiderius, escaped by flight, entered the sea, and went to Constantinople. After subjugating and organizing Italy, Charles left a Frankish guard in Pavia and returned triumphantly to Francia. When he reached the place called [Col. 0053D] Hengilinheim, he sent four troops into Saxony. Three engaged the Saxons in battle and, with God’s help, proved victorious; the fourth troop did not fight, but returned to Francia with much booty. The king celebrated Christmas at Quierzy and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 775, the king held a synod at the estate called Düren. From there, proceeding into Saxony, he captured the fortress of Sigiburg, rebuilt Heresburg, and came to the river Weser at a place called Brunisberg. There the Saxons met him, wishing [Col. 0054A] to defend the bank of the aforesaid river. With the Lord’s help and the Franks fighting, the Saxons were put to flight, the Franks occupied both banks, and many Saxons were killed. Then the king divided the army, took part of it with him, and went as far as the river Oker. There all the eastern Saxons came with their duke Hassio, gave hostages according to the king’s pleasure, and swore oaths. As he was returning, the Angarians came to the district called Bucki with their duke Bruno and did what the eastern Saxons had done. Meanwhile the Saxons fought with the Franks who had remained above the river Weser; by God’s generosity the Franks won the victory, and many of the Saxons were killed. [Col. 0054B] Hearing this, the king again attacked the Saxons with an army, inflicted a great slaughter, and captured abundant booty from the Westphalians, who were compelled to give hostages. After receiving the hostages and capturing much booty, the king returned to Francia. There he was informed that Rotgaud the Lombard, setting aside his allegiance and oaths, intended to rebel against him. He immediately set out for those regions and celebrated Christmas at the estate called Sélestat in Alsace.

*At the same time* [Note: [Col. 0053] “At the same time the duke of Venice, etc., through the end, is found in codex 7 in the lower section.] the duke of Venice, because of the envy and plots of certain Venetians who gave him grounds to wish to hand Venice over to King Charles, was captured by his own men [Note: [Col. 0053] “captured by all his own men,” according to the codex.] and sent into exile at Constantinople to the emperor Constantine. [Col. 0054C] The same emperor carefully investigated the matter and clearly recognized the Venetians’ deceitful plots. He considered their accusations worthless and made that same duke Anthipatros a patrician. He sent him back to Venice with an envoy and a letter of his own and honorably restored him to his proper seat. After the death of the aforementioned Constantine, however, the rebels tried to kill the duke. The duke, shrewdly anticipating their plan, immediately sent word to the emperor Nicephorus. When the emperor perceived this crime, he promptly sent the patrician Nicetas to Venice to investigate the matter. When Nicetas arrived there and the offenses had been exposed, he arrested twelve of those faithless men. Taking them back with him, he sent them to prison by the emperor’s command, there to end their lives. 7.]

[Col. 0054D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 776, King Charles entered Italy and headed for the territory of the Friulians. He ordered Rotgaud the rebel to be captured and beheaded, came to the city of Treviso, and celebrated Easter there. Having settled affairs and left Frankish guards in the cities that had shown hostility toward him, he returned safely to Francia. Meanwhile the Saxons, learning of the king’s absence, gathered together as usual after breaking their oaths. They attacked the fortress of Heresburg and deceitfully urged the Franks to leave the fortress and go peacefully to their homeland. But when the Franks gave no assent to their deceitful counsels, the Saxons prepared siege engines, surrounded the stronghold with a siege, and fought with all their strength, but accomplished nothing. One day, when they had again prepared for battle with renewed fighting, the glory of God visibly appeared above the church building that stood inside the fortress, witnessed by many Christians and pagans alike. For two shields appeared above the aforementioned basilica, blazing with a blood-red color and moving as though being shaken in battle. When the pagans saw this sign, they were immediately filled with fear and dread and turned to flight. They fell into such madness that, with drawn swords, they stabbed one another with their weapons. The more terrified they were by fear and fled, the more the Christians were strengthened and praised the almighty Lord, who saves [Col. 0055B] those who hope in him.

Leaving that place in great confusion, they came to another fortress called Desuburg [Note: [Col. 0055] Everyone can see that Regino misunderstood the words of the Lorsch Annals and that the passage can refer to no other fortress than Eigiburg.]. They wished to act similarly there, but, with God’s help and the Franks resisting them bravely, they achieved nothing. The townsmen pursued them as far as the river called the Lippe and killed many of them. The king then came to Worms, held a synod and a public assembly there, and, when the council had been dissolved, immediately penetrated the borders of Saxony. Like a huge storm, he laid everything low and broke into the fortifications. Terrified, the Saxons came to the place where the Lippe rises, surrendered themselves and their homeland to the king, and promised that they would become Christians. Then the king, together with the Franks, restored the fortress of Heresburg and another fortress above the [Col. 0055C] Lippe. There the Saxons came with their wives and little children, an innumerable multitude, and were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity. After this they gave as many hostages as the king demanded. Once the fortresses had been repaired and guards assigned, Charles returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at Heristal and Easter at Nijmegen.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 777, the king entered Saxony and held an assembly at a place called Paderborn. All the Saxons gathered there except Widukind, who had fled with a few Saxons to the region of the Northmen. At the same place there also came Saracens from the regions of Spain, whose names were Ibina, Larabi, and the son of Devizefi, who was already called Joseph, together with his son-in-law. There too a multitude of Saxons was baptized and gave oaths according to custom, under penalty of losing their freedom and all their inheritance unless they preserved the Christianity they had received and the loyalty to the king and his sons that they had promised, as well as loyalty to the Franks. Charles returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at Douzy and Easter in Aquitaine, at the estate called Cassinogilum.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 778, Charles entered Spain with an army. He first came to the city of Pamplona and then proceeded to the city of Zaragoza, where an innumerable multitude from Burgundy, Austrasia, Bavaria, Provence, and Septimania gathered to aid the Franks, along with part of the Lombards. When the city had been surrounded by a siege, the terrified Saracens gave hostages and an immense weight of gold. After the Saracens had been expelled from Pamplona, its walls demolished, and the Vascones subjugated, he returned to Francia.

Meanwhile the Saxons, hearing that Charles was separated from them by such a great distance of land, rebelled again at Widukind’s urging, according to their custom. They came as far as the fortress of Düren, which is adjacent to the city of Cologne, devastating everything with slaughter, plunder, and fire. [Col. 0056B] When this was reported to the returning king, who was already staying at the city of Auxerre, the prince sent one troop of picked men to resist their violence. When the Saxons heard that the king was safe and that the Franks were approaching, they turned to flight. The Franks followed them immediately and found them above the river called the Adour, at a place called Lihesi. There the battle began and ended; with the Lord’s help the Franks were victorious, and a multitude of Saxons was killed. The king celebrated Christmas at Heristal and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 779, Charles came to the estate called Compiègne, where Hildebrand, duke of Spoleto, presented himself with gifts and submitted himself to Charles’s rule. In the same year he held a synod [Col. 0056C] at Düren. After this he entered Saxony and came as far as the Lippe. The Saxons tried to resist at a place called Buochol, but achieved nothing. When the way had been opened, he subjugated the Westphalians and all the Saxons who lived beyond the Weser. The king came to a place called Medofulli, where he received hostages and oaths from the Saxons who had defected from him. He returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas in the city of Worms and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 780, Charles entered Saxony and came to Heresburg. From there he went to the place where the Lippe rises and held a synod there. Proceeding onward, he came to the river Elbe. On the journey, the Bardengauvians and many of the North Thuringians were baptized [Col. 0056D] at a place called Horheim, beyond the river Oker. He reached the place where the river Jora flows into the Elbe. After arranging matters among both Saxons and Slavs, he returned to Francia. Having decided to go to Rome for prayer together with his wife Hildegard, he celebrated Christmas in the city of Pavia.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 781, Charles proceeded on his journey and celebrated Easter at Rome. There his son Pippin was baptized by Pope Hadrian, who himself lifted him from the sacred font. The same pontiff anointed his two sons as kings: Pippin as king over Italy and Louis over Aquitaine. Returning from there, Charles came to Milan, where his daughter Gisla was baptized by Archbishop Thomas, who himself lifted her from the sacred font. When these matters had been completed, he returned to Francia.

At that time the apostolic envoys, the bishops Formosus and Damasus, were sent, together with the king’s envoys, the chaplain Siculfus and the master Euvardus, to Duke Tassilo. They admonished and charged him, by apostolic authority, to remember his former oaths and to act in no other way than he had formerly promised under oath to King Pippin and his sons. Tassilo agreed to these admonitions, took hostages from the king, and came to Worms, where he renewed his oaths and gave twelve hostages. [Col. 0057B] [But the aforesaid Tassilo did not keep his promises for long.] The king celebrated Christmas at Quierzy and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 782, Charles came to Cologne, crossed the Rhine, and held a synod where the Lippe rises. All the Saxons gathered there except the rebel Widukind. Envoys of King Godfrey of the Northmen also came there: Altdenus and Hosmundus, and likewise envoys of the Avars sent by the Cagan and Jugur. When the assembly had concluded, the king returned to Francia. The Saxons again violated their faith, took up arms, and did so at Widukind’s urging. At that time the king had sent his envoys Adalgisus, Geilo, and Conrad, powerful men, to lead an army of Franks and Saxons against the few Slavs [Col. 0057C] who still remained in rebellion. When the aforementioned leaders were already on the march and heard that the Saxons had rebelled, they turned their arms against them. Battle was joined, and they killed many of the Saxons. In that battle two commanders fell, namely Adalgisus and Geilo, at the mountain called Suntdal.

When the emperor heard this, he went there with the Franks whom he could gather in haste and reached the place where the river Alara flows into the Weser. Then all the Saxons gathered again, submitted themselves to the power of the aforesaid king, and surrendered for execution four thousand five hundred men who had chiefly fomented that rebellion. Widukind, however, fled to the region of the Northmen. After the seditious men had been put to death or condemned to exile, the king [Col. 0057D] returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at the estate of Düren and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 783, Queen Hildegard died on the day before the Kalends of May, which at that time fell on the eve of the Lord’s Ascension. The king again entered Saxony because the Saxons had rebelled once more. With a few Franks he came to Thietmalli, where the Saxons bravely prepared for battle in the field. Then the king attacked them with the Franks and inflicted such a great slaughter that very few escaped by flight. After completing the victory, the king came to Paderborn, [Col. 0058A] where he assembled his army and again attacked the Saxons, who had joined together above the river called the Asa. Battle was again joined there, and no fewer Saxons fell than had fallen in the earlier battle. The king then crossed the Weser and reached the Elbe. After this he returned to Francia. In the same year Queen Bertha died on 12 July. When the king had reached Worms, he took Queen Fastrada in marriage. He celebrated Christmas at Heristal and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 784, Charles entered Saxony because the Saxons had rebelled again, together with part of the Frisians. He reached Huculvi, going around and devastating everything. There was an exceptionally great flood of waters. He therefore entered [Col. 0058B] through Thuringia from the eastern side against the Eastphalians. He left his son Charles with a strong force against the Westphalians. The king, entering Thuringia, reached the river Elbe, and from there went to Tagnfurt, then to Scaininge, from which place he returned to Francia. The Westphalians assembled near the Lippe. The king’s son met them in the district called Dragini, joined battle with them, defeated them bravely, and returned to Worms to his father. The king, having consulted his faithful men, entered Saxony again in winter and celebrated Christmas at Skidrioburg in the Wizzigau, above the river Ambra, at the estate called Liuhidi.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 785, the king came to Adrine, above the river Weser, where the river Wachna flows into it. Because of the excessive flooding, he returned from there to Heresburg. There he ordered his wife Fastrada to come with his sons and daughters, and remained there throughout the winter. He also celebrated Easter there and sent troops against the Saxons many times, plundering their camps. In May he held a synod at Paderborn. Then, proceeding on his journey without opposition, he traversed all Saxony. He came to Bardengau and from there sent for Widukind and Abbio [Note: [Col. 0057] “Abbio”: witnesses 4, 5a, d, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12; the others read “Albion.”]. He caused both to come to him and bound them by oath to come to him in Francia. After receiving hostages, they came to the king at Attigny, where they were baptized. Then all Saxony was subjugated to the Franks. At the same estate the king celebrated Christmas and Easter likewise.

[Col. 0058D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 786, Charles sent his army into the region of Brittany together with his envoy Odulfus, master of the cooks. The Franks captured many fortresses and brought their leaders before the king at Worms in a public assembly. Then the king, seeing that he had peace on every side, went to Rome for prayer and to confer there with the emperor’s envoys. He celebrated Christmas in the city of Florence.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 787, Charles came to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Hadrian. He remained there for several days. When Duke Heregisus of Benevento heard this, he was terrified by fear and sent his son Romuald to the king with great gifts, asking for peace and promising to do his entire will. But the apostolic did not at all believe these assurances; rather, he urged the king to enter the territory of Benevento, which he did. When he reached Capua, Grimoald left Benevento and withdrew to Salerno, where he fortified himself. From there he sent his son Grimoald—for the king was keeping Romuald with him—with great gifts, offering hostages and promising complete loyalty, provided only that the king cease attacking him. Then the king, after consulting his faithful men and priests, so that the bishoprics and monasteries might not be utterly devastated, chose twelve [Col. 0059B] hostages and a thirteenth, the aforesaid duke’s son Grimoald. After accepting the gifts, all the Beneventans swore allegiance to him. He returned to Rome and there celebrated Easter with the bishop of the apostolic see.

Envoys of Tassilo also came to the same place: Bishop Arnus and Abbot Henry. They asked the pope to make peace and settle the dispute between King Charles and Duke Tassilo. The apostolic struggled greatly over this matter. The king replied to their requests that he had sought this for a long time but had been unable to obtain it. Nevertheless, so that he might not appear disobedient to the apostolic admonitions, he declared that, in the presence of that same pope, he wished to establish peace with those envoys. But when they refused and said that they did not dare to give a definitive judgment on behalf of their lord and that they had not been sent for this purpose, the apostolic, seeing their deceit and recognizing the duke’s instability, angrily anathematized the aforementioned Tassilo and all who favored him, unless he observed in every respect the loyalty that he had promised to King Pippin and his son Charles. Through the same envoys he charged that man and warned that, through his obstinacy and treachery, Christian blood should not be shed and the land laid waste. If the duke was unwilling to obey in any way, then Charles and his army would be absolved by God and Saint Peter, and whatever was perpetrated in his duchy by fire, homicide, or any other evil would all be charged against Tassilo and his accomplices; the king and the Franks would be without blame.

After these words had been spoken, the envoys of Tassilo were absolved. The king completed his prayer at the threshold of the apostles, received the blessing, and set out for Francia. He reached Worms, where his wife Fastrada was, assembled a synod, and explained to the priests and nobles of the kingdom the reasons for his journey and how Tassilo’s cunning had been exposed before the supreme pontiff. After consulting his faithful men, he sent word to that same Tassilo, admonishing him to obey the apostolic exhortations.
