When Tassilo refused to obey, the king moved his army toward Bavaria and came to the place called the Lechfeld, above the city of Augsburg. The eastern Franks, Thuringians, and Saxons came along the Danube to a place called Faringa. King Pippin came from Italy with an army to Trent. [Col. 0060A] Then Tassilo perceived that he was surrounded on every side and saw that the Bavarians were more loyal to Charles than to himself. Hemmed in on all sides, he came to Charles, surrendered himself into his hands for service, returned to him the duchy entrusted to him by King Pippin, and confessed that he had sinned and acted wrongly in every respect. Renewing his oaths, he gave twelve chosen hostages and a thirteenth, his son Theodo. The king received the hostages, returned to Francia, and celebrated Christmas at Engilinheim and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 788, the king assembled a synod at the aforesaid estate. Tassilo came there, and the Bavarians began to accuse him of having violated the loyalty he had promised, at the urging of his wife Liutberga. Tassilo could not deny the charges brought against him; rather, it was proved that he had later sent word to the Avars and had plotted against the life of the king’s faithful men. Finally he confessed that he had said that, even if he had ten sons, he would rather lose them all than remain as he had sworn. On these and many other grounds, he was condemned to death by everyone. When all were calling for the capital sentence, the king, moved by mercy because Tassilo was his kinsman, obtained from those same faithful men of God that he should not die. When the king asked him what he wished to do, he prostrated himself on the ground and requested permission to enter a monastery, so that he might mourn his sins there. His son Theodo did likewise. They were therefore tonsured and sent to a monastery. The few Bavarians who had sided with Tassilo were sent into exile.

[Col. 0060C] In the same year war was waged between the Greeks and the Lombards, under the leadership of Hildebrand of Spoleto, Grimoald of Benevento, and Winegisius, who had been sent by the king with the Franks. The Greeks were put to flight, and the Franks and Lombards were victorious. At the same time battle was joined between the Avars and the Franks who lived in Italy; by God’s generosity the Franks won the victory. A third battle was fought between the Avars and the Bavarians in the field of Ibora. The king’s envoys Grahamanus and Odocar were there with some Franks, and, with God’s help, victory belonged to the Franks and Bavarians. All these matters were brought about by the aforementioned Tassilo and his wife Liuthirga. A fourth battle was fought against the Avars, who wished to avenge those who had fallen in the battle mentioned above; but, with God’s help, victory [Col. 0060D] went to the Christians. After this Charles came to Regensburg, where he arranged the marches and borders of the Bavarians. From there he returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at the palace of Aachen and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 789, the king crossed the Rhine at Cologne and entered Saxony. He came to the river Elbe, where he built two bridges and constructed wooden-and-earth fortresses on both sides of the bridge. From there he advanced into the territory of the Slavs and subjugated the Slavs known as the Wiltzi to his rule. Franks and Saxons were with him on that expedition, while the Frisians came by ship along the river Havel. The Slavs called Surbi [Col. 0061A] and Abotrites were also with him; their prince was named Wisan. After receiving hostages, he returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at Worms and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 790, the king undertook no expedition. He celebrated Christmas in the aforesaid city and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 791, Charles went to the region of the Bavarians and came to Regensburg, where he ordered his army to assemble. There, with the counsel of the nobles of the kingdom, he decided to go into the kingdom of the Avars because of the intolerable evil that they had inflicted upon the peoples of Gaul and upon the churches of God. He came with the army as far as the river Enns, where they kept a three-day fast with litanies, [Col. 0061B] praying for the safety of the army, for God’s help, and for vengeance upon their enemies.

The king held the southern bank of the Danube, while the Saxons with certain Franks and a very large multitude of Frisians held the northern bank. Proceeding in this manner, they came to where the aforementioned Avars had prepared fortifications: on the southern side at Chumberg, and on the northern bank at a place called Camp. That is the name of the river that flows into the Danube there. When the Avars saw the army on both banks and the fleet coming through the middle of the river, such confusion fell upon them, by God’s doing, that they abandoned the defenses of their fortifications and sought hiding places in flight. Thus, with Christ as their leader, both armies entered Pannonia without injury. The king reached the river called the Rába, devastating everything with slaughter, fire, and plunder. From there he returned to Regensburg, celebrated Christmas there, and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 792, the Felician heresy was condemned. Engilbert brought Felix, its proponent, into the presence of Pope Hadrian, and after confessing, he renounced the heresy. In the same year no expedition was undertaken. Only a bridge was constructed over boats for crossing the rivers, secured with anchors and ropes and fastened so that it could be joined and dismantled. The king celebrated Christmas at the same place, Regensburg.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 793, Charles departed from Regensburg and came to the great ditch between the rivers Altmühl and Regnitz. There the envoys of the supreme pontiff came into his presence with great gifts. There he was also informed that the Saxons had again violated their faith and promises in their customary manner. From there he entered the river Main by ship through the Regnitz and celebrated Christmas at Würzburg.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 794, the king celebrated Easter at Frankfurt. There he assembled a great synod of the bishops of Gaul, Germany, and Italy, at which the apostolic envoys, Bishops Theophilus and Stephen, were present. At this synod the Felician heresy was condemned for the third time. They wrote that condemnation in a book on the authority of the holy Fathers, and all the priests copied the book with their own hands. At the same time Queen Fastrada died [Col. 0062A] and was honorably buried in the monastery of Saint Alban. The pseudo-synod of the Greeks, which they had held concerning the worship of images, was rejected by the pontiffs.

After this the king entered Saxony, dividing the army into two parts: he himself went through Thuringia, while his son Charles crossed the Rhine at Cologne. The Saxons gathered at a place called Finisfelt and prepared themselves for battle. When they heard that they were surrounded from two directions, God scattered their plans. Although they deceitfully promised that they were Christians and would be loyal to the king, the king returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at the palace of Aachen and Easter likewise.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 795, the king came to Mainz and held his assembly at the estate called [Col. 0062B] Cuffinstein, in the suburb of that city. When he heard that the Saxons, according to their custom, had invalidated their promise concerning the observance of Christianity and the maintenance of loyalty to the king, he entered Saxony with an army and reached the river Elbe at a place called Hliuni. In those days Wizzam, king of the Abotrites, had been killed there by the Saxons. There also came envoys of Thudun, who held great power among the people and kingdom of the Avars, affirming that Thudun himself wished to surrender himself, his land, and his people to the king and to receive the Christian faith under the king’s direction. The king, therefore, having afflicted the Saxons to a great extent and devastated their land, received hostages and returned to Francia. He celebrated Christmas at Aachen and Easter likewise.

[Col. 0062C] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 796, Pope Adrian died, and Leo immediately succeeded him in the pontificate. He at once sent envoys to the king with gifts, and also sent the keys of the confession of Saint Peter and the standard of the city of Rome.

Henricus, duke of the Friulians, having sent his men with the Slav Wonomir into Pannonia, unexpectedly despoiled Iring, leader of the Avar people, after their rulers had long exhausted one another in civil war. Caganus and Jugoro were killed in internal slaughter. The same duke sent Charles, at the palace of Aachen, the treasure of the ancient kings, accumulated over the long span of many centuries. After receiving it and giving thanks to the giver of all good things, he sent a large part of it to Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles, through Abbot Engilbert. He distributed the remaining part among his leading men, whether clergy or laity, [Col. 0062D] and his other faithful followers.

At that time Thudun, in accordance with his promise, came to the king with a large part of the Avars and surrendered himself, his people, and his homeland to the king. He and his people were baptized, and, having received gifts, they returned to their own country.

At that time the king entered Saxony with an army, and King Pippin entered Pannonia with an army. An embassy from King Pippin came to his father in Saxony and reported that, after the killing of their former leaders, the Avars had set over themselves a king named Kaja, and that Pippin was preparing to fight him. The king, having traversed Saxony, withdrew into Francia and gladly saw at the palace of Aachen his son Pippin returning from Pannonia and bringing the portion [Col. 0063A] of the treasure that had remained. [And in the same place he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord, and likewise Easter.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 797, the city of Barcelona in Hispania, which had long before defected from the Franks, was restored to the Franks by Thatim, its governor. For he came to the palace and surrendered the city, together with himself, to the king.

At that time an expedition was made into Saxony. The army crossed the whole country as far as the ocean, through all the marshes and pathless places. Having returned from Adulo—for this is the name of the place where the ocean washes Saxony—the king, after taking the entire Saxon people into submission through hostages, returned to the palace of Aachen. There he received Abdella the Saracen, son of Ibin, a great king who, driven from his kingdom by his brother, was living in exile in Mauretania [Col. 0063B] and had commended himself to the king.

At the same place there also came an envoy of Nicetas, who at that time ruled Sicily, named Theophilus, bearing a letter from the emperor. The king received him honorably and released him after several days.

In the middle of November, however, the king entered Saxony with an army for the winter. He established a camp beside the river Weser and ordered the camp to be called Heristell. Envoys of the Avar nation came there with great gifts. From that place he ordered Abdella the Saracen to go into Hispania with his son Ludowic, and sent his own son Pippin back to Italy. He himself spent the whole winter there arranging affairs in Saxony, and there celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and Easter.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 798, an envoy of Haldifonsus, king of Galicia and Asturias, named Frola, came to the king [Col. 0063C] and presented a pavilion of marvelous size.

At Easter itself, the Nordliudi, who lived beyond the Elbe, having raised a revolt, seized the royal envoys who were then staying among them to administer justice. They slaughtered some of them and kept the others for ransom.

Accordingly, the king assembled an army and went from Heristell to a place called Minden. After taking counsel, he took up arms against the deserters and traversed all Saxony between the Elbe and the Weser, laying it waste. The Nordliudi engaged in battle with Transaco, duke of the Abrodites, and Hebruinus, the king’s envoy, and were defeated. Four thousand of them were killed in that battle; the rest who fled began to negotiate the terms of peace.

The king [Col. 0063D], after taking hostages from the Saxons, returned to Francia. When he reached Aachen, he received an embassy sent from Constantinople by the Greeks. The envoys were Michael, formerly patrician of Phrygia, and the priest Theophilus, bearing a letter from the empress Irene. Her son, the emperor Constantine, had been seized and blinded by his own people.

This embassy, however, concerned only peace. When he released them, he also released with them Sisinnius, brother of Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, who had long before been captured in battle in Italy.

In this year the star of Mars did not appear in the entire sky. The Balearic Islands were ravaged by the Moors and Saracens. Aldefonsus, king of Galicia and Asturias, having plundered Lisbon, the last city of Hispania, sent the king, during the winter, through his envoys Froja and Basilicus, coats of mail, [Col. 0064A] mules, and captive Moors. He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the same place, and likewise Easter.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 799, the Romans seized Pope Leo during the greater litany, blinded him, and cut out his tongue by the roots. Placed in custody, he escaped at night over a wall. He then came to the king’s envoys, who were at that time staying at the basilica of Saint Peter—namely, Wirundus the abbot and Winigisus, duke of Spoleto—and was taken to Spoleto.

The king entered Saxony and settled with his camp at Paderborn. From there, dividing the army, he sent his son Charles with half of it to meet the Slavs and to receive the Saxons who had come from the Nordliudi, in Bardengau [Col. 0064B].

In the same place he received Pope Leo with the greatest honor. While awaiting the return of his son Charles, he dismissed Pope Leo with the same honor with which he had received him; Leo immediately set out for Rome.

After receiving his son safely, the king returned to Aachen. There the envoy of Michael, governor of Sicily, named Daniel, came to him and was then dismissed with great honor.

In the same year the nation of the Avars defected from the faith they had promised. Einricus, duke of the Friulians, after achieving many victories successfully, was ambushed and overcome near Tharsatica, a city of Liburnia.

At the same time Gerold, who was count and governor of Bavaria, was killed in battle with the Avars [and was buried at Reichenau]. Concerning him it is read in the vision of Witinus that he was numbered among the martyrs [Col. 0064C].

The Balearic Islands, which had been ravaged by the Moors and Saracens, requested and received aid from the Franks and were defended against the raiders’ attacks. The standards of the Moors, captured in battle, were also presented to the king.

Count Wido, who held the March against the Britons, entered Brittany with his companions, traversed the whole country, and brought it into submission. To the king, on his return from Saxony, he presented the weapons of the dukes who had surrendered, with each man’s name written on them. Thus all Brittany, something that had never happened before, was subjected to the Franks.

In the same year a certain monk came from Jerusalem and brought the king many relics from the patriarch of Jerusalem. Azan, governor of the city called Oscaclavis, sent gifts to the king. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in [Col. 0064D] the same palace.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 800, the king released the monk from Jerusalem and sent with him Zacharias, a priest from his palace. Through him he sent a large sum of money to those holy places where the Lord had dwelt bodily.

In mid-March he left Aachen and surveyed the coast of the Gallic Ocean. In the sea itself, which was then infested by pirates, he established a fleet and arranged garrisons. He celebrated Easter at Saint-Riquier. From there he again traveled along the ocean coast to the city of Rouen. After crossing the Seine, he went to Tours, to Saint Martin, for the sake of prayer, and stayed there several days because of the poor health of his wife Liutgard [Col. 0065A], who there died and was buried. She died on the day before the Nones of June.

Returning by way of Orléans and Paris, he came to the palace of Aachen. In the same year, on the day before the Nones of June, there was, contrary to the usual course of nature, a harsh frost covered with ice; and likewise on the seventh day before the Ides of July. Nevertheless, it caused no harm to the crops.

In August he held an assembly at Mainz. From there he set out with an army and came to Ravenna, where he stayed seven days, then directed his journey toward Rome, having sent his son Pippin with an army into Benevento.

When he reached Rome, Pope Leo and the Roman senate met him on the day before the Nones, at Nomentum, twelve miles from the City, and received him with the greatest humility and honor, dining with him in the same place. The pope then went ahead of him to the City. [Col. 0065B] On the following day he stood on the steps of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. He sent out to meet the king the standards of the city of Rome with crosses and relics, and arranged in suitable places groups of pilgrims and citizens who were to sing praises as the king approached. Then, with the clergy and bishops, he humbly received him before the steps of the church. After giving a blessing, he led him into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter while everyone sang psalms.

This took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. Seven days later the king summoned an assembly and openly explained why he had come to Rome. From then on he devoted himself daily to the tasks for which he had come, among them the greatest and most difficult: investigating the accusations brought against the supreme pontiff.

When the case had been examined, and no accuser or lawful witness appeared who would undertake the burden of the dispute, the aforesaid pontiff, carrying the Gospel, climbed the ambo in the presence of all the people in the house of Saint Peter. Invoking the name of the Holy Trinity, he cleared himself by oath of the accusations brought against him [Col. 0065C].

On the same day the priest Zacharias came to Rome with two monks, one from the Mount of Olives and the other from Bethlehem. The bishop of Jerusalem had sent them to the king, and they brought, as a blessing, the keys of the Lord’s tomb and of the place of Calvary, as well as the keys of the city together with a standard. The king received them kindly, kept them with him for several days, and dismissed them in April after rewarding them. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 801, [Col. 0065D] when the king rose from prayer before the confession of Saint Peter on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord, Pope Leo placed a crown on his head. The entire Roman people acclaimed three times:

“Life and victory to Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor of the Romans!”

After the acclamations he was worshiped according to the custom of the ancient rulers, and, the title of patrician having been removed, he was called Emperor and Augustus.

A few days later he ordered those who in the preceding year had deposed the pontiff to be brought before him. After an inquiry had been conducted according to Roman law, they were condemned as guilty of treason to the capital sentence. Nevertheless, the pope, moved by pious affection, interceded for them with the emperor. Their lives and bodily integrity were spared; but, because of the magnitude of their crime, they were carried away into exile.

The leaders of this faction were Paschalis the moneyer and Campullus the treasurer, along with many other Roman nobles, all of whom were condemned by the same sentence [Col. 0066A].

After arranging all the affairs and business of the city of Rome and of the whole of Italy—not only public matters but also ecclesiastical ones—and after again sending Pippin his son on a hostile expedition against the Beneventans, the emperor himself left Rome after Easter, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May. He came to Spoleto, and while he was staying there, on the second day before the Kalends of May, at the second hour of the night, a great earthquake occurred, by which all Italy was violently shaken. In that earthquake the roof of the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, with a large part of its beams, collapsed.

In the same year certain places around the Rhine, in Gaul, and in Germania trembled from an earthquake, and pestilence arose because of the mildness of the winter season.

The emperor came from [Col. 0066B] Spoleto to Ravenna, stayed there several days, and proceeded to Pavia. There it was announced to him that the envoys of Aaron Amir al-Mu’minin, king of the Persians, had entered the port of Pisa. Sending men to meet them, he had them presented to him between Vercellae and Ivrea.

One of them was a Persian from the East, an envoy of the king of the Persians; the other was a Saracen from Africa, an envoy of the emir Abraham, who held territory at Fossato on the borders of Africa. They announced that Isaac the Jew, whom the emperor four years earlier had sent to the king of the Persians with Lantfrid and Sigimund, had returned with great gifts. Lantfrid and Sigimund had died on the journey.

The king therefore sent the notary Herchenbald into Liguria to prepare ships, on which the elephant and the other things being brought could be transported. He himself, [Col. 0066C] after celebrating the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist at Ivrea, crossed the Alps and returned to Gaul.

That summer the city of Barcelona in Hispania was captured, having by then been besieged for a little more than two years. Its governor Zatun and many other Saracens were taken prisoner. In Italy, too, the city of Teate was captured and burned, and its governor Rotselmus was taken prisoner. The castles belonging to that city were received into submission. Zatun and Rotselmus were condemned to exile.

In October Isaac the Jew returned from Africa with the elephant and entered the port of Veneris. Since he could not cross the Alps because of the snow, he wintered at Vercellae. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 802, the empress Irene [Col. 0066D] sent from Constantinople an envoy named Leo to the emperor to confirm peace between the Franks and the Greeks. The emperor sent Jesse, bishop of Amiens, and Count Elingaud to Constantinople to establish peace with her. Easter was celebrated in the same palace.

In the same year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, Isaac arrived with the elephant and the other gifts sent by the king of the Persians and appeared before the emperor. The elephant’s name was Ambulator.

The city of Ostona in Italy was received into submission. Luceria, too, exhausted by a prolonged siege, surrendered, and a Frankish garrison was placed there.

During the summer the emperor devoted himself to hunting in the Ardennes. After sending an army into Saxony, [Col. 0067A] he ravaged the Saxons beyond the Elbe.

Grimald, duke of the Beneventans, besieged at Luceria Count Winigisus of Spoleto, who commanded the garrison and had been weakened by illness. He received him into surrender, captured him, and treated him with great honor. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 803, an earthquake occurred at the palace of Aachen, followed by an epidemic. Winegisus was released by Grimald.

The emperor’s envoys returned from Constantinople, and with them came envoys of the emperor Nicephorus, who at that time governed the state. Their names were Michael the bishop, Peter the abbot, Calistus, and Candidatus. They came to the emperor in Germania, beside the river Sala, at a place called Saltz, and accepted a pact for [Col. 0067B] the establishment of peace in Christ.

After being dismissed with a letter from the emperor, they came to Rome and from there returned to Constantinople. The emperor, however, went to Bavaria. After settling the affairs of Pannonia, he returned to Aachen and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 804, the emperor wintered at Aachen. In the summer he went with an army into Saxony and transferred to Francia all the Saxons who lived beyond the Elbe and in Wihmodia, together with their women and children. He gave the trans-Elbian districts to the Abrodites.

At the same time Godefrid, king of the Danes, came with his fleet and all the cavalry of his kingdom to a place called Sliestorp, on the border between his kingdom and Saxony. He had promised to come to a conference with the [Col. 0067C] emperor, but, frightened by the advice of his men, he did not come nearer; instead, he sent through envoys whatever he wished to say.

The emperor was seated above the river Elbe, at a place called Holdunsteti. After sending an embassy to Godefrid concerning the fugitives whom he was retaining, he came to Cologne in mid-September. From there he entered the Ardennes, occupied himself with the pleasures of hunting, and returned to Aachen.

In mid-November it was announced to him that Pope Leo wished to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord with him wherever the emperor desired. The emperor gladly accepted this. He immediately sent his son Charles to Saint Maurice and ordered him to receive the pope honorably. He himself set out to meet Leo at the city of Reims. Having received him there, he escorted him as far as Quierzy, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with him there. He then brought him to Aachen and, after honoring him with great gifts, had him escorted by his own men through Bavaria as far as Ravenna [Col. 0067D].

The reason for his arrival was this: it had been reported to the emperor that the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ had been discovered in the city of Mantua. The emperor sent to the pope, asking him to investigate the truth of the matter. The pope, taking this as an opportunity to leave Rome, first set out for Lombardy, ostensibly for the aforesaid investigation; then, suddenly taking another route, he reached the emperor. He stayed with him for eight days and, as has been said, returned to Rome.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 805, Cacanus, prince of the Avars [Col. 0068A], approached the emperor and requested that a place be given to him for habitation between Savaria and Carantania, since he could not remain in his former settlements because of the attacks of the Slavs. The emperor received him kindly and granted his request.

At the same time he sent an army with his son Charles against the Slavs called Bohemians. They ravaged their entire land and killed their duke, whose name was Letho.

The emperor came to Theodonis Villa and proceeded from there as far as Mount Romaric. He occupied himself there with hunting, then returned to Theodonis Villa and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 806, Wilharius and Beatus, dukes of Venice, together with Paul, duke of Iadera, and Donatus, bishop of that city, [Col. 0068B] envoys of Dalmatia, came into the emperor’s presence with great gifts. After settling matters in Venice and Dalmatia and dismissing their envoys, the emperor held an assembly with the leading men and nobles of the Franks concerning the establishment and preservation of peace among his sons and the division of the kingdom.

After the division had been made, he divided his empire into three parts among his three sons, so that each might know which part he ought to defend and govern if he survived him [the father]. Concerning this division he made a testament. It was confirmed by the Franks with oaths and sent to Pope Leo, so that he might ratify these decrees with his own hand; and this was done.

Afterward, having left each of his two sons in the kingdom assigned to him—namely Pippin and Ludowic—the emperor departed from Theodonis Villa [Col. 0068C]. Traveling by boat along the Moselle, he entered the Rhine and came to Nijmegen in Batavia. He stayed there throughout Lent and celebrated Holy Easter.

From there, returning to Aachen, he sent his son Charles with an army into the land of the Slavs called the Sorabs, above the river Elbe. In that encounter the Slav Miliduoc was killed, and the army constructed two castles, one on the bank of the river Sala and the other above the Elbe.

After suppressing the Slavs, Charles entered Bohemia from this side with the Bavarians and Alamanni and ravaged most of their land.

In the same year a fleet sent by Pippin from Italy went to the island of Corsica against the Moors who were ravaging it. The Moors did not await its arrival but withdrew. One of the Franks, however, named Hademarus, [Col. 0068D] count of the city of Genoa, was killed by the Moors while fighting rashly.

In Hispania the Navarrese and the people of Pamplona, who in earlier years had gone over to the Saracens, were received into allegiance.

A fleet was sent by the emperor Nicephorus to recover Dalmatia, under the command of the patrician Geta [Note: [Col. 0067] “Geta patrician” in witnesses 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7; “Getra patrician” in witness 8; “Niceta patrician” in witnesses 4, 9, 10, 11, and 12.].

The envoys who had been sent to the king of the Persians for almost four years were transported past the stations of the Greek ships and reached Tarvisium without any of their adversaries perceiving it.

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the palace of Aachen. In the same year there was an eclipse of the moon on the fourth day before the Nones of September. The sun was then stationed in the sixteenth degree of Virgo, while the moon remained in the sixteenth degree of Pisces [Col. 0069A].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 807, a solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Ides of February, with both heavenly bodies standing in the twenty-fifth degree of Aquarius. In the same month, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, a lunar eclipse occurred. During that same night armies of marvelous size appeared in the sky, with the sun remaining in the eleventh degree of Pisces and the moon in the eleventh degree of Virgo.

Again, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, a lunar eclipse occurred at the third hour of the night, with the sun placed in the fifth degree of Virgo and the moon in the fifth degree of Pisces.

Ratbert, the emperor’s envoy, who was returning from the East, died. Also present was an envoy of the king of the Persians named Abdella, together with monks from Jerusalem who were serving as the envoys of Thomas, the patriarch. Their names were George and Felix.

George was abbot of the Mount of Olives and was German by nationality; his parents had called him Engilbald. They came to Aachen to the emperor bearing gifts that the aforesaid king had sent to the emperor: a pavilion and awnings for a court, sprinkled with varied colors and of marvelous size and beauty [Col. 0069B].

Everything was made of fine linen—both the awnings and their ropes—dyed in different colors. Among the aforesaid king’s gifts were also many cloaks of silk, exceedingly precious, perfumes, balsam, and ointments.

He also sent a clock made of brass, marvelously constructed by mechanical art. The cycle of twelve hours revolved by means of a water-clock, with an equal number of bronze balls that fell when the hours were completed and, by their fall, caused a cymbal beneath them to resound. In the same clock there were also riders of the same number, who emerged through twelve windows when the hours were complete and, as they came out, closed the same number of windows that had previously been open [Col. 0069C]. There were many other features in the aforesaid clock as well.

Among the gifts there were also two bronze candlesticks of marvelous size and height. Everything was deposited at Aachen.

The emperor kept the envoy and the monks with him for some time, then sent them into Italy and ordered them to await the season for navigation there.

In the same year he sent Burchard, count of his stable—a title that we corruptly call constable—with a fleet to Corsica, to defend it against the Moors who were carrying on raids there.

The Moors, coming out of Hispania [Col. 0069D] according to their custom, first landed in Sardinia. There they engaged the Sardinians in battle, losing many of their own—for it is reported that three thousand fell there—and reached Corsica by a direct course.

There, in a certain harbor of the island, they again fought a battle with the fleet commanded by Burchard. They were defeated and put to flight, losing thirteen ships and having many of their men killed.

That year they were so harassed by adverse fortune everywhere that they themselves declared that this had happened to them because, in the preceding year, contrary to all justice, they had carried away sixty monks from the island of Patalaria and sold them in Hispania. Some of these monks returned to their own places through the emperor’s generosity.

[Col. 0070A] The patrician Nicetas, who was stationed in Venice with the Constantinopolitan fleet, made peace with King Pippin and obtained a truce until the month of August. He then broke camp and returned to Constantinople. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen, and likewise Easter.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 808, the winter was exceedingly mild and pestilential. At the beginning of spring the emperor departed for Nijmegen. After celebrating Easter there, he returned again to Aachen.

There it was announced to him that Godefrid, king of the Danes, had transported forces across into the land of the Abrodites. Against him he sent his son Charles with an army, ordering him to resist the mad king if he attempted to attack the borders of Saxony.

After capturing several castles of the Slavs, Godefrid returned to his homeland with great losses among his forces [Col. 0070B]. For although he had driven out Drasco, duke of the Abrodites, and had captured and hanged another duke, Godelaib, by treachery, and had made two parts of the Abrodites tributary to himself, he nevertheless lost the best and most courageous of his soldiers. Among them was his brother’s son, named Reginbald, who was killed, together with many leading Danes, during the assault on a certain town.

The emperor’s son built a bridge across the Elbe and, with as much speed as he could, transported across it the army under his command against the Hilinones and Smeldingi, who had themselves defected to King Godefrid. After ravaging their fields on every side, he crossed the river again and withdrew into Saxony with his army unharmed.

With Godefrid on the aforesaid expedition were the Slavs called Wiltzi. Because of the ancient enmity [Col. 0070C] that they customarily had with the Abrodites, they willingly joined themselves to his forces. When Godefrid returned to his kingdom, they too went home with the booty they had taken among the Abrodites.

Before returning, Godefrid destroyed the trading settlement that had been established on the ocean coast. In the Danish language it was called Reric, and it provided great benefit to his kingdom through the payment of customs. After transferring the merchants from there and setting out with his fleet, he came with his entire army to the harbor called Liestorph.

After staying there several days, he decided to fortify with a rampart the border of his kingdom facing Saxony. Accordingly, he extended the fortification along the entire northern bank of the Eider River, from the eastern inlet of the sea, which they call Hostarsal, to the western ocean, leaving only one gate through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and brought in [Col. 0070D].

After dividing the work among his dukes, he returned home.

Meanwhile, the king of the Northumbrians from the island of Britain, named Eardulf, driven from his kingdom and homeland, came to the emperor while he was still staying at Nijmegen. After explaining the purpose of his arrival, he set out for Rome. On returning from Rome, he was restored to his kingdom through the envoys of the Roman pontiff and the emperor.

The apostolic envoy was Adulphus, a deacon from Britain and a Saxon by nationality. With him the emperor sent two abbots: Rotfrid the notary and Nantharius of Saint Othmar.

After his envoys had built two castles above the Elbe and arranged garrisons in them against the incursions of the Slavs [Col. 0071A], the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen, and likewise Easter.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 809, a fleet sent from Constantinople first reached Dalmatia and then Venice. While it was wintering there, part of it came to the island of Comacina. After engaging in battle with the garrison stationed there, its men were defeated and put to flight by the inhabitants.

The duke who commanded the fleet, named Paul, attempted to negotiate with King Pippin concerning the establishment of peace between the Franks and the Greeks, as though this had been entrusted to him. But Willarius and Beatus, dukes of Venice, thwarted all his efforts and even prepared ambushes for him. When he learned of their treachery, he departed.

While these things were happening in Italy, King Ludowic entered Hispania with [Col. 0071B] an army in the western regions and besieged the city of Tortosa, situated on the bank of the river Ebro. After spending a considerable time trying to capture it, and seeing that it could not be taken quickly, he abandoned the siege and withdrew into Aquitaine with his army unharmed.

After Eardulf, king of the Northumbrians, had been restored to his kingdom, the envoys began their return journey. The deacon Adulphus was captured by pirates, but was later ransomed and returned to Rome.

In Tuscany, Populonium, a maritime city, was plundered by Greeks called Orobitae. The Moors also entered Corsica from Hispania and, on Holy Saturday of Easter itself, plundered a certain city. They left nothing there except the bishop and a few old and sick people.

Meanwhile, through [Col. 0071C] certain merchants, Godefrid, king of the Danes, sent word to the duke who governed Frisia that he had heard the emperor was angry with him because he had led an army into the land of the Abrodites and avenged his injuries. He added that he wished to deny the charge brought against him—that he had broken the promised treaty. He also asked that the emperor send his envoys across the Elbe, near the borders of his kingdom, and that he himself come there with his men, so that, after the causes at issue had been examined on both sides, whatever required correction might be amended there without opposition.

When this was reported to the emperor, he did not refuse. A conference was held with the leading Danes beyond the Elbe, and although many matters were brought forward by both sides, the affair was not brought to any conclusion.

Thrasco, duke of the Abrodites, after giving his son as a hostage to Godefrid at the latter’s request, gathered a force and obtained aid [Col. 0071D] from the Saxons. He attacked his neighbors, the Wiltzi, and ravaged their fields with sword and fire. Returning home with immense booty, and receiving still stronger aid from the Saxons, he captured the principal city of the Smeldingi. Through these successes he compelled all who had defected from him to return to his alliance.

Accordingly, when many reports reached the emperor concerning the boasting and arrogance of the Danish king, he decided to build a city beyond the Elbe and place a Frankish garrison in it. After gathering men for this purpose throughout Gaul and Germania, equipping them with arms and the other necessities of war, and ordering them to be led through Frisia to the appointed place [Col. 0072A], Thrasco, duke of the Abrodites, was treacherously killed by Godefrid’s men in the trading settlement of Reric.

After the site for establishing the city had been examined, the emperor appointed Count Egbert to carry out the undertaking and ordered him to cross the Elbe and occupy the place. It lies on the bank of the river Sturia and is called Essesfelt. It was therefore occupied by Egbert and the Saxon counts, and fortification began around the Ides of March.

While these things were happening concerning the Danes, Count Aureolus, who lived beyond the Pyrenees on the border between Hispania and Gaul, opposite Huesca and Zaragoza, died. The governor Amoroz entered his place, and sent an embassy to the emperor [Col. 0072B], promising to surrender himself and all his people to the emperor’s service.

A lunar eclipse occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.

## 810

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 810, the prefect Amoroz sought a conference with the emperor on the border between Gaul and Spain. At that conference he promised that he would commend himself and all his people into the emperor’s hands. Although the emperor agreed, the matter remained uncompleted because of many intervening circumstances.

The Moors, having gathered a very large fleet from all Spain, first landed in Sardinia and then in Corsica. Finding no garrison there, they ravaged almost the entire island. While these events were taking place, King Pippin, incited by the treachery of the Venetian leaders, harassed the island itself by land and sea. After subjugating Venice and receiving its leaders into surrender, he sent the same fleet to devastate the shores of Dalmatia. But when Paul, prefect of Cephalonia, arrived with the eastern fleet to bring aid to the Dalmatians, the royal fleet returned to its own territory.

Ruodthrud, the emperor’s elder daughter, died on 6 June.

The emperor was staying at Aachen when he was informed that a fleet of two hundred ships from Northmen-land had landed in Frisia, fought three battles with the Frisians, and, having won, imposed tribute upon the defeated. It was said that one hundred pounds of silver had already been paid by the Frisians and that King Godefrid was directing all these operations. This report so stirred the emperor that, sending messengers throughout all the surrounding regions to assemble an army, he himself immediately left the palace and began to proceed in that direction.

After crossing the Rhine at a place called the Lippe, he decided to await the forces that had not yet assembled. While he remained there for several days, the elephant that Aaron, king of the Saracens, had sent him died suddenly. When the forces had finally assembled, he hastened with all possible speed to the river Aller. Having set up camp, he awaited the outcome of King Godefrid’s threats; for that tyrant, puffed up by a spirit of arrogance, boastfully declared that he wished to engage the emperor.

[Note: The passage from “he awaited the outcome of King Godefrid’s threats” through “puffed up” is preserved in witnesses 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12. Witnesses 1, 2, and 5 read “the king, puffed up,” omitting the intervening words. Manuscript 3 emended the passage as follows: “and there he set up camp, angered by King Godefrid’s threats, since he had arrogantly boasted.”]

But while the emperor was stationed at the place just mentioned, reports from various quarters were brought to him. It was announced that the fleet which had been ravaging Frisia had returned home; that Godefrid had been killed by one of his own retainers; that a fortress called Hohbuochi, adjoining the river Elbe, in which Odo, the emperor’s envoy, was stationed and which served as a garrison for the eastern Saxons, had been captured by the Wiltzi; that Pippin, his son and king of Italy, had died on 8 July; and that two embassies from different parts of the world—one from Constantinople and the other from Córdoba—were approaching on a mission of peace.

When he received these reports, he arranged matters in Saxony as the circumstances of the time required and returned to Aachen.

During this expedition there was such a severe epidemic among the cattle that scarcely any animals survived for so great an army; indeed, all of them perished, down to the last one. Nor did this occur only there: throughout the entire empire animals of this kind died.

Arriving at Aachen in October, he received the embassies mentioned above and made peace with the emperor Nicephorus and with Abulaz, king of Spain. He restored Venice to Nicephorus, and received Count Heinric, formerly captured by the Saracens, after Abulaz had sent him back.

In that year the sun and moon were eclipsed twice: the sun on 9 June and on 30 November; the moon on 21 June and on 24 December.

The island of Corsica was again ravaged by the Moors. Amoroz and Abdiraman, son of Abulaz, was expelled from Zaragoza and compelled to enter Huesca; the source has the singular verb. After Godefrid had died, as we have said, Hemming, his brother’s son, succeeded to the kingdom and made peace with the emperor.

## 811

When the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 811 had ended and Arsafio, the imperial spatharius and envoy of the august emperor Nicephorus, had departed, the emperor sent envoys to Constantinople to confirm the same peace: Haido, bishop of Basel; Count Hugh of Tours; Aio the Lombard of Friuli; and with them a certain Leo, a spatharius by rank and a Sicilian by birth, and Willarius, duke of Venice.

Of these two latter men, one had fled from Sicily to the emperor at Rome ten years earlier, when the emperor was there; wishing to return, he was sent back to his homeland. The other, having been stripped of his office because of his treachery, was ordered to be taken to Constantinople to his lord.

The peace agreed upon by the emperor and Hemming, king of the Danes, was maintained only by oath and in arms because the severity of winter closed the roads between the two sides, until, with the return of spring and the roads opened, twelve leading men from each side—Franks and Danes—arrived at the river Eider. There, after they had exchanged oaths according to their own rite and custom, the peace was confirmed.

The nobles on the Frankish side were Walach, Burchard, Bernhard, Egbert, Theoderic, Ano, Osdag, and Wichman, all counts. On the Danish side there were first Hemming’s brothers, Ankwin and Angantyr, and then other men held in honor among their people, whose names we have thought it unnecessary to record.

After the emperor had established peace with Hemming and had held the general assembly at Aachen according to custom, he sent three armies into three regions of his kingdom. He sent one across the Elbe against the Linones; it both ravaged them and restored the fortress of Hohbuochi, which the Wiltzi had destroyed in the preceding year. He sent another into Pannonia to settle the disputes between the Huns and the Slavs. He sent the third against the Bretons to punish their treachery. All three armies, having achieved success, returned home.

The emperor himself went to Boulogne to inspect the fleet that he had ordered to be constructed and built in the preceding year. There he restored the lighthouse that had been established in ancient times to guide the courses of ships, and at its summit he lit a fire during the night. From there he came to the river Scheldt and, at a place called Ghent, inspected the ships constructed for the same fleet. He arrived at Aachen around the middle of November, where the envoys of Hemming, king of the Danes—Aovin and Hebbi—met him, bearing the king’s gifts and peaceful words.

Also waiting at Aachen for his arrival were those who had come from Pannonia: Canizauci, prince of the Avars; Thudun; and other princes and leaders of the Slavs living along the Danube. They had been ordered to come into the presence of the emperor by the Frankish leaders who had been in Pannonia.

Meanwhile Charles, the emperor’s elder son, died on 4 December.

## 812

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 812, Hemming, king of the Danes, died. When Sigefrid, Godefrid’s nephew, and Anilo, Heriold’s nephew, both wished to succeed him, and they could not agree about the division of the kingdom, they assembled their forces and engaged in battle; both men died.

Anilo’s party, however, gained the victory and established his brothers Heriold and Reginfrid as kings. The defeated party was necessarily compelled to follow them and did not refuse to accept the same men as rulers. It is reported that 10,940 men fell in that battle.

The emperor Nicephorus, after many notable victories, died in the province of Moesia in a battle fought against the Bulgars. Michael, his son-in-law, became emperor. He received at Constantinople the envoys of our lord emperor who had been sent to the emperor Nicephorus, and dismissed them. With them he sent his own envoys: Michael the bishop, Arsafius, and Theognostus the protospatharius. Through them he confirmed the peace begun by Nicephorus.

When they came to the emperor at Aachen, they received from him in the church the written treaty. According to their custom—that is, in the Greek language—they sang his praises, calling him “Emperor” and “Basileus.” When they came to Rome on their return journey, they again received the same little book of the treaty or alliance from Pope Leo in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter.

After dismissing them, the emperor solemnly held a general assembly at Aachen and sent Bernhard, Pippin’s son and his own grandson, into Italy. Because of the report that a fleet from Africa and Spain was said to be coming to ravage Italy, he ordered Wallo, the son of his cousin Bernhard, to accompany him until the outcome of events brought security to his men.

Part of this fleet came to Corsica and part to Sardinia. The section that came to Sardinia was almost entirely destroyed.

The fleet of the Northmen attacked the island of Ireland. After engaging in battle with the Scots and killing many of them, the rest fled.

Grimald, duke of the Beneventans, paid the emperor 25,000 gold solidi as tribute.

In the same year an expedition was undertaken against the Wiltzi, and hostages were received from them.

Heriold and Reginfrid, kings of the Danes, sent an embassy to the emperor, asking for peace and requesting that their brother Hemming be sent back to them.

In this year there was an eclipse of the sun after midday on 15 May.

## 813

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 813, the emperor wintered at Aachen. When spring began, he sent Hamalarius, who held the bishopric of Trier, and Peter, abbot of the monastery of Nonantula, to Constantinople to confirm the peace with Michael.

Afterward, having held a general assembly, he summoned Ludowic, his son, from Aquitaine and placed upon him the crown of imperial dignity. He appointed his grandson Bernhard over Italy and ordered him to be called king.

By his command councils were also held by bishops throughout Gaul concerning the condition of the churches. One was convened at Mainz, another at Reims, a third at Tours, a fourth at Chalon, and a fifth at Arles. The decrees made at each of them were confirmed by the emperor. Anyone wishing to know them may find them in the cities mentioned above, although copies of them are also kept in the palace archive.

At the same time certain Frankish and Saxon nobles were sent across the Elbe to the borders of the Northmen, in order to make peace with them according to their request and return the king’s brother to them. After oaths had been given on both sides, peace was established.

At that time, however, the kings were not at home. They had gone with an army to Westerfalt, the farthest region of their kingdom, situated between the north and the west and facing toward the northern extremity of Britain. Its leaders and people disdained their rule.

After the kings had subdued them, returned, and received their brother sent by the emperor, the sons of King Godefrid and certain of the leading Danes—who had long been exiles among the Swedes after abandoning their homeland—gathered forces from every direction and made war upon them. When bands of people from throughout the Danish land flocked to them, they engaged the kings in battle and expelled them from their ancestral kingdom.

In the same year the emperor Charles died. He was honorably buried at Aachen in the basilica of the holy Savior and of holy Mary, Mother of God, which basilica he himself had caused to be built from its foundations with magnificent workmanship.

His son Ludowic received the imperial scepters.

I found the events set out above in a certain little book composed in a common and rustic manner of speech. I corrected part of it according to the rules of Latin, and I also added some things that I had heard from the account of elders.

The remainder that follows has been written down through the efforts of my smallness, just as I found it recorded in books of chronicles.

[Note: “In the books of the Theonic [German] language” in witness 2; “in the books of the Theotonic [German] language” in witness 1; “in the books of the Theutonic [German] language” in witness 3.]

Or as I was able to learn by hearing it from the report of our fathers.

[Note: “I was able to learn.” The material absent here is found at the beginning of this book; witness 7 adds “and concerning Ludowic.”]

I have committed very little to writing concerning the times of the emperor Ludowic, because I found no written accounts and heard from the elders nothing worthy of being entrusted to memory. Of the deeds of the emperor Hlotharius and his brothers, the kings of the Franks, I have written more. But when the narrative reached our own times, I extended the account at greater length. For, as Jerome says, things seen are related in one way and things heard in another; and what we know better, we also present better.

## DCCCXVIII (818)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 818, Bernhard, son of Pippin and king of Italy, was summoned to the emperor at Aachen, seized by treachery, and first deprived of his eyes and then of his life.

This Bernhard had a son named Pippin, who fathered three children: Bernhard, Pippin, and Heribert. Heribert killed Count Rodulf, son of Balduin, in our own times, and not long afterward was himself killed by Balduin, a retainer of Balduin, Rodulf’s brother.

[Note: “Brother” is absent from witnesses 2, 5c, d, and e; witness 7 reads “brother.”]

[Note: The name appears as *Rodulfum … Rodulfi* in witnesses 1 and 2; as *Ruodulfi … Ruodulfi* in 5d, 7, and 10; as *Rodulphum … Rodulphi* in 3; as *Rodolfum … Rodolfi* in 8; as *Roudolfum … Roudolfi* in 9; as *Ruodolfum … Ruodolfi* in 11; as *Ruodulfum … Ruodulfi* in 12; and as *Rudolphum … Rudolphi* in 5c and e.]

[Note: The name Balduin appears as *Balduuini*, etc., in 5d, 7, 8, and 10; as *Bardwini* in 9 and 11; as *Wardwini* in 12; as *ab Aldwino* in 1, 3, 5c, d, e, 6, 7, 9, 10, and 11; and as *ad Aldwino* in 12.]

That Balduin still holds the duchy in Flanders.

[Note: “Balduin, Rodulf’s brother, held the duchy in Flanders in the years 879–918.”]

## DCCCXXIX (829)

[Note: “A.D. 836” in witness 7.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 829, Tancrad, the second abbot of the monastery of Prüm, died, and Marcward succeeded him in its administration, a prudent man devoted to sacred religion.

[Note: The name appears as *Pruniensis* in witnesses 9, 10, 11, and 12.]

[Note: He appears for the last time in a charter of Ludowic and Lotharius from the year 826. Hontheim, *History of Trier* I, p. 175.]

[Note: The name Marcward appears as *Marcuardus* in witness 2; *Marcunardus* in 1, 3, 5, and 6; *Marquardus* in 11; *Marchwardus* in 9 and 12; and *Marcuuaidus* in 10.]

[Note: He is first named in a charter of the emperor Ludowic for the monastery of Prüm in the year 835. Hontheim, cited work, p. 178.]

## DCCCXXXVI (836)

[Note: The year numbers written by Regino are indeed erroneous. These events occurred in the years 818, 833, and 834; Ebo, however, was deposed in 835.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 836, the Bretons violated their treaties and began to rebel under their leader named Murman. The emperor led an army against them, but did not prevail decisively.

[Note: “They began to violate” in witness 6. The entire year is absent from witness 2.]

## DCCCXXXVII (837)

[Note: The year numbers written by Regino are indeed erroneous. These events occurred in the years 818, 833, and 834; Ebo, however, was deposed in 835.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 837, Murman, king of the Bretons, died, and at Ingelheim the emperor entrusted the rule of that people to Nomenoius.

[Note: The name appears as *Numenoid* in witness 7; *Numendio* in 9, 10, 11, and 12.]

## DCCCXXXVIII (838)

[Note: The year numbers written by Regino are indeed erroneous. These events occurred in the years 818, 833, and 834; Ebo, however, was deposed in 835.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 838, Hludowic was deprived of the empire by his own men and, after being deprived, was handed over to custody. The monarchy of the kingdom was granted by election of the Franks to Hlotharius, his son.

[Note: Witnesses 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 read “by election of the brothers.”]

Then he was again rescued from custody by his son Ludowic and by the Franks and restored to the imperial seat.

This deposition occurred for the most part because of Judith’s many forms of fornication, she being his wife.

[Note: “Because of her great fornication” in witnesses 1 and 3.]

## DCCCXXXIX (839)

[Note: The year numbers written by Regino are indeed erroneous. These events occurred in the years 818, 833, and 834; Ebo, however, was deposed in 835.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 839, Hlotharius abandoned Francia and went to Italy. Ebbo, bishop of Reims, was deposed in a general synod, and many others who had conspired in the emperor’s deposition were condemned to exile.

## DCCCXL (840)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840, the emperor Hludowic, while pursuing his son Ludowic across the Rhine, fell ill. He was put on a ship and carried down the river Main into the Rhine; there, on an island near Ingelheim, he died.

[Note: The river-name appears as *Moin* in witnesses 1, 2, and 3; *Mogonum* in 5 and 8; and *Magonum* in 9–12.]

From there he was carried to Metz and honorably committed to burial in the basilica of Saint Arnulf.

[Note: The place-name appears as *Mediomatricum* in witnesses 2 and 5–6; *Medio Martio* in 3; and “the city of Mediomatricum” in witnesses 7–12.]

[Note: “Arnolfi” in witnesses 2, 3, and 5.]

Immediately Hlotharius, returning from Italy, seized the empire.

[Note: Witness 6 and following read “immediately”; witnesses 3, 5, and 11 read “Italy”; witnesses 7–12 preserve “returning.”]

## DCCCXLI (841)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 841, Hludowic and Charles, indignant that they had been entirely deprived of their father’s kingdom, gathered an army from every direction and soon attacked their brother in battle at Fontenay.

[Note: Witnesses 7 and 9–12 read “attacked their brother in battle.”]

In that battle the strength of the Franks was so diminished and their famous valor so weakened that thereafter they were sufficient neither to enlarge the boundaries of the kingdom nor even to defend their own.

[Note: Witnesses 9–12 read “their splendid valor.” Witness 5c reads “not only not to enlarge.”]

At last, not without serious loss among their own men, Charles and Hludowic were victorious.

[Note: Witnesses 7–12 read “yet not without serious loss.”]

## DCCCXLII (842)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 842, the three brothers mentioned above divided the Frankish empire among themselves.

The western kingdoms fell to Charles, from the British Ocean as far as the river Meuse. The eastern kingdoms fell to Hludowic, namely all Germany as far as the waters of the Rhine, together with certain cities and their neighboring districts across the Rhine, because of the abundance of wine.

[Note: The text has “Ythenum” and “Ytheni” in place of *Rhenum* and *Rheni* in witness 7.]

Hlotharius, who was both the eldest by birth and called emperor, received the kingdom lying between the two others. From his name it is still called the kingdom of Hlotharius.

[Note: The name appears as *Lotharii* in witnesses 1, 2, 7, and 8; *Lotharii regnum* in 3; *Lothar* in 6; *Lotharia* in 9–12; and *Lotharingia* in 5. Witnesses 2, 3, 5, and 6 read “and all” rather than “and also all.”]

He also received the whole of Provence, as well as all the kingdoms of Italy with the city of Rome itself. That city is now venerated by the whole holy Church with a special privilege because of the presence of the apostles Peter and Paul; formerly, because of the unconquered power of the Roman name, it had been called the mistress of the world.

[Note: A note in an old hand in the margin of witness 3, drawn from the Fulda Annals under the years 844 and 846, reads: “In the year 844 Lotharius killed Gestionulus, king of the Slavs, and subjected the Slavs to himself. In the year 846 King Ludowic subdued Pannonia, and on his return ravaged the Bohemians.”]

## DCCCXLVII (847)

[Note: “851” in witnesses 9–12.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 847, Hetti, bishop of Trier, departed from this world, and Thietgaud obtained his see.

[Note: Witnesses 7 and 9–12 read “archbishop.”]

[Note: The name Hetti appears as *Hetto* in witnesses 5 and 9; *Hecti* in 7.]

[Note: He occurs for the last time in the year 846 in Hontheim, cited work, p. 184.]

[Note: The name Thietgaud appears as *Thietgandus* in witness 5; *Tiehtgaudus* in 1; *Thioetgaudus* in 3; and *Thitgaudus* in 2.]

## DCCCLI (851)

[Note: “852” in witnesses 9–12.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 851, Queen Hirmingardis, wife of the emperor Hlotharius, died. She was a venerable matron acceptable to God, and she had borne three sons to Hlotharius: Hludowic, Hlotharius, and Charles.

[Note: “She bore” in the text.]

[Note: According to Hrabanus’s epitaph, on 20 March. Compare the Bertin Annals under the year 853.]

[Note: The name appears as *Herimingardis* in witnesses 1, 2, and 5; *Hermingardis* in 3; *Ermengardis* in 4; *Yrmingardix* in 7; and *Irmingardis* in 8–12.]

## DCCCLIII (853)

[Note: “The year 843.” Compare the contemporary author of the *Fragment of the History of Armorican Britain*, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum* III, 381, and Bouquet VII, 46.]

[Note: The year number is absent from witnesses 7 and 10; witnesses 1 and 2 have 854.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 853, the Northmen, sailing around the British Sea, occupied the mouth of the Loire. In a sudden invasion they attacked the city of Nantes, ravaging everything with slaughter, fires, and plunder. On Holy Saturday, while celebrating baptism according to custom in the basilica, they killed the city’s bishop and slaughtered the clergy.

[Note: Witness 5 reads *nortmani, britani, cum mare* (“Northmen, Britons, with/by sea”; the reading is uncertain); it also reads “on Holy Easter” and “first toward Angers.”]

They devastated the entire surrounding region. First they occupied Angers, then the city of Tours, and, like a monstrous storm, they overthrew everything and consumed everything. They also burned by fire the church of the most distinguished bishop Martin.

[Note: Witnesses 5 and 6 read “they burned.”]

At that time, as they say, the fleet of the Northmen first reached the shores of the Loire.

In the same year Egil was appointed abbot of the monastery of Prüm.

[Note: *Pruniensis* in witnesses 9–12.]

[Note: Compare the Bertin Annals under the year 852 and following years, and the Fulda Annals under the year 851 and following years.]

Around this time Charles captured Pippin, king of Aquitaine and his nephew, after the Aquitanians themselves betrayed him. They did so because, once the peace had been broken, that province was being ravaged by its own inhabitants and many crimes were being committed there with impunity.

After taking Pippin, Charles, with the counsel of the bishops and nobles, had him tonsured and sent him, dressed in monastic clothing, to the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons.

[Note: “With two monks agreeing and at the same time providing assistance” in witness 1.]

From there he escaped with the agreement and help of two monks. But after being captured again, he was committed to custody in the extremely well-fortified fortress at Senlis.

[Note: Witness 5 reads “captured on the island of Nectis”; witness 7 reads “in the forest of Nectis.”]

[Note: Senlis.]

This Pippin was the son of Pippin, son of the emperor Hludowic. It is said that his father, the emperor Hludowic, while Pippin was still a boy, wished to promote him to the clerical office

[Note: Witness 7 reads “at that age”; witness 2 reads “while he was still a little boy, wished.”]

and entrust him to Drogo, bishop of Metz—his maternal uncle, that is, the boy’s uncle—to be instructed in both the liberal and ecclesiastical disciplines.

[Note: Witnesses 7–12 read “to his brother, that is, the boy’s paternal uncle.”]

[Note: Witnesses 1, 2, 3, (4), 5, and 6 read “to Drogo, bishop of Metz, his maternal uncle, that is, to be entrusted to him.” Witness 6 adds “to instruct him.”]

But Hlotharius, the boy’s brother, opposed his father’s wishes

[Note: “Opposed” is absent from witness 5.]

and by no means allowed him to be tonsured; instead, he forcibly snatched him from his father’s hand.

For that boy, as they say, was of extraordinary beauty.

[Note: Witnesses 7–12 read “of marvelous beauty.”]

Later, when the emperor Hludowic, his father, divided the empire among his sons, he granted him only the province of Aquitaine.

[Note: “The emperor Hludowic” is absent from witnesses 1, 3, and 6. “Among his sons” is absent from those witnesses and from witness 5.]

But it did not turn out well for him that he had been recalled from the worship and service of God. For, devoting himself day and night to drunkenness and feasting, he eventually lost his mind and fell into a manic illness. He ended his present life in disgrace, leaving as his successor his son Pippin, whom we mentioned a little above.

[Note: Witnesses 4 and 7–12 read “the service of God”; witnesses 5 and 7–12 read “withdrawn from service.” Witnesses 7 and 9–12 read “into a mad illness”; witnesses 11 and 12 read “into madness.” “A little” is absent from witnesses 7 and 9–12.]

## DCCCLV (855)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 855, Hlotharius summoned the leading men of the kingdom and divided the empire among his sons. He gave Italy to Hludowic and had him called emperor. To his namesake, Hlotharius, he granted the kingdom that is called after his own name. To Charles, who was younger by birth, he gave the kingdom of Provence.

After arranging and ordering the affairs of the kingdom, he bade farewell to his people, left this world, and, coming to the monastery of Prüm, cut off the hair of his head. Having taken on the habit of holy conduct, he ended his final day in the profession of religious life, on 29 September.

[Note: Witnesses 1, 2, 3, and probably 6 read “divided his empire among his sons.” Witnesses 5 and probably 6 read “he left his people and the world.” Witness 4 reads “the monastery of Prüm”; witnesses 5 and probably 6 read “to the monastery of Prüm.”]

## DCCCLVI (856)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 856, King Hlotharius took Queen Thietbirga in marriage. [Note: Witness 5 consistently reads *Thietbergam*.] From this union the greatest disaster befell not him alone but also his entire kingdom, as will become clearer than daylight in what follows.

[Note: Witnesses 1, 3, 4, and 6 read “in the following things.” Witnesses 11 and 12 give the year as 855, in a place erased.]

## DCCCLVIII (858)

[Note: “The year 863.”]

[Note: Witnesses 11 and 12 give the year as 856, in an erased place; witnesses 1, 2, and 10 give it as 859.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 858, King Charles, son of the emperor Hlotharius, died. He had ruled Provence, and from the kingdom he had held there arose a considerable dispute between King Hlotharius and his uncle Charles.

[Note: Witnesses 7–12 read “his paternal uncle.”]

## DCCCLIX (859)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 859, Hlotharius entrusted Abbot Hucbert with the duchy between the Jura and Mount Jovis, because he was then considered exceptionally faithful, being related to him through Thietbirga’s sister.

[Note: The name appears as *Huberto* in witness 7; *Hugberto* in 3, 11, and 12.]

[Note: “The duchy” is absent from witnesses 5 and 7.]

[Note: “Mount” in witness 7.]

## DCCCLX (860)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, Egil voluntarily resigned the abbacy of Prüm, and Ansbald succeeded him in its administration, a man distinguished by every holiness and goodness.

[Note: Witness 2 reads “Exgil”; witness 5 reads “Auspaldus.”]

[Note: Ansbald first appears in the charters in the year 861. Hontheim, cited work, p. 198.]

In these times Hludowic the Elder, brother of the emperor Hlotharius, fought many wars with great bravery against the peoples of the Slavs. For he entered the realms of the Moravians and subdued everything by arms, capturing their prince named Rastiz.

[Note: Witness 3 reads *Mirahensium* for *Marahensium*.]

Because he had violated the treaties, he also ordered that his eyes be gouged out.

[Note: Witnesses 7–12 read “to be gouged out.” Witness 2 reads “he ordered his eyes to be gouged out.”]

[Note: Rastiz was captured in the year 870. Fulda Annals.]

[Note: The name appears as *Rastix* in witness 1; *Rastrix* in 3; *Rastitz* in 2, 5, and 6; and *Rastri* in 11.]

At that time a great conflagration of discord and lawsuits broke out among Charles’s leading men.

[Note: Witnesses 9–12 read “they kindle a conflagration.”]

Finally Lambert, who held the duchy between the Loire and the Seine, treacherously killed Vivian, a powerful man.

[Note: For the year 848, see the British Chronicle in Bouquet VII, 221, or the year 849 in the Bertin Annals.]

[Note: The name Vivian appears as *Vixinianus* in witness 7 and as *Juvianus* in the manuscript of Saint-Godehard.]

[Note: The event belongs to the year 851, according to the Aquitanian or Memmian Chronicle and the Chronicle of Angoulême.]

[Note: The name Gauzbert appears as *Ganzbertus*, etc., in witness 5 and as *Gausbertus*, etc., in witnesses 9–12.]

Then Count Gauzbert, with others, likewise treacherously slaughtered Lambert.

[Note: “Count Gauzbert likewise treacherously” in witness 5; “with others treacherously” in witnesses 7–12; “with many others” in witness 7.]

[Note: The event belongs to the year 852, according to the Bertin Annals.]

Gauzbert himself was beheaded by Charles’s command.

[Note: The event belongs to the year 853; compare the Aquitanian or Memmian Chronicle and the Chronicle of Angoulême under the year 852.]

When the Bretons saw that the land had been left without leaders and deprived of counsel, they took up arms, invaded the borders of the Frankish kingdom, crossed the Loire, and advanced as far as Poitiers. They devastated everything with slaughter, plunder, and fires, and, laden with enormous booty, returned to their own country.

To suppress the insolent presumption of this undertaking, Charles entered Brittany with a large army.

[Note: Compare note 29. The Saxons were the Saxons of Bayeux, already mentioned by Gregory of Tours.]

Battle was joined. The Saxons who had been hired were placed in the front line to receive the winding charges of the swift horses. But at the first attack, terrified by the Bretons’ javelins, they hid themselves within the battle line.

The Bretons, as was their custom, riding here and there on horses trained for this kind of fighting, attacked the tightly packed Frankish line. With all their strength they hurled javelins into its midst; then, pretending to flee, they nevertheless drove their javelins into the breasts of those pursuing them.

[Note: Witness 5 reads “riding about”; witnesses 1, 3, and 9–12 read “the closely joined Frankish line.” Witnesses 6 and 8–12 read “into the middle.” Witnesses 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 preserve “pretending to flee”; witness 3 has “of those pretending to flee”; witness 7 has a corrupt “now fleeing”; witnesses 9–11 have “now having been put to flight”; witness 12 has “nor having been put to flight.”]

The Franks were accustomed to fight at close quarters with drawn swords, but they stood stunned, shaken by the novelty of a danger they had never before experienced. They were fit neither to pursue nor, because they were not gathered into one body, to remain safe.

[Note: Witness 5 reads “who, the less”; witnesses 1–6 read “by a novelty not previously experienced”; witnesses 1–4 read “the coming night brought the battle to an end.”]

Nightfall brought the battle to an end. Many Franks were killed, very many wounded, and countless horses perished.

On the following day the battle began again, but ended in a more grievous misfortune.

[Note: Witness 4 reads “but ended in the former misfortune.”]

When Charles saw this, he was overcome by extreme terror and secretly fled during the night, without the army’s knowledge, abandoning his pavilion, tents, and all the royal equipment.

When morning came and the army learned that the king had fled, it was filled with overwhelming fear and thought of nothing but flight. The Bretons rushed upon them with a shout and attacked the Frankish camp, filled with every kind of wealth. They seized all the equipment of war, pursued the fleeing Frankish columns, and cut down with the sword or captured alive everyone they encountered. The rest were saved by flight.

Thus enriched by the Franks’ possessions and equipped with their weapons, the Bretons withdrew into their own land.

## DCCCLXI (861)

[Note: Compare the Bertin Annals under the years 859 and 861.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 861, Charles held an assembly at Compiègne. There, with the counsel of the nobles, he entrusted to Count Rodbert the duchy between the Loire and the Seine, against the Bretons. Rodbert governed it with great energy for some time.

[Note: The name appears as *Redbertus* in witness 7; *Roudbertus* in 9; *Rudbertus* in 10; *Ruodbertus* in 3 and 11; *Ruodpertus* in 12; *Robertus* in 4; *Rudpertus* in 2; and *Rotbertus* in 1.]

[Note: Witness 7 gives the year as 862; the year number is absent from witness 10.]

## DCCCLXII (862)

[Note: “The year 851.” Compare the Bertin Annals.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 862, Nomenoius, king of the Bretons, was struck down by divine will.

[Note: The name appears as *Numeneus* in witnesses 1–3, 5, and 7; *Numeneius* in 4; *Nomeneius* in 8; *Nomecieus* in 9, 11, and 12; *Dometieus* in 10; and *Nomenoi* below in witnesses 9–12, *Nomenei* in 8, and *Numenoi* in 2. Witness 7 reads *Nomenoi Herispoius*.]

For when he was devastating the churches of God and cruelly ravaging the borderlands because they remained faithful to Charles, one day, as he was about to mount his horse in order to complete the wickedness he had begun, he suddenly saw Saint Maurilio the bishop standing before him. [Note: “Saint” is absent from witnesses 7 and 9–12.] With a stern expression and terrifying eyes, the bishop repeatedly said to him:

“Cease now, cruel robber, from devastating the churches of God.”

After saying this, he raised the staff he was carrying in his hand and struck him on the head. His men carried him back to the house, and he ended his life together with his kingdom.

This Maurilio was bishop of the city of Angers, whose boundaries adjoined the borders of Brittany; for that reason they were severely ravaged by the Bretons.

[Note: *Maurilo* in witness 5; “they were being ravaged” in witness 5; “the city of Angers” in witnesses 7–12.]

Herispoius, son of Nomenoius, obtained his father’s kingdom.

[Note: The name appears as *Herispius* in witness 5.]

## DCCCLXIII (863)

[Note: “The year 851.” Compare the Bertin Annals.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 863, Charles again entered the borders of the Bretons with an immense army, but he prevailed far less than he had wished. Finally, however, he made peace with them.

[Note: Witnesses 7–12 read “Charles indeed”; witnesses 7–12 read “finally, when”; and witnesses 7–12 read “he himself, however.”]

After hostages and oaths had been exchanged on both sides, King Herispoius came to him and submitted himself to his rule. Charles honored Herispoius with great gifts and allowed him to return to his kingdom. Charles himself returned to Francia.

## DCCCLXIV (864)

[The supplied source ends here.]

### 864

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 864 [Note: [Col. 0082D] Cf. the Annals of Fulda and Bertin under 863.], King Lothair began to seek ways by which he might separate Queen Theutberga from his company. He hated her on account of Waldrada [Note: [Col. 0081] In codex 7 Waldrada’s name is sometimes written *Vuldrada*, as also in the Annals of Fulda.] who had been his concubine while he was still a young man in his father’s household. Indeed, inflamed by the devil, he loved her with an excessive passion.

Accordingly, King Lothair first approached Gunthar, bishop of the city of Cologne, who at that time was chief chaplain, through agents secretly introduced; then he attacked him in person with every kind of stratagem concerning this dispute. To make him more readily give his consent, he promised to take the bishop’s niece in marriage, provided only that, with the authority and permission of the aforesaid bishop and of the other bishops, he could somehow repudiate the aforementioned Theutberga [Note: [Col. 0081] “On whatever occasion” in manuscript 4.].

Gunthar, being light-minded and thoughtless in his actions, was immediately drawn wholeheartedly into the affair [Note: [Col. 0081] “With an incitement” in manuscript 5; “into the affair” is absent in manuscripts 1–3, 5, and 6.], seduced, as later became clear, by a vain hope. Again, Gunthar addressed Thietgaud, archbishop of Trier, on this matter [Note: [Col. 0083] Manuscript 5 reads “he addresses, knowing” (*alloquitur sciens*)]. Knowing him to be a simple man, and not particularly learned in the divine Scriptures or practiced in canonical decrees, he produced certain passages from the pages of both Testaments. Expounding them otherwise than ecclesiastical rule teaches, he dragged the unwary man with him into the pit, “the blind leading the blind.”

What more need be said? Everything that seemed necessary for this scheme was done. They convened the council of Metz [Note: [Col. 0083D] In 860 it was held at Aachen, not at Metz; Col. 0083: manuscript 5c/e reads “convenes” (*convocat*)]. They placed the queen in the midst of the assembly, as though she had been canonically summoned [Note: [Col. 0083] “Summoned canonically” in manuscripts 7 and 12.]. They produced witnesses together with written documents; these witnesses, laying serious charges against her [Note: [Col. 0083] “Were laying” in manuscript 5], declared among other things that Theutberga had confessed that she had defiled herself by incestuous intercourse with her own brother.
