Immediately the decrees of the Fathers concerning incestuous persons were recited. Theutberga was not only separated from her lawful husband, but every marital union was also forbidden her; penance was imposed according to the measure of her alleged guilt, and by such a criminal contrivance the king’s long-desired wish was fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0083] “And so criminal” in manuscripts 7–12.].

Not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0083D] 862. Cf. the Council of Labbé, vol. VIII, and the Annals of Bertin for this year.], they again assembled a synodal gathering at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0083] “At Aachen” in manuscripts 4 and 5]. There the king presented a written statement of his complaint. It contained an account of how he had been deceived concerning a certain woman named Theutberga by the schemes of factious and treacherous men; indeed, he emphatically repeated that he had endured the judgment of separation by the decision of the bishops.

If she were fit for the marriage bed, and had not been polluted by the destructive stain of incest, and if she had not been publicly condemned by a confession from her own mouth, he would willingly retain her. But he declared himself incontinent and unable to endure the ardor of youthful age without sexual union.

When volumes from various councils had been brought forward, many passages concerning incestuous persons were repeated [Note: [Col. 0083] The words from “When volumes…” through “were repeated” are absent in manuscripts 7–12.]. After these had been read, they pronounced the following definitive sentence:

> “We believe that she was neither a suitable nor a legitimate wife, nor prepared by God as a wife, since she is proved by a public confession to have been marked by the incestuous crime of fornication. Therefore, for our glorious prince, because of his most devoted zeal in divine worship [Note: [Col. 0083] “Most devoted assertion” in manuscripts 2, 4, and 5] and his most victorious protection of the kingdom, to whom not only we but also every canonical authority has forbidden an incestuous marriage [Note: [Col. 0083] The base text has “also canonical authority”; manuscripts 7–12 read “every canonical authority”], we do not deny that a lawful marriage has been granted by God, in accordance with the indulgence of the Apostle’s saying: ‘It is better to marry than to burn.’”

When these matters had thus been carried out, Waldrada now appeared in public, surrounded by a multitude of attendants, and the whole royal palace resounded with the cry that Waldrada was queen. Gunthar’s niece [Note: [Col. 0083] Manuscript 5 consistently writes *Guntherius*] was summoned to the king, and, as they say, he violated her once; then, amid laughter and the mockery of everyone, she was sent back to her uncle.

Thereupon, through the efforts of Queen Theutberga’s brothers, all these matters were brought to the attention of Pope Nicholas, who at that time presided over the Roman Church.

### 865

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Cf. the Annals of Bertin under 863.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 865, Hagano [Note: [Col. 0083] “Agano” in manuscript 10] and Rodoald [Note: [Col. 0083] “Rodojaldus” in manuscripts 9–12], legates of the apostolic see, were sent into Gaul to investigate whether the matter was as it had been reported to the supreme pontiff. When they came into Francia, they were corrupted by money and favored iniquity more than equity.

Nevertheless, when they reached the king and had explained to him the reasons for their mission, they received this answer from him: that he had done nothing other than what the bishops of his kingdom had indicated at the general synod should be done [Note: [Col. 0083] “Had demonstrated” in manuscript 4.].

The same legates advised the king to send to the apostolic see those bishops who had presided over that synod [Note: [Col. 0083] “To send the bishops who had presided over that synod” in manuscripts 7–12; “who” is absent in manuscript 8], so that they might satisfy the universal pope by word and writing. The legates, enriched with immense wealth, returned to Rome and reported to the pontiff what they had seen and heard in Gaul. They added [Note: [Col. 0083] The text from “They added” through “disciplines” is absent in manuscript 4] that they had found no learned bishop in Lothair’s kingdom who had been thoroughly trained in canonical disciplines [Note: [Col. 0083] “Who was somewhat trained in canonical disciplines” in manuscripts 7–12.].

Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0084D] 864. Cf. the Annals of Bertin], the archbishops Thietgaud and Gunthar set out for Rome, intending both to demonstrate the king’s innocence in the aforesaid matter [Note: [Col. 0083] “To demonstrate the matter” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12] and to show that they, together with the other co-bishops, had acted according to ecclesiastical and apostolic decrees [Note: [Col. 0083] “And apostolic” is absent in manuscript 7]. They deserved to be branded with the epithet of folly [Note: [Col. 0083] “Indeed” (*quidem*) in manuscripts 7–12; “eulogy” in manuscripts 9–12], since they imagined that they could deceive the see of Peter [Note: [Col. 0083] “The apostle Peter” in manuscript 7] by some perverse doctrine—a see that had never been deceived [Note: [Col. 0083] “Nor had it deceived itself” in manuscript 5] and could never be deceived by any heresy.

When they had therefore come into the presence of Pope Nicholas, they presented a written statement containing the acts of the synods that they had established at Metz and Aachen [Note: [Col. 0083] “In the city of Metz or at Aachen” in manuscripts 7–12; “in the city of Metz and at Aachen” in manuscripts 2 and 5]. When it had been read aloud by a notary before everyone, the pontiff asked whether they confirmed these writings by their words [Note: [Col. 0083] “Whether they refuted them in words” in manuscripts 7–12; “whether they were refuting them in words” in manuscript 4]. They replied that it seemed inappropriate for them to wish to invalidate by words what they had confirmed with their own hands [Note: [Col. 0083] “To defame by words” in manuscripts 1 and 3].

Thus, without either rejecting or accepting their assertion [Note: [Col. 0084]—], they were ordered to go to their lodgings until they should be summoned again. After a few days had intervened [Note: [Col. 0085] “After a few days had indeed intervened” in manuscripts 7–12], they were summoned to the synod that the pope had convened. There their writings were condemned and anathematized, and by the judgment of all the bishops, priests, and deacons [Note: [Col. 0085] “Deacons” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12], they themselves were deposed and deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity.

Thus shamefully dishonored, they approached the emperor Louis, brother of King Lothair, who at that time was staying in the region of Benevento. By written and spoken complaints they cried out that they had been unjustly deposed, that an injury had been done to the emperor himself and to the whole holy Church, since it had never been heard or read anywhere that any metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0085] “Metropolitan bishop” in manuscripts 1 and 3] had been degraded without the prince’s knowledge or without the presence of other metropolitans.

They added many other things, blaspheming the same pope [Note: [Col. 0085]—], which we have thought it superfluous to enumerate here. They imagined that through the emperor’s support and intercession they could at once erase the stain of the accusation brought against them and recover the status of their former dignity [Note: [Col. 0085] “That the stain might be erased” in manuscript 5]. But their hope was disappointed, although the emperor wished in every way to help them.

Thietgaud, patiently enduring the sentence of his deposition pronounced by the apostolic see, presumed to have no contact whatsoever with the sacred ministry, in accordance with the preceding custom. Gunthar, however, inflated by the spirit of pride, did not shrink from arrogantly usurping the office forbidden to him, making light of the apostolic excommunication.

They therefore returned to Francia covered with the shame they deserved [Note: [Col. 0085] “Driven back with confession” in manuscript 5]. When they had again, and a third time, approached the apostolic see for the sake of restoration and reinstatement [Note: [Col. 0085] “The apostolic see for the sake of restoration and reinstatement” in manuscripts 7–12], they were finally overtaken by illness in Italy [Note: [Col. 0085] “Into Italy” in manuscript 7] and died as exiles and wanderers, with only lay communion granted to them.

### 866

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 866 [Note: [Col. 0085D] Cf. the Annals of Fulda and Bertin under 865.], Bishop Arsenius, the apocrisiarius [Note: [Col. 0086D] That is, a referendary, chancellor, or legate] and counselor of Pope Nicholas, was sent to Francia as his representative. When he arrived, he exercised such authority and power as though the supreme pontiff himself had come.

Finally, after a gathering of the bishops had been convened, he addressed King Lothair and ordered him to choose one of two alternatives: either to be reconciled with his lawful wife, renouncing the company of Waldrada the concubine, or immediately to be struck by the sword of anathema—he himself and all who offered him support in this crime.

Compelled by this necessity [Note: [Col. 0085] “Driven or constrained by necessity” in manuscript 5], whether he wished it or not, he received Queen Theutberga in marriage, inserting an oath that he would henceforth keep her as the rights of equity prescribe a legitimate wife must be kept; that he would not separate from her, nor, while she lived, bring another woman over her.

After this, by the authority of God and of Saint Peter and by the command of the apostolic lord, he ordered Waldrada to go to Rome so that she might strive to give an account for herself [Note: [Col. 0085] “Ought to give an account” in manuscripts 7–12]. He also declared to everyone that Engiltrude [Note: [Col. 0085] “Also” is absent in manuscripts 1–3, 5, and 6], once the wife of Count Boso [Note: [Col. 0085] “Buso” and other forms in manuscript 5], had been excommunicated by the apostolic see because she had abandoned her own husband and followed Wanger, her vassal, into Gaul [Note: [Col. 0085] “Had followed” in manuscripts 2, 3, 5, and 6; “had followed” in manuscripts 7–12]. He renewed this excommunication with all the bishops who were present.

After this, the same Engiltrude [Note: [Col. 0085] “Engildruda” in manuscript 5; “Engiltrudis” in manuscripts 4 and 7. The words of Engiltrude’s oath are not found in manuscript 4; “Hengiltrudis” in manuscript 7] presented herself to the aforesaid Arsenius in the city of Worms, where the aforementioned bishop had met King Louis.

In the presence of that legate she therefore swore an oath containing the following:

> “I, Engiltrude, daughter of the late Count Mathfrid, who was the wife of Count Boso, swear to you, Lord Bishop Arsenius, legate and apocrisiarius of the supreme holy Catholic [Note: [Col. 0085] “Apocrisiarius of the holy Catholic” in manuscripts 7–12] and apostolic see, and through you to my lord Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0085] “Through you” is absent in manuscripts 7 and 9–12; “through you” in manuscript 8], my lord supreme pontiff and universal pope, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by these four Gospels of Christ God [Note: [Col. 0085] “Of Christ God” is absent in manuscripts 9–12; “The Gospels of Christ” in manuscripts 7 and 8], which I kiss with my mouth [Note: [Col. 0085] “I kiss” in manuscript 7] and touch with my own hands [Note: [Col. 0085] “I touch with my hands” in manuscripts 7–12], that from now on I shall abandon the wickedness which I practiced against the aforementioned Boso, my husband [Note: [Col. 0085] “That wickedness having been abandoned” in manuscripts 7–12], and, like the sheep that was lost, I shall return to the holy Catholic and apostolic Church [Note: [Col. 0085] “The Catholic and apostolic Church” in manuscripts 7–12], under the same obligation by which Lord Nicholas, supreme pontiff and universal pope, bound me. I shall go to the Italian kingdom [Note: [Col. 0085] “The Italian kingdom” in manuscripts 2 and 7–12], either with you or before you, wherever you shall provide; and whatever the apostolic lord commands or determines, I shall fulfill, nor shall I refuse to carry it out [Note: [Col. 0085] “To depart” in manuscripts 9 and 12; “to proceed” in manuscripts 11 and 10].”

But she did not fulfill this terrible oath. For she went with Arsenius as far as the waters of the Danube, and there arranged to go to some relative for assistance with horses [Note: [Col. 0085] The wording from “she went” through “assistance with horses” is absent in manuscripts 7–12]. She promised that she would return to the same legate at the city of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0085] “That she would return to him” in manuscript 7].

Turning back her steps on such a pretext [Note: [Col. 0085] “Turning back” in manuscript 5], she went from Alamannia back into Francia. When the aforesaid Arsenius learned this, he sent a letter to all the archbishops and bishops [“priests” in manuscript 7], and to all the faithful of God’s holy Church dwelling in Gaul, Germany, and Neustria [Note: [Col. 0085] “Nustria” in manuscript 2; “Nestria” in manuscripts 9–12].

He adjured them all by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed princes Peter and Paul, and of the lord pontiff and universal pope [Note: [Col. 0087] “Nicholas” in manuscripts 8–10], that no one should receive her into his parish. Rather, they were to proclaim her publicly in all their churches as wholly excommunicated, excluded from all communion with Christians, and bound by the chain of anathema [Note: [Col. 0087] “Bound until” in manuscripts 7–12], condemned among the impious and criminal, until she should receive worthy penance before the presence of the apostolic lord for her destructive conspiracies and the perjury she had committed.

Having recalled these matters briefly, let us return to the grievous case of King Lothair.

The legate of the apostolic see, having set affairs in Gaul in order [Note: [Col. 0087] “Having received and settled affairs” in manuscripts 7–12], returned to Rome, from which he had come. Again, while Waldrada and her accomplices were struggling against him, the king’s mind was stirred against Theutberga. Anger was aroused, and upon the smoldering ashes of discord and hatred a great fire was kindled anew.

She was despised, abhorred, and rejected [Note: [Col. 0087] “Abominated, accused as guilty” in manuscript 5]. The crime of adultery was laid against her, and every artifice of ingenuity was employed to discover how she might be punished as though she were guilty.

Foreseeing that the danger of death threatened her, she secretly fled and, coming to King Charles, entrusted herself to his protection. When Pope Nicholas learned of this through the spread of the report [Note: [Col. 0087] The letters of Nicholas are absent in manuscript 4], he sent King Charles a letter of praise and encouragement [Note: [Col. 0087] “Of exhortation and praise” in manuscript 4] containing the following [Note: [Col. 0087D] Among the letters of Nicholas, no. 33; Bouquet]:

> “Among the other religious defenders of the holy Church and vigorous champions of truth [Note: [Col. 0087] “Defenders of truth” in the abbreviated witnesses], we recall that no one has been more concerned than Your Piety over the distress of Theutberga, the glorious queen, and that no one has felt more compassion for her troubles.”

After an appropriate exhortation he added:

> “We do not wish Your Excellency to remain unaware that King Lothair has subjected Theutberga, his wife, to such varied afflictions and forced her under innumerable pressures, contrary to the oaths he had sworn [Note: [Col. 0087] “Contrary to the oaths prescribed” in manuscript 5d and manuscripts 8–12; “contrary to the written oaths” in manuscripts 1 and 7], that she has now written to us under compulsion saying that she wishes to be stripped of her royal dignity or of marriage [Note: [Col. 0087] “Of dignity without marriage” in manuscript 5; “dignity” in manuscript 7] and to be content with a private life alone [Note: [Col. 0087] “Despised” in manuscript 7]. We wrote back to her [Note: [Col. 0087] “We wrote” in manuscripts 5 and 7–12] that this could not happen unless her husband Lothair chose the same life [Note: [Col. 0087] “Her husband Lothair chose the same life” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12].

“But, as we have learned from the report of many [Note: [Col. 0087] “From the account” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12], Lothair himself has decided to hold an assembly [Note: [Col. 0087] “He decides” in manuscripts 7–12], and is planning to subject the same Theutberga to his own examination and judgment [Note: [Col. 0087] “To his own judgment” in the abbreviated witnesses]. If by the artifices of his falsehood or by argumentative evasions he can make her appear not to have been his lawful wife, he wishes to remove her from himself completely. But if he wishes to admit her as his own wife, he then intends to accuse her as though she had committed adultery, and for this reason to drive his own man and Theutberga’s man into single combat [Note: [Col. 0087] “Monachiam” in manuscript 5]. If the queen’s man should fall, he plans to kill her without delay.

“Your wise judgment, we believe, already perceives how contrary these things are to every divine law. But we too wish to make a brief demonstration concerning this matter. First, we assert that Theutberga ought not to be summoned again to answer concerning the dispute already concluded, since what has once been rightly decided and settled by the interposition of oaths ought not to be reopened, except perhaps where there is greater authority [Note: [Col. 0087] “Perhaps there” in manuscript 5].

“Furthermore, since she is seeking refuge in the Church and constantly requesting ecclesiastical judgment, she ought not to be subjected to secular judgment [Note: [Col. 0087] “To the judgment of secular persons” in manuscripts 1 and 3].

“After this, since we have been summoned as judges by both parties—that is, by both Lothair and Theutberga—and since we have dealt with the dispute of both, it is not fitting to flee to other judges in this matter. According to the sacred canons, one may not appeal from judges whom common consent has chosen; and where an appeal is permitted, it may be made only to a higher authority [Note: [Col. 0087] “Where there is a higher authority” in manuscripts 1 and 3].

“Since, therefore, there is nowhere a higher authority than that of the apostolic see, which has dealt with the case of both parties, we do not know whether anyone may judge its judgment or reopen its sentence.”

And after a little he said:

> “But as for Lothair’s accusation that Theutberga committed adultery, who does not see that it is full of deceit? For if, as he himself boasts, she is not his wife, what concern is it of his to fabricate an accusation of adultery against her, since she could not have committed adultery [Note: [Col. 0087] “Could not have” in manuscripts 1–3 and 5–12] if she was not someone’s wife [Note: [Col. 0087] “If she does not exist as a wife” in manuscripts 5, 7, and 9–12]? But if Lothair accuses her of adultery, and punishment is prepared if she is convicted [Note: [Col. 0087] “If she is defeated” in manuscript 5], it is necessary that he acknowledge her as his wife.”

And after some intervening material:

> “Moreover, whether judgment is to be conducted concerning the marital bond or concerning the crime of adultery, there is no way that Theutberga can legally enter into conflict with Lothair or undertake a legitimate contest in the dispute unless she is first restored for a time to her own control and freely reunited with her relatives [Note: [Col. 0087] “To her own control and also to her relatives” in manuscripts 2, 3, 5, and 6].

> “Among them, a place must also be provided where no violence from a multitude need be feared [Note: [Col. 0087] “Where no violence” in manuscript 5], and where it will not be difficult to produce the witnesses or other persons whom both the holy canons and the venerable laws of the Romans require in disputes of this kind.

> “But we do not say that these things are to be done, since above we have taught that they cannot be done without our decree and arrangement.”

The same most holy pontiff, therefore, inflamed by the zeal of God with which the priest Phinehas had once been inflamed [Note: [Col. 0089] “Phinehas” is absent in manuscript 5], excommunicated Waldrada on the very day of the Purification of holy Mary, Mother of God, in the basilica, and separated her from all fellowship with Christians. He also sent a letter to all the bishops established throughout Germany and Gaul, containing the reasons and manner of her excommunication [Note: [Col. 0089D] Among the letters of Nicholas, no. 27; Bouquet]. For the sake of brevity, he preferred to set down its meaning rather than the sequence of its words [Note: [Col. 0089] “It was decided to set down the meaning rather than the sequence of words for the sake of brevity” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12; codex of Saint Godehard].

> “We had indeed decided to temper the measure of punishment against Waldrada, the adulteress who persistently remained impenitent, less strictly, and to pronounce against her a sentence of just punishment not proportionate to so great a crime [Note: [Col. 0089] “For the crime” in manuscripts 2, 5, and 12], unless she had resolved to remain forever in the mire of adultery [Note: [Col. 0089] “In the mire of adultery” in manuscripts 1 and 3].

> “But because she has despised our warnings and repeated exhortations, because she has neither acknowledged nor confessed her guilt, because she has not sought pardon by sending a legation to us, although we have undertaken to deal with her case, and finally because, when she ought to have approached us by the direct route and sought the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, she has turned back after Satan, she does not cease to plot deceit against Queen Theutberga, having begun to devise her destruction [Note: [Col. 0089] Manuscripts 1–3 read: “and does not cease from devising the destruction begun against Queen Theutberga”].

> “Together with the excellent Apostle we say—and this must often be repeated against her and those like her—that according to her hardness and impenitent heart she is storing up wrath for herself on the day of wrath.

> “Therefore we excommunicate her for her deeds [Note: [Col. 0089] ‘We have excommunicated her’ in manuscript 5d], until she has given satisfaction to the Church of Christ and especially to us, who principally have charge of her and who have begun to deal with and investigate her case; until, by accepting our counsel, she removes every sinister suspicion; and from participation in the precious body and blood of the Lord, and from every fellowship of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0089] ‘Of the holy Church’ is absent in manuscripts 7 and 9–12], by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by the authority of our mediocrity, we have made her wholly alien, together with all her accomplices, communicants, and supporters [Note: [Col. 0089] ‘And by the authority of our mediocrity we have made her wholly alien’ in the abbreviated witnesses].

> “We remember that we promulgated this sentence on the fourth day before the Nones of February and sent it to you in writing. So that our labor may not be in vain [Note: [Col. 0089] “Laver” in manuscripts 5a and 5d; “our labor in vain” in the abbreviated witnesses], let your fraternity raise spiritual arms with us against the aforesaid adulteress and her communicants. Let each of you publicly proclaim her and her supporters excommunicated in his parish [Note: [Col. 0089] ‘Her supporters with one voice’ in manuscripts 3, 5, 7, and 9–12], until she submits to worthy penance according to our special judgment [Note: [Col. 0089] ‘According to our judgment’ in manuscripts 7–12].”

The same most reverend pontiff also sent a letter to King Lothair [Note: [Col. 0090D] No. 34 among the letters of Nicholas; Bouquet], containing the following:

> “When we heard from our returning legate of the beginning, so to speak, of your correction, we gave fitting thanks to God and prepared our mind to return suitable thanks to you as well [Note: [Col. 0089] “Suitable thanks” is absent in manuscripts 7 and 9–12]. But, alas, adverse reports arriving [Note: [Col. 0089] “Arriving” is absent in manuscript 5] swiftly opposed the purpose of this intention of ours [Note: [Col. 0089] “Opposed it” in manuscript 3].

> “Therefore we have been compelled to change our tone; and we who had resolved to open our mouths in thanksgiving [Note: [Col. 0089] “To open them in thanksgiving” in manuscript 5] are forced to direct the office of our tongue still toward mourning and reproaches [Note: [Col. 0089] “Toward mourning and reproaches” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12].

> “For we have learned that you, who have persisted in crime for a long time and have greatly harmed the Church of God, are still doing harm; and that you who were in filth are still becoming filthy. Indeed, as we think, it is not enough for you merely to have committed adultery unless you add this also: that you plunge the souls of men, entangled in the snares of perjury [Note: [Col. 0089] “Souls through perjury” in manuscripts 5 and 9–12], into ultimate destruction.

> “But what wonder if you have brought ruin upon the souls of a few through perjury [Note: [Col. 0089] “Brought souls to ruin” in manuscripts 1–3 and 6], when, placed in such exalted position, through the example of your adultery [Note: [Col. 0089] “Of your adulteress” in manuscript 5] you have hurled so many thousands of people into the chaos of perdition?

> “As for Theutberga’s futile effort, willingly or unwillingly, to establish, as though giving testimony on Waldrada’s behalf, that she was your legitimate wife, who could possibly need her testimony in this matter, when we rather think what is just and understand what is equitable: that even after Theutberga’s death you can neither lawfully nor according to any rule take Waldrada as your wife or be permitted to do so?

> “Therefore, whether Waldrada was ever your legitimate wife, the Church of God has no need of Theutberga’s satisfaction. But we know one thing: neither we nor that same Church of God, by the authority of God who will judge adulterers [Note: [Col. 0089] “By the authority of God” is absent in manuscript 5d], will in any way leave you unpunished if you ever take Waldrada back, even after Theutberga has died [Note: [Col. 0089] “Who will judge adulterers, and if” in manuscript 5d].”

And after a little he said:

> “Therefore, with the greatest care, cherish and love the aforementioned Theutberga, your wife, as your own flesh; and watch attentively that you do not consent to separate her from yourself by any means. If she wishes to depart from you, rebuke her—indeed, correct her [Note: [Col. 0089] “Correct her, indeed rebuke her” in manuscript 5]—and strive by every means to turn her back from such an intention.

> “But if, out of love of chastity, she seeks separation and demands the dissolution of the marital union [Note: [Col. 0091] “She demands” in manuscript 1; “she requests” in manuscripts 7 and 9–12], it is certain, as the Apostle says: ‘For the woman has no authority over her own body, but the man has.’ But if you too, pursuing chastity, wish to dissolve the union for the sake of religion, we permit it, provided that it is not done hypocritically.

> “For although it is written, ‘What God has joined, let no human separate,’ God, and not a human being, separates when, in view of divine love, marriages are dissolved with the consent of both spouses. If you wish to proceed in this way, we grant permission with a willing spirit and readily give our assent; but we forbid your mutual separation if it is to be done otherwise.

> “Furthermore, if infertility is alleged, consider the ninety-year-old Sarah, and Anna, and likewise Elizabeth [Note: [Col. 0091] “Elizabeth” in manuscript 5c and “Elizabeth” in manuscript 5a/e]. Yet perhaps it is not infertility that causes such barrenness [Note: [Col. 0091] “Fecundity” in manuscript 5d], but iniquity.

> “Therefore, most glorious king, be content with your own wife, and seek no other woman’s company besides hers. Accept our counsel, then, and embrace our admonitions as those of an affectionate father. Restrain your mind, tongue, and body from every depravity, above all avoiding communion with Waldrada, your concubine and the woman you formerly repudiated, and consigning her company to perpetual oblivion [Note: [Col. 0091] “To obligation” in manuscripts 2 and 5a/d].

> “For she has been excommunicated and, until she appears before us, separated from all fellowship with Christians, as the entire West already knows; and very soon the East too, together with the other regions, will not be unaware of it through our legates [Note: [Col. 0091] “And already also” in manuscript 3; “and already” in manuscript 2; other variants preserve the same sense].

> “Therefore you must beware lest you too be struck by the same sword of sentence as she, and, because of the passion for one little woman and the desire of a very brief time [Note: [Col. 0091] “Struck by the sentence because of passion and a very brief…” in manuscript 5d], be dragged, bound and fettered, to sulfurous stench and everlasting destruction.”

And after a brief interval the letter concludes as follows [Note: [Col. 0091] “The letter concludes as follows” is absent in manuscripts 7–12]:

> “Let what we have now written to you suffice, as though our words, reproving your transgressions, had passed between you and us. For the rest, beware lest at some time, in accordance with the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 0091] “According to the commandment” in manuscript 5], we bring two or three witnesses against you—or rather, lest we report this to the holy Church, and, what we do not desire, you henceforth become like a heathen and a tax collector.”

Behold, from many matters we have taken care to note a few, so that those who did not know might thereby become partly informed, while those who did know might not be burdened in every respect.

What end the ravages of this destructive disease, refusing to be healed by the apostolic antidote, brought about, and how great the losses inflicted on the kingdom by this deadly contagion were—as the aforementioned most holy pope, inspired by the Holy Spirit, had foretold [Note: [Col. 0091] Manuscript 5 reads, “the aforementioned pope made [them] by this contagion”]—will be demonstrated in its proper place in what follows [Note: [Col. 0091] Manuscript 5 reads “we shall demonstrate”; it also has “he had foretold what [is] in what follows”].

Additional apparatus omitted above:

- At the oath of Engiltrude, manuscript 7–12 reads “of the count, to you lord” (*comitis tibi domno*) for “to you, Lord Bishop Arsenius”; and the words from “whatever the apostolic lord commands” through “I shall fulfill” are absent in manuscripts 7–12.
- Arsenius is called “the oft-mentioned” (*saepedictus*) rather than merely “aforesaid” in manuscripts 7–12. At his injunction, manuscript 4 reads “the blessed apostles,” while manuscripts 7–12 read “the holy princes Peter,” for “the blessed princes Peter and Paul.”
- In Nicholas’s letter to Charles, manuscripts 7–12 read “he decides to hold” rather than “he has decided to hold” an assembly; manuscripts 5, 7, and 9–12 read “by both parties alike, that is, by both” at the appeal passage. In the account of Waldrada’s excommunication, manuscript 3 has “and sent” rather than “sent.”
- In the sentence against Waldrada, manuscripts 1–3, 5, and 6 add *ac* (“and”) before “from participation in the precious body and blood”; manuscripts 7–12 place “This sentence” after the phrase concerning her accomplices, communicants, and supporters.
- In Nicholas’s letter to Lothair, manuscript 5 reads “returning to” (*revertenti*) for “returning”; manuscripts 7–12 add “and” before “toward mourning and reproaches” and omit “still” (*adhuc*); manuscript 5c/e reads “lest with us” (*ne cum nobis*) for “lest at some time we.”
- In the concluding authorial notice, manuscripts 7–12 read “how” (*qualiter*) for “what kind of” (*qualem*), manuscript 5d reads “how great” (*quantoque*) for “what great,” and manuscript 5 reads “we shall demonstrate” for “will be demonstrated.”

Around this time [Note: [Col. 0091D] Years 858 and 859. Cf. the Annals of Fulda and Bertin.], King Louis [Note: [Col. 0091] The words “king of his brother” are absent in manuscript 7.] entered the kingdom of his brother Charles with an army, eager to subject the western kingdoms to his rule and to seize from his brother [Note: [Col. 0091] “to seize from his brother”: manuscript 7 and manuscripts 9–12; “to his brother”: manuscript 8; the words from “from his brother” through “had bound himself before God” are absent in manuscript 4.] the portion due to him, which had properly fallen to him by lot and by the cord of inheritance; forgetting the bonds of brotherhood and blood relationship, forgetting the pact which they had long ago established by mutual agreement [Note: [Col. 0091] “he had established”: manuscripts 3 and 5.], and also forgetful of the oaths by which he had bound himself before God with great execrations.

They had supplied, for committing this crime, the tinder of such opportunities and inducements [Note: [Col. 0091] “had supplied” (*praebuerat*): manuscripts 1–3, 5, and 6; *talem* (“such,” singular): manuscripts 5 and 6; *occasionem* (“opportunity,” singular): manuscripts 3, 7, and 9–12.]. Charles, as we have already stated [Note: [Col. 0091] “Charles, who also, as”: manuscript 5.], struck down some of the more distinguished men of the kingdom, either publicly condemned to the sword [Col. 0092B] or destroyed through deceit after being tricked [Note: [Col. 0091] “deceived”: manuscript 7]. The others, fearing that they might suffer the same fate, appealed to King Louis, who was staying beyond the Rhine, and enticed his mind toward acquiring his brother’s kingdom, promising that they themselves, together with the kingdom, would surrender to his authority [Note: [Col. 0091] “of the same man”: manuscript 5; “would subject”: manuscript 7.].

Since the minds of kings are greedy and always insatiable, he was easily brought by this persuasion to hope; and, as we have said, he entered the borders of the kingdom with a strong force. Charles, perceiving that the strength of the kingdom had deserted him [Note: [Col. 0091] “the men of the kingdom”: manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, and 9–12; the reading is uncertain.], sought a hiding place for his flight in the farthest boundaries of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0091] Manuscript 5 reads “a hiding place for the flight of Aquitaine”; manuscript 2 has “of Aquitaine,” corrected from “of Eugia.”]. Louis obtained the kingdom as he had begun to do, and reached as far as the city of Sens [Note: [Col. 0091] “as far as the city of Rethel”: manuscript 5]. After dismissing his army to return to Germany and their homes, he began to arrange affairs with the nobles of the kingdom. But suddenly fortune changed. For the princes who had introduced him into the kingdom, seeing that he was proceeding toward them quite differently from what they had expected [Note: [Col. 0091] “seeing that he was proceeding toward them”: manuscripts 7–12.], struck by repentance, returned to Charles.

Charles, rejoicing that he had recovered strength from desperate circumstances, gathered forces from every side and attempted to attack his brother in war. When Louis saw that he had been abandoned both by those whom he had brought with him and by those whom he seemed to have acquired there, he promptly took flight and, with the requisite confusion, left the borders of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0091] “the borders of the kingdom”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12.].

At this time Abbot Hubert [Note: [Col. 0091] “Hubert”: manuscript 5; “Eubert”: manuscript 7.], brother of Queen Theutberga, began to rebel against King Lothar. Having gathered a strong band of marauders, he began to practice plunder; and after killing or driving away Lothar’s faithful men who possessed the neighboring places, he distributed their fields and estates among the followers of his faction. [Col. 0092D]

To suppress such recklessness, King Lothar led out an army once, twice, and a third time; he also frequently sent a force with commanders of armed men [Col. 0093A]. Yet he could not extinguish this presumption at all, because the inaccessible places [Note: [Col. 0093] “the inaccessible places were between”: manuscript 5.] between the Jura [Note: [Col. 0093] *Jurum*; *Juram* in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5.] and the Pennine Alps [Note: [Col. 0093] “the Apennine Alps”: manuscript 5] provided the rebels with an exceptionally strong refuge. Because of the hollows of the valleys and the precipitous mountains, they offered the king and his army extremely narrow paths and difficult access [Note: [Col. 0093] Some manuscripts omit the passage from “they provided” through “difficult access.” Other readings are: “the inaccessible places between the Jura and the Apennine Alps are the strongest fortifications for the rebels and provide those entering with difficult access”; or, “they are the strongest fortifications for the rebels, yet provide travelers with difficult passage.” The copy of St. Godehard reads “providing access.”].

Nevertheless, this same acephalous Hubert [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Acephalous” means one who acknowledges neither his head—namely, a king—nor a monastic rule; a rebel, or a married cleric.] was finally killed by Count Conrad [Note: [Col. 0093] “Chuonrad”: manuscript 3; “Chonrad”: manuscript 7; “Chunrad”: manuscripts 9–12] near the castle called Orbe [Note: [Col. 0093D] Orbe, north of Lausanne.].

## 866

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 866 [Note: [Col. 0093] Some copies read 867: manuscripts 3, 8, and 9–12; these copies likewise increase each subsequent number by one.] [Note: [Col. 0093D] The year 857. Cf. the Annals of Bertin.], Herispoius [Note: [Col. 0093] “Herisposius”; elsewhere “Herisposios”: manuscript 5; “Hierispoius”: manuscript 7], king of the Britons, was killed by his own men, and the duke Solomon was installed in his place. For this man was energetic and warlike and suited to rule the kingdom in both appearance and character [Note: [Col. 0094D] Year 863. Cf. the Annals of Bertin.].

Charles prepared for a third invasion of the Britons with an army [Col. 0093B]. But when he had approached the borders of the people and heard that they were prepared to resist with all their strength, he suddenly changed his mind and chose rather to accept peace than to wage war. Thus, after making an agreement with Solomon—the same agreement he had previously made with Herispoius—he departed [Note: [Col. 0093] “he withdrew”: manuscript 4; “he departed”: manuscript 5d.].

## 867

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 867 [Note: [Col. 0094D] Cf. the Annals of Bertin, year 866, and those of Fulda, year 867], the Northmen, occupying the bank of the Loire River [Note: [Col. 0093] “the bank”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12], began once more to ravage cruelly the provinces of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0093] “occupying Nantes”: manuscript 5], Angers, Poitiers, and Tours. Against them, Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 0093] “Rothert”: manuscript 7; “Rodbert”: manuscript 8; “Robert”: manuscript 4; “Rutbert”: manuscripts 11 and 12; “Rothbert”: manuscript 10; “Rubert”: manuscripts 5c and 5e], who held the march [Note: [Col. 0093] “the marquisate”: manuscripts 2–5], and Ramnulf [Note: [Col. 0093] “Rannulf”: manuscripts 1, 3, and 4; “Ranulf”: manuscripts 5 and 6; “Ramolf and Ramnulf”: manuscript 2; “Ramnolf”: manuscript 8; “Arnulf”: manuscript 7], duke of Aquitaine, gathered a multitude and drew up their battle line.

When the Northmen realized that they were being pursued by the army [Note: [Col. 0093] “that the army was pursuing them”: manuscript 5], they hastened back to their fleet with the greatest speed [Col. 0093C]. But when they saw the multitude of their pursuers approaching and recognized that they could not escape, they entered a certain village, where they fortified themselves as much as the time permitted. In that village there was a very large basilica built of stone, into which most of the Northmen entered with their leader, named Hasting.

Ruotbert and Ramnulf, with their companions, attacked them [Note: [Col. 0093] “attacked”: manuscripts 1, 2, and 5] and without delay slaughtered all whom they found outside the basilica [Note: [Col. 0093] “found”: manuscripts 1 and 3; “found them”: manuscripts 2 and 5; “find”: manuscript 4]. When they reached the church [Note: [Col. 0093] *vero* (“indeed”): manuscripts 7–12], they saw that the place was fortified and noticed that a considerable crowd of pagans was hiding inside [Col. 0094A]. After deliberating for a short while, they established a camp all around it and set up tents, intending on the following day, after constructing embankments and bringing up siege engines, to attack the enemy with all their strength; for the sun was already declining toward sunset.

Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 0093] *quoque* (“too”): manuscripts 7 and 9–12], burning with excessive heat, removed his helmet and cuirass so that, having gathered some air, he might cool himself for a while [Note: [Col. 0093] “might be cooled”: manuscript 5]. While each man was attending to the arrangement of the camp, suddenly the Northmen burst out from the fortification and, with an enormous shout, attacked Ruotbert and his companions [Note: [Col. 0093] “his companions”: manuscript 5c; “and his companions”: manuscripts 7–12]. [Note: [Col. 0093] “They attacked”: manuscripts 3, 5, and 6.]

Although sudden and unexpected events in war commonly throw even the bravest men into confusion, they nevertheless seized their weapons as quickly as possible, received the enemy courageously, and forced them, as they gave way, to return to the basilica. [Col. 0094B] Ruotbert, running up without helmet or cuirass, fought incautiously and pursued the enemies too eagerly [Note: [Col. 0093] “beyond”: manuscripts 3 and 5]. He was killed at the entrance of the church, and the Northmen dragged his already lifeless body inside.

Ramnulf, meanwhile, standing at a distance and watching the outcome, was severely wounded by an arrow shot through a window of the basilica by one of the Northmen. His men carried him out of the battle [Note: [Col. 0093] “having carried him out”: manuscript 5d], and he survived scarcely three days.

With this unhappy misfortune the battle was joined and ended [Note: [Col. 0093] “was joined and ended”: manuscript 5]. The army, deprived of its head and filled equally with confusion [Note: [Col. 0093] “with grief”: manuscript 4] and sorrow, broke off the siege that same hour and returned home. The Northmen, exulting, directed their steps toward the fleet [Note: [Col. 0093] “their steps”: absent in manuscript 5d].

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Year 866. Cf. the Annals of Bertin.] Not long afterward, after an interval of time [Note: [Col. 0093] “a long time”: manuscript 1], Abbot Hugh [Note: [Col. 0093] “Hugh”: manuscript 3] was appointed in Ruotbert’s place—a vigorous, humble, just, peace-loving man, grounded in every moral virtue [Col. 0094C]. For Odo [Note: [Col. 0093] “Oudo”: manuscripts 9 and 11; “Udo”: manuscripts 5, 6, 7, and 10] and Ruotbert, the sons of Ruotbert, were still children when their father died, and therefore the dukedom was not entrusted to them.

At the same time, the people of the Saracens, coming from Africa into Benevento [Note: [Col. 0093] “Beneventum”: manuscript 4; manuscripts 5c, 5e, and 8], invaded nearly the whole of that region, laying everything waste with slaughter, plunder, and fires. Against them [Note: [Col. 0094D] Year 866. Cf. Erchempert, *History*, chapter 32, and the Annals of Bertin, year 866], Emperor Louis gathered an army. Fearing that the strength of the kingdom might perhaps not suffice against the countless multitude of the enemy [Col. 0095A], he sent envoys to his brother Lothar in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0095] “Lothar” is absent in manuscript 5], earnestly requesting that, with God’s help and the valor of the Franks, he assist him in weakening the strength and restraining the audacity of that most wicked people.

Lothar did not hesitate at all, but gathered an army from every side with great diligence and came to his brother’s aid with all possible speed. Many battles were fought there, not only bravely but also successfully, with God bringing assistance. Meanwhile, Lothar’s army was worn down by a severe pestilence. Dissolved by unaccustomed heat and unseasonable weather, it was seized by the disease of dysentery or lientery [Note: [Col. 0095] “clientery”: manuscripts 1–3, 5, and 7–12; “elientery”: manuscript 4. Lientery is a form of diarrhea.] [Note: [Col. 0095D] From Greek λύω (*lýō*, “I loosen”) and ἔντερα (*éntera*, “intestines”), the same as dysentery.], and an innumerable multitude died from this affliction. Many others also perished from the bites of spiders [Note: [Col. 0095] *araniarum* (“of spiders”), corrected from *a ranarum* (“from frogs”) in manuscripts 1 and 3.]. Thus it was already made clear at that time that because of hardness and an unrepentant heart [Note: [Col. 0095] “of heart” (*cordis*): manuscripts 8–12.], God was opposed not only to Lothar but also to his entire kingdom. Accordingly, Lothar returned to Francia, not without the grave loss of his men, as has been said.

## 868

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 868, Nicholas, the most holy and blessed pope [Note: [Col. 0095D] Cf. the Annals of Bertin, year 867], after many labors for Christ and many struggles for the inviolable condition of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0095] “and after many”: manuscripts 1 and 5; “and after” is absent in manuscripts 2 and 4; absent in manuscript 5d], departed to the heavenly kingdoms, there to receive from the most generous Lord an unfading crown of glory for the faithful administration of the stewardship entrusted to him. Many things worthy of report could have been said about his deeds pleasing to God, had we not resolved, in our concern for brevity, to record the causes of events more summarily than to explain them [Note: [Col. 0095] “to expound”: manuscript 4].

Indeed, after blessed Gregory, no prelate elevated to pontifical honor in the city of Rome up to the present seems comparable to him [Col. 0095C]. He commanded kings and tyrants and presided over them with authority as though he were lord of the world. To bishops and religious priests who observed the Lord’s commands he appeared humble, gracious, devout [Note: [Col. 0095] “devout and merciful”: manuscripts 7–12], and gentle; toward the irreligious and those straying from the right path he was terrible and full of severity. Thus he may rightly be believed to have been another Elijah, raised up in our times by God [Note: [Col. 0095] “to have risen again”: manuscript 5; “to have risen up again”: manuscript 2], if not in body, then in spirit and power [Note: [Col. 0095] The words from “so that he may rightly be believed” through “power” are absent in manuscript 4].

Adrian succeeded this man of most holy memory in the pontificate. When King Lothar learned this through a reliable report [Note: [Col. 0095] “through a reliable report” is absent in manuscripts 7–12. Only the substance of this letter is reported in manuscript 4], he sent him a letter in these words [Col. 0095D]:

“An unfavorable and unambiguous report [Note: [Col. 0095] “an ambiguous report”: manuscripts 1–3]—remaining, so to speak, unaltered—has pierced the ears of our serenity with keen force, announcing that the lord Nicholas, of blessed memory, has departed from this valley of tears at Christ’s summons, to be crowned, as we believe, immeasurably among the saints. It is not surprising that all Christian religion should grieve over so great a pontiff and that the whole ecclesiastical order [Note: [Col. 0095] Absent in manuscripts 1–3] should mourn so prudent a pope.

In truth, we grieve even more, because we entrusted to so kindly a father the causes of our accusation and the fraudulent complaints of our rivals, so that he might weigh and determine them with the scales of equity and justice, at least for a time and in part. But, as we sorrowfully repeat, the snares and feigned deceptions of our enemies had greater force with his holiness than our simple and sincere defense.

For we, proclaiming unceasingly in letters and words, and repeating the same through various embassies, humbly requested that both we and our accusers might deserve a hearing before his pontificate according to divine and human laws [Note: [Col. 0095] “of his pontificate”: manuscripts 5c and 5d; “before the pontiff”: manuscript 5c], presenting our presence, as reason demands. But we were always rejected.”

And a little later:

“But because almighty God, the prince of shepherds, has exalted the summit of your pontificate in that holy see, if time smiles upon us [Note: [Col. 0095] “if time permits”: manuscript 3], we desire your presence in many ways, and to be encouraged by your conversations worthy of God and to obtain your honey-sweet blessing [Note: [Col. 0095] “to obtain it at the end”: manuscripts 1, 3, and 6].”

And at the end of the same letter:

“Meanwhile, we entreat you in every way to deign to make our highness certain through your letters of your desirable prosperity, and to grant us the gift of your dear sonship [Note: [Col. 0095] “to grant”: manuscript 2].”

To this the aforesaid pope replied that the see of Saint Peter was always prepared to receive worthy satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0095] “to perceive”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12; “to receive”: manuscript 8], and had never rejected what divine and human laws justly decreed. Therefore, if Lothar knew himself to be free from the charges brought against him, he ought to approach the apostolic see with complete confidence, so that he might receive the blessing he desired. But if he acknowledged his guilt, he should nevertheless hasten to come without hesitation, in order to accept remedies appropriate to repentance.

In these times [Note: [Col. 0095D] Cf. the Annals of Fulda, years 866 and 867; the Annals of Bertin, year [Col. 0096D] 866], the fiercely warlike people of the Bulgars [Note: [Col. 0095] *vulgarorum*: copy of St. Godehard; *ulgorum*: manuscript 7; *vulgorum*: manuscripts 9–12; *bulgarum*: manuscripts 1 and 5; *bulgarorum*: manuscript 5d], abandoning idols and renouncing pagan superstitions, believed in Christ for the most part [Note: [Col. 0095] “from the greatest part”: manuscript 9; “from the large part”: manuscripts 3 and 10; “Christ instead of ‘the greatest part’”: manuscripts 1–3 and 6; “in instead of ‘the greatest part’”: manuscript 7; “and instead of ‘the greatest part’”: manuscript 5], and, washed in the saving water of baptism, entered the Christian religion.

Priests and religious men were sent from the apostolic see to that people [Col. 0096D] [Note: [Col. 0096D] In the month of August, in the fourteenth indiction—that is, in the year 866. Cf. the *Life of Nicholas I*, chapter 68.], to instruct the still-uncultivated people in divine commands and, cultivating their unformed barbarism with sacred teachings, to prepare for Christ a dwelling pleasing to him [Col. 0097A].

So that the work of this truly holy devotion might achieve a successful result, Louis, the most Christian king who ruled the Germans, provided no slight assistance [Note: [Col. 0097] “support”: copy of St. Godehard]. They relate concerning the king of this people that, after receiving the grace of baptism, he advanced to such perfection [Note: [Col. 0097] “that, in such perfection”: manuscript 3; “that such”: manuscripts 5c, 5e, and 7] that by day he would appear before the people dressed in royal ornaments, but by night, clothed in sackcloth [Note: [Col. 0097] “clothed in sacred vesture”: manuscripts 5a and 5e; “in sacred clothing”: manuscripts 5c and 5d; the copy of St. Godehard reads “clothed in a sackcloth garment.”], he would secretly enter the church and lie prostrate in prayer on the pavement of the basilica, with only a hair shirt spread beneath him.

Not long afterward, warned by divine inspiration [Note: [Col. 0097] “moved”: manuscript 5], he abandoned his earthly kingdom so that he might reign eternally with Christ in heaven. After appointing his elder son as king in his place [Note: [Col. 0097] *in* (“in [his place]”) is absent in manuscript 5; *in suum locum* (“into his place”): the copy of St. Godehard and manuscripts 5, 7, and 9–12; *rege* (“with his son as king”): manuscript 6; “appointing his elder son as king”: manuscripts 1 and 5; “with his son, who was older, as king”: manuscript 3 and the copy of St. Godehard], he cut off the hair of his head, assumed the habit of holy conduct [Col. 0097B], and became a monk [Note: [Col. 0097] He was not yet a monk in the following year, for his legate attended the Council of Constantinople in 869. Bouquet.], devoting himself day and night to almsgiving, vigils, and prayers.

Meanwhile, his son, whom he had made king, departing far from his father’s intention and practice, began to practice plunder, to devote himself to drunkenness, feasting, and lust, and with every effort to recall the newly baptized people to the rites of paganism. When his father heard this, inflamed by excessive zeal, he laid aside the sacred habit, resumed the military belt, and, dressed in royal clothing and joined by men who feared God, pursued his son. He soon captured him without difficulty, gouged out his eyes [Note: [Col. 0097] “he captured him, and after his eyes had been torn out”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12], and sent him to prison.

Then, having summoned his entire kingdom, he made his younger son king, declaring before everyone that he too would suffer the same fate if he deviated in any respect from upright Christianity [Col. 0097C]. After carrying out these actions, he laid aside the belt, resumed the habit of holy religion, entered a monastery [Note: [Col. 0097] “into the monastery”: manuscripts 1–3 and 6; “returned to the monastery”: manuscript 4], and spent the remainder of his present life [Note: [Col. 0097] “of the present life” is absent in manuscript 2] in holy conduct [Note: [Col. 0097] “he led out”: manuscript 7].

## 869

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 869, Lothar set out for Rome [Note: [Col. 0097] “King Lothar set out for Rome”: manuscript 7]. When he arrived there, he was honorably received by Pope Adrian. The pontiff asked him whether he had thus far observed with complete vigilance the admonitions of the pious father, Lord Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0097] “preserved thus far with diligence”: manuscripts 7–12], and had guarded the oath he had sworn with an unbroken covenant [Note: [Col. 0097] “and had guarded it, which he had sworn”: manuscripts 1 and 2; “who had sworn it”: manuscripts 3, 6, 7, and 9–12].

Deceived by him who did not stand in truth, who is not only a liar but also the father of all lies, Lothar replied that he had observed everything as though it had been divinely commanded him. When the nobles and leading men who had come with him testified to the same, and no opposing person could be found who dared to enter into a legitimate dispute against royal authority, the universal pope continued:

“If truth supports the words of your testimony, we render manifold thanks to almighty God with every joy of mind. It remains, therefore, dearest son, that you approach the confession of Saint Peter, where, with God’s favor, we shall offer the saving sacrifice for the safety not only of your body [Note: [Col. 0097] “not only for the safety of your body”: manuscripts 3, 4, 5c, and 5e] but also of your soul. You ought to share in it with us, so that through this participation you may deserve to be incorporated into the members of Christ, from which you seemed to have been cut off [Note: [Col. 0097] “from which you seemed to have been cut off”: manuscripts 5, 6, and 5e; “to have been cut off”: manuscripts 5d and 6].”

When the solemnities of the Mass had ended [Note: [Col. 0097] “when the solemnities of the Mass had ended”: manuscript 4; “when the solemn solemnities of the Mass had ended”: manuscripts 7–12; “when the solemn rite of the Mass had ended”: manuscripts 5c and 5d; “when the office of the Mass had ended”: manuscript 3], the supreme pontiff invited the same king to the table of Christ. Taking the body and blood of the Lord in his hands [Col. 0098B], he addressed him as follows:

“If you recognize yourself innocent of the crime of adultery forbidden and prohibited to you by Lord Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0097] Absent in manuscript 5], and have firmly resolved never during the days of your life to engage in wicked intercourse with Waldrada, your concubine, whom you formerly repudiated, approach confidently and receive the sacrament of eternal salvation, which will profit you for the remission of sins.

“But if your conscience accuses you and proclaims that you are wounded by a mortal injury [Note: [Col. 0097] “your conscience accuses you of being mortally”: manuscripts 5c and 5d], or if you are planning in your mind to return again to the mire of adultery [Note: [Col. 0097] “the mire”: manuscripts 4, 5c, 5d, and 7–12], do not presume to take it at all, lest what divine providence prepared for the faithful as a remedy should happen to you for judgment and condemnation [Note: [Col. 0097] “come upon you for judgment”: manuscripts 2–6 and 11].”

But he, mentally deranged, hardened, and blinded at once, received without reconsideration the communion of the body and blood of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0097] “of the Lord” is absent in manuscripts 7 and 9–12] from the pontiff’s hand, not fearing that saying which declares: “It is a fearful thing [Note: [Col. 0097] Absent in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5] to fall into the hands of the living God.” For “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.”

Then the same pontiff turned to the king’s followers and supporters and offered communion to each one in these words:

“If you have not given favor to your lord and king Lothar [Note: [Col. 0097] *fautorem* (“a supporter”), for *favorem* (“favor”): manuscripts 2 and 5] in the alleged crime of adultery, nor given your consent, and have not shared communion with Waldrada or with others excommunicated by this apostolic see, may the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ profit you unto eternal life!”

Therefore, whoever knew himself guilty in these matters and nevertheless rashly presumed to receive communion offered under such a declaration was struck by divine judgment and taken from this life [Col. 0098D] before the beginning of the following year [Col. 0099A]. The very few who abstained from communion scarcely escaped the danger of death [Note: [Col. 0099] “escaped”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12].

Lothar, moreover, after leaving Rome, was seized by illness. When he reached the city of Piacenza [Note: [Col. 0099] “the city of Piacenza”: manuscripts 2, 3, and 5–12], he died on the sixth day before the Ides of August. Such slaughter occurred among the people of the aforesaid king that the strength and nobility of his entire kingdom seemed not to have perished through pestilence but to have fallen by the sword of an enemy. At that time this population was so abundant that, multiplying like thickly sown crops, it had filled the borders of the empire like a swarm [Note: [Col. 0099] “a certain swarm”: manuscripts 4 and 5].

When Charles [Note: [Col. 0099] Here and elsewhere this Charles is called Charles the Bald in manuscript 4] learned through a reliable report that King Lothar had died, he immediately attempted to seize his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0099] “he immediately attempted to seize his dominion”: manuscript 5]. Reaching Metz [Note: [Col. 0099] “Mitas”: manuscripts 1–3, 6, and 8], he was favorably received by Adventius, bishop of the aforesaid city, and by certain other leading men [Note: [Col. 0099] “by certain others” is absent in manuscripts 4 and 7–12], and was raised to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0099] “having been raised”: manuscript 5]. Departing from there, he entered the palace at Aachen, since it seemed to be the seat of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0099] “the seat of the king”: manuscript 5]. Many more people flocked to him there [Note: [Col. 0099] “flocked”: manuscript 5].

At that time the city of Trier and Cologne Agrippina lacked bishops. For, as we have already said, the prelates of both cities had been taken from this life in Italy. After the king had taken counsel with the leading men, he placed Bertulfus, nephew [Note: [Col. 0099] “a relative”: manuscript 3] of the aforesaid Bishop Adventius, over the church of Trier.

It was arranged that this man should obtain episcopal dignity through the intervention and assistance of the aforementioned Adventius, who at that time possessed great influence with the king [Note: [Col. 0099] “who at that time had great influence with him”: manuscripts 7–12], because, by flattering him, he supported him too ambitiously in acquiring the affairs of the kingdom [Col. 0099C].

At Cologne Agrippina the king attempted to place Abbot Hilduin in the episcopal chair [Note: [Col. 0099] “to prefer Abbot Hilduin”: manuscripts 7–12; “to appoint him”], and had him ordained priest at the palace in Aachen by Francon [Note: [Col. 0099] “Francion”: manuscript 2], bishop of the diocese of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 0099] “by the bishop of Tongeren”: manuscripts 7–12], for the title of Saint Peter of the aforesaid metropolis.

While these things were being done in Lothar’s kingdom, King Louis, detained by illness, lay sick in bed in the territory of the Bavarians. When he heard from his brother that the kingdom in question had been invaded in this way, he took it badly and sent envoys with all haste, asking him earnestly to cease from this reckless invasion and not, through an undue presumption, to usurp alone what equally belonged to both by hereditary right.

He urged him to leave the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0099] “but to leave the kingdom”: manuscripts 3 and 5d] until God, restoring his former health [Note: [Col. 0099] “health”: manuscripts 7–12], should permit him to come, so that they might confer together and, by common agreement, determine the condition of that kingdom according to what the rights of justice and equity dictated.

After sending these envoys with such a command, Louis secretly dispatched Liudbert [Note: [Col. 0099] “Luidpert”: manuscript 3; “Luitpert”: manuscript 10; “Luipert”: manuscript 7; “Lutbert”: manuscripts 9, 11, and 12], archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0099] “Mogontiac”: manuscript 7; “Mogontiac”: manuscripts 9–12; “Mainz”: manuscripts 1 and 3; “Magoncia”: manuscript 2], to Cologne. He urged him to strive by every means to forestall Hilduin’s ordination and to attempt to consecrate as bishop, through election by the citizens, someone from the clergy of that city [Note: [Col. 0099] “to attempt” is absent in manuscripts 7 and 9–12; also absent in manuscripts 4 and 8].

Taking other bishops with him, Liudbert proceeded directly to the fortress of Diuza [Note: [Col. 0099] “Duizam”: manuscripts 3 and 6–12; “Diuza”: manuscripts 1 and 2; “Duiza”: manuscripts 5a–5d]. Fearing that the supporters of Charles might perhaps be plotting an ambush against him [Note: [Col. 0099] “that an ambush might be constructed by the supporters”: manuscripts 5c and 5e], he did not cross the Rhine at all. Instead, he sent messengers instructing the more honorable members of the clergy and the nobler members of the people to meet him at the same fortress.

When they had carried out his orders, the bishop addressed them on behalf of the king, advising them to look to their own interests and, as quickly as possible, to choose a prelate from their own flock [Note: [Col. 0099] “from the flock belonging to him”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12]. He said that he had been sent for this purpose: whoever they decided should be appointed by common agreement, he would immediately consecrate.

They replied that the episcopate had been given to Hilduin [Note: [Col. 0099] “that Hilduin was bishop”: manuscript 5], that he had already been ordained priest for that very see, and that nearly all of them had accepted his authority by giving their hands. No reason permitted them to choose another [Note: [Col. 0099] “no reason permitted”: manuscript 5].

He answered them in turn: “If you despise the election granted to you by the king [Note: [Col. 0099] “granted to us … to us”: manuscript 5], it lies within the king’s judgment and power to give you whichever bishop he wishes [Note: [Col. 0099] Some manuscripts read “nevertheless … a bishop,” with the remainder absent in manuscripts 4, 6, and 8]. But know for certain that before three days have passed you will have a bishop other than Hilduin [Note: [Col. 0099] “you have”: manuscript 6].”

When they heard this, they unanimously elected Willibert, a venerable man. Although he strongly refused and shrank from the office [Col. 0100C], the aforesaid bishop consecrated him [Note: [Col. 0099D] Year 870, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. Cf. the Annals of Cologne] together with his fellow priests. Then, accompanied by all the clergy and people, he crossed the waters of the Rhine and honorably placed him in the episcopal see [Note: [Col. 0099] “and honorably placed him in the see”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12]. After everything had been properly completed, he withdrew with all speed [Note: [Col. 0099] “after everything had been completed, each returned to his own”: manuscript 5c].

When Charles learned of the ordination, he was inflamed with enormous fury and immediately set out for Cologne. For while these things were being carried out by Louis’s envoys, Hilduin was staying at the palace in Aachen [Note: [Col. 0099] “at the palace of the king”: manuscripts 7–12] in royal service. Bishop Willibert and all who had agreed to his ordination crossed the Rhine and avoided the king’s fury. When the king found no one against whom he could take vengeance for his wrongs [Note: [Col. 0099] “against whom he could avenge himself”: manuscripts 4 and 5], he returned by the road on which he had come.

Meanwhile, Louis again sent envoys, asking Charles to withdraw from the kingdom. But when Charles did not yield at all, Louis finally sent from Saxony the archbishop Liudbert and Bishop Altfrid [Note: [Col. 0101] “Adalfrid”: manuscript 7], [Note: [Col. 0101C] Bishop of Hildesheim], a most prudent man [Note: [Col. 0101] “from Saxony, of Hildesheim”: the copy of St. Godehard], instructing Charles to choose one of two alternatives: either to withdraw quickly from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0101] “to depart, or”: manuscripts 7–12; likewise the copy of Freising; cf. Aretin, *Contributions to History and Literature*, vol. 7, p. 240], or that he would have to fight with his brother, Louis.

They approached him with such skill of intellect and such firmness that he withdrew without delay and retreated into his own kingdom. After this, the aforesaid kings planned to hold a meeting at the place called Marsana [Note: [Col. 0101C] Mersen], beside the Meuse.

## 870

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 870 [Note: [Col. 0101] The copy of St. Godehard reads 871; by the same method it increases the numbers 871, 872, 874, 876, 877, 878, 879, 880, and 889], Louis and Charles, coming to Marsana together with their nobles and leading men, divided among themselves in equal portions the kingdom formerly belonging to Lothar [Note: [Col. 0101] “in portions among themselves”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12; manuscript 8 is similar].

Since nearly everyone knows how this division was made [Note: [Col. 0101] “since it is known”: manuscript 5], we considered it superfluous to record it [Note: [Col. 0101] The words from “how” through “record” are absent in manuscript 4].

After the meeting had ended, Charles went to Heristellium [Note: [Col. 0101] “Haristallium”: manuscripts 7–12], because that palace had fallen to him in his portion [Note: [Col. 0101] “because the same palace had fallen to him”: manuscript 5; “because that palace had fallen to him”: manuscripts 7–12; “the same … to him”: manuscript 8]. Louis, meanwhile, returned to the palace at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0101] “Aachen”: manuscript 5], where he lay in bed for nearly two months, overcome by poor health.

Finally, coming from the eastern regions and entering the territory of the Ripuarians, he turned aside for lodging at a certain royal estate called Flameresheim [Note: [Col. 0101] “Flamersheim”: manuscript 5] [Note: [Col. 0102C] An unknown village.]. When he had climbed onto the upper floor of the house, surrounded by a crowd of attendants, the upper floor itself, which had been weakened by extreme age and decay [Note: [Col. 0101] “by age and rot”: manuscripts 5–12], suddenly collapsed when its beams broke. The king was severely crushed beneath the ruins, so that two of his ribs were separated from their proper joint [Col. 0101C] [Note: [Col. 0101] “joint”: manuscripts 7 and 9–12].

When everyone rushed to him and thought that he had perished, he himself rose from the place where he had fallen and presented himself to his men, asserting that he had suffered no harm. Concealing his illness beyond what could be believed [Note: [Col. 0101] “pretending”: manuscript 5d], he set out the following day for Marsana to meet his brother [Note: [Col. 0101] “the following day he went to meet his brother at Marsana”: manuscripts 7, 8, and 9–12].

Such was the hardness and courage of this prince that, although some people could hear the crash of the broken ribs striking against one another, nevertheless no one heard him draw a sigh or utter a groan on that account [Note: [Col. 0101] “nevertheless no one perceived him suffering because of it”: manuscripts 11 and 12, and perhaps 9 and 10; “no one, however, heard him sigh on that account”: manuscripts 5 and 7].

[Col. 0102A] At the same time [Note: [Col. 0101] “At the same time,” and the rest through the end of the year: in codex 8, Adalgisus’s flight follows in the year 873. “At that time,” 5.], [Note: [Col. 0102C] Year 873, Annals of Bertin.] Charles deprived his son Carloman of his eyes. For the aforesaid king had received three sons from Queen Hirmindrude [Note: [Col. 0101] *hirmandrude* 5a d.; *irmandrude* 7, 9; *irmendruda* 10; *irmindrude* 11, 12; *hirmentrude* 4.], namely Charles, Carloman, and Louis. But two of these perished miserably [Note: [Col. 0101] “They perished; one wishing to test,” 7, 9–12.]: Charles, led on by youthful frivolity, wishing to test the boldness and often-praised steadfastness of Albuin, Bivin’s brother [Note: [Col. 0101] “Bivin’s brother” is absent in 1–3, 5, 6.] [Note: [Col. 0101] *buuini*, 9; *buouini*, 11, 12.], and of Betto, pretending to be someone else, attacked Albuin alone one evening when he was returning from the hunt, as though he intended to seize violently the horse on which Albuin was riding [Note: [Col. 0101] *sedebat* is absent in 2, 5.]. Albuin, imagining anything rather than that he was the king’s son, drew his sword and struck him in the head from the front, immediately knocking him to the ground; then, after piercing him with many wounds, he left him half alive, carrying away with him both his arms and his horse [Col. 0102B] [Note: [Col. 0101] “his own horse with him,” 5.]. His limbs having therefore been weakened [Note: [Col. 0101] “his limbs having been weakened,” 7–12.], and his face disfigured, he survived only a short time. When Albuin learned that the man against whom he had committed such deeds was the king’s son [Note: [Col. 0101] “the king’s son,” 4, 5.], he quickly fled and avoided the danger of death [Note: [Col. 0101] “avoided the danger,” 7, 9–12.].

Carloman, moreover, while still a very young boy, was tonsured at his father’s command and made a cleric. Then, as time went on [Note: [Col. 0101] *est deinde* (“then he is”) in 5; *dehinc* (“thereafter”) in 7, 9–12.], although unwilling and compelled, he was ordained to the office of deacon in his father’s presence. He publicly read the Gospel and, according to custom, ministered to the bishop celebrating Mass. After this, withdrawing by apostasy from ecclesiastical religion, casting away and scorning [Note: [Col. 0101] “casting away and scorning,” 7, 9–12.] negligently the grace that had been given him through the laying on of hands, he became another Julian. For, gathering no small band of robbers, [Col. 0102C] he began to ravage the churches of God, attack the things that belong to peace, plunder everything, and perpetrate unheard-of evils. Because of these acts he was frequently rebuked by his father, but he did not in any way cease from the perversity he had begun [Note: [Col. 0101] Codex S. Godeh.: “he did not cease from the perversity he had begun”; *ullatenus accepta pravitas* in 5.]. Finally, by his father’s command, his eyes were torn out [Note: [Col. 0101] “His eyes were torn out,” 7.], as we have mentioned above: by the just judgment of God, he lost outward light, having driven from his breast the inner light, which is Christ; he was sent into the outer darkness, having willingly surrendered himself to inward darkness [Note: [Col. 0101] The passage from “into the outer darkness” through “had surrendered himself” is absent in 4.]. Thus deprived [Note: [Col. 0101] “and thus deprived,” 5.] he went to his uncle Louis [Note: [Col. 0101] “paternal uncle,” 4, 7–12.], mournfully lamenting before him the sorrows of his miseries [Note: [Col. 0101] “of his miseries” is absent in 4.] and calamities [Note: [Col. 0101] “and” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0103] “and calamities” is absent in 7, 9–12.] [Note: [Col. 0103] *deplorans qui m.*, 7, 9–12 (reading uncertain).] [Col. 0103A]. Moved by compassion, Louis granted him the monastery of Saint Willibrord at Absternacum [Note: [Col. 0103] *afternacum* 3; *absternatum* 5; *absternacum* 1, 2, 4; *epternacum* 7, 9–12.] [Note: [Col. 0103C] Echternach near Trier, where Saint Willibrord was buried.] for the support of his present life; there he died and was buried not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0103] “died and was buried,” 5c.].

## DCCCLXXI

In the year 871 of the Lord’s incarnation, Pope Adrian [Note: [Col. 0103C] Compare the Annals of Bertin, year 872.] departed to the Lord, and John attained the summit of the supreme pontificate [Note: [Col. 0103] “the summit of the pontificate,” 5; “the summit of the pontificate.”].

In those days Adalgisus, duke of Benevento, corrupted by the persuasions of the Greeks, raised his hand against the emperor Louis. Indeed, at his urging, many cities of the provinces of Samnium, Campania, and Lucania withdrew from Louis and submitted themselves to Greek rule. When the emperor learned this, he transferred his army into the province of Samnium [Col. 0103B] [Note: [Col. 0103] “the province of the Samnites,” 5c.], intending to attack Benevento [Note: [Col. 0103] Codex S. Godeh.: *peritus harum provinciarum capit Beneventum* (“[he] takes Benevento, [the] head of these provinces”; corrupt or uncertain reading).], the chief city of these provinces, a very rich and wealthy city.

When Adalgisus sensed that the army was approaching, terrified by fear he resorted to crafty devices. Leaving Benevento, he voluntarily presented himself to the emperor, professing that he was—and always had been—ready to serve him. He confirmed under oath that he had never given his assent to the deserters [Note: [Col. 0103] “given assent to the deserters,” 7, 9–12.]. Then he won the king over by gifts and was soon restored to his former favor.

The emperor transferred troops into Campania and Lucania against the cities that had revolted, and received them into submission without difficulty, except Capua [Note: [Col. 0103] *excepta*, 4, 5c, 8.], which, because it had been built of squared stone [Note: [Col. 0103] *quadrato*, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7.], gave its citizens the courage to resist. It was therefore surrounded by a siege [Note: [Col. 0103] “gave them courage; it was surrounded by a siege,” 7.], and every entrance for going in or out [Note: [Col. 0103] “or going out” is absent in 5.] was completely blocked. The surrounding region [Note: [Col. 0103] “the surrounding region” is absent in 5.] was devastated, everything was plundered with hostile rapacity, and finally the vines, olive groves [Note: [Col. 0103] “the vines and olive groves,” 5d.] and other [Note: [Col. 0103] “the olive groves and the other,” 7–12.] fruit-bearing trees were cut down by the roots.

The Capuans, their situation desperate, approached the city’s bishop. They lifted onto a bier the body of Saint Germanus, the bishop whose soul the venerable Father Benedict had seen being carried into heaven by angels in a sphere of fire [Note: [Col. 0103] “in a fiery sphere,” 4, 7, (8), 9–12.] [Note: [Col. 0103] “had seen being carried,” 7, 9–12.]. Then, opening the gates, they went as suppliants to the emperor’s camp, asking that, through the intercession of that saint, he grant them pardon.

The Augustus, because he overflowed with every affection of compassion, was moved by mercy, graciously forgave their errors and transgressions [Note: [Col. 0103] “their guilt and transgressions,” 1; “their errors and transgression,” 5c.], and ordered the army to withdraw its hand from destruction [Note: [Col. 0103] “to withdraw its hand,” 7, (8), 9–12.].

After the Greeks had been expelled, he stationed guards from among his retainers in the cities he had recovered [Col. 0104A], and thus departed for Benevento [Note: [Col. 0103] “and thus into Benevento,” 7, 9–12; *sic* is absent in 1–3, 5, 6.], where he had decided to remain for a while. The army, wearied by the long siege of the cities, began to sigh for its native soil and, desiring rest after its labors, to recall before the eyes of its mind the sweet embraces of wives [Note: [Col. 0103] “marriage,” 5a.] and children [Note: [Col. 0103] “embraces,” 5d.], and for this reason to melt away little by little each day [Note: [Col. 0103] “each day little by little,” 7–12.].

Meanwhile Adalgisus [Note: [Col. 0103] “in the meantime, Adalgisus,” 7–12.], crafty by nature, addressed the emperor: why was he wasting the strength of his men when there was no reason to do so? Why did he permit the fields and villages subject to his rule to be laid waste like those of an enemy? It was fitting both that the weary be granted the rest they desired [Note: [Col. 0103] “that they be granted what they desired,” 5; “that it be granted,” 2.] and that the region, which was already almost [Note: [Col. 0103] “which was almost,” 5d, 7.] devastated, be saved by the ruler’s clemency.

Bent by these suggestions, the emperor dismissed most of the army [Note: [Col. 0103] “the army, and most of it,” 5; “for the most part,” 7; “for a very large part,” 4.] and permitted it to return to its own country [Col. 0104B] [Note: [Col. 0103] “to go back to its own country,” 1–3, 5, 6.]. He himself remained in the same place with a few men [Note: [Col. 0103] “but he himself remained,” 7–12.], suspecting no adversity [Note: [Col. 0103] “suspecting no evil,” 7–12.].
