When Adalgisus saw that the king had been deprived of the strength of his forces [Note: [Col. 0103] “the king deprived of his strength,” 5c.], he gave birth to the wickedness he had long conceived. With the followers of his conspiracy [Note: [Col. 0103] “conspirators,” 5.], he attempted to seize the palace in which the emperor was resting at midday.

Awakened by the noise and shouting of the attackers, the king leapt from his bed, seized his weapons, and, with a very few guards of his person, went in confusion toward the doorway of the house in the sudden assault. Blocking the entrance with weapons, he kept the enemy away from the threshold.

When Adalgisus realized that the doors of the house could not be entered without danger, he withdrew from the entrance and ordered the palace to be burned. Meanwhile the king asked that a truce be granted him [Note: [Col. 0103] “the king asked for a truce,” 5.] and earnestly begged for peace. He was answered that he would obtain what he requested only if he first swore under oath that he would never, during the days of his life, enter the territory of Benevento, nor ever exact vengeance for the injury he was then suffering.

The relics of the saints having been brought, and constrained by necessity, he swore the oath demanded of him. Immediately, on the following day, he left Benevento [Note: [Col. 0103] “he left Benevento on the following day,” 7–12.].

## DCCCLXXII

In the year 872 of the Lord’s incarnation, the emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0104C] These events occurred in 873, since Pope John was not ordained until December of 872.] came to Rome. There, holding an assembly, he complained before the supreme pontiff about the many acts of Adalgisus’s tyranny. Then [Note: [Col. 0103] *tunc* is absent in 1, 2, 7.] Adalgisus was declared by the Roman senate to be a tyrant and an enemy of the commonwealth, and war was also decreed against him [Note: [Col. 0103] *etiam* is absent in 1, 2.].

Pope John, by the authority of God and Saint Peter, absolved the emperor from the oath [Col. 0105A] by which he had bound himself. He affirmed that the emperor was not harmed by what he had done under compulsion to escape the danger of death, and that an oath should not be called an oath when it had been uttered, even with many curses, against the safety of the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0105] “had been approved,” 2, 5.]. By these exhortations he stirred the ruler’s spirit to renewed struggles [Note: [Col. 0105] “the spirit is provoked,” 5.].

Nevertheless, lest he be called a perjurer by his own people, the emperor himself did not proceed against the tyrant, but sent the queen with an army. Adalgisus, gathering from reliable indications [Note: [Col. 0105] *certis* is absent in 9–12.] that war was being prepared against him with the greatest forces [Note: [Col. 0105] *visceribus*, “with innermost forces,” 2, 5.] and that he had been proclaimed an enemy and a tyrant, was shaken by fear, conscious of his wickedness [Note: [Col. 0105] “terrified by fear,” 5.]. Placing his hope of life in flight, he withdrew to the island of Corsica and hid there for a time [Note: [Col. 0105] “lay hidden,” 5, 7–12.].

## DCCCLXXIII

In the year 873 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0105] “of the incarnation,” 874 in 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9–12. The whole account of the locusts is absent in 4.], an immeasurable multitude of locusts came from the east in the month of August and devastated almost the whole of Gaul. They were larger than other locusts and had six wing-blades each [Note: [Col. 0105] “they had,” 7, 9–12.]. And—marvelous to say [Note: [Col. 0105] “it is marvelous to say,” 5.]—they moved through the air in ordered ranks like a battle line of an army, or, settling upon the earth, pitched camp [Note: [Col. 0105] “measured out,” 2; “measured,” 5.].

Their leaders went ahead of the army by a day’s journey, as though to survey suitable places for the multitude. Around the ninth hour they settled where the leaders had arrived the previous day, and did not move from the occupied place until the sun showed its rising. Then they departed in their companies, so that one might observe military discipline in these small animals.

They fed on the crops, which they devoured so completely [Col. 0105C] that they appeared to have been consumed as if by a monstrous storm. The extent of their daily march was four or five miles [Note: [Col. 0105] “miles,” 5.]. They reached as far as the British Sea, covering the surface of the earth [Note: [Col. 0105] “the British [Sea] and the surface,” 5c e.], into which [Note: [Col. 0105] “which,” 1, 3, 5c e.]—by God’s will—they were driven by the violent blast of the winds [Note: [Col. 0105] “by the blast of the winds,” 7, 9–12.] and carried into the depths, where they were submerged [Note: [Col. 0105] “drowned,” 5, 8.].

But cast back by the tide and the ocean’s ebb, they filled the maritime shores, and such a mass was formed that they were heaped and piled up like mountains [Note: [Col. 0105] “like a mountain,” 7–12.]. From their stench and putrefaction the air was corrupted and generated a dreadful plague among the neighboring peoples, by which many perished [Note: [Col. 0105] “by which many perished” is absent in 7–12.].

At the same time Charles was besieging the city of Angers. Finally, after the Northmen had killed Robert and Ramnulf, and several other men of noble stock [Note: [Col. 0105] “several” is absent in 5.], who had defended the borders of their homeland with arms—God being hostile to the inhabitants of the land—and no one being found who could resist their violence [Note: [Col. 0105] *inviolentiae* in 2, an apparent variant or corruption of *violentiae* (“violence”).] [Col. 0106A], they were enticed by the plunder of a few cities or regions [Note: [Col. 0105] *ex praeda singularum regionum* (“from the plunder of individual regions”) in 1–3, 5; *vel regionem direptionem et ex praeda singula* (“or the plundering of a region and from individual booty”) in 7.]. Looking in their minds toward the wealth of all the others, they entered the city of Angers, finding it empty because the citizens had dispersed in flight. When they saw that it was extremely well fortified and impregnable because of the nature of its site, they rejoiced and decided that it would be a very secure refuge for their own forces and those of their people against nations that had challenged them in war.

They immediately brought their ships up the Mayenne River [Note: [Col. 0105D] The Mayenne.] and fastened them to the wall. With women and children, as though they intended to live there, they entered the city, repaired what had been destroyed, renewed the ditches and ramparts [Note: [Col. 0105] “the rampart,” 1, 3, 5c e; “the valleys,” 7.], and, sallying forth from it, devastated the surrounding regions in sudden raids [Note: [Col. 0105] “sudden marches,” 5c d.]. When this disastrous plague, shut up in the heart of his kingdom, was reported to Charles, he immediately gathered an army from all the kingdoms subject to his rule, as though to extinguish a common fire. He set up camps around the city and encircled it with a siege.

Since the Mayenne River washed the city wall on the side facing Brittany [Note: [Col. 0105] “washed,” 5.], he sent word to Salomon, king of the Britons, to gather auxiliaries and come quickly, so that they might attack the common enemy with common forces. Taking many thousands of Britons with him, Salomon pitched his tents on the bank of the Mayenne River [Note: [Col. 0105] “pitched,” 1–3, 5, 6.].

Thus, with the city surrounded on every side by the siege, they fought everywhere with the utmost courage for many days, and applied new and ingenious kinds of siege engines. But the king’s effort did not achieve a successful result [Note: [Col. 0105] “an affected result,” 5a.], because the configuration of the place did not easily permit access, and the strong force of the pagans, since the matter concerned their lives, resisted with the utmost effort [Col. 0106C] [Note: [Col. 0105] “resisted with the utmost effort,” 7.].

The army, an immense multitude, was worn down by the tedium of the long siege, hunger, and a severe disease. Seeing that the city was impregnable, the Britons attempted to divert the river from its channel, so that, after drying up its natural course, they could attack the ships of the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0105] “could not attack,” 5c.].

They therefore began to dig a ditch of extraordinary depth and width. This caused the Northmen so great a fear [Note: [Col. 0105] “so great a fear,” 1–5.] that, without delay, they promised Charles a vast sum of money if, after lifting the siege, he would allow them free departure from his kingdom. The king, overcome by shameful greed, accepted the money and, withdrawing from the siege [Note: [Col. 0105] “and from the siege,” 7–12.], opened the roads to the enemy [Note: [Col. 0105] “the road,” 4, 5.].

They boarded their ships and returned to the Loire. But they did not, as they had promised, withdraw from his kingdom [Col. 0106D]. Remaining in the same place, they perpetrated deeds much worse and more savage than those they had committed before [Note: [Col. 0105] “they committed” instead of “they had committed,” 4; “they committed,” 5, 7, 9–12.], [Note: [Col. 0105] “perpetrated” is absent in 5, 7.].

## DCCCLXXIV

In the year 874 of the Lord’s incarnation, the emperor Louis, who ruled the kingdom of Italy, died [Note: [Col. 0107D] He died in the following year.]. This ruler was pious and merciful, devoted to justice, pure in simplicity, a defender of the churches of God [Note: [Col. 0107] “of God” is absent in 5.], a father to orphans and the fatherless, a lavish giver of alms, humbly submitting himself to the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0107] “a humble servant of the servants of God,” 1–3, 5.], so that his righteousness might endure forever [Note: [Col. 0107] “forever and ever,” 5.] and his horn might be exalted in glory [Note: [Col. 0107] “might be exalted forever,” 7, 9–12.].

In the same year Salomon, king of the Britons, was treacherously killed by Pasquitanus [Note: [Col. 0107] *parquitano* and *partiquano*, 7; *pastiquano*, 8–12; “consistently,” apparently meaning the form is stable.] and Vurfandus [Note: [Col. 0107] *wurfando*, consistently in 11, 12.], his dukes. After his death, when these two wished to divide his kingdom between themselves but disagreed over the division, because the greater part favored Pasquitanus’s side, both renewed the war with all their strength.

Although Pasquitanus had the larger multitude, he hired auxiliaries from the Northmen with money and mingled them with his army to increase its strength. Then he set out for battle against his rival.

When Vurfandus’s retainers [Note: [Col. 0107] “Vurfandus’s soldiers,” see 6.] saw that the strength of the kingdom had passed to Pasquitanus, they began to flee from him, so that scarcely a thousand remained with him in the battle line. Even these began to advise him to withdraw [Note: [Col. 0107] “to withdraw ... to turn aside,” 5.] and avoid the danger of death, saying that with a few men he could not withstand an innumerable multitude.

He answered them: “Far be it, my excellent fellow soldiers, that today I should do what I have never done—namely, turn my back on my enemies and allow the glory of our name to be disgraced [Note: [Col. 0107] “turn my back, so that our glory ...,” 5c e.]. It is better to die nobly than to preserve life in disgrace. Nor should we despair of victory; let us test the strength of fortune against the enemy. For safety is not in multitude, but rather in God.”

With his companions encouraged by such exhortations [Note: [Col. 0107] “his companions encouraged”; *animarum sociis* in 5a d., apparently an error for *animatis sociis*.], he charged more than thirty thousand of the adversaries, as they say [Note: [Col. 0107] “as they report,” 6.] [Note: [Col. 0107] “they charge,” 4, 5.]. A shout was raised to heaven, and battle was joined with the utmost courage.

Vurfandus and his men broke into the enemy’s densely packed line [Note: [Col. 0107] *consertissimam*, “most tightly joined,” 5d.]. Just as meadow grass falls before the sharp edge of a sickle, and abundant crops are thrown down when a storm rages violently [Note: [Col. 0107] “rages,” 4.], so he cut down and struck down everything with the sword. Rarely in that kingdom, in any battle, was so much blood shed [Note: [Col. 0107] “in any,” 1–3, 6.].

When Pasquitanus saw his men being slaughtered like animals, he fled with the few whom the sword had not yet consumed. The Northmen who had been summoned to his aid entered the monastery of Saint Melanius [Note: [Col. 0107] *melanii*, 7–12; *menelai* in Codex S. Godeh.] the bishop, and there fortified themselves in the customary manner. As night came on, they dispersed in flight and returned to their ships.

This battle was fought in the fields beside the city of Redon [Note: [Col. 0107] *rodonis*, 2, 5.] [Note: [Col. 0108D] Rennes.].

Vurfandus was illustrious by birth among his people, but more illustrious through the proofs of his virtues than through nobility [Note: [Col. 0107] “in the trials of his virtues” is absent in 3; “in the trials of his virtues and nobility,” 4, 5.]. These were so great in him [Note: [Col. 0107] “in him they were,” 4.] that, in greatness of spirit and glory of strength, he seemed to be second to no one among his people, as we have said [Note: [Col. 0107] “he may seem,” 2, 5a d.]. To demonstrate his boldness and constancy of mind, it seemed worthwhile to relate one example among many.

When King Salomon had once, in winter, pitched camp against the Northmen in order to defend the borders of his kingdom from their incursions [Note: [Col. 0107] “the aforesaid Vurfandus defended,” 4.], and had remained there for many days, a conversation arose one day among his companions about the boldness and stubbornness of the Northmen. The aforesaid Vurfandus, presuming beyond his strength, boastfully declared that, if the king withdrew with the army, he alone [Col. 0108B] would dare to remain there with his men and stay for three days after the king’s departure [Note: [Col. 0107] “after the king’s death,” 3, 5, 7; *dicessum*, 2; “after his departure,” 9–12.].

The camp of the Britons was only eight miles [Note: [Col. 0107] “miles,” 5.] from the fleet of the Northmen. The words Vurfandus had uttered, apparently lightly, were reported—I do not know by whom—to Hastingus, the pagan commander [Note: [Col. 0107] “the commander of the pagans,” 4, 7–12.].

Not long afterward, after giving five hundred cows, Salomon made peace with the Northmen. Having received hostages and preparing to return to his kingdom, he was addressed by Hastingus’s envoy as follows:

“It has been reported to my lord that you have such a man who boasts that, when you depart, he alone with his men dares to remain in this place. If, therefore, he is as great as he thinks himself, let him remain without hesitation, because my lord wishes to see him and desires to know this bold man.”

The king asked Vurfandus whether he had made such a claim. He replied that he had said such things and wished to prove them by deeds [Note: [Col. 0107] “wished to prove that he would do the same,” 1–3, 5.]. Immediately he asked permission to remain there.

The ruler rebuked him, asking why, held by such foolish obstinacy, he wished to die for words foolishly uttered into the wind [Note: [Col. 0107] “for proverbs foolishly spoken into the wind,” 5.], and to hand his men over to death. But he did not yield in any way, asserting that, unless the king granted him permission to remain, he would never again be faithful to him.

When Salomon perceived that his resolve was unalterable [Note: [Col. 0107] Codex S. Godehardi: “that Salomon’s mind was irrational.”], he wished to give him assistance from among his own retainers. Vurfandus refused to accept it, affirming that, if he had anyone other than his own men with him, what he had promised would no longer be true.

The king withdrew into his kingdom with all his forces, while Vurfandus remained in the same place with nearly two hundred men [Note: [Col. 0107] “nearly two hundred,” 7.], and waited there for five days.

On the sixth night Hastingus released a certain captive from his bonds [Note: [Col. 0107] “released from his bonds,” 7.] and sent him to Vurfandus, ordering him to meet Hastingus at the ford of a certain torrent between the third and second hours of the following day [Note: [Col. 0109] “between the third and second hours,” 1; “hours,” 5, 5.]. Vurfandus, without hesitation, ordered his companions to take up their arms and proceeded without delay to the appointed place.

Seeing that the ford of the torrent would be like a boundary between his men and the enemy, he refused to remain there in any way. Instead, after wading across the deep water, he advanced voluntarily to meet the enemy.

The Northmen, amazed at the man’s courage and boldness [Note: [Col. 0109] “courage and boldness,” 7–12.], withdrew from him and did not dare to challenge him to battle [Note: [Col. 0109] “to wound him in battle,” 5.]. He waited there fearlessly until the sixth hour [Note: [Col. 0109] “until the sixth hour,” 1; “until the hour six,” 7, 9–12.]. When he saw that no one from the opposing side [Note: [Col. 0109] “that no one of the opposing side was coming,” 7.] would come, he returned with his men to their own territory.

His spirit was no less unconquerable in the face of death than in the face of the enemy. Finally, after the victory had been completed [Col. 0109B], he was brought to the point of death, weighed down by illness [Note: [Col. 0109] “gravely ill,” 4, 5.].

When Pasquitanus became aware of his illness [Note: [Col. 0109] “his health,” 1–3, 5c e.], he gathered his strength again and attacked Vurfandus’s supporters in battle [Note: [Col. 0109] Perhaps *ipsius* (“of himself / his own”), 6; *aggredi parat* (“prepares to attack”), 6–12.]. Terrified by fear [Note: [Col. 0109] “terrified with fear,” 1–3, 6.], they fled to their commander and with tears revealed Pasquitanus’s threats to him, asking for advice against the danger that threatened.

He urged them to advance boldly against the enemy, carrying his standard, and promised them victory. When they replied that without his presence they did not dare to engage the adversaries, he recovered the breath that had almost departed together with the strength of his body. Since he could go neither on foot nor on horseback [Note: [Col. 0109] *nec* is absent in 4, 7–12.], he ordered them to carry him on a bed and place him before the enemy’s battle line, so that he might thus enter the contest.

When his retainers had done this [Note: [Col. 0109] “had done this for him,” 5c d e.], the enemy immediately turned to flight [Col. 0109C]. After the victory had been won, when they wished to carry him back home, the breath that merely fluttered in his breast escaped between the hands of the soldiers.

A few days later Pasquitanus himself also died. After the successive deaths of these two men, Judicheil [Note: [Col. 0109] *uuidicheil*, 1, 3; *indicheil*, 5; *indichel*, 8.]—born of the daughter of King Herispoji [Note: [Col. 0109] *herispoi*, 1, 3; *herispon*, 5.]—and Alanus, the brother of the aforesaid Pasquitanus, divided Brittany between themselves. There were also many quarrels and wars between them.

But Judicheil was killed in a battle which he had waged against the Northmen more boldly than prudently [Note: [Col. 0109] *uuidicheilo*, 1, 3; *indicheile*, 3; *vidicheile*, 8; *iudicheil*, 7.]. All Brittany passed into Alanus’s possession [Note: [Col. 0109] “into Alanus’s power,” 4, 5; *Brittonia* (“Brittany”), 7.], and he has governed it vigorously up to the present [Note: [Col. 0109D] He died in the year 907.].

In the same year [Note: [Col. 0109D] Charles immediately went to Rome after the death of the emperor Louis; in the year 875 he was crowned on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.] Charles proceeded to Rome. After giving great gifts to the apostolic lord John [Note: [Col. 0109] “to John,” 1, 9.] and to the Romans, he was created emperor [Col. 0109D].

## DCCCLXXVI

In the year 876 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0109] *A. d. i.*; 877, 3; 886, 5d, 9–12.], King Louis closed his final day at the palace of Franconofurt on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. He was buried [Note: [Col. 0109] “buried,” 1–3, 5, 6.] in the monastery of Saint Nazarius, which is called Lorsch [Note: [Col. 0109] *lorasam*, 1, 2; *loraszam*, 3.].

This ruler was a most Christian prince, Catholic in faith, adequately instructed not only in secular but also in ecclesiastical disciplines. He was a most ardent executor of the things that belong to religion, peace, and justice [Note: [Col. 0109] This clause is absent in 3.]. Most shrewd in understanding [Note: [Col. 0109] Codex S. Godeh.: “very prudent in understanding.”], most provident in counsel, and temperate with the moderation of discretion in granting or withdrawing public dignities, he was most victorious in battles [Note: [Col. 0109] “in battle,” 1–3, 5.], more devoted to the equipment of arms than to banquets. His greatest wealth consisted of weapons of war; he valued the hardness of iron [Col. 0110B] more than the glitter of gold.

No useless person had influence with him, and in his eyes a useful person was very rarely displeasing. No one could corrupt him with gifts [Note: [Col. 0109] “the glitter of gold; with him no one could corrupt him with gifts,” 7.]. No one obtained an ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0109] “an ecclesiastical dignity up to an ecclesiastical dignity” and the remainder are absent in 7.] or worldly dignity through money. Rather, ecclesiastical dignity was obtained through upright conduct and holy way of life [Note: [Col. 0109] “the church,” 2, 5, 6.], and worldly dignity through devoted service and sincere fidelity [Note: [Col. 0109] “worldly,” 2, 5, 6.].

This most glorious king, whose memory is blessed, had a queen named Emma, joined to him in marriage [Note: [Col. 0109] “in matrimony,” 7.]. She was noble by birth, but—what is more worthy of praise—far more distinguished in nobility of mind. By her he had three sons of the highest promise: Carloman, Louis, and Charles, who, by a fortunate succession, governed the reins of the empire after their father’s departure [Note: [Col. 0109] “after their father’s death,” 7; “departure,” 1.].

When Charles heard that his brother had departed from the world [Note: [Col. 0109] “But when Charles heard,” 5.], he was filled, they say, with excessive rejoicing. He supposed that the portion of Lothair’s kingdom which that brother had held would pass according to his own wishes [Note: [Col. 0109] *in suos libitos*, “according to his own wishes,” 7; Codex S. Godeh.: “to his own children,” 1, 3, 5, 6.]. He therefore gathered an army with all possible speed and, entering the kingdom with all his forces, came to the palace at Aachen. After remaining there a few days, he departed for Cologne.

While these events were taking place in the aforementioned kingdom [Note: col. 0109: *cum* (“while”) in witnesses 1 and 2], Carloman, the firstborn son of Louis, had entered the borders of Italy, wishing to bring it under his own and his father’s dominion [Note: col. 0109: *Carolomannus* in witness 5, consistently; *intravit* (“entered”) in witnesses 1–3]. For the Emperor Louis had already, as we have said, been taken from this life, and Charles, bearing the Emperor’s name, had withdrawn from Italy [Note: col. 0109: *excesserat* (“had departed”) in witnesses 1, 2, 4, 5, 7–10, and 12]. Charles, his brother, however, was staying in Alamannia.

Louis, moreover, who had been present at his father’s death and had celebrated his funeral rites with fitting honor, was residing at Frankfurt, the principal seat of the eastern kingdom. When it was announced to him that Charles, his uncle [*patruus*, “paternal uncle,” in witnesses 3, 4, and 8], after occupying the boundaries of his father’s kingdom, had pitched camp beside the waters of the Rhine [Note: col. 0111: “the river Rhine” in witness 5], he was inflamed with immense fury. At once he sent envoys to him, begging him to remember their brotherhood and kinship; to remember the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he and his brother had invoked before several witnesses when they divided the kingdom between them, having with awe promised one another peace by mutual agreement; and, fearing to take so great a name in vain [Note: col. 0111: *nomen tantum* (“so great a name”) in witnesses 7 and 9–12; “that he remember the oath he had sworn to his brother; that he be content with his allotted portion,” and so forth, in witness 4], to render his vows to the Lord, so that the pact they had made with one another [Note: col. 0111: “the pact which both had made,” in witnesses 5c and 5e] might remain inviolable.

He begged him to spare the sword and, infected by so dreadful a desire, to shudder all the more fearfully at shedding human blood; to be content with his allotted portion and peacefully enjoy the allotment of his inheritance divinely granted to him [Note: col. 0111: “and not invade what belonged to another, but let justice, charity, and concord hold the highest place between him and his nephews,” in witness 4], invading, removing, or disturbing no one else’s rights. Let there be in so great a man no swelling of empty glory [Note: col. 0111: *tipus* (“swelling”) in witnesses 8–12 and 9g; *triumphus* (“triumph”) in witness 7; *typus* in the remaining witnesses], no arrogance of the brow, no ambition to usurp another’s boundaries; but let justice, charity, and concord reign, and let peace hold the highest place altogether [Note: col. 0111: *pacis* (“of peace”) in witness 5] between him and his nephews.

But Charles despised such admonitions [Note: col. 0111: *hujus commodi* (“of this advantage/benefit”) in witness 5], asserting that he had made a pact with his brother, not with his nephews. Meanwhile Louis gathered an army from Saxony, Thuringia [Note: col. 0111: *Turinga* in witness 7], and eastern Francia, so that one might recognize in the son not merely his father’s features but also the refinement of his mind and the ingenuity of his abilities [Note: col. 0111: *filio tantum* (“in the son only”) in witness 5; *recognosceret* (“might recognize”) in witness 5d]. With great preparation he placed his camp opposite Cologne, facing Charles’s camp on the bank of the river [Note: col. 0111: *omni* (“all”) is absent in witness 5]. He himself, however, crossed the Rhine with all his military strength between Confluentes and Andernach [Note: col. 0111: *Confluentes et Arduennam* (“Confluentes and the Ardennes”) in witness 5], and crossed it [*transiit*] in witness 5.

Nor was there anyone who failed to report to Charles that his nephew had crossed the Rhine with all his forces [Note: col. 0111: *nec fuit* (“nor was there”) in witness 7]. Then Charles first realized that he had been deceived by Louis’s camp. He therefore moved his army without delay [Note: col. 0111: *ita* (“thus”) in witness 6; *vero* (“however”) in the remaining witnesses except 5d, which lacks the conjunction], and, with fifty thousand men and more, as they say, advanced against him for battle in the district of Mayen, not far from Andernach [Note: col. 0111: *Andernaco* in witness 5], at a castle [Note: col. 0111: “Andernach, situated approximately in the middle of the Mayen district. Compare the map in D. Gunther’s *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, vol. II.].

But the king is not saved by great strength, for a horse is deceptive as a means of safety [Note: col. 0111: *salvatur ex multa* (“is saved from great strength”) in witness 5]. When the battle began, Count Reginar, who carried the royal standard, was killed in the first charge. Louis’s densely packed ranks were broken through by their companions, and, just as fire driven into stubble rages and devours everything in an instant [Note: col. 0111: *stipulam* (“stubble”) in witnesses 3 and 5; *immissus fuerit* (“may have been driven in”) in witnesses 2 and 3a/d], so they crushed the enemy’s forces with the sword [Note: col. 0111: *conterunt et terrae* (“they crush and [cast] to the earth”) in witnesses 5c and 5e, as well as 1 and 3], and threw them to the ground [Note: *conteruntur* (“they are crushed”) and *prosternuntur* (“they are thrown down”) in witness 6]. Charles’s army, severely beaten, turned its back, and victory belonged to Louis.

When Charles saw his men fleeing, he too saved his life by flight, belatedly reflecting how great a danger it is to wish to violate, through the ambition of immoderate desire, the rights of equity strengthened by the institutions of divine and human law [Note: col. 0111: *violare* (“to violate”) in witnesses 4 and 5]. This slaughter took place on 8 October.

Afterward the three brothers mentioned above met at a place called Sualfeld [Note: col. 0111: *Saulifelt* in witnesses 5c and 5d; *Salevelt* in witnesses 11 and 12; *Sualivelt* in witnesses 4, 7, and 8; *Sualivent* in witnesses 9 and 10]. There they divided their father’s kingdom [Note: col. 0112: this was a district beside the river Altmühl, where Charles the Great had dug a ditch; it was part of the larger district of Ries]. Carloman received Bavaria, Pannonia, and Carantum, which is corruptly called Carantania [Note: col. 0111: *Karnotum* in witnesses 11 and 12; *Caruntum* in witness 8], as well as the kingdoms of the Slavs, the Bohemians, and the Moravians [Note: col. 0111: “and of the Moravians” is absent in witnesses 1 and 3]. Louis received eastern Francia, Thuringia, Saxony, Frisia [Note: col. 0111: *Frisia* in witnesses 5c, 5e, 2, 3, 7, and 9–12], and part of Lothair’s kingdom. Charles, moreover, received Alamannia as his portion and certain cities from Lothair’s kingdom [Note: col. 0111: “Charles received Alamannia and certain cities” in witness 5; “some cities” in witnesses 1–3; *in partem* (“as a portion”) in witness 4].

## 877

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, Charles the Elder went to Rome for the second time. There he had long before purchased the title of Emperor from John, the pontiff of the Apostolic See, at an enormous price; and he gained possession of the kingdom of Italy more by passing through it than by enjoying it.

Returning from Rome to Lombardy [Note: col. 0111: *Roma in Barcham* (“from Rome to Barcham”) in witnesses 1 and 2; *in Bracham* in witness 3], he took Hirmingard, the daughter of the Emperor Louis, as wife for Boso, the brother of Queen Richildis [Note: col. 0111: *Buosoni* in witness 2; *Rihhilae* in witness 7; “Boso, brother of Germanchildis” in the R manuscript and witnesses 2 and 5; “Boso, brother of Richildis” in witness 3 and the Freising manuscript]. The day of the wedding was celebrated with such preparation and such magnificence of entertainments that, they say, the joys of the celebration exceeded all bounds.

He further gave Provence to Boso and, placing a crown upon his head [Note: col. 0111: *coronam* (“a crown”) in witnesses 1, 4, and 9–12], ordered him to be called king, so that he might appear to rule over kings in the manner of the ancient emperors [Note: col. 0111: the words “from the city of Rome onward” are absent in witness 4].

After a few days had passed, he entered Pavia. While he was applying his mind to the administration of public affairs [Note: col. 0111: *cum disponendis* (“while arranging”) in witnesses 1, 2, and 5], he was suddenly [*repentine*, “suddenly,” in witnesses 1, 2, and 5–6] informed that Carloman had entered Lombard territory [Note: col. 0113: “Lombard dominion” in witnesses 1 and 5; “Lombard kingdoms” in witness 3] with a great multitude of armed men.

Immediately stricken with panic, he crossed the Ticino and the Po and hastened with all speed to return to Gaul. But before he reached the lofty ridges and narrow passes of the Alps, he was struck by illness; death immediately followed [Note: col. 0113: *subsecuta est* (“followed”) in some manuscripts] and brought his life to an end.

There is, however, a report that a certain Jew named Sedechias gave him a deadly cup [Note: col. 0113: “a Jew named Sedechias who was called...” in witness 7]. This man had remained especially close to him because he was said to possess exceptional skill in treating bodily illnesses. Yet this charlatan [Note: col. 0113: variants read *hic sicarius plane erat* (“this man was plainly an assassin”) in witness 5; *hic sicca planta erat* (“this dry plant was”) in witness 2 and the Saint-Godehard manuscript; *hic sicopanta erat* (“this sycophant was”) in witness 7; and *hic sicut prebatus erat* (“this was as the aforesaid [man]”) in witnesses 9–12] practiced deception and deluded people’s minds by magical tricks and incantations.

He died on the day before the Nones of October [Note: col. 0113: “he died on the Nones of October” in witness 4]. His body was lifted onto a bier [Note: col. 0113: “was lifted” in witnesses 3 and 5] and carried out of Italy by his followers. But because an intolerable stench from the rotting corpse weighed upon those carrying it, they were compelled to commit it to the earth [Note: col. 0113: “he compelled it to be committed to the earth” in witness 5]. After some years his bones were transferred and honorably buried at Paris, in the monastery of Saint Denis. His son Louis succeeded him in the kingdom.

## 878

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 878, a great eclipse of the moon occurred in October, on the fifteenth day [Note: col. 0113: “on the fifteenth day” in witness 4]. In the same month a solar eclipse also occurred, on the twenty-ninth day [Note: col. 0113: the twenty-eighth in witness 5d], around the ninth hour.

A few days later [Note: col. 0113: compare the *Annals of Bertin*, year 879], King Louis, Charles’s son, who was called the Stammerer because his speech was more impeded and slower, was taken from this life. This prince was a simple and gentle man, a lover of peace, justice, and religion.

While he was still flourishing in the bloom of youthful age, he had joined to himself in the bond of marriage a certain noble girl named Ansgard [Note: col. 0113: “a noble girl” in witnesses 4 and 5]. By her he had two children, outstanding in graceful appearance and in the strength of their spirit: one was called Louis, the other Carloman.

But because he had united her to himself without the knowledge and consent of her father, she was afterward forbidden him by that same father [Note: col. 0113: *postmodum ei* (“afterward to him”) in witnesses 7–12; *est* (“was”) is absent in witness 5] and, after an oath had been sworn, was permanently separated from his companionship [Note: col. 0113: “from their companionship” in witness 2]. The same father then gave him Adalheid in marriage [Note: col. 0113: forms include *Adheleidis* in witnesses 4, 5c, 5e, and 8; *Adaltheidis* in witnesses 1 and 2; *Adelheith* in witness 3; *Adalcheidis* in witness 7]. When he died, the king left her pregnant by him. At the completion of her term, she gave birth to a boy, whom she named after his grandfather and caused to be called Charles.

## 879

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 879 [Note: col. 0113: 829 in witness 6], Boso, whom we mentioned a little earlier [Note: col. 0113: the passage from “Boso...” through “the enemies had often attempted both” is absent in witness 4], on hearing of Louis’s death, departed from Provence and attempted to occupy all Burgundy [Note: col. 0113: “Boso, whose...” in witness 7]. Finally, he drew a number of bishops into an alliance, partly by threats and partly by persuasion. Entering Lyon, he was anointed king over the aforementioned kingdom of Burgundy by Aurelian, metropolitan of that city [Note: col. 0113: *metropolitano* (“metropolitan”) in witness 5], and by other bishops.

He treated Louis’s young sons as nothing and despised them as though degenerate, because their mother had been rejected and repudiated at Charles’s command. This action brought him continual calamity [Note: col. 0113: *continuum clam odium* (“continual hidden hatred”) in witness 5; *Claudium* in witness 2] and the cost of dangers rather than any profit of glory and dignity [Note: col. 0113: “the action brought him greater...” in witnesses 1–3 and 5].

For the young men already mentioned, Louis and Carloman, were raised to the kingdom through the diligence and efforts of Abbot Hugh and the other nobles [Note: col. 0113: *sublimatorum et* (“of those who raised them, and...”) in witness 5], and they pursued this same Boso with every effort throughout their lives. Nor did they alone, but also other kings of the Franks in succeeding times, bear his name with such severity [Note: col. 0113: “bear his name so severely” in witnesses 7 and 9–12] and hold him in such hatred that, for his irrecoverable downfall and death, not only princes and commanders but even their attendants were bound by oaths and curses.

He was nevertheless a man of such penetrating intelligence that, although, as has been said, he was continually attacked by many kings and kingdoms [Note: col. 0113: “and kingdoms” is absent in witness 3 and the Saint-Godehard manuscript], he could never be captured or outwitted by anyone. He was also so moderate that, although those favoring him were condemned to proscription and deprived of all their possessions, he was never attacked by the ambushes of his own soldiers nor betrayed by their treachery, even though his enemies had often attempted both [Note: col. 0113: “although the enemies of both sides had often fought among themselves” in witness 3 and the Saint-Godehard manuscript; *saepe certassent* (“had often contended”) in witnesses 2 and 5].

At that time Louis, who ruled Austrasia, having learned of the death of his namesake, decided to invade his kingdom [Note: col. 0113: *disponit* (“decides”) in witnesses 7–12]. After crossing the Meuse, he occupied the borders of the empire. The two brothers mentioned above met him with a strong force [Note: col. 0113: *concurrerunt* (“ran together to meet”) in witness 2]. But as embassies passed back and forth, no battle was fought; instead, peace was strengthened.

So that Louis might withdraw from them as their ally, the young men granted him in full the portion of Lothair’s kingdom that his grandfather and father had held, and added the abbey of Saint Vedast at Arras. After the agreement had been made and oaths given, as that king was returning to his kingdom [Note: col. 0113: *in regnum cum idem* (“into the kingdom, when that same...”) in witnesses 7 and 9–12; compare the *Annals of Fulda*, year 880], he suddenly encountered an innumerable multitude of Northmen near Carbonaria [Note: col. 0113: *Cabonariam* in witnesses 1 and 2; *Carbonaria* in witness 7], at a place called Thimiun [Note: col. 0115: forms include *Thimnin*, *Thimuin*, *Thurium*, *Thimum*, and *Timum*; this was Thuin on the Sambre], returning to their fleet with enormous booty.

He engaged them at once and, with God’s favor, struck the greater part of them down with the sword. The survivors, scattering in flight [Note: col. 0115: “the survivors fled” in witnesses 1–3], fortified themselves in the royal fisc mentioned above [Note: col. 0115: “in the aforementioned royal fisc” in witnesses 1 and 3]. There Hugh, the king’s son born of a concubine, while fighting too carelessly [Note: col. 0115: *incautus* (“careless”) in witness 6], was severely wounded, seized by the enemy, and surrendered his soul amid the hands of his adversaries [Note: col. 0115: “fell amid the weapons of his adversaries” in witness 5].

The king, believing that his son was still being kept alive by the enemy, ordered the army to cease its assault, so that he might recover him alive by whatever means. Meanwhile night came on [Note: col. 0115: “night came upon them from above” in witnesses 1–3 and 5] and forced the king and his men to return to the camp.

The Northmen burned the corpses of their own men in the flames, fled during the night, and made their way to the fleet. At dawn the king rose, and when he found his son dead, he was overwhelmed by immense grief. He ordered his body, placed in a coffin [Note: col. 0115: “placed in a place” in witnesses 1–3 and 5–6], to be carried to the monastery at Lorsch [Note: col. 0115: forms include *Lorsheim*, *Jorasam*, and *Joresham*] and buried there.

## 880

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 880, King Carloman, crippled by paralysis, ended his last day on the seventh day before the Nones of April. He was buried with due honor in Bavaria [Note: col. 0115: *Baioariam* (“Bavaria”) in witness 1], at a place called Ötting [Note: col. 0115: *Huodingas* in witnesses 7–12; Altenötting on the Inn].

This most excellent king was learned in letters, devoted to the Christian religion, just, peaceable, and adorned with every moral excellence [Note: col. 0115: “of honorable appearance” in witness 6]. His bodily beauty was remarkable, and his physical strength was astonishing in a man; he was no less distinguished in greatness of spirit [Note: col. 0115: witness 5 omits the phrase following *magnitudine*, “very many ... exceedingly many”].

He waged many wars with his father and still more without his father [Note: col. 0115: *quoque* (“also”) in witness 6], in the kingdoms of the Slavs, and always carried away the triumph of victory. He enlarged the boundaries of his empire by extending them through the sword. To his own people he appeared gentle, to his enemies terrifying; gracious in speech, adorned with humility, and endowed with extraordinary skill in arranging the affairs of the kingdom. In every respect he seemed to lack nothing required by royal majesty [Note: col. 0115: “so that it seemed entirely that nothing was lacking in him within the competence of royal majesty” in witness 5; *in regiae maiestatis competentia* (“within the competence of royal majesty”) in witness 4].

He had no offspring from a lawful marriage because of his wife’s infertility. But from a certain noble woman he fathered a son of exceptionally handsome appearance, whom he ordered to be called Arnolf [Note: col. 0115: *Arnolphus* in witness 5, consistently; *Arnulphus* in witness 4; *Arnulfus* in witness 8], in memory of the most revered Arnolf, bishop of the church of Metz, from whose holy stock the lineage of his own family and that of other Frankish kings had sprung [Note: col. 0115: variants read “the stock of others,” “the stock of other Frankish kinsmen,” and related forms].

This seems not to have happened by chance but through some foreshadowing and portent of future events [Note: col. 0115: “which did not continue until...” is absent in witness 8]. For from him the genealogy of kings, divinely provided [Note: col. 0115: *siquidem genealogia* in witnesses 1–3, 5, and 7], began to flourish through the intervals of time with favorable successions of increase [Note: col. 0115: *successionibus* (“successions”) in witness 5], until in the great Charles it attained the highest summit of empire, not only among the Franks but also among various peoples and kingdoms.

After his death [Note: col. 0115: “after his death” in witness 2], with fortune changing, the glory of worldly affairs—which had advanced beyond expectation—began gradually to dissipate in the same manner in which it had arisen [Note: col. 0115: “fortune withdrew, and the glory ... began in the same manner in which it had advanced” in witnesses 7 and 9–12]. At last, when not only kingdoms were failing but the royal stock itself was perishing—partly through premature death and partly withering through the infertility of marriages [Note: col. 0115: *conjugium* (“marriage”) in witness 5c]—this man alone of so numerous a posterity of kings was found capable of taking up the scepters of the Frankish empire. This will become clearer in what follows, in its proper place [Note: col. 0115: *suo loco* (“in its proper place”) in witness 6].

When Louis learned that his brother had died [Note: col. 0115: the passage from “Louis, having learned...” through “was created Emperor” is absent in witnesses 7–12; “his brother” is absent in witnesses 4, 5, 6, and 8–12], he entered Bavaria and came to Regensburg [Note: col. 0115: *Rastibonam* in witnesses 5 and 6]. There all the nobles of the kingdom, gathering to him, submitted themselves to his rule. The same king granted Arnolf Carantania [Note: col. 0115: *Corantanum* in witness 5], which his father had granted him long before. In it stood a very strongly fortified castle called Mosaburg [Note: col. 0115: forms include *Mosburh*, *Mosburch*, *Mosburgk*, *Mosaburh*, *Mosaburt*, and *Mosaburc*], because the place, surrounded by an impassable marsh, offered those approaching it extremely difficult access [Note: col. 0115: it was a parish and ancient castle in lower Carinthia, a German mile from Klagenfurt, not far from Lake Klagenfurt].

## 881

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 881, Charles departed from Alamannia and occupied the territory of the Lombards. Within a few days he received all Italy into submission. Arriving at Rome, he was favorably and with great glory created Emperor by John, pontiff of the Apostolic See, and by the Roman Senate.

At that time a fleet of Northmen entered the river Waal [Note: col. 0115: *Walam* in witnesses 1, 3, and 5] and moored at the royal palace of Nijmegen [Note: col. 0115: *Neumago* in witness 5; *Niumago* in witnesses 4 and 8], where they established their camp. When this was reported to Louis [Note: col. 0115: *perlatum est* (“was reported”) in witness 5], he came with his army without delay and enclosed the fortress in a siege.

After fighting had been joined for several days, he did not prevail to any great extent, because the palace, immense in size and remarkable in its construction, provided the enemy with an extremely secure refuge. In this engagement Eberhard the Saxon, son of Count Meginhard [Note: col. 0117: *Everhardus* in witnesses 1, 4, and 8; *Saxo* (“the Saxon”) is absent in witnesses 7 and 11, while the Saint-Godehard manuscript has *Saxi*; *Meguinardi* in witness 1; *Meginardi* in witness 4; *est adversarius* (“is an enemy”) in witnesses 1–3 and 5], was captured by the enemy and led away as a prisoner [Note: col. 0117: *ducitur* (“is led away”) in witnesses 1, 2, and 5]. His mother Evesa [Note: col. 0117: forms include *Enessa*, *Enesse*, and *Eversa*] later recovered him unharmed by paying a great price.

Finally, after receiving a promise that, if he abandoned the siege, the Northmen would immediately leave his kingdom [Note: col. 0117: “immediately depart from his kingdom” in witnesses 3–5], the king withdrew with all his forces. After his departure, the pagans burned the palace and its fortification with fire [Note: col. 0117: the word order “burning ... with flames” varies among witnesses], boarded their ships [Note: col. 0117: some witnesses read “their ships having been burned”], and returned to the mouth of the Rhine.

In the same year, in November, two kings of the Northmen, Godfrey and Sigifrid [Note: col. 0117: *Sigefridus* in witnesses 2–5], settled with an immeasurable multitude of infantry and cavalry at a place called Ahslon [Note: col. 0117: forms include *Haslon*, *Haslou*, *Aslon*, and *Haslion*], beside the Meuse [Note: col. 0117: *Mosa* in witness 7; see the *Annals of Fulda*].

At their first attack they ravaged the neighboring places, burning the city of Liège, the fortress of Trajectum (Maastricht) [Note: col. 0117: *Terjectum* in witness 2; *Traectum* in witness 7; *Trejectum* in witnesses 4 and 8], and the town of Tongeren. In a second incursion they poured into the territory of the Ripuarians [Note: col. 0117: *effusi* (“pouring forth”) is absent in witnesses 7 and 9–12], devastating everything with slaughter, plunder, and fire [Note: col. 0117: “burning everything” in witnesses 4 and 5]. They burned Cologne, Bonn [Note: col. 0117: the marginal note identifies Bonn, Zülpich, Jülich, and Neuss], and the cities with their adjacent castles, namely Zülpich, Jülich [Note: col. 0117: variants include *Julpiacum*, *Juliacum*, *Viliacum*, *Vilpiacum*, and *Vilipiacum*] and Neuss [Note: col. 0117: *Nuis* in witness 5; *Musa* in witness 3]. After this they reduced the palace at Aachen and the monasteries of Inden, Malmedy, and Stavelot to ashes [Note: col. 0117: witness 5 reads *idem Amalimundarias et Stabilius* (“the same [places], Amalimundarias and Stabilius”)].

## 882

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 882, traversing the Ardennes, they entered the monastery of Prüm on the very day of the Epiphany of the Lord. Staying there for three days, they ravaged the entire surrounding region.

At that place an innumerable multitude of foot soldiers, gathered into a single column from the fields and villages, attacked them as though intending to fight [Note: col. 0117: variants read “as though intending battle,” “with a multitude,” and “as though intending to storm them”]. But when the Northmen saw that the common rabble was not so much unarmed as devoid of military discipline [Note: col. 0117: variants include “not merely monstrous,” “not merely unarmed,” and other forms], they rushed upon them with a shout and struck down so many that it seemed that brute animals, not human beings, were being slaughtered.

After accomplishing this, they returned to their camp laden with booty. When they departed, the fire that had been lit in various dwellings and remained burning, since there was no one to extinguish it [Note: col. 0117: one witness adds “and no one was...”], consumed the monastery.

While these things were taking place, King Louis, weighed down by illness, died at Frankfurt on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [Note: col. 0117: compare the *Annals of Fulda*]. He was buried beside his father in the monastery at Lorsch [Note: col. 0117: forms include *Jorosan*, *Jorasam*, *Jorasheim*, and *Joresham*; one witness reads “he was buried at Joresheim beside his father in the monastery”].

He had taken Queen Liutgard [Note: col. 0117: *Juogardem* in witness 1; *Juidgardam* in witness 5a] in marriage, and by her had an only son, whom he named Louis after himself. But, as we have already related [Note: col. 0117: variants rearrange the clause concerning his entry into Bavaria], after his brother’s death he entered Bavaria to obtain his brother’s kingdom and was staying at Regensburg. There the same little boy fell from a window of the palace [Note: col. 0117: “fell from a window” in witnesses 1–5], broke his neck, and immediately expired.

This death, not only premature but also dishonorable [Note: col. 0117: “not so much premature as dishonorable” in witness 4; “so dishonorable” in witnesses 1–3 and 5; “so premature a death” in witness 3], brought the greatest grief not only to the king and queen but also to the entire royal household [Note: col. 0117: “the entire royal house” in witnesses 2, 5e, 6, 7, and 9–12].

When the Northmen heard of the king’s death, they celebrated with excessive rejoicing and now thought not of battle but of plunder. Accordingly, they rushed out with all their strength from their fortification [Note: col. 0117: corrupt variants read “with every warning,” “with every haste,” “with every admiration,” and other forms] and occupied the most noble city of Trier in Gaul on the Nones of April, the most sacred day of the Lord’s Supper [Note: col. 0117: compare the account of Trier’s destruction in the *Gesta Trevirorum*, which has nearly the same wording].

There they refreshed their bodies, weary from the journey, until the holy day of Easter, and demolished the entire territory of the city all around, down to the ground [Note: col. 0117: “the entire encampment” in witness 5]. Then, burning the city with fire, they directed their line toward Metz.

When Walo, bishop of that city [Note: col. 0117: “the bishop of the city” in witnesses 5, 6, 8, and 9–12; the name Walo is absent in witnesses 1–3, 6, 7, and 9–12], learned this, he went out to meet them voluntarily for battle, joining to himself Certulf, bishop [Note: col. 0117: *Bertolfus* in witness 3 and *Bertulfus* in witnesses 5 and 7–12], and Count Adalhard [Note: col. 0118: Bertulf was archbishop of Trier; Adalhard is called count of Metz by writers of Lorraine, not incorrectly. The *Gesta Trevirorum*, after Count Adalhard, add Remich].

When the battle began, the Northmen emerged victorious. The bishop Walo fell in the battle [Note: col. 0117: “in battle” is absent in witnesses 1–3 and 5], and the others fled. Abandoning the expedition they had begun, the pagans returned to their fleet with great booty and the utmost speed.

At that time the Emperor Charles was staying in Italy. From there he was pressed by various embassies from Germany and Gaul to hasten to receive the kingdoms that belonged to him by hereditary right and to come to the aid of the endangered empire, which, having lost its head, was a laughingstock to its enemies.

He delayed not at all. He came to Francia with all his forces and, together with the Lombards, Bavarians, Alamanni, Thuringians, Saxons, Frisians, and all the kingdoms subject to his rule, began to besiege the Northmen at the place mentioned above. But his efforts achieved little, although, as we have said, an immeasurable multitude from diverse kingdoms and peoples had gathered together [Note: col. 0119: *confluxit* (“had gathered”) in witnesses 1–3, 5, 7, and 9–12], while heavenly indignation raged against the people profaning the Christian religion.

Finally, the Northman king Godfrey promised that he would become a Christian on the condition that Frisia be granted to him as a royal benefice [Note: col. 0119: *Frisia* in witnesses 5, 7, and 9–12] and that Gisla [Note: col. 0119: *Gissa* in witness 5e], the daughter of Lothair, be given to him as wife. Having obtained what he desired [Note: col. 0119: *optavit* (“he desired”) in witnesses 4–6], he was baptized and received from the sacred font by the Emperor.

A vast amount of gold and silver was paid to Sigifrid and the other Northmen, and on these terms they departed from the borders of the kingdom.

## 883

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 883 [Note: col. 0119: 888 in witnesses 9, 11, and 12], King Louis, Carloman’s brother [Note: col. 0119: “king” is absent in witness 5], died at Saint Denis and was honorably buried there. All the peoples of Gaul mourned him with immense lamentation.

For he was a man of the greatest courage [Note: col. 0119: “a man” is absent in witnesses 2–5; “of the greatest courage” is absent in witnesses 2 and 7–12], and he defended the kingdom subject to him powerfully and manfully against the attacks of the pagans [Note: col. 0119: *infestatione* (“harassment”) in witness 3]. Among the many things he accomplished bravely, special praise is given to the battle that he waged with all his strength against the Northmen at a place called Saucourt [Note: col. 0119: forms include *Sodaltcurt*, *Sodalcurth*, and *Sodalcurch*; this was Saucourt, a town in Picardy]. In that engagement, they say, he struck down more than eight thousand of the enemy with the sword [Note: col. 0119: “eight thousand men with the sword” in witnesses 1–3 and 5].

His brother Carloman obtained his kingdom.

At the same time Bertulf, bishop of Trier, departed to the Lord on the sixth day before the Ides of February [Note: col. 0119: variants give the Ides of September, the second day before the Ides of February, or the Ides of February]. In the episcopal chair he was succeeded, by the election of the clergy and the entire people, by the most reverend bishop Ratbod [Note: col. 0119: forms include *Rabbodus*, *Radbodus*, and *Rapodus*], on the sixth day before the Ides of April [Note: col. 0119: the seventh day before the Ides of April in witnesses 2, 5, and 6].

In these same days the bishop Ruodbert [Note: col. 0119: variants include *Rutbertus*, *Rudpertus*, *Ruopertus*, *Rupertus*, *Ruothpertus*, *Rotbertus*, *Routbertus*, and others] was consecrated by that same bishop Ratbod in the church of Metz, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: col. 0119: “by the same archbishop Ratbod” in witnesses 7–12].

Around this time Hugh, the son of Lothair, was introduced by certain promoters of discord and litigation in the hope of recovering his father’s kingdom. All who hated justice and peace flocked to him, so that within a few days [Note: col. 0119: *ut paucis* (“so that [in] few”) in witness 5] an innumerable multitude of plunderers submitted to his rule [Note: col. 0119: “had submitted” in witness 5].

Among them, certain leading men of the kingdom, led astray by a vain hope, approached him after giving their pledge: namely, Counts Stephen, Ruodbert, Wicbert [Note: col. 0119: *Witbertus* in witness 5], and Thietbald, and Albéric and his brother Stephen [Note: col. 0119: one witness gives the sequence “Ruodbert, Wicpert, Albéric, and his brother Stephen”; *ejus* (“his”) is absent in witnesses 7 and 9–12].

Such plunder and violence were committed by these men in the kingdom that there was no difference between their wickedness and that of the Northmen, except that they abstained from slaughter and arson. Thus Almighty God, angered, opposed the kingdom of Lothair and so utterly destroyed the strength of that kingdom through such accumulating calamities that the prophecy of the most holy Pope Nicholas, as well as the curse he had pronounced upon that kingdom, might be fulfilled [Note: col. 0119: “the prophecy and also the curse” in witnesses 1 and 5].

At this time the same Hugh killed Count Wicbert, who had favored him from the beginning of his life [Note: col. 0119: this clause is absent in witnesses 1–3]. A few days later he ordered Bernarius, a noble and entirely faithful man, to be murdered treacherously, having been captivated by the beauty of his wife, whom he immediately took to himself in marriage [Note: col. 0119: “took her in marriage without delay” in witnesses 1–3 and 5].

The woman was called Friderada [Note: col. 0119: variants include *Friderath*, *Fridera*, *Friderach*, and *Friderat*.]. Before she was joined to Bernarius, she had been married to Engilram, a powerful man [Note: col. 0119: forms include *Engilrannus*, *Engelrannus*, and *Engelgrammus*]. By him she had borne a daughter, whom Count Richwin afterward took in marriage; he too later ordered her beheaded because of an adulterous act committed.

## 884

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 884, the Northmen who had withdrawn from Ahslon [Note: col. 0119: *Aslon* in witness 6; “who had withdrawn far from here” in witnesses 9–12] entered the river Somme [Note: col. 0119: variants include *Sonus* and *Somnus*] and settled there. Since Carloman could not withstand their frequent incursions, he promised money if they would withdraw from his kingdom.

At once the hearts of that greedy people burned to obtain the money. They demanded twelve thousand weights of pure and tested silver and promised peace for the same number of years. After receiving so vast a payment, they loosened the ropes from the shore, boarded their ships, and returned to the sea-coast.

Meanwhile Carloman went hunting. There he was severely wounded by a boar and, shortly afterward, lost his life together with his kingdom. He was buried at Saint Denis.

Some say, however, that he was wounded by one of his own attendants, who was carrying weapons carelessly [Note: col. 0119: *ferente* (“carrying”) in witnesses 1–3 and 5c/e]. Because the man had committed the deed unwillingly and not deliberately, the matter was concealed from the king [Note: col. 0119: *celatum est* (“was concealed”) in witnesses 4 and 5], so that an innocent man might not be handed over to death.

## Supplemental exact-form apparatus for the unresolved scopes

These entries supply the forms and witness assignments that the inline apparatus had compressed. They follow the relevant narrative lemmas and do not regularize corrupt readings.

### Opening battle and division

- At *movit ergo absque mora exercitum, et cum quinquaginta...* (“he therefore moved the army without delay, and with fifty thousand...”), witness 5 reads *exercitum cum*, joining “army” directly to “with.”
- At *vires adversariorum ferro conterunt, terrae prosternunt* (“they crush the enemy’s forces with the sword and cast them to the ground”), witnesses 5c, 5e, 1, and 3 read *conterunt et terrae* (“they crush and [cast] to the earth”); witness 6 has the passives *conteruntur . . . prosternuntur* (“they are crushed . . . they are cast down”).
- At *convenerunt* (“they met”), witness 5 reads *cum venerunt* (“when they came”).

### Year 879

- At *a multis, ut dictum est* (“by many, as has been said”), witness 3 reads *multis sicut dictum* (“by many, as stated”).
- In *Nec solum illi, verum etiam alii reges* (“not only they, but also other kings”), *alii* (“other”) is absent in witness 3; *et regnis* (“and kingdoms”) is absent in witness 3 and the Saint-Godehard manuscript.
- At *Per idem tempus* (“at the same time”), witness 5 reads *Per id* (“through/at that [time]”).
- At *Adolescentes, quippe ut foederatus...* (“the young men, indeed so that, as an ally...”), witness 5 has the corrupt *quo impetu f.* (“by what attack/impulse f.”).
- At *Hugo*, witness 3 has the shortened name-form *Hug*.
- At *exercitum* (“the army,” accusative), witnesses 2 and 5 have nominative *exercitus* (“the army” as subject).
- The Thimiun place-name evidence is: *Thimnin* in 5; *Thimuin* in 2 and the Saint-Godehard manuscript; *Thurium* in 7; *Thimum* in 4, 8, 9, and 10; *Timum* in 11 and 12. The editorial note identifies it as Thuin on the Sambre.
- At Lorsch the readings are *Lorsheym* in 5, *Jorasam* in 3 and the Saint-Godehard manuscript, and *Joresham* in 4.

### Year 881

- At *Per idem tempus* (“at the same time”), witness 5 reads *per id*.
- The river-name *Wal* has the inflected form *Walam* in witnesses 1, 3, and 5. Nijmegen appears as *Neumago* in 5 and *Niumago* in 4 and 8. At *perlatum esset* (“had been reported”), witness 5 reads *perlatum est* (“was reported”).
- At Eberhard’s capture, witnesses 1–3 and 5 read *est adversarius* (“is an enemy”) for *est ab adversariis* (“is by enemies”). The name is *Everhardus* in 1, 4, and 8. *Saxo* (“the Saxon”) is absent in 7 and 11; the Saint-Godehard manuscript reads *Saxi*. The father’s name is *Meguinardi* in 1 and *Meginardi* in 4. Witnesses 1, 2, and 5 read present *ducitur* (“is led away”).
- The mother’s name is *Enessa* in 5a/d, *Enesse* in 5c/e, and *Eversa* in 7. For *quem postea* (“whom afterward”), 1 and 5 read *quoad postea* and 2 reads *quod postea*.
- For the promised withdrawal, witnesses 3, 4, and 5 read *continuo e regno* (“at once from the kingdom”). The burning phrase is *flammis exurentes* (“burning with flames”) in 4 and 7–12. At *navibus ascensis* (“having boarded the ships”), witnesses 2, 4, 5, and 7 read *navibus accensis* (“the ships having been burned/set alight”).
- *Sigifridus* is spelled *Sigefridus* in witnesses 2–5. Ahslon is *Haslon* in 2, 4, 8, 9, 11, and 12; *Haslou* in 5; *Aslon* in 7; *Haslion* in 10. The Meuse is *Mosa* in 7.
- Trajectum is *Terjectum* in 2, *Traectum* in 7, and *Trejectum* in 4 and 8. *Effusi* (“having poured forth”) is absent in 7 and 9–12. Witnesses 4 and 5 read *inc[ensis] omnia* (“everything having been burned”). Bonn is *Bonnam* in 5c/e; the marginal note lists “Bonn . . . Zülpich, Jülich, Neuss.”
- At Zülpich, witness 7 reads *scilicet Julpiacum* (“namely Zülpich”). Jülich is *Juliacum* in 4 and 7, *Viliacum* in 8–12, *Vilpiacum* in 1–3, and *Vilipiacum* in 5. Neuss is *Nuis* in 5 and *Musa* in 3. Witness 7 explicitly reads *Aquis palatium* (“the palace at Aachen”). For Inden, Malmedy, and Stavelot, witness 5 has the corrupt/place-name sequence *idem Amalimundarias et Stabilius* (“the same [places], Amalimundarias and Stabilius”).

### Year 882

- At the Prüm attack, witnesses 1–3 read *eos quasi pugna...* (“them as though battle...”); witnesses 1, 2, 4, and 5 also transmit *multitudine* (“with/by a multitude”); witness 5 reads *eos expugnatura* (“a force about to storm them”). At *non tantum inerme* (“not so much unarmed”), witnesses 2, 7, and 9–12 read *non tantum inorme* (“not so much monstrous/enormous”), and 8 has *innerme*. *Militari* (“military”) is absent in 1–3, 5, and 6.
- At the burning monastery, witness 5a/d reads *extingueret et m.* (“should extinguish it, and m.”), a truncated continuation.
- The burial place is *Jorosan* in 1 and 3, *Jorasam* in 2, *Jorasheim* in 8–12, and *Joresham* otherwise; witness 5 (with 1–3 cited) reads *sepultus est in Joresheim juxta patrem in coenobio* (“he was buried at Joresheim beside his father in the monastery”). Liutgard is *Juogardem* in 1 and *Juidgardam* in 5a.
- The first alternate reading for the son’s death, in witnesses 1, 2, 4, and 5, is *sed ut . . . Bajoariam ingressus* (“but, as . . . having entered Bavaria”). Witness 3 reads *sed ut . . . fratris dum ad ingressus est* (“but, as . . . of his brother, while he entered toward...”), an incomplete/corrupt rearrangement. Witnesses 1–5 have *fenestra cecidit* (“he fell from the window”).
- For the death’s character, witness 4 has *quantum inhonesta* (“as much dishonorable”); witnesses 1–3 and 5 have *sed inhonesta* (“but dishonorable”); witness 3 also reads *quae tam immatura mors* (“which, so premature a death”). The household form is *domo* in 2, 5e, 6, 7, and 9–12.
- At the Northmen’s rush, 1, 2, and 5 read *cum omni ammonitione* (“with every admonition”), 3 *cum omni festinatione* (“with every haste”), and 5c/e *cum omni admiratione* (“with every amazement”). The verb is *exibunt* (“they will go out”) in 2, *exibant* (“they were going out”) in 3, and *exeunt et* (“they go out, and”) in 6.
- At Easter, witnesses 4 and 5 read *sanctum diem* (“the holy day”); witness 5 has *omne tentorium* (“the whole encampment/tent”) for *omne territorium* (“the whole territory”). Metz is *Mediomatricum* in 5. At “when he learned,” 5 has *reperisset* (“he had found”).
- For Walo, witnesses 5, 6, 8, and 9–12 have *urbis episcopus* (“bishop of the city”); the name *Walo* is absent in 1–3, 6, 7, and 9–12. Certulf is *Bertolfo* in 3, 5, and 7–12. The marginal note identifies Bertulf as archbishop of Trier and Adalhard as count of Metz, adding that the *Gesta Trevirorum* place Remich after Count Adalhard. Adalhard is *Andalhardo* in 5. Walo is *Walla* in 1–3 and 5, *Wiala* in 7, *Walu* in 11, and *Walo* in 4 and 8; *in praelio* (“in battle”) is absent in 1–3 and 5.

[Fragmentary opening: the supplied section begins within the annal preceding 885.]

The Northmen, having learned of the king’s death, immediately returned to the kingdom. Accordingly, Abbot Hugo and the other nobles sent envoys to them, declaring that the promise and pledge given had been violated. They replied that they had made a treaty with King Carloman, not with anyone else; whoever he might be who succeeded to his kingdom, he would have to pay the same number and amount of money if he wished to hold the realm quietly and peacefully. Terrified by such demands, the leading men of the kingdom sent envoys to Emperor Charles, inviting him of their own accord into the kingdom. As he approached, they went out to meet him at Gundolf’s estate; after giving the customary pledges by hand and oath, they subjected themselves to his authority.

[Variant readings: “who succeeded him in the kingdom” (7, 9–12); “who succeeded him in his kingdom” (6). “Gundolf’s” is read as *Gundulphi* (4), *Gundfi* (8), and *Gundolphi* (5). “They subjected themselves” is read “they submitted” (5).]

In the same year, the Northmen who had come to Chinheim from Denmark, while Godefrid was absent, sailed up the Rhine and, after occupying the town of Duisburg, built a fortification there in their customary manner. They remained in it throughout the winter. Against them Duke Henry established a camp and did not allow them to carry out raids in any way. When spring returned, they burned their camp and withdrew to the coastal regions.

[Variant readings: “Chinheim and Denmark” (2, 5a, d); “Chinheim and Denemarca” (5c, e); “Denimarca” (4, 7–12). “They sailed up the Rhine toward Nijmegen” is found in one codex. The town is called “Dinsburg” (5), “Duisburg” (11, 12), and “Duusburh” (7). “In it” is read “in her” (5). “They burned the camp and withdrew to the coastal regions” is also transmitted as “they burned the camp and withdrew to maritime places” (5c, e).]

[In those same days, the Northmen left the Somna and, returning again into the kingdom of Lothar, encamped at a place called Lovon [Löwen], on the border of that kingdom. By continuous raids they exhausted both kingdoms. To restrain their wickedness, the emperor sent an army against them once and again, but nothing worth remembering was accomplished against the rapacity of such violent men.]

[Variant readings: “from the Sono” (5). “Lovon” is also written “Louen” (5). “By continuous raids they harassed that kingdom” (1–3, 5, 6). “More violent” (5a, d). “Rapacity” is absent in manuscript 2. The whole passage from “In those same days” through “was accomplished” is absent from manuscripts 8–12; compare below under the year 886.]

DCCCLXXXV.

In the year 885 of the Lord’s incarnation, Hugo, intending to rebel against the emperor, secretly sent envoys to Godefrid in Frisia. He was related to Godefrid by marriage, since he had married Godefrid’s sister. Hugo urged him to send word to his homeland, gather a strong force of auxiliaries from every side, and come to his aid with all his strength, so that he might be able to recover his father’s kingdom by force of arms. If this were successfully accomplished through Godefrid’s exertion and courage, Hugo promised him half of the kingdom as a reward.

[Variant readings: “Frisia” (5c, e). “He should send auxiliaries” (5c, e); “he should send and auxiliaries” (3–12). “So that he might be able” (1–3, 5, 6). “As though by a just arrangement” (1–3, 5, 6); “as though according to reason” (5c, e). The names are written “Gerolfus and Gardolfus” (1, 3, 5c, d), “Gerulfus and Gardulfus” (4), and “Gerulfus and Cardulfus” (8).]

Godefrid, as though infected by the poison of these persuasive promises, sought an opportunity by which he might withdraw from his allegiance to the emperor as if on just grounds. He immediately sent Gerolfus and Gardolfus, counts of the Frisians, as envoys to Caesar. Through them he conveyed that, if the emperor wished him to remain in the allegiance he had promised, he should grant him Confluentes, Andernach, and Sinzig, together with several other royal estates devoted to imperial service, for his own use, because wine abounded in those places, whereas the land he had received from the prince’s generosity to possess was by no means productive of wine.

[Variant readings: “Confluentem” (4, 5). “Sinzig” is also written “Sucicha” (5a, d) and “Sucicham” (5c, d). “And several other estates devoted to imperial service” (5); “and several other borders devoted to imperial service” (5). “To himself” is read “to him” (3, 4, 8, 12). “Because wine, which abounded in those places” (7, 9–12); “because wine was abundant in those places” (1–3, 5). “Which he had received to possess through the prince’s generosity” (2); “which he might receive” (7, 9–12).]

He was doing this with the intention that, if the things he requested were granted, he might introduce his own men into the heart of the kingdom and observe the course of events; but if they were denied him, he could nevertheless, offended by what was forbidden him, rage more plausibly, as though justice demanded it, and take up the causes of rebellion.

[Variant readings: “If the things requested were granted” (7, 9–12); “if the requests were granted” (7, 9–12). “Might mingle his men” is read “might be mingled” (2, 5a, d, 7, 9–12). “But if they were also denied” (5); “but if they were denied” (5); “but if these too were denied” (4, 9–12). “Offended by the things forbidden him” (2, 3, 5); “offended by those forbidden things” (7). “Take up the cause of rebellion” (5a, d, 1–3); “take up the causes of rebellion” (1–3).]

When the emperor perceived their cunning schemes and the conspiracies of their factions, he discussed the matter in a more far-sighted council with Henry, a most prudent man, considering by what stratagem he might destroy the enemy whom he had introduced into the extremities of the kingdom. Knowing that there were places inaccessible to an army because of the innumerable channels of its various waters and its impassable marshes, he decided to test his skill rather than his strength.

[Variant readings: “Knowing that there were inaccessible places” (1–3, 5). “Rather by strategy than by force” (1–5); “rather than through strength” (1–5).]

He therefore dismissed the envoys, who were left in suspense by his answer, and permitted them to return to Godefrid, asserting that through his own messengers he would provide answers concerning all the matters of their embassy—answers suitable both to himself and to Godefrid—provided only that Godefrid persevered in the allegiance he had begun.

After this he sent Henry to the same man. To conceal the deception that was being prepared, he sent with him Willibert, the venerable bishop of Cologne. Henry secretly instructed his followers that, as they hurried through Saxony, they should not meet him in a formed body but come to him separately, at the place and on the day he had appointed for them.

[This refers to Henry.]

He himself came to Cologne with very few men and, taking the aforesaid bishop with him, immediately set out for Batavia.

[Variant readings: “He sends him” (5); “he sends him so that…” (5). “With him” is absent in manuscripts 1–3. “He came to Cologne, taking the aforesaid bishop with him.” “Batavia” is also written “Batuva” (5d) and “Baccua” (3).]

When Godefrid heard of their arrival, he went out to meet them at a place called Herispich [now the place called Heerwen], where the waters of the Rhine and the Waal branch off from a single channel and, moving farther apart from one another, surround the province of Batavia with their currents.

[Variant readings: “Herispihc” (2), “Herispirch” (9, 11, 12), and “Arispich” (10).]

Entering this island, the bishop and the count heard many things from Godefrid and gave many replies on the emperor’s behalf. The day was declining toward sunset; when the conference ended, they left the island and returned to their lodgings, intending to come back on the following day.

Henry urged the bishop that on the next day he should summon Gisla, Godefrid’s wife, out of the island and endeavor to call her back to a desire for peace. Meanwhile, Henry himself would discuss with Godefrid the case of Count Everhard, whose property Godefrid was violently taking from him.

[Variant readings: “Gissa” (5e) and “Gisala” (7). “To recall her to a desire for peace” (2, 3, 5). “Eberhard” (5). “Whose property” (2, 5).]

Then he persuaded Everhard to rise in the assembly and publicly denounce the injustice he was suffering. If the savage man of that barbarous people uttered some harsher and more insulting word against him, Everhard was to draw his sword without delay and strike him on the head with all his force, before he could be lifted from the ground.

[The text appears to have lost something after “strike him”; perhaps a phrase such as “so that he might immediately be slaughtered by Henry’s men.”]

What more need be said? Godefrid, first struck by Everhard and then pierced by Henry’s followers, died; and all the Northmen found in Batavia were slaughtered.

[Variant reading: “Were being slaughtered” (7–12).]

Not many days later, Hugo, drawn by promises to Gundolf’s estate on the advice of Henry, was captured by treachery. On the emperor’s orders, Henry had his eyes torn out, and all who supported him were disgraced. After this he was sent to a monastery in Alamannia, the monastery of Saint Gall; later he was recalled from there to his homeland. Finally, in the time of King Zwentibold, my own hand tonsured him in the monastery of Prüm—for at that time I was the keeper, though unworthy, of the Lord’s fold in that place. There, not many years later, he died and was buried.

[Variant readings: “Alamannia” (3, 5c, d, 7, 9–12); “the monastery” (1, 3–5, 7, 9–12). The king’s name is written “Zwentibold” (1), “Zwendebold” (3), “Zundibolch” (5), “Zeindibach” (7, 9), “Zunentibolch” (4), “Zuendibolcho” (8), and “Zendibachi” (10–12). “Prüm” is also written “Brumia” (7).]

DCCCLXXXVI.

[The same narrative occurs above under the year 884 in almost the same words. Since it is omitted there in manuscripts 9–12, Regino appears, after gaining a clearer understanding of the facts, to have omitted the vague sentence “In those same days” and restored the narrative to its proper place.]

In the year 886 of the Lord’s incarnation, the Northmen left the Somna River and, returning again into the kingdom of Lothar, established their camp and settlements at a place called Lovon, on the border of the two kingdoms. By continuous raids they exhausted both kingdoms. To restrain their inborn wickedness, the emperor sent an army against them once and again, but nothing worthy of mention was accomplished against the rapacity of such violent men.

[Variant readings: “Somna” (5), “Sanno” (5a), and “Sonno” (5c).]

In the same year, Ansbald, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, a man of the highest holiness and devotion, passed to the heavenly homeland on 12 July. Farabert, a venerable father, succeeded him in the governance of the monastery on 6 August.

[Variant: “Sarabertus” (5).]

DCCCLXXXVII.

In the year 887 of the Lord’s incarnation, the Northmen, withdrawing from Lovon, entered the Seine. Arriving at Paris, they established their camp and surrounded the city with a siege. Against them the emperor sent Duke Henry with an army in the spring, but he accomplished nothing. For, it is said, there were thirty thousand or more enemy soldiers, nearly all strong warriors.

[Variant readings: “They entered the Seine at Paris” (5c, d); “they entered the Seine, encamped on the border of that kingdom, and arrived at Paris” (9–12).]

Again, in summer, before the crops were gathered into sheaves, the same Henry came to Paris with the armies of both kingdoms. While the legions surrounded the city, he himself approached with very few men, went around the fortification, examined the position of the place, and sought an approach by which an engagement between the army and the enemy might be exposed to less danger.

The Northmen, hearing that the army was approaching, had dug ditches one foot wide and three feet deep around their camp. They had covered them with refuse and straw, leaving untouched only the paths necessary for movement. A few marauders who were hiding in the hollows beside the roads saw Henry approaching, quickly rose from the places where they had concealed themselves, and challenged the man with weapons and shouting.

[Variant readings: “Seeing Henry approaching, they quickly…” (5). “From the places in which they had hidden” (4, 5); “from places in which they had hidden” (4, 5).]

He, in the greatness of his courage, unable to endure the indignity of the affair, rushed upon them. Immediately the horse he was riding stumbled into the hidden ditches, and he fell to the ground with it. The enemy hastened toward him and, before he could be lifted from the spot, pierced him with their weapons and slaughtered him without delay in the sight of the entire army. They took away his arms and carried off some of his spoils.
