[Variant readings: “Into blind ditches” (1, 3, 5); “into uncertain ditches” (1, 3, 5); “into foul ditches” (2). “With him” is read “with himself” (5a, d), and “him into the ground” (1, 5). In manuscripts 1–3 the phrase “before he could be lifted from the place” is absent; manuscript 3 inserts “swiftly” after “with the utmost haste.”]

When the battle lines attacked, the lifeless corpse was scarcely recovered. It was carried by his men as far as Soissons and buried in the basilica of Saint Medard. The army, having lost its commander, returned to its own territory.

[Variant readings: “Suessionis” is also written “Sessionis” (7) and “Suuessionis” (5a, d). “It was carried away” (2, 5).]

At the same time, Abbot Hugo, a man of great power and great prudence, died at Orléans and was buried at Saint-Germain in Auxerre.

[Variant: “A man of great piety” (5). The place is also written “Autissiodurum” (2), “Autisiodure” (1), “Antisiodorum” (5, 8), and “Abisiodorum” (7, 9–12).]

The command he had held and vigorously governed was entrusted by the emperor to Odo, son of Robert. At that time Odo was count of Paris and, together with Gozlin, bishop of that city, defended it with all his strength against the unceasing attacks of the Northmen.

[Variant: “To Odo, Robert’s son” (1, 3). The name is written “Gozlinus” and “Gozlini” (1, 2), and “Gozelinus” and “Gozelino” (3).]

In those same days the aforesaid Bishop Gozlin departed from this world amid the pressures of the sieges. Haschirus was appointed by the emperor in his place as bishop.

[Variant readings: “Haschirus” (5), “Aschirus” (4), “Haischericus” (8), and “Aschirinus” (3). “By the emperor” is absent in manuscript 7.]

After this the emperor traveled through the peoples of Gaul and came to Paris with an immense army. There he established a camp against the enemy, but accomplished nothing in that place worthy of imperial majesty.

[Variant readings: “Worthy of the emperor’s majesty” (2); “worthy of the emperor’s majesty” (6); “worthy of imperial majesty” (9–12); “worthy of the emperor” (7). Manuscript 3 reads: “nothing worthy was done by the emperor in that place.”]

Finally, he granted the Northmen the lands and regions beyond the Seine for plundering, because the inhabitants of those places refused to obey him, and withdrew. He proceeded by a direct route into Alamannia.

[Variant: “He withdrew into Alamannia” (5).]

First, he drove Liudward, bishop of Vercelli, a man especially dear to him and his only counselor in administering public affairs, from his side in disgrace, charging him with adultery because he involved himself too familiarly, more than was proper, in the queen’s private affairs.

[Variant readings: “Liutward” (3), “Ludward” (4), “Liward” (8–10), “Lifard” (11), and “Litsard” (12). “Because he was inserted into the queen’s private affairs more intimately than was proper” (6). “With honor” (2).]

Then, after a few days had passed, he summoned his wife Richard, for that was the name by which the Augusta was called, before an assembly on the same matter. In a remarkable declaration, he publicly protested that he had never had carnal intercourse with her, although she had been joined to him in a lawful marriage for more than ten years.

She, on the contrary, declared that she was free not only from intercourse with him but from intercourse with any man, and boasted of the integrity of her virginity. She confidently affirmed that she would prove this by the judgment of almighty God, if her husband wished it, either by single combat or by the ordeal of heated ploughshares; for she was a religious woman.

[Variant readings: “With her” is absent in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5. “Remarkable to say” (7); “remarkable in speech” (9–12).]

After the separation had taken place, she withdrew to the monastery that she had built on her own property, intending to serve God.

[Variant readings: “To the monastery” (5). “In the monastery of Andlau, a convent of the handmaids of God in Alsace” (8). “After this deed” (1, 5); “she, having carried out this deed” (1, 5).]

When these things had happened, the emperor began to fall ill in body and mind. In November, around the feast of Saint Martin, he therefore came to Tribur and summoned a general assembly there.

The leading men of the kingdom saw that not only the strength of his body but also the faculties of his mind were deserting him. They voluntarily drew Arnolf, the son of Carloman, into the kingdom, and, suddenly conspiring, deserted the emperor and hurried together to the aforesaid man, so that within three days scarcely anyone remained who would offer him even the offices of ordinary human kindness.

[Variant readings: “Even words of human kindness” (7). “Food alone” (1, 3, 5); “food nevertheless” (1, 3, 5).]

Only food and drink were provided at the expense of Bishop Liudpert.

[Liudpert of Mainz.]

The spectacle was worthy of wonder, and astonishing as an example of the changing lot of human affairs. Previously, when favorable fortune had caused everything to overflow beyond what he could have imagined, he had drawn to himself so many and such great kingdoms of the empire without the sweat of labor or the struggles of war that, after the great Charles, he seemed inferior in majesty, power, and wealth to none of the Frankish kings.

Now, however, as he failed amid adversity—almost as a display of human frailty—all that fortune had heaped upon him was dishonorably taken away in a moment, though that same fortune, smiling on him with prosperous success, had once brought it to him gloriously.

[Variant readings: “As though in a display” (5); “destroying,” rather than “failing” (4, 7, 9–12).]

He therefore sent to Arnolf, reduced from an emperor to a needy man. With his fortunes desperate, he thought not of the dignity of the empire but of his daily sustenance, and humbly requested only enough food to support his present life. He also sent his son Bernhard, whom he had fathered by a concubine, with gifts, and entrusted him to Arnolf’s protection.

[Variant readings: “Whom he had fathered from a concubine” (6). “With presents” (5).]

A pitiable spectacle of human affairs: to see the wealthiest emperor deprived not only of the adornments of fortune but also of human assistance.

Arnolf the king granted him several royal estates in Alamannia, from which his maintenance might be provided. He himself, having successfully arranged affairs in Francia, returned to Bavaria.

[Variant readings: “Arnolf granted him” is absent in manuscripts 1 and 5. “Royal estates in Alamannia” (5). “Estates of the royal court in Alamannia” (7).]

In the same year, Witgar, bishop of the city of Augsburg, died. Adalbero, a man of noble birth and great intelligence and prudence, obtained his episcopal seat and succeeded him in the bishopric.

[Variant: “He succeeded him in the episcopate” (5).]

DCCCLXXXVIII.

In the year 888 of the Lord’s incarnation, the Emperor Charles, third of that name and dignity, died on the day before the Ides of January and was buried in the monastery of Reichenau.

[Variant: “DCCCLXXXVIIII” (2, 10). The text should read: “he died on the Ides of January,” that is, 13 January. Compare the Annals of Fulda and the Necrology of Saint Gall. “Buried in” is absent in manuscripts 7 and 9–12. “Reichenau” is written “Augea” and “Augia” (2), and “the island of Augia” in manuscript 3 and in the Saint Gall–Göttweig codex.]

This prince was most Christian: he feared God and kept his commandments with all his heart; he obeyed ecclesiastical decrees with the greatest devotion; he was generous in almsgiving; he was continually devoted to prayer and the melodies of the psalms; he was tirelessly intent upon the praises of God; and he entrusted all his hope and counsel to divine providence. Consequently, everything came together for him with fortunate success, so that all the kingdoms of the Franks, which his predecessors had acquired with great labor and not without bloodshed, he received to possess with the greatest ease, within a short period of time, without conflict and without anyone offering resistance.

[Variant readings: “Which his predecessors had acquired with labor for the good” (7); “which they had acquired with labor” (7, 9–12). The span from the first “everything” through the second is absent only in manuscript 3.]

That toward the end of his life he was stripped of his dignities and deprived of all his possessions was, as we believe, a trial—not only for purification, but, what is greater, for testing. For, as they say, he endured it with the greatest patience, offering vows of thanksgiving in adversity just as in prosperity. Therefore he has either already received, or without doubt will receive, the crown of life that God promised to those who love him.

[Variant: “Which God promised” (3).]

After his death, the kingdoms that had obeyed his authority, as though deprived of their lawful heir, fell apart from their former unity. They no longer awaited their natural lord; instead, each prepared to have a king created from its own midst. This caused great disturbances of war—not because the princes of the Franks were lacking in nobility, courage, or wisdom, and therefore unable to rule kingdoms, but because equality among them in birth, dignity, and power increased their discord. No one so far surpassed the others that they were willing to submit to his rule.

For Francia would have produced many capable princes to guide the kingdoms, had fortune not armed them against one another for mutual destruction through their rivalry in virtue.

[Variant: “Unless fortune had armed us through rivalry in virtue for mutual destruction” (7).]

Accordingly, one faction of the Italian people made Berengar, son of Everhard, who held the duchy of Friuli, its king; another faction decided that Wido, son of Lambert, duke of Spoleto, should likewise be raised to royal dignity.

[Variant readings: “Berengar” (9–12); “son of Everhard” (5). “The duchy of the men of Friuli” (5). “Wido” is also written “Guido” (5). “Lambert, duke of Spoleto” (8, 9–12).]

From this dispute of dissensions there later arose such slaughter on both sides, and so much human blood was shed, that, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, the kingdom divided against itself nearly suffered the misery of desolation.

In the end Wido emerged victorious and expelled Berengar from the kingdom. Driven out, Berengar went to King Arnolf and sought his protection against his enemy. What Arnolf did, and how he twice entered the kingdom of Italy with an army, will be related in its proper place.

[Variant readings: “He therefore went to Arnolf” (5); “Arnolf went to him” (3). “He entered” (5d); “he entered twice” (5).]

Meanwhile, the peoples of Gaul gathered together and, with Arnolf’s consent, made Odo king over them. Odo was the duke and son of Robert, whom we mentioned shortly above. He was a vigorous man, distinguished above all others by the beauty and height of his stature and by the greatness of his strength and wisdom. He ruled the commonwealth manfully and proved an indefatigable defender against the unceasing depredations of the Northmen.

[Variant: “Otto” (5).]

At about the same time, Ruodolf, son of Conrad and nephew of Abbot Hugo, whom we mentioned above, seized the region between the Jura and the Pennine Alps. At Saint-Maurice, having associated with himself certain leading men and several priests, he placed a crown upon his own head and ordered himself to be called king.

[Saint-Maurice on the Rhône, in the district of the Valais.]

After this he sent envoys throughout the entire kingdom of Lothar and, through the persuasive arguments and promises of bishops and noblemen, charmed their minds into favoring him.

When this was reported to Arnolf, he immediately attacked him with an army. Ruodolf slipped away in flight through the narrowest paths and sought safety in the most secure rocky places. Thus, every day of his life, Arnolf and his son Zwentibold pursued the same Ruodolf, but they could not harm him, because, as was stated above, the inaccessible places, passable only to solitary ibexes, kept the closely packed ranks of the pursuers far from entering.

[Variant readings: The unsigled printed reading *prioribus* means “earlier men,” against *primoribus*, “leading men.” “All his days of life.” “Passable only by solitary tracks” (3); “passable only by paths” (6). “The compact ranks” (1–8); “the connected ranks” (1–8).]

[This was written after the death of Zwentibold.]

In the same year, the Northmen who were besieging the city of Paris accomplished a marvelous and unheard-of deed, not only in our age but also in the age before it. When they realized that the city was impregnable, they began to labor with every strength and every device, so that, leaving the city behind them, they might convey their fleet upstream on the Seine with all their forces, enter the river Yonne, and penetrate without obstruction into the territory of Burgundy.

[The Yonne.]

But since the citizens resolutely prevented them from ascending the river, they dragged the ships over dry land for more than two thousand paces. Having thus avoided every danger, they plunged them once more into the waters of the Seine. After leaving the Seine a little farther on, they entered the Yonne as they had planned and, sailing with the utmost speed, arrived at Sens. There they established their camp and for six continuous months enclosed the same city in a siege. They devastated almost all Burgundy with plundering, slaughter, and fires.

[Variant readings: “With the fleet and with all their forces” (3); “the fleet with all their forces” (3). “And thus, having avoided every danger” (5c, e); “thus they dragged them” (5c, e). “Again plunged the fleet into the Seine” (6); “again plunged them into the waters of the Seine” (5c, e). “Leaving the Seine, they entered the Yonne” (1, 2); “leaving the Seine, they entered the Vienne” (one manuscript).]

But because the citizens resisted bravely, and God protected them, they were entirely unable to capture the aforesaid city, although they had repeatedly attempted it with every exertion and with every kind of skill in the use of machines and devices.

[Variant: “They did not obtain it, although…” (7, 9–12).]

During the very hardships of the siege, Everhard, metropolitan of that place, a man radiant with the splendor of complete holiness and wisdom, was released from the bonds of the body and passed to the heavenly homeland. Waltharius was raised to his episcopal seat, the nephew of Waltharius, bishop of Orléans, though he was far inferior to his predecessor in character, religious devotion, and devotion to philosophy.

[The passage beginning “During the very hardships of the siege” is absent from manuscript 4. “To his episcopal seat” is also transmitted as “to the episcopate” (1–3, 5).]

DCCCLXXXIX.

In the year 889 of the Lord’s incarnation, the Hungarian people, exceedingly savage and more cruel than any beast—a people previously unheard of in past ages because previously unnamed—emerged from the Scythian kingdoms and from the marshes that the Tanais, by its overflowing, extends to an immense distance.

[Variant readings: “The Hungarians” (2); “the kingdoms of the Hungarians” (9, 12); “the Scythian kingdoms” (5e, 2).]

Before we pursue the cruel deeds of that people with the pen, it may not seem superfluous, following the statements of historians concerning the situation of Scythia and the customs of the Scythians, to recall a few things.

Scythia, as they say, stretches toward the east. On one side it is enclosed by the Pontus, on another by the Riphaean Mountains, and at its rear by Asia and the river Ithasi.

[Ithasi is the reading of Justin’s manuscripts; Bongars introduced “Phasis” instead. The passage from “Scythia, as they say” through “they wear” is drawn from Justin, Book II, chapter 2.]

It extends greatly in length and breadth. Among the people who inhabit it there are no boundaries between one another, for they rarely cultivate the land. They have no houses, roof, or fixed dwelling, but always pasture herds and flocks and are accustomed to wander through uncultivated deserts.

They carry their wives and children with them in wagons, using leather coverings as shelters against rain and winter in place of houses.

[Variant readings: “They carry them in wagons” (5a, d). “Using wagons as shelters against rain” (4). “For the sake of winter, they use covered wagons as houses” (6).]

Among them no crime is more serious than theft. For, for people possessing flocks, herds, and provisions without the protection of a house, what would remain among the forests if theft were permitted?

[Variant readings: “What except gold would remain?” (5). “What besides the forests?” (4). “What would remain for them?” (3, 6). “What would remain?” (8, 9–12).]

They do not desire gold and silver in the same way as other mortals. They devote themselves to hunting and fishing, and they eat milk and honey.

[“They devote themselves to hunting and fishing” is absent from Justin. The passage is marked as an editorial addition.]

The use of wool and clothing is unknown to them. Although they suffer continual cold, they wear only the skins of wild animals and mice.

[Variant readings: “They are ignorant of the use of wool and clothing” (3); “of garments” (7).]

They sought the empire of Asia three times, yet remained forever either untouched or unconquered by foreign rule. They became famous no more for the courage of their men than for that of their women, since the men founded the Parthian and Bactrian kingdoms, while their women founded the kingdoms of the Amazons. Thus, for those considering the deeds of the men and women, it is uncertain which sex among them was the more illustrious.

[Variant readings: “Untouched by foreign rule” (2, 7); “unconquered” (5d); “unseen” (5d). “Which sex was more illustrious” (2).]

They drove Darius, king of the Persians, shamefully away from Scythia in flight; they slaughtered Cyrus with his entire army; and in the same manner they destroyed Sopirion, the commander of Alexander the Great, together with all his forces. They heard the weapons of the Romans but did not experience them.

They are hardened by labors and wars, and their bodily strength is immense.

[Variant: “The strength of their bodies” (3, 5). The passage from “They sought the empire of Asia” through “their bodily strength is immense” is from Justin, Book II, chapter 3.]

They abound in such a multitude of peoples that their native land is not sufficient to feed them. For the more the northern region is removed from the heat of the sun and chilled by snowy cold, the healthier it is for human bodies and the more suited to the propagation of peoples. Conversely, the nearer every southern region is to the sun’s heat, the more it always abounds in diseases and the less suitable it is for raising mortals.

Thus it happens that such multitudes of peoples arise beneath the northern axis that, not without reason, that entire region from the Tanais as far as the west is generally called Germania, although its individual places are also known by their own names.

[Variant readings: “The northern region” (1, 2, 4, 5, 7–12). “Beneath the northern axis” (1); “beneath the arch” (2, 3); “beneath the northern one” (3). “The region from the Tanais” (5); “the region from the Tanais River” (5). “Although individual places in it are called by their own names, the whole is often counted as Germania” (5c, e); “the whole is often named Germania” (1, 2, 5a, d); “the whole is often called Germania” (3, 4).]

From this populous Germania, countless bands of captives are frequently carried away and sold for a price to southern peoples. Many peoples have also often emerged from it, because it produces so many mortals that it can scarcely feed them; these peoples have afflicted not only parts of Asia but especially nearby Europe.

Everywhere, the cities destroyed throughout Illyricum and Gaul bear witness to this, but above all unhappy Italy, which has experienced the savagery of nearly all those peoples.

[Variant readings: “Wretched Italy” (3, 6). “Illyria” (5). The passage from “For the northern region” through “experienced the savagery of nearly all those peoples” is drawn from Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book I.]

## Complete source-ordered apparatus

The following register translates every supplied apparatus note in source order. Latin forms are retained because spelling, case, number, omission, and word order are often the substance of the reading; witness numbers and editorial attributions follow the supplied source.

- **N001 — at “whoever should succeed Carloman in his kingdom”.** `[Col. 0121] qui ei in regnum succ. 7. 9---12 qui ei in regnum ejus succ. 6.` — 7 and 9–12 read ‘who succeeded him in the kingdom’; 6 adds the possessive, ‘who succeeded him in his kingdom.’
- **N002 — at “in regnum invitant, eique advenienti ad Gundolfi”.** `[Col. 0121] gundulphi 4. gundfi 8. gundolphi 5.` — Name spellings: *Gundulphi* (4), corrupt/abbreviated *Gundfi* (8), and *Gundolphi* (5).
- **N003 — at “juxta morem datis, ejus ditioni se subjiciunt”.** `[Col. 0121] se subdiderunt 5.` — 5 reads ‘they submitted themselves.’
- **N004 — at “anno Nordmanni qui in Chinheim ex Denemarca”.** `[Col. 0121] chinheim et denemarca 2. 5a. d. chinheim et denemarcam 5c. e. denimarca 4. 7---12.` — Place-name and case variants: ‘Chinheim and Denmark’ (2, 5a,d), ‘Chinheim and Denemarca’ (5c,e), and *Denimarca* (4, 7–12).
- **N005 — at “venerant, absentiente Godefrido, Rhenum navigio”.** `[Col. 0121] rhenum in niumaga navigio cod. S. Godeh:` — The Saint-Godehard manuscript reads ‘by ship up the Rhine to Nijmegen.’
- **N006 — at “ascendunt, et Diusburch”.** `[Col. 0121] dinsburch 5. duspurch 11. 12. duusburh 7.` — Duisburg is spelled *Dinsburch* (5), *Duspurch* (11–12), and *Duusburh* (7).
- **N007 — at “loco more solito construunt, et in eo”.** `[Col. 0121] in ea 5.` — 5 reads ‘in it/her’ (*in ea*).
- **N008 — at “vernali tempore, castris exustis, maritimis locis”.** `[Col. 0121] exustis ad maritima loca 5c. e.` — 5c,e read ‘after burning [them/the camp], toward the coastal places.’
- **N009 — at “recipiunt. [His etiam diebus Nordmanni a Somna”.** `[Col. 0121] a sono 5.` — 5 reads ‘from the Sono’ (*a Sono*), a river-name variant.
- **N010 — at “Hlotharii revertentes, in loco qui dicitur Lovon”.** `[Col. 0121] louen 5.` — 5 spells Louvain *Louen*.
- **N011 — at “the place called Lovon”.** `[Col. 0121C] Löwen.` — Editorial identification: Löwen (Louvain).
- **N012 — at “confinio ejusdem regni, et continuis incursionum infestationibus”.** `[Col. 0121] continuis ejusdem regni infest. 1---3. 5. 6.` — 1–3, 5, and 6 read ‘with continual attacks upon that same kingdom.’
- **N013 — at “sed nihil dignum memoria adversus tantam violentorum”.** `[Col. 0121] violentiorum 5a. d.` — 5a,d read ‘of the more violent men.’
- **N014 — at “rapacitatem”.** `[Col. 0121] rapacitatem deest 2.` — The word *rapacitatem*, ‘rapacity,’ is omitted by 2.
- **N015 — at “actum est”.** `[Col. 0121] His etiam diebus etc. usque actum est deest 8---12. cf. infra a. 886.` — The whole clause from ‘In those same days’ through ‘was accomplished’ is omitted by 8–12; compare the annal for 886.
- **N016 — at “contra imperatorem, legatos ad Godefridum in Fresia”.** `[Col. 0121] frisiam 5c. e.` — 5c,e read the place-name in the accusative, *Frisiam* (‘Frisia’).
- **N017 — at “hortaturque ut in patriam mitteret, et auxiliatorum”.** `[Col. 0121] mitteret auxiliorum 5c. e. mitteret et auxiliorum 3---12.` — 5c,e read ‘he should send auxiliaries’; 3–12 have the awkward ‘he should send and [of] auxiliaries.’
- **N018 — at “ferret, quatenus regnum paternum evindicare armis potuisset”.** `[Col. 0121] posset 1---3. 5. 6.` — 1–3, 5, and 6 read ‘he might be able.’
- **N019 — at “fomitem inquirit, qualiter ac si justa ratione”.** `[Col. 0121] ac si juxta rationem 1---3. 5. 6.` — 1–3, 5, and 6 read ‘and as though according to reason.’
- **N020 — at “fidelitate imperatoris se subducere praevaleret, statimque Gerolfum”.** `[Col. 0121] gerolphum et gardolphum 1. 3. 5. c. d. gerulfum et gardulfum 4. gerulfum et cardulfum 8.` — Name spellings: Gerolf/Gardolf (1,3,5c,d), Gerulf/Gardulf (4), and Gerulf/Cardulf (8).
- **N021 — at “dirigit, mandatque, si vellet, ut in ea”.** `[Col. 0121] vellet cum ea 5.` — 5 reads ‘if he wished, with it/her.’
- **N022 — at “quam pollicitus fuerat”.** `[Col. 0121] pollicitus est 6.` — 6 reads ‘he promised.’
- **N023 — at “sibi commissos ab incursione propriae gentis defensaret”.** `[Col. 0121] defenderet 5c. e.` — 5c,e read ‘he would defend.’
- **N024 — at “Confluentes”.** `[Col. 0121] confluentem 4. 5.` — 4 and 5 read the accusative place-name *Confluentem* (Coblenz).
- **N025 — at “Andrenacum et Sincicha”.** `[Col. 0121] sucicha 5a. d. sucicham 5c. d.` — Sinzig appears as *Sucicha* (5a,d) and accusative *Sucicham* (5c,d).
- **N026 — at “et nonnullus alios fiscos obsequiis”.** `[Col. 0121] alios fines obsequiis 5.` — 5 reads ‘other territories devoted to services,’ instead of ‘other fiscal estates devoted to services.’
- **N027 — at “imperialibus deditos sibique”.** `[Col. 0121] sibi 3. 4. 8. 12.` — 3,4,8,12 read ‘to him’ (*sibi*), rather than the compound ‘and to himself.’
- **N028 — at “propter vini affluentiam, quae in his locis”.** `[Col. 0121] qui in his locis 7. 9---12.` — 7 and 9–12 read ‘which in these places,’ changing the relative clause’s attachment.
- **N029 — at “exuberabat”.** `[Col. 0121] locis erat 1---3. 5.` — 1–3 and 5 read ‘there was [wine] in the places.’
- **N030 — at “eo quod terra quam ex”.** `[Col. 0121] ex deest 7. 9---12.` — 7 and 9–12 omit *ex*, ‘from/by,’ before the prince’s generosity.
- **N031 — at “munificentia principis possidendam perceperat”.** `[Col. 0121] perciperet 2.` — 2 reads subjunctive *perciperet*, ‘he might receive,’ instead of ‘he had received.’
- **N032 — at “animi intentione, ut si petita sibi largirentur”.** `[Col. 0121] petita larg. 7. 9---12.` — 7 and 9–12 abbreviate the clause to ‘the requested things were granted.’
- **N033 — at “suos in visceribus regni immiscere”.** `[Col. 0121] immisceri 2. 5a. d. 7. 9---12.` — 2, 5a,d, and 7,9–12 read passive *immisceri*, ‘be mingled/inserted,’ rather than ‘mingle [his men].’
- **N034 — at “varios eventus speculari; si autem et denegarentur”.** `[Col. 0121] autem denegarentur 5. autem ei denegarentur 4. autem ea denegarentur 9---12.` — 5 reads ‘but were denied’; 4 ‘but were denied to him’; 9–12 ‘but those things were denied.’
- **N035 — at “nihilominus offensus in sibi prohibitis”.** `[Col. 0121] prohibitos 2. 3. 5.` — 2,3,5 read accusative *prohibitos*, yielding ‘offended at the persons/things forbidden,’ rather than ‘at what was forbidden him.’
- **N036 — at “quasi justitia dictante, rationabilius desaevire”.** `[Col. 0121] racionabilius dictante desevire 7.` — 7 reads ‘might rage more reasonably, with [justice] dictating,’ with the spelling *racionabilius/desevire*.
- **N037 — at “rebellionisque causas”.** `[Col. 0121] causa 5a. d. causam 1---3.` — 5a,d read singular nominative ‘cause’; 1–3 singular accusative ‘a cause,’ against plural ‘causes.’
- **N038 — at “introduxerat, extinguere posset, et sciens esse loca”.** `[Col. 0121] sciens loca 1---3. 5.` — 1–3 and 5 read ‘knowing the places [to be inaccessible].’
- **N039 — at “impenetrabiles paludes, magis in arte quam virtute”.** `[Col. 0121] quam ex virtute 1---5.` — 1–5 add *ex*: ‘more by art than from strength.’
- **N040 — at “quae sibi et eidem Godefrido essent decentia”.** `[Col. 0121] essent convenientia 4. 5.` — 4 and 5 read ‘were suitable/fitting.’
- **N041 — at “Heinricum ad eundem virum mittit; et ut”.** `[Col. 0121] mittit ut 5.` — 5 omits the conjunction: ‘he sends [him] so that…’
- **N042 — at “eo Willibertum, venerabilem episcopum Coloniae Agrippinae. Qui”.** `[Col. 0121C] Id est, Heinricus.` — The pronoun ‘who’ refers to Henry.
- **N043 — at “occurrerent, loco et die quo eis condixit”.** `[Col. 0121] quo eis concidit 1---3. quos eis constituit 6. quos eis edixit 5. quo se ei concidunt 7.` — Readings for the rendezvous: ‘where he met them’ (1–3), ‘which he appointed for them’ (6), ‘which he proclaimed to them’ (5), and corrupt ‘where they meet him’ (7).
- **N044 — at “ipse cum perpaucis Coloniam venit, et assumpto”.** `[Col. 0121] assumpto cum 5.` — 5 reads ‘having taken with [him],’ explicitly supplying ‘with.’
- **N045 — at “secum”.** `[Col. 0121] secum deest 1---3.` — 1–3 omit *secum*, ‘with him.’
- **N046 — at “praefato episcopo, mox in Batuam”.** `[Col. 0121] battuam 5d. baccuam 3.` — Batavia is spelled *Battua* (5d) and *Baccua* (3).
- **N047 — at “obviam procedit ad locum qui dicitur Herispich”.** `[Col. 0121] herispihc 2. herispirch 9. 11. 12. arispich 10.` — Herispich is spelled *Herispihc* (2), *Herispirch* (9,11,12), and *Arispich* (10).
- **N048 — at “the place called Herispich”.** `[Col. 0122C] Modo ibi exstat locus Heerwen.` — Editorial geographical note: the place now existing there is Heerwen.
- **N049 — at “Heinricus episcopum hortatur, ut die subsequenti Gislam”.** `[Col. 0123] gissam 5e. gisalam 7.` — The queen’s name is *Gissam* (5e) and *Gisalam* (7), accusative forms of Gissa/Gisala.
- **N050 — at “insulam evocaret, eamque ad pacis studium provocare”.** `[Col. 0123] studium revocare 2. 3. 5.` — 2,3,5 read ‘to recall her to zeal for peace,’ rather than ‘rouse her.’
- **N051 — at “satageret, interim ipse cum Godefrido causam Everhardi”.** `[Col. 0123] eberhardi 5.` — 5 spells Eberhard *Eberhardi*.
- **N052 — at “comitis agitaret, cujus rerum”.** `[Col. 0123] cui rerum 2. 5.` — 2 and 5 read ‘to whom the possession of property…,’ changing ‘whose property.’
- **N053 — at “et barbarae gentis homine durius et contumeliosius”.** `[Col. 0123] contumeliosis 5d.` — 5d reads plural/adjectival *contumeliosis*, ‘insulting [words].’
- **N054 — at “gladio eum summo annisu in capite percuteret”.** `[Col. 0123] percutit 4. 5.---Post vocem percuteret aliquid excidisse videtur, e. g. ab hominibus Heinrici protinus trucidandum.` — 4 and 5 read present *percutit*, ‘he strikes.’ The editor suspects lost words after *percuteret*, perhaps ‘to be killed at once by Henry’s men.’
- **N055 — at “Evarharde primo percussus, et a satellitibus Heinrici”.** `[Col. 0123] et satellitibus 5.` — 5 reads ‘and by the attendants,’ rather than ‘by Henry’s attendants.’
- **N056 — at “Nordmanni qui in Batua reperti sunt, trucidantur”.** `[Col. 0123] trucidabantur 7---12.` — 7–12 read imperfect passive ‘were being slaughtered.’
- **N057 — at “omnesque faventes dehonestantur. Post haec in Alamannia”.** `[Col. 0123] alamanniam 3. 5c. d. 7. 9---12.` — Alamannia appears in the accusative *Alamanniam* in 3,5c,d,7,9–12.
- **N058 — at “in monasterio”.** `[Col. 0123] monasterium 1? 3.-5. 7. 9---12.` — 1?,3–5,7,9–12 read accusative *monasterium*, ‘[sent] to the monastery.’
- **N059 — at “sancti Galli mittitur, inde postea”.** `[Col. 0123] interim postea 5d.` — 5d reads ‘meanwhile, afterward.’
- **N060 — at “in patriam revocatur; novissime, temporibus Zuendebolchi”.** `[Col. 0123] zuendebochi 1. zuendeboldi 3. zundibolchi 5. zeindibachi 7. 9. zunentibolchi 4. zuendibolcho 8. zendibachi 10. zendibachi 11. 12.` — Numerous spellings of King Zwentibold are transmitted: *Zuendebochi, Zuendeboldi, Zundibolchi, Zeindibachi, Zunentibolchi, Zuendibolcho,* and *Zendibachi* with the listed witnesses.
- **N061 — at “regis, in Prumia”.** `[Col. 0123] brumia 7.` — 7 spells Prüm *Brumia*.
- **N062 — at “Anno Dominicae incarnationis 886, Nordmanni”.** `[Col. 0123C] Cum eadem narratio supra an. 884 iisdem fere verbis occurrat, ibi tamen in codicibus 9-12 omittatur, Regino vagam illam sententiam, His [Col. 0124C] etiam diebus, veritate magis perspecta, omisisse, et narrationem suo loco restituisse videtur.` — Because nearly the same story occurs under 884 but is omitted there by 9–12, the editor thinks Regino later removed the vague opening ‘In those same days’ and restored the story to its proper year.
- **N063 — at “a Somna”.** `[Col. 0123] sanno 5a. sonno 5c. d.` — The Somme is written *Sanno* (5a) and *Sonno* (5c,d).
- **N064 — at “Hlotharii revertentes, in loco qui dicitur Lovon”.** `[Col. 0123] loven 5. ita et infra.` — 5 spells Lovon/Louvain *Loven* here and below.
- **N065 — at “tantam violentorum rapacitatem actum est. Eodem anno”.** `[Col. 0123] Eodem anno usque idus aug. deest 4.` — 4 omits the whole text from ‘In the same year’ through ‘the Ides of August.’
- **N066 — at “Julii, cui successit in regiminis loco Farabertus”.** `[Col. 0123] sarabertus 5.` — 5 reads the abbot’s name *Sarabertus*.
- **N067 — at “887, Nordmanni a Lovon recedentes Sequanam ingrediuntur”.** `[Col. 0123] ingrediuntur parisiis 5c. d. ingrediuntur, castra metati sunt in confinio ejusdem regni et parisius 9.---12.` — 5c,d read ‘they enter [the Seine] at Paris’; 9–12 add that they encamped on the kingdom’s border and [came to] Paris.
- **N068 — at “idem Heinricus cum exercitibus utriusque regni Parisius”.** `[Col. 0123] parisiis 5c. e. ita fere semper.` — 5c,e regularly use *Parisiis*, ‘at Paris.’
- **N069 — at “venit, et circumstantibus legionibus ipse cum perpaucis”.** `[Col. 0123] paucis 7. 8.` — 7 and 8 read simply ‘with a few,’ instead of ‘with very few.’
- **N070 — at “perquirit, quo exercitui cum hostibus minus periculosus”.** `[Col. 0123] periculosis 5a. d.` — 5a,d read plural *periculosis*, ‘dangerous [ways/encounters],’ rather than singular ‘less dangerous.’
- **N071 — at “concavis viarum itineribus, videntes Heinricum appropinquare, cito”.** `[Col. 0123] appropinquantem quare cito 5.` — 5 reads ‘seeing [Henry] approaching, why/wherefore quickly…’; the transmitted *quare* is awkward in context.
- **N072 — at “surgunt a locis in quibus”.** `[Col. 0123] locis quibus 4. 5.` — 4 and 5 read ‘from the places where [they had hidden].’
- **N073 — at “voce lacessunt. Ille animi magnitudine indignitatem rei”.** `[Col. 0123] rei deest 5.` — 5 omits *rei*, ‘of the matter,’ after ‘indignity.’
- **N074 — at “eos irruit, et mox in caecis foveis”.** `[Col. 0123] mox incertis foveis 1. 3. 5. mox incestis 2.` — 1,3,5 read ‘at once into uncertain/unseen ditches’; 2 has corrupt *incestis*, ‘unclean/incestuous,’ for the ditch adjective.
- **N075 — at “equus cui insidebat impegit, et cum ipso”.** `[Col. 0123] cum ipse 5a. d.` — 5a,d read ‘with himself’ (*cum ipse*) instead of ‘with him.’
- **N076 — at “in terram”.** `[Col. 0123] eum in terra 1. 5.` — 1 and 5 read ‘him onto the ground.’
- **N077 — at “corruit; hostes summa cum festinatione advolantes”.** `[Col. 0123] festinatione advolantes antequam deest in codd. 1---3; quorum loco cod. 3. post summa vocem celeritate inseruit.` — 1–3 omit ‘flying up in greatest haste, before…’; 3 instead inserts ‘swiftly’ after ‘greatest.’
- **N078 — at “et aspiciente universo exercitu, absque mora”.** `[Col. 0123] mora eum 5.` — 5 adds the object: ‘without delay [they slaughter] him.’
- **N079 — at “exanime eruitur, et a suis usque Suessionis”.** `[Col. 0123] sessionis 7. suuessionis 5a. d.` — Soissons is spelled *Sessionis* (7) and *Suuessionis* (5a,d).
- **N080 — at “deportatum”.** `[Col. 0123] deportatur 2. 5.` — 2 and 5 use present passive *deportatur*, ‘is carried away,’ instead of perfect ‘was carried.’
- **N081 — at “revertitur. Eodem tempore Hugo abba, magnae potestatis”.** `[Col. 0123] magnae pietatis 5.` — 5 reads ‘a man of great piety,’ rather than ‘great power.’
- **N082 — at “vir et”.** `[Col. 0123] vir magnae 7.` — 7 moves ‘man of great’ to the following phrase, yielding ‘a man of great prudence.’
- **N083 — at “Aurelianis moritur, et apud sanctum Germanum Antisiodoro”.** `[Col. 0123] autissioduro 2. autisiodure 1. antisiodoro 5. (8.) abisiodoro 7. autissiodoro 4. 9-12.` — Auxerre is transmitted as *Autissioduro, Autisiodure, Antisiodoro, Abisiodoro,* and *Autissiodoro* in the listed witnesses.
- **N084 — at “Ducatus quem tenuerat et strenue rexerat, Odoni”.** `[Col. 0123] adoni filio 1. 3.` — 1 and 3 read ‘to Odo, [Robert’s] son.’
- **N085 — at “Parisiorum comes erat, et cum Gozzilino”.** `[Col. 0125] gozlinus . . gozlini 1. 2. gozelinus . . gozelino 3.` — Gozlin’s name and case forms are *Gozlinus/Gozlini* (1,2) and *Gozelinus/Gozelino* (3).
- **N086 — at “in cujus loco substitutus est ab imperatore”.** `[Col. 0125] ab imperatore deest 7.` — 7 omits ‘by the emperor.’
- **N087 — at “Haschiricus”.** `[Col. 0125] aschiricus 4. haischericus 8. aschirinus 3.` — Bishop Haschiricus is spelled *Aschiricus* (4), *Haischericus* (8), and *Aschirinus* (3).
- **N088 — at “castra posuit, sed nil dignum imperatoria majestate”.** `[Col. 0125] imperatore majestati 2. imperatoris m. 6. imperatoriae majestati 9-12. imperator in 7.` — Majesty readings: 2 has corrupt ‘to the emperor, to majesty’; 6 ‘of the emperor’s majesty’; 9–12 ‘to imperial majesty’; 7 breaks the phrase as ‘the emperor in…’
- **N089 — at “in eodem loco gessit”.** `[Col. 0125] dignum ab imperatore in eodem loco factum est 3.` — 3 reads ‘nothing worthy was done by the emperor in that place.’
- **N090 — at “he went straight to Alamannia”.** `[Col. 0125] alamanniam recessit 5.` — 5 reads ‘he withdrew to Alamannia.’
- **N091 — at “Et primo quidem”.** `[Col. 0125] quidem tempore 1. 7.` — 1 and 7 add *tempore*: ‘at the first time.’
- **N092 — at “Liudwardum”.** `[Col. 0125] liutwardum 3. ludwardum 4. liwardum 8-10. lifardum 11. litsardum 12.` — Liudward’s name appears as *Liutwardum, Ludwardum, Liwardum, Lifardum,* and corrupt *Litsardum* in the listed witnesses.
- **N093 — at “quod reginae secretis familiarius quam oportebat immisceretur”.** `[Col. 0125] oportebat insereretur 6.` — 6 reads ‘because he was inserted [into the queen’s affairs] more intimately than was proper,’ a passive construction.
- **N094 — at “a suo latere cum dedecore”.** `[Col. 0125] decore 2.` — 2 reads *decore*, ‘with honor,’ rather than *dedecore*, ‘with disgrace.’
- **N095 — at “repulit; deinde paucis interpositis diebus, conjugem Richardem”.** `[Col. 0125] ricgardem 4.` — 4 spells the empress’s name *Ricgardem*.
- **N096 — at “re in concionem vocat, et, mirum dictu”.** `[Col. 0125] mira dictu 7. 9-12.` — 7 and 9–12 read neuter/plural *mira dictu*, ‘wonderful things to tell,’ rather than singular *mirum dictu*.
- **N097 — at “protestatur, nunquam se carnali coitu cum ea”.** `[Col. 0125] cum ea deest 1. 2. 5.` — 1,2,5 omit ‘with her’ from the denial of carnal intercourse.
- **N098 — at “fiducialiter adfirmat; erat enim religiosa femina. Facto”.** `[Col. 0125] femina ea acto 1. 5.` — 1 and 5 transmit corrupt *femina ea acto* around ‘she was a religious woman / the separation having been effected.’
- **N099 — at “dissidio, in monasterio”.** `[Col. 0125] monasterium 5. discidio in Andelam monasterium ancillarum Dei in Alsatia 8.` — 5 reads ‘to the monastery’; 8 expands: ‘after the separation, to Andlau, a monastery of God’s handmaids in Alsace.’
- **N100 — at “ab eo diffugere, Arnolfum, filium Carlomanni, ultro”.** `[Col. 0125] ultra 5d.` — 5d reads *ultra*, ‘beyond/further,’ instead of *ultro*, ‘of their own accord.’
- **N101 — at “qui saltem”.** `[Col. 0125] saltim 7. 9-12` — 7 and 9–12 spell *saltem* ‘at least’ as *saltim*.
- **N102 — at “officia humanitatis”.** `[Col. 0125] saltim vel verba humanitatis 7.` — 7 reads the awkward alternative *saltem vel verba humanitatis*, ‘at least, or words of human kindness.’
- **N103 — at “impenderet. Cibus tantum”.** `[Col. 0125] cibus tamen 1. 3. 5.` — 1,3,5 read ‘food, however,’ instead of ‘food alone.’
- **N104 — at “et potus ex Liudperti episcopi”.** `[Col. 0125C] Moguntini.` — Editorial identification: the bishop was of Mainz.
- **N105 — at “sumptibus administrabatur”.** `[Col. 0125] administrabatur illi 6.` — 6 adds the beneficiary: ‘was supplied to him.’
- **N106 — at “regna sine laborum sudoribus, sine laborum certaminibus”.** `[Col. 0125] sudoribus et certaminibus 5.` — 5 joins the two nouns under the repeated negative: ‘without exertions and struggles,’ rather than ‘without exertions, without struggles.’
- **N107 — at “postponendus, ita nunc adversa velut in ostentatione”.** `[Col. 0125] ostensione 5.` — 5 reads ‘in a display [of human frailty].’
- **N108 — at “fragilitatis humanae deficiens”.** `[Col. 0125] destruens 4. 7. 9-12.` — 4 and 7,9–12 read *destruens*, ‘destroying,’ rather than *deficiens*, ‘failing.’
- **N109 — at “quae fortuna”.** `[Col. 0125] fortuna deest 7. 9-12.` — 7 and 9–12 omit *fortuna*, ‘fortune,’ leaving the subject implicit.
- **N110 — at “reduced from emperor to needy man”.** `[Col. 0125] egenus ex 5.` — 5 reads ‘made needy from [being] emperor,’ emphasizing his fall from emperor to pauper.
- **N111 — at “dirigit etiam Bernhardum filium, quem ex pellice”.** `[Col. 0125] quem de pellice 6.` — 6 reads ‘whom he had by/from a concubine.’
- **N112 — at “susceperat, cum exeniis”.** `[Col. 0125] xeniis 5.` — 5 spells gifts *xeniis*.
- **N113 — at “etiam humanae opis egentem. Concessit autem ei”.** `[Col. 0125] deest 1. 5.` — 1 and 5 omit ‘to him’ in ‘Arnolf granted [to him].’
- **N114 — at “Arnolfus rex nonnullos fiscos”.** `[Col. 0125] fiscos cortis regia in 7.` — 7 reads ‘fiscal estates—the royal court—in Alamannia,’ an expanded description of the royal estates.
- **N115 — at “feliciter rebus, in Bajoariam revertitur. Eodem anno”.** `[Col. 0125] eodem anno usque successit deest 7.` — 7 omits the entire passage from ‘In the same year’ through ‘succeeded.’
- **N116 — at “et ei in episcopatu”.** `[Col. 0125] episcopatum 5.` — 5 reads accusative *episcopatum*, ‘succeeded to the episcopate.’
- **N117 — at “successit. DCCCLXXXVIII. Anno Dominicae incarnationis 888”.** `[Col. 0125] DCCCLXXXVIIII. 2. 10.` — 2 and 10 give the year as 889 (*DCCCLXXXVIIII*) instead of 888.
- **N118 — at “tertius hujus nominis et dignitatis, obiit pridie”.** `[Col. 0125] Legendum obiit die Idus Januar. CF. Ann. Fuld. et Necrologium Sangallense.` — Editorial correction: read ‘he died on the Ides of January’; compare the Annals of Fulda and the Saint-Gall necrology.
- **N119 — at “Idus Januar., sepultusque”.** `[Col. 0125] sepultusque in 7. 9-12.` — 7 and 9–12 add *in*: ‘was buried in…’
- **N120 — at “est in Augea”.** `[Col. 0125] augia 2. augia insula 3. cod. S. Godeh.` — Augea/Reichenau appears as *Augia* (2), ‘the island Augia’ (3), and likewise in the Saint-Godehard manuscript.
- **N121 — at “monasterio. Fuit vero hic”.** `[Col. 0125] deest 7. 9-12.` — 7 and 9–12 omit only *hic*, ‘this [prince],’ not the adjective ‘most Christian.’
- **N122 — at “Christianissimus princeps, Deum”.** `[Col. 0125] princeps Deum 4.` — 4 reads ‘the prince [fearing] God,’ changing the word order.
- **N123 — at “divinae dispensationi committens, unde et ei omnia”.** `[Col. 0125] omnia usque omnia deest 3.` — 3 omits the whole span from the first *omnia* (‘all things’) through the second *omnia*; no other witness is assigned this omission.
- **N124 — at “sine sanguinis effusione cum magno labore acquisierant”.** `[Col. 0127] in bonum cum labore acquisierant 7.` — 7 reads ‘which they had acquired for good with labor,’ displacing ‘for good’ from the following clause.
- **N125 — at “spatio sine conflictu, nullo contradicente, possidenda perceperit”.** `[Col. 0127] perceperat 7. 9-12.` — 7 and 9–12 read imperfect *perceperat*, ‘he had received,’ instead of perfect/subjunctive ‘he obtained.’
- **N126 — at “finem vitae dignitatibus nudatus bonisque omnibus spoliatus”.** `[Col. 0127] bonisque spoliatus 2.` — 2 abbreviates ‘stripped of all goods’ to ‘stripped of goods.’
- **N127 — at “ut ferunt, patientissime toleravit, in adversis sicuti”.** `[Col. 0127] toleravit in adversis, sicuti 5.` — 5 reads ‘he endured [it] in adversity, just as…’
- **N128 — at “et ideo coronam vitae, quam repromisit Deus”.** `[Col. 0127] quam promisit deus 3.` — 3 reads ‘which God promised,’ rather than ‘which God promised in return.’
- **N129 — at “each kingdom sought a king from its own midst”.** `[Col. 0127] unusquisque 7.` — 7 reads singular *unusquisque*, ‘each one,’ instead of neuter ‘each [kingdom].’
- **N130 — at “de suis visceribus regem sibi creari”.** `[Col. 0127] creare 9-12.` — 9–12 read infinitive *creare*, ‘to create,’ instead of passive ‘to be created [king].’
- **N131 — at “aequalitas generositatis, dignitatis ac potentiae discordiam augebat”.** `[Col. 0127] augebant 1. 2. 5.` — 1,2,5 use plural *augebant*: nobility, dignity, and power ‘increased discord.’
- **N132 — at “fortuna eos, aemulatione virtutis, in perniciem mutuam”.** `[Col. 0127] fortuna nos aemulatione . . . mutua 7.` — 7 reads ‘unless fortune had armed us/them, through rivalry in virtue, for mutual ruin’; *nos* is transmitted and awkward.
- **N133 — at “armasset. Igitur quaedam pars Italici populi Berengarium”.** `[Col. 0127] berngarium 9-12.` — 9–12 spell Berengar *Berngarium*.
- **N134 — at “filium Everhardi”.** `[Col. 0127] ennarhardi 5.` — 5 has corrupt *Ennarhardi* for Everhard.
- **N135 — at “qui ducatum Forojulanorum”.** `[Col. 0127] foro julianorum 5.` — 5 separates Friuli as *Foro Julianorum*, ‘the forum/territory of the Julians.’
- **N136 — at “tenebat, regem sibi statuunt, quaedam Widonem”.** `[Col. 0127] guidonem 5.` — 5 spells Wido *Guidonem* (Guido).
- **N137 — at “filium Lantperti, ducem Spolitanorum”.** `[Col. 0127] lantperti spolitanorum ducis (8.) 9-12.` — 8 and 9–12 read ‘Lambert, duke of the Spoletans,’ with genitive *ducis*.
- **N138 — at “humanus sanguis effusus, ut juxta Dominicam vocem”.** `[Col. 0127] vocem dominicam 7. 9-12.` — 7 and 9–12 reverse the order: ‘the word of the Lord.’
- **N139 — at “regno expulit. Pulsus itaque Arnolfum regem adiit”.** `[Col. 0127] itaque ad arnolfum 5. arnolfum adiit 3.` — 5 reads ‘therefore [he went] to Arnolf’; 3 ‘he went to Arnolf.’
- **N140 — at “qualiter Italiae regnum bis cum exercitu penetraverit”.** `[Col. 0127] penetravit 5d.` — 5d uses finite *penetravit*, ‘he penetrated,’ instead of subordinate ‘how he had penetrated.’
- **N141 — at “suo in loco”.** `[Col. 0127] suo loco 5.` — 5 reads ‘in its proper place.’
- **N142 — at “in unum congregati, cum consensu Arnolfi Odonem”.** `[Col. 0127] ottonem 5.` — 5 names Otto rather than Odo.
- **N143 — at “Nordmannorum indefessus propugnator extitit. Per idem tempus”.** `[Col. 0127] per id tempus 5.` — 5 reads ‘at that time.’
- **N144 — at “de quo supra meminimus, provinciam inter Jurum”.** `[Col. 0127] juram 5.` — 5 gives accusative *Juram* for the Jura.
- **N145 — at “et Alpes Penninas”.** `[Col. 0127] alpes apenninas 3.` — 3 reads ‘the Apennine Alps’ instead of the Pennine Alps.
- **N146 — at “occupat, et apud sanctum Mauritium”.** `[Col. 0127C] Saint-Maurice ad Rhodanum in Vallensium pago.` — Editorial identification: Saint-Maurice on the Rhône in the Valais district.
- **N147 — at “adscitis secum quibusdam primoribus”.** `[Col. 0127] prioribus.` — The unsigled printed reading is *prioribus*, ‘earlier men,’ against *primoribus*, ‘leading men’; it is not assigned to witness 5.
- **N148 — at “rupium locis salutis praesidium quaesivit; omnibus itaque”.** `[Col. 0127] omnibusque 5.` — 5 reads ‘and on all [the days].’
- **N149 — at “diebus vitae suae”.** `[Col. 0128C] Haec igitur post Zuendibaldi obitum scripta sunt.` — Editorial note: these words were written after Zwentibold’s death.
- **N150 — at “Ruodolfum persecuti sunt, nec tamen eum laedere”.** `[Col. 0127] tamen laedere 7. 9---12.` — 7 and 9–12 read ‘yet [they could not] injure him.’
- **N151 — at “loca inaccessibilia, quae in multis solis hibicibus”.** `[Col. 0127] quae solis ybicibus 3.` — 3 reads ‘which are passable only to ibexes.’
- **N152 — at “pervia sunt”.** `[Col. 0127] quae semitis tantam pervia 6.` — 6 transmits corrupt ‘which, by paths, [are] so passable,’ instead of ‘passable to ibexes.’
- **N153 — at “insequentium confertas acies”.** `[Col. 0127] consertas acies 1---8.` — 1–8 read *consertas acies*, ‘joined/close-packed battle lines,’ against *confertas*, ‘dense ranks.’
- **N154 — at “quatenus urbe post tergum relicta, classem cum”.** `[Col. 0127] classe et cum 3.` — 3 adds a conjunction: ‘the fleet and with all their forces.’
- **N155 — at “Sequanam sursum possent evehere, et sic Hionnam”.** `[Col. 0127] sursum possent evehere et sic hionnam deest 1---3. 5.` — 1–3 and 5 omit ‘could carry [the fleet] upstream and thus [enter] the Yonne.’
- **N156 — at “entering the river Hionna”.** `[Col. 0128C] Yonne.` — Editorial identification: *Hionna* is the Yonne.
- **N157 — at “plusquam duorum passuum milibus trahunt, et taliter”.** `[Col. 0127] trahunt taliter 5c. e.` — 5c,e read ‘they drag [the ships], and in this way…’
- **N158 — at “declinato omni periculo, iterum eas Sequanae”.** `[Col. 0127] ite rum classem Sequanae 6.` — 6 reads ‘again the fleet [into] the Seine,’ rather than ‘again them into the Seine’s waters.’
- **N159 — at “fluentis immergunt; et post”.** `[Col. 0127] immergunt. post 5c. e.` — 5c,e punctuate ‘they immerse [them]. After…’
- **N160 — at “paulum Sequanam relinquentes, Hionnam”.** `[Col. 0127] relinquentes in ennam 1. 2. r. in vi viennam.` — 1,2 read ‘leaving [them] in the Yonne’; one reading has ‘in the Vienne,’ both altering ‘leaving the Seine, [they enter] the Yonne.’
- **N161 — at “ut disposuerant”.** `[Col. 0127] disposuerant intrant 11. 12.` — 11 and 12 add present *intrant*: ‘as they had planned, they enter.’
- **N162 — at “Sed civibus fortiter repugnantibus, Deo protegente, nequaquam”.** `[Col. 0127] nequaquam usque quamquam deest 7.` — 7 omits the span from ‘by no means’ through ‘although.’
- **N163 — at “quanquam”.** `[Col. 0129] nequaquam eam obtinuerunt quanquam (7) 9.---12` — 7 and 9–12 read ‘they did not obtain it, although…’
- **N164 — at “et machinamentorum ingenio id multipliciter pertentassent. Inter”.** `[Col. 0129] Inter ipsas etc. deest 4.` — 4 omits the passage beginning ‘Amid the very…’ (the siege and the bishop’s death notice).
- **N165 — at “ad coelestem patriam transiit; in cujus cathedra”.** `[Col. 0129] cathedram 1 ---3. 5.` — 1–3 and 5 use accusative *cathedram*, ‘to the episcopal chair,’ rather than ablative ‘in the chair.’
- **N166 — at “philosophiae studio. DCCCLXXXIX. Anno Dominicae incarnationis 889”.** `[Col. 0129] DCCCLXXVIIII. 7. 9---12.` — 7 and 9–12 give the year as 879, a plainly divergent numeral for 889.
- **N167 — at “gens Hungarorum”.** `[Col. 0129] hungarium 2. ungarium 7.` — 2 spells ‘Hungarians’ *Hungarium*; 7 *Ungarium*.
- **N168 — at “inaudita quia nec nominata, a Scythicis regnis”.** `[Col. 0129] ungariorum 9. 12.` — 9 and 12 read ‘of the Hungarians’ (*Ungariorum*) where the printed text has ‘Scythian realms.’
- **N169 — at “et a paludibus quas Thanais”.** `[Col. 0129] scythis regnis 5e. scithis regnis 2.` — 5e and 2 read ‘from Scythian realms’ with spellings *Scythis/Scithis regnis*.
- **N170 — at “priusquam ipsius gentis acta crudelia stilo persequamur”.** `[Col. 0129] tanais 5c. e.` — 5c,e spell Tanais *Tanais* (without the printed aspirated form *Thanais*).
- **N171 — at “moribus historiographorum dicta sequentes, aliquid commemoremus. Scythia”.** `[Col. 0129C] Scythia ut aiunt usque induuntur desumpta ex Justino, lib. II, cap. 2.` — The span ‘Scythia, as they say’ through ‘they wear’ is taken from Justin, Book II, chapter 2.
- **N172 — at “ut aiunt, in orientem”.** `[Col. 0129] praesequamur 5a. d.` — 5a,d read *praesequamur*, ‘before we pursue [the narrative],’ instead of *persequamur*. Although printed here after *in orientem*, it belongs in sense to the preceding narrative-introduction clause.
- **N173 — at “extensa, includiditur”.** `[Col. 0129] oriente 1. 2. 4. 5. 7.---12.` — 1,2,4,5,7–12 read *oriente*, ‘on the east,’ relocating the geographical term from ‘extends toward the east’ to the following boundary clause.
- **N174 — at “altero-montibus Riphaeis, a tergo Asia et Ithasi”.** `[Col. 0129] induitur 5.` — 5 reads *induitur*, ‘is clothed/surrounded,’ apparently a displaced or corrupt variant of *includitur*, ‘is bounded’; the apparatus prints it here after *Ithasi*.
- **N175 — at “Asia and the river Ithasi”.** `[Col. 0129C] Ithasi, lectio codicum Justini, pro quo Bongars induxit phasi.` — Justin’s manuscripts read *Ithasi*; Bongars emended it to *Phasi* (the Phasis River).
- **N176 — at “multum in longitudinem et latitudinem. Hominibus hanc”.** `[Col. 0129] itasi 8. 11. 12. ethasi 7.` — The river-name forms are *Itasi* (8,11,12) and *Ethasi* (7).
- **N177 — at “et pecora semper pascentibus; et per incultas”.** `[Col. 0129] latitudinem, omnibus hanc 2. 5a. d.` — 2 and 5a,d displace words to ‘in breadth; all [the inhabitants]…’
- **N178 — at “Uxores liberosque secum in plaustris vehunt, quibus”.** `[Col. 0129] per multas 5a. d.` — 5a,d read ‘through many [wastes],’ instead of ‘through uncultivated wastes.’
- **N179 — at “coriis”.** `[Col. 0129] quibus deest 1---5a. d. 6---12.` — All listed witnesses omit *quibus*, ‘which/in which,’ before ‘covered with hides.’
- **N180 — at “causa tectis”.** `[Col. 0129] carris imbrium 4. tecti 9---12.` — 4 reads ‘wagons against the rains’; 9–12 read ‘covered,’ changing the attachment of the participle.
- **N181 — at “pro domibus”.** `[Col. 0129] hiemis causa pro tectis domibusqus 6.` — 6 reads ‘for winter, [using] covered wagons as houses.’
- **N182 — at “tecti munimento pecora et armenta alimentaque habentibus”.** `[Col. 0129] habent. Aurum 5. quid nisi silva 7. quid praeter silvas 4. quid illis 3. 6. quid eis superesset 8. quid superesset 9---12.` — Readings after ‘they have’: 5 begins ‘Gold’; 7 ‘what except woodland’; 4 ‘what besides woods’; 3,6 ‘what would remain for them’; 8 ‘what would remain to them’; 9–12 ‘what would remain.’
- **N183 — at “inter silvas superesset, si furari liceret? Aurum”.** `[Col. 0129] si figurari liceret aurum 2.` — 2 reads corrupt ‘if it were permitted to fashion [it], gold…’ instead of ‘if it were permitted to steal, gold…’
- **N184 — at “mortales appetunt, venationum et piscationum exercitiis inserviunt”.** `[Col. 0129C] Venationum et piscationum exercitiis inserviunt. [Col. 0130C] Haec desiderantur in Justino.` — The sentence ‘They devote themselves to hunting and fishing’ is absent from Justin and is an addition in this text.
- **N185 — at “vescuntur. Lanae his usus ac vestium ignotus”.** `[Col. 0129] lanae usus ac vestium ignari sunt 3. vestimentorum 7.` — 3 reads ‘they are ignorant of the use of wool and clothing’; 7 substitutes ‘garments.’
- **N186 — at “pellibus tantum ferinis ac murinis induuntur. Imperium”.** `[Col. 0130C] Imperium Asiae usque corporum immensae, ex Justino lib. II, cap. 3.` — The span ‘They sought the empire of Asia’ through ‘immense strength of body’ is from Justin, Book II, chapter 3.
- **N187 — at “ipsi perpetuo ab alieno imperio aut intacti”.** `[Col. 0129] inacti 2. 7.` — 2 and 7 read *inacti*, ‘inactive,’ instead of *intacti*, ‘untouched [by foreign rule].’
- **N188 — at “invicti”.** `[Col. 0129] invisi 5d.` — 5d reads *invisi*, ‘unseen/hated,’ instead of *invicti*, ‘unconquered.’
- **N189 — at “sit, uter apud eos sexus illustrior fuerit”.** `[Col. 0129] inlustrior sit 2.` — 2 uses present subjunctive: ‘which sex may be more illustrious.’
- **N190 — at “Darium, regem Persarum, turpi a Scythia summoverunt”.** `[Col. 0129] summa moverunt 2. 5d.` — 2 and 5d corrupt ‘drove [Darius] from Scythia’ (*summoverunt*) as *summa moverunt*, ‘moved the highest things.’
- **N191 — at “omni exercitu trucidaverunt, Alexandri Magni ducem Sopiriona”.** `[Col. 0129] zopyriona 5c. e.` — 5c,e spell Zopyrion *Zopyriona*.
- **N192 — at “pari ratione”.** `[Col. 0129] patri ratione 2.` — 2 has corrupt *patri ratione*, ‘by the father’s method,’ for *pari ratione*, ‘in like manner.’
- **N193 — at “arma. Laboribus et bellis asperi, vires corporum”.** `[Col. 0129] corporis 3. 5.` — 3 and 5 read singular ‘strength of the body.’
- **N194 — at “eos genitale solum non sufficiat alere. Septemtrionalis”.** `[Col. 0130C] Septentrionalis usque experta saevitiam, ex Pauli Diac. Hist. Langob. lib. I.` — The span ‘The northern region’ through ‘experienced [their] savagery’ is taken from Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book I.
- **N195 — at “et propagandis gentibus coaptata; sicut et contra”.** `[Col. 0129] et econtra 5.` — 5 adds *et*: ‘and conversely.’
- **N196 — at “unde fit, ut tantae populorum multitudines arcto”.** `[Col. 0129] actos 1. archos 2 archi 3.` — The northern-axis phrase appears as corrupt *actos* (1), *archos* (2), and *archi* (3), against *arcto* (‘northern’).
- **N197 — at “non immerito universa illa regio Thanai tenus”.** `[Col. 0129] thanaitenus deest 7. 9---12. regio a thanai fluvio 5.` — 7 and 9–12 omit ‘as far as the Tanais’; 5 reads ‘the region from the river Tanais.’
- **N198 — at “nuncupentur nominibus, generali tamen vocabulo Germania vocitetur”.** `[Col. 0129] germaniae sepe annumerabitus 5c, e. germaniae saepe innumerabitur 1. 2. 5a. d. germania nominetur 3. germaniae saepe nominetur 4.` — Germania clause variants: 5c,e ‘is often counted among Germania’ (corrupt spelling); 1,2,5a,d ‘will often be counted as Germania’; 3 ‘is named Germania’; 4 ‘is often named Germania.’
- **N199 — at “Ab hac ergo populosa Germania saepe innumerabiles”.** `[Col. 0129] vocabulo nortmanniae saepe innumerabiles 7.` — 7 reads ‘under the name Northmania, often innumerable [bands]…,’ changing Germania to Northmania.
- **N200 — at “captivorum turmae abductae, meridianis populis pretio distrahuntur”.** `[Col. 0129] pretio traduntur 5.` — 5 reads ‘are handed over for a price’ rather than ‘are sold/distributed for a price.’
- **N201 — at “ea, pro eo quod tantos mortalium germinat”.** `[Col. 0129] germinae 5a. d.` — 5a,d have corrupt *germinae* for *germinat*, ‘produces.’
- **N202 — at “hoc ubique urbes erutae per totam Illyricum”.** `[Col. 0129] illiriam 5.` — 5 reads *Illiriam*, a spelling of Illyricum/Illyria.
- **N203 — at “Galliamque, sed maxime miserae Italiae”.** `[Col. 0129] misera italia 3. 6.` — 3 and 6 read singular ‘wretched Italy,’ rather than genitive ‘of wretched Italy.’

From the aforesaid places, therefore, the people in question were driven from their own settlements by neighboring peoples called the Pechenegs [Note: [Col. 0129] *Pecinati* in witness 2; *Pezinati* in 6; *Pecenati* in 7; *Pecenaci* in 8–12. *Vocabuntur* in 7.], because they surpassed them in number and strength, and because their native land, as we have said above, was overflowing with such a multitude [Note: [Col. 0129] “Overflowing with such a multitude” is absent in witness 3.] that it was insufficient for habitation. Driven out, then, by their violence, they set out to seek lands that they might inhabit and establish as settlements, bidding farewell to their homeland. At first, wandering through the wastelands of the Pannonians and Avars [Note: [Col. 0131] “Of the Pannonians and roads” in witness 7.], [Note: [Col. 0131] “The wasteland of the Avars” in witness 7.], they sought their daily sustenance by hunting and fishing [Note: [Col. 0131] “And by grazing” in witnesses 2, 5a, d, and 9–12.]; then they burst into the territories of the Carantanians, Moravians, and Bulgars [Note: [Col. 0131] “Bulgars” in witnesses 4, 5, 7, and 8.] with repeated incursions, killing very few by the sword but many thousands with arrows, which they shoot from horn bows with such skill that their blows can scarcely be guarded against.

For they do not know how to fight at close quarters in battle formation or to take cities by siege [Note: [Col. 0131B] “At close quarters … you must face danger,” from Justin, book XLI, chapter 2.]. They fight either by advancing their horses or by turning their backs [Note: [Col. 0131] “They fight or” in witness 2.]; often, too, they pretend to flee, and they cannot fight for long. Otherwise they would be unbearable if their strength and endurance were as great as their attack. Usually, in the very heat of battle [Col. 0131B], they abandon the fighting and shortly afterward renew the combat from their flight, so that precisely when you think you have won, you must then face danger. Their manner of fighting is all the more dangerous because it is unfamiliar to other peoples [Note: [Col. 0131] “More unfamiliar” in witnesses 3–6.]. The only difference between their conflict and that of the Britons is that the former use missiles, while the latter use arrows.

They live not in the manner of human beings but of beasts. For, as rumor has it [Note: [Col. 0131] “For indeed” is absent in witnesses 2 and 5.], they eat raw meat, drink blood, and, dividing into pieces the hearts of the people whom they capture, devour them as though for a remedy. They are moved by no compassion and stirred by no bowels of pity. They cut their hair with iron down to the skin [Note: [Col. 0131] “They ride horses at all times” is absent from the manuscripts and all editions alike. Manuscript 1 has: “They cut the hair down to the skin, and usually ride upon them, deliberate, halt, and converse”; 2: “They cut the hair down to the vine, and usually ride upon them and converse”; 3: “They usually curry horses excessively”; witness 6 has supplied nothing, and therefore, together with 5, 7, and 9–12, should be read as: “They neither cut the hair down to the skin with iron, nor usually ride upon them, deliberate, halt, and converse”; 4: “They cut the hair with iron up to the crown. They usually ride upon them, halt, measure out, and converse”; 8 finally: “They cut the hair down to the skin, and usually ride horses, halt, converse, and deliberate. I am prevented from accepting the reading of the Saxon annalist, which seems to restore the text with the slightest alteration, because Regino’s words are not copied by the annalist with such fidelity but are usually abridged or altered. Since the word ‘them’ also occurs in the complete sentence of Justin, and since the disagreement of the manuscripts shows that not one corrupted word but several have dropped out at this point, I sought a remedy from Justin himself. Yet, considering Regino’s practice in adopting the words of others, I did not think that Justin’s complete sentence should be accepted, for I very much doubted whether the words ‘They ride horses at all times; horses are their battles, their banquets, their public and private duties’ would also suit the Hungarians. Moreover, the editions of Justin have not *deliberate* but *trade*, to which manuscript 4, the Annals of Metz, comes closest with *measure out*. That *deliberate* is the genuine reading of both Justin and Regino is established sufficiently and abundantly by the connection of the sentences.”]. They ride horses at all times [Note: [Col. 0131B] “They ride horses at all times” through “they usually,” from Justin, book XLI, chapter 3.]; they usually ride upon them, deliberate, halt, and converse.

They teach their free men and slaves to ride and shoot arrows with great diligence [Note: [Col. 0131B] “Free men … teach,” ibid., chapter 2.] [Note: [Col. 0131] “To ride and shoot” in witnesses 1–3, 5, 6?, and 7.]. Their minds are swollen, seditious, deceitful, and precocious [Note: [Col. 0132B] “Their minds” through “more ready to act than to speak,” from Justin, book XLI, chapter 3, where, however, the reading is: “For they assign violence to men and gentleness to women.”]. For they assign the same ferocity to women as to men; they are always restless, whether in external or domestic disturbances, silent by nature, and readier to act than to speak [Note: [Col. 0131] “Readier” in witnesses 1, 5, and 6?]. By the cruelty of this most accursed people, therefore, not only the regions mentioned but also the kingdom of Italy was devastated for the greater part.

In the same year the Northmen withdrew from the city of Sens and came again to Paris with all their forces. When the citizens completely prevented their descent down the river [Note: [Col. 0131] “Course” in witnesses 1–3 and 5.], they once more established their camp and attacked the city with all their strength, but, with God providing aid, they accomplished nothing. After a few days they again sailed up the Seine with their fleet, entered the river Marne, burned the city of Troyes with fire, and ravaged everything around them as far as the cities of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0131] “Verdensem” in witness 5; “Virdenensem” in witness 2.] and Toul [Note: [Col. 0131] “Ravaging” in witnesses 2 and 5.].

In those same days Liudpert, bishop of the city of Mainz, was taken from human affairs [Note: [Col. 0131] “Bishop from affairs” in witnesses 1–3 and 5.]. In his place Sunzo [Note: [Col. 0131] “Sinzo” in witness 7.] was appointed, a religious and simple man, sufficiently instructed in sacred letters [Note: [Col. 0131] “Sufficiently instructed” in witnesses 1–3 and 5.], who had been brought up and lived from early youth in the monastery of Fulda [Note: [Col. 0131] “In Fulda” in witnesses 1, 3, 5, and 8–12.] under the rule of an abbot [Note: [Col. 0131] “Had lived there” in witness 5.] [Note: [Col. 0131] “Had been … through the support” is absent in witnesses 1–3, 5, and 8–12.], through the support of Boppo [Note: [Col. 0131] Also written *Bobpo* in witnesses 1 and 2, *Poppo* in 3 and 6, *Boppo* in 7, and *Poppo* in 5 and 8–12.], duke of the Thuringians, and with the approval of King Arnolf.

## 890

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 890 [Note: [Col. 0131] “891” in witness 7.], King Arnolf granted to Zuendibold [Note: [Col. 0131] The name appears variously as *Zuendibolch*, *Zundeboldus*, *Zundibolch*, and *Zundibohlc* in witness 2; *Cendebolt* in 3; *Zundebolch* and *Zundeboldus* in 5; *Zuendiboldus* and *Zuendibolche* in 7; *Zuentibolh* and *Zuentibolcus* in 4; *Zuendibolh* and *Zuendibolc* in 8; and *Zendebolch*, *Zendibolch*, and *Zuendibolch* in 9–12.], king of the Moravian Slavs, the duchy of the Bohemians, who until then had had a prince of their own lineage and people over them and had preserved their promised fidelity to the kings of the Franks by an unbroken treaty [Note: [Col. 0131] “They preserved” in witnesses 5a and d.], because he had been bound to him by friendship before he was raised to the summit of royal power. Finally, he lifted from the sacred font his son, whom he had begotten by a concubine, and had him called Zuendibold after his own name.

This event provided no small stimulus for discord and defection. For the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0133] “Bohemians” in witness 4, again in 4, and in 7–12; *Boheimi* in 2; *Bohemani* in 3; *Bohemi* in 5; *Boemi* in 8–12.] also withdrew from the allegiance they had maintained for so long, and Zuendibold, perceiving that considerable strength had accrued to him through the addition of another kingdom, was puffed up by arrogant pride and rebelled against Arnolf. When Arnolf learned this, he entered the kingdom of the Moravians with an army and cut down to the ground everything he found outside the cities. Finally, when the other fruit-bearing trees also began to be cut down by the roots [Note: [Col. 0133] “Finally, while the others …” in witness 5; “Finally, and the others …” in witnesses 1, 2, and 9–12; “Finally, then, and the others …” in witness 7; “Finally, and so forth …” in witness 6.], Zuendibold asked for peace [Note: [Col. 0133] “Asks for peace” in witness 5.], and, having given his son as a hostage, obtained it only late [Note: [Col. 0133] “This peace” in witness 5.].

At the same time the Northmen left the Marne and returned to Paris. Since the descent of the river was entirely blocked by the bridge [Note: [Col. 0133] “By the bridge” is absent in witness 3.], they established their camp for the third time and again attacked the aforesaid city. But the citizens, hardened by the continuous labor of construction [Col. 0133B] and watchfulness [Note: [Col. 0133] “For the citizens, hardened by the continuous labor of construction” in witness 5.] and trained by the constant conflicts of war, resisted boldly [Note: [Col. 0133] “Audaciously” in witnesses 7–12.]. The Northmen, their affairs desperate, dragged their ships overland with great toil and, thus regaining the riverbed, crossed by fleet to the shores of Britain.

They besieged a certain castle in the territory of Coutances [Note: [Col. 0133] “Constantinensis” and similar forms in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], [Note: [Col. 0133C] Coutances.], called Saint-Lô [Note: [Col. 0133C] Saint-Lô.]. Completely cutting off access to the spring, they caused the townspeople to waste away from thirst, and a surrender followed, on the terms that, with their lives alone granted, everything else would be taken. When the Northmen had left the fortification, the treacherous people violated the faith and promise they had given [Note: [Col. 0133] “Violated” in witnesses 7–12.] and slaughtered everyone without restraint; among them they killed the bishop of the church of Coutances.

At that time there was a considerable dispute between Alan and Indicheil, dukes of the Britons [Note: [Col. 0133] “Dukes” in witnesses 2, 5a, and d.], concerning the division of the kingdom [Col. 0133C]. In this schism [Note: [Col. 0133] “Schism” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.] and division, the pagan Northmen, finding the Britons divided not so much in lands as in minds [Note: [Col. 0133] “Mountains” in witnesses 5c and e.], attacked them confidently. While the Britons waged each man’s private war rather than a common war for all [Note: [Col. 0133] “A common war for everyone” in witnesses d, b, and 7–12.] and each refused to bring aid to the other, as though the victory of one would not belong to all, they were grievously harmed by the enemy; they were cut down everywhere, and all their possessions were plundered as far as the river Blavet [Note: [Col. 0133] “As far as Blavilla” in witness 1; “Blavita” in 3 and 5; “Blaverta” in 7.], [Note: [Col. 0134C] Blavet, at whose mouth lie Port-Louis and Lorient.].

Then, for the first time understanding how great a ruin discord brought upon themselves and how much strength it gave their adversaries [Note: [Col. 0133] “Would administer” in witnesses 5a and d.], they confirmed one another through messengers, announced the time and place for setting out [Note: [Col. 0133] “They announced the place to him” in witness 5.], and prepared for war with united forces. Thus Judicheil, who was the younger, wishing to exalt the glory of his name [Note: [Col. 0133] “Of his name” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], engaged in battle without waiting for Alan and his companions, killed many thousands of the enemy, and forced the rest to flee to a certain village. When he imprudently pursued them farther than was proper, he was killed by them, unaware that to conquer is good [Note: [Col. 0133] “Ignorant that victory is good” in witness 5.], but to over-conquer is not [Note: [Col. 0133] “To prevail completely is not good” in witness 5.]; for despair is dangerous.

After this Alan, having gathered all Britain, made such a vow that, if by divine power he could overcome his adversaries, he would send a tenth part of all his goods to God and Saint Peter at Rome. When all the Britons likewise promised this vow, he advanced to battle and, when the fighting began, routed the enemy with such slaughter [Note: [Col. 0133] “Poured out” in witnesses 4 and 5.] that scarcely four hundred men out of fifteen thousand [Note: [Col. 0133] “Out of twelve thousand” in witnesses 3, 7, and 9–12.] returned to the fleet.

At this time, when the most holy and most prudent bishop Willibert, wise in divine and human affairs [Col. 0134B], had been taken from this life [Note: [Col. 0133] “At this time … the bishop” is absent in witness 4.], Herimannus [Note: [Col. 0133] “Hermannus” in witnesses 1 and 5.], a venerable man, was placed over the church of Cologne by election of the clergy and people [Note: [Col. 0133] “Of the clergy and people” is absent in witness 7.]. Around this same time Salomon [Note: [Col. 0133] “Salemon” in witness 3.], bishop of the church of Constance, departed from the world. He was succeeded by Salomon, who at that time held the abbacy of Saint Gall, a man distinguished not only by nobility but also by the virtues of prudence and wisdom; he is recognized as the third bishop of that city to bear this name [Note: [Col. 0133] “Of that same name” in witnesses 7 and 9–12; “of this name” in witnesses 2 and 5.].

## 891

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 891 [Note: [Col. 0133] “890” in witnesses 2, 9, 11, and 12.], the Northmen, severely weakened by two successive battles in Britain, transferred their fleet to the kingdom of Lothar and, having pitched camp [Note: [Col. 0133] “Having pitched camp” in witnesses 5, 6, 7, and 9–12.], set about plundering. King Arnolf sent an army against them and ordered it to pitch its tents above the Meuse and prevent the enemy from crossing the river.

But before the army could assemble at the appointed place near the castle of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 0134C] Maastricht.], the Northmen, holding the upper reaches, crossed the Meuse near Liège. Leaving the hostile expedition behind them, they dispersed through the woods and marshes adjoining the palace at Aachen; they killed everyone they met and seized numerous wagons and vehicles in which provisions were being carried to the army [Note: [Col. 0133] “Numerous” is absent in witnesses 4 and 5.].

When news of this reached the army, which had almost assembled on that very day, the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0133] “Almost” is absent in witness 6; “well” in witness 7.], not so much trembling as astonishment seized everyone’s minds. The princes summoned an assembly and deliberated not so much about the danger as about the uncertain situation [Col. 0135A], unsure whether the Northmen, entering the territory of the Ripuarians [Note: [Col. 0135C] “Unsure whether”—namely, whether the Northmen were heading toward the territory of the Ripuarians, and so forth.], were making for Cologne [Note: [Col. 0135] “Ripuarians” in witness 7.], or, crossing through Prüm, were directing their course toward Trier [Note: [Col. 0135] “Trier” in witnesses 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 12; “Prüm” in witness 2; “directing their course” in witnesses 7–12.], or, fearing the multitude gathered against them [Note: [Col. 0135] “The multitude gathered” in witnesses 1–5 and 11.], were crossing the Meuse and hastening to their fleet. Meanwhile night came on and dissolved the assembly.

The next day, when dawn displayed the rays of its light [Note: [Col. 0135] “When dawn grew bright” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], all armed themselves and, raising their standards, marched equipped for battle downstream [Note: [Col. 0135] “Downstream, in hope” in witness 6.]; [Note: [Col. 0135] “Equipped” is absent in witnesses 1–5 and 8.]. When they had crossed the torrent called the Geule [Note: [Col. 0135] “Gulid” in witness 5; “Jugila” in 3.], [Note: [Col. 0135C] It flows into the Meuse near Maastricht, today called the Geule.], the battle lines halted together. They then decided, so that the entire army would not be wearied to no purpose [Note: [Col. 0135] “So that it would be wearied” in witnesses 2, 6, and 8; “but so that it would be …” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], that each nobleman should send twelve of his men, who, formed into one column, would seek out the enemy.

While they were discussing this, the Northmen’s scouts suddenly appeared [Col. 0135B] [Note: [Col. 0135] “Suddenly” is absent in witnesses 7–12.]. When the whole multitude, without consulting its leaders, pursued them in confused order, it encountered bands of infantry in a certain little village [Note: [Col. 0135] “A certain village” in witnesses 1 and 2; “a certain farm” in witness 3.]. The infantry, gathered into one mass, easily drove back those who came upon them scattered and forced them to retreat [Note: [Col. 0135] “While they pursued … they encountered” in witness 5.].

Then, as the quivers rattled according to custom, a cry was raised to heaven and battle was joined. The Northmen’s horsemen, hearing the shouting, hurried up with the utmost speed, and, as the battle grew heavier [Note: [Col. 0135] “With the battle made heavier” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], the Christian army, because of its sins, alas, turned its back. In that battle Sunzo, bishop of the city of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0135] “Of Mainz” in witness 5; “of the city of Mainz” in witness 7.], and Count Arnolf fell, along with an innumerable multitude of noblemen. After achieving victory, the Northmen stormed the camp, filled with every kind of wealth [Note: [Col. 0135] “Filled with every kind of wealth” in witnesses 1 and 2.], slaughtered those whom they had captured in battle, and returned to their fleet laden with booty. This slaughter took place on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0135] “The seventh day before the Kalends” in witnesses 7–12.].

While these things were happening, King Arnolf was staying in the borderlands of Bavaria, suppressing the insolence of the Slavs. When the slaughter of his men and the victory of the enemy were reported to him, he first grieved excessively over the faithful who had been lost [Note: [Col. 0135] “Was saddened” in witnesses 7–12.] and, with a groan, voiced his complaint that the Franks, hitherto unconquered [Note: [Col. 0135] “Until then” in witnesses 1, 3, 4, and 5.], had turned their backs on their adversaries. Then, turning the disgrace of the event over in his spirited heart [Note: [Col. 0135] “Turning the event over in his mind” in witnesses 7–12.], he was inflamed against the enemy. He gathered an army from the eastern kingdoms, quickly crossed the Rhine, and established his camp along the banks of the Meuse.

After several days the Northmen, elated by their previous battle, set out with all their strength to plunder. The king advanced against them with troops equipped for battle. Seeing the battle lines approach, they fortified themselves in their customary manner with wood and a mound of earth beside the river called the Dyle [Note: [Col. 0135C] Dyle.], and taunted the army with laughter and reproaches, repeating amid insults and mockery that they should remember the Geule, their shameful flight, and the slaughter they had inflicted, since they would shortly suffer the same things.

The king, angered to fury, ordered the army to descend and fight the adversaries on foot [Note: [Col. 0135] “To be fought” in witnesses 2, 4, 5a, d, and 9–12.]. They immediately leapt down from their horses, gave a shout of encouragement, burst into the enemy’s fortification, and, as God supplied them strength from heaven, cut them down with the sword to the point of annihilation [Col. 0136B] [Note: [Col. 0135] “They burst in and cut them down to destruction” in witness 6.] and cast them upon the ground, so that from the innumerable multitude scarcely anyone remained to carry adverse news back to the fleet. Having successfully completed the undertaking, Arnolf returned to Bavaria.

In the same year Hatto [Note: [Col. 0135] Also *Hattho* in witness 2; *Atho* in 7; *Hatho* in 9; *Atto* in 10.], a venerable abbot, was consecrated metropolitan of the church of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0135] “Metropolitan bishop” in witness 2 and in 9–12.]. Until then he had been the father of many monks in the monastery of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0135] “He was” in witnesses 5, 7, and 9–12.].

## 892

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 892 [Note: [Col. 0135] “891” in witness 10.], in the month of February, the Northmen who had remained with the ships crossed the Meuse, entered the district of the Ripuarians [Note: [Col. 0135] “They entered and” in witnesses 4 and 5.], and, devouring everything according to the cruelty innate in them, reached as far as Bonn [Note: [Col. 0135] “Bonn” in witness 5; “as far as Bonn” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.].
