From there they departed and occupied a certain village called Landulfesdorf [Note: [Col. 0135] The name appears as *Landulfesdorph* in witness 1; *Landulfestorph* in 2; *Landolfasdorf* in 7; *Landuluestorph* in 4; *Landolfestorp* in 8; *Landolfesdorf* in 9, 11, and 12; *Landofesdort* in 10; and *Landolfesdorff* in 5; “is called” in witness 5.], [Note: [Col. 0136C] Hontheim thinks that this is the present-day Leudesdorf opposite Andernach, on the right bank of the Rhine (History of Trier I, p. 220a); but I should think it must be sought on the left bank, from our passage.], where a Christian army met them, but accomplished nothing worthy of being ascribed to valor [Note: [Col. 0135] “Anything worthy of valor” in witness 5d.].

When night came, the Northmen withdrew from the aforesaid village. Fearing an enemy attack, they did not dare to commit themselves to more open and level country [Note: [Col. 0135] “To more open and level places” in witnesses 7–12; “open or level places” in witness 8.], but always kept to the woods. Leaving the army behind them on their left and to the rear, they directed their battle line with all possible speed toward the monastery of Prüm [Note: [Col. 0135] “Of Prüm” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4.]. As they were already rushing upon it [Note: [Col. 0135] “Already” is absent in witness 5.], the abbot and the community of brothers scarcely escaped by flight.

The Northmen entered the monastery, ravaged everything, killed some of the monks, slaughtered a great number of the household, and led the rest away captive [Note: [Col. 0137] “Led them away” in witnesses 4 and 5.]. Leaving from there, they entered the Ardennes, where they attacked a certain castle newly built on a prominent mountain, into which an innumerable multitude of common people had fled [Note: [Col. 0137] “Into which” in witnesses 1–5.]. They stormed it without delay and, after killing everyone [Note: [Col. 0137] “After the people had been killed” in witnesses 1, 2, 5, and 9–12.], returned to the fleet with immense booty. With their ships laden and all their forces aboard, they returned to the lands across the sea.

At the same time Farabert, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, voluntarily laid down the pastoral office with the king’s permission [Note: [Col. 0137] “For the same time … we shall take care to record” is absent in witness 4.], and I, although unworthy, succeeded him in the administration by election of the brothers, according to regular authority. I did not, however, remain there long [Note: [Col. 0137] “In which, nevertheless, I remained” through “I endured” is absent in witnesses 1–3 (and perhaps 4) and 6.]; through the actions of rivals, I had to endure Richarius, the brother of Gerhard and Mathfrid [Note: [Col. 0137] The names appear as *Gerahrdi and Mahtfridi* in witness 7; *Gerardi et Mathfredi* in 10; after *Gerhardi*, the words are absent in 9 and 12; after *Gerhardi* they are absent in 11; *Geuchardi* in 8.], as the successor imposed upon my office, though he was jealous of my undertaking.

I ask that it not seem burdensome to the reader if I retrace the matter from its beginning and plainly explain how such a business was brought to completion [Note: [Col. 0137] “I ask” through “calumnious complaint” is absent in witnesses 7–12.]. For it seems absurd that I, who have proposed to explain the actions of others and the causes of events, should pass over in silence the business that concerns me [Note: [Col. 0137] “Because I have proposed to explain the actions of others” in witnesses 1, 3, and 5.]. [Note: [Col. 0137] After this word, the entire account of Regino’s election and deposition has fallen out. Its omission is clearly indicated by the words *praeterita decuit* (“was proper to pass over”), *extiti* (“I was”), *compulit* (“compelled”), and *ponerem* (“I should set down”), used in the sentence that follows.]

**[Much is missing.]**

I especially ask pardon of the reader on bended knees [Note: [Col. 0137] “With knee bent” in witness 3.], because in this account I have been more verbose than was proper [Note: [Col. 0137] “Of the reader” in witnesses 1 and 5.]. Necessity compelled me [Note: [Col. 0137] “Necessity demands” in witnesses 5c and e; *com* [lacuna] in witness 2; “compelled” is absent in witnesses 5c and d.], so that I might set down not only the deeds but also the words in their order [Note: [Col. 0137] “I should speak of the words in order” in witnesses 2 and 5.], on account of the calumnious complaint of those who were envious and opposed [Col. 0137C].

It is enough to have recalled briefly a few things from many concerning past causes and times that have gone by. For we have decided to remain silent about recent times because, if we set forth the truth of the events in full with our pen, we shall undoubtedly incur the hatred and offense [Note: [Col. 0137] “We shall incur offense” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.] of certain people who are still alive; but if, departing from the truth, we write otherwise than the matter stands, we shall nevertheless incur the charge of flattery and falsehood, since the facts are known to almost everyone. We therefore leave it to later generations to explain these matters more fully [Note: [Col. 0137] “More fully this” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.]; but, lest we be blamed for having passed over everything untouched [Note: [Col. 0137] “Lest we seem, or be blamed, to have passed over it” in witness 7; “lest we seem to have passed over it” in witnesses 9–12.], we shall take care to record only a portion of the deeds, in summary.

In the aforesaid year, therefore, in the month of July, Count Waltgarius [Note: [Col. 0137] “Waltharius” in witness 5.], nephew of King Odo [Note: [Col. 0137] “Grandson of Otto” in witness 5; “grandson of King Rudolf” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], namely the son of his uncle Adalhelm [Note: [Col. 0137] “Adalhalm” in witness 2.], raised the arms of rebellion against that same king with the counsel of certain men. He entered Laon [Note: [Col. 0137] “Having entered Laon” in witness 5.], and strove with all his effort to oppose the royal authority [Note: [Col. 0137] “He raised the arms of the region with all his effort, and, having entered Laon, with all his effort [opposed] the royal …” in witness 7.]. When Odo learned of this [Note: [Col. 0137] “When Odo” in witness 7.], he surrounded the city with a siege and received its surrender without delay. Then, when all the leading men who were present there had adjudged the matter, he ordered that Waltgarius [Note: [Col. 0137] “Walgarius” in witness 5.] be beheaded, because at a public assembly he had drawn his sword against the king and his lord.

After this he set out for Aquitaine against Ramnulf [Note: [Col. 0137] Also *Ramnolfus* in witnesses 2, 5, and 12; *Arnulfus* in another source; *Ranulfus* in witnesses 7.], his brother Gozbert [Note: [Col. 0137] “Gozbert Ebulon” in witnesses 5c and e.], and Ebulon [Note: [Col. 0137] “Eubulon” in witnesses 9–12.], abbot of Saint-Denis, and several others who refused to obey his commands, in order to suppress their insolence.

Likewise, in the same year, in the month of August, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0137] “August” in witness 5; “Kalends” is absent in witnesses 2 and 5.], Count Megingaud [Note: [Col. 0137] “Megingandus” in witness 5.], nephew of the aforesaid King Odo, was treacherously killed by Alberic [Note: [Col. 0137] “Albric” in witness 2.] and his companions in the monastery of Saint Xystus, which is called Rotila [Note: [Col. 0137] “Sotila” in witnesses 1, 2, and 5; “Rottila” in witnesses 7–12.], [Note: [Col. 0137] This seems to be Rethel on the Moselle; Browerus, however, says in his Annals of Trier II, no. 28, that it lies on the bank of the Moselle near Sierck.]. His body [Note: [Col. 0137] “His body” through “was buried” is absent in witnesses 1–4.] was carried to Trier and buried at Saint Maximin.

At the same time Arnt [Note: [Col. 0137] “Arn” in witnesses 7–12. In manuscript 8, the whole passage from “Arnt” through “succeeded him” is assigned to the year 889.], venerable bishop of the church of Würzburg, went to battle against the Slavs at the urging and persuasion of Poppo [Col. 0138C], duke of the Thuringians, and was killed in that battle. His see was obtained by Ruodulf [Note: [Col. 0137] “Rodulfus” in the Frisian manuscript.], although noble, yet utterly foolish, namely the brother of Counts Chuonrad and Gebehard [Note: [Col. 0137] The words “although noble, yet utterly foolish” are absent in witnesses 1–4 and 6; “namely” is absent in witnesses 1–6; “of Count Chuonrad” is absent in witnesses 1–4 and 6.], and he succeeded him in the episcopate.

Arnolf granted to his son Zuendibold part of the honors of Count Megingaud [Note: [Col. 0137] “Of Count Meginhard” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.].

Boppo [Note: [Col. 0137] “Poppo” in witnesses 3, 5, and 7–12; “Popo” in witness 4.], duke of the Thuringians [Note: [Col. 0137] “Of the Thuringians” frequently in witness 7.], was stripped of his dignities, and the duchy that he had held was entrusted to Chuonrad. Chuonrad held it for a short time and returned it of his own accord [Note: [Col. 0139] “He held it because he returned it of his own accord” in witnesses 9–12.]. Then it was entrusted to Count Burchard [Note: [Col. 0139] “Burkard” in witnesses 11 and 12.], who has governed it vigorously up to the present [Note: [Col. 0139] *qui eum* (“who governed it”) in witnesses 5, 6?, and 7–12; “who governed it vigorously for some time” in witness 8.].

While King Odo was staying in Aquitaine, the princes of the Franks deserted him for the greater part [Note: [Col. 0139] “For the most part” in witnesses 3 and 7.]. Through the actions of Bishop Folco [Note: [Col. 0139] “Falco” in witness 5.], [Note: [Col. 0139] “Archbishop” in witnesses 2, 4, 5, and 7–12.], and Counts Heribert [Note: [Col. 0139] “Heripert” in witness 7.] and Pippin, [Note: [Col. 0139C] Heribert and Pippin were grandsons of Bernard, king of Italy.] Charles, son of Louis, born, as we have mentioned above, to Queen Adalheid [Note: [Col. 0139] “Adelheid” in witness 5.], was raised to the kingship in the city of Rheims. [Note: [Col. 0139C] Charles was crowned king on 28 January 893. Regino does not notice that the author from whom he copied this account apparently began the year at Easter. Bouquet.]

## 893

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 893, Arnolf left Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0139] “Bavaria” in witness 5.] and came to Frankfurt. Crossing the Rhine, he visited for the greater part the cities that lie in the kingdom of Lothar. On this journey immense gifts were offered to him by the bishops.

Odo, having settled affairs in Aquitaine, returned to Francia and, together with his brother Ruodbert [Note: [Col. 0139] “Rodebert” in witness 5.], drove out Charles and pursued the defectors [Note: [Col. 0139] “Defectors” in witnesses 2, 4, and 5a, d.].

Ebulo, abbot of Saint-Denis, died from a stone’s blow while attacking too fiercely a certain castle situated in Aquitaine. Odo recalled the monastery of Saint-Denis to his service.

Unable to withstand Odo’s strength, Charles humbly sought the protection of Arnolf. In the summer [Note: [Col. 0139] “For indeed” is absent in witnesses 1, 2, and 6.], the aforesaid king held a public assembly in the city of Worms [Note: [Col. 0139] “At Worms” in witnesses 5c and e.], where Charles came and won Arnolf’s favor with great gifts [Note: [Col. 0139] “With many gifts for himself” in witnesses 7 and 9–12; “many” in witness 8.], and received from his hand the kingdom that he had usurped. It was also ordered [Note: [Col. 0139] “For it was also ordered” in witnesses 1 and 2.] that the bishops and counts who resided around the Meuse should bring him aid and, leading him into the kingdom, enthrone him on the royal seat.

But neither of these measures benefited him at all [Note: [Col. 0139] “Prevailed” in witness 2.]. When King Odo heard this, he sat with an army along the bank of the river Aisne [Note: [Col. 0140C] The Aisne, also called the Axona.], and did not allow Arnolf’s forces to enter the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0139] “To enter Arnolf’s kingdom” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.]. The king’s dukes, seeing that Odo was manfully prepared for battle [Note: [Col. 0139] “Prepared to fight” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], withdrew from him [Note: [Col. 0139] “Withdrew” in witness 1.] and returned to their own territories. Charles, however [Note: [Col. 0139] “However” is absent in witnesses 2 and 3.], withdrew into Burgundy. When Odo returned to Paris, Charles again occupied the borders of the kingdom and harassed Odo’s faithful; thus, in turn, many on both sides perished, great wickedness was committed, and innumerable acts of robbery and continual plunder took place.

## 894

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 894 [Note: [Col. 0139] “893” in witnesses 9–12.], Arnolf entered the territory of the Lombards with a strong army. Around the Purification of Saint Mary he captured by force the fortress called Bergamo and hanged Ambrose, count of that city, from a tree before the gate of the city [Note: [Col. 0139] “Before the city gate” in witnesses 7 (8) and 9–12.]. Such fear fell upon the remaining cities that no one dared to resist, but all came out to meet him as he approached.

He reached as far as Piacenza, then turned [Note: [Col. 0139] “He turned” in witnesses 1 and 5.] across the Pennine Alps, entered Gaul, and came to Saint-Maurice [Note: [Col. 0139] “And reached Saint-Maurice” through “he arrived” in witnesses 1–3 and 5.]. He could not harm Rudolf, whom he was seeking, because Rudolf had climbed into the mountains and hidden himself in the safest places [Note: [Col. 0139] “In safe places” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.]. Arnolf’s army severely harassed the region between the Jura [Note: [Col. 0139] Also *Juram* in witnesses 1?, 3?, 5, and 6?] and Mount Jupiter [Col. 0140B].

After this he came to Worms and held an assembly there [Note: [Col. 0139] “There” in witnesses 2 and 6; “where” in witness 4.], wishing to place his son Zuendibold [Note: [Col. 0139] “His son” is absent in witnesses 1, 2, 4, and 6.] over the kingdom of Lothar; but on that occasion the leading men of the aforesaid kingdom gave no assent.

When the assembly had been dissolved and the same prince had come to Lorsch [Note: [Col. 0139] “Lorassam” in witness 3; “Lauresham” in 7; “Lauresheim” in 8–12.], through the intervention of Louis, son of Boso, whose mother was Ermengard [Note: [Col. 0139] “Irmingard” in witnesses 7 and 9–12.], he granted certain cities with their adjoining districts, which Rudolf held. But this too came to nothing for him, because he was in no way able to wrest them from Rudolf’s power.

In the same year Guido, who ruled Italy and bore the name of emperor, died. His son Lambert [Note: [Col. 0139] “Lampertus” in witnesses 5a, c, and e; “Lambertus” in witness 5d.] obtained the kingdom and, coming to Rome, had the imperial diadem placed upon him by the bishop of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0139] “Placed upon him by the apostolic bishop” in witness 5.].

At the same time Hildegard, daughter of King Louis, brother of Carloman and Charles, was accused before Arnolf by certain persons [Note: [Col. 0139] “At” in witness 3; “before Arnolf” in witnesses 1, 5c, and e.], deprived of her royal possessions, and, after her deprivation, sent into exile in the monastery of women called Chemissem [Note: [Col. 0139] “Cremisse” in witness 8.], [Note: [Col. 0140C] This is Chiemsee; compare the Annals of Fulda under the year 895.] But not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0139] “Of time” in witnesses 1 and 5.] she returned to favor [Note: [Col. 0139] “Returns” in witness 2.] and recovered most of what was hers [Note: [Col. 0139] “Began to recover” in witnesses 2 and 5a, d.].

Around this same time Zuendibold, king of the Moravian Slavs, a man among his people most prudent and exceptionally clever in mind, ended his final day. His sons held his kingdom unhappily for a short time, while the Hungarians ravaged everything to the ground [Note: [Col. 0139] “Hungarians” in witnesses 3 and 7.].

## 895

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 895, a great synod was held at Tribur against many secular persons who were attempting to diminish episcopal authority. There twenty-six bishops [Note: [Col. 0141] “Twenty-three” in witnesses 9–12.], seated together with the abbots of the monasteries, confirmed in writing very many decrees concerning the condition of the holy Church.

After this Arnulf came to Worms, where the leading men from all the kingdoms subject to his authority came to meet him, and he held a public assembly. At this assembly, with everyone agreeing and applauding, he placed his son Zwentibold over the kingdom of Lothar.

At the same assembly King Odo came to Arnulf with great gifts and [Col. 0141B] was received by him with honor. After Odo had obtained everything for which he had come, as he was returning to his kingdom, his lodging officers encountered Bishop Folco and Count Adalung midway on the road, coming to Arnulf with gifts sent by Charles. The officers attacked them with a shout. The bishop escaped by flight; Adalung was mortally wounded, and the baggage was plundered. The aforesaid count was buried in Trigorium, in a village called Belthomus.

In the same year Zwentibold, having gathered an immense army and wishing to enlarge the boundaries of his kingdom, came to Lugdunum Clavatum, as though he were going to bring aid to Charles against Odo, and surrounded the city with a siege. But he could not capture it at all, although for many days [Col. 0141C] they fought fiercely with all their strength. When he heard that Odo was approaching with an army—for at that time Odo was staying in Aquitaine—he withdrew with all his forces and retreated into his own kingdom. At that time Ludelmus, a venerable man, was consecrated bishop of the church of Toul by Archbishop Rathbod and his suffragan bishops.

## 896

In the year 896 of the Lord’s incarnation, Arnulf, entering Italy for the second time, came to Rome and captured the city of Rome by force, with the consent of the supreme pontiff. This was unheard-of in earlier centuries [Col. 0142A] because it had not happened, except that the Gauls, the Senones, under their leader Brennus, had done so once long before the birth of Christ. Lantbert’s mother, who had been left behind by her son to defend the city, secretly fled with her people. When Arnulf entered the city, he was received with great honor by Formosus, bishop of the apostolic see, and was crowned before the Confession of Saint Peter and created emperor.

On his return he was afflicted by paralysis and languished from this illness for a long time. In the same year Lantbert, son of Wido, whom we mentioned a little above, died, and Louis, son of Boso, invited by the Lombards, left his province and entered Italy.

About the feast of Saint Andrew, [Col. 0142B] Count Alberic, who had killed Megingaud, was killed by Stephen, Walon’s brother.

## 897

In the year 897 of the Lord’s incarnation, Counts Stephen, Odacar, Gerard, and Matfrid lost the honors and dignities which they had received from the king. Zwentibold came to Trier with an army and divided among his own followers the land formerly held by the men mentioned above, reserving for himself the monastery at Horrea and the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Metz.

After this he consulted his father through envoys about the woman whom he desired to marry. At his father’s urging he sent a messenger to Count Otto and asked for his daughter, named Oda, in marriage. [Col. 0142C] Otto gladly granted his request and gave him his daughter, whom Zwentibold took as his wife after Easter, when the marriage had been celebrated. In the same year Arnulf came to Worms and held an assembly there. Zwentibold came to meet him, and through the emperor’s intervention Stephen, Gerard, and Matfrid were reconciled with Zwentibold.

At that time a great quarrel of discord and an irreconcilable conflict of hatred arose between Rudolf, bishop of Würzburg, and the sons of Duke Henry—Adalbert, Adalhard, and Henry—from small and insignificant causes; and, as from a very tiny spark [Col. 0143A] a huge fire is kindled, it grew day by day and spread without limit. While they exalted themselves beyond what was fitting on account of the nobility of their flesh, the great number of their relatives, and the magnitude of their earthly power, they broke out into mutual slaughter. Countless men on both sides perished by the sword; hands and feet were mutilated; and the regions subject to them were devastated to the ground by plundering and fires.

## 898

In the year 898 of the Lord’s incarnation, King Odo was struck by illness, and in January, on the third day of that month, he died. He was buried at Saint-Denis with the honor due to his burial. The princes assembled together [Col. 0143B] and by common counsel and agreement set Charles up as king over them.

In the same year Zwentibold, at the prompting—I do not know whose—of some person, drove away Reginar, his most trusted and only counselor. Having forbidden him the honors and hereditary possessions that he held in his kingdom, he ordered him to leave the kingdom within fourteen days. He, accompanied by Count Odacar and certain others, together with women, children, and all their property, entered a very secure place called Durfos and fortified himself there.

When the king learned this, he gathered an army and tried to storm the fortress, but he was completely unsuccessful because of the marshes and the many channels through which the river Meuse flows at that place. When the king withdrew from the siege, [Col. 0143C] the aforesaid counts approached Charles and introduced him into the kingdom with an army. Zwentibold, although he understood only late that he had been surrounded, fled with a few men. Charles came by the direct route to Aachen [*Tucicha*, a place-name reading in witness 6] and then proceeded to Nijmegen.

Meanwhile Zwentibold came to Bishop Francon of Liège, took him and all his people with him, crossed the Meuse, and came to Florichingas. There all the nobles of the kingdom who were in those regions flocked to him. Rejoicing that, although his affairs had seemed desperate, he had recovered his strength, he regained confidence and set out against his rival for battle.

Returning from Nijmegen, Charles came to Prüm and from there moved his forces against Zwentibold. [Col. 0144A] But when the armies on both sides drew near, no battle was fought; instead, envoys intervened and peace was secured, oaths were sworn, and Charles, having forded the Meuse, returned to his own kingdom.

While these events were taking place in Francia, numerous engagements occurred in Italy between Louis and Berengar, and many dangerous battles followed one another in turn. Finally Louis put Berengar to flight and entered Rome, where he was crowned by the supreme pontiff and proclaimed emperor.

At about the same time Duke Eberhard, son of Meginhard, was treacherously slaughtered by Waltgar the Frisian, son of Gerulf, while he was going hunting. The duchy which he had held was entrusted by the emperor to his brother Meginhard.

[Col. 0144B]

## 899

In the year 899 of the Lord’s incarnation, Zwentibold held a conference with the nobles of Arnulf and Charles and with his own men at Saint Goar. From Arnulf’s kingdom there were Archbishop Hatto and Counts Conrad and Gebehard; from Charles’s side, Bishop Haschiric and Count Odacar. What was dealt with privately at that assembly, without the king’s presence, was later made perfectly clear by the outcome.

In the same year Richarius was appointed abbot of the monastery of Prüm. I have delayed recording here what was done against me because I feared that, provoked by injuries, [Col. 0144C] I might appear to exaggerate the causes of my persecution beyond what Christian patience permits, and because a lengthy account—complex and involved—might weary those who heard it. As I stated above, I have endeavored to record the events themselves, not to unravel the causes of those events through precise indications of reasoning. And since in the actions of others we strive for brevity, in our own we must beware the fault of verbosity.

Zwentibold again came with an army to Durfos and attempted with all his strength to storm the fortification. But when his efforts made no progress, he ordered the bishops to excommunicate Reginar, Odacar, and their associates. When they refused to pronounce the sentence of excommunication, [Col. 0145A] he used threats, reproaches, and insults against them; and thus, when the siege was lifted, each party returned to its own place.

At that time Odilbald, a holy man and bishop of the church of Utrecht, was taken from human affairs and passed to the heavenly kingdom. Ratbod, a venerable bishop, was appointed in his place.

Near the end of this year, Emperor Arnulf departed from this world on the third day before the Kalends of December and was honorably buried at Odingas [9–12 instead read: “in Regensburg, in the basilica of the martyr Saint Emmeram, whom he himself greatly venerated during his life”], where his father also lies buried.

## 900

In the year 900 of the Lord’s incarnation, the princes and nobles who had been under Arnulf’s authority [Col. 0145B] assembled at Forchheim. They made Louis, son of the aforesaid ruler, whom he had begotten in a legitimate marriage, king over them, and, after crowning him and clothing him in royal ornaments, raised him to the summit of kingship.

While these events were occurring in Germany, an irreconcilable disagreement arose between Zwentibold and the leading men of the kingdom because of the continual devastations and plunderings taking place in the kingdom, and because Zwentibold, conducting affairs with women and men of low status, was casting down the more honorable and noble men and stripping them of honors and dignities. For this reason he became hated by everyone.

They therefore went over eagerly to Louis, introduced him into the kingdom, and at Theodonis villa, having given him their hands, [Col. 0145C] submitted themselves to his rule. When Louis crossed the Rhine, Zwentibold gathered together as many men as he could and went around the cities of the kingdom, devastating everything with fires and plunder. He thought that, by doing things still more savage and worse, he might bring back to himself the deserters who had abandoned him because of his arrogance and monstrous wickedness.

Louis was summoned back into the kingdom, and the same Zwentibold was killed in battle near the Meuse by Counts Stephen, Gerard, and Matfrid on the Ides of August. In the same year Count Gerard took Oda, the wife of Zwentibold, as his wife.

[Col. 0146A]

## 901

In the year 901 of the Lord’s incarnation, the people of the Hungarians entered the territory of the Lombards and cruelly devastated everything with slaughter, fires, and plunder. When the inhabitants of the land tried to resist their violence and bestial fury by gathering into one army, an innumerable multitude perished under showers of arrows; very many bishops and counts were slaughtered.

Liudward, bishop of the church of Vercelli, formerly the closest confidant and privy counselor of Emperor Charles, taking with him the wealth and incomparable treasures in which he abounded beyond any possible estimate, was striving with every effort to escape their bloody savagery when, unaware, he fell among them and was immediately killed. [Col. 0146B] The wealth carried with him was plundered.

In the same year Count Stephen, Walon’s brother, while sitting in seclusion and relieving his bowels during the night, was gravely wounded by a poisoned arrow shot through the window of his chamber by someone. From this wound he died that same night.

## 902

In the year 902 of the Lord’s incarnation, Adalbert, together with his brothers Adalhard and Henry, gathered a strong force and advanced to battle against the brothers Eberhard, Gebehard, and Rudolf, whom we mentioned shortly above. He sallied forth from the fortress called Babenberg.

The opposing brothers bravely received his attack, broke through the line with weapons, and struck down all whom they encountered. [Col. 0146C] They did not stop until they forced the enemy army to flee. In this battle Henry was killed, Adalhard was captured, and afterward was beheaded on Gebehard’s orders. Eberhard too, pierced by many wounds, fell in the battle. When the conflict was over, his men found him among the corpses of the slain, carried him home, and a few days later he himself died.

## 903

In the year 903 of the Lord’s incarnation, Adalbert drove Bishop Rudolf from the church of Würzburg and [Col. 0147A] cruelly devastated the property and possessions of that church. He also forced the sons of Eberhard, together with their mother, to leave the inheritances and honors granted to them by royal favor, compelling them to withdraw beyond the Spessart.

About this time Folco, archbishop of Reims, was killed by a certain Winemar, a follower of Count Baldwin of Flanders. The cause of this murder is said to have been the following.

The aforesaid Baldwin had invaded the fortress of Arras, namely the abbey of Saint Vaast, without anyone granting it to him. King Charles took it away from him and bestowed it as a benefice on Bishop Folco. Baldwin took this badly and sent Winemar to the aforementioned bishop, begging him not to seize for himself, [Col. 0147B] out of greed, the honors which Baldwin had hitherto held and possessed. He also promised immense gifts if, through the bishop’s help and intervention, he could obtain the aforesaid possession.

But when the bishop gave no assent and answered, I know not what, more harshly and bitterly than was proper, Winemar, stirred up by the devil and inflamed with excessive rage, left him. He entered a certain forest with his companions, and when Folco was returning from the king at the palace of Compiègne, he attacked him and slaughtered him without delay.

Heriveus was raised to the see of Reims. Together with many other bishops, he excommunicated that same Winemar and condemned him to perpetual anathema for so unheard-of a crime.

## 905

In the year 905 of the Lord’s incarnation, [Col. 0147C] Louis, son of Boso, whom we mentioned above as having assumed the imperial title, expelled Berengar from Italy and subjected the whole kingdom to his authority.

Seeing that no one either could or dared resist him, and presuming on his security beyond what was proper, he began to consider matters of peace and quiet. Having dismissed his army, he entered Verona with very few men, at the urging of Adalhard, bishop of that city. The citizens immediately informed Berengar of this; at that time he was an exile in Bavaria.

Without delay Berengar gathered forces from every direction, reached Verona, and [Col. 0148A] captured the unsuspecting man by deceit. After capturing him, he deprived him of his sight. For the citizens who favored Berengar opened the city gates to him and received him within the walls during the night. Thus, unexpectedly and without forethought, Louis was deprived not only of his kingdom but also of his eyes.

At last Berengar obtained the kingdom of Italy, stained by much slaughter and long sought through disastrous and ill-fated battles, with this kind of triumph. In May of the same year a comet appeared, and in August this change of kingdom took place.

## 906

In the year 906 of the Lord’s incarnation, Count Conrad sent his son Conrad with a considerable force of armed men [Col. 0148B] to attack Gerard and his brother Matfrid, because they had violently seized Conrad’s honors and those of his brother Gebehard—namely, the possessions of Saint Maximin and of Saint Mary at Horrea. An army from the kingdom of Lothar joined them.

They advanced as far as the district of Bliesgau, devastating with plunder and fires the inheritance and possessions of the aforesaid brothers and their followers. Gerard and Matfrid, sending an embassy from the fortress in which they had fortified themselves, asked for peace. When peace had been granted until the octave of Easter and oaths had been exchanged on both sides, the army withdrew to its own territory.

While these events were taking place in the kingdom of Lothar, the elder Conrad was stationed in Hesse, at a place called Fritzlar, with a large crowd of infantry and cavalry, [Col. 0148C] keeping watch because he suspected repeated incursions by Adalbert. His brother Gebehard, meanwhile, was in the Wetterau with everyone whom he could gather, awaiting the same Adalbert’s sudden attack.

The outcome fully bore out their fears. Adalbert, perceiving that the strength of his opponents had been weakened because they were divided into three groups, rejoiced that the favorable and long-desired moment had arrived. Having gathered his allies, he immediately took up arms. First he pretended that he intended to move his forces against Gebehard, both to frighten him with war and to make his brother more secure. [Col. 0149A] Then, with all possible speed, he directed his battle line against Conrad.

When Conrad learned this too late, he divided his followers into three troops and advanced against him without hesitation. When the battle was joined, two troops—one of infantry and the other of Saxons—immediately turned their backs. Although Conrad vainly encouraged them with a great shout not to yield to the enemy under any circumstances, but to fight with all their strength for the safety of their wives and children and the defense of their homeland, he himself, with the third troop, animated his companions and rushed upon the enemy. But immediately, in the first assault, he was pierced by many wounds and killed.

Adalbert, having won the victory, pursued the fugitives with his companions and struck down an innumerable multitude, especially infantry, with the sword. For three continuous days he traversed the whole region, [Col. 0149B] destroying everything with slaughter and plunder. After accomplishing this, and with his companions loaded with spoils and immense booty, he returned to the fortress of Babenberg.

This slaughter took place on the third day before the Kalends of March. His sons came with their mother, lifted Conrad’s body, and buried him in the fortress called Wileneburg.

About July of the same year King Louis held a general assembly at Triburias, a royal estate. He ordered the often-mentioned Adalbert to appear there, so that he might give an account of himself in the presence of the leading men of the kingdom, at last accept the terms of peace which he had hitherto hated, lay aside the tyranny of his cruelty, and cease, even if late, from plunder, slaughter, and fires.

[Col. 0149C] But he gave no assent at all to these salutary admonitions. When the king saw that his mind was hardened and that he was obstinate in the wickedness of the rebellion he had begun, [Col. 0150A] he gathered an army from every direction and surrounded him in the fortress called Terassa.

Meanwhile Egino, who had been his inseparable companion in every wickedness, abandoned his association and went over to the king’s camp with all his men. When the siege had consequently dragged on somewhat longer, Adalbert, broken in spirit, resorted to crafty devices. He began to devise every possible means by which the siege might be lifted, so that, once the army had returned home, he might obtain the freedom he desired and spread far and wide the plots which he was turning over in his heart, together with those who favored him.

He therefore opened the gates and came out of the fortification with a very few men. He voluntarily presented himself to the king, humbly begged pardon for his offenses, and promised reform. But when the treachery being prepared [Col. 0150B] had been exposed by his own men, he was handed over to custody. He was brought before the entire army with his hands bound, and, by the judgment of all, received the death sentence on the fifth day before the Ides of September. His possessions and estates were confiscated for the treasury and distributed by royal gift among the nobles.

After affairs in eastern Francia had been settled, the king came to Metz. There, at a public assembly, he condemned Gerard and Matfrid to proscription.

From there he departed and went to the city of Strasbourg. There he restored to harmony the bishop and the people, who were divided among themselves. Then, crossing the Rhine, he proceeded by the direct route into Alamannia.

At about the same time Baltrammus, bishop of the church of Strasbourg, and Ludelmus, bishop of the church of Toul, [Col. 0150C] departed from this world. They were succeeded in the episcopal sees by Otbert in the city of Strasbourg and Drogo in Toul.

[Col. 0151]

# CONTINUATOR OF REGINO

## PERTZ’S PREFACE

*(Monumenta Germaniae historica*, vol. I, *Scriptores*, p. 614)

[Col. 0151A] The man who provided Regino’s *Chronicle* with a continuation in the tenth century wished to keep his name concealed. Nevertheless, he should be regarded as a monk of Saint Maximin at Trier, in which monastery we have said that Regino’s work was written, since he knows its affairs thoroughly and takes them to heart, and since it is clear that he enjoyed the companionship of the monk Adalbert.

Simlerus and some later writers call him Romerius, but without any reason that they have disclosed. I believe they were misled in this no less than by the fact that various writers—Simlerus, Possevinus, Vossius, and others—say that the work extends variously to the years 972, 977, 1453, 1457, 1467, or 1477, although in no edition does it go beyond the year 967.

Whoever the author may be, he appears to have begun writing after the year 939, relying on the Annals of Reichenau and the Alamannic Annals insofar as they extended. But the matters which he himself experienced and added are of much greater value and, given the scarcity of historians in that century, [Col. 0151B] must be regarded as extremely important, since neither Liutprand’s *History* nor what Widukind of Corvey recorded can in any way be compared with them. For this reason they were frequently copied in succeeding centuries by Hermann, Siegfried, Otto of Freising, and others.

I have reviewed the aids to this edition in the preface to Regino above, columns 9 and following.

II. habes, ubi tamen finibus justo arctioribus circumcluditur; nam villa Belthomus ibi [Col. 0142C] omissa, est hodiernum Beltem, e septentrione vici Castellaun positum.

   This is the district of Trechirgowe, on the left bank of the Rhine, from Bacharach to Confluentes. Its outline is given in the distinguished Gunther’s Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus, volume II; there, however, it is enclosed within unduly narrow boundaries. The village of Belthomus, omitted there, is the present-day Beltem, situated north of the village of Castellaun.

126. **903.** [Col. 0147] spetheshart 1. 3. spehtesharth 2. spectheshart 5. speteshart 10---12. spetitheshart 8. spechtheshart 4.

   Forms of the Spessart’s name: spetheshart in 1, 3; spehtesharth in 2; spectheshart in 5; speteshart in 10–12; spetitheshart in 8; spechtheshart in 4.

127. **903.** [Col. 0147C] Spessart nemus.

   The Spessart forest.

128. **903.** [Col. 0147C] Cf. Ann. Vedastinos an. 900.

   Compare the Annals of Saint-Vaast under the year 900.

129. **903.** [Col. 0147] folcho archiepiscopus 9---12. fulco 2.

   “Archbishop Folcho”: 9–12, omitting “of Reims”; Fulco in 2.

130. **903.** [Col. 0147] winimaro etc. 3. 5. 7. 8. winimate 9---12.

   Winimaro, etc., in 3, 5, 7, 8; winimate in 9–12: forms of Winemar’s name.

131. **903.** [Col. 0147] balduvini 7. constanter.

   Balduvini, “of Baldwin,” consistently in 7.

132. **903.** [Col. 0147C] Flandrensis

   Of Flanders.

133. **903.** [Col. 0147] atrebatis 3.

   Atrebatis, a form of Arras’s name, in 3.

134. **903.** [Col. 0147] ingentia bona 5d.

   “Immense goods,” instead of “immense gifts”: 5d.

135. **903.** [Col. 0147] praeberet nescio 2.

   “He granted … I do not know,” without et, “and”: 2.

136. **903.** [Col. 0147] henricus 1? 5c. e. herineus 5a. d. heinbertus 9. heimbertus 10. hembertus 11. 12. hireneus 8.

   Forms of Heriveus: henricus in 1? and 5c, e; herineus in 5a, d; heinbertus in 9; heimbertus in 10; hembertus in 11, 12; hireneus in 8.

137. **903.** [Col. 0147] condemnavit. Quae hinc inde sequuntur, omnia desunt in codice 4.

   After “condemned,” everything that follows from this point is absent in manuscript 4.

138. **905.** [Col. 0147] DCCCCV. 3. 7---12. et cod. Fris.; in codice 1. prima manu DCCCCIIII. recentiori vero DCCCCV. 2. 5. DCCCCIV; de codice 6. mihi non constat.

   905 in 3, 7–12, and the Freising manuscript. In 1 the original hand wrote 904 and a later hand 905. Manuscripts 2 and 5 have 904. “I do not know about manuscript 6.”

139. **905.** [Col. 0148C] Hoc anno quae narrantur accidisse, probat Muratorius in Annalibus ad h. a.

   Muratori, in his Annals under this year, proves that the events narrated occurred in this year.

140. **905.** [Col. 0147] nullum esse aut posse nocere ultra 5.

   “That there was no one, or [no one] could harm [him] … beyond”: 5, instead of the wording that no one could or dared resist him.

141. **905.** [Col. 0147] adelardo 1. adelhardo 5. adalardo 7.

   Forms of Adalhard’s name: adelardo in 1; adelhardo in 5; adalardo in 7.

142. **905.** [Col. 0147] tractis 2. undique deest 3.

   Tractis, “drawn,” instead of contractis, “gathered,” in 2; undique, “from every direction,” is absent in 3.

143. **905.** [Col. 0147] insperato 5c. e. inspirate 1---3.

   Insperato, “unexpectedly,” in 5c, e; inspirate, an altered or defective form in this context, in 1–3.

144. **905.** [Col. 0147] diu quaesitum deest 3.

   Diu quaesitum, “long sought,” is absent in 3.

145. **905.** [Col. 0147] cometa 7. 9---12. cometes 8.

   Cometa in 7, 9–12; cometes in 8: forms for “comet,” instead of cometae, “of a comet.”

146. **906.** [Col. 0147] anno ut supra 1---3. anno d. i. DCCCCV. 5. anno d. i. DCCCCVI. 7---12. et cod. Frising de codice 6. nobis non constat.

   “In the year as above” in 1–3; “in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 905” in 5; “in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 906” in 7–12 and the Freising manuscript. “We do not know about manuscript 6.”

147. **906.** [Col. 0147] fratris videlicet 7. 9---12. fratris sui 8.

   “Namely, of the brother”: 7, 9–12; “of his own brother”: 8. The following narrative explicitly identifies Gebehard as Conrad’s brother.

148. **906.** [Col. 0147] pagum blesiacum 5c. e. pagum blasiacum 3.

   Pagum blesiacum in 5c, e; pagum blasiacum in 3: accusative forms for the district of Bliesgau, instead of pago Blesiaco.

149. **906.** [Col. 0148C] Cujus caput Bliescastel.

   Its chief place is Blieskastel.

150. **906.** [Col. 0147] octavis 2. 7. 9---12.

   Octavis, a plural form for “octave,” in 2, 7, 9–12, instead of octava.

151. **906.** [Col. 0147] hesia 2. henessia 7.

   Forms of Hesse: hesia in 2; henessia in 7.

152. **906.** [Col. 0147] frideslar 1. 3. 5. 7---12.

   Frideslar, a form of Fritzlar’s name, in 1, 3, 5, 7–12.

153. **906.** [Col. 0147] fratrem . . . . gerhardum 5.

   Fratrem … gerhardum, “brother … Gerhard,” accusative forms, in 5, instead of the nominative “brother … Gebehard.”

154. **906.** [Col. 0147] wederabia 1? wenteibacum 3. wedereina 2. wetreiba 7. wedria 8. wedereia 9---12.

   Forms of the Wetterau: wederabia in 1?; wenteibacum in 3; wedereina in 2; wetreiba in 7; wedria in 8; wedereia in 9–12.

155. **906.** [Col. 0148C] Die Wetterau.

   The Wetterau.

156. **906.** [Col. 0147] extenuatas sentiens 1. 2.

   “Perceiving [the forces] diminished,” without esse, “to be”: 1, 2.

157. **906.** [Col. 0147] gerhardum 5.

   Gerhardum, “Gerhard,” in 5, instead of Gebehardum.

158. **906.** [Col. 0149] verterunt 7.

   “They turned,” instead of “they turn”: 7.

159. **906.** [Col. 0149] gladio perstrinxit 6.

   “He struck/cut with the sword”: 6, instead of “struck down with the sword.”

160. **906.** [Col. 0149] honeratis 2. honoratis 7. oneratisque 9---12.

   Honeratis, “loaded,” as spelled, in 2; honoratis, “honoured,” in 7; oneratisque, “and loaded,” in 9–12.

161. **906.** [Col. 0149] spoliis, ingenti 7. 9---12.

   “With spoils, immense [booty],” without ac, “and”: 7, 9–12.

162. **906.** [Col. 0149] abenberc 7. bababenberch 2.

   Forms of Babenberg: abenberc in 7; bababenberch in 2.

163. **906.** [Col. 0149] castro 3. 5. castrolo 2.

   Castro, “fortress,” in 3, 5; castrolo, an altered diminutive form, in 2, instead of castello.

164. **906.** [Col. 0149C] Weilburg.

   Weilburg.

165. **906.** [Col. 0149] venientes. . . vocatur deest 7---12.

   The passage from “His sons came” through “is called” is absent in 7–12, omitting the recovery and burial of Conrad’s body.

166. **906.** [Col. 0149] driburias 2.

   Driburias, a form of Triburias’s name, in 2.

167. **906.** [Col. 0149] villam regiam 7.

   Villam regiam, “royal estate,” accusative, in 7, instead of villa regia.

168. **906.** [Col. 0149] et rapinis 1---5? 3. 7.

   “And plunder,” without a, “from.” The witness list is printed as “1–5? 3. 7.”

169. **906.** [Col. 0149] saltim 2.

   Saltim, “at least,” an alternative spelling, in 2.

170. **906.** [Col. 0149] trassa corr. terassa 2. teras 7. tedresse corr. tharesse 9. tarase corr. tarasse 10. tharesse 11. 12. tetrassa 5.

   Forms of Terassa: trassa corrected to terassa in 2; teras in 7; tedresse corrected to tharesse in 9; tarase corrected to tarasse in 10; tharesse in 11, 12; tetrassa in 5.

171. **906.** [Col. 0149C] Jam anno 903 in diplomate regis pro ecclesia Wirzeburgensi nominatur. Postea monasterium factum esse, Hofmannus in Annalibus Bambergensibus affirmat.

   It is already named in a royal charter of 903 for the church of Würzburg. Hofmann, in his Bamberg Annals, states that it later became a monastery.

172. **906.** [Col. 0149] interea regino 7. egio 3. egeno 8.

   “Meanwhile Regino” in 7; egio in 3; egeno in 8: variants of Egino’s name.

173. **906.** [Col. 0149] omni familiaritate 3.

   “In all intimacy/familiarity,” instead of “in every wickedness”: 3.

174. **906.** [Col. 0149] libertate potius 1. 2. 5. 7.

   Libertate potius, “freedom … rather,” in 1, 2, 5, 7, replacing potitus, “having gained.” There is no source word meaning “advantage.”

175. **906.** [Col. 0149] exigens 2.

   Exigens, “demanding/driving out,” instead of exiens, “going out”: 2.

176. **906.** [Col. 0149] se regi 5.

   Se regi, “himself to the king”: 5, replacing ultro regi, “voluntarily to the king,” at this point.

177. **906.** [Col. 0149] dejecta 2.

   Dejecta, “cast down,” instead of detecta, “exposed”: 2.

178. **906.** [Col. 0149] mancipatur 2? 5.

   “Is handed over,” instead of “was handed over”: 2? and 5.

179. **906.** [Col. 0149] adductus ab omnibus capitalem 5e.

   “Brought forward, by all … capital [sentence]”: 5e, abbreviating the construction by omitting “judging.”

180. **906.** [Col. 0149] VIo idus 7.

   The sixth day before the Ides, instead of the fifth: 7.

181. **906.** [Col. 0149] nobiles 7. 9---12.

   Nobiles, “nobles,” instead of nobiliores, “the more noble”: 7, 9–12.

182. **906.** [Col. 0149] dona. . . distributa 5c. e.

   Dona … distributa, “gifts … distributed”: 5c, e, instead of dono, “by a gift,” and distributae, agreeing with the possessions.

183. **906.** [Col. 0149] ita in 5.

   Ita in, “thus in”: 5, instead of itaque in, “therefore in.”

184. **906.** [Col. 0149] mediomatricum 5.

   Mediomatricum, an alternative inflection for Metz, in 5.

185. **906.** [Col. 0149C] Exstat diploma regium Ludhelmo Tullensi [Col. 0150C] episcopo concessum Kalendis Septembribus hujus anni, actum Tullo civitate, apud Calmet Hist. Lotharing. I, 332; quod si pro genuino habetur, rex Adalberti punitioni non adfuisse censendus est, Et Ludhelmus III id. Sept. hujus anni obiit. Cf. Hist. episc. Tullensium apud Calmet., Probatt. p. 130.

   A royal charter granted to Ludhelm, bishop of Toul, on the Kalends of September of this year survives in Calmet, History of Lorraine I, page 332, dated at the city of Toul. If it is accepted as genuine, the king must be considered not to have been present at Adalbert’s punishment. Ludhelm died on the third day before the Ides of September of this year. Compare the History of the Bishops of Toul in Calmet, Proofs, page 130.

186. **906.** [Col. 0149] ibique deest 5.

   Ibique, “and there,” is absent in 5.

187. **906.** [Col. 0149] regressus 1---3? 5.

   Regressus, “having returned,” instead of egressus, “having departed”: 1–3? and 5.

188. **906.** [Col. 0149] strasburgensem 1. 5. argentanam civitatem 3.

   Strasburgensem in 1, 5, a spelling of “of Strasbourg”; argentanam civitatem, “the city of Argentana,” in 3.

189. **906.** [Col. 0149] baltrannus 1. 5.

   Baltrannus, a form of Baltrammus’s name, in 1, 5.

190. **906.** [Col. 0149] luidhelmus 5. 9---12. liuthelmus 7.

   Forms of Ludelmus: luidhelmus in 5, 9–12; liuthelmus in 7.

191. **906.** [Col. 0149] tulliensis ecclesiae 5.

   “Of the church of Toul”: 5, with Tulliensis as spelled.

192. **906.** [Col. 0149] drugo 5. 10. druogo 2. druoso 9. 11. 12.

   Forms of Drogo: drugo in 5, 10; druogo in 2; druoso in 9, 11, 12.

193. **906.** [Col. 0149] tulliensi. anno Dominicae incarnationis DCCCCVIII. 7. tullensi. Hac voce desinunt codices 1. 2. 3; in hoc additur Explicit, et rubro colore Explicit chronica Reginonis. Deo gracias. Quam et nos subjicimus, continuatio ignoti cujusdam scriptoris, extat in codice 6. post verba: Explicit chronica reginonis abbatis, in codice 7. (et Frisingensi, cf. Aretin l. c. p. 239) interjecto: Hucusque regino. Haec quae secuntur nos addidimus, in 9. 10. 11. 12. eadem sententia, mutato addidimus in addimus, legitur: codex 11. voces anno Dominicae incarnationis DCCCCVIII. temere statim post druogo in tulliensi, cod. 12. anno Dominicae incarnationis DCCCCVII. inter regino et Haec inserit. In editionibus: Tullensi. «Hucusque Regino. Haec vero quae sequuntur addita fortasse sunt ab alio quopiam monacho.»

   7 reads: “at Toul. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 908.” At the word Tullensi, “at Toul,” manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 end; in the last, “Here ends” is added, and in red: “Here ends Regino’s Chronicle. Thanks be to God.” The continuation by an unknown writer, which we too append, is found in 6 after “Here ends the Chronicle of Abbot Regino”; in 7, and in the Freising manuscript (compare Aretin, cited work, page 239), the inserted notice reads: “Thus far Regino. What follows we have added.” In 9, 10, 11, and 12 the same sentence is read with addidimus, “we have added,” changed to addimus, “we add.” Manuscript 11 rashly places “in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 908” immediately after “Drogo at Toul”; 12 inserts “in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 907” between “Regino” and “What follows.” The editions read: “at Toul. Thus far Regino. But what follows was perhaps added by some other monk.”

194. **Pertz’s preface.** [Col. 0151B] Cf. an. 934, 950.

   Compare the years 934 and 950.

195. **Pertz’s preface.** [Col. 0151B] Cf. an. 961, 962.

   Compare the years 961 and 962.

196. **Pertz’s preface.** [Col. 0151B] De Wilhelmi, Ottonis filii, nativitate an. 928, antequam an. 954 archiepiscopus Moguntinus crearetur, relatum fuisse, vix crediderim.

   I can scarcely believe that William’s birth in 928, the son of Otto, was recorded before he was made archbishop of Mainz in 954.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 907 [Note: [Col. 0152B] Compare the Annals of Reichenau and Alamannia.], the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0151] “Bavarians … Hungarians … Liutbald … Arnulf” 5.] engaged the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0151] “with the Hungarians … Liutbald” 11, 12.] and were struck down in great slaughter; in this engagement Duke Liutbald [Note: [Col. 0151] “Liutbald” 9, 10.] was killed, and his son [Note: [Col. 0151] “his” is absent in 9–12.] Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0151] “Arnolf” 9, 10.] succeeded him in the duchy [Note: [Col. 0151] “in the duchy” 5c, e, 8.].

## 908

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 908 [Note: [Col. 0151] In codices 9–12, the words “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation” occur before the number of every year; in codex 7 they are written occasionally up to the year 917, but are otherwise omitted. That the same practice existed in the codices from which the editions were derived is shown by the number 915, which introduces the final entry for the year 915.], the Hungarians again crossed the borders and ravaged Saxony and Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0151] “ravaged. The Hungarians” 9–12; the number of the year 909 is absent.] [Note: [Col. 0152B] Compare the Annals of Reichenau.].

## 909

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 909, the Hungarians entered Alamannia [Note: [Col. 0151] “attacked” 8.] [Note: [Col. 0152B] Compare the Annals of Reichenau.].

## 910

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 910, the Franks engaged the Hungarians on the border between Bavaria and Francia [Note: [Col. 0151] “with the Hungarians” 9, 11, 12], and were miserably either defeated or put to flight [Note: [Col. 0152B] Compare the Annals of Alamannia and of Cologne.]. In this battle Count Gebeard [Note: [Col. 0151] “Gebelhard” 5; “Gebehard” 8–12.] perished, leaving two sons, still boys, Udo and Hermann [Note: [Col. 0151] “Hermann” 8; “Herimann” 5, 9–12.], who later became famous and noble in Francia [Note: [Col. 0151] “and great and noble” 7.].

## 911

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 911, King Louis [Note: [Col. 0151] “Emperor” 7.], son of Emperor Arnulf, died; and Conrad, son of the Conrad who had been killed by Adalbert, succeeded him in the kingdom, since the royal line had now failed [Note: [Col. 0152B] Compare the Annals of Reichenau for the years 911, 913, 915, 917, 919, and 923.].

## 912

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 912, the Hungarians again, with no one resisting, ravaged Francia and Thuringia. Archbishop Hatto [Note: [Col. 0151] The deaths of Otto and Hatto are reported under the year 914. 8.] [Note: [Col. 0151] “Hatho” 7.] died, a man so energetic and prudent; Heriger succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0151] “Heringer” 5c, d; “Herger.”]. Otto, duke of the Saxons, died.

## 913

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 913, there was an exceptionally severe winter. The Hungarians ravaged parts of Alamannia, and near the river Inn [Note: [Col. 0151] “near the river” 7; “at the river Inn” 8.] they were killed by Bavarians and Alamanni [Note: [Col. 0151] “and Alans” 7.]. In the same year Einhard [Note: [Col. 0151] “Enilhard” 7; “Everhard” 5.], bishop of Speyer, was blinded by Counts Bernhard [Note: [Col. 0151] “by Bernhard” in the Frisian codex; “by Erenhard” 5; “by Werinharius” 8; “by Erinhard” 9; “by Bernard” 10; “by Erenard” 12.] and Conrad.

## 914

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 914 [Note: [Col. 0151] “Otbert is killed.” This is assigned to the year 914 in 7, 9–12, and the Frisian codex; in the others, to 913.], Otbert, bishop of Strasbourg [Col. 0153A] [Note: [Col. 0153] “prelate” 9–12], is killed. Bishop Solomon was captured.

## 915

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 915, the Hungarians ravaged all Alamannia with fire and sword, but traversed all Thuringia and Saxony and reached the monastery of Fulda [Note: [Col. 0153] “all” is absent in 5.].

## 916–917

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 917 [Note: [Col. 0153] “915” 7, 10; “916” 8–12.], the Hungarians passed through Alamannia into Alsace and reached the borders of the kingdom of Lotharingia. Erchanger [Note: [Col. 0153] “Otthager” 7; “Freckanger” 6.] and Berthold [Note: [Col. 0153] “Berthold” 9–12.] were beheaded [Note: [Col. 0153] “Duke Erchanger and Berthold his brother, and Liutfrid, were punished by decapitation on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February” 7.]. Arnulf, duke of the Bavarians, rebels against the king.

## 918

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 918, King Conrad celebrated the Nativity of Saint John at the monastery of Herolvesfeld [Note: [Col. 0153] “Herovesfeld” 8; “Herolfelt” 7.] [Note: [Col. 0153C] The name had already been contracted to Hersfeld and Hirschfeld.].

## 919

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 919, King Conrad died, a man gentle and prudent in every respect [Note: [Col. 0153] Absent in 5c, e.] and a lover of divine religion. When he perceived that the day of his death was approaching, he summoned his brothers and relatives—namely, the leading men of the Franks—and announced to them that his death was near. So that no division might arise in the kingdom when a king was chosen after him [Note: [Col. 0153] “and in … let there not be a king after him” 7.], he warned them in a fatherly voice. He also ordered them to choose Henry, duke of the Saxons, son of Otto, an energetic and industrious man and an outstanding pursuer of peace; and he testified that no other man equally worthy of this office could be found. He transmitted to him through those same men the scepter, crown, and other ornaments of royal dignity, on the condition [Note: [Col. 0153] “the agreement having been completed” 5a, d.] that he protect and preserve the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0153] “the kingdom” 7.]. As he himself departed from this life [Note: [Col. 0153] “departing from this life” 5; 6.] [Col. 0153C] [Note: [Col. 0153] “departing” 6.], he was buried with an honorable [Note: [Col. 0153] “honored” 5, 7, 9.] burial in the monastery of Fulda. Yet during the few years in which he reigned [Note: [Col. 0153] “for the few … years” 5.], he was wearied by many struggles against the Bavarians, Alamanni, and Saxons who rebelled against him [Note: [Col. 0153] “was driven into exile” 5a, c, e.], although, by God’s favor, he overcame them before his death.

## 920

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 920, Henry was elected king with the consent of the Franks, Alamanni, Bavarians, Thuringians [Note: [Col. 0153] “Thuringians” is absent in 5d.] and Saxons; he began his reign by establishing discipline for the preservation of peace. For in those times many people, even nobles, devoted themselves assiduously to robbery.

## 921

In Upper Francia [Note: [Col. 0153] “the upper regions” 7.], grave and internal conflicts raged between Ruodbert, usurper of the kingdom, and King Charles. Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0153] “Meanwhile he persists” under the year 922 in 8.] King Henry vigorously devoted himself to establishing peace and suppressing the savagery of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0153] “for peace and suppression” absent in 7.].

## 922

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 922 [Note: [Col. 0153] “in the year 923” 8.], such a battle was fought at Soissons between Ruodbert and Charles that the victors seemed almost to be on both sides. Nevertheless Charles thrust a lance into the sacrilegious mouth of Ruodbert in such a way that, passing through his split tongue [Note: [Col. 0153] “divided tongue” 7, 9, 11, 12; “spread tongue” 5a, d; “split tongue” 10.], it penetrated the back of his neck.

## 923

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 923, the most precious treasure of the Lord’s blood came to Reichenau on the sixth day before the Ides of November. Abbot Haycho of Fulda [Note: [Col. 0153] “Haicho” 5.] died, and Hiltibert succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0153] “Iltibert” 7; “Hildebert” 8–12; “Hilbert” 5.]. Charles, intending to usurp Alsace and those parts of Francia along the Rhine as far as Mainz, advanced hostilely as far as Paternisheim [Note: [Col. 0153] “Patennichheim” 5.] [Note: [Col. 0153C] Pfeddersheim.], a village near Worms [Col. 0154B]. From there, when the king’s faithful men had gathered at Worms, he fled in a manner unworthy of a king. [Note: [Col. 0153] “He had driven out the king” 6.] In the same year King Henry [Note: [Col. 0153] “king” absent in 7.], together with Archbishop Ruotger [Note: [Col. 0154C] Of Trier.], Duke Giselbert, besieged the city of Metz, and compelled Widger [Note: [Col. 0153] “and, as it were, Widger” 7.] [Note: [Col. 0154C] Bishop of Metz.], although he resisted for a long time, to obey him. The most holy man Hermann, bishop of Cologne, died, and Wigfrid succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0153] “Wugfrid” 9, 11; “Winfred” 10.].

## 924

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 924, the Hungarians ravaged eastern Francia. Kings Charles and Henry met at the fortress of Bonn; making peace between themselves, they entered into a treaty, and Charles returned, promising never again to usurp the kingdom of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0153] “Lotharingian.”] [Note: [Col. 0153] “to usurp it, he went forth” 6; “promising, he returned” 5.]. In the same year he was seized by Heribert and placed in custody [Col. 0154C] [Note: [Col. 0153] “into custody” 5, 9, 11, 12.].

## 925

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 925, while King Henry held the kingdom of Lotharingia, gathered and firmly established under his authority [Note: [Col. 0153] “the Lotharingian kingdom” 7; “the kingdom” for this reason in 5.], King Charles died in the custody in which he was being held. He is said to have been a man of dull understanding and less suited to the needs of the kingdom. Since everyone had also abandoned his son—for at that time, after his father had been captured, he had gone into exile in Ireland [Note: [Col. 0153] “Hybernia” 5a, d; “Hibernia” 5c, e, 9–12.]—they chose a certain Rudolf as king. In the same year Bishop Witger died, and Benno, one of the ordinary clergy of Strasbourg, who had once lived an eremitical life in the Alps, was elected as his successor [Note: [Col. 0153] “to him” is absent in 5d.].

## 926

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 926, the Hungarians ravaged all Francia, Alsace, [Col. 0155A] Gaul, and Alamannia with fire and sword [Note: [Col. 0155C] Compare the Annals of Reichenau under the year 926.]. Burchard [Note: [Col. 0155] “Purchard” 7, 10.], duke of Alamannia, was killed in Italy [Note: [Col. 0155C] Compare the Annals of Reichenau.]. Heriger, a prelate worthy of God, died, and Hildibert, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0155] “Hildipert” 7.]. The duchy of Alamannia was entrusted to Hermann, who married Burchard’s widow [Note: [Col. 0155] “who married Wida, Burchard’s widow” 5.].

## 927

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 927, Benno, who is also called Benedict [Note: [Col. 0155] “who is Benedict” 5.], was blinded by the people of Metz. After a synod had been held at Duisburg [Note: [Col. 0155] “the people of Duisburg” 5; “Duisburg” 11, 12; “Duisburg” 10.], all the perpetrators of that deed [Note: [Col. 0155] “the perpetrator” 7.] were excommunicated, and the noble Adalbero was appointed bishop in his place.

## 928

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 928, King Henry invaded the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0155] “Bohemians” 9; “Boenos” 10.] with hostile intent and, with God’s aid, defeated them decisively. At that time a son, William [Note: [Col. 0155] “Willielmus” 7; “Willelmus” 10.], was born to Otto, the king’s son. The winter was exceptionally severe [Note: [Col. 0155C] Compare the Annals of Reichenau under the year 927.] [Note: [Col. 0155] “A winter arose, exceptionally severe” 7.]. Ruotger, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0155] “Ruodhger” 7.], died, and Ruodbert succeeded him.

## 929

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 929, Duke Giselbert [Note: [Col. 0155] “Gisilbert” 9; “Giselbert” 11, 12.] married Gerberga, daughter of King Henry.

## 930

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 930, Otto, son of King Henry, married Edith, daughter of the king of the English.

## 931

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 931, King Henry made the king of the Obodrites and the king of the Danes Christians [Note: [Col. 0155C] Compare the Annals of Reichenau under the years 931, 932, 934, 936, 937, 938, and 939.]. In the same year, having been summoned to Francia by Eberhard [Note: [Col. 0155] “King Habelishard” 7.] and other counts or bishops of Francia [Note: [Col. 0155] “when they were summoned” 7.], the king was honored individually by each of them in their houses or in the fitting seats of their churches with banquets and gifts [Note: [Col. 0155] “was honored” 932; “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 933, the Hungarians” 5.].

## 932

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 932, after many cities in eastern Francia and Alamannia [Note: [Col. 0155] “and in Alamannia” 5.] had been consumed by fire and sword, the Hungarians crossed the Rhine near Worms and, devastating Gaul as far as the Ocean Sea, returned through Italy.

## 934

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 934, King Henry struck down the Hungarians in great slaughter and captured many of them [Note: [Col. 0155] “struck down most of them” 7.]. In the same year he invaded and defeated the Slavs called the Ucrani [Note: [Col. 0155] “Uncrani” 5; “Werani” 11, 12.] [Note: [Col. 0155C] Their country is still called the Uckermark.] and made them tributary to himself. The church of Saint Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0156C] Of Trier.] fell in a storm: when, by election and the king’s clemency [Note: [Col. 0155] “by election and …” 9–12.], it had been restored to the monks [Note: [Col. 0155] “it fell, but by clemency … restored” 5c, e.], Ougo [Note: [Col. 0155] “Hugo” 7; “Ogo” 9–12; “Ougo” 8.], formerly provost, was elected abbot of that place, and the monks living there irregularly [Note: [Col. 0155] “the irregular monks” 7.] [Note: [Col. 0155] “dwelling” 6.] were expelled.

## 935

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 935, King Henry was struck by paralysis.

## 936

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 936 [Note: [Col. 0155] The year number is absent in 7 and 11.], a synod was held at Erfurt [Note: [Col. 0155] “Erfurt” 5; “Erfesfurth” 9, 11, 12; “Epesfurth” 10.] in Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0155] “Tiringa” 7; “Tyringa” 9; “Thuringia” 5.] by numerous bishops. King Henry, an outstanding pursuer of peace and a vigorous persecutor of the pagans, after achieving many victories bravely and manfully, having extended the boundaries of his kingdom in every direction [Col. 0156B] [Note: [Col. 0155] “the boundaries” 7.], died on the sixth day before the Nones of July. His son Otto was elected as his successor with the consent of the leading men of the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0155] “is appointed” 7.] Archbishop Hildibert died, and Frederick succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0155] “Friderich” 5a, d.]. Archbishop Unni [Note: [Col. 0156C] Of Bremen.] died, and Adaldag succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0155] “Adalgarius” 5c, e, 7, 9–12; “Adalgisus” 5a, d.].

## 937

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 937, the monastery of Saint Gall and the monastery of Saint Boniface [Note: [Col. 0155] “Boniface” 5, 9–12.] were burned by fire. Rudolf, king of the Burgundians [Note: [Col. 0155] “of the Burgundians” 5.], and Arnulf, duke of the Bavarians, died. Grave and internal conflicts arose between Henry, the king’s brother, and Eberhard, duke of the Franks, because of the enmity that had arisen between their vassals [Note: [Col. 0155] “vassals” 5; “knights” 6.].

## 938

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 938, the sons of Duke Arnulf rebelled against the king out of ambition for the duchy [Col. 0156C] [Note: [Col. 0155] “rebelled” 5.]. He himself marched into Bavaria to subdue them; but, unable to pacify them as he wished, he returned. Meanwhile the king’s brother Henry was seized by Eberhard in the fortress of Badalikki [Note: [Col. 0155] “Badaliki” 7, 10; “Badaliggi” 11, 12; “Balebike” 8.] [Note: [Col. 0156C] Belike, a town to the north, not far from the Rur and Arnsberg.]. After Henry had nevertheless been released soon afterward, Eberhard was sent into exile at Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0155] “Hildineshem” 7; “Hildinesheym” 5; “Ildineseim” 10; “Hildinisheim” 11, 12.]. Returning once again to Bavaria, the king subjected them all to himself and sent Eberhard, son of Arnulf, who was more rebellious than the others, into exile. The Hungarians were again ravaged with great slaughter by the Saxons.

## 939

In the year 939 [Note: [Col. 0155] “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 934” 7.], Eberhard was recalled from exile, and the entire kingdom was thrown into confusion by enmities [Note: [Col. 0157] “enemies” 5, 7, 9, 12.] and rebellions. For Eberhard and Giselbert conspired with Henry, the king’s brother, against the king; and certain wicked and God-hating ecclesiastical men also joined their faction, while they disturbed everywhere all the laws of peace and concord. When the king went to Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0157] “King Lotharius” in the Saint Godehard codex; “the king of Lotharingia” 7; “the king” 9, 11, 12; “Lotharingian” 10.], where the center of the rebellion then lay [Note: [Col. 0157] “when they go” 7.], Giselbert, wishing but unable to prevent the king from crossing the Rhine together with the king’s brother, engaged the king’s supporters near Biertan [Note: [Col. 0157] “Bieran” 10.] [Note: [Col. 0157C] Birthen, on the road leading from the town of Xanten to Rheinberg. See the distinguished Wedekind, Notes, etc., p. 205.] with his allies [Note: [Col. 0157] “with his allies” 9, 11, 12.]. With God granting victory, many of his men were killed and others put to flight, and he and the king’s brother sought the safety of flight. Pursuing them, the king reached Caprimons [Note: [Col. 0157C] Chevermont, on the right bank of the Meuse, about 4,000 paces from Liège. Wedekind, cited above, pp. 209–211.] and surrounded the fortress located there with a firm siege on every side.

Meanwhile Louis, king of Roman Gaul, son of Charles, at the urging of the king’s enemies, invaded Alsace under the pretext of seeking the kingdom of Lotharingia, which his father had lost; there he acted wherever he could, more like an enemy than a king [Note: [Col. 0157] “was able” is absent in 6.]. King Otto could not bear this patiently, so he lifted the siege of Caprimons [Note: [Col. 0157] The final words “the siege of Caprimons” in codex 6.] and, going to Alsace, expelled King Louis. After expelling him, he besieged the strongly fortified fortress of Breisach [Note: [Col. 0157] “Brisac” 5.] [Note: [Col. 0158C] Altbreisach, formerly situated on the left bank of the Rhine. Wedekind, cited above, p. 207.]. There, the succession of future generations will not be unaware of how many brave and warlike deeds were performed on both sides [Note: [Col. 0157] “were performed” 7; “the deeds were accomplished, which the future” 5.] [Note: [Col. 0157] “of later generations” 7.].

Thereupon Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, and Ruodhard, bishop of Strasbourg, having pitched their tents in the siege and abandoned the baggage of the forces they had brought, secretly fled by night. Going to the city of Metz, they hoped to meet Giselbert and Henry, as they had conspired to do. But things turned out very differently for them [Note: [Col. 0157] “turned out, because” 9–12; “turned out when” 5.], since the emptiest hope deceived them [Note: [Col. 0157] “their hope” 9, 11, 12.].

For when Giselbert and Eberhard were about to cross the Rhine with their men near the fortress of Andernach [Note: [Col. 0157] “crossed” 7.], Counts Udo and Conrad [Note: [Col. 0157] “Conrad, son-in-law of the emperor” in the Saint Godehard codex.] and the other faithful men of the king [Note: [Col. 0157] “faithful to the king” 5.] engaged them in battle to prevent them from crossing [Note: [Col. 0157] “in a military engagement” 5.], and they were soon overtaken by the swift course of death [Note: [Col. 0157] “the danger of death” 7.]. For Eberhard was killed, and Giselbert was drowned and perished in the Rhine; many of their companions were killed, while the rest were put to flight or captured.

When this was heard, the garrison of Breisach [Note: [Col. 0157] “the garrison of Brisach” 7.] submitted to royal domination [Note: [Col. 0157] “to domination” 7.], and the fortress was relieved from the siege [Note: [Col. 0157] “the garrison submits; the fortress” 5d.]. [Col. 0158A] Then the king again went to Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0157] “the king” absent in 5.] and subjected everyone to his authority. He also received his brother, who came to him after laying down his arms, with his customary mercy: he forgave him everything in which he had offended against him and kept him with himself in fraternal affection [Note: [Col. 0157] “in fraternal affection with him” 5.].

After all the Lotharingians had been subdued, the bishop of Metz tried for some time to resist. Therefore, at Thionville, he destroyed the chapel of the lord Emperor Louis the Pious, begun on the model of the chapel at Aachen, so that it might neither be completed nor regarded as a defense. Yet he did not remain longer in this kind of rebellion [Note: [Col. 0157] “of this kind” 7.]. Immediately, by God’s favor, the whole kingdom turned toward the king, as though from the very entrails of faith, and when the enemies had been destroyed, peace and concord were renewed.

Archbishop Frederick was sent to the monastery of Fulda [Col. 0158B], and Ruodhard of Strasbourg was sent to the monastery of Corbie. Meanwhile, while the events just described were taking place, Lady Queen Edith [Note: [Col. 0157] “Egid” 5a, c, e.] [Note: [Col. 0158C] Wife of Otto.] was staying at the monastery of Lorsch [Note: [Col. 0157] “Lauresheim” 5.].

At this same time Dancmar [Note: [Col. 0157] “Danemar” 5, 7, 9, 10; “Denemar” 11, 12; “Tancmar” 8.] [Note: [Col. 0158C] The death of Thancmar is reported under the year 938 by the Annals of Saxony.], the king’s brother by a concubine, rebelled [Note: [Col. 0157] “rebelling at Merseburg” 5, 7, 9.] and was killed in the fortress of Eresburg [Note: [Col. 0157] “at Erisburg” 10; “at Hersburk” 11, 12.]; his other followers were mutilated or hanged. This disturbance was not confined to one [Note: [Col. 0157] “one” 5.] province alone, but moved here and there throughout all the provinces of Saxony and Francia [Note: [Col. 0157] “Wigman was in motion” 5.]. Wigman the Saxon, who had rebelled [Note: [Col. 0157] “rebelling, but reconciled” 5.], was reconciled. King Louis married Gerberga, Giselbert’s widow.

## 940

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 940, the duchy of Lotharingia was entrusted to Henry, the king’s brother [Note: [Col. 0157] “brother” 7.], but he was soon expelled from it by the Lotharingians; Count Otto succeeded him in the same duchy. Also [Note: [Col. 0157] “And” absent in 5, 9–12.] Bishop Frederick was recalled from Fulda.

## 941

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 941, Henry, the king’s brother [Note: [Col. 0157] “the king’s” absent in 5.], conspired against the king with certain Saxons [Note: [Col. 0157] “sighed” 7.]. The king ordered those of them who seemed most prominent to be beheaded. He committed his brother to custody at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0157] “Ingleheim” 7.]. Because Archbishop Frederick appeared to be a participant in this conspiracy [Note: [Col. 0157] “who” 5d.], he cleared himself in a public examination by receiving the body and blood of the Lord before the people in the church.

## 942

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 942, the king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 0159] “at Frankfurt” 5.]. There his brother, secretly fleeing his custody through Ruodbert, a deacon of the church of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0159] “custody” 5d.], came at dawn, before daylight [Note: [Col. 0159] “before the time of light”; “already before dawn” 7.], and lay at the feet of the king as he entered the church. Having received pardon, he obtained the mercy for which he prayed [Note: [Col. 0159] “for which he had prayed” 9–12.]. A distinguished synod was held at the fortress of Bonn [Note: [Col. 0159] “at the distinguished fortress” 7.] by twenty-two bishops. At Trier, the basilica of Saint Maximinus was dedicated. A star resembling a comet was seen for fourteen nights, and an immense mortality of cattle followed.

## 943

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 943, Duke Otto died, and Conrad [Note: [Col. 0159] “of Conrad” 5.], son of Werinher [Note: [Col. 0159] “of Werinher” 7; “Wernher” 11, 12; “Weriner” 10.], succeeded him in the duchy.

## 944

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 944 [Col. 0159B], during the Rogation days, the king held a judicial assembly at Duisburg [Note: [Col. 0159] “at Duisburg” 5c, d; “at Duisburg” 5a, d.] [Note: [Col. 0159C] Situated on the Rhine.] with the leading men [Note: [Col. 0159] “the prior men” 7.] of the Lotharingians and Franks. There, through the faction of Duke Conrad, Ruotbert, archbishop of Trier, and Richarius [Note: [Col. 0159] “Richkarius of Tongeren” 7.], bishop of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 0159] “Tungerensis” 5.], were accused before the king of infidelity, but were soon freed from the charge brought against them.

The body of Saint Servatius was also carried there by clerics from Utrecht, because of the many injuries inflicted upon them by Count Immo. The Hungarians were slaughtered by the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0159] “by the Bavarians” is absent in 5, 8–12.] and Carantanians at a place called Wels [Note: [Col. 0159] “at the place Wels” is absent in 5, 8–12.] [Note: [Col. 0159C] Wels in Austria.] with such great slaughter that they had never before been so weakened by our people [Note: [Col. 0159] “disgraced them” 9–12.]. Count Adalbert, son of Matfrid, was killed by Ido [Note: [Col. 0159] “Ydo” 7.].

## 945

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 945, Bishop Richarius died, and Ougo [Col. 0159C] [Note: [Col. 0159] “Ogo” 5; “Ugo” 7.] the abbot of Trier succeeded him in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0159] “the bishopric” 5.]. Hermann [Note: [Col. 0159C] Duke of Alamannia.] and Duke Conrad, who had some enmity between them, were reconciled in the presence of the most pious king at Kassel [Note: [Col. 0159] “Castella” 7; “in the fortress” 9–12; “Casella” 8.] [Note: [Col. 0159C] Kassel, opposite Mainz.]. Bertald [Note: [Col. 0159] “Berthold” 9–12.] [Note: [Col. 0160C] Compare the Brief Annals of Saint Emmeram under the year 947.], duke of Bavaria, died, and Henry, the king’s brother, succeeded him in the duchy [Note: [Col. 0159] “to him” is absent in 5d.].

## 946

In the year 946, King Louis, expelled from his kingdom by his own people, sought help and approached King Otto, obtaining what he had desired. For the king entered Gaul with a strong force [Note: [Col. 0159] “with a strong hand” 5.], and had the city of Reims, Laon [Note: [Col. 0159] “Laudanum” 9–12; “Lugdunum” 5d.] [Note: [Col. 0160C] Laon.], and many other strongly fortified castles restored to Louis. He himself advanced hostilely as far as Rouen [Note: [Col. 0159] “Rotomacum” 7; “Rotomagum” 9–12.]. From there, after almost all the leading men of the kingdom, except Hugh son of Ruodbert, had been subjected to their king, he returned to his homeland [Note: [Col. 0159] “to his homeland” is absent in 9–12.].

## 947

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 947 [Note: [Col. 0159] 946 in 11, 12.], Lady Queen Edith died and was buried at Magdeburg amid the greatest mourning of the king and all his people [Note: [Col. 0159] “with great mourning at Magdeburg” 11, 12; “with great mourning at Magdeburg” 9; “with great mourning” (the name is written in the margin) 10; “with honor” 5a, d; “at Magdeburg” 6; “at Magdeburg” 5c, e.]. Duke Conrad, at that time dear to the king above almost all others, took Liutgard [Note: [Col. 0159] “Luitgard” 5a, d; “Luidgard” 5c, e.], the king’s daughter, in marriage. Liutolf [Note: [Col. 0159] “Ludolf” 5.], the king’s son, with fitting ceremony, joined Ita, daughter [Note: [Col. 0159] “with ceremony, his third daughter” 5.] of Duke Hermann, to himself in marriage.

## 948
