In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 948 [Note: [Col. 0159] 947 in 11, 12.], a synod of thirty-four bishops was held at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0159] “Ingelheim, of thirty-three bishops” 7.] [Col. 0160B] [Note: [Col. 0159] “by thirty-four bishops” 5, 9–12.]. Bishop Marinus [Note: [Col. 0159] “Martin” 5.], legate of the Roman Church, presided, and the illustrious kings Otto and Louis were present. At this synod, many matters useful to the Church were promulgated. The case of Hugh [Note: [Col. 0159] “Hugo” 7.], son of Heribert, who had expelled Archbishop Artald and seized the seat [Note: [Col. 0159] “the seats” 5.] of the church of Reims [Note: [Col. 0159] “of Reims” 7.], was also examined, and he was condemned by the judgment of all the bishops who were present [Note: [Col. 0159] “who had been present” 5, 9–12.]. Count Conrad, called Curcipoldus, son of Eberhard, a wise and prudent man, died.

## 949

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 949, Waldo, bishop of Chur, died [Note: [Col. 0159] “The bishop of Chur died” 9, 11, 12.], and Hardbert succeeded him. Count Uto died. With the king’s permission, whatever benefices or prefectures he possessed, he divided among his sons as though they were an inheritance. Duke Hermann, the wisest and most prudent among his people, died on the fourth day before the Ides of December [Note: [Col. 0159] “the third day before the Ides” 6, falsely; compare the Necrology of Saint Gall.]. In the same year, a daughter, Mathilda, was born to Liutolf, the king’s son.

## 950

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 950, the king celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary at Frankfurt. From there he went to Worms, where he kindly received the widow of Duke Hermann, who had come to him; he also entrusted the duchy of Alamannia to his son Liutolf [Note: [Col. 0159] “to his son Liudolf” 5.].

There Conrad, son of Count Gebehard [Note: [Col. 0159] “son of Hebehard” 7; “son of Gebeard” 10; “son of Eberhard” 5.], because he claimed that he had slept with a certain niece of the king [Note: [Col. 0159] “because he himself claimed that he had slept with the king’s niece” 10.], was defeated in single combat by a certain Burchard the Saxon, and it became clear that he had lied [Note: [Col. 0161] “he made it clear that he had lied” 5.].

In the same year the prince of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0161] “of the Bohemians” 5.] Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 0161] “Bolizlao” 9–12; “Bolizlaus” 5.] rebelled against the king. The king marched against him with a very strong force and subjected him entirely to his own authority. Ruodhard, bishop of Strasbourg, died, and Udo [Note: [Col. 0161] “to him Vido” 6; “to him Oido (Oudo?)” 9–12.], son of Count Udo, succeeded him in the episcopate. Rihgowo [Note: [Col. 0161] “Rihgonno” 5; “Rihguuo” 10; “Richguuo” 9, 11, 12.], bishop of Worms [Note: [Col. 0161] “Ribgauuior, bishop of Mainz” 7.], died, and Anno succeeded him. Archbishop Ruodbert labored greatly to acquire the abbey of Saint Maximinus, but by God’s favor he did not prevail [Note: [Col. 0161] “not” is absent in 5e.].

## 951

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 951, King Otto, wishing to go to Italy, equipped himself for this journey with much preparation, because he had decided to free Adalheid [Note: [Col. 0161] “Adalheid” 5.], widow of Lothair, king of Italy, daughter of King Rudolf, from the bonds and custody in which she was being held by Berengar [Note: [Col. 0161] “from the custody which” 6.], to take her in marriage, and together with her to acquire the Italian kingdom [Note: [Col. 0161] “so that he might acquire it” 5.].

His son Liutolf anticipated this journey with the Alamanni. Wishing to please his father if anything were done there energetically at his entrance, he accomplished nothing of what he had hoped, but rather, without consulting his father, offended him [Note: [Col. 0161] “showing” 7.] and thus became the source of the entire ensuing rebellion [Note: [Col. 0161] “the source of all the rebellion against himself” 7.] and discord.

For his uncle, Duke Henry, envious of all his honors and prosperity, sent his envoys from Bavaria through Trent [Note: [Col. 0161] “for three years” 5, 7, 9, 11, 12.] into Italy and turned away from him the minds of all the Italians he could influence. The result was that no city or fortress which had subsequently been open to the king’s bakers and cooks would open to the king’s son, and he suffered every kind of hardship and trouble there.

Soon afterward the king entered the Italian kingdom and, with God assisting him, became possessor of all Italy. Lady Adalheidis [Note: [Col. 0161] “Adalheid” 5.], a queen beloved by God, was also freed from custody by her own prudence, through God’s favor, and, with God auspiciously guiding the event, was joined in marriage to the fortunate King Otto.

Then Duke Liutolf [Note: [Col. 0161] “Rudolf” 5c, e.], distressed by what we have recorded, returned to his homeland without consulting his father, together with Archbishop Frederick.

## 952

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 952 [Note: [Col. 0161] 951 in 7.], the king, having expelled Berengar and wintering in Italy with his faithful men, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Pavia. Having thus arranged the affairs of the kingdom, he returned to his homeland in spring, but left Duke Conrad behind in Italy to pursue Berengar [Note: [Col. 0161] “abandoned” 10.].

Returning from Italy, Duke Liutolf celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with royal magnificence at Saalfeld [Note: [Col. 0161] “the Nativity of the Lord at Saalfeld” 5; “Saalfeld” 11, 12.] [Note: [Col. 0161] Saalfeld in Thuringia, formerly a royal estate.], where he kept Archbishop Frederick and all the leading men of the kingdom who were at hand with him [Note: [Col. 0161] “celebrates” 5d.]. This banquet soon began to seem suspicious to many, and it was said that more destruction than benefit was being deliberated there.

After Duke Conrad had been left to pursue Berengar, Berengar, on the duke’s advice, came of his own accord to the king in Saxony. Yet he obtained none of what he desired; instead, through the plotting of Duke Henry, the king’s brother, he barely received permission to keep his life and homeland [Note: [Col. 0161] “the king’s” is absent in 5a, c, e; “the king’s brother, he barely” is absent in 5d.] and returned to Italy. For this reason Duke Conrad too, greatly offended, defected from the loyalty owed to the king.

Then Archbishop Frederick and Duke Conrad became friends, for previously they had been enemies of one another. Nevertheless, in the same year, in the middle of August, a public assembly of Franks, Saxons, Bavarians, Alamanni, and Lombards was held at Augsburg, a city of the province of Rhaetia. There the aforesaid Berengar, together with his son Adalbert, surrendered himself entirely into royal vassalage [Note: [Col. 0161] “Adalbert, he surrendered himself to the king” 7.] [Note: [Col. 0161] “He gave Italy in vassalage to the royal authority” 7.] and again received Italy to govern with the king’s favor and gift. Only the marches of Verona and Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0161] “Aquileian” 5d, 7; “Aquilian” 11.] were excepted; these were entrusted to Henry, the king’s brother.

Nevertheless, when Berengar returned to Italy, he turned all these matters against the bishops, counts, and other leaders of Italy. Pursuing all of them with hatred and enmity, he made them his bitterest enemies.

## 953
A.D. 953. The king celebrated Christmas at Frankfurt. From there, advancing into Alsace [Note: [Col. 0161] “into Alsace” precedes “from there” in 7.], he gave his mother-in-law Berta—namely, the mother of the lady Queen Adelheid—the abbey at Erenstein [Note: [Col. 0161] “the abbey at Merenstein” in 5; “at Erenstein” in 9; “Nerestein” in 7; “at Heresteim” in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0161] Situated on the River Ill, between Strasbourg and Schlettstadt.]. By then the hostilities and secret plans formed against him had begun to appear openly, and each person began to disclose what they had woven together in their hearts [Note: [Col. 0161] “had drawn together” in 7 and 10.]. For as he was returning from Alsace and preparing to celebrate Easter at Ingelheim, his son Liutolf and Duke Conrad, having gathered wicked supporters—especially young men—from Francia, Saxony, and Bavaria, had conspired [Note: [Col. 0161] “had breathed the plan” in 7; “conspired” in 5c and 5e.] and were fortifying whatever strongholds or castles they could [Note: [Col. 0161] “wherever” in 5d.] for the rebellion that was to come. Nor was it now being done secretly what they were aiming at [Note: [Col. 0161] “for it was being done secretly” in 10.], but they were displaying open signs of rebellion.

When the king therefore reached Ingelheim, he judged it unsafe to celebrate Easter among his enemies, since only a few of his faithful men were with him [Note: [Col. 0163] “reached Ingelheim, but with only a few” in 9, 11, and 12.] [Note: [Col. 0163] “tute” in 5a, 5c, and 5e; “tuto” in 5d; “tutus” in 7; “tutius” (“more safely”) in 10; “tocius” in 9 and 11; “tutum” in 8 and the Saxon Chronicler.]. He withdrew from there to Mainz, where, after waiting for a long time before the gates in a manner unbefitting a king, and with Archbishop Frederick already conspiring with them, he scarcely obtained admission to the city. Then Liutolf and Conrad came to him there with feigned humility [Note: [Col. 0163] “with humility shown there” in 5.], as later became clear, and said that they had done nothing of the sort against him [Note: [Col. 0163] “in opposition” in 5.]; but they did not deny that, if his brother Henry came to Ingelheim at Easter, they would seize him. The king received this calmly and moderately, reached Cologne by boat, and, proceeding from there, celebrated Easter at the village of Dortmund [Note: [Col. 0163] Dortmund in Westphalia.] [Note: [Col. 0163] “Droomannus” in 5, 7, 9, and 11; “Deoomannus” in 12; “Drotmannus” in the Saxon Chronicler and in 8.].

After Easter, having gathered a multitude of his faithful men, he returned to Cologne. There he encountered the Bishop of Metz, in whom Liutolf and Conrad seemed to place their greatest hope and confidence, and all the Lotharingians except a few whose hearts were set on plunder and robbery. Those who came to him, abandoning his enemies [Note: [Col. 0163] “his friends” in 5.], he received with kindly affection and gathered them together, firm and steadfast in their loyalty. Having arranged these matters, he returned to Saxony; and after likewise strengthening and securing his affairs there, he again returned to Francia with a hostile force.

When Archbishop Frederick heard this, he withdrew to Mainz and entrusted the city to the king’s enemies for its defense [Note: [Col. 0163] This clause is absent in 5.]. He himself entered Brisach castle [Note: [Col. 0163] “Brisica” in 7; “Brisacum” in 5.], always a refuge of those rebelling against God and the king, and remained there for nearly the whole summer, awaiting the outcome.

Then the king, hearing that Mainz—the metropolitan and royal city of Francia—had been handed over to his enemies, hastened there as quickly as he could. Having gathered a multitude of his faithful men, both Franks and Saxons and Lotharingians, he surrounded it with a firm siege [Note: [Col. 0163] “royal” in 5c and 5e.]. His brother Henry also came from Bavaria to bring the king assistance, although there he acquired more disadvantage than advantage for himself [Note: [Col. 0163] “although for himself” in 5c; “for himself” is absent in 5; “his own” in 7.]. For meanwhile Liutolf, through the machinations of Arnold [Note: [Col. 0163] “Arnulf” in 9–12.], the brother of his wife Judith [Note: [Col. 0163] “Judith” in 7; “Juditta” in 9–12.], turned the Bavarians away from him; and, having been admitted into Regensburg, he plundered all Henry’s treasures there and distributed them to his own men for plunder.

Putting this misfortune of his brother before his own concerns, the king lifted the siege of Mainz and set out for Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0163] “Bavaria,” without “set out,” in 7.]. He besieged Regensburg and remained at that siege almost until Christmas. In the same year Wigfrid, archbishop of the church of Cologne, died; his successor was Brun [Note: [Col. 0163] “Brunus” in 7; “Bruno” in 5.], the king’s brother, who assumed, together with the episcopate, the duchy and government of the whole kingdom of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0163] “succedens a totius” in 7; “and kingdom” in place of “and government” in 5, 11, and 12.]. Liutgard, the king’s daughter, died.

## DCCCCLIV

A.D. 954. Abandoning the siege, the king celebrated Christmas in Saxony and, when Lent again approached, returned to Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0163] “again” in 7.]. There Archbishop Herold [Note: [Col. 0163] “Heroldus” in 7; Archbishop of Salzburg.] was blinded by the king’s brother [Note: [Col. 0163] “was, and” is absent in 5; “and” is absent in 7 and 10.]. By God’s favor, as the strength of the enemies diminished, the entire power of Bavaria and so much of Alamannia soon turned toward him that Regensburg was restored to the king [Note: [Col. 0163] “so that Regensburg” in 7.] and the rebels themselves declared that they neither wished nor were able to do anything against him [Note: [Col. 0163] “or might be able to do” in 7.].

Frederick also came to clear himself by oath, declaring that he had done nothing against his royal loyalty; but the king, full of every kind of mercy, released him from this oath [Note: [Col. 0163] “from this” is absent in 5.]. In the same year Duke Conrad, together with the Lotharingians under Duke Brun [Note: [Col. 0163] “Brunus” in 7; “Brunone” in 5c and 5e.], was about to engage in battle in the district of Blesensis, near the village of Rimilinga [Note: [Col. 0163] “Rumilinga” in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0163] The village Remeling exists east of Sarreguemines and the Saar, and south of the Blies and the town of Blieskastel.]; but at the last moment the encounter was abandoned, since it was against the king, as God willed it to happen.

The Hungarians, crossing the Rhine during Lent under the leadership of the king’s enemies, invaded Gaul and inflicted unheard-of evils upon the churches of God [Note: [Col. 0163] “the church” in 5c and 5e], then returned through Italy. Archbishop Frederick died, a man vigorous in holy religion and highly praiseworthy in every respect, except that in this one matter he seemed blameworthy: wherever even a single enemy of the king arose, he immediately placed himself beside him [Note: [Col. 0164] “a man altogether” in 10; “Arnstadt” in 9, 11, and 12.]. His successor was the king’s son William, unanimously elected by the people and clergy at Arnstadt [Note: [Col. 0164] In Thuringia, in the diocese of Mainz. It is also mentioned in the Life of Saint Bruno, chapter 30.].

At that time Liutolf was recalled to the king’s favor. He returned to his father the vassals he had held and the duchy; Burchard succeeded him in the duchy. Conrad also, stripped of all the wealth he had possessed, was admitted to the king’s favor after renouncing the duchy, content with his life, homeland, and estate [Note: [Col. 0163] “life” is absent in 5c and 5e.]. Otto, Liutolf’s son, was born.

## DCCCCLV

A.D. 955 [Note: [Col. 0163] “945” in 7.]. The Hungarians came forth in so immense a multitude that they said they could be defeated by no one unless the earth opened up and swallowed them or heaven overwhelmed them [Note: [Col. 0163] “they went out” in 9–12; “the earth swallow them” in 5.]. Conrad, formerly duke, was killed there, and by God’s favor such a slaughter of them was inflicted by the king’s army beside the River Lech [Latin *Lichum*; “Lechum” in 9, 11, and 12.] that among our people no such victory had ever before been heard of or achieved.

Returning from there, the king directed his army against the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0165] “directed his armies” in 5.]. Having gained a similar victory there, he struck them down in a vast slaughter. Wigmann was expelled. Henry, the king’s brother, after recovering his fortunes when all seemed lost, recovered the duchy of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0165] “of the Bavarian” in 5d.] and died. To his son Henry the pious king gave the duchy and the march. Otto, the king’s son [Note: [Col. 0165] “the king’s” in 10–12.], was born [Note: [Col. 0165] “He gave it. In the year of the Lord 956: Otto” in 7.].

## DCCCCLVI

A.D. 956. The king, living in peace and leisure, held a royal assembly at Cologne with a very large gathering of his faithful men. At that time a severe pestilence was raging throughout all parts of the kingdom and destroyed countless people everywhere. Among those who died were Ruodbert, archbishop of Trier, and Hadamar [Note: [Col. 0165] “Adamarus”; “Atto” in 7.], abbot of Fulda. Henry succeeded the former in the episcopate, and Hatto succeeded the latter in the abbacy.

In the same year Liutolf was sent to Italy to suppress the tyranny of Berengar [Note: [Col. 0165] “to condemn” in 7.]. Within a short time, after Berengar had been expelled, he became the possessor of almost all Italy. The abbey of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch [Note: [Col. 0165] “Saint Nazarius at Lorsch” in 11 and 12; “Nazarius at Laursheim” in 9 and 10.] was restored to the right of election.

## DCCCCLVII

A.D. 957 [The supplied text reads “757,” apparently erroneously.] The king again invaded the Slavs. Liutolf died in Italy; his body was brought back from there and honorably buried by his venerable brother, Archbishop William, at Saint Alban’s in Mainz. Willerus [Note: [Col. 0165] “Willihelmus” in 9, 11, and 12.], abbot of Trier, died; Witkerus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0165] “Wikerns” in 5 and 7.].

At that time the most merciful king restored the abbey of Saint Peter at Wissembourg [Note: [Col. 0165] “Wirtzburg” in 5; “Wizenbus” in 7; “Wizenburc” in 10; “Wizemburk” in 11 and 12.] [Note: [Col. 0165] In Alsace.] to its former dignity through his zeal for holy religion. Under his predecessors it had long been deprived of the gift of election and privilege, and he appointed the venerable man Geilo [Note: [Col. 0165] “Gelionem” in 5; “Gedonem” in 7; “Heilonem” in 10.] abbot of that monastery.

## DCCCCLVIII

A.D. 958. The king celebrated Easter at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0165] “celebrates” in 7; “at” is absent in 5a, 5c, and 5e.]. From there he came by boat to Cologne to hold a royal assembly there. In the same year Count Reginher was arrested through the agency of Archbishop Brun [Note: [Col. 0165] “of Brun” in 7; “of Bruno” in 5c and 5e.] [Col. 0166A] and was sent into exile among the Slavs.

With the consent of Herold, Frederick was ordained archbishop of the church of Juvavum [Note: [Col. 0165] “Viennensis” in 5; “Uanensis” in 7; “Viuanensis” in 11; “Juvaviensis” in 10.] in the presence of the king at Ingelheim, during the octave of Easter, after a synod of sixteen bishops had been held there. Alewicus [Note: [Col. 0165] “Aleniucus” in 5; “Alwicus” in 9, 11, and 12.], abbot of the monastery of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0165] “Augeensis” in 9–12.], died; Ekkehardus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0165] “Ekkihardus” in 5; “Eggehardus” in 11 and 12.]. Gralo [Note: [Col. 0165] “Garolo” in 7; “Gralo” in 9 and 11; “Graio” in 12; “Cralo” in 5; the words “Gralo … succeeded” are absent in 10.], abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, died; Burchard succeeded him.

## DCCCCLIX

A.D. 959. The king again invaded the Slavs, where Thietmar was killed [Note: [Col. 0165] “Dietmarus” in 11 and 12.]. Envoys of Helena [Note: [Col. 0165] Helena, that is, Olga, queen of the Russians.], queen of the Rus’, who had been baptized at Constantinople under the emperor Romanus, came to the king, as later became clear, with deceitful intentions. They requested that a bishop and priests be ordained for that people [Note: [Col. 0165] “be ordained” is absent in 5.]. In the same year Hagano [Note: [Col. 0165] “Hagatio” in 5; “Hageno” in 11 and 12.], abbot of Hersfeld, was struck by paralysis.

## DCCCCLX

A.D. 960. The king celebrated Christmas at Frankfurt. There Libutius [Note: [Col. 0165] “Libunus” in 7; “Libentius” in the codex of Saint Godhard.] from the monks of Saint Alban’s was ordained bishop for the people of the Rus’ by the venerable Bishop Adaldag [Note: [Col. 0166C] Archbishop of Bremen.] [Note: [Col. 0165] “archbishop” in 9–12.]. Gunther was appointed abbot at Hagano’s request [Note: [Col. 0165] “at Hageno’s request” in 11 and 12.].

In the same year the king again went against the Slavs. Envoys also came from the Apostolic See: John the deacon and Azo the scriniarius, summoning the king to defend Italy and the Roman state from Berengar’s tyranny [Note: [Col. 0165] “to defend it” in 5e.]. Walbert, archbishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 0165] “Waltbertus” in 5; “Walpertus” in 7.], Waldo, bishop of Como [Note: [Col. 0165] “Uuldo” in 7.], and Margrave Opertus [Note: [Col. 0165] “Eupertus” in 7.], fleeing Berengar, also came to the king in Saxony. Nearly all the other counts and bishops of Italy likewise begged him by letters or envoys to come and free them [Col. 0166C].

Geilo, abbot of Wissembourg [Note: [Col. 0165] “Wirzenburgensis” in 7; “Wirtzburgensis” in 5.], died; Gerricus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0165] “Gerric” in 7; “Herrichus” in 5d.].

## DCCCCLXI

A.D. 961. The king celebrated Christmas in the city of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0165] “the city” is absent in 5a.] [Note: [Col. 0165] “celebrated at Regensburg” in 5c and 5e.]. There Poppo, bishop of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 0165] “archbishop” in 5.], very dear to the king, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0165] “the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March” in 8–12; the Fulda Necrology, in Leibniz and Schannat, has “the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March”; 7 has “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March”; the Würzburg Chronicle has “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March”; Baluz.]. His kinsman Poppo succeeded him in the episcopate.

Libutius, who in the preceding year had been delayed from the journey by certain postponements, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March of the present year [Note: [Col. 0165] “his own successor in the episcopate” in 9–12.]. Adalbertus, from the monks of Saint Maximinus, succeeded him in the ordination, to be sent abroad, through the machination and counsel of Archbishop William, although he had trusted that William would treat him better [Note: [Col. 0167] “had trusted in him” in 10; “had seemed to trust in him” in 9, 11, and 12.] and although he had never committed any offense against him [Note: [Col. 0167] “had committed” in 5d.].

The most pious king sent him honorably to the people of the Rus’, equipped with all the resources he needed [Note: [Col. 0167] “equipped with the body he needed” in 7.]. The king, preparing to go to Italy, gathered a very large multitude of his faithful men at Worms. There, with the consent and unanimity of the magnates of the kingdom and of the entire people, his son Otto was elected king. Proceeding from there, he was likewise elected king at Aachen by the agreement and election of all the Lotharingians.

After his son had been ordained [Note: [Col. 0167] “after his son, however, had been ordained” in 7.], the father returned to Saxony. Having arranged the affairs of the kingdom, he entrusted his son to Archbishop William to protect and educate, and thus made his way into Italy through Bavaria and Trent [Note: [Col. 0167] “Trent” in 7, 9, 11, and 12; “Terrentum” in 5.].

There he encountered nearly all the counts and bishops of Italy. Received honorably by them, as was fitting, he entered Pavia with authority and without any resistance, and ordered the palace destroyed by Berengar to be rebuilt. Berengar, Willa, and their sons, however, were shut up in whatever fortifications or castles they could find, and dared to advance nowhere outside against the king [Note: [Col. 0167] “what they heard” in 9–12; “however” is absent in 5 and in 9–12.].

In the same year Gotefrid, bishop of Speyer, died; Otgerus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0167] “Othgerius” in 10.]. A solar eclipse occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. The king sent Hatto, abbot of Fulda, ahead to Rome to build dwellings for him.

## DCCCCLXII

A.D. 962. The king celebrated Christmas at Pavia [Note: [Col. 0167] “at Pavia” is absent in 5, 7, and 9–12, although 7 and 11 leave a space; the word is written above the line in one witness.]. Proceeding from there, he was favorably received at Rome and, amid the acclamation of the entire Roman people and clergy, was called and ordained emperor and Augustus by the apostolic John, son of Alberic. The pope also detained him with much affection and promised that throughout his life he would never desert him; the promise nevertheless produced a result far different from what it professed [Note: [Col. 0167] “professed” in 7.].

When the Emperor Augustus was returning from the Roman city [Note: [Col. 0167] “Roman” is absent in 5.] and celebrating Easter at Pavia, Berengar fortified himself on a certain mountain called Saint Leo [Note: [Col. 0167] Saint Leo in the Urbino Legation, near San Marino.], having drawn forces to himself from every direction. Willa shut herself in on an island in Lake Maggiore [Note: [Col. 0167] “Willa into Lake Maggiore” in 7.] [Note: [Col. 0167] The island of Saint Julius lies not in Lake Verbano but in Lake Orta, west of Lake Verbano.], on an island called Saint Julius [Note: [Col. 0167] “called Saint” in 7.].

Their sons, Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0167] “Alpertus” in 7.] and Wido [Note: [Col. 0167] “Guido” in 5.], wandered uncertainly here and there, although they still held certain strongholds with their followers: namely, the castle of Garda [Note: [Col. 0167] “Grad” in 5; “Gard” in 9–12.] [Note: [Col. 0167] Garda, on the shore of Lake Garda.], Travallium [Note: [Col. 0168] Muratori conjectures that Valle Travaglia was in the mountains toward Lake Verbano.], and an island [Note: [Col. 0167] “Travallium island” in 11 and 12.] in Lake Como [Note: [Col. 0168] Lake Como.].

Willa was attacked first. After every exit from the lake had been closed, she was worn down by daily attacks from slingers, archers, and other instruments of war. Besieged for not quite two full months, she was captured; finally, through the emperor’s clemency, she was released and allowed to go wherever she wished [Note: [Col. 0167] “he was released … to whom” in 5c and 5e.]. With all possible speed she went to Berengar and persuaded him by every means not to surrender to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0167] “that he should not give himself” in 7; “in every way” in 5 and 7.].

In the same year Adalbert, who had been ordained bishop for the Rus’, returned, unable to accomplish anything in the matters for which he had been sent and seeing that he had exhausted himself in vain. Some of his men were killed on the return journey; he himself escaped only with great difficulty. Coming to the king, he was received affectionately and was embraced and supported by the God-beloved Archbishop William, as brother by brother [Note: [Col. 0167] “as brother by brother” is absent in 5 and 7.], in return for the very troublesome journey William had plotted for him.

Reginbert, a servant of God, died [Note: [Col. 0168C] The Saxon Chronicler adds: “He built the abbey of Saint Blaise in Swabia.”]. When letters had also been sent to the emperor on his behalf, it was ordered that his return be awaited at the palace. In the same year Adalbero, a venerable man and bishop of Metz, died [Note: [Col. 0167] “Adalpero” in 7.].

## DCCCCLXIII

A.D. 963. The king again celebrated Christmas and Easter at Pavia. Meanwhile Adalbert, rushing here and there [Note: [Col. 0167] “wandering” in 5.], drew to himself as many people as he could from every direction; he also entered Corsica [Note: [Col. 0167] “coming to Corsica, he entered there” in 9, 11, and 12.], seeking to defend himself there. He repeatedly urged the Roman pontiff to come to his aid.

While these things were happening, the emperor set out from Pavia and besieged Berengar on Mount Saint Leo [Note: [Col. 0167] “Berengar again” in 10.]. He spent the entire summer there, repeatedly surrounding the mountain on every side and preventing any exit or entrance.

Meanwhile Pope John, consigning to oblivion the promises he had made to the emperor, defected from him [Note: [Col. 0167] “defects” in 5.] and, favoring Berengar’s or Adalbert’s party, admitted Adalbert into Rome. When the emperor heard of these fraudulent schemes, he abandoned the siege around the mountain and marched toward Rome with his army. Fearing his arrival, those within Rome seized a great deal of Saint Peter’s treasure and sought the means of flight.

Then the Romans divided into several factions [Note: [Col. 0167] “Rome … divided” in 5.]. Some favored the emperor—for many complained that they were being oppressed by the aforesaid pope with numerous injuries [Note: [Col. 0167] “for many indeed” in 5.]—while others courted the apostolic, although they held different opinions. Nevertheless, they admitted the emperor into the city with the honor due to him and, after giving hostages, subjected themselves entirely to his authority.

The emperor then gathered a great number of bishops and convened a synod. Acting on their advice, he sent a delegation and, by canonical authority, recalled the fugitive apostolic to the pontifical and apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0169] “the fugitive” in 5.]. Since John stubbornly refused in every way [Note: [Col. 0169] “in all ways” in 3 and 7.], the Roman people, by common consent, elected and ordained in his place Leo, the protoscriniarius, a vigorous and capable man.

Nearly all the bishops of Romania [Note: [Col. 0169] “of Rome” in 5, 9, 11, and 12.] and Italy attended this synod. Angelfred, patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0169] “Ingalfred” in 7.], was also present; he died there at that time. From our people there also attended Adaldag [Note: [Col. 0169] “Landtwardus” in 5a and 5d; “Landwardus” in 5c and 5e.] and Archbishop Henry [Note: [Col. 0169D] Of Trier.], Lantwardus [Note: [Col. 0169] “Adaldadus” in 9 and 11; “Adaldaldus” in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0169D] Of Minden.] and Bishop Otgerus [Note: [Col. 0170D] Of Speyer.].

Afterward John, also called Octavian, seeing that he had been deposed, was moved to late repentance and separated himself from Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0169] “moved by Adalbert” in 5.]. Adalbert returned to Corsica. In the same year the castle of Garda in Italy was captured [Note: [Col. 0169] “Karda” in 7; “Gard” in 5 and 9–12.]. Among our people, the Slavs called Lusinzani [Note: [Col. 0169] “Lunsinzani” in 5 and 9–12.] [Note: [Col. 0170D] Lusatians.] were also subjugated.

## DCCCCLXIV

A.D. 964. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Rome. Berengar and his men, besieged on Mount Saint Leo, were defeated, and the castle itself was subjected to the emperor’s authority. Berengar and Willa were sent to Bavaria.

The Romans again defected from the emperor in their customary manner [Note: [Col. 0169] “in their customary manner” is absent in 9–12.]. Joining themselves by conspiracy to several other castellans from outside, they attempted to kill him. But when their ambush was exposed, on the very day on which they were plotting to destroy him, he anticipated the death prepared for him. On the third day before the Nones of January, with only a very few of his men, he attacked them and struck down no small number of them within the city walls [Note: [Col. 0169] “struck them down within the walls of the city” in 11 and 12; “inside the walls” in 5.].

On the following day the Romans came again [Note: [Col. 0169] “Rome” in 5a and 5c–d.], gave one hundred hostages, and swore upon the body of Saint Peter that they would remain faithful to the emperor and the pope. The emperor then remained among them for a full additional week [Note: [Col. 0169] “a week” in 5.], before departing to organize the duchies of Spoleto and Camerino. At Pope Leo’s request he sent the hostages back to the Romans. Ungrateful for these favors [Note: [Col. 0169] “although he himself” in 9 and 11.], while he was not far from the city they admitted John, also called Octavian, and did not fear to annul the loyalty they had promised to the emperor and the pope.

Pope Leo, scarcely escaping with a few men and stripped of all his possessions, went to the emperor, who was stationed in the duchy of Camerino [Note: [Col. 0169] “the duchy” in 7.], and celebrated Easter there [Note: [Col. 0169] “went to him and there” in 9 and 11.].

John, also called Octavian, cruelly mutilated John the deacon and Azo the scriniarius [Note: [Col. 0169] “Aton” in 7.]. He seized Otger, bishop of Speyer, flogged him, and detained him with himself for some time, though under harsh conditions. Later he immediately sent him away in the hope of obtaining pardon from the emperor [Note: [Col. 0169] “the emperor’s pardon” in 9 and 10; “to the emperor” in 11 and 12.], but this hope deceived him through divine dispensation. For he died on the second day before the Ides of May.

Then the Romans, greatly fearing the emperor’s arrival, elected a certain Benedict, a deacon of the Roman Church, forgetting their loyalty and election of Lord Leo, and installed him, once ordained, in the Apostolic See. When the emperor heard this, he gathered a multitude of his faithful men from every direction [Note: [Col. 0169] “with him from every direction” in 11 and 12.], went to Rome, and fortified it with a firm siege on every side so that no exit would be possible.

But the aforesaid Benedict, the false-named apostolic, encouraged the Romans to resist the emperor for a long time. Threatening excommunication against the emperor and his faithful men, he climbed the city walls and comported himself with a more arrogant pride than was fitting for an apostolic [Note: [Col. 0169] “showed himself more arrogantly than was fitting for an apostolic” in 5.].

At last, constrained by hunger and the siege, the Romans repented that they had erred and acted unjustly against the emperor [Note: [Col. 0169] “had erred and acted against” in 5.]. On the vigil of the Forerunner, the ninth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0169] “the Forerunner, that is, the ninth day before the Kalends” in 5; “the sixth day before the Kalends” in 5d.], they opened the city gates. After admitting the emperor with the honor due to him, they handed over the sacrilegious and perjured Benedict to the emperor’s authority [Note: [Col. 0169] “subjected him to his authority” in 9, 11, and 12.] and restored Lord Leo to the Apostolic See.

Then Pope Leo, having gathered a synod of many bishops [Note: [Col. 0169] “a synod” in 7.], deposed the same Benedict, the invader of the Roman See, from the rank he had usurped, by the judgment of all. He cut away the pontifical pallium that Benedict had placed upon himself [Note: [Col. 0169] “cut off” in 5c and 5e.], seized the pastoral staff from his hand, and broke it into pieces before everyone. At the emperor’s request he allowed him to retain only the rank of deacon [Note: [Col. 0169] “allowed him only the rank” in 5.].

After celebrating the Nativity of blessed John and the feast of the holy apostles, the emperor returned from the Roman city and encountered on his return a more unfavorable omen than he had hoped. For such plague and mortality attacked his army that scarcely even a healthy person hoped to remain alive from morning until evening or from evening until morning [Note: [Col. 0169] “from evening until morning” in 5.].

In this pestilence died Henry, archbishop of Trier; Gerricus [Note: [Col. 0169] “Gerrich” in 9, 11, and 12.], abbot of Wissembourg [Note: [Col. 0169] “Wirtzburgensis” in 5; “Wirziburgensis” in 7; “Wizburgiensis” in 9; “Wiziburgensis” in 10; “Wirzeburgiensis” in 11 and 12.]; and Godefrid, duke of Lotharingia, together with an innumerable multitude of others, noble and lowborn alike.

At last, when the pestilence ceased through divine mercy, the emperor reached Liguria. There, during the autumn season, devoting himself to peace and leisure, he exercised himself in hunting.

In the same year Duodo [Note: [Col. 0171] “Dudo” in 11 and 12.], chaplain of the palace, was seized by Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0171] “two of the palace chaplains by Alpert” in 7.]. After being beaten with whips, he was taken to Corsica, but was released not long afterward.

At that time Waldo, bishop of Como, captured an island in Lake Como and destroyed the fortifications on it from the foundations [Note: [Col. 0171] “the fortifications, or it, from the foundations” in 7.]. This was the beginning of evils for Count Udo [Note: [Col. 0171] “a message for the count” in 5.]. For he had received Hatto [Note: [Col. 0171] “Atto” in 7.], the island’s guardian, into his allegiance; and after the island had been destroyed, he could not reconcile Hatto to the emperor as he had wished [Note: [Col. 0171] “reconcile him” in 5.]. Taking this badly, he turned all his hostility against Bishop Waldo and resolved to take revenge on him if he could.

Erchanbert [Note: [Col. 0171] “Erkanbertus” in 5; “Encharbertus” in 7.] was appointed abbot of the monastery of Wissembourg [Note: [Col. 0171] “Wirtzburgensis” in 5; “Wirziburgensis” in 7; “Wiziburgensis” in 10.] in place of his brother Gerricus [Note: [Col. 0171] The words from “Erchanbert” through “was appointed” are absent in 9, 11, and 12.].

## DCCCCLXV

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 965, the emperor celebrated Christmas at Pavia. After the feast was completed, he immediately returned to his homeland, having arranged the affairs of the kingdom in Italy. His son King Otto [Note: [Col. 0171] “king” is absent in 5.] and Archbishop William met him at the border of Francia and Alamannia, in the village of Heimbodesheim [Note: [Col. 0171] “Heimbogesheim” in 7; “Heimbodesheym” in 5; “Heimbodeseim” in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0171] Today Heimsheim or Heimsen, midway between Stuttgart and Pforzheim.], and received him there with great joy.

Proceeding to Worms, he encountered there his brother Archbishop Brun [Note: [Col. 0171] “his Brun” in 11 and 12; “his Brunian archbishop” in 5; “Brun, archbishop of Cologne” in the codex of Saint Godhard.] on the Purification of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0171] “of the Most Holy Virgin Mary” in 5.]. Thus he spent the whole of Lent in Francia and celebrated Easter at Ingelheim with great joy.

From there [Note: [Col. 0171] “from there” in 5.] he reached Cologne by boat. He treated his mother, the lady Matilda, his sister, Queen Gerberga, and her son, King Lothair, who had come to meet him, with fitting affection and honor there [Note: [Col. 0171] “with fitting affection and honor toward him” in 7.], and then set out for Saxony [Note: [Col. 0171] “set out again” in 5.].

He also brought with him into Francia that Benedict who had been deposed from the Roman city and entrusted him to Archbishop Adaldag for safekeeping. He kept two daughters of Berengar in the palace, treating them with suitable honor alongside the lady empress.

In the same year certain Lombards, following their customary practice, defected from the emperor and brought Adalbert back into Italy [Note: [Col. 0171] “into Italia” in 7; “introduced” in 9 and 11; “led him back” in 10.]. Then the emperor sent Burchard, duke of the Alamanni, into Italy. To engage Adalbert wherever he might be found, Burchard sailed down the Po with the Lombards loyal to the emperor and with the Alamanni through the Jusum [Note: [Col. 0171] “with the Alamanni through the Jusum” in 7; “with the Alamanni, apparently ‘visum,’ through the Jusum” in 5; “with the Alamanni through the Jusum and the Po” in 7. Concerning the word *Jusum*, compare Adelung or Du Cange.], and brought his ships to land in the region where he had heard Adalbert was [Note: [Col. 0171] “they had heard” in 5.].

Adalbert rushed upon them at their first landing from the river. His brother Wido and many others fell there. Adalbert himself barely escaped by flight [Note: [Col. 0171] “by flight” is absent in 5.], entered certain mountainous places, and concealed himself there from the emperor.

The duke, therefore, rejoicing in this victory, returned to his homeland and reported to the emperor what had happened to him [Note: [Col. 0171] “what had happened there” in 7; “reported” in 7.].

Meanwhile Wido, bishop of Modena [Note: [Col. 0171] “Wido of Metz” in 5 and 7.], pretending with foxlike cunning to be faithful to the emperor and loudly claiming that he would betray the emperor’s enemies to him, undertook Adalbert’s embassy and attacked the emperor in Saxony [Note: [Col. 0171] “in Saxony” in 7.]. He was not granted an audience or conversation with the emperor, however, but was allowed to return in disgrace. Below the Alps, beyond Chur, he was arrested, sent back to Saxony, and handed over to the custody of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0171] “to the custody of the Slavs” in 7; the phrase is absent in 5c and 5e.].

Uodo, bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0171] “Odo” in 7; “Udo” in 5 and 11.], died; Erchanboldus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0171] “Hercanboldus” in 7; “Erkanboldus” in 5; “Erchandoboldus” in 10; “Eripkanboldus” in 9.].

In the same year Lord Pope Leo died. The Roman envoys—namely, Azo the protoscriniarius and Marinus, bishop of the church of Sutri [Note: [Col. 0171] “Martinus of Sutri” in 5d.]—approached the emperor in Saxony [Note: [Col. 0171] “into Saxony” in 5.] to ask him to appoint whichever man he wished as Roman pontiff. They were honorably received and sent back. Otger, bishop of Speyer [Note: [Col. 0171] “Hothkerus” in 7.], and Liuzo [Note: [Col. 0171] “Luzo” in 11 and 12; “Linzo” in 5.], bishop of Cremona, were sent by the emperor to Rome with them.

Then John, bishop of the church of Narni, was elected by all the Roman people and enthroned as pontiff of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0171] “was elected and enthroned” in 5.]. Immediately he persecuted the leading Romans with a more elevated spirit than was proper, and within a short time found them exceedingly hostile and enraged against him. For he was seized by the prefect of the city and a certain Rotfred [Note: [Col. 0171] “Rothfred” in 10.], expelled from the city, and committed to custody in Campania.

Finally, in this year, when the emperor was returning from Italy, Thiodricus [Note: [Col. 0171] “Thiedericus … Thiedericus” in 5; “Theodericus” in 10; “Tyodericus” in 11.]—a deacon of the church of Trier [Note: [Col. 0171] “subdeacon” in 10.]—was appointed successor to Henry, archbishop of Trier; and Diedericus [Note: [Col. 0171] “Diedericus” in 10; “Dietricus” in 9.], the emperor’s cousin, was appointed successor to Adalbero, bishop of Metz.

Archbishop Brun [Note: [Col. 0171] “Bruno” in 5.], the emperor’s full brother, a man most worthy both of the duchy and the episcopate, died on the fifth day before the Ides of October. Folchmarus succeeded him in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0171] “Folthmarus” in 5; “Flokmarus” in 11 and 12.]. In the same year Gero, the best and most distinguished of the margraves of our time [Note: [Col. 0171] This phrase is absent in 5c and 5e.], died. King Lothair married the lady Hemma [Note: [Col. 0171] “Henima” in 5.].

## DCCCCLXVI
In the Year of Our Lord 966 the emperor celebrated Christmas at Cologne and arranged all the affairs of the kingdom of Lotharingia as seemed best to him. Erchanbert, abbot of the monastery of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 0173] “Witzenburgensis,” 7, etc.], died, and the emperor, at the monks’ election, placed Adalbert, ordained bishop for the Rugians, over that monastery. Starchandus [Note: [Col. 0173] “Stanchardus,” 7; “Starkandus,” 5.] died; he was bishop of the church of Rubloc [Note: [Col. 0173] “Rubolocensis,” “Ruolocensis,” 10.] [Col. 0173C] [Eichstätt]. Reginold succeeded him in the episcopate. Count Udo, who had entered into a conspiracy with Adalbert, son of Berengar, and was preparing to go to Italy to blind Waldo, bishop of Como, was convicted of treason against the imperial majesty and expelled from the kingdom under oath not to presume to enter any part of it thereafter. Witker [Note: [Col. 0173] “Witgerus,” 11, 12; “Wikerus,” 5, 7.], abbot of the monastery of Trier, died; Asolf succeeded him in the abbacy. The emperor, preparing to go to Italy once more, celebrated the Assumption of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0173] “of the Most Holy Virgin Mary,” 5.] at Worms. There, having held a council with all the leading men of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0173] “counsel,” 5d.], he crossed the Alps through Alsace and Chur [Note: [Col. 0173] “descending the Alps,” 7.] and entered Italy. He sent Sigolf [Note: [Col. 0173] “Sigelfus,” 7; “Sigalfus,” 8.], bishop of Piacenza, and certain Italian counts who had defected from him on Adalbert’s account in the previous year, to the transalpine regions of France or Saxony, to be held in custody. Then the Romans, fearing the emperor’s arrival, released Pope John from the custody in which he had been held, since Rotfred had by then died, and, asking pardon for the wrongs they had inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 0173] “requesting,” 5d.], restored him to his office and see. In the same year Count Eberhard died. In the same year [Note: [Col. 0173] From “anno” through the second “anno” is absent in 11, 12.] Berengar, formerly king of Italy, died in exile and was buried at Babenberg [Note: [Col. 0173] “Babenberch,” 9; “Babenberc,” 10.] in royal fashion; [Col. 0173C] his widow Willa, before he was buried, assumed for herself the veil of a religious woman [Note: [Col. 0173] “the veil for herself,” 5c, e.]. Count Udo, having forgotten his oath, entered Francia, from which he again returned without accomplishing anything.

**DCCCCLXVII.**

In the Year of Our Lord 967 the emperor celebrated Christmas at Rome [Note: [Col. 0173] “Christmas is celebrated,” 7.] and, except for the prefect of the City, who had fled, ordered thirteen of the leading Romans who seemed to have been responsible for the expulsion of Lord Pope John [Col. 0174A] [Note: [Col. 0173] “14 from,” 7.] to die by hanging [Note: [Col. 0173] “expulsions,” 7.]. Proceeding from there through Spoleto, he went to Ravenna. There, celebrating Easter [Note: [Col. 0173] “celebrated,” 7.] with Lord Pope John, he gathered there very many bishops from Italy and Romania. After holding a synod, he devised many measures for the benefit of the holy Church, and restored to the apostolic John the city and territory of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0173] “of the Ravennates,” 5, 9–12.] and many other possessions that had been taken from Roman pontiffs over a long period. He then sent him back to Rome with great joy, while he himself withdrew into the regions of Tuscany and Lucania [Note: [Col. 0173] “and Lucania” is absent in 5.].

Meanwhile Pope John and the emperor sent letters of invitation to King Otto [Note: [Col. 0173] “to Otto,” at several points, 5.] [Note: [Col. 0173] “sent [them] that [he] with,” 10.] and ordered him to hasten to celebrate Christmas at Rome with them [Note: [Col. 0173] “and with them,” 7; “that he should hasten,” 7.]. The king then came to Worms to arrange the affairs of the kingdom before his journey to Italy, and at his first assembly there, with God’s favor, gave many indications in advance both of his future prudence and of his clemency [Note: [Col. 0173] “of his,” absent in 5.]. Thus, after celebrating the Nativity of the Forerunner and the feast of the apostles at Frankfurt, he returned to Saxony, intending to hasten his journey. At that time Asulf, abbot of Trier, was taken from the present life, and Thietfrid was chosen as his successor. At that time also Lord Archbishop William, seized by a slight illness, soon recovered through God’s mercy. While the lord emperor was staying in Italy, envoys of Nicephorus [Note: [Col. 0173] “Nicephorus,” 5; “Nicophorus,” 11, 12.], emperor of the Greeks, came to him at Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0173] “met him,” 9, 11, 12.], bringing honorable gifts and asking peace or friendship from him. After receiving them honorably and sending them back suitably, the lord emperor dispatched his own envoy to the same Greek emperor at Constantinople, to join in marriage to his son, King Otto, the emperor’s stepdaughter, namely the daughter of Romanus, the emperor [Note: [Col. 0173] “Nicephorus,” 5; “Nicophorus,” 11, 12.]. The envoy returned again to the emperor in the same year before Christmas [Note: [Col. 0173] “who therefore returned in the same year,” 7.]. In the same year, as the month of September began [Note: [Col. 0173] “September,” 9–12.], King Otto, setting out for Rome [Note: [Col. 0173] “setting out” is absent in 9–12.], departed with a suitable retinue and celebrated the feast of Saint Michael at the city of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0173] “with a suitable retinue he departed and celebrated the feast,” 7.].

# TWO BOOKS OF REGINO, ABBOT OF PRÜM, ON ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE AND THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

(Edited by Stephanus Baluzius of Tulle; corrected against a very ancient manuscript and illustrated with notes.)

[Col. 0175]

# BALUZIUS’S PREFACE

## I

The holy Church of God is governed partly by divine law and partly by apostolic and ecclesiastical law. Again, some matters are regulated by order and canon, while others have been established by custom. In ancient times, moreover, it had been arranged that no priest should be permitted to be ignorant of these things, so that, warned by them, they might discharge their office seriously and diligently. It is unnecessary to recall how great the contempt for the holy canons and how great the forgetfulness of them had been over many generations. The provinces of our world know this: they attribute the diminution of their dignity to the neglect of the ancient rules.

At last, however, sound discipline began to flex its muscles and, as it were, to revive under the rule of the excellent prince Francis I, Most Christian king of the Franks. Following his example, other princes also encouraged letters and those devoted to learning. The canons of the councils were first published at Paris in 1524 by my most learned countryman Jacques Merlin; to him we also owe the first edition of Origen’s works. Later they were published by Crabbe and Surius in Germany, and then at Venice, Rome, Cologne, and elsewhere. Indeed, each nation wished to possess a corpus of its own councils. It is generally acknowledged that the first place in this respect belongs to Spain, whose councils were published in the most elegant typography in 1593 by the most learned and highly distinguished man García de Loaysa, archbishop of Toledo.

He was followed by that unique ornament and glory of the Gallican Church, and a man of the highest judgment, Jacques Sirmond, who in 1629 published the ancient councils of Gaul, arranged in three volumes, with incredible labor and diligence. They are frequently used throughout the universal Church. Inspired by these great examples, the Englishman Henry Spelman, who excelled in this field of study, gathered together the councils of the British islands. He published part of them during his lifetime in 1639 and left the remainder to be published by his heirs after his death. From the care of such learned men it can easily be understood how important it is to devote oneself to these most holy studies, which greatly contribute to the proper ordering of Christian life and to reforming the depraved morals of the last times for the better.

## II

Our ancestors, endowed with profound understanding, recognized this when they decreed that every priest should keep a book of canons with him—not for mere curiosity, but so that he might use it in all ecclesiastical cases. Accordingly, those who first prepared collections of canons published nothing apart from the ancient canons, so much so that they omitted the apostolic canons because their authority had not yet been established.

Such was the old collection that the universal Church used before the time of Justinian, containing only the Greek synods. Since the Latin translation of this book, which the Western Churches used, was obscure and confused, Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, undertook a new one. In it, besides the fifty apostolic canons and the decrees of the Greek councils contained in that collection, he also added the canons of Chalcedon, then those of Sardica and Africa, and finally the decrees of the Roman pontiffs from Siricius down to his own time.

## III

Isidore, bishop of Seville, later imitated Dionysius’s work. Besides the material contained in Dionysius’s collection, he transferred into his own collection various African councils and then the Gallican and Spanish synods, inserting also letters of those pontiffs who held the Roman see after Damasus. The diligence of later generations enlarged this collection with the councils held in Spain after Isidore’s time.

The illustrious and most excellent man in every kind of distinction, Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, had seen one copy of that collection—perhaps the very one that still exists in the library of the church of Urgell in the province of Tarragona. In it there are no letters of the Roman pontiffs from before the times of Damasus and Siricius.

Later, in the age of Charlemagne, those famous and celebrated letters attributed to the ancient pontiffs were inserted into this collection. Archbishop Riculfus of Mainz was the first to bring them into this part of the world, having obtained them from that good Spanish merchant. In that century there was much dispute concerning the authority of those letters. The Gallican bishops brought a case against them because they understood that the letters contradicted the ancient rules. Yet the fortune of the Roman people prevailed.

After that time, nothing was more frequently heard in Christian ears than the authority and mention of these letters, so that those who subsequently composed collections of canons and decrees also used them as though they were sound merchandise, though not everyone did so. Rabanus, although he was abbot of Fulda in the diocese of Mainz and, being himself archbishop of Mainz after Otgar, was therefore Riculfus’s successor, did not use those letters, as Antonius Augustinus correctly observed.

## IV

The authority of those letters certainly seems to have been great at the time when the synod was held at Reims against Arnulf, bishop of that place—that is, in the year 991. Yet if anyone examines the matter more closely, he will observe that the bishops did not openly resist those decrees—for that is what they are called in the Acts of the synod—but, understanding that they were contrary to our ancient institutions and customs, they eluded their force and authority with plainly exceptional prudence.

The memory of the illustrious achievements of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, had not yet died out among the Gallican bishops. He had engaged in frequent and major struggles with the attempts of the pontiffs of the eternal city. Hincmar fell upon the very difficult times of Nicholas I and Adrian II, who spared no diligence and no labor in order to exalt immeasurably the dignity of their see, which is undoubtedly great and splendid.

Above all, in every case, opportunely or inopportunely, they pressed those letters upon their opponents. The letters had not yet lost the favor of novelty, while their credibility and authority had been increased by the astonishing and remarkable silence of the men of that age. Whenever they were brought forward against our customs, Hincmar did not openly contradict them. Instead, he tried to soften their harshness with words full of reverence and, as far as possible, to reconcile them with the ancient rules. If that was impossible, he diminished their authority by comparing them with the ancient canons and by adducing passages from letters that had unquestionably been written by the Roman bishops whose names they bore.

Those who undertook Arnulf’s defense at the Council of Reims introduced almost no other arguments than those forged letters, which provided that a bishop could not be judged without the authority of the Roman bishop, and declared null and void any judgments that happened to be issued while this procedure was disregarded.

But the bishops were not greatly moved by this parade of great names. This is shown by the fact that, although at first they treated the decrees of the Roman pontiffs that were brought forward with great reverence, even though they clearly understood them to be false, when they reached the point at which it was certain that the bishops would not tolerate a new law gaining strength against the ancient rules, and when they had no means of evading the manifest words of those decrees by interpretation, they freely opposed those decrees with the African canons that had legislated concerning the judging of bishops within their own province. For this reason they also copied, at the end of the Acts, the Sixth African, or Carthaginian, Council.

## V

I know that I am reporting something new, because until now the Acts of the Council of Reims have been published without this African council. Yet it can easily be inferred from the same Acts that it was omitted from them, or from the table of chapters. There, after the protest and deposition of the priest Adalger—a point at which the Council of Reims ends in the published editions—the following is read:

“African council, in which the procedure concerning the Roman bishop is ascertained.”

Then, at the end of chapter 27, the Fathers, speaking of this same African council, establish the following:

“Since this council is distinguished, illuminated by the presence of blessed Augustine, refined by skillful deliberations, and has supplied this synod with the force of multiple argument, we have judged it useful to append it in full to these Acts.”

You and I, reader, owe this observation to Hermann Conring, the most learned of the Germans. He wrote to me that this African council forms chapter 56 of that synod in the most ancient manuscript of the Julia Academy, and he also sent me, copied in his own hand, various readings of the complete Acts.

You understand, then, that an excellent and authentic edition of this same Council of Reims can subsequently be produced; we promise to provide it in our new collection of councils. Now let us return to the ancient collectors of canons.

## VI

After the ninth century, those who devoted themselves to the study of canon law, wishing both to learn and to teach, also published canonical collections. Yet in them they did not publish the synods and letters of the Roman pontiffs in full and in chronological order, as the ancients had done. Instead, dividing these synods and letters into certain titles and chapters, they also added a great deal from councils held in Gaul, Germany, and Spain, as well as elsewhere. They included sayings of the holy Fathers, plainly believing that the authority of such holy and learned men would lend their collections the greatest possible dignity.

The distinguished man François Florent believed that Burchard, bishop of Worms, and Ivo of Chartres were the first to use this method. Nor is it surprising that so learned a man thought this, since no collector of canons and decrees older than those two bishops had yet been published. Nevertheless, Abbot Regino of Prüm had provided the example. Burchard and Ivo obtained much from him, but especially Burchard, who seems to have transferred approximately 670 chapters from Regino’s collection into his own.

## VII

Regino undertook this collection at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, for the use of that archbishop and of the entire diocese of Trier. The title of the work makes it clear that this was the intention of Rathbod and Regino. Moreover, in the third chapter of the second book there is a synodal oath prescribing that synodal cases must not be concealed from the bishop of Trier or from his representative. This sufficiently indicates that the collection was made for the use of that diocese.

But because the collection was recommended for its usefulness, various copies of it were subsequently made and circulated to different places.

## VIII

In composing this work Regino used a method that was by no means ordinary. He divided it into two books, evidently following the example of Martin of Braga. In the first he treats ecclesiastical matters and persons; in the second, the life and conduct of laypeople. Regino himself explains this in the epilogue of the first book and the preface to the second.

Together the two books contain nearly nine hundred chapters, as Trithemius also observed. At the front of the first book is an inquiry according to which bishops were to question people about the life of clerics; at the beginning of the second is an inquiry to be conducted by the bishop concerning laypeople.

These general inquiries are followed by canonical authority—that is, the authority of canons, decrees, and other holy institutions—by which the chapters contained in each inquiry may be supported and approved.

These are Regino’s words after the inquiry in the first book:

“What we have set out above, chapter by chapter, as matters to be investigated must be strengthened by canonical authority.”

In the second book, before chapter six, that is, after the inquiry concerning the life of laypeople, he writes:

“These chapters that we have noted in order must be strengthened by canonical decrees.”

To prove these chapters he cites the canons of councils; the decrees of the Roman pontiffs; and the sayings of the holy Fathers Basil, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Cassian, Ferrandus, Benedict, Fructuosus, Aurelian, Theodore, Bede, and Rabanus.

He also adduces laws from the Theodosian Code—or rather, the words of Anianus, its interpreter. He frequently uses the authority of the Capitularies of the Frankish kings Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and Charles the Bald, as well as the Law of the Burgundians and the Law of the Ripuarian Franks.

As we have said, he praises the letters of the Roman pontiffs, frequently citing those that are unquestionably believed to be genuine. He rarely cites the pseudepigraphal and spurious letters, perhaps merely so as not to seem to despise them. From this we can easily conclude that Regino did not think very highly of those letters.

It cannot be said that they were unknown to him, since he occasionally uses their authority, and since it is also clear that he took a great deal from Isidore’s collection. Yet I do not wish anyone to infer from this that Dionysius Exiguus’s collection was unknown to him. Although he received much from Isidore, he very frequently cites the canons of the Greek synods from Dionysius’s translation, and rarely from the ancient version preserved in Isidore.

## IX

Besides the authorities discussed up to this point, I believe that Regino also used some older collection in which both the ancient canons and the genuine letters of the Roman pontiffs were recorded, together with the Gallican councils that are frequently mentioned by Regino—namely, the councils of Nantes, Reims, and Rouen.

I seem to have inferred this from the following. In the first book, chapter 117, when citing a passage from the decrees of Innocent I, he says that he took it from the letter of Pope Innocent, chapter 387. Again, in the same book, chapter 61, when describing the first canon of the Council of Nantes, he places this in the title:

“From the Council of Nantes, 419.”

These things, I say, persuade me that Regino then had in his hands a collection in which, as in the collection of Cresconius, the canons of councils were mixed with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs in one continuous series of numbers.

Someone might suspect that this collection was not different from the books of the Capitularies, in which the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the canons of the Council of Nantes are very frequently cited, and that the two chapters mentioned above were copied in the sixth or seventh book.

The fact that this canon of Nantes is not read there today, and that neither of those two books has survived as far as the number 419 cited by Regino, should not delay anyone. Those books are very mutilated and incomplete, as we shall note below. The ancient scribes removed much from them while copying, and those who later published them in print cut out much that seemed superfluous to them.

## X

Regino also frequently praises the canons of the Council of Tribur. It is worthwhile to say something about them separately. Since he cites many canons that do not exist today in the published editions, some that differ somewhat from the edited texts, and finally many that he has condensed into an epitome in his customary fashion, we must consider how much confidence should be placed in him: whether the Triburian canons reported by him, which no longer exist, should be accepted, or rejected as spurious.

Since the good faith of the man is established for us from other evidence, it is easy to believe that he also acted in good faith regarding the canons of the Council of Tribur, in whose composition he may himself have participated. This is especially likely because the matter was so recent that no one could have lied about it except the most shameless of men.

That council was held not far from Prüm shortly before Regino prepared his collection, as he himself testifies in the second book of his Chronicles:

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 895, a great synod was held at Tribur against very many laymen who were attempting to diminish episcopal authority. There twenty-six bishops, sitting with the abbots of monasteries, confirmed in writing many decrees concerning the condition of the holy Church.”

There is therefore no doubt that the Triburian canons reported by Regino are genuine, and that they will one day be published together with the others.

## XI

We have appended two ancient appendices to Regino’s collection. The first comes from an old Parisian manuscript whose antiquity and authority are known to us; the second comes from the Helmstedt edition.

The eminent man and eager investigator of these matters, Joachim Hildebrand, who first published Regino, copied the latter from an old manuscript of the Julia Academy and attached it to Regino’s second book in a continuous numerical series. In our edition, however, it follows the chapter numbered 446. He honestly added this notice:

“Up to this point the chapters were numbered in the manuscript copy. To the chapters that follow, collected satirically, we have added the number and title.”

From this it can be concluded that these chapters are not Regino’s and were added in antiquity by some student.

That they are not Regino’s is also proved by the Parisian manuscript. At its beginning, where the chapter headings of these books are written out, the table ends entirely with chapter 446:

“How can I do penance for seven years of penance?”

For this reason we have separated these appendices from Regino’s work and assigned separate numbers to each. Burchard appears to have seen both of them, since several chapters from each appendix are read in his work.

## XII

Just as Regino had received certain material from Halitgar and Rabanus, so Burchard received a large part of his collection from Regino. So that no one may think I say this without evidence, the matter must be established by arguments that are neither obscure nor ambiguous—provided I first mention that Antonius Augustinus correctly observed that Burchard should be criticized because he did not draw each item from the sources themselves, but from the streams and pools of others.

For this reason, to begin with, we have marked in parentheses the passages transferred from Regino into Burchard’s Decree, so that the reader may compare them with one another. I do not deny that some passages are occasionally different in Burchard. But the number of those that are entirely similar is far greater. I shall cite several passages from which it will be clear that Burchard used Regino’s collection.

## XIII

In the Parisian manuscript Regino, book I, chapter 61, reports the first canon of the Council of Nantes as follows:

“From the Council of Nantes, 419.”

Burchard, however, has:

“From the same”—that is, from the Council of Nantes, which he had praised in the preceding chapter—“chapter 419.”

Ivo of Chartres attempted to correct this, plainly believing that the error had been made not by Burchard but by a scribe; for there could not be so many chapters belonging to one council. Thus, in part II, chapter 122, when reporting this same canon, he states that it was taken “from the Council of Nantes, chapter 19.”

## XIV

In Regino, book I, chapter 202, we read:

“It must also be preached how the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary.”

This passage was taken from the first book of the Capitularies, where both the printed and manuscript copies read, “from Mary, ever virgin.” Since Burchard reports the same passage without that phrase, it is clear that he received it from no other source than Regino, from whom that word had undoubtedly fallen out through carelessness while writing.

## XV

Again, in the same book, chapter 369, several matters are reported from the Council of Soissons, or from the chapters of Charles the Bald. In the old Parisian manuscript this chapter is divided into two parts, whereas it is not divided in the Helmstedt edition or in the Capitularies of Charles the Bald.

Accordingly, when Burchard copied Regino, he reported it as divided. Ivo later followed him in part III, chapters 233 and 234, as did the author of the first collection of Decretals, chapter 2, “On the Exchange of Property.”

The same occurred with chapter 81 of the first book of the Capitularies, which Regino divided into three parts in book I, chapter 371; Burchard later reported it in the same order.

The same applies to chapter 88, which Burchard, following Regino, reported as divided into five parts; in Regino it appears in book I, chapter 396 and the following chapters.

## XVI

In book II, chapter 103, Regino reports the ninth canon of the Council of Elvira, concerning a faithful woman who leaves her faithful adulterous husband in order to marry another man.

The reading that we have retained in Regino is monstrous. Where the true reading is “and takes another husband,” it reads “and takes an adulterous man.” The sense of the canon itself first rejects this reading, as do the authority of the manuscript and the editions of the Council of Elvira. The authority of all the ancient writers also confirms the good reading.

But because the Helmstedt edition had “adulterous” at this point, and because it was therefore clear that the corrupt reading found in Burchard had flowed from that error, we preferred the former reading to the genuine one, so as to preserve untouched the sources from which Burchard derived his own streams.

## XVII

Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, had written to Pope Damasus that certain monks and nuns, having abandoned their profession of holiness, had mingled themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious intercourse.

Siricius, replying to the letter written to his predecessor, responded that these shameless and detestable persons should be expelled from the community of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches.

When Regino reports this passage in book II, chapter 164, he omits the first part and confines himself to the response of Siricius. Yet, in order to convey the sense of the chapter, he interpolates these words repeated from the first part:

“namely, monks and nuns who, having abandoned their profession of holiness, have mingled themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious intercourse.”

We have enclosed these words in parentheses. Since Burchard reports the passage exactly as it appears in Regino, it is reasonable to believe that he copied it from this collection.

## XVIII

In book II, chapter 188, Regino cites chapter 102 of the first book of the Capitularies. In copying it, however, he omitted the words “of the parents and,” which ought to stand after the words “of their religious priests and their parents,” since they occur in all the books of the Capitularies, both printed and manuscript.

Thus an error made by Regino while writing caused Burchard also to omit these two words in his Decree.

## XIX

The following observation clearly shows that Burchard took from Regino the first chapter of his tenth book, which is chapter 363 of Regino’s second book, where a passage is reported from the Council of Ancyra.

Regino then placed the words “Whence above” in the title of the following chapter. Burchard, thinking that these words indicated that the following chapter too had been taken from the Council of Ancyra, cites it as “from the Council of Ancyra, chapter 1,” adding the number from his own work.

In reality it does not belong to the Council of Ancyra, but to a capitulary of one of our kings, as we shall note there.

The same mistake caused Burchard to attribute to the Council of Rouen chapter 407 and the two following chapters of Regino’s second book, because their title says, “Whence above.”

By these words Regino meant that the same subject was being treated there as had been treated in the preceding chapter. As for these final chapters, it is certain that they do not belong to the Council of Rouen and are nothing other than formulas of excommunication that were then in use.

## XX

It would be endless to pursue everything. We have already sufficiently occupied ourselves with this matter, since it will be easy from now on for anyone who values knowing such things to establish them by comparing the chapters found in Regino and Burchard.

For us it is enough to have opened a path toward discovering the origins of so many false attributions in Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian. From this it may meanwhile be concluded that it was highly worthwhile to publish this work of Regino.

## XXI

Many things also seem to prove that Ivo of Chartres used Regino’s collection, but above all the formal letters found at the end of Regino’s first book. Ivo could not have received them from Burchard, since they are not found in Burchard. He therefore copied them from Regino, changing or adding nothing.

## XXII

Regino also gave Ivo the example of using the authority of the Capitularies. When Burchard compiled his work from Regino, he preferred to attribute the chapters he took from him to certain councils or ancient Fathers rather than to our kings. The designation “Frankish,” by which the kings of Germany still gloried in Regino’s and Widukind’s time, had ceased to be used in Burchard’s age, and all reverence for these Capitularies had accordingly been stripped from the Saxons.

Burchard cites the Capitula of Charlemagne only once, in chapters 218 and 19 of book I, adding that they had been praised by the bishops at Aachen; otherwise he might perhaps not have used them.

Ivo’s situation was different, since he lived among the Franks and had himself been born in Francia. Nevertheless, these two men—Regino and Ivo—although they frequently praise the books of the Capitularies, do not cite them in the order in which they are now printed, but according to the ancient manuscripts. Hincmar of Reims, Isaac of Langres, Fulbert of Chartres, and others likewise do this.

As a result, the order of these books now appears confused in the published editions. Some chapters that belong, for example, to the third book are no longer found in the third but in the first; again, chapters that ought to occupy position 92 in the first book are now found at 98.

Finally, the sixth book formerly contained at least 456 chapters and the seventh 476, as is clear from Isaac of Langres. Today, however, the sixth contains only 330 chapters and the seventh 377.

It cannot be argued that Isaac is in error here, since in these passages Sirmond’s edition agrees remarkably with the most ancient manuscript of the Royal Library, in which the same collection of Isaac is contained. Moreover, the sixth book of the Capitularies consists of 436 chapters in the most ancient manuscript of the Colbert Library.

Finally, the most learned men have observed that Ivo, in part XVI, chapter 344, cites chapter 383 of the seventh book of the Capitularies. Since Juretus could not find this chapter in the books of the Capitularies, he went so far as to suppose that Ivo had used manuscripts more extensive than the copies that have been printed.

We shall discuss all this matter fully and carefully when we publish a corrected edition of these and the other books of the Capitularies, based on the most ancient copies. Meanwhile, we have noted various things about Regino in passing; they may provide learned men in advance with some taste of the work we are undertaking.

XXIII. It remains for us to say something about this edition of ours, so that readers may know what has been accomplished here by us—provided that we first mention that the first edition of Regino was published at Helmstedt in 1659 by that most distinguished man whom I named above, Joachim Hildebrand, from a very ancient manuscript that had belonged to Matthias Flacius Illyricus. That manuscript also contains the Council of Rheims against [Col. 0182C] Arnulf. Thus, when Flacius cites Regino’s collection in the tenth century of his *Ecclesiastical History*, he cites this manuscript, which is now held at Helmstedt in the library of the Julia Academy.

A most distinguished and learned man who shared a copy of that edition with me also pointed out that it ought to be given to François Muguet, the Parisian printer, so that it might be reprinted in his most elegant type for the public benefit of all. The printer did not object. But I thought that the first thing to be done was to compare the Helmstedt edition with some old manuscript copy, if one could be found in this seat of good letters, Paris.

Fortune favored my plan. For, while I was at that same time looking for something else in the book *On Penance*, published by the most learned John Morin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Our Lord Jesus Christ, I noticed that he occasionally cited this collection of Regino from an old manuscript written, as he himself believes, in the time of Otto I. Having received this indication, and having no doubt that the book still existed in the library of the Paris Oratory, I asked the most distinguished writer of the *Annals of the Church of France*, Charles Le Cointe, a priest of that same congregation, where the old manuscript of Regino cited by Morin was now kept, and requested that he show it to me.

He, being in every respect courteous and exceedingly polite, and privately my friend, replied that he had the manuscript in the library and soon placed it in my hands. The book is truly most ancient, nearly contemporary with Regino, as Morin rightly conjectured. I compared it with the printed edition and corrected, restored, and completed Regino in almost innumerable places.

It is unfortunate that eight leaves are missing from that manuscript: namely, part of chapter 200 of Book II and everything that follows down to the seventh paragraph of chapter 246. We supplied this gap from the Helmstedt edition, as we explain there.

XXIV. I added notes to the chapters of this collection that are found in Burchard, and, insofar as possible, indicated from what source each item was taken—whether from the canons of councils, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, the books of the *Capitularies*, or many other places that there is no need to list here.
