Those who wish to examine this work of ours fairly will understand how much tedium I had to swallow in carrying it out, and how assiduously, for how long, and with what hardship I had to labor.

XXV. I had resolved to abstain entirely from writing notes. But since, while reading, many things occurred to me that seemed to require explanation, I was forced to abandon my plan and to continue offering this service to those curious about such matters. I shall consider myself to have received a sufficiently ample reward for my labor if they honor my notes with their approval.

XXVI. In accordance with our usual practice, the notes ought to have been followed by an appendix of the ancient documents mentioned in them [Col. 0183B]. We compiled it from the illustrious monuments of ancient times, so that it may fairly be affirmed that it is not unworthy to be joined to Regino’s work.

[Col. 0184A] In this matter we were wonderfully assisted by Antonius Vion Herovallius, who, because of his love for letters and for those devoted to letters, is always accustomed to encourage and foster our studies. While he is most distinguished for all his other virtues, he has deservedly won the affection and respect of all of us who cultivate the liberal arts for this reason above all: he not only most willingly extends his favor to those who seek it, but voluntarily offers and presses himself upon them so that, with a generous hand, he may give everything sent to him from the various cities and provinces of this flourishing kingdom.

You also owe much, reader, to the learned printer François Muguet, who spared neither diligence nor expense so that you might possess that golden collection of Regino both in a truly corrected form, as it is, and in a most elegant one. He promises you the same zeal and diligence in the edition of the *Capitularies*, when we have enough leisure to undertake its preparation.

[Col. 0184B] Farewell, reader, and use this book for the greater glory of God, for the salvation of your soul, and finally for the benefit of Holy Church.

[Col. 0183]

## Eulogies of Regino

### Regino, Book II of the Chronicles, under the year 892

[Col. 0183B]

At that time Farabert, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, voluntarily resigned the pastoral office with the king’s permission; and I, although unworthy, succeeded him in its governance by election of the brethren, according to the authority of the Rule. I did not remain there long, however, for, through the efforts of my rivals, I was forced to endure as my successor in that office Richarius, the brother of Gerhard and Matfrid, who was hostile to me.

### Under the year 899

In the same year Richarius was appointed abbot of Prüm. I postponed recording here how I was treated, lest, provoked by the injuries I suffered, I should appear to have exaggerated the causes of my persecution beyond what Christian patience permits.

### Sigebert, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[Col. 0183C] Regino, abbot of Prüm, wrote for Albero I, bishop of Metz, a chronicle chiefly containing the deeds of the Franks, which he continued from the birth of Christ to the year of Christ’s birth 908.

### John Trithemius, in the *Hirsau Chronicle*, under the year 892

Farabert, abbot of Prüm, voluntarily resigned his abbacy with the consent of the king of the Franks. Regino, a monk of that same monastery, succeeded him—a man most distinguished in life and learning. Among the other small works of his intellect, he wrote a chronicle of past events for Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, beginning with the origin of the world and continuing to his own times: certainly a most celebrated work and one highly worthy of learned men’s reading.

### Under the year 899

Regino, abbot of Prüm, was deposed, as he writes in his Chronicle. He did not state the causes of his deposition [Col. 0183D], but he says this: “In the year of the Lord 889, Richarius became abbot,” and so forth. From these words we may conjecture that he was removed from the abbacy amid injuries, although we do not know the causes.

### The same author, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Regino, abbot of the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a Teuton by nationality, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in secular letters, easily held first place among the teachers of Germany in his time. He wrote works of great authority, of which I have found only those listed below.

For Albero I, bishop of Metz, he wrote a history or chronicle in ten books, from the birth of Christ to the year 908, chiefly containing the deeds of the Franks and Germans. He also wrote two books *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*: “First of all, inquiry must be made.” I have not yet seen anything else.

He wrote the aforementioned work, entitled *On Ecclesiastical Discipline and Christian Religion*, at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier. From the decrees of the holy Fathers and of general councils he compiled it in two books and clearly divided it, according to custom, into nearly nine hundred chapters under headings.

He flourished under Emperor Arnold in the year of the Lord 910.

### The same author, in *Catalogue of Illustrious Men of Germany*

[Col. 0184C] Regino, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, of the Order of the holy Father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally educated in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, and devout in life and conduct, easily held first place among the teachers of his time.

For Adelbero, bishop of Metz, he wrote, in ten books, a history of the deeds of the Franks and Teutons, from the birth of Christ to his own times. At the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, he compiled from the decrees and judgments of the Fathers and of general councils a distinguished canonical work entitled *On Ecclesiastical Discipline and Christian Religion*, in two volumes and two books.

He also composed one book of many elegant sermons, one book of letters to various persons, and many other works that have not yet come to our notice through reading. He flourished in the time of Emperor Arnold, in the year of the Lord 910.

### Bellarmine, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[Col. 0184D]

Regino, abbot of Prüm, appears to have flourished at the beginning of the year 900. For he wrote two books of Chronicles from the coming of the Lord to the year 908 of the same Lord, as he himself testifies at the beginning of his work. But another anonymous author continued it to the year 967.

He is also said to have written two books *On Christian Discipline*, which I do not think are extant.

### Gerard John Vossius, in Book II of *On Latin Historians*

[Col. 0185A]

In the age of that same Louis, and likewise under Emperor Conrad—who succeeded Louis in 912 and ruled for seven years—Regino flourished, abbot of the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier.

He composed two books of Chronicles, in which he chiefly treats Frankish affairs. We have manuscripts of them at Cambridge, both in the library of the University and in that of St Benedict’s College, according to Thomas James. But there he is called not Regino, but simply (*haplōs*, “simply”) “the abbot of Prüm.”

Sigebert says of him in chapter 112 of his *Catalogue*: “Regino, abbot of Prüm,” and so forth, “to the year 908 of the birth of Christ.” There I would prefer to subtract one year, although in Trithemius one also reads “98” for “908.”

Certainly, before the year 907, and even today in Regino, one finds these words: “Thus far Regino.” But another author continued this Chronicle to the year 957, or rather to Otto II, who began to reign in 972.

He also composed books *On Ecclesiastical Doctrine* from the decrees of the holy Fathers and of general councils. These manuscripts are preserved at Vienna in the Imperial Library.

Trithemius’s error arose from the fact that Regino’s preface reads: “I divided this Chronicle into two little books, beginning from the first year of the Lord’s Incarnation and completing the work begun up to the present year, which is reckoned from the [read: aforementioned] Incarnation of the Lord as 908.” But it is sufficiently clear, from what we have said, that through the fault of the copyist the number of the year is greater than it should be. For this is how it is found both in the manuscripts, as we have reported, and in the old and recent printed editions.

The appendix to Regino that I mentioned appears to have Romerius as its author.

### John Morin, in the appendix to his book *On Penance*, p. 39

We very frequently cite Regino’s collection, which we possess. It is a collection of canons divided into two books. From its script it can easily be inferred that it was written before the year 1000, scarcely afterward.

We attribute it to Regino the abbot because the beginning of the collection, written in capital letters, bears this title:

> Here begins the little book on disciplines, collected at the command of Rathbod of Trier by Regino, abbot of the monastery, from the divine councils and decrees.

Trithemius mentions this collection in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Regino. He says:

> He wrote a history or chronicle in ten books. He also wrote two books *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, and so forth. He wrote the aforementioned work, entitled *On Ecclesiastical Discipline and Christian Religion*, at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, compiling it from the decrees of the holy Fathers and of general councils in two books, and clearly dividing it, according to custom, into nearly nine hundred chapters under headings.

Our manuscript is divided in this way. The first book contains 454 chapters; the second contains somewhat more, because certain items were added after Regino’s death—for example, a decree issued at Conofurth in the year 952, in the ninth indiction, by King Otto in the fifteenth year of his reign, with the consent of the bishops, counts, and other faithful, ordering that ravishers of virgins and widows be anathematized and deprived forever of every hope of marriage.

There are also several other reasons why the number of chapters slightly exceeds that recorded by Trithemius. It therefore appears that this copy of the collection was written during the reign of Otto I.

It was compiled and published in the year 906. This may be inferred from the end of Book I, especially chapter 447 and those that follow, where an entire formula for composing *formatae*—official ecclesiastical letters—is reported from the Council of Nicaea.

Two copies of the formula are then provided: one from Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, writing to Robert, bishop of Metz, and commending to him Gislemar, a priest ordained by Rathbod; it is dated the Ides of October in the year 906 of the Incarnation. The other is from Dado, bishop of Verdun, to Rathbod of Trier, likewise dated in that year.

Regino flourished at the same time. For, as he himself testifies in his Chronicle, he was elected abbot of Prüm in 892, though unsuccessfully, since many opposed him. He finished his Chronicle in 906, the year in which he includes the copies of these *formatae*.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, saw this collection [Col. 0186C] and used it in his *Decree*. For he transferred those two copies of the letters *verbatim* from this collection into his own work—not merely their method of transcription from the Council of Nicaea, as you can see in the final three chapters of the sixth part of the *Decree*.

[Col. 0185]

## 1–21. The Little Book on Ecclesiastical Disciplines and the Christian Religion

Collected, in God’s name, from various councils of the holy Fathers and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, at the command of the lord Rathbod, metropolitan bishop of the city of Trier, by Regino, formerly abbot of the monastery of Prüm. Amen.

## Book I

### Admonition concerning the following inquiry

[Col. 0185] Among the *Capitula* of Hincmar, first published in the appendix to volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*, the second title concerns the matters that masters and deans must investigate in each church and report to the bishop.

These *Capitula* of Hincmar are identical with those that are read in this Inquiry. Therefore either Regino took them from fuller *Capitula* of Hincmar, which we do not yet possess, or Hincmar took them from an ancient formula from which Regino later copied them also; I would consider the latter explanation closer to the truth. If anyone thinks otherwise, he is free to follow his own judgment.

### Here begins the inquiry concerning the matters that the bishop or his ministers ought to investigate in their district or territory, throughout the villages, rural settlements, and parishes of his diocese

[Col. 0187A]

First of all, inquiry must be made in whose honor the basilica was consecrated, or by whom it was consecrated. Next, the church itself must be inspected, to see whether it is well roofed and vaulted, and to ensure that no pigeons or other birds nest there because of the uncleanness of their droppings or the disturbance caused by their nuisance.

2. Of what metal are the bells of that church?

3. Is hay, grain, or anything of that kind brought into the church?

4. Then one must approach the altar and examine what its coverings are like: how many are new, how many old, and how clean they are.

5. Of what metal are the reliquaries and crosses covered? Or are the relics carefully stored in the altar? Are the reliquaries secured with locks and keys?

6. Of what metal are the chalice and paten? Are they clean of every impurity, and where are they kept?

7. Is the corporal made of the purest and cleanest linen, and where is it stored?

8. Is there a prepared place in the sacristy or beside the altar where water may be poured when these things are washed? Is a vessel suspended there in which the priest may wash his hands after receiving the Body and Blood of the Lord? And does the priest, deacon, or subdeacon first wash the corporal there?

9. Inquiry must be made whether the pyx containing the sacred oblation for the viaticum of the sick is always kept upon the altar.

10. Does he possess a complete Missal [perhaps “Psalter,” as in the *Capitula* of Walter of Orléans, chapter 7], a Lectionary, and an Antiphonary? For without these Mass cannot be celebrated completely.

11. It must also be seen how many other books are there, and whether they are well [*retiati*, uncertain; the Helmstedt edition and Hincmar read *recitati*, “read aloud”]; how many priestly vestments there are and of what kind; and whether they are clean or kept in a clean place.

12. Inquiry must be made concerning the lights of the church, and how many candlesticks it has.

13. Investigation must be made whether the church possesses a holding with twelve *bonvaria* [a term of uncertain meaning, perhaps units of agricultural property], apart from the cemetery, and a courtyard containing the church and the priest’s house, and whether it has four bondservants.

14. How many free holdings does it possess, and how many servile holdings or dependent tenants, from which the tithe is paid?

15. It must also be considered whether the churchyard is properly enclosed, so that it may not be polluted by any uncleanness.

### Concerning the life and conduct of the priest

16. Inquiry must be made whether the priest has a cell beside the church, or whether there are suspicious little doors in the surrounding area.

17. Is he suspected concerning any woman, or does he keep some woman secretly introduced into his house?

18. Does he visit the sick? Does he reconcile them? Does he anoint them with holy oil according to the Apostle? Does he communicate them with his own hand and not through some layman? If he gives Communion to a layman or woman to carry to the sick person, this is forbidden.

19. Does he demand a reward or gift for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead?

20. Above all, this must be investigated: whether, through the priest’s negligence, any infant has died in the parish without baptism.

21. Does he sing Mass in houses outside the church?

22. Is he drunken or quarrelsome?

23. Does he carry weapons during an uprising?

24. Does he devote himself to playing with dogs or birds?

25. Does he drink in taverns?

26. Does he have a cleric who reads the Epistle or the lesson, responds at Mass, and sings psalms with him?

27. Does he rise every night during the nocturnal hours to perform the morning praises?

28. Does he announce Prime, Terce, Sext, and None at the appointed times by the church bell, and sing the prescribed office?

29. Are the solemn rites of Mass not celebrated before the third hour?

30. Does the priest, God forbid, presume to celebrate Mass after he has taken food or drink?

31. Does he have a thurible, and does he offer incense in the sacrifice of the Lord?

32. Does he announce the word of the Lord to the people?

33. Does he celebrate Mass at the appointed time, namely around the third hour of the day, and afterward fast until midday, so that, if necessary, he may sing Mass for guests and travelers who arrive?

34. Does he care for the poor, travelers, and orphans, and, according to his ability, invite them to his meal?

35. Does he prepare holy water every Sunday [Col. 0188D] before the solemn rites of Mass, in a clean vessel and with a ministry appropriate to the occasion, so that the people entering and standing in the church may be sprinkled with it?

36. Does he presume to give a chalice, paten, priestly vestment, or book as security to a tavern keeper [or innkeeper] or merchant?

37. Does he publicly accept from anyone living in sin or incest a gift, or any temporal profit—or rather spiritual harm—in order to conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or his ministers?

38. Does he bring someone insufficiently penitent to reconciliation out of favor, familiarity, or kinship, and give him a certificate of reconciliation?

39. When summoned for the anniversary, thirtieth, seventh, or third day of a dead person, does he presume to become drunk and to drink “in the love of the saints” or of the person’s soul; to compel others to drink; to gorge himself at another’s prayer; or to engage in disorderly applause and laughter, shameful jokes, and indecent songs?

40. If, when he was advanced to ecclesiastical office, he possessed no patrimony, did he afterward purchase estates? What is their legal status?

41. Does he exact usury and act as his lord’s steward?

42. Does he sing Mass without receiving Communion?

43. Does he allow a woman to approach the altar and, which is not permitted, to touch the Lord’s chalice?

44. Was he ordained for money, or did he obtain for a price the church in which he ministers?

45. Did he previously possess another church and, after abandoning it, move to another for the sake of profit?

46. Does he hold several churches without the assistance of other priests?

47. Does he sing Mass in another parish [Col. 0189C] without the consent or request of the copriest?

48. Does he receive a tithe belonging to another?

49. Does he invite a penitent to eat meat and drink wine, unless he has presently made almsgiving on his behalf?

50. Does he write documents, or act as his lord’s steward?

51. Does he baptize indiscriminately?

52. Does he lack stone baptismal fonts or another vessel prepared for this purpose, in which nothing else is done?

53. Does he ensure that the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed are taught to all his parishioners?

54. Concerning the Greater Litany.

55. Concerning the Rogation days.

56. Does he announce that the fast of the Four Times of the year must be observed by the people in every respect?

57. On the Wednesday before Lent, does he invite the people entrusted to him to confession and impose penance upon them according to the character of their offense—not from his own judgment, but as it is written in the *Penitential*?

58. At the three seasons of the year—Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—does he admonish all the faithful to approach the Communion of the Body and Blood of the Lord?

59. Does he also admonish them at what times married people ought to abstain from their own wives?

60. That no cleric is to go to weddings.

61. From the offerings presented by the people on Sunday and feast days, after Mass has been completed, does he distribute *eulogiae*—blessed portions—to the people?

62. Does he travel without a stole or orarium?

63. Does he set aside clerical clothing and use lay attire?

64. Does he mix water with wine in the sacrifice of the Lord?

65. After Mass has been completed, does the priest himself consume the remainder of the Body and Blood of the Lord with fear and reverence? And, if he has no deacon or subdeacon, does he wash and wipe the chalice and paten with his own hands?

66. Does he presume to sing Mass without an alb, or wearing the alb that he uses daily for his ordinary purposes?

67. Are the tithes divided into four portions?

68. Has he presumed to sell, exchange, or alienate by any means whatever a church’s property, possession, or bondservant?

69. Does he teach that Sunday and the other feasts are to be celebrated without servile labor from evening to evening?

70. Does he admonish the people never to sing in the churchyard or lead women’s dances there, but, when they enter the church, to hear the word of God in silence?

71. Under a solemn adjuration by almighty God, does he forbid the devilish songs that the common rabble customarily sings over the dead during the night, and the bursts of laughter [Col. 0190C] in which they indulge?

72. Does he instruct those making offerings to bring a candle or anything else they wish to the altar before Mass, or before the Gospel is read?

73. But let each person offer only one offering at the offertory, for himself and all his own.

### What must be asked of the priest

74. After all these matters have been carefully investigated, the priest himself must then be questioned by the bishop or his representative:

75. Was he born of free parents or of servile condition?

76. Was he born or ordained in the same parish or in another?

77. If he is from the same parish, inquiry must be made by which bishop he was ordained, or for which place he was designated.

78. If he is a slave, let him produce his charter of freedom.

79. If he is from another parish, let him produce letters of recommendation, which they call a *formata*.

80. Is any part of his body mutilated? Has he cut off any part of himself?

After this, inquiry must be made concerning the ministry entrusted to him.

81. Does he have written with him an exposition of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer according to the teaching of the orthodox Fathers? Does he fully understand it? And does he diligently instruct the people entrusted to him by preaching from it?

82. Does he understand the prayers of the Mass, including the preface of the Canon and the Canon itself, and can he recite them from memory and distinctly?

83. Can he read the Epistle and Gospel well and at least explain their literal meaning?

84. Does he know how to recite the words and divisions of the psalms regularly from memory, together with the customary chants?

85. Does he know by heart the sermon of Athanasius, bishop, on the faith of the holy Trinity, which begins, “Whoever wishes to be saved,” and does he understand its meaning and know how to express it in ordinary words?

86. Can he recite clearly, appropriately, and rationally the exorcisms and prayers for making a catechumen, for consecrating the font, and the remaining prayers over male and female persons, both in the singular and plural?

87. Likewise, does he know the rite for baptizing those who are sick and in need of immediate assistance?

88. Does he know how to read or recite from memory the rite of reconciliation according to the manner canonically reserved to him, as well as the rite of anointing the sick and the prayers appropriate to that need?

89. Likewise, does he know the rite and prayers for funeral ceremonies and the rites performed for the dead?

90. Does he know by heart the exorcisms and blessings of salt and water?

91. Does he know the nocturnal and diurnal chant?

92. Does he understand the lesser computus—that is, the epacts, concurrents, regular numbers, Paschal limits, and the rest?

93. Does he possess a Martyrology from which he can announce the feasts of the saints to the people on the appointed days?

94. Does he possess Gregory’s forty homilies, and does he read and understand them diligently? Or, if he cannot have them, does he possess the sermon of that teacher concerning the seventy disciples sent by the Lord to preach, and does he read and understand it carefully, recognizing that he has been advanced to the ecclesiastical ministry in the likeness of the seventy disciples?

95. Does he possess the Roman *Penitential*, or that edited by Bishop Theodore or by the venerable priest Bede, so that, according to what is written there, he may question the person confessing or impose upon the penitent the appropriate measure of penance?

### The inquiry ends here

These matters, which we have set out above as points to be investigated, must be strengthened by canonical authority.

### That the provisions of the canons be observed by all without prejudice

From the Council of Meaux, held in the time of Charles the Younger, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 845, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, title 10.

I. (*Council of Meaux*, chapter 34; *Burchard*, Book I, chapter 61.) Let the provisions of the canons be observed by all without prejudice, and let no one in ecclesiastical proceedings or judgments be guided by his own opinion, but by their authority.

In explaining or preaching the divine Scriptures also, let each person follow the understanding of the holy Catholic and most approved Fathers. In their writings, as blessed Jerome says (*Letter to Laeta*), the truth of the faith does not waver.

### What sort of minister a bishop ought to have beside him

From the same council, title 11.

II. (*Council of Meaux*, chapter 35; *Burchard*, Book I, chapter 83.) Let every bishop strive, according to his ability, to have beside him a man who, according to the most sincere and pure understanding of the Catholic Fathers, may continually instruct and form the priests of the parishes in faith, observance of God’s commandments, and the doctrine of preaching, lest the house of the living God, which is the Church, remain without the lamp of the divine word.

Let such a man also be one whom love of money does not trouble, and whom disreputable morals or blameworthy conduct does not make contemptible [Note: In the commonly circulated canons of the Council of Meaux, where Regino and Burchard have “blameworthy conduct makes contemptible,” one reads “blameworthy conduct dangerously devastates.” What follows in Regino and Burchard is not found in that canon of the Council of Meaux.].

For this reason, when Moses laid before God his complaint that he could not bear the great burden imposed upon him, he heard the Lord say:

> Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and their teachers; and I will take from your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you, and you alone may not be burdened. (Numbers 11)

What do we understand in Moses except the high priesthood, and in the seventy men except the priests? By taking from Moses’s spirit and giving it to them, the Lord plainly shows that those who have been called by the bishop in God’s presence to bear the burden of the people with him ought to think and will the same things as the bishop, and cooperate with all their strength in the portion of the burden assigned to them. For this signifies that they receive not another spirit, but the spirit of that same Moses.

### On the same matter

From the synodal *Capitula* of Emperor Charles, title 103.

III. (*Book I of the Capitularies*, chapter 109.) We therefore admonish bishops, whether personally or through representatives, to provide the peoples diligently with the nourishment of the divine word; for, as blessed Gregory says (*Book I, Letter 24*), a priest arouses the anger of the hidden Judge against himself if he goes about without the sound of preaching.

### What should be requested from the king so that bishops may have time at a suitable season for the ministry entrusted to them

From the aforementioned council, title 4.

IV. (*Council of Meaux*, chapter 28, and in the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald, title 7.) Let royal magnificence grant bishops greater freedom to carry out the ministry in their parishes than they have hitherto possessed because of various disturbances.

Let the bishops themselves turn the leisure granted to them not to their own pleasures, but to divine and dutiful business, so that, by devoting themselves to preaching, correction, and strengthening, they may diligently repair in the future what has hitherto been neglected throughout the parishes.

### That bishops not neglect the people entrusted to them for the sake of their own repose

From the same council, title 5.

V. (*Council of Meaux*, chapter 28; *Burchard*, Book I, chapter 28.) Care must be taken that bishops, withdrawing to more remote places for the sake of their own repose and neglecting their ministry, do not abandon their own cities. Rather, let them either travel through their parishes with effective diligence in their office, or live canonically and religiously in their cities with their sons.

They must also compel the priests entrusted to them to be adorned, according to their ministry, with doctrine, chastity, sobriety, and hospitality.

### Concerning bishops who rarely or never visit in person the peoples entrusted to them

From the same council, title 6.

VI. (*Council of Meaux*, chapter 29.) The blameworthy—indeed damnable—custom of certain bishops must be corrected in every way: they visit the peoples entrusted to them either rarely or never in person, according to the evangelical, apostolic, and ecclesiastical order, although the Lord says:

> I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me.

(Ezekiel 3), together with the other things contained in the divine word.

### That a bishop travel through his diocese

From the Council of Braga, title 7.

VII. (*Second Council of Braga*, chapter 1; *Burchard*, Book I, chapter 85.) It pleased all the bishops, and they agreed, that as they travel through each church and diocese they should first examine the clergy: how they observe the order of baptism and of the Mass, and how they perform each of the offices in the Church.

If they find everything correct, thanks be to God. But if not, they must teach the ignorant and prescribe in every respect that, as the ancient canons command, twenty days before baptism catechumens should undergo the exorcisms of purification. During those twenty days the catechumens must be specially taught the Creed, which is “I believe in God.”

### What ought to be taught to the laity

[Col. 0193D] (*From the same Council of Braga II, chapter 1.*) After the bishops have examined or instructed their clergy, on the following day they should summon the people of that church and teach them to avoid the error of idols and various crimes—namely, homicide, adultery, perjury, false testimony, and the remaining deadly sins—and not to do to another what they do not want done to themselves.

They should also teach them to believe in the resurrection of all human beings and in the day of judgment, on which each person will receive according to his works. After this, the bishop should depart from that church and proceed to another.

### That a bishop travel through his parish with only a few companions

From the Council of Toledo, title 5.

VIII. (*Seventh Council of Toledo*, chapter 4; *Burchard*, Book I, chapter 86.) When a bishop visits his diocese, he must not burden anyone by the size of his retinue. He must never exceed fifty mounts in his conveyance, nor have permission to remain in any one basilica for more than one day [Note: See the Third Council of Valence, chapter 17.].

### That, if a bishop cannot fulfill this duty, he should send his representatives

From the same council, title 6.

IX. (*Fourth Council of Toledo*, chapter 36; *Burchard*, Book I, chapter 87.) If a bishop, whether detained by illness or occupied with other affairs, cannot fulfill this duty, he should send priests of approved life or deacons to investigate the revenues of the basilicas, their repairs, and the life of those serving them.

### That bishops visit their diocese

From the synodal *Capitula* of Charles Augustus.

X. [Note: [Col. 0193D] See Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapters 94, 109, [Col. 0194D] 365, and volume II of the Councils of Gaul, p. 248, chapter 32.] Bishops are to visit the parishes entrusted to them and there diligently inquire about incest, parricides, adulteries, and other evils contrary to God and which Christians ought to avoid; within those parishes they are also to take care to repair the churches that require it. Likewise, they are to provide with the utmost diligence for both those churches which we have granted to them as benefices and those belonging to others.

That a bishop is to accept only two solidi when he makes his circuit of his parish. From the Council of Braga, title 10.

XI. (10, q. 3, c. 1.) It has been decided that no bishop, when visiting his dioceses, is to take anything from the churches, apart from the honor of his see, that is, two solidi; nor is he to demand a third part of any offering of the people in parish churches. Rather, that third part is to be reserved for the lights or repair of the church, [Col. 0194C] and an account of it is to be rendered to the bishop each year. For if the bishop takes that third part, he has taken away the church’s light and its repairs.

Concerning bishops who demand the price of servitude without visiting the parishes. From the council held at Tribur in the time of King Arnulf, title 26.

XII. (BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 229.) A complaint of the common people was brought before the holy synod: certain bishops were unwilling to travel through their parishes each year in order to preach or confirm, yet they demanded that those responsible for providing the lodgings which they ought to have used on their journey redeem them by another payment. This double disgrace—negligence and greed—was a great horror to the holy synod; and they decreed that no one should henceforth practice such a device of avarice, and that bishops should be more diligent in visiting their flocks.

Concerning the same matter. From the synodal capitularies of Emperor Charles, title 94.

XIII. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 100.) Lest bishops, on the pretext of preaching or confirming, become a burden to the peoples, after being admonished by us [*adm. a n.*], they promised that henceforth they would take care to avoid this and, at the appropriate time, carry out their ministry [*min. s.*] insofar as their means allowed, among those [*apud hos*] whom they could benefit, so that their journey, insofar as it depended on them, would not be troublesome or burdensome [Note: [Col. 0195D] The order of this chapter is disturbed in Regino. Here we have presented the reading of the Paris manuscript. The Helmstedt edition is not much different. We give the variant readings in brackets; but the entire passage should be restored from the books of the *Capitularies*, both printed and manuscript, as follows: “Lest bishops, etc., and at the appropriate time carry out their ministry, insofar as their means allowed, so that their journey, insofar as it depended on them, would not be troublesome or burdensome to those whom they can and ought to benefit.”].

37 Concerning the immunity of churches. From the same capitulary, title 103.

XIV. (Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 9, chapter 4.) It is to be announced to all and ordered by our envoys that all churches and priests are to remain under the immunity, privilege, authority, and disposition of the bishops of the respective parishes in which they are located, in accordance with canonical authority.

[Col. 0195B] That all basilicas are under the authority of the bishops. From the Council of Orléans, title 13.

XV. (First Council of Orléans, chapter 17; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 8.) It has been decided, in accordance with the rule of the earlier canons, that all basilicas which have been built in various places or are built daily are to remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated.

Concerning parishes. From the Council of Chalcedon, title 19.

XVI. (Council of Chalcedon, chapter 17; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 148.) The rural parishes or estates belonging to individual churches are to remain undisturbed for those bishops who are known to retain them, especially if they have governed them for thirty years without force while holding them under their administration [Col. 0195C]. But if within thirty years a dispute has arisen or arises concerning them, those who claim to have been injured are permitted to contest the matter before the holy synod of the province.

What sort of ministers bishops ought to leave in their cities. From the capitularies of Charles the Younger, title 5.

XVII. (Capitula of Carloman, title 2, chapter 7.) Since bishops, occupied with the common needs of our churches and of the whole kingdom, both theirs and ours, are unable by themselves to oversee everything that is perpetrated within the boundaries of their parishes, we decree that whenever bishops depart from their own city, each is to leave in his city such assistants as will carry out all these matters in his city with the greatest prudence [Col. 0195D], so that the poor, redeemed by the blood of Christ, may always find someone present in the city from whom they can receive an answer and consolation. In the villages and small settlements far removed from the city, each bishop is to appoint reverend and prudent priests, disciplined in every moral virtue, who will modestly perform in his place the duties established above, and to whom the other, younger, and less cautious priests may bring their cases.

[Col. 0196A] Concerning the thirty-year prescription. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

XVIII. (Gelasius I, letter 10, chapter 1; Book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 175; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 149.) It has also seemed good to add that if anyone—God forbid—should lawfully claim for himself the resources of the Church or dioceses held by other bishops, the law of thirty years has closed the matter; for the authority of our princely sons has likewise been promulgated in such a way that, after thirty years, no one may appeal concerning something excluded by the passage of time established by law.

Concerning things possessed for thirty years. From the capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 7.

XIX. (Additions IV, chapter 34; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 150.) No testimony is to be accepted concerning church property which they have possessed for a period of thirty years without any interruption [Col. 0196B]; rather, it is to be maintained in the same manner in which things belonging to the royal fisc are customarily maintained.

Concerning the recording of periods of time. From the same, chapter 9.

XX. (Burgundian Law, title 79, chapters 2–3.) If anyone says that land was violently taken from him by another, and proves this before the number of thirty years has been completed, and the occupation of the property has been established, and he has been able to bring a claim, the property is to be restored to the party making the claim. But if, after thirty years have been completed, the land is said to have been occupied by anyone and was not previously reclaimed, he is to understand that nothing is to be restored to him.

Also concerning the same matter. In the same place.

XXI. (Ibid., chapter 5.) Since the law requires provision to be made for everything pertaining to the peace of all, no case concerning any property which has not been resolved within thirty years may afterward be brought by any legal process; for it is clear that the aforesaid number of years ought to be sufficient for anyone to seek and receive whatever was owed to him.

40 Also concerning the same matter. In the same place.

XXII. (Interpretation of the single law of the *Theodosian Code*, concerning tenants and colonists.) If anyone has held another man’s colonus on his estate for thirty years, let him claim him as his own. Whoever is found within thirty years is to be reclaimed by his lord, together with the sons owed to him and all his peculium. If he has died, however, his lord is to receive his peculium. But if a female colonus (*colona*) has remained under another’s dominion for twenty years, she is not to be claimed by her former lord. Two-thirds of the offspring are to follow the male colonus, but one-third the female colonus. For if offspring were produced within twenty years, while the female colonus still belonged to her lord, they are not to be denied to those reclaiming them, since this has been established in the newer laws. Certainly, lest the marriage be separated, we decree that the lord of the colonus is not to be denied the substitute woman together with one-third of the offspring.

[Col. 0197A] Concerning the consecration of a church. From the Council of Worms.

XXIII. (Second Council of Braga, chapter 5; Council of Worms, chapter 3; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 37.) It has been decided that whenever a bishop is invited by one of the faithful to consecrate churches, he is not to demand any gift from the founder as though it were owed; but if the founder himself offers something from his own vow, he is not to refuse it. Nevertheless, each bishop is to remember that he must not dedicate a church unless he has first received, confirmed by a written charter, the endowment of the basilica and the service owed to it. For it is no less reckless to consecrate a church without lights or substantial support for those who are to serve there than it would be to consecrate a private house as a church [Note: [Col. 0197D] See Book III of the Lombard Laws, title 1, chapter 45.].

Concerning the freedom of churches. From the *Capitularies*, title 81.

[Col. 0197B] XXIV. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 91; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 52; WALTER of Orléans, chapter 9.) It has been decreed that one complete mansus is to be assigned to each church without any service obligation, and that the priests established there are to perform no service from the tithes, the offerings of the faithful, the houses, the courtyards, or the gardens situated beside the church, nor from the aforesaid mansus, except ecclesiastical service. If they possess anything more, they are to render from it the service owed to their lords.

Concerning the boundaries of churches. From the same, chapter 117.

(Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 155.) Each church is to have a boundary specifying from which villages it is to receive tithes.

Concerning new churches. Chapter 87.

[Col. 0197C] XXV. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 93.) It has been decreed concerning new villages and the new churches newly established in them that the tithes from those villages are to be assigned to the same churches.

Also from the same, chapter 5.

XXVI. (Capitulary of Charlemagne at Salz, chapter 3; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 7.) Whoever wishes to build a church on his own property is to have permission to do so with the consent and will of the bishop in whose parish it will be. Nevertheless, it must be provided in every way that the older churches do not on this account lose their due or their tithe; rather, payment is always to be made to the older churches.

42 Also concerning the church mansus. From the same capitulary.

XXVII. (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 45.) Concerning a single mansus given to a church, from which certain men demand service for themselves contrary to the statutes: whoever is accused on this account is to be compelled by the count or the royal envoys to restore to the priests whatever has been taken from it, together with the legal penalty.

Concerning the same matter. From the Synod of Meaux, chapter 63.

XXVIII. (Council of Meaux, chapter 63.) In accordance with canonical authority and the constitution of Lord Emperor Louis, concerning the church land, mansus, and bondservants which he established in his capitularies, or if anyone has bestowed something upon a church for a place of burial: no one is to compel any priest to pay any rent from the tithes or offerings of the faithful, nor is anyone, of whatever order or dignity, to take anything from them or demand any temporal repayment. If anyone does so, let him be deprived of communion until he has made satisfaction, and let him be compelled by royal authority to correct the matter according to law.

Also concerning the privilege of churches.

XXIX. (Sixth Council of Arles, chapter 20; Book II of the *Capitularies*, chapter 36; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 9.) Churches established in ancient times are not to be deprived either of tithes or of any possession, so that these may be assigned to new oratories.

43 Concerning churches or altars of doubtful status, and that superfluous altars are to be removed from a church. Chapter 65.

XXX. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 151; BURCHARD, Book III, [Col. 0198B] chapter 10.) Churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain are to be consecrated; and superfluous altars are to be destroyed and removed from the church.

Concerning ecclesiastical honor. Chapter 142.

XXXI. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 148.) Bishops are to see what due service priests render to their lords on behalf of their churches.

That the endowments of all churches belong to the bishop. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 19.

XXXII. (Third Council of Toledo, chapter 19; Book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 213; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 20.) Many, contrary to the provisions of the canons, demand that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they consider the endowment which they have contributed to the churches not to belong to the bishop’s administration [Col. 0198C]. This practice was displeasing in the past and is prohibited in the future; rather, everything is to belong, according to ancient custom, to the bishop’s administration and authority [Note: [Col. 0198D] See Book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 69.].

Whence churches are to be restored and service rendered to the bishop. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

XXXIII. (Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 27; Book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 290; Riculf, chapter 11; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 137.) Four portions are properly to be made from both revenue and the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago: one is to be the bishop’s, another the clergy’s, a third the poor’s, and the fourth assigned to the building and repair of the church [Col. 0198D]. Of these, just as it is the priest’s responsibility, so the cleric must understand that he is not to demand insolently anything beyond the amount assigned to him. The restoration of the places is to make clear that what has been assigned to ecclesiastical buildings has truly been devoted to that work; for it is a sacrilege if, while sacred buildings are left without support, the bishop converts to his own profit the funds designated for them.

Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Simplicius, chapter 2.

XXXIV. (Decrees of Simplicius, chapter 2.) From the revenues of the Church or the offerings of the faithful, only one portion is to be allotted to the bishop; two are to benefit the buildings of the church and the distribution to pilgrims and the poor; the remaining portion is to be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each.

Concerning the honor of the church of God. From the synodal capitularies, title 69.

XXXV. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 71.) It has pleased us to admonish each bishop to see to it throughout his parish that the church of God receives its due honor, and that the altars likewise be venerated according to their dignity; that the house of God and its sacred altars not be accessible to dogs; that the vessels consecrated to God be held in great veneration; and that the sanctified offerings be collected with the greatest care by those who are worthy.

Also concerning the restoration of the churches of God. From the capitularies of Emperor Louis, chapter 40.

[Col. 0199B] XXXVI. (Book IV of the *Capitularies*, chapter 40.) Concerning the construction or restoration of churches, the count and the bishop, or the abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves choose for this purpose, are to make an assessment, so that each of them receives for the work and restoration only as much as he is known to possess from the property of the churches. Likewise, our vassals are either to contribute jointly only as much labor as they possess church property, or each individually according to the amount he holds. Or, if they agree to give silver for carrying out the work, they are to pay in silver according to the estimated value of the work; with this money the head of the church can hire laborers and purchase materials for the aforesaid restoration. Whoever has neglected to give the ninth and the tithe is first to restore them with the legal penalty [Col. 0199C], and in addition pay our ban, so that, chastened in this way, he may beware of losing his benefice by repeating the offense.

Concerning the same matter. Also from the *Capitularies*, title 22.

XXXVII. (Book II of the *Capitularies*, chapter 22.) In works for the restoration of churches, whether in carrying them out or redeeming the obligation, the bishop’s will is to prevail. Nevertheless, it must in no way remain undone that, as we have often ordered, this or that payment be made to the various parts of the churches. Let this also be known to all: whoever acts negligently in this matter and is found negligent before us is to undergo precisely what we ordered in our capitulary on this matter, with the common counsel of our faithful.

[Col. 0199D] 46 Concerning places formerly sacred. From the same capitulary, chapter 54.

XXXVIII. (Book IV of the *Capitularies*, chapter 53.) Concerning places long ago made sacred and now defiled by filth: insofar as possible, they are to be restored to their former condition.

Concerning destroyed churches. From the same, chapter 3.

XXXIX. (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 144; Book III of the Lombard Laws, title 1, chapter 47.) Concerning destroyed churches: bishops and royal envoys are to investigate whether they were destroyed through negligence or impossibility; and wherever negligence is found, those who ought to have restored the church are to be compelled by episcopal authority to make amends. But if this occurred through impossibility—whether because there are more churches than necessary or because they are larger than can be restored from the property belonging to them—the bishop is to find a way by which they can suitably be repaired and maintained.

Concerning the same matter. From the synodal capitularies of Charles the Younger, chapter 62.

XL. (Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 6, chapter 66.) The servants of the churches, subject to whatever authorities they may be, where no better custom or more devout arrangement exists from the time and command of Lord Louis, or certainly of Lord Charles or even Pippin, are at least to be permitted to serve that same church for twenty days each year, without harassment, in repairing its ruins. Where a more generous arrangement or better custom exists, it is not to be diminished on account of this consideration of our necessity.

47 Also concerning the same matter. From the capitulary of Louis, chapter 5.

XLI. Your diligence must nevertheless watch over this: churches entrusted to priests must not, insofar as their resources permit, be neglected in their restoration or in the provision of lights. And just as you prohibit others from taking anything from the mansi assigned to the church lights, so you and your archdeacons, by taking nothing from those same mansi, are to provide an example to others. Rather, let them be allowed to serve the purpose for which they were given, so that everything, as stated, may through your authority and zeal be devoted to the restoration of churches and the lights.

Concerning tithes. Chapter 162.

XLII. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 149.) Tithes are to be under the authority of the bishop, so that they may be distributed by the priests.

Concerning the same matter. From chapter 157.

XLIII. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 163.) Those who hold the benefices of churches are to give to the church whose property they are the ninth and the tithe from them; and those who hold such a benefice are to labor on half of it and give tithes from their share to their own priest.

Concerning the same matter.

XLIV. Newly cleared fields made beside cultivated lands are to pay tithes to the ancient church [Col. 0200D]. And if, more than four or five miles away in the wilderness, any person of standing has brought some newly cleared land under cultivation and has built a church there with the consent of his bishop, after the consecration of the church he is to provide a priest; and under that priest’s direction he is to pay the tithes from the same cultivated land to that church [Note: [Col. 0199] This chapter is not found in Regino’s manuscript.].

Also concerning the ninths and tithes. From the same, chapter 36.

XLV. (Second Council of Chalon, chapter 19; Book II of the *Capitularies*, chapter 38.) Those who, after repeated admonitions and preaching by the priests, have neglected to give tithes are to be excommunicated [Col. 0201A]. We do not wish them to be bound by an oath, because of the danger of perjury.

Also concerning the ninths and tithes. From the same, chapter 21.

XLVI. (Book II of the *Capitularies*, chapter 21.) Concerning the ninths and tithes—about which both our father and we have frequently admonished people in various assemblies, and concerning which we have ordered in our capitularies how they are to be observed—we wish and command that from every cultivated product, and from wine and hay, the ninth and the tithe be faithfully and fully paid by all. As for the tithe from livestock, the custom observed until now is to be followed by all. If, however, there is a bishop who wishes to accept money for this, it is to remain within his authority, according to the agreement made between him and the person who is to make the payment.

[Col. 0201B] Also concerning the ninths and tithes. From the same, chapter 5, Book V.

XLVII. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 145.) Concerning those who for many years have neglected to give the ninth and the tithe, either in part or altogether: we wish them to be compelled by our envoys to pay, according to the former custom, the ninth and the tithe of one year, together with the legal penalty, and in addition our ban [Col. 0201C]. It is also to be announced to them that whoever repeats this negligence is to know that he will lose the benefice from which this ninth and tithe ought to have been paid.

Also concerning the same matter. Chapter 6.

XLVIII. (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 145; and Additions IV, chapter 73.) Whoever takes a tithe away from the church to which it is owed by right and presumptuously gives it to another church, whether because of gifts, friendship, or any other reason [Col. 0201C], is to be restrained by the count or our envoy, so that he restores the amount of that tithe together with the legal penalty.

Also concerning the same matter. Chapter 7.

XLIX. (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 46; Law of the Lombards, Book III, title 3, chapter 8; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 154.) Concerning tithes which the people refuse to give unless they are redeemed from them in some manner: bishops are to prohibit this. If anyone is found to be contemptuous and unwilling to obey either the bishop or the count, if he is our man, he is to be compelled to come into our presence; the others are to be restrained, so that unwillingly they restore to the church what they negligently refused to give voluntarily.

Also concerning the same matter. Chapter 9.

L. (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 147.) Concerning those who have neglected to cultivate the lord’s fields in order not to pay the ninth and tithe from them, and for this reason have taken other people’s lands to cultivate: we wish them to pay, for three years, that grain with the legal penalty [Col. 0201D]. If anyone on this account is contemptuous either of the count or of our envoys, he is to be compelled, under sureties, to come to the palace.

Also concerning the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 62.

LI. Those who are obliged from ecclesiastical property to pay the ninth and the tithe and to restore the church’s roofs and repairs according to ancient authority and custom, and who not only neglect this but abandon it contemptuously [Col. 0202A], while subjecting the clergy to hunger and want and allowing ecclesiastical buildings to be destroyed through dilapidation, are to be separated from ecclesiastical communion until they diligently strive to correct what they neglected through negligence. If they repeat the offense, then, after making satisfaction for the excommunication, they are to be compelled by royal authority according to the ancient legal edict: “Whoever neglects the rent shall lose the field.”

Also concerning tithes. From the capitularies of Charles.

LII. (Capitulary at Salz, chapter 2.) Where baptismal churches existed from ancient times and a pious endowment was made, tithes are in every respect to be granted according to what the bishop of that parish has ordered. If, through donations by kings or by other God-fearing and worthy men, certain properties have been assigned to bishoprics or monasteries, and from those properties tithes were formerly given to the original churches, that ancient donation or endowment is to remain firm and stable. Nevertheless, as we said above, whoever appears to possess those properties is to pay the tithes from them.

That hay, grain, and wine are not to be stored in a church. From the same, chapter 142.

LIII. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 150.) No priest is to presume to store grain, hay, or wine in a church [Note: [Col. 0201] See Theodulf, chapter 8, and Ahyto, chapter 21.].

Concerning the same matter. From the sayings of Saint Augustine, bishop.

LIV. In an oratory no one is to do anything except what it was made for; hence it received its name. Or if perhaps some people, at the appointed hours, are free and wish to pray, those who think that something else ought to be done there are not to impede them.

Also elsewhere.

(Rule of Tournai, chapter 15; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 80.) In an oratory nothing at all is to be done except the worship of God through prayer and psalmody, so that both the name and the work continually devoted to it may correspond.

Also concerning the same matter. From the sayings of Saint Benedict.

LV. (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 52; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 81.) Let this be an oratory, as it is called; nothing else is to be done or stored there.

That no one is to presume to hold a feast in a church. From the Council of Carthage.

LVI. (BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 83.) No bishop or cleric is to feast in a church, unless perhaps, while traveling, he remains there because of the necessity of lodging. The people too are, insofar as possible, to be prohibited from such banquets [Col. 0202D].

52 Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Laodicea.

LVII. (Council of Laodicea, chapter 28; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 82.) It is not proper to hold an agape in divine dwellings, that is, in churches, or to eat inside them or spread couches there.

That no one is to presume to sell wine in a church. From the Council of Tours.

LVIII. (BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 84.) It has been reported to the holy synod that certain priests establish taverns in the churches entrusted to them—which is sacrilegious—and neither sell wine through tavern-keepers nor permit it to be sold [Col. 0203A]. Thus, where only prayers, the word of God, and the praise of God ought to resound, banquets and drunkenness take place; there are laughter, applause, and shameful words; there are quarrels and disputes. How contrary this is to God, the Lord God himself demonstrates: when he found sellers and buyers and money-changers sitting in the temple, he made a whip from cords and drove them all out of the temple. If he drove out of the temple even those things which appeared to be lawfully sold there and were bought in order to be offered to the Lord in that same temple, what do you think will happen concerning such a pestilential presumption and contempt of God? And if not only priests but all clerics are commanded not to enter taverns, who can tolerate the churches of God becoming taverns [Col. 0203B]? Therefore the synod absolutely forbids this from happening in the future. If it does happen, the priest is to be deposed; laymen, deprived of communion, are to be expelled from the church which they have dishonored [Note: [Col. 0203] See the Capitulary of Riculf of Soissons, chapter 13.].

53 Concerning the same matter.

LIX. (BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 85.) Meanwhile, what the Lord says must not be taken lightly: “My house is a house of prayer” (Isaiah LVIII). If the house of God is called a house of prayer, it ought to be what it is called, and nothing else ought to be done or stored there. For where the Lord’s body is consecrated, where the presence of angels is unquestionably present, where the relics of the saints are reverently kept, nothing dishonorable should appear that might offend the eyes of those who come to pray, nor should anything be seen there that pertains to temporal profit [Col. 0203C]; rather, everything should be holy, everything clean, and everything pertain only to ecclesiastical service.

That altars are to be covered with the cleanest linens; and that priests are to preach to women so that they provide linen with which the altar may be clothed. From the Council of Reims, chapter 5.

LX. (BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 97.) Care must be taken that the table of Christ—that is, the altar, where the Lord’s body is consecrated, where his blood is consumed, where the relics of the saints are kept, and where the prayers and vows of the people are offered by the priest in the sight of God—be honored with every form of veneration and most carefully covered with the cleanest linens and coverings. Nothing is to be placed upon it except reliquaries containing the relics of the saints and the four Gospels. When Mass has been completed, the chalice and the book of the sacraments, together with the priestly vestments, are to be stored under lock in a clean place [Col. 0203D].

54 Concerning the preparation of altar linens. From the *Capitularies*.

(Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 152.) Priests are to preach throughout their parishes to women, so that they prepare linens for the altars.

That no priest is to receive another’s parishioner for Mass. From the Council of Nantes, 419.

LXI. (Council of Nantes, chapter 1; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 92.) On Sundays and feast days, before celebrating Mass, priests are to ask the people whether a parishioner of another church is present who wishes to hear Mass there after despising his own priest [Col. 0204A]. If they find such a person, they are immediately to expel him from the church and compel him to return to his own parish. They are likewise to ask whether there are any people in disagreement who have an irreconcilable dispute among themselves. If any are found, they are immediately to be reconciled. If they refuse to accept peace, they are to be expelled from the Church until they return to charity. For we cannot offer a gift or offering upon the altar until we have first been reconciled with our brother. When these matters have been carried out, the priests are properly to perform the solemnities of Mass.

Also from the same council. From the *Capitularies*.

(Council of Nantes, chapter 2; Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 153; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 91.) No priest is to receive another’s parishioner for Mass, unless he is on a journey or has a legal hearing there.

Concerning the offerings of the faithful at the altar.

LXII. If the faithful offer anything at the altar, once received by the minister it is to be placed behind the altar.

55 That nothing else is to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice except what the Lord ordained. From the Canons of the Apostles, title 3.

LXIII. If any bishop or priest offers upon the altar, contrary to the Lord’s ordinance, anything else in the sacrifice—that is, honey, milk, strong drink instead of wine, prepared foods, birds, animals, or legumes—acting against the Lord’s constitution, he is to be deposed from his rank.

Which kinds of things are to be offered at the altar, not for the sacrifice but for a simple blessing. From the Canons of the Apostles, title 4.

LXIV. (BURCHARD, Book VI, chapter 6.) Nothing may be offered at the altar, when the sacred offering is celebrated, except new ears of grain, grapes, oil, and *thymiama*, that is, incense.

That things which cannot be offered in churches are to be brought by the faithful to the priests’ houses. In the same place, title 5.

LXV. All other fruits or firstfruits are to be sent to the house of the bishop or priest and are not to be offered on the altar. It is certain, however, that they are to be divided among bishops, priests, deacons, and the other clerics.

What ought to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice. From the Council of Worms, chapter 29.

[Col. 0204D] LXVI. (Third Council of Braga, chapter 2; Council of Worms, chapter 4; BURCHARD, Book V, chapter 2.) Pure water is not to be offered in the Eucharist, as some are deceived for the sake of sobriety [Col. 0205A], but wine mixed with water. For wine was also present in the mystery of our redemption, when he says, “I will not drink of this fruit of the vine” (Matthew XXVI), and he gave it mixed with water after the supper. Moreover, water flowed from his side together with blood; this expressly shows wine from the true vine of his flesh mixed with water. Therefore, when the teacher of truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples, we understand that he provided only bread and the chalice under this sacrament. Consequently, nothing else is to be offered except bread and wine mixed with water.

The Lord’s chalice, mixed with wine and water, ought to be offered, because we understand the people in the water, while the blood of Christ is represented in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ, and the congregation of believers is joined and attached to him in whom it has believed. This union and conjunction is so mingled in the water and wine in the Lord’s chalice that the mixture cannot be separated. For if anyone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to be without us. But if there is water alone, the people begin to be without Christ. The Lord’s chalice cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed with each other.

Concerning the Lord’s chalice. From the Council of Reims, title 8.

[Col. 0205B] LXVII. (BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 96, and Distinction 1, *On Consecration*, chapter 45.) The Lord’s chalice, together with the paten, is to be made entirely of silver if it is not made of gold. Nor should priests, persuaded by greed, plead poverty or inability, since one part of everything belonging to the church is to be spent on the construction and repair of the church itself [Col. 0205C]. The people are also to be admonished to offer something among the gifts of the Lord, as the ancient people under Moses are read to have done in the Lord’s tabernacle. If anyone is extremely poor, he is at least to have a pewter chalice. A chalice is not to be made of bronze or brass, because, through the force of the wine, it produces verdigris, which provokes vomiting. No one is to presume to sing Mass with a wooden chalice.

Concerning the Lord’s corporal. From the council mentioned above.

[Col. 0205C] LXVIII. (BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 98.) The corporal upon which the sacred offering is sacrificed is to be made of the cleanest and purest linen; no material of another kind, whether more precious or cheaper, is to be mixed with it, because the Lord’s body was wrapped in the tomb not in all-silk cloths, but only in a clean shroud. The corporal is never to remain on the altar; it is to be placed either in the Sacramentary or, together with the chalice and paten, stored in a very clean place. When it is washed by a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, it is first to be washed in the church, in a place and vessel prepared for this purpose, because it has been imbued with the Lord’s body and blood. Afterward it is to be washed by the laundress in a clean place [Helmstedt edition: “stored”].

Concerning the Eucharist. From the synodal capitularies, chapter 155.

[Col. 0205D] LXIX. (Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 161; Capitula of Walter of Orléans, chapter 7; BURCHARD, Book V, chapter 10.) The priest is always to have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever anyone falls ill, or a little child falls ill, he may immediately give him communion, lest he die without communion.

Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Tours.

LXX. (BURCHARD, book V, chapter 9.) Every presbyter shall have a pyx, or a vessel worthy of so great a sacrament, in which the Lord’s body may be carefully kept as viaticum for those departing from this world. This sacred offering must be dipped in Christ’s blood, so that the presbyter may truthfully say to the sick person: “May the body and blood of the Lord profit you,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0205D] See Hug. Menard, notes on the *Book of Sacraments*, p. 378.] It shall always be kept on the altar, because of mice and wicked people; and it shall always be changed every third day—that is, the presbyter shall consume that one, and another consecrated on the same day shall be substituted in its place—lest, if kept longer, it should perhaps become moldy, which God forbid.

### Concerning the offerings, that they be renewed from Saturday to Saturday. From the same source.

LXXI. (BURCHARD, book V, chapter 12.) This also seems necessary to add: that the offerings presented on the altar should always be renewed from Saturday to Saturday, because the loaves of the Presence, which were placed upon the Lord’s table, were always changed from Saturday to Saturday.

### That the chrism should always be kept under lock and key. In the same place.

LXXII. (BURCHARD, book IV, chapter 80.) Moreover, this too must be observed in every way: that the sacred chrism and consecrated oil always be kept under lock and key, lest anyone faithless or unclean touch that by which we are incorporated into Christ, by which all the faithful are sanctified, and by which kings and priests are anointed; or lest some treacherous person steal it in order to overturn God’s judgment, as we have learned by experience. [Note: [Col. 0205D] See the Council of Metz of the year 888, chapter 6.]

### If a presbyter gives chrism to overturn a judgment. From the Capitularies, title 55.

[Col. 0206C] LXXIII. (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 55; Lombard Laws, book III, title 27, chapter 1.) A presbyter who gives chrism in order to overturn a judgment shall, after being deposed from his rank, lose his hand.

### That no presbyter give any gift for chrism. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 45.

LXXIV. (BURCHARD, book V, chapter 77.) No bishop or any ecclesiastical minister shall receive any gift on account of the sacred chrism, neither money nor any little presents that are improperly demanded from presbyters by the bishops’ ministers. Nevertheless, it is fitting that presbyters visit and honor their bishops at a suitable time with voluntary offerings.

### That every presbyter bring two flasks to the city on the Lord’s Supper. From the Capitularies, title 156.

LXXV. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 162; BURCHARD, book IV, chapter 75.) On the Lord’s Supper, the presbyter shall bring two flasks with him: one for chrism, the other for oil, for anointing catechumens or the sick, according to the apostolic teaching [Note: [Col. 0205D] The Helmstedt edition and the Paris manuscript that we used agree at this point. The books of the Capitularies, however, vary. In the printed editions, as well as in Burchard and in the old manuscript of the Colbert Library [Col. 0206D], and also in ours, it is prescribed that the presbyter bring three flasks with him. But in the old manuscript from which the first Paris edition was produced, and also in the most ancient book of the monastery of Ripoll, it is read exactly as follows: “On the Lord’s Supper, the presbyter shall bring two flasks with him: one for chrism, the other for oil, for anointing catechumens [Col. 0207D] or the sick, according to the teaching,” etc. Regino followed this latter reading. On the other hand, in the old pontifical manuscript of the church of Rouen, quoted by Hugh Menard in his notes on the *Book of Sacraments*, p. 80: “Early in the morning, let the mansionarii arrange everything necessary for the consecration [Col. 0208D] of the chrism, placing in the sacristy three flasks filled with the purest oil: one for oil for the sick, another for chrism, and the third for oil for anointing catechumens.”] Thus, when someone falls ill, he may bring in the presbyters of the Church, who shall pray for him and anoint him, and so forth (James 5).

[Col. 0207A] ### Concerning presbyters who live far away. Also from the source cited above, chapter 93.

LXXVI. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 99; BURCHARD, book IV, chapter 79.) Concerning the presbyters who were accustomed to come to the cities on the Lord’s Supper to receive chrism, it has been decreed that, from among those who live far away, one out of eight or ten be chosen by the bishop, to carry the chrism he has received carefully to himself and his companions. Those who live no farther than four or five miles from the city shall come in person, as usual, to receive the chrism; but for the sake of instruction they shall be summoned to the city at another time outside Lent, on account of the congregations entrusted to them.

### That no one receive another bishop’s chrism. From the Council of Vaison, chapter 3.

[Col. 0207B] LXXVII. (Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 310; BURCHARD, book IV, chapter 78.) In each territory, presbyters or ministers shall request chrism from their own bishops every year as Easter approaches—not from neighboring bishops merely as they please, nor through just any ecclesiastical person. But if some necessity or the ministers’ occupation prevents this, it may be done through a subdeacon, since it is dishonorable to entrust what is highest to inferiors. It is best, however, that the person who will use it in administering it should himself receive it. If something prevents this, then at least the person whose duty it is to arrange the sacristy and receive the sacraments [Note: [Col. 0208D] See the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 36.]

### That no minister depart without chrism.

LXXVIII. (First Council of Orange, chapter 2; BURCHARD, book [Col. 0207C] IV, chapter 75.) None of the ministers who has received the duty of baptizing ought ever to proceed without chrism, because it has been agreed among us that a person is chrismated once in baptism. Concerning one who, through any necessity, has not been chrismated in baptism, the priest shall be admonished at confirmation.

62 ### Concerning the sacred fonts. From the source cited above.

LXXIX. (Capitula of Hincmar, year 852, chapter 3; BURCHARD, book IV, chapter 13; Capitularies of Agyto, chapter 7.) If a presbyter cannot have stone fonts, he shall have a suitable vessel solely for the office of baptism, and it shall never be carried outside the church. Likewise, separate vessels shall be kept for washing the corporal and the altar cloths; nothing else shall be done in them. [Note: [Col. 0208D] See below, chapter 271 of this book.]

[Col. 0207D] ### That no presbyter presume to sing Mass without priestly vestments. From the Council of Rheims.

LXXX. No presbyter shall presume in any way to celebrate Mass without an amice, alb, stole, maniple, and chasuble. These sacred vestments must be perfectly clean and kept in a clean place inside the church. Nor, when wearing them, may the presbyter go outside the church, because divine law forbids this.

[Col. 0208A] ### That no presbyter pawn consecrated vessels or vestments. From the source cited above, chapter 11.

LXXXI. (HINCMAR, in the Capitula issued in the year 852, chapter 11; BURCHARD, book III, chapter 104; Capitularies of Theodulf, chapter 18.) No presbyter shall presume to give a chalice, paten, altar cloth, priestly vestment, or book as security to a tavern keeper, merchant, any layman, or a woman, unless the most urgent necessity compels him. For so great is the sanctity of the sacred ministry that, without prejudice to the deeper meaning of the mystery, the Lord even through the prophet forbade a priest to go out among the people wearing the sacred vestments, but required him to leave them inside the holy place when returning from divine conversation. And if the sacred canons forbid a person to enter taverns for drinking, how much less ought sacred objects of the ministry to be exposed to the touch of the unclean, or still less given as security, as Pope Stephen, martyr, taught according to Hilary in his Decretals.

## HEREAFTER, CONCERNING THE LIFE OF PRIESTS

### That a bishop and presbyter have lodging not far from the church. From the Council of Carthage.

LXXXII. (Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 14.) A bishop shall have a small lodging not far from the church.

### That presbyters nowhere be allowed to lodge indiscriminately. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 36.

LXXXIII. Presbyters shall nowhere be allowed to lodge indiscriminately, nor shall they presume to do so in any way; rather, they shall diligently remain continually at their own churches, in order to provide the faithful with the sacred mysteries and ministries [Col. 0208C], nor shall they be permitted to live elsewhere. Nor shall women have any residence [Sirmond and the manuscript read: association] in places where presbyters have had any regular access. If they take this lightly, they shall be judged as transgressors, as shall those who act contrary to the prohibitions.

64 ### Concerning the continence of priests. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1.

LXXXIV. (BURCHARD, book II, chapter 108; Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 10.) If a presbyter takes a wife, he shall be deposed from his order. But if he has fornicated or committed adultery, he must be expelled still more severely and reduced to penance. Likewise, if a deacon falls into the same sin, he shall be removed from the rank of the ministry [Col. 0208D].

### Concerning the same matter. From the same council.
