LXXXV. (Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 9; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 49.) If a presbyter, having been overtaken by bodily sin, confesses that he committed the offense before ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in the other duties on account of his good conduct. If he has not confessed this himself and cannot be openly convicted, the matter shall be left to the judgment of his authority.

[Col. 0209A] ### Concerning the same matter. From the canons of the apostles.

LXXXVI. (Apostolic Canons, chapter 25; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 189; book XVII, chapter 39.) A presbyter or deacon who is caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or murder shall be deposed, but shall not be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord does not judge twice.”

### Likewise.

LXXXVII. The priests and deacons of the Lord, and all who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, shall abstain from wives.

### Concerning the same matter.

LXXXVIII. (BURCHARD, book II, chapter 118.) Moreover, the Church must observe entirely what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites not have intercourse with women, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry; and it is written: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

### Concerning the same matter.

LXXXIX. (BURCHARD, book II, chapter 117.) Concerning presbyters and deacons, the discipline of the divine laws is that those who are incontinent, having been placed in such offices, be deprived of all ecclesiastical honor and not admitted to a ministry that ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

### Likewise.

XC. (Council of Nicaea, chapter 3; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 109.) The great council entirely forbade any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, except perhaps a mother, sister, or aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion.

### Concerning the same matter. From the Decrees of Pope Siricius, title 12.

XCI. (Decrees of Siricius, chapter 12; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 110.) We do not permit any women to be in the homes of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them specifically on grounds of kinship alone.

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 25.

XCII. (Sixth Council of Carthage, chapter 25.) Bishop Aurelius said: “We add, dearest brothers, moreover, since a report had been made concerning the incontinence of certain clerics—even lectors—with respect to their own wives, that it was resolved, as has also been confirmed by various councils, that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries [Col. 0209D], and deacons, presbyters, and even bishops, according to their respective statutes, abstain from their wives, so that they may appear to be as though they did not have them. If they do not do this, they shall be removed from ecclesiastical office. The other clerics, however, shall not be compelled to this except at a more mature age.”

### Concerning the same matter. From the Decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 7.

XCIII. (Decrees of Siricius, chapter 7.) We have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, long after the time of their consecration, have fathered offspring both from their own marriages and from shameful intercourse [Col. 0210A], and defend their crime by this argument: that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are said to have been granted the capacity to beget children. Let whoever he may be who follows lust and teaches vice now tell me: if he thinks that in the law of Moses the restraints of licentiousness were everywhere loosened by our Lord for the sacred orders, why does He warn those to whom the Holy of Holies was entrusted, saying: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy”? Why also were priests ordered to live far from their homes in the temple during the year of their service? Clearly for this reason: so that they could not have carnal intercourse even with their wives, and, shining with integrity of conscience, might offer an acceptable gift to God. After their period of service had been completed, the use of their wives was permitted solely for the sake of producing offspring, because no one except someone from the tribe of Levi was commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry.

### Concerning the same matter. Chapter 92.

XCIV. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 98; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 3.) The bishops have decreed concerning presbyters that those who permit women to live indiscriminately with them, and thereby become marked by suspicion of a bad reputation, if they do not correct themselves after being admonished, shall be struck with canonical censure as contemptuous of the sacred canons. [Note: [Col. 0209D] Regino rightly cites this chapter if the ancient manuscripts are taken into account. For this chapter, which is chapter 98 in the editions, is chapter 92 in the Colbert and Ripoll manuscripts, where six chapters that appear in the editions are absent from Book I [Col. 0210D]. In the old manuscript of the Royal Library, from which the first Paris edition was produced, it is numbered 91.]

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Worms, chapter 38.

XCV. (Council of Worms, chapter 9.) It was resolved that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons abstain from wives, so that they may not beget children. If they violate this decree [Col. 0210C], they shall be expelled from the honor of the clergy.

### Concerning the same matter. From the Decrees of Pope Leo.

XCVI. (Decrees of Leo I, chapter 17; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 114.) The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or lectors, they were lawfully able both to marry and to beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them began to be forbidden. Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual one, they ought neither to dismiss their wives nor to possess them as though they did not have them, so that both the love of marriage may remain intact and marital intercourse may cease.

### Concerning the same matter. From the sayings of Saint Pope Gregory.

XCVII. Those who dedicate their bodies to chastity shall not permit women to live with them.

[Col. 0210D] ### Likewise, Saint Augustine.

XCVIII. “For this reason I do not want my sister to be with me: because the women who are with my sister are not my sisters.”

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Worms, chapter 9.

XCIX. (Council of Worms, chapter 2.) Therefore, if priests have fallen into the snare of fornication and the crime has been most clearly demonstrated, they can no longer retain the honor of the priesthood, according to the authority of canonical institution.

[Col. 0211A] ### Which women may live in the homes of clerics. From the Council of Agde.

C. (Council of Agde, chapter 10; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 112.) We also prescribe by special ordinance, for the protection of life and reputation, that no cleric be joined to any unrelated woman by any form of comfort or intimacy. Not only shall no unrelated woman enter his house, but he himself shall not have the power to visit an unrelated woman. He shall be free to live only with his mother, sister, daughter, or niece, if he has one; concerning these relationships, it is impious to suspect anything other than what nature has established.

### That female servants or freedwomen not manage the clerics’ storerooms or perform secret service. From the Council of Agde.

[Col. 0211B] CI. (Council of Agde, chapter 11; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 113.) It was resolved that female servants or freedwomen be removed from the storeroom, from secret service, and from the same residence in which the cleric lives.

### Concerning intimacy with unrelated women. From the Council of Orléans.

CII. (Third Council of Orléans, chapter 4.) Therefore we decree that no bishop or cleric have within his house any woman, except the female relatives named by the earlier canons. A specific prohibition is also issued concerning them: if any cleric incurs adverse suspicion or the people’s reproach because of any woman, he shall immediately dismiss her if he has her within his house [Col. 0211C]. If she is in fact unrelated and independent, he shall make every effort to dismiss her, so that the infamy that has arisen may be removed. If any bishop or cleric refuses to avoid what has been written above, he shall be punished for disobedience with three years’ excommunication. If he is found guilty of adulterous intercourse, the provisions of the earlier canons concerning his degradation from honors shall be observed.

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Tours.

CIII. (First Council of Tours, chapter 4; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 291; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 116.) Since no place must be given to the devil, we have decreed that this must especially be guarded against: that no cleric have intimacy with unrelated women, or give people any opportunity for evil speech or thought. For it has frequently happened through this indecent occasion that the devil, who lies in wait like a lion in his lair, exults over the downfall of God’s servants [Col. 0211D]. If any cleric, after his bishop’s prohibition, wishes to persist in illicit intimacies with unrelated women, he shall be held excluded from communion.

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 6.

CIV. (Council of Nantes, chapter 3; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 291; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 116.) It must be prohibited and forbidden with every form of warning that no priest have in his house those female persons concerning whom suspicion may arise, as is also contained in the canon. Nor should he have even those whom the canons permit, because, at the devil’s instigation, a crime is frequently found to have been committed even with them, or with their attendants—namely, a mother, aunt, or sister [Col. 0212A]. But if someone has among these women a needy person who requires the presbyter’s support, he shall provide her with a house in the village or settlement, far from the presbyter’s residence, and there supply her with what is necessary. This too, however, must be prohibited in every way according to canonical authority: no woman shall presume to approach the altar, minister to the presbyter, or stand or sit within the rails.

### Concerning the visitation of the sick by a presbyter. From the source cited above.

CV. (Council of Nantes, chapter 4; BURCHARD, book XVIII, in the Argument.) When a priest hears that someone in his parish has fallen ill, he shall go to him as quickly as possible. Having entered the room, he shall sprinkle blessed water over the sick person and throughout the room, with the antiphon “Thou shalt sprinkle me, O Lord,” and the verse “Let God arise.” Then he shall say the prayer: “O God, who have bestowed upon your priests, above others, so great a grace.” Then he shall sing seven psalms with prayers for the sick. After this he shall order everyone to withdraw outside the room. Approaching the bed on which the sick person lies, he shall address him gently and kindly, urging him to place all his hope in God; to endure God’s scourge patiently; to believe that these things have come about for his purification and correction; to confess his sins; to promise amendment if the Lord grants him life; to vow penance for the faults he has committed; to arrange his possessions while he still retains understanding and reason; to redeem his sins by almsgiving; to forgive those who have sinned against him; to hold fast to the right faith and belief; and never to despair of God’s mercy. When the sick person’s mind has been strengthened by these and similar exhortations, the priest shall give a blessing and depart, intending to return shortly afterward, and shall allow the sick person time to reflect upon his sins.

### Concerning the sick who confess their sins and seek reconciliation. From the source cited above.

CVI. (Council of Nantes, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 3.) A sick person who, with death pressing upon him, confesses his sins shall be reconciled by the priest on this condition: that, if the Lord grants him life and restores his health, he perform penance in every way according to the nature of his offense.

### Concerning the reconciliation of the sick. From the Council of Nicaea.

[Col. 0212D] CVII. (Council of Nicaea, chapter 13; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 6.) Concerning those who are approaching death, the ancient and regular leniency shall still be observed, so that if someone is departing from the body, he may not be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. If, though considered hopeless, he receives communion and partakes of the offering, and then recovers, he shall be among those who receive only the communion of prayer. In general, to anyone placed at the point of death who asks that the grace of communion be granted to him, the bishop ought properly to give it from the offering.

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Leo.

CVIII. (LEO I, letter 91; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 4.) For those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger [Col. 0213A], immediately implore the help of penance and reconciliation, neither satisfaction should be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can impose neither measures nor times upon God’s mercy, and no conversion is prevented from coming to him even at death, as the Spirit of God says through the Prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.” And elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.” Likewise: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” Therefore, in dispensing God’s gifts, we must not be difficult, nor disregard the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very impulse to repent has been conceived through God’s inspiration, so that they may recover from the devil’s snares, by whom they are held captive for his will.

[Col. 0213B] ### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Africa.

CIX. (Second Council of Carthage, chapter 4; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 13.) Bishop Aurelius said: “If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, then, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter ought certainly to consult the bishop and, at his command, reconcile the person in danger. We ought to strengthen this matter by sound counsel.”

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Celestine.

CX. (Decrees of Celestine I, chapter 15; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 1.) True conversion to God in those placed at the point of death must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the time, as the Prophet asserts: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.” Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the judge to whom he knows that all hidden things will be revealed.

### Concerning those who become mute before the priest comes to them. From a letter of Pope Leo.

CXI. (SAINT LEO, letter 91, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 9; Riculf, chapter 10.) The needs of such persons must therefore be aided in this way: neither the act of penance nor the grace of communion is to be denied them, if they are shown, even after losing the power of speech, to seek it through signs of sound understanding. But if they have been so weakened by illness that what they had shortly before requested they are unable to indicate in the priest’s presence [Note: [Col. 0213] This chapter has a corrupt reading in Regino. It should therefore read: “what they had requested, but are unable to indicate in the priest’s presence,” etc.], the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them; nevertheless, they shall receive both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation [Col. 0213D].

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Carthage.

CXII. (Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 78; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 23.) Penitents who have received the Eucharistic viaticum during illness must not consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands, if they survive.

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Siricius.

CXIII. (Decrees of Siricius, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 8.) We wish to aid all who have fallen through bodily weakness, when they begin to depart to the Lord, with the viaticum of communion.

[Col. 0214A] ### Concerning penitents who die suddenly. From the Council of Vaison, chapter 65.

CXIV. (First Council of Vaison, chapter 2; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 24.) The offering of those who, after receiving penance, die suddenly while proceeding along the course of a good life without communion is to be received; their funerals and, thereafter, their memory are to be attended with ecclesiastical devotion.

### Concerning those deprived of communion who have died. From a letter of Pope Leo.

CXV. (Decrees of Leo I, chapter 20; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 52.) Their case must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the death of such persons was not delayed until the remedy of communion [add: “not”]. But we, who did not give communion to them while they were alive, cannot give communion to them after their death.

[Col. 0214B] 75 ### Concerning the anointing of the sick. From the Council of Tours.

CXVI. After the sick person has been relieved of the burden of sins through confession and reconciled by the priest, he is to be anointed in God’s name with sanctified oil, first on the chest and then between the shoulder blades, with the prayers belonging to this holy anointing, so that, according to the Apostle, the prayer of faith may save the sick person, etc.

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Innocent, chapter 387.

CXVII. (Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 8; BURCHARD, book XVIII, chapter 2.) Blessed James the Apostle wrote in his Epistle: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5). There is no doubt that this must be understood as referring to sick believers, because they may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism, which, having been prepared by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but by all Christians for anointing themselves or their own people in a time of need. We regard as superfluous, however, the addition that raises doubt about the bishop, when there is no doubt that this is permitted to the presbyter. For this reason presbyters are mentioned: because bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot go to all the sick. But if a bishop either is able or considers someone worthy of a visit, he may without hesitation bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one who prepares the chrism itself. This cannot be poured upon penitents [Col. 0214D], because it is a kind of sacrament. For how can it be thought that one kind may be granted to those to whom the remaining sacraments are denied?

### Concerning the same matter. From the sayings of Bede the presbyter.

CXVIII. “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord, and the prayer of faith will save the sick person.” The apostles are also read to have done this in the Gospel, and now the custom of the Church maintains that the sick are anointed by presbyters with consecrated oil and are healed with prayer accompanying it. Not only presbyters but, as Pope Innocent writes [Col. 0215A], all Christians may use the same oil to anoint themselves or their own people in a time of need. This oil, however, may be prepared only by bishops. When he says “with oil in the name of the Lord,” he means oil consecrated in the name of the Lord—or certainly that, when they anoint the sick person, they must likewise invoke the Lord’s name over him. “And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” Many are afflicted with illness or even death of the body because of sins committed against the soul. Thus the Apostle says to the Corinthians, because they were accustomed to receive the Lord’s body unworthily: “For this reason many among you are weak, and many sleep.” If, therefore, the sick are in sins, and have confessed them to the presbyters of the Church, and have striven with a perfect heart to abandon and amend them, they will be forgiven. For sins cannot be forgiven without a confession of amendment [Col. 0215B]. Hence it is rightly added: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

### Concerning holy communion. From the source cited above.

CXIX. After the sick person has been anointed with the holy unction, he must immediately be refreshed with the body and blood of the Lord, so that, although there is despair concerning his bodily life, he may be revived in soul or deserve eternal life. For the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” And: “Unless you eat, you will not have life in yourselves.” Therefore the holy canons prescribe that communion be denied to no faithful person placed at the point of death.

### That a presbyter not hand holy communion to a layman or woman for delivery. From the Council of Rheims.

[Col. 0215C] CXX. (BURCHARD, book V, chapter 30, and Distinction 2, *On Consecration*, chapter 29.) It has come to our attention that certain presbyters so greatly despise the divine mysteries that they hand the sacred body of the Lord to a layman or woman for delivery to the sick. To those who are forbidden to enter the sacristy and to approach the altar, the Holy of Holies is entrusted. How horrible and detestable this is, the prudence of all religious persons recognizes. Therefore the synod absolutely forbids such rash presumption to occur any further. Rather, the presbyter himself must communicate the sick person. If he acts otherwise, he shall be liable to jeopardy of his rank.

78 ### That no payments be demanded for baptizing. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

[Col. 0215D] CXXI. (Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book IV, chapter 71.) Let them fix no prices for those to be baptized and signed, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions, since we are commanded to give freely what we have received freely. Therefore let them make no effort to demand anything at all from those mentioned above, lest, deterred either by poverty or provoked by indignation, they disdain to approach the means of their redemption; and let them be certain that those who are found to have committed prohibited acts, or who have not corrected their offenses of their own accord, will incur the danger of losing their own honor.

### That no one demand anything for burial. From a letter of Pope Gregory.

CXXII. (SAINT GREGORY, book VII, indiction 2, letter 55; Capitularies of Agyto, chapter 24.) It is utterly grave and far removed from a priest’s duty to seek payment for earth granted to corruption and to wish to make profit from another’s grief [Col. 0216A]. After, by God’s authority, we attained the honor of the episcopate, we entirely prohibited this vice in our own Church and did not permit the wicked custom to be resumed, remembering that when Abraham requested from Ephron, son of Seor, the price of a burial place for burying his wife’s body, he refused to accept payment, lest he appear to have gained a profit from a corpse. If a pagan man showed such consideration, how much more ought we, who are called priests, not do this? Therefore I warn that this vice of avarice must not again be attempted even among others. But if you sometimes permit someone to be buried in your church, and his parents, relatives, or heirs voluntarily wish to offer something for lights, we do not forbid you to accept it. We absolutely forbid asking for or demanding anything, lest—something most irreligious—either the Church be called, God forbid, a commercial institution, or you appear to rejoice in human deaths if you seek profit in any way from their corpses.

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 72.

CXXIII. (Capitularies of Theodulf, chapter 9; Riculf, chapter 19; Agyto, chapter 23; BURCHARD, book III, chapter 158.) No one shall presume to bury any dead person in a church as though by hereditary right, unless the bishop or presbyter has judged the person worthy according to the quality of his conduct or life. Nor shall anyone cast the bones of any dead person out of his tomb or violate anyone’s burial in any way through rash daring. Rather, each person shall be allowed to await the coming of his Judge in the grave prepared and granted to him by God. This is especially so since not only divine laws but also human laws, in the human commonwealth, judge violators of tombs guilty of death. Nor shall they in any way attempt, to use the words of Saint Gregory, to seek payment for earth granted to corruption or to make profit from another’s grief. But if relatives or heirs should voluntarily wish to offer something in the church as alms for the deceased, we do not forbid its acceptance. We entirely forbid asking for or demanding anything, lest—something most irreligious—the Church be called, God forbid, a commercial institution, or we appear to rejoice in human deaths if we strive to seek profit from them in any way [Col. 0216D].

### That no one bury a dead person in a church. From the Synodal Capitularies, title 156.

CXXIV. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 159.) Henceforth no one shall bury a dead person in a church.

### Concerning the same matter. Chapter 46.

CXXV. (Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 47; Sixth Council of Arles, chapter 21.) The regulation established by the ancient Fathers concerning the burial of the dead in basilicas shall be observed.

### From the Council of Nantes.

(Council of Nantes, chapter 6; BURCHARD, book III, chapter 159.) [Col. 0217A] It must be prescribed, according to the authority of the canons, that they demand no gift for tombs or for people being buried, unless perhaps the person being buried, while alive, ordered that something from his possessions be given to the church in whose courtyard he is buried, or, after his death, those entrusted with giving his alms should voluntarily wish to give something from his possessions. Nevertheless, nothing at all is to be demanded by those presbyters or by those who preside over places and villages. It must also be prohibited, according to the institutions of our forefathers, that people be buried inside a church; rather, they are to be buried in the courtyard, portico, or vestibule of the church. Inside the church, or near the altar where the body and blood of the Lord are made, they shall have no permission whatsoever to bury.

[Col. 0217B] 81 **On the same matter. From the Council of Tribur.**

**CXXVI.** (Council of Tribur, chs. 15–16.) If it can be done, the dead are not to be buried anywhere except near a church, and henceforth nothing is to be demanded as the price of burial.

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CXXVII.** (BURCHARD, book IV, ch. 101.) It has been said that in certain places it was customary for money to be given for the reception of chrism, for baptism, and for communion. The holy synod detested and anathematized this seed of the Simoniac heresy, and decreed that henceforth nothing be demanded either for ordination, chrism, or baptism, or for burial or communion, but that the free gifts of Christ be distributed freely [Burchard: “let the gifts be given freely”].

[Col. 0217C] **On children who have died unbaptized through negligence. From the Penitential, ch. 17.**

**CXXVIII.** A woman who has given birth, whose child has died unbaptized through negligence, shall do penance for one year and shall never be without some form of penance [Note: [Col. 0217D] See below, book II, ch. 60 and following.]. If the priest responsible was summoned to baptize the child and neglected to come, he himself shall be chastised by the judgment of his bishop in proportion to the condemnation of his soul. Moreover, all the faithful are permitted—and indeed it is commanded—that wherever they find unbaptized persons apparently at the point of death, they rescue every soul from the devil through baptism: that is, they are to baptize them simply with blessed water in the name of the Lord, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, immersing them or pouring water over them. Therefore those who are able—especially the faithful and, above all, monks—ought to possess the knowledge of baptizing; and if they go anywhere farther away, they should always carry the Eucharist with them.

**On the same matter.**

**CXXIX.** (BURCHARD, book IV, ch. 46; CAPITULARY OF THEODULF, ch. 17.) Let priests consider how great a danger it is for innocent souls to be excluded from the kingdom of God through their negligence. For if there is joy in heaven over one sinner who does penance, what do you think—how great will be the anger and indignation [Col. 0218A] against him who through his negligence has closed the gates of paradise to the innocent? Therefore priests must take the greatest care lest, through their negligence, they separate from heavenly blessedness the souls for whom Christ’s blood was shed. But if—God forbid—it should happen, the one through whose neglect it occurred shall submit himself, throughout the days of his life, to the grief of severe penance.

**On the same matter. Hence the preceding source.**

**CXXX.** Whoever’s little child has died without baptism through negligence shall do penance for three years, the first of these on bread and water.

**That offerings are not to be made in private houses, and that Masses are not to be sung outside a church. From the Council of Laodicea.**

**CXXXI.** (Council of Laodicea, ch. 58; Additions III, chs. 4 and [Col. 0218B] 41; BURCHARD, book III, ch. 60.) Offerings ought not to be celebrated in houses by bishops or priests.

**Hence the preceding source.**

**CXXXII.** (BURCHARD, book III, ch. 61.) It has been reported to us that certain laymen order priests to celebrate Masses in their own houses, and that amid the running about of dogs and packs of prostitutes the mysteries of holiness are more polluted than consecrated. Therefore we command that no priest presume to sing Mass outside a church, unless perhaps the necessity of travel requires it. In such a case we permit Masses to be celebrated in a tent or under the open sky, in a clean place far removed from every impurity—and never without a consecrated altar-stone.

[Col. 0218C] **On the same matter. From a letter of Pope Anacletus.**

**CXXXIII.** (BURCHARD, book III, ch. 71.) When priests offer sacrifice, they ought not to do so alone, but should bring witnesses with them, so that they may be shown to offer sacrifice perfectly to God in places consecrated to the Lord. For the authority of divine law says: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God has chosen” (Deut. XII). [Note: [Col. 0217D] Compare below, chs. 339 and 340 of this book. See book VI of the Capitularies, chs. 198 and 205; book VII, [Col. 0218D] chs. 99, 312, and 334; and Additions II, chs. 7 and 10; and the Capitular of Riculf of Soissons, ch. 2.]

**On drunken clerics. From the Council of Agde.**

**CXXXIV.** (Council of Agde, ch. 41; BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 2.) Accordingly, whoever is found to have been drunk shall, as the ecclesiastical order permits, either be removed from communion for thirty days or be subjected to corporal punishment [subdendum: “given over to punishment”].

**On the same matter. From Bishop Fructuosus.**

[Col. 0218D] **CXXXV.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 9.) If anyone endowed with ecclesiastical ordination, or a monk, is found to be a drunkard, he shall do penance on bread and water for three months.

**On the same matter.**

**CXXXVI.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 6.) If a bishop or any ordained person has made a practice of drunkenness, let him either cease or be deposed.

**On the same matter.**

**CXXXVII.** If a layman has been drunk, he shall do penance for three days on bread and water.

[Col. 0219A] **General judgments concerning all drunkards and winebibbers. By Jerome the holy priest and Ephraem the Syrian deacon.**

**CXXXVIII.** (JEROME, Letter to Eustochium; BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 12.) Flee wine as though it were poison, lest drunkenness overcome you and, stripping you of your virtues, make you naked. For wine, as Holy Scripture says (Ecclus. XIX), causes even the wise to apostatize. Consider Noah, a wise and holy man: how, having become drunk, he lay naked in sleep (Gen. IX). Consider the patriarch Lot, who through drunkenness shamefully had intercourse with his daughters (Gen. XIX). Hence blessed Basil says: “Many have been captured by demons through wine; and drunkenness is nothing other than the most manifest demon.” Hence the prophet says: “Fornication [Col. 0219B] and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. IV). For drunkenness produces disturbance, gives birth to madness of mind, and kindles the flame of lust, as the Apostle testifies: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. V). But if anyone acts contrary to these statutes of the saints, let him perform worthy and prolonged penance, because this is one of those sins that separate a person from the kingdom of God, as the Apostle Paul says: “Neither will drunkards possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI).

**On the same matter. From the sayings of Saint Benedict.**

**CXXXIX.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 1.) Nothing is so contrary to a Christian as gluttonous excess, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI).

**On the same matter. From the Capitularies, title 161.**

[Col. 0219C] **CXL.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 167.) Concerning drunkenness: first of all, let the elders guard themselves against it and set a good example of sobriety for their juniors.

**Likewise from book III, ch. 38.**

**CXLI.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 38.) No drunk person shall presume to plead his case in the mallus or give testimony; nor shall a count hold a judicial session unless he is fasting.

**From the same source, ch. 72.**

**CXLII.** (Book III of the Capitularies, ch. 72.) In the army, no one is to ask [force; from the manuscript of Ripoll] his equal or any other person to drink. Whoever is found drunk in the army shall be excommunicated in such a way that he may drink only water until he recognizes that he has acted wrongly.

**From book I of the Capitularies, title 138.**

**CXLIII.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 144.) No one is permitted to force another to drink.

86 **From the Apostolic Canons, title 42.**

**CXLIV.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 5.) A bishop, priest, or deacon who devotes himself to gambling and drunkenness must either cease or certainly be condemned. A subdeacon, lector, or cantor who does similar things must either cease or be deprived of communion. The same applies to a layman.

[Col. 0220A] **From the Penitential, ch. 19.**

**CXLV.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 13.) Whoever vomits through drunkenness, if he is a priest or deacon, shall do penance for forty days; if a monk, thirty days; if a cleric, twenty days; if a layman, fifteen days.

**From the canons.**

**CXLVI.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 6.) If a bishop or any ordained person has the vice of drunkenness, he must either cease or be deposed.

**From another Penitential.**

**CXLVII.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 14.) If a layman has vomited through drunkenness, he shall abstain from meat, wine, and beer for three days.

**CXLVIII.** (BURCHARD, book XIV, ch. 15.) If anyone has made another drunk through wickedness, he shall do penance for forty days.

**Concerning those who vomit the Eucharist.**

**CXLIX.** (BURCHARD, book V, ch. 46.) If anyone vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony, he shall do penance for forty days. Clerics, monks, or deacons shall do penance for forty days; priests, seventy; bishops, ninety. If he vomits because of illness, he shall do penance for four days.

87 **Concerning clerics singing during meals. From the African Council.**

**CL.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 62; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 170.) Clerics who sing during meals are to be removed from office [Note: [Col. 0219D] See Addition IV to the Capitularies, ch. 47; the Capitular of Riculf of Soissons, ch. 14; and the Capitular of Ahyto of Basel, ch. 46.].

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

[Col. 0220C] **CLI.** (BURCHARD, book II, ch. 171.) If any cleric or monk speaks scurrilous, jesting, or laughter-provoking words, let him be corrected most severely.

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CLII.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 60; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 172.) Scurrilous clerics and jesters with obscene speech are to be removed from office [Note: [Col. 0220D] See the Council of Toledo IV, ch. 23; the Council of Agde, ch. 70; Addition IV to the Capitularies, ch. 46; and the Capitular of Bishop Ahyto of Basel, ch. 44.].

**Concerning clerics who curse.**

**CLIII.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 57; BURCHARD, book X, ch. 66.) A cursing cleric, and especially a priest, shall be compelled to ask pardon. If he refuses, he shall be degraded and shall never be restored to office without satisfaction.

**Concerning clerics who swear oaths.**

**CLIV.** Clerics who swear oaths are to be excommunicated.

[Col. 0220D] **On the same matter. Hence the preceding source.**

**CLV.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 61; Addition IV, ch. 48; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 175.) A cleric who swears by creatures is to be rebuked most severely. If he persists in the vice, he is to be excommunicated.

88 **Concerning abusive or cursing persons.**

**CLVI.** If anyone injures another by abuse, a curse, or even an accusation, he shall be cleansed by the most appropriate satisfaction. If he repeats this vice, it shall be expiated by the most fitting penance, according to the measure of the fault.

[Col. 0221A] **On the same matter.**

**CLVII.** (BURCHARD, book X, ch. 51.) The Apostle says: “Neither will those who curse possess the kingdom of God.” If anyone has committed this sin, let him do penance as greatly as the crime he committed, which separates him from the kingdom of God.

**Concerning slanderers.**

**CLVIII.** (BURCHARD, book X, ch. 63.) If anyone is quick and ready to slander, saying what is not true, let him do penance for seven days on bread and water, separated from fellowship with his brothers.

**Concerning quarrels and fights.**

**CLIX.** (BURCHARD, book X, ch. 62.) If anyone loves quarrels or fights, or has openly insulted a brother, let him do penance at the discretion of his superior for as long as a protracted penance is required to expiate the offense.

[Col. 0221B] **Hence the preceding source.**

**CLX.** (BURCHARD, book X, ch. 53.) Whoever has been quarrelsome or murmuring shall do penance, at the discretion of his superior, for as long as the quality of the fault endures.

89 **Hence the preceding source.**

**CLXI.** (BURCHARD, book X, ch. 55.) If anyone appears to be quarrelsome, since the Apostle says, “We have no such custom, nor the churches of God” (I Cor. XI), let him be marked until he is corrected.

**Concerning the wanton or proud.**

**CLXII.** Whoever has been wanton and proud shall do penance for three days on bread and water.

**On the same matter.**

**CLXIII.** (BURCHARD, book X, ch. 56.) If anyone has been wanton in speech, let it be expiated by three days of penance [Note: [Col. 0221] See the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, ch. 15.].

**Concerning those who murmur.**

**CLXIV.** (Rule of Saint Basil, ch. 71; Concordance of Rules, ch. 8, § 9; BURCHARD, book X, ch. 54.) The Apostle says: “Do everything without murmuring” (Phil. II). Let the one who murmurs be a stranger to the unity of the brothers, and let his work be rejected.

**Hence the preceding source.**

**CLXV.** (Rule of Saint Basil, ch. 93; BURCHARD, book X, ch. 52.) If anyone has been a murmurer, let him beware lest he incur the punishment of the murmurers, of whom the Apostle says: “Nor should you murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (I Cor. X). According to the measure and deed of the sin, let him do penance by the judgment of the priest, since the Apostle’s sentence fully declares this.

**If anyone slanders his superior. From the sayings of Saint Basil.**

**CLXVI.** (Rule of Saint Basil, ch. 43; BURCHARD, book X, ch. 67.) If anyone slanders the one who presides, let him be separated from the assembly of the church for seven days and do penance, like Miriam, Aaron’s sister, who slandered Moses.

**Concerning seditious clerics. From the Council of Toledo.**

**CLXVII.** (Council of Toledo IV, ch. 45.) Clerics who have taken up arms in a sedition are to be deprived of their rank and confined in a monastery as a penalty [Note: [Col. 0221] Loaisa’s edition reads: “handed over to penance.” Elsewhere: “handed over perpetually.”].

[Col. 0222A] **Concerning clerics who resort to mutual slaughter. From the Council of Ilerda.**

**CLXVIII.** (Council of Ilerda, ch. 11; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 216.) If any clerics have resorted to mutual slaughter, the bishop shall punish them with the greatest severity, in proportion to the insult inflicted upon the dignity of their offices by such an excess.

**Hence the preceding source.**

**CLXIX.** (Rule of Saint Aurelian, ch. 13; Concordance of Rules, ch. 75, § 2; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 217.) If a brother has dared to lay hands upon a brother, let him receive legitimate discipline.

**On the same matter. From the sayings of the saints.**

**CLXX.** (Rule of Saint Ferreolus, ch. 21; Concordance of Rules, ch. 75, § 2.) A cleric or monk inflamed against another—which is most disgraceful—must not presume to lay hands on him, except those to whom correction belongs. Whoever transgresses this shall be subject to canonical discipline.

**On the same matter. From the Council of Agde.**

**CLXXI.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 67; Council of Agde, ch. 69; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 17.) Seditious persons are never to be ordained, nor usurers, nor those who avenge their own injuries.

**Hence the preceding source.**

**CLXXII.** (BURCHARD, book II, ch. 190.) If anyone consecrated in any ecclesiastical rank has become a violent assailant, let him be corrected most severely. If he does not amend, let him do penance for three months on bread and water.

**On the same matter. From the Apostolic Canons.**

**CLXXIII.** (Apostolic Canons, ch. 28.) We command that a bishop, priest, or deacon who strikes faithful persons who have committed offenses or unbelievers acting wickedly, wishing by such means to make himself feared, be removed from his office, since the Lord nowhere taught us this. On the contrary, when he himself was struck, he did not strike back.

**That clerics are not to carry weapons. From the Capitularies, book I, title 72.**

**CLXXIV.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 70; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 212.) Priests and deacons must be told in every way that they are not to carry weapons, but should place their confidence more in God’s protection than in arms.

**On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux.**

**CLXXV.** (Council of Meaux, ch. 37; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 211.) All who appear to belong to the clergy shall not take up military weapons or go about armed, but shall give expression to the name of their profession through religious conduct and religious dress. If they despise this, they shall be punished by the loss of their own rank, as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, since they cannot serve both God and the world as soldiers.

92 **That a bishop, priest, or deacon is not to keep dogs for hunting.**

**CLXXVI.** (Council of Agde, ch. 55; Council of Epaon, ch. 4; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 213.) A bishop, priest, or deacon is not permitted to keep hunting dogs or hawks. If anyone of such rank is discovered pursuing this practice, then, if he is a bishop, he shall suspend himself from communion for three months; a priest for two months; and a deacon for one month, from every office or from communion.

**That clerics are not to enter taverns. From the Council of Laodicea.**

**CLXXVII.** (Council of Carthage III, ch. 27; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 130.) Clerics are not to enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.

**Hence the preceding source.**

**CLXXVIII.** (Council of Laodicea, ch. 24; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 131.) Those devoted to the sacred ministry—from priests down to deacons and the rest of the ecclesiastical order, that is, subdeacons, lectors, cantors, exorcists, and doorkeepers—as well as those among the continent and monks, ought not to enter taverns.

**On the same matter. From the decrees of Augustine.**

**CLXXIX.** No cleric, as the decrees of the canons prohibit, may dare to enter a tavern in order to obtain food or drink. Whoever violates this shall be corrected by the severest discipline as a despiser of the holy canons.

93 **On the same matter. From the Council of Carthage.**

**CLXXX.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 48; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 210.) A cleric who strolls through the fairs or the marketplace for no purpose of buying something shall be removed from his office.

[Col. 0223C] **Concerning clerics’ vigils. From the Council of Carthage.**

**CLXXXI.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 49.) A cleric who is absent from the vigils without bodily weakness shall be excommunicated and deprived of his stipend until he is seen to have been corrected.

**On the same matter. From the Council of Elvira.**

**CLXXXII.** (Council of Elvira, ch. 21; Council of Agde, ch. 64.) If anyone living in a city has not come to church for three Sundays, let him be excommunicated until he is seen to have been corrected.

**On the same matter. From the Council of Toledo.**

**CLXXXIII.** (Council of Toledo I, ch. 5.) If a priest, deacon, or any cleric assigned to a church, while in a city or in a place where there is a church—whether a castle, village, or estate—does not come to the church for the daily sacrifice, he shall not be regarded as a cleric if, after being corrected, he does not amend [Note: [Col. 0223D] The Council of Toledo reads: “If, after being corrected, he has not wished to obtain pardon from the bishop through satisfaction.”].

**On the same matter. From the Council of Agde.**

**CLXXXIV.** (Council of Agde, ch. 64.) Clerics who neglect to attend church or fulfill their office are to be given communion as strangers.

94 **On the same matter. From the decrees of Saint Benedict.**

**CLXXXV.** (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 16; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 105.) As the Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII). This number seven will be fulfilled by us if, at the hours of matins, prime, terce, [Col. 0224A] sext, none, vespers, and compline, we perform the offices of our service, for the Prophet spoke of these. Concerning the nocturnal vigils he says the same: “At midnight I arose,” and so forth (ibid.). Therefore at these times let us offer praises to our Creator for the judgments of his justice.

**From the Council of Vannes.**

(Council of Vannes, ch. 14; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 153.) A cleric who lives within the walls of a city and, without illness, is absent on that day from the morning hymns shall be excluded from communion for seven days.

**That Masses are not to be celebrated before the third hour. From a letter of Pope Telesphorus.**

**CLXXXVI.** (BURCHARD, book III, ch. 63, and Distinction 1 on Consecration, ch. 48.) The celebration of Masses is not to take place before the third hour of the day, because it was at that same hour that the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the apostles, except on the night of the holy Nativity.

**That the faithful are not to dine before the third hour.**

**CLXXXVII.** (Addition IV, ch. 49; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 185, and Distinction 44, ch. 12.) Clerics or religious laypeople ought not to begin banquets before the holy third hour of the day; nor should clerics ever eat before a hymn has been said, and after the meal they should give thanks to God the author.

**That the sacraments of the altar are to be celebrated by those who are fasting. From the African Council.**

**CLXXXVIII.** (African Council, ch. 8; CAPITULARY OF AHYTO, ch. 10.) The sacraments of the altar are to be celebrated only by those who are fasting, except on the one anniversary day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. For if, in the afternoon, a memorial is to be made for deceased bishops or others, it is to be done by prayers alone, if those who perform it are found already to have eaten.

**That after the bishop’s address during the solemn celebration of Mass the people are to be invited to prayer. From the Council of Laodicea.**

**CLXXXIX.** (Council of Laodicea, ch. 19; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 69.) First, after the bishops’ addresses, prayer ought to be offered separately for the catechumens. After the catechumens have departed, a prayer is to be made for those who are doing penance. When these have also approached the priest’s hand and departed, the three prayers of the faithful are to be completed, so that the first is fulfilled in silence, while the second and third are completed with the customary acclamations.

**On the same matter.**

**CXC.** (BURCHARD, book II, ch. 70.) It is necessary [Note: [Col. 0224D] Compare below, ch. 204 of this book; see the first letter of Amulo.] that on feast days or Sundays, after the sermon delivered to the people during the solemn celebration of Mass, the priest admonish everyone, according to apostolic instruction, to pour out prayers together to the Lord for various needs: for kings and the rulers of the churches, for peace, for pestilence, for the sick who lie bedridden in that parish, and for the recently dead. In these prayers, the people are to say the Lord’s Prayer silently one by one, while the priest solemnly completes the appropriate prayers after each admonition. After this, the sacred offering is to be celebrated. For the Apostle says: “I urge first of all that prayers, supplications, thanksgivings, and so forth be made” (I Tim. II).

**That no priest is to presume to sing Mass alone. From the Council of Nantes.**

**CXCI.** (BURCHARD, book III, ch. 68.) The holy council has decreed that no priest presume to sing Mass alone [Note: [Col. 0225D] See book V of the Capitularies, ch. 93.]. To whom does the Lord say, “The Lord be with you,” or “Lift up your hearts,” or “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” when there is no one to respond? Or in the Canon, “and all who stand around,” when no one is present? Or whom does he invite to prayer when he says, “Let us pray,” if there is no one praying with him? Either, therefore, these words must be completely suppressed, and not only will the sacrifice be imperfect, but whoever he may be will incur the terrible sentence: “If anyone takes away from this, God will take away his share from the book of life” (Apoc. XXII). Or, if he whispers these words to walls and partitions, it will be ridiculous. Therefore this dangerous superstition must above all be driven out of monasteries of monks. Let superiors see to it that priests in monasteries have assistants in celebrating Masses. Whoever transgresses this shall be suspended from office.

97 **Concerning priests who, after celebrating Mass, do not communicate. From the Apostolic Canons.**

**CXCII.** (Apostolic Canons, ch. 9; BURCHARD, book III, [Col. 0225C] ch. 79.) If any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone from the priestly order, after making the offering, does not communicate, let him state his reason. If it is reasonable, let him obtain pardon; but if he gives no reason, let him be deprived of communion, as one who has become a cause of injury to the people.

**That the faithful laypeople ought to communicate. Hence the preceding source.**

**CXCIII.** (Apostolic Canons, ch. 10; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 67.) All faithful Christians who enter the church on Sunday and hear the writings of the apostles and the Gospel, but do not remain in prayer until Mass is completed and do not receive holy communion, should, as those who stir up disturbances in the church, be deprived of communion.

**Hence the preceding source.**

[Col. 0225D] (BURCHARD, book II, ch. 68.) All who enter the church of God and hear the holy Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer and through some intemperance turn away from receiving holy communion, are to be removed from the church until they show the fruits of penance through confession.

**Concerning diligence regarding the Lord’s body. From a definition of ecclesiastical dogmas.**

**CXCIV.** (BURCHARD, book V, ch. 15, and Distinction 2 on Consecration, ch. 13.) I neither praise nor blame receiving communion of the Eucharist daily; nevertheless, I urge that communion be received every Sunday. If, however, the mind is disposed toward sinning, I say that reception of the Eucharist burdens it more than it purifies it. Therefore, although someone is tormented by sin, if he has no further desire to sin, makes satisfaction with tears and prayers before communicating, and, trusting in God’s mercy, approaches the Eucharist without fear and in confidence, this is what I say concerning one who is not weighed down by mortal sins [Note: [Col. 0225D] See Hincmar at the end of Letter 40.].

**Likewise Saint Augustine to Januarius.**

(AUGUSTINE, Letter 118; BURCHARD, book V, ch. 16.) Someone may say that the Eucharist should not be received daily, while another may affirm that it should be received daily. Let each person do what he piously believes, according to his faith, ought to be done. For Zacchaeus and the centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either place himself above the other, when one joyfully received the Lord into his house (Luke XIX), while the other said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII). Both honored the Savior, though not in the same way; both were wretched through sins, and both obtained mercy. This is the significance of the fact that the manna tasted in each person’s mouth according to his own will.

**On the same matter. From a letter of Pope Clement.**

**CXCV.** (CLEMENT, Letter 2; REMEDIUS OF CHUR, ch. 1; BURCHARD, book V, ch. 11.) Certainly, as many offerings should be made on the altar as ought to be sufficient for the people. If any remain, they are not to be kept until the next day, [Col. 0226C] but are to be consumed with fear and trembling through the diligence of the clerics. Those who consume the remnants of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy are not immediately to come together to eat ordinary foods, nor should they think of mixing with the holy portion food that, digested through the intestines, is expelled into the privy [Note: [Col. 0225D] See Rabanus’ letter to Heribald, ch. 33.]. Therefore, if it is distributed in the morning on the Lord’s Day, the ministers who have consumed it shall fast until the sixth hour; and if they received it at the third or fourth hour, they shall fast until evening. Thus, by secret sanctification, the sacraments are to be guarded eternally.

**From the Capitularies, book I, ch. 32.**

(Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 138.) All the faithful are to communicate and to wait for the final prayer of intercession [Note: [Col. 0226D] In the manuscripts of Ripoll and Colbert, and also in the Royal manuscript from which the first Paris edition was issued, it reads: “let them wait without another prayer of intercession.”].

[Col. 0226D] **From book II, ch. 34.**

(Council of Chalon II, ch. 46; book II of the Capitularies, ch. 40; BURCHARD, book V, ch. 14.) Great discernment must be exercised in receiving the Lord’s body and blood. For care must be taken lest, if it is postponed too long, this lead to the destruction of the soul, since the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI). But if it is received without discernment, we must fear what the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks [Col. 0227A] unworthily eats judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI). In accordance with the Apostle’s words, a person must test himself and thus eat of that bread. That is, abstaining for several days from the works of the flesh and purifying body and soul, he should prepare himself to receive so great a sacrament, following the example of David (I Sam. 21), who would never have received the loaves of the presence from the priest unless he had confessed that he had abstained from marital relations since yesterday and the day before [Helmaestadt edition: “had practiced abstinence”].

**From the same book.**

(Book II of the Capitularies, ch. 45; BURCHARD, book V, ch. 17.) Laypeople are to communicate, if not more frequently, at least three times a year, unless someone is prevented by some very serious crime: namely, at Easter, at the Nativity of the Lord, and at Pentecost.

**Concerning priests who do not communicate.**

(Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 6; BURCHARD, book III, ch. 78.) It has been heard that certain priests celebrate Mass and do not communicate, although this is expressly said to be forbidden in the Apostolic Canons. Or how can he rightly say, if he has not communicated, “We have received the sacraments, O Lord,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0227D] This chapter is absent from the Helmaestadt edition and was added from a Paris manuscript].

**That the people are not to leave the church before Mass is finished. From the Council of Arles.**

**CXCVI.** (Council of Orléans I, ch. 26; BURCHARD, book III, ch. 29.) When people assemble in the name of God to celebrate Mass, they are not to depart before the solemnity of Mass is completed; and wherever a bishop is present [Note: [Col. 0227D] The Helmaestadt edition reads: “And where a bishop is not present,” and so forth. See the Council of Orléans III, ch. 29; book VII of the Capitularies, ch. 201; and Addition [Col. 0228D] IV, ch. 42.], they are to receive the priest’s blessing.

[Col. 0227C] 101 **On the same matter. From the Council of Carthage, ch. 147.**

**CXCVII.** (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 24; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 66.) If, while a priest is speaking in the church, anyone leaves the assembly, let him be excommunicated.

**That women are not to enter the sacristy. From the Council of Laodicea.**

**CXCVIII.** (Council of Laodicea, ch. 44; BURCHARD, book III, ch. 100.) Women ought not to approach the altar or touch those things that are assigned to the offices of men [Note: [Col. 0228D] See book VII of the Capitularies, chs. 134, 175, and 189; the Capitular of Bishop Theodulf of Orléans, ch. 6; the Capitular of Ahyto, ch. 11; and his Chapters, ch. 16.].

**From a letter of Pope Leo.**

(Decrees of Gelasius, ch. 26; BURCHARD, book III, ch. 101.) We have nevertheless heard with indignation that such contempt for divine matters has arisen that women are asserted to minister at the sacred altars [Col. 0227D] and that everything assigned exclusively to the service of men is being entrusted to a sex to which it does not belong.

**On the same matter. From the Council of Tours.**

**CXCIX.** (BURCHARD, book III, ch. 76, from the Council of Rouen, ch. 2.) It has been reported to us that certain priests, after celebrating Mass, refuse to consume the divine mysteries that they have consecrated and hand the Lord’s chalice to little women who offer at Mass, or to certain laymen who do not know how to judge the Lord’s body—that is, to distinguish spiritual food from carnal food. The faithful understand how contrary this is to all ecclesiastical religion. Therefore we forbid all priests to presume to do this in the future. Instead, either the priest himself is to consume it reverently, or he is to hand it to a deacon or subdeacon, who are ministers of the altar, to collect it. He must also see to it that he communicates them first with his own hand. He is not to place the Eucharist in the hands of any layman or woman, but only in the mouth, with these words: “May the body and blood of the Lord benefit you for the remission of sins and eternal life.” Whoever transgresses this, because he despises almighty God and dishonors him as far as he is able, shall be removed from the altar.

**That every priest who governs a church is to have a censer [Col. 0228B] and incense. Hence the preceding source.**

**CC.** (BURCHARD, book III, ch. 227, from the Council of Rouen, ch. 1.) At the time when the Gospel is read, and after the offertory has ended, incense is to be placed over the offering, as a sign of the death of the Redeemer.

**Concerning priests’ preaching. From Book I of the Capitularies, title 76.**

**CCI.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 82.) Each of you, dearly beloved and venerable shepherds of the churches of God, must also see to it that the priests whom you send through your parishes to govern and preach to the people of God preach honorably, and that you do not allow anyone to devise and preach to the people novelties or noncanonical matters from his own understanding and not according to the sacred Scriptures [Col. 0228C]. You yourselves must also preach what is useful, honorable, and right, and what leads to eternal life; and instruct others to preach these same things.

103 **What priests are to preach.**

**CCII.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 82; BURCHARD, book II, ch. 59.) First of all, everyone in general must be taught to believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one almighty God, who made all things, and that there is one deity, substance, and majesty in the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

(BURCHARD, book II, ch. 60.) It must also be preached that the Son of God became incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary for the salvation of the human race; that he suffered, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; and that at the end of the world he will come to judge all people according to their own works. The wicked will be sent with the devil into eternal fire, while the just will be with Christ in eternal life.

(BURCHARD, book II, ch. 61.) It must also be preached that all people will rise again in their own flesh.

(BURCHARD, book II, ch. 65.) It must also be preached for which crimes people are cast down with the devil—those which the Apostle lists: fornication, impurity, debauchery, [Col. 0229A] the service of idols, sorcery, and so forth. Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. Therefore these things must be prohibited with every effort.

(BURCHARD, book II, ch. 64.) It must also be preached concerning love of God and neighbor; faith and hope in God; humility, patience, chastity, kindness, mercy, almsgiving, and confession, so that one may forgive one’s brothers from the heart. Those who do these things and others like them will obtain the kingdom of God.

**On the same matter. From the same book I, ch. 154.**

**CCIII.** (Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 168; WALTER OF ORLEANS, ch. 7; BURCHARD, book XIX, ch. 99.) Every priest is to have chapters concerning greater and lesser vices, by which he may be able to recognize and preach to his subjects that they must beware of the devil’s snares.

[Col. 0229B] **On the same matter. From the same source, ch. 159.**
## CCIV

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 165; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 72.)* Priests are to admonish the people to give alms and to pray for the various scourges which we continually suffer on account of our sins [Note: [Col. 0229] See above, chapter 190 of this book.]

### On the same matter. From chapter 160.

## CCV

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 166.)* The priests themselves, each according to his order, are to strive to preach and teach the people entrusted to them.

### Admonition to Bishops. From Book II, chapter 5.

## CCVI

*(Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 5.)* Apply great diligence to the priests entrusted to your care, so that they may be thoroughly instructed by you regarding how they ought to live and how, by example and word, they may benefit the people committed to their pastoral care; [Col. 0229C] and compel them by your authority to strive to do so.

### That every priest who holds a church should have a cleric. From the Council of Nantes.

## CCVII

*(BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 56; Capitularies of THEODULF, chapter 20.)* Every priest who governs a congregation shall have a cleric who can sing, read the Epistle and the Lesson, and maintain a school. He shall admonish his parishioners to send their sons to the church to learn the Psalter, so that he himself may educate them in all chastity.

### That every priest should solemnly perform the canonical hours. From the same source, chapter 19.

## CCVIII

*(CAPITULARIES OF HINCMAR, title I, chapter 9; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 104.)* After the priest has completed the morning office, he shall perform the duty of his service by singing Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, yet in such a way that afterward, at the appropriate hours and as circumstances permit, these offices shall be completed publicly either by himself or by the scholars. Then, after the Masses have been celebrated and the sick visited, he shall go out to rural labor fasting, so that he may again be able to assist the needs of travelers and guests, of all who are passing through, and also of the sick and the dead, until the appointed hour, according to the season and the opportunity.

### That the priest should care for guests. See above.

## CCIX

*(HINCMAR, same source, chapter 10.)* The priest shall care for guests, especially the poor and weak, as well as orphans and travelers; he shall invite them daily to his own meal, as circumstances permit, and provide them lodging [Note: [Col. 0229] See the Capitulary of Riculf of Soissons, chapter 12.]

### From the same chapter.

*(CAPITULARIES OF CARLOMANNUS, title 2, chapter 12; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 167.)* To remove every occasion of robbery, we decree that priests, who ought to display a good example of charity to all, should be hospitable, in accordance with the Lord’s and the Apostle’s command, and should show kindness to travelers, because by hospitality certain persons pleased God when they received angels as guests. The Lord will also say to the elect on the day of judgment: “I was a guest, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25). Job likewise says: “My door was always open to the traveler” (Job 31).

### On blessed water. From a letter of Pope Alexander.

## CCX

*(ALEXANDER I, Letter I, chapter 5; REMEDIUS OF CHUR, chapter 24; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 53.)* We bless water sprinkled with salt for the people, so that all who are sprinkled with it may be sanctified; and we command all priests to do the same. For if the ashes of a heifer, when sprinkled, sanctified and cleansed the people (Hebrews 9), how much more does water, sprinkled with salt and consecrated by divine prayers, sanctify and cleanse the people? And if the barrenness of water was healed when salt was sprinkled upon it by the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 2), how much more will water consecrated by divine prayers remove the barrenness of human things, sanctify and cleanse the defiled, multiply other good things, avert the snares of the devil, and protect a person from the deceits of apparitions.

### On the same matter. From the council mentioned above, chapter 5.

## CCXI

*(HINCMAR, same source, chapter 5; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 52.)* Every Sunday each priest shall prepare blessed water in his church, before the solemn celebration of Mass, in a clean vessel suitable for so great a mystery. The people entering the church shall be sprinkled with it; and those who wish may take some of it in their own small vessels and sprinkle it throughout their houses, fields, and vineyards, and also over their livestock and their fodder, as well as over their food and drink.

### On priests who conceal the faults of sinners or bring insufficiently penitent persons to reconciliation. See above.

## CCXII

*(HINCMAR, same source, chapter 13; BURCHARD, Book XIX, chapter 100; Penitential Book, in Stevartius, p. 711.)* No priest shall accept a gift or any temporal profit—or rather, spiritual injury—from anyone who sins publicly or is involved in incest, in order to conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or his ministers. Nor, out of regard for any person, kinship, or friendship, shall he refuse to make the matter known to the bishop, thereby sharing in another’s sins. Nor shall he presume to accept from any penitent a gift, favor, or advantage, or bring an insufficiently penitent person to reconciliation and provide him with a certificate of reconciliation, while, through any kind of ill will, excluding from reconciliation another who is doing penance more worthily; for this is simoniacal and contrary both to God and to human beings [Note: [Col. 0231] See the Capitulary of Riculf of Soissons, chapter 9.]

### From the Penitential Book.

*(BURCHARD, Book XIX, chapter 121.)* Whoever conceals a brother’s sin that leads to death, and neither reproves him nor tells the Church of God so that he may be corrected, shall do penance for as long as he consented to it.

### On priests who are invited to dinner by the faithful. See above, chapter 14.

## CCXIII

*(HINCMAR, same source, chapter 14; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 161.)* No priest, when priests have gathered at the anniversary, thirtieth, seventh, or third day of a deceased person, or at any other summons for a clerical assembly, shall presume to make himself drunk. Nor shall he presume to pray or drink in honor of the saints or of the deceased person’s soul, or compel others to drink; nor shall he gorge himself through another’s drinking. He shall not presume to introduce disorderly applause, laughter, empty stories, or songs, or indecent jokes, nor permit a bear or female dancers to perform before him. Nor shall he consent to have demons’ masks, commonly called *talamascas*, carried before him, because this is diabolical and forbidden by the sacred canons.

### On quarrels and fighting among priests.

## CCXIV

*(HINCMAR, same source; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 103.)* Every priest must take the greatest care, if he wishes to rejoice in the dignity of his office, not on any occasion to provoke or incite an equal or anyone else to anger and quarrelling by any word, much less to fighting or killing; nor, if provoked, may anyone rush into such conduct, because at such banquets and drinking parties the devil always insinuates himself.

### On priests’ banquets.

## CCXV

*(HINCMAR, same source; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 162.)* When priests gather for a banquet, the dean or one of their senior members shall begin a verse before the table and bless the food. They shall then sit according to their order, showing honor to one another, and shall bless the food and drink in turn. One of their clerics shall read something from Holy Scripture, and after the meal they shall likewise sing a sacred [Paris manuscript: “second”] hymn, following the Lord’s example, as it is recorded that he did at the supper. Thus all the priests shall conduct themselves, especially in such places, so that our ministry may not be disgraced [Burchard: “so that their ministry may not be disgraced”; Helmstedt manuscript: “so that our ministry may not be disgraced.”]

### On the Kalends, when priests gather together. See above, chapter 16.

## CCXVI

*(HINCMAR, same source, chapter 15; RICULF, chapter 20; CAPITULARY OF AHYTO, chapter 29; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 164.)* When priests gather together at the Kalends, after the divine service and the necessary conference have been completed, they shall not sit there at tables as though for a meal [Burchard: “as though for a full meal”], and burden one another with such dishonorable banquets, because this is indecent and burdensome. Often, returning late to the churches, they gain more harm from reproach and incur more mutual weariness than they derive benefit there. For Paul reproved the Corinthians for such a gathering (1 Corinthians 11), since they came together improperly to eat the Lord’s Supper. Likewise, those who come together under the pretext of the Lord’s Supper—that is, for a conference concerning the word—and are joined by [the corrupt printed reading: “exuri aetate ventrisca”; Helmstedt edition, Burchard, and Hincmar: “for the sake of bodily appetite, according to truth”] are considered blameworthy before God and human beings. Therefore, when everything has been completed, whoever wishes may break bread with charity in his brother’s house together with the brothers, and each may take a single drink; above all, they shall not touch the cup more than three times. Then they shall return to the churches.

### On those who are ordained having nothing. From the Council of Carthage.

## CCXVII

*(Code of the Canons of the African Church, chapter 32; JESSE OF AMIENS, chapter 6; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 120.)* It has been decided that bishops, priests, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained while possessing nothing, and who during the time of their episcopate or clerical office acquire fields or any estates in their own name, shall be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they have transferred those same properties to the church.

### On the same matter. From Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 150.

## CCXVIII

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 156; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 121.)* Every priest shall leave to his own church the property he acquires after the day of his consecration.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Reims.

## CCXIX

*(CAPITULARIES OF HINCMAR, title 2, chapter 18; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 118.)* It must be investigated whether a priest who possessed no patrimony when he was advanced to ecclesiastical orders later purchased estates, and to whom those estates belong, since, according to canonical authority, they ought to belong to the church to which he was promoted from a state of having nothing.

### From the Council of Orange, chapter 54.

*(Council of Agde, chapter 54; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 119.)*

When a priest holds a diocese, he shall draw up a document assigning to the church what he has purchased, or withdraw from the administration of the church he holds [Note: [Col. 0231] This chapter is not present in the manuscript.]

### On the revenues or offerings of the church.

## CCXX

*(CAPITULARIES OF HINCMAR, title 2, chapter 19.)* It must be investigated whether, taking advantage of the preceding chapter, any priest has purchased property under another name from the church’s revenues, offerings, or the vows of the faithful, and has built structures there or deposited there what belongs to the church; whether he has permitted women to frequent the place; or, more shamefully, has kept there women who practice their wool-working and manage the household, and whether the priest, frequently coming there, has stayed in the same place. This is done contrary to the decrees of the canons. For just as a priest must not practise usury in his own name, so neither may he do so in another’s name, much less commit fraud with ecclesiastical resources, since this is sacrilege and a crime equal to that of Judas the thief, who carried away and stole the sacred offerings.

### On usury. From the apostolic canon.

## CCXXI

*(Apostolic Canon, chapter 44; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 119.)* A bishop, priest, or deacon who exacts interest from debtors must either cease or certainly be condemned.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Nicaea.

## CCXXII

*(Council of Nicaea, chapter 17; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 120.)* Since many persons under ecclesiastical rule pursue avarice and shameful profits, forgetting the Scripture that says, “Who has not given his money at interest,” and, when lending money, demand hundredfold returns, the holy synod has justly decreed that if anyone is found receiving interest, demanding *hemiolia*, that is, one and a half times the principal, or devising anything of this kind, he shall be deposed from the clergy for the sake of shameful profit and shall be excluded from the rule.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Laodicea.

## CCXXIII

*(Council of Laodicea, chapter 5.)* Priests and clerics must not practise lending at interest or receive what is called *sescupla*, that is, the principal together with half of the principal [Note: [Col. 0233D] See the Capitularies of Ahyto of Basel, chapter 17.]

### On the same matter. From a letter of Leo.

## CCXXIV

*(Decrees of LEO I, chapter 3; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 123.)* We have also judged that this must not be passed over: some, seized by the desire for shameful profit, practise [the manuscript reading: “usurious punishment”; Leo I’s first letter reads “deal in money,” which I consider more correct] usurious punishment and wish to grow rich through lending at interest [Note: [Col. 0233D] It should be noted here that, where the manuscript of the Region has *usurariam exercere poenam* (“practise usurious punishment”), Leo I’s first letter reads *exercere pecuniam* (“deal in money”), which I consider more correct. The Helmstedt edition has neither *poenam* nor *pecuniam*. Ivo, Part VI, chapter 65, and Gratian, 14, question 4, chapter 76, read *pecuniam* (“money”).]. We grieve that this applies not only to those established in clerical office, but also to lay people who wish to be called Christians.

### That clerics should not practise lending at interest under another’s name. From the same letter.

## CCXXV

*(LEO I in the Decrees, chapter 4; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 121.)* It must also be expressly warned that, just as no cleric may practise lending at interest in his own name, so no one should presume to do so in another’s name.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Tarragona.

## CCXXVI

*(Council of Tarragona, chapter 2; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 122.)* Whoever wishes to remain in the clergy shall not engage in the practice of buying cheaply and selling more dearly.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Elvira.

## CCXXVII

*(Council of Elvira, chapter 18.)* Bishops, priests, and deacons shall not leave their places for the purpose of trading, nor travel through the provinces in pursuit of markets. To obtain their livelihood, however, they may send a son, freedman, hired servant, or friend. If they wish to trade, they shall trade within the province.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Carthage.

## CCXXVIII

*(Third Council of Carthage, chapter 16; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 151.)* It has been decided that bishops, priests, and deacons shall not be leaseholders or agents, nor seek their livelihood through any disgraceful or dishonorable business, because it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2).

### On the same matter. From the same council.

## CCXXIX
