*(Third Council of Carthage, chapter 16; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 124.)* It has likewise been decided that if a cleric lends money, he shall receive money; if he lends a commodity, he shall receive the same commodity, in the quantity that he gave.

### From Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 36.

## CCXXX

*(Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 37; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 125.)* Priests must themselves abstain from shameful profits and usury, and must also instruct the people subject to them to abstain from them.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Chalcedon.

## CCXXXI

*(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 3; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 145.)* It has come to the attention of the holy synod that certain persons who appear to have been chosen for the clergy become leaseholders of other people’s possessions for the sake of shameful profits and undertake secular business under their supervision, setting little value on the ministry of God while running about the houses of secular persons and, out of avarice, assuming responsibility for patrimonies. The holy council therefore decreed that henceforth no one—neither bishop, cleric, nor monk—shall lease possessions or involve himself in secular business, apart from the administration of ecclesiastical property.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 49.

## CCXXXII

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 49; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 146.)* No layperson shall presume to involve the priests of his churches in shameful stewardship or, according to the Apostle, in secular and dishonorable business, nor take them elsewhere with him [Sirmond: “elsewhere”; likewise in our old manuscript], so that they are compelled to neglect the ministry entrusted to them. If anyone presumes to act contrary to these prohibitions, let him be excommunicated.

### On those who have been ordained through payments. From the apostolic canon.

## CCXXXIII

*(Apostolic Canon, chapter 50.)* If any bishop, priest, or deacon has obtained this dignity through payments, let both him and the person who ordained him be deposed and cut off from communion in every way, just as Simon Magus was by Peter.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Chalcedon.

## CCXXXIV

*(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 2; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 112.)* If any bishop has performed an ordination for money and reduced the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be sold, to a price, and has ordained a bishop, priest, or deacon for money, he shall be subject to the peril attached to his own order; and the person ordained shall gain nothing from that ordination but shall be excluded from the dignity. If anyone has acted as an intermediary by giving or receiving payments, then, if he is a cleric, he shall fall from his own order; if a monk or layperson, he shall be anathematized.

### On the same matter. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

## CCXXXV

*(Decrees of GELASIUS, chapter 24; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 22.)* Those who are proven to have purchased the sacred dignity, despite being unworthy by their merits, must be excluded when convicted, because the condemnation of Simon, attested by Holy Scripture, involves equally the giver and the receiver.

### On the same matter. From a letter of Pope Hormisdas.

## CCXXXVI

*(BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 23.)* We therefore join this to what precedes, so that the blessing bestowed through the laying on of hands, which is believed to come from God, may not be purchased for a price; for Simon, wishing to buy the Holy Spirit by payment, was struck down by the apostle’s detestation (Acts 8).

### On the same matter. From the Council of Nantes.

## CCXXXVII

*(Council of Nantes, chapter 7; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 106.)* We forbid all ministers of ecclesiastical dignity to presume, corrupted by any gift or favor, secretly and furtively to introduce a cleric from another parish for ordination. If anyone does so, then, according to the decree of Chalcedon, the person ordained shall lose the gift of the Holy Spirit which he attempted to steal; and the intermediary, if a cleric, shall fall from his own order; if a layperson or monk, he shall be anathematized.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 43.

## CCXXXVIII

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 43; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 21.)* It must be guarded against and most diligently prevented, and bishops, kings, all higher authorities, and all supporters, electors, consenters, and ordainers in ecclesiastical rank must be forbidden by the power of Christ’s blood, that no one should obtain a place of governance through the simoniacal heresy by any faction, cunning, promise, advantage, or payment, whether directly or through an intermediary. For the Holy Spirit, among other testimonies, says through the mouth of Saint Gregory (Book VII, indiction 2, letter 110): “Why does he not consider that the blessing is turned into a curse for him?” And elsewhere (Book IV, indiction 14, letter 51): “I say this in sorrow and announce it with groaning: the priesthood, which has fallen inwardly among you, will not be able to stand outwardly for long.”

### That a gift may also proceed from the tongue. From the sayings of Pope Gregory.

## CCXXXIX

*(SAINT GREGORY, Homily 4 on the Gospels; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 113.)* There are some who do not accept monetary rewards for ordination, yet bestow sacred orders for human favor. These people certainly do not give freely what they receive freely, because they seek the coin of favor in return for the office of holiness they have conferred. Thus, when Isaiah described the just man, he said: “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah 33). For one kind of gift proceeds from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue. A gift from service is submission improperly rendered. A gift from the hand is money. A gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore, the person who confers sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift only when, in divine matters, he seeks not merely no money but also no human favor [Note: [Col. 0235D] See Saint Gregory, Moralia, Book IX, chapter 17, and Book XII, chapter 25.]

### That priests should not give gifts in order to obtain churches. From Book I of the Capitularies.

## CCXL

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 146.)* No priest shall give a gift upon entering a church [Note: [Col. 0235D] See the Capitulary of Theodulf, chapter 16; the Capitularies of Bishop Ahyto of Basel to his priests, chapter 12; and the Capitulary of the same man, chapter 33.]

### On priests or clerics who seize or overthrow the churches or benefices of other priests through payments.

*(Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 146; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 114.)* It has been decreed and absolutely prohibited that if any priest is caught giving or having given gifts to a cleric or layperson, or giving money to anyone so that he may seize the church of another priest, he shall, for this desire or robbery motivated by shameful profit, be deposed from the clergy and excluded from the rule. For if, out of mercy, the bishop wishes to confine him for a long period in the misery of prison, doing penance there for what he has done and remaining there until satisfaction is made, and afterward, if he has corrected himself and promised not to do such things again, to treat him more humanely, he may do so if he wishes and if the man himself is found worthy.

### That no one should install or expel a priest from a church. From the same Capitularies, chapter 41.

## CCXLI

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 147; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 111.)* No layperson shall presume to install or expel a priest from a church except with the consent of the bishop [Note: [Col. 0236D] See the Council of Vienne under Formosus, chapter 4, and the Council of Engelheim, chapter 4.]

### From the same source.

It also appears necessary to prohibit clerics and laypeople from presuming to give any priest a church without the permission and consent of his bishop.

### Also from the same source.

*(Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 43; Addition IV, chapter 72; Book III of the Lombard Laws, title 1, chapter 43.)* Concerning those who establish priests in their churches without the bishop’s consent, or expel them from the churches, and who, after being admonished by the bishop or by any royal envoy, refuse to obey: they are to be ordered to pay our fine by a security pledge and to come to the palace through sureties, so that we may then decide whether we wish them to pay that fine or to undergo another punishment.

### On churches divided among coheirs. From the same source.

## CCXLII

*(Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 44; Book III of the Lombard Laws, title 1, chapter 44; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 41.)* Concerning churches divided among coheirs, it must be considered that if the coheirs wish to retain and honor them according to the bishop’s direction and admonition, they may do so. But if they refuse, it shall remain within the bishop’s power either to permit the churches to continue in that condition or to remove the relics from them.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Tribur.

*(Council of Tribur, chapter 32; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 40.)* If several heirs quarrel over a common church, the bishop shall order the sacred relics to be removed and the church to be closed until they establish a priest there by common agreement and provide the means by which he may live.

### That several priests should not be established in one church. From the Council of Reims, chapter 8.

## CCXLIII

*(BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 44.)* Each priest shall be content with the one church in which he was ordained, and no one shall presume to minister in two churches [Note: [Col. 0237D] This chapter was added from a manuscript. It is not found in the Helmstedt edition. See Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 73, and Addition II, chapter 8.]

### From the council mentioned above.

*(BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 45.)* Just as there ought to be a priest in each church, so that church itself, which is called his bride or wife, cannot be divided among several priests; rather, it shall have only one priest, who will govern it chastely and sincerely. Therefore, we forbid anyone to presume to divide a church between two or more persons, because Christ’s church ought to be a wife and bride, not a prostitute, as Pope Calixtus testifies [Note: [Col. 0238D] See Addition III of the Capitularies, chapter 25] [7, question 1, chapter 39].

### That laypeople should not hold churches or receive tithes. From the Council of [Meaux], chapter 65.

## CCXLIV

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 75.)* It is entirely unworthy that you, who by God’s authority surpass the other children of the Church in royal dignity, should appear negligent in carrying out the things that belong to God. It would therefore have been fitting for you not to entrust the chapels of your estates to laypeople, but rather to those who would treat these sacred places more religiously and render you the service owed to you. We therefore warn and exhort you not—God forbid—to incur the danger of anathema by presuming to take the tithes, but to strive to correct this.

### On the same matter. From the same chapter.

## CCXLV

*(Council of Meaux, same source.)* If you give your chapels to priests or ecclesiastical men, and they receive the Lord’s tithes, let them use them appropriately to maintain the church buildings and lights; and let the parish priests receive the parish tithes and diligently attend to the needs of the people.

### On the same matter. From the same source.

## CCXLVI

*(Council of Meaux, same source.)* But if laypeople hold your chapels, it is contrary to reason and authority that they themselves should receive the tithes, keep dogs or female astrologers (*genitiarias*) at their expense, and maintain their own households from funds intended for the restoration of churches. Rather, let the priests provide the churches with lights, receive guests and the poor, and earnestly implore God’s mercy for you and for the condition of your kingdom.

### On those who abandon the churches to which they have been advanced and transfer to others. From the Council of Nicaea.

## CCXLVII

*(Council of Nicaea, chapter 16; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 98.)* Whoever rashly and dangerously leaves his church—whether a priest, deacon, or anyone at all subject to ecclesiastical rule—without keeping the fear of the Lord before his eyes or recognizing the rule of the Church, must by no means be received into another church. Rather, every necessity should be imposed upon him so that he returns to his own parish. If he does not do so, he must be deprived of communion.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 10.

## CCXLVIII

*(BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 96.)* It is not permitted for a cleric to be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities: both in the church in which he was originally ordained and in the one to which he has fled as though it were more important, out of a desire for empty glory. Those who do this must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and minister there alone [Note: [Col. 0238D] See Addition III of the Capitularies, chapter 50.]

### Also from the Council of Antioch.

## CCXLIX

*(Council of Antioch, chapter 21; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 73.)* A bishop must not move from one parish to another, whether he rush there of his own accord or is compelled by the people. Rather, he must remain in the church which he first received by lot from God and must not transfer from it.

### On the same matter. From the Decrees of Pope Calixtus.

## CCL

*(CALIXTUS, Letter 2; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 49; also in GRATIAN, 7, question 1, chapter 39.)* Just as another man’s wife, while her own husband is alive, is not permitted to be violated, judged, or disposed of by anyone except her own husband, so neither may the wife of a bishop or priest—that is, unquestionably his church or parish—while he lives, be judged or administered by another, nor may another enjoy intercourse with her. Hence the Apostle says: “The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but when her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband” (Romans 7). Likewise, the church, which is called the priest’s wife, is bound to him while he lives; but after his death she may marry in the Lord, that is, according to the rule. For if she marries another while he is alive, she will be judged an adulteress.

### That no one should usurp another’s parish. From a letter of Pope Calixtus.

## CCLI

*(CALIXTUS, same source.)* No one shall usurp another’s boundaries, nor presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner; for such judgment or excommunication will be neither valid nor effective, since no one is bound or condemned by the sentence of any judge other than his own. No primate or metropolitan shall usurp the church or parish of a diocesan bishop, or presume to excommunicate or judge anyone from that bishop’s parish without his counsel or judgment. Rather, let him observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors and confirmed by us.

### Also from the same letter.

*(CALIXTUS, same source; Capitularies of ADRIAN I, chapter 43.)* If any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything outside his own parish, except with the counsel and consent of all the bishops of the province, he shall be subject to the penalty attached to his rank, and whatever he has done in this way shall be considered invalid and void.

### On clerics placed in charge of hospices for the poor. From the Council of Chalcedon.

## CCLII

*(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 8; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 2.)* Clerics placed in charge of hospices for the poor, or those ordained in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, shall remain under the authority of the bishops who are in each city, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, and shall not defiantly withdraw from their own bishop. Those who dare to overturn this arrangement and refuse to submit to their own bishop shall, if clerics, be subject to canonical correction; if laypeople or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.

### That a priest should not have more than one church. From Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 86.

## CCLIII

It has been decreed that each church shall have its own priest wherever this can be arranged with the bishop’s provision. *(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 92; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 46.)*

### On the same matter. From the Council of Nantes.

## CCLIV

*(Council of Nantes, chapter 8; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 47.)* Just as a bishop may have no more than one city and a man one wife, so a priest may have only one church. Therefore, no priest shall presume to have several churches unless perhaps he has under him, in each of them, other priests who solemnly perform the offices by night and by day and complete the celebrations of Mass according to the daily rites [Note: [Col. 0239D] See Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 73.]

### That no priest should receive another priest’s parishioner.

## CCLV

*(Council of Nantes, chapter 2; Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 153; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 91.)* No priest shall receive another priest’s parishioner at Mass unless the person is traveling or has legal business there [Note: [Col. 0239D] This chapter is not found in the Helmstedt or Paris manuscripts. Since the table of chapters prefixed to the Paris manuscript showed that this chapter was missing here, we have transferred it to this place from Book I of the Capitularies. See above, chapter 61.]

### From the Council of Carthage.

*(First Council of Carthage, chapter 7; Addition IV, chapter 22.)* Bishop Cassian said: “Let your dignity decree that no cleric or layperson shall communicate in another congregation without letters from his own bishop.”

### On the same matter. From Book I of the Capitularies, title 187.

## CCLVI

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 154.)* No priest shall presume to sing Mass in another’s parish unless he is traveling; nor shall he dare to receive a tithe belonging to another.

## CCLVII

### On the same matter.

[Note: [Col. 0240D] This chapter is absent from the Helmstedt and Paris manuscripts. Since nothing certain occurred to us that we could restore, we judged that nothing should be rashly presumed. If anyone nevertheless wishes to fill this gap, let him use chapter 33 of the Fourth Council of Carthage.]

### That a bishop should not ordain in another bishop’s parish. From the Council of Antioch.

## CCLVIII

*(Council of Antioch, chapter 22; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 71.)* A bishop shall not enter another city that is not subject to him, nor approach a possession that does not belong to him, nor perform an ordination there, except perhaps with the counsel and consent of the bishop of the region.

### That no priest or layperson should invite a penitent to drink wine or eat meat. From Book I of the Capitularies, title 151.

## CCLIX

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 157.)* No priest or layperson shall invite a penitent to drink wine or eat meat unless, for the present occasion, he has first given one or two denarii on the penitent’s behalf, according to the character of the penance.

### That no priest should write documents. From the same source.

## CCLX

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 158; RICULF, chapter 15.)* No priest shall write documents or become the leaseholder of his lord.

### That no one, despising a lesser church, should aspire to a more important one. From the Synod of Meaux.

## CCLXI

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 30; BURCHARD, Book III, chapter 48.)* If anyone of priestly rank, despising a lesser church, ambitiously and improperly aspires to a more important one, the canonical judgment concerning him shall be upheld.

### On baptism and the time at which it is to be celebrated. From the apostolic canon.

## CCLXII

*(Apostolic Canon, chapter 49; BURCHARD, Book IV, chapter 22.)* If any bishop or priest does not baptize according to the Lord’s command in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but in three principles without a beginning, or in three Paracletes, let him be deposed.

### On the same matter. From the same source.

## CCLXIII

*(Apostolic Canon, chapter 50; BURCHARD, Book IV, chapter 23.)* If any bishop or priest does not celebrate the threefold immersion of the one mystery, but immerses only once in baptism, which appears to be given in the Lord’s death, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say, “Baptize in my death,” but: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

### That baptism should be administered at Easter and Pentecost. From a letter of Pope Leo.

CCLXIV. (Decrees of Leo I, c. 11; BURCHARD, book IV, [Col. 0241A] c. 2, 12.) Since it is therefore most clearly evident that these two times—namely, Easter and Pentecost—are the proper seasons for those chosen to be baptized in the Church, we admonish Your Love not to mix any other days into this observance. For although there are also other festivals on which much reverence is owed in honor of God, nevertheless we must preserve the observance dictated by the mystical rationale of the principal and greatest sacrament, without prohibiting the permission by which aid is offered through baptism at any time to those in danger. Thus we defer the free vows of those who are safe and living in security and peace to these two festivals, joined and related to one another, so that in danger of death, in the peril of siege, in the straits of persecution, or in fear of shipwreck, we may at no time deny anyone this unique safeguard of true salvation. [Col. 0241B] 127

### On the Baptism of Pregnant Women. From the Council of Neocaesarea.

CCLXV. (Council of Neocaesarea, c. 6; BURCHARD, book IV, c. 31.) A pregnant woman ought to be baptized whenever she wishes. For the woman giving birth communicates nothing in this matter unknowingly, since each person’s own intention is declared in confession.

### Those Whose Baptism Is Unknown Are to Be Baptized. From the Council of Carthage.

CCLXVI. (Council of Carthage V, c. 5; book VII of the Capitularies, c. 307; BURCHARD, book IV, c. 45.) It was likewise decreed concerning infants that, whenever wholly reliable witnesses cannot be found to testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and they themselves, because of their age, are not competent to answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized without any scruple. [Col. 0241C]

### Concerning Those Who Have Been Baptized but Die without Confirmation. From the Council of Elvira.

CCLXVII. (Council of Elvira, c. 77; BURCHARD, book IV, c. 92.) If a deacon governing a congregation without a bishop or presbyter has baptized anyone, the bishop must complete them through blessing. But if they have departed from this world before that, each may be justified according to the faith in which he believed.

128

### Concerning Those Who Have Been Rebaptized. From the Council of Lérida.

CCLXVIII. (Council of Huesca, c. 9.) Concerning those who, through transgression, have been rebaptized without any necessity or compulsion: it was decreed that the statutes of the Council of Nicaea be observed with regard to them; that is, they are to pray for seven years among the catechumens and for two among the Catholics, and afterward they are to communicate with the faithful in the offering and the Eucharist.

### That Baptism Is to Be Administered Only at Easter and Pentecost. From the Council of Worms.

CCLXIX. (Council of Worms, c. 1; BURCHARD, book IV, c. 7.) Let every member of the faithful know that the sacrament of holy baptism is to be administered only at the festival of Easter and at Pentecost, except to those whom the urgency of danger threatens with death and to whom such remedies must be supplied lest they perish eternally.

[Col. 0242A] From the Council of Meaux, chapter 18.

CCLXX. (Council of Meaux, c. 48; BURCHARD, book IV, c. 14.) Let no presbyter presume to baptize except in villages and baptismal churches, and at the appointed times, unless there is a cause of illness or definite necessity; and let the villages retain their authority and due privileges.

### Concerning Sacred Fonts. As Above.

CCLXXI. (BURCHARD, book IV, c. 13; also in GRATIAN, Distinction 4, *De consecratione*, c. 106.) Every presbyter who cannot have stone fonts shall have a suitable vessel devoted solely to the office of baptism. Likewise, separate vessels shall be kept for washing the corporal and for the altar cloths, and nothing else shall be done in them. [Col. 0242B] [Note: [Col. 0241D] See above, chapter 79 of this book.]

129

### That Every Presbyter Instruct His Parishioners in the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. From the Council of Reims, title 20.

CCLXXII. (BURCHARD, book II, c. 62.) Every presbyter shall either personally teach all his parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer or instruct others to teach them. [Note: [Col. 0242D] See the Capitular of Theodulf, c. 22; the Capitular of Ahyto, c. 97; book V of the Capitularies, c. 103; and book VI, c. 172.] When they come to confession during Lent, he shall have each person recite these from memory, and he shall not admit anyone to holy communion before that person knows how to recite them from the heart. For no one can be saved without knowledge of these things. In the one, Christian faith and belief are contained; in the other, what we ought to pray and ask of God is expressed. That no one can be saved without faith the Lord showed when he said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI). No one, however, can believe what he does not know or has not heard. For Paul says: “How will they believe in him whom they have not heard?” (Romans X). Nor is faith alone in the heart sufficient unless it is also expressed in words, as the same Apostle testifies: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X).

Let no one make an excuse on the grounds of dullness of understanding or weakness of intellect, for these matters are so simple that no one is so dull or barbarous that he cannot learn them and recite them in ordinary words; yet they are so great that whoever can fully grasp their meaning may believe them sufficient for eternal salvation. (Capitular of THEODULF, c. 22, and book VI of the Capitularies, c. [Col. 0242D] 172.)

This also must be observed: no one is to receive an infant from the sacred font in baptism before reciting the same Creed and the Lord’s Prayer in the presence of a presbyter; and the presbyter is to announce to all godparents that they are obliged, when their godchildren reach the age of understanding, to teach them these same things.

### From Book II of the Capitularies.

CCLXXIII. (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, c. 47; book II of the Capitularies, c. 39.) We command that every godparent and the spiritual relatives instruct their spiritual children in the Catholic faith. [Col. 0243A] [Note: [Col. 0243D] See the Capitular of Bishop Ahyto of Basel, chapter 18, and also his Capitula, chapter 25, in volumes VI and VIII of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*.]

### From the Same, Chapter 49.

CCLXXIV. (Council of Arles VI, c. 19; book II of the Capitularies, c. 46.) Parents should earnestly strive to teach their children, and godparents those whom they receive from the font: the former because they have begotten them and they have been given to them by the Lord; the latter because they have become sureties for them.

### Concerning the Greater Litany. From the Council of Mainz.

CCLXXV. (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, c. 33; book V of the Capitularies, c. 86; BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 6.) It was agreed that the Greater Litany should be observed by all Christians on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, as we have found by reading and as our holy fathers established: not riding, not dressed in costly garments, but sprinkled with ashes and clothed in sackcloth, unless illness prevents it. [Col. 0243B] [Note: [Col. 0243D] See the Council of Aachen of the year 836, chapter 10.]

### Concerning the Rogation Fast.

CCLXXVI. (BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 7.) When, because of the sins of the people of Gaul, they were being harshly slaughtered by the rabid fury of wolves (the Helmstedt edition reads: “were being ravaged”), and they could find no remedy for this scourge, the bishops of Gaul are said to have assembled at the city of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0244D] See Alcuin, chapter 20 of *On Divine Offices*, and Walafrid Strabo, chapter 28 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*] and jointly decreed that they should undertake a three-day fast.

When the Lord mercifully removed the plague, these days became an annual observance, to be celebrated throughout the provinces of Gaul before the day of the Lord’s Ascension. Let us too observe these days with the greatest reverence and devotion, with abstinence of the flesh and humility of heart: not so that we may escape the rage of visible wolves, but so that we may be able to overcome the temptations of invisible ones—that is, of unclean spirits. [Col. 0243C] [Note: [Col. 0244D] See Caesarius of Arles, homily 37.]

Let no one wear costly garments on these days, when we ought to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Let drunkenness and feasting, such as occur among the common people, be prohibited. Let no one presume to ride, but let everyone walk barefoot. Let women by no means lead dances; instead, let all together sing “Kyrie eleison” and with contrition of heart beseech God’s mercy for sins, for peace, for pestilence, for the preservation of the crops, and for other necessities. For these are days of abstinence, not of rejoicing.

[Col. 0243D]

### Concerning the Fast of the Four Seasons. From the Council of Mainz.

CCLXXVII. (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, c. 34; book V of the Capitularies, c. 86; BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 2.) We establish that the four seasons of the year are to be observed by all with fasting: in March, during the first week; in June, during the second; in September, during the third; and in December, during the fourth week, whichever full week precedes the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity—that is, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Let everyone come to church at the ninth hour 132 with litanies for the solemn celebration of Mass.

[Col. 0244A]

### Concerning the Vigils of the Saints.

CCLXXVIII. (BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 16.) When presbyters announce the holy festivals to the people, they should also urge them in every way to observe the fasts of the vigils.

### Concerning an Imposed Fast. From the Council of Mainz.

CCLXXIX. (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, c. 35; book V of the Capitularies, c. 87; BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 4.) If anyone, in pride, despises an imposed fast and refuses to observe it with the other Christians, the Council of Gangra commands that he be anathematized.

### From the Council of Gangra.

CCLXXX. (Council of Gangra, c. 19; BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 5.) If any of those who practice continence, without bodily necessity, proudly abolishes the common fasts handed down and observed by the Church, impelled by the spur of his own thinking, let him be anathema.

### Concerning the Same Matter. In the Same Place.

CCLXXXI. Whoever violates an imposed fast without serious necessity should remember Jonathan, son of King Saul, who, disregarding his father’s curse, ate a little honey from the end of his staff and therefore deserved the sentence of death (I Samuel XIV).

### Likewise from Book I of the Capitularies, Chapter 47.

CCLXXXII. (BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 17.) Let the fasts established by priests in the Church not be relaxed without a reasonable necessity.

133

### Concerning Famine and Pestilence.

CCLXXXIII. (Book I of the Capitularies, c. 118; BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 18.) If famine, pestilence, unseasonable weather, or any other kind of tribulation occurs, do not wait for our edict; immediately implore God’s mercy.

### What Usury Is.

CCLXXXIV. (Book I of the Capitularies, c. 125; BURCHARD, book II, c. 126.) Usury is when more is demanded than is given; for example, if you give ten solidi and demand more, or if you give one bushel of grain and demand something in addition to it.

### Likewise, Chapter 123.

CCLXXXV. (Book I of the Capitularies, c. 129.) Those practice shameful profit who, for the purpose of making gain, strive dishonestly to gather various things by different deceptions.

[Col. 0244D]

### What Interest Is.

CCLXXXVI. (Book I of the Capitularies, c. 130.) A loan (*fenus*) is something advanced. A just loan is one in which no more is demanded than the amount advanced.

### Concerning the Same Matter. In the Same Place, Chapter 125.

CCLXXXVII. (Book I of the Capitularies, c. 131; BURCHARD, book II, c. 127.) Whoever, at harvesttime or vintage, buys grain or wine not out of necessity but out of greed—for example, buys one bushel for two denarii and stores it until it can be sold for four denarii, or six, or more—this we call shameful profit.

134

### Concerning Confession and Penance.

CCLXXXVIII. (BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 2.) Presbyters ought to admonish the people subject to them that everyone who feels himself wounded by the deadly injury of sin should hasten, on the Wednesday before Lent, to the life-giving mother Church. There, with complete humility and contrition of heart, he should simply confess what he has done wrong, receive the remedies of penance according to the measure established by canonical authorities, and be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Nor should only the person who has committed some mortal sin hasten to come to his own priest. Every person who recognizes that he has stained with the blemish of sin the spotless tunic of Christ, which he received in baptism, should come likewise and, with a purified mind [Burchard: “with purity of mind”], humbly confess all the transgressions and sins by which he remembers having incurred God’s displeasure. Whatever the priest enjoins upon him, he should heed diligently and observe with the utmost care, as though it had been spoken by the mouth of almighty God himself.

### Concerning Penitents. From the Council of Africa.

CCLXXXIX. (Council of Carthage III, c. 32; book V of the Capitularies, c. 53; BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 40.) If a penitent’s crime is public and notorious and has disturbed the entire Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse. [Col. 0245C]

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council of Agde.

CCXC. (Council of Agde, c. 15; BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 27.) At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon their heads, as has been established everywhere. But if they do not cut their hair or change their garments, let them be excluded. [Helmstedt edition: “But if they are unwilling to cut their hair or change their garments, let them be excluded.”]

### Likewise, Concerning the Above. From the Same Council.

CCXCI. (BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 26, and Distinction 50, c. 64.) At the beginning of Lent, all penitents who are undertaking or have undertaken public penance are to present themselves before the bishop at the gates of the city church, clothed in sackcloth, barefoot, and with their faces cast down to the ground, proclaiming by their clothing and expression that they are guilty. The deans—that is, the archpresbyters of the parishes—must be present there with witnesses, namely, the presbyters of the penitents, who must carefully observe their conduct. According to the measure of the fault, the bishop shall impose penance upon them through the prescribed stages.

After this he shall introduce them into the church and, prostrated on the ground with all the clergy, sing with tears the seven penitential psalms for their absolution. Then, rising from prayer, he shall, in accordance with what the canons command, lay hands upon them, sprinkle blessed water over them, first cast ashes upon them, and then cover their heads with sackcloth. With groaning and frequent sighs [Col. 0246A] he shall declare to them that, just as Adam was expelled from paradise, so they too are expelled from the Church on account of their sins. After this he shall order the ministers to drive them outside the church doors.

The clergy, however, shall accompany them with the responsory: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” etc. (Genesis III), so that, seeing that the holy Church has been shaken and stirred by their crimes, they may not regard penance lightly. On the holy day of the Lord’s Supper, they are to present themselves again at the thresholds of the church.

### On the Imposition of Penance. From the Council of Mainz.

CCXCII. (Council of Mainz under Rabanus, c. 31; BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 28.) The measure and duration of penance for those confessing their sins must be imposed by priests either according to the regulations of the ancient canons, the authority of the holy Scriptures, or ecclesiastical custom. For those who impose certain light and unusual forms of penance for serious sins “sew cushions,” according to the prophetic saying, “under every elbow,” and “make pillows under the head of persons of every age,” to catch souls. But a distinction must be maintained between penitents who sin publicly and those who sin secretly. For one who sins publicly ought to be punished with public penance and, according to the order of the canons, excommunicated and reconciled in proportion to his merit.

### How Bishops or Presbyters Ought to Receive a Penitent. From the Roman Penitential.

CCXCIII. (BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 33.) Whenever Christians approach penance, we impose fasts, and we too ought to share their fast by fasting with them for one or two weeks, or as much as we can, so that it may not be said to us, as the Lord says to the teachers of the Jewish law: “Woe to you, lawyers, who load people with burdens difficult to bear, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with one of your fingers” (Luke XI).

### Likewise, Shortly Thereafter.

CCXCIV. (BURCHARD, in the same place.) Whenever you give counsel to a sinner, immediately impose penance upon him as well: how long he must fast or redeem his sins by almsgiving. Otherwise, you may forget what he has already told you, and it may again be necessary for you to question him; perhaps he will be ashamed to confess a second time, and may then be found liable to further judgment.

[Col. 0246D]

### That No One Else May Presume to Impose Penance or Hear Confession Except a Bishop or Presbyter. From the Same Source.

CCXCV. “Rise, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.” Brother, the Lord Jesus Christ, who said to his disciples, “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVIII), has willed that we, although unworthy, be numbered among them. May he himself, through our ministry, absolve you from all your sins—whatever you have negligently committed in thought, word, or deed—and, once freed from the bonds of sin, deign to lead you to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

We also, dearest brother, according to the authority entrusted by the Lord to us unworthy men, absolve you from every bond of offenses, so that you may merit eternal life through him who lives, etc. [Col. 0247A] [Note: [Col. 0247D] This chapter is not found in the manuscript.]

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 153.) For just as no one except bishops and presbyters, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, ought to offer sacrifice, so no others ought to usurp the judgments concerning penitents.

### That a Deacon, If Necessary, May Receive a Confession.

CCXCVI. (HALITGAR, in the preface to book VI; BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 154.) If necessity arises and no presbyter is present, let a deacon receive the penitent for holy communion.

### Likewise, Concerning Receiving Confession. From the Penitential of Archbishop Theodore or Presbyter Bede.

[Col. 0247B]

CCXCVII. (HALITGAR, in the same place; BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 2.) When bishops or presbyters receive the confessions of the faithful, they ought to humble themselves and pray with the groaning and tears of sorrow, not only for their own offenses but also for the brother’s fall. For the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Corinthians XI).

### As Above.

CCXCVIII. (HALITGAR, in the same place; BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 2.) When someone comes to a priest to confess his sins, the priest should tell him to wait a little while, until he enters the church or his room to pray. If there is no suitable place for this, he should say the following prayer in his heart.

### Prayer.

CCXCIX. (HALITGAR, in the same place; BURCHARD, in the same place, c. 3.) Lord almighty God, be gracious to me, a sinner, so that I may be able to give you worthy thanks: for in your mercy you have made me, unworthy as I am, a minister of the priestly office, and have appointed me, insignificant and humble, as a mediator to pray and intercede before our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, for those who sin and return to penance.

Therefore, Lord and ruler, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, who does not desire the death of sinners but that they be converted and live, receive my prayer, which I pour out before the sight of your clemency for your male and female servants who have come to penance. Grant them the spirit of compunction, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held bound, and return to you through worthy satisfaction, through the same Lord.

When the person who has come to penance sees the priest sorrowful and weeping over his crimes, he himself should be struck more deeply with fear of God, grieve more intensely, and dread his sins more greatly. [Note: [Col. 0247D] This passage reads as follows in an old manuscript of the monastery of Ripoll: “When that brother who has come to penance sees this humility of the priest, he dreads his sins more greatly and fears his crimes more deeply. After this, the priest should receive him charitably, make him sit humbly beside him, and draw him gently with words such as these: ‘Brother, do not be ashamed to confess your sins,’” etc. [Col. 0248D].]

### Order for Imposing Penance. As Above.

CCC. (BURCHARD, in the same place.) After this, question him gently and kindly. 140

“Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?”  
Response: “I believe.”

“Do you believe that these three persons are one God?”  
Response: “I believe.”

“Do you believe that in this very flesh in which you now are, you will rise on the day of judgment and receive either the good or the evil that you have done?”  
Response: “I believe.”

“Do you wish to forgive the sins of those who have sinned against you, since the Lord says: ‘If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins’ (Matthew VI)?”  
Response: “I do.”

And carefully inquire whether he is guilty of incest or has been unfaithful to his lord. If he does not wish to renounce incest, you cannot give him penance; but if he does, you may.

Once these matters have been addressed, the priest should speak affectionately to the penitent in these words:

“Brother, do not be ashamed to confess your sins. For I too am a sinner, and perhaps I have committed deeds worse than yours. I offer this admonition because, as blessed Gregory says (*Moralia*, book XXII, c. 9), it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling into it and, after committing it, not to reveal it by confession, but to defend it by denial and, when convicted, to multiply it by defending it.

“Although, at the devil’s prompting, we do not fear committing abominable crimes, we are ashamed, at his same persuasion, to confess in words the very things we have carried out in deed without any shame. Before a human being, who is like us and perhaps subject to the same passions, we are embarrassed to say what we did not fear to commit, without any blush of mind, as a detestable action before the Lord, who sees everything.

“Let us therefore freely confess what we committed under no compulsion. But if we conceal our crimes, they will be revealed by him who is both the accuser [Ripoll manuscript: ‘author’] and instigator of sin. For he urges us here to sin; once we have sinned, he accuses us. If, therefore, in this life we forestall him and become accusers of our own crime, we shall escape the wickedness of the devil, our enemy and accuser, as Paul testifies when he says: ‘If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged’ (I Corinthians VI).”

When the priest sees him feeling ashamed, he should continue:

“Perhaps, dearest brother, not everything you have done now comes to mind. I shall question you. Take care not to presume to conceal anything at the devil’s prompting.”

Then he should question him in the following order:

“Have you committed homicide, whether by accident or deliberately, or in revenge for your parents, or at the command of your lord, or in open war? If you did it voluntarily, you must do penance for seven years; if unwillingly or by accident, for five years. If in revenge for a parent, for one year, and during the following two years, three Lents and the appointed fast days. If in war, for forty days. If you are free and, at the command of your lord, killed an innocent slave, you must do penance for one year, and during two other years, three Lents and the appointed fast days. If the slave deserved death, let him do penance for forty days.

“Have you cut off someone’s hands or feet, torn out someone’s eyes, or wounded someone? For mutilation, you must do penance for one year; for a wound, let him do penance for forty days.

“Have you committed perjury, whether out of worldly greed, or under compulsion and necessity, or through obstinacy, or on account of your parents; or have you done so unknowingly; or have you knowingly led others into perjury? If you knowingly swore falsely and led others into perjury, you must do penance for seven years. If unknowingly, for one year and three Lents. If for the sake of life or bodily members, for three Lents.

“Have you committed theft, sacrilege, breaking and entering, or robbery, taking what was not yours? If you broke into houses by night and carried away livestock, or something of greater value worth forty solidi, you must do penance for one year and restore its value. If you do not restore it, do penance for two years. If you committed a greater theft, you must do penance for three years; if you did it repeatedly, for seven years. For a small theft, twenty days; for a child, ten days. If you took something from a church, which is sacrilege, do penance for seven years.

“Have you committed adultery with another man’s wife or betrothed, or corrupted a virgin, whether with a nun or a woman dedicated to God, or with an unattached woman—that is, without a husband—or with your own maidservant? If you committed adultery with another man’s wife or with a nun, do penance for seven years; if with a virgin, for two years; if with a widow, for one year. If you abandoned your own wife and joined yourself to another, do penance for seven years; if with an unmarried woman, for three Lents and the appointed fast days; if with your own maidservant, you must do penance for forty days.

“Did you have intercourse from behind with your wife or maidservant? If you did so, you must do penance for forty days.

“Did you have intercourse with your wife during the forty days before childbirth? You must do penance for forty days.

143

“Did you have intercourse on the Lord’s Day? You must do penance for three days.

“Did you abduct a virgin or widow? You must do penance for three years.

“Did you commit fornication as the Sodomites did, with animals, or with your mother or sister? You must do penance for fifteen or twelve years.

[Col. 0249D]

“Did you defile yourself with your wife during Lent? If you did so, you must do penance for one year or give twenty-six solidi as alms. If it happened through drunkenness, do penance for forty days.

“This too must be guarded against: twenty days before the Nativity of the Lord and Pentecost, on every Lord’s Day, and after conception has become apparent, a man must abstain from his wife.

[Col. 0250A]

“Did you give false testimony out of greed or unknowingly? Do penance for one year.

“Did you cut off any bodily member? Do penance for three years.

“Did you hate your brother? For as long as you remained in that hatred, do penance on bread and water.

“Did you slander anyone to his lord or to his peers out of envy? Do penance for forty days.

“Did you violate a grave by theft? Do penance for two years.

“Did any negligence on your part occur concerning the Lord’s sacrifice? Do penance for one hundred and forty days.

“Did you consult magicians, soothsayers, enchanters, or diviners, or make vows at trees or springs? Do penance for three years.

144

“Did you take any money from the Church? Either restore fourfold or do penance for three years.

[Col. 0250B]

“Did you cause someone’s ruin through an unjust accusation? Do penance for three years.

“Did you lead or send someone into captivity? Do penance for three years. [Note: [Col. 0249D] The Helmstedt edition reads: ‘Did you lead or send any Christian man into captivity? Three years.’ Burchard, in book XIX, has a somewhat fuller version and differs in some respects: ‘Did you lead, send, or sell any person into captivity, except for the sake of the common peace? If you did so, bring him back, if you can. If not, do penance for two years on the appointed fast days.’ [Col. 0250D].]

“Did you burn another person’s house or threshing floor? Do penance for three years.

“Did you vomit because of drunkenness? Do penance for fifteen days. If because of strife, for forty days. If unknowingly, do penance for six days. [Note: [Col. 0250D] The Helmstedt edition reads: ‘Did you vomit because of drunkenness? Do penance for fifteen days. If because of strife, for forty. If unknowingly, do penance for seven days. Likewise, if you have eaten blood.’]

“Did you eat carrion or meat torn apart by beasts? Do penance for forty days. Likewise, if you have eaten blood.

“Did you drink from a liquid in which a mouse or weasel was found dead? Do penance for forty days.

“Did you despise an imposed fast in the Church or the decrees of your lords? Do penance for forty days. If during Lent, for one year.

145

“Did you suffocate or otherwise crush your infant? You must do penance for five or three years.

“Did you drink any magical potion—that is, herbs or other substances—to prevent yourself from having children, or give such a potion to another; or did you wish to kill someone with a deadly drink; or teach another to do this; or taste a man’s semen so that he would burn with love for you; or drink chrism, or give it to another to subvert God’s judgment, and so forth? If you have done anything of this kind, do penance for seven years.

“Did you voluntarily kill your offspring? Do penance for ten years. If you killed a son or daughter, for twelve. If in the womb before conception, for one year; if after conception, for three years. If your infant died without baptism through your negligence, do penance for one year, and never be without some form of penance.

“Did you do anything that pagans do on the Kalends of January, in the form of a little deer or a little heifer? Do penance for three years.

“Did you do or say anything, in any undertaking you began, by means of divination or magical art? Do penance for one year.

“Did you place your son on a roof or on a furnace for the sake of some healing, or burn grain where a dead person had been? Do penance for five years.

“Did you sing demonic songs over the dead? Do penance for twenty days.

“Did you join yourself to a woman during menstruation? Do penance for forty days.

“Did you marry your wife after she had given birth, before forty days had been completed? Do penance for thirty days.

146

“Did you receive the Lord’s sacrifice without first abstaining from intercourse with your wife for five or seven days? Do penance for twenty days.

[Col. 0251B]

“Did you do any work on the Lord’s Day? Do penance for seven days.

“Did you slander or curse anyone out of envy? Do penance for seven days.

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 6; Capitular of THEODULF, c. 31.) I shall now explain to you the eight principal vices: pride, vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, greed, gluttony, and lust. If you recognize yourself as guilty of any of these, undertake penance. For all vices arise from them. [Note: [Col. 0251] These words are absent from the Helmstedt edition and the manuscript; they have been added from Burchard and others.]

From pride, which is the beginning of every sin and the queen of all evils, arise every disobedience, every presumption, every obstinacy, quarrels, heresies, and arrogance.

From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing at one’s neighbor’s misfortunes, and distress at his prosperity.

From anger arise quarrels, swelling of the mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness, and wandering of mind.

From greed arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, and hardness of heart toward mercy.

From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding.

From lust arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present world, and horror and despair concerning the future.

## Address.

[Col. 0251D]

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 7.) Therefore, if you have been proud until now, humble yourself before God. If you have loved vainglory, consider lest you lose an eternal reward for the sake of passing praise. If the rust of envy has consumed you until now—envy being the greatest and most detestable of sins, because the envious person is compared to the devil, who envied the first man the gift that he himself had lost through his own fault—do penance, and count the progress of others as your own.

If sadness overcomes you, meditate upon patience and long-suffering. If the disease of greed weighs upon you, consider that it is the root of all evils and is compared to idolatry; therefore you ought to be generous. If anger troubles you, anger which rests in the bosom of fools, you must rule your spirit and drive it away from you through tranquility of mind. If gluttony pulls you toward devouring, pursue sobriety. If lust does so, vow chastity.

Then let the penitent prostrate himself on the ground and say with tears:

“Both in these matters and in any others through which human frailty may sin against God and its creator—by thinking, speaking, acting, taking pleasure, or desiring—I acknowledge and confess that I have sinned in all things and am guilty before God above all people. I also humbly beseech you, priest of God, to intercede for me and for my sins before our Lord and creator, so that I may merit to obtain pardon and indulgence for these and all my crimes.”

148

Then the priest should rise and sing Psalm XXXVII. Then Psalms L and LIII. He should prostrate himself on the ground and say this prayer:

## Prayer

“I beseech, Lord, the majesty of your clemency and mercy that you may now deign to remit the sins and crimes of that servant of yours who confesses them, and forgive the faults of the past. You who brought back upon your shoulders the lost sheep, you who were appeased by the prayers and confession of the tax collector, may you also, Lord, deign to be appeased by this servant of yours. Look favorably upon his prayers, so that you may remain propitious to him in his confession. May his weeping and petition swiftly entreat your perpetual clemency, and, once restored to the holy altars, may he again be devoted to eternal and heavenly glory—you who live, etc.”

Then the following should be added:

“May almighty God be your helper and protector, and grant forgiveness for your past, present, and future sins.” (BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 7.)

## Preface of Bede on Remedies for Sins

We have excerpted these matters concerning remedies for sins from the records of earlier authorities. In all of them, however, we have relied not on the authority of a censor but rather on the counsel of one who shares in compassion. We earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ that, in everything he finds noted here, he carefully discern the sex, age, condition, status, person, understanding, and even the very heart of the penitent, and that, according to these considerations and as he sees fit, he judge each matter individually.

For it is necessary to correct all offenses: some by abstaining from foods, others by giving alms, still others by frequently bending the knees, standing in the form of a cross, or performing some other action of this kind that contributes to the cleansing of sins. All these matters must depend upon the judgment of a discerning judge.

## Concerning Penitents. From the African Council

### CCC.I

(Halitgar, Book III, chapters 1 and 11; Third Council of Carthage, chapter 31.) The bishops shall determine the periods of penance for penitents according to the difference among their sins.

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

### CCC.II

(Halitgar, in the same place, chapter 1; Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 74; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 35.) A priest shall impose the laws of penance upon one who implores penance, without showing preference on account of his person.

## That Penance Be Given to Married Persons by Mutual Consent. From the Council of Arles

### CCC.III

(Second Council of Arles, chapter 22; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 111.) Penance must be given to married persons only by mutual consent.

## From the Council of Laodicea

### CCC.IV

(Council of Laodicea, chapter 2; Halitgar, Book III, chapter 15; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 41.) Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes: if, by persevering in prayer, confession, and penance, they have achieved a complete conversion from their evils, after a period of penance proportionate to the quality of their offense has been imposed upon such persons, communion shall be granted because of the mercy and goodness of God.

## On the Same Matter

### CCC.V

(Halitgar, Preface to Book VI; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 32.) If you see someone approaching penance who is standing in penance earnestly and continually, deal with him more leniently at once.

[Note: In the old manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll, after the words “deal with him more leniently,” the following is added: “But if you see him negligent and lukewarm, release him more slowly.”]

## From the African Council

### CCC.VI

(Third Council of Carthage, chapter 32; Burchard, Book XIX, chapters 40 and 70.) A presbyter shall not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop’s absence, under the pressure of necessity, compels him to do so.

## From a Letter of Pope Innocent

### CCC.VII

(Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 7; Halitgar, Book III, chapter 13; Burchard, Book XVIII, chapter 18.) Concerning penitents who are doing penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones: if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that their penance is to be remitted on the Thursday before Easter. But if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, his penance is to be remitted before Easter.

## From the Council of Carthage

### CCC.VIII

(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 75; Burchard, Book XV, chapter 38.) Negligent penitents are to be received more slowly.

## That No Bishop Receive a Penitent from Another City or Parish, or Reconcile Him without the Testimony of a Bishop or Presbyter. From a Letter of Pope Felix

### CCC.IX

(Felix III, Letter 7, chapter 6.) The greatest care must be taken that none of our brother bishops, fellow bishops, or even presbyters receive in another person’s city or diocese a penitent, one placed under the authority of a priest, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter to whose parish he belongs.

## That Hands Not Be Laid upon Presbyters and Deacons as upon Penitents. From the Council of Carthage

### CCC.X

(Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 11; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 72.) It has been confirmed that, whenever presbyters or deacons are convicted of some serious offense for which it is necessary to remove them from ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them as upon penitents or as upon faithful laymen.

## That Penance Not Be Denied to Clerics. From the Council of Arles

### CCC.XI

(Second Council of Arles, chapter 29.) Penance must not be denied to clerics who desire it.

## How Presbyters and Deacons Are to Do Penance. From a Letter of Pope Leo

### CCC.XII

(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 16; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 71.) It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated to the priestly dignity or the rank of deacon should receive a remedy for penance through the laying on of hands for some crime of theirs, according to what is written: “If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 1.) Therefore, for such fallen persons, private withdrawal is to be sought in order to obtain the mercy of God; there, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.

## That Penitents Abstain from Business. From a Letter of Pope Leo

### CCC.XIII

(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 23; Halitgar, Book III, chapter 6; Rabanus, Letter to Heribald, chapter 15; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 95.) The nature of business either excuses or condemns it, since there is honorable profit and disgraceful profit. Nevertheless, it is more useful for a penitent to suffer losses than to be entangled in the dangers of business, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the commerce between buyer and seller.

## That after Laying Aside His Belt No Penitent Return to Secular Military Service. From the Same Source

### CCC.XIV

(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 24; Halitgar, in the same place, chapter 7; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 66.) It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules, after undertaking penance, to return to secular military service, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God …,” and so forth. Therefore, one who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Arles

### CCC.XV

(Second Council of Arles, chapter 25; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 67.) Those who, after adopting the purpose of holy religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, shall not receive communion without penance. We also order that they not be admitted to clerical office.

## Again from the Same Source

### CCC.XVI

Whoever presumes to assume secular clothing shall be expelled from the Church.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Toledo

### CCC.XVII

(Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 7. See the Decrees of Siricius, chapter 5; First Council of Orléans, chapter 13; and Halitgar, Book III, chapter 8.) Concerning those who, after completing penance, return to their former sins: the councils of the ancient fathers decree that those who, after doing penance, return like dogs and swine to their former vomit and wallowing places shall be held condemned as excommunicated and anathematized until they return to the remedies of penance and to the order they abandoned.

## On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Saint Gregory

### CCC.XVIII

(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 65.) Whoever remembers that he has committed unlawful acts should also strive to abstain from lawful ones, so that by this he may satisfy his Creator; whoever has committed what is forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what is permitted.

## On the Same Matter. From a Letter of Leo

### CCC.XIX

(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 22; Halitgar, Book III, chapter 5; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 43.) One who asks pardon for unlawful acts must also abstain from lawful ones, as the Apostle says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Corinthians 6).

[Note: See Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, chapter 15.]

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Toledo

### CCC.XX

(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 158.) Things that are repeated through frequent transgression are also condemned by frequent judgment.

## On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Basil, Bishop

### CCC.XXI

(Rule of Saint Basil, chapter 27; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 39.) A penitent should be received from the heart in the manner shown by the Lord when he says: “He called his friends and neighbors and said: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (Luke 15).

## Hence the Preceding Matter

### CCC.XXII

(Rule of Saint Basil, chapter 18.) The penitent should receive within himself the attitude of the one who said: “I have hated iniquity and abhorred it” (Psalm 118).

## What True Penance Is. From the Sayings of Saint Augustine

### CCC.XXIII

Nothing makes penance genuine except hatred of sin and love of God. When you repent in such a way that what was formerly sweet to you in life becomes bitter in your heart, and what previously delighted you in the body torments you in your heart, then you truly repent.

## How We Ought to Regard the Unrepentant. Hence the Preceding Matter

### CCC.XXIV

(Rule of Saint Basil, chapter 28; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 64.) Toward one who does not repent of his sin, we ought to behave as the Lord commanded when he said: “Let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18); and as the Apostle orders: “Withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that I delivered to you” (2 Thessalonians 3).

## That Clerics Not Attend Weddings

### CCC.XXV

(Council of Vannes, chapter 11; Council of Agde, chapter 39; Burchard, Book II, chapter 134.) Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and others thereafter who are not permitted to take wives must also avoid the banquets of other people’s weddings. They must not mingle with gatherings where love songs and shameful songs are sung, or where obscene movements of the body are displayed in choruses and dances, lest hearing and sight, assigned to sacred mysteries, be polluted by the contagion of shameful spectacles and words.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Mainz, Chapter 39

### CCC.XXVI

(Burchard, Book II, chapter 132.) Those who are not permitted to take wives must avoid the banquets of other people’s weddings.

## On the Same Matter. From the Decrees of Saint Martin the Pope

### CCC.XXVII

(Martin of Braga, chapter 59; Burchard, Book II, chapter 135.) Priests and clerics are not permitted to watch any spectacles at weddings or banquets. Rather, before they enter those spectacles, they ought to rise and depart from there.

[Note: See above, chapter 213.]

## The Times during Which Married Persons Must Abstain from Their Wives. From the Council of Elvira

### CCC.XXVIII

(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 155.) The Synod of Elvira says: During the three Lents of the year, on Sunday, and on Wednesday and Friday, married couples must abstain from one another. Likewise, they must not have intercourse during those days for as long as the wife is pregnant—that is, from the day the child begins to move in the womb until the birth. After the birth, abstinence is required for thirty-three days if the child is a son, but for fifty-six days if it is a daughter.

## On the Same Matter. From a Penitential

### CCC.XXIX

A married man shall abstain for forty days before Easter and Pentecost, or before Christmas, and throughout every Sunday night, and on Wednesday and Friday, and from the time conception becomes evident until after the child is born. After the birth of the child, the wife shall abstain from church for thirty days if it is a son, and for forty days if it is a daughter. A woman shall abstain from her husband for three months before childbirth and for forty days after childbirth. Whoever marries during these days shall do penance for twenty days.

## On the Same Matter

### CCC.XXX

(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 76.) Whoever has intercourse with his wife during the Lent before Easter and refuses to abstain from her shall do penance for one year [Helmstedt edition: five years of penance], or shall give his payment, namely twenty-six solidi, to the church or distribute it among the poor. If it happened through drunkenness and contrary to custom, he shall do penance for forty days.

## That One Must Abstain from One’s Spouse before Communion

### CCC.XXXI

(Burchard, Book V, chapter 22.) Every person must abstain from his own wife for seven, or five, or three days before sacred communion.

## Concerning Eulogies to Be Given to the People by a Presbyter. From the Council of Nantes

### CCC.XXXII

(Council of Nantes, chapter 9; Burchard, Book V, chapter 27.) From the offerings presented by the people and remaining after consecration, or from the loaves that the faithful offer to the church, or certainly from his own loaves, the presbyter shall suitably have portions cut and placed in a clean vessel. After the celebration of Mass, those who were not prepared to communicate may receive eulogies from it every Sunday and on feast days. The portion from which the presbyter is going to distribute the eulogies shall first be blessed with these words:

### Prayer

(Burchard, Book V, chapter 28.) Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, deign to bless this bread with your holy and spiritual blessing, so that it may be health of mind and body for all, and protection against every disease and all the snares of enemies. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, the bread of life, who came down from heaven and gives life and salvation to the world, and who lives and reigns with you.

Care must also be taken that crumbs do not fall carelessly.

## That Presbyters Travel Wearing a Stole. From the Synod of Tribur

### CCC.XXXIII

Presbyters must not travel unless dressed in a stole or orarium. If, while traveling, presbyters are stripped, wounded, or killed when not wearing a stole, the perpetrators shall pay a simple compensation. But if they were wearing a stole, the compensation shall be triple.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Mainz

### CCC.XXXIV

(Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, chapter 28; Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 81, and Book VI, chapter 169; Burchard, Book II, chapter 101.) Presbyters shall use oraria without interruption, because of the distinction of priestly dignity.

## That Clerics Not Wear Lay Clothing. From the Council Mentioned Above

### CCC.XXXV

(Burchard, Book II, chapter 208.) Clerics must not wear lay clothing—that is, a mantle or tunic without a cloak—nor costly and inappropriate footwear or other vain novelties. They must walk about in religious and decent attire.

[Note: See the Capitular of Ahyto, Bishop of Basel, chapter 15.]

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Adrisphach in Bavaria, Chapter 41

### CCC.XXXVI

No cleric shall wear lay clothing or presume to bear arms, except insofar as this is suitable to his religious calling.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Carthage

### CCC.XXXVII

(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 45; Burchard, Book II, chapter 209.) A cleric must demonstrate his profession both by his dress and by his manner of walking. Therefore, he must not seek elegance in clothing or footwear.

## That Presbyters Not Obtain Churches for a Price. From the Council of Mainz

### CCC.XXXVIII

(Rabanus, Letter to Heribald, the same, chapter 19; Burchard, Book III, chapter 110.) Whoever has obtained a church for a price shall be deposed in every way, since one is known to act contrary to the discipline of ecclesiastical rule when, by means of money, he expels another presbyter lawfully ordained to a church and claims it for himself in this manner.

[Note: See above, chapter 240.]

## That Sacrifice Is Not to Be Offered Everywhere. From a Letter of Pope Anacletus

### CCC.XXXIX

[Note: See above, chapters 132 and 191.] When priests celebrate the sacrifice, they must not do so alone, but must bring witnesses with them, so that they may be shown to offer sacrifice perfectly to God in places consecrated to the Lord. For the authority of the divine law says: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God has chosen” (Deuteronomy 12).

## Where Mass Is to Be Celebrated. From the Council of Saint Sylvester

### CCC.XL

(Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 198.) No presbyter shall presume to celebrate Mass except in places consecrated by a bishop, if he wishes thereafter to participate in the priesthood.

[Note: This chapter is found in the epilogue known as that of the Roman Council celebrated under Pope Sylvester, and from there in Gratian, Distinction 1, “On Consecration,” chapter 15. See the Capitular of Theodulf, Bishop of Orléans, chapter 11; the Capitular of Ahyto, Bishop of Basel, chapter 8; and his Capitula, chapter 14. See also Additions I to the Capitularies, chapter 10.]

## That Tithes Be Divided into Four Portions. From the Synod of Vannes

### CCC.XLI

(Council of Nantes, chapter 10; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 290; Burchard, Book III, chapter 138.) Presbyters must be instructed and likewise admonished, so that they understand that the tithes and offerings they receive from the faithful are the provisions of the poor, guests, and pilgrims, and that they are to use them not as their own but as entrusted property. They must know that they will render an account of all these things in the sight of God, and that, unless they faithfully administer them to the poor and to those mentioned above, they will suffer loss [manuscript codex: “will cause losses”; Sirmond’s edition: “will suffer them”].

The holy canons establish how these things are to be distributed: namely, four portions are to be made from them—one to support and repair the church building, another to be distributed to the poor, a third to be held by the presbyter and his clerics, and a fourth to be reserved for the bishop, so that whatever he orders from it may be done with prudent counsel.

## If a Bishop or Presbyter Presumes by Any Means to Alienate Church Property. From the Council of Braga

### CCC.XLII

(Second Council of Braga, chapter 17; Burchard, Book III, chapter 179.) If a presbyter or deacon is found to have sold anything from the church’s furnishings, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been decided that he shall not be retained in the ecclesiastical order. Nevertheless, the matter is to be left to the judgment of the bishop, whether he is worthy or unworthy to be received back into his rank.

## That No Prelate May Permanently Alienate a Large or Small Possession of the Church. From the Decrees of Pope Symmachus

### CCC.XLIII

(Third Roman Council under Symmachus, chapter 4.) No prelate of the Apostolic See may transfer to the rights of anyone, by perpetual alienation or exchange, a rural estate, whatever its size or smallness.

[Note: See the Council of Paris, Book I, chapter 17.]

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

### CCC.XLIV

(From the same Roman Council, chapter 1.) Houses established in any cities, whose condition necessarily requires considerable expense for their maintenance, may indeed be exchanged, if it should happen that revenues are offered, provided that the exchange is made according to a just valuation and in fear of divine judgment.

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

### CCC.XLV

(From the same Roman Council, chapter 6; Burchard, Book III, chapter 180.) If any presbyter attempts in any way to alienate permanently anything belonging to the legal property of his title, except gold, silver, or gems, and also clothing, if there is any, or any movable things that may have been added and do not pertain to divine ornaments, the donor, alienator, and seller shall be punished by loss of their rank.

## Again, Chapter 6

### CCC.XLVI

(From the same Roman Council, chapter 7.) Moreover, whoever asks for and receives church property, or whoever signs the document of a presbyter, deacon, or defender who gives it, shall be struck with the anathema by which God, when angered, strikes souls.

## That Presbyters Not Sell Church Property in the Places Where They Are Established. From the Council of Carthage

### CCC.XLVII

(Council of Carthage, chapter 33; Burchard, Book III, chapter 178.) It has likewise been decided that presbyters must not sell church property where they are established without the knowledge of their bishops, just as a bishop may not sell church estates without the knowledge of the council and his presbyters. If there is no necessity, neither may a bishop seize the property of the mother church, nor may a presbyter [seize church property; the printed text is corrupt: “licet matricis ecclesiae nec presbytero rem, etc.”].

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

### CCC.XLVIII

(Council of Carthage, chapter 26.) It has been decided that no one shall sell church property. But if it has no revenues and some extreme necessity compels such action, the matter must be reported to the primate of that province, so that, together with the appointed number of bishops, he may judge whether it should be done. If he does not do this, the seller shall be held guilty before God and the council and, having lost his rank, shall be punished.

## From the Decrees of Saint Martin the Pope

### CCC.XLIX

(Martin of Braga, chapter 14; Burchard, Book I, chapter 215, and Book III, chapter 181.) If any bishop, compelled by no necessity recognized by ecclesiastical reason, presumes to sell anything of the church’s property in his clergy [without the knowledge of the clergy], or where there happens to be no presbyter, he shall be compelled to restore those things to their own church. He shall be deposed when brought before the judgment of the bishops and, as one guilty of theft or robbery, deprived of his rank.

## What the Relatives of One Who Enriched a Church from His Own Property Ought to Do If They Foresee That Something from His Gifts Has Been Defrauded from the Church. From the Council of Toledo

### CCC.L

(Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 1; Burchard, Book III, chapter 182.) The whole amount of church property, just as it grants the giver a remedy of pardon, so rightly prepares punishment for the fraudulent person. Therefore, no priest or minister shall take anything from church property that the faithful donate in any place, or attach it to his own right or to the unity of his own see.

However, so that greater security may be maintained in this matter, the relatives of the person who built or enriched the church shall be permitted to exercise careful vigilance with good intention.
