If they foresee that a priest or minister is defrauding anything from the collected property, they should restrain him either through an honorable meeting of admonition or by reporting to the bishop or judge that such matters must be corrected. If the bishop attempts to do such things, they shall take care to report them to his metropolitan. If the metropolitan does so, they shall not delay informing the king’s ears.

The heirs themselves, however, may not claim authority over these same things as though they possessed a private right; they may not commit robbery, fraud, or any violence. If anyone presumes to disregard these admonitions, he shall restore what he has wickedly seized with shame and shall endure a sentence of excommunication for a year.

## Concerning Small Plots and Small Vineyards. From the Council of Agde

### CCC.LI

(Council of Agde, chapter 45.) If necessity requires it, a bishop may, without the counsel of his brothers, dispose of small plots or little vineyards that are of little use to the church or are situated far away.

## That Fugitives Who Are Slaves of the Church May Be Disposed Of. From the Same Council

### CCC.LII

(Council of Agde, chapter 46; Burchard, Book III, chapter 188.) Fugitives who are also slaves, abandoning their homes or families, and who, even if recalled, cannot be kept, may likewise be disposed of by the bishop, if he wishes or if they have deserved such treatment.

## If Anyone Dares to Suppress Royal Charters or Commands or Hand Them over to Adversaries. From the Council of Agde

### CCC.LIII

(Council of Agde, chapter 26; Burchard, Book III, chapter 183.) If any cleric presumes, with blameworthy and punishable obstinacy, either to suppress or deny documents by which the possession of the church is secured, or perhaps to hand them over to adversaries, he shall restore from his own resources whatever loss has been inflicted upon the Church through the withholding of the documents [Helmaestad edition: “through the removal of the documents”; Sirmond: “through the absence of the documents”], and shall be deprived of communion.

Those, however, who, to the detriment of the church, having been impiously solicited by traitors, receive the instruments of the holy Church [Sirmond: “those solicited [by] traitors”] shall be struck by the same sentence.

## Concerning the Bishop’s Testament and Its Validity. From the Same Council

### CCC.LIV

(Council of Agde, chapter 51; Burchard, Book I, chapter 212.) If a bishop, having drawn up a testament, assigns anything from property belonging by right to the church, it shall have no validity unless he supplies an equal amount from resources belonging to his own right.

## Concerning Manumissions in the Church. From the Same Council

### CCC.LV

(Council of Agde, chapter 56.) Slaves given to monks may not be manumitted by the abbot. For it is unjust that, while the monks perform daily rural labor, their slaves should enjoy the leisure of freedom.

[Note: See the Rule of Saint Ferreolus, chapter 36.]

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Toledo

### CCC.LVI

(Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 67; Burchard, Book III, chapter 189.) Bishops who contribute nothing of their own property to the Church of Christ must not presume to make freedmen, to their own condemnation, from the families belonging to the Church. For it is impious that one who has not contributed his own possessions to the Church of Christ should inflict loss upon it. Accordingly, a successor bishop shall recall such freedmen to the right of the Church without any opposition.

[Note: See the First Council of Seville, chapters 1 and 2, and the Council of Mérida, chapter 20.]

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Council

### CCC.LVII

(Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 68; Burchard, Book III, chapter 176.) A bishop who wishes to manumit a slave belonging by right to the Church, without retaining ecclesiastical protection, shall offer before the council of the Church over which he presides two slaves of equal merit and peculium, with the priests subscribing to the exchange, so that the decision of the person making the exchange may be found valid and just.

Such a freedman shall be denied the right to bring an accusation or give testimony against the Church to whose jurisdiction he belonged. But if he presumes to do so, it is decreed that, while the exchange remains in force, he shall be recalled into the servitude of his own Church.

## Concerning the Freedmen of the Church. From the Same Council

### CCC.LVIII

(Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 72; Burchard, Book III, chapter 186.) Freedmen who have been manumitted by anyone and entrusted to the protection of the Church shall be protected by priestly defense from the insolence of anyone, whether in the condition of freedom they are known to possess or in the peculium they are known to have.

## Concerning Ecclesiastical Treasures. From Book I of the Capitularies, Title 117

### CCC.LIX

(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 123.) Each bishop, abbot, and abbess must carefully inspect the ecclesiastical treasures, lest through the bad faith or negligence of the custodians anything of the gems, vessels, or remaining treasure be lost.

## That No One Presume to Alienate Immovable Church Property. From Book I, Chapter 19

### CCC.LX

(Emperor Justinian, Novel 7, chapter 1; Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 29; Burchard, Book III, chapter 164.) No one may alienate immovable church property, whether a house, field, garden, rural slave, or *panes civiles*—literally, “civil breads,” a wording that is uncertain—nor bind it to creditors by way of a special mortgage.

[Note: See Book III of the Decretals, title 13, chapter 5.]

The word “alienation” includes a sale, donation, exchange, and a perpetual emphyteutic contract. But all priests must abstain entirely from such alienation, fearing the penalties threatened by the Leonine constitution (Book 14 of the Code, “On Sacred Churches”).

## If the Prince Wishes to Make an Exchange Involving Church Property. From the Same Chapter, 30

### CCC.LXI

(Justinian, Novel 7, chapter 2; Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 30; Burchard, Book III, chapter 165.) If the prince wishes to grant an immovable possession to a holy place and receive another immovable possession from it, and in this way conclude an exchange, he may do so by a divine pragmatic sanction promulgated by him.

[Note: See the same work, title 19, chapter 1.]

## Concerning Ecclesiastical Precariae. From the Council at Belvacum, Title 21

### CCC.LXII

(Council of Meaux, chapter 21; Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 6, chapter 6; Burchard, Book III, chapter 166.) Precariae and exchanges made during the periods when churches were widowed, by those who had occupied the places of bishops, shall be rescinded. If such transactions are to be made, they must be made with ecclesiastical or civil authority.

## On the Same Matter. Chapter 22

### CCC.LXIII

(Council of Meaux, chapter 22; Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 6, chapter 7; Burchard, Book III, chapter 167.) No one shall presume to make a precaria from church property unless, for whatever suitable amount is given from his own property, he receives twice that amount from church property, solely in his own name, if he wishes to hold both his own and church property in usufruct.

But if he relinquishes his own property for the present, he shall take three times that amount from church property in usufruct, solely in his own name. For it is fitting that everyone manage these things as a steward of another’s property, not as a giver of his own.

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

### CCC.LXIV

(Council of Meaux, chapter 22; Burchard, Book III, chapter 168.) No one may be compelled by any authority to make a precaria from property dedicated to God and his saints, since reason and custom establish that no one is obliged to make a benefaction from his own property to someone whom he does not wish to benefit, contrary to utility and reason.

## That Precariae Be Renewed Every Five Years. From the Same Source

### CCC.LXV

(Council of Meaux, chapter 22; Burchard, Book III, chapter 169.) Precariae shall be renewed every five years, according to ancient custom and authority.

## Concerning Exchanges. From the Same Source, Chapter 23

### CCC.LXVI

(Council of Meaux, chapter 23; Burchard, Book III, chapter 171.) Exchanges of church property must be secured as valid and, if they must be made in any way, examined with the greatest precision. Those made without due consideration, in accordance with the canonical decree of Pope Hilary (chapter 1), and whatever the preceding bishop illicitly permitted or others illicitly committed, must be corrected by the successor.

[Note: See the Third Council of Valence, chapter 21, and Book III of the Lombard Laws, title 10, chapter 3.]

## That Commands Not Be Issued Concerning Ecclesiastical Benefices or Precariae. From the Council at Saint-Médard, Chapter 40

### CCC.LXVII

(Council of Meaux, chapter 22; Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 6, chapter 7; Burchard, Book III, chapter 175.) Neither reason allows nor authority in any way permits royal commands to be issued concerning ecclesiastical precariae. For royal majesty must necessarily judge it unworthy to confirm commands in ecclesiastical law unless they are requested by an ecclesiastical ruler.

That guardian of the Church must take the greatest care lest, forgetful of his order and ecclesiastical communion, he request that a royal command be issued, out of any kind of flattery, contrary to authority concerning any matter. Even if he does so, he must not be heard; and if he should obtain such a command, it must be rescinded by royal discretion and episcopal judgment, while the unjust petitioner must be suitably punished for his unjust petition before the prince.

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Chapter

### CCC.LXVIII

(Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 9, chapter 7, section 11, in the council at Saint-Médard.) Let our faithful know that in the synod we granted the venerable bishops that we would in no way issue commands confirming our authority over ecclesiastical benefices or precariae, even if any superior of a monastery should make an unreasonable request. Therefore, let each person restrain himself from making an unreasonable request.

## That Exchanges of Church Property Not Be Made without the King’s Consent, and That Church Slaves Be Exchanged Only for Freedom. From the Same Source, Chapter 12

### CCC.LXIX

(Capitula of Charles the Bald, in the same place, section 12; Burchard, Book III, chapter 172.) Our representatives shall announce throughout their respective jurisdictions that no superior may presume to make exchanges of church property or church slaves without our permission and consent.

### Another Provision

(Capitula of Charles the Bald, in the same place; Burchard, Book III, chapter 173.) Nor may anyone exchange church slaves except for freedom: namely, slaves given in exchange for an ecclesiastic must remain in the Church’s servitude, while the ecclesiastical person who is exchanged must enjoy perpetual freedom.

[Note: The words that follow “enjoy perpetual freedom” are not found in the acts of the Council of Soissons, from which Regino cites them, nor in the Capitula of Charles the Bald, nor finally in the Capitular of Compiègne that we published in the appendix to Lupus of Ferrières, which was copied from the Capitula published in that synod of Soissons. They are nevertheless also found in Burchard, who undoubtedly took them from Regino.]

For what has once been consecrated to the Lord can no longer be transferred to human uses. For the law says: “If anyone changes it, both what he changes and what has been changed shall be sacrificed to the Lord” (Leviticus 27).

## Again from the Capitula at Quierzy

### CCC.LXX

(Burchard, Book III, chapter 174.) It seems unjust and impious that slaves whom faithful men or women have consecrated to God and his saints for the remedy of their souls should again be reduced to secular servitude through commerce involving any gift, price, or exchange, since canonical authority permits only fugitive slaves to be disposed of.

Therefore, all rectors of churches must take the greatest care that one person’s almsgiving does not become another person’s sin. For just as it is indecent for a free person to become a slave, so it is absurd for one who has fallen from ecclesiastical dignity to become subject to human servitude.

## Concerning Sunday. From the Capitularies of Charles

### CCC.LXXI

(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 81; Burchard, Book II, chapter 82.) We also decree, in accordance with what the Lord commanded in the law, that servile works not be performed on Sundays, just as my father commanded in his synodal edicts.

[Note: See Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 200; Additions I, chapter 9; and Additions II, chapter 9.]

Men must not engage in rural labor, cultivate vineyards, plow or reap the fields, cut hay, build hedges, grub up roots in the forests, cut down trees, work in quarries, build houses, work in gardens, assemble at court hearings, hold markets, or engage in hunting.

## What May or May Not Be Done on Sunday. From the Same Source

### CCC.LXXII

(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 81; Burchard, Book II, chapter 83.) Three kinds of carting work may be done on Sunday: military carts, carts carrying provisions, or transport service; and, if there should be need, the body of anyone may be carried to the grave.

## Again Concerning Sunday. From the Same Council
### CCCLXXIII

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 81; Burchard, book II, chapter 84.)* Women shall not perform textile work on Sunday; they shall not cut out garments, sew, or card wool.

[Note: In the commonly circulated editions of the Capitularies, and in the Royal manuscript from which the first Paris edition was produced, the reading is: “Likewise, women shall not perform textile work, nor cut out garments, nor sew, nor make embroidery; nor shall they card wool,” etc. The Colbertine manuscript reads “or make acupile”; the Rivipullensis, “make acupicula”; ours, “nor let aucupiculae be made.” Instead of the reading found here, *nec verveces tondere* (“nor shear wethers”), the editions of the Capitularies have *berbices*. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts have *verveces* or *vervices*, including the one from which the first Paris edition was prepared.]

It is not permitted to beat flax, or to wash clothing in public, or to shear wethers, so that honor and rest may in every respect be rendered to Sunday. Rather, let them assemble from everywhere for the solemn celebration of Mass and praise God for all the good things that he has deigned to bestow upon us on that day. [Col. 0264C]

### That there should be no market on Sunday. From a council.

### CCCLXXIV

*(Council of Mainz, A.D. 813, chapter 37; Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 88; Burchard, book II, chapters 81 and 85.)* We have decreed that all Sundays are to be observed with complete reverence and that people are to abstain from unlawful work; that no market is to be held on them, nor a court-session in which anyone is judged to death or punishment, nor oaths sworn. [Note: See Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 28, and the Capitularies of Riculfus of Soissons, chapter 18.]

### From Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 139.

### CCCLXXV

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 145; Burchard, book II, chapter 86.)* A market shall be held nowhere on Sunday. [Note: See Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 49, chapter 1.]

### That no bishop or person of lower rank should presume to judge a case on Sunday. From the Council of Tarragona.

### CCCLXXVI

*(Council of Tarragona, chapter 4; Burchard, book II, chapter 87.)* No bishop, presbyter, or cleric shall dare to take up and decide on Sunday the business of any case whatsoever, except only that the solemn rites appointed for God may be performed.

### On the festivals of the year. From Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 23.

### CCCLXXVII

*(Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 35.)* We decree that the following feast days be celebrated during the year: the Lord’s Day of Easter together with the entire week; the day of the Lord’s Ascension; Pentecost, likewise as at Easter; one day for the apostles Peter and Paul; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the Assumption of Saint Mary; Saint Michael’s day; Saint Remigius’s; Saint Martin’s; Saint Andrew’s; four days at the Nativity of the Lord; the Lord’s Octave; the Epiphany of the Lord; and the Purification of Saint Mary. We also decree that the festivals of those martyrs or confessors whose bodies rest in each parish be observed. [Note: See Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 164, and Book VI, chapter 186.]

### 173. On the same matter. From the Council of Adrispach.

### CCCLXXVIII

We decree that the following feast days be celebrated: Easter, and likewise Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. Before Mass, permission is given to plough and sow, cultivate a garden or vineyard, and enclose a hedge. From all other work, however, we decree that people abstain. After Mass, they are to be free from work. Pentecost likewise as at Easter; Saint Lawrence; the Kalends of November; All Saints; and likewise the dedications of churches. [Note: See the Council of Mainz held in the year 813, chapter 36.]

### On not kneeling on feast days. From the Council of Nicaea.

### CCCLXXIX

*(Council of Nicaea, chapter 20; Burchard, book II, chapter 88.)* Since there are some who kneel on Sunday and on the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed uniformly in different places, the holy council has decreed that vows should be offered to the Lord while standing.

### As above.

### CCCLXXX

Presbyters are to announce to the congregations that during Lent and the fast of the Four Seasons they should kneel only for the solemn celebration of Mass, when the deacon gives the announcement. On Sundays, by contrast, and on the other feast days, from vespers until vespers, they shall not kneel, but shall pray standing and bowed. No one shall presume to pray with only one knee pressed to the ground, as the Jews are said to have done in mockery of the Lord during his Passion; rather, he shall fix both knees to the earth. For the Apostle says: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians III).

### That shameful songs be forbidden to the congregations. From the Council of Arles.

### CCCLXXXI

*(Third Council of Toledo, chapter 23.)* The irreligious custom that the common people have been accustomed to practice during the festivals of the saints must be completely eradicated: namely, that people who ought to attend to the divine offices should devote themselves to dances and shameful songs, harming not only themselves but also disturbing the services of the religious. The holy council entrusts the care of removing this practice from all Spain to the priests and judges. [Col. 0266A]

### That devilish songs not be sung at night over the corpses of the dead. As above.

### CCCLXXXII

*(Burchard, book X, chapter 34.)* Laypeople who keep vigil over a funeral shall do so with fear, trembling, and reverence. No one shall presume there to sing devilish songs, or to engage in the games and dances that the pagans devised under the instruction of the devil. [Note: See Book VI of the Capitularies, chapters 193 and 194, and the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 22.]

For who does not know that it is devilish, not only alien to the Christian religion but also contrary to human nature, to sing there, rejoice, become drunk, and let one’s face break into laughter, setting aside all piety and affection of charity, as though exulting over a brother’s death, when mourning and lamentation ought to resound in tearful voices over the loss of a beloved brother? Indeed, we read in many places that the fathers of the Old and New Testaments lamented the deaths of holy men with weeping, but nowhere that they rejoiced because they had departed from the world.

For the whole of Egypt mourned the patriarch Jacob for seventy days. And Joseph and his brothers, when they carried their father into the land of Canaan for burial and celebrated the funeral rites, filled the threshing-floor of Atad—which is situated beyond the Jordan—with great and intense mourning for seven days (Genesis L). So great was the mourning that the place received its name from it.

And we read concerning blessed Stephen that devout men buried him, or made arrangements for his burial, and made great mourning over him (Acts VIII). Therefore such foolish merriment and destructive songs must be utterly forbidden by God’s authority. If anyone wishes to sing, let him sing “Kyrie eleison.” Otherwise, let him be completely silent. If he does not wish to be silent, let him immediately be expelled by everyone, or be ordered not to have permission to remain there any longer, but to depart and go to his own dwelling. On the following day, however, let him be punished in such a way that the others may be afraid.

### That a bishop should in no way ordain clerics belonging to another parish. From the Council of Antioch.

### CCCLXXXIII

*(Council of Antioch, chapter 22; Burchard, book I, chapter 107.)* A bishop shall not appoint presbyters or deacons subject to another bishop, unless perhaps with the counsel and consent of the bishop of the region. If anyone attempts to do such a thing, his ordination shall be invalid, and he shall be disciplined by the synod.

### 176. That no one should ordain another’s cleric. From the Council of Nicaea.

### CCCLXXXIV

*(Council of Nicaea, chapter 16; Burchard, book I, chapter 109.)* If any bishop audaciously attempts to take a cleric belonging to another and ordain him in his own church, without the consent of the bishop from whom he departed, such an ordination shall be declared invalid. [Editio Helmaestadiensis: “to take one belonging to another, or a deacon,”—incorrect.]

[Col. 0267A] ### On the same matter. From the Council of Africa.

### CCCLXXXV

*(Council of Africa, chapter 57; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 21; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 11.)* It has likewise been decreed that whoever has read even once in a church shall not be retained for the clerical order by another church.

### That ordinations should not be performed absolutely. From the Council of Chalcedon.

### CCCLXXXVI

*(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 6; Burchard, book II, chapter 6.)* No one is to be ordained absolutely as a presbyter or deacon, or to any ecclesiastical rank, unless the church of the city or estate, shrine of the martyrs, or monastery to which the person being ordained is assigned is specifically declared. Those who are ordained absolutely: the holy synod has decreed that such imposition of hands is to be considered invalid, and that they may nowhere minister, to the injury of the one who ordained them. [Col. 0267B]

### Likewise, that no one be ordained absolutely. From Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 25.

### CCCLXXXVII

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 25.)* No one is to be ordained absolutely or without a declaration establishing the place to which he is ordained.

### 177. On examination before ordination. From the same source, chapter 136.

### CCCLXXXVIII

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 142.)* Presbyters are not to be ordained before they have been examined.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 52.

### CCCLXXXIX

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 52.)* Those from our parishes who request ordination either to a title or absolutely are in no way to be ordained unless they have first resided for at least one year in a definite and religious place, or even in a city, so that certainty concerning their life, conduct, and learning may be established. No one shall presume to ordain anyone absolutely, as the holy canons have decreed. [Note: See below, chapter 442 of this book.]

### That those ordained should receive letters from their ordainers. From the Council of Africa.

### CCCXC

*(Council of Africa, chapter 56; Burchard, book II, chapter 46.)* It has been decreed that all who henceforth are ordained throughout the African provinces shall receive letters from their ordainers, signed by their hands and containing the consul and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning those who are later or earlier.

### That no one should presume to ordain another’s slave. From a letter of Pope Leo.

### CCCXCI

*(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 1.)* Those who have no dignity of birth or character to commend them are not to be admitted indiscriminately to sacred orders; and those who have been unable to obtain freedom from their masters are not to be promoted to the dignity of the priesthood, as though servile baseness could attain this honor. It is believed that one can be pleasing to God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his own master. And shortly afterward:

He who is to be enrolled in the divine army must be free from other obligations, so that he may not be withdrawn by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, in which his name is inscribed.

[Col. 0268A] ### On the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 26.

### CCCXCII

*(First Council of Orléans, chapter 8; Council of Worms, chapter 40.)* If a slave, in the absence or ignorance of his master, but with the bishop’s knowledge, has been ordained deacon or presbyter, he shall remain in clerical office, while the bishop shall pay his master double compensation. [Note: See the Council of Mainz under Charles the Great, chapter 23.]

But if the bishop did not know that he was a slave, those who give testimony concerning him or request that he be ordained shall be held liable to a similar compensation. [Note: The first part of this chapter is mutilated and therefore makes no sense. The gap should accordingly be supplied from editions of the Council of Orléans as follows: “If a slave, in the absence or ignorance of his master, and with the bishop knowing that he is a slave, has been ordained deacon,” etc. On the ordination of slaves, see below, chapter 396 of this book.]

### That no minister should secretly introduce a cleric from another parish for ordination. From a letter of Pope Innocent.

### CCCXCIII

*(Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 14.)* No bishop shall presume to ordain a cleric from another church unless he has done so after being entreated by the prayers of the other bishop, or unless that bishop, having been entreated, has wished to grant permission. The Council of Nicaea also established that one church should not receive a cleric rejected by another.

### Likewise, concerning slaves to be ordained. From the Council of Toledo.

### CCCXCIV

*(Council of Toledo, chapter 73; Burchard, book I, chapter 25.)* Those who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from them shall, if they are free from crime, be freely admitted to the clerical order, since they are known to have been released by direct manumission. Those, however, who have been manumitted while retaining an obligation of service, because they remain bound in servitude to their patrons, are in no way to be promoted to ecclesiastical rank, lest, whenever their masters wish, they become slaves out of clerics.

[Col. 0268C] ### Likewise from the Capitularies, title 84.

### CCCXCV

*(Council of Paris, book I, chapter 22, and Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 178.)* If laypeople offer to bishops clerics of commendable life and learning so that they may be consecrated and appointed in their churches, the bishops shall not reject them for any reason whatsoever.

### On the ordination of slaves. From the same source, chapter 82.

### CCCXCVI

*(Capitulary of Aachen of Louis the Pious, chapter 6; Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 88; Burchard, book II, chapter 31; Ivo, part VI, chapter 232.)* Concerning the ordination of slaves, who are indiscriminately and without due consideration promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, it has been agreed by all that the sacred canons must be followed. It has therefore been decreed that henceforth no bishop shall presume to promote them to sacred orders unless they have first obtained freedom from their own masters.

And if any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master, or by employing witnesses hired or bribed with money, or by any cunning or fraud, has attained ecclesiastical rank, it has been decreed that he be deposed and that his master receive him.

But if a grandfather or father, migrating from one country to another, has begotten a son in that province, and the son was raised there and promoted to ecclesiastical rank, while it was unknown whether he was a slave [Sirmond: “if it had remained unknown”; our old manuscript: “he did not know”], and afterward his master came and acquired him by legal process, it has been decreed that, if his master wishes to grant him freedom, he shall remain in his rank.

But if the master wishes to remove him from the Lord’s camp by the chain of servitude, he shall lose his rank, because, according to the sacred canons, a base person remaining in that condition cannot exercise the dignity of the priesthood.

### On the peculium of slaves.

### CCCXCVII

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 88; Burchard, book II, chapter 23; Ivo, part VI, chapter 38.)* Concerning the property or *peculium* of those who are granted freedom by their own masters so that they may lawfully be promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, it has been decreed that it shall remain in the power of the masters whether they wish to grant it to them or claim it for themselves.

### On the peculium of the ordained.

[Col. 0269B] ### CCCXCVIII

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 88; Burchard, book III, chapter 122.)* If, however, he acquires anything after ordination, the rule established by the canons concerning consecrated persons who possess nothing is to be observed.

### On the slaves of churches.

### CCCXCIX

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 88; Burchard, book II, chapter 32; Ivo, part VI, chapter 133.)* Concerning the slaves of churches, it has been decreed by common agreement that the archbishops established in the individual provinces shall possess our written authority, and their suffragans shall keep a copy of it. Whenever someone useful from the household of the church is found who is to be ordained, this authority shall be read aloud on the ambo before the people, and before the priests and the entire clergy, in front of the altar’s horn, as it is contained in our authority. With every form of deceit removed, he shall obtain freedom, and only then shall he be promoted to ecclesiastical ranks.

### On the households of monasteries.

### CCCC

*(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 88.)* The same procedure is also to be followed concerning those whom laypeople wish to promote from the household of the churches to sacred orders. The same form is likewise to be observed concerning those whom the superiors of canons or monks request for ordination.

### Model of the act of freedom mentioned above.

### CCCCI

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 26; Ivo, part VI, chapter 127.)* Ecclesiastical authority openly admonishes, and royal majesty also gives its assent to canonical religion, that whenever any church chooses to promote someone from its own household to sacred orders, his freedom should be solemnly confirmed, in the presence of priests, canons, and noble laymen, by the subscription of the person to whom he is subject, under a written deed of freedom. [Note: See volume II of Goldast’s *Rerum Alamannicarum*, chapter 7, page 37.]

Therefore I, in the name of God, bishop, or abbot, or any other person, with Christ’s approval and with the consent of the rector of that holy church, establish by this deed of authority that a certain servant of our church, named that man, who has been offered for sacred orders, is free at the altar’s horn in the presence of noble men, so that from this day and time forward he may remain completely free and secure from every bond of servitude, as though he had been begotten or born of free parents.

Let him proceed to whatever status he canonically chooses, according to his will, so that henceforth he owes neither to us nor to our successors any service arising from a servile condition. Rather, throughout all the days of his life, under a definite and complete freedom, let him exist always as fully free and secure, like the other Roman citizens, by this deed of manumission and freedom.

Concerning his own *peculium*, whatever he possesses or may henceforth acquire, let him freely do with it whatever he wishes according to canonical authority. And so that this document of freedom may possess inviolable firmness, we have confirmed it with our own hand.

[Col. 0270B] ### Model of the freedom of one’s own slave.

### CCCCII

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 30; Ivo, part VI, chapter 131.)* Whoever releases a bond and service owed to him does not doubt that a reward will come to him from the Lord in the future. Therefore I, in the name of God, that man, for the salvation of my soul or for eternal recompense, in the church of Saint Peter, or of that other saint, in the presence of the bishop, or of the priests and noble laymen present there, before the horn of the altar of that church, release my slave, that man, by this deed of release and freedom, from every bond of servitude.

Thus, from this day forward, let him be free and remain free, as though he had been born or begotten of free parents. Let him proceed to whatever status he prefers, or whatever canonical authority permits him, and, like the other Roman citizens, let him live a free life.

To none of my heirs or heirs-to-be, nor to any other person, shall he owe any service of slavery or freedom, except to God alone, to whom all things are subject, or for whose love I have devotedly offered him to his service.

His *peculium*, however, whatever the Lord has given him and whatever, with God’s help, he may be able to acquire by his labor in the future, let him possess permanently as granted to him, so that he may do with it whatever pleases him according to ecclesiastical ordinances.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, one of my heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this deed of freedom or in any way seek to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of God and be made an outsider from the thresholds of the holy Church of God. Moreover, let him pay sixty solidi to the person against whom he has brought the action, and let him be unable to establish whatever he claims. But let this freedom of mine, confirmed by the hands of other good men and supported by stipulation, remain unshaken forever.

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 27; Ivo, part VI, chapter 128.)* The deed of freedom written above must contain not only the name of the person who requests that it be made, but also the names of the priests and noble laymen who were present there, arranged in order and bearing marks impressed by their own hands. Without their attestation, the document, deprived of the authority of witnesses, is considered worthless.

It must also have the place, day, year, consul, and indiction noted at the end or in the margin in this form:

“Executed in that city, in the house of Saint Peter, on those Kalends, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation so-and-so, while that king was reigning, and while that bishop was presiding in the chair of the aforesaid city, in that monastery, in that indiction, happily, in the name of God. Amen.”

For Roman authority says (*Interpretation of Book I, title 1, of the Theodosian Code, On the Constitutions of Princes*): “Whatever laws have been issued without a day and consul are invalid.”

### That manumission ought to take place in a church.

### CCCCIII

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 28; Ivo, part VI, chapter 129.)* Laypeople must also be instructed so that they know that they can in no way manumit their own slaves elsewhere when they have decided to enroll them in the Lord’s army, except in a holy church, according to the procedure stated above.

For how can clerics who are strangers to secular law obtain freedom outside the church? And since they are forbidden to proceed to a secular court, how can they be released from the yoke of servitude by secular judgment?

But perhaps someone says: “A person is not permitted to become a cleric unless, before undertaking clerical office, he possesses the dignity of freedom.” He speaks the truth. Therefore what can be weakened or censured must be guarded against.

### As above.

### CCCCIV

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 29; Ivo, part VI, chapter 130.)* It is not only those who are to be promoted to the clerical order who must be manumitted in a church; those whom anyone wishes to emancipate for the salvation of his soul must likewise be released in a church according to secular law and commended to the protection of that same church. For it is written in the Pact of the Franks.

### On the same matter. From the Pact.

### CCCCV

*(Chapter 58 of the Ripuarian Law.)* We also wish this: if any Ripuarian Frank wishes to make his slave free, for the salvation of his soul and according to Roman law, he shall hand over the slave with the documents into the hand of the bishop in the church, before presbyters, deacons, or the whole clergy and people. The bishop shall order the archdeacon to have documents written for him according to Roman law, by which the churches live. [Editio Helmaestadiensis: “by which the Church is governed.”]

Both he and all his descendants shall remain free and shall live under the protection of the church. They shall pay all the income of their status to the church and shall hold a court nowhere except at the church where they were released. If they die without children, they shall leave no heir other than the church.

### On the same matter. From Roman law.

### CCCVI

*(Interpretation of Book I and the Theodosian Code, On Manumission in a Church.)* The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Hosius, bishop of Córdoba:

Whoever wishes to manumit slaves in the holy church need only wish to release his slaves in the presence of priests; he should know that, once they have received freedom, they are Roman citizens. For if clerics wish to grant freedom to their slaves, even if they do so outside the presence of priests, or if the slaves are released only by spoken words and without a written document, their freedom shall nevertheless remain complete and unimpaired, just as it is for Roman citizens.

### That the deed of freedom should be read on the ambo. From the Council of Tribur.

### CCCCVII

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 21.)* No one of servile condition is to be promoted to sacred orders unless he has first obtained lawful freedom from his own masters. The deed of this freedom shall be publicly read on the ambo before ordination; and if no one objects, he shall be duly consecrated.

Furthermore, if he falls from his rank, he shall have the condition that he possessed before attaining that rank. [Note: This chapter does not appear in the commonly circulated editions of the Council of Tribur. It is found, however, both in Burchard and in an old manuscript collection of canons in the Royal Library. The final part, which is mutilated in Regino, should be supplemented from Burchard and that old collection as follows: “Moreover, a slave not canonically consecrated, after he has fallen from his rank, shall have the condition that he possessed before attaining that rank.”]

### On ordination. From the Council of Neocaesarea.

### CCCCVIII

*(Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 11; Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 50; Burchard, book II, chapter 10.)* A presbyter shall in no way be ordained before his thirtieth year, even if he is very worthy; this age must be observed. For our Lord was baptized in the thirtieth year of his life.

### On deacons. From the Council of Carthage.

### CCCIX

*(Third Council of Carthage, chapter 4; Burchard, book II, chapter 11.)* It has likewise been decreed that before the age of twenty-five neither deacons are to be ordained nor virgins consecrated.

### Whoever cuts off part of his finger should not be a cleric. From a letter of Pope Felix.

### CCCCX

*(Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 28; Burchard, book II, chapter 14.)* Whoever deliberately cuts off part of his finger is not admitted to the clergy by the canons. But if this happens to someone by accident, he may become a cleric; and if he is found already in the clergy, he is not to be expelled. [Note: See Innocent III, Book X, letter 124.]

### That the unlearned should not be ordained. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

### CCCCXI

*(Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 16; Burchard, book II, chapter 18.)* No one shall presume to promote the unlearned, or those diminished in any part of the body, to the clergy; for one who lacks learning cannot be fit for sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective may be offered to God. Likewise, concerning those who mutilate themselves. *(Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 17.)*

### That criminals should not be admitted to the clergy. From the same letter.

### CCCCXII

*(Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 18; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 50.)* Criminals are not to be admitted to the clergy. For the Apostle says: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy V).

[Col. 0273A] ### That those entangled in demonic and similar afflictions should not exercise sacred ministries. From the same letter.

[Note: Chapter 412 served as the heading in the Helmstedt edition. Since that heading did not fit chapter 413, which deals with an entirely different subject, we have separated the chapters so that nothing might delay the reader. We then added headings to these two chapters from our own sources.]

### CCCCXIII

*(Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 19; Burchard, book II, chapter 20.)* We have indeed discovered that unlawful things break out to such an extent that those entangled in demonic and similar afflictions are permitted to handle the most sacred mysteries. And shortly afterward:

If divine law forbids one wounded or disabled in body from touching holy things, how much less is it fitting that dispensers of the heavenly gift be mentally stricken—which is the worse condition? [Note: See Book VIII of the Capitularies, chapter 51.]

### On the sons of concubines, that they should not be admitted to the clergy. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.

### CCCCXIV

*(Third Council of Orléans, chapter 9; Burchard, book II, chapter 19.)* Concerning those who have sons by concubines, and who have had legitimate wives, and after their wives’ deaths have publicly joined themselves to concubines, we have judged that this rule must be observed: just as we do not remove those who, through ignorance, have already been ordained as clerics, so we decree that such men are not to be ordained in the future.

### On the abductors of virgins and widows. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 61.

### CCCCXV

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 64.)* Abductors of virgins and widows [Note: See below, Book II, chapter 159] who afterward, with the consent of the parents, took them into marriage as though betrothed, under the name of a dowry, shall be subjected to public penance. After the public penance, so that they do not fall into worse things, they shall again come together and strive thereafter to devote themselves to almsgiving and to every other action of a saving way of life, until by mutual consent they are able to abstain from conjugal relations.

### On illegitimate sons.

### CCCCXVI

*(Council of Meaux, chapter 64, and Gratian, part I, question 7, chapter “Tali conjugio.”)* Sons begotten from such a disreputable union before the less commendable marriage are in no way to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignity; nor are those born from such a marriage to be admitted to ecclesiastical orders, unless perhaps the greatest advantage or necessity of the Church requires it, or an evident preeminence of merits commends them.

### On the same matter. From Roman law.

### CCCCXVII

*(Institutes of Gaius, title 4.)* If anyone contracts incestuous or unlawful marriages, he has neither a wife nor children. [Note: See Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 8, chapters 4 and 5.] For those who are born from such a conception, although they appear to be born, are considered in no way to have a father and are treated as though they had been conceived in adultery.

### Ecclesiastical dignity does not admit sons born from illicit intercourse.

### CCCCXVIII

Therefore those whom the public laws do not admit, but reject as though sprinkled with the stains of infamy, and despise as if degenerate, ecclesiastical dignity in no way receives—especially since nothing stained can properly be offered to God or applied to his service.

### That no one should receive another’s cleric. In the Apostolic Canons.

### CCCCXIX

*(Apostolic Canons, chapter 16.)* If a bishop in whose presence it is established that another’s clerics are staying receives them as clerics, perhaps disregarding as worthless the prohibition imposed against them, he shall be deprived of communion as a teacher of disturbance.

### That no one should receive an alien cleric. From the decrees of Bishop Leo.

### CCCCXX

*(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 39.)* No one shall receive or solicit another’s cleric against the will of his bishop, unless perhaps the matter is agreed between the giver and the recipient as an act of charity. For he is guilty of a grave injury who dares to reject or retain what is more useful or more precious from his brother’s church. [In Leo’s letter: “to entice.”]

### On clerical fugitives.

### CCCCXXI

*(Decrees of Leo I, chapter 39.)* Therefore, if the matter concerns someone within the province, the metropolitan shall compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. But if he has withdrawn farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of your command. [Note: The Helmstedt edition and the Paris manuscript read, “he shall be recalled by the authority of his command.” But the sense is opposed to this. Moreover, all editions of Leo’s letters read *tui* (“your”). The matter here concerns the authority of Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, in the provinces of Illyricum. See Book V, *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 27, section 5.]

### As above.

### CCCCXXII

*(Rule of Saint Ferreolus, chapter 20; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 26.)* It has been decided that a fugitive cleric, or a monk abandoning discipline, should be recalled as a contemptuous person.

### 191. On the same matter. From the sayings of Bishop Basil.

[Col. 0274C] ### CCCCXXIII

*(Burchard, book II, chapter 228.)* If anyone discovers that a person, unable to endure ecclesiastical discipline, is planning flight, and does not immediately report him, let him have no doubt that he shares in the betrayal. He is to be excluded from the assembly of the brethren for as long as the fugitive can be recalled.

### That clerics should travel with letters from their bishop. From the Apostolic Canons.

### CCCCXXIV

*(Apostolic Canons, chapter 13; Burchard, book II, chapter 136.)* If any cleric or layperson travels to another city and is received without letters of commendation, both the one who received him and the one received shall be deprived of communion.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Antioch.

[Col. 0274D] ### CCCCXXV

*(Council of Antioch, chapter 7; Burchard, book II, chapter 137.)* No traveler is to be received without peaceful letters—that is, letters of commendation.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Chalcedon.

### CCCCXXVI

*(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 13; Burchard, book II, chapter 139.)* Traveling clerics and readers are nowhere to minister in another city without letters of commendation from their own bishop.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Agde.

### CCCCXXVII

*(Council of Agde, chapter 52; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 149; Burchard, book II, chapter 44.)* No one shall grant communion to a presbyter, deacon, or cleric traveling without letters from his bishop.

### 192. On the same matter. From the Council of Chalcedon.

### CCCCXXVIII

*(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 11; Burchard, book II, chapter 143.)* We have decreed that all the poor and needy who require ecclesiastical assistance are, when they travel, to be commended only with a letter of proof or with ecclesiastical letters of peace, and not with letters of commendation, because letters of commendation ought to be issued only to persons of higher standing.

### On the same matter. From the same council.

### CCCCXXIX

*(Council of Agde, chapter 38; Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 130, and Book VII, chapter 195; Burchard, book II, chapter 142.)* A cleric without letters of commendation from his bishop shall have no permission to wander about. The same rule of the present judgment is also to be observed among monks.

### On the same matter. From the Apostolic Canons.

### CCCCXXX

*(Apostolic Canons, chapter 34.)* No bishop, presbyter, or deacon traveling from elsewhere is to be received without letters of commendation. When they bring written documents, they are to be examined carefully and then received.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Sardica.

### CCCCXXXI

*(Council of Sardica, chapter 18.)* Bishop Januarius said: “Let your holiness also establish that no bishop may solicit the minister of another bishop’s city and ordain him in his own parishes.”

### As above.

### CCCCXXXII

*(Council of Sardica, chapter 19.)* Bishop Hosius said: “We have also unanimously established this: whoever from another parish wishes to ordain another’s minister without the consent and will of that minister’s bishop shall have an ordination that is not valid.”

### On the same matter. From the Council of Laodicea.

### CCCCXXXIII

*(Council of Laodicea, chapter 41; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 59; Burchard, book II, chapter 45.)* A priest or cleric ought not to travel without canonical letters.

[Col. 0275D] ### On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 50.

### 434. (Council of Meaux, canon 50)

Presbyters or any clerics are not to be received into another parish without a canonical letter (*formata*), nor retained there, nor even permitted to minister. Those accused of wrongdoing, however, are to be excluded and expelled by everyone from the parishes in which they lie concealed, until they return to the bishop from whom they are known to have fled.

[Note: The Helmstedt edition and the Paris manuscript agree on this passage. In the commonly printed editions of the Council of Meaux, however, it reads: “and let them be expelled from the parishes in which they wish to remain, until …” We possess an ancient manuscript in which the canons of this Council of Meaux are written; there the passage reads: “and let them be expelled from the parishes in which they wish to remain,” etc.]

### On the same matter. From the same council.

### 435. (Council of Meaux, canon 51; Burchard, Book II, chapter 144)

Those who come with their superiors from other provinces to our provinces without a canonical letter are not to be permitted to minister. Even if they have brought one, and are found suitable to minister, they are to be instructed in how religiously and diligently they should perform the sacred ministry [the Helmstedt edition reads: “how they should perform it,”] and in which places they ought not to exercise it.

### On the same matter. From the same source.

### 436. (Council of Meaux, same place)

Clerics, if they are presented for ordination by such men, must be instructed to send them back to the bishops from whose parishes they were taken, so that they may either be ordained there or bring canonical letters from the bishop of whose diocese they are, as canonical authority teaches.

The Council of Nicaea established that this procedure should be observed among bishops in the preparation of letters.

### 437. (Ivo, part VI, chapter 453)

No one who has even slight knowledge of the Greek language is unaware that the elements of the Greek alphabet also express numbers. Therefore, lest any fraud of falsification be rashly attempted in the preparation of canonical letters—which Latin custom calls *formatae*—the 318 Fathers assembled at Nicaea most beneficially devised and established the following: that canonical letters should have this method of calculation or reckoning, namely, that the first Greek letters of “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” should be included in the reckoning: Π, Υ, Α. These letters represent the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one.

The first letter of the name of the apostle Peter is also to be included, namely Π, which signifies eighty. The first letter of the name of the writer of the letter; the second, of the person to whom it is written; the third, of the recipient; the fourth, of the city from which it is written; and the number of the indiction of the current period are likewise to be included. Thus, when all these Greek letters—which, as we have said, express numbers—have been added together, the letter is to contain whatever total has been obtained.

In addition, the letter is to contain separately the number ninety-nine, which according to the Greek letters is expressed by ΑΜΗΝ. Thus the three letters mentioned above, Π, Υ, Α, together with the first letter of Peter’s name, Π, produce the numbers 561. Π, which is the first letter in the name of the supreme Father, counts as 80. Υ, which is the first letter in the name of the Son, counts as 400. Α, which is the first letter in the name of the Holy Spirit, signifies 1. If Π, the first letter in Peter’s name, that is, 80, is added, the result is 561.

ΑΜΗΝ, written at the end of the aforesaid letter, signifies 99. Α counts as 1, Μ as 40, Η as 8, and Ν as 50; together they make 99. If the entire total is joined together, the letter contains the number 660.

But for the benefit of those who know less, the Greek letters themselves should apparently be set down together with their proper numerical values.

The numbers are counted as follows: *mia* [one], *dia* [two], *tria* [three], *tessera* [four], *pente* [five], *exa* [six], *epta* [seven], *ogda* [eight], *nea* [nine], *deca* [ten], *icosi* [twenty], *triepta* [thirty], *serenta* [forty], *nirenta* [fifty], *exenta* [sixty], *ebdominta* [seventy], *ogdominta* [eighty], *enneminta* [ninety], *ecaton* [one hundred], *diacos* [two hundred], *tetracos* [three hundred], *pentacos* [four hundred], *exacos* [five hundred], *ebdacos* [six hundred], *ogdacos* [seven hundred], *ennacos* [eight hundred], etc.

[Note: These forms are very corrupt. But since they are easy to correct, we have preferred to change nothing.]

### Model of a canonical letter

### 438. (Ivo, part VI, chapter 434)

In the name of Π, the Father, and Υ, the Son, and Α, the Holy Spirit.

Rathbodus, humble servant of the holy Church of Trier and of its people, to Rotbertus, reverend bishop of the holy Church of Metz: in Christ, the prince of shepherds, a lasting share in the joy of prosperity and the glory of perpetuity.

Faithfully observing the most salutary decrees of the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, we canonically approach your God-worthy and devout fraternity, and, under the designation of a canonical letter, reverently come before your holiness, informing you that we have given these letters of dismissal to the present priest of ours, named Gislemarus. Having been ecclesiastically educated in our diocese, we advanced him from the clerical order to the rank of presbyter, so that, fortified by these canonical letters and with our permission, he may lawfully dwell in your parish under the protection and governance of your beloved affection. We entrust him to you to be canonically fostered and governed in the bosom of holy Mother Church.

We have therefore decided to secure this letter on every side with Greek letters and have judged it appropriate to seal it with the ring of our Church.

May Christ, the prince of shepherds, through the intercession of blessed Peter, to whom the Lord’s sheepfold was specially entrusted, long preserve your fraternity unharmed for the care of his flock. Amen.

Π. Υ. Α. Π. Ρ. Ο. Ϲ. Υ. Θ. ΑΜΗΝ.

The sum of these is 1,539.

Given at Trier on the Ides of October, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 906, in the ninth indiction.

Π. Υ. Α. Π. Δ. Ρ. Δ. Θ.

### Another letter

### 439. (Ivo, part VI, chapter 435)

To the most reverend and most holy Rathbodus, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, Dado, devoted servant of Christ’s flock in the Church of Verdun, sends in the Lord, the true King, the highest happiness and blessedness.

(Burchard, Book II, chapter 227.) Since the holy Catholic Church is ready to follow the teachings of the Gospel, which say, “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man,” etc.; and since the Apostle commands us to pursue hospitality and to share in the needs of holy men, nevertheless—[read: “on account of those who have”] a seared conscience, saying that they are simple when they are filled with diabolical cunning, and claiming that they travel from place to place as an act of piety when in fact their own wickedness has made them fugitives, and saying that they are uncertain about the sacred ministry when they are not—it has been established by the holy Fathers that no foreign and unknown cleric is to be received by any bishop or enthroned in his Church unless he has from his own bishop a letter which the canons call a *formata*.

Therefore we make known to your fatherhood that the present brother of ours, the bearer of these letters, named Adruinus, was not expelled by us on account of his wickedness. Rather, at the request of our brothers, because he had belonged to our household [Note: See above, chapter 399], we gave him the freedom canonically received from the horn of the altar, and ordained him to the priesthood. We also prepared these letters of dismissal or commendation for him and send him to your most beloved fraternity, so that he may be able to remain in your parish under your sacred governance and protection.

I, Dado, humble bishop, in the name of Π, the Father, and Υ, the Son, and Α, the Holy Spirit, and in the unity of the holy Church, in which the power of binding and loosing was given to Peter, absolve the presbyter Adruinus of the city of Verdun, and, in the ninth indiction, give you permission, Rathbodus, venerable archbishop, to enthrone him in whatever church of your parish you wish.

May almighty God deem it worthy to preserve your beloved fatherhood, adorned with the flowers of virtue. Amen.

Π. Υ. Α. Π. Δ. Α. Ρ. Δ. Θ.

778.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 906, in the ninth indiction.

### On ordination. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

### 440. (Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 11; Ivo, part VI, chapter 74)

Let them know that the ordinations of presbyters and deacons, which ought to be performed only at fixed times and on fixed days, are to be celebrated toward evening on the Saturday fast of the fourth [read: that is, the first and fourth] month, the seventh, and the tenth, and also at the beginning of Lent and on the middle day of Lent. Let no one presume to prefer any presbyter or deacon for any advantage whatsoever to those who were ordained before them.

### How a bishop ought to conduct an ordination. From the Council of Nantes.

### 441. (Council of Nantes, chapter 11; Burchard, Book II, chapter 1)

When a bishop is preparing to conduct ordinations, all those who wish to enter the sacred ministry are to be summoned to the city on the Wednesday before the ordination itself, together with the archpresbyters who are to present them. Then the bishop must send from his side priests and other prudent men who are knowledgeable in divine law and experienced in ecclesiastical decrees. They are carefully to investigate the life, lineage, homeland, age, education, place where each was brought up, whether he is well educated, and whether he is instructed in the law of the Lord.

Above all, they must investigate whether he firmly holds the Catholic faith and can affirm it in simple words. Those entrusted with this task must take care lest, out of favor or desire for any gift, they depart from the truth and bring before the bishop’s hands someone unworthy or insufficiently suitable to receive the sacred orders.

If they do so, the one who approached unworthily will be removed from the altar, while those who attempted to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, already condemned before God, will lose their ecclesiastical dignity.

They are therefore to be carefully examined for three successive days. Then, on Saturday, those who are found approved are to be presented to the bishop.

### From the Council of Meaux

### 442. (Council of Meaux, chapter 52; Burchard, Book II, chapter 4)

Those who are requested for ordination are in no way to be ordained unless they have remained for at least one year in a definite and religious place, or even in a city, so that certainty may be gained concerning their life, conduct, and teaching.

[Note: See above, chapter 389.]

### How a bishop who is to be ordained is to be examined. From the Council of Carthage.

### 443. (Council of Carthage IV, chapter 1; Burchard, Book I, chapter 8; Ivo, part V, chapter 62; Gratian, Distinction 23, chapter 2)

The man who is to be ordained bishop must first be examined as to whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, temperate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, always careful in his own affairs, humble, approachable, merciful, educated, instructed in the law of the Lord, cautious in understanding the Scriptures, and trained in ecclesiastical doctrines.

Above all, it must be determined whether he affirms the teachings of the faith in simple words: namely, whether he confirms that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God; whether he proclaims the whole Trinity to be one divinity, of one essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; whether he declares each individual person in the Trinity to be fully God and all three persons to be one God; and whether he believes that the divine incarnation took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit but in the Son alone.

Thus, he must believe that the one who was the Son in the divinity of God the Father became, in humanity, the son of a human mother: true God from the Father, true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul; that in him the two natures—man and God—are one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord; and that he, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is the [creator], author, lord, and ruler of all creatures.

He must believe that Christ suffered with a true suffering of the flesh, died with a true death of his body, and rose with a true resurrection or resumption of his flesh [elsewhere: “and a true resumption of his soul”], in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

He must also be asked whether he believes that the God of the New and Old Testaments—that is, of the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles—is one and the same author; whether the devil became evil not by creation but by choice; whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh which we bear, and not of another; whether he believes that judgment will take place and that each person will receive punishments or rewards for what he has done in this flesh; whether he does not condemn marriage; whether he does not condemn second marriages; whether he does not blame the eating of meat; whether he communicates with penitents who have been reconciled; whether in baptism all sins are forgiven, both the original sin contracted and those voluntarily committed; and whether no one outside the Catholic Church can be saved.

When he has been examined and found fully instructed in these matters, then he is to be ordained.

[Note: Regino shortened the final part of this chapter. Yet it is of great importance, and we have therefore judged it appropriate to restore it here for the benefit of readers. The first chapter of the fourth Council of Carthage reads as follows: “When he has been examined in all these matters and found fully instructed, then, with the consent of the clergy and laity and the assembly of all the bishops of the province, especially with the authority or presence of the metropolitan, he is to be ordained bishop.” Burchard and Ivo, because they received their text from Regino, give the ending of this chapter in shortened form. Gratian appears to have obtained it from another source rather than from these collections, since he cites the passage in full.]

How presbyters or deacons are to be examined before or after ordination, and how they are to be questioned concerning their ministry, has already been set out sufficiently at the beginning of this little book, where it is written what is to be required of a presbyter. Therefore it seems superfluous to repeat and reiterate what is already known to have been recorded.

**The First Book Ends.**

**The Second Book Begins.**

In the preceding book we noted in part what a bishop or his ministers ought to do with ecclesiastical persons and what ought to be investigated in his synod. Now, as the Lord grants, let us go through what ought to be done, or is necessary to be done, with secular persons and laypeople.

### How a bishop ought to go around his parish. From the Council of Rouen.

### I. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 90)

When a bishop travels through his diocese, the archdeacon or archpresbyter ought to precede him by one or two days through the parishes he is going to visit. After summoning the people, he must announce the arrival of their own shepherd and, by the authority of the holy canons, strictly command and threateningly proclaim that all must unfailingly attend his synod on the appointed day; for anyone absent without serious necessity is unquestionably to be excluded from Christian communion.

Then, taking with him the presbyters who ought to provide service to the bishop in that place, he should strive to correct and amend whatever he can concerning lesser and lighter cases, so that when the bishop arrives he will not be wearied by easier matters or need to remain there longer than the expenses permit.

For the Lord says to Moses concerning such helpers: “That they may bear the burden of the people with you, so that you alone may not be burdened” (Numbers 11). Blessed John the Baptist also preceded the Lord’s coming by preaching, saying: “Do penance,” etc. (Matthew 3). And again: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (ibid.).

Since the bishop appears to act in Christ’s place, he must therefore be received with joy, fear, and the highest reverence by the people subject to him, so that what the Apostle says to the disciples may deservedly be said of them with praise: “I bear you witness that you received me as an angel of God, as Jesus Christ” (Galatians 4).

### Concerning the jurors of the synod. As above.

### II. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 91)

When the bishop is seated in the synod, after a suitable address he should call into the midst of the assembly seven men from the people of that parish—or more or fewer, as he judges expedient—men who are mature, honorable, and truthful. After bringing forward the relics of the saints, he must bind each of them by the following oath.

### Synodal oath

### III. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 92)

From this moment onward, whatever you know or have heard, or may later investigate, that has been done in this parish, or may in future be done, against the will of God and proper Christianity—if it occurs during your lifetime, and comes to your knowledge by any means—if you know or are informed that it is a synodal matter and pertains to the bishop’s ministry, you must not conceal it in any way from the bishop of Trier or from his envoy whom he orders to investigate it, whenever he questions you about it: neither for love, nor for fear, nor for reward, nor because of kinship.

So may God help you and these relics of the saints.

### Let the others swear likewise.

(Burchard, same place, chapter 93.) You shall observe this oath which this man has sworn concerning a synodal matter, insofar as you know or have heard it, or may investigate it from this day forward.

So may God help you.

### The bishop’s address

### IV. (Burchard, same place, chapter 94)

See to it, brothers, that you render your oaths to the Lord. For you have not sworn to a human being but to God your creator. We, who are his ministers, do not covet your earthly possessions but seek the salvation of your souls. Take care that you conceal nothing, lest another’s sin become your condemnation.

After this he is to question them in the following order.

### V. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 94)

1. Is there in this parish a homicide who has killed a person willingly, or for the sake of greed or plunder, or by accident, or unwillingly and under compulsion, or in revenge for relatives—which we call a feud—or in war, or at the command of his lord, or has killed his own slave?

2. Is there anyone who is a parricide or fratricide, who has killed his father, mother, brother, sister, maternal uncle, or any relative?

3. Is there anyone who has killed a presbyter, deacon, or any cleric, or cut off one of his limbs?

4. Is there any man or woman who has crushed his or her own infant, or suffocated it under the weight of clothing? And did this happen before baptism or after baptism? Or did an infant become ill and die without baptism through the negligence of its parent?

5. Is there any man or woman who has caused another woman’s fetus to be expelled? Or has any woman, of her own will, expelled her own fetus and caused an abortion?

6. Is there any woman who, having conceived through fornication and fearing that it would be discovered, has thrown her own infant into water or hidden it in the earth—an act they call *morth*?

7. Is there anyone who has killed his wife without legal process or certain proof?

8. Is there any woman who has killed her husband or another person with poisonous herbs or deadly potions, or taught another to do so?

9. Is there any man or woman who has done this, or taught another to do it, so that a man cannot beget children or a woman conceive?

10. Is there anyone who has killed his own slave outside judicial proceedings, or any woman who, inflamed by jealous fury, has killed her own female slave?

11. Is there anyone who, driven on by the devil, has killed himself?

12. If someone wounded people in war and does not know whether anyone died from that wound; and if someone is accused of having killed a person but denies it.

13. If anyone participated in a plan for a person to be killed but was not present at the deed, and yet the person was killed through his counsel and encouragement.

14. Is there anyone who has mutilated another’s hands, feet, tongue, or testicles, or torn out another’s eyes?

Next, inquiry is to be made concerning adultery and fornication.

15. If any married man has committed adultery with another man’s wife; or if any wife has committed adultery with another woman’s husband.

16. If any man who has a wife has at the same time kept a concubine, whether his own female slave or another woman.

17. If any man has abandoned his lawful wife and taken another in marriage.

18. If any woman has abandoned her own husband and joined herself to another.

19. If, after a divorce has taken place, they separate from one another and remain in that condition.

20. If anyone, without his wife’s consent, abandons a lawful marriage and enters a monastery.

21. If anyone abandons his wife, even though she is culpable, without the bishop’s judgment.

22. If any woman has committed fornication with the knowledge of her husband.

23. If any man without a wife has committed fornication with another man’s spouse; or if any woman without a husband has committed fornication with another woman’s husband.

24. If any man without a wife has committed fornication with a woman who has no husband.

25. If a lay virgin has committed adultery with a young man.

26. If anyone has not taken the girl to whom he was betrothed and has broken the pledge of betrothal.

27. If anyone has abducted another man’s betrothed and joined her to himself.

28. If anyone has carried off any woman—virgin or widow—and joined her to himself in marriage; and whether there are any who consented to or assisted in this.

29. If anyone has committed adultery with a Jewish woman; or if a Jew or pagan has committed adultery with a Christian woman.

30. If anyone has abducted a nun or a widow consecrated to God and taken her in marriage; or, if they consented, has committed fornication with them.

31. If anyone is accused of having committed adultery with a woman while her husband was alive and, when he soon afterward died, is known to have taken the same woman.

32. If any woman says that her husband cannot have intercourse with her, and for this reason seeks separation and wishes to take another husband.

33. If anyone has committed adultery with his spiritual mother or taken her in marriage; likewise, if he has committed adultery with his goddaughter whom he received from the sacred font or held before the bishop.

34. If anyone has taken a close relative or blood relation in marriage, or committed fornication with her.

35. If anyone irrationally—that is, against nature—has sexual relations with males or with mute animals.

36. If any woman has practiced procuring or pandering.

37. If anyone in his own house connives with his own female slaves or *geneciarii* [textile workers] in committing adultery.

### Concerning theft and sacrilege

38. Inquiry is to be made whether anyone is a thief or sacrilegious person who has broken into God’s churches, stolen anything from a church, publicly carried it off, or secretly taken it; or whether anyone is a robber, plunderer, or despoiler of God’s church. Although such matters must be corrected and compensated according to human law, penance nevertheless belongs to the bishop.

### Concerning perjury

39. Inquiry is to be made whether anyone is perjured, or has knowingly sworn falsely for the sake of earthly gain; and whether he did so unknowingly or under compulsion, at the command of his lord, or to ransom his limbs and life; or whether anyone knowingly not only swore falsely but also led others into perjury.

### Concerning false testimony

40. Inquiry is to be made whether anyone has knowingly given false testimony against another, since this is a capital crime, and what harm anyone suffered as a result of that testimony.

41. Inquiry is to be made whether anyone has stolen a free person, another’s slave, or a foreigner and outsider; whether he has deceived someone by flattery, sold him, and sent him into captivity outside his homeland; or whether anyone has sold a Christian slave to a Jew or pagan, or whether Jews themselves sell Christian slaves.

### Concerning enchanters and diviners

42. Inquiry is to be made whether anyone is a magician, soothsayer, enchanter, diviner, or sorcerer.

43. (Burchard, Book X, chapter 32.) If anyone makes vows to trees, springs, or certain stones as though to altars, or brings a candle or any offering there, as though some divinity existed there capable of bringing good or evil.

44. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 94, §43; and Book X, chapter 18.) Inquiry is to be made whether any swineherd, cowherd, hunter, or other such person says diabolical charms over bread or herbs and over certain abominable bindings, and hides them either in a tree or throws them at a fork in the road or a crossroads, in order to free his own animals from plague and destruction and bring loss upon another’s. No faithful person can doubt that all these things are idolatry, and therefore they must be utterly eradicated.

45. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 94, §44; Book X, chapter 29.) Inquiry is to be made whether there is any woman who claims that by certain magic practices and incantations she can alter people’s minds—that is, turn hatred into love or love into hatred, or damage or steal people’s possessions. And if there is any woman who says that, transformed into the likeness of women and accompanied by a troop of demons, she rides on certain beasts on appointed nights and is counted among their company, such a woman is to be expelled from the parish in every way.

### Concerning carrion and blood

46. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 94, §45 and following.) Inquiry is to be made whether anyone eats blood, carrion, or flesh torn apart by a beast.

47. If anyone refuses to return to peace because of hatred, or has sworn—which is contrary to God—that he will never be reconciled to his brother, which is a sin unto death.

48. If anyone drinks a liquid in which a weasel, mouse, or some other unclean animal has been killed.

49. If anyone does not observe the Lenten fast, or the fast of the Ember Days, or the Greater Litany or Rogations, or a fast imposed by the bishop on account of any affliction.

50. (Burchard, Book X, chapter 25.) If there is anyone who drinks, eats, or carries upon himself something which he believes can turn aside God’s judgment.

51. (Burchard, Book X, chapter 17.) If anyone at the Kalends of January has done something invented by pagans, and observes days, the moon, or months, and hopes that their effective power can turn something either for the better or for the worse.

52. If anyone, when beginning any work, says something else there, or performs something else by any magical art, instead of doing everything in the name of the Lord, as the Apostle teaches. For we must not invoke demons for our assistance, but God. Likewise, when gathering medicinal herbs, one ought to say the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and nothing else.

53. Inquiry is also to be made whether women, in their spinning or in setting up their looms, say or observe anything except, as was stated above, doing everything in the name of the Lord.

54. If anyone unjustly retains offerings—that is, alms belonging to deceased relatives.

55. If anyone sings diabolical songs over a dead person during the night, and drinks and eats, as though rejoicing over his death; and whether the dead are kept elsewhere in nightly vigils except in a church.

56. If there is any Christian who does not receive Communion three times a year—that is, at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—unless he has been removed from Communion by the judgment of the bishop or priests on account of deadly crimes.

57. Is there anyone who performs any work on Sunday or on the principal feast days; and do all unfailingly attend matins, Mass, and vespers on those days?

58. If anyone treats excommunication as nothing, and whether anyone has fellowship with an excommunicated person.

59. If anyone has not observed the measure of penance imposed upon him.

60. If anyone dishonors, strikes, or curses his father or mother.

61. If anyone vomits after receiving the Eucharist because of drunkenness.

62. If there is anyone who withholds his tithe from God and his saints.

63. If there is anyone so perverse and estranged from God that he does not even come to church on Sunday.

64. Whether swineherds and other herdsmen come to church on Sunday and hear Mass. Likewise on other feast days.
