[Note: This is how the Helmstedt edition and Burchard, Book I, chapter 94, §63, read. The Paris manuscript, however, reads: “Whether swineherds … come.” Likewise, “on the principal feast days.” A manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll, containing the decrees of Pope Eutychianus, reads: “Whether swineherds and other herdsmen do not come to church on Sunday and do not hear Mass. Likewise on other feast days.”]

65. If anyone does not come to confession even once a year—that is, at the beginning of Lent—and undertake penance for his sins.

66. If there is anyone who pursues constant drunkenness. For drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God.

67. If anyone, despising his own presbyter, comes to church in another parish, receives Communion there, and gives his tithe there.

68. Inquiry is to be made concerning beggars who travel through the lands, and whether each person feeds a poor person from his own household.

69. (Burchard, Book I, chapter 93, §68 and following.) Whether in each parish there are deans appointed throughout the villages—truthful men who fear God—who admonish the others to go to church for matins, Mass, and vespers, and to perform no work on feast days; and whether, if any of them transgresses, they immediately report it to the presbyter. The same is to be done concerning sexual immorality and every evil deed.

70. If there is anyone who, disregarding the bishop’s or his own presbyter’s ban and excommunication, treats them as nothing.

71. Whether the parishioners render their presbyter the honor due to him, or whether anyone dishonors him by word or deed and disregards his admonitions.

72. If there is anyone who refuses hospitality to a foreigner or traveler.

73. Inquiry is to be made concerning which festivals they observe.

74. Whether godparents teach their godchildren the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or have them taught.

75. If four or five or more people have killed one person.

76. If there is anyone who opposes the bishop or his ministers so that peasants or slaves are not beaten naked with rods on account of crimes committed.

77. Inquiry is to be made whether anyone wishes to regard as his own slave a foreigner who fled his homeland because of pagan attacks or persecution, merely because he stayed in his house and served him for days or years in the place of a hired laborer, and whether he dares to sell or give him to anyone.

78. If anyone sells his grain or wine using an unjust measure, although the Lord says: “Let your bushel be fair and your sextarius fair.”

79. It must also be declared how grave an offense it is to demand interest and seek to grow rich from another’s loan, and that the sacred canons command such people to be expelled from the Church.

80. If anyone kills a Jew or pagan out of greed.

81. If anyone, while insane, kills a person.

82. If anyone cuts down a tree and, while engaged in necessary work, someone coming beneath the tree is unexpectedly crushed.

83. If anyone pursues conspiracies and seditious plots.

84. If anyone presumes to harass a church or cleric.

85. Inquiry is to be made concerning lay deserters and traitors.

86. Inquiry is to be made concerning confraternities and associations of brotherhoods, and how they are conducted in the parish.

87. If anyone presumes to sing obscene and laugh-provoking songs around a church.

88. If anyone, upon entering a church, is accustomed to devote himself to stories and does not listen attentively to the divine words, and whether he leaves the church before Mass is finished.

89. Whether men and women offer the offering—that is, bread and wine—at Masses; and, if the men do not, whether their wives offer on their behalf, for themselves and all their household, as is contained in the canon.

These chapters, which we have noted in order, ought to be strengthened by canonical decrees.

### On the penance of homicides. From the Council of Tribur.

### VI.

Penance for homicides is not to be carried out according to differing customs, as previously, but according to one custom in each bishopric.

### As above

(Burchard, Book I, chapter 1.) If anyone has committed homicide willingly, persuaded by the devil, he ought, according to the decrees of the canons and the judgment of the bishops, to receive such penance.

First of all, he must not have permission to enter the church for the next forty days; he must walk barefoot and use no vehicle; he must wear woolen garments without breeches; he must carry no weapons; and during these forty days he must take nothing except bread [Col. 0287C] and salt, and drink only pure water. He must have no communion in food or drink with the other Christians or with another penitent before the forty days have been completed; and no one else may eat from the food that he takes. After consideration of the person’s status or illness, however, something from fruits, vegetables, or legumes may be granted out of mercy, as seems appropriate—especially if someone committed the homicide under compulsion and not willingly. He must also be absolutely forbidden, by canonical authority, to have intercourse with any woman during these days, to approach his own wife, or to sleep with any man. He must remain near the church, before whose doors he is to bewail his sins day and night; and he must not go from place to place, but remain in one place during these [Col. 0287D] forty days. If he happens to have people lying in wait for his life, his penance is to be postponed meanwhile until peace with his enemies has been restored to him by the bishop. If he is held by illness so that he cannot perform penance properly, the penance is to be postponed until he has been restored to health. If, however, he is held by a long 217 illness, it will belong to the bishop’s judgment to determine how he should arrange to heal the guilty and sick man. When the forty days have been completed, he is to wash with water, resume the clothing and footwear that he had cast off, and cut his hair.

### What he must observe during the first year

VII. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 2.) During the first year after the forty days, he must abstain throughout that entire year from wine, mead, [Col. 0288A] honeyed beer, meat, cheese, and fatty fish, except on feast days celebrated in that bishopric by the whole people, and except perhaps when he is on a long journey, on campaign, detained for a long time at the lord’s court, or detained by illness. In such cases he may redeem Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday by one denarius, or by the value of one denarius, or by feeding three poor persons—provided, however, that he uses only one of these three alternatives. After he has returned home or has been restored to health, he is to have no permission to redeem the abstinence.

### What he must observe during the following two years

VIII. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapters 3–4.) When the year has been completed, he is to enter the church and be granted the kiss of peace. In the second and third years he is likewise to fast, except that he has the power to redeem Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday [Col. 0288B] wherever he may be. In all other respects he must carefully observe everything prescribed for the first year.

218. ### What he must observe during the remaining four years

IX. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 5.) Four years then remain, during each of which he must fast for three Lents. One is before Easter, with the other Christians, abstaining from wine, mead, honeyed beer, cheese, and fatty fish. The second is before the Nativity of Saint John. If anything remains of the forty days, he is to complete it after the mass of Saint John. He is to fast the third before Christmas, as stated above. During the four years just mentioned, he may eat whatever he wishes on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, but he must observe Wednesday and Friday in every respect and must not redeem them in any way [Col. 0288C]. When these observances have been completed, he is to receive Holy Communion.

### Concerning one who committed homicide deliberately. From the Council of Ancyra

X. (Council of Ancyra, canon 21; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 1; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 13.) Those who have committed deliberate homicide are indeed to submit themselves continually to penance, but they are to attain completion only toward the end of life.

219. ### On the same matter. From the Council of Reims

XI. (Council of Reims, year 630, canon 9; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 14.) If someone voluntarily commits homicide—not resisting violence, but using force—and kills an innocent person who was simply going on his way, no communion whatsoever is to be granted to him. Nevertheless, if he performs penance, the communion of the viaticum is not to be denied him at the end of his life [Col. 0288D].

### On the same matter. From the Council of Agde

XII. (Council of Agde, canon 37; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 29.) Accordingly, we have judged that homicides and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion, unless they have washed away the crimes they committed by the satisfaction of penance.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Nantes

XIII. (Council of Nantes, canon 17; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 12.) If someone has deliberately and treacherously killed a man, let him submit himself to perpetual penance. If it is established that this was done publicly, and he is a layman, let him be removed for five years from the communion of prayers; after five years let him be received into the communion of prayers [Note: [Col. 0287D] The following passages are not extant in the manuscript codex]; [Col. 0289A] but let him not offer at the same time, nor touch the Lord’s body. After persevering for fourteen years, let him then be received into full communion with offerings.

### On the same matter. From the same source

XIV. (Council of Nantes, in the same place.) In Exodus the Lord says concerning homicides: “If anyone deliberately and treacherously kills a man, you shall drag him away from my altar, so that he may die” (Exodus 21).

### Concerning homicides committed unintentionally. From the Council of Ancyra

XV. (Council of Ancyra, canon 22; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 2; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 15.) Concerning homicides committed unintentionally, the earlier decision prescribed that completion should be attained after seven years of penance, whereas the second prescribed completion of a period of five years.

[Col. 0289B] 220. On the same matter. From a letter of Rabanus to Bishop Heribald

XVI. (RABANUS, Letter to Heribald, chapter 4; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 23.) For we read concerning those who have killed a man unintentionally that God, through the lawgiver, appointed cities of refuge, so that those who fled to them would be saved from the avenger of his neighbor’s blood and would not die. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: “This shall be the law concerning the homicide whose life is to be preserved. If someone strikes his neighbor without knowing it, and it is shown that he had borne no hatred against him yesterday or the day before, but had gone with him innocently into the forest to cut wood, and, while cutting the wood, the axe had slipped from his hand, or the iron had fallen from its handle and struck and killed his companion, let him flee to one of the cities mentioned above [Col. 0289C] and live” (Deuteronomy 19).

### On the same matter. From the Council of Worms, chapter 5

XVII. (Council of Worms, canon 29; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 21.) It often happens that, while someone is engaged in necessary work and cuts down a tree, a person coming beneath it is crushed [Note: [Col. 0289D] See the Saxon Law, chapter 11, and the Lombard Law, book I, title 9, chapter 5.] and therefore, if this occurred through the will or negligence of the person cutting down the tree, he must submit entirely to penance as a homicide. But if this occurred not by his intention but through his negligence, then indeed [Note: [Col. 0290D] From an old manuscript codex of the Royal Library.] [this sentence concerning him] does not apply; rather, while the one man was perhaps occupied with necessary work, the other unexpectedly came beneath the tree and was crushed beneath it, the tree-cutter is not held liable as a homicide.

[Col. 0289D] 221. On the same matter. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 17

XVIII. (Council of Tribur, canon 36; BURCHARD, book VI, [Col. 0289D] chapter 22.) If two brothers cut down trees in a forest, and, when the fall of one tree was approaching, one brother called “Beware!” to the other, and the latter, fleeing, fell into the tree’s crushing fall and died, the surviving brother is to be judged innocent of his brother’s blood.

### On the same matter. From the same source

XIX. (Council of Tribur, canon 37.) If a mother places an infant beside the hearth, and another man pours water into a cauldron, and, when the water has boiled, the infant dies after being scalded by it, the mother is to do penance for negligence, while the other man is to be free from liability.

[Col. 0290A] ### On the same matter. From the same source, chapter 20

XX. (Council of Tribur, canon 52.) In the case of homicides committed unintentionally, the severity of the penance to which those who commit them are to submit is to remain in the bishop’s judgment.

### On the same matter. From the same source

XXI. (Council of Tribur, canon 53; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 36.) If someone unintentionally kills his own son, he is to do penance according to the rule for homicides committed unintentionally.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Nantes

XXII. (Council of Nantes, canon 18; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 16.) If someone commits homicide by accident and without intending it, he is to do penance for forty days on bread and water. After these have been completed, he is to be separated from the prayer of the faithful for two years; he is not to offer within the communion of prayer, but he is nevertheless not to communicate. 222. After five years [Col. 0290B] he is to be received into full communion. Abstinence from food is to remain at the priest’s discretion.

### He who kills a man through a blood-feud. From the Penitential, chapter 14

XXIII. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 32.) Whoever kills a man in revenge for his brother or other relatives is to do penance for one year, and during the following two years is to observe three Lents and the appointed fast days, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

### On the same matter. From the same source

XXIV. Whoever suddenly kills a man through anger, quarrelling, and drunkenness is to do penance for four years.

### On the same matter. From the same source

XXV. If a free man, at the command of his lord, kills a slave, he is to do penance for forty days. If a free man, at the command of his lord, kills an innocent man, he is to do penance for one year and during two further years observe three Lents and the appointed fast days.

### Concerning those who kill their slaves without a judge. From the Council of Agde, chapter 35

XXVI. (Council of Agde, canon 62; RABANUS, Letter to Heribald, chapter 3.) If someone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, he shall cleanse the guilt of blood by excommunication for two years.

### Concerning parricides and fratricides. From the Council of Mainz

XXVII. (Council of Worms, canon 30; BURCHARD, book X, chapter 34.) We decree that parricides and fratricides 223 are to persevere for the course of one year in prayer before the doors of the basilica, [Col. 0290D] imploring the Lord’s mercy. When the year has been completed, they are to be brought into the church; nevertheless, they are to stand among the hearers until the period of one year has ended. When these things have been completed, if the fruit of penance is seen in them, let them become participants in the Lord’s body and blood, so that they may not be hardened by despair. They are not to eat meat for all the days of their lives. They are to fast every day until the ninth hour, except on feast days and Sundays. They are to abstain from wine, mead, and honeyed beer for three days each week. They must not dare to carry weapons, except against pagans; and wherever they wish to go, they are not to be taken by any vehicle, but are to travel on their own feet. We place the duration of this penance in the judgment of the bishops, so that they may lengthen or shorten it according to their conduct. They are not to be separated from their wives, if they have wives. If they do not have wives and cannot maintain continence, they are to take legitimate women in marriage, lest they appear to fall into the abyss of fornication. If, however, the end of their lives comes before the courses of the two years mentioned above have been completed, the viaticum is not to be denied them. [Note: [Col. 0291D] In the excerpts from Burchard published by Stevartius, this chapter is attributed to a letter of Pope Nicholas to Charles, archbishop of Mainz, and his suffragans; whereas in Burchard’s *Decree* it is attributed to the Council of Tribur, where it is not found, nor is it found in the Council of Mainz, from which Regino cites it. The final part of this chapter, namely what follows the words “may lengthen or shorten it,” is not found in the editions of Burchard, although it does occur in the excerpts published by Stevartius. From this it may be inferred that the author of these excerpts used a copy of Burchard’s *Decree* more extensive than the commonly published editions. This final part of the chapter, which, as we have noted, is absent from the commonly published editions of Burchard, is found in chapter 30 of the Council of Worms.]

[Col. 0291B] 224. Also concerning parricides. From another Council of Mainz, chapter 20

XXVIII. (RABANUS, *Penitential*, chapter II, and Letter to Heribald, chapter 7; Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 20; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 35.) By the judgment passed between Cain and his brother Abel, the Lord showed how detestable a crime parricide is [Col. 0291B]. But because in our times parricides, as fugitives, wander through various places and devote themselves to various vices and the allurements of gluttony, it seems better to us that, remaining in one place, they should chastise themselves by strict penance, if perhaps they may deserve, through the Lord’s goodness, to receive pardon for their crime.

### That weapons and marriage are forbidden to parricides

XXIX. (Council of Mainz, in the same place; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 35.) For they are not permitted thereafter to take up the military belt or to be joined in marriage, because the sacred canons do not consent to this for them.

[Col. 0291C] 225. Concerning one who kills a man performing public penance. From Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 17

XXX. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 18.) Whoever kills a man performing public penance is to pay our ban threefold and pay his wergild to his nearest relatives. [Note: [Col. 0292D] See below, chapter 190 of this book.]

### Concerning one who kills a man in a church

XXXI. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 13; Book I of the Lombard Laws, title 9, chapters 2, 29, 30, 35 and following.) If someone kills men in a church either for a trivial reason or without reason, he is to pay compensation for the life. But if two men have quarreled outside, and one flees into a church, and there, defending himself, kills the other; and if he has no witnesses to this act, let him swear with twelve legitimate witnesses that he killed him while defending himself; after this he is nevertheless to be compelled to pay six hundred solidi to the church which he had polluted by that homicide, as well as our ban. The man who was killed is to lie without compensation [Col. 0291D]; thereafter the killer is to receive, according to canonical judgment, a penance appropriate to the crime he committed. [Note: [Col. 0292D] In a very old manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll, containing the first five books of the Capitularies, the following words are added immediately after “he is to receive a penance appropriate to the crime he committed”: “that is, for twenty-one years; for seven of these he is to make satisfaction on bread and water at the church door, removed from the prayer and communion of the faithful; for the other seven he is to be joined to the prayer of the faithful; after the remaining seven have passed, full communion is to follow completely. His abstinence is to be moderated by priestly provision. If he is his own slave,” and so forth.] If his own slave [Col. 0292A] committed this act, he is to be examined by the ordeal of boiling water to determine whether he did it willingly or in self-defense. If his hand is burned, his master is to pay to the church according to the slave’s wergild; or, if he wishes, he may hand him over to that same church. In the case of an ecclesiastical slave, a fiscal slave, or a beneficiary slave, we decree that his wergild is to be paid for him once; on a second occasion, the slave is to be handed over for punishment. Nevertheless, the inheritance of a free 226 man who has been sentenced to death on account of such a crime is to pass to his legitimate heirs. If a homicide of this kind is committed in the churchyard of a church whose door has been consecrated to the relics of the saints, it is likewise to be compensated and expiated. But if it has not been consecrated, compensation is to be made in the same way as for what is committed in violated immunity [Col. 0292B].

### Concerning injuries to priests or clerics. From the same source, chapter 14

XXXII. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 14; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 40, chapter 6.) The shedding of blood in a church with a staff, if the victim is a priest, is to be compensated threefold: two parts to the priest himself, the third as a peace-fine to the church, and in addition our ban. The same applies to a deacon: compensation is to be made threefold according to his wergild, together with our ban. For a subdeacon or a cleric of any order, payment is to be made threefold according to his wergild, and in addition our ban.

[Col. 0292C] 227. Concerning a blow

XXXIII. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 14; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 40, chapter 6.) Likewise, a blow without bloodshed against a cleric of any order is to be compensated threefold, and in addition our ban. Whoever has nothing with which to pay the church is to hand himself over to the service of that church until he has paid the whole debt.

### If someone strips a cleric. From the Council of Tribur

XXXIV. (Council of Tribur, canon 7.) If anything is perpetrated against clerics or churches—that is, if someone strips or wounds a cleric, or inflicts any injury, or takes away or withholds the church’s tithes—if it has not first been duly punished through secular power, the bishop is to summon those wrongdoers to his synod and impose a fitting correction. If they refuse to come, they are to be excommunicated.

[Col. 0292D] ### If someone beats a cleric. From the same source

XXXV. If someone beats, disables, or injures a cleric in any way, let him perform canonical penance and make [Col. 0293A] legal compensation, according to what is written in the Capitularies.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Toledo

XXXVI. (Council of Toledo I, canon 11.) If someone of the powerful strips a cleric or a religious person, and the bishop orders him to come before him to be heard, but he refuses, letters are immediately to circulate among all the bishops of the province whom they can reach, so that he may be regarded as excommunicated until he is heard and returns what belongs to another.

[Col. 0293B] 228. Concerning fighting and homicide in a churchyard. From the Council of Tribur

XXXVII. (Council of Tribur, canons 4 and 6; BURCHARD, book III, chapter 195.) If someone engages in a fight or commits homicide in a churchyard, whatever is to be paid in compensation for violated immunity is to be paid to the altar, whoever the church may belong to.

### Concerning fighting in a church. From the same source

XXXVIII. If someone strikes a cleric in a church with a staff or sword so that blood flows, or strikes him without shedding blood, compensation is to be made according to what is written in the Capitularies—that is, threefold according to his wergild. [Note: [Col. 0293D] See above, chapter 132.]

### That laymen are to receive no portion of the property of their deceased priests. From the same source, chapter 2

XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0293D] See below, in the second appendix, chapter 39.] It has also been reported to the holy synod that certain laymen act wickedly against their priests, claiming for themselves portions of the property of dying priests, just as they would from their own slaves. We therefore forbid this from happening any longer. Rather, just as priests have been made free to receive ordination and perform the divine office, so nothing is to be demanded from them except the service of God [Col. 0293C]. They are not to appropriate anything from the priests’ private property; but from two portions let the priests do what seems right to them, and let them leave the third to the churches they serve, in accordance with the commands of the canons.

[Col. 0293D] 229. Concerning the compensation for a priest if he is killed. From the same source

XL. (Council of Tribur, canon 4.) If a priest is wounded or beaten but escapes death, the entire compensation is to go to the priest. If he dies, the compensation is to be divided into three portions: one portion is to be paid to the altar served by the priest, another to the bishop, and the third to the priest’s relatives.

### On the same matter. From Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 49

XLI. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 15; BURCHARD, book [Col. 0293D] VI, chapter 11.) The compensation for priests who have been killed is to be paid to the bishop of whose parish they are members, according to the capitulary of our glorious father Charles, specifically so that the bishop may assign half of the priest’s wergild to the needs of the church over which he presided, and distribute the other half rightly as alms on his behalf; for no heir of his appears nearer to us than the one who joined him to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0293D] See the note of the Roman corrector on the chapter “All priests,” 17, 9, 4.]

### Concerning one who kills a priest. From the Council of Worms

XLII. (Council of Worms, canon 26; BURCHARD, book VI, [Col. 0294A] chapter 8.) Whoever voluntarily kills a priest is not to eat meat or drink wine for all the days of his life; he is to fast until evening, except on feast days and Sundays; he is not to take up weapons or mount a horse; he is not to enter a church for five years [Note: [Col. 0294D] See Morin, book VII, *On Penance*, chapter 7, sections 8–9], but is to stand before the church doors. After five years he is to enter the church, but is not yet to communicate; rather, he is to stand or sit among the hearers. When the course of twelve years 230 has been completed, permission to communicate is to be granted to him, and the restriction on riding is to be lifted. In the remaining observances, however, he is to continue for three days each week, so that he may deserve to be purified more completely.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 24

XLIII. (Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 24; BURCHARD, [Col. 0294B] book VI, chapter 7.) Whoever kills a priest is to be assigned twelve years of penance according to the canons. If he denies it, then, if he is free, he is to swear with twelve men; but if he is a slave, he is to purify himself over twelve red-hot plowshares. Once convicted of the offense, he is to lay aside the military belt until the end of his life and lose his wife.

### Concerning one who kills a degraded priest. From the same council

XLIV. (Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 25; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 9.) It has been reported to us that certain men who formerly said that they had been priests, and who afterward, having been degraded for their sins, traveled through various places seeking the intercession of the saints by performing penance, have been murdered. We deny all ecclesiastical [Col. 0294C] communion to their killers until they have discharged worthy penance for their offense according to the judgment of the bishops.

### Concerning the homicides of clerics. From Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 25

XLV. Whoever kills a subdeacon is to pay 300 solidi. Whoever kills a deacon, 400. Whoever kills a priest, 600. Whoever kills a 231 bishop, 900. Whoever kills a monk is to pay 400 solidi.

### If an ordained person commits homicide. From the Penitential

XLVI. (HALITGAR, book VI, chapter 1.) If a bishop or any ordained person commits homicide, he is to do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water.

### If someone consents or gives counsel that a man be killed. From the same source

[Col. 0294D] XLVII. (HALITGAR, in the same place.) If someone consents to a homicide and gives counsel for it, and the deed is carried out, he is to do penance for seven years. If it is not carried out, he is to do penance for three years.

### If someone kills his relative or his lord. From the same source

XLVIII. If someone kills his neighbor and relative, he is to do penance for ten years. The same applies if someone treacherously murders his elder and lord.

### From the sayings of the deacon Ferrandus

XLIX. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 31, and in GRATIAN [Col. 0295A], Distinction 1, *On Penance*, chapter 23.) Those who think that only those who kill a man with their hands are homicides, and not rather those through whose counsel, deceit, and urging men are destroyed, dangerously deceive themselves. For the Jews did not kill the Lord with their own hands, as it is written: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John 18). Nevertheless, the Lord’s death is imputed to them, because they crucified him with their tongue, saying: “Crucify him” (Luke 23). Hence one 232 Evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour (Mark 15), another at the sixth (Luke 23): the Jews crucified him at the third hour with their tongue, and the soldiers at the sixth with their hands. Therefore, whoever hands over a man kills him, as the Lord says: “The one who handed me over to you has the greater sin” [Col. 0295B] (John 16). Hence the Psalmist says: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56). Therefore, let those through whose counsel blood is shed submit themselves to penance, if they wish to merit forgiveness.

### Concerning those who regard homicide committed in war as nothing. From a letter of Rabanus to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, concerning the battle fought at Fontenay

L. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 23.) Some excuse the homicide that was recently committed in the rebellion and battle of our princes, as though no one needed to perform penance for it because it was carried out at the command of the princes and brought to an end by God’s judgment. We know indeed that God’s judgment [Col. 0295C] is always just and worthy of no reproach. Nevertheless, those who wish to defend this wicked slaughter must consider whether they can excuse as innocent before God those who, on account of avarice—which is the root of all evils and is compared with the service of idols—and on account of favor toward their temporal lords, despised the eternal Lord and, scorning his commands, committed homicide not by accident but deliberately. Hence it is written in Exodus: “If someone deliberately and treacherously kills his neighbor, you shall drag him away from my altar 233” [Col. 0295D] (Exodus 21). And in Deuteronomy: “If someone, hating his neighbor, lies in wait for his life, and rises up against him and strikes him so that he dies, and he flees to one of the cities mentioned above, the elders of that city shall send and seize him from the place of refuge, and hand him over to the hands of the neighbor whose blood was shed, and he shall die; you shall not pity him” (Deuteronomy 19). Who, then, would say that the man whom the Lord judged worthy of death is not guilty? How can one who insists that what God commanded is void not be opposed to the law? Yet amid these matters it must be understood that there is a great difference between a legitimate prince and a rebellious tyrant.

### On the same matter. From the Penitential

LI. If someone kills a man in a public war, he is to do penance for forty days.

[Col. 0296A] ### Concerning a cleric who kills his neighbor. From the same source

LII. If a cleric commits homicide and kills his neighbor out of deliberate hatred, he is to do penance in exile for seven years.

### Concerning parricides. From the Penitential

LIII. If someone commits this crime, some have judged that he should do penance for seven years, or that he should perform fourteen years of penance; others, until the end of his life, like Cain, if he has committed a similar act.

### From the same source

LIV. Whoever disables and disfigures a man is to pay the expenses of physicians and make restitution for the scar and for his labor until he is healed, 234 and is to do penance for half a year. If he has nothing with which to make restitution, he is to do penance for one year.

[Col. 0296B] ### Concerning the mutilation of limbs. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5

LV. (Council of Toledo II, canon 6; BURCHARD, book I, chapter 201.) Those who administer the Lord’s sacraments are not permitted to exercise a judgment of blood [Note: [Col. 0295D] See the Penitential of Rabanus, chapter 30]. Therefore such excess must be prohibited with the greatest care, lest, driven by impulses of indiscriminate presumption, they either presume, by their own judgment, to judge a matter punishable by death, or themselves inflict mutilations on any persons, or order them to be inflicted. If any of them, forgetful of these precepts, does such a thing either among the dependents of his own church or against any persons, let him be deprived both of the honor and place of his order and be confined in the prison of perpetual damnation [Col. 0296C]. Nevertheless, communion is not to be denied him when he departs this life, on account of the Lord’s mercy.

### What discretion the rulers of churches must exercise, lest through undisciplined correction they incur the charge of homicide

LVI. (Fourth Addition to the Capitularies, chapter 6.) Since, according to the decree of ancient institution, benevolence ought to be applied more than severity toward those who are to be corrected, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power,

[Col. 0296D] 235. ### Concerning parricide. From Book IX of the Theodosian Law

LVII. (Interpretation of Book I of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Parricide*.) If someone kills his father, mother, brother, sister, sons, daughters, or other relatives, then, with all other kinds of torture set aside, a sack made of hides, called a *culleus*, is to be made; once he has been placed in it, snakes are also to be enclosed with him; and, if the sea is not nearby, he is to be thrown into any pool. Condemned to this punishment, he is never at any time to receive burial.

### Concerning a mistress who kills a female slave. From the Council of Elvira

LVIII. (Council of Elvira, canon 5; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 19.) If a mistress, inflamed by the fury of jealousy, kills a female slave, so that she gives up her soul in torment within the third day—since it is uncertain whether she killed her deliberately or by accident—it has been decided that, if deliberately, she may be admitted to communion after seven years; if by accident, after [Col. 0297A] five years, once she has performed the prescribed penance.

### If a slave is killed by his master while being punished with blows. From the Theodosian Law

LIX. (Interpretation of Book I of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning the Correction of Slaves*.) If a slave dies while his master is punishing his offense, the master is not held guilty of homicide, because he is guilty of homicide only if he is proved to have wished to kill him. For correction is not considered a crime.

### Concerning the crushing of infants. From the Council of Mainz

LX. (BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 58.) If someone carelessly crushes his own infant [Col. 0297B] 236, or suffocates it under the weight of clothing, and this happens after baptism, he is to do penance for forty days on bread and water, vegetables, and legumes, and abstain from his spouse. Afterward he is to do penance for three years on the appointed fast days and observe three Lents each year. But if the infant was crushed before baptism, he is to do penance for the first forty days as above and afterward complete five years.

### If an infant dies unbaptized through the mother’s negligence. From a letter of Rabanus to Reginbald, chorepiscopus

LXI. (BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 59; Council of Ancyra, canon 20.) Concerning infants found dead with their father and mother, when it is not apparent whether the infant was killed or suffocated by the father or mother, or died a natural death, the parents are not to be secure on that account or without penance. Nevertheless, [Col. 0297C] consideration of compassion must be exercised toward them when not intention but the outcome was the cause of death. But if they are not unaware that they themselves were the child’s killers, they must know that they have sinned grievously, as is confirmed in the Council of Ancyra. Some judge that such a person’s penance ought to be three years, one of which is to be spent on bread and water, while during the time of penance he is to guard himself from every form of sexual indulgence.

### Concerning a woman whose son dies unbaptized through negligence. From the Penitential, chapter 17

LXII. A woman who has given birth, whose son dies unbaptized through negligence [Col. 0297D] 237, is to do penance for one year and is never to be without some form of penance. If it happened through the negligence of a priest, see the first book, chapter 128.

[Col. 0297D] ### Concerning women who kill their own offspring. From the Council of Ancyra

LXIII. (Council of Ancyra, canon 20; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 3; RABANUS, Letter to Heribald, chapter 8; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 54.) Concerning women who fornicate and kill the offspring they have borne, or who act to cause what they have conceived in the womb to be expelled, the ancient ruling indeed removes them from the Church until the end of life. But now we define more humanely that a period of ten years of penance is to be granted to them according to the prescribed stages.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Lérida

LXIV. (Council of Lérida, canon 2; RABANUS, Letter to Heribald, chapter 9; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 52.) Those who have sought to kill children wrongly conceived through adultery, whether before or after birth, or who have crushed them in their mothers’ wombs with various potions [Col. 0298A], are to be granted communion after the course of seven years—both sexes, namely the father and mother who committed adultery—provided that throughout all the days of their lives they persist in tears and humility.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Elvira

LXV. (Council of Elvira, canon 63; RABANUS, Letter to Heribald, chapter 8; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 51.) If a woman, while her husband is absent, conceives through adultery and kills the child after the crime, it has been decided that communion is scarcely to be given to her even at the end of life, because she has doubled the offense.

### If a woman causes her offspring to be expelled. From the Penitential

LXVI. If a woman voluntarily loses her offspring in the womb before 238 forty days [Col. 0298B] have passed, she is to do penance for one year. But if she kills it after forty days, she is to do penance for three years. If she loses it after it has become animate, she is to do penance as for homicide. Yet there is a great difference between whether she acts as a poor woman because of the difficulty of raising the child, or for a fornicatory reason, in order to conceal her crime.

### If a woman kills her son or daughter. From the same source

LXVII. If a woman voluntarily kills her son or daughter, she is to do penance for ten years for homicide.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Rouen

LXVIII. (BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 53; Ivo, part X, chapter 103.) There are certain women—as has come to the notice of the holy council—who, having conceived through fornication [Col. 0298C], and fearing that the crime they had secretly committed would become known, killed the infants they had borne and covered them with heaps of earth or threw them into the water. How great an outrage this is is demonstrated by the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Elvira, and Lérida. Accordingly, they decree that communion is scarcely to be given to such women even at the end of life. But treating them more humanely, it has been decided that, after ten years of penance, such women may be received into communion.

### That adulterous infants are to be exposed before the church door

*[The supplied source ends here, with this heading incomplete.]*
### LXIX. (BURCHARD, book III, chapter 200)

Since such acts are very often perpetrated at the devil’s prompting, with the weakness of the flesh taking delight in them and therefore consenting, we wish, as it were, to remedy one deadly potion with another [239], lest the crimes of adultery and homicide be doubled. We therefore advise that every priest publicly announce in his parish that, if any woman, secretly corrupted, should conceive and give birth, she must by no means, at the devil’s urging, kill her son or daughter. Rather, by whatever means she can, she should have the child carried before the doors of the church and abandoned there, so that, brought before the priest on the following day, it may be received and nourished by some faithful person. In this way she may escape the guilt of homicide and, what is more serious, of parricide. For whoever kills his son or daughter is to be regarded in every respect as a parricide.

### On the same matter. From the Theodosian Law, book V, chapter 7.

### LXX. (Interpretation 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On Exposed Children*) [Col. 0299A]

Whoever, knowing it to have been exposed immediately after birth and with the father, mother, or master aware of it, takes up an exposed child and raises it by his own labor shall have the child in his power, whether he wishes the one he has nourished to be freeborn or enslaved.

### On the same matter. From the same source.

### LXXI. (Interpretation 2; Theodosian Code, same title)

Whoever, knowing the master or patron to be aware of it, takes up an exposed boy or girl out of mercy shall retain it in his ownership, provided that the bishop or clergy have subscribed a formal record concerning its recovery. No one may later claim as his own a child whom he is proved to have exposed to death.

### On the same matter. From the same source.

### LXXII. (Single law of the Theodosian Code, *On Those Who Nourish Children of Another Blood*) [Col. 0299B]

If anyone raises an infant of another blood, he shall have the power to hold and possess it. Certainly, if the master or father wishes to reclaim the child after it has been raised, he must either give the nurse a slave of equal value, or the nurse shall receive from him the price of the child, according to the value of the one who was nourished. [Note: [Col. 0299D] See book IV of the Visigothic Laws, title 4, chapter 1.]

### On homicides. From the Council of Tours.

### LXXIII. (Council of Tours I, canon 7; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 30)

Homicides are absolutely not to be admitted to communion until their crimes have been expiated through the confession of their penance.

### On those who kill their spouses. From the Council of Mainz.

### LXXIV. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 38)

If a husband has killed his wife, or a wife her husband, let an impartial judgment be applied to them, as the Lord says: “You shall not show partiality to the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful” (Leviticus XIX). And shortly afterward: “You shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not accept anyone’s person, because the judgment is God’s” (Deuteronomy I). Therefore, when either of them is accused of such a crime, if the accused denies it, let the matter be examined by the same impartial judgment.

### On the same matter. From book III of the Capitularies, chapter 89.

### LXXV. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 67)

Let homicides within the realm not be committed, as they are forbidden by the law of the Lord, either for the sake of vengeance, or greed, or brigandage. Wherever such persons are found, let our judges punish them according to the law and by our command. Let no one be killed except by command of the law.

### 241. On the same matter. From the same source.

### LXXVI. (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 149; book II of the Lombard Laws, title 13, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 37) [Col. 0299D]

Whoever, after abandoning his own wife—or after she has been killed without legal cause and without certain proof—takes another wife shall lay down his arms and perform public penance. If he proves obstinate, let him be arrested by the count, bound in chains, and placed in custody until the matter is brought to our attention.

### On the combat of two men, which our people call “the field,” customarily undertaken on account of an alleged adultery. From Pope Nicholas’s letter to King Charles.

### LXXVII. (NICHOLAS I, letter 50; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 51)

We do not accept trial by single combat as part of the law, since we do not find that it was commanded. Although we read that certain persons engaged in it, as sacred history records the combat of the holy David and Goliath, divine authority nowhere sanctions it as something to be observed as law. Those who pursue this and similar practices seem to be merely tempting God.

### On the same matter. From the same letter.

### LXXXVIII. (BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 50)

Yet, as we have learned from the report of many, King Lothair is planning to hold an assembly and intends to subject Queen Theutberga to his own examination and judgment. If he can, by the artifices of his falsehood, present her as not having been his lawful wife, he wishes to separate her from himself completely. But if not, he wishes to receive her as his own wife and then accuse her as though she had committed adultery; [242; Helmstedt edition: *pro* for *per*] for this reason he plans to compel his own man and Theutberga’s man to single combat. If the queen’s man should fall, he intends to put her to death without delay. We believe that your great prudence has already perceived how completely these actions contradict every divine law.

### On parricides. From the Capitularies.

### LXXIX. (Addition IV, chapter 85; book I of the Lombard Laws, title 10, chapter 4) [Col. 0300C]

If anyone, out of greed for property, kills his father, mother, brother, sister, nephew, or any other relative, let the inheritance of the murdered person pass to the rightful heirs. Let the murderer’s inheritance, however, be confiscated to the treasury. Let the murderer himself, at the bishop’s direction, be subjected to public penance.

### On those who are bound in irons. From the same source.

### LXXX. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 79)

Let the *mangones* and *cotiones*, who wander about this land without any legal authority, not be allowed to roam about deceiving people; nor should those who are bound and fettered in irons be allowed to do so—those who say that a priest has imposed upon them the obligation to wander as vagrants and fugitives through the realms. It seems better to us that they remain in one place, working, serving, and showing patience, according to what has been canonically imposed. [Note: [Col. 0299D] This chapter is not found in book I of the Capitularies in the oldest handwritten codices—not in the Royal manuscript, from which the first Paris edition was produced, nor in the Ripoll manuscript, nor finally in the Colbert manuscript. In both places, however, it is found in the appendix to book IV, chapter 34. Moreover, the commonly printed edition of this chapter, which the ancient codices also prefer, differs greatly from the version transmitted by Regino. It should be noted that where Regino has “and showing patience,” the Capitularies read “and performing penance.”]

### On restraining feuds.

### LXXXI. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 27; book I of the Lombard Laws, title 9, chapter 34)

If anyone, compelled by some necessity, commits homicide, let the count in whose jurisdiction the deed was committed arrange both the payment of compensation and the pacification of the feud by oath. If one party refuses to consent to this—whether the one who committed the homicide or the one who ought to receive the compensation—let him compel the person who resists to appear before us, so that we may send him into exile for whatever period we deem appropriate, until he is corrected there and dares no longer disobey his count, and until greater harm does not arise.

### On a woman who kills a man by witchcraft. From the Penitential, chapter 15.

### LXXXII.

If a woman kills anyone by magical art—that is, by means of a potion or some other art—let her do penance for seven years. If she is a poor woman, let her do penance for four years.

### On the same matter. From the Council of Elvira.

### LXXXIII. (Council of Elvira, canon 6; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 26)

If anyone kills another by magic, since he could not accomplish the crime without idolatry, he is not to receive communion even at the end of his life. [244]

### Hence the foregoing.

### LXXXIV. (HALITGAR, book VI, chapter 5)

If anyone causes another’s death by magic, let him do penance for seven years and give many alms.

### On the same matter.

### LXXXV. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 39)

If a woman kills her husband with poison on account of fornication, or causes him to be killed by any art, let her do penance for ten years, because she has killed her lord and master.

### On those who persuade someone to be killed. From Roman law: Paul’s *Sentences*, book V, chapter 25.

### LXXXVI. (Paul’s *Sentences*, book V, chapter 23)

Those who commission a killing—that is, those who order or persuade others to kill—are to be punished just as homicides are.

### [Col. 0301C] On the same matter.

### LXXXVII. (Same source)

A person who kills someone is sometimes acquitted; another who does not kill is nevertheless treated or condemned as a homicide. For it is each person’s intention, not merely the deed, that must be punished. Therefore, whoever wished to kill but was unable to carry it out because of some accident is to be punished as a homicide. But whoever accidentally kills a person through the unintentional discharge of a weapon is acquitted.

### On one who castrates a man. From the same source.

### LXXXVIII. (Same source)

Whoever castrates a man for the sake of lust or commerce, and delivers him after castration, whether he is a slave or a free man, shall be punished by death. [245]

### Hence the foregoing.

### LXXXIX. (BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 57)

If anyone, either to satisfy lust or out of a plan prompted by hatred, does something to a man or woman—or gives something to drink—so that the person cannot beget or conceive and no offspring may be born from him or her, let him be treated as a homicide.

We have included all this from Roman law so that a priest may assess from the law the appropriate form of penance in such transgressions. For canonical authority agrees with Roman law in most respects.

### On those who are circumcised. From the same law, chapter 24.

### XC. (Paul’s *Sentences*, book V, chapter 22)

Roman citizens who permit themselves or their slaves to be circumcised according to the Jewish rite shall be deprived of their property and deported to an island; physicians shall be punished by death.

### [Col. 0302A] If a Jew circumcises a slave of another nation. From the same source.

### XCI. (Same source)

If Jews circumcise slaves acquired from another nation, they shall either be deported into exile or punished by death.

### On those who kill themselves. From the Council of Braga, chapter 15.

### XCII. (Council of Braga I, chapter 16; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 6; BURCHARD, book XIX, chapter 130)

It has been decided that no commemoration is to be made in the offering for those who inflict death upon themselves, whether by the sword, poison, throwing themselves from a height, hanging, or any other means; nor are their bodies to be escorted to burial with psalms. Many have presumed to do this out of ignorance. It has likewise been decided that the same is to be done with those who are punished for crimes. [Note: [Col. 0301] See book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 10, and book VII, chapter 344.]

### [Col. 0302B] On those who are hanged on the gallows. From the Council of Mainz.

### XCIII. (Council of Mainz under Archbishop Rabanus, chapter 27; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 76)

Certain brothers asked whether the bodies of those who are hanged on the gallows for their crimes, after having made confession to God, ought to be carried to churches, whether offerings should be made for them, and whether Masses should be celebrated—or not. We answer them: If communion must be given at the end of life, according to the command of the canons, to all who make a pure confession of their sins and perform worthy penance, why should it not be given to those who undergo the extreme penalty for their sins? For it is written: “The Lord does not judge the same thing twice.”

### [Col. 0302C] On thieves and robbers apprehended. From the Council of Tribur.

### XCIV. (Council of Tribur, chapter 31; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 59; also in Gratian 13, question 2, chapter 31)

If thieves and robbers are killed while stealing or plundering, it has been judged that no prayer should be offered for them. But if, after being apprehended or wounded, they confess to a priest or deacon, we do not deny them communion.

### 247. On one who kills a Jew or pagan out of greed.

### XCV. (Council of Worms, chapter 27; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 33)

Whoever kills a Jew or pagan out of hatred or greed ought to do penance as a homicide, since this is no minor fault. For the ancient people were not at all commanded to wage war even against foreign nations unless they had rejected the peace offered to them.

### If someone kills a man while insane. From the same source.

### XCVI. (Council of Worms, chapter 28; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 25; also in Gratian 15, question 1, chapter 12)

If anyone kills someone while insane, and later returns to a sound mind, a lighter penance must be imposed upon him than upon one who commits such an act while of sound mind. Although penance must be imposed upon him—because the infirmity itself was the cause of the sin, even if it is perhaps believed to have arisen through some hidden cause—it should nevertheless be lighter than that imposed upon one who killed someone while sound, by as much as there is a difference between the sound and the insane, and between the rational and the irrational.

### [Col. 0303A] If several people kill one man. From the Council of Mainz.

### XCVII. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 42)

If four or five men, or even more, quarrel with one man, and he dies after being wounded by them, whoever inflicted the wound is to be judged a homicide according to the statutes of the canons. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Regino cites this chapter from the Council of Mainz; Burchard and the old collector of canons in the Royal Library cite it from the Council held at Verberie, chapter 991. In both places it is longer than in Regino.]

### 248. On one accused of homicide when it cannot be proved. From the same source.

### XCVIII. (BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 24)

Where it can be clearly shown that a particular person committed homicide, let a judgment of proportionate penance be imposed upon him according to canonical authority. But if it cannot be proved by clear indications that he is a homicide, and he himself is unwilling to confess, let the matter be reserved for the judgment of almighty God, to whom all hidden things are manifest. [Col. 0303B] Nevertheless, let it be declared that he is unworthy of ecclesiastical communion until he confesses the crime he committed and strives, through confession and suitable penance, to obtain absolution from it.

## HEREAFTER, ON ADULTERY AND FORNICATION. From the Council of Ancyra.

### XCIX. (Council of Ancyra, canon 19; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 9; Council of Worms, chapter 44)

If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he ought to attain completion through seven years of penance, according to the former stages.

### On one who keeps a concubine while having a wife. From the Council of Toledo.

### C. (Council of Toledo I, chapter 17)

A man who has a wife and also keeps a concubine is not to receive communion. But a man who has no wife and keeps a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided that he is content with the union of one woman only—whether wife or concubine, as he chooses. Otherwise, while he continues in that way, he is to be expelled until he stops and returns to penance.

### On divorce. From a letter of Pope Innocent.

### CI. (Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 26; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 21; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 72)

Your affection also inquired about those who, after a divorce has intervened, have joined themselves to others in marriage; it is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. Those, however, who, while their wife is still living—although the marriage may seem to have been dissolved—hasten to another union cannot fail to appear adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons joined to them seem themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery.” Therefore all such persons are to be kept from the communion of the faithful.

### On women who leave their husbands. From the Council of Elvira.

### CII. (Council of Elvira, chapter 8; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 62)

Likewise, women who, without any prior cause, have left their husbands and joined themselves to another are not to receive communion even at the end of their lives.

### On an adulterous husband. Hence the foregoing.

### CIII. (Council of Elvira, chapter 9; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 63)

Likewise, a faithful woman who has left a faithful adulterous husband and marries an adulterer is to be prohibited from marrying. If, however, she does marry, she is not to receive communion before the man whom she left has departed from this world, unless the necessity of illness should compel communion to be given. [Note: [Col. 0303D] This is a canon of the Council of Elvira, transmitted by all the collectors of decrees—Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian. Yet the reading that is not the better one seems to have prevailed. For here in Regino, and likewise in Burchard and Ivo, part VIII, chapter 199, it reads, “and marries an adulterer.” On the contrary, in all editions of the canons of Elvira, in Rabanus’s third chapter of the *Penitential* addressed to Otgar, in the oldest manuscript of Regino used for this edition, and finally in an old manuscript collection of canons preserved in the Royal Library, it plainly reads, “and marries another.” This reading is confirmed by Rabanus himself in his letter to Heribald, chapter 21, where he has “and marries another.” In Gratian, however, the ancient editions read, “and takes another husband.” We have therefore preferred the corrupted reading to the genuine one, so as to preserve untouched the sources from which Burchard derived his streams.]

### [Col. 0304B] On separation. From the Council of Africa.

### CIV. (Council of Africa, chapter 69; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 10; RABANUS’s Penitential, chapter 3; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 64)

It has been decided that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may join themselves to another, but that they must remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they refuse, they are to be brought to penance; in this matter, the promulgation of an imperial law is to be sought.

### 251. On the same matter. From Augustine’s statements on the Sermon on the Mount.

### CV. (BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 71; also in Gratian 32, question 7, chapter 5)

The Apostle Paul says: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (1 Corinthians VII). It can happen that she departs for the reason for which the Lord permitted it. Or if a woman is permitted to dismiss her husband even apart from the cause of fornication, what shall we answer concerning what he says afterward, “and let the husband not dismiss his wife”? Why did he not add “except for the cause of fornication,” which the Lord permits, unless he wishes the same form to be understood: that if he dismisses her—which is permitted on account of fornication—he should remain without a wife or be reconciled to his wife? And shortly afterward: “The Lord, however, permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication. But because he permitted it, he did not command it.”

### On the same matter. From book I of the Capitularies, chapter 43.

### CVI. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 43; book II of the Lombard Laws, title 13, chapter 4)

Let neither a wife dismissed by her husband take another husband while her husband is alive, nor a husband take another wife while his former wife is alive.

### [Col. 0305A] On lawful marriages. From Jerome’s statements.

### CVII. (36, question 2, chapter 8)

Three lawful marriages are read of in Scripture. The first lawful marriage is that of a chaste virgin, given lawfully in marriage to a man while remaining a virgin. The second is that of a virgin discovered in the city by a man and joined to him by force. If her father wishes, the man himself shall provide her dowry according to whatever amount the father determines, and shall pay the price of her chastity. But if she had a betrothed before she was discovered, she shall be given to him. The third is this: if the aforementioned daughter has been discovered and her father is unwilling, he shall take her away from the aforementioned man, give her to another, and provide her dowry; and she shall be lawfully married to him. Yet the first is preferred to these two (27, question 2, chapter 13).

A fourth lawful marriage is added. When his wife has died, a man may take another—not one who has been divorced or betrothed to another man. The same should be observed by a woman. Paul clearly teaches this: “The woman,” he says, “who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband as long as her husband lives,” and so forth. A fifth is added: when either a man or a woman, by mutual consent, has embraced religious life, the other may enter a new marriage, but with a girl or a boy.

We believe that the council assembled at Compiègne in the time of King Pippin followed this authority; in its sixteenth chapter we read the following decree.

### CVIII. (Council of Compiègne, chapter 13)

If a man dismisses his wife and gives her permission, for the sake of religious life, to serve God within a monastery and receive the veil—as we have said, for God’s sake—her husband may, if he wishes, take a lawful wife. The woman is to do the same.

But this judgment is shaped by canonical and apostolic documents, as has been shown above. We are also instructed by the decrees of Pope Nicholas, who writes to King Lothair as follows:

### 253. If a married person wishes to abandon the world. From a letter of Nicholas.

### CIX. (NICHOLAS I, letter 67; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 53)

Therefore take the greatest care to cherish and love your wife Theutberga as your own flesh, and watch vigilantly that you do not consent to her being separated from you in any way. If she wishes to leave you, rebuke her—indeed, correct her—and strive in every way to turn her back from such an intention. But if, out of love of chastity, she seeks separation and demands the dissolution of the marital bond, it is certain, as the Apostle says, that “a woman does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does.” Yet if you too, pursuing chastity, wish to dissolve the union under the pretext of religion, we grant this, provided that it is not done deceitfully. For although it is written, “What God has joined, let no human being separate,” God, and not a human being, separates when, out of regard for divine love and by the mutual consent of both spouses, marriages are dissolved. If you wish to proceed in this way, we freely permit it and readily give our assent. Otherwise, however, we prohibit your mutual separation.

### On the same matter. From the statements of Bishop Basil.

### CX. (BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 45)

If a married person wishes to convert and enter a monastery, he is not to be received unless he has first been released by his spouse, who professes chastity. For if she, while he is alive, marries another through lack of self-control, she will undoubtedly be an adulteress; nor is such a man’s conversion acceptable to God when it is followed by the violation of the marital bond. Such people therefore follow Christ without guilt, after abandoning the world, only if they have consent regarding chastity by mutual agreement.

### On those who dismiss their spouses without judgment. From the Council of Agde.

### CXI. (Council of Agde, chapter 25; book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 226)

Those secular persons who, without any serious fault, dismiss or have dismissed the marital union, and who put forward no credible grounds for separation, but dismiss their marriages in order to presume upon another’s marriage or an unlawful union, are to be excluded from the communion of the Church and from the assembly of the people, because they stain the fidelity of marriage—provided that they have abandoned their wives before stating the cause of separation before the bishop of the province and before being condemned by judgment.

### That every dispute which seeks to be tried by ecclesiastical judgment must not pass to secular judgment. From a Capitular.

### CXII

It has been decreed that any disputes which have begun to be heard by ecclesiastical judgment and authority must not pass to secular judgment, where the parties might renew their appeal, but must be concluded by ecclesiastical sanctions. For it is not permitted to appeal from judges chosen by common consent to other judges, unless a higher authority exists, according to canonical procedure. If, however, a case has first been aired in secular judgment—that is, in the count’s court—it is to be settled according to secular law, without prejudice to the privilege of ecclesiastical law.

### 255. On the same matter. From Pope Nicholas’s letter to King Charles.

### CXIII. (NICHOLAS I, letter 50; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 49)

Queen Theutberga wrote to us that she wished to be released from royal dignity and from the marital union, and desired to be content with a solitary private life. We replied that this could not otherwise be done unless her husband Lothair chose the same life. And shortly afterward: Theutberga must not be compelled to make a renewed reply concerning the dispute already settled, because what has once been properly decided and determined by the intervention of oaths must not be reconsidered, except perhaps where a higher authority is involved.

### On ecclesiastical judgment.

### CXIV. (NICHOLAS I, same letter)

Furthermore, since she seeks refuge in the Church and constantly seeks ecclesiastical judgment, she ought not to be subjected to secular judgment. After this, when we have been called as judges by both parties—that is, by the king as well as by the queen—and have dealt with the dispute between them, it is not appropriate to rush to any other judges concerning this matter. For according to the sacred canons, it is not permitted to appeal from judges whom common consent has chosen; and where an appeal is permitted, it may be made only where there is a higher authority. Since there is nowhere any authority higher than that of the apostolic see, whose authority has dealt with the case of both parties, we do not know whether anyone may judge its judgment or reconsider its sentence.

### 256. That no one presume to reopen a judged case. From book III of the Capitularies, chapter 31.

### CXV. (Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 31)

If anyone presumes to reopen a case already judged in the assembly, and is there convicted by witnesses, let him either pay fifteen solidi or receive fifteen blows from the *scabini* who previously judged the case.

### That a woman accused of adultery, if she is to enter a legal combat with her husband, must for a time be restored to her own control. From a letter of Pope Nicholas.

### CXVI. (NICHOLAS I, letter 50; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 52)

Furthermore, whether judgment is to be conducted concerning the marital bond or the crime of adultery, there is no reason to suppose [Sirmond: “no reason permits”] that Theutberga can enter into conflict with Lothair or undertake the lawful contest of the dispute unless she has first been restored for a time to her own control and freely associated with her own relatives. A place must also be provided among them where no violence from a crowd need be feared, and where it will not be difficult to produce the witnesses and other persons required in such disputes both by the holy canons and by the venerable Roman laws.

We have said this in order to show what kind of legal conflict Lothair imagines he can enter into with a person whom he daily harasses and crushes within his own chambers; whom, whenever he wishes, he leads out to judgment; whom, whenever he wishes, he takes back into confinement; and who, when brought out, must profess whatever he commands, and so forth. Therefore she must be entrusted to her own freedom, liberated from every oppression and power of the man with whom she is to enter into conflict, and allowed to use what is hers *liberter* [*licenter*, “freely”]. She who wishes to show herself free from the accusations brought against her must also avoid suspicious persons.

### That a bishop’s sentence must not be reconsidered. From Roman law.

### CXVII. (Law 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On Episcopal Judgments*)

The Emperor Constantine says: Whatever has been settled by the sentence of bishops is to be held sacred and venerable, and it is not permitted to reconsider thereafter a matter decided by the sentence of bishops.

### If a woman has conspired with others in the death of her husband. From the council held at Verberie in the time of King Pippin, chapter 6.

### CXVIII. (Council of Verberie, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book VI, chapter 41)

If a woman conspires with others in the death of her husband, and her husband himself kills a man while defending himself, and can prove this, then, as it seems to us, the husband may dismiss that wife and, if he wishes, take another. The woman who plotted the ambush, however, having been subjected to penance, must remain without hope of marriage.

### On a free man who takes another’s female slave. From the same source, chapter 7.

### CXIX. (Council of Verberie, chapter 6; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 26)

If a free man takes another person’s female slave as his wife, believing that she is freeborn, and the woman is later found to be enslaved, he must redeem her from slavery if he can. If he cannot, he may, if he wishes, take another wife. A free woman may do the same with another person’s male slave.

### 258. If a slave has his own female slave as a concubine. From the same source, chapter 8.

### CXX. (Council of Verberie, chapter 7)

If a male slave has his own female slave as a concubine, he may, if he wishes, dismiss her and take as his wife an equal female slave belonging to his master.

### On a freedman who keeps his master’s female slave. From the same source.

### CXXI. (Council of Verberie, chapter 8)

If a slave, after receiving his freedom from his master, later commits adultery with his master’s female slave, then, whether he wishes it or not, he shall have her as his wife if his master so wishes.

### [Col. 0308B] If a male and female slave are separated for purposes of sale. From the same source.

### CXXII. (Council of Verberie, chapter 19)

If a male and female slave have been separated for the purpose of sale, they are to be exhorted to remain as they are if we cannot bring them together.

But Roman law appears to prescribe much better rules concerning this particular matter.

### On the same matter. In Roman law, chapter 25.

### CXXIII. (Interpretation of the single law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Division of Common Property*)

In the division, it says, of the property of patrimonial or fiscal lords, or of private persons, special care must be taken that, since it is unjust for children to be separated from parents and wives from husbands when possession passes to anyone, slaves who have been joined together—that is, a wife with her children and husband—must, with substitutes provided, belong to one person when it is necessary to exchange what must be exchanged. Those responsible for arranging such matters must take particular care that separation cannot occur at all.

The same rule also appears to apply in sale or purchase: when someone buys a husband, he should also buy his wife at the same time, unless she happens to be another person’s female slave. Concerning this matter, the law commands and forbids that no slave—whether privately owned, ecclesiastical, or belonging to the treasury—take another’s female slave in marriage; likewise, another’s female slave must by no means take a male slave. If she does so, such a marriage is to be considered invalid and counted as adultery. [Note: [Col. 0307D] See book II of the Lombard Laws, title 12, chapter 10.]

### If a husband, driven by a definite necessity, has fled outside the duchy. From the council mentioned above.

### CXXIV. (Council of Verberie, chapter 9; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 54)

If anyone, compelled by unavoidable necessity, flees to another duchy or province, or follows his lord, to whom he cannot refuse the faith and loyalty he has promised, and his wife, although she is able and in a position to do so, refuses to follow him out of love for her relatives or property, she must remain unmarried at all times, as long as the husband whom she did not follow remains alive. But he who, compelled by necessity, remains in another land, if he does not hope ever to return to his own country, may, if he cannot remain continent, take another wife, though with penance.

### [Col. 0309A] On one who permits his wife to receive the veil. From the same source, chapter 22.

### CXXV. (Council of Verberie, chapter 21; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 46)

Whoever permits his wife to receive the veil must not take another wife.

### 260. If a woman receives the veil without her husband’s permission. From the decree issued at Compiègne.

### CXXVI. (Council of Compiègne, chapter 3; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 16; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 47)

If a woman places the veil upon her head without her husband’s permission, he may, if he wishes, receive her back into marriage.

### On a man who takes a wife in another province. From the same source, chapter 8.

### CXXVII. (Council of Compiègne, chapter 6)

A Frankish man received a benefice from his lord in another province and took his vassal with him. Afterward the lord himself died there, and the aforementioned vassal remained there. Another man then received that benefice; and, so that he might securely retain the vassal, he gave him a woman from that benefice, and he kept her for some time. When that lord treated him harshly, he left his wife and returned to the relatives of his deceased lord, and there took a wife. It was decided that he should keep the woman whom he took later.

### On a wife previously defiled. From the same source, chapter 10.

### CXXVIII. (Council of Compiègne, chapter 7)

If anyone takes a wife and, finding her defiled, abandons her and takes another, it has been decreed that he must return to the first one in every respect. For it may also have happened that, when he took her, he himself was not a virgin; nor is a woman bound by the law of her husband until she has been joined to her husband. The woman whom he took later may marry whomever she wishes.

### 261. That the insane must not be joined in marriage. From Roman law.

### CXXIX. (PAUL, book II of the *Sentences*, title 19; BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 30)

Neither an insane man nor an insane woman can contract marriage; but if a marriage has been contracted, it is not to be dissolved.

### If persons in sound mind have contracted marriage. From the same source.

### CXXX. (BURCHARD, book IX, chapter 28)

If persons in sound mind have contracted marriage and one of the two is later afflicted by madness, insanity, or some illness, their marriage cannot be dissolved on account of that illness. The same judgment is to be applied to those who are blinded by enemies or have their limbs mutilated.

### If anyone’s wife has committed adultery. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 21.

### CXXXI. (Council of Nantes, chapter 12)

If anyone’s wife commits adultery, and this is discovered and made public by her husband, he may dismiss his wife on account of fornication, if he wishes; but she must perform public penance for seven years. Her husband, while she is alive, may under no circumstances take another wife. If he wishes to be reconciled with the adulteress, he has permission to do so, but only on the condition that he performs penance together with her. After the penance has been completed, both may approach communion after seven years. The same rule is to be observed in the case of a woman if her husband has committed adultery against her.

### [Col. 0310A] If unmarried persons have committed fornication. From the same source, chapter 22.

### CXXXII. (Council of Nantes, chapter 13)

If a woman without a husband or a man without a wife commits fornication, they shall perform penance for three years.

### What if one absolved person and one married person have committed adultery? From the same source.

### CXXXIII. (Council of Nantes, canon 14; Burchard, book IX, chapter 70)

But if a man without a wife commits adultery with another man’s wife, or if a woman without a husband commits adultery with another woman’s husband, the one who violated the marriage bond shall do penance for seven years, as stated above; the one who is not bound by the law of marriage shall do penance for five years. For equal penance ought not to be imposed on those for whom the embrace of marriage could have sufficed to satisfy their lust, and on those who, lacking a spouse and driven by the heat of lust, fell into fornication.

### Concerning the same matter. From a Penitential.

### CXXXIV
