If anyone without a wife defiles himself with another man’s wife, he shall do penance for two years. The same is to be observed concerning women.

### If a married man keeps his own female slave.

### CXXXV

If a married man keeps his own female slave, he shall do penance for one year; or, in another year, he shall observe three forty-day fasts and the prescribed fast-days, and for the preceding three months he shall abstain from his own wife. The female slave, if she suffered violence, shall do penance for forty days; if she consented, she shall observe three Lents and the appointed feast days during the year.

[Col. 0310C] 263

### If a layman has fornicated with a laywoman. From the same source.

### CXXXVI. (Burchard, book IX, chapter 68)

If a layman has fornicated with a laywoman—that is, if both are free from the law of marriage—he shall do penance for three years. And the more frequently and carelessly they have committed these sins, the more both the period and the form of penance shall be increased.

### Concerning a married man who has repeatedly fornicated. From the Council of Elvira.

### CXXXVII. (Council of Elvira, canon 47; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 22; Burchard, book IX, chapter 67)

If a believer who has a wife has committed adultery not once but repeatedly, he is to be visited at the point of death. If he promises that he will cease, communion is to be given him. But if, after recovering, he again commits adultery, it has been decided that he should no longer mock others concerning the communion of peace.

[Col. 0310D]

### Concerning one who has fallen once. From the same council.

### CXXXVIII. (Council of Elvira, canon 69)

If someone who has a wife should perhaps fall once, it has been decided that he shall do penance for that matter for five years and then be reconciled, unless the necessity of illness compels communion to be given before the appointed time. This is also to be observed concerning women.

### Why husbands do not receive communion with adulterous wives. From a letter of Pope Innocent.

### CXXXIX. (Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 24; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 21; Burchard, book IX, chapter 77)

It has also been desired that it be known why husbands who receive communion do not associate with adulterous wives, while, conversely, wives appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands. Concerning this matter, the Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not easily accuse their husbands of adultery, and their hidden sins do not receive punishment. Husbands, however, customarily bring adulterous wives more freely before priests. Therefore communion is denied to women once their crime has been disclosed. But when the crime committed by men remains hidden, no one is easily excluded on the basis of suspicions; he will certainly be removed if his wickedness is exposed. Since, therefore, the cause is equal, when proof is lacking the application of punishment sometimes comes to rest.

### If a wife has committed adultery with her husband’s knowledge. From the Council of Elvira.

### CXL. (Council of Elvira, canon 70; Burchard, book IX, chapter 69)

If a wife has committed adultery with her husband’s knowledge, it has been decided that she is not to be given communion even at the point of death. But if he abandons her, she shall receive communion after ten years.

[Note: See the Lombard Laws, book I, title 32, chapter 6.]

### If anyone has committed adultery with a Jewess or a pagan woman. From the same source.

### CXLI. (Council of Elvira, canon 78)

If a believer who has a wife has committed adultery with a Jewess or a pagan woman, he shall be excluded from communion. But if another man marries her, after five years, once he has completed the prescribed penance, he may be admitted to the Lord’s communion.

[Note: The Helmstedt edition and the Paris manuscript consistently read “if another man has married her.” In Rabanus, however, in his letter to Heribald, chapter 26, the reading is “if he has married her.” This agreement caused us not to alter that reading. For I suspected that the word “married” was corrupt in Regino, because the editions of the Council of Elvira print “if he has exposed her.”]

265

### Concerning procuring. From the same council.

### CXLII. (Council of Elvira, canon 12)

If a woman, a relative, or any female believer practices procuring, because she has sold another person’s body—or rather her own—it has been decided that she is not to receive communion even at the point of death.

[Col. 0311C]

### That no Jew may marry a Christian woman. From the Theodosian Law, book IX.

### CXLIII. (Interpretation of book 5 of the Theodosian Code, concerning adulterers)

Neither may a Jew marry a Christian woman, nor a Christian a Jewish woman. If anyone does so, he shall be prosecuted, upon anyone’s accusation, as though for adultery.

### That no one may accuse another man’s wife. From the same book, chapter 4.

### CXLIV. (Interpretation of book 2 of the Theodosian Code, concerning adulterers)

In a case of adultery, no one may accuse an unrelated woman; rather, her relatives to whom the matter pertains may do so—that is, her full brother, her cousin on the father’s side, her paternal uncle, and her cousin. The others, however, before the formal accusation, may, if the accused woman agrees, earn pardon through compensation.

### Concerning husbands who bring accusations. From the same source.

[Col. 0311D]

### CXLV. (The Theodosian Code, same title; Burchard, book XVI, chapter 37)

Husbands, certainly, are also permitted to accuse on the basis of suspicion.

266

### That a household may be subjected to interrogation concerning adultery. From the same source.

### CXLVI (Interpretation of book 4 of the Theodosian Code, same title)

In cases of a wife’s adultery, husbands are permitted to inquire by means of torture of the entire household—that is, both their own household and the wife’s—provided that the slaves in question are proved to have been present or to have been in the same house at the time when the offense is alleged to have been committed. The same applies if a husband complains that his adulterous wife had plotted his death. Likewise, the households of both parties are to be interrogated under punishment if the husband has in any way plotted the death of his wife.

### If a freeborn woman has united herself with her own slave. From the same source, chapter 6.

### CXLVII. (Interpretation of the single law of the Theodosian Code, Concerning a woman who has joined herself to her own slave)

If a freeborn woman has secretly united herself with her own slave, she shall be punished capitally. The slave, too, who has been convicted of adultery with his mistress shall be burned by fire. Slaves are also permitted to accuse of this crime; and if they prove it, they shall obtain their freedom; if they do not, they shall be punished. The woman’s inheritance shall be assigned to her children, if she has had them by her husbands, or to the relatives who inherit according to law.

[Col. 0312B]

### When a wife may be killed. From book II of Paul’s Sentences, chapter 27.

### CXLVIII. (Paul, Sentences, book II, title 27)

A husband may kill a wife caught in adultery only if he catches the adulterer in his own house.

### Concerning one liable for procuring. From the same source.

### CXLIX. (Paul, same work)

It has been decided that a man who does not immediately dismiss a wife caught in adultery should be prosecuted as liable for procuring.

267

### Concerning delay in a case of adultery. From the same source.

### CL. (Paul, same work)

In a case of adultery, if the matter is manifest, a requested delay cannot be granted [in Paul: “a requested delay cannot be obtained”].

### Concerning lay virgins. From the Council of Elvira.

### CLI. (Council of Elvira, canon 14; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 23; Burchard, book IX, chapter 14)

If virgins have not preserved their virginity and have taken as husbands the very men who violated them, since they violated only the marriage bond, they shall be reconciled after one year of penance. If they have known other men, since they have committed adultery, they shall do penance for five years and then approach communion.

### Concerning those who break the pledge of betrothal. From the same source.

### CLII. (Council of Elvira, canon 54)

If parents have broken the pledge of betrothal, they shall abstain for three years. If, however, the same betrothed man or woman has been found guilty of a serious crime, the parents shall be excused.

### Concerning the blessing of the betrothed bride. From the Council of Carthage.

### CLIII. (Council of Carthage IV, canon 13; Burchard, book IX, chapter 5)

When the betrothed man and woman are to be blessed by a priest, they shall be presented by their parents or by the paranymphs. Once they have received the blessing, they shall remain virgins that same night, out of reverence for the blessing itself.

268

### That no one may take another man’s betrothed. From a letter of Pope Siricius.

### CLIV. (Decrees of Siricius, chapter 4; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 15; Burchard, book IX, chapter 31)

You have asked concerning the violation of marriage whether one man may take into marriage a girl betrothed to another. We absolutely forbid this from happening, because, among the faithful, the blessing that the priest bestows upon those about to marry is like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by such a transgression.

### Concerning abducted and betrothed girls. From the Council of Ancyra.

### CLV. (Council of Ancyra, canon 10; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 18; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 20; Burchard, book IX, chapter 38)

It has been decided that betrothed girls who have subsequently been abducted by others are to be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by their abductors.

### Concerning the same matter. From book I of the Capitularies, chapter 99.

### CLVI. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 105; Capitular of Aachen of Louis the Pious, chapter 24; Burchard, book IX, chapter 37)

Accordingly, it has been decided and decreed by the sacred assembly that the abductor shall be punished with public penance. But if the betrothed man does not wish to receive the abducted woman, and she did not consent to the same crime, she shall not be denied permission to marry another. But if she also consented, she shall be subject to the same sentence. If, after this, they should presume to unite with one another, both shall be anathematized.

[Col. 0313B]

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 69.

### CLVII. (Council of Meaux, canon 68; Burchard, book IX, chapter 32)

The ancient and synodal judgment concerning those who abduct another man’s betrothed women is to be observed. Even if perhaps such an event is found in the Church, so that the bishops ought to treat something more humanely in accordance with the requirements of salvation and religion [the bishops should treat it], nevertheless, as canonical authority teaches, to use its own words: “because the earlier decision defined the matter more harshly, whereas the later one treated it somewhat more humanely,” under no circumstances should we descend to the greatest indulgence: the taker of another man’s betrothed woman shall not pass without public penance, and he shall pay the betrothed man the legally prescribed compensation.

If she refuses to obey this, let her be anathematized without any resistance. Her supporters, however, shall do penance by episcopal decree, according to the measure of their guilt. But if—which we do not wish—someone from the ecclesiastical order has openly shown himself to be a consenting party to or an intermediary in such a marriage, let him be expelled from his own order. And if plausible suspicions arising from this matter have been brought against him, let him clear himself canonically.

### Concerning those who are not betrothed. From book I of the Capitularies, chapter 98.

### CLVIII. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 104; Capitular of Aachen of Louis the Pious, chapter 23; Burchard, book IX, chapter 36)

Concerning girls who have been abducted but are not yet betrothed, it is written in the Council of Chalcedon:

> “The holy synod has decreed that those who abduct girls under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or assist the abductors, shall, if they are clerics, fall from their own order; but if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

These words make clear how the authors of this evil are to be condemned, since the participants and assistants are struck with such an anathema; and, in accordance with canonical authority, the abductors can in no way lawfully claim the abducted women for legitimate marriage.

270

[Col. 0314A]

### Concerning abductors of virgins and widows. From the Council of Meaux.

### CLIX. (Council of Meaux, canon 64)

Concerning abductors of virgins or widows, who later also by the will of their parents, and so forth: see above, in the first book, concerning the ordination of clerics, chapter 416.

### Concerning the same matter. From the same source, chapter 65.

### CLX. (Council of Meaux, canon 65; Burchard, book IX, chapter 39)

But if those who have not yet taken as wives the women whom they abducted, with their parents’ consent, under the aforementioned designation of betrothal or dowry, then, once this decree has been proclaimed in everyone’s hearing, they shall separate from their union and be subjected to public penance; the abducted women, however, shall be legally restored to their parents.

After they have completed public penance, if age and incontinence require it, they may be joined in a lawful marriage agreed upon by both sides. For in these matters we are not establishing a rule; rather, to use the words of the great Leo, we are considering what is more tolerable. But if one of the married parties dies, the one who performed public penance and survives shall not presume to marry again, unless perhaps the bishop foresees granting some indulgence by which he may remove the more serious offense.

[Col. 0314B]

### Concerning the same matter. From the same source, chapter 66.

### CLXI. (Council of Meaux, canon 66; Council of Rome under Gregory II, canons 10 and 11)

But whoever thereafter presumes to abduct virgins or widows shall, according to the synodal decree of blessed Gregory, be anathematized together with their accomplices, and the abductors shall remain without marriage perpetually.

271

[Col. 0314C]

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Symmachus.

### CLXII. (Symmachus, letter 5, chapter 4; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 16; Burchard, book IX, chapter 34)

We therefore detest the abductors of widows or virgins because of the enormity of so great a crime, pursuing with particular severity those who have attempted to join sacred virgins to themselves in marriage, whether willingly or unwillingly. Because of the atrocity of so utterly wicked a crime, we order that they be suspended from communion.

[Thus also in an old royal manuscript.]

### Concerning those who abduct nuns. From the aforementioned council, chapter 67.

### CLXIII. (Council of Meaux, canon 67; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 52)

Those who abduct consecrated virgins or widows and, as the crime progresses, take them into marriage shall be subjected to public penance. Both shall remain perpetually without any hope of marital union. But if—which God forbid—they presume to renew the marriage, they shall be subjected to a more severe punishment and expelled still further. If they should perhaps refuse to obey the salutary admonitions, let them be anathematized.

[Note: In the Helmstedt edition one reads, “let them be handed over to public penance and compelled to return to the religious habit. Both,” and so forth. The reading of the Paris manuscript, however, is the one preferred by this edition of ours. In both places this passage is mutilated; it should be supplemented as follows from Sirmond’s edition and our old manuscript: “let them be subjected to public penance, according to the measure foreseen by the bishop. Let the women themselves be confined in suitable places of penance, and return to the religious habit,” and so forth.]

272

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Siricius.

### CLXIV. (Decrees of Siricius, chapter 6; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 29)

We order that shameless and detestable persons—namely, monks and nuns who, having cast aside their commitment to holiness, have mingled in unlawful and sacrilegious intercourse—be expelled from the communities of monasteries and from the assemblies of churches, so that, confined in their own prisons and lamenting such a great crime in continual mourning, they may be refined in the purifying fire of repentance, and so that, at least at the point of death, they may be helped through the grace of communion, solely out of regard for mercy.

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Gregory.

### CLXV. (In Gratian, 27, question 1, chapter 15)

It has come to us that a certain most wicked man, at the devil’s prompting, persuaded a woman consecrated to God to leave the monastery; and after she had been recalled by a certain man from whom she had departed, that same most wicked man, by an unjust persuasion, again drove her from the monastery and continues to keep her shamelessly with him. We wish her to be recalled and confined in the monastery by the authority of your bishopric.

### Concerning the same matter. From a letter of Pope Gelasius.

### CLXVI. (Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 20; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 32)

We have learned that certain men have joined themselves to sacred virgins and, after their consecrated commitment, entered into incestuous and sacrilegious unions with them. It is just that such men be immediately expelled from sacred communion and not received except through public and private penance. Nevertheless, communion as viaticum is not to be denied to those departing from this world, provided that they have repented.

[Col. 0315C] 273

### That a bishop should enter a monastery of monks or women. From the Council of Rouen.

### CLXVII. (Burchard, book VIII, chapter 66)

The bishop is to enter frequently the monastery of monks and of nuns, and, while sitting with serious and religious persons in their assembly, is carefully to examine their life and conduct; and if he finds anything blameworthy, he is to strive to correct it. He shall also investigate the chastity of the nuns with precision. If he finds one who, having neglected her commitment to chastity, has shamelessly intercourse with a cleric or layman, she shall be sternly restrained with beatings and confined in private custody, where she may suitably repent of what she has wrongly done.

By the authority of the holy canons, he shall prohibit any layman or cleric from having access to their cloisters and private dwellings, and priests likewise, except only for Mass. Once Mass has been completed, they shall return to their own churches. Moreover, he shall publicly and privately proclaim how great a sacrilege it is to violate another person’s bride, and how much more guilty of lese-majesty is the one who corrupts the bride of almighty God.

[Note: The final part of this chapter is mutilated; it is to be restored from Burchard as follows: “how great a sacrilege it is to presume to violate Christ’s bride. For if the one who violates a human being’s bride is held guilty, how much more,” and so forth.]

274

### That an abbess should not leave the monastery. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 16.

### CLXVIII. (Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 16; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 80)

An abbess shall by no means leave the monastery except with the permission of her bishop, unless perhaps she is compelled by a royal command. And whenever she goes outside, she shall take the greatest care concerning the nuns whom she takes with her, so that no opportunity for sinning is given to them.

### What nuns ought to do. From the same source.

### CLXIX. (Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 16; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 77)

The nuns established in the monastery shall devote themselves to reading and singing, and shall solemnly celebrate the canonical hours together. All of them, except those whom illness confines, shall sleep in the dormitory; they shall come every day to the chapter meeting and to the conferences; and they shall diligently observe the rule established for them by the holy Fathers.

### Concerning the vigilance to be exercised over nuns. From the Council of Seville.

[Col. 0316B]

### CLXX. (Second Council of Seville, canon 11; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 53)

This precaution is to be observed concerning everyone: they must be kept away from the personal quarters of the virgins and must not be granted familiar permission even to approach the vestibule. Nor should the superior speak with one of them alone; rather, he should do so in the presence of two or three sisters, so that visits are infrequent and conversation brief.

### That clerics or continent men should not enter among virgins. From the Council of Carthage.

### CLXXI. (Third Council of Carthage, canon 25)

Clerics or continent men are not to approach widows or virgins except by order or permission of bishops or priests—and not even the bishops and priests alone, but only when clerics or other serious Christians are present.

275

### Concerning corrupted nuns. From a letter of Pope Innocent.

### CLXXII. (Decrees of Innocent I, chapter 10; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 19; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 13)

Those who are spiritually married in Christ, if they later marry publicly or corrupt themselves secretly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has departed from this world. For if this rule is observed concerning human beings—namely, that a woman who marries another while her husband is alive is regarded as an adulteress, and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of the men has died—how much more must it be observed concerning one who had previously joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward transferred herself to human embraces.

[Col. 0316D]

### Concerning secular widows. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 61.

### CLXXIII. (Council of Meaux, canon 70; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 50)

Those women who appear to live as nuns under the veil of religion, but who, living instead in luxury, are reckoned as dead in the eyes of God, roam through the provinces, inquisitive and talkative [1 Timothy 5]. If they are accused of serving lusts and other carnal desires and pleasures, and can be openly exposed, they shall, by episcopal authority and royal power, be compelled to reside in such places under religious supervision, where, if they perform worthy penance, they may also obtain its fruitful benefit.

But if they cannot be openly exposed, they shall be compelled legally to clear themselves before the Church of the evil reputation they have acquired; and, so that thereafter they may live more religiously and conduct themselves in monasteries, they shall be restrained by episcopal decree and royal power. For concerning such women the Apostle says: “When they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry” (same passage).

[Note: This chapter differs greatly from the commonly published editions of the Council of Meaux. Nevertheless, it is read as we have published it in Regino’s manuscript and in the Helmstedt edition, except that in that edition, through an obvious scribal error, the following words have been omitted: “its fruitful benefit. But if they cannot be openly exposed, before the Church,” and so forth.]

### Concerning the same matter.

### CLXXIV. (Burchard, book VIII, chapter 41, and Ivo, part VII, chapter 59)

Concerning widows the Apostle says:

> “Command,” he says, “that widows be irreproachable. Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, who has testimony in good works, if she has raised children,” and so forth. “Avoid younger widows. For when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have rejected their first faith. At the same time they learn to be idle, going about from house to house—not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive, saying things that ought not to be said. Therefore I wish younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no opportunity for reproach. For some have already turned back after Satan” (1 Timothy 5).

### Concerning the same matter. From Roman law.

### CLXXV. (Novel of Majorian, title 8)

We are moved by the obstinacy of widows who, having borne no children, condemn their fertility by refusing to restore the household through a second marriage, and choose a solitary life—not, as may be inferred, from love of religion and chastity, but the freedom of living in power and wantonness. People who solicit them, under a pretended show of religion, or cunning flatterers, encourage them in every kind of license.

In order to recall such women to a more honorable way of life, we enact that a woman deprived of her husband by his death, if she is forty years old and still able by age to bear children, shall marry within five years. If, after the five years have elapsed, she remains a widow, she shall immediately divide her property with her relatives; or, if these should perhaps be lacking, she shall divide her estate with the treasury [in the Novel: “estate” (patrimonium)].

### That nuns should not go to the palace or public assemblies. From the Council of Nantes.

### CLXXVI. (Council of Nantes, canon 19; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 85)

Since the Apostle says, “Let women keep silent in the church, for it is not permitted to them to speak” (1 Corinthians 14), it seems astonishing that certain little women, acting shamelessly with hardened brows against divine and human laws, continually attend general councils and public assemblies, and disturb rather than arrange the affairs of the kingdom and the interests of the commonwealth.

It is indecent and even blameworthy among barbarian peoples for women to discuss men’s cases; yet women who ought to have discussed matters concerning their wool-working and textile labor, while seated among their female companions, arrogate to themselves in a public assembly, as though seated in the senate, senatorial authority.

This disgraceful presumption appears imputable more to their supporters than to the women themselves. Therefore, since divine laws, as shown above, contradict this practice, and human laws likewise prohibit it—so that women may pursue no matter in public other than their own case—the Theodosian law says (Interpretation of book 5 of the Theodosian Code, concerning advocates and procurators):

> “Women shall in no way have authority to conduct cases beyond their own, nor shall they undertake the prosecution of anyone else’s case.”

Accordingly, by canonical authority we forbid any nun, virgin, or widow to attend general assemblies unless she has been summoned by the prince or by her own bishop, or unless perhaps the necessity of her own case has compelled her—and even then, with the permission of her bishop.

### When a virgin is to receive the veil. From the Council of Africa.

### CLXXVII. (Council of Africa, canon 93; book I of the Capitularies, chapter 46; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 18; Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 12)

Virgins are not to receive the veil before the age of twenty-five, unless perhaps the necessity of endangered virgin chastity requires it. And, as Pope Gelasius says, they are not to be consecrated except on Epiphany, on Easter in white garments, and on the feasts of the apostles—unless the urgency of impending death requires it.

### Concerning the same matter. Gelasius.

### CLXXVIII. (Decrees of Gelasius, chapter 13; book I of the Capitularies, chapter 59; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 36)

No bishop should presume to veil widows.

(Council of Tribur, canon 24; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 10)

Virgins who, before the age of twelve and without the knowledge of their mundburds, have placed the sacred veil upon their heads, and whose mundburds have consented to this by remaining silent for an entire year and a day, shall remain in the holy commitment. If, during that year and day, they bring a complaint on their own behalf, their petition shall be granted—unless perhaps, touched by the fear of God, they remain in the religious habit with their permission.

279

### Concerning the same matter. From the same council.

### CLXXIX. (Council of Tribur, canon 23; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 35)

Concerning widows who, of their own free will, receive from the altar the veil of sacred religious life, the holy synod has decreed that they remain in the same commitment. For we decree that it is not lawful, after they have once consecrated themselves to the Lord beneath the veil and made offerings among the veiled women, to permit them again to lie to the Holy Spirit.

### Pope Zacharias, chapter 7.

[Col. 0318D]

(Burchard, book IX, chapter 13)

No one may dare to abduct a virgin or widow in order to marry her, except the man to whom she has been betrothed. If anyone should presume to do this with such rashness, let him be anathema.

[Note: This chapter is not found in the Paris manuscript.]

### Also concerning nuns. From the same council.

### CLXXX

If a nun decides, for the profit of her soul and with the permission of her abbess, to go to another monastery and remain there, the synod has decreed that this is permitted. But if she seeks another place in flight from discipline, she shall be compelled to return.

[Col. 0319A]

### Concerning concubines. From a letter of Pope Leo.

### CLXXXI. (Decrees of Leo I, chapters 18 and 19; Burchard, book IX, chapter 1)

Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. Therefore, a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another.

To cast a slave woman away from the marriage bed and take a wife of certain free birth is not a doubling of marriage but an advance in respectability. For there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to a marriage when it is shown that there was no nuptial ceremony. Unless perhaps that woman appears both to have been made free, lawfully endowed, and honored by a public wedding.

### That wives should be restored to husbands returning from captivity. From a letter of Leo.

[Col. 0319B]

### CLXXXII. (Decrees of Leo I, chapter 42; Burchard, book IX, chapter 55)

Women who, after their husbands had been captured and led into captivity, married other men, believing their husbands to have been killed, ought, when their former husbands return from captivity, to be joined to them, so that each person may be restored to what he lawfully possessed, each may receive what belongs to him, and the marriage bonds may be renewed.

### Concerning the same matter. From the same source.

### CLXXXIII. (Decrees of Leo I, chapters 43, 44, and 45; Burchard, book IX, chapter 56)

A man who appears to have taken the wife of a captive man in marriage is not proved to be culpable. And if the men returning from captivity are not offended by their wives’ incontinence and wish to receive them back into marriage, they shall have full freedom to do so.

[Col. 0319C]

But if a woman refuses to return to her former husbands, having been captivated by love for her later husbands, she shall be deprived of ecclesiastical communion.

281

### Concerning incestuous unions. From the Council of Lérida, chapter 4.

### CLXXXIV. (Council of Lérida, canon 4; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 20; Burchard, book VII, chapter 3)

Concerning those who defile themselves with incestuous pollution, it has been decided that, for as long as they persist in that detestable and unlawful sexual union, they shall be admitted in the church only as far as the Mass of the catechumens. With them, too, no Christian ought to take any food, as the Apostle commanded.

### From the Council of Toledo.

(Council of Toledo II, canon 5; Burchard, book VII, chapter 6)

Taking salutary precautions, we decree that no believer should desire to join in marriage with a blood relative, so long as he recognizes the lines of kinship through the succession of generations. For it is written: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relative to uncover her nakedness” (Leviticus 18).

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Agde.

### CLXXXV. (Council of Agde, canon 61; Sixth Council of Arles, canon 11; Burchard, book VII, chapter 4)

We reserve absolutely no pardon for incestuous unions, unless they have healed the adultery through separation. We judge such cases as follows: if anyone has violated through carnal union his brother’s widow, who had previously almost been his sister; if anyone has taken his brother’s wife’s full sister; if anyone has taken his stepmother, his cousin, his maternal uncle’s daughter or his widow, his paternal uncle’s daughter, or his stepdaughter; such persons, for whom an unlawful union is prohibited, shall, after performing penance, have the freedom [that is, the power] to enter into a better marriage [that is, a lawful one].

[Note: See Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, chapter 20.]

282

### Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Rome.

### CLXXXVI. (Council of Rome under Gregory II, chapter 3 and following; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 22; book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 127)

Pope Gregory said:

> “If anyone takes a handmaid of God, that is, a nun, in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his spiritual godmother in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his niece [Paris manuscript: ‘his brother’s wife’] in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes in marriage a woman from his own kindred or one whom a relative has had, let him be anathema. If anyone abducts a widow as a wife, or those who consent to him do so, let him be anathema. If anyone abducts a virgin as a wife without having betrothed her, or those who consent to him do so, let him be anathema.”

And to all these statements the entire council answered three times: “Amen.”

### Concerning judgment. From the Council at Confluentes. Charles to Louis.

### CLXXXVII. (Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 30, chapter 5)

Our daughter Judith, a widow established under ecclesiastical protection and royal mundburd according to divine and human laws, Baldwin abducted as his wife. After a lawful judgment, the bishops of our kingdom excommunicated him according to the holy canons and the decree of Saint Pope Gregory, who says:

> “If anyone abducts a widow as a wife, or those who consent to him do so, let him be anathema.”

283

### Concerning women who lose their husbands. Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 96.

### CLXXXVIII. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 102; book II of the Lombard Laws, title 6, chapter 4; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 42; Ivo, part VII, chapter 60)

Concerning women who lose their husbands, it is pleasing that they should not, as previously, veil themselves indiscriminately; instead, they shall wait thirty days after their husband’s death. After the thirtieth day, they shall choose what they ought to choose, with the advice of their bishop—or, if the bishop is absent, with the advice of their other religious priests and their friends.

And because we were asked by the sacred assembly to protect, by our authority, those who are performing public penance and women who lose their husbands until they decide what they should do, we have decreed that special chapters concerning them be drawn up and inserted into the chapters of secular law.

[Note: This passage is mutilated in Regino, Burchard, and Ivo. For in book I of the Capitularies, chapter 102, both in the printed and manuscript copies, and also in the Capitular of Aachen of Louis the Pious, chapter 21, after the words “religious priests,” one reads “and their parents and friends.” From this it must be inferred that Burchard and Ivo copied their texts from Regino.]

### Concerning the same matter. From book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 16.

### CLXXXIX. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 17; book II of the Lombard Laws, title 6, chapter 3)

Whoever joins himself to a widow, whether against her will or with her consent, within the first thirty days of her widowhood shall pay sixty solidi. And if he has taken her against her will, he shall pay her the compensation prescribed by her law and shall not touch her thereafter.

284

### Whoever kills a person performing public penance. From the same source, chapter 17.

### CXC. (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 18; book I of the Lombard Laws, title 9, chapter 31)

Whoever kills a person performing public penance shall pay three times the amount of our ban and shall pay his wergeld to his relatives.

[Note: See above, chapter 30 of this book.]

### That a brother should not ascend upon his deceased brother’s bed. From the Council of Orléans.

### CXCI. (First Council of Orléans, canon 18; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 20)

A brother must not ascend upon the bed of his deceased brother, nor may anyone, after losing his wife, dare to join her sister to himself.

### Concerning the violation of a betrothed woman’s sister. From the Council of Ancyra.

### CXCII. (Council of Ancyra, canon 24)

A certain man had a betrothed woman and violated her sister, making her pregnant. He later took the betrothed woman as his wife. The woman who had been violated, however, killed herself with a noose. Those who were aware of the matter were ordered, after ten years of satisfaction, to be received according to the established degrees of penance.

### Of the woman who married two brothers. From the Council of Neocaesarea

**CXCIII.** (Council of Neocaesarea, canon 2; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 14; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 1.) If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be excluded until death; nevertheless, at the point of death, communion is to be granted to her out of mercy. But if a man or woman persists in such a marriage, penance will be difficult during the life that remains.  
[Note: [Col. 0321D] See below, book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 296.]

**285. Of the same matter. From the Council of Elvira**

**CXCIV.** (Council of Elvira, canon 62.) If anyone, after the death of his wife, takes her sister, and she is a believer, it has been decreed that he abstain from communion for five years, unless death compels otherwise.

### Of the same matter. From a decree of Pope Martin

**CXCV.** (Martin of Braga, canon 79; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 2.) If any woman marries two brothers, or any man marries two sisters, they are to be separated from communion until death; at death they are to receive the viaticum out of mercy.  
[Col. 0321D]

### Of a goddaughter and a godmother. From a letter of Rabanus to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, chapter 20

**CXCVI.** (Burchard, book XVII, chapter 24.) Concerning what you asked—whether the man [and] his goddaughter (the wording is incomplete), the man who has had intercourse with his spiritual godmother, and the man who baptized his son and whose wife received him from the font may afterward remain in such a union—we have judged this altogether unlawful. For it is written in the Council of Mainz, canon 55 (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, canon 55; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 100; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 25):

> “Let no one receive his own son or daughter from the baptismal font, nor take his goddaughter or godmother as wife, nor the woman whose son he has held before the bishop for confirmation. But wherever this has happened, let them be separated.”

### If anyone takes a widow as his wife. From the same source

**CXCVII.** (Rabanus, same work; Council of Mainz under Rabanus, canon 56; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 101; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 9.) If anyone takes a widow as his wife and afterward fornicates with his stepdaughter, or marries two sisters, or if any woman marries two brothers, or fornicates with a father and son, we command that such unions be anathematized and dissolved, and that they never again be joined in marriage, but that this be done under severe discipline.  
[Note: [Col. 0322D] This chapter has been added from a manuscript; it is not present in the Helmstedt edition.]

### Of the man who violates his goddaughter. As above

**CXCVIII.** (Rabanus, same work; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 26.)  
[Col. 0322B] How detestable and abhorrent a crime it is for any Christian to defile his goddaughter is attested by Saint Pope Gregory in his *Dialogues* (book IV, chapter 32). There he reports that a certain man defiled his goddaughter and, because he neglected to do penance, was suddenly struck down by a grievous illness and died; after he had been buried, not only his body but also the entire tomb was consumed by an invisible fire.

### Likewise concerning incestuous unions and their penance. From the Council of Mainz

**CXCIX.** (Rabanus, same work; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 18.) If anyone fornicates with two sisters, or with his stepmother, or with his paternal aunt, or with his mother, or with the daughter of his paternal uncle or maternal uncle, or with the daughter of his paternal or maternal aunt, or with his niece, or with his godmother or goddaughter, whether the one whom he received from the font or held before the bishop, and if any woman fornicates in the same manner, let that person abstain from entering the house of God for one year. During that same year, except on Sundays and feast days, let him use only bread, water, and salt; let him bear no weapons and give no kiss; let him receive the sacrifice only as a viaticum and in no other circumstance.

For the following six years, let him indeed enter the house of God, but let him not use meat, wine, or beer, except on feast days. As for weapons, the kiss, and the sacrifice, let him observe what was stated above. Thereafter, for two years, whenever he eats meat, let him abstain from every drink capable of causing drunkenness; and if he drinks such a beverage, let him not eat meat, except on the principal feast days. Regarding weapons, the kiss, and the sacrifice, let him observe the previously stated rule.

From then until his death, except on the aforesaid feast days, let him abstain from meat on three ordinary weekdays every week, and let him properly observe the three Lents each year. As for weapons, let him observe what was stated above. Let him never afterward enter into marriage.

This same penance is to be imposed on parricides, fratricides, and kinsmen, as well as on those who willingly kill an innocent person through fraud and greed—what they call *morchidum*.

### In which degree the faithful may marry. From a letter of Rabanus to Bishop Humbert

**CC.** Concerning marriages, and how kinship is to be honored, the Lord speaks in Leviticus, saying: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relation, to uncover his nakedness” (Leviticus XVIII). Since the Lord wished to separate his people from the contaminations of the nations, he first prohibited anyone, in a general expression, from approaching a near blood relation, lest he uncover that person’s nakedness. Then he subdivided that general prohibition, more or less, into twelve categories; these nevertheless do not extend beyond the third or fourth generation.

Hence, I think, it happened that Gregory responded to Augustine, when he asked about this, that marriages could already lawfully be contracted in the third or fourth generation. Likewise, in the *Capitula* of Archbishop Theodore of the English people, which he composed concerning necessary matters, we find that marriage is permitted in the third degree of fleshly kinship according to the Greeks, and in the fifth according to the Romans.

Nevertheless, they would not dissolve marriages contracted within the third degree if they had previously been arranged by persons unaware of the prohibition. In the same way, a man would be joined in marriage to those related to him by blood, and after the death of his wife to her blood relatives.

This Theodore, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, was ordained bishop at Rome by Pope Vitalian and sent to Britain. He had therefore been fully instructed in the customs of both the Eastern and Western Churches. Nothing could have escaped him concerning the lawful observances then held by the Greeks and Romans, especially since he was perfectly trained in both languages.

As for the writings of the Roman pontiffs in more recent times, which state that the use of marriage should be deferred until the sixth or seventh generation, it must be believed that they commanded this more from human custom than from divine law. For when Isidore, in his *Etymologies*, asserted that one should abstain from blood kinship until the sixth generation and then enter into lawful marriage, I think he did so because, tracing the line of genealogy, he judged that blood relationship should be maintained as far as the point to which he carried the order of counting. Thus he sanctioned a return to marriage for the renewal of the family and the confirmation of the right of friendship, once the order of kinship had ceased to be counted.

Above all, however, it must be considered that the rigor of discipline should be tempered in such a way that, through excessive correction, the accumulation of sin is not increased. For we know that the one who established the observance of the law of kinship in the Law commanded in the Gospel that the bond of marriage not be dissolved.

If, whenever any degree of proximity or kinship, however distant, could be found between married persons, the marriage were immediately dissolved, I fear that adultery and the crime of fornication would multiply. For when companionship with his equal is denied to a married adolescent or young man, and no consolation is provided by which he might preserve continence, he may, inflamed by lust and instigated by the devil, defile himself through repeated fornication, and thus his soul may be plunged into the abyss of eternal death.

Therefore, since you wished me, in my lowliness, to write to you what I thought about this matter, I believe that, given the weakness of the present age, we should follow more closely what Bishop Theodore, proceeding midway between Gregory and Isidore, defined in his *Capitula*: that marriage should already be permitted in the fifth generation, because divine law does not contradict this, nor do the sayings of the holy Fathers prohibit it.

But if, even within the fifth generation, a union has been contracted by persons unaware of the prohibition, it seems better to me that, with the humiliation of penance, they should satisfy God, if the married man does not wish to remain continent.

### Of the same matter. Gregory to Augustine

**CCI.** (In Bede, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 27, section 6.) It is necessary that the faithful of the third or fourth generation also be permitted to join themselves lawfully. For they must altogether abstain from the second generation, as we stated above.

### Of the same matter. From a letter of Rabanus to Reginbald, chorepiscopus

**CCII.** Concerning what you asked—if a father and son, or two brothers, or an uncle and nephew, have fornicated with the same woman, what should be done—it is clear that this must be punished with severe vengeance, since it is found to be a grave crime. For every act of adultery is forbidden where it is written: “You shall not commit adultery.” How much more so when the woman is a relative, or the wife or concubine of a relative?

Hence it is written in Leviticus: “If anyone commits adultery with another man’s wife, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death. Whoever lies with his stepmother or with his daughter-in-law, and whoever takes both daughter and mother, and whoever takes his sister, shall be put to death” (Leviticus XX).

If the Law commanded that the shamefulness of incest be punished by a sentence of death, how will the incestuous person escape penance for his sin in the Gospel, where there is perfect justice? Hence the Apostle says: “Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you suppose, will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified as unclean, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Hebrews X.)

Accordingly, Theodore judged that one who committed incest ought to do penance for twelve years. Others prescribe fifteen years, others ten, others seven. But you, following the footsteps of the ancient Fathers, should moderate the period of penance only for those who have performed penance devoutly and with tears; the others should observe the prescribed period.

### Of the man who made himself a slave. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 11

**CCIII.** (Burchard, book IX, chapter 75.) It was reported to the holy synod that a free man had taken a free woman as his wife and, after fathering children, had made himself someone’s slave on the pretext of divorce. The question was whether he was necessarily required to keep the woman, and, if he kept her, whether she too ought to be subjected to slavery according to secular law.

It was judged that the wife should by no means be dismissed; nevertheless, on account of Christ’s law, the woman should not be reduced to slavery, since the man had made himself a slave without the consent of his wife, whom he had taken as a free husband.

### Likewise concerning incest. From the same source

**CCIV.** (Council of Tribur, canon 44; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 15.) It was likewise judged that a certain man had violated a woman whom his brother afterward took as his wife. They decreed that the man who had violated her and concealed from his brother that he had violated her, because he had doubled his sin, should be punished with stricter penance; that such a marriage ought to be dissolved; that, while those men were alive, the woman should not have the power to marry; but that, out of mercy, marriage should be granted to them.

### If anyone has intercourse with his maternal aunt’s daughter, and so forth. From the same source

**CCV.** (Burchard, book XVII, chapter 20.) [Col. 0325B] It was likewise asked whether, if anyone has had intercourse with the daughter of his maternal aunt or maternal uncle, paternal aunt or paternal uncle, he may, if married, continue to use marriage, or, if unmarried, take a wife. It would be just, as some earlier statutes provide, that such persons abstain from marriage forever. But, out of consideration for human weakness, it seemed appropriate that after penance they should not be entirely deprived of marriage; nevertheless, so monstrous a fornication must be punished with the greatest severity, as Saint Pope Nicholas and the other Roman pontiffs decreed, lest, with their consciences driven to despair, they sin still more.

### Likewise concerning incest. From the same source

**CCVI.** (Burchard, book XVIII, chapter 4; Roman Penitential, title 3, chapter 5.) In the husband’s bed, while the wife was absent, the wife’s sister went there. The husband, thinking that she was his own wife, slept with her. Concerning this, it was judged that, if he could establish with true certainty that he had committed the crime unknowingly, he should perform the penance assigned to him and be permitted to retain his lawful marriage; but she should be afflicted with deserved punishment and deprived of marriage forever.  
[Note: [Col. 0325D] The Helmstedt edition reads *veram non probaverit* (“if he has not proved it true”), entirely contrary to the meaning of the canon. Since we lacked the assistance of the manuscript codex, which is defective at this point, we have adopted the true reading from Burchard and from the Roman Penitential edited by Antonio Agustín.]

### 293. Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCVII.** (Council of Tribur, canon 43; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 16.) A certain man fornicated with a woman. Later, his son, unaware of what his father had done, violated the same woman. When the father learned of this, he confessed concerning himself and his son. They decreed that it was better for those who had fallen in this way, with appropriate penance, to be permitted lawful marriages, lest they perhaps commit a worse offense; but stricter action was to be taken against the fornicating woman.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCVIII.** (Council of Tribur, canon 45; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 5.) If anyone fornicates with two sisters, and one sister does not know that the other has previously been violated by the same man, or if he himself did not realize that the woman was the sister of the one whom he had previously violated, then, if they perform worthy penance and are unable to remain continent, marriage is not to be denied to them after seven years. But if they were not ignorant of the matter, they are to abstain from marriage until death.

[Col. 0326A] ### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCIX.** (Burchard, book XVII, chapter 6.) If anyone fornicates with two sisters, let the man do penance for all the days of his life. But the sister who did not know about the other sister is to have permission to marry.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCX.** (Council of Tribur, canon 44; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 13.) If a man fornicates with a woman, and his brother, unaware of it, takes her as his wife, the brother is to do penance because he concealed the crime from his brother, and after penance he may marry. But the woman is to do penance until death.  
[Note: [Col. 0326D] See book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 296.]

### 294. Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXI.** (Council of Tribur, canon 43; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 14.) If one brother fornicates with a woman and [Col. 0326B] another brother, unaware of it, has intercourse with the same woman, the woman is to do penance for all the days of her life; but after penance, the brother who was unaware of the crime may take her in marriage, if he wishes.  
[Note: [Col. 0326D] See the Council of Compiègne under Pippin, chapter 8, and book X of the Capitularies, chapter 19.]

### Of separation. From the Council of Verberie in the time of Pippin

**CCXII.** (Council of Verberie, canon 1; Council of Compiègne, canon 1.) Let them be separated in the third degree. But if they are found to be joined in the fourth degree, we do not separate them; rather, we prescribe penance for them. Nevertheless, if the union has not yet taken place, we grant no permission for them to join in the fourth degree.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXIII.** (Council of Verberie, canon 2.) If anyone remains with his stepdaughter, he may have neither the mother nor the daughter of that woman, and neither she nor he may ever join himself or herself to anyone else. Nevertheless, his wife, if she wishes and cannot remain continent, may marry another, provided that, after learning that her husband had committed adultery with her daughter, she has no sexual relations with him.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXIV.** (Council of Verberie, canon 10; Burchard, book XVIII, chapter 11.) If anyone sleeps with his stepmother, they can in no way proceed to marriage. If her husband wishes, he may take another wife, if he cannot remain continent. Likewise, one who has slept with his stepdaughter or with his wife’s sister may remain married.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXV.** (Council of Verberie, canon 12; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 3.) Whoever sleeps with two sisters, one of whom had previously been his wife, is to have neither of them, and the adulterers are never to be joined in marriage to them.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXVI.** (Council of Compiègne, canon 8; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 17.) If anyone sleeps with his brother’s wife, let the adulterer and the adulteress remain without marriage for all the days of their lives. But the man whose wife she was may, if he wishes, take another wife.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXVII.** (Council of Compiègne, canon 10; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 5; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 18.) If anyone violates his son’s betrothed, and afterward the son marries her, the father is not afterward to have a wife, nor is that woman to have a husband. The son, who was unaware of his father’s crime, may take another wife.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXVIII.** (Burchard, book XVII, chapter 22.) If anyone has held his step-son or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, he is to be separated from his wife and never take another. The same applies to the woman.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXIX.** (Council of Compiègne, canon 14; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 12.) If anyone has fornicated with both mother and daughter, while the mother did not know about the daughter and the daughter did not know about the mother, he is never to take a wife. But they, if they wish, may take husbands. If the women knew of this, they are to remain without husbands forever.

### 296. Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXX.** (Council of Compiègne, canon 15; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 7.) Likewise, concerning two sisters: the man who remained in adultery with one and publicly took the other is not to have a wife until the day of his death; but the woman who did not know is to take a husband.

### If anyone flees because of a feud. From the same source

**CCXXI.** (Council of Compiègne, canon 18; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 6.) If anyone flees to other countries because of vengeance and leaves his wife, neither he nor she is to be joined to another.

### Likewise concerning incest. From the same source

**CCXXII.** (Council of Metz under Pippin, canon 1; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 7.) If anyone commits incest with a close female relative, let him lose his property, if he has any; and if he does not wish to reform, let no one receive him into his house or give him food. Whoever does so is to pay sixty solidi to the king. If he has no money, let him be sent to prison if he is free; if he is a slave, let him be beaten with many blows.

### Likewise concerning parricides. From the same source

**CCXXIII.** If a free man kills his father or mother, his brother or uncle, let him lose his own inheritance. And if anyone commits adultery with his mother, sister, or paternal aunt, let him lose his inheritance.

### Likewise concerning incest. From the same source

**CCXXIV.** (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, canon 53; book V of the Capitularies, chapters 98 and 152; Third Council of Tours, canon 41.) Let the bishops take care to investigate incestuous persons. If they do not wish to repent, let them be expelled from the Church until they return to penance. If they refuse to obey the priests, they must be restrained through secular discipline.

### Of the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 29

**CCXXV.**  
[Note: [Col. 0327D] See above, chapter 197 of this book.]

If anyone takes a widow as his wife and afterward fornicates with his stepdaughter, or marries two sisters; or if any woman marries two brothers, or if anyone fornicates with a father and son, or violates his brother’s widow, his niece, his stepmother, his daughter-in-law, his cousin, his uncle’s daughter, his uncle’s widow, or his stepdaughter, we command that they be separated and never again joined in marriage.

### Of the same matter. From the same source

**CCXXVI.** (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, canon 54; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 99; Burchard, book VII, chapter 18.) We also prohibit anyone from being joined in marriage beyond the fourth generation. But where a marriage has taken place after the prohibition was issued, let them be separated.

### Of the same matter. From the Council of Worms

**CCXXVII.** (Council of Worms, canon 33.) If anyone has fornicated with two sisters, or with two brothers, or with those persons whom Holy Scripture prohibits, and has performed worthy penance but cannot remain continent, he may take a lawful wife or husband.

### If anyone has fornicated with his spiritual godmother. From the same source

**CCXXVIII.** (Council of Worms, canon 34.) If anyone has fornicated with his spiritual godmother, let him be struck with anathema until he has performed worthy penance. The same applies if he has fornicated with the woman whom he received from the font or whom he held before the bishop. But if he has a lawful wife, let him not dismiss her.

### Likewise concerning incest. From the same source

**CCXXIX.** (Council of Worms, canon 36.) If anyone has fornicated with his stepdaughter, after the marriage has been dissolved let him perform penance. Specifically, for a period of three years let him be suspended from the body and blood of the Lord; let him not eat meat or drink wine, and let him fast every day except feast days and Sundays.  
[Col. 0328C] The same rule is to be observed concerning women who have secretly given themselves in intercourse to their father and concerning the son, and by those who recognize that they have secretly defiled themselves with two sisters.

### That unlawful marriages are to be dissolved under oath. From the Council of Tribur

**CCXXX.** (Council of Tribur, canon 49.) We wish those whose unlawful marriages must be severed to confirm by oath that they will not live together at one table or under one roof, nor enjoy any familiar conversation, except in public or in church. Let them divide the possessions they held in common, so that no suspicion can arise or grow.

### How the oath concerning kinship is to be investigated

**CCXXXI.** (Burchard, book VII, chapter 25.) Concerning the kinship which they say exists between that man and this woman, his wife: whatever you know or have heard about it, reckon from your neighbors or your ancestors. You shall conceal nothing from your bishop, or from his messenger whom he has ordered to investigate this matter—not by any device, nor out of fear, reward, or kinship—whenever he questions you about it. So may God help you.

### Of the same matter

**CCXXXII.** (Burchard, book VII, chapter 26.) This is the oath which that man swore concerning the kinship reckoned between him and his wife: you shall observe it insofar as you know or have heard about it. So may God help you.

### Oath concerning the separation of incestuous persons

**CCXXXIII.** (Burchard, book VII, chapter 27.) From this day forward you shall swear that, by no device, you will join yourself to this kinswoman of yours, named [so-and-so], who until this day has been your wife contrary to the law and to right Christianity—not in marriage, nor in adultery or fornication. You shall not eat or drink with her at one table, nor remain under one roof, except perhaps in a church or in some public place where no evil suspicion can arise, so that there, in the presence of witnesses, you may speak together for a definite necessity.

You shall not take another wife, unless perhaps, after completing your penance, permission has been granted to you by your bishop or his messenger.  
[Col. 0329B] So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.

### Invocation of judgment

**CCXXXIV.** (Burchard, book IX, chapter 79.) Concerning the charge brought against me in this synod, that I had committed adultery or fornication with this woman: I did not do so, nor do I acknowledge myself guilty in this matter. So may God help me at this judgment of his.

### Oath after penance has been assigned for committed sexual misconduct

**CCXXXV.** (Burchard, book IX, chapter 80.) From this day forward, with the woman with whom you committed adultery or fornication, for which you received discipline or penance, you shall commit adultery or fornication no more, nor take her as your wife, unless perhaps, after completing your penance, permission has been granted to you by the bishop or his messenger. So may God help you.

### Of the man who is said to have been accused of committing adultery with a married woman while her husband was alive. From the Synod of Meaux

**CCXXXVI.** (Council of Meaux, canon 69; Burchard, book IX, chapter 65.) The man who is accused of having committed adultery with another man’s wife while her husband was alive, and who is known to have taken her soon after her husband’s death, is to be subjected in every way to public penance. After his penance, the aforesaid rule is also to be observed concerning him, if appropriate, unless perhaps he or the woman is accused of having killed the man who died, or kinship or some other criminal act prevents it.

If this is proved, let them remain permanently in penance, without any hope of marriage. But if he denies that he committed adultery with the same woman while her husband was alive, and neither of them is guilty of the aforesaid homicide, and he cannot in any way be convicted by credible witnesses, let them legally clear their reputation and use the marriage they have contracted, if no other consideration, as we have said, prevents it.

### Of the same matter. From the Council of Tribur

**CCXXXVII.** (Council of Tribur, canon 40; Burchard, book IX, chapter 66.) It was reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man had violated another man’s wife, and had moreover given the adulteress, while her husband was alive, an oath that, after her lawful husband’s death, if he survived, he would take her as his wife; and this was indeed done. We therefore prohibit and anathematize such a marriage.

### Invocation concerning the death of a husband or wife

**CCXXXVIII.** Concerning the charge brought against you in the presence of this bishop and in this synod: that through your action and your counsel your husband, or her husband, received death and lost his life—it is altogether not so. You did nothing against his life or limbs, nor did you conspire with others in anything for which, according to ecclesiastical judgment, you ought rightly to receive the remedies of penance, or according to worldly law suffer death or any other harm. So may God help you at this judgment.

### Oath or invocation concerning an alleged homicide

**CCXXXIX.** Concerning what has been charged against you in the presence of your bishop, whose parishioner you are: that you killed that man together with other men who followed you, for the purpose of seizing his possessions and taking his wife in marriage—it is not true. You neither alone nor together with other men killed that man, nor did you conspire with others so that he would lose his life or limbs, nor did you do anything in connection with his death for which you ought rightly to receive penance or punishment, or pay any compensation. So may God help you.

### Oath concerning the reconciliation of married persons

**CCXL.** (Burchard, book IX, chapter 81.) From this day forward, you shall hold this woman, your wife, named [so-and-so], whom you unjustly dismissed, with such care as a rightful husband ought to show his wife, in affection and due discipline. You shall not separate her from yourself by any evil device, nor take another wife while she lives. So may God help you.

### Of the same matter

**CCXLI.** (Burchard, book X, chapter 82.) From now on you shall hold and embrace this man, your husband, whom you unjustly dismissed, and you shall be subject and obedient to him in service, love, and fear, just as a wife ought rightly to be subject to her husband. You shall never separate yourself from him, nor, while he lives, join yourself to another man in marriage or adultery. So may God help you.

### Of those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse. From a letter of Rabanus, chapter 29

**CCXLII.** (Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 29; book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 55; Burchard, book X, chapter 40.) Concerning what you asked about those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse: whether the man may take another wife or the woman another husband. It is written of them:

> “If a man and a woman have joined themselves, and afterward the woman says concerning the man that he cannot have intercourse with her, if she can prove through a lawful judgment that this is true, let her take another.”

### Of the same matter. From the Council of Verberie in the time of King Pippin, chapter 17

**CCXLIII.** (Council of Verberie, canon 17; Burchard, book IX, chapter 41.) If a woman complains that her husband has never had intercourse with her, let them go to the cross; and, if it is true, let them be separated, and let her do what she wishes.

### Of the same matter

**CCXLIV.** (Council of Compiègne, canon 17; Burchard, book IX, chapter 42.) If anyone takes a wife and has had her for some time, and the woman says that he did not have intercourse with her, while the man says that he did, the truth is to rest on the man’s assertion, because the man is the head of the woman.

### Of the same matter. From the Council of Tribur

**CCXLV.** (Council of Tribur, canon 41; Burchard, book IX, chapter 43.) If a man takes a wife but, being unable to have intercourse with her, his brother secretly violates her and makes her pregnant, let them be separated. But, in consideration of their weakness, let mercy be shown to them for marriage, only in the Lord.

### Of fornication with various persons. From the Roman Penitential, and from those of Bishop Theodore and the priest Bede

**CCXLVI.**  
[Col. 0331B] If an adolescent sins with a virgin, let him do penance for one year.

If it happened only once and by accident, let his penance be lightened, and let him do penance only until the full year has elapsed.

If an adolescent under thirty years of age commits fornication, let him observe three Lents and the regular fast days.

If, because of this sin, they have been deprived of human service, let them do penance for forty days.

If a married man fornicates with a virgin, let him do penance for two years, first of all by remaining continent from his wife. If she consented, a measure of penance is also to be added for the wife.

If a layman fornicates with a laywoman, let him do penance for three years; and the more frequently it occurred, the more time is to be added.

[Col. 0331C] Let a layman who defiles himself with a servant of God do penance for two years. If he fathers a son by her, let him do penance for three years. If he is unmarried, let him observe three Lents and the regular fast days. If they are canons and fornicate, let them do penance for one year; if frequently, two years.

Let one who is in an ecclesiastical grade do penance for three years. If a monk without a grade, or a canon who holds a grade, fornicates with a lay girl, let them do penance for three years. If with a consecrated woman, let them do penance for seven years. Monks who commit fornication while holding a grade are to do penance for seven years. If a monk takes a laywoman as his wife, let them do penance for three years, and let her do penance for two years and the regular fast days. If a child is born, let him do penance for four years. If he kills, let him do penance for seven years.

[Col. 0331D] If a bishop fornicates, let him do penance for eight years. Others have judged that penance should last twelve years. After the third year, let him perform lighter penance.

**305.** If a priest fornicates with a girl, let him do penance for four years, with three Lents each year, and Wednesdays and Fridays on bread and water. If he fornicates with a servant of God, let him do penance for seven years.

(Burchard, book XVII, chapter 39.) If a bishop, priest, or deacon is caught in fornication, perjury, or theft, let him be deposed; nevertheless, let him not be deprived of communion, because the Lord does not punish the same offense twice.  
[Note: [Col. 0331D] From canon 25 of the Apostles.]

### Likewise concerning incest

**CCXLVII.** If an adolescent takes his sister as his wife, let him do penance for five years. If he takes his mother, seven years. And for as long as he lives, let him never be without continence [read: penance].

### Likewise, another rule

Whoever fornicates with his mother is to do penance for fifteen years.

Whoever fornicates with his daughter or sister is to abstain from all meat and do penance for fifteen years.

If a mother fornicates with her young son, let her abstain from meat for three years and fast one day each week until evening.

### Likewise

Whoever has relations with his mother and daughter, two sisters, his father’s or brother’s wife, his paternal or maternal cousin, his niece or female cousin, or whoever is joined to another in the first, second, or third generation—we wish to instruct such persons that they are to separate.

And, for the sake of the Church’s new planting, let them do penance for seven years: during the first three years, three days each week, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; forty days before Easter; twenty days before the feast of Saint John; and twenty days before Christmas.

During the remaining four years, let them fast on Wednesday and Friday, and for fourteen nights before the feast of Saint John and the same number before Christmas. If anyone wishes to redeem the obligation, let him give one denarius, or the value of one denarius, for each day. If he is poor, let him give half a denarius.

### Of the defilement of boys

**CCXLVIII.** Boys who defile one another with their hands are to do penance for forty days; older persons, one hundred days. Boys who defile one another between the thighs are to do penance for one hundred days; older persons, three Lents and the regular fast days. If a young child is violated by an older person, let him do penance for seven days. If he consented, twenty days. A boy who voluntarily pollutes himself is to do penance for thirty days; a young man, forty days.

### Of abstaining during menstruation

**CCXLIX.** Whoever marries a menstruating woman is to do penance for forty days.

### As above

If anyone has intercourse with his wife from behind, let him do penance for forty days. If he has intercourse with her anally, let him do penance for three years, because it is the crime of sodomy. Men who fornicate between the thighs are to do penance for one year. If anally, three years. If they are boys, let them do penance for two years.

### 307. Of women’s fornication

**CCL.** (Burchard, book XVII, chapter 27.) A woman who fornicates by any contrivance, whether with herself or with another woman, is to do penance for three years.

### As above

(Burchard, book XVII, chapter 28.) If a consecrated woman fornicates with another consecrated woman by any device, let her do penance for seven years.

### Of lustful embraces

**CCLI.** (Burchard, book XVII, chapter 42.) Whoever is polluted through lustful embraces of a woman or through a kiss is to do penance for thirty days. Whoever indecently touches the flesh of the same woman is to do penance for three months. Whoever is polluted through obscene speech is to do penance for seven days.

A presbyter, if he has kissed a woman out of impure desire, shall do penance for twenty days. If he has been polluted, he shall do penance for forty days. Whoever is polluted in the church through sleep shall do penance for three days. Whoever has been polluted in sleep by his own will shall rise and sing the seven penitential psalms, and do penance for thirty days. Whoever wished to sin in sleep but was not polluted shall sing thirty-four psalms.

## On the Emission of Semen

**CCLII.** *(BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 43.)* If a cleric emits semen without touching himself, he shall do penance for seven days. If he touches himself with his hand, for twenty days. If he is a deacon, for thirty days. If he is a presbyter, for four weeks. A presbyter [Col. 0333B], if he emits semen through thought, shall do penance for seven days. A monk likewise. Whoever voluntarily emits semen in a church, if he is a cleric, shall do penance for fourteen days; if a monk or deacon, for thirty days; if a presbyter, for forty days; if a bishop, for fifty days.

## On Fornication with Quadrupeds

**CCLIII.** *(BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 32.)* Whoever sins with an animal shall do penance for one year. Some judge ten years, some seven, some four, and some one hundred days.

Likewise.

If any cleric has fornicated with a quadruped, he shall do penance for two years; a subdeacon, three; a deacon and a monk, five; a presbyter, seven; and a bishop, ten years.

[Col. 0333C] ## On Sodomites

**CCLIV.** *(HALITGAR, book VI, chapter 25; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 34.)* Whoever has fornicated as the Sodomites did: some have judged ten years, some seven, and others one. Boys: one hundred days. Others have judged that, if it is habitual, a layman shall do penance for five years, a cleric for seven, a subdeacon and monk for eight, a deacon for ten, a presbyter for twelve, and a bishop for thirteen years.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Ancyra

**CCLV.** *(Council of Ancyra, chapter 15; RABANUS, letter to Heribald, chapter 32; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 7; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 30.)* Concerning those who have acted or are acting irrationally: all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, be admitted to communion in prayer. After a further five years—that is, after twenty years—they shall receive the sacraments of the offering. But all who, after the age of twenty, having wives, have fallen into this sin shall, after doing penance for twenty-five years, be admitted to communion in prayer. After a further five years—that is, after thirty years—they shall receive communion.

[Col. 0333D] ## On the Same Matter. From the Same Council

**CCLVI.** *(Council of Ancyra, chapter 16; book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 273; HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 8; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 31.)* Those who have lived irrationally and have polluted others, marked with the leprosy of their crime: the holy synod commanded that they pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.

[Col. 0334A] ## On the Same Matter. From Book I of the Capitularies, Chapter 19

**CCLVII.** *(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 49; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 33.)* If any are found who sin against nature with quadrupeds or males, they are to be restrained by harsh and strict penance. Therefore the bishops or presbyters by whom the judgment of penance is imposed shall strive by every means to eradicate this evil from its roots.

## On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Basil

**CCLVIII.** *(BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 35.)* A cleric or monk who pursues adolescents or children, or who has been convicted of an obscene act by a kiss or on some other occasion, shall be publicly beaten and lose his tonsure.
