After being shamefully shaved, his face shall be smeared with spittle; bound tightly with iron chains, he shall be worn down by the confinement of prison for six months, and for three days each week he shall be allowed to take food consisting of barley bread only, in the evening. After this, for another six months he shall live apart under the custody of a spiritual superior in a small dwelling, devoting himself to manual labor and prayer and subjecting himself to vigils and weeping. He shall always walk under the custody of two spiritual brothers and shall thereafter be joined to young men neither in private conversation nor in counsel.

[Col. 0334B] ## On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Isidore

**CCLIX.** *(BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 36.)* If any of the young men, or any suspicious person, plays with children, let him be worn down by prolonged penance.

[Col. 0334C] ## On the Same Matter. As Above

**CCLX.** *(BURCHARD, book VII, chapter 37.)* If any brother is caught playing with boys and forming friendships with those of an immature age, he shall be admonished a third time to remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not cease, he shall be corrected with the utmost severity.

## On the Same Matter. From the Theodosian Law, Book 9

**CCLXI.** *(Interpretation of book 6 of the Theodosian Code, “On Adulterers.”)* It is disgraceful to condemn a male body made womanly to endure the passive role of the other sex. For such persons appear to have nothing distinguishing them from women. You shall expiate such a crime by avenging flames in the sight of the people.

*[Helmstedt edition: “they shall expiate.”]*

[Col. 0334D] ## On the Union of the Faithful. From the Council of Worms

**CCLXII.** *(Council of Worms, chapter 32; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 80; BURCHARD, book VII, chapter 2.)* In the union of the faithful we do not define the number of generations; but we establish this, that no Christian may take a wife from his own consanguinity or kinship so long as the relationship is remembered, known, or retained in memory.

We have briefly surveyed these matters concerning the various forms of fornication from diverse little works, leaving it to the judgment of priests to determine what is more healthful and useful when assigning penances.

[Col. 0335A] ## That Adulteries May Not Be Committed in the Houses of the Faithful. From the Council of Meaux

**CCLXIII.** *(Council of Meaux, chapter 74.)* Let powerful men, and especially powerful women, take care that adulteries, lustful concubinage, and incestuous adulteries do not flourish in their houses. Let them ensure that their presbyters [old manuscript: *sui presbyteri*, “their presbyters”], who go with them to the chapel, possess such authority, so that in their houses they cut away every vice and compel everyone to know and regularly recite the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, because the parish presbyters and the ministers of the bishops will strive to provide this for persons of lesser and lower status.

## On the Same Matter. From Book III of the Capitularies

[Col. 0335B] **CCLXIV.** *(Council of Chalon II, chapter 18; book II of the Capitularies, chapter 38; book II of the Lombard Laws, title 3, chapter 10.)* It has been reported to us that in certain places bishops and counts accept pledges from incestuous persons and from those who do not pay tithes, and from presbyters for certain negligences, and divide the money among themselves. We have decreed that this must be abolished altogether, lest an opportunity be given to avarice.

[p. 312] ## HEREAFTER, ON THEFT AND ROBBERY. From a Penitential

**CCLXV.** *(HALITGAR, book IV, chapter 29.)* Whoever, overcome by greed, commits theft shall return what he has taken and do penance for five years.

## On the Same Matter. From Roman Law

**CCLXVI.** Money belonging to the church, if stolen or carried off, shall be repaid fourfold; popular goods, twofold.

*[Note: See volume IX of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 57, chapter 54, and Gratian, 17, question 4, canon 16.]*

[Col. 0335C] ## On the Same Matter. From a Penitential

**CCLXVII.** Whoever has often committed theft shall do penance for seven years.

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

**CCLXVIII.** *(HALITGAR, book VI, chapter 4; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 58; GRATIAN, 17, question 4, canon 17.)* If anyone has committed capital theft—that is, has taken quadrupeds or broken into houses—he shall do penance for seven years and return what was stolen. But if anyone has committed a lesser theft once or twice, he shall return what he took and do penance for one year on bread and water. If he cannot make restitution, he shall do penance for three years.

As above.

If anyone has violated a tomb, he shall do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

[Col. 0335D] [p. 313] ## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Toledo

**CCLXIX.** *(Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 46; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 63.)* If any cleric is caught demolishing tombs, he must be removed from the clerical order as one exposed in such a crime and assigned to three years of penance.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Agde

**CCLXX.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 5.)* If any cleric commits theft from the church, let communion as a stranger be granted to him.

[Col. 0336A] ## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

**CCLXXI.** *(EXCERPTS OF EGBERT, chapter 68; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 64.)* If any cleric or monk commits theft—which can more properly be called sacrilege—we have judged that the following order should be established: a younger man who is beaten with rods and found guilty of so great a crime shall never receive ecclesiastical office. But if one already ordained is caught in this offense, let him be deprived of the dignity of his rank. For the lightness of his act, it may be sufficient for him, once he has fulfilled the satisfaction of penance, to receive communion alone.

*[Note: This chapter is not found among the canons of the Synod of Agde. Nevertheless, Egbert of Canterbury, who is much older than Regino, cites it as coming from the Council of Agde.]*

## On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Jerome to Titus

**CCLXXII.** *(BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 55.)* A thief is judged not only in major matters but also in minor ones. For it is not what has been taken by theft that is considered, but the thief’s intention. Just as in fornication the fornication is not different because the woman is beautiful or deformed, enslaved or freeborn, poor or wealthy—for whatever she may be, it is one fornication—so in theft, however much someone may have taken, he incurs the crime of theft.

[Col. 0336B] [p. 314] ## On the Same Matter. Sayings of Augustine

**CCLXXIII.** *(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus, question 39; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 53.)* The Lord said to Moses: “Let each person receive from his neighbor, male and female, vessels of silver and gold and clothing,” and so forth. No one should think that an example is thereby provided for stripping one’s neighbor. God commanded this, for he knew what each person ought to suffer. Nor did the Israelites do it on their own; at God’s command they rendered service. It is like when an attendant kills someone whom the judge has ordered killed: if he does this voluntarily, he is certainly a murderer, even if he kills someone whom he knows the judge ought to have killed.

Likewise, Augustine.

[Col. 0336C] *(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus, question 71; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 54.)* To take secretly is punishable; to seize openly is punishable by a much greater penalty. Thus taking from one who is unwilling, whether secretly or publicly, has its own prohibition. For the name “theft” properly includes every unlawful appropriation of another’s property. The one who prohibited theft did not permit robbery; rather, he intended robbery also to be understood under the name of theft. By naming a part, he signified the whole: whatever is taken from one’s neighbor.

## On the Same Matter. From the Capitularies

**CCLXXIV.** *(Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 96, and in the Chapters of Charles the Bald, title 20, chapters 27.)* If anyone commits robbery within the kingdom, or forcibly takes anything from any of our faithful or from one of their men, he shall pay legal compensation threefold to the person from whom he took it and shall additionally pay our ban. Afterwards he shall be brought before us by the count, so that, confined in the *bastiniacum*, he may suffer punishment until it pleases us. If the act was public, he shall perform public penance for it according to the decrees of the holy canons. If it was secret, he shall perform penance for it on the advice of the priests, since, as the Apostle says, robbers will not possess the kingdom of God unless they truly repent of it. But those who have taken anything belonging to churches shall be judged more severely, because the taking of sacred things is sacrilege, and whoever takes anything from them is called a sacrilegious person. Such persons, expelled from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, are to be held and firmly marked as excluded until they have made satisfaction to the church they injured.

*[Note: The final part of this chapter differs from the edition found in the books of the Capitularies. It agrees, however, with the version presented by the Chapters of Charles the Bald.]*

[Col. 0337A] ## On the Same Matter. From a Penitential

**CCLXXV.** *(BURCHARD, book I, chapter 65.)* If anyone steals anything belonging to the ministry of the Church in any manner, he shall do penance for seven years.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Worms

**CCLXXVI.** *(Council of Worms, chapter 15; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 66.)* It often happens that thefts are committed in monasteries. Therefore we establish that, whenever the brothers themselves must purge themselves of such matters, Mass shall be celebrated by the abbot, or by someone else in the presence of the brothers. When the Mass has been completed, all shall receive communion with these words:

“May the Body of the Lord be for you today as a test.”

*[Note: This canon is very different from the editions commonly circulated of the Council of Worms. Nevertheless, Burchard followed this reading, and Gratian followed him. Thus the final part reads as follows in the canons of the council: “And so, at the final celebration of Mass, for their purification, let them receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that by this means they may show themselves innocent.” See the Mass of Judgment in François Pithou’s *Glossary*, under the entry “Judgment by boiling or cold water.”]*

[Col. 0337B] [p. 316] ## On a Criminal Case. From the Same Source

**CCLXXVII.** *(Council of Worms, chapter 10; BURCHARD, book II, chapter 199.)* If a criminal charge—homicide, adultery, or sorcery—is imputed to a bishop or presbyter, he must handle the Mass in each case, publicly recite the Secret, receive communion, and show himself innocent of each charge imputed to him. If he does not do this, he shall be regarded as excluded from the thresholds of the church for five years.

## On Robbery and Violence. From a Capitular

**CCLXXVIII.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, title 20, chapters 3 and 4, and title 29, chapter 4.)* Bishops ought to have briefly written down the judgments of evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic authority concerning robbery and violence, as well as the canonical and apostolic decrees, and they shall publicly reread these to everyone. The royal envoys shall likewise make known to all the legal judgments, the chapters of our predecessors, and our own chapters concerning this matter. The bishops of God, by episcopal authority, shall forbid depredations and robberies to everyone. Our envoys and counts shall also firmly strive, by our ban, to prohibit these things to all, so that everyone may know that if anyone presumes to do such a thing, he will receive episcopal judgment according to the divine judgments; he will be compelled to make amends according to the laws and royal chapters; and according to the judgment of our faithful he will receive a fitting punishment.

[Col. 0337D] ## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

**CCLXXIX.** *(Ibid., chapter 7.)* If—God forbid—someone should arise who sets aside the fear of God, despises ecclesiastical authority, and rejects royal power, whoever he may be, let him know that, both according to canonical authority, he will be alienated from the assembly of all Christians and from the fellowship of the holy Church in heaven and on earth, and that, by royal power and the unanimity of all the faithful of the kingdom, he will be pursued as an enemy of God and a devastator of the kingdom until he is exterminated from the kingdom.

## As Above

[p. 318] **CCLXXX.** *(Ibid., chapter 10.)* Let robbers hear what the Lord says through Isaiah: “The robbery of the poor is in your house.” And through the Apostle: “Neither robbers, nor murderers, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God.” Therefore let them consider what a great and grievous sin robbery is, since the holy Apostle compared it with adultery and homicide. He also says: “If anyone is a fornicator, or an adulterer, or a robber, or a murderer, a Christian may not even eat with such a person before satisfaction has been made.” And blessed John the Apostle forbids greeting such a person, saying: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, nor receive him into your house. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works.” Let them hear what was written at the Council of Toledo. See chapter 36.

**CCLXXXI.** “If,” they say, “anyone among the more powerful strips a cleric or a poor person, see above where homicide is discussed.”

Let robbers and plunderers of ecclesiastical property hear what the holy Anacletus, ordained by the Apostle Peter, says.

## On the Same Matter. Anacletus

[Col. 0338C] **CCLXXXII.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, same place; BURCHARD, book XVII, chapter 18.)* “Whoever,” he says, “takes anything from a father is a participant in homicide.” Without doubt our father is God, who created us. Our mother, however, is the Church, which spiritually gave birth to us in baptism. Therefore whoever takes, robs, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s money is a murderer and is reckoned a murderer before God. For whoever takes away the Church’s property commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.

Likewise Pope Urban and martyr says:

**CCLXXXIII.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, same place.)* Ecclesiastical possessions and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. If anyone robs them, he is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira; and such a person ought to be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

[p. 319] Likewise Pope Lucius.

[Col. 0338D] **CCLXXXIV.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, same place; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 19.)* By apostolic authority we anathematize, expel from the thresholds of the holy Church, and condemn as sacrilegious those who rob ecclesiastical possessions and resources; and not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who act but also those who consent are judged guilty.

[Col. 0339A] ## On the Same Matter

**CCLXXXV.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, same place; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 91.)* Augustine says: Whoever steals and robs anything from the church is compared with Judas the betrayer.

## Written in the Canons

**CCLXXXVI.** *(Council of Gangra, chapter 7; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 21.)* If anyone wishes to take or give the offerings of the church outside the church without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, let him be anathema.

## On the Same Matter. From the Council of Meaux, Chapter 61

**CCLXXXVII.** *(Council of Meaux, chapter 61; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 61.)* Let those who seize ecclesiastical property—who are known not only to retain that property against authority but also cruelly to lay it waste, and who strip the church’s resources through various exactions and revenues, while also mercilessly stripping, devastating, and oppressing the poor, neighbors, and those living around them—like robbers, who according to the Apostle *(1 Corinthians 6)* are excluded from the kingdom of God, make satisfaction through public penance for their criminal and public sin. If they refuse to do this, and are neither exhorted nor compelled to do so by royal power, a terrible apostolic sentence shall be pronounced against them, which says: “If anyone is named a brother and is a robber, let no one presume to eat with such a person” *(1 Corinthians 5)*. For it is wicked and sacrilegious—as Pope Symmachus writes, in the sixth Roman synod under Symmachus, and blessed Gregory after him writes to Sabinus the subdeacon *(Saint Gregory, book VIII, Indiction 3, letter 6)*—and it is contrary to the laws, if anyone attempts to retain for the profit of his own evil will what has been left to venerable places. According to the decrees of the canons, he must be excluded from all ecclesiastical communion as a sacrilegious person until he strives to correct what he has done through worthy satisfaction.

## On Those Who Violate Sacred Places. From the Same Source

[Col. 0339D] **CCLXXXVIII.** *(Council of Meaux, chapter 60; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 22.)* Let those who violate monasteries, places consecrated to God, and churches, and who remove deposits or anything else from them, and who not only dishonor priests and ecclesiastical men but also afflict them in various ways, be subjected as sacrilegious persons to canonical judgment and excommunicated.

## How a Bishop Should Summon Plunderers to a Synod. As Above

**CCLXXXIX.** *(Chapters of Carloman, title 2, chapter 5; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 13.)* The bishop in whose parish someone has committed an injustice shall, once, twice, and a third time if necessary, summon him canonically through his messenger, by his admonition, to correction or settlement and to penance, so that he may make satisfaction to God and to the church he has injured. But if he despises and scorns his admonition and his most salutary invitation, let him strike him with the pastoral rod—that is, with the sentence of excommunication—so that he may be separated from the communion of the holy Church and of all Christians until he has made suitable satisfaction and worthy amends. The same bishop must make this excommunication known to his superior and to all his fellow bishops, so that they do not receive him until he has made worthy satisfaction.

*[Note: At the end of this chapter Burchard added certain words which, in my opinion, he undoubtedly thought necessary: namely, that when a Christian had been excommunicated, this should be brought to the knowledge of all the parishioners. Thus, at the end of the chapter, after the words “to all his fellow bishops,” Burchard added “and to all his parishioners.” These words, however, are not found in Regino or in the Chapters of Carloman, from which this chapter was taken.]*

## On Those Who Belong to Another Parish. From the Same Source

[Col. 0340B] **CCXC.** *(Chapters of Carloman, same place, chapter 6; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 45; Ivo, part XIV, chapter 109; GRATIAN, 6, question 3, canon 5; First Collection of Decretals, book V, title 14, chapter 1.)* Concerning those who have a benefice or inheritance within a parish but belong to another bishop’s parish, and who, while traveling from one place to another, commit robberies and depredations: it has pleased us and our faithful that they be excommunicated and not leave the parish before they have made worthy amends for what they committed. Their excommunication must be reported to their superior and to their own bishop, so that they do not receive them before they return to the place where they committed the robbery and fully make amends for everything.

[p. 322] *[Note: In the Chapters of Carloman, in Burchard, and also in Ivo and Gratian and in the First Collection of Decretals, this chapter is printed in a version very different from that presented by Regino’s collection. There is no mention there of the king’s faithful, just as there is none in the following chapter. Moreover, in the old manuscript of Regino that we used, the words “and our faithful” have been erased with a knife in these two chapters, though clear traces of the former reading remain.]*

## On the Same Matter. As Above

**CCXCI.** *(Chapters of Carloman, same place, chapter 8; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 12.)* It has pleased us and our faithful, for the sake of common welfare and pressing necessity, that no bishop take it amiss if another bishop excommunicates his parishioner on account of such depredation.

## On the Same Matter. From the Same Source

**CCXCII.** *(Chapters of Carloman, same place, chapter 10.)* But if anyone has regarded royal power and episcopal authority as nothing, and, while rebellious, is killed in the course of robbery, none of our faithful who kills him shall incur a feud on account of him or pay any compensation for his death.

## If a Bishop Does Not Excommunicate a Plunderer. From the Council at Pîtres

**CCXCIII.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, title 29; Council of Toledo VI, chapter 7.)* According to chapter 7 of the Council of Toledo, if the bishop to whom those who act in such ways against God and the peace of the Church are known to belong delays, through any gift, favor, or negligence, either admonishing or excommunicating them—so that he may receive those who return, or cast out from the Church those who despise the admonition—he shall be regarded as excommunicated from the college of the others until he publishes a sentence of their correction or condemnation. For unless we strive together so that justice may be preserved in every matter, neither the king, as father of his country, nor the bishops, as the people’s mediators and reconcilers, nor those who are called Christians because we share the name of Christ, can be what we are called in the sight of God.

*[In the Chapters of Charles the Bald: “if he has not wished to admonish them, so that he may receive those who return, or …”]*

## Likewise, on Robbers. From the Council of Mainz

**CCXCIV.** *(Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 6; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 23.)* Whoever, raised up by the arrogance of pride, treats the house of God with contempt, and dishonorably handles possessions consecrated to God and placed under the protection of royal immunity for the honor of God, or presumes to violate them, or commits fires or devastations with reckless boldness, shall, as an invader and violator of the Church of God, which is the house of the living God, be cut off from the communion of all the faithful. It is also fitting that he feel the indignation of the lord king, whose goodwill he has despised and whose ordinance he has violated.

[p. 324] ## That Bishops Ought to Protect and Defend the People. From the Council of Toledo

**CCXCV.** *(Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 32; BURCHARD, book XV, chapter 1.)* Let bishops have no doubt that care for protecting and defending the people has been entrusted to them. Therefore, when they see judges and powerful men acting as oppressors of the poor, let them first rebuke them by priestly admonition [the reading *commonitione* is preferred]. If they refuse to be corrected, let them report their insolence to the king’s ears, so that those whom priestly admonition does not bend toward justice may be restrained from wrongdoing by royal power.

## Likewise, on Wrongdoers. From the Council of Tribur, Chapter 8

**CCXCVI.** *(Council of Tribur, chapters 3 and 8.)* Some complained about certain wrongdoers whose wickedness is so excessive that they pay no attention to the admonition of priests, despise the bishops’ ban, disdain coming when summoned to the synod three or four times, and finally regard receiving communion as nothing. Concerning such persons it was also established in a Capitular that they should be referred to royal judgment. And it pleased the devout King Arnulf and the holy synod that whoever, after due excommunication, so despises God and Christianity should be pursued by secular power; and, if they are killed, let them lie without compensation.

[p. 325] ## On the Same Matter. From the Council at Soissons

**CCXCVII.** *(Second Council of Soissons, chapter 12.)* It was also obtained from the most devout prince Charles that any incestuous persons and other reprobates who avoid examination by the bishops be brought before them by public judges, lest the impunity of vices continue to nourish the enticement to sin.

## From the Council at Lauriacum in the Pagus of Anjou, in the Year 844, Indiction 6, Chapter 1, in October

*[Note: See volume III of the Councils of Gaul, p. 36.]*

**CCXCVIII.** *(BURCHARD, book XV, chapter 7.)* If anyone is found to be a public transgressor of divine law, or a despiser of the church’s just and reasonable judgments because of manifest crimes, and a contradictor of the constitutions of the holy Fathers, then, if he delays obeying the bishops’ admonitions, let him be anathematized.

## From the Same Source, Chapter 2

**CCXCIX.** If anyone is proved to act deceitfully, craftily, and perniciously against royal dignity, let him be anathematized unless he makes the most worthy satisfaction.

## From the Same Source, Chapter 3

**CCC.** *(BURCHARD, book XV, chapter 22.)* If anyone presumes, with a stubborn and arrogant spirit, to contradict or resist royal power—which according to the Apostle *(Romans 13)* is from God alone—and refuses to obey its just and reasonable commands in accordance with God, ecclesiastical authority, and civil law, let him be anathematized.

[p. 326] ## As Above, Chapter 4

**CCCI.** Whoever, inflamed by the torches of pride or angered by insolence, violates these provisions which we have unanimously defined for the tranquility of holy Mother Church and with priestly severity, and which we have confirmed with our own hands, it pleases us that all such persons be anathematized.

## If a Man Is Accused and Denies It. From the Council of Tribur

**CCCII.** *(Council of Tribur, chapter 22; BURCHARD, book XVI, chapter 19.)* If a noble or freeborn man is accused in the synod and denies it, if they know him to be faithful, he shall clear himself by oath. If he has previously been caught in theft and perjury, he shall not be admitted to an oath. Rather, like one who is not freeborn, he shall clear himself by boiling water and red-hot iron.

## That No One May Excommunicate Another’s Parishioner. From a Letter of Pope Zephyrinus

**CCCIII.** *(Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 159; BURCHARD, book XVI, chapter 13.)* No one shall be judged in his absence, because human and divine laws prohibit this. For no sentence against any of them—that is, the accusers—shall bind them unless it has been pronounced by their own judge, since the laws of the secular world also order that this be done.

*[Note: See book VII of the Capitularies, chapters 229 and 266.]*

## On the Same Matter. From the Theodosian Law

**CCCIV.** *(Interpretation of the single law of the Theodosian Code, “On Judgments.”)* In private cases the following rule shall be observed: no one shall be bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own.

[p. 327] ## From the Same Source, Chapter —

*(Interpretation of book II of the Theodosian Code, “On Judgments.”)* No one at all shall be heard who wishes to divide the presentation of one case between two judges.

## On the Same Matter. From the Capitularies

**CCCV.** *(Chapters of Charles the Bald, title 26, chapter 6.)* Let no bishop alienate a sinful person from the Church, the Christian religion, or communion until he has admonished him, according to the evangelical precept, to return to correction and penance. But if he remains incorrigible, let the bishop make this known to the royal power, so that he may be compelled. If he is not corrected even in this way, then, according to the canonical laws, let him be separated from ecclesiastical communion.

[Col. 0343A] ## On the Same Matter. In the Synod of Meaux, Chapter 55

**CCCVI.** *(Council of Meaux, chapter 56; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 16.)* Let no bishop deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. Let no one impose an anathema without the consent of the archbishop or fellow bishops, and without giving priority to evangelical admonition, except where canonical authority teaches that it should be imposed; for anathema is a condemnation to eternal death and must be imposed only for a mortal crime and upon one who could not otherwise be corrected.

[p. 328] ## That a Bishop Should Not Excommunicate Anyone Quickly in Anger. From a Letter of Pope Evaristus

**CCCVII.** *(Council of Tribur, chapter 22; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 9.)* Almighty God, in order to restrain us from the hasty pronouncement of judgment, although everything is naked and open before his eyes, nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom on hearsay before he had clearly learned what was being said. Hence he says: “I shall go down and see whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” *(Genesis 18)*. By his example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing judgment, or to judge rashly, carelessly, and without investigation in any way.

[Col. 0343C] ## On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Gregory

**CCCVIII.** *(SAINT GREGORY, book XIX of the *Moralia*, chapter 23.)* Blessed Job says: “I investigated most carefully the case that I did not know” *(Job 29)*. The rulers of the churches and those who conduct public trials must take the greatest care not to be driven by light-mindedness or fury into hasty judgments when issuing sentences. Rather, after the cases have first been carefully examined, once the matter that was unknown has fully come to their knowledge, let them consult divine and human law and, without respect of persons, pronounce a definitive sentence according to what is established there. Hence Moses, whenever he entered the tabernacle, always referred the complaints of the people to the Lord, and proposed judgments according to what the Lord commanded—clearly instructing us not to pronounce a sentence of condemnation or justification from our own heart, but from the divine oracle.

[p. 329] ## On the Same Matter. From the Theodosian Law, Book II, Chapter 18

**CCCIX.** *(Interpretation of book I of the Theodosian Code, “On Judgments.”)* When a judge begins to hear a case, he shall patiently receive the assertions and responses of the litigants and investigate everything through a full examination. He shall not wish to oppose the litigants with his judgment before they themselves, after everything has been completed, no longer have anything to put forward in the hearing or dispute. They ought frequently to be questioned, lest something perhaps remain overlooked.

[Col. 0344A] ## That No One Can Pardon What Someone Sins Against God. From the Sayings of Jerome

**CCCX.** *(JEROME on Matthew, chapter 18; BURCHARD, book XI, chapter 15; Ivo, part XIV, chapter 85.)* Attention must be paid to what the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you.” It is one thing to sin against us and another to sin against God. If someone sins against us, we have the power to forgive him. But if someone sins against God, it is not within our discretion. For it is written: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” *(1 Samuel 2.)* On the contrary, we are kind and merciful in the matter of an injury to God, and we pardon an offense against God with impunity and without the fitting punishment of penance, as though his willing and unwilling were within our power; yet what is committed against us—even a lightly spoken word of insult—we do not allow to pass without punishment. Therefore, for God’s sake, let us forgive what has been committed against us; but what has been committed against God, since we cannot forgive it, let us punish according to the custom [manuscript: “constitution”] of the holy Fathers and in accordance with canonical authority.

## HEREAFTER, ON PERJURY. From a Capitular

**CCCXI.** *(Capitulary of Aachen of Charles the Great, chapter 63; book I of the Capitularies, chapter 63; BURCHARD, book XII, chapter 2.)* We have it written in the law of the Lord: “You shall not commit perjury in my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God, nor take the name of the Lord your God in vain” *(Leviticus 19)*. Therefore all must be admonished carefully to avoid perjury, not only at the altar or upon the relics of the saints, but also in ordinary speech. Likewise, care must be taken that no one honor gold more than the altar, lest the Lord say to him: “Fool, which is greater, the gold or the altar that sanctifies the gold?” *(Matthew 23)*

Likewise, as above.

**CCCXII.** *(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 63; book II of the Lombard Laws, title 55, chapter 22; BURCHARD, book XII, chapter 12.)* Moreover, it seems proper to us that whoever dares to swear by holy things should do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God; and that children who have not reached the age of reason should not be compelled to swear.

Likewise.

[Col. 0344D] **CCCXIII.** *(Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 63; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 51, chapter 4.)* Whoever has once committed perjury shall thereafter be neither a witness, nor admitted to an oath, nor an oath-taker in his own case or that of another.

**On the same matter. From the council at Pîtres.**

**CCCXIV.** *(Capitulary, Book III, chapter 8.)* No one shall promise fidelity by oath to anyone other than us and his own particular lord, for the benefit of us and of his lord, except for those oaths which, according to justice and the law, one person owes to another.

**From the same source, chapter 10.**

*(Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 10; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 51, chapter 2, and title 58.)* Concerning perjuries: they are to be guarded against, and witnesses are not to be admitted to an oath before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, they shall be separated from one another and questioned individually. Nor shall the accuser alone be permitted to choose witnesses in the absence of his opponent in the case. Absolutely no one shall be admitted to an oath or testimony unless fasting. Witnesses shall be chosen from that very district and from the neighboring hundreds. If anyone is convicted of perjury, he shall lose his hand or redeem it.

**On the same matter. From the same source, chapter 58.**

**CCCXV.** *(Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 58; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 55, chapter 26.)* Oaths that have been pledged to the palace shall be completed at the palace. If the oath-bound men refuse to come, they shall be compelled to come by a lordly command, a written summons, or a seal.

**From Book IV, chapter 26.**

[Col. 0345B] *(Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 28.)* Where there was an ancient custom, and where a public court is held, there the oaths shall be sworn.

**That a bishop should not swear over the sacred objects. From the council of Meaux, chapter 37.**

**CCCXVI.** *(Council of Meaux, chapter 38.)* Henceforth no bishop shall presume to swear over the sacred objects—a practice which the holy patriarchs sought and instituted for the sake of the mystery. Faith is preserved not through the hesitation and malice of the one demanding it, but in sincere charity. Whoever, seduced in any way, presumptuously dares to transgress this shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank.

**Again, concerning perjury. From the same source, chapter 38.**

**CCCXVII.** *(Council of Meaux, chapter 39; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 1.)* Let everyone be more attentively informed how detestable and hateful to God is the manifold confusion of oaths and perjuries, through which many souls of the faithful are known to have been lost throughout this entire kingdom. For this evil is so great that at the shrines of the martyrs—where the illnesses of many are healed—perjurers, even though they sometimes do not appear to be visibly tormented, are nevertheless seized by demons through God’s just judgment. As Saint Gregory says *(Homily 32 on the Gospels)*: “The sick come to their bodies and are cured, while perjurers are tormented by a demon.”

**At what time oaths are to be sworn. From the council at Pîtres.**

**CCCXVIII.** *(Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 31, chapter 33.)* We have decreed, with the consent and counsel of our faithful, that from the very day on which the oath is received, after forty days and forty nights—that is, on the forty-second day of the six weeks—the person who received that oath shall swear it lawfully, on that same weekday, in the appointed places. If that day falls within Lent, no one shall presume to swear. Whoever presumes to do so shall pay our ban and thereafter perform penance according to episcopal judgment. We command that Lent itself be observed from the beginning of the fast, on that Wednesday, until the Monday after the octave of Easter.

[Col. 0346A] **That oaths should not be sworn on the Wednesday before Lent. From the council held at Saint-Médard.**

**CCCXIX.** *(Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 9, chapter 7, § 8; and volume III of the Councils of Gaul, p. 89.)* Let our envoys firmly announce, in our name, to the counts and to all officials of the realm that from the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent until after the octave of Easter they must not presume to hold a public court, except for matters of agreement and reconciliation, nor may anyone swear an oath. Likewise, they shall observe the period from the Wednesday before the Nativity of the Lord until after the consecrated days, as well as the fasts of the Four Seasons and the Rogations. No one shall hold a public hearing or swear an oath on the Lord’s Day.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] This last clause, which is found both in the Helmstedt edition of Regino and in the Paris manuscript, is not present in the Acts of the council of Soissons or in the Capitularies of Charles the Bald. [Col. 0346D]]

[Col. 0346B] **Concerning a cleric who commits perjury. From the council of Orléans.**

**CCCXX.** *(Third Council of Orléans, chapter 8.)* If a cleric has given an oath and is subsequently exposed by evident facts as having committed perjury, he shall be punished by excommunication for two years.

**Concerning those who bind themselves by oath not to return to peace. From the council of Lérida.**

**CCCXXI.** *(Council of Lérida, chapter 7; Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 33; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 17.)* Whoever has bound himself by oath never to return to peace shall, on account of his perjury, be separated from the body and blood of the Lord for one year, and shall atone for his guilt by fasts and almsgiving. Let him hasten, however, to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

**Again, concerning perjury. From the writings of Jerome.**

[Col. 0346C] **CCCXXII.** *(Burchard, Book XII, chapter 16.)* Herod promised under oath to give the dancing girl whatever she might ask of him. If he says that he did it because of his oath, what would he have done if she had demanded the death of his father and mother? Would he have done it or not? Therefore, what he would have rejected in the case of his own family, he ought also to have rejected when it concerned the prophet.

**On the same matter. From the writings of the presbyter Bede.**

**CCCXXIII.** *(Bede, Homily 44, on the Beheading of Saint John; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 18.)* If it should happen that we have rashly sworn something which, if kept, would lead to a worse outcome, let us recognize that it must be changed according to the sounder counsel; and, when necessity presses, it is better for us to commit perjury than, by keeping a formal oath, to turn aside into another and greater crime.

**On the same matter. From a Penitential.**

[Col. 0346D] **CCCXXIV.** *(Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 28; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 8.)* Whoever knowingly commits perjury shall do penance for seven years and thereafter receive communion.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] See Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, chapter 8.]

**From the Penitential, as above.**

**CCCXXV.** If anyone commits perjury, he shall not thereafter be admitted to an oath.

**335. On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CCCXXVI.** *(Rabanus, Letter to Heribald, chapter 18; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 11.)* If anyone suspects that he is being led into perjury, yet swears with his consent, he shall do penance for two years.

**From the preceding source.**

**CCCXXVII.** *(Burchard, Book XII, chapter 3.)* If anyone commits perjury out of greed, he shall sell all his possessions and distribute them to the poor; then, entering a monastery, he shall submit himself to perpetual penance.

**From the preceding source.**

**CCCXXVIII.** If anyone commits perjury, laymen shall do penance for three years, clerics for five, subdeacons for six, deacons for eight, priests for ten, and bishops for twelve years.

**On the same matter. From the Capitularies, title 14.**

**CCCXXIX.** *(Capitulary 111 of Louis the Pious, title 7, chapter 6, and Fourth Addition, chapter 77; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 51, chapter 14.)* Whoever is proved to have knowingly induced witnesses to commit perjury shall be brought under sureties to the palace, where, together with our faithful, we shall consider what should be done with such people. It shall be the bishops’ responsibility to determine the penance.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] The final part of this chapter is not given in Capitulary 111 of Louis the Pious or in the Fourth Addition to the Capitularies. [Col. 0348D] Nevertheless, it is found in the Helmstedt edition of Regino and in the old manuscript codex that we used.]

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CCCXXX.** *(Burchard, Book XII, chapter 4.)* Whoever commits perjury because he was compelled by his lord, if he did so knowingly, shall do penance for three Lents and the legally prescribed weekdays.

**336. On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CCCXXXI.** *(Rabanus, Letter to Heribald, chapter 18; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 5.)* Whoever commits perjury upon the hand of a bishop or priest, or upon a consecrated cross, shall do penance for three years.

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

[Col. 0347C] **CCCXXXII.** *(Rabanus, same letter; Burchard, Book XII, chapter 5.)* If, however, it is upon an unconsecrated cross, he shall do penance for one year. But if it is upon a man’s hand, among the Greeks it amounts to nothing. Whoever has been deceived and has sworn in ignorance, but later comes to know the truth, shall do penance for three Lents.

**From the same source.**

*(Burchard, Book XII, chapter 6.)* If anyone commits perjury under coercion, whether to ransom his life or for any other cause or necessity, he shall do penance for three Lents. Others judge that he should do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

**Concerning false testimony. From the council of Orléans.**

**CCCXXXIII.** *(Third Council of Orléans, chapter 8; Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 165.)* If a cleric commits theft or gives false testimony, since these are capital crimes, he shall be degraded from his order after communion has been granted.

**On the same matter. From Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 22.**

**CCCXXXIV.** *(Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 23; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 51, chapter 11.)* If anyone has a dispute with another concerning any matter, and witnesses have been produced against him by judicial process, if he suspects them of being false, he may set against them other witnesses whom he can obtain and who are better. If the two parties disagree with one another so completely that neither is willing in any way to yield to the other, two men shall be chosen from among them to fight in the field with shields and clubs. The champion who is defeated shall, on account of his perjury, have his right hand cut off. The other false witnesses shall redeem their hands. Two parts of this payment shall be made by the person who brought the accusation, and the third as the fredus. This applies to a secular case. In ecclesiastical cases, where one party’s matter is secular and the other’s ecclesiastical, the same procedure shall be followed. Where both parties’ matters are ecclesiastical, if their superiors cannot reconcile them, their advocates shall pursue their cases in the public court before the count. The witnesses, however, must be from that very county.

**On the same matter. From the preceding source, chapter 32.**

**CCCXXXV.** *(Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 32; Addition of Charlemagne to the Salic Law, chapter 11; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 51, chapter 3.)* The best person in the district or city shall be selected to give testimony, and he must be someone against whom the person against whom he is to testify can bring no accusation.

**On the same matter. From the same source, chapter 52.**

**CCCXXXVI.** *(Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 52; Book II of the Lombard Laws, title 51, chapter 6; Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 35.)* Witnesses shall not be hired for a reward to give testimony. No one shall give testimony unless fasting. Before they swear, the witnesses shall be examined separately concerning what they intend to say about the matter on which they must give testimony.

**On the same matter. From the council of Agde.**

**CCCXXXVII.** *(Second Council of Arles, chapter 24; Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 21; Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 34.)* Those who have been convicted of falsely charging their brothers with capital crimes shall not receive communion until death, unless they repent with fitting satisfaction.

**338. On the same matter. From the council of Elvira.**

**CCCXXXVIII.** *(Council of Elvira, chapter 75; Burchard, Book II, chapter 195.)* If anyone attacks a bishop, priest, or deacon with false accusations and cannot prove them, communion shall not be given to him even at the end of his life.

**On the same matter. From the council of Seville.**

**CCCXXXIX.** *(Council of Epaon, chapter 13; Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 24.)* If a cleric is convicted of false testimony, he shall be judged guilty of a capital crime.

**On the same matter. From the council of Agde.**

**CCCXL.** *(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 55; Fourth Addition, chapter 20; Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 33.)* Let a bishop excommunicate the accusers of his brothers. If they correct their fault, he shall receive them back into communion, but not into the clergy.

**On the same matter. From the council of Elvira.**

**CCCXLI.** *(Council of Elvira, chapter 74; Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 18.)* A false witness shall be excluded according to the nature of the crime. If the accusation he made did not concern a capital offense, and he proves what he had kept silent about for a long time, he shall be excluded for two years. If he does not prove it, it has been decreed that he shall be excluded for five years in the assembly of the clergy.

**On the same matter. From the council of Agde.**

**CCCXLII.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 37; Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 30; Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 17.)* False witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless they wash away the crimes they have committed by the satisfaction of penance.

**From the preceding source.**

**CCCXLIII.** *(Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 16.)* Let false witnesses know that, if false testimony were not a capital crime, the Lord would by no means have counted it among the principal crimes in the Gospel. For he says: “From the heart come murders, adulteries, thefts, and false testimonies.” Therefore a false witness must likewise repent and be excommunicated, just like an adulterer, thief, or murderer.

**Concerning one who has stolen a human being. From the letter of Bishop Rabanus to Reginbald, chorepiscopus.**

**CCCXLIV.** You first asked what should be done with one who, by enticement, stole a Christian person and handed him over and sold him to a pagan people. I then replied that it seemed to me that the man thereby incurred the guilt of homicide. Later, while reading the divine law, I found this stated in Deuteronomy: the murderer must repay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and so forth *(Deuteronomy XIX)*. And again: “If anyone is caught enticing his brother, one of the children of Israel, and selling him after receiving a price, he shall be put to death” *(Deuteronomy XXIV)*. Therefore it seems to me that, just as the divine law establishes an equal sentence for a murderer and for a thief who sells a person, so canonical authority likewise requires that the person who has stolen, enticed, and sold his brother be punished in the same manner as one who has unjustly killed his neighbor—that is, a Christian person.

**On the same matter. From the Theodosian Law, Book IX.**

**CCCXLV.** *(Interpretation of the single law in the Theodosian Code concerning the Fabian law.)* Those who have stolen the children of others and transported them anywhere, whether freeborn or enslaved, shall be punished by death.

**That a Jew may not possess a Christian slave.**

**CCCXLVI.** Careful observance must be required so that no Jew may possess a Christian slave, nor presume to transfer him to his own religion.

**CONCERNING ENCHANTERS, SORCERERS, AND DIVINERS. Concerning those who seek divinations. From the council of Ancyra.**

**CCCXLVII.** *(Council of Ancyra, chapter 23; Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 25; Hincmar, On the Divorce of Lothar, response to question 17; Burchard, Book X, chapter 5.)* Those who seek divinations and follow pagan custom, or introduce such people into their houses to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of expiation, shall be subject to the five-year rule, according to the established degrees of penance.

**From the council of Braga.**

**CCCXLVIII.** *(Second Council of Braga, chapter 71; Hincmar, same work; Burchard, Book X, chapter 6.)* If anyone, following pagan custom, introduces diviners and fortune-tellers into his house, supposedly to drive out an evil or discover magical practices, he shall do penance for five years.

[Col. 0350A] **From the writings of Pope Gregory.**

**CCCXLIX.** *(Roman council under Gregory I; Burchard, Book X, chapter 23.)* If anyone observes soothsayers, haruspices, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema.

**341. From the council of Carthage.**

**CCCL.** *(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 89; Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 27; Hincmar, same work; Burchard, Book X, chapter 7.)* Anyone who serves auguries or enchantments is to be separated from the assembly of the Church. The same applies to one who clings to Jewish superstitions.

**On the same matter. Pope Gregory.**

**CCCLI.** *(Saint Gregory, Book IX, Letter 47; Burchard, Book X, chapter 4; also in Gratian, 26, question 5, chapter 8.)* It has come to our attention that you have pursued certain enchanters and fortune-tellers with the utmost diligence. Know that your zeal has been pleasing to us. It should be your careful concern to seek out such people, and to correct with strict punishment all those enemies of Christ whom you find.

**On the same matter. From the council of Toledo.**

**CCCLII.** *(Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 29; Burchard, Book X, chapter 48.)* If a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone belonging to the clerical order is discovered consulting magicians, haruspices, soothsayers, augurs, fortune-tellers, or those who profess to determine lots, he shall be deposed from the honor of his rank, subjected to monastic discipline, and there perform perpetual penance for the sacrilege he has committed.

**On the same matter. From Roman law.**

[Col. 0350C] **CCCLIII.** *(Interpretation of Book III of the Theodosian Code, concerning sorcery; Burchard, Book X, chapter 28.)* Sorcerers, enchanters, those who send storms, and those who disturb human minds through the invocation of demons shall be punished by every kind of penalty.

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CCCLIV.** *(Interpretation of Book IV of the same title; Burchard, Book X, chapter 30.)* Whoever, out of curiosity concerning the future, consults either an invoker of demons, or diviners—whom they call soothsayers—or a haruspex who gathers auguries shall be punished by death.

**On the same matter. From a Penitential.**

**CCCLV.** *(Burchard, Book X, chapter 31.)* Whoever celebrates nocturnal sacrifices to demons or invokes demons by enchantments shall be punished by death.

[Col. 0350D] **CCCLVI.** Those who serve auguries or divinations shall do penance for five years. Those who send storms shall do penance for seven years.

**CCCLVII.** *(Rabanus, Letter to Heribald, chapter 30; Burchard, Book X, chapter 24.)* If a woman has practiced divinations or diabolical enchantments, she shall do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days, according to the nature of the offense.

**From the same source.**

**CCCLVIII.** *(Burchard, Book X, chapter 9.)* All who observe auguries or lots falsely called those of the saints, or divinations, or any kind of writings, or who make or fulfill vows at a tree, stone, or any object other than a church, shall be excommunicated. If they come to penance, clerics shall do penance for three years and laymen for one and a half years.

**Concerning trees, springs, and stones consecrated to demons. From the council of Nantes.**

**CCCLIX.** *(Council of Nantes, chapter 20; Burchard, Book X, chapter 10.)* Bishops and their ministers must strive with the utmost zeal to ensure that trees consecrated to demons—which the common people worship and hold in such veneration that they do not dare cut off a branch or shoot from them—are uprooted and burned. Stones too, which people deceived by demonic illusions venerate in ruined and wooded places, where they make and bring offerings, must be dug up completely and thrown into a place where their worshipers can never venerate them.

Let everyone be told what a great crime idolatry is: whoever venerates and worships these things denies his God, as it were, and renounces Christianity. Such a person must undertake penance as though he had worshiped idols. Everyone must also be forbidden to make a vow, or to carry a candle or any gift elsewhere while seeking health, except to the church of the Lord their God. For it is written: “Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God.” We know how many threats the Lord uttered through his prophets against the ancient people, because they sacrificed in sacred groves and offered sacrifice on high places. Whoever transgresses these commands has lost the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Therefore he must be entirely cut off from the fellowship of the holy Church and, unless he has duly repented, must not be received back.

**On the same matter. Rabanus.**

**CCCLX.** *(Rabanus, Letter to Heribald, chapter 30; Burchard, Book X, chapter 13.)* Concerning those who sacrifice to demons, we have the regulations of Bishop Theodore, in which it is written: “Those who sacrifice to demons in small matters shall do penance for one year. Those who do so in great matters shall do penance for ten years.”

**344. On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CCCLXI.** *(Rabanus, same letter; Burchard, Book XI, chapter 14.)* If a woman places her son on a roof or in a furnace for the sake of curing a fever, she shall do penance for seven years. Whoever causes grains to be burned where a person has died, for the health of the living and of the household, shall do penance for five years.

**Concerning menstrual blood. Rabanus to Heribald.**

**CCCLXII.** *(Rabanus, same letter; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 152.)* You also asked about the following: the woman who mixed her menstrual blood into food or drink and gave it to her husband to eat; the woman who drank her husband’s semen in a beverage; and the woman who burned a piece of a human skull in fire and gave it to her husband to avoid illness—what penance should punish them? In our judgment, they should be struck with the same sentence as magicians and soothsayers, since they are known to have practiced magical art.

[Col. 0352A] **On the same matter. From the council of Ancyra.**

**CCCLXIII.** *(Rabanus, same letter, chapter 25; Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 29.)* If a woman has committed fornication with a woman, she shall do penance for three years. Likewise, the woman who mixes her husband’s semen into food so that she may receive more of his love shall do penance.

**From the preceding source.**

**CCCLXIV.** *(Burchard, Book X, chapter 1.)* Bishops and their ministers must strive with all their strength to eradicate completely from their parishes the harmful magical and sorcerous art of divination, invented by the devil. If they find any man or woman pursuing such a crime, they shall expel him or her, shamefully dishonored, from their parishes.

For the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretic after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted” *(Titus III)*. Those are perverted and held captive by the devil who, having abandoned their Creator, seek assistance from the devil. Therefore the holy Church must be cleansed of such a plague.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] See the Capitula of Herard of Tours, chapter 3.]

Nor should this be omitted: certain wicked women, turned backward after Satan and deceived by demonic illusions and phantasms, believe and profess that during the hours of night they ride upon certain beasts with Diana, the pagan goddess, and an innumerable multitude of women; that they traverse many stretches of land in the silence of the dead of night; that they obey her commands as their mistress; and that on appointed nights they are summoned to serve her. Would that these women alone had perished in their faithlessness and had not dragged many with them into the destruction of unbelief.

[Col. 0352C] For an innumerable multitude, deceived by this false opinion, believes these things to be true, and by believing deviates from the right faith. It falls back into pagan error when it supposes that some divinity or divine power exists outside the one God. Therefore priests must preach with all urgency to the people in the churches entrusted to them, so that they may know that such things are entirely false, and that such phantasms are inflicted upon the minds of unbelievers not by a divine spirit but by an evil one.

For Satan himself, who transforms himself into an angel of light, when he has seized the mind of some poor woman and subdued her to himself through unbelief and lack of faith, immediately transforms himself into the forms and likenesses of various persons. Deceiving in dreams the mind that he holds captive, now showing joyful, now sorrowful, now familiar, now unfamiliar persons, he leads it through every kind of pathless place. When only the spirit suffers this, the unbelieving mind supposes that it happens not in the mind but in the body.

[Col. 0352D] For who is not carried outside himself in dreams and nocturnal visions, seeing while asleep many things he has never seen while awake? Who, then, is so foolish and dull as to suppose that all these things, which occur in the spirit alone, also happen in the body, when the prophet Ezekiel saw the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body, and the apostle John saw and heard the mysteries of the Apocalypse in the spirit, not in the body, as he himself says: “Immediately I was in the spirit” *(Revelation IV)*? Paul too does not dare to say that he was caught up in the body.

[Col. 0353A] Therefore it must be publicly announced to all that whoever believes such things and things like them has lost the faith; and whoever does not have right faith in God belongs not to God but to the one in whom he believes—that is, the devil. For it is written concerning our Lord: “All things were made through him” *(John I)*. Therefore whoever believes that anything can happen, or that any creature can be changed or transformed for better or worse into another form or likeness, except by the Creator himself, who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an unbeliever.

**347. That Christians should not observe pagan traditions. From the writings of Ambrose.**

**CCCLXV.** *(Saint Ambrose, on chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Galatians; Burchard, Book X, chapter 11.)* The Apostle says: “You observe days and months and seasons and years. I fear that I may have labored over you in vain.” Those observe days who say, for example: “One must not set out tomorrow; after tomorrow, nothing should be begun,” and in this way they are accustomed to be more easily deceived.

Those observe months who examine the course of the moon, saying: “On the seventh moon no tools should be made.”

[Note: [Col. 0353D] See Augustine, Letter 119 and the Enchiridion, chapter 79.]

“Again, on the ninth moon a purchased slave ought not to be brought home.” Through such practices adverse events are more readily accustomed to occur.

They observe seasons when they say: “Today is the beginning of spring, and therefore it is a festival.” “The day after tomorrow is the Vulcanalia.” And again: “Tomorrow it is not permitted to leave the house.”

They observe years when they say: “The Kalends of January are the new year,” as though the years were not completed every day.

[Col. 0353C] This superstition must be far from the servants of God.

[Note: [Col. 0354D] See Hincmar, volume I, p. 656.]

**On the same matter. From the council of Braga.**

**CCCLXVI.** *(Second Council of Braga, chapter 72; Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 26; Hincmar, On the Divorce of Lothar, response to question 17; Burchard, Book X, chapter 13.)* Christians may not observe pagan tradition, worship the elements, or examine the moon, the course of the stars, or the empty deception of signs in order to build a house, plant crops or trees, or arrange marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God” *(Colossians III)*.

**348. Concerning the gathering of herbs. From the same source.**

**CCCLXVII.** *(Second Council of Braga, chapter 74; Halitgar, same work; Hincmar, same work; Burchard, Book X, chapter 20.)* In gathering medicinal herbs it is not permitted to observe any omens or use enchantments, but only to do so with the divine creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that God and our Lord Jesus Christ may be honored.

**Concerning women’s weaving. From the same source.**

**CCCLXVIII.** *(Second Council of Braga, chapter 75; Halitgar, same work; Hincmar, same work; Burchard, Book X, chapter 19.)* Christian women may not observe vanity in their weaving, but must invoke God as their helper, since he has given them the wisdom to weave.

[Col. 0354A] **Concerning carrion. From a Penitential.**

**CCCLXIX.** *(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 88.)* Whoever eats unclean meat, carrion, or meat torn apart by a beast shall do penance for forty days. If anyone ate it under the compulsion of hunger, he shall do much lighter penance.

**CCCLXX.** Whoever knowingly eats what has been obtained by fraud, seizure, or theft shall do penance for seven days if he is poor, and for forty days if he is powerful. The sick, if they know what they have eaten, shall do penance for fifteen days.

**CCCLXXI.** *(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 106.)* Whoever eats or drinks something contaminated by a domestic animal—that is, by a dog or cat—shall do penance for two days.

**Concerning liquids. From the same source.**

**CCCLXXII.** *(Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 106.)* If anyone gives someone a liquid in which a mouse or weasel has died, he shall do penance for seven days if he is a layman. If they are in a monastery, they shall sing two hundred psalms. Whoever later learns that he drank such a beverage shall sing one psalter.

**349. Concerning blood.**

**CCCLXXIII.** If anyone eats the blood of an animal, he shall do penance for forty days.

**Again, that no one should eat blood.**

**CCCLXXIV.** The faithful must be admonished that no one presume to eat blood. For at the beginning, when God gave human beings permission to eat meat, we read that blood was forbidden. For the Lord said to Noah and his sons: “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood. For I shall demand an account of the blood of your lives from every beast and from human beings” *(Genesis IX)*.

This is forbidden not only very frequently in the Old Law, but also in the New Testament, where the apostles, after much deliberation, write to the gentiles of the primitive Church that they should abstain from the defilements of idols, fornication, things strangled, and blood.

Explaining this, Jerome says: “According to the literal meaning, these precepts apply to every Christian, so that he does not eat carrion, whether of birds or of livestock, whose blood has in no way been poured out.”

The letter sent by the apostles from Jerusalem necessarily instructs us to observe these things [Col. 0354D] *(Acts XV)*, as well as meat seized by a beast, since it too has likewise been strangled; and blood—that is, not eating meat with the blood.

[Col. 0354D] If these commands were written for those coming from pagan life, as the very beginnings of faith and because of their long-established pagan custom, as though these observances were sufficient for their salvation, who would disregard them as a transgressor? It must also be considered that what is strangled and blood are equated with idolatry and fornication. Therefore everyone must be told how great a sacrilege it is to eat blood, since it is compared with idols and fornication. If anyone violates these commands of the Lord and the apostles, [Col. 0355A] he shall be suspended from ecclesiastical communion until he has duly repented.

**Concerning those at odds. From the council of Carthage.**

**CCCLXXV.** *(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 93; Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 31; Burchard, Book V, chapter 38.)* The offerings of brothers who are at odds with one another shall be received neither in the sacristy nor in the treasury.

**On the same matter. From the council of Agde.**

**CCCLXXVI.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 31; Halitgar, same work, chapter 32; Burchard, Book X, chapter 61.)* It has also been decreed that, as often happens, whoever has separated from another through hatred or a prolonged dispute, and cannot be recalled to peace despite sustained efforts, shall be expelled from the assembly of the Church by the most just excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] See above, Book I, chapter 61.]

**On the same matter. From the writings of Isidore.**

[Col. 0355B] **CCCLXXVII.** *(Burchard, Book X, chapter 57.)* If anyone remains discordant, quarrelsome, and at odds through hatred, he shall remain, until he returns to harmony, alien from the assembly and fellowship of the Church, as the canons command.

**351. On the same matter.**

**CCCLXXVIII.** *(Burchard, Book X, chapter 58.)* If anyone, hating another, does not return to peace, he shall be excommunicated on bread and water and separated from the Church, as the holy Fathers decreed.

**On the same matter. From the council of Carthage.**

**CCCLXXIX.** *(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 25; Burchard, Book I, chapter 62.)* If fear of God does not reconcile bishops who are at odds, let a synod reconcile them.

**On the same matter. From the same source.**

**CCCLXXX.** *(Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 26; Burchard, Book I, chapter 101.)* A bishop must strive to encourage brothers who are at odds—whether clerics or laymen—toward peace rather than toward judgment.

**Concerning the subversion of God’s judgment.**

**CCCLXXXI.** *(Burchard, Book X, chapter 25.)* If anyone eats, drinks, or carries upon himself something by which he thinks he can subvert God’s judgment, and this is proved against him, he shall receive the same sentence as magicians, soothsayers, and enchanters: namely, he shall be punished by penance of seven or five years.

[Note: [Col. 0356D] See Book III of the Lombard Laws.]

**Concerning offerings for the dead. From the council of Vaison.**

**CCCLXXXII.** *(Council of Vaison, chapter 4.)* Those who retain offerings for the dead and delay handing them over to the churches are to be expelled from the church as unbelievers.

[Col. 0355D] **From the same source.**

**CCCLXXXIII.** If anyone defrauds others of their offerings, they must be admonished to return what they fraudulently took. If they refuse to return it, they shall be separated from the fellowship of the Church until they do so, as the holy synod has decreed.

**From the council of Agde.**

**CCCLXXXIV.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 4; Burchard, Book III, chapter 140.)* Clerics or laymen who presume to retain offerings given or bequeathed by their parents, or who entrust to churches or monasteries something they themselves have donated and then attempt to take it away, shall be excluded from the churches until they return it, as killers of the poor.

[Col. 0356A] **From the same source.**

**CCCLXXXV.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 26.)* If any cleric voluntarily causes harm to the Church, he shall repay it from his own resources and be deprived of communion.

**Concerning the dead.**

**CCCLXXXVI.** If anyone sings diabolical songs over a dead person during the night, and so forth, see Book I, chapter 383.

**CONCERNING COMMUNION. That the principal festivals should be celebrated in the cities. From the council of Agde.**

**CCCLXXXVII.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 18; Burchard, Book V, chapter 23.)* Laymen who do not receive communion at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be regarded as Catholics, nor counted among Catholics. See Book I, chapter 93.

**On the same matter. From the council of Orléans.**

**CCCLXXXVIII.** *(First Council of Orléans, chapter 25.)* No citizen may celebrate the solemnities of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost in the countryside, unless it is established that illness kept him there.

**On the same matter. From the council of Agde.**

**CCCLXXXIX.** *(Council of Agde, chapter 63.)* Citizens who neglect to attend their bishops in their cities on the festivals of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost, in order to receive communion or a blessing, shall be deprived of communion for three years.

[Col. 0356C] **Concerning decans to be sent through the parishes. From the council of Rouen.**
### CCCXC. (BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 239)

The people are to be admonished that on Sundays and feast days everyone must without fail attend Vespers, the nocturnal vigils, and Mass. Decans are also to be appointed in the cities and in the public villages—truthful men who fear God—who will admonish the idle and negligent to hasten to the service of God without excuse. These decans are to be bound by an oath that, regardless of any intervening consideration—whether affection, fear, kinship, or a gift—they will not conceal the negligent and transgressors, but will disclose their individual faults to the priests.

It will be the priests’ responsibility to correct their vices with zeal and divine love, together with the requisite discipline, just as the priests themselves do not wish to receive the sentence of just condemnation for the faults of others. Feast days are likewise to be celebrated from evening to evening, without servile labor and with due honor.

### Concerning the Excommunicated. From the Sayings of Cassian

### CCCXCI

If anyone has been suspended from prayer on account of his fault, no one may have permission to pray or speak with him before he has been reconciled. For whoever, through ill-considered compassion, presumes to join him in prayer or conversation before he has been received back by his superior likewise becomes condemned.

### Concerning the Same Matter. Isidore, as Above

### CCCXCII. (Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 17; BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 31)

No one is permitted to pray, speak, or eat with an excommunicated person.

### Hence, Above

### CCCXCIII. (BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 32)

If any brother has spoken either openly or secretly with an excommunicated person, he immediately incurs with him the common penalty of excommunication.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Bishop Fructuosus

### CCCXCIV. (Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 14; BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 33)

Let no one speak with an excommunicated person, support him by any sort of compassion or pity, or presume to encourage him in contradiction or arrogance.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Rule of Saint Benedict

### CCCXCV. (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 26)

If anyone in any way associates himself with an excommunicated brother or sends him a message, let him incur a punishment of excommunication of the same kind.

### Likewise

### CCCXCVI. (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 25)

That brother who is held by the guilt of a more serious fault is to be suspended both from the table and from the oratory. No one is to associate with him, either in companionship or in conversation.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council of Antioch

### CCCXCVII. (Council of Antioch, canon 2; BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 34)

It is not permitted to share in communion with the excommunicated; nor is one to pray together with those who assemble in houses while avoiding the prayers of the Church. But if anyone from the clergy is discovered to be sharing communion with the excommunicated, he too is to be deprived of communion.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council of the Apostles

### CCCXCVIII. (Apostolic Canons, canon 11; BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 35)

If anyone has prayed with an excommunicated person, even in a house, let him be deprived of communion.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council of Nicaea

### CCCXCIX. (Council of Nicaea, canon 5; BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 36)

Concerning those who are deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the laity: let the regular sentence of the bishops prevail, so that those who are cast out are not received by others. Let inquiry also be made, lest the person appear to have been excluded from communion through the bishop’s faintheartedness, contentiousness, or some other fault.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council of Antioch

### CCCC. (Council of Antioch, canon 6; BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 37)

If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he is not to be received by other bishops until he has been reconciled with his bishop.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council of the Apostles

### CCCCI. (Apostolic Canons, canon 12)

If anyone has prayed together with a condemned cleric as though he were a cleric, let him be condemned.

### Concerning Those Condemned by a Synod. From the Council of Antioch

### CCCCII. (Council of Antioch, canon 4; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 199)

If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any priest or deacon condemned by his own bishop, dares to undertake anything belonging to the ministry, he is in no way to have either hope of restoration or an opportunity for satisfaction, even in another synod.

### Concerning an Excommunicated Person Who Presumes to Share in Communion. From the Council of Carthage

### CCCCIII. (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 28, and Fourth Addition, chapter 35; BURCHARD, Book I, chapter 200)

It was likewise decreed by the entire council that whoever has been excommunicated for his negligence—whether a bishop or any cleric—and during the period of his excommunication has presumed to receive communion before a hearing, is to be judged to have pronounced upon himself the sentence of condemnation.

### If a Bishop Wishes to Expel Someone from the Church. From the Council of Sardica

### CCCCIV. (Council of Sardica, canon 17)

If a bishop wishes to expel his cleric from the Church, care must be taken that an innocent man is not condemned. Therefore, he is to have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and his case is to be heard and examined more carefully, since a hearing ought not to be denied to one who asks for it. The bishop, moreover, should patiently accept that his sentence either be proved or corrected.

### Concerning Those Who Have Been Deposed, If They Dare to Exercise the Ministry Once Entrusted to Them. In the Apostolic Canons

### CCCCCV. (Apostolic Canons, canon 29)

If any bishop, priest, or deacon, who has been justly deposed for specified crimes, dares to exercise the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be completely cut off from the Church.

### Concerning an Accused Priest. From the Council of Rouen

### CCCCVI

No bishop is to remove an accused priest from the office of Mass unless, having been summoned by letter on a fixed day to present his case, he has entirely failed to appear—that is, within the space of a month. If he does not appear after a second month, then he is to be suspended from office until he gives an account on his own behalf. For if laymen are not canonically excommunicated unless they have been summoned and admonished three times, it seems unworthy that priests, who belong to a higher order and dignity, should be denied what ecclesiastical regulation mercifully permits to laymen. A priest is considered to be removed from office to the same extent that a layman is considered to be excluded from the Church’s communion. For from the grounds on which laymen are excommunicated, priests are removed from the office of the altar. See chapter 289.

### How a Bishop Ought to Excommunicate Infidels. Hence, Above

### CCCCVI. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 2, from the Council of Rouen)

When a bishop has determined to excommunicate or anathematize an infidel on account of definite and manifest crimes, after the reading of the Gospel he is to address the clergy and people as follows.

### Address

### CCCCVIII. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 2; also in the CENTURIATORS, century 10, chapter 6)

Let your charity know, my brothers, that a certain man, whose name is such-and-such, at the devil’s prompting, setting aside the Christian promise that he professed in baptism, has turned through apostasy to Satan, whom he renounced together with all his works. He does not fear to devastate and plunder Christ’s vineyard—that is, his Church—violently oppressing and killing Christ’s poor, whom he redeemed with his precious blood, and seizing their goods.

Since he ought to have been a son of this Church of ours, over which by God’s authority we preside, because in it he was reborn through water and the Holy Spirit and numbered among God’s adopted sons—although he is now a son of the devil by imitating the devil—we have been concerned lest, through pastoral negligence, any of the sheep entrusted to us should perish, for which we might be compelled to render an account at the fearful judgment before our Lord Jesus Christ, the chief Shepherd. For he himself gravely threatens us, saying: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3).
