Accordingly, we sent to him our priest and letters of admonition, once, twice, and a third time, canonically inviting him to correction, satisfaction, and repentance, and reproving him with paternal affection. But he—alas!—because the devil hardened his heart, despised the salutary admonitions and, persisting in the evil he had begun, puffed up by a spirit of pride, disdains to make satisfaction to the Church of God whom he has injured.

We therefore have the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands concerning such transgressors and violators of the holy religion and peace that Christ himself gave and left to his disciples. Through these commands we are instructed concerning what we ought to do with such transgressors. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him” (Matthew 18).

Brothers, whoever sins against the holy Church sins against each one of us. For if the Church, once healed, is one body whose head is Christ, while each of us is a member of the other, and “if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12), then without doubt he sins against us who injures our members.

The Lord therefore commands that a brother—that is, a Christian—who sins against us should first be rebuked privately, then reproved with witnesses, and finally confronted publicly in the assembly of the Church. But if he despises these three admonitions and charitable corrections and scorns to make satisfaction, then, he says, “let him be to you as a heathen” (Matthew 18)—that is, a gentile and pagan—so that he is no longer regarded as a Christian but as a pagan.

Elsewhere the Lord commands that a member which is loosened from its framework, separated from the bond of charity, and every body that causes scandal, be cut off and cast away, saying: “If your eye, or your hand, or your foot causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you” (ibid.). The Apostle says: “Remove the evil from among you” (1 Corinthians 5). Again: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Corinthians 7). Elsewhere he excludes the rapacious from the kingdom of God, saying: “Nor will the rapacious possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). And elsewhere: “If anyone is called a brother”—that is, a Christian—“and is a fornicator, or adulterer, or murderer, or rapacious, with such a one you must not even eat” (1 Corinthians 5).

John, beloved above the other disciples of Christ, forbade such a wicked man to be greeted, saying: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, and do not receive him into your house. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John 10).

Therefore, fulfilling the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, let us cut off from the body of the Church, by the sword of excommunication, the rotten and incurable member that does not accept treatment, lest the remaining members of the body be infected, as if by poison, with so deadly a disease (Decrees of Siricius, chapter 7).

### Excommunication

### CCCCIX. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 3; also in the CENTURIATORS, same location)

Because he despises our admonitions and frequent exhortations; because, having been summoned a third time according to the Lord’s command to correction and repentance, he has scorned to come; because he has neither recognized nor confessed his fault; because, although he is our parishioner, he has neither sent a delegation to us, who are conducting his case, nor asked for pardon; and because, with the devil hardening his heart, he persists in the evil he began and, as the Apostle says, “according to his hardness and impenitent heart treasures up wrath for himself on the day of wrath”—therefore, by the judgment of almighty God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; and of all the saints; and also by the authority and power of our lowliness, divinely conferred upon us to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, we separate him, together with all his accomplices, fellow communicants, and supporters, from receiving the precious body and blood of the Lord and from the fellowship of all Christians.

We exclude him from the threshold of holy mother Church in heaven and on earth, decree that he is excommunicated and anathematized, and judge him condemned with the devil, his angels, and all the reprobate in eternal fire—unless perhaps he comes to his senses from the devil’s snares, returns to correction and repentance, and makes satisfaction to the Church of God whom he has injured.

Let everyone answer three times: “Amen”; or “Let it be, let it be”; or “Let him be anathema.”

Twelve priests are to stand around the bishop and hold burning lamps in their hands. At the conclusion of the anathema or excommunication, they are to throw the lamps onto the ground and trample them underfoot.

After this, the bishop is to explain the excommunication itself to the people in ordinary words, so that all may understand how terribly he has been condemned and may know that from that hour onward he is to be regarded not as a Christian but as a pagan. Whoever associates with him as though he were a Christian, eats or drinks with him, kisses him, or has familiar conversation with him—unless perhaps he makes an effort to call him to satisfaction and repentance—or whoever receives him into his house or prays together with him, is without doubt likewise excommunicated.

Afterward, letters are to be sent to the priests throughout the parish setting forth the manner of the excommunication. They are to be instructed to announce that excommunication publicly to the people entrusted to them on Sundays after the reading of the Gospel, so that no one through ignorance may associate with the excommunicated person.

The excommunication must also be made known to the other bishops. For the Council of Toledo commands (Council of Toledo I, chapter 11) that writings should immediately circulate among all the bishops of the province, to whichever of them they can reach, so that the excommunicated person may be heard. His lord must also be informed of the excommunication [Note: See above, chapter 289 of this book].

### Another Address of Excommunication

### CCCCX. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 4; also in the CENTURIATORS, same location)

You have heard, beloved, how many and how dreadful were the works of depravity and iniquity that this man, instigated by the devil, did not fear to commit, and how, through apostasy, he withdrew with a profane mind from the worship of the entire Christian religion.

You have heard how he was canonically summoned to make satisfaction but delayed coming; how, although frequently admonished to recover from the devil’s snares by which he is held bound, he contemptuously refused to hear the most salutary admonitions with the ears of his heart stopped.

The Lord says in the Gospel concerning such a contumacious brother who refuses to accept ecclesiastical correction: “If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you,” he says, “as a heathen and a publican” (Matthew 18)—that is, he is no longer to be counted among Christians but among pagans.

Paul, therefore, following the teaching of the Lord and Master, reproves the Corinthians for maintaining fellowship with criminals and wicked men, saying: “You are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has committed such a deed may be removed from among you” (1 Corinthians 5)—that is, let the one who has committed such a crime be separated from your fellowship.

And he adds: “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit; I have already judged, as though present, him who has done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled and my spirit is with you, with the power of my Lord Jesus, to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (ibid.).

And shortly afterward: “I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators” (ibid.). Immediately he adds: “If anyone is called a brother”—that is, a Christian—“and is a fornicator or rapacious, with such a one you must not even eat” (ibid.). Elsewhere: “Remove the evil from among you” (1 Corinthians 7). And: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Corinthians 5).

For one diseased sheep contaminates the entire flock, a little leaven corrupts the whole mass, and often one rotten member infects the entire body. Therefore, so destructive a pest must be uprooted from the body of the Church.

### Excommunication

### CCCCXI. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 5; also in the CENTURIATORS, same location)

Therefore, instructed by the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, by the judgment of the Father, and of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, and by the authority and power granted by God to the apostles and the successors of the apostles, together with you we exclude the aforementioned most wicked man from the threshold of holy mother Church and separate him from all Christian fellowship and communion. We decree that he is separated forever—that is, in the present age and in the age to come.

Let no Christian say “Hail” to him or presume to kiss him. Let no priest dare to celebrate Mass with him or give him the most sacred body and blood of the Lord. Let no one associate with him in fellowship or in any business.

If anyone associates with him and shares in his evil works, let him know that he has been struck by a similar anathema—except for those who associate with him for the purpose of turning him back from error and calling him to satisfaction. He remains so separated unless perhaps he comes to his senses, is moved by God’s grace to turn to the remedy of repentance, and humbly makes worthy satisfaction to the Church of God whom he has injured.

### Another, More Terrible Excommunication

### CCCCXII. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 6; also in the CENTURIATORS, same location)

Following canonical institutions and the examples of the holy Fathers, we separate those violators of the churches of God—namely, robbers, plunderers, and murderers—from the bosom of holy mother Church in the name of the Father and of the Son, and by the power of the Holy Spirit, as well as by the authority divinely conferred upon bishops through Peter, chief of the apostles; and we condemn them with the anathema of perpetual malediction.

Let them be accursed in the city and accursed in the field; accursed be their granary and accursed their remnant; accursed be the fruit of their womb and the fruit of their land. Accursed be those who enter and accursed those who depart. Let them be accursed in the house and fugitives in the field. Let all those curses come upon them which the Lord threatened through Moses to send upon the people who transgressed the divine law. Let them be “anathema maranatha”—that is, let them perish at the second coming of the Lord.

Let no Christian say “Hail” to them. Let no priest presume to celebrate Mass or give them holy communion. Let them be buried with a donkey’s burial and become dung upon the face of the earth.

And just as these lamps thrown today from our hands are extinguished, so may their lamp be extinguished forever—unless perhaps they come to their senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God whom they have injured through correction and worthy repentance.

### Brief Excommunication

### CCCCXIII. (BURCHARD, Book VI, chapter 7; also in the CENTURIATORS, same location)

Following canonical institutions and the examples of the holy Fathers, we expel those violators of the churches of God from the bosom of holy mother Church and from the fellowship of all Christians, by the authority of God and the judgment of the Holy Spirit, until they come to their senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God.

### How a Bishop Reconciles or Receives an Excommunicated Person

### CCCCXIV. (BURCHARD, Book XI, chapter 8)

When an excommunicated or anathematized person, moved to repentance, asks for pardon and promises amendment, the bishop who excommunicated him is to come before the doors of the church, together with twelve priests, who are to stand around the excommunicated person on either side. Those to whom injury or damage was inflicted are also to be present. There, according to divine and human laws, the damage committed must be repaired, or, if it has already been repaired, this must be confirmed by their testimony.

The bishop is then to ask whether he wishes to undertake the penance prescribed by the canons for the crimes he has committed. If, prostrate on the ground, he asks pardon, confesses his fault, implores penance, and promises to take care concerning the future, then the bishop is to take him by his right hand, lead him into the church, and restore to him communion and Christian fellowship.

After this, the bishop is to impose penance upon him according to the nature of his fault and send letters throughout the parish, so that all may know that he has been received into Christian fellowship. He is also to make this known to the other bishops.

No bishop, however, is to presume to excommunicate or reconcile another bishop’s parishioner without the knowledge or consent of that person’s own bishop.

### Concerning One Who Dishonors His Father or Mother. From the Council of Rouen

### CCCCXV

If anyone strikes or curses his father or mother, since he has committed capital crimes, let him undertake public penance for it, as for more serious sins. For the Lord says: “Whoever curses father or mother shall be put to death” (Exodus 2). Whoever the Lord judges worthy of death is without doubt held to be a murderer and ought to repent as a murderer.

### Concerning Cowherds and Swineherds, That They Should Come to Mass at Least on Sundays. Hence, Above

### CCCCXVI. (BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 71)

The priests must admonish the people subject to them to ensure that cowherds, swineherds, and other shepherds or ploughmen who remain continually in the fields or woods and therefore live like animals are made or permitted to come at least to Mass on Sundays and other feast days. For Christ also redeemed these people with his precious blood.

If they neglect this, they must know without doubt that they will have to render an account for their souls. For when the Lord came into this world, he did not choose orators and the more noble people, but took fishermen and uneducated men as his disciples, to show in deed what he affirms in the Gospel in words: “What is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.” And, without prejudice to a higher understanding, the birth of our Redeemer was first announced by an angel to shepherds.

Concerning confession, penance, tithes, drunkenness, and vomiting after the Eucharist, the matter has been explained above in the first book.

### Concerning How the Poor Are to Be Supported. From the Council of Tours

### CCCCXVII. (Council of Tours II, chapter 5)

Let each city feed the poor and needy with suitable provisions according to its means. Let the neighboring priests as well as the citizens each support his own poor person, so that the poor themselves may not wander through other cities.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From Book I of the Capitularies, Chapter 118

### CCCCXVIII. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 124)

Concerning beggars who travel throughout the regions: we wish each of our faithful to support his own poor person from his benefice or household and not permit him to go anywhere begging. Wherever such people are found who are able to work with their hands but do not do so, let no one presume to give them anything.

### Concerning One Who Despises the Bishop’s or Priest’s Ban. Hence, Above

### CCCCXIX

Whoever, in his arrogance, despises the ban or excommunication of his bishop or priest is to be completely uprooted from the Church. For the Lord says to Moses: “The person who, in his arrogance, transgresses the commandment of the Lord shall perish from among his people” (Numbers 15).

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10). Moses also says to the rebellious: “Your murmuring is not against me but against the Lord” (Exodus 16). Dathan and Abiram were swallowed alive because they rose up against that same Moses and despised his command. Therefore such a crime must be punished with the greatest severity.

### Concerning a Priest Who Has Been Degraded. From the Twelfth Council of Toledo, Chapter 6

### CCCCXX. (Council of Verneuil under Pippin, chapter 9; Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 42; BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 179)

If any priest has been degraded by his bishop or suspended from office for specified crimes, and through contempt and arrogance has presumed to undertake anything belonging to the ministry forbidden to him, and afterward, having been corrected by his bishop, has persisted in the presumption he began, let him be excommunicated in every way and expelled from the Church.

Whoever knowingly shares communion with him is likewise to know that he is excommunicated. The same is to be observed concerning excommunicated clerics, laymen, and women.

If anyone despises all these measures and the bishop is entirely unable to correct him, let him be condemned to exile by the judgment of the king.

### That No One Should Deny Lodging to a Traveler. From the Council at the Palace of Verneuil

### CCCCXXI

It pleased us and our faithful that priests should admonish their parishioners to be hospitable themselves, to deny lodging to no one making a journey, and to remove every opportunity for robbery. They are not to sell anything more dearly to travelers than they are able to sell it in the market.

If they wish to sell at a higher price, let the travelers report this to the priest, and, at his command, let them sell to them humanely.

### Concerning One Who Dishonors a Priest. Hence, Above

### CCCCXXII. (BURCHARD, Book II, chapter 229)

If anyone dishonors his own priest or insults him by word or deed, let him be kept away from the threshold of the church until he makes satisfaction through worthy penance. For the Apostle says: “Let the priests who preside be considered worthy of double honor” (1 Timothy 5). He says elsewhere: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them,” and so forth (Hebrews 13).

### If Anyone Contradicts the Bishop So That Servants Are Not Beaten with Rods on Account of Their Crimes. From the Council at Saint-Médard

### CCCCXXIII. (Council of Soissons II, act 8, canon 9)

Our envoys are to announce to everyone throughout the individual parishes that, if a bishop or the bishop’s ministers flog peasants with rods on account of their crimes, they must do so, for the fear of others and the correction of the offenders themselves, with such discretion and without any improper pretext as was determined in the synod, so that the offenders may undertake penance even unwillingly and not perish eternally.

If the lords of these peasants take this badly and wish to exact some vengeance on that account, or presume to oppose action against those same peasants so that they may not be coerced, they must know that they will both pay our ban and, together with ecclesiastical excommunication, suffer our harshest royal penalty (*harmiscara*).

### Concerning Refugees. From the Council of Charles and Lothair at Valence, Chapter 10

### CCCCXXIV. (Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 12, chapter 9)

Concerning the refugees who, because of the oppression of the Northmen or Bretons, have fled into parts of these kingdoms: our lords have decreed that they are to suffer no violence, oppression, or exaction from any official of the state. They are to be permitted to seek their livelihood until peace is restored and either they return to their own places or their lords receive them.

No one is to presume to place them in servitude because they have remained with someone as hired workers; nor is anyone to demand a census or tribute from them. If any official of the state or anyone else is found to be doing or to have done anything against this command of mercy, he is to pay our ban on that account.

### Hence, Above

### CCCCXXV

It has come to the ears of the priests that refugees who have barely escaped the hands of the pagans, having lost all their possessions, are unjustly oppressed by certain people in our regions and reduced to servitude contrary to divine and human laws, although the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not oppress the resident aliens in this place, and I will dwell with you” (Jeremiah 7). And again: “You shall not grieve the resident alien” (Exodus 20), together with many similar passages.

Such people are therefore to be severely corrected, and the resident aliens are to be rescued from their hands, according to what is written: “Rescuing the needy from the hand of one stronger than he,” and so forth (Psalm 34).

For among their Christian brothers, that is, among Christians, resident aliens ought to be hired workers, not slaves. If they are reduced to servitude, what benefit was it for them to escape the hands of the pagans, if they have not escaped the yoke of captivity and harsh servitude? Therefore priestly compassion must struggle against this cruelty, lest divine anger consume the Christian people on account of so monstrous a wickedness.

### That Just Measures Are to Be Used. From the Capitular at Pîtres

### CCCCXXVI. (Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 31, chapter 20)

Let the counts and all officials of the state, as well as our other faithful, ensure that a just *modius* and an equal *sextarius*, according to Sacred Scripture and the Capitularies of our predecessors, are used for buying and selling in the cities, villages, and estates; and let them obtain their measures from our palace according to ancient custom.

If anyone is accused of falsifying a measure, then, if he is a free man, let him clear himself by oath according to his law; or, if he is found guilty, let him pay our ban, and let the officials of the state confiscate what he intended to sell using the unjust measure.

If the accusation concerns a peasant or slave, let him submit the matter to the judgment of God; and if he is convicted, let him lose the object—that is, the thing by which he falsified the measure—and in addition let him be beaten with rods on his bare skin.

Whether slave or free, after the legal penalty has been imposed, let him also undergo episcopal judgment, because he acted against God’s prohibition. For Scripture says: “Let your *modius* be just and your *sextarius* equal” (Leviticus 19). Elsewhere: “The Lord hates diverse measures” (Proverbs 20). And again: “Who has not given his money at interest” (Psalm 14). This sin is counted among those capital sins of which the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 5) that whoever commits them may not eat with such a person as a Christian.

Likewise, in the cities, villages, and markets, let the officials of the state ensure that those who sell bread and meat by *deneradas* and wine by *sextarii* cannot falsify the measure. Instead, let them require the bakers who sell bread to make as many measured loaves from the same *modius* as the bishops or abbots receive from their own bakers from a just *modius* in each city.

If they are found to falsify or diminish the measure, let them both suffer the loss and be beaten with rods.

The men entrusted with ensuring that the measures are not diminished must also be dealt with. If they are convicted of perjury, because they swore that they ought not to have consented to this, let them be punished according to the law: either let them lose a hand, or redeem it, or suffer a severe penalty; afterward let them receive public penance from the bishop for their perjury.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From Book III of the Capitularies, Chapter 90

### CCCCXXVII. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 74)

Let everyone have equal measures and equal weights, whether in cities or in monasteries, for giving and receiving from one another, as we have the commandment in the law of the Lord [Note: See Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 148].

### Concerning Conspiracies. From the Council of Chalcedon

### CCCCXXVIII. (Council of Chalcedon, canon 18; BURCHARD, Book X, chapter 18)

The crime of conspiracy or confederacy is altogether prohibited even by secular laws. Much more, therefore, is it fitting to admonish that this not occur in the Church of God. If any clerics or monks are found to be forming a conspiracy, confederating, or laying ambushes for bishops or clerics, let them be completely cut off from their proper rank.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From Book I of the Capitularies, Title 28

### CCCCXXIX. (Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 29)

Neither clerics nor monks are to form a conspiracy or lay ambushes against their shepherd.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From the Council at Pîtres

### CCCCXXX. (Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 29, chapter 4)

We bishops likewise prohibit this by the authority of God and the sacred canons, just as the holy pontiffs of the Council of Chalcedon, numbering 630, prohibited conspiracies, and just as the other councils of bishops forbade such pernicious acts. Those who commit them are, by the judgment of those who now reign with God in heaven, separated both from the heavenly Church and from the fellowship of Christians, unless through worthy fruits of repentance they return to the point at which they can be reunited with the holy Church.

### Concerning the Same Matter. From Book III of the Capitularies, Chapter 9

### CCCCXXXI. (Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 9; Book I of Lombard Law, title 17, chapter 11)

Whoever presumes to form conspiracies and confirms any conspiracy by an oath is to be judged in three ways.

First, wherever some evil has been perpetrated through it, the authors of the deed are to be killed. Their helpers, however, are each to be flogged by the others, and they are to cut off one another’s noses.

Where no evil has been perpetrated, they are nevertheless to be flogged among themselves and to cut one another’s hair in turn.

If the conspiracy has been formed by joining right hands, then, if they are free men, they are either to swear with suitable oath-takers or, if they cannot do this, to pay the composition required by their law. If they are slaves, let them be flogged.

### Concerning Confraternities or Associations. From the Council of Nantes
### CCCCXXXII. On collections or confraternities, which they call associations

(Concil. Nannet., c. 15; HINCMAR, *Capitula*, tit. 1, c. 16.)

Concerning collections or confraternities, which they call associations, as we have admonished orally and now expressly command in writing: let only so much be done as pertains to what is right, to authority and usefulness, and to the salvation of the soul. Let no one—neither priest nor any of the faithful—in our parish dare to go beyond this, namely, in any religious service: in offerings, lights, mutual prayers, funerals, almsgiving, and the other works of piety.

But meals and banquets, which divine authority forbids, at which drunken excesses, improper exactions, shameful and empty merriment, and quarrels often arise—and, as we have experienced, sometimes even homicide, hatred, and dissension—these we utterly prohibit. Whoever presumes to act against this decree, if he is a presbyter or any cleric, shall be deprived of his rank; if he is a layman or woman, he shall be separated from the Church until satisfaction has been made.

If it should be necessary for such confraternity members to meet together, or if someone happens to have a disagreement with his equal and needs to be reconciled, so that this cannot be done without a gathering of priests and others, then, after the matters belonging to God and fitting for Christian religion have been completed, and after the proper admonitions, if it happens that all come together for refreshment in true charity and mutual fraternal consolation, we permit such things to be done in this manner: with modesty, temperance, sobriety, and the harmony of peace preserved, as is fitting for brothers, let everything be done for the building up of brotherhood, and for the praise and glory of God and thanksgiving.

Let this saying of the Savior be observed with the utmost care: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21). Those who wish may receive *eulogiae*—blessed portions—from the presbyter; and, breaking bread only, let each receive one individual drink, and let no one presume that anything more should take place. Thus let each return to his own home with the Lord’s blessing.

### If a presbyter dies, a neighboring presbyter must not obtain his church from the senior layman

From the same source.

### CCCCXXXIII

(Concil. Nannet., c. 16; HINCMAR, *Capitula*, tit. 2, c. 17; BURCHARD, book III, c. 229.)

If any presbyter dies, let a neighboring presbyter obtain that church from the senior layman neither by entreaty nor by any gift, since the benefice previously existed as an established title in its own right; nor may he obtain a chapel without consulting the bishop. (Decrees of LEO I, c. 38.) If he does so, let him accept the sentence determined against him, just as canonical authority has decreed concerning a bishop: whoever through ambition has sought a greater city shall lose the one he held and shall in no way obtain the one he attempted to usurp.

### On liquid into which a mouse has fallen

From the *Penitential*.

### CCCCXXXIV

If a mouse falls into liquid, let it be removed, sprinkled with holy water, and the liquid consumed. But if the mouse is found dead, let all that liquid be thrown away. If there is a large quantity of liquid, let it be purified, sprinkled with holy water, and consumed if necessary. If a dead mouse is found in flour, curdled milk, or honey, let what is around it be thrown outside, and let the remainder be consumed.

### If someone violates a tomb, and other matters

As above.

### CCCCXXXV

If someone violates a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

If someone has made magical bindings—which is detestable—let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

If someone has eaten carrion or something sacrificed to idols, let him fast for twelve weeks.

If someone has voluntarily cut off any member of his own body, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

If someone has exacted interest of any kind, let him likewise do penance.

If someone by violence or by any evil device or wrongful means has invaded or taken another person’s property, let him likewise do penance.

If someone has sold a human being by an evil or wrongful act, let him likewise do penance.

If someone has voluntarily burned another person’s threshing floor or house with fire, let him likewise do penance.

If someone, in anger, has struck another person and shed blood or disabled him, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water.

### If an excommunicated person dies

As above.

### CCCCXXXVI

(HALITGAR, book VI, c. 10; BURCHARD, book XI, c. 51.)

If an excommunicated person dies who had already confessed but was unable to come to the priest because death overtook him at home or on the road, let his relatives make an offering for him at the altar and give a ransom offering for captives.

### Concerning one who has stolen out of necessity

### CCCCXXXVII

(BURCHARD, book XI, c. 56.)

If someone has stolen food, clothing, or livestock out of necessity, because of hunger or nakedness, let him do penance for four weeks. If he returns what he stole, he shall not be compelled to fast.

### Concerning the price of redemption

### CCCCXXXVIII

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 22.)

If someone is perhaps unable to fast but has the means of redemption, then, if he is wealthy, let him give twenty solidi for seven weeks. If he does not have enough to give that much, let him give ten solidi. If he is extremely poor, let him give three solidi.

Let no one be troubled because we have ordered twenty solidi or less to be given: if he is wealthy, it is easier for him to give twenty solidi than for a poor man to give three. But let each person consider to whom he ought to give it—whether for the redemption of captives, upon the holy altar, to God’s servants, or to the poor as alms.

### What should be done for one month

From the preceding material.

### CCCCXXXIX

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 19.)

For one month of penance on bread and water, a person should recite 1,200 psalms kneeling; if not kneeling, 680. Every day, if he wishes and cannot abstain, let him eat at the sixth hour; except on Wednesday and Friday, let him fast until the ninth hour, and let him consume neither meat nor wine. Let him receive the remainder.

### What should be done for one week

As above.

### CCCCXL

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 18.)

For one week, let him recite 300 psalms while kneeling, or let him sing the psalms continuously in one place.

### What should be done for one year

### CCCCXLI

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 20.)

Whoever does not know the psalms and cannot fast should, for one year of the penance that he ought to perform on bread and water, give twenty-six solidi as alms. Every week he should fast for one day until the ninth hour—that is, Wednesday—and another day, Friday, until evening. During the three Lents, let him reckon the amount he consumes and give half of it as alms.

### Also concerning the price for one year

### CCCCXLII

In the first year, some allowed four three-day fasts; others, twelve three-day fasts—that is, once each month. Some said that the three-day fasts should be performed with scourging and vigils throughout the three days.

### Concerning the redemption of one day

### CCCCXLIII

The price for one day is a charitable meal (*agape*) for two or three poor people, or one denarius. Others prescribe the entire Psalter in summer, but in winter, spring, or autumn, fifty psalms. Some judged that it should be twelve blows or strokes.

### Also concerning the redemption of one day

### CCCCXLIV

Whoever is able to fulfill what is written in the *Penitential* should give thanks to God. But for whoever cannot fulfill it, we offer the following counsel through the mercy of God.

First, for one day on bread and water, let him sing fifty psalms while kneeling; or, standing in one place, let him recite seventy; or let him give one denarius; or let him feed three poor people.

Some say: fifty blows or fifty psalms for one day; in autumn, winter, or spring, one hundred blows or fifty psalms; in summer, one Psalter or one hundred blows.

### Also concerning the redemption of three years

### CCCCXLV

(BURCHARD, book XIX, c. 23.)

Whoever cannot perform penance in the manner described above should give twenty-six solidi in alms in the first year, twenty in the second, and eighteen in the third—that is, sixty-four solidi.

Let wealthy people do for their sins what Zacchaeus did. For he said to the Lord: “Lord, I give half of all my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything unjustly, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19).

Let them also set some of their slaves free, redeem captives, and forgive from the heart those who sin against them. Whoever has committed unlawful acts should also abstain from lawful pleasures and afflict his body with fasts, vigils, and frequent prayers. For a joyful flesh drew us toward sin; when afflicted, it leads us back to forgiveness.

### How can I perform seven years of penance?

From the sayings of Saint Boniface, bishop.

### CCCCXLVI

One three-day fast in place of thirty days, together with the recitation of 120 psalms.

For one day: fifty psalms and five *Pater nosters*.

For three days: one Psalter and fifteen *Pater nosters*.

Also, for one day, recite three times “Blessed are the undefiled” (*Beati immaculati*), six times “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*), and prostrate oneself on the ground seventy times, saying the *Pater noster* each time.

If someone does not know the psalms, then for one day let him prostrate himself on the ground one hundred times, saying each time, “Have mercy on me, O God,” and, “Forgive, Lord, my sins.”

The singing of one Mass can redeem twelve days; ten Masses, four months; twenty Masses, nine months; thirty Masses, twelve months.

For one week, let 300 psalms be recited while kneeling.

Whoever does not know the psalms and cannot fast should reckon the amount he consumes each day and give half of it as alms.

Here we have set out, in order, the differing opinions of various Fathers concerning remedies for sins or the easing of penance, leaving it to the judgment of the prudent priest to determine what will be more healthful and beneficial for the penitent soul.

## APPENDIX ONE

### 384–385. The text of the chapters begins

### On forged writings and doubtful narratives

From Book I of the *Capitularies*.

### I

(Book I of the *Capitularies*, c. 78.)

Forged writings and doubtful narratives, or those that are altogether contrary to the Catholic faith—such as the very wicked and utterly false letter which they say fell from heaven in Jerusalem—are neither to be believed nor read, but are to be burned.

### On preparing altar cloths

From the same source.

### II

(Book I of the *Capitularies*, c. 152; BURCHARD, book II, c. 115.)

Let presbyters preach throughout their parishes that women should prepare linen cloths for covering the altars.

### Concerning those who are forbidden even to propose fornication

From the Council of Neocaesarea.

### III

(Council of Neocaesarea, c. 4.)

If someone, desiring a woman, has proposed to lie with her, but his intention has not reached fulfillment, it is evident that he has been freed by God’s grace.

### A layman who dismisses his wife is to be deprived of communion

From the Council of the Apostles.

### IV

(Apostolic Canon 48.)

If a layman dismisses his own wife and marries another, or one dismissed by another man, let him be deprived of communion.

### Concerning those who abandon marital intercourse as though it were sinful

From the Council of Gangra.

### V

(Council of Gangra, c. 14.)

If any woman, leaving her own husband, wishes to depart and curses marriage, let her be anathema.

### Concerning women who use men’s clothing

From the same source.

### VI

(Council of Gangra, c. 15.)

If any woman, instead of her customary feminine dress, assumes masculine clothing, let her be anathema.

### Concerning those who despise their children under the pretext of Christianity

From the same source.

### VII

(Council of Gangra, c. 15.)

If anyone abandons his children and does not nourish them but neglects them under the pretext of continence, let him be anathematized.

### Concerning those who fast on Sunday

From the same source.

### VIII

(Council of Gangra, c. 18; BURCHARD, book XII, c. 19.)

If anyone fasts on Sunday for the sake of continence, let him be anathema.

### Concerning those who condemn people who eat meat

From the same source.

### IX

(Council of Gangra, c. 2.)

If anyone condemns, with religion and faith, a person who eats meat, apart from blood (that is, without blood), meat sacrificed to idols, and strangled meat, let him be anathema.

### That commemorations of martyrs should not be held on fast days

From the Council of Laodicea.

### X

(Council of Laodicea, c. 51; BURCHARD, book XIII, c. 10.)

It is not fitting to celebrate the anniversaries of the martyrs during Lent; rather, their holy commemoration should properly be held on Saturdays and Sundays.

### That the arrangement should remain firm if fiscal slaves have built churches

From the Council of Toledo.

### XI

(Council of Toledo III, c. 15.)

If any fiscal slaves should happen to build churches and enrich them from their poverty, let the bishop see to it that this is confirmed by royal authority at his request.

### That the possessed should be exorcised every day

From the Council of Carthage.

### XII

(Council of Carthage IV, c. 90; BURCHARD, book II, c. 223.)

Every day let the exorcists lay hands upon the possessed.

### On the food of the possessed

From the same source.

### XIII

(Council of Carthage IV, c. 92; BURCHARD, book III, c. 213.)

Let daily food be supplied by the exorcists to the possessed who sit in the house of God.

### Concerning slaves who flee to a church

From the Council of Orléans.

### XIV

(Council of Orléans I, c. 3; BURCHARD, book III, c. 192.)

If a slave has fled to a church on account of any fault [manuscript codex: cause], and has received an oath from his master concerning the fault committed, he must immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service.

If, after he has been handed back to his master upon the giving of the oath, he suffers any punishment for the same fault, let the master be regarded as excluded from communion with Catholics for his contempt of the Church and violation of faith.

### On names to be recited at Mass

From a letter of Innocent.

### XV

(Decrees of INNOCENT I, c. 2.)

Regarding the names to be recited, let this be observed: first, let the offerings of those who offer them be commended, and then let the names of those whose offerings they are be pronounced amid the sacred mysteries of the Mass.

### That fasting should properly be observed every Saturday

From the same source.

### XVI

(Decrees of INNOCENT I, c. 4.)

That one ought to fast on Saturday is demonstrated by the clearest reasoning. For if on Sunday, because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, we celebrate not only Easter but also, in every weekly cycle, repeatedly observe the image of that day; and if on Friday we fast because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not to omit Saturday, which appears to lie between the sorrow and joy of that period.

For it is certain that during those two days the apostles were both in mourning and hidden because of fear of the Jews. Therefore, just as one must fast on Friday, so one must also act on Saturday, because both days display sorrow, just as Sunday displays joy.

### Legitimate fasting may be relaxed only in the greatest necessity

From the preceding material.

### XVII

(IVO, part IV, c. 32.)

Certainly, the legitimate fasts—that is, Wednesday and Friday—are not to be relaxed except for great necessity, because on Wednesday Judas conceived the betrayal of the Lord, and on Friday the Lord was crucified.

Thus the person who does not fast on these days will appear either to betray the Savior along with the betrayer or to crucify him along with those who crucified him.

### That prisoners should be visited by the ecclesiastical officials on Sundays

From the Council of Orléans.

### XVIII

(Council of Orléans V, c. 20.)

Out of regard for mercy, we have thought it right to establish that defendants confined in prison for whatever offenses should be visited by the ecclesiastical official on Sundays, so that the necessities of those in bonds may be mercifully relieved according to the Lord’s command, and suitable food supplied from the church’s household.

### That women should not presume to teach publicly or baptize

From the same source.

### XIX

(Council of Carthage IV, cc. 99 and 100; BURCHARD, book VIII, c. 83.)

A woman, however learned and holy she may be, must not presume to teach men in an assembly. Likewise, she must not baptize.

### Those who flee to a church must not be handed over

From the same council.

### XX

(Council of Arles II, c. 30.)

Those who have fled to a church ought not to be dragged away; rather, their masters should persuade them to leave after promising pardon. If they inflict anything punitive upon those leaving the church, let them be excommunicated as enemies of the Church.

### Concerning the accused and accusers

### XXI

(BURCHARD, book II, c. 196.)

Furthermore, this must be observed in every way by the entire ecclesiastical order: no one should presume to bring an accusation against a brother in a council or synodal assembly unless he has first set down in writing, in due order and in his own hand, the charge of the accusation itself and the causes of the dispute, signed it, and presented it to the bishop or sacred synod, so that the controversies of the litigants may be resolved justly and canonically.

For, as Roman authority testifies, no one may be made a defendant or brought to judgment unless an inscription has first been formally made; and just as punishment constrains one convicted of a crime, so it constrains the accuser if he has not proved what he alleged.

### On the same matter

From the Council at Saint Medard.

### XXII

(Council of Soissons II, act 1; BURCHARD, book II, c. 197.)

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, said to his accusers:

“What is your petition, brothers?”

“We ask,” they replied, “that mercy be shown us by your fatherly authority concerning the administration of ecclesiastical orders. We were advanced to them by the late Lord Ebbo, but by your authority we have been suspended.”

Hincmar, archbishop, said:

“Do you have a written petition of complaint or request, as ecclesiastical tradition requires?”

They replied that they had no written petition in hand.

Hincmar, archbishop, said:

“The authority of ecclesiastical laws is such (2, q. 1, c. 9) that in cases concerning actions they always require a written document. Thus the person who approaches the sacred font is ordered to give his name; the person advanced to the highest priesthood is elected by a decree confirmed by the hands of all; and the ordained person is ordered to receive letters from those who ordained him.

Likewise, one who is separated from ecclesiastical fellowship because of any offense is either received or cast out by a written petition. The person who is accused, excommunicated, or reconciled is likewise accused or reconciled in writing.

And so, in other matters of this kind, writing is demanded to such an extent that, as blessed Gregory writes in his memorandum to John the defensor, drawing from Roman laws (book VI, letter 54), ‘a sentence issued without writing does not even deserve to bear the name of a sentence.’

Therefore, brothers and sons, you ought, according to ecclesiastical authority, to set forth your complaint in the form of a written petition, sign it with your own hands, and present it to the sacred synod, so that you may receive an appropriate and canonical response.”

Then the brothers themselves composed a written petition, signed their names to it, and presented it to Bishop Hincmar, who at that time was presiding over a synod together with Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, and Amalric, likewise archbishop of Tours, in the presence of the glorious King Charles.

### On the same matter

### XXIII

(Interpretation of book 9 of the Theodosian Code, *On Accusations and Inscription*.)

In both civil and criminal proceedings, a written declaration of the accusation, composed by the accuser’s own hand, must precede the accusation.

### On the same matter

### XXIV

(Interpretation of book 9 of the Theodosian Code, same title.)

Whoever brings a charge against another concerning a capital crime must not be heard by the judges before signing that he will himself undergo the same punishment that he seeks to impose upon the defendant.

### Also, from the preceding material

### XXV

(Interpretation of book 15 of the Theodosian Code, same title.)

In criminal cases or charges, no one may accuse through an agent; the person who makes the accusation must accuse in person, with an inscription made beforehand. The judges themselves are to be punished, and their office condemned, if they have believed that anyone should be subjected to investigation without a prior inscription.

### From the same source

### XXVI

(Interpretation of book 19 of the Theodosian Code, same title.)

Before the inscription, no one becomes a criminal. Once the inscription has been made in due order, the defendant is then to be accepted by the judge and handed over to custody together with the accuser.

### Concerning those who have inflicted an injury or dishonor upon a bishop

From Book VI of the *Capitularies* of King Charles, chapter 99.

### XXVII

(Book VI of the *Capitularies*, c. 98.)

If anyone inflicts an injury or unjust dishonor upon a bishop, let him pay compensation for his life, and let everything he appears to possess be joined to the Church over which he is known to preside. Let him also pay us our royal fine threefold, that is, sixty solidi; or let him be permanently assigned to service in our treasury until he is able to redeem himself threefold according to his *wergild*.

The holy Church consists in its priests. Therefore those who inflict injury or insult upon bishops or other priests must be punished with a severe penalty. For slander against priests concerns Christ, in whose place they exercise an embassy in the Church.

### What penance should be imposed upon those who kill a thief or robber?

### XXVIII

(BURCHARD, book XI, c. 60; IVO, part XIII, c. 46; also in GRATIAN, 13, q. 2, c. 32.)

If a thief or robber could be captured in the act of plunder without killing him, but is nevertheless killed—since they were created in the image of God and baptized in his name—those who killed them shall not enter the church for forty days.

Clothed in woolen garments, they shall abstain from the forbidden foods and drinks, from sexual intercourse, swords, and riding. On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, they shall eat in moderation, taking in turn some kind of legumes, vegetables, and fruits, small fish, and a moderate amount of beer.

But if truthful witnesses establish that they killed members of the devil without intending hatred, in order to free themselves and their possessions, then, according to the indulgence, they shall abstain for forty days from the church, meat, wine, and marriage, giving generously in alms.

If he is a presbyter, he shall not be deposed; nevertheless, he shall do penance throughout all the days of his life [manuscript codex: “doing penance”].

### That offerings must not be made anywhere except in the Church

### XXIX

(Council of Gangra, c. 7; Book VII of the *Capitularies*, c. 5; BURCHARD, book V, c. 144, and book XI, c. 21.)

If anyone wishes to receive or give the Church’s offerings outside the church without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.

### Against those who say that Saint Gregory, Roman pope, did not intend marriages contracted within the fourth degree to be dissolved when answering Augustine, bishop of Canterbury

Excerpt from the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II, chapter 37.

### XXX

(EXCERPTS OF EGBERT, cc. 130–131; BURCHARD, book VII, cc. 19–20.)

When Gregory, Roman pope, was asked by Augustine, bishop of the English people, to what degree of generation the faithful ought to marry, he replied by way of dispensation:

“A certain earthly law in the Roman commonwealth permits a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, to intermarry. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot arise from such a marriage. Therefore it is necessary that the fourth and sixth generations of the faithful should be permitted to marry one another. But from the second degree, which we mentioned, they must abstain altogether.”

Yet, after a long time, when Felix, bishop of Messana in Sicily, asked whether Gregory had written to Augustine that marriages contracted within the fourth degree among the English should by no means be dissolved, the most humble Father Gregory gave, among other things, the following explanation:

“Know with complete certainty that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people—your foster son, as you remember—concerning consanguineous unions, I wrote specifically for him and for the English people, who had recently come to the faith, and not as a general rule, so that they would not retreat from the good they had begun because they feared excessive severity. The whole city of Rome is therefore a witness to me in this matter.

“I did not write these instructions to them with the intention that, once they had been firmly established in the faith, they should not be separated if they were found to be within their own consanguinity, or that they should join in marriage within the line of affinity, that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, while they were still neophytes, they needed first to be taught unlawful matters very gradually, instructed by words and examples, and then, in a reasonable and faithful manner, to be excluded from such practices.

“For, according to the Apostle, who says, ‘We gave you milk for food,’ we allowed them to observe these things only for the present, not for the future, and only for the periods specified, so that the good planted while its root was still weak would not be burned up but might gain some strength and be preserved until perfection.”

For this reason I, John, have taken care to touch upon these matters, so that those who contract unlawful marriages under the pretext of a new dispensation may recognize that this most learned man did not regularly approve marriage within the fourth degree, but permitted it indulgently and only for a time.

### Concerning presbyters or deacons who are not to be deposed by one bishop

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 13.

### XXXI

(Council of Seville II, c. 13.)

We learned that a certain Fratiganus, a presbyter of the Church of Córdoba, had once been unjustly deposed by his bishop and condemned to exile even though innocent. When we restored him again to his order, we decreed this anew against such presumption: in accordance with the synodal judgment of the ancient Fathers, none of us may dare to depose any presbyter or deacon without examination by a council.

A bishop may bestow honor upon priests and ministers, but he alone cannot take it away. A presbyter cannot be condemned by one person alone, nor can one judge strip him of the privilege of his honor; rather, this must be done by the superior synodal judgment and according to what the canon has prescribed concerning them.

### That abbots should be subject to bishops and monks to abbots; also concerning wandering monks

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 15.

### XXXII

(Council of Orléans I, c. 19; BURCHARD, book I, c. 67.)

For the sake of religious humility, abbots shall remain under the authority of bishops; and if they do anything outside the Rule, they shall be corrected by the bishops. Once a year, after receiving a summons, they shall assemble at the place chosen by the bishop.

Monks, however, shall be subject to abbots with all obedience and devotion. If anyone proves disobedient through obstinacy and presumes to wander about in various places or to possess anything privately, let the abbots take away everything he has acquired, according to the Rule, for the benefit of the monastery.

Those who have wandered about shall be brought back under custody, wherever they are found, with the bishop’s assistance, as fugitives. Let that abbot know that he will be held responsible who has not disciplined such persons with regular correction, or who has received another man’s monk.

### Concerning the limits of the authority that bishops may exercise in monasteries

From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 50.

### XXXIII

(Council of Toledo IV, c. 51.)

It has been reported to this council that monks are being subjected to servile labor by episcopal command and that the rights of monasteries are being usurped through unlawful presumption, contrary to the canonical decrees, so that almost the entire monastery becomes a possession and Christ’s distinguished portion is reduced to disgraceful servitude.

Therefore we admonish those who preside over churches not to presume such things any longer. In the monastery, priests should claim for themselves only what the canons prescribe: namely, to appoint abbots over the holy way of life, establish the other offices, and collect what is done outside the Rule [*colligere*; read *corrigere*, “correct”].

If some of them presume to do what the canons forbid concerning monks, or attempt to usurp anything from the monastery’s property, the sentence of excommunication will not be lacking against those who thereafter do not withdraw from their unlawful acts.

### Concerning those whom their parents dedicated to clerical service from infancy, if they later wish to marry

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 119.

### XXXIV

(Council of Toledo I, c. 1.)

Concerning those whom their parents’ will has devoted to divine service from the earliest years of infancy, we decree that this must be observed: as soon as they have been tonsured or assigned to the ministry of readers, they must be instructed in the church’s household by the official under the bishop’s supervision.

Nevertheless, they shall retain the freedom of their own will concerning whether they choose to dedicate themselves to the clerical office. When they have completed their eighteenth year, the bishop shall inquire, in the presence of all the clergy and people, about their wish to seek marriage.

If, by God’s inspiration, they prefer the grace of chastity and promise to observe their profession of chastity without the obligation of marriage, they shall, as aspirants to the strictest life, be placed under the Lord’s light yoke. First, they shall undertake the ministry of subdeacon, which they may receive from the twentieth year after their profession has been tested.

If they have completed their twenty-fifth year blamelessly and without offense, they may be promoted to the office of deacon if the bishop confirms that they are capable of fulfilling it knowledgeably.

### That a deacon should not be ordained before twenty-five and a priest before thirty

From the Fourth Council of Arles, chapter 1.

### XXXV

Because it is known that the decrees of the ancient Fathers concerning the ordination of clerics have not been observed in full, as is appropriate, lest the priests of the Lord be wearied by the importunate and disorderly petitions of various people and compelled to transgress commands so often given, they determine that this must be observed among them: no bishop may presume to ordain a deacon before he has completed twenty-five years.

No layman may receive the honor of the episcopate or presbyterate before the conversion mentioned above or before the age of thirty.

### That penitents and bigamists are not to be ordained

From the same source, chapter 3.

### XXXVI

Let no one presume to ordain a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a woman previously married to another into the honors mentioned above.

Although these provisions are established by nearly all the canons, nevertheless, lest importunity or an unjust recommendation—as we have already said—creep in upon any priest when he is petitioned, it was necessary for the priests of the Lord now to impose a stricter rule upon themselves.

Therefore, whoever from this day onward presumes to ordain a cleric contrary to the provisions stated above must not, once this has been proved against him, celebrate Masses for an entire year. If anyone refuses to observe this and, acting against the agreement of the brothers, presumes to celebrate Masses, let him know that he is separated from the charity of all the brothers.

For it is fitting that the person who scorns to observe what the holy Fathers established for salvation should feel the severity of ecclesiastical discipline.

[**Note:** Several words are missing in this canon. According to the edition of the canons of this Council of Orléans, the following should be inserted: “Once this has been proved, let him not presume to celebrate Masses for an entire year. If anyone refuses to observe this and, acting against the agreement of the brothers, celebrates Masses,” and so forth. This was a scribal error.]

### At what age deacons should be ordained

Chapter 13.

### XXXVII

(Council of Agde, c. 16.)

A bishop must in no way entrust the blessing of the diaconate to anyone younger than twenty-five. If married young men agree to be ordained, the consent of their wives must likewise be sought, so that, after the marital chamber has been set apart and religious observance has been undertaken, they may be ordained once they have converted together.

### At what age bishops and presbyters should be consecrated

From the same source, chapter 17.

### XXXVIII

No metropolitan may presume to ordain a presbyter or bishop before the age of thirty—that is, before he has reached the age of a mature man—for fear that, because of age, they may, as has sometimes happened, be blamed for some error.

### At what age priests should be ordained

From the canons of the ancient Eastern Fathers, chapter 20.

### XXXIX

(Council of Neocaesarea, c. 11; MARTIN OF BRAGA, c. 20; BURCHARD, book II, c. 10.)

If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he must in no way be ordained a presbyter, even if he is very worthy, because the Lord himself was baptized in his thirtieth year and then began to teach. Therefore the person who is to be ordained must be kept until this legitimate age.

### On the ordination of a bishop

From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 19.

[Col. 0378B] **XL.** A pernicious custom must by no means be passed over in silence. It has disregarded the ordinances of the Fathers and thrown the entire order of the Church into confusion: some seek the priesthood through canvassing, others assume the episcopate by offering gifts; some, moreover, entangled in crimes or devoted to secular military service, have reached the dignity of the highest sacred order though unworthy. Concerning their case and removal, a ruling ought indeed to have been established. But lest the Church suffer the greatest disturbance, leaving aside what has already occurred, we believe that the following must henceforth necessarily be inserted from the canonical regulations concerning those who are not to be promoted to the priesthood:

Namely, those who have been detected in any crime; those stained by a mark of infamy; those who have confessed, through public penance, to having committed some crimes; those who are noted as having been baptized or rebaptized in heresy; those who have castrated themselves, or who are known naturally to lack something through bodily defect or deformity; those who have entered into a second marriage or contracted numerous marriages; those who have married a widow or a woman abandoned by her husband, or who have been husbands of women corrupted by others; those who have kept concubines for fornication; those subject to servile status; those who are unknown; those who are neophytes or laymen; those devoted to secular military service; those bound by obligations to a municipal curia; those ignorant of letters; those who have not yet reached thirty years of age; those who have not advanced through the ecclesiastical grades; those who seek office by canvassing; those who strive to obtain office by gifts; and those who are chosen for the priesthood by their predecessors.

Nor henceforth shall he be a priest whom neither the clergy nor the people of his own city have elected, or whom neither the authority of the metropolitan nor the concurrence of the neighboring priests has sought out. Therefore, whoever is henceforth presented for the priestly order, and who, after examination concerning the matters mentioned above, is found guilty of none of them and proves to be of commendable life and doctrine, shall, in accordance with synodal or decretal ordinances, be consecrated on a Sunday with the consent of all the clergy and citizens by all the bishops of the province, or at least by three of them, with letters of consent from those who are absent [Col. 0379A] and especially with the authority or presence of the one established in the metropolitan city.

A bishop is to be consecrated with the bishops of his province wherever the metropolitan has chosen; but the metropolitan only in the metropolitan city, with the bishops of the province assembled there. If anyone should henceforth strive, contrary to the prohibitions of the canons stated above, to aspire unworthily to the priestly rank, he shall, together with those who ordain him, be subjected to the danger of losing the dignity they have obtained.

403 **That widows are not to be veiled. From the general decrees of Pope Gelasius.**

**XLI.** *(Decrees of Gelasius, ch. 13; Book I of the Capitularies, ch. 59.)* Let no bishop presume to veil widows, since neither divine authority authorizes it nor the form of the canons prescribes it. It is therefore absolutely not to be usurped; rather, ecclesiastical support is to be provided for them in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed [Col. 0379B].

**That widows, as stated above, are not to be veiled. But if, after professing continence, they violate it by changing their purpose, let them themselves give an account before God on their own behalf. Chapter 21 of the same author.**

**XLII.** *(Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 34.)* For concerning widows, whom no one is to veil under any blessing, we have already judged it appropriate to discuss the matter at length and sufficiently. If, by their own will and with an unstable mind, they trample upon the chastity they previously professed in marriage, they will share in the danger, since, according to the Apostle, they have made their first faith void. By what satisfaction they ought to appease God is evident.

For just as, if she perhaps could not remain continent, she was in no way forbidden by the Apostle to marry, so, after deliberation with herself, she ought to preserve the pledge of chastity promised to God. We, however, ought to impose no snare upon such women; we should only set before them the exhortations of eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may give an account before God on their own behalf. For one must beware of what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies concerning their morals and actions. We pass over explaining it more plainly, lest the unstable sex appear to be not so much deterred as admonished [Col. 0379C].

**Concerning widows who sin after professing continence. The fourth Council of Carthage in Africa, held by 214 bishops, in the year 436.**

**XLIII.** *(Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 104; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 29.)* Just as the reward of chastity is good, so it must be guarded with greater observance and injunction, so that if any widows—whether still placed in their younger years or left by a husband at a mature age—devote themselves to God, cast off secular clothing, and appear in religious dress before the testimony of the bishop and the Church, but afterward pass over to secular marriage, they shall, according to the Apostle Paul, incur condemnation, because they have dared to make void the faith of chastity which they vowed to God.

Such persons, therefore, are excluded from the communion of Christians and are not to share even in meals with Christians. For if adulterous wives are liable to guilt before their husbands, how much more will widows, who vowed religious devotion to God, be branded with the crime of adultery if, through lustful pleasure, they corrupt the devotion they freely offered to God [Col. 0379D] and pass over to a second marriage?

Even if they have been seized by someone through an assault of violence, and afterward consent, through the pleasure of lust, to remain married to the ravisher or violent man, they are nevertheless to be held liable under the condemnation stated above. For concerning such women the Apostle says: “When they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made their first faith void” (1 Timothy 5).

I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have subscribed. Donatianus, of Taleptum, of the first see.

**Concerning widows who have professed continence, if they marry or are carried off. The Council of Orange, held by seventeen bishops in the year 477, title one, chapter 27.**

**XLIV.** *(First Council of Orange, ch. 27; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 43.)* A profession of preserving widowhood, made before the bishop in the secretarium, after the bishop has imposed the widow’s garment, is not to be violated. Its violator, or the woman herself who abandons such a profession, is rightly to be condemned.

**Here begin the chapters which, in the name of God, the holy synod held in the city of Toledo, chapter 10.**

**XLV.** *(Third Council of Toledo, ch. 10; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 44.)* In view of the protection of chastity—which ought especially to advance through the encouragement of the council—and with the consent of our glorious lord King Reccared, this holy council affirms that widows who wish to preserve chastity are not to be compelled by any force to enter a second marriage.

But if, before professing continence, they choose to marry, let them marry those whom they freely wish to have as husbands. The same condition shall apply to virgins: they are not to be compelled to accept husbands against the will of their parents or their own will. If anyone hinders the purpose of chastity of a widow or virgin, let him be regarded as excluded from holy communion and from the thresholds of the church [Col. 0380C].

406 **Concerning sacred men and women who transgress their religious commitment. The Council of Toledo.**

**XLVI.** *(Sixth Council of Toledo, ch. 6; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 14.)* The course from the will is easy, and nature imitates vices. Therefore, whoever, man or woman, has once assumed religious dress, whether voluntarily; or any man devoted to the Church’s choir, or woman assigned to a monastery of girls—if either sex violates the commitment, the offender is to be compelled unwillingly to return to it: the man is to be tonsured [Col. 0380D], and the girl is to enter the monastery.

But if, under any protection, they wish to remain deserters, they are to be held exiled from the company of Christians by priestly judgment, so that no place in common remains for them. The universal synod long ago also established that widows who abandon their professions or their dress are to be condemned by the judgment stated above.

**That widows or virgins who have professed continence are not to marry. Likewise, from the letter of the same Pope Gelasius to the bishops of Sicily.**

**XLVII.** *(Symmachus, Letter 5, ch. 5; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 46.)* We do not permit widows to pass over to marriage if they have remained for a long period in a religious commitment. Likewise, we forbid virgins to marry when it is established that they have spent many years of their lives in monasteries [Col. 0381A].

**Concerning those who have taken into marriage women veiled and consecrated to God. Chapter 23.**

**XLVIII.** *(Council of Tribur, ch. 23; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 38.)* If anyone marries a woman consecrated with the sacred veil and afterward, following her dedication to God, enters into incestuous and sacrilegious relations with her, then, as is read in the constitutions of Pope Gelasius, chapter 20, it is immediately right that he be expelled from sacred communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance.

Nevertheless, if he repents, a viaticum is not to be denied to those departing from this world. At the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 16, those who commit this act are to be excommunicated. Mercy is to be granted to those who confess, by the authority of the bishop.

[Col. 0381B] In the letter of Pope Siricius, chapter 6, it was judged that women veiled and consecrated to God who, having cast aside their religious purpose, secretly joined themselves through sacrilegious contact, or publicly and openly bore children from illicit embraces, are to be expelled from the company of monasteries and from the assemblies of churches, so that, shut away in prisons, they may mourn such an enormous crime with continual lamentation.

Therefore, by the word of the Lord and by canonical authority, we decree in this holy synod that they be completely separated and bound by oath never again to dwell under one roof, nor to enjoy familiar conversation, except in church and in public, nor to have any communion with one another from which a suspicion of seductive desire or a scandal arising from lustful conduct could justly emerge. If anything must also be divided between them, let them divide it, and let each make provision for his or her own share [Col. 0381C].

**Concerning veiled widows. Of Pope Gelasius.**

**XLIX.** *(Council of Tribur, ch. 25; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 36.)* Let no bishop presume to veil widows, as was established in the decrees of Gelasius, chapter 13, since neither divine authority nor the form of the canons prescribes it. But if a woman has professed continence by her own will, as is read in chapter 21 of the same Gelasius, let her intention give an account on her own behalf before God. For just as, according to the Apostle, if she could not remain continent she was in no way forbidden to marry, so, after deliberation with herself, she ought to preserve the pledge of chastity promised to God.

Supported by the authority of this paternal judgment, we establish and freely decree in this holy assembly that if a woman has voluntarily imposed a veil upon herself, even though it was not consecrated, and has offered an oblation to God in the church among veiled women, then, whether she wishes it or not, she must henceforth retain the habit of sanctity, even if she wishes to confirm by oath that she imposed the veil upon herself on such terms and for such a purpose that she would not afterward be able to remove it [Col. 0381D].

**Likewise concerning veiled widows. From the African council, chapter 89.**

**L.** A widow who has placed a sacred veil upon her head, prayed in church among the other veiled women, and offered an oblation with them has professed that she will remain in the same habit. Having pledged never to remove the veil of religion, she must not presume to depart from religious observance. We wish your holiness good health in Christ [Col. 0382A].

**Concerning a man who entered a monastery against his wife’s will and has already been tonsured, and must be returned without exception. From the Register, Part I, chapter 180, to Adria, notary of Palermo.**

**LI.** *(St. Gregory, Book IX, indiction 4, Letter 44; Burchard, Book IX, ch. 48.)* Agathosa, the bearer of this letter, has complained that her husband was converted to the monastery of the abbot Urbici against her will [409]. Since this undoubtedly pertains to the fault and disrepute of that same abbot, we command Your Experience to investigate the matter carefully, lest perhaps he was converted with her consent, or she herself promised to change her way of life.

If you discover that this is so, see to it that he remains in the monastery and compel her, as she promised, to change [Col. 0382B]. But if none of these circumstances exists, and if you find that the aforesaid woman has not committed some crime of fornication on account of which a man is permitted to leave his wife, you must without excuse return her husband to her—or, if he has already been tonsured, return him to her entirely—lest his conversion become an occasion of perdition for the wife left in the world.

For although secular law prescribes that, for the sake of religious conversion, a marriage may be dissolved even against the will of one party, divine law does not permit this. For, except on account of fornication, it grants a man no permission whatsoever to leave his wife. Since, after the union of marriage has made a man and woman one body, one part cannot be converted while the other remains in the world.

[Col. 0382C] **That a bishop must relinquish his dignity if he had a concubine while he was established in sacred orders. From a letter of Saint Gregory, chapter 43.**

**LII.** *(St. Gregory, Book II, indiction 11, Letter 83; Burchard, Book I, ch. 195.)* He writes to Andrew, bishop of Tarentum, saying:

“Whoever, conscious of his guilt, strives to appease the eternal Judge by worthy penance will look upon the tribunal of the eternal Judge without fear. We have learned with manifest certainty that you had a concubine [410], concerning whom a contrary suspicion has also arisen in the minds of some. But because judgment ought not to be absolute in matters that are uncertain, we have chosen to entrust this matter to your conscience.

Therefore, if you recall that, while established in sacred orders, you were defiled by intercourse with her, then, having laid aside the dignity of the priesthood, do not presume in any way to approach the exercise of ministry [Col. 0382D]. Know that you minister at the peril of your soul and that you will undoubtedly render an account to our God if, conscious of this crime, you wish to remain in the order you occupy while concealing the truth.”

**Concerning ravishers of virgins and widows. Likewise concerning abbeys that possess the right of election and those that do not.**

**LIII.** In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 952, in the ninth indiction, it was established at Frankfurt by the most glorious King Otto, in the fifteenth year of his reign, with the consent of the bishops, counts, and many other faithful men, on the authority of the holy canons and Fathers and with the constitutions of the preceding kings set forth before them, that no oppression or abduction of virgins or widows be carried out by any men [Col. 0383A].

Those who abduct them under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the ravishers, are to be punished: if they are clerics, they are to fall from their own rank; if laymen, they are to be anathematized; and the ravishers are to remain without hope of marriage. If afterward they presume to unite themselves, both parties are to be anathematized.

It was likewise enacted by the aforesaid king that no abbey which possesses the right of election in its own capacity may be given either to a monastery or to anyone as private property. Those, however, which lack the right of election may, by the king’s donation and privilege, be transferred to another monastery that remains under his protection [411].

**What it means to minister to Christ.**

**LIV.** *(St. Augustine, Tractate 51 on John.)* “If anyone ministers to me, let him follow me.” With what fruit, what reward, what recompense? “And where I am,” he says, “there my minister will be also.” Let him be loved freely, so that the price of the work by which one ministers to him may be to be with him. For where can one be well without him, or when could one be ill with him?

Listen more clearly: “If anyone ministers to me, my Father will honor him.” With what honor, except that he may be with his Son? For what does he say above? “Where I am, there my minister will be also.” He shows that this is what he means when he says, “My Father will honor him.” For what greater honor can one adopted receive than to be where the Only-Begotten is—not made equal to the divinity, but joined to eternity?

But what it means to minister to Christ, for which work so great a reward is promised, we ought rather to investigate. For if we should think that ministering to Christ means preparing the things necessary for his body, cooking or setting food before him at dinner, or giving him a cup and mixing his drink, those who were able to have him present in the body did this, such as Martha and Mary, when Lazarus was one of those reclining at table.

But in this way even Judas, the lost man, ministered to Christ. For he himself also kept the money box.
