And although he wickedly stole from what was put into it, necessities were nevertheless prepared through him as well [412]. Hence the passage in which, when the Lord said to him, “What you are doing, do quickly,” some thought that he had ordered him to prepare necessities for the feast day or to give something to the needy.

The Lord would therefore in no way speak of such ministers when he said, “Where I am, there my minister will be also. If anyone ministers to me, my Father will honor him,” since we see Judas, who ministered in such ways, rejected rather than honored.

Why, then, do we seek elsewhere what it means to minister to Christ, instead of recognizing it in these very words? For when he said, “If anyone ministers to me, let him follow me,” he wished this to be understood as though he had said: “If anyone does not follow me, he does not minister to me.” Those, therefore, minister to Jesus Christ who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. This is what “Let him follow me” means. They walk in his ways, not their own. As it is written elsewhere: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked.”

If he gives bread to the hungry, he ought also to do so from mercy, not boastfulness—“with the left hand unaware of what the right hand is doing”—that is, so that the intention of self-seeking may be removed from the work of charity. Whoever ministers in this way ministers to Christ, and rightly it will be said to him: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.”

He should perform not only works pertaining to bodily mercy, but every good work for Christ’s sake. Then indeed they will be good, because Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The minister serves Christ even unto that great work of charity which consists in laying down one’s life for the brethren [in Augustine: “to everyone who believes. A minister of Christ is, even unto”]; for of this also he will say to his members [in Augustine: “to lay down. For this is also to lay down one’s life for Christ, because he too, for his members ...”; Col. 0384B]: “When you did it for these, you did it for me.”

Indeed, concerning such a work he deigned both to make himself a minister and to call himself one, when he said: “The Son of Man did not come to be ministered to, but to minister, and to lay down his life for many.” Therefore each person is Christ’s minister in the same way that Christ is a minister. The Father will honor the one who ministers to Christ with that great honor: that he may be with his Son, and that his happiness may never fail.

When, therefore, you hear, brothers, the Lord saying, “Where I am, there my minister will be also,” do not think only of good bishops and clerics. You too, according to your capacity, minister to Christ by living well, giving alms, and preaching his name and teaching to those to whom you can.

Thus each head of a household may understand by this name that, for Christ’s sake and for eternal life, he ought to show fatherly affection toward his entire household: admonishing, teaching, exhorting, correcting, showing kindness, and exercising discipline. In this way, in his own house, he fulfills an ecclesiastical and, in a certain sense, episcopal office, ministering to Christ so that he may be with him eternally.

Many from among you also minister in that greatest ministry of suffering: many bishops, clerics, young men and virgins, old men together with the young. Many married men and women, many fathers and mothers of families, while ministering to Christ, have laid down their lives in his martyrdom and, when the Father honored them, received glorious crowns [Col. 0384C].

414 **Concerning clerics who seek the monastic commitment. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 50.**

**LV.** *(Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 50; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 21.)* Clerics who seek the monastic commitment and desire to follow a better life ought to be granted free entry by the bishop into monasteries. Their purpose must not be hindered when they strive to pass over to the desire for contemplation [Note: [Col. 0383D] See the Council of Zaragoza, chapter 6.].

**Decree concerning widows. From a letter of blessed Pope Gregory sent to Archbishop Boniface, in which, among other matters, the following is read:**

**LVI.** *(Additions IV, ch. 65; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 45; Ivo, Part VII, ch. 63.)* Concerning widows who depart from their commitment to widowhood, about whom your affection, dearest brother, wished to consult us, I believe you know that they were long ago condemned by Saint Paul and by many holy Fathers unless they convert. We likewise judge, by apostolic authority, that they are to be condemned and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the church until they obey their bishops and return, whether unwillingly or willingly, to the good work they began [Col. 0385A].

Concerning veiled virgins who have gone astray, we have the following decree from our predecessor of holy memory, Innocent:

“Those who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always pretended to remain in the virginal commitment—although they have not been veiled—if they marry, must perform penance for some period, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract of good faith is ordinarily dissolved in no way, how much more cannot this promise, which she made with God, be dissolved without bondage,” and so forth.

For if virgins not yet veiled are punished with public penance in this manner and excluded from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, how much more must widows, who possess more advanced age and more mature wisdom and judgment, who have often associated with men, who have permitted themselves to be veiled, assumed the religious habit, and finally apostatized and returned to their former vomit, be expelled by us, by all the faithful, and by the men of our order from the thresholds of the church and from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, and be handed over to prisons, in the manner that, according to the Apostle Paul, such a person is handed over to Satan so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord?

For concerning such women the Lord also speaks through Moses: “Remove the evil from your midst.” Concerning them the Prophet says: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Psalm 57).

Concerning such women and those like them, and those who consent to them—for not only those who do such things but also those who consent are guilty—the Lord speaks through that same prophet David, saying: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49), and many similar things.

Such persons, therefore, are unmistakably shown to be adulteresses, because, having abandoned their immortal bridegroom, they have returned like dogs to their own vomit, becoming apostates, polluting themselves with unlawful and sacrilegious contact, and clinging to mortal men.

Moreover, according to the Apostle Paul, because they abandoned their commitment to widowhood, dared to break the faith they had pledged with God, and violated their first faith, they are to be condemned by us, by you, and by the remaining men of our order—namely, by each one in his own diocese. As stated above, they are to be expelled from the thresholds of the church and from the company of the faithful until satisfaction [Col. 0385D].

We command all the faithful to abstain entirely from the companionship and association of such women. It has also seemed good to us that, so long as they persist in that detestable, unlawful, and sacrilegious carnal union, no Christian—except those whom the bishop, with a specific purpose of correction, has ordered—may communicate with them in any way or approach the house [Col. 0386A] in which they are. No faithful person may eat with them, as the Apostle already mentioned has commanded. If anyone among them should presume to attempt or dare anything of this kind, let him be struck with the same sentence of excommunication as they.

**Concerning a widow who temporarily imposed a veil upon herself under the pretext of religion. Chapter 5.**

**LVII.** *(Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 47.)* Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother Adalwin, archbishop of the holy Church of Salzburg:

Concerning the woman about whom you asked, who, after her husband’s death, placed the sacred veil upon her head and pretended under that veil to be a religious woman, but afterward returned to marriage, it seems good that she should do penance for her wicked deception and return to what she promised and began in the sacred ministry [Col. 0386B], since she wished through hypocrisy to disturb ecclesiastical discipline and did not remain lawfully in her vow [417].

For if we agree that everyone may counterfeit all ecclesiastical sacraments as he wishes, so that they do not truly take place, the entire ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion, the rights of the Catholic faith do not stand, and the sacred canons are not rightly observed.

For what did it profit Simon Magus to receive sacred baptism deceitfully and pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when his fraud was exposed through the Apostle and what would befall him was declared? For he says: “May your money perish with you. Your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God that perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8).

Therefore, unless such people repent, we judge that they must be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished [Col. 0386C].

**Concerning men and widows or virgins doing penance who, after turning aside, become laypeople, change their clothing, or enter marriage. The Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 55.**

**LVIII.** *(Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 27.)* Whoever among secular people, after receiving penance, tonsured himself and then, transgressing again, became a layman is to be seized by his bishop and recalled to the penance from which he withdrew. If some are irrevocably committed to penance and do not return even when admonished, they are truly to be condemned before the Church as apostates by the sentence of anathema [Col. 0386D].

The same applies to those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, after their parents’ death, voluntarily devoted themselves to religion, but afterward assumed secular dress. Once seized by a priest, they are to be recalled to religious observance after first performing penance. If they cannot return, they are truly to be subjected to the sentence of anathema as apostates.

This rule is also to be observed regarding sacred widows and virgins and women doing penance who have put on the habit of a religious woman and afterward either changed their clothing or passed over to marriage [418].

**Concerning the distinction between secular and religious widows. Likewise from the same council, chapter 56.**

**LIX.** There are two kinds of widows: secular and religious. Secular widows are those who, while still intending to marry, have not removed their lay clothing. Religious widows are those who, having already changed their secular dress, have appeared in religious attire before a priest or the Church. If these pass over to marriage, they will not be without condemnation, according to the Apostle, because, having first vowed themselves to God, they afterward abandoned their commitment to chastity.

**She who has cast off religious clothing is to be compelled to return to the habit and confined in a monastery. From Gregory’s Register, to Vitalian, bishop of Siponto.**

**LX.** *(St. Gregory, Book VII, indiction 1, Letter 9; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 49.)* If you had known that, as a bishop, you ought to be a guardian of the religious habit, you would not, while placed there, have permitted the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, of glorious memory, to return to secular dress after casting off her religious garments, nor would you have sent us a perverse letter [Col. 0387B].

But because you are weighed down by excessive negligence and sluggishness, an unlawful act has presently been committed there with impunity, to your disgrace. For, as we have said, if you had been vigilant, the punishment of the most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her fault did.

Since you are so dull and so negligent that, unless you have experienced canonical correction upon yourself, you do not know how to preserve strictness and discipline in others, we shall show, at a suitable time, if it pleases the Lord, how vigilant you ought to be [variant: “we shall demonstrate”].

Therefore, upon receiving this present letter, awaken and, once roused, at least carry out what, oppressed by sloth, you have delayed until now. Let it be your urgent task to seize the aforesaid woman together with Sergius the defensor, and immediately not only to restore her, without any excuse, to the habit she has wickedly despised, but also to thrust her into a monastery where she can be kept under the strictest custody. Show such vigilance concerning her that, through your strictness, she may understand how wicked was the act she committed [Col. 0387C].

If any layman should attempt, by some stratagem, to resist you in this matter—which we do not believe—suspend him from participation in the most holy [variant: “most sacred”] communion, and hasten to report it to us, so that, since he did not recognize how execrable was the deed he presumed to commit by his own reflection, he may learn it through the manner of his correction.

In all these matters, show yourself so cautious and diligently vigilant that your negligence does not double your fault, but that your vigilance may at least somewhat lessen it [Col. 0387D].

420 **Concerning the same matter. Gregory to our defensor Sergius.**

**LXI.** *(St. Gregory, Book VII, indiction 1, Letter 10.)* If you were a man, or possessed any strictness, you ought to have been so much a guardian of regular discipline that you would correct by punishment the things unlawfully committed there before news of them reached us.

But while excessive folly makes you negligent, we are offended not only by those matters but are also provoked to avenge your sluggishness. Therefore, setting aside every delay and every excuse, hasten, together with our brother and fellow bishop Vitalian, to seize the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, of glorious memory. Having cast off the religious garments she had voluntarily assumed, she has disfigured herself with secular clothing [Col. 0388A]. Restore her again to the religious habit and send her to a monastery where she may be kept under the strictest custody. Do not permit her custody to be relaxed in any way until you receive another letter from us.

For if you are negligent or slow in this matter in any way, know that punishment will be inflicted upon you with the utmost severity, so that, as punishment reveals it, you may learn what you do not know from yourself. For, as we have said, if you possessed human intelligence, you ought already to have understood and carried out—with punishment—the things you are now ordered to do.

**Concerning women who have changed religious clothing in their own homes and afterward chosen marriage: what is to be done. The Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 57.**

**LXII.** *(Book VII of the Capitularies, ch. 257; Burchard, Book VIII, ch. 48.)* Concerning widows and girls who have changed the habit of religion in their own homes, whether by the action of their parents or by themselves: if afterward they believe they should enter marriage contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the commands of the canons, let both parties be held suspended from communion until they amend what they have unlawfully done. If they neglect to amend it, let them be separated forever from communion and from the table of all Christians [Note: [Col. 0387] This is not found among the canons of the councils of Toledo.].

**That ecclesiastical custom is to be held as law. Written by our holy Father Basil in chapter 27 of his sermons to blessed Amphilochius concerning the Holy Spirit.**

[Col. 0388C] **LXIII.** *(Burchard, Book III, ch. 127.)* We have received some ecclesiastical institutions from the Scriptures and others from apostolic tradition, confirmed through successive ministers. Who among those even slightly acquainted with the sacred Scriptures would hesitate that equal authority and the same pious effect belong to both?

For if we attempt to regard as worthless the customs of the Church handed down by the Fathers without written documents, those who clearly see how much religion would suffer by such contempt will recognize the danger. To begin with, what writing taught the faithful to mark themselves with the sign of the saving cross? What writing commended the many words of prayer and consecration spoken over the bread and the cup? For we say in the mysteries not only what is contained in the Gospel or what the Apostle has handed down in secret, but we also add many other things, as though they belonged to one great whole and contributed to the completion of the mysteries.

What written text prescribed that we pray facing the East? We bless the baptismal font and the oil of anointing. To this is added the fact that we immerse those whom we baptize three times, anoint them with oil, and instruct them by words to renounce Satan and his angels.

From where, then, do these and many other practices of the same kind come, unless from a silent and mystical tradition handed down by the Fathers and observed in the mysteries according to ecclesiastical custom with reverent diligence—more carefully preserved in silence than published in writing? [Col. 0388D]

**Likewise, chapter 29.**
### LXIV. (BASIL, in the letter to Amphilochius, chapters 27 and 29) [Col. 0389A]

My day would fail me if I undertook to explain each of the Church’s customs individually. What more is there to say? Who taught us in writing the very confession of faith by which we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, except that the piety of faith follows the tradition of baptism, and that, just as we are baptized, so also we believe? Which passage of Scripture commanded us to pray standing on feast days, but not in this way on weekdays? Therefore, if the Church’s practice piously preserves so many things handed down without writing through a mystical observance, I consider it not absurd, but rather apostolic, also to hold firmly to traditions that have not been written.

“I commend you,” says the Apostle, “because you remember me in everything and hold the traditions as I handed them on to you.” And again: “You hold the traditions which you received, whether through word or through letter.” Therefore, although every word is to stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses, we have preferred to rely on different examples, so that it may become more convincingly clear to the learned that the observance of ecclesiastical custom, handed down from our forebears, must be held as law.

## 423 APPENDIX II

[Col. 0389]

The first eighteen chapters of this second appendix, which survive in the Helmstedt edition, are entirely the same as the first twenty-eight chapters of the first appendix, which we published from an old Paris manuscript, except for chapter nine, which is absent from the Helmstedt edition and was added from the Paris manuscript. Thus only twenty-seven of those twenty-eight chapters belong to this second appendix; for that reason we have wished to omit them here, lest there be a useless repetition. We shall, however, faithfully reproduce the Helmstedt edition, except that, insofar as possible, we shall note where the chapters were taken from—a practice not followed in the Helmstedt edition. We shall also present within brackets the variant readings that are of some importance.

## 424 HERE BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE CHAPTERS

[Col. 0389B]

### That a priest must not be harassed. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8.

#### XXVIII

It has been reported to the holy synod that very frequent and serious harassments are inflicted upon Christ’s priests and upon other clerics of lower rank by wicked Christians. Therefore the holy council has decided, so that such things may not occur thereafter, to strike them with a spiritual weapon: if anyone inflicts any injury or accusation upon a cleric, he is to be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church until he has made worthy satisfaction.

#### XXIX

From the Council of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0389D] This chapter is absent from our manuscript.]

### Concerning the departure of clerics.

#### XXX

Since we are confident that you direct your brotherhood according to the statutes of the canons and the rigor of discipline, we have considered it necessary to entrust you with investigating this matter: lest freeborn clerics who possess a more capable and sharper intellect cross over to places renowned for superior knowledge and learning, whether for the sake of study [or enrichment], or in order to seek what is useful for the Church and for themselves [unless the Church’s advantage has been secured].

The envy of bishops often prevents this, when they oppose to such men chapter 20 of the Council of Chalcedon, where it is said that clerics serving in one church ought not to be appointed in the church of another city, while through envious obscurity they suppress what follows, where those who have moved to another church out of necessity are excepted.

A man who is constrained by hunger is surely pressed by great necessity; and he who is oppressed by the injury of ignorance needs to be refreshed by the teaching of knowledge. Finally, the bishop must carefully distinguish between a fugitive and a student, so that the former may not find a place in which to hide, while the latter is not prevented from changing his place for the better and from going “from strength to strength” [Col. 0390B], but is raised up by the assistance of charity, which never fails. Therefore, if until now they have piously and justly run the straight course along the path of life, we have judged that permission to seek more perfect places for the sake of religion ought not to be denied them.

### Concerning hatred toward brothers.

#### XXXI

If anyone has unjust hatred toward his brother, God separates him from His kingdom and removes him from heaven; for hatred is neither removed from him by suffering, nor expiated by martyrdom, nor erased by the shedding of blood. To slander another out of hatred, for the sake of one’s own advantage, is more contrary to nature than death, pain, or other evils of this kind.

### Saint Gregory, and likewise Augustine, on hatred.

#### XXXII

A great and wondrous saying: how a man’s love for his own soul can be directed toward its destruction, and hatred toward its preservation. If you love wrongly, then you have hated. If you hate rightly, then you have loved. Happy are those who hate in order to guard, lest they lose through loving.

### Pope Gregory on fallen priests.

#### XXXIII (GREGORY THE GREAT, book I, letter 42)

Concerning fallen priests, or anyone from the clergy, we wish this to be observed: you must not become involved in their possessions through any contamination. Instead, seek the poorest regular monasteries, which know how to live according to God, and hand over the fallen to those monasteries for penance, so that the possessions of the fallen may be administered in the place where they are assigned to perform penance [variant: “may make progress”]. In this way those who take care of their correction may receive support from their possessions. But if they have parents, their possessions are to be given to their legitimate parents, provided nevertheless that the maintenance of those who have been assigned to penance is adequately supplied.

[Col. 0391A] If any priests or laymen [deacons], monks, clerics, or any others from the ecclesiastical household should fall, we wish them to be assigned to penance, but their possessions are not to be withdrawn as ecclesiastical property [or: “not withdrawn from ecclesiastical jurisdiction”]. They are nevertheless to receive enough for their own use to sustain them in performing penance, lest, if they are stripped, they become burdensome to the places to which they have been assigned. If they have parents who possess property, their possessions are to be handed over to those parents, so that they may be preserved in the Church [variant: “under the Church’s jurisdiction”].

(The same, book IV, indiction 13, letter 31.) No lord is to inflict violence upon priests through secular power; rather, with excellent consideration, because they are servants of Him whose servants they are, he should rule them in such a way that he also shows them the reverence they deserve. For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and sometimes angels. Through Moses it is said concerning the man who is to be brought to judgment: “Bring him before the gods,” that is, before the priests. And again: “You shall not slander the gods” (Exodus 22), that is, the priests. The prophet says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

Why, then, is it surprising if your piety deigns to honor those whom God Himself, in granting them honor in His utterance, calls either angels or gods? Ecclesiastical history testifies that when accusations against bishops were brought before the emperor Constantine of blessed memory, he accepted the written accusations. Then, summoning the bishops who had been accused, he burned the writings he had received in their presence, saying: “You are gods, appointed by the true God. Go and settle your cases among yourselves, because it is not fitting for us to judge gods.” In ancient times there were rulers in the commonwealth who, although they did not know the true God, worshiped gods of wood and stone; nevertheless, they granted the greatest honor to their priests.

For this reason Gregory deposed no priest except for crimes; rather, according to the seriousness of their offenses, he deprived them of communion in a lenient manner.

Whenever, therefore, there was something to be examined concerning the crimes of priests, Gregory, with the greatest strictness and great caution, seeking the details of each case, issued his judgment with greater reluctance than readiness. He said: “While all matters require the anxious investigation of truth, those matters which concern the removal of priests from their ranks must be weighed with particular strictness, since in them an attempt is made not merely against men established in humble office, but, in a certain sense, against a divine blessing. For it is sufficiently grave and unbecoming that, in a doubtful matter, a definite judgment should be pronounced.”

### That the priests of the Lord must not be compelled to swear, as the common people are accustomed to do. Pope Cornelius to Rufus, bishop of the East.

#### XXXIV (POPE CORNELIUS, letter 2; BURCHARD, book I, chapter 193)

We have learned that an oath has hitherto been required from supreme priests and others for the sake of right faith, but we have not found that they swore voluntarily. Therefore the holy Apostle James speaks while most earnestly forbidding oaths, saying: “But above all things, my brothers . . . do not swear” (James 5). In these words, dearest brothers, the Lord Himself forbids swearing; that is, an oath ought not to be imposed, except for the sake of right faith.

All the apostles especially forbid oaths; so do the holy men, our predecessors, who presided over this holy universal and apostolic Church before us; and so do the prophets and the other holy teachers scattered throughout the world to preach.

### Witnesses in an ecclesiastical dispute.

#### XXXV

Every dispute that arises concerning ecclesiastical matters is to be settled according to divine law on the evidence of two or three witnesses, since the Lord says: “One person must not stand against another, but every word must stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18). The same applies to the separation of married persons: three truthful men are to testify to it if seven cannot be found.

### Concerning a physician who treated badly.

#### XXXVI

A physician, treating an infant carelessly, caused him to become lame. It was asked whether such a man could merit a rank in the clergy. It was judged that this kind of disability, if he displayed other good attainments, ought not to prevent him from receiving a rank.

### Concerning the tonsure of clerics.

#### XXXVII (Council of Tribur, chapter 27; BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 97)

If a cleric has received the tonsure after dismissing his wife, and if he is without rank and has not been handed over by his parents to any monastery, then, if he is permitted to have a wife, he must be tonsured again, and he must not dare to neglect the tonsure throughout his life. But one whom his parents have handed over, who reads in the Church, may neither marry nor leave the monastery. If he departs, he is to be brought back. If he abandons the tonsure, he is to be tonsured again. If he takes a wife, he must be compelled to dismiss her.

### Concerning girls made nuns.

#### XXXVIII (Council of Tribur, chapter 24; BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 98)

If a girl, before completing twelve years of age, voluntarily takes the sacred veil for herself, her parents or guardians may immediately invalidate what she has done, if they wish. But if they allow a year and a day to pass without objecting, thereafter neither they nor she will be able to change this. Moreover, if a young woman or young man, at a more mature age, chooses to serve God, the parents have no power to forbid it.

### Concerning laymen who seize the property of dying priests.

#### XXXIX [Note: [Col. 0391D] See above, book II, chapter 59.]

It has also been reported to the holy synod that certain laymen act improperly toward their priests, claiming shares in the property of dying priests just as they do in the property of their peasants. We therefore forbid this from happening any longer. Just as priests have been made free to receive their rank and perform the divine office, so nothing is to be demanded from them except the service of God. They are not to appropriate anything from the priests’ personal property; rather, the priests may dispose of two-thirds as they wish. The third part, according to the commands of the canons, they are to leave to the churches which they serve.

### Concerning the holding and tithes.

#### XL (Council of Worms, chapter 50; book I of the Capitularies, chapter 91; BURCHARD, book III, chapter 52)

It has likewise been decreed in the Capitularies that from a church holding, or from tithes, or from offerings, or from houses or courtyards situated beside the church, they are to perform no service other than ecclesiastical service. If they possess anything beyond this, they are to render service from it to their lords.

### That no one from a servile condition is to be promoted to the clergy.

#### XLI [Note: [Col. 0393D] See above, book I, chapter 407.]

No one from a servile condition is to be promoted to the sacred orders unless he has first obtained legitimate freedom from his own masters. The charter of this freedom is to be read publicly in the ambo before his ordination; and if no one objects, he is to be duly consecrated. But if afterward they fall from their rank, they are to return to the condition in which they were before receiving that rank.

### Concerning ecclesiastical goods. From a canonical letter.

#### XLII

No bishop, priest, deacon, or even cleric may have the power to sell church estates, nor may he give them to any of his relatives. Whoever does so must, with all speed, restore the price, and the estates must return to the sacred places to which they belong. But if, disregarding this provision, anyone should presume to do so, he must leave his own possessions in that church and be cast out himself, since divine reason requires that those who receive churches to govern them should receive them not to scatter but to preserve.

In the same way, they are to have no power to alienate or sell anything by any means, nor to give it to deputies without the consent of their bishop, nor to leave it to their children. Whoever presumes to do so, as we have decreed above, if he has property of his own, must restore an equal amount. If he has none, he is to be stripped of everything and expelled. The possessions themselves, however, are to return to the church whose property they are.

### Concerning the patrimony of clerics. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 21.

#### XLIII [Note: [Col. 0393D] See above, book I, chapter 219.]

It must be investigated whether, when a priest who had no patrimony was advanced to ecclesiastical order, he afterward acquired estates, and to whose right they belong—whether they ought to belong to the Church. For every priest must leave to the Church the property that he acquires after the day of his consecration. But if he purchases property in another person’s name and builds structures there, or places there anything belonging to the Church for God, this evil is committed contrary to the decrees of the canons, because it is sacrilege, and he is recognized as being guilty of the same crime as . . . the thief who stole sacred offerings.

### Concerning women who have exchanged their clothing for religious dress in their own homes, and who afterward choose sexual intercourse: what is to be done.

#### XLIV (Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 257; BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 48)

Concerning widows and girls who have exchanged their clothing for the religious habit in their own homes, whether from the action of their parents or on their own initiative [Note: [Col. 0394D] See above in Appendix I, chapter 62], and who afterward believe that they should enter marriages contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the commands of the canons: both parties are to be held suspended from communion until they correct what they have unlawfully done. But if they neglect to correct it, they are to be separated forever from communion and from the fellowship of all Christians.

### Concerning widows. A letter of blessed Pope Gregory sent to Boniface, archbishop, in which the following decree is read among other things.

#### XLV (BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 45)

Concerning widows who depart from their professed state of widowhood, about whom your affection, dearest brother, wished to consult us, I believe you know that they were long ago condemned by Saint Paul and by many holy Fathers unless they convert. We likewise judge, by apostolic authority, that they must be condemned and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the Church until they obey their bishops and return, willingly or unwillingly, to the ban they began [variant: “the good course”] [Note: [Col. 0394D] See above in Appendix I, chapter 56].

### Concerning virgins who have not been veiled.

#### XLVI (BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 45)

We have the following decree from our predecessor of holy memory, Innocent:

“But those who, although not yet covered with the sacred veil, have always professed that they remain in their virginal state: if they marry, even though they have not been veiled, they must perform penance, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved by no means, how much more must this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment.”

And further [etc.]. For if virgins who have not yet been veiled are punished by public penance in this manner and excluded from the gathering of the faithful until satisfaction, how much more ought widows—who are of a more mature age and possess greater maturity of wisdom and judgment, who have often associated with men, who have allowed themselves to be veiled and have assumed the religious habit, yet have apostatized and returned to a worse vow [variant: “their former vomit”]—to be expelled by us and by all the faithful from the thresholds of the Church and from the gathering of the faithful until satisfaction, and handed over to prison, so that, according to blessed Paul, they may be handed over to Satan, “so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

Concerning such women the Lord also speaks through Moses, saying: “Remove the evil from your midst.” Concerning them the prophet says: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Psalm 57). Concerning such women, and those like them and those who consent to them—for not only those who commit acts are guilty, but also those who consent to the perpetrators—the Lord speaks through the same prophet David, saying: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49). And there are many other passages of the same kind.

Such persons are therefore plainly shown to be adulteresses, since [variant: “because”], having abandoned their immortal bridegroom, they have returned like dogs to their own vomit and, having become apostates, defile themselves with unlawful and sacrilegious contamination by attaching themselves to mortal men. They must also be condemned by us, according to the same Apostle Paul, because they have . . . abandoned the profession of widowhood, dared to break the faith which they pledged to God, and violated their first faith. They must likewise be expelled by you and by the other men of our order—each from his own diocese—from the thresholds of the Church and from the gathering of the faithful until satisfaction, as was said above [Note: [Col. 0395] See above in Appendix I, chapters 47–56].

### That clerics must not associate with the company of widows. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 102.

[Col. 0395B]

#### XLVII (Council of Carthage I, chapter 102; BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 55)

The bishop, or the priest who presides over the parish, is liable to guilt if younger widows or religious women are placed in the company of clerics for the sake of supporting their present life.

### Concerning widows supported by the stipends of the Church. Chapter 103.

#### XLVIII (Ibid., chapter 103)

Widows who are supported by the Church’s stipend ought to be continually engaged in the work of God, so that they may assist the Church both by their merits and by their prayers.

### Concerning widows who violate their professed continence. Chapter 104.

#### XLIX (Ibid., chapter 104)

Just as the reward of chastity is good, so it must be guarded with greater observance and command, so that if any widows—although still in their younger years, and left by a husband at a mature age—devote themselves to God, cast off secular clothing in the presence of the bishop, and afterward return to the world, they may be condemned, because they dared to annul the faith of chastity which they vowed to God.

Such persons are therefore to be excluded from the communion of Christians and are not to share in meals with Christians. For if married adulteresses are liable to their husbands on account of the guilt of adultery, how much more will widows, who have vowed religious devotion to God, be branded with the crime of adultery if, through lustful will, they corrupt the devotion which they voluntarily offered to God and pass to a second marriage? Even if they are seized by someone through an act of violence and afterward, through the pleasure of lust, consent to remain in the marriage of their abductor or violent husband, they are still to remain liable to the condemnation mentioned above.

Of such women the Apostle says: “When they have become wanton, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have annulled their first faith” (1 Timothy 5).

### Concerning widows who have professed widowhood before the bishop. From the Council of Orange, chapter 9.

#### L (Council of Arles I, chapter 27; BURCHARD, book VIII, chapter 43)

We decree that the profession of preserving widowhood must be made before the bishop and that the habit imposed must in no way be violated. The abductor of such a woman, or the woman herself who abandons such a profession, is rightly to be condemned.

### Concerning virgins who are veiled under the age of twenty-five because necessity requires it. From the Eighth Council of Carthage in Africa, chapter 26.

#### LI (Council of Milevis II, chapter 26; Council of Carthage VII, 7, chapter 93)

It has been decided that if any bishop veils a virgin because her chastity is endangered—when a suitor or abductor is feared, or if she has been troubled by some fear of death lest she die unveiled—or if her parents require it, or if the Church or those responsible for her care veil a virgin under twenty-five years of age, the council’s decree concerning that number of years is not to be held against her.

[Col. 0396B]

### A woman who has received the sacred veil may not abandon it.

#### LII (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 113)

In whatever manner a woman has received the sacred veil upon her head—whether with the canonical permission of her husband, after his death, voluntarily, or unwillingly—she must remain in it entirely and must not abandon it.

### Concerning those who receive Communion.

#### LIII

Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily, or immoderately, or disorderly, will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. “Guilty” means deserving to be condemned by the sacrifice itself, because he has despised so great a mystery as something worthless.

It is written: “Every clean person shall eat them. The soul that has sinned shall be cut off from its people as unclean.” “Unworthily”—as the Lord says: “If you are standing before the altar and there you remember,” and so forth. The conscience must first be examined to see whether it reproves us in anything; afterward we ought to offer or receive Communion.

Some say: “The Lord does not turn away the unworthy person, but the person who receives unworthily.” But if a worthy person who approaches unworthily is held back, how much more one who cannot receive worthily? Therefore it is necessary to cease from vices, so that you may receive the holy body of the Lord in a holy manner.

“Let him examine himself”—that is, let him inquire whether he is worthy. Whoever eats has become guilty in two ways: of presumption and of sin. “Not discerning”—that is, not distinguishing it from other foods. (In Rabanus, at the end of the first book *On the Ministers of the Church*.)

Therefore, when the plague of sin and the force of the disease are so great that the medicines of the body and blood of the Lord must be deferred, each person ought, by the authority of the bishop, to be removed from the altar to perform penance, and by that same authority to be reconciled. For this is what it means to receive the body and blood of the Lord unworthily: to receive it at a time when one ought to be performing penance.

For holy, religious, and God-pleasing bishops, when they enter beneath God’s roof, are accompanied there by the Lord through them, as though they were receiving God. And when you enjoy the bread of life and the cup, when you eat the Lord’s body and drink His blood, then the Lord enters beneath your roof. But wherever He enters unworthily, He enters there for judgment upon the one who receives Him.

[Col. 0397A]

### When a priest dies, what is to be observed concerning his possessions. From the Council of Lérida.

#### LIV (Council of Lérida, chapter 16)

Although the ancient authority of the canons has by no means been silent concerning this matter, which we decree should be established by a salutary ordinance, but has expressly commanded that, when a bishop of any Church dies, no one should rush indiscriminately and according to his own desire to seize the possessions he left at his death or overturn his household, but that the priest present at the funeral should carefully secure everything pertaining to its use and preservation, nevertheless, because this very ordinance is—what is worse—known to be violated by many clerics, so that when a priest dies they violently seize and carry away whatever is found in the bishop’s house, disregarding the proper affection and setting aside every strictness of discipline, we have now decided to preserve among us the full force of this decree or ordinance.

When a bishop has died, or is even still in his final hours, no cleric of any order, office, or rank is to presume to remove anything from his house or attempt to seize anything, movable or immovable, belonging to the ecclesiastical property that is recognized as the household’s equipment. He must suppress, remove, and conceal nothing by theft, force, or deceit.

Rather, the person entrusted with the household, taking with him one or two most faithful clerics as advisers, must preserve everything until the time when the bishop’s successor is appointed, and must provide the clerics found in the household with their customary food.

The succeeding bishop, having received these things, must use them according to the arrangements made by his predecessor, or according to what God inspires him to do, for those whom he knows to have faithfully obeyed the discipline and charity of his predecessor.

If afterward any cleric of whatever order, on any pretext, is proved to have taken anything from the Church’s household or from its entire property, or perhaps to have concealed anything through deceit, he is to be condemned as guilty of sacrilege by a lengthy anathema, so that scarcely even communion among strangers may be granted to him.

For it is harsh that those who are known to have labored in the service of the Lord together with the bishop of the chief see should be in any way tormented by the contempt of those who are known to have been concerned with, served, and devoted themselves to the bishop’s possessions.

[Col. 0397D]

### Concerning accused priests, and likewise concerning palace nobles and *gardingi*. From the Council of Toledo.

#### LV (Council of Toledo XIII, chapter 2)

An additional matter has come before our assembly, one that must be driven away with all the greater weight of synodal judgment insofar as it brings greater slaughter and ruin upon the peoples. For in the course of past times we have seen, and lamented, many men fall from the office of the palace order. A forced confession cast them down from their honor, and the judgment imposed by the faction of kings [variant: “sanction”] subjected them either to death or to perpetual disgrace.

Intending to abolish this intolerable evil and this horrifying crime of impiety, the mind of our religious prince introduced it for reconsideration by the general judgment of all the bishops and established that it should be restrained by the authority of synodal penance [or: power] that avenges wrongdoing.

Therefore, decreeing a judgment fitting his devotion, we have established this common rule: henceforth no one from the rank of the palace order or from the assembly of holy religion is, through the cunning of royal subtlety, the impulse of profane power, or the opposition of anyone’s malicious will, to be removed from the honor of his order or from service in the royal household without a manifest and evident indication of his guilt. He is not to be bound in chains, subjected to interrogation, tormented by any kind of torture or beating, deprived of his possessions, handed over to prison custody, or dismissed through unjust pretexts introduced from one side or the other, by which a forced, secret, or fraudulent confession might be extracted from him.

Rather, the accused person, while retaining the rank of his order and not yet suffering any of the harmful measures [variant: “honors”] mentioned above, is to be brought before a public examination of priests, elders, and also *gardingi*, and carefully investigated. If found liable for the detected guilt, he is to receive the legal penalties; or he is to appear proved liable by the judgment of all.

Those, however, who are found to be staying in places from which suspicion of a harmful refuge might arise, or those whom it is more necessary to guard because of disturbance in the land, must remain under free custody, without any injury from chains or other mistreatment. Nevertheless, after all terror has been removed, they are to be held under vigilant and careful custody, so that the time when they ought to be judged is in no way prolonged through deceit, with the result that, separated for a very long time from their wives, relatives, and possessions, they might appear to have made their confession unwillingly.

Even if such a confession has been made, it will have no force by any means. Rather, according to the procedure stated above, that alone will be accepted as true which has been acknowledged from his mouth and confirmed by the general judgment.

The same procedure is to be observed concerning other freeborn persons who do not hold palace offices [variant: “have attached themselves to them”], yet appear to bear the title of freeborn dignity. Even if they are beaten by the prince with blows from whips for minor offenses, as commonly happens, they will not thereby lose their testimony or be deprived of the possessions due to them.

If anything is alleged against them concerning the crime of infidelity, they are likewise to be judged according to the procedure set out above. If any king henceforth rashly neglects to observe this synodal decree—which we trust was promulgated by the divine Spirit—or deliberately chooses to disregard it, so that any of the designated persons is condemned otherwise than has been prescribed, killed through a military force contrived against him [or: maliciously amassed by trickery], or removed from his rank and deprived of his position, he, together with all who willingly consent to him, is to be punished with perpetual anathema in the sight of God the almighty Father, His only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, and is to be excluded [variant: “condemned”] to burn in divine or eternal fires.

Moreover, whatever has been done contrary to this rule of our judgment concerning any person, or whatever has been decided concerning the possessions of an accused person, is to have no force, so that the person judged otherwise than we decree may neither lose the dignity of his testimony nor be deprived of the benefit of his own property.

Nevertheless, these and similar statutes do not remove from princes the power of domestic correction [variant, corrupt: “for while they promulgate these and other [measures], princes’ power of domestic correction . . .”]. For, specifically concerning those laymen whom no guilt of infidelity binds, but who are found either sluggish in the duty of their service or harsh—or rather negligent—in the tasks entrusted to them, the prince may correct such persons without any disgrace to them, without damage to their property, and without changing their service; he may transfer others whom he approves into their place [variant, corrupt: “those entrusted with such persons”].

### That no one is to be condemned without an accuser. From the Sixth Council of Toledo, title 40.

[Col. 0399B]

#### LVI (Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 11)

It is right that the lives of the innocent not be stained by the ruin caused by accusers. Therefore, whoever is accused by anyone must not be handed over to punishment before the accuser is presented and the judgments of the laws and canons are sought [or: the judgment of the law and canons is sought]. If the person is found unfit to bring an accusation, no judgment is to be made on the basis of his accusation, except where the matter concerns the life of the royal majesty.

[Note: [Col. 0399] This does not belong to this canon of Toledo.]

Accordingly, after enmities, ambushes, lies, and every kind of disgraceful act or crime have been removed, the question is how the priests who have been accused are to be convicted or defended. The Apostle says to Timothy: “Do not receive an accusation against a priest except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Timothy 5).

In the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews: “In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true” (John 3). Concerning accusers of clerics, the canons provide sufficient material, especially in the Council of Carthage, where the faith and conduct of the accuser are to be investigated.

But if priests and deacons have been accused, they are to take with them a lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places, whom the accused have requested from the bishop. Together with them, six are to examine the cases in the name of the presbyterate, and three in the name of the diaconate.

[Col. 0399]

## NOTES OF STEPHEN BALUZE ON REGINO’S BOOKS ON ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE

[Col. 0399]

## 444–523 ON THE LIFE OF REGINO

[Col. 0399C]

Regino’s native country was German, as Trithemius writes—by conjecture, I believe. For he saw that Regino had been a monk and abbot of the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, which, together with all its royal estates and vassals, had been added to the kingdom of Germany under the agreements made in 870 between Charles the Bald, king of Western Francia, and Louis, king of Eastern Francia—that is, Germany—as is clear from title 37 of Charles’s Capitularies.

At that time the Normans, devastators of Gaul and Germany, entered the kingdom of Arnulf, who had succeeded Louis’s son Carloman, his own father. In the year 892 they finally reached the monastery of Prüm. Farabert was then its abbot. Accompanied by some of his monks, he yielded to circumstances and fled. All who were found in the monastery were either slaughtered or carried into captivity by the barbarians. Afterward, having stormed and plundered a nearby castle, they returned to their fleet with immense booty; loading their ships, they departed with all their forces, as Regino writes in the second book of his *Chronicle*, to the regions across the sea—that is, to Western Francia.

After receiving news of this disaster, Farabert, overcome by weariness with human affairs, decided to resign his office. At that time this was not permitted except with the authority of the rulers, since all monasteries were under their power, as we said in our note on letter 29 of Lupus of Ferrières. Thus, whenever an abbot of a monastery died or withdrew from its administration, the king in whose domain the monastery was situated appointed a new abbot in his place. The situation was different if the monastery had been granted, by royal authority—that is, by charter and privilege—the right to elect an abbot. In that case the monks could elect an abbot, and he was not appointed from the palace.

Farabert therefore went to King Arnulf. Having obtained from him permission to relinquish the government of the monastery of Prüm, he voluntarily abandoned the pastoral charge. The monks of Prüm, as we learn from Regino, possessed royal authority—that is, a royal diploma by which they had been granted the right to elect an abbot from among themselves. Accordingly, after the community had been convened, the monks’ votes and voices converged upon Regino, a man—as may be gathered from his books *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*—most worthy of that charge and that dignity.

Yet, because among mortals nothing is undertaken with such great and extraordinary unanimity that it does not always have some opponents and detractors, after several years he was deposed through the machinations of his rivals, as he himself reports—namely, in the year 899. It is entirely reasonable to think that this was done with the authority of the ruler. For at that time, and long afterward, abbots were deposed by rulers without synodal order, solely on their own authority, as could be demonstrated by many examples.

Regino had begun to relate this disaster of his in the second book of his *Chronicle*. Whether it happened that the account did not survive to the present time because the monks of Prüm deliberately destroyed it, so that once envy had subsided and died its memory might not preserve so great a disgrace; or whether Regino did not complete what he had intended; or whether the account perished through the injuries of time—it is difficult to say. One thing may be affirmed: there is a lacuna in this place in Regino.

As I investigated the reasons for the deposition of so outstanding a man, nothing seemed more probable to me than his love of the old discipline. He had become burdensome and irritating to his monks because he made excessive mention of the ancient rules, and thus had earned their hatred for a thoroughly just reason. What could be more unjust, more disgraceful, or more absurd than that, at a time when wretched people were afflicted by domestic and foreign wars, their repose after so many disasters should be disturbed by the most unwelcome recollection of trivial matters, useful neither to the public nor to private interests?

They therefore alleged before the ruler—who was still Arnulf at that time—that Abbot Regino was useless and harmful to his monastery, being too devoted to literary studies. He was, as Giraldus Cambrensis once said of Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, a good monk but a bad abbot, one who knew neither how to govern nor how to benefit others. They demanded that he be removed and another be appointed in his place.

But lest anyone think that I am mistaken in this conjecture, or that the monks of Prüm could have been so foolish and mad as to hate their abbot because he was devoted to literary studies, I shall show by a very notable example from the same century that I am speaking truth. The example is provided by the person of the great man Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, in that same kingdom of Germany.

The author of the *Chronicle of Hildesheim* has taught us that Rabanus was expelled and driven from his monastery in 842. Elsewhere, in our notes on the fortieth letter of Servatus Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, we have proved with the most certain arguments that in that year he relinquished the administration of the monastery of Fulda.

I shall not state the reasons for which he was expelled; an old manuscript, cited by Nicolaus Serarius in the fourth book of his *Moguntine Affairs*, page 643, states them: “In the year 842 Rabanus was driven from the abbacy of Fulda, the monk-brothers alleging that he was too studious, too intent upon the Scriptures, and neglected temporal matters.”

Trithemius sharply attacks this foolishness and dishonesty of the monks in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, attributing it to the prompting of the devil. These are his words concerning Rabanus: “At last, offended by the dishonesty of his monks, who said that he was too intent upon the Scriptures and neglected temporal matters, and since the devil was at work in them, they conceived displeasure against him, taking scandal at the very thing in which they ought chiefly to have been edified. Therefore, giving place to anger and unwilling to remain any longer with ungrateful sheep, he abandoned the monastery and its inhabitants.”

But let us return to Regino.

The monks of Prüm therefore attacked Regino with these frivolous accusations and asked Arnulf to take him away from them. Their request was aided by the extremely troubled condition of the state. Since Arnulf was occupied with continual wars and therefore needed soldiers more than learned men, the monks of Prüm took advantage of this most opportune circumstance. Through Counts Gerard and Matfrid, who possessed great influence at Arnulf’s court, they undoubtedly created the expectation that, if they could obtain from the ruler Regino’s deposition and the right of election, they would elect their brother Richarius.

That monks in those times were accustomed to use such devices in order to win the favor of those who held the chief position of dignity or influence among the rulers of human affairs is attested by Ratpert in the third chapter of the first book of *The Origin and Fortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*. We also learn from book IV, chapter 15, of Liutprand that magnates were accustomed to exploit periods of disturbance in order to ask rulers to grant them abbeys.

There is no doubt that Gerard and Matfrid dared much for Richarius’s benefit. Arnulf therefore saw these two very powerful men pressing the matter so that their brother Richarius might occupy Regino’s seat when it became vacant. He yielded, allowed himself to be overcome, and deprived Regino of the abbacy in order to gratify Gerard and Matfrid, whose assistance and support he needed amid the kingdom’s present disorder. It was rightly observed in former times that the circumstances and tendency of the times are of the greatest importance in public affairs.

Thus Regino became a simple monk from an abbot, and Richarius, still very young, was placed in his position in the year 899, as we have said. Fulcuinus vigorously attacks his dreadful deeds and conduct, scarcely worthy of an abbot, in chapter 19 of *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*.

Regino afterward lived as a private man, amusing himself with his books and always writing something. To his leisure and repose we owe that distinguished work *On Ecclesiastical Discipline and the Christian Religion*, which he composed at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, around the year 906. After completing that work, he prepared and finished his *Chronicle* in 908, as he himself confirms in his letter to Adalbero, bishop of Metz, to whom he dedicated that work.

I have not been able to discover whether he survived for many years afterward. There is, however, someone who thinks that he lived at least until 912.

At the time when Regino was still abbot of Prüm, Hugh, son of King Lothair, was captured by Arnulf through treachery. First, according to the custom of those times, he was deprived of his sight; then he was thrown into the monastery of Saint Gall; finally, in the time of King Zwentibold, he became a monk at Prüm. Regino himself bears witness to this in these words: “Finally, in the time of King Zwentibold, he was tonsured by my hand in the monastery at Prüm. For at that time I was, though unworthy, the guardian of the Lord’s fold in that same place.”

Let this suffice concerning the man’s life.

## NOTES ON THE TITLE OF THE BOOKLET

### “The booklet begins”

This is the true title of these books. The Vienna manuscript cited by Hildebrandus has it in precisely this form, as does the Paris manuscript that we used. Trithemius’s authority also confirms it. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, when he discusses these books of Regino, he writes: “He also wrote the aforesaid work, entitled *On Ecclesiastical Discipline and the Christian Religion*, at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier.”

Since the title was absent from the manuscript of the Julia Academy, and he still had no certain information about the Vienna book, Hildebrandus gave these books the title *On the Ecclesiastical Discipline of Ancient Germany*. Later, when the title from the Vienna manuscript had been sent to him, he placed this at the head of the book: *The Two Books of Regino of Prüm on Ecclesiastical Discipline, Especially That of the Ancient Germans*.

We considered it our duty not to depart from the wording of the ancient manuscripts. Before proceeding further, however, I think learned readers will find it useful if I set out here the title of these books as it now appears in the very old Paris manuscript, and then the title as it must originally have been. It reads there as follows:

> THE BOOKLET BEGINS, COLLECTED ON ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINES AND [THE CHRISTIAN] RELIGION AT THE COMMAND OF RATHBOD OF TRIER, BY REGINO, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY, FROM COUNCILS AND DECREES, SUCCESSFULLY, IN THE NAME OF GOD. AMEN.

The most learned Joannes Morinus printed this title in the appendix to his book *On Penance*, page 39, as follows:

> The booklet begins, collected on disciplines at the command of Rathbod of Trier, by Regino, abbot of the monastery, from divine councils and decrees.

Clearly, he lacked a manuscript in which the complete title was preserved. For this manuscript contains only the middle portion of the title, namely the part that was supposed to be written in black characters.

Ancient scribes, for the sake of elegance, sometimes wrote book titles in black ink and sometimes in vermilion—that is, red ink—hence the term *rubric* for a title. Sometimes they used both, so that the first line was black, the second red, the third black again, and so on; or the reverse. Perhaps the person who wrote the book did not himself apply the vermilion to the second lines, but entrusted them to another craftsman. Consequently, it could sometimes happen that the second lines were not copied through the negligence of the scribes or for some other reason, as happened in this book of Regino.

To make the matter clearer, it seemed worthwhile to present here the title of these books as it must have stood in the Paris manuscript, adding from the Vienna manuscript the lines missing from ours:

> THE BOOKLET BEGINS ON ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINES AND THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION, COLLECTED AT THE COMMAND OF THE LORD RATHBOD, METROPOLITAN BISHOP OF THE CITY OF TRIER, BY REGINO, FORMERLY ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF PRÜM, FROM VARIOUS COUNCILS OF THE HOLY FATHERS AND DECREES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, SUCCESSFULLY, IN THE NAME OF GOD. AMEN.

It should also be noted that those ancient scribes sometimes used blue or green in place of vermilion, as may be seen in the oldest manuscript books.

### In the same place — “Rathbod”

He was archbishop of Trier, as the title states, ordained in 883, on 7 April, as Regino reports in the second book of his *Chronicle*. I think he should be trusted on this point rather than Trithemius, who writes in the *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle* that Rathbod was ordained in 886.

He had been abbot of Mettlach. Then, in 889, the abbey of Saint Servatius at Maastricht was united with the church of Trier through the favor and authority of Arnulf, king of Germany, as is clear from his decree, published by Wilhelm Kyriander from the *Deeds of Trier* and afterward by Aubertus Miraeus. The succeeding kings confirmed this donation. Concerning Rathbod, see also what is written in the *Fulda Annals* under the year 900.

### In the same place — “Formerly abbot”

It should be read *abbate quondam*, “formerly abbot.” The error arose from a transposition of the words.

## NOTES ON THE CHAPTERS OF THE INQUIRY

### “The inquiry begins”

In the old Paris manuscript, only the following words are found, the lines that were to be rubricated in vermilion having been omitted:

> OR HIS MINISTERS SHOULD INQUIRE IN HIS [DIOCESE’S] VILLAGES AND PARISHES.

We supplied the remainder partly with the help of the two words *Finit inquisitio*, “the inquiry ends,” which occur after the *Inquiry* in the Paris manuscript, and partly from the Helmstedt edition, which has at this point:

> Instruction concerning what the bishop or his ministers were formerly required to inquire about during visitations through the villages, districts, and parishes of his diocese.

### “His ministers”

That is, archdeacons and archpriests, who, under the bishop, are responsible for the churches. The *Chartulary of Saint-Denis of La Chapelle* in the diocese of Bourges, chapter 26, says: “The monks, very often making accusations, came into the presence of Lord Richard and lodged a complaint against his minister, the archpriest.” See Regino, book II, chapter 1.

It is certain that the term “the bishop’s ministers” means archdeacons and archpriests, as we have said. Nevertheless, it is worth adding the testimony of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, in letter 27 to Stigand, bishop of Chichester: “The clerics of our villages,” he says, “who are located in your diocese, have complained to us that your archdeacons, having found opportunities, demand money from them, and have already received it from some.”

And below: “We therefore command you to have what was wrongly taken returned without delay, and, in the interest of preserving charity, to prohibit your ministers from presuming to do this any longer.”

From another letter of the same Lanfranc, letter 32, we also gather that in his time the communion of the Lord’s body and blood was customarily given to children. When consulted about this by Domnald, bishop of Ireland, he replied as follows:

> “Indeed, you should know, with every ambiguity entirely removed, that neither the churches across the sea nor we English hold the opinion about children that you suppose. For we generally believe that it is greatly beneficial for all people of every age, both living and dying, to strengthen themselves by receiving the Lord’s body and blood.”

See the notes of the distinguished Luca Dacher on this passage.

### Chapter 1 — “First of all”

Hildebrandus had no doubt that this *Inquiry* belonged to the collection of canons published by him. It is now certain, however, that Regino placed it at the beginning of the first book, as we demonstrated in the preface. Moreover, it exists in Regino’s manuscript in the order in which we published it, namely, after the title of the work. Finally, when Trithemius discusses this very composition and, as is his custom, reports its opening words, he shows that this was its beginning: “First of all, it must be inquired into.”

In the brief preface placed at the beginning of the first book, we already noted that this *Inquiry* was the formula according to which bishops and their ministers questioned priests throughout the parishes, and that Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, also used this formula.

What was then stated briefly and almost in passing, merely to give the learned reader a taste of this *Inquiry*, must now be explained somewhat more fully because of the importance of the subject, scarcely any subject in this field of study being more illuminating.

First, it is certain that in ancient times bishops were responsible for visiting their own parishes every year in person, if this could be done without serious inconvenience. If not, they were at least to send priests or deacons of reputable life who would inquire into the revenues of the basilicas, their repairs, and the conduct of those serving them, as is written in Regino, book I, chapter 9. We have recently discussed this matter at greater length in our notes on Agobard.

The priests who governed the parishes were therefore required once a year to render an account of their stewardship to the bishop or his ministers, both concerning the Catholic faith and the administration of the sacraments and concerning the good condition of the basilicas. No priest was permitted to be ignorant of the canons.

Later, in an uneducated age, when priests were for the most part devoid of ecclesiastical learning and all reverence for the ancient canons, which had become obsolete through age, had been stripped away, it was necessary to compose for them a very brief summary of their rules, so that no one could defend himself under the pretext of ignorance. For this reason the *Admonition* now circulated under the name of Leo IV was published. It contains rules for ecclesiastical conduct and teaching.

Before saying more about it, it is worthwhile to observe that the priests of rural churches were accustomed to come to the city every year on Maundy Thursday for two reasons: first, to undergo an inquiry concerning their ministry; and second, to receive chrism, to use Hincmar’s words from his *Capitula*, title 5, chapter 5.

At the same time, in accordance with the institution of Prince Carloman at the synod attended by Saint Boniface, they were required to render an account of their ministry to the bishop, as is clear from his decree preserved in book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 2:

> “We have also decreed, in accordance with the canons of the holy fathers, that every priest residing in a parish be subject to the bishop in whose parish he resides, and that every Lent he render and display to the bishop an account and description of his ministry, whether concerning baptism, the Catholic faith, prayers, or the order of the Masses.”

Boniface also reports this decree in letter 105 to Cuthbert.

The *Capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours*, chapter 73, says: “So that they may learn, let priests come to the city or to designated places during Lent.”

Later this was changed, and priests were forbidden to come to the city during Lent for the sake of learning, as is clear from Regino, book I, chapter 76. Hence in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 108, it is written simply, without any indication of the season:

> “That every priest render an account of his ministry to his own bishop each year, both concerning the Catholic faith and baptism and concerning the entire order of his ministry.”

Although the time at which priests were to come to the city for the inquiry concerning their ministry and to render an account of their stewardship had been changed, the regulation remained that priests were to come once a year to the bishop in the city and attend his synod, as is also clear from the sixth Council of Arles, chapter 4.

At this synod, after the Gospel had been read, a deacon publicly read the *Admonition* mentioned above, as is clear from the edition of that *Admonition* prefixed to Burchard’s decree, where it reads:

> “The *Admonition* to be read at the synod, after the Gospel, by the deacon, while the bishop and the others sit in order.”

This same practice is confirmed by our old manuscript, where the following is found:

> “Afterward the Gospel is read in the customary manner. ‘Looking at his disciples, Jesus said to Simon Peter: If your brother sins against you.’ Let the seven psalms follow, together with whatever prayers may be appropriate. When these have been completed, while the bishop and the others sit in order, let the deacon read this *Admonition*: ‘Brother priests,’ etc.”

Later it was introduced that the bishop should read it if he wished. For in the *Roman Order*, when this point is reached, instead of our manuscript’s “let it be read by the deacon,” it says: “Let this *Admonition* be read by the bishop himself or by the deacon in his person.”

Finally, when they no longer wished the deacon to act here as the bishop’s minister, they removed all mention of him from this passage. Thus in the *Roman Pontifical* of Augustinus Patricius of Piccolomini, bishop of Pienza, and in the editions printed afterward, it reads without any mention of the deacon:

> “Finally, while the pontiff is still seated in the aforementioned chair with his mitre, if he wishes, he admonishes and exhorts the assembled people in words such as these: ‘Dearest brothers,’” etc.

But let us return to antiquity.

The bishop then, at the synod of each parish, when carrying out the duty of visitation, questioned the priests according to the headings contained in that *Admonition*. I have called the bishop’s visitation a “synod,” relying on the authority of the Council of Rouen. There, as Regino cites it at the beginning of book II, archdeacons and archpriests who visit the parishes with the bishop are instructed that, when he is about to visit a church, they should precede him by one or two days and admonish the people that all must come without fail on the appointed day to his synod.

“But why,” you will ask, “was it necessary for the people to be present in the church with the bishop when he visited the parishes of his diocese?”

First, because the bishop was going to investigate the life and conduct of the priests and the subordinate clergy, he needed the testimony of the Christian people who were governed there in Christ’s place. Moreover, at that synod the bishop also questioned them about the lives of the laypeople: whether anyone had committed incest, adultery, or murder; whether anyone had seized another’s property; and many similar matters, as is clear from Regino, book I, chapters 7 and 10, and book II, chapter 5. This was the reason for assembling the ecclesiastical people.

There is no doubt that the strength of ecclesiastical discipline lay in that holy care and diligence of the ancient bishops. When it collapses, everything must necessarily collapse for the worse and be carried backward in ruin.

To come to the matter itself, we may therefore conclude that the *Inquiry*, like the *Admonition*, did not belong to any one diocese but was general to all, and was consequently adopted throughout all the regions of the West.

That the *Admonition*, to which the headings of the *Inquiry* correspond, was used everywhere throughout the provinces of our world may be inferred from the fact that, as we have already noted, it is set out at the beginning of Burchard’s work and in our old manuscript as the formula of the matters that each bishop was to announce to the priests sitting in synod in the city.

This opinion is also confirmed by the present practice of the Church, according to which that *Admonition*, although greatly altered and changed from the ancient one, is read by a mitred bishop seated in his diocesan synod.

Moreover, since it was used in ancient times in various regions and dioceses, it is reasonable to think that bishops adopted it from a common formula. That it was known in Tarraconensian Spain may be abundantly inferred from the fact that it is found copied in the very old manuscript of the monastery of Ripoll in the diocese of Vic.

For Italy, Bishop Rather of Verona provides evidence, since he inserted it in full into his synodal sermon, which was published in the second volume of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*.

Finally, that it penetrated Germany is shown by the edition of Burchard mentioned above and also by the old manuscript of the monastery of Neresheim in the diocese of Augsburg, where it appears under the title of a synodal sermon. Marcus Welser first gave this sermon to Jacob Gretser for publication at the end of the *Apology for Baronius*, page 457; afterward Severinus Binius included it in the second edition of the Councils.

Welser is mistaken in thinking that Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, was the author of this sermon merely because the Neresheim manuscript was written in 1009. I say he is mistaken because what has already been said makes it easy to infer that the *Admonition* is much older than Saint Ulrich.

It is commonly believed that it was composed by Pope Leo IV, to whom some old manuscripts attribute it. I, however, think it is older than Leo and emerged at precisely the same time as the *Inquiry*.

I am entirely of the opinion that, since the *Inquiry* contains certain matters directed against pagans and against customs and superstitions derived from paganism, it was composed in the age of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz—or at least not long afterward—and was subsequently enlarged and corrected according to the various customs of the churches, the provinces, and the peoples.
