Meanwhile, we owe much to Regino, who preserved this distinguished monument of antiquity for us intact and thus made possible the present observation.

It would be desirable that, just as the *Admonition* is retained for the most part, so the *Inquiry* might be restored to use by the most holy bishops of our age, so that there might be one form of discipline everywhere, and so that the wretched priests of rural churches—who are utterly ignorant of most of the matters contained in the *Admonition* and the *Inquiry*—might be led to know and study those things which they absolutely must know if they are to avoid the anger of the supreme shepherd, the shepherd of our Lord Jesus Christ’s shepherds.

For how many people today, especially in the provinces far removed from the civilization of the Parisian soil, are acquainted with these matters? But this is the bishops’ concern, not the clerics’. Let them look to it themselves. I absolve myself of responsibility.

### Chapter 10 — “A complete Missal”

Thus the Paris manuscript and the Helmstedt edition; all editions of the *Admonition* also agree. Walter of Orléans, however, chapter 7, has: “A Missal, a Psalter.” This reading is supported by chapter 72 of book I of the *Capitularies*: “The Gospel, the Psalter, and the Missal.” See also Bede in the second chapter of his book *On Remedies for Sins*.

### Chapter 11 — “Retiati”

The Helmstedt edition and Hincmar’s *Capitula* have *recitati*, “recited,” which, as I think, makes no sense. The subject here is not the recitation of the divine office, but whether the books necessary for the divine service were properly bound and assembled.

Just as they took the greatest care to ensure that those books were correctly copied and thoroughly emended, as is clear from various passages of the *Capitularies* and from the institutions of bishops of that age, so they certainly had to ensure that the books could not be scattered through negligence if they were not properly bound and assembled. For this reason the bishop inquired throughout the parishes whether they had been properly *retiati*, “netted” or “bound.”

They called them *retiati*, I think, by comparison with nets made from sinews, taking the part for the whole. For books are bound along the spine to cords or bands.

### Chapter 12 — “Cerarios”

Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 128, and book III of the *Lombard Laws*, title 5, chapter 1, say: “Concerning wax-sealers, tabularies, and chartularies, let the practice observed for a long time be maintained.”

Lindenbrog interprets *cerarii* as those who seal letters with wax; Spelmann follows him. Here, however, the word has a very different meaning in Regino.

There is no doubt that it was then customary—and the practice is still observed today among the people of Limoges—for each church to possess a fixed number of candles, candles that equaled a man’s height and were so thick that a person could scarcely embrace or grasp them with both hands: masses of candles, as Vigilantius calls them in Jerome.

As I have said, the churches of Limoges possess more or fewer candles of this kind according to their means. They last for many years and are called *cires*, a word that signifies nothing more than this kind of candle.

They were kept inside the church in a designated place, always, however, displayed before the faithful. They were lit on the principal feast days and also carried in processions. For these things are still done today, evidently according to an ancient institution.

Since those candles lasted a long time, they were counted among the furnishings of the Church. For this reason they formerly inquired how many *cerarii* each church possessed.

### Chapter 13 — “Bonvaria”

The Helmstedt edition has *bona arva*, “good fields.” Hincmar’s *Capitula*, title 2, chapter 2, says: “If he possesses a holding having twelve *bunnuaria*.” The same Hincmar, in the *Opusculum of Fifty-Five Capitularies*, chapter 1, concerning the estate of Attola, says: “It has only two and a half *bunnuaria* of arable land, and of other land, etc., four and a half *bunnuaria*, which altogether amount to seven *bunnuaria* of arable land.”

The Emperor Lothair, in book III of the *Lombard Laws*, title 1, chapter 46, orders that, according to the constitution of his father Louis, each church be given “one holding with twelve *bunvaria* of arable land.”

A decree of Charles the Bald for the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu says: “A royal holding with ten *bunvaria*.”

A charter of Macharius and Gondrada for the church of Cambrai, in Balderic, book I, chapter 52, says: “A royal holding with cultivated lands, to which four *bunvaria* of arable land belong.”

The *Glossary of Papias* says: “*Bunvarium*, a certain measure of land, like an acre.”

Thus, by a holding possessing twelve *bunvaria*, one should understand a holding containing as much arable land as is required for sowing twelve measures of grain.

This interpretation is supported by an old charter of Jonas, bishop of Autun, published in volume VIII of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, page 147, where, instead of the twelve *bunvaria* found here, it reads: “I also give, at the place called Biat, arable land for twelve measures.”

### Chapter 18 — “To a layman or a woman”

An ancient synodal *Admonition* says: “And let no one presume to give communion to a layman or a woman to carry to the sick.”

The distinguished Henri Valois, failing to notice that this *Admonition* is much older than the time of Rather, bishop of Verona, and Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, inferred from this passage that the practice of giving communion to laymen and women to carry to the sick continued in the Church until the tenth century. A learned man who recently published a history of the Eucharist later adopted this conjecture.

The argument is false. For if this method of reasoning were permitted, we would necessarily infer in the same way something that everyone knows to be entirely false—namely, that the practice of sending the Eucharist to the sick through laymen and women still continues in the Church, since the synodal *Admonition* read every year by bishops in their diocesan synods throughout all the churches of the West contains the following statement in the Roman Pontifical: “Let no one presume to give communion to a layman or a woman to carry to the sick.”

See below, book I, chapters 120 and 199.

### Chapter 26 — “To give as security”

To hand over as a pledge, *donner en gage*, “to give as security.” In Hincmar’s time and in the following centuries they also used *vadimonium* for this, as will be noted below. Hence *invadiare*, “to pledge” or “to engage.”

### Chapter 39 — “In the love of the saints”

Below, book I, chapter 213: “Nor to pray in the love of the saints or to drink for the sake of the soul itself.” See Caesarius of Arles, homily 6, among those recently published by us.

“Indecent jokes.” Below, book I, chapter 213, *vel turpia joca*, “or indecent jokes.” This was the expression then used instead of the grammatically correct *turpes jocos*. Those who attempt to correct it according to the rules of grammar are therefore mistaken.

The Council of Reims under Charlemagne, chapter 17, and Addition III to the *Capitularies*, chapter 18, say: “That bishops and abbots not permit indecent jokes to be made in their presence.”

The *Capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours*, chapter 18, says: “That priests and clerics not permit indecent jokes to be made in their presence.” Likewise, *diabolical games* in the same work, chapter 114.

### Chapter 40 — “If he has no patrimony”

See what we have said on this subject in our notes on the third book of Salvian *Against Avarice*, page 425 of the latest edition.

### Chapter 42 — “If he celebrates Mass”

Below, book I, chapter 199: “It was reported to us,” etc.

This was undoubtedly prohibited so that the sacrifice would not appear incomplete if priests did not communicate in the Lord’s body. In ancient times they considered this offense so serious that, among the other grave accusations brought against John XII at the council held at Rome in 963, Liutprand’s continuator, book VI, chapter 7, reports that he was accused of having celebrated Mass on one occasion without receiving communion.

“Peter,” he says, “a cardinal priest, testified that he had seen him celebrate Mass without receiving communion.”

### Chapter 51 — “If he baptizes indifferently”

That is, whether he baptizes without necessity at a time other than Easter or Pentecost.

### CAP. 57.—“From his own heart”

The Inquiry intends this: when a presbyter has received a penitent’s confession, he should impose penance upon him according to the measure of his fault, not “from his own heart”—that is, not from the impulse of his own mind, not from some sudden movement of his spirit and will, but according to what is written in the Penitential, in which all remedies for sins and all punishments are contained. For this reason it is decreed below, in chapter 95 of this Inquiry, that every presbyter should possess a Penitential, “so that according to what is written there he may question the person confessing, or impose upon the one who has confessed the appropriate measure of penance.” And Charlemagne, at the end of the Capitulary promulgated at Salz, admonishes that each presbyter “should be instructed in the canons and know his Penitential well.” How far, however, we are from the modesty of those times! [Col. 0411C]

### CAP. 66.—“With that white garment”

An ancient synodal admonition states: “Let no one presume to sing Mass in the white garment which he uses for his ordinary purposes.” The Capitulary of Riculf, bishop of Soissons, chapter 7, says: “We absolutely forbid anyone to use in the sacred mysteries that white garment which he wears for daily or secular use.” From this it follows that in ancient times presbyters were always dressed in a white garment, and were distinguished by this mark from clerics of the lower orders, who were forbidden to use the white garment outside the time of the offering or of reading. The Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 4, says: “Let the deacon use the white garment only at the time of the offering or of reading.”

### CAP. 69.—“If he should observe the Lord’s day”

See the notes on Agobard, [Col. 0411D] p. 20, and on the Councils of Narbonnese Gaul, p. 45.

### 539. “Freeborn”

That is, of free status. Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 29, says of Abbot Aredius: “He was a resident of the city of Limoges, born not of mediocre parents of his region, but very freeborn”—that is, noble. Hence a slave or tenant who had obtained freedom through his lord’s grant was called *ingenuus*, “freeborn,” and was said to have been granted *ingenuitas*, “free status.” Hence the charter of freedom in the books of the Capitularies, in the Lombard laws, and elsewhere.

### “Of servile status”

That is, if he were a hereditary slave, born of slaves. For Saint Leo, writing to the bishops established in Campania, Picenum, and Tuscany, had forbidden anyone bound by hereditary status or by any other condition to be admitted to holy orders, unless perhaps the petition or will of those who claimed some power over them should intervene. This passage is quoted in Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 34. Hence the expression “a slave from birth” occurs in Letter 107 among the letters of Boniface. Finally, in a letter of the clergy of Ravenna to Charles the Younger, published by Cordesius, they say that it was the custom in the Church of Ravenna that anyone about to be ordained to the dignity of the priesthood should be asked whether he was subject to servile or hereditary status.

Thegan writes in chapter 44 of his *Deeds of Louis the Pious* that Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, came from the stock of hereditary slaves. I think, however, that by the term “slaves,” besides the word’s proper meaning, tenants were also understood—that is, those who from their origin owed labor to the lords of estates and villages for the cultivation of the fields. Since the lords needed a very large number of such tenants, they did not want them to become clerics, lest their own interests suffer some loss. But after these conditions changed, tenants too became clerics without their lords’ consent.

Nevertheless, I find in an old register of the royal archives of Paris a transaction, as it is called, concluded in the year 271 between the lady and the tenants of Vendopera, commonly Vandeuvre. Among other provisions, it states that the sons of the inhabitants of that place could not be offered for the clerical state without the consent of the lords; otherwise, those promoted to ecclesiastical orders contrary to this were to be deprived of their paternal inheritance. These are the words of the old document:

“And they shall not be able to make their children clerics except by the will of the said lady and of the aforesaid lord and of their heirs. And those who do so shall be at the mercy of the aforesaid lady and lord. And they agree that the cleric who is made against the will of the lord shall receive nothing from the goods of the father or mother; rather, those goods shall belong to the lord.”

Finally, it is clear from letters of Philip IV that this right still existed among the Franks in his age; we shall publish those letters in the appendix to the ancient acts. See also the old formulas of an uncertain author, chapter 8, and the chapter beginning *The more willingly*, “On servants not to be ordained,” from Book X of the *Registers* of Innocent III, Letter 73.

### CAP. 83.—“To read well”

Such was the misfortune of that age that it was necessary for bishops to ask presbyters whether they knew how to read well. This happened not only with lower-ranking presbyters, but sometimes even with those who were elected to the highest priesthood. Charles the Bald bears witness to this in his letter to Pope Nicholas, speaking of Gislemar, who had been elected to the pontifical dignity in the Church of Rheims:

“When he had sat down before the bishops to be examined, a Gospel text was brought before him. Although he could read it to some extent, when they all recognized that he understood nothing, he was rejected and cast out by everyone as though he were foolish.”

The bishops assembled at the Council of Valence in 855 lament the same condition in these words:

“And because, through our sins, bishops are ordained in the cities without examination or scrutiny, almost ignorant of learning and falling short of the apostolic command.”

Hincmar shows in chapter 36 of his later work against Gottschalk that this passage was written against them. What, then, do those do today who prepare editions of the divine books, except expose the ignorance of the presbyters of our age by marking accents in Missals and Breviaries? Is this not done because they think that those books may fall into the hands of presbyters who do not know how to read well, and therefore must be aided by the marking of accents?

### CAP. 84.—“By heart”

That is, from memory, *par cœur*. The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 9, says: “After these things, let the reading of the Apostle follow, to be recited by heart.” The Capitulary of Ahyto, bishop of Basel, chapter 4, says: “Let the faith of Saint Athanasius be learned by the priests and recited by heart on Sunday at the first hour.” [541] The following chapter of this Inquiry easily explains this passage. See below, Book I, chapter 272.

### CAP. 89.—“For the observances of the dead”

That is, in the public prayers made for the dead. Bede, Book XI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 3, says: “Their observances are solemnly celebrated.” The Capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours, chapter 116, say: “Concerning prayers, almsgiving, and the celebration of Masses to be performed for the faithful departed.”

Thus *agenda* was so called from *agere missam*, “to perform Mass.” Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 101, says:

“Whoever has an oratory in his house may pray there. Yet he must not dare to celebrate Mass there, nor permit anyone else to perform it, without the permission or dedication of the bishop of that place.”

The Second Council of Carthage, chapter 9, says:

“Any presbyter who wishes to celebrate the observances in any place without consulting the bishop is acting against his own dignity.”

This passage is cited in Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 234, and in Addition IV, chapter 50, where *agendam* is read instead of *agenda*, the reading found in editions of the African council. In Book V, chapter 38, however, *agenda* is read both in the printed books and in the manuscripts. See the most learned Hugh Menard in his notes on the *Concordia of the Rules*, p. 355.

### CAP. 92.—“The computus”

The Capitula of Herard, chapter 125, say: “Let the presbyters learn the computus.” The bishops of that time took the greatest care to ensure that none of the presbyters was ignorant of the computus, so that by this means they could easily determine the epacts, the concurrent days, the Dominical letters, movable feasts, and other matters of this kind. There exists on this subject a dialogue of Rabanus, dedicated to the monk Macarius, which is mentioned by the monk Rudolf and by Trithemius. [Col. 0413D]

### “Let him know”

That is, “let him understand” or “be knowledgeable.” Boniface, Letter 132, to Zachary, says: “I ought to possess and understand the counsel and command of your authority, that is, of the apostolic see.” Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 100, and Ivo, Part VI, chapter 300, say: “Priests who do not properly understand how to fulfill their ministry.” Jonas, bishop of Autun, in volume eight of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 146, has *pro posse et sapere*, “according to ability and understanding.” Rather of Verona, in volume two of the same *Spicilegium*, p. 305, writes:

“If you wish to go to the church of Saint Michael, know this, says Bishop Rather: Saint Michael does not receive you more willingly on Monday than on another day.”

Hence *sapientia*, “wisdom,” is used for knowledge or skill below, Book III, chapter 368.

## NOTES ON THE CAPITULA OF BOOK I

### “From the synodal capitula”

There were therefore two kinds of royal capitula. Some were simply royal—that is, conceived and established in the prince’s council. Others were synodal: certainly royal, but produced in synods, and for the most part concerned with ecclesiastical matters, as these are.

Hincmar, in Letter 39 and in his book on the divorce of Lothair and Theutberga, in his response to the sixth question, says:

“Nor should this be passed over, since we read that the ordeal by cold water was forbidden in the Capitula of the Emperors—but not in those synodal capitula which we have received from particular synods.” [Col. 0414B]

### CAP. 5.—“For his own peace”

There is no doubt that a greater burden of affairs falls upon a bishop when he is in the city than when he lives in a rural parish, especially if that parish is very far from the city. For this reason, it sometimes seemed to certain men, who were moved by a desire for a freer and quieter life, that they should abandon the principal see and withdraw to some rural parish.

The Fifth Council of Carthage restrained the rashness of such men. It states:

“It has been decided that no one shall have the right, after abandoning the principal see, to withdraw to any church established in the diocese.”

Charlemagne regarded this rule as so important that he wished it to have the force of law in Gaul, prescribing in Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 41:

“Let it not be permitted for a bishop to neglect the principal see of his parish and to frequent another church in his diocese more often.”

Burchard quotes this passage from the Council of Rouen, chapter 16, in Book I, chapter 81. He did not wish to cite it from the books of the Capitularies.

Those, therefore, who sought private withdrawal for the sake of their peace also, for the sake of their peace and pleasures—as Hincmar sharply complains in Letter 45, chapter 26—had chorepiscopi under them. While the bishops themselves devoted themselves to hunting, fowling, and the other amusements of the world—which Agobard testifies was customary among most bishops of that age—the chorepiscopi supplied their place in every episcopal ministry and entirely relieved them of the episcopal burden.

Thus the Fathers of the Council of Meaux, who in this chapter inveigh against bishops withdrawing to more remote places for the sake of their peace, later, in chapter 44, condemn those who entrust their ministry to chorepiscopi. They say that this evil arose from the bishops’ laziness. Earlier, too, Charlemagne had warned, in Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 119, that chorepiscopi had been appointed by bishops who were unlearned and devoted to their own quiet and pleasures. Let our bishops see whether this complaint applies to them—whether they are more devoted to their pleasures than to the care of the Lord’s flock.

### CAP. 11.—“It has been decided”

From the Second Council of Braga, chapter 2.

### “Two solidi”

That is, for the right of visitation, as we say today. Perhaps relying on this right, Gausbert, bishop of Cahors, who held that see around the year 945, granted certain properties to the church of Saint Mary of Carbonac and added this condition to the deed of donation:

“But each year, on the feast of Saint Stephen, which is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, two solidi shall be paid to our side and to that of our successors.” [Col. 0415A]

### CAP. 12.—“Delivered”

This chapter is no longer found today among the canons of the Council of Tribur. It is nevertheless also cited by Burchard, although he took it from Regino. It is certainly a holy constitution, and one worthy of the holiest bishops. Before them, Charles the Bald had acted similarly in the Capitulary of Toulouse, chapter 6, as had the bishops assembled at Valence in the Viennese province in 855. See Book V of the *Concordia*, chapter 51, § 7.

### “Lodgings”

That is, provisions or hospitality, as a later age called them. Elsewhere, however, the word *mansiones* means buildings and lodging places. Gregory of Tours, Book III, chapter 15, says: “He entered his lord’s lodging.” Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 82, says: “If anyone should forbid a person traveling somewhere a lodging.” And there are hundreds of similar examples elsewhere.

Hence *mansionaticum* means the right of hospitality owed to a lord at the expense of the possessor—that is, provision or maintenance. See Sirmond in his notes on the Capitula of Charles the Bald, p. 105.

### CAP. 23.—“Unless he has first provided a dowry”

Book I of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*, p. 526, says:

“This is the dowry and endowment with which the church of Estigenfeld was endowed and consecrated by Archbishop Erhenald, when he was at once abbot and bishop.”

To illustrate this Worms canon, it will be worthwhile to cite the letter of Jonas, bishop of Autun, concerning the endowment and consecration of the basilica of Saint Sebastian at Mont Buznin. It is certainly a splendid monument of antiquity, and there will be no more suitable place for publishing it than in the appendix to the ancient acts. We shall therefore give it there after the notes.

For the present, we shall observe that laymen who founded and endowed churches retained for themselves the churches they had endowed, as well as the power to bestow the benefice when the church was vacant, as patrons. Consequently, those who wished to obtain churches from patrons acquired them either with money paid down or through shameful services.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, vigorously denounces this utterly depraved custom in his *Capitula*, title 4, chapter 5. He writes plainly that presbyters who did such things were bringing themselves and their dependents—namely, the clerics educated and raised in their churches—under a curse, since, by giving a reward to the patrons, they purchased sin for themselves and for them.

Again, laymen who founded churches founded them with the intention of being able to have presbyters on their estates who would celebrate the divine offices and mysteries for them, so that they would not have to go to the parish churches within whose boundaries those new churches were built. Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, complains bitterly of this in chapter 11 of his book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*. For this reason, as I said, they retained for themselves the power to bestow the benefice.

To obtain this more easily from the bishops, who were forbidden to consecrate new churches until it was established that they had been endowed, they assigned some portion of their fields as the church’s endowment. Hence it can easily be concluded that the conjecture of the distinguished Francis de Roye, former official of Angers, is entirely correct: he thinks that the founder was called the patron because he was once the lord of those from whom the Church was founded.

From the letter of Jonas, bishop of Autun, however, we conclude that the opinion of those who think that founders of churches were called patrons because of the protection they were expected to provide is not unreasonable. The founder of the church of Mont Buznin adds this condition in the deed of endowment:

“Namely, on this condition: that so long as I, or one of my nearer lawful heirs, shall appear to survive, we may hold it throughout our lifetime, not so much by right of lordship and inheritance as by right of defense and protection, under our *mundeburdium*.”

Certainly Innocent III, in the Lateran Council, chapter 45, observed that the right of patronage had been devised as an aid to defense, as the same former official correctly noted.

### CAP. 24.—“An entire *mansus*”

That is, one containing twelve *bunvaria*, as was stated in the Inquiry. Hence Hincmar of Rheims complains that Attola’s estate contained only seven *bunvaria* of arable land.

Adrian Valesius, that most distinguished scholar, is therefore correct when, in Book XXV of his *History of the Franks*, he discusses the properties which Charles Martel took from the bishop of Auxerre. Robert writes that only one hundred *mansi* were left to the bishop; Valesius interprets these *mansi* as having contained approximately twelve *jugera* each.

### “Some service”

This law shows that fields and possessions belonging to the church were exempt from the payment of taxes and dues—namely, the *mansus* mentioned shortly before, and absolutely all property belonging to the church. A later age called this the presbyteral fisc, the presbyteral or priestly fief, and also the presbyteral ministry.

But if the presbyters who govern those churches possess certain fields as their own property, those fields are subject to the relevant obligations. See the exceptions of Egbert, archbishop of York, chapter 25.

### CAP. 27.—“According to his law”

That is, whoever was convicted of having done these things was not only to restore what had been taken away; in addition, the fine prescribed by the law was to be imposed upon him—that is, by the law according to which the presbyters lived.

For at that time in the Frankish kingdom, just as there were different peoples, so there were different laws. The Franks lived according to their own law, the Lombards according to theirs, likewise the Burgundians and Saxons according to theirs, and the Goths according to theirs, and so on with the others, as we have said in our discussion of Agobard’s book against the law of Gundobad.

Different laws, moreover, prescribed different fines. Nothing is more common in the books of Regino and in the books of the Capitularies than such expressions as “let them restore according to their law,” “let them settle according to their law,” and similar phrases. The word *law* therefore means here a fine.

A charter concerning Balbiniac in an old cartulary of the church of Autun says:

“But if perhaps they should stretch out their lawless hands toward anything belonging to the aforesaid church, within forty days from the time when they had been summoned to account they shall restore the thing taken without a fine. But if restitution is not made within forty days, after the forty days the capital penalty shall return together with the legal fine.” [Col. 0417A]

### CAP. 36.—“For the work”

A most just law. For what could be fairer than that those who possess the goods of a church should supply the expenses for restoring that same church? But if this law were in force today, all those who hold tithes as fiefs and all those who possess pensions, as they are called, established upon ecclesiastical benefices would each be obliged, according to his share, to repair the churches. Yet this would inflict the gravest injury upon the right that is now public.

### “Ninths and tithes”

That is, a fifth part of the produce from estates which laymen held from churches as fiefs, whatever sort of estates they might have been. The most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, correctly explains this in Book I of his *History of Béarn*, chapter 28, § 15.

Hence the “vesting of ninths and tithes” occurs in a diploma of King Carloman for the church of Orléans. Hence Lambert, bishop of Le Mans, writes to Hildebrand, bishop of Sées, that he had excommunicated a certain Rainon, who retained the ninth and tithe of his church.

### “Our ban”

That is, the lord’s ban, the royal ban. Here *ban* means the same as law, fine, or compensation, as we say today: “He will pay the fine.” [Col. 0417C]

Below, in chapters 214, 324, and 368, there is the bishop’s ban. Elsewhere *ban* sometimes means an edict or public proclamation made by a herald; at other times it means confiscation, proscription, or exile, as Sirmond notes on the Capitula of Charles the Bald.

### “Benefice”

A fief, specifically an ecclesiastical one, as is clear from the words of the law and is also shown by chapter 43 of this book, as well as chapter 47. For the most part these benefices were hereditary, as is clear from the books of the Capitularies.

There is a remarkable passage on this subject in the dialogue *On the State of the Church*, which the distinguished John Cordesius, canon of Limoges, published together with the letters of Hincmar. The dialogue reads:

“In the regions of Saxony and Germany, it is believed that some shadow of justice is still preserved in this matter. For when a bishop has been enthroned, all who hold benefices of the Church lay them down at the feet of the enthroned bishop, leaving it in the power of the bishop whom they wish to honor with the ancient benefice and whom they wish to strip of it.” [Col. 0417D]

See our notes on the Capitulary of Compiègne of Charles the Bald.

### CAP. 41

This chapter is taken from Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 5.

### CAP. 44.—“Newly cleared fields”

This constitution has two parts. First, it establishes that tithes from newly cleared land are to be paid to the churches within whose boundaries the new fields have been established. Then it orders that if a person of great nobility or rank should clear some new land in a woodland and build a church there, the tithes of that newly cleared land should belong to the newly built church.

The prince nevertheless requires that the new fields whose tithes are withdrawn from the ancient church be more than four or five miles distant from that old church. Thus fields that were nearby owed their tithes to the ancient churches.

Later, the Roman pontiffs, in order to relieve the poverty and need of monks, freed them from paying tithes on newly cleared fields which they cultivated with their own hands. Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, writing to the Cistercians, in Peter of Blois, Letter 82, says:

“If the lord pope at some time privileged you by a special indulgence, while your order rejoiced in poverty and willingly poured out the resources of its poverty for the uses of the needy, it could be tolerated for a time—although what had been introduced for the sake of necessity resulted in a common injury. But now, when your possessions have increased even beyond measure, these privileges are judged to be instruments of ambition rather than of religion.” [Col. 0418B]

John of Salisbury, Book VII of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, chapter 21, says:

“At first, while religion rejoiced in poverty and poured out the resources of its want for the needs and uses of others, privileges were granted to possessions. But once necessity had ceased and charity had grown cold, they were judged instruments of avarice rather than of religion.”

Since those fields had become the object of great resentment because they had everywhere increased beyond measure, people later began to ask what should be understood by the term *novale*. Consulted on this matter by the bishop of Zaragoza, Innocent III replied that *novale* should mean land newly brought under cultivation, of which there was no memory that it had ever previously been cultivated.

This definition is found in the chapter beginning *What is meant by novale?*, “On the meaning of words,” from Book X, Letter 110, of Innocent himself.

A serious controversy arose again under Gregory IX. For lands that had been called *novalia* during Innocent’s pontificate seemed to have lost the designation *novalia* under Gregory. Some people in Gaul therefore argued that monks should pay tithes on them. The canons of Arles consulted the oracle of the apostolic see on this question.

Gregory replied that land of which there was no memory that it had ever been cultivated, but which religious men had newly brought under cultivation, was perpetually to be regarded, with respect to exemption from the payment of tithes, as subject to the law of newly cleared land. This is in the chapter beginning *To the consultation*, “On privileges and the excesses of those privileged.”

Thus it was no longer newly cleared land, since over time it had passed into the condition of ordinary fields. Yet it was always *novale* with respect to tithes: that is, so far as the payment of tithes was concerned, it enjoyed the privilege of newly cleared land.

### CAP. 46.—“From the nourishment”

Namely, of animals. For tithes are also owed to the churches from these. Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 40, says:

“It has been considered that from the produce of the earth and the nourishment of animals, ninths and tithes are to be paid in addition to other payments.”

Book V, chapter 146, says:

“It has been decreed that ninths and tithes are to be paid from the produce of the earth, the nourishment of animals, and all dues, except those from gardens.”

At a later time, however, the Roman pontiffs freed monks from paying tithes on the nourishment of animals. See the chapter beginning *On the part*, “On tithes.”

It is surprising that no dispute was once raised against monks on this matter, since we read in Peter of Blois and John of Salisbury of extremely serious complaints from earlier times on precisely this subject. Peter of Blois, Letter 82, has Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, rebuking the Cistercian monks as follows:

“Why do you have your lands and animal nourishment privileged to the injury of others, so that you may take away what belongs to another? Did Abel not regard the Lord from the nourishment of his animals? Are you more righteous than the first righteous man, so that you may rise up against God’s justice?” [Col. 0419B]

John of Salisbury, Book VII of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, chapter 21, says:

“‘We are protected,’ they say, ‘by an apostolic privilege, through whose benefit we retain the tithes from the nourishment of animals and from our labors. Certainly, everything is permitted to the apostles, but it is by no means expedient for everything to be done by those who act as apostles. Granted that they freely conceded this to you. You must see whether you rightly sought it. Did Abel not regard the Lord from the nourishment of his animals? And perhaps tithes are more properly rendered from animals, since they arise without our cultivation. For there is more labor in sowing and reaping crops.’”

### CAP. 51.—“The roofs in good repair”

That is, roofs. Anastasius, in his life of Gregory IV, says: “He made all its roofs new and in good repair,” and frequently uses the expression elsewhere.

### CAP. 52.—“Baptismal churches”

Below, chapter 271: “except in villages and baptismal churches.” The expression “baptismal titles” occurs in a charter of Louis and Lothair for the Church of Rheims, preserved by Flodoard, Book II, chapter 19:

“Outside, also, in the same parish, in the fortress of Voncé, a baptismal title, and likewise in the same parish a title of Saint John, also baptismal.”

### CAP. 56.—“From these banquets”

See what we have said on this subject in our notes to the sixth homily of Caesarius, bishop of Arles, among those which we have published.

### CAP. 60.—“Nothing upon it”

This constitution orders that upon the altar on which the Lord’s body is consecrated nothing else should be placed except boxes containing the relics of saints and the Gospel book. It therefore seems to prohibit the placing of images upon the altar on which the Lord’s body is consecrated.

In my opinion, this was also the view of the Gallican Fathers assembled at the Council of Tours in 567. They established the following in canon 3:

“Let the body of the Lord be placed upon the altar not in an order of images, but under the sign of the cross.”

### “The Sacramentary book”

Below, chapter 68: “Let the corporal be placed in the Book of Sacraments.” Consider how great the reverence for this book was among the ancients and how carefully it was guarded. Finally, Flodoard, Book III, chapter 5, praises Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, who distinguished himself by so many outstanding deeds, because he “decorated with ivory and silver the Book of Sacraments, as well as the Lectionary, which he had caused to be written.” See our notes on Agobard, p. 90.

### CAP. 61.—“Let them expel him immediately”

A harsh and extremely severe discipline, if judged by the standards of our times. A Christian goes to another church rather than his own on a feast day in order to hear Mass there, and he is ordered to be expelled from the church that is not his, so that he will be forced to return to his own. Such was the discipline of that age.

Things have now changed. Yet this practice is not so ancient that even in the year 1202 Christians were not forbidden to leave their own churches and carry their offerings to other churches. An old charter drawn up that year exists in the cartulary of Saint Bertin at Sithiu. It reads:

“And if any of the parishioners of Peterse or Calais should often come there to Mass, and, after being admonished by his own presbyter, should not correct this, he shall be publicly excommunicated.”

### “Those who are at variance”

How much was then done out of charity! If any Christians were at odds, they were immediately reconciled, if this could be accomplished with the agreement of the parties. Those who refused to be reconciled with their brothers were forbidden entry into the church until they returned to peace.

The Capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours, chapter 120, say:

“Let those who are at variance be expelled from the church until they return to peace.”

And the person who had come forward to make satisfaction in charity was received. Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 171, says:

“It has been decreed that no one involved in a dispute between persons should dare to approach the Lord’s altar or receive the grace of holy communion before they have been reconciled; rather, the time during which they had remained in discord shall be compensated by an equal period of penance. But if one of them, while the other refuses, should come forward to make satisfaction in charity, let him be received into the church as a peacemaker from the time when he is shown to have hastened toward reconciliation.”

See the *Concordia of the Rules*, chapter 12, § 17, and Regino, Book II, chapters 375 and following.

### CAP. 66.—“In water before the people”

From Letter 63 of Saint Cyprian. Etherius and Beatus also cite Cyprian on this matter in Book I against Elipandus, in Stevartius, p. 92, as does Rabanus in Book I of *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 31.

### CAP. 67.—“That the chalice…”

An ancient synodal admonition states:

“Let no one dare to sing Mass in a wooden or glass chalice.”

Formerly Jerome praised Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, because he carried the Lord’s blood in glass. According to Baronius, the glass chalice was in use from apostolic times. Later, says the same cardinal, it was forbidden because of the danger posed by the fragile material. An example of this exists in Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 46, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*.

Baronius thinks that this Rheims canon, in which the use of a glass chalice was forbidden, was enacted in the synod held at Durocortorum of the Remi by order of Charlemagne.

### CAP. 69.—“A sick little child”

In ancient times the Eucharist was also given to children, at least to those who were dying, so that they would not die without communion or the viaticum. For this reason, those entrusted with the office of baptizing are instructed always to carry the Eucharist with them whenever they go farther away. Walter of Orléans, chapter 7, says:

“Let the presbyter always have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever someone falls ill, or a little child becomes sick, he may communicate him immediately, lest he die without the viaticum.”

Indeed, in a very ancient manuscript Pontifical preserved in the library of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims, written, according to the judgment of the most learned and highly expert theologian Antonius Faure of Paris, during the age of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, the infant is ordered to be confirmed and communicated at the same time as he receives the grace of baptism.

These are the words of the old book:

“Then let him baptize the infant under a threefold immersion, invoking the Holy Trinity only once, saying: ‘And I baptize you in the name of the Father,’ and he immerses him; ‘and of the Son,’ and he immerses him; ‘and of the Holy Spirit,’ and he immerses him a third time. Immediately afterward let the infant be confirmed and communicated by the bishop, who says: ‘The body and blood of the Lord.’”

Likewise, in the most ancient manuscript Pontifical of the Church of Sens, written around the year 980 and supplied to us by the distinguished Antonius Vion of Hérouval, the following is read in the rite for the baptism of infants:

“Then the priest baptizes under a threefold immersion, invoking the Holy Trinity only once, saying: ‘And I baptize you in the name of the Father,’ and let him immerse him once; ‘and of the Son,’ and let him immerse him again; ‘and of the Holy Spirit,’ and let him immerse him a third time.

“When he has risen from the font, let the presbyter make the sign of the cross with chrism using his thumb, saying this prayer: ‘Almighty God, Father of our Lord…’ And the infant is clothed in his garments, while the presbyter says: ‘Receive the white garment…’

“If a bishop is present, he must immediately confirm the infant with chrism and afterward give him communion. If the bishop is absent, let the presbyter communicate him, saying: ‘May the body of the Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life.’”

In a letter of Jesse, bishop of Amiens, concerning the order of baptism, it is prescribed that after the threefold immersion the bishop should confirm the child on the forehead with chrism, and finally that he should be confirmed or communicated with the body and blood of Christ, so that he may be able to be a member of Christ.

Finally, the learned Hugh Menard notes on the Book of Sacraments, p. 144, that in ancient times bishops, after baptizing, immediately conferred the sacrament of confirmation. This was also observed by the illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, in his notes on the Council of Clermont, p. 312 of our edition.

On p. 298 he notes that the communion of Christ’s body continued to be given to children until the time of Paschal II, and that the Eucharist was given to them dipped in the blood because of the weakness of their age.

Cellotius, in his notes on the Capitula of Walter of Orléans, shows from Augustine and Cyprian that it was an ancient custom in the Church to give the body and blood of the Lord to boys and girls. It is therefore surprising that, after so many testimonies, he dared to write that the universal Church had never accepted this custom without the mark of novelty.

Although that practice has now fallen out of use, it cannot be inferred from this that it was never accepted. For there are many practices that flourished in one age and were abandoned in another—such as the giving of the chalice to a layperson approaching communion, and the giving to the sick of the Eucharist dipped in the Lord’s blood, concerning which Regino speaks in the following chapter, along with many others.

### Chapter 70—The Viaticum

Communion, as we were saying shortly before. The petition of the monks of Fulda presented to Charlemagne, chapter 5: “That they may not die without confession and the necessary viaticum of life.”

### Chapter 72—Kings and Priests

Privilege of Louis VII for Theobald, bishop of Paris: “We know that, by the authority of the Old Testament, and also in our own times by ecclesiastical institution, only kings and priests are consecrated through the anointing of sacred chrism. [Col. 0422B] It is fitting, moreover, that those who alone, above all others, are appointed to govern God’s people after being joined through the most holy anointing of chrism should provide for themselves and their subjects by supplying both temporal and spiritual necessities, and, by providing them, should in turn supply one another.”

### Chapter 74—Eulogies

Offerings, gifts.

### Chapter 77—Through a Subdeacon

This constitution orders that chrism should be requested from the bishop not by just any ecclesiastic, but specifically by one of those who are constituted in the priestly order, and that it should then be carried to the church to which the minister who came to request it belongs. If, however, the circumstances of the time were such that neither a priest nor a deacon could travel to the city for this purpose, it was then permitted to entrust this responsibility to subdeacons. [Col. 0422C] For they were approaching the priesthood; and, since they ministered at the sacred altars, they handled the sacred mysteries, as the Sixth Council of Carthage says in Regino, book I, chapter 92.

There is no doubt that the same persons are intended by canon 36 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, where it reads: “The priests who govern churches throughout the dioceses are to request chrism before the solemnity of Easter, not from just any bishops but from their own, and not through a junior cleric, but either in person or through the one who keeps the sacrarium.”

Again, in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 310, it is decreed that chrism is “not to be handed over to anyone else except only to priests, deacons, or thoroughly faithful subdeacons. For it is unworthy that anyone else should receive it except those who will use it when administering it.”

[Col. 0422D] Later centuries departed greatly from this rule. For it became customary not only to send clerics of the lower orders to request chrism from the bishop, but also laymen. Wishing to remedy this abuse, Raymond, bishop of Elne, decreed the following in his diocesan synod in 1380:

“Although it had previously been wisely decreed that no rector or parish priest should be sent for the holy chrism before the solemnity of Easter unless he were constituted in the sacred orders, as the canonical sanctions require, yet because this is observed by many not at all, and indeed they send mere laymen for it, we therefore establish by the present constitution that any parish priest who does the contrary shall incur a penalty of twenty solidi [Col. 0423A] in current money, which we order to be assigned to the fabric of the church of Elne.”

### Chapter 78—At Confirmation

From this it may be inferred that the practice of confirming children immediately after they had been baptized did not prevail always or everywhere. This should doubtless be understood to apply when they had been baptized outside the presence of the bishop. See Marca’s notes on the Council of Clermont, p. 312 of our edition.

### Chapter 81—By the Most Just Necessity

For example, for the redemption of captives; Cyprianus shows in book I of his Life that this was done by Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

**Vadimonium.** A pledge, security. See the Addition to chapter 14 of book IV of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*.

**Pope Stephen.** In his first letter, in Isidore Mercator. [Col. 0423B] It is therefore clear that the Council of Reims from which these two chapters were taken was held after the time of Charlemagne—if, indeed, any council was held in which these decrees were enacted, rather than their having been taken from the Capitularies of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, which still exist.

For it is possible that Regino believed these provisions had been established by Hincmar in a Council of Reims because he perhaps read in his manuscript that they had been enacted in a synod of Reims—namely, a diocesan synod, not a provincial one. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent these same provisions from having been decreed in some provincial synod held by Hincmar, so that the authority of the enactments might be greater.

For chapter 213 of Regino’s first book, which appears to have been taken from the Capitularies [Col. 0423C] of Hincmar, is cited by Vossius in book II of *On the Vices of Speech* as an abridged epitome from an ancient Council of Reims. And below, chapter 120 of this book contains another canon from a Council of Reims, which is plainly shown by the wording to have been issued in some council. Perhaps chapter 60 of this first book, as well as chapter 272, should also be referred to that same Council of Reims.

**According to Hilary.** In Hincmar: “As holy Pope and martyr Stephen taught Saint Hilary in his decretals.” Burchard and Ivo, part II, chapter 139: “As holy Pope and martyr Stephen [taught] Saint Hilary,” and so forth. Regino should therefore be corrected on the basis of these witnesses.

### Chapter 86—Or Homicide

This clause does not occur in the ancient editions of the Apostolic Canons. It does, however, occur in Gregory of Tours, book V, chapter 19, from a new quire that had recently been appended to the book of canons. Hence it came about that two editions of the Apostolic Canons subsequently circulated: in one the clause concerning homicide was present, while in the other it was absent.

Halitgarius, when citing that Apostolic Canon in book V, chapter 4, includes the clause concerning homicide; Regino may perhaps have taken it from him. Gregory IV also seems to have had it in his manuscript, as we said in the note on Agobard. Isidore, by contrast, does not have it; nor does Rabanus in his letter to Heribaldus; nor, finally, does Hincmar, who transcribes that canon in letter 49, chapter 3.

### On Chapter 97

This chapter was taken from book III, chapter 7, of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory.

### Chapter 98

In Saint Gregory, book VII, indiction 2, letter 39. See Posidonius, *Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 26, and Hincmar, letter 48, chapter 10.

### Chapter 104—For Whom There Is a Necessity

The distinguished Joachimus Hildebrand added this interpretation to the passage: “If a priest should have a need to procure sustenance for one of his female relatives.” He appears to have understood it as referring to a woman whose assistance and service the priest needs in procuring the necessities of life.

The true and genuine meaning of this passage, however, as far as I can infer, ought to be this: if the priest’s mother, aunt, or sister is so poor that, without his assistance and support, she has no means of living, she may indeed remain in the same locality in which the priest resides, but at a distance from his dwelling; and the priest should send to her whatever is necessary for her support.

The *Capitula* of Herard, archbishop of Tours, chapter 19: “They are to detest the company of women, as well as their access and service. Otherwise, as despisers of the canons, they are to be deposed from their order. And for those whom they decide must be supplied with necessities, they are to arrange houses far away, in which they are to provide assistance not personally but through ministers.”

Priests, however, were evading this constitution in Hincmar’s time, as he himself explains in letter 48, chapter 33, in these words:

“Certain priests acquire property after their ordination from the revenues of the church, or from the offerings and vows of the faithful; they construct buildings on it and place there what belongs to the church. In these same estates they receive women to practice their weaving and manage the household. On this account they neglect their churches, return to those estates, and live there contrary to the decrees of the canons.”

See below, in Regino, chapter 220.

**No woman at the altar.** Below, chapter 120: “and those who are forbidden to enter the sacrarium or to approach the altar.”

These matters ought to be impressed upon the women of our own time, who not only stand within the chancel rails but also approach the very altar, as though they ought to celebrate the divine mysteries with the priests. [Col. 0424D] No one resists this abuse, although the Fathers provided nothing with greater care than that such things should not be permitted to women.

Nor do I doubt—indeed, I say that I do not doubt—that if this most devout sex were taught that such conduct is wrong and contrary to the mind of the Church, it would most willingly abstain from that corrupt practice of an evil custom.

Formerly, as we noted in our remarks on the Councils of Narbonese Gaul, impious boldness had advanced so far that women stood beside the altars and, often during the very time of the offering, shamelessly received in the sight of all what was being offered to God upon the altar. If, after being admonished, women subsequently abstained from this crime, it is to be hoped that our own women will readily change their practice if they understand that greater irreverence toward God [Col. 0425A] and the Church is committed when they break through beyond the altar rails. I thought it appropriate to offer this admonition, so that at least in this matter the life of Christians may be corrected.

### Chapter 105—Let Him Redeem It with Alms

Later they called this the redemption of sins. Paschal II, in his letter to Norigaud, bishop of Autun: “For the redemption of sins, we decree and absolutely confirm, according to the apostolic decrees, that those who are dying should give alms in the church in which they received the sacraments of the faith.”

From this source, for the most part, arose the possessions, estates, and lands by which the Church was enriched and enlarged, as we said in our note on Agobard.

### Chapter 115—That the Matter Be Deferred

It should unquestionably be read: “that the remedy should not be deferred,” as we pointed out. This is how the published editions of the letters of Saint Leo read, as do most manuscript codices.

Nevertheless, in Isidore’s Collection, from which Regino appears to have taken the passage, it reads as it has been printed here. In an old manuscript codex of the Royal Library, and also in another very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in which the collection of Dionysius is contained, among the decrees of Saint Leo from which this chapter was taken, it is written exactly as follows: “until the remedy of communion is deferred.”

Halitgarius also has this reading in book III, chapter 14, both in Canisius’s edition and in the old manuscript of the monastery of Corbie, and likewise in the edition issued by Colvenerius under Rabanus’s name, in volume VI of Rabanus’s works.

### Chapter 119—Afterward

From this passage alone it may be established that in former times the viaticum was customarily given after extreme unction.

### Chapter 123—Unless Someone Whom the Bishop …

As a general rule, it was formerly forbidden for anyone to be buried inside a church, as Gretserus explains at length in book II of *On Christian Burial*, chapter 8. This privilege is still retained by the church dedicated to Saint Saturninus in the city of Toulouse.

For Augustine of Canterbury was not buried in the church, but in the northern portico of the church, as Bede relates in book II, chapter 3, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

Later, however, it became permissible to bury inside a church bishops, abbots, worthy priests, and faithful laymen, as the Council of Mainz held under Charlemagne says—that is, righteous men who, by the merit of their lives, had acquired such a place for their dead bodies through the way they had lived, to use Theodulf’s words.

I observe that these practices remained in force for a very long time. Yet the ancient stone tomb of Ademar, viscount of the Turenne family and lay abbot of the monastery of Tulle, who flourished during the reign of King Rudolph, appears still to be in the church of Tulle.

There were, in truth, many reasons that would have allowed him to be buried in the church. First, he had been the restorer of the monastery and had ordered it to be the sole heir of all his property; and, moreover, he was doubtless renowned for his reputation for holiness. For to this day he is called “saint” by the people of Tulle.

Although it is not necessary that he was buried in the church at the time when he died, it may nevertheless be that his tomb is now inside the church. Something similar may have happened to him as in the account found in Bede concerning the body of Saint Augustine: it was placed outside beside the church because the church had not yet been completed or dedicated; but as soon as it was dedicated, the body was brought inside and decently buried in its northern portico.

In that portico, too, the bodies of all the succeeding archbishops were buried, except for only two, namely Theodore and Berhtwald, whose bodies were placed in the church itself because the aforementioned portico could not contain more.

Perhaps Ademar had originally been buried in a small tomb beside the humble church that then existed at the monastery. When the church was rebuilt and enlarged two hundred years later, and the bodies of the dead had begun to be brought inside the church, it was easy for the monks of Tulle, out of respect for the man’s holiness and his immense benefactions, to enclose his tomb within the church.

For it is at the far end of the church, in a corner—that is, in a place very remote from the altar they call the high altar. The following was formerly written on the tombstone, and is still read today:

> + XPE SERVA TUUM PER SECLA ADEMARUM. AMEN. +

“+ O Christ, preserve your Ademar through the ages. Amen. +”

### Chapter 125—Exedra

Thus reads an old Parisian manuscript, in place of what the Helmstadt edition has: “outside the church.” Burchard, Ivo, an old manuscript collector of canons in the Royal Library, and Gratian support this correction, which is otherwise necessary; Gratian reads *in exedris*, “in the exedrae.”

For the canon decrees that no one is to be buried in the church, but in the church’s atrium, portico, or exedra. Therefore, if the commonly published reading of the Synod of Nantes were correct, the person who had generally forbidden the dead to be buried inside the church would have ordered them to be buried outside the church in vain. Accordingly, there were three places outside the church in which the bodies of the dead could be buried: the atrium, the portico, and the exedra.

The *atrium* properly means the empty space remaining from the area or ground on which the church was built, and thus the atrium surrounds the entire church. When ecclesiastical authors speak of an atrium, however, they usually mean that part of the atrium nearest the doors, where the vestibule is located.

Below, book II, chapter 31: “If in the atrium of a church, whose door has been consecrated with the relics of the saints,” and so forth.

Anastasius, in the *Life of Sergius II*: “When that king joined him, and ascended all the steps of that most sacred church of blessed Peter, he approached the aforementioned pontiff, who was standing in the atrium above the steps beside the church doors with the entire clergy and the Roman people.”

Ditmar of Merseburg, in book I of his *Chronicles*: “When he came to the atrium of the dead, he saw in it a great multitude offering gifts to the priest who was standing before the temple doors, and stopped there first.”

Anastasius, in the *Life of Donus I*: “He paved the upper atrium of blessed Peter the Apostle, which is before the church in the form of a four-sided portico, with great marble slabs.”

Some read this passage as follows: “He paved the upper atrium of blessed Peter the Apostle, which is called paradise and is before the church,” and so forth.

For the atrium was sometimes called *paradise*, as Heribertus Rosweydus demonstrates at length in his notes on Paulinus. There, following Breul, he also notes that the atrium of the church of Paris, now commonly called the *parvis*, is called *paradise* in the ancient charters of that same church.

An old charter of Saint Victor of Marseille, published in the *Annals of Marseille*, p. 296, explains why the atrium was called paradise. Thus *parvisius* was formed from *paradise*.

Matthew Paris uses this word. His words under the year 1250, p. 798 of the latest London edition, are: “Therefore, to pay that sum, the poor man, who had been teaching in the schools for many days, was compelled, by selling little books in the parvis, to prolong his hungry and wretched life.”

This practice still continues: books are commonly sold in parvises, especially in the parvis of the church of Paris. Vossius is therefore mistaken when he interprets *parvisius* here as “a school for little children.”

A *portico* is a place suited for walking, such as the cloisters of churches and monasteries. In ancient times, however, the location of porticoes was uncertain. Although today they are everywhere at the side of the church, in some places formerly they were between the church and the vestibule, and in others on both sides of the temple, as Eusebius testifies concerning the temple of Tyre in book X, chapter 4, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Hence Bede’s “northern portico,” in book II, chapter 3, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, and Rabanus’s “northern and southern” porticoes in his description of the church of Fulda.

It may be inferred from the passage quoted above from the *Life of Pope Donus* that at Rome the portico of Saint Peter’s Basilica was in front of the church doors, where the atrium is said to have been before the church in the form of a four-sided portico. The same may be inferred from Isidore, book XV, chapter 3, of the *Etymologies*, who notes that the atrium received its name because three porticoes were added to it on the outside.

If we attend to the origin of the word, an *exedra* was a place surrounding the church in which one could sit and rest. In the temple of Tyre, exedrae had been established outside that part of the church in which we place the high altar, around the choir, so that they were subsequently joined to the doors through which one entered the middle of the temple.

I believe that the exedrae formed part of the church walls—that is, that seats were made in the wall around the church—as we still see in some churches. Later, when some people wished to be buried in that projecting wall, they built chambers and vaults in the exedra, in which their bodies were laid. Several such chambers can still be seen around the church of Tulle.

Bartholomew of Brescia therefore correctly observed, in 13, q. 2, chapter *Praecipiendum*, that exedrae are certain vaults attached externally to the walls of a church.

The use of exedrae ceased when, as the abuse grew, everyone began to sit openly and publicly in the church, including laymen and women. Hence the many different interpretations of this word, since nothing certain could be established concerning a feature that had already fallen out of use through antiquity.

To return, then, to the point from which we digressed: there were three places outside the church in which the bodies of the dead could be buried—namely, the atrium, the portico, [Col. 0428A] and the exedra.

In those times, the more honorable place of burial was in the atrium, before the church door—that is, in the most distinguished part of the atrium. Gretserus notes in book II of *On Christian Burial*, chapter 8, that Constantine the Great wished to be buried in the vestibule of the church of Constantinople, and that many emperors and pontiffs were subsequently buried in the same place.

Concerning the emperor Otto II, Leo of Monte Cassino testifies in book II, chapter 9, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* that he was buried in the atrium of the church of blessed Peter the Apostle. In book IV, chapter 8, speaking of Elgaita, the wife of Duke Robert, he says that she wished to be buried in the church’s paradise before the Basilica of the Apostle Peter.

Thus in ancient times the tombs of the counts of Toulouse were in the atrium of the church of Saint Saturninus, near the door, where they can still be seen, until, by the authority of Urban II, their cemetery was established in the atrium of the Golden Basilica.

To use local examples, the vestibule of the church of Tulle was formerly designated as the burial place of the bodies of the viscounts of Turenne, whose merits and benefactions toward that church were extensive and magnificent; their tombs still remain after so many centuries.

In some places, however, the portico was the most honorable place of burial. For we read in Bede, book II, chapter 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, that Augustine and the other archbishops of Canterbury were buried in the portico of the church of Canterbury until it became necessary to bury them inside the church because that portico could contain no more.

Besides the atrium before the principal door of the church, in which eminent men were buried, there was another atrium in which people of every condition were buried. That atrium was properly a cemetery.

An old charter of Archambald, viscount of Comborn, for the monastery of Tulle: “Gaucelin of Petrabuferia himself later devoutly fulfilled this at the entrance of the cemetery of Saint Martin, which is before the door of the church of Saint Julian the Martyr.”

### Chapter 129—Through His Own Negligence

The synodal statutes of Simon, bishop of Sodor, chapter 4: “Let chaplains take care lest, through negligence, any infant—God forbid—die without baptism.”

### Chapter 132—A Consecrated Altar Slab

The *Capitula* of Hincmar, title 3, chapter 3: “Let every priest who needs one have a slab, suitably and honorably prepared according to his means, of marble, black stone, or the finest *litium*, and bring it to us for consecration. When necessary, let him carry it with him, so that he may celebrate the sacred mysteries upon it according to ecclesiastical rite.”

As an incidental observation, *litium* appears to be a type of black stone commonly used for covering roofs. Nicot, from the French word *ardoise*, called it *ardosia*; Monetus called it *lithostilben*.

In later centuries that consecrated slab, which priests were to use when celebrating the sacred mysteries outside the church, was called a portable altar. The Roman Pontifical contains an order for the consecration of a slab or portable altar.

### Chapter 142—In the Army

“In the army,” as he will say immediately. The provision forbids any of those serving as soldiers to compel others to drink, specifically to the point of drunkenness. Otherwise, no law prohibits friends from drinking with one another, provided that the matter remains within the bounds of sobriety.

### Chapter 169—Discipline

That is, private correction by scourging.

The distinguished Joannes Morinus believed that this kind of penitential punishment or remedy was unknown in the Church before the year 950, and that the example was set by Dominic Loricatus, whose superhuman virtue and endurance Peter Damian celebrates.

But in the Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop of Arles, I read the following in chapter 41: “For any fault, if it is necessary to receive the discipline of the scourge, the prescribed number is never to be exceeded—that is, thirty-nine.”

The Council of Mainz held under Charlemagne decreed in chapter 45: “We wish those who neglect to learn these things to receive fitting discipline, whether they are corrected by fasting or by some other punishment.” This chapter is transcribed in book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 95.

That is, from among those who have been enrolled in the clergy and, by that title, distinguished from the people.

The petition of the monks of Fulda presented to Charlemagne, chapter 4: “That the reception of broken bread before food should not be rejected as a daily practice, according to the examples of the preceding Fathers.”

See the eighth homily of Caesarius of Arles.

### Chapter 199—Torunensi

So that no one may think there is a typographical error here, I note that it is written this way both in the Helmstadt edition and in the Parisian manuscript that we used for this edition.

**With these words.** Above, chapter 70: “The body and blood,” and so forth. In the age of Robert, king of the Franks, they said, as Helgaud testifies in his *Life*: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation for you in soul and body.”

That formula is not used in recent times. For when we receive Communion, the priest says only this to us: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.”

### Chapter 203—Let Him Have Capitula

That is, if we wish to express it in the language of our own times, a *Summa of Cases of Conscience*.

### Chapter 208—The Duty of Their Servitude

His office, as we would say today.

Stevartius preserves an elegant preface by an ancient writer on the Psalms, addressed to Bathuric, bishop of Regensburg, who lived under Charlemagne. In it he sharply rebukes certain bishops of his time who, devoted to their pleasures for the entire day, recited their office partly when going to bed and partly while dressing in the morning.

I wish to quote the man’s own words:

“Others, however, who—as it is shameful to say—even include bishops, spending the whole day at banquets and cups, and devoting themselves almost until the middle of the night, or until the crowing of the roosters, or even later, to various drinks in an effort to satisfy their desire—such men, being more concerned to please human beings than God, lazily perform the night vigils before going to sleep, then immediately lie down in bed until the time for eating and drinking returns.

“On rising, when they put on their clothes, they perform the daytime offices, thinking that it can be enough for them if only they chant them somehow.”

But let our bishops not think that I have said this about them, as though I wished to disparage them. I shall use toward them the same words that the same author uses toward Bathuric:

“For in reporting such things, he says, I do not wish to mark you out, but, with the greatest humility and submission, I presume to admonish you not to share in them.”

### Chapter 213—With a Bear

On the Kalends of January, people were accustomed to transform themselves into beasts, wild animals, or monsters, as learned men long ago established from a homily of Maximus, bishop of Turin, on the Kalends of January.

They therefore assumed the forms of stags and calves, and also of bears, so that they might imitate more freely and licentiously the mad wantonness of dumb animals.

Later, when this had been forbidden by both ecclesiastical and civil laws, Christians transferred this madness from the Kalends of January to the days preceding the beginning of Lent. See the Synod of Auxerre under Aunacharius, Zachary’s letter to Boniface—the 142nd among the letters of Boniface—and Carloman’s edict at the beginning of book V of the *Capitularies*.

**Talamascas.** That is, masks, as explained earlier. Vossius reports this chapter in abridged form from an old Council of Reims in book II of *On the Vices of Speech*: “We prohibit under anathema the demons’ masks, which the common people call *talamascas*.”

Hence our word *masque* for a mask. From the same source arose the usage by which secret marks in writing—through which we wish something to be concealed from others, though not from the person to whom we are writing—are called *talamascas* in a fragment of Odo Aribertus concerning the murder of Bernard, count of Barcelona, part of which we published in our notes on Agobard: “I shall write the remaining matters, which it is dangerous to disclose, in talamascas.”

In this passage, instead of what the Helmstadt edition has—“which the common people call *dalamaschas*”—we have followed the authority of the Parisian manuscript and Hincmar, and also wished not to disrupt the sources from which Burchard took his text; we therefore printed “which the common people call *talamascas*.”

The person who copied the Helmstadt manuscript in ancient times appears to have had before his eyes the Council of Reims cited by Vossius.

### Chapter 216—Priests on the Kalends

The constitution of Riculf, bishop of Soissons, chapter 20: “We have also decreed that it is most reasonable that, on a fixed day in each month—that is, on the Kalends of each month—the priests should assemble together throughout the individual deaneries. When they assemble, they are not to devote themselves to food or drink, but are to confer about their ministry, their religious conduct, and the events that occur in their parishes.”

**Let them receive individual *biberes*.** Below, book II, chapter 432: “Let each person receive one *biber* each.” That is, individual cups of wine, as Vossius interprets it.

The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 35: “Those serving for the week are to receive, in addition to the prescribed allowance, one *biber* each.”

The Rule of Saint Aurelian, in the epilogue: “Daily provisions: three at the refreshment, two at dinner, and two at supper. *Biberes* at the refreshment—that is, in summer, unmixed wine—and three small cups (*caldelli*).” And below: “Two *biberes* at dinner.”

Ekkehard, in book *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 11: “At last the abbot invites them together to the brothers’ nones, for which *biberes* had been prescribed.”

From these passages it is clear that the Helmstadt edition incorrectly reads “let each receive one freely.” It is likewise incorrect in Burchard: “let them make each person drink one.”

**More than a third time.** See book V of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 51, section 2.

An ancient synodal admonition: “Know that the property and resources which you acquire after the day of your ordination belong to the church to which you have been assigned.”

Paschal II, in his letter to Norigaud, bishop of Autun: “Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that no priest,” and so forth, as below in the Appendix of Ancient Acts, title 21.

### Chapter 230—Usury

The Council of Soissons, held in 1078 under Manasses, archbishop of Reims: “That no cleric or Christian layman shall receive usury. And if anyone has accepted another person’s property as a pledge and has already obtained his principal from it, let him return the property itself and take nothing more.”

### Chapter 241—To Repledge

This is exactly how Regino’s manuscript reads. The Helmstadt edition has instead: “that those liable to our ban, through sureties, …”

Our emendation is also confirmed by the books of the *Capitularies* and the *Book of Lombard Law*. “They repledge the ban,” as Sirmond says: those who have been condemned by judgment to a penalty of the ban give a pledge for it.

A charter of Queen Matilda for the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu: “The aforesaid arbiters also judged that if a peasant had closed his door against the abbot’s officer and assessors, the assessors and the officer were permitted to open the door by forcing it, and to carry away the pledge, even after breaking open chests, if they did not find it outside the lock.”

Lindenbrog and Spelman explain *rewadiare* as “to release.” See Vossius, book IV of *On the Vices of Speech*.

**Armiscaram.** The Helmstadt edition has *aruscaram*, which Hildebrand interprets as an arbitrary penalty. Below, book II, chapter 423: “They will endure our most severe *harmiscara*.”

Sirmond notes in his remarks on the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald that *harmiscara* was a heavier fine, which a prince could impose at his discretion and outside the ordinary procedure. See Vossius, book II of *On the Vices of Speech*, who rightly criticizes Vitus Amerbach here.

### Chapter 242—If There Are Several

This is an abridgment of canon 32 of the Council of Tribur, as Regino generally reports the canons of that synod.

The matter there concerns the right of patronage. The canon therefore orders that if there are several patrons of one church, and they cannot reach agreement among themselves concerning the priest who is to govern and administer it, the bishop is to close the church and prohibit the celebration of sacred services in it until harmony returns among the patrons. This had previously been established in the Second Synod of Chalon.

In Burchard, book II, chapter 43, and in the first collection of the *Decretals*, chapter 1, *On the Right of Patronage*, however, this canon—which is found published among the canons of the Council of Chalon—is attributed to the Council of Metz.

Burchard and Bernardus Circa appear to have transcribed this canon of Metz from different exemplars, since their readings differ in several places in the same chapter. It is therefore possible that it was also issued in some synod of Metz.

Later, this law was altered by the authority of Innocent III, Roman pontiff. He decreed that if a dispute concerning the right of patronage arose among laymen, and it was not settled within four months who possessed the right, the diocesan bishop should thereafter not delay appointing a suitable person to the church.

This constitution is found in Innocent III, book I, letter 521, and hence in chapter *Cum propter*, *On the Right of Patronage*.

### Chapter 243—To Be Divided Among Several

This is an ancient rule, as could be proved by many examples, established by the same law that forbade two bishops to exist in one Church.

But because some people occasionally departed from this rule, it was at times necessary to admonish them not to abandon the most sacred institutions. Yet the abuse often revived, to such an extent that one church was sometimes entrusted simultaneously to two priests, with the consent and authority of the bishops.
