There are letters of Rodhmund, bishop of Autun, issued around the year 940, by which he entrusts the chapel of Saint Germanus of Centissa to two clerics, “so that during the days of their lives they may hold, govern, and possess it.” The complete charter will be published below in the Appendix of Ancient Acts.

### Chapter 246—But If

Burchard, book III, chapter 239, reports this canon as coming “from the Council of Reims in the presence of Emperor Louis, chapter 5,” although it belongs to the Council of Meaux. Burchard evidently thought he could change everything.

Canes or *Genitiarias*. I think the word *genitiarias* is used here spitefully, to suggest that the tithes received by laymen had been diverted to wicked uses—namely, to the expenses of dogs and whores. This conjecture is supported by chapter 132 of this book, where we read: “among the roaming of dogs and the herds of whores.” [Col. 0433A] Moreover, among the various chapters on which laymen were formerly questioned by the bishop, this also appears below, in chapter 37: “If anyone in his own house consents to commit adultery with his own maidservants or *geneciariae*.” Finally, the author of the *Dialogue on the State of the Church*, published by Cordesius together with the letters of Hincmar, rebuking secular men who possessed ecclesiastical revenues, reproaches them in these words: “You will eat the tithes and offerings of the faithful with your wives and maidservants—and, what is worse, some of you with whores.” Otherwise, the word *genitiariae* is an honorable term, meaning the same as “maidservant.” Below, Book II, chapter 176, from the Council of Nantes: “residing among their maidservants.” King Louis of Bavaria, in the second volume of the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, p. [Col. 0433B] 12: “568 slaves within the court, among boys and women; *geneciae*, twenty-two in number.” Title 80 of the Alemannic Law: “Concerning him who has intercourse with a female servant, a *vestiaria* and *geneciaria*.” The law explains what a *geneciaria* maidservant is: “And if anyone has intercourse against her will with a girl from the upper *genecium*, let him pay six solidi. If anyone has intercourse against her will with one from another *genecium*, let him pay three solidi.”

Thus *genitiariae* were called maidservants because they had been placed in the *genecium*, or gynaeceum—that is, in that part of the house where the women, to use the words of the Council of Nantes, attended among themselves to their spinning and textile and feminine work. It can be inferred from the passage of the Alemannic Law just cited that there were two kinds of *genecia*, upper and lower—that is, as [Col. 0433C] Spelmannus interprets it, more honorable and more servile. The very learned scholar thinks that the *genecium* was a place intended for the punishment of women, just as it was formerly customary to put men in a mill as a punishment. Indeed, in Book II of the Lombard Law, title 37, chapter 7, we read that in ancient times the punishment imposed on corrupted nuns was that they should be handed over to the *genecium*; and that this law was consequently abrogated by the emperor Lothair, lest, if they were placed in the *genecium*, they should afterward have a place for committing adultery with several men.

Since these women also spun threads and wound skeins, which are included under the term “women’s work,” they are called “spindling maidservants” (*pensiles ancillae*) in Book II of the Lombard Law, title 9, chapter 2. There it is prescribed to the officers of the state that a free woman who has voluntarily married a slave should be led into [Col. 0433D] the court—that is, the king’s palace—and placed among the *pensiles* maidservants. This, then, was the punishment of a woman who had joined herself to a slave.

It remains for us to investigate what distinction there was between the two *genecia*. Spelmannus left this part untouched. In the upper *genecium*, therefore, there were undoubtedly placed the native maidservants—that is, those who had not sinned but had been born from slaves in the houses of their mistresses. These women were treated more honorably. Those who had sinned, however, were perhaps placed in workhouses and were not even admitted into the presence of their mistresses; they attended within the house to whatever was more degrading, fortunate if they were still permitted to live or were not subjected to exile.

[Col. 0434A] 569. TO CHAPTER 254.—“A priest one.” See the Notes on Letter 29 of Lupus of Ferrières.

TO CHAPTER 259.—“Let him invite the penitent.” See the first homily of Caesarius of Arles.

TO CHAPTER 285.—“What tribulation.” Whenever some prodigy occurred, they expiated it with fasts, prayers, and the celebration of Masses. Boniface the martyr, Letter 72, is entirely on this subject: “You priests, remember to celebrate those Masses which are customarily held for storms.” There is a Mass “for any tribulation” in the Book of Sacraments. Recently, however, I found another in an old manuscript codex, which I thought should be published in the Appendix of Ancient Acts.

“Our edict.” From this it seems possible to infer that extraordinary fasts and supplications, which were imposed outside the regular order, [Col. 0434B] were sometimes decreed only with the authority of the ruler. For the ruler would have imposed the necessity of awaiting an edict in vain if this had not been the case. Charlemagne, in the brief collection of capitularies published by Sirmond in the second volume of the Councils of Gaul, p. 262: “First, it must be recalled that last year we held three three-day fasts, praying God that he might deign to show us in what respects our conduct before him ought to be amended; and this we now desire to do.” Louis the Pious, in the third capitulary of Aachen, chapter 3: “We believe that you remember how this year, on the advice of the priests and our other faithful men, we ordered a general fast to be celebrated throughout our entire kingdom.” And below: “We wish that a general three-day fast, [Col. 0434C] to be celebrated on the Monday after the octave of Pentecost, be proclaimed and universally observed by all with the greatest devotion.” See the Sixth Council of Paris, in its letter to the emperors Louis and Lothair, and Book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 184.

CAP. 286.—“He lends.” He accommodates; he lends on loan. In French, *qui prête*. Ruricius of Limoges, Book I, Letter 7, to Bassulus of Cahors, as I believe, a bishop: “I signify that I have returned the book which you had lent.” Book II of the Visigothic Law, title 5, chapter 2: “If anyone has lent another person a beast of burden or a horse or another animal.” Title 54 of the Salic Law: “If anyone has lent another something from his property and is unwilling to return it.”

570 CAP. 289.—“Apse.” The Helmstedt edition has *absidem*. Both forms are used, but *absida* is more frequent. Commonly, however, they interpret *absida* as the bishop’s seat or throne in the church. I agree that the throne was, as it still is, in the apse—that is, within the space near the high altar, which is generally separated from the rest of the church by screens. But since, in Anastasius’s *Life of Leo III*, I find that he enclosed and adorned the windows of the apse with glass of various colors, I am compelled to understand *absis* as referring to that space which, as I have said, is near the high altar and separated from the rest of the church by screens. See the *Glossary* of François Pithou and Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*.

CAP. 290.—“Hair shirt.” Ruricius calls it an ecclesiastical garment [Col. 0435A] in Book II, Letter 20. See our notes on the homilies of Caesarius of Arles.

CAP. 291.—“Let them expel.” According to the ancient custom of the Church, which removed penitents from the assembly and communion. The first homily of Caesarius of Arles is especially notable on this matter. Later, however, the Roman pontiffs violated this rule for the benefit of monasteries.

“He incites us to sin.” It can easily be inferred from Ruricius of Limoges that this formula is ancient. In Book II, Letter 12, he writes: “But to whom shall we first confess or disclose our iniquities before the Lord, if not to the devil, who is both the instigator and the accuser of sins? For he incites us to sin. When we have sinned, he accuses us. Therefore, in confessing our crimes, let us anticipate him in this world, so that he may have nothing to bring against us in the future.” [Col. 0435B]

“You have killed offspring.”—This passage is obscure. For it imposes ten years of penance on parents who have voluntarily killed their children, but immediately orders those who have killed a son or daughter to do penance for twelve years. Yet no one should suppose that there is an error here, since this reading is consistent in the Helmstedt edition and in the Paris manuscript, and also in the old penitential book which Morinus published from a very ancient Sicilian codex. Some light, however, can be shed on this difficulty by Burchard, in whose Book XIX we read: “You have done what certain women are accustomed to do: while committing fornication, 571 they wish to kill their offspring and act by their magical practices and herbs to cast out what has been conceived in the womb; you must do penance for ten years during the prescribed [Col. 0435C] periods.” And below: “Have you voluntarily killed a son or daughter after birth? If you have, you must do penance for twelve years during the prescribed periods.”

“Before conception.” That is, you caused yourself not to conceive by means of deadly potions and herbs; do penance for one year. But if, after you had conceived, while you were pregnant, you expelled the contents of your womb, then you must do penance for three years. The Angevin Penitential published by Morinus: “If a woman voluntarily loses her offspring before forty days, let her do penance for one year. But if after forty days, for three years. But if after it has become ensouled, let her do penance as a homicide.” See Burchard, Book XIX.

“Vegula.” See Hugh Menard’s Notes on the Book of Sacraments, p. 252.

[Col. 0435D] “Of your clemency and mercy.” The Paris manuscript and Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 7, as well as Halitgarius in Book VI, have this reading exactly. The Helmstedt edition, however, reads: “your clemency and mercy, so that for your servant…” Morinus has: “your clemency and your mercy and your majesty, so that for your servant…” The reading of the Paris manuscript is further confirmed by the *Penitential Book* of Egbert, archbishop of York, in Morinus’s Appendix, p. 19, and by the Dionysian codex published there, p. 70. In ancient times there were various forms of absolution, which the same Morinus treats at length and with learning. For the present, however, I thought it appropriate to publish in the Appendix of Ancient Acts the ancient forms of absolution that were in use in the age of Gregory XI and [Col. 0436A] Boniface IX, which I recently discovered in an old manuscript codex of the Royal Library.

CAP. 316.—“Whoever.” That is, whoever among those who had received penance and had assumed the clothing of penitents. Otherwise, that constitution would be ridiculous.

CAP. 327.—“Spectacles.” Masked men; *des mascarades* (“masquerades”). For these are the spectacles of recent times. See above, where *talamascas* were discussed.

CAP. 328.—“The Synod of Helibern.” In two very old manuscript codices, one Royal and the other belonging to us, it reads: “It is called the Synod of Ebernia. During the three Lents,” etc. 572 The old collection of Irish canons, published in volume IX of Dacheray’s *Spicilegium* [Col. 0436B] from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Corbie, Book XLIV: “The Irish Synod. During the three,” etc. The most illustrious archbishop of Paris, Peter de Marca, had seen an old manuscript codex in which this chapter was said to have been copied from an Irish council. Those are therefore mistaken who attribute that constitution to the Council of Eliberis. It should also be noted that several other canons attributed by Burchard and Ivo to the Council of Eliberis are found in the collection of the monastery of Corbie. From this an argument may be drawn concerning the others that are not found among the generally accepted canons of the Synod of Eliberis. Elsewhere we shall discuss at length the whole matter treated in this chapter.

CAP. 332.—“Eulogies.” That is, blessed bread, as we would say today. [Col. 0436C]

CAP. 333.—It appears in Burchard, Book VI, chapter 33.

CAP. 335.—“Cotta.” The Helmstedt edition has *collum*. But the Paris manuscript clearly has *cotta*. Burchard and Ivo, Part VI, chapter 283, have *cotto* or *cappa*. The Council of Metz, held in the year 888, chapter 6: “That no cleric carry weapons or put on lay clothing; that is, that he wear neither *cottos* nor cloaks without a cape, and that laymen not wear capes.” Bishop Conrad, in the *Chronicle of the Affairs of Mainz*, in Reuber, p. 453: “Arnold, as he was inaugurating the beginnings of his episcopate, taking the finest purple from the wardrobe, made garments for himself—a tunic, a *sorcotium*, and a cloak—so that he might appear more glorious at the emperor’s court.” [Col. 0436D]

A *cotta* or *cottus*, therefore, was a long garment, but one that lacked a hood, as we say today. This was lay clothing, which clerics are forbidden to wear. Spelmannus and Vossius, however, maintain that the word *cotta* signifies a hiding place, cave, hut, cottage, hovel, and even the monks’ cells and dormitory. Vossius is certainly mistaken when, in Book II, Letter 15 of Peter Damian, he interprets *cottus* as a poor bed or little couch, since the passage concerns a monastic garment under which that monk whispered Compline every day in bed. For monks were not permitted to remove their clothing when they went to bed. The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 22: “Let them sleep clothed and girded with belts or cords.” The Rule of the Master, [Col. 0437A] 573 chapter 11: “When they sleep, let them sleep clothed and girded.”

CAP. 336.—“From the Council of Adrisphach.” The title of this chapter indicates that the place was in Bavaria. But it does not explain in what part of Bavaria it was situated or at what time that council was held. Perhaps it should be understood as the council which Boniface of Mainz wrote to Gregory III that he intended to celebrate beside the bank of the Danube, as is read in the fifth letter of Gregory himself, which is Letter 130 among the Bonifacian letters. [Col. 0437B] There the matter concerns the people of Bavaria, about whom Boniface had written to Gregory. That Bavaria had been entrusted to Boniface by Gregory and confirmed by Zachary is shown by a letter of that same Zachary addressed to him, which is Letter 143 among the Bonifacian letters; and Wilibald also writes this in the ninth chapter of his *Life* of Boniface. Perhaps, then, Boniface held a council beside the Danube at Adrisphach. This is my conjecture, though it is not especially certain.

Below, in chapter 378 of this book, there is another decree of the same synod. Perhaps chapters 380 and 382 also belong to it, following Regino’s customary practice of placing in the title the words “From the foregoing” whenever he takes several items discontinuously from a preceding council. This sometimes gave Burchard an opportunity for error.

CAP. 342.—“Concerning ecclesiastical ministrations.” That is, concerning the goods and property of the church, as the sense requires and as the title of the chapter further shows. Below, chapter 275: “If anyone in any way steals something from the ministry of the church, let him do penance for seven years.” Thus, in an old agreement [Col. 0437C] between the monks of Tulle and those of Aurillac, the goods and property of the church are understood by the term “presbyteral ministry”: “The presbyteral ministry of the church of Saint Amantius of Faurcius, and three manses in the same court.” See what we said above concerning the presbyteral fisc in the notes on chapter 24.

CAP. 347.—“Without the knowledge of the council.” That is, of the clergy, below, chapter 349. They sometimes used the word *concilium* when they meant the clergy. Below, chapter 357: “before the council of the Church.” The emperor Constantine: “Let everyone have permission, departing from the most holy and venerable Catholic council, to leave behind whatever property he wished.” Bishops therefore were not permitted to sell the property of churches without the advice and consent of their brothers, except perhaps small plots of land or vineyards, or property of little use to the church or situated far away, 574 [Col. 0437D] as the Council of Agde determined.

CAP. 349.—“In his clergy.” It should undoubtedly be read, “without the knowledge of the clergy.” Yet because Martin of Braga, from whom this chapter was taken, Burchard in two places, and Ivo of Chartres, Part III, chapter 172, retained the reading “in his clergy,” we too thought that it should be retained, especially since both the Helmstedt edition and the Paris manuscript expressly display it.

CAP. 362.—“Precariae.” “Those who obtained a church property for usufruct,” writes Sirmond, “subject to an annual rent, customarily received it by *precaria* and *praestaria*. The rector of the church gave the *praestaria*, granting the property as a loan [Col. 0438A] and explaining under what conditions he granted it; the petitioner requested the *precaria*, receiving the property on that tenure and professing that he would fulfill the rent and other conditions imposed.” This is certainly true. Yet it is equally certain that the terms *precaria* and *praestaria* were formerly confused, because property held by *precarium* was said to be *praestata* or *praestita*, that is, handed over for a fixed period—*prêtée* (“lent”).

In Book I of the *Antiquities of Fulda*, in Pistorius, p. 459, a certain man, while making a donation of three slaves to the monastery of Fulda, informs Abbot Ratgar that he is giving those slaves on the condition “that I too may have them, for as long as I endure the course of this life, for my support, through your *precaria*.” There are almost innumerable examples of this kind in these books of the *Antiquities of Fulda* [Col. 0438B] and elsewhere. A charter of Solomon, abbot of Saint Gall, in Goldast’s second volume of the *Alemannic Affairs*, p. 69: “It pleased us that the property which Ingelbold handed over to us should, by this *precaria*, be lent back by us to him.” Above, p. 65: “a *praestaria* renewed for five years,” in accordance with the law on the renewal of *precariae* which Regino cites below in chapter 365 of this book. Thus those who lent property also granted *precariae*. Moreover, in place of these terms they also used *precation*, *petition*, *praestation*, and *benefice*, as is clear from the cited books of the *Antiquities of Fulda*.

CAP. 363.—“As a usufructuary.” That is, by *precaria*. For those who were formerly said to possess by *precaria* were later said to hold the property of churches as usufructuaries, as is clear from the same books of the *Antiquities of Fulda* [Col. 0438C]. To hold by *precarium* and to hold as a usufructuary mean the same thing.

575 This chapter is not divided in the Helmstedt edition or in the chapters of Charles the Bald, from which it was taken. The Paris manuscript, therefore, presents it divided in the manner in which we have edited it. First, the authority of the ancient codex caused us to depart from the Helmstedt edition at this point. Moreover, we had to proceed in this way in order to show the origin of this division, since the chapter is found divided in the same way in Burchard and Ivo as in the Paris manuscript. But Burchard, having decided not to use the authority of the capitularies of the Frankish kings, preferred to attribute the two parts of this chapter to the Council of Mâcon and to the Council at Carisiacum. This [Col. 0438D] misled Ivo, who, describing Burchard in Part III, chapters 233 and 234, claims that he himself received those constitutions from the Council of Mâcon and from the Council at Carisiacum. Thus, by Burchard’s art and industry, it came about that most of the chapters were thought to have been issued in certain synods, although they actually derived from the authority of our kings.

—“Except for liberty.” Perhaps this decree was directed against the barbarous and foolish custom of certain people who exchanged the churches’ slaves and bondsmen for mute animals, such as horses, as Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, testifies in the hundredth letter among the Bonifacian letters.

CAP. 376.—“No bishop.” This canon [Col. 0439A] forbids anyone among those constituted in the clergy to judge any case on Sunday. It appears to have been enacted so that no one, being called away from prayer, would neglect the Church of God. Agano, bishop of Autun, knew this rule. Nevertheless, on the very sacred day of Pentecost he undertook to judge a certain case. It should be understood, however, that the matter was so important that it disturbed the Church. Thus, although he stated that on so great a day one ought to devote oneself not to secular but to divine duties, he said that he had undertaken to judge that case because of its gravity, “also fearing,” he said, “the divine judgment if the matter were not mitigated by our authority.” We shall publish Agano’s complete charter, since it contains many things worthy of notice, in the Appendix of Ancient Acts.

[Col. 0439B] CAP. 378.—“Before Mass.” Today the practice is different. For if circumstances arise that make it necessary to permit farmers 576 or other workers to attend to their work on Sundays or feast days, this is no longer permitted before Mass but after it has been celebrated.

CAP. 382.—“Let him be banned.” Let him be cast out; let him be expelled.

CAP. 394.—“Whoever is free.” From this canon, which in fact belongs to the Fourth Council of Toledo, arose a considerable number of spurious canons wrongly attributed to the Toledan councils, although they do not and cannot occur in them. Regino had cited this one from the Council of Toledo. Then he referred to chapter 396—which, like chapter 395, was taken from Book I of the *Capitularies*—with the words “From the same,” that is, from the same book of the *Capitularies*. [Col. 0439C]

Burchard, either because he did not notice this or because he had decided to make no mention of the books of the *Capitularies*, cited chapter 396 from the Council of Toledo, chapter 82. He then attributed to the same council chapters 397, 398, 399, 402, and the two following chapters, because Regino’s codex did not indicate where they had been taken from. From this Burchard inferred that all of them had been taken from the Council of Toledo. Ivo and Gratian followed Burchard. But Loaysa refused to acknowledge those chapters as Toledan canons, although he included them at the end of the First Council of Toledo, sufficiently indicating in these words that he did not think they had been enacted in the Toledan councils: “Fragments cited, whether corruptly or falsely, under the title of the Toledan councils, since they are not found in those councils.”

[Col. 0439D] CAP. 399.—“Of the household of the Church.” That is, from the church’s slaves and bondsmen. See Book IV of the Visigothic Law, title 5, chapter 7.

CAP. 402.—“Who owes.” This formula also appears, in a slightly different form, in Marculf, Book II, chapter 32, and likewise in the chartulary of the monastery of Uzerche among the people of Limoges.

CAP. 403.—“By secular law.” Book II, chapter 112: “let him be brought to an end according to secular law”; and chapter 238: “according to secular law, may you suffer death.” There secular law is distinguished from ecclesiastical law—that is, civil law from canon law. But at that time they preferred to speak in this way. In the preface to the *Capitularies*, laws are divided into secular and ecclesiastical. The first two books belong to ecclesiastical law; the two following books to secular law. The first [Col. 0440A] 577 concerns bishops and clerics of the subsequent orders and monks; the second, laymen.

CAP. 404.—“In the pact of the Franks.” Burchard included this entire chapter in his *Decretum*, as usual, from the Council of Toledo, but did not transcribe the pact. Thus this passage will be obscure to anyone reading Burchard unless he seeks assistance from Regino, who immediately placed the pact here. He understands it as the pact made by the Franks with the Ripuarians. At that time they used this solemn term to signify a treaty or agreements of peace—what we would today call a *traité de paix ou d’alliance* (“treaty of peace or alliance”).

The Synod of Dingolfing, chapter 7: “That no one be deprived of his inheritance except for the three causes that shall be written in the pact.” Einhard, speaking under the year 812 of the envoys of Emperor Michael of Constantinople sent to Charlemagne: “When they came to the emperor at Aachen, [Col. 0440B] receiving from him in a letter the written text of the pact, they returned from there to Rome and in the basilica of Saint Peter received the same little book of the pact or treaty again from Pope Leo.”

CAP. 443.—“Whoever is a bishop.” This chapter requires some attention on our part. For it was taken from the ancient statutes of the Church, which were formerly read to each bishop at his consecration. Atto of Vercelli calls them the Ancient Statutes of the Easterners in his eighth letter, where he states that they had been numbered in one hundred chapters, and that their beginning was “Whoever is a bishop,” etc. Severinus Binius had seen two copies of these statutes, one belonging to the monastery of Gembloux and the other [Col. 0440C] to Saint Bavo at Ghent. It is therefore all the more surprising that he did not publish them. For although they are generally written in the Fourth Council of Carthage, they do not occur there in the order in which they are read in the ancient books. Regino, because he took these materials from that Council of Carthage, did not cite the Ancient Statutes of the Church. Since the matter is important and those statutes long remained in force in the Church, we shall eventually publish them from a very ancient manuscript codex.

NOTES ON THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK II

CAP. 1.—“From the Council of Rouen.” Regino frequently cites the canons of some Council of Rouen, which nevertheless are not found in the collections of councils. For, besides this canon, 578 Regino refers from the same council to chapters 68, 69, 167, 390, 406, 415, and 416 [Col. 0440D] of this second book. That council must have been ancient, since it was held before Regino. It may even be earlier than the year 858, since Herard of Tours uses certain words that occur in this chapter, as will be said immediately. But elsewhere there will be a more suitable place to discuss these matters.

“Synod.” That is, an assembly to be held in the church when the bishop comes to it to conduct a visitation. There were therefore two kinds of synod, as we said above. One was held by the bishop in the city, to which priests from rural parishes were required to come for an inquiry into their ministry. The other was held by the bishop or his ministers in each church when they carried out the duty [Col. 0441A] of visitation; there the priests rendered an account of their ministry, and the synodal cases of each parish were judged. Below, chapter 234: “Concerning what has been charged against me in this synod,” etc. And chapter 238: “Concerning what you have been accused of in the presence of this bishop in this synod,” etc.

I think that the canon of the Council of Tribur which Regino cites below, chapter 296, should be understood as referring to this latter synod. Richard, archbishop of Bourges, who lived during the reign of Philip I, king of the Franks, even calls an assembly held for the dedication of a certain church a council, because he undoubtedly did there what bishops at that time customarily did when they went around their dioceses.

“Let them attend without delay.” The Chapters of Herard, archbishop of Tours, chapter 133: “Let those summoned attend the synod without delay. Otherwise, let them be condemned.” [Col. 0441B]

“By no means in an easy matter.” In accordance with the rule of Saint Gregory, who writes thus to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, Book II, Indiction 10, Letter 4: “If there should perhaps be certain difficult matters which cannot at all be resolved by the judgment of your Fraternity, let these alone demand our judgment, so that, relieved of minor matters, we may devote ourselves more effectively to the greater cases.”

CAP. 2.—“A bishop in synod.” Burchard attributed this material, and what follows up to chapter 6, 579 to Pope Eutychian; it is likewise attributed to him in an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll. Yet it is evident from this that the material was copied into the old codex from Burchard’s *Decretum*, since the numbers written there [Col. 0441C] are those found in Burchard. The title reads: “The decretal institution of Pope Eutychian: what bishops ought to inquire into at a synod. Chapter XCI.” Then: “The synodal oath, XCII.” Afterwards: “The oath of the others, XCIII.” And so with the rest.

Therefore, before Burchard, these texts were not said to belong to Pope Eutychian; and in reality they cannot be his, since they contain much that clearly reflects the age of Charlemagne, whereas Eutychian sat in Rome toward the end of the third century. They were so little known in the age of Charlemagne—at least under the name of Eutychian or of any other Roman pontiff—that they are found neither in the collection of papal letters with which Riculfus, archbishop of Mainz, filled Gaul and Germany [Col. 0441D], nor are they cited by Regino as Eutychian’s. It likewise happened that those who prepared the collections of councils, although they indiscriminately published everything prefixed with the venerable names of ancient Roman pontiffs, nevertheless omitted these decrees of Eutychian.

My opinion is that these texts are not from any council or from the decrees of any Roman pontiff, but were a formula according to which bishops were to question laymen in each parish. Moreover, this formula was invented at the same time as the inquiry into the life of the clergy that is placed at the beginning of Book I.

CAP. 3.—“A synodal case.” That is, a matter belonging to the bishop’s cognizance, which should be judged in the episcopal court, namely, for the imposition of penance, [Col. 0442A] as is clear from chapters 238, 278, 318, and 426 of this second book. An unpublished old charter concerning the peace of the church of Morin, drawn up in the time of Callistus II: “But if the bishop or his legate should be injured or disturbed in the place where synodal cases are customarily litigated, and should be unable to settle the synodal matters peaceably, it has been determined by canonical judgment that thereafter all should come together to the mother church, there to administer justice in all matters concerning which they have been admonished through the bishop’s legation.”

CAP. 5, § 1.—580 “Feud.” That is, open and mortal hostility undertaken because one of a person’s relatives had been killed, as Sirmond correctly explains, and as is also clear from this passage of Regino [Col. 0442B] and from chapter 221. Sometimes, however, *faida* simply means hostility, even when no killing is involved, as in Book II of the Lombard Law, title 13, chapter 2. A constitution on restraining feuds appears below, chapter 81.

From *faida* is derived *faidosus*, that is, one who is suffering a feud and whose life is not secure because of mortal enmities. From the same source came the word *faiditus*, which properly means a rebel and traitor, proscribed and exiled for that reason, as we noted in the notes on the Councils of Narbonnese Gaul. Vossius is mistaken, for he was misled by a corrupt reading found in Peter the monk of Vaux-de-Cernay, in chapter 85 of the *History of the Albigensians*, where *faydici* are mentioned after the *ruptarii*, [Col. 0442C] and also by a marginal note in which it is written, “perhaps *fatidici*.” He therefore thought that the passage concerned people who promised to predict the fates of others, whereas it concerns *faiditi*, that is, proscribed or banned traitors. Hence *faidimentum*, “treason.”

§ 6. “What they call *morth*.” Book I of the Lombard Law, title 9, chapter 15, and title 36, chapter 1: “If a royal slave commits *morth*, we decree that he shall pay compensation for the person according to the value at which that person has been assessed, and that the slave himself shall be hanged over the grave of the dead man, so that vengeance may be taken on him and the matter brought to an end.”

§ 53. “For weaving webs.” The Helmstedt edition has *ordinandis* (“for arranging”); the manuscript codex has *ordiendis* (“for weaving”). Isaiah, chapter XXV: “The web which he has woven.”

§ 55. “Except in a church.” Thus, during those times, the bodies of the dead were carried to the church and kept there during the night watches. This practice was later changed. But it is not easy to determine exactly when this alteration took place. The distinguished Laurentius Bochellus, in Book III of the *Decrees of the Church of Gaul*, title 18, chapter 11, reports a decree from the synodal statutes of the Church of Rheims, in which it is prescribed that the bodies of the dead “not be watched over in the church at night, because of the evil practices that might result from this and that often occurred in former times.” Then, in chapter 30 of the same title, he sets out 581 another decree from the synodal statutes of the Church of Troyes, in which it is written: “Let parish priests forbid their parishioners to keep vigil in the church at night when the bodies of some of the dead [Col. 0443A] are brought there or elsewhere, because of the evil practices committed there and that occurred in former times.”

But the distinguished author did not note the time when these statutes were enacted. Even earlier, the Council of Eliberis had decreed in canon 35: “Women are not to keep vigil in the cemetery, because they often secretly commit crimes under the pretext of prayer.”

CAP. 6.—Burchard copied this material at the beginning of Book VI, from the Council of Tribur. Yet he uses Regino’s wording, which is more elegant than the readings in the received editions of the Synod of Tribur. He initially attributed the material to Pope Melchiades, to whom no one else has attributed it. But when he saw that Regino repeated it from canonical sanctions and from the judgment of bishops, he thought that the “judgment of bishops” belonged to the canons of the Council of Tribur, while the “canonical sanctions” must be attributed to some Roman pontiff. Then, conveniently, the name of Melchiades undoubtedly occurred to him. Such was the man’s character.

CAP. 9.—“The Mass of Saint John.” That is, the feast.

### Chapter 41

This chapter does not appear in the oldest book of the Capitularies in the Royal Library, from which the first Paris edition of the Capitularies was published; nor does it appear in the Colbertine manuscript, or finally in the Rivipullensian manuscript. Nevertheless, since it was published from an old book, and since this collection of Regino, as well as an old manuscript collection of canons in the Royal Library, confirms it, there is no doubt that it once existed in the books of the Capitularies.

Whether, however, it was copied into Book IV, as the common editions of the Capitularies have it; into Book II, as Regino cites it; or finally into Book V, as in the old collection just mentioned, is difficult to determine. In that collection it reads:

> Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 90. For slain priests, payment shall be made to the bishop to whose parish they belong.

From this we may infer that the diligence of copyists sometimes caused many things to be omitted from the new copies they made of the Capitularies, although those things still existed in the older copies.

As is his custom, Burchard does not cite this chapter from the books of the Capitularies, but from the Council of Tribur, chapter 5. In fact, chapter 4 of that council establishes a payment of compensation for a murdered priest. Nevertheless, everything there differs from the meaning of this chapter.

Burchard was therefore misled because he thought that the chapters following chapter 37 of this book—which is expressly taken from the canons of the Council of Tribur—belonged to the same council until one reached the constitution of the Council of Worms. This is the source and origin—something that must often be said—of many errors in Burchard.

Yet in this passage he also seems not to have acted in good faith. For what is said there about the Capitularies of Charlemagne he omitted, lest anyone should think that he had taken this chapter from the books of the Capitularies. Thus Ivo and Gratian, who do not have that clause appended in their editions, were deceived by Burchard.

### Chapter 43

“Together with twelve.” In Burchard and Gratian it reads, “together with seventy-two, he shall swear.” But in the Council of Mainz, from which this chapter was taken, it reads, “together with twelve, he shall swear.” It is also found in this form in Regino, both in the Helmstedt edition and in the Paris manuscript.

Moreover, it is absurd to compel anyone to find so many compurgators. Finally, it is clear from Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 23; Book IV, chapters 13 and 26; and Book V, chapter 201; as well as from Book I of the Law of the Lombards, title 13, chapter 3; title 16, chapter 2; title 25, chapter 73; and Book II, title 1, chapter 2; title 14, chapter 1; and title 55, chapters 2, 3, 5, and 33; and finally from title 53 of the Law of the Alamanni and titles 8 and 52 of the Law of the Burgundians, that ordinarily only twelve were then employed.

Nevertheless, the author of the Annals of Fulda, under the year 898, reports that seventy-two oath-helpers were used in the case of Queen Ota, if the reading is correct.

> “Let him lose his wife.”

In Burchard and Gratian, and also in Book V of the Decretals, it reads, “and let him remain without hope of marriage”—a very significant difference, as everyone can see. Certainly, chapter 24 of the Council of Mainz, from which, as we have said, this chapter was taken, has “and let him lose his wife.”

### Chapter 61

“Reginbald, chorepiscopus.” He supported Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, in bearing the episcopal burden, as is evident from Rudolf’s *Life of Rabanus* and from an old inscription published by Brower in Book II, chapter 15, of the *Antiquities of Fulda*. It reads:

> “In the year of the Lord 808” (read: 838), “in the fifteenth indiction, this oratory was dedicated by order of Otgar, archbishop, by Reginbald, chorepiscopus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October.”

Moreover, Rabanus’s letter written to him, which Regino cites here, has not yet been published in full. Regino reports other fragments of it below, in chapters 202 and 344. Reginbald’s epitaph appears among the poems of Rabanus.

After Reginbald’s death, Thiotmar became chorepiscopus of Mainz, as Rabanus testifies in a letter written to him, which appears at the beginning of his book *On the Sacred Orders*. These are his words:

> “And because I chose you as my co-worker in the sacred ministry, I urge you to make known to those who have been ordained to the priesthood and who must exercise the priestly ministry what I cannot explain publicly before many people because of the weakness of my body—you, who are younger in age and stronger in body.”

Thus the old manuscript of the Royal Library from which we recently published Rabanus’s book *On Chorepiscopi* belonged to that same Thiotmar, since the following words were anciently written at the front of the book:

> “Thiotmar, chorepiscopus, acquired this.”

Since the occasion has arisen, something should also be said about that book. The priest Rudolf mentions it in the *Life of Rabanus*:

> “There are also other little works of his,” he says, “which he found it necessary to compose in response to questions from various people. One of them is on the ordination of chorepiscopi; concerning this he wrote a book to Archbishop Drogo.”

But to return to Thiotmar: he had previously been a monk of Fulda under Rabanus, as the same Rudolf teaches in these words:

> “A certain priest from among our monks, named Theotmar, was sent by the abbot to Archbishop Otgar for certain matters.”

### Chapter 69

“Before the door.” This canon commands that children whose mothers do not wish to be recognized should not be killed, but should be exposed before the church door, so that afterward they may be taken in by some faithful person and brought up. See Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 142, and Burchard, Book III, chapters 201 and 202.

### Chapter 75

This chapter does not appear in Book III of the Capitularies as it is printed today, but in Book I. Nevertheless, it is found at the end of Book III in the old manuscript from which the first Paris edition of the Capitularies was produced; likewise in the Rivipullensian manuscript and also in the Colbertine manuscript.

In none of the old manuscripts that I have seen does it appear in Book I. And, what is remarkable, it does not appear in the manuscript used by those who prepared the first Paris edition. The same thing happened with the chapter on equal measures and weights, as we shall note below at chapter 427 of this book.

### Chapter 77

“They call it the field.” This has been emended from the Paris manuscript. The Helmstedt edition had, “which they call the chapter.”

A diploma of King Robert, cited by François Pithou, says:

> “The law of judicial combat, which is commonly called the field.”

The Synod of Dingolfing, chapter 24, says:

> “Whoever, after the judgment in the aforesaid combat—which we call *Camfwic*—has been completed, presumes to rise against the complainant with like vengeance, shall swear the oath called *ahteid* in church with the three compurgators named above.”

Hence *camphio* occurs in Book II, title 55, chapters 11 and 24, of the Law of the Lombards; and *campio* in Book I, titles 3 and 4, chapter 6, of the same law. See Lindenbrog’s *Glossary*.

### Chapter 80

“*Cotiones*” [a technical term of uncertain sense]. Hence Hincmar, Letter 5, to Charles the Bald:

> “Even those *cocciones* [the same uncertain term] themselves commit robberies.”

See Pithou’s *Glossary*.

### Chapter 81

“For restraining.” Thus the old manuscript reads, and the books of the Capitularies agree with it. The Helmstedt edition reads: “Concerning the feuds of co-heirs.”

### Chapter 100

“Not human.” Innocent III used the same manner of argument to show that the transfer, deposition, and resignation of bishops belong by divine law to the supreme pontiff. For he says that God reserved the dissolution of a carnal marriage to his own judgment alone, whereas the spiritual bond is stronger than the carnal one; therefore no one except the Roman pontiff can touch these matters.

> “For,” he says, “a spiritual marriage is dissolved not by human authority, but by divine authority when, through the authority of the Roman pontiff, who is known to be the vicar of Jesus Christ, a bishop is removed from the Church by transfer, deposition, or even resignation.”

This constitution appears in Book I of the letters of Innocent III, Letter 532, and from there in the chapter *Inter corporalia*, *On the Transfer of a Bishop*. See Book I of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 26, §8.

### Chapter 114

“Since we, from both sides.” It should be noted here that Pope Nicholas did not assume jurisdiction over the divorce of Lothair and Thetberga solely by privilege of his see, but because he had been chosen judge by both parties.

This observation is important for refuting the argument of Innocent III. Writing to Philip Augustus about his divorce from Ingelburge, and referring to the example of Lothair, Innocent says that what Nicholas did against Lothair he himself had done by virtue of his office and authority:

> “Do you think, illustrious king, that although our aforesaid predecessor surpassed us in merit and wisdom, we are inferior to him in office and authority?”

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the year 1208.

### Chapter 126

“Without permission.” See the notes on Agobard’s *Apology*, chapter 9.

### Chapter 130

In Paul, Book II of the *Sentences*, title 19, this chapter is expressed as follows:

> “Neither a madman nor a madwoman can contract marriage; but a marriage that has been contracted is not dissolved by madness.”

Anianus added this interpretation to that sentence:

> “If persons have contracted marriage while of sound mind, and madness or insanity has subsequently come upon one of the two, their marriage cannot be dissolved because of this illness.”

These words alone are found in Paul and his interpreter. What follows, therefore, in Regino and Burchard may perhaps have been taken from a letter of Nicholas I to Charles, archbishop of Mainz. Fragments of it are reported by Luitprand—or someone else—in the *Life of Nicholas I*; by Burchard in excerpts published by Stevartius, p. 687; and by Gratian, Distinction 50, chapter 33, and Causa 32, question 7, chapter 25.

Burchard attributes that last chapter—the one we are now discussing—to Nicholas himself. But in Gratian there is an added clause not found in Regino or Burchard. The Gratian edition reads:

> “The same must be thought concerning those who are blinded by their adversaries, or whose limbs are cut off, or who have been mutilated by barbarians.”

See Antonius Augustinus, Book II of *On the Correction of Gratian*, dialogue 18.

### Chapter 158

“On that same night.” This canon exhorts a man and his new bride to abstain from marital intercourse on the first night of their marriage. In some dioceses this exhortation was later turned into an obligation.

For example, at Abbeville, in the diocese of Amiens, there was formerly a custom that those who had recently married were not permitted to have intercourse during the first three nights after the wedding. The Paris Parlement abolished this custom by its decree of 1501, on 11 March:

> “As for not sleeping with his wife for three nights at the beginning of the marriage, the petitioners shall have relief while the case is pending, and the newly married may freely sleep with their wives during the first three nights.”

Stephen Poncher, bishop of Paris, inserted that entire decree into his *Synodal Statutes*. I think, however, that the printer made an error in the edition of the *Synodal Statutes* of Stephen Poncher, bishop of Paris, and that the decree is a full century older.

For in an old collection of legal decisions by Matthieu Chartier, advocate of Paris, which I possess in manuscript, the following is found:

> “The first day of March 1401: the decision issued against the bishop of Amiens concerning the taxation of the sacraments and other ecclesiastical matters.”

Then, in another old manuscript which the distinguished Antoine Vion of Herouval once shared with me, the following appears in exactly these words:

> “In the year 1409, on the nineteenth day of March, it was declared by decision of the court that the prohibitions made at the request of the attorney general and the mayor and aldermen of Abbeville in Ponthieu, by virtue of certain royal letters, against the bishop of Amiens and the curates of that town—namely, against the said bishop, so that he should neither take nor exact money from newly married persons in order to give them permission to sleep with their wives on the first, second, and third nights of their marriage, and the other matters contained in the said decision—were good and valid; and that the opposition of the said bishop had been entered without exception, except with regard to the general exceptions, concerning which it was declared that the prohibitions had been made without cause.
>
> “And it was declared that each of the said inhabitants might sleep *cum uxoribus suis*—with their wives—on the first night of their marriage without the bishop’s permission; and that inhabitants who died might be buried without the permission of the bishop and his officials, unless there were a canonical impediment.
>
> “Furthermore, the heirs and executors of the will of any deceased person could not be compelled or required to carry out the ordinances made by the officials of the said bishop, or by the bishop himself, concerning the wills made by such intestates; but the bishop could charitably admonish them to do what was beneficial for the soul of the intestate.
>
> “And the heirs or executors of the will of any deceased person could, within one year of the death, submit its execution to the secular or ecclesiastical court, together with many other matters contained in the decision.”

Thus Innocent III, Book X, Letter 85, restrained the avarice of the bishop of Le Puy, who prevented the lawful marriages of widows until they had redeemed his consent with money.

“*Genitiarias*” (“female astrologers”). See above, Book I, chapter 246.

### Chapter 178

“Mundiburdi.” That is, guardians, as below in chapter 38 of the Second Appendix. The common version of canon 24 of the Council of Tribur, from which this chapter was taken, designates guardianship by the term “protection.” *Mundeburdis*, or *mundeburdium*, means guardianship, defense, or protection. The Laws of the Lombards use *mundualdus* for *mundiburdus*, or guardian.

### Chapter 179

“From the altar.” For they themselves had to take the veil from the altar and place it upon themselves; this was forbidden to bishops.

### Chapter 199

“Morchidum.” Thus the Helmstedt edition reads; so does the Paris manuscript, Burchard, the Roman Penitential of Antonius Augustinus, title 3, chapter 8, and finally Ivo, Part IX, chapter 70, in all editions.

Nevertheless, Lindenbrog and Voss confidently read *mortridum* in Ivo, as though that were the only reading found there, although they cite no ancient manuscript as the authority for their emendation.

It therefore seemed that the old reading should be retained. Following the agreement of so many books, we also restored it in chapter 20 of Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, where Stevart’s edition had *mordicum*. Although that word is corrupt, it indicates that *morchidum* was originally written in that letter.

*Morchidum*, therefore, as Antonius Augustinus correctly observed, means “homicide.” It is not, however, derived from *caedes* (“slaughter”), as he thought, since *morchidum* is not a Latin word but a Germanic one, as Rabanus teaches in the passage just cited.

### Chapter 200

“Let crime increase.” After those words, eight leaves are missing from the Paris manuscript, namely, up to the seventh paragraph of chapter 246. The Helmstedt edition therefore conveniently supplied this gap. Wherever it seemed not to be free from error, we corrected it from the common editions of the Councils or of the writers from whom the chapters copied onto those eight missing leaves had been taken. We also used Burchard and an ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which contains several fragments of Rabanus’s letters to Bishop Humbert and to Reginbald, chorepiscopus. In some places we were also assisted by the Roman Penitential edited by Antonius Augustinus.

### Chapter 112

“Geniculo.” That is, generation or offspring. See Book VI of the Capitularies, chapters 80 and 128; the Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 30; and Book II of the Law of the Lombards, title 14, chapter 1. They also used *genu* for *geniculum*, as in the *Capitula* of Haito of Basel, chapter 21, and elsewhere.

### Chapter 222

“Sixty solidi.” The punishment for one who received an incestuous person was here, in Regino, eleven solidi. Since we lacked the assistance of a manuscript at this point, we corrected it from other sources.

In the Council of Metz under Pippin, from which this passage was taken; in the printed and manuscript books of the Capitularies; and finally in the canons of Isaac, bishop of Langres, both printed and manuscript, title 4, chapter 1, it is consistently written that whoever transgressed this law was to pay sixty solidi to the king.

This was the *bannus dominicus*, or royal fine, as is evident from various passages in the Capitularies. The error in Regino therefore arose from a transposition of the numerals: XI instead of LX.

### Chapter 231

“Count.” *Nar­rare*, “to recount”; French *compter*, “to count.”

### Chapter 243

“To the cross.” Judgment by the cross was later prohibited by the law of Charlemagne, found in Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 108, and Book II of the Law of the Lombards, title 55, chapter 32. Nevertheless, this practice continued to be observed, as is clear from Agobard.

“Into human servitude.” There was therefore some form of lust that reduced free men to servitude, just as was noted above concerning women at chapter 246 of Book I. Thus in Book VIII, title 6, chapter 11, of the Law of the Visigoths, the counterfeiter of money loses his freedom and is assigned to servitude.

### Chapter 262

“These things concerning many.” These are Regino’s words.

### Chapter 274

“Bastiniacum.” In Book VI of the Capitularies and in the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald, *bastonico* is read. They interpret this as the strictest custody. I think it refers to a royal prison, such as those now called *conciergeries*.

Moreover, the clause beginning “but afterward,” and continuing up to “let him suffer the penalties,” does not appear in the Helmstedt edition. It was therefore added from the Paris manuscript.

### Chapter 276

“The body of the Lord.” Others have already observed that one of the various forms of judgment formerly used in doubtful cases was the body of the Lord. Helgald, at the beginning of his *Life* of King Robert, teaches that this practice was condemned by Robert in a letter written to Leotharic, archbishop of Sens.

Nevertheless, Lambert of Hersfeld testifies that the custom was still retained in the time of Gregory VII. Under the year 1077 he says that Gregory, after celebrating Mass and completing the sacred offering, summoned the king to the altar and, holding the body of the Lord before him, spoke at length about his innocence and finally added:

> “So that, by a brief act of satisfaction, I may remove from everyone every scruple of scandal, behold, let the body of the Lord which I am about to receive serve me today as a test of my innocence. May almighty God, by his judgment today, either absolve me from suspicion of the crime charged against me, if I am innocent, or destroy me by sudden death, if I am guilty.”

After prefacing these and other terrifying words, as is customary, and praying that God would be present as the most just judge of his cause and the defender of his innocence, he took part of the body of the Lord and ate it.

See the following chapter of Regino, which concerns the same subject. See also the appendix added to Regino’s *Chronicle* under the year 841.

### Chapter 282

“He commits sacrilege.” See the notes on Agobard’s *On the Administration of Ecclesiastical Property*, chapter 18.

### Chapter 292

“Let him bear a feud.” French: *Porte inimitié*, “he bears enmity.” See Sirmond’s notes on the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald.

### Chapter 295

“Communion.” It should be read *commonitione*, “admonition,” as we noted. For in the common canons of the Fourth Council of Toledo, *admonitione* is written where Regino has *communione*. Immediately afterward, the canon calls “admonition” what it had called “communion” in this passage.

Below, in chapter 408, we read: “But if those three admonitions,” and so forth. The Paris manuscript, however, has: “But if those three communions.”

From this it follows that the words *communio* and *commonitio* were formerly accustomed to be interchanged, and that the emendation introduced by the illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, into the letter of the Italian Council to Theodosius is legitimate. Sirmond had printed:

> “from which flow the rights of every venerable admonition,”

whereas Marca restored:

> “from which flow the rights of every venerable communion.”

### Chapter 297

“Impunity for vices.” Lupus of Ferrières, in his *Book on Three Questions*, p. 210:

> “The hope of impunity is a great enticement to sin.”

It is established that Lupus attended this Synod of Soissons, during whose second session he disclosed to the synod the proceedings concerning the deposition of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims.

Since he was therefore present at the synod, and since his words are found in this canon, I am compelled to wonder whether he may not have been the author of the canons of this Synod of Soissons, just as he was the author of the canons found at the palace of Verneuil.

For, as we said long ago in connection with Lupus’s Letter 60, the Gallican bishops held him in such high regard that they regarded him almost as a maker of canons and in some sense considered his presence at synods necessary. Again, Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans used his services when they wrote to Pope Nicholas against Herimann, bishop of Nevers—Letter 130 among the letters of Lupus.

### Chapter 309

“*Contione* or *contentione*.” In the Theodosian Code, only *in contentione* is found. This was therefore a copyist’s note. Unable to determine which reading should be preferred—*contione* or *contentione*—he inserted both, leaving the judgment to the reader.

Ancient copyists used to do this, as we have demonstrated with numerous examples in connection with Salvian, p. 403, and Lupus of Ferrières, pp. 346 and 451.

The same remedy may perhaps be applied to this passage of Minucius Felix:

> “while they build altars to unknown divinities and to the spirits of the dead.”

Desiderius Herald thought that the final phrase was superfluous or corrupt. What if we read:

> “to unknown divinities or to the spirits of the dead,”

so that this too is a copyist’s note?

In Saint Gregory, Book IV, Letter 53, the printed text reads in this way: “from consideration or comparison of this matter it is properly inferred.” In place of this, the oldest manuscript of Saint-Remigius at Reims has only:

> “it is inferred from comparison of the matter.”

These minor details are sometimes of great importance.

### Chapter 312

“He dares to swear.” In Regino, both in the Helmstedt edition and in the Paris manuscript, the consistent reading is:

> “upon holy things he dares to swear.”

It is written in the same way in Burchard, who unquestionably copied Regino.

Nevertheless, in all the books of the Capitularies, both printed and manuscript, it reads:

> “upon holy things he is required to swear,”

which gives an excellent sense, and this alone is the correct reading.

The reading of the same chapter preferred by Regino, in which there is no mention of the Gunebodigni, is confirmed by the oldest books of the Capitularies in the Royal and Colbertine Libraries, as well as by Burchard, Ivo of Chartres, Part XII, chapter 23, an old manuscript collection of canons in the Royal Library, and Gratian, Causa 22, question 5, chapter *Parvuli*.

For nowhere does the clause added to this passage in the edition of the Capitularies appear:

> “as the Gunebodigni do.”

Yet this clause is found in the edition of Vitus Amerbach, as well as in the Paris editions, the old manuscript of the monastery of Ripoll, and finally the book of Lombard laws.

Amerbach notes that in the manuscript he used, the word *Guntbodigni* had been written above *Gunebodigni*; neither word, however, appears in chapter *Parvuli*, Causa 22, question 5. He says:

> “It signifies some nation, people, or family.”

The otherwise very learned Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, was no more successful than Amerbach in explaining this word. In Book I of *On the Correction of Gratian*, dialogue 13, seeking to determine what the word *Gunebodigni* means, he invents the notion that they were enemies of Charlemagne.

Yet the *Gunebodigni*—that is, those who lived under the law of Gundobad, namely, the Burgundians—were not enemies of Charlemagne, since they were subject to his empire.

That they were people who used the law of Gundobad is sufficiently shown by the word itself and is also clear from the cited book of Lombard laws. There, in place of what the editions of the Capitularies have as *Gunebodigni*, we read:

> “as those living under the law of Gundobad do.”

See our notes on Agobard’s book *Against the Law of Gundobad*.

### Chapter 314

“Excepting these *sacr.* [sacred …].” This was the ordinary manner of speaking at that time. Below, in chapter 358, *excepto ad ecclesiam* (“except at the church”), and in Book III of the Law of the Visigoths, title 5, chapter 1, the common editions read:

> “*exceptis illis personis*” (“excepting those persons”).

Instead of this, the oldest manuscripts of the monastery of Moissac and of the church of Albi have:

> “*excepto illas personas*” (“excepting those persons”),

with *excepto* governing the accusative *illas personas*.

### Chapter 315

“Indiculum.” This was then the common name for a ruler’s diploma issued for immediate use. French: *une lettre de cachet*, “a sealed letter.”

Boniface of Mainz, Letter 104, to King Pippin:

> “A certain servant of our Church came to us with your *indiculum*,”

and so forth. See the notes on Agobard’s *On the Insolence of the Jews*.

### Chapter 334

“With shields and clubs.” See Book II of the Law of the Lombards, title 55, chapter 29.

### Chapter 346

“A Christian slave [the source breaks off].” See the notes on Agobard’s *On the Insolence of the Jews*.

### Chapter 358

“Vows at tree[s …].” The *Capitulary of Charlemagne concerning the regions of Saxony*, chapter 20:

> “If anyone makes a vow at springs, trees, or groves, or offers anything according to pagan custom, and eats in honor of demons,”

and so forth.

Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 64:

> “Likewise, concerning trees, stones, or springs, where foolish people make lights or perform other observances, we command absolutely that this most wicked custom, hateful to God, wherever it is found, be removed and destroyed.”

See again Book VII, chapter 236.

These statutes were enacted after the time of Saint Boniface, who took care to eradicate that superstition, as Othlo of Fulda relates in Book I of his *Life*. Boniface himself, in Letter 128, also admonishes the peoples of Germany wholly to reject and abandon the omens or amulets of groves and springs. See Pithou’s *Glossary*, under *Luminaria* (“lights”).

### Chapter 363

Regino took this canon from the same place from which he had taken the preceding three chapters, namely, from Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre.

Because Rabanus had cited it from the Council of Ancyra, Regino too claims to have taken it from there, and Burchard and Ivo followed him.

Nevertheless, this canon is not from the Council of Ancyra, but without doubt from some old Penitential Book.

### Chapter 364

In Regino this chapter is entitled:

> “From the preceding.”

This was clearly placed there so that readers would understand that the following chapter dealt with the same subject as the one treated shortly before, namely, the magical practices of women.

Burchard then followed Regino. When he was preparing his collection, taking most of it from Regino, he was misled by the false heading of the preceding canon, which is wrongly attributed to the Council of Ancyra. He therefore thought that the words “from the preceding” referred to the Council of Ancyra.

Ivo of Chartres, Part XI, chapter 30, copied them from Burchard, and Gratian, Causa 26, question 5, chapter 12, who say that they received this canon from chapter 1 of the Council of Ancyra.

Antonius Augustinus, a man highly skilled in these matters, correctly observed in Book I of *On the Correction of Gratian*, dialogue 14, that this heading is false, and that a large part of the chapter is found in Augustine’s *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 28—namely, everything between the words “certain criminal women” and “and with Ezekiel.”

If conjecture is permissible, I think this chapter was certainly taken from some previously unpublished capitulary of one of our kings. For it plainly bears the manner of speech of those times. At that period such chapters were customarily filled with testimonies and passages from the sacred Scriptures, the canons, and the ancient Doctors, as is obvious to everyone.

### Chapter 365

“*Strumenta*.” *Instrumenta*, “documents.” A decree of Louis the Pious for the church of Paris:

> “Because through the carelessness and negligence of the guardians of that church, the documents of the charters had been burned, consumed by fire, or lost.”

And below:

> “The slaves who had been handed over to that church by the aforesaid documents of the charters.”

A decree of Louis the Transmarine for the church of Autun:

> “And if the documents of those matters or charters should be held immediately at hand.”

### Chapter 412

“Through Peter.” This is an ambiguous manner of speaking, by which it may be meant either that authority was bestowed upon bishops by Christ in the person of Peter, or that Peter alone received that power and afterward shared it with the bishops. Some Roman pontiffs were imbued with this conviction.

The true and genuine meaning of the passage, however, is that bishops received their authority from Christ in the person of Peter, who at that time represented the whole Church in a figurative universal person, as Augustine says.

### Chapter 416

“Concerning confession.” These are Regino’s words.

### Chapter 424

This chapter does not appear among the capitula announced at Valence in the year 853, which are preserved in the manuscript of the capitularies of Charles the Bald.

It is found, however, among the capitula enacted immediately after the assembly held at Valence, at Servais, where it is clear from the preface that those capitula were reread. Concerning this matter, see the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald, title 13, chapter 6, and title 13, chapter 31.

### Chapter 426

“By the judgment of God.” That is, by the judgment of boiling or cold water, or of heated iron.

In ancient times, as Aventinus observes in Book IV of the *Annals of Bavaria*, this meant “to be wise, to have faith in God, and to place all hope in him.” Now, however, these practices are counted among the foolishness and insanities of those centuries.

Aventinus therefore concludes that the same act often received different names in different ages: in one place, piety; elsewhere, error.

“Or let them redeem it.” Namely, the hand which they were about to lose because of this crime. Above, chapter 314 of this book:

> “If anyone is convicted of perjury, let him lose his hand, or redeem it.”

And chapter 334:

> “But let the other false witnesses redeem their hands.”

### Chapter 427

We already noted, at chapter 75 of this book, that the order of the Capitularies had been disturbed and that a chapter which appears in the fourth book in the manuscripts had been thrown into the first book, although Regino also cites it from the fourth.

The same happened with this chapter on weights and measures, which Regino reports from Book III of the Capitularies. For it does not appear in Book I of the manuscript from which the first Paris edition was produced; nor in the Rivipullensian manuscript; nor finally in the Colbertine manuscript.

In both places it is found at the end of Book III. In the old manuscript from which the first Paris edition was produced, it is numbered 87; in the Rivipullensian manuscript, 92; and in the Colbertine manuscript, finally, 90, as Regino cites it.

### Chapter 432

“Individual beavers.” See above, Book I, chapter 216.

## Notes on Appendix I

### Chapter 1

“The most wicked letter.” He means the letter which the heretic Aldebert published, but which was reread and condemned at the Roman Council held under Pope Zacharias.

That letter began:

> “Here begins the letter of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, which fell at Jerusalem; and this letter was found by the archangel Michael at the gate of Ephraim,”

and so forth.

### Chapter 39

The author of this appendix cites this canon from the *Canons of the Ancient Oriental Fathers*, chapter 20—that is, from Martin of Braga’s collection. Burchard, however, reports it from a letter sent by Pope Fabian to the Orientals, where it does not occur. In fact, it is from the Council of Neocaesarea, whence Martin of Braga transferred it into his collection.

### Chapter 40

“He who is under servile condition.” Since these matters ceased long ago to be included in the Pontifical Books—in which, formerly, in the order for celebrating sacred orders, an admonition was first read that excluded certain persons from sacred orders according to the canons, especially slaves unless they had obtained freedom from their masters—it seemed worthwhile to publish at the end of these notes a fragment from an old manuscript Pontifical Book, now preserved in the Royal Library, so that from it at least we may gather the ancient practice.

### Chapter 43

“On the crime of adultery.” This was then the name given to the offense of widows who, after assuming the religious habit, entered into marriage.

The same women are discussed in chapter 56 of this appendix and chapter 46 of the Second Appendix, where such widows are plainly shown to be adulteresses. See also the celebrated history of a certain widow who fell into this form of adultery, in our notes on Agobard’s apologetic book on behalf of the sons of Louis the Pious.

### Chapter 44

This canon of Orange reads as follows in the first volume of the Councils of Gaul:

> “But the abductor of such women,”

and so forth.

The edition of Isidore published by Merlin has:

> “But the repudiator of her,”

The manuscript of Regino has:

> “But her robber,”

from which we produced *robatorem*, “robber.”

In ancient times, *robatores* were called those who forcibly took away some object. At first, as Spelman correctly notes, the word was used of those who had taken *robes* or *raubes*—that is, garments—from travelers.

In title 19, chapter 10, of the Salic Law, as Voss cites it in Book II of *On the Vices of Language*:

> “If anyone attacks another on the road and robs him.”

As the same author notes in Book I, *raubare* is corrupted from the Latin *rapere*, “to seize.” Therefore, whether we read *raptorem*, “abductor,” or *robatorem*, “robber,” the meaning remains the same. Nevertheless, we have thought that readers should be informed of the matter.

### Chapter 50

This chapter is not found among the common African canons. In Ivo, Part VII, chapter 145, and Gratian, Causa 27, question 1, chapter 34, it is cited from a letter of Pope Nicholas to Charles, archbishop of Mainz, and his suffragans.

It is certainly possible that these words were written by Nicholas but taken from some African canon which, like many others, is no longer available to us.

### Chapter 53

The very distinguished scholar Joannes Morinus cites this passage in the appendix to his book *On Penance*, page 39, and calls it a decree “at Conofurth.” The learned man was evidently misled by the fact that the book, written in large letters, has at the end of one line *infra*, and in the next *Conofurth*, which he read as *infra Conofurth*. Yet everyone can see that the final syllable of the preceding line must be joined to the first word of the following one, so that it should be read *Franconofurth*. What Franconofurth is, everyone understands.

“Nuendum.” Thus it is written in the old manuscript. For this, *petendum* (“to be sought” or “requested”) seems to be the proper reading—unless, perhaps, *nuendum* has the same force. [Col. 0454C]

### Chapter 57

*Adalwino.* It is astonishing how far the name of the bishop to whom this letter of Nicholas was written, and even the name of the see over which he presided, has deviated from the original. In Burchard it is said to have been written to Adalwin, archbishop of the holy Church of Vivenensis. In Ivo, Part VII, chapter 65, it is addressed to Adalwin, archbishop of the holy Church of Viennensis; but in the margin of the latest edition, “Vivanensis”; and in chapter 152, to Aluminus, bishop of Junariensis. In Gratian, Distinction 27, chapter 6, it is addressed to Albinus, archbishop of the Church of Vienne. In that place the Roman correctors note that these names vary greatly in the manuscripts, both in Burchard and in Ivo.

Ignorance of the true and legitimate address was the cause of error for the most learned archbishop of Tarragona, Antonio Agustín. For, in Book II of his *On the Correction of Gratian*, Dialogue 17, attempting to correct Gratian at this point, he supposes that Albinus, to whom he read that letter of Nicholas as having been written, was the same person whom some call the archbishop of Januensis and others the bishop of Jovanensis.

But in order at last to put an end to such great disagreement, the correct reading must be established. The letter, therefore, was written to Adalwin, archbishop of Juvavum, as is confirmed by the manuscript of Regino and also by an old anonymous collector of canons in manuscript in the Royal Library. That Juvavum is the same as Salzburg is too well known to require testimony. Moreover, it is certain that Adalwin held the see of Salzburg from the beginning of Nicholas’s pontificate, and that in the year 870 he attended the Council of Cologne. At this time there was certainly no archbishop named Albinus or Adalwin at Vienne. [Col. 0454D–0455A] Ado succeeded Agilmar in 859 and died in 874. [Col. 0456A]

[Col. 0455]

## 597–601. APPENDIX OF ANCIENT ACTS MENTIONED IN THE NOTES

### I. LETTER OF POPE ZACHARIAS TO THEODORUS, BISHOP OF TICINUM

From an old manuscript of the Royal Library.

Zacharias, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother Theodorus, bishop of the Church of Ticinum.

Your venerable fraternity presented us with a written petition in which you asked us whether it is permissible for a son whose father had received another man’s daughter from the sacred font—that is, his spiritual daughter, as it is cruel to say—to take her in marriage; you asserted that this had happened in your region in a particularly scandalous manner.

But your holy fraternity knows well that the Lord commanded Moses, saying: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father; you shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother; you shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, nor the nakedness of the daughter of your father. It is your nakedness.” Nakedness is said to be uncovered when we are commanded to abstain from our own blood relationship. [Col. 0455B]

How much more, with every occasion or argument set aside, must we strictly guard ourselves from the spiritual daughter of our father, lest anyone who has failed to restrain the reins of lust and has become involved in such a crime incur the anger of divine judgment. Therefore everyone must carefully avoid involvement in such a crime, lest they perish eternally.

But those who, despising the salvation of their souls, have entered into this impious marriage out of ruinous presumption, your fraternity should strive by every means to separate and subject to a fitting penance, so that, rescued from eternal damnation, you may win their souls, with the Lord’s help.

Regarding the children who are said to have been born from them, you asked whether they may be joined in marriage. But why should these children be prohibited from marriage, or compelled to do penance for such a matter, since they are declared free from condemnation on this account? For “the father shall not bear punishment for the son, nor the son for the father,” as the Lord says through the prophet: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it shall die.” [Col. 0455C]

But, dearest brother, let what has been said about them suffice. Take care, however, that you do not permit those subject to you to act otherwise, lest you be found to have strayed from the right path.

### II. ANCIENT SYNODAL ADMONITION, TO BE READ BY A DEACON AFTER THE GOSPEL TO THE BISHOP AND TO THE OTHERS SEATED IN ORDER

Now published in an emended form from two very ancient manuscript codices, one belonging to the monastery of Ripoll and the other to us.

Brother priests and priests of the Lord, you are co-workers in our order. We, although unworthy, occupy the place of Aaron, while you occupy the place of Eleazar and Ithamar. We act in the place of the twelve apostles, while you represent the seventy disciples. We are your shepherds, while you are shepherds of the souls entrusted to you. We shall render an account of you to the supreme Shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall render an account of the peoples entrusted to you. Therefore, beloved, consider your danger. Accordingly, we admonish and beseech your fraternity to commit to memory what we suggest to you and to strive to put it into practice. [Col. 0455D–0456A]

First of all, we admonish you that your life and conduct be irreproachable: namely, that your dwelling be near the church and that you have no women in your house. Rise every night for the nocturnal offices. Sing your office at the appointed hours. Celebrate the Masses reverently. Receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence. Wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands.

Let no one sing Mass unless he is fasting. Let no one sing who does not receive Communion. Let no one sing without an amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. Let these vestments be clean and not used for any other purposes. Let no one presume to sing Mass in the alb that he uses for his ordinary purposes. Let no one dare to sing Mass in a wooden or glass chalice.

Let no woman approach the altar or touch the Lord’s chalice. The corporal must be perfectly clean. The altar must be covered with clean linens. Nothing should be placed upon the altar except reliquaries and relics, or perhaps the four Gospels, or a pyx containing the Lord’s body for the viaticum of the sick. Let the other items be stored in a clean place.

Each of you must possess a complete Missal, a Lectionary, and an Antiphonary. A place must be prepared in the sacristy or near the altar where water may be poured out when the sacred vessels are washed. There also let a clean vessel filled with water be suspended, so that the priest may wash his hands there after Communion.

Let the churches be well roofed and vaulted. Let the churchyard often be fortified. Let no one sing Mass outside the church, in houses, or in unconsecrated places. Let no one sing Mass alone. Every priest must have a cleric or a student who will read the Epistle or lesson, answer him at Mass, and sing psalms with him.

Visit the sick, reconcile them, anoint them with holy oil according to the Apostle, and give them Communion with your own hand. Let no one presume to give Communion to a layman or woman to carry to a sick person.

Let none of you demand a payment or gift for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead. Take care that through your negligence no infant dies without baptism.
