The altar must be covered with clean linens, at least three separate ones; nothing may be placed upon it except relics, sacred objects, and things suitable for the sacrifice.

Each of you must possess a Missal, Breviary, and Martyrology. Your churches must be well roofed and clean. In the sacristies or secretaries, or near the high altar, there must be a place prepared for pouring out the water used to wash the corporals and sacred vessels and the hands after you have handled the holy chrism or the oil of catechumens or of the sick.

A vessel containing clean water must hang there for washing the hands of priests and others who are about to perform a sacred act or divine office, and a clean cloth must be nearby for wiping them. [Col. 0460C–0461A]

The churchyards must be well secured. Let no one obtain a church through secular power without our knowledge and consent. Let no one leave the church to which he has been titled and transfer to another for the sake of gain. Let no one presume to acquire several churches without a title and contrary to the provisions of the sacred canons.

Under no circumstances may one church be divided among several people. Let no one celebrate outside the church in unconsecrated places. Let no one receive another’s parishioner for Communion without the permission of his own priest. Let no one celebrate Mass in another’s parish without the permission of its own priest.

During the celebration, each person must sign the chalice and the offerings with the sign of the cross—not with a circular motion or wavering of the fingers, as some do, but with joined and extended fingers—and thus bless them.

The chalice and paten must be of gold or silver, not of bronze, brass, glass, or wood. Each priest must have a cleric or student who sings psalms with him, reads the Epistle and lesson, and answers at Mass.

The priest himself must visit and reconcile the sick, give them Communion with his own hand, according to the Apostle, and anoint them with holy oil. Let no one presume to give Communion to a layman or woman to carry to a sick person.

Let no one demand a payment or gift for baptizing infants, reconciling adults or the sick, or burying the dead. Through your negligence, let no infant die without baptism or adult without Communion.

Let none of you be drunk or quarrelsome. Let no one carry weapons. Let no one devote himself to games involving dogs or birds. Let no one drink in taverns.

Let each of you announce to his people as much of the Gospel as he understands on Sunday and the other feast days. Preach the word of the Lord. Care for the poor, strangers, widows, and orphans, and invite the strangers to your meal. Be hospitable, thereby providing others with a good example.

Every Sunday, before Mass, bless water with which the people may be sprinkled; have a vessel for this purpose alone.

Do not give sacred vessels or priestly vestments as pledges to a merchant or tavernkeeper. Do not bring an unworthy penitent to reconciliation for any reason, nor give him a certificate of reconciliation.

Do not exact interest. Do not alienate the goods you acquired after your ordination, because they belong to the church. No one may sell, exchange, or alienate by any means any object, possession, or slave belonging to the church.

Let no one receive another’s tithe. Let no one invite a penitent to eat meat or drink wine unless he gives alms for him at that time.

Each of you must have clean stone baptismal fonts. If he cannot have stone fonts, let him keep another vessel assigned solely to this purpose.

Make known to all your parishioners that they must observe the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Make known that they must observe the fasts of the Four Ember Seasons and the other commands of the Church.

On the Wednesday before Lent, invite the people to confession, and impose penance upon those who confess according to the character of their offenses. Three times a year—that is, at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—admonish all the faithful to approach Communion of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, and see to it that no one fails to communicate at least at Easter.

Exhort married people to abstain from their wives at appointed times. Let none of you wear red, green, or lay clothing.

Teach the people to celebrate Sunday and the other festivals without servile labor, from vespers to vespers. Prohibit the songs and dances of women in the churchyard. Under solemn adjuration by Almighty God, forbid the incantations that the common people customarily perform over the dead during the night.

Do not communicate with excommunicated persons, and let none of you presume to celebrate for them or in their presence. Announce this also to the people. Let no one from the people take a wife into his household unless the wedding has first been publicly celebrated at a time permitted by the Church.

Forbid everyone to approach a woman who has been abducted or a blood relative, or to take another man’s betrothed. [Col. 0461B–0462A]

Have swineherds and other shepherds come to Mass at least on Sunday. Exhort godparents to teach their godchildren, or have them taught, the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

Carefully preserve the sacrament of the Eucharist, the holy chrism, the oil of catechumens, and the holy oil, or oil of the sick, in the church, in a clean, suitable, and secure place, under sacred and trustworthy custody.

Each of you must keep with him an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer according to the traditions of the orthodox Fathers, and must understand them, as well as the prayers of the Mass, the Epistles, the Gospels, and the Canon. From these, by preaching, he must diligently instruct the people entrusted to him, especially those who do not believe correctly.

He must recite the Introit of the Mass, the prayers, the Epistle, the Gradual, the Gospel, the Creed, and the other non-secret prayers in a loud and intelligible voice. He must read the Secrets and the Canon slowly and distinctly in a subdued voice.

He must pronounce the words and divisions of the Psalms regularly and intelligibly, together with the customary canticles. He must know by heart the Creed of Saint Athanasius concerning the Trinity and the Catholic faith.

He must distinctly recite, in the plural or singular as appropriate, the exorcisms and prayers for making catechumens and the remaining prayers over a male and a female. He must observe according to the canonical form the order for baptizing, assisting the sick, reconciliation, commending the soul, and conducting the funeral rites of the dead.

He must read the exorcisms and blessings of salt and water correctly. He must know the daytime and nocturnal chant. He must also know the lesser computation for finding the Sunday letter, the interval of the day of Easter, and the dates of the principal movable feasts.

Now, dearest brothers, we wish you to strive to fulfill by good works what you have received through our tradition, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. [Col. 0462B]

### V. ORDER FOR CELEBRATING THE SACRED ORDERS ACCORDING TO THE BOOK OF BROTHER DANIEL, CARMELITE, BISHOP OF MOTENSIS

From an old manuscript of the Royal Library.

[Col. 0462C]

The bishop, fully vested in pontifical vestments and about to say Mass with the proper order of ministers, should proceed to the altar. After the first collect has been said, let those to be ordained in the following manner be called, either personally or through another.

For the title of Saint Mary of the House, let the doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes to be ordained come forward. The same procedure is followed for all the grades to be ordained.

Then, seated on his seat, let him read, or have another read, the following prohibition:

“By the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Church, we forbid publicly and strictly prohibit, under the power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and under penalty of excommunication and anathema, that anyone suffering from a defect of age or birth now presume rashly to approach the sacred orders.

“No one unless accepted by us. No slave unless restored to freedom by his master. No one using false letters and without the permission of his bishop or prelate. No one who has contracted with any woman by words expressing the present tense. No apostate. No excommunicated person. No one who has advanced by skipping an order. No bigamist. No irregular person. No Simoniac.

“No epileptic, no one mutilated in any limb, no one whose body is gravely deformed, and no one burdened by any incurable illness. Likewise, no one who has any other lawful impediment, unless a merciful dispensation has first been granted to him.

“Likewise, let no one presume to put himself forward to receive an order if he has not been canonically examined. And let no one, after receiving one order, presume to receive another without the proper permission and without any fraud.” [Col. 0462D]

### VI. AN ANCIENT CONFESSION OF PENITENTS

From an old manuscript of the Colbert Library.

[Col. 0463A]

#### Here begins the confession of penitents

In dread of the multitude of my offenses and the enormity of my crimes, and trusting in your goodness and ineffable mercy, I confess to you, my Creator and Redeemer, who promised that after guilt forgiveness and pardon may be obtained through a pure and tearful confession: I confess that, born in sins, I have until now lived in sins throughout the whole period of my life, thinking, speaking, and acting.

For I again subjected myself, at the devil’s persuasion, to the works and pomp of the devil, which I had renounced at baptism, and afterward I have always lived shamefully and negligently.

#### On pride

First of all, through pride, which is the root of all evils, I grievously defiled my character, life, and actions. Through pride, in words, thoughts, deeds, desires, behavior, and in all the other ways that I cannot enumerate, I confess that I have gravely sinned in the sight of God against God, against religion, and against my own vocation and purpose.

#### On vainglory
## On Vainglory

I confess that I have also sinned in many ways through vainglory, and that I sin daily because of it: for I continually embrace and covet beyond measure the glory of the world, secular dignities, and pleasures in my sins; and through it I have sinned in the other vices that arise from it—namely, in disobedience, by disobeying the commands of God and the orders of elders and teachers; in boasting, by exalting my spirit in many vanities; in hypocrisy, by keeping one thing in my heart and displaying another with my mouth; in contention, by uselessly pressing an argument contrary to reason; in obstinacy, by brazenly persisting in matters in which one ought not; and in presumptuous novelty, by rashly undertaking new and previously unfamiliar things. I confess that I have grievously sinned.

## On Envy

I confess that, above all men, I am guilty and criminal on account of envy, through which the devil first deceived humanity and through which death entered the world: for by envying the goods of others and grieving over their advantages, I have often saddened their spirits and, whenever I could, harmed their prosperity. And when I could not harm them, I nevertheless endured their good fortune resentfully.

Through envy I also recognize and confess that I have sinned in the other vices arising from it: in hatred, by retaining enmity and hatred in my heart against many; and in exultation, by rejoicing at the adversity of my neighbors, at their troubles and impediments, in opposition to them.

[Col. 0463D]

## On Anger

I know and confess that I have often sinned through anger and am guilty, because I did not bear the slight injuries inflicted by others with the equanimity I ought to have shown. Instead, as far as I could, I provoked both my own spirit and the spirits of others to anger and vengeance.

Through this I recognize and confess that I have sinned grievously in the other vices arising from anger: in quarrels, by stirring up not only myself but also others to disputes and contentions; in mental swelling, by proudly inflaming my spirit against the slightest and humblest complaints of others; in insults, by slandering others; in indignation, by becoming indignant at matters over which I ought not to have been indignant; and in blasphemies, by blaspheming many in anger without cause.

## On Sadness

I know and confess that I have sinned considerably through sadness, because I have usually saddened myself uselessly and without cause. And when I ought to have been sad and mourning over my sins, I have felt sadness over vain matters that offered no benefit.

Through this I confess that I have often sinned in the other vices arising from sadness: in malice, by harboring ill will against many; in faintheartedness, by losing the vigor and strength of my spirit through sadness; in despair, by despairing of the mercy and compassion of God; in torpor regarding God’s commands, by lacking attentiveness and zeal for his commandments; in wandering of mind toward unlawful things, by pursuing idleness and occupying my mind with illicit matters.

[Col. 0464A]

## On Gluttony

I confess that I have sinned, and that I sin daily, through gluttony of the belly—dangerously and damnably—because I have hitherto filled my belly with food and drink beyond measure and beyond what bodily necessity and need require, and I do not cease to fill it daily. What could have satisfied me and many other needy people, I alone have consumed through excessive eating and gluttony.

Therefore, through this I confess that I have sinned very grievously in the other vices arising from it: in foolish joy, by rejoicing and taking pleasure in vanities; in buffoonery, by devoting myself to and delighting in jokes and laughter; in loquacity, by speaking in many ways about things that do not contribute to usefulness; and in dullness of understanding, by losing the intelligence of my mind through excessive greed for food and drink.

## On Avarice

I confess that I am exceedingly guilty through avarice, because contrary to God’s command I have excessively desired, and continue to desire, possessions; what I have possessed I have retained, and continue to retain, with excessive greed; and I have not assisted and served the needs and necessities of my neighbors as I ought and could have done.

Through this I confess that I have sinned quite grievously, and sin daily, in the other vices arising from it: in betrayal of others, especially by betraying and revealing the secrets and hidden matters of an elder; in fraud, by secretly taking away the property of others; in covetousness; in deceit, by devising and uttering lies; in perjury, by invoking the holy name of God and his saints and swearing falsely; in restlessness, by failing to possess a quiet and peaceful spirit; and in hardness of heart against mercy, by not distributing alms to the poor as I ought and could have done.

[Col. 0464C]

## On Lust

I confess that I am guilty and criminal through lust beyond all other men and beyond what the human mind can comprehend. For after I reached the age at which I could perpetrate this evil, or consent to those wishing to perpetrate it, I lived perpetually in shame and lust, and in sodomy, under the excessive persuasion of the devil.

By defiling others through wicked deeds and the crime of sodomy, and by consenting to those who wished to defile me, I most shamefully and—words themselves cannot express it—most heinously polluted the temple of my body, as the most wretched and most criminal of men.

Through this I also confess that I have sinned in the other vices arising from lust: in blindness of mind, by failing to understand what was useful and necessary; in thoughtlessness, by doing many things lightly, wantonly, and without consideration; in inconstancy, by lacking stability and constancy in good works; in rashness, by carrying out many things with a precipitate and inconsiderate mind; in love, by seeking and fulfilling the pleasures and desires of my flesh and my own wishes beyond what I ought; in hatred of God, by resisting his commands and failing to love him as God ought to be loved; in attachment to the present age, by fixing love and desire beyond what was fitting upon secular and carnal pursuits; and in dread and despair of the age to come, by neither thinking about nor striving for the future life.

[Col. 0465A]

And not only in these things, but also in all the other matters not mentioned here, I confess that I have sinned and transgressed grievously and most unhappily in the sight of God. I know that, unless divine mercy comes to the aid of wretched me, I am utterly lost in thought, speech, deed, and will.

Therefore, before the earth swallows me up with Dathan and Abiron, and before heavenly fire consumes me with the Sodomites, I flee to you, Lord God and my Creator, who do not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn and live. To you, who spared the thief believing on the cross, and the publican and the harlot when they confessed, I humbly ask for forgiveness and pardon.

Most merciful one, do not put my face to shame; do not abandon me into the hands of those seeking my life. Look favorably upon me and hear me, wretched and sinful as I am, crying out and fleeing to you. Open the bosom of your compassion and the door of your mercy. Raise up the one dead in sins; give life to the one buried in transgressions; and do not reject the one whom you deigned to create in your image and redeem with the precious blood of your Son.

You promised forgiveness to penitents. You declared that there is greater joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons. Through your holy prophet you promised us that, on whatever day a sinner should turn, his sins would be forgiven.

Therefore I hold fast to your pledges and rejoice in your promises; with complete hope and confidence I flee to your immeasurable clemency. Spare my evils, my sins, and my crimes. Your mercy is greater than my misery. Hear me, Lord; be appeased, Lord; attend and act. Incline your ear, my God, and hear my prayer. Open your eyes and see my contrition.

Although I am a sinner, I am nevertheless your creature; I have been redeemed by the blood of your only-begotten Son. I am not worthless to you for salvation, since I was not worthless to you for redemption. But in your compassion have mercy and forgive. Through that same Son.

[Col. 0465C]

### Another Prayer

O God, light of minds, drive from me the night of foolishness and grant me the day of wisdom. Let the sun of truth, the sun of justice, arise; appear from the deepest recesses of your nature, which surpass all understanding, in the sky of my soul and above the earth of my heart.

Extinguish the images of bodies and the phantoms of my vain thoughts. Create the offspring of my understandings in the womb of my mind. Pour out your Spirit upon the waters of my formlessness, so that, turned toward you and conformed to your Son, I may see you through yourself, and all things beneath you.

O purest truth, see yourself in me; understand yourself in me. Through myself I see nothing but vain, fleeting, and perishable things; I see nothing but false and bodily forms. Through myself I am nothing but death and a dark, shadowy abyss, incomplete.

In you I am insofar as I am; in you I live insofar as I live; in you I understand insofar as I understand. For you are supreme understanding, supreme essence, supreme life: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; threefold unity, simple Trinity; infinite in yourself without end; one God, forever and ever. Amen.

## VII. Mass for Tribulation

From an old manuscript codex of the Colbert Library.

At the appropriate hour let the litanies be sung, with the chant agreeing with the matter. Then the Mass: “Remember your mercies.” Psalm: “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul. My God, in you I trust.”

### Prayer

O God, who do not despise the groaning of the contrite and do not reject the devotion of those who mourn, attend to our prayers, which we pour out for tribulation. Mercifully receive them and grant that whatever adversities, whether diabolical or human, are plotted against us may be reduced to nothing, so that, harmed by no persecutions but rescued from every tribulation and distress, we may continually give joyful thanks in your holy Church. Through the Lord.

Gradual: “Help.” Verse: “For not …”

### Reading from the Prophet Daniel

In those days Daniel prayed, saying:

“Lord God, do not despise your people, nor take away your mercy from us, for the sake of your beloved Abraham, your servant Isaac, and your holy one Israel, to whom you spoke, promising that you would multiply their offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore.

For, Lord, we have been reduced to fewer than all the nations, and today we are humbled throughout the whole earth because of our sins. At this time there is neither prince nor prophet nor leader, neither sacrifice nor offering nor incense nor place [lacuna].

[The rest is missing.]

## VIII. Letter of Jonas, Bishop of Autun, Concerning the Endowment and Consecration of the Church of Mont Buznin

From an old chartulary of the church of Autun.

[Col. 0466B]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ. Jonas, bishop of Autun, with divine mercy going before him.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church, present and future, that the venerable man Reimbodo, together with his son, whose name is Lifericus, touched by divine clemency, and with the advice of our predecessor, Bishop Altheus, built a chapel from their own property in the county of Autun, in the vicariate of Isiotre, at the place called Mont Buznin, and brought it to completion. They petitioned our goodwill that we might solemnly consecrate this chapel, constructed by their labor, according to ecclesiastical order, so that divine worship might continually be performed there.

We therefore considered their devoted intention and most humble petition and arranged, according to canonical laws, that an endowment should be provided from which the house of God might suitably be supported. Fulfilling this with the most devout will, according to the arrangement of our exhortation, they nobly granted to that place, from their own property and as reason dictated, the possessions set out below, for the love of God and the veneration of his saints.

Having received their reasonable and praiseworthy petition, we judged that it should be consecrated according to ecclesiastical order for the work of almighty God. By God’s authority we dedicated it on the Ides of October with solemn rite, in honor and veneration of Saint Sebastian the martyr and the other saints.

Therefore I, Ragamboto, together with my son Hilferic, following the counsel and consideration of the lord and venerable Jonas, the aforementioned bishop, endow the aforesaid chapel with our own property for the love of God and the remedy of our souls, and wish it to remain endowed forever.

Accordingly, for the use and service of the aforesaid basilica, which we constructed for the love of God and asked to have consecrated, we give and wish it to be [lacuna] forever—that is, around the basilica, before its entrance, a field of one modius situated below the ditch and extending as far as the dead gutter; and on the eastern side, arable land with a meadow and an attached property amounting to five modii, while preserving the atrium of the church itself.

Likewise, we give in full the estate held by Bernoinus, together with the aforesaid male serf and his wife named Bertildis, and their offspring, with all its boundaries. We likewise transfer to this place another estate in that county or territory, in the village called Villaris, which came to us from Altmarus by title of sale, acquired for us by our grandfather Hilferic, together with a female servant named Leobertane and her offspring, with all its appurtenances, attached property, and whatever belongs or appears to belong to it.

We also transfer a meadow acquired from Abulmarus for the honor of the aforesaid chapel. All the things named above, in honor of almighty God and in veneration of his saints, whose memory and power are commemorated there, we transfer for the use and support of the basilica named so often above, and pass them from our right into the right and ownership of the basilica and its rectors, granting them to serve it perpetually.

And so that it may remain forever free and undisturbed from every temporal domination and harassment by heirs in the service of the Lord, with complete and fullest willingness we hand over both the chapel and the properties belonging to it to the mother church of Saint Nazarius and its rectors. We decree that they are subject to ecclesiastical law and perpetually devoted to it, so that in every administration and exercise of authority the bishop and his ministers may deal with them according to ecclesiastical laws, just as with the other properties granted to that mother church.

On this condition, however: as long as we or one of our nearest lawful heirs remains alive, we may hold them throughout our lives not by right of domination or inheritance but for defense and protection, under the mundeburdum. Each year we shall pay to the representatives of Saint Nazarius, on the very day of the Lord’s Supper, when the chrism is prepared, one pound of wax.

But so long as we, or any of our heirs’ successors, preserves the aforesaid chapel with the complete integrity of its possessions for the honor of the church, possesses it in keeping with its custody, and pays the synodal census to the representatives of Saint Nazarius at the appointed time, the bishop shall have no license, if moved by anger or greed, to alienate the right of our inheritance or that of our successors, divert it to his own uses, or disturb it.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, any of our heirs, or any person introduced for the purpose, should attempt by evasion to raise or bring any complaint against this gift and endowment of ours to the house of God, or divide the property of the same church, or, inflamed by diabolical greed, attempt to divert it to his own use, or prove slow or negligent in paying the census stipulated above, then he shall be compelled to make restitution according to law. If he refuses, he shall be forced to pay one pound of gold to the mother church, or to the party against whom he has brought suit, together with the enforcing treasury; and, in addition, he shall obtain no effect for what he claims, with the stipulation appended.

And so that this charter of our gift and endowment, which we have handed over to the mother church of Saint Nazarius with the readiest hearts, may possess complete, perfect, and unshaken validity for all time, we have not only confirmed it below with our own hands, but have also delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of the religious canons of that church and of noble faithful laymen.

## IX. Letter of Lambert, Bishop of Le Mans, to Hildebrand, Bishop of Sées

From an old manuscript codex of the Colbert Library.

To the magnificent bishop Hildebrand, venerable for his holy merits, Lambert, an unworthy bishop: eternal happiness in the Lord.

We inform your fatherhood that a certain detestable man of an erroneous faction, named Raino, presumptuously dares to retain and defraud our church of its ninth and tenth. It is established that, concerning these audacious and atrocious deeds, he has been warned by us and by our Church not once or twice but frequently. Yet he has in no way wished either to obey the warnings or to satisfy our Church.

Therefore, by divine authority, together with the holy and glorious martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and all the saints, we hold the aforesaid sacrilegious Raino, together with his entire household, excommunicated and anathematized, excluded from the thresholds of the Church and from the Christian community, until he ceases from these wicked acts and satisfies our Church.

For this reason we presume to admonish your blessedness by this letter of our insignificance, so that, just as he has been generally excommunicated by us, he may likewise be considered excluded and excommunicated by you and by your entire Church. As for the form of excommunication, how … [the text is lacunose] … I believe that your fatherhood is in no way without knowledge of it.

I wish your holiness always to prosper in Christ.

## X. Testament of Riculfus, Bishop of Elne

From the chartulary of the church of Elne.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the year 915 of the incarnation of the Word, indiction 3, Riculfus, by the grace of God bishop of the see of Elne, gives to the house of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr of Christ, mother church of the people of Roussillon, Conflent, and Vallespir, and to my successors serving the Lord there.

Therefore I, Riculfus, by the grace of God bishop of the see of Elne, give to the aforesaid church the sacred vestments that I acquired, and books, and chalices with patens, and things belonging to the worship of God, whose names are as follows:

Two gold crosses with precious gems; one ivory reliquary; silver chalices, one gilded with a paten, another without a paten, and another daily-use chalice; one excellent silver *Sion*; two censers with silver chains; four silver candelabra; two bronze basins; one small vessel for preparing chrism, with a water vessel; one bronze handled vessel for holy water; one pair of chests for preserving sacred vestments; one ivory comb; two ivory tablets; two pairs of boots and sandals; four gold-embroidered amices; five albs, three bright and two plain; four *roques*, one purple with gold, another pale in the Greek style, and two others made in Greece; five belts, one with gold and precious gems and the other four with gold; four gold-embroidered stoles, one of them with little bells; six gold-embroidered maniples, one of the six with little bells; three excellent episcopal chasubles, one *dioprasius* and the other two of *orodona* [textile terms]; one gold ring with precious gems; one pair of gloves [the text reads *vuantos*, uncertain]; four shirts for the Gospel Book and Missal, one purple with gold; four other pale corporals; four cloths; one embroidered cloth; three dalmatics; two cloaks, one purple and the other *bition* [uncertain textile term]; two *toalias olicias* [uncertain textile terms], one with silver; two Spanish nails or clasps [uncertain reading]; one silver altar; one *facistergium*; one pallium cushion.

The number of books, by their titles, is as follows: one Gospel Book; three Missals; one Missal and Lectionary in a single volume; another Missal with Antiphonary in a single volume; one work of Smaragdus; two books of Gospel and Epistle traditions; one book of Rabanus, an exposition of the Gospels and Epistles; one Heptateuch; one book containing an exposition of Genesis; one book of Solomon; one book of Maccabees; one volume containing Job, Tobit, and the twelve Minor Prophets; one book containing Tobit, Judith, and Esther; one excellent Martyrology; one Psalter; two books of Canons; gatherings of canons; one book of Augustine against five heresies; two books of prayers; one computus cycle; one book of Sentences on various cases; two books of law, one Roman and the other Gothic; excellent gatherings in one volume containing lucid expositions of Genesis, Kings, Maccabees, and the Prophets; two gatherings for consecrating a church; two gatherings for visiting the sick; one gathering for ecclesiastical ordinations; one medical book.

Of these things, and of other things by testament—which I have solemnly attested—I give to the aforesaid church of Saint Eulalia in the county of Roussillon, Conflent, and Vallespir whatever I have acquired in those places or, with God’s help, may acquire, whether by purchase or exchange, and so forth.

This deed of donation was made on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the eighteenth year of the reign of King Charles, son of Louis.

[Note: [Col. 0467] Error in the years of Charles’s reign. Therefore XXIII should be read in place of XVIII.]

## XI. Manumission of Constantia

From the chartulary of the monastery of Uzerche.

[Col. 0469A]

Whoever releases the bond of servitude owed to him should know that the Lord will be his recompense at the future judgment, as the reward for this act.

Therefore I, Rainardus, named below, considering the weakness of my condition, hereby free a certain female servant born in my household, named Constantia, for the love of God and for the remedy of my soul and of the souls of my father and mother, from every yoke of servitude. After this day, throughout the four corners of the earth, she shall have the license and power to choose whatever lord she wishes in all matters; she shall go for herself and live for herself, and shall remain free and released all the days of her life.

Certainly, if anyone—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or relatives, or any person introduced for the purpose—should presume to raise any complaint against this release, may he first incur the anger of almighty God and of all the saints, and likewise share with Dathan and Abiron in hell. Let this release nevertheless remain firm and stable for all time.

This release was made in the month of March, while King Charles was reigning.

Signature of Rainardus, who requested that this release be made or confirmed.

## XII. Testament of Lord Ademar, Viscount of Scalas and Abbot of Tulle

From the chartulary of the church of Tulle.

[Col. 0469B]

… First, therefore, I leave and return to Saint Martin and to the monks serving him in the aforesaid monastery the old abbey, which, as has already been said, had come to me from my father’s great-grandfather: namely, the church of Saint Julian built beside the same monastery; the church of Saint Peter of the castle of that village; the church of Saint Martin of Laguena; the church of Saint Fortunata; the church of Saint Mary of Lagarda; the church of Saint Amantius; the church of Saint Bonitus of Verni; the church of Saint Martial of Faurcensis; the church of Saint Bonitus of Avalosa; the church of Saint Mary of Selliacum; the church of Saint Julian of Porcaria; and the church of Saint Laurence of Gorsa, together with the associated estates, villages, meadows, woods, and everything belonging to that abbey.

Although I possessed all these unjustly and not without guilt, I willingly abandoned them, making satisfaction to God and his saints. So that merciful and almighty God may deign to grant forgiveness both to me and to all my parents, present, past, and future, for the sins of this place and of the others, and so that the aforesaid holy place may be restored completely to its former condition, I have decided to assign to it the best and most precious things from my own right, since I had no legitimate son.

The first of these is my castle of Scalas, with its entire castellany and all its fiefs, churches, my estate of Cannacum, the villages situated around it, the estates, woods, waters, all rights of entry and exit, and male and female servants.

I also give the vicariates of Navensis and Spaniacensis, everything I possess in the vicariate of Beennatensis, the church of Saint Pardulfus, Placiacum, the church of Acuto Monte, the church of Saint Martin situated between the Dour and the Dordogne, and the church of Albuciacum with the estates and vineyards of Murell.

I give my castle of Mulsedonum with its entire castellany and the church of Saint Martin situated beneath it. In the vicariate of Argentadensis, I give my estate of Longor, with the vineyards of Cortoiolum, fishponds, meadows, fields, and my village called Grandis Campus.

I give the allod that my father acquired from Count Raymond [above the line: “of Perteus”] in the vicariate of Spaniacensis or Faurcensis; Marcum; Abilensis; the church of Saint Bonitus; and the village in the vicariate of Brivensis called Pauliacum, with its vineyards and everything belonging to it.

[Col. 0470A]

I also give the village called Marcus, with its vineyards and everything likewise belonging to it; in that vicariate, my estate where Eliseus is said to have lived, with its vineyards, meadows, and everything belonging to it; the village called Clarafaga; Biareni; the village called Vallis; the village called Grandis Rivus; the village called Betelanita; the village called Bedenas; the chapel called Novavilla, with its estate and everything belonging to that estate; one estate in the village of Confulentum; the village called Colia in the vicariate of Spaniacensis; the church of Brancellae; the church of Saint Julian of Garriga; and one estate in the vicariate of Tornensis, in the village called Montilium—all of which are situated in the county of Limoges. I give these to Saint Martin and his monks of Tulle.

In the county of Quercy, likewise, after my death and that of my brother Gauzbertus and my wife Gauzla, I give to Saint Martin and to the monks serving him in the monastery of Tulle my castle of Foliosum, situated in the vicariate of Casiliacensis; my estate of Vairiacum, with the church of Saint Stephen, formerly called Saint Boicius; the church of Saint Martin; the church of Saint Germanus; and the church of Saint Mary of Macerias.

I also give Cambonum, with the vineyard of Faga; four estates of Ampulliaccum; my plantation situated beside Saint Michael; the vineyards of Celsiacum; the villages and woods; the waters; all rights of exit and entry; male and female servants and free persons; and everything belonging to that castle or estate.

I give also the beautiful castle, the church of Calessum, the estates of Cambonancum, Mairacum, Buxariae, Matrona, Vichiracum, Vogaironum, and Longor, with the vineyards of Cortoiolum, with the *vitis ad piscandum* (fishing apparatus; reading uncertain); my estate of Croissia, with its church and all its appurtenances; the church of Mairinacum; Pardinae; Beceda; the church of Saint Medardus; Cloiols; the ditch of Amalgerius; the village called Vilaris; the other village called Mons Joviniani; Vedrivineae; and the estates of Juliacum, situated in the aforesaid county of Quercy. These also I leave to Saint Martin and the church of Tulle.

[Col. 0470D]

This too should be known: in the forest of Borma, belonging to the estate of Vairiacum, a certain portion has been granted as a fief to vicarii bearing the name Borma, solely for the construction of a fortification, for the protection and defense of the possessions of Saint Martin existing all around—not for claiming any supposed proprietary right there. This includes the church of Saint Peter of Borma, similarly so called, with certain properties belonging to it, and whatever they possess in the riverbank and in the water, including devices suitable for catching fish.

All these things, therefore—both those that I have hitherto possessed unjustly and those belonging to me by hereditary right—I, Ademar, have left or donated to Saint Martin and the monks serving him, for the salvation of my soul, of my wife Gauzla, of my father and mother, and of all my relatives and friends, both those still dwelling in this age and those who have already departed from it; moreover, for our king Rodulfus and our lord Count Ebalus [of Perteus], with whose consent we have completed all this; and finally, especially for those who shall be guardians and defenders of the aforesaid place and its inhabitants.

I, Ademar, viscount, sensing that the end of my present life was approaching, and also seeing that I had no legitimate son to whom I might lawfully leave my extensive possessions, began, with God’s inspiration, to consider how I might use eternally in the future the property that I had used temporarily in the present age.

I confidently believe that this will happen if I leave to the holy Church, namely the bride of Christ, what I cannot leave to a temporal heir, so that when he himself, the judge of the living and the dead, comes to judge, he may deign to grant me an eternal reward in return for the temporal support of his bride.

For this reason, therefore, I leave to God and to his holy Church, for the salvation of my soul, as stated above, and for the souls of all my relatives, friends, and lords, including those who shall defend this document of mine, all the things written below.

In addition to the properties described above, these include my estate of Tauriacum with its church; what I possess at Molle; my lands of Bulciacum, which belong to Vairacum; whatever I acquired from the priest Sigibertus at Gintracum and Salle; my village Maisit; my estate where Adalrandus lives at Laustanica; my estates of Madriniacum and Pariacum with their churches; Verniae; Mespelium; Cassaniae; Potentins; Coozono; Presangae; my village Caminus with its church; Laus; one vineyard at Rofiniacum; my allod of Blaviniacum; two estates at Nantiliacum; a vineyard at Pardina which belonged to Donadeus; what I possess at Altudere and Dezenatum; my plantation at Pogium with its attached estates and the vineyard I acquired from Arnaldus; the church of Saint Albinus; Taurini; Cassaniae; one estate at Laustangas where Berdandus is said to have lived; the estates at Brancatum; my vineyard at Donzenacum; the estate of Brasc, which I purchased from Rotbertus; the vineyard of Maurian Valley; one estate at Calzfurnum; one vineyard at Lineriaccum; my allod in the vicariate of Cambolivensis; the forest of Mala Vallis; the village of Ribaus with the forest of Monbresme; the estate where Ingelbertus lives near Vairacum; one estate at Argentadum; Camelariae; Cuculonia; Vinzacum; three estates at Dauza and Pedania, with the vineyard Bernardus planted; Valannonus; and Alix.

[Col. 0471C]

I leave the following among certain of my relatives and friends: Floriacum and Montelium; my vineyard at Scopiacum; my vineyards at Detnatum and Damella; my estates of Angulus and Taraiasa; one estate at Spaniacum; one vineyard at Blandina; my allod of Montaniacum, with the vineyards I acquired from Witardus; one vineyard at Quinconum; my estate of Rete; the allod at Verniola; and my allod of Scorbinum.

Although at various times I have given or altered many gifts, either orally or in writing, to various churches and to people both related to me and counted among my friends and faithful, I nevertheless wish this written testament to remain and endure in this world as valid, firm, and unchangeable. Amen.

The monks, moreover, are under the king’s protection for the purpose of keeping the place safe, and are to pay nothing except prayers.

[Col. 0471D]

Furthermore, I call upon and adjure all my relatives and successors, and all the neighbors of that monastery, present and future, by the fearful name of the holy Trinity and by the merit of Saint Martin and Saint Laudus, who was carried there, that no one presume to disturb either the monks or any of their property, or in any way bring them under secular authority.

But if anyone should attempt to possess God’s inheritance, let him be cursed throughout the whole world, and let it be said of them:

“My God, make them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind, and let them be confounded forever and ever.”

Let them not be coheirs with Christ unless they repent, but sharers in the fate of Pharaoh, who said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not release Israel.”

As for the princes to whom this document is presented, I adjure them by the judgment of the living and the dead to strive in every way to defend it, remembering that everyone who moves boundaries—that is, the ordinances of his fathers—is accursed.

And so that this authority may remain more firmly established, we requested that our lord Ebalus [count of Perteus] confirm it by his authority.

[Col. 0472A]

Signature of Count Ebalus and of his son William.

Signature of Ademar, who requested that this be done.

Signature of Odolricus, viscount of Saint-Cyr.

Signature of Gauzbertus, viscount.

Signature of Rotbertus.

## XIII. LETTER OF RODHMUND, BISHOP OF AUTUN, CONCERNING THE CHAPEL OF CENTISSA, GRANTED TO TWO CLERICS

From the old cartulary of the church of Autun.

In the name of the Lord, the eternal God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Rodhmund, by the mercy of that same God, humble bishop of the Aedui. We wish to make known to all the faithful of God and of the holy Church, present and future, that while we were residing in the aforesaid city, the leaders of that same church—Udolmannus the dean, Radaldus the abbot and provost, and Almarus the archdeacon—came into our presence, entreating our serenity and showing us that they held a certain chapel which they wished to entrust to two brother clerics, Girardus and Wichardus, provided that they proved worthy of obtaining our consent.

This chapel is situated in the county of Beaune, in the village of Centissa, and is consecrated in honor of Saint Germanus, confessor of Christ. Therefore, in order to resist the trickery of secular persons, they desired that their arrangement be strengthened by the authority of our written charter. Accordingly, we ordered this testament of our charter to be made. By its authority we decree, and by decreeing we affirm, that the aforesaid chapel of Saint Germanus, with the consent of the canons of that same place, shall be held, governed, and possessed by the two aforesaid brother clerics, Girardus the canon and Wichardus, for as long as they live, on the condition that they pay the synod dues and do not neglect to deliver, in the month of March, a census of five solidi for the use of the canons.

So that the grant of this cession may possess fuller firmness in the name of God, we have confirmed it with our own hands and ordered it delivered to our faithful for ratification. Done successfully at Autun in the Lord. Amen.

Rodmundus, sinful bishop of the holy church of Autun, subscribed.

Girardus, cardinal archdeacon, subscribed.

Udolmannus, most humble deacon, subscribed.

Radaldus, abbot and provost, subscribed.

Gerardus, abbot, subscribed.

Almarus, archdeacon, subscribed.

Teutho, abbot, subscribed.

Hugo, humble levite and precentor, subscribed.

Arnulfus, abbot, subscribed.

Heldegrimus, archpriest, subscribed.

Geraucus, archpriest, subscribed.

Warnerius, schoolmaster, subscribed.

Heriveus subscribed.

Rodmundus subscribed.

Constantius, schoolmaster, subscribed.

Optadus subscribed.

Boso, priest, subscribed.

Teotbertus, priest, subscribed.

I, Vuido the levite, wrote and subscribed this in place of Suavius the chancellor.

Issued on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the twelfth indiction, in the first year of King Lothair’s reign.

## XIV. AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE MONKS OF TULLE AND AURILLAC

From the cartulary of the church of Tulle.

Let it be known to all the brothers of the monasteries, namely those of Aurillac and Tulle, present and future, that Raimundus, abbot of Aurillac, and Bernardus, abbot of Tulle, had disputes with one another.

Abbot Joannes, who is known to have been a kinsman of Saint Geraldus, held both churches together. He gave to the church of Saint Martin of the monastery of Tulle certain possessions belonging to him by right, which had come to him from his parents: namely, the priestly ministry of the church of Saint Amantius of Faurcio; three manses in the same estate—the mansus of Geraldus, the mansus of Frudinus, and the mansus of Rotgerius; fifteen taxable pigs in the same estate; and the royal fines which Joannes annually received from the hand of the king of the Franks in the castle of Tulle.

He also gave five other manses in the parish of Argentado. Abbot Joannes gave these possessions, named above, to the church of Saint Martin and to the monks serving God there on this condition: every year, on the feast of Saint Geraldus, the brothers of Tulle were to pay the brothers of Aurillac three pounds of pepper or spices.

While he was alive, as our fathers were accustomed to relate, this was paid without any opposition. After his death, however, litigation arose very often. At last peace was made in this manner:

I, Raimundus, abbot of Aurillac, recognizing, with the counsel of my brothers, that this was burdensome for the brothers of Tulle, at their request and humble entreaty, remit to Bernardus, our brother and abbot, and son and monk of our congregation, and to his successors, the entire annual census.

## XV. [Note: [Col. 0473C]

This excommunication was recently published from the same codex from which we transcribed it, in volume ten of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 635. Since, however, it has not until now been sufficiently known when it was issued or for what reason—and since the matter is also especially relevant to our purpose—we have judged it appropriate to reprint it here together with our observations.

In the year 976, when Anastasius, archbishop of Sens, had died, Ragenardus, count of that city, who wished to bring the episcopate into his own family, disrupted the election of a new bishop for a period of five months. At last Seguinus, the son of Ragenardus’s sister, was elected and consecrated against Ragenardus’s will at Auxerre on the third day before the Ides of June. When Seguinus subsequently came to Sens, Ragenardus prevented him from entering the city.

When the archbishop himself saw this, as Clarius says in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living* of Sens, he placed the whole province under interdict from the Kalends of October until the beginning of Lent. It was therefore at that time that this excommunication was issued against Count Ragenardus and his son Rodmundus—whom the same Clarius calls Frotmundus—because, after Seguinus had received the archiepiscopal blessing, they had not permitted him to enter the holy place of the church of Sens, as is read in the excommunication.

After Seguinus’s death, which occurred in the year 999, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, the church of Sens was again thrown into turmoil. For when Count Frotmundus, who had succeeded his father Ragenardus not long before, wished Bruno to be given to Sens as bishop, while at the same time many clerics also—as Clarius says, that is, canons—were seeking the bishopric out of ambition, a great schism arose in the Church. Neither Bruno nor any of the canons who wished to become bishops could attain that dignity, since the votes of the electors converged upon Leothericus the archdeacon.

For this reason Frotmundus, angered against him, closed the gates to him after his consecration when he approached his own see, and denied him entry into the city, as is read in Tavellus. Since the causes for excommunication were then the same as those that had led Seguinus to issue this decree against Ragenardus and his son Rodmundus, it was decided to use the same formula, changing the names. Thus, in some places the names in the earlier excommunication were erased with a knife, and in their places were substituted the names of those who had recently been excommunicated, generally above the line. In one place, where we have arranged for dots to be printed interspersed among the letters, the names of two canons have been inserted into the body of the sentence rather than above the line.

We wished to record these matters here with the greatest care so that the dates and names of the two excommunications might be distinguished. We also had everything added to the second excommunication printed in a different type, except for those two words interspersed with dots. Although they belong to the second excommunication, the form of the letters in that line could neither be changed nor ought to have been changed. Thus, the continuous text belongs to the excommunication of Seguinus. The additions above the lines, printed in a different type, together with the two words interspersed with dots, were added in the time of Leothericus. Wherever the names of the excommunicated persons had been erased so completely that they could not be read at all, we substituted dots for their names.]

### EXCOMMUNICATION OF RAGENARDUS, COUNT OF SENS, RENEWED AGAINST GAUZFRIDUS AND GEILO, CANONS OF SENS

From an old Pontifical Book of the church of Sens, now in the possession of the distinguished man Antonius Vio of Herouval.

Immense grief drives us to groaning, and unspeakable sorrow moves us to weeping, when we see those whom Christ’s Passion redeemed from the yoke of the devil, whom holy baptism purified from the filth of sins, and whom it joined to the body of the Catholic Church, now once again voluntarily subjecting themselves to the ancient enemy; and not merely inflicting persecution upon the members of Christ, but also plotting war against the very author and lord of all creation.

For those who ought to have been builders and defenders of the holy Church, now afflicted by the devil’s poisonous fury and driven on by bestial rage, having set aside all fear of the Lord and neglected the remedy of repentance, do not fear to tear apart churches dedicated to the honor of God, to the perpetual Virgin Mary, and to Saint Stephen, and to leave them without a shepherd, violently usurping what ought to be used to restore the holy Church of God.

We also admonish, and by admonishing adjure, that the incorrigible, and those entangled in pestilential and shameful conduct, just as they are estranged from good morals, so also become strangers to the fellowship of the faithful.

Therefore let the universal Church know the fiercest enemies and wicked tyrants, the worst adversaries and persecutors of the holy Church of God: Gauzfridus and Geilo [the later substitutions], Ragenardus and his son Rodmundus [the erased earlier names], and their canons—their comrades in command, invaders of ecclesiastical property, despisers of God, transgressors of the holy canons, and opponents of their shepherd.

Unless they correct themselves as quickly as possible and faithfully restore what they have taken by making satisfaction, we bind them, together with all the saints living in heaven through their merits and shining on earth through miracles; and, according to the power of binding and loosing granted to us despite our unworthiness, we excommunicate them and pierce them with the sword of anathema.

Furthermore, we excommunicate G. a. u. z. f. r. i. d. u. m., G. e. i. l. o. n. e. m., Grobertus the deacon, who unjustly usurps my archdeaconry, Vuangerius, Arricus, then Ansellus, likewise Ansellus, Hugo, Ansegisus, Balduinus, [lacuna].

We anathematize these men and all those who, after I had received the archiepiscopal blessing, did not permit me to enter the holy place of the church of Sens, following the custom of my predecessors, abandoning the truth and adhering to falsehood: by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by the authority granted to us by God.

Let them have no portion among Christians, and let them not enter the church of God; nor let Mass be celebrated for them by anyone who does not wish to be subject to the same penalty. No offering or commemoration shall be made for them or for their offenses unless they have made satisfaction. Let them receive no share, whether alive or dying, in incense, frankincense, or even the sacred light, but let their portion be with the wicked, those swollen with opposition to God and tearing apart the saints.

Let their portion and inheritance be unending fire and perpetual torment. Let them be accursed in the city; accursed in the countryside. Amen. Let them be accursed in their houses; accursed in their villages. Amen. Accursed in the woods; accursed in the waters. Amen. Let them be accursed in the lanes, accursed in the streets, and in every place. Amen.

Unless they are corrected, let them be clothed in manifold curses. Amen. Let no priest visit them at the point of death, nor let them be buried in Christian cemeteries; but, like foul-smelling corpses, let them be cast out. Amen.

Let their granaries be accursed, and let their remains be accursed. Amen. Let those entering and departing be accursed. Amen. The Lord shall strike them with want, fever, cold, and heat, and shall pursue them until they perish. As this lamp is extinguished before the eyes of men, so may their lamps be extinguished forever. Amen.

## XVI. LETTER OF RICHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, CONCERNING THE CONSECRATION OF THE CHURCH OF VIPPLES

From the cartulary of the monastery of La Chapelle in the diocese of Bourges, chapters 36 and 86.

In the name of Almighty God, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of all the saints.

Let all the sons of the Catholic Church know that I, Richard, archbishop of the see of Bourges, came to a certain village of my archbishopric called Vipples, in order to consecrate an altar in the principal church of that village, namely the parish church, established in honor of Saint Martin, and to hold a council there.

In order to place the aforesaid church, in which the altar stood, in the hands of the ministers of God and to remove it from the hands of laymen, I did not wish to consecrate the altar or even place the stole around my neck until the laymen who had been receiving a share of the offerings of this church and of the upper church adjoining it had promised in my presence and that of all those standing around that they would accept nothing further from them.

After this had been done, I assigned the same church and another adjoining it to God, Saint Dionysius, Prior Hugo, and the monks of La Chapelle. Radulfus of Paciaco had already given them whatever he possessed in that church, both inside and outside, with the consent of Hunbaldus of Uriac, from whom, according to the old custom of laymen, the church was said to hold; and with the consent of Rotgerius the archdeacon, Gosfridus the archpriest, and all the other clerics and laymen present, many of whom had gathered for the consecration and council.

By the authority of God, Saint Peter, Saint Stephen, and our archiepiscopal authority, I assigned it with the episcopal staff. I also gave Prior Hugo of La Chapelle, as a memorial of this gift, a portion of the relics of that church, which had been taken from a well on that same day and which he was to carry to his own church. I ordered this charter to be sealed with our own seal.

This was done in the time of King Philip, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign.

[Signatures]

Richard, archbishop.

Hunbaldus of Uriac.

Amblardus Guillebaldi.

Rotgerius, archdeacon.

Gosfridus, archpriest.

Andreas, archdeacon.

Petrus of Giis.

Radulfus, cleric.

Rotgerius, chaplain.

Bernardus, cleric.

Aimericus, cleric.

Petrus lo Grogn.

Rotgerius Malevizini.

Aimericus of Guiranda.

Araldus of la Coldra.

Radulfus Malevizini.

Hunbaldus of Agia.

Dalmacius Chabri, and many others who were present.

Benedictus, monk of Saint Gildasius, who wrote this charter.

## XVII. JUDGMENT OF AGANO, BISHOP OF AUTUN, AGAINST RAGINARDUS

From the old cartulary of the church of Autun.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God. Agano, by the grace of God bishop of the Aedui.

The words of divine instruction admonish everyone that whenever ecclesiastical property is withheld by anyone, it ought to be restored when equity demands it. Therefore, let the unanimous universal community of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own community know that, while we were passing through Beliniacum in the summertime, we encountered, along the course of our journey, men belonging to that jurisdiction, who complained before us in mournful voices about our brother Raginardus.

They said that he judged them by new and unheard-of laws; that he imposed excessive payments and great exactions, which he demanded daily; and that he had also raised up evil customs during his time in that jurisdiction. There was much distress and no mercy, and there was no one to help. Many complaints were also brought to our ears by the clerics traveling with us concerning the injuries inflicted by him day after day, the unlawful additional burdens, and the various oppressions imposed by his servants.

Since the distinguished feast of Pentecost was approaching after the completion of the annual cycle, and since we knew that many nobles, as well as nearly all the leading men of the region, would be present at Autun on that day, and that the most pious duke of Burgundy, namely Hugo, would also come in a great company, our paternal care judged it appropriate to defer those complaints patiently for a while, until everyone had gathered for the aforesaid day and we had been joined by our lord and most religious father Roclenus, bishop of the holy see of Chalon.

Then, with his pious counsel, the intolerable yoke of wickedness could be lightened through our shared compassion and common authority, so that the people of God entrusted to us might, under our protection, preserve law, justice, and their dignity, breathe freely, and be permitted to live peacefully and justly and to devote themselves securely and faithfully to the interests of Saint Nazarius and his clerics.

Accordingly, through the generosity of heavenly piety, physically and in the name of God, on the eve of the aforesaid feast that most reverend person joined himself to our humility. For, moved first by divine love and veneration for the most blessed martyr Nazarius, he had resolved to visit the desired thresholds of that most sacred temple. By God’s grace, he had been deemed worthy to fulfill his great desire to complete this journey and see us, and he rejoiced.

While we were being refreshed, as thirsty men, by the sweet streams of speech from his sacred mouth, and were being instructed in a fatherly manner by his holy admonitions, we took care to explain to his holiness those matters that would contribute to the increase of the common good if corrected by our judgment of just severity, but that would harm the same community if, through equal negligence, the things requiring correction remained uncorrected.

Accordingly, that illustrious Father and most blessed shepherd, learning through our truthful report what was unknown to his sacred simplicity, began with us to deliberate deeply about how, by common consent, the unjust oppressions and unlawful additional burdens might be abolished through his cooperation, our episcopal action, and the duke’s intervention.

For it appeared just to the diligence of all our faithful that, since divine mercy had united persons of such great dignity—namely, princes of the Christian soldiery—in concordant goodwill, whatever the blind greed of wicked rulers had impiously inflicted upon their subjects should be corrected as quickly as possible by applying the rule of justice, and that they should obtain all good things in the name of God, remaining and being confirmed by our most fortunate grant.

After the vigils of the past night had been celebrated, when the aforementioned day of Pentecost was already dawning, and when, according to custom, we had gathered together after the first hour of the day, nearly the entire multitude of the clerics of the aforesaid martyr Nazarius assembled there and earnestly demanded, in vibrant voices, the clemency of our piety.

They said that the jurisdiction of Beliniacum had been deprived of the benefit of law, justice, and mercy, and had been so afflicted by the many oppressions and additional burdens imposed by the aforesaid Raginardus that it could no longer bear such a prolonged and intolerable evil.

Moved by their immense cries and sufferings, and also fearing divine judgment if our authority did not relieve them, although on such a day we ought to be occupied not with secular but with divine duties, we nevertheless ordered that the aforesaid Raginardus with his men, as well as our faithful and leading men, should attend to this business and come into the chapter-house. In their presence we promised that we would hear the complaints of the clerics.

When they had come, the most noble men of the neighboring cities were also summoned to our council for this matter. Therefore, while we were seated in the chapter-house of Saint Nazarius together with the venerable clerics, our religious fellow bishop, and our beloved nobles, with the duke of Burgundy also present with his fur-clad nobles, the complaints of the clerics were brought forward.

Again and again they said that the aforesaid village and its inhabitants were burdened and nearly ruined by the excessive weight of evil customs and by the continual exactions that the aforesaid Raginardus always demanded. From every mansus possessed by an inhabitant, a pig and a lamb, a hen and a chick, hay and grain, money, and whatever else was necessary were customarily extorted.

The men of the jurisdiction had been reduced to this condition, and their lives had been placed in such danger that all cried out—as human life is always inclined to complain—that they would be reduced to extreme poverty or entirely stripped of their property. This was especially so because the tyrannical fury of robbers afflicted them without respite, and their lords, in whose benefices they lived, also burdened them with the payment of a similar census. Moreover, because their sins demanded it, a miserable and dreadful outcry was heard everywhere concerning both a pestilence among the animals and the barrenness of the land.

After the case of both sides had been discussed and the reasoning of each party heard, although there was one common cry from all, we nevertheless wished to examine the complaints of each person in our presence. Once the truth of the matter had been learned, we finally discovered that the men of Saint Nazarius had suffered such great evils from the abominable oppression of the aforesaid Raginardus and his men that law and justice were not truly maintained among them except in name; and not only had they been made strangers to justice in practice, but no limit at all was being observed in these evils.

Then, whatever we learned had been unlawfully imposed upon them by the aforesaid lord, we released for the sake of the common good and declared invalid. By our common authority we prohibited the evil customs from being rendered any longer. We established and designated the just custom that was properly to be preserved and paid by all, and we declared that, if it could be done, we wished to grant them remission of everything—that is, of both the just and the unjust customs.

But because our frequently mentioned brother did not wish to consent to this, after lengthy deliberation and common consultation, and at the acclamation and request of the people themselves, we provided the following remedy: namely, that the excessively burdensome total should be reduced, the injustices annulled, and that from each occupied mansus each inhabitant should pay six denarii and one obol, together with two sextarii of oats, each year.

In this way, neither would the loss to our jurisdiction be excessive, nor would the aforesaid Raginardus appear to be deprived of everything altogether.

When nearly all the men of Saint Nazarius were prepared to swear that this was the true and just custom, and that they held no more and no less in the jurisdiction than had been stated above, Giroardus, the dean and steward, swore on behalf of all that the entire custom consisted of six denarii with one obol and two sextarii of oats, as stated, and that no one owed him more or less.

Overcome and confounded by this oath, Raginardus, together with his men whom he had prepared to speak for him, having nothing to say against it, on the advice of us and of his brothers, abandoned to Saint Nazarius, for the salvation of his soul and those of his parents, his evil occupations, wicked exactions, and everything else of the same kind beyond the rightful custom.

He willingly made a gift of them, humbly placed it upon the saint’s altar, abandoned every claim and whatever evil custom he had been accustomed to exercise in the jurisdiction, and agreed in every respect with the will of the clerics.

The clerics, for their part, voluntarily gave him three hundred solidi of denarii, since he promised to observe and faithfully maintain this agreement, and since he caused his wife, children, and successors to approve this gift.

We therefore confirm by a written act of our authority the validity of this donation, assigned to the uses of the aforesaid canons. Under threat of excommunication, we prohibit by episcopal authority anyone from daring to violate this privilege. We decree and establish by the authority of this decree that what had been lost and restored, and which the church now possesses, shall possess without delay for all time; and, as it was in ancient times, so shall it remain inviolably in its dominion forever.

If, however, some rash and presumptuous person—which we do not at all believe will happen—should attempt to resist this decree fortified by our authority, we first adjure him to turn back quickly from the injury he has begun. Then, if he refuses, we bind him with the bond of anathema and hand him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.

But whoever proves to be its guardian shall enjoy eternal joys and receive rewards with the angels in the heavens.

So that the *chirograph* of this testament of ours may not be violated by anyone, but may be more firmly secured and established by greater stipulation, we have signed it below with the mark of our sign, and have had it strengthened by the hands and signs of our distinguished faithful, both clerics and laymen.

Done publicly at the city of Autun. This privilege was made in the month of May, on the very day of Pentecost, on the first day of the week, in the fifth indiction, under Agano the bishop, Hugo the duke, Philip the king, and Gregory the universal pontiff.

[Signatures]

Sign of A. P., bishop of Chalon.

Sign of Hu., duke.

Sign of Ho., his brother.

Sign of P., of Glenne.

Sign of V., of Colchis.

Sign of A., of the Island.

Sign of Hu., of Mount Saint John.

Sign of B., of Montfort.

Sign of G., Bruni.

Sign of Vv., of Archis.

Sign of Vv., dean.

Sign of Hu., abbot.

Sign of S., provost.

Heldierius the commentator wrote this in place of Sevinius the chancellor.

## XVIII. LETTER OF RICHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, CONCERNING THE PRIESTLY FISC OF THE CHURCH OF LANATICUM

From the cartulary of the monastery of La Chapelle, chapters 37 and 177.

Since things established in the present time are commonly handed over to oblivion as times succeed one another, and since disputes arise from oblivion, it is necessary, for the purpose of putting an end to the quarrels of posterity, that the deeds of the present time be committed to writing and thus transmitted to the knowledge of future generations.

Therefore I, Richard, humble minister of the church of Bourges, make known that Hunbaldus, lord of Uriac, and Willelmus Albus and his brother Galterius, having come into the presence of our highness, humbly and devoutly placed in our hands the priestly fisc and church of Lanaticum, which Hunbaldus himself and his *fiscales*—men of the fisc—had long held according to the customs of laymen. They acknowledged themselves guilty before God and us concerning what they had unjustly possessed.

We, whose duty it is to order churches for the honor of God and to enlarge monasteries, with the counsel of our ministers and clerics, and with the will and petition of Hunbaldus of Uriac, restored this church, together with its priestly fisc, to the monastery of La Chapelle, since it had been its right, as the authentic privileges of the kings of the Franks and of the pontiffs testify.

After this, we summoned into our presence four legitimate men of that church’s parish, who were the eldest men of the entire parish: namely, two priests of that church, Dacbertus and Rotgerius, and two laymen, Leodegarius Vizo and Aimericus of Porta.

We entreated these four men and adjured them under anathema to distinguish the priestly fisc from the other lands. They did so willingly, at the command and on the advice of Lord Hunbaldus and by our authority.

They declared and showed that everything consisting of meadows, gardens, and houses situated below the village between the two roads belonged to the priestly fisc; likewise the land extending from the meadows to the course of the water; all the streets extending from the village gate to the street of Bernardus Balbus; the house of Geraldus Malepellus; the barn and garden behind Geraldus’s house; the garden of Bernardus Culicocus; the barn, courtyard, and houses contained within that same courtyard up to the oven; the house of Martinus; the garden of Lenaticum; the house and courtyard of Archembaldus Petit; three eminae of land situated between La Chapelle and Lenaticum in one valley; a sextarada of land above the meadow of Segreie, where the elderberry tree is; the *olca* of Lenpaut; a sextarada of land at the crossroads; and the *olca* below the crossroads.

The whole tithe of Monte Vilano also belongs to this same fisc, as does the entire tithe of Tristangis, from Calvello as far as the public road descending from the gallows, and half the tithe of Coctum and Cortada.

Everything that has been shown and listed belongs to the priestly fisc. So that these matters might be firm and remain forever, we ordered a charter to be made and sealed with our own seal.

This was done at La Chapelle of Saint Dionysius on the day of the Ascension of the Lord, in the time of Philip, king of the Franks.

[Signatures]

Richard, archbishop.

Hunbaldus of Uriac.

Dea, his wife.

Hugo, prior.

Geraldus, monk.

Iterius, archdeacon of Bourbon, and others.

## XIX. GIFT OF THE CHURCH OF LENATIA TO THE MONASTERY OF LA CHAPELLE IN THE DIOCESE OF BOURGES

From the cartulary of the same monastery, chapter 101.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Let the love of all Christians know that Hunbaldus of Uriac assigned to God, Saint Dionysius, and the monks of La Chapelle the church of Lenatia and the fisc of that same church, in its entirety, just as the priests Dacbertus and Rogerius held it from that church, together with the whole tenure (*tenor*) which they held for the church, with the consent of the Blancs of Domairac—namely Amelius Blancus, his brother Guillelmus, Hunbaldus, and Galterius—and with the consent of those of Paciaco, namely Willelmus his brother and Geraldus, who held the aforesaid property from the Blancs.

For this tenure to be known more clearly, it is necessary to state it item by item: all the meadows and the land lying between the two roads below the village and extending to the water, together with the gardens and houses; all the streets extending from the gate to the street of Rogerius of Trugnac; the barn and garden of Vizo; the garden of Joannes of Lenacia; the barn, courtyard, and houses contained within that same courtyard up to the oven, just as Rotgerius the chaplain held them; the house and garden of Boerellus; the barn and courtyard of Stephanus of Terail, as they are set out there; the marsh and land above the village, just as Rotgerius the priest held them; a sextaria of land above the meadow of Segrechia, where the elderberry tree is; the *olca* situated below the crossroads; and the garden of Clavellus.

Everything listed here belongs to the priestly fisc.

Now let us list the gifts that were given to the church as alms: an emina of land situated at the meadow of Caprarius; an emina of vineyard at the Red Mountain; half an emina given to Saint Sulpicius by the mother of Araldus of the Crossroads; three eminae of arable land beside the road; one sextarada of land at the Rock, between the two places; one *plantea* of land at the Pear Tree of the Mill; one sextarada from Prospe, between the two places; a *cartalata* of land at Boniol; and half a *cartalata* at the Hill.

The witnesses are these:

Sign of Hunbaldus of Uriac.

Sign of his wife.

Sign of Hugo the monk.

Sign of Rotgerius the chaplain.

Sign of Amblardus Galdet.

Sign of Joannes of Saint Caprasius.

Sign of Petrus of Saint Caprasius.

Sign of Leodegarius Vizi of Lenatia.

Sign of Geraldus of Lenatia.

## XX. AGREEMENT CONCERNING THE CHURCH OF CASIMANSI FOR THE MONASTERY OF LA CHAPELLE IN THE DIOCESE OF BOURGES

From the cartulary of the same monastery, chapters 38 and 96.

Our ancestors, seeing that many things had been handed over to oblivion through antiquity and that their possessions had been diminished, decided that these matters ought to be commemorated by the testimony of writing. Therefore, agreeing with their prudence, we wish the restoration of the church of Casimansi—which took place before the time of [Col. 0480B] Archbishop Richard, who deprived the churches of the power of laymen—[lacuna] to be made known by this testament.

Let it therefore be known to all that Hunbald of Paciacum, Raibod of Berra, and the others who had usurped the aforesaid church for themselves, as was being done in those days, recognizing the right of Saint Dionysius, which he claimed by the gift of the kings of the Franks, returned it, abandoning every claim. Indeed, the aforesaid Richard, who, as has already been said, completely withdrew the churches from the hands of laymen, knowing that this church had been given by the aforementioned kings to Saint Dionysius at the request and command of Pope Alexander, under whom he himself remained, permitted the monks of Capella to possess it in its entirety.

Later, in the time of Archbishop Aldebert, Dacbert, archpriest of Saint Desideratus, who held it in the hands of laymen, seeing that he could not retain it except by the favor of the prior and the other monks—who had recovered it by ecclesiastical sentence and rescued it from the power of its claimants—released it without reservation [Col. 0480C]. Wishing, however, to receive it from them with goodwill during his lifetime, he obtained from Radulf, the prior then in office, at the request of the aforesaid archbishop, that it be granted to him for his lifetime with the advice of the monks, while retaining for them a share of the church’s revenues by way of acknowledgment: namely, six solidi from the priestly benefice at Easter; on the following day, the procession; half of the offering on the feast of Saint Mary in August; a third part on All Saints’ Day; likewise on the day after Christmas; and everything on the feast of the Purification, except the loaves.

This was done on the condition that after Dacbert’s death the monks would possess the church free from claims, except that, if a priest from his family succeeded who was considered suitable for such an office, he would, at the monks’ pleasure, be made its chaplain, possessing the same rights as the preceding chaplains.

Under this agreement, Dacbert also transferred to the monks, to be possessed after his departure, a certain house in that village necessary for the church, together with its appurtenances. In it Rotger Baraton held two census-payments, which Dacbert himself likewise held as a fief. Nevertheless, he ordered that, if the monks could do so, they should hold them in the same way; otherwise, by returning them, they would have the house free. He also gave a certain vineyard in the same village. Therefore Radulf, the prior, gave him a chalice of gold and silver.

Three charters were made concerning this agreement. One was divided by chirograph: one part was delivered to the archpriest and the other to the prior; in addition, each party received another complete copy.
