This was enacted at Capella in the time of Philip, king of the Franks, and Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges.

## XXI. LETTER OF PASCHAL II TO NORIGAUD, BISHOP OF AUTUN

From the old cartulary of the church of Autun.

Paschal, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Norigaud, bishop, and to his canonically appointed successors, forever.

Since, by the dispensation of divine judgment, we have been promoted—though unworthy—to the rank of this office, so that we may hold the place of the chief of the apostles in governing the Church, we must labor and strive with all our strength to imitate, with the most faithful devotion and devout faith, his admonitions and instructions in arranging ecclesiastical affairs.

His faith and distinguished love were pleasing to God to such a degree that the Son of God wished to establish and confirm, upon the immovable foundation of his faith, his Church, redeemed by his precious blood, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” He also granted him such a privilege of power that, at his discretion, things to be bound or loosed in heaven and on earth would be loosed. This succession of his power he himself granted to blessed Clement, and through him to all who should justly preside over his see and undertake to order the Church of God according to canonical regulation.

Strengthened by the authority of this faith [Col. 0481B], we confirm to you, beloved brother Norigaud, and to all your canonically appointed successors, everything that appears to pertain to the Church of Autun, in which we believe you have been canonically ordained: churches, parishes, cemeteries, priests, and all ecclesiastical orders, as well as estates and all other movable and immovable possessions that have been acquired or may justly be acquired. You and your successors shall be permitted to possess all these things as freely as your predecessor is proven to have possessed them peacefully and justly on the day before his death.

By apostolic authority we further decree that no priest, whether living or dying, or transferring to another religious life or to a life of retirement, may remove or diminish the goods that he has been able to acquire from the day of his ordination in the church in which he was ordained. Rather, he must allow them to remain untouched and unimpaired in that same church in which they were acquired.

By the same authority we prohibit anyone from receiving into communion or restoring to divine offices those whom you have excommunicated or removed from the divine offices because of their offenses [Col. 0481C]. We also decree that no one may demand any payment whatsoever from anyone for the place or space of burial.

For the redemption of sins, we establish and entirely confirm, according to apostolic decrees, that those who are dying should give alms in the church in which they received the sacraments of the faith. If anyone, whether living or dying, wishes to transfer to another church, let him leave to the mother church, according to apostolic decrees, a portion of whatever he has decided to give for the salvation of his soul.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person should presumptuously attempt to act against this page of our constitution, we judge and confirm that such a person, as guilty of sacrilege, is to be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church of God. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that church, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the rewarder of the good [Col. 0481D] the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen.

Written by the hand of John, notary of the sacred Lateran palace.

I, Paschal, bishop, have subscribed for the Catholic Church.

I, Walter, unworthy bishop of the Alban Church, have subscribed.

I, Albert, cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed.

I, Bernard, unworthy cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

I, Alberic, by the grace of God humble priest of the title of the Apostles at the Chains, have subscribed in confirmation.

I, Augustine, unworthy cardinal of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Ones, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Leo, scribe, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0482A] 1100, and in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Paschal II.

## XXII. AGREEMENT OF THE MONKS OF SAINT BERTIN AT SITHIU WITH THE PARISHIONERS OF CALAIS

From the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Bertin.

Let all of you know that an agreement has been reached between us and our parishioners, the masters of the church of Calais, as follows: the lepers of that parish shall have their own priest, whom we shall appoint there with the counsel of the parish priest and the consent of the burgesses of Calais. He shall swear that he will be faithful to the church of Saint Bertin and to the parish church.

To enable him to do this better, the masters of those same lepers have assigned him annual revenues of ten pounds. He must be content with these and may not usurp anything belonging to the rights of the parish. If someone traveling past turns aside to the same house in order to hear Mass and offers something, it belongs not to the chaplain but to the lepers.

If any parishioner from Peterse or Calais frequently comes there to Mass, and, after being admonished by his own priest, does not correct this behavior, he shall be publicly excommunicated; and whatever he has offered, the chaplain of the lepers shall restore under oath to the parish priest and shall not receive him thereafter.

The same chaplain shall accept no payment from anyone in order to grant him a seventh-day, thirtieth-day, or anniversary observance. He shall promise this by corporal oath. If he is found to have violated any of these provisions, or is found to be an infamous person, we shall remove him and substitute another in his place in the manner stated above.

In the cemetery of the aforesaid lepers, no one may be buried except a leper, or a healthy person who, after making a solemn vow with them, has worn the religious habit for some period of time. For whatever they cultivate or raise within the bounds of their dwelling, which contains approximately six measures of land [Col. 0482C], they shall not be obliged to pay tithes.

Enacted in the year of the Lord 1202.

## XXIII. MANUMISSION OF NICOLAS OF MARISIAC

From the royal archive of Paris.

Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks. We make known to all present and future that, moved by piety, by these present letters we manumit our beloved Nicolas, son of John of Marisiac and of Mary of Faverolles, his wife, the bearer of this document, who is our personal bondman, so that he may be able to obtain the clerical tonsure.

As testimony of this matter, we have caused our seal to be affixed to these present letters. Enacted at Valles-Comtesse, in the year of the Lord 1312, in the month of June.

## XXIV. OLD FORMS OF ABSOLUTION FOR PENITENTS

From an old manuscript codex of the Royal Library.

### Absolution from punishment and guilt in the time of Lord Gregory XI

May our Lord Jesus Christ, through his mercy, absolve you. And I absolve you from the bonds of excommunication, from association with the excommunicated, and from all general sentences imposed by law, by a human authority, or even by canon, and from all transgressions and all your sins of which you are truly contrite and have confessed, or which do not come to your memory.

I also dispense you from irregularity, if you have incurred any by involving yourself in divine matters while bound by any sentence whatsoever, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, of our lord Pope Bo., and of holy mother Church. And I grant you full indulgence of all your sins, insofar as the Lord wills and the keys of holy mother Church extend, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

### Another form of absolution

After the *Confiteor* and *Misereatur* have been said, the absolving priest shall say:

And I, by the authority of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of our lord the pope, etc., grant you, who are present in the sincerity of Catholic faith, contrite in heart and fully confessed with your mouth, full indulgence from all excommunications, suspensions, and interdicts, and from the irregularities thereby incurred, and from all your sins [I grant you], insofar as the keys of holy mother the Roman Church extend, and also by the authority entrusted to me, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

### Another form

By the authority of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of our lord Pope Bo., and also by the authority which I exercise, I absolve you from the bond of excommunication, if you have incurred it through association or through a slight laying-on of hands, and from all general sentences—not, however, those specially reserved by the aforesaid lord Pope Bo., but those promulgated generally, whether by human authority or by law—and from the sentence of suspension and interdict.

I dispense you from irregularity, if you have contracted any through celebrating the divine offices or involving yourself in divine matters. I restore you to the sacraments of the Church and to the communion of the faithful, together with the divine prayers.

By the same authority I absolve you from those sins that you have confessed to me, and from all others that you do not remember, which, when you recall them, you intend to confess, and from your negligences, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

# REGINO, ABBOT OF PRÜM, ON HARMONIC INSTRUCTION

## NOTICE

(From Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, on music.)

We publish this according to two copies of one and the same codex in the Paulina Library at Leipzig. One of them was communicated to me by Father Joannes Baptista Martini, of the Order of Friars Minor, a Bolognese; the other I owe to the courtesy of Friedrich Wilhelm Marpurg of Berlin, and to the industry and care of the distinguished Andreas Belli, professor and librarian at Leipzig. I was unable to see the manuscript itself, or autograph, and therefore could not decide what ought to be done with the *Tonary* appended to this letter to Ratbod, archbishop of Trier, since no one was willing to undertake its description because of the unfamiliar forms of the ancient musical signs. Meanwhile, whatever has come into our hands we place here before the reader’s eyes.

## SUMMARY

1. The occasion and rationale of the *Tonary* appended to this letter.  
2. The anomalies of the modes, or eight tones.  
3. The eight tones, or musical modes.  
4. Tone and natural and artificial music.  
5. Music in the movement of the heavenly bodies.  
6. Natural music and its effects.  
7. Artificial music, first in instruments.  
8. The etymology of music.  
9. What voice is, and what sound is.  
10. Consonances and intervals.  
11. According to Pythagoras’ discovery.  
12. The seven liberal disciplines.  
13. The names of strings or intervals.  
14. Tetrachords.  
15. The consonances which they contain.  
16. The names and origin of the consonances.  
17. Tones and the smaller intervals.  
18. The distinction between practical and theoretical musicians.  
19. The syllables *Nonannoeane*, etc.

# HERE BEGINS THE LETTER ON HARMONIC INSTRUCTION SENT TO RADBOD, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, BY REGINO THE PRIEST

To the most excellent lord Radbod, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, Regino offers devoted service forever.

## 1.

Since I had often seen the chorus of those singing psalms in the dioceses of your Church resounding with confused voices because of the dissonance of the tone, and since I had seen your reverence frequently disturbed by this matter, I took up the Antiphoner and, carefully turning through it in order from beginning to end, assigned to their proper tones, as I believe, the antiphons that I found written in it [Col. 0485A]. I also took care to insert in distinct orders the divisions of the tones—that is, the differences [Note: [Col. 0485D] The differences of the eight tones are customarily written on the final syllables of the doxology “Glory be to the Father,” etc., at the end of each psalm, namely in the vowels *euouae* of the two [Col. 0486D] final words *saeculorum. Amen*.]—that are customarily made on the final syllable in the verse, so that the singing might be graceful and appropriate, as they have been handed down to us by our predecessors and as the experience of the discipline of harmony itself has shown.

Some people also add other divisions, which we consider superfluous [alternative: “to be such”]. But, lest we be criticized by overly scrupulous musicians, we have tried to note them below or above in the margin, leaving it to the judgment of the skilled cantor whether he wishes to regard them as necessary or [alternative: superfluous] unnecessary.

I have not only distinguished the antiphons according to suitable tones, but have also worked with the greatest care to associate with consonant tonal correspondences the introits for Masses and the communions, as well as the responsories that are sung during the night hours in praise of God [alternative: divine praise] [Col. 0485B].

## 2.

The skilled cantor must know that the consonance of the tones is not easily recognized in certain antiphons. For there are some antiphons that we call *nothae*, that is, degenerate and illegitimate: they begin in one tone, are in another in the middle, and end in a third. We have explained their dissonance and ambiguity in their proper places in the brief treatise that follows.

Nevertheless, so that the principle may become clearer, we insert several examples here. “Before me no God was formed” (*Ante me non est formatus Deus*). “From the moment the voice was made” (*Ex quo facta est vox*). “From Egypt I called” (*Ex Aegypto vocavi*). “To you, Lord, I lifted up my soul” (*Ad te, Domine, levavi animam meam*). “Zion, you shall be renewed” (*Sion, renovaberis*). “O death, I shall be your death” (*O mors, ero mors tua*). “Go now and do not sin” (*Vade jam et noli peccare*). These aforesaid antiphons begin in the seventh tone, while some end in the first and others in the fourth tone.

Likewise, the antiphons “Do not remember” (*Ne reminiscaris*) and “Then the paralytic took up his bed” (*Tulit ergo paralyticus*) begin in the third tone but end in the fourth. Similarly, “Why have you pulled down?” (*Quare detraxistis*) and many other examples begin in the third tone but end in the sixth. “Who hates his life” (*Qui odit animam suam*) and “And looking upon them” (*Et respicientes*) begin in the third but end in the eighth. “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine” (*Quod uni ex minimis meis*) begins in the seventh but ends in the first, and there are many similar examples.

But not only are antiphons mixed with these ambiguities and uncertainties of tone; some introits also begin in one tone but end in another. Thus “O God, attend to my help” (*Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*) begins in the eighth tone but ends in the seventh. Likewise, “Receive gladness” (*Accipite jocunditatem*) and “When God went forth” (*Deus dum egrederetur*) begin in the eighth but end in the fourth. “Let my mouth be filled” (*Repleatur os meum*) and “The charity of God” (*Charitas Dei*) begin in the third and end in the fourth. “Judge, Lord, those who harm me” (*Judica, Domine, nocentes me*) begins in the fourth but ends in the seventh. “Your victorious hand” (*Victricem manuum tuam*) begins in the third but ends in the eighth. “The Lord led out his people” (*Eduxit Dominus populum suum*) begins in the fourth but ends in the eighth. “Behold, the eyes of the Lord” (*Ecce oculi Domini*) begins in the third but ends in the fourth. “The Lord will speak” (*Loquetur Dominus*) begins in the third but ends in the fourth. “The just man will not be disturbed” (*Justus non conturbabitur*) begins in the second but [Col. 0486A] ends in the first. “The Lord speaks words” (*Dicit Dominus sermones*) begins in the third and ends in the first, along with many similar examples.

The prudent cantor must observe above all that he should always attend more to the beginning of an antiphon, introit, or communion in its tonal sound than to its ending. Conversely, in responsories he should consider the ending and conclusion in the consonance of the tone more than the beginning.

## 3.

In natural music—that is, in the song performed in divine praises—four principal tones are found, which are named in Greek as follows: authentic *protos*, authentic *deuterus*, authentic *tritus*, and authentic *tetrardus*. From their sources flow four others, called: *plaga proti*, *plaga deuteri*, *plaga triti*, and *plaga tetrardi*.

For from the authentic *protos* arises or is derived *plaga proti*. In the same way, the remaining three take their beginning from the other three; they are, so to speak, their members. They may be interpreted as follows:

- authentic *protos*, that is, first authority—understood, in natural music;
- authentic *deuterus*, that is, second authority;
- authentic *tritus*, that is, third authority;
- authentic *tetrardus*, that is, fourth authority;
- *plaga proti*, that is, part of the first tone;
- *plaga deuteri*, that is, authority [better: part] of the second tone;
- *plaga triti*, that is, part of the third tone;
- *plaga tetrardi*, that is, part of the fourth tone.

Within these eight tones is contained and comprehended not only all the spiritual harmony of melody but also every natural song.

## 4.

Many people hear a tone and perhaps do not know what a tone is, why it is called a tone, or how far natural musical tone differs from artificial musical tone. Natural music has four principal tones. Artificial music, however, has five tones and two semitones, which nevertheless do not complete a full tone, since they cannot be divided into equal parts. One is larger and the other smaller, and for this reason they do not admit equal divisions.

These five tones together with the two semitones are constituted by the three consonances of musical perfection: the *diapente*, *diatessaron*, and *diapason*. Likewise, from the four principal tones of natural music four others arise; like streams flowing from springs and branches proceeding from the root of a tree, they derive their origin from them in a certain way.

Nothing of this sort happens in artificial music. A tone does not generate another tone from itself, nor does one surpass another in authority; rather, all are divided among themselves by equal divisions [alternative: dimensions], namely by the sesquioctave proportion, except for the semitones.

It must also be observed that in natural music all eight tones are whole and perfect, although they differ from one another in authority. They admit no semitone, nor *diesis*, nor *apotome*, nor *tristemorium*, nor *tetrastemorium* [Note: [Col. 0487D] *Diesis* (δίεσις) is the first difference of tones perceptible to the senses, or the smaller semitone. *Apotome* (ἀποτομή) is the greater semitone; *tritemorium* (τριτημόριον), the third part of a tone; *tetrastemorium* (τεταρτημόριον), the fourth part of the same tone. See Boethius.]; for it is in these divisions that the tone of artificial music is divided.

From this dissonance it is evident that those eight often mentioned entities called tones ought rather to be called modes, or differences or tropes of the consonances of musical modulation. Mixed from grave and acute sounds in a beautiful variety of harmonic delight, and as though sprinkled with certain flowers, they render the sweetness of the melody agreeable and pleasing.

Moreover, the entire skill of musical discipline is measured and confined by arithmetic rules. It proceeds by the numerical proportions of double, quadruple, sesquialter, sesquitertian, or sesquioctave ratios. These dimensions, as I think, are difficult to find in the tones mentioned above. For all whole and perfect tones must differ from one another by equal dimensions, that is, by an eighth of themselves. This distance can be demonstrated between the numbers eight and nine. The number nine contains the whole number eight within itself and, in addition, its eighth part, namely one. Musicians call this difference an interval; arithmeticians call it a sesquioctave proportion. An interval is the distance between an acute and a grave sound.

Thus a tone either exceeds another tone or is exceeded by another tone by an eighth of itself. But what the relation of the tones or of the consonances mentioned above is, and how the musical consonances are found, or how they are fitted together or separated from one another, we shall demonstrate more clearly below. Meanwhile, the preceding discussion should be accepted with only moderate confidence; certainty will come when, through clear demonstration, those things that seemed ambiguous have been revealed.

Since natural and artificial music have been mentioned, the less-experienced musician may ask what distance there is between natural and artificial music. The answer is that, although the modulation of every harmonic discipline is one and the same in the sounds of its consonances, one kind of music is natural and another artificial.

Natural music is that which resounds through no musical instrument, no touch of the fingers, and no human impulse or contact, but, breathed into it by God and taught by nature alone, modulates sweet modes. It occurs either in the movement of the heavens or in the human voice. Some add a third instance: in an irrational creature, through sound or voice.

## 5.

The Pythagoreans infer by the following argument that music exists in the movement of the heavens. “How,” they say, “can it happen that the heavenly mechanism, moving so swiftly, travels in silent and noiseless motion? Even if that sound does not reach our ears, it cannot in any way happen that motion so swift is without sound, [Col. 0488A] especially since the courses of the stars are joined with such great coordination and harmony that nothing can be conceived as so joined and connected.

Some are carried higher, others lower, and all revolve with equal impetus, so that an ordered arrangement of courses is produced through unequal inequalities. From this it is conjectured that an ordered pattern of modulation exists in the movement of the heavens. Consonance, which governs all musical modulation, cannot exist without sound. Sound, however, is not produced without some impulse or blow. Again, a blow does not occur unless motion has preceded it.

Some movements are faster and others slower. If movement is slow and varied, it produces grave sounds; if it is swift and dense, acute sounds must necessarily be produced. For in an immobile thing no sound is ever made. Therefore musicians define sound in this way: sound is an undissolved striking of the air continuing as far as the hearing.

Thus both acuteness and gravity arise from several movements.

From this conjecture astrologers or musicians say that, between the outermost sphere and the circles of the seven planets, all musical consonances are completed. From Saturn to the celestial sphere, they say, the most acute sound is produced; from the earth to the lunar circle, the gravest, although some think otherwise. Finally, they assert that from Saturn to the sphere the sound is graver, while from the earth to the lunar circle it is more acute, because what is narrower and shorter must necessarily resound more acutely, just as, conversely, what is longer resounds more gravely.

Between Saturn’s circle and the moon, throughout the entire breadth of the planets, there is a variety of different tones, and all the consonances of music are perfected. Martianus represents all this figuratively in the book that he composed on the marriage of Philology and Mercury, placing it in the grove of Apollo, who himself is the sun, the moderator of heavenly music. For he says: “The more elevated summits,” that is, the higher branches, “stretched out” [that is, greatly extended], “resounded with an acute sound,” that is, a subtle and slender one.

Whatever was near and adjacent to the earth shook—meaning drove and struck back—the branches that were more inclined and lower and nearer to the earth; a hoarse gravity [Col. 0488D] answered them. But the middle parts of the forest, with the spaces joined to one another, sang together with double accompaniments.

*Concentus* is the united association of similar voices; *succentus* is different sounds that agree very closely with one another, as we see in an organ. He says “with double accompaniments, and sesquialter, and also sesquitertian” accompaniments. Here he touches on three consonances: *diapason*, *diatessaron*, and *diapente*. “With octaves,” he says, “joined without distinction,” that is, without an interval, “by connections,” that is, by consonances. Here he touches upon the tone, although *limmata*, that is, semitones, intervene. Here he touches upon the two semitones. From all these things the sum of the whole of music is composed. But all this will be demonstrated more clearly in its proper place.

Nor should it be omitted that the strings, or chords, are also compared with heavenly music. Musicians have assigned *hypate meson* to Saturn. *Parypate* is likened to the Jovian circle. They assigned *lichanos meson* to Mars. The sun holds *meson*. Venus possesses *trite synemmenon*. Mercury governs *paranete synemmenon*. The moon’s circle holds the example of *nete*. This is according to Boethius [Note: Book I, chapter 27].

Cicero, however, arranges them in the opposite order. In the *Dream of Scipio* he asserts—and nature dictates—that the outermost bodies sound gravely on one side and acutely on the other. For this reason, that highest star-bearing chariot of heaven, whose revolution is more rapid, moves with an acute and excited sound, while the lunar and lowest sphere sounds most gravely. The earth, ninth, remaining immobile, always clings to one position.

Thus, in this passage Cicero places the earth as a kind of silence, namely as immobile. Next to it, the moon, which is closest to silence, he assigns the gravest sound, so that the moon is *proslambanomenos*, the string that resounds most gravely; Mercury is *hypate hypaton*; Venus, *parypate hypaton*; the sun, *lichanos hypaton*; Mars, *hypate meson*; Jupiter, *parypate meson*; Saturn, *lichanos meson*; and the celestial sphere, *mese*.

Compared with Mercury, therefore, the moon sounds a tone. The same moon creates the consonance *diapente* with Mars, *diatessaron* with the sun, and *diapason* with the celestial sphere. Behold, in the movement of the heavens, the sum of all music.

Let these few remarks on heavenly music suffice. If anyone wishes to know these matters more fully, let him read the second book of Macrobius, the excellent philosopher, on the aforementioned *Dream of Scipio*. We add only this: not merely the philosophers of the pagans but also the earnest preachers of the Christian faith agree about this heavenly harmony.

## 6.

Having passed over these matters, we must turn to the contemplation of human music. No one who understands himself doubts that music is naturally joined to all human beings, to every age, and to both sexes. For what age or what sex does not delight in musical songs? It is characteristic of humanity to take pleasure in sweet modes and to be irritated by their opposites.

Infants and young people, as well as the elderly, are so naturally entangled in musical modulations by a kind of spontaneous feeling that there is absolutely no age devoid of the enjoyment of sweet song. Although some people cannot sing learnedly or sweetly for others, they nevertheless sing something sweetly to themselves, even if without sweetness.

It should also be understood that human character is recognized through music. A wanton and impudent mind delights in more wanton modes, or, by frequently hearing them, is softened and rendered effeminate. Conversely, a harder and fiercer mind either rejoices in harsher modes or is incited by them. It cannot happen that soft things are joined to hard things, or hard things to soft, or that they take pleasure in one another; rather, as has been said, similarity of character produces love and delight [Col. 0490A]. For the harsher peoples delight in harsher modes, while the gentle and peaceful delight in milder ones.

Thus the entire disposition of character is governed and directed by songs, so that one sings both for the advance into battle and likewise for the retreat, with the trumpet’s song first arousing and then calming the courage of the mind. Song brings sleep and takes it away; it also introduces and removes cares and anxieties. It arouses anger, recommends clemency, and even cures bodily illnesses.

It is well known how often song has restrained angry minds and how many remarkable things it has accomplished amid afflictions of body or soul. Finally, as Cicero relates, when drunken young men, incited by the sound of flutes, were breaking down the doors of a chaste woman in order to violate her chastity [Col. 0490B], Pythagoras understood that the sound of the Phrygian mode had stirred the young men’s minds to lust. He was then observing the course of the stars and immediately hurried up and advised the flute-player to change the mode and play a spondaic rhythm. When she had done this, the slowness of the modes and the gravity of her playing caused their raging insolence to subside.

What we produce from the books of the pagans we can affirm from our own sources. When an evil spirit tormented King Saul, David took up the psaltery and mitigated the fierceness of his breast with sweet and pleasing modes. What shall we say about the prophet Elisha? When he had been questioned by a king and understood that at that moment the spirit of prophecy was not in him, he ordered a psalmist to be brought. While the psalmist played before him, the Spirit suddenly descended upon him [Col. 0490C], and he prophesied.

Thus, just as it is certainly evident that in war the minds of combatants are inflamed by the sound of trumpets, so there is no doubt that a more moderate and gentler mode of song can temper mental disturbance. From all these things it clearly and indubitably appears that music is naturally joined to us in such a way that, even if we wished, we could not be without it. Therefore the mind’s attention must be raised, so that what is naturally implanted within us may also be comprehended by knowledge.

It remains now to examine the third kind of natural music, which we mentioned above as existing in irrational creatures. The philosophers hold the following opinion about it. “It is not surprising,” they say, “that music has such great dominion among human beings, since birds too—nightingales, swans, and others—practice song as though according to a certain discipline of the musical art.” Thus Virgil says of swans: “They give melodies through their necks,” and so forth.

Some birds of land or water, attracted by song, willingly run into nets or bird traps. Nor should one overlook the fact that the shepherd’s pipe commands the flock’s feeding, movement, and rest. It is also said that in the sea the Sirens produce sweet songs.

Rightly, therefore, music captures everything that lives, because the heavenly soul by which the universe is animated took its origin from music, as Plato and his followers hold. These remarks on natural music have been presented briefly.

[Col. 0491A] **7.** It remains briefly to consider artificial music. Artificial music is that which has been devised and discovered through human art and ingenuity, and which consists in certain instruments. It too is divided into three kinds, namely, stringed, wind, and percussion instruments. Stringed music is produced by the tightening of strings, as, for example, in the lyre, cithara, harp, and similar instruments. Wind music is driven by breath or air, as in pipes, bagpipes, flutes, organs, and similar instruments. Percussion music is produced in certain hollow bronze vessels and other instruments when they are struck with a blow or by percussion, from which different sounds are produced, as in cymbals, drums, and so forth.

Anyone wishing to possess knowledge of this art must understand that, although natural music greatly precedes artificial music, [Col. 0491B] no one can recognize the power of natural music except through artificial music. Therefore, although our discussion began with natural music, it must end with artificial music, so that through a visible thing we may be able to demonstrate an invisible one.

**8.** Having briefly pre­liminarily stated these matters, reason now demands that we examine music itself more carefully. First, we must say from what it is called music. Music is called *musica* from the *musa*, the instrument which the Gauls call the *cornemuse*, we call the *utriculus*, and the Germans *Cactpfeife* or *Dudelfact*, and which the ancients judged worthy of preference over all musical instruments, either because, as they say, it was first invented by nature, or rather because the whole perfection of music is contained in it. For all consonances and tones can be demonstrated through its upper holes, and the greater and lesser semitones through its two lower holes.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Concerning this musical instrument, *musa*, which the Gauls call *cornemuse*, we call *utriculus*, and the Germans *Cactpfeife* and *Dudelfact*, see Du Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, s.v. *Musa*. Other etymologies of *musica* are found throughout the earlier writers.]

[Col. 0491C] *Musica* is said to derive from *musa*, just as *grammatica* derives from *gramma*, *rhetorica* from *rhetoreion* (ῥητόρειον), that is, abundance of expression, *arithmetica* from *arithmos*, that is, number, *geometria* from *ge* (γῆ), that is, earth, and *astrologia* from *astron*, that is, star.

**9.** But before we distinguish the parts of the musical discipline, let us first say something about voice and sound. Although every voice is a sound, not every sound can rightly be called a voice. That creature, therefore, which is breathed upon by vital spirit produces a voice; that which is driven by a blow, strike, or breath produces a sound.

Every voice is either *syneches* [Note: [Col. 0492D] *Synechēs* (συνεχής); another reading is *synaphēs* (συναφής), incorrectly, in view of what follows.]—that is, continuous, as when speakers, or those reading aloud, run through words continuously—or *diastematikē* [Note: [Col. 0492D] *Diastematikē* (διαστηματική), divided by intervals; opposed here to *synechēs* (σηνεχής). See Coelius Rhodiginus, book V, chapter 24.]—that is, suspended with an interval, as when we suspend the voice in singing. It is the latter that is now under discussion; in it we serve not words but melodic patterns.

**10.** It must be understood that consonance is produced from voice or tone. Yet one must also observe that in voices or sounds which do not clash through any inequality there is no consonance at all. Consonance is defined as follows: consonance is the harmonious union of different voices brought together into one. Alternatively, consonance is a mixture of a high and a low sound, reaching the ears pleasantly and uniformly.

Conversely, dissonance is the harsh and unpleasant striking upon the ear produced by two sounds mingled with one another. Although the sense of hearing judges consonance, reason weighs it. Whenever two strings are tightened, and one of them sounds lower while the other sounds higher, and when struck together they produce a somehow mingled and pleasant sound, so that the two voices seem to unite and grow together into one, then what is called consonance occurs. But when, struck together, each strives to oppose the other and they do not blend into a single pleasant sound composed of the two, then what is called dissonance occurs.

There are only six numerical ratios that create consonances or by which consonances are distinguished: the *epitritus*, *hemiolius*, *duplaris*, *triplaris*, [Col. 0492B] *quadruplus*, and *epogdous*.

The *epitritus* occurs when, of two numbers, the greater contains the whole of the lesser and, in addition, its third part, as four is to three. For four contains three and a third of three, namely one. In arithmetic this number is called *sesquitertius*, and from it arises the *symphonia*, that is, consonance, called in music the *diatessaron*.

The *hemiolius* occurs when, of two numbers, the greater contains the whole of the lesser and, in addition, half of it, as three is to two. For three contains two and their half, namely one. In arithmetic this number is called *sesquialter*, and from it arises the *symphonia* called the *diapente*.

The *duplaris* number occurs when, of two numbers, the lesser is contained twice in the greater, as four is to two; from this double ratio arises the *symphonia* called the *diapason*.

The *triplaris* occurs when, of two numbers, the lesser is contained three times in the greater, as three is to one; from this triple ratio arises the *symphonia* called the *diapason with diapente*.

The *quadruplaris* number occurs when, of two numbers, the lesser is contained four times in the greater, as four is to one; this number produces the *symphonia* called *bis diapason*.

The *epogdous* is a number that contains the lesser within itself and, in addition, its eighth part, as nine is to eight, because nine contains eight and, in addition, an eighth part of it, namely one. Arithmeticians call this number *sesquioctavus*. This number produces the sound that musicians have called a tone.

The sound lesser than a tone the ancients wished to call a semitone. It must not, however, be understood as half a tone, just as in letters we do not take a semivowel to mean half a vowel. Moreover, by its nature a tone cannot be divided into two equal parts. Since it consists of the number nine, and nine cannot be divided equally, the tone refuses to be divided into two halves.

They therefore called a semitone a sound lesser than a tone, which was found to differ from it by as small an interval as that separating the numbers 243 and 256. Some ancient Pythagoreans called this semitone a *diesis*, but later usage established that the lesser sound should be called a *diesis*. Plato called the semitone a *limma*.

These are the parts into which all music is resolved. There are therefore five symphonies, that is, consonances: the *diatessaron*, *diapente*, *diapason*, *diapason with diapente*, and *bis diapason*. All musical consonances therefore consist either in a double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter, or sesquitertian numerical proportion. What is sesquitertian in numbers is called *diatessaron* in sounds; what is sesquialter in numbers is called *diapente* in voices; what is double in numbers is called *diapason* in consonances; what is triple is *diapason with diapente*; and what is quadruple is *bis diapason*.

The attentive reader should recognize that consonances placed upon consonances produce other consonances. For when diapente and diatessaron are joined, they create the consonance diapason. If diapente is joined to this—that is, to diapason—the consonance named from both terms is produced, namely diapason and diapente. If diatessaron is added to this, *bis diapason* is produced.

It must further be understood that if diapason and diatessaron are joined, they produce no consonance. It immediately falls into the superpartient type of inequality and preserves neither the order of multiplicity nor the simplicity of superparticularity. How this can be demonstrated would take too long to insert here. Whoever wishes to know it more fully should read Boethius’ second book *On the Institution of Harmony*.

For the present, it is enough briefly to recall that consonance arises from unequal numbers. There are five kinds of inequality, which differ from one another in their inequality in these ways: one number is exceeded by another through multiplicity, through a single part, through several parts, through multiplicity and a part, or through multiplicity and several parts. Whoever wishes to examine these kinds of inequality should read the first book of Boethius’ *Arithmetic*.

It must be noted, however, that of the five kinds of inequality mentioned above, only two are employed to form harmonic consonances, namely the multiple and the superparticular. A number is called multiple when it contains the lesser number twice or four times. From this are formed the consonances of diapason. A number is called superparticular when it contains the whole lesser number and, in addition, half, a third, or an eighth part of it. From this arise the consonances of diapente and diatessaron, as well as the tone. It follows that one cannot become a perfect musician unless one has first been thoroughly instructed in the rules of arithmetic.

With these matters set forth for clarification, let us examine the aforementioned consonances through tones. The diatessaron consonance consists of two tones and a semitone, and is produced from the epitritus, that is, the sesquitertian ratio.

The diapente consonance consists of three tones and a semitone, and is produced from the hemiolius, that is, from a half and a whole. For the Greeks call “half” *hēmi* and “whole” *holon*.

The diapason consonance consists of six tones and is produced from the double ratio, since the diapason symphony is made from diapente and diatessaron. For it was shown above that diatessaron consists of two tones and a semitone, and diapente of three tones and a semitone—that is, of five tones and two semitones.

Diapason with diapente consists of nine tones and a semitone, and is produced from the triple ratio. *Bis diapason* contains twelve tones and is produced from the quadruple ratio. We have stated these things about tones according to Macrobius; Cassiodorus, however, asserts in his *Secular Letters* that there are fifteen tones, according to the number of strings placed in the *bis diapason* consonance. We shall demonstrate them later, when we begin to discuss the strings and their names.

**11.** It must be understood that the often-mentioned consonances were not discovered by human ingenuity, but were revealed to Pythagoras through a certain divine prompting. Since that philosopher possessed an ardent intellect and had long been consumed by inquiry into the manner in which he might firmly and consistently discern the principles [variant: monuments] of consonances, it happened that, while passing by the workshops of smiths, he heard hammers being struck, producing in a manner a single harmony from different sounds.

Astonished, he approached the matter he had been seeking. After long consideration, he supposed that the difference in tones was produced by the varying weights of the striking objects. To test this, he ordered the hammers to be exchanged. Once they had been exchanged, the difference in the sounds withdrew from the men and followed the hammers. He then devoted all his attention to examining their weights.

One hammer was found to weigh twelve units, another nine, a third eight, and a fourth six. The hammers weighing twelve and six units therefore produced the diapason consonance in the double ratio. The twelve-unit hammer with the nine-unit hammer, and the eight-unit hammer with the six-unit hammer, produced the diatessaron consonance according to the epitritian, that is, sesquitertian, proportion. The nine-unit hammer sounded with the eight-unit hammer in the sesquioctave proportion, producing a tone.

Pythagoras then returned home and, through various examinations, determined that the entire principle of the symphonies consisted in the dimensions just described. Sometimes he fitted equal weights to strings and judged their consonances by ear; sometimes he applied double, half, and other proportions to the lengths of reeds or pipes; and often he struck cymbals made with different weights using a hammer, according to the method described above.

From all these experiments he gathered the most complete certainty through varied experience, and rejoiced greatly that he had discovered nothing different. Since the whole summit of harmonic learning consists in the consonances recognized by divine gift, they ought therefore to be known both to the mind and to the ears. For these matters are gathered in vain through reason and knowledge, as the distinguished author Boethius testifies, unless they are thoroughly familiar through use and practice.

**12.** There are, in fact, seven liberal disciplines. Three of them—grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic—are grasped through reason and natural understanding; they are not seen by the eye or pointed out by the finger, because their power lies in speech, while speech, that is, human utterance, can be heard but cannot be seen.

The remaining four—arithmetic, geometry, music, and astrology—cannot be fully comprehended by the mind unless they are seen by the eye and demonstrated by the finger.

**13.** For this reason it seems useful and entirely necessary for us first to discuss briefly the strings and their names, and to place each string’s tone beneath it. Then, when we begin to discuss the consonances mentioned above more clearly and distinctly, we shall be able to send a sober singer to those strings, so that he may see with his eyes and touch with his finger what he has received from us through word and writing by ear.

For the sake of brevity, we omit the invention of the strings and the manner in which their number was increased by different people at different times. Let the strings on which the *bis diapason* consonance is completed and demonstrated be arranged in order as follows:

*Proslambanomenos*, and *Prosmelodos*. *Hypate hypaton*. *Parypate hypaton*. *Lichanos hypaton*. [Col. 0495C] *Hypate meson*. *Parypate meson*. *Lichanos meson*. *Mese*. *Paramese*. *Trite diezeugmenon*. *Paranete diezeugmenon*. *Nete diezeugmenon*. *Trite hyperboleon*. *Paranete hyperboleon*. *Nete hyperboleon*.

The names of the strings written above require interpretation because they are Greek.

*Proslambanomenos* therefore means “acquired” or “added,” since, because *mese* was not located in the middle so as to be able to join the two diapasons, but lay closer to the *hypatai*, this one string was added above the *hypatai hypaton*. Hence by some it is also called *prosmelodos*, that is, “joined or added to the melody.”

*Hypate hypaton* means “chief of the chief strings,” with “strings” understood. For this was always the first string. Before *proslambanomenos* was added, it was the string producing the lowest sound. Hence some interpret it as “the greatest of the great” or “the lowest of the low.”

*Parypate hypaton* is called the third string, as though placed beside *hypate*, that is, gathered alongside it. It may also be interpreted as “the subordinate chief of the chief strings.”

*Lichanos hypaton* is so called because *lichanos* in Greek means the index finger. [Col. 0496A] The Greeks call it *lichanon* from licking. Just as, in singing, the index finger—which is the *lichanos*—was found at the string that was third from *hypate*, that string itself was therefore also called *lichanos*.

**14.** This tetrachord, because it is formed from longer and thicker strings and produces a lower sound, is called the principal tetrachord. It is followed by *hypate meson*, that is, “chief of the middle strings,” with “strings” understood.

*Parypate meson* means “subordinate chief of the middle strings,” or “placed beside the chief of the middle strings.”

*Lichanos meson* means “the third of the middle strings.”

Then *mese* is placed in the eighth position. *Mese* means “middle,” either because it is always in the middle between seven and seven, or because it is the end of the preceding diapason and the beginning of the following one, and is counted as two strings. Although the eighth string sounds the first diapason consonance, there are not for this reason sixteen strings in the *bis diapason*, but only fifteen, because *mese*, as we have said, fills the place of the sixteenth string.

*Paramese* means “placed beside the middle.”

*Trite diezeugmenon*: *trite* means “third from *mese*”; *diezeugmenon* means “of the disjoined” or “separated” strings, with “strings” understood. When two tetrachords are joined by one intervening middle string, this is called in Greek *synemmenon*, that is, “joined.” Hence it is also called *synaphē*, that is, “connection,” whenever two tetrachords are continued and joined by one shared middle boundary.

Conversely, *diezeuxis* is called “separation,” whenever two tetrachords are separated and differ from one another by a full tone.

*Paranete diezeugmenon* is so called because it is placed beside *nete*, that is, the last of the disjoined strings. It is followed by *nete diezeugmenon*, that is, the lower or last of the disjoined strings.

*Trite hyperboleon* means “third of the high,” with “strings” understood.

*Paranete hyperboleon* means “joined to *nete*,” that is, placed before the last of the high strings.

*Nete hyperboleon* is interpreted as “the last of the high strings.”

These three final and most recent strings produce a sound sharper and thinner than that of the other strings; hence they are called “the high” or “excellent” strings.

**15.** Let us now see how all the consonances are found in these fifteen strings. *Proslambanomenos* is separated from the second string, *hypate hypaton*, by a complete tone. *Proslambanomenos* is itself the eighth from *mese*, and sounds with it—that is, with *mese*—the diapason consonance.

The same *proslambanomenos* sounds with the fourth string, *lichanos hypaton*, the diatessaron consonance. *Lichanos hypaton* sounds with *mese* the diapente symphony, and is the fifth string from it.

Again, *mese* is separated by a tone from *paramese*. The same *mese* produces with *nete diezeugmenon*, which is the fifth string from *mese*, the diapente consonance called the symphony of diapason and diapente.

The aforementioned *nete diezeugmenon* produces with *nete hyperboleon*, the fourth string, the diatessaron consonance.

Again, *proslambanomenos* with *nete hyperboleon*, that is, the first string with the fifteenth, sounds the *bis diapason* consonance.

There you have, in the fifteen strings, all the tones and all the consonances. On more careful examination of the subtlety of the musical discipline, no more than five tetrachords are found: *hypaton*, *meson*, *synemmenon*, *diezeugmenon*, and *hyperboleon*. They may be interpreted as follows: *hypatai*, the chief strings; *mesai*, the middle strings; *synemmenai*, the joined strings; *diezeugmenai*, the disjoined strings; and *hyperboleai*, the high or excellent strings.

It would take too long to demonstrate all these matters more fully here. For we have not proposed to explain the whole fullness of harmonic instruction in this letter, since even the distinguished author Boethius was scarcely able to explain its intricate subtlety in five books. [Col. 0497B] We note only that the five aforementioned tetrachords extend across twenty-eight strings.

**16.** Having set forth these matters concerning the strings and their names, it is now time to discuss the names of the consonances and their sounds somewhat more plainly and clearly for those who understand less. Although we have already mentioned most of the matters relating to music, the names are Greek and therefore require an interpreter.

*Diatessaron* can be rendered in Latin as “from four.” This is not because it consists of four numbers or parts, since it is made from the hemiolius, that is, from a half and a whole, but because it is composed of four sounds or voices separated from one another by a definite interval.

The diatessaron is therefore a consonance of four voices but of three intervals. What an interval is was shown above: it is the distance between a high and a low sound.

When a greater voice contains a lesser voice wholly within itself and, in addition, a third part of the lesser voice or tone, it produces a diatessaron consonance, which always occurs in the fourth string. Thus *proslambanomenos* sounds with *lichanos hypaton* the diatessaron, as was shown above.

*Diapente* means “from five.” *Dia* is the Greek preposition meaning “from,” and *pente* means “five.” *Diapente* is so called because it is completed from five voices or sounds. It consists of five voices but four intervals.

Thus, when the greater voice precedes the lesser voice by its whole quantity and, in addition, surpasses half of the voice exceeded, whether in height or in depth, this symphony is called diapente, and it always occurs in the fifth string. For *lichanos hypaton* sounds with *mese* the diapente consonance.

*Diapason* may be interpreted as “from all,” since it is formed from all semitones, tones, and consonances. Indeed, diapason consists of diapente and diatessaron.

When the greater voice exceeds the lesser voice by twice its quantity, whether in the extension of height or in the lowering of depth, this symphony is called diapason, and it always occurs in the eighth string. For *proslambanomenos* sounds with *mese* the diapason consonance, and it is more principal and honorable than the other consonances.

Furthermore, the diapason-and-diapente consonance is formed when the greater voice or sound exceeds the lesser voice or sound by three times its quantity in height or depth. It always occurs in the twelfth string. Thus *proslambanomenos* sounds with *nete diezeugmenon* the consonance of diapason and diapente.

The *bis diapason* consonance occurs when the greater voice or sound exceeds the lesser voice or sound fourfold in height or depth. It always occurs in the fifteenth string. For *proslambanomenos* sounds with *nete hyperboleon* the *bis diapason* consonance.

**17.** A tone is produced when the greater voice or tone possesses the whole of the lesser voice or sound and, in addition, its eighth part. It always occurs in the second string. Thus *proslambanomenos* sounds with *hypate hypaton* a tone.

It must be understood that what is called *epogdous* in arithmetic is called a tone in music. *Epogdous* is said as though it were *epi-ogdous*, that is, “above the eighth.”

A tone is divided into two semitones—not because the semitones are altogether equal halves, but because that which does not reach the complete measure is commonly called “half.” This can be demonstrated very easily. Let the sesquioctave proportion be represented by eight and nine. No intermediate natural number lies between them. Let us therefore multiply both by two. Twice eight makes sixteen; twice nine makes eighteen. Between sixteen and eighteen there is one natural number, namely seventeen.

Let these three numbers be arranged in order: sixteen, seventeen, and eighteen. Sixteen compared with eighteen retains the sesquioctave proportion and therefore produces a tone. But the seventeenth number, which lies between them, does not divide this proportion into equal parts.

Compared with sixteen, seventeen contains sixteen and, in addition, its sixteenth part, namely one. Again, if seventeen and eighteen are compared, eighteen contains seventeen and, in addition, its seventeenth part, namely one. It does not therefore exceed the lesser and fall short of the greater by equal parts. The lesser part is seventeenth; the greater is sixteenth. Both parts, however, are called semitones: one is the greater and the other the lesser.

We could insert here an abundant and manifold account of the numbers in which these semitones are found or demonstrated, and record the differing opinions of various authors. We omit this for two reasons: either lest the discourse of a letter grow to the size of a book, and someone object to us, “When the wheel was turning, the amphora began to be shaped; why does a pitcher emerge?”; or lest we create greater difficulty and blunt the understanding of our readers rather than instruct them with clear proofs.

Although the semitone and its divisions are a very small part of harmonic instruction, they are the most difficult of all difficult matters and require laborious exposition. In a matter naturally obscure, therefore, whoever pours out more in explanation than is necessary adds darkness rather than removing density.

It is enough to know this: half a semitone is called a *diesis*, and is a quarter of a tone. Likewise, *tetrastemoria* is called a quarter of a tone, while *tritemoria* is called a third of a tone.

The greater part of a tone, that is, the greater semitone, is called *apotome* by the Greeks; we may call it “division” or “cutting.” It is natural that whenever something is cut in such a way that it is not divided into equal parts, the greater part exceeds the half by as much as the lesser part falls short of the half. If an apotome is therefore added to a semitone, the greater semitone is produced.

A complete tone therefore consists of an apotome and a semitone. Moreover, the semitone differs from the apotome by a comma. For this reason, the apotome is nothing other than the lesser semitone plus a comma. If someone removes two lesser semitones from a tone, the remainder is a comma.

A comma is the final sound lying beneath the threshold of hearing. The Pythagorean Philolaus defines the smaller intervals of tones as follows: “A diesis,” he says, “is the interval by which the sesquitertian proportion exceeds two tones. A comma is the interval by which the sesquioctave proportion exceeds two dieses, that is, two lesser semitones. A schisma is half a comma; a diaschisma is half a diesis, that is, half a lesser semitone.”

From these statements it follows that although a tone is principally divided into a lesser semitone and an apotome, it is also divided into two semitones and a comma. Thus it can be divided into two diaschismata and a comma.

A complete half-tone, which is a semitone, consists of two diaschismata—one lesser semitone—and a schisma, which is half a comma. Although the whole tone is joined from two lesser semitones and a comma, anyone wishing to divide it completely should take one lesser semitone and half a comma. The lesser semitone is divided into two schismata; half a comma is one schisma.

It was therefore correctly said that a complete half-tone can be divided into two diaschismata and one schisma. Hence a complete semitone appears to differ from the lesser semitone by one schisma; the apotome, however, differs from the lesser semitone by two schismata, for it differs by a comma. Two schismata make one comma.

We have set out all this in order to show the difficulty of semitones, which can be expressed and demonstrated more readily through numerical proportions than through the variety of sounds. If anyone is a curious investigator of such profound and intricate subtlety, let him read the third book of the often-mentioned Boethius *On the Institution of Harmony*. There he may perhaps not only satisfy his curiosity but also test his own ability. For if he proves capable of grasping these matters, he may know that nothing in the seven liberal disciplines will be difficult for him.

Let us therefore omit what only a few can understand and speak of what the understanding of many can grasp. It must be understood that although there are eight tones that complete the diapason consonance, there are no more than seven different sounds separated from one another by a tone, because the eighth is the same as the first in the double ratio. The ninth is the same as the second in the double ratio, and so with the rest.

Knowing this, Virgil says:

> I have a pipe joined from seven unequal reeds.

A pipe is therefore made from seven unequal reeds, because the whole consonance is completed from seven dissimilar voices or sounds. Hence some maintain that there are only seven tones.

As for Martianus’ introduction of nine Muses in *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury*, singing different songs, this pertains to the heavenly harmony, which is understood to have nine orders: seven on account of the seven planets, [Col. 0500B] an eighth for the heavenly sphere, and a ninth for the earth.

The eight together sound all the consonances; the ninth, namely the earth, remains silent in perpetual silence because it is immobile. Hence, when eight Muses had been carried upward in the heavenly circles, the ninth, namely Thalia, remained on earth.

For when Urania had entered the heavenly sphere, Polyhymnia the circle of Saturn, Euterpe that of Jupiter, Erato that of Mars, Melpomene that of the Sun, Terpsichore that of Venus, Calliope that of Mercury, and Clio that of the Moon, so that they might sound sweet melodies there, Thalia alone was left behind. She sat in the very richness of the flowering field—that is, in the circle of the earth—because her bearer, the swan who carried her, unable to bear the burden and unwilling to fly upward, sought the nourishing waters dear to him.

Thalia is interpreted as though from *theton lia*, that is, “placing forth shoots,” which beautifully suits the earth, since it germinates green grass and produces seed.

Some say that the nine Muses are so called because there are nine functions of the human voice. Every utterance is formed by these nine things: first, by the contact of the four teeth; by the striking together of the two lips; by the plectrum of the tongue; by the hollow of the throat; and by the breathing of the lungs. If any one of these is lacking, the voice will not be perfect.

**18.** But behold: while trying to demonstrate the tones, we have wandered farther into the vast and profound forest of musical instruction. It is enveloped in such dense darkness that it seems to have withdrawn from human knowledge.

Very few people can weigh its power and nature through certain reasoning, yet those who understand something of it cannot demonstrate it fully through manual work. Conversely, many can work it with their fingers or produce it through the sound of their voice, yet they scarcely understand its power and nature at all.

Indeed, if you ask a cithara-player, lyre-player, or anyone else knowledgeable about musical instruments to show you the consonances or the relation of the strings, and how one string is joined to another by a fixed numerical proportion, none of them will give you any answer at all. He will confess only that he does these things as he received and learned them from his teacher.

Since music hides itself for the most part from both the learned and the ignorant, it lies concealed, as it were, in the depths. Hence, they say, the story of Orpheus and Eurydice was invented.

Orpheus loved the nymph Eurydice, and, soothing her with the sound of his cithara, took her as his wife. While the shepherd Aristaeus pursued her out of love, she fled and fell upon a serpent, and died. When her husband learned of this, he tried to recall her from the underworld to the upper world by the sound of his cithara, but he was entirely unable to do so.

Orpheus is said to derive from *oreon phōnē*, that is, “excellent voice.” *Eurydice* is interpreted as “deep discernment.” Orpheus therefore wishes to recall Eurydice from the underworld through the sound of his cithara, but he cannot prevail, because human ingenuity attempts to penetrate the depth of harmonic subtlety, to judge and distinguish it through definite principles, and to recall it to the light—that is, to knowledge. But it, fleeing human understanding, lies hidden in the darkness of ignorance.

Meanwhile, it must be understood that the person who merely performs music with his hands is not called a musician. The true musician is the one who knows how to discuss music by nature and to unravel its meaning through definite principles.

Every art and every discipline naturally possesses reason in a more honorable form than the craft that is exercised by the hand and through the work of the craftsman. It is much greater to know what someone does than to do what one has learned from another. Bodily craftsmanship serves like a servant; reason commands like a mistress.

The knowledge of music is therefore more glorious in the understanding of reason to the extent that the mind surpasses the body. Consequently, since reason does not need the act of performing, the work of the hands is nothing unless it is directed by reason.

To this may be added the following: bodily craftsmen received their names not from the musical discipline but rather from the instruments themselves. A *citharoedus* is named from the cithara, a *lyricus* from the lyre, a *tibicina* from the tibia, and the others are named from their respective instruments. A musician, however, receives his name not from any instrument but from music itself.

A musician, therefore, is one who, after considering the matter through reason, has acquired knowledge of singing not through servile performance but through the authority of contemplation. Whoever is entirely ignorant of the power and reason of harmonic instruction vainly claims for himself the name of singer, even if he knows how to sing extremely well.

For a person who merely reads a lesson is not called a teacher; the teacher is the one who explains the lesson. And although boys may recite the words of the psalms from memory, they nevertheless remain strangers to their knowledge, because they do not understand their mystical meanings.

Just as it is not enough for learned men in visual matters to observe colors and shapes unless they also investigate their properties, so it is not enough to delight the mind with musical songs unless one also learns by what proportion of sounds or voices they are joined to one another.

We have touched briefly upon a few matters from among many, lest we provide musicians and skilled singers with cause to laugh at our ignorance. We do not, however, propose these matters for Walcaudus to read, nor do we urge his mind to learn such things; for “the lyre is played to the ass in vain.”

We know that you are an outstanding and perfect singer, and it is with your excellent wisdom and with other skilled singers that our conversation and reasoning are concerned. Let the words of this letter speak only to you and to the very few other musicians who may happen to read them. We exclude the rest in such a way that those unable to grasp these matters intellectually may also seem unworthy to read them.

19. Furthermore, lest we seem to have left untouched anything relevant to the undertaking we have taken up, we place at the end the following matter, which ought to have been mentioned above in its proper place, had memory not failed us. Some ask what those words signify by which, in natural music, we distinguish the sonority of the tones [Col. 0502C]—namely, *Nonannoeane*, *Noeais*, *Noioeane*, and similar expressions—and whether their meaning can be interpreted. To this one must answer that they admit absolutely no interpretation; indeed, they signify nothing. They were discovered by the Greeks solely so that, through their diverse and dissimilar sounds, the marvelous variety of the tones might be apprehended by ear and mind alike. But now this lengthy discourse awaits its conclusion.

May divine Providence deign to preserve Your Excellence, for the benefit of all His holy Church, safe and sound through many cycles of years! Most Reverend Father.

**In the Year of Our Lord 915. Bertarius, priest of Verdun. Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun, by Bertarius and an Anonymous author, monks of Saint-Vanne.**

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. I, p. 36, from the edition of D. G. Waitz.)*

[Col. 0501]

## D. G. WAITZ’S PREFACE

[Col. 0501D] Several monks, writing at different times, composed a history of the bishopric of Verdun. The earliest of them were Bertarius and his continuator, who are to be published here; Laurentius and the others who followed him are to be included in another volume [Col. 0503A]. Bertarius, a priest [Note: [Col. 0503C] Preface.] and canon of Saint-Vanne [Note: [Col. 0503C] Hugo of Flavigny, in Labbe, I, p. 123.], associated with Bishop Hatto, who governed the Church of Verdun from 846 to 878 [Note: [Col. 0503C] Chapters 2, 3.], was instructed by Hatto’s successor Berharius “in human and divine books” [Note: [Col. 0503C] Chapter 19.] and was also familiar with Dado, who succeeded Berhardus [Note: [Col. 0503C] Wassebourg, *Antiquitez de la Gaule Belgicque*, first volume, fol. 174, calls him Dado’s chaplain; I do not know on what authority.]. For when, in his time, the principal church of Verdun was burned and the books and Lives of the saints were destroyed, Bertarius—“though worn down by illness and sorrow”—undertook to compose a brief history of the bishops, which he dedicated to Dado [Note: [Col. 0503C] Preface. The author of the *Life of Saint Paul* says that he undertook this task at Dado’s request: Mabillon, *Acta*, II, p. 272.]. Since Dado was elected bishop in the first days of the year 880 [Note: [Col. 0503C] Dado himself reckons the year 893 as the thirteenth of his ordination; see below. His predecessor died on December 31, apparently in 879. Rivet, *Hist. litt.*, VI, 154, thought that Dado had already been elected in 879, because in the second year of his ordination he received a diploma from King Louis, who died in 882 (Bertarius, chapter 20); but Bertarius expressly says that this occurred not after two full years had elapsed, but in the second year. We regret that the diploma itself has been lost.], the thirty-seventh year after that fire falls in 916 or 917, and it is likely that Bertarius wrote his history shortly thereafter, although [Col. 0503B] he did not carry it beyond the time of King Arnulf.

Deprived of more abundant sources, he was able to offer only the briefest account [Note: [Col. 0504C] “In abbreviated speech,” Preface; “with marvelous brevity,” *Life of Saint Paul*, in Mabillon, *Acta*, II, p. 272. For this reason Laurentius calls the work a catalogue or an excerpt from a codex.] of the affairs of Verdun, since he appears either not to have known or to have rejected the stories that we read in later writers concerning the earliest bishops of Verdun. Nevertheless, he consulted several earlier Lives of the saints: those of Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 1.], Servatius [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 1.], Lupus of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 3.], and Maximinus of Micy [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 4.]. He cites the “Deeds of the Franks” [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 5.], but by this name he meant not the work commonly bearing that title, in which these matters are not found at all [Note: [Col. 0504C] Even in the epitome of Fredegar’s history, only a brief notice of this matter is found.], but the history of Gregory of Tours. Yet in certain matters he differs even from that work [Note: [Col. 0504C] Compare my notes on chapters 5 and 6.], and he did not repeat everything that Gregory relates about the bishops of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0504C] For example, what is found in Gregory IX, 8 and following.], so that, although he sometimes copied Gregory’s actual words [Col. 0503C] [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 7.], he seems rather to have retained Gregory’s narrative in memory than to have consulted the book itself. He inserted into his work poems by Fortunatus addressed to Bishop Agericus [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapter 6.]. He also seems to have had a catalogue of the bishops at hand [Note: [Col. 0504C] At the end of chapter 7.], while he keenly regretted the absence of their Lives, which he had heard existed [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapters 4 and 12.]; he also consulted diplomas preserved in the churches on several occasions [Note: [Col. 0504C] Chapters 8 and 12.].

What happened in the time of Hatto, Bertharius, and Dado he himself witnessed [Col. 0504A], but he also treats these matters very briefly, devoting only a few lines to Dado. Perhaps he was influenced by the fact that Dado himself had left an account of these bishops and of his own time. I have judged a fragment of it, preserved by Wassebourg, worthy of insertion here [Note: [Col. 0504C] Although, if this writing existed in its entirety, I found no trace of it in the library of Verdun, I have no doubt whatever that the fragment is genuine.].

> “In the year 893 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, while the most glorious lord Arnulf was reigning as king in the fifth year of his reign, and in the thirteenth year of my ordination, in the ninth indiction [Note: [Col. 0504C] The year is 893. Arnulf’s year is the sixth, and the indiction the eleventh.], I, Dado, bishop of the Church of Verdun, began to reflect in my mind upon the various vicissitudes of the present age, to recall to memory the deeds of earlier pontiffs, and diligently and profitably to investigate them from the faithful of our Church. For this reason I recorded in writing the deeds of orthodox bishops, so that the memory of those whose names we believe to be eternally written in heaven might remain eternal with us.
>
> [Col. 0504B] “Lord Hatto, therefore, was our predecessor in the time of the emperor Lothar and likewise of his son Lothar; his tenure continued until the first year of King Charles. This venerable pontiff bestowed many things upon the Church worthy of remembrance; we have thought it useful to commend a few of them to writing. For he obtained from King Lothar possessions lying in many places, namely, in the county of Verdun, Alberevilla, and so forth. The same venerable bishop also began this new basilica; it was honorably completed by his successor, namely our uncle, Lord Berhardus the bishop. He too assumed the governance of this church in the time of Charles and governed it successfully until the time of King Louis the German.
>
> “To recall briefly a few of his worthy deeds, this illustrious pastor, Lord Bechardus—our uncle—was extraordinarily zealous in ecclesiastical disciplines, beyond what could be believed or accomplished. He was exceedingly devoted to the episcopal ministry and the religious life, and bestowed very many things upon this Church, which now bear eternal witness to his zeal. He gave, and so forth. In the basilica of Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus he also installed eight canons and gave them the properties belonging to that Church, just as he then held them in his own dominion, together with a tenth of the rams which are received for our use from the hundred of Bras at the appropriate times. He also gave that altar one priestly vestment adorned with gold, namely a *platena*, that is, one made of *dirotanum* with drops, and so forth. He also placed one pallium over the tomb of that holy patron, and so forth.
>
> [Col. 0505A] “We too, who by divine disposition succeeded him and, in the time [Note: [Col. 0505C] *ipse*, edition.] of Lord King Louis, undertook the governance of this Church after our uncle, and after his death assumed Lord Charles, his brother, the emperor, and have now reached the time of the most glorious King Arnulf, their nephew, have judged it most beneficial to add to this work whatever, with God’s help, I have been able to add to the church entrusted to me—its properties and dependents, all its ecclesiastical ornaments. He gave, and so forth. All these things Lord Charles the emperor, in the solemn manner of the aforesaid Church, assigned and granted for perpetual possession. The most glorious King Arnulf likewise gave to the aforesaid Church, by a charter of his authority, the abbey called Montfaucon, built in honor of Saint Germanus and situated in the county of Doulain, with everything belonging to it,” and so forth.”

Since the catalogue of the bishops of Verdun, to which Dado is said to have added this material, appears to have been lost, Bertarius’s brief summary of the history is consequently all the more valuable. Laurentius found only a few matters from his own age to add to Bertarius’s work. Hugo of Flavigny, taking Bertarius’s narrative as his foundation [Note: [Col. 0505C] What he copied from Bertarius, whose “memorial antiquity” carried great authority for him, is found in Bertarius, chapter 4.], gathered much material from everywhere and handed down to posterity a richer harvest of Verdun’s history, but for the most part he stitched together false, fabulous, and historically unworthy tales. The author of the *Life of Saint Paul* likewise praises Bertarius as an author of considerable antiquity, but also charges him with negligence, since he did not write everything he had learned [Note: [Col. 0505C] “The authority of this man and his antiquity, which should not be despised, seem sufficient to lend considerable credibility to the belief that these things happened so. But because he himself states (chapter 8) that he had read and seen many things depicted which, through negligence, were not written down, he too is rightly reproached with negligence, since he failed to record, for the edification of posterity, what he had read or seen depicted.—Mabillon, *Acta*, II, p. 273.].

Bertarius’s year of death is unknown. Perhaps he was still alive under Barnoinus, who assumed the bishopric in 925. For in Wassebourg’s account we read the beginning of a *polyptych* of Verdun, drawn up in Barnoinus’s time [Col. 0505C]:

> “Continual salvation to the brothers of the Church of Verdun, serving Christ under canonical authority in the house of the blessed Virgin. Since many tribulations in our time oppressed this bishopric of Verdun, two especially monstrous calamities, demanded by our own evil merits, cast it down from its proper condition. One occurred when, in the time of Bishop Dado, of venerable memory, a hateful fire consumed almost the entire city and struck the church of Saint Mary to the ground. And, alas, the flames consumed all the ecclesiastical ornaments, together with the archive, the apostolic privileges, the decrees of the bishops, and the documents and writings of ecclesiastical properties, commonly called *pulegia*.
>
> “As an addition to so great an evil, when the venerable Bishop Barnoinus, the nephew of Lord Dado, succeeded to the same place, in the first year of his ordination the most savage people of the Hungarians unexpectedly attacked that bishop. Having burned almost all the villages, they either put to death or consigned to captivity the people found outside the fortified towns. Pressed by these two grievous calamities, the venerable canons and elders of the same place gathered together—namely, Ewenardus the provost, Bertarius the dean, together with the archdeacon Leutfredus and Odilo, and with a few peasants who had remained in the brothers’ villages after the aforesaid devastation. Lest the ancient institution, the revenues of the villages, and their censuses be utterly erased through ignorance, they judged it worthwhile, for the common benefit of those living now and those to come, to draw up this *pulegium* through diligent investigation concerning the canons’ properties.
>
> “But *pulegium*, as it seems to me, signifies or sounds in the Latin language as nothing other than ‘public law’ or ‘popular law.’ If anyone has interpreted this more correctly, I, Sarovardus the chancellor, obeying the commands of my superiors who placed me in charge of this work, humbly yield to his understanding.”
