[Col. 0506B] If the Bertarius called the dean here is the same person as the historian [Note: [Col. 0505C] So Wassebourg, fol. 174.], whom we saw already grown to adulthood in Hatto’s time, he must have died at an advanced age. He was buried in the cemetery of Saint-Vanne [Note: [Col. 0505C] Hugo of Flavigny, p. 123. In a diploma of Otto II, a mill given by Bertarius the canon to the church of Saint-Vanne is confirmed.].

A monk of Saint-Vanne [Note: [Col. 0506C] Chapter 9.] continued the history begun by Bertarius down to the year 1047, when Bishop Theoderic was in office [Note: [Col. 0506C] Chapter 11.]. He appears to have known almost nothing about the early years of the tenth century; afterward, however, he set out the affairs of Verdun in a sufficiently accurate narrative, although it was neither copious nor continuous. He reported what he had heard from others [Note: [Col. 0506C] “I heard from many informants,” chapter 2; “I heard from the abbot of this place,” chapter 3.] or had seen himself, using a florid style, but, like Bertarius, he almost entirely neglected to record the dates of events [Note: [Col. 0506C] I have labored greatly to establish these. Those given by Wassebourg are generally based on no foundation. Calmet copied them and added new errors. I found the history of Verdun composed by Roussel neither in the royal library nor in the Göttingen library.]. He nowhere indicates that he possessed written sources apart from diplomas granted to churches, and it is probable that no other monuments of Verdun’s history existed in his time. Laurentius later continued his narrative; Hugo of Flavigny partly copied it and partly expanded it. The author who composed the *Life of Abbot Richard* [Note: [Col. 0506C] Mabillon, *Acta*, VI, 1, p. 519.] also seems to have drawn several things from this work [Note: [Col. 0506C] Chapters 4, 5, 9. From the Continuation, chapters 9, 20. From the Continuation, chapter 11.]. Since he himself clearly never saw Richard, but says that he will write “what we have learned through a faithful account from those who themselves saw and knew these things with certainty,” he appears to have lived after Richard’s time; whereas the author of the continuation ended his history only two years after Richard’s death, so that the author of the Life could not have used it.

In publishing this work I used the following manuscript:

[Col. 0507A] 1. Verdun no. 3, parchment, a very large folio volume, formerly belonging to Saint-Vanne of Verdun, into which six leaves from the end of the twelfth century have been inserted. Folios 159–162 contain the History of Bertarius and his continuator, joined together and distinguished by no title. This excellent book was shared with me by the distinguished Clouet, librarian of the city of Verdun, and by his son, a most learned and cultivated man, professor at the college and seminary, who supported my labors with the greatest generosity and exceptional courtesy. While staying at Verdun, I compared it most carefully with the printed editions and restored the authentic text from it.

2. Verdun no. 36, parchment, thirteenth century, a small folio, folios 116 and following, contains the same work of Bertarius and his continuator, but greatly altered [Note: [Col. 0507A] Thus at the end of chapter 2 it reads in altered form: “To this miracle Lord Bishop Hatto came on the same day, and together with him we saw his legs and thigh flayed as far as the buttock, as though he had nothing there except bones in his legs and thigh. Yet he had scarcely arrived in a vehicle; now, an old man full of days, he returned on foot and in good health” [Col. 0508A]. At the beginning of chapter 4: “When Saint Firminus had died, the inhabitants of this city rebelled against Lothar, king of the Franks. When he had been besieged by him,” and so forth.], corrupted by errors and faults [Col. 0508A], so that it could scarcely be used, except in a few places, for correcting the wording. The codex seems to have belonged to the monastery of Saint Paul; at the end it adds certain material concerning the church of Saint Agericus that had been taken from that monastery, which I did not wish to omit.

Bertarius’s History, frequently cited by Wassebourg, was first published by D’Achery in *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 251, from a copy made by Barthélemy Senocq of Verdun from the codex of Saint-Vanne and sent to D’Achery; D’Achery appended the continuation. Calmet (*History of Lorraine*, vol. I, proofs, p. 194) and de la Barre, in the second edition of the *Spicilegium* (II, p. 234), then reproduced both works. A French translation, prepared by J.-J. Caiot, appeared at Verdun in 1775 [Note: [Col. 0508A] *Historical Almanac of the City and Diocese of Verdun*, 1775, octavo, p. 67.].

[Col. 0507]

## HERE BEGINS THE EXCERPT OF LORD BERTARIUS [Note: [Col. 0507] *Bertharii* in manuscript 1.] THE PRIEST, FROM THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF VERDUN, ADDRESSED TO LORD DADO, BISHOP OF THAT SEE

[Col. 0507B] To my most reverend and holy lord, Lord Dado [Note: [Col. 0507] *Donno* in manuscript 1.], illustrious bishop of the Church of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0507] I have written it this way throughout; manuscript 1 usually has *ecclesia*.], Bertarius [Note: [Col. 0507] *Bercarius* in manuscript 1.], your priest, praying devoutly for you, wishes eternal happiness in Christ.

Since during your time, over thirty-six years, through your good zeal and illustrious reputation, many benefits came to us, now, however, because our sins have demanded it, our principal church has been consumed by fire, and the books and memorials of our holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0507] *Nostrarum* later corrected to *nostrorum*.] have for the most part been given over to the same flames. Lest the sacred memory, venerable zeal, and holy work of your predecessors be utterly consigned to oblivion, although worn down by illness and sorrow, I have judged it worthwhile to gather, in abbreviated form, what I have read and heard from the faithful concerning your holy predecessors [Col. 0507C]—pleasant for you, and useful for posterity.

### 1

We read that in this church, built in honor of the holy Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0507] *Contructa* in manuscript 2; the words *quae—constructa in* are erased in manuscript 1.], thirty bishops have already preceded us; the first is called Saint Sanctinus. We have undertaken here to record what we understand about him. For we read [Note: [Col. 0507C] Compare Hincmar’s letter concerning Saint Dionysius, in Surius V, p. 660, where it is not said, however, that Sanctinus came to Verdun. Calmet I, p. XLI, mentions another legend in which these matters are related.] that Saint Dionysius sent Sanctinus, bishop of the Church of Meaux [Note: [Col. 0507] *Meldensem* in manuscript 2.], and the priest Antoninus to Rome, carrying the account of his passion, to Saint Clement. Their journey passed through this city, and on going and returning they preached the word of God here for the first time. They say that for this reason he is placed first in the succession of bishops of this Church. It is also read in the Life of Saint Servatius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0507C] This Life appears to have been lost. See J. Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 210, and concerning the synod of Cologne, *Councils*, ed. Labbe II, p. 615, where a fragment of the Life of Saint Servatius is also published, p. 617.], where the deposition of the archbishop of the Church of Cologne is discussed, that Sanctinus, bishop of the city of Claves, was present [Note: [Col. 0508C] Compare Calmet I, pp. XXXV–XLIV.]. Yet we nowhere find where his body was buried, except at Meaux.

### 2

After him, we read that there were Saint Maurus, Saint Salvinus, and Saint Arator. The frequent miracles at their tombs display their merits. For the monuments of these saints were divinely revealed to Saint Agericus, and by him were honorably and most reverently arranged. We can relate very many things concerning them that we saw with our own eyes. In the time of the younger King Lothar and Lord Hatto, bishop of our city, relics of these most holy men were taken and, in our own time, brought to the monastery of Tholey [Note: [Col. 0508C] Tholey, near Saint-Wendel.], which is subject to this Church [Col. 0509A].

God is witness to my conscience that I cannot recall, much less set down in writing, all that, from childhood to mature age, I saw divine mercy accomplish through the merits of these saints at their tombs: how many blind were given sight, how many deaf were healed, how many lame were made upright, how many possessed persons were freed [Note: [Col. 0509] *Leberati* in manuscript 1.], how many sick were cured of various ailments. Nevertheless, I shall gather some examples in brief.

Two crippled persons, who entered their church to pray, were immediately straightened through the merits of these saints. A certain woman named Emma, deprived for many days of the light of the present age, was given sight there in my presence. Likewise another woman, who was mute, began to speak after Matins had been completed, while I was listening. A certain man who had been crippled for forty years and had lain for many years in the portico of the church of Saint Stephen at Metz was carried in a vehicle and brought to the tombs of these saints. During the first part of the night he began to utter sounds; continuing to utter them until Matins, he deserved to regain his health.

When Lord Bishop Hatto and I came to this miracle on the same day, we saw together with him that his thigh and leg had been flayed as far as the buttocks, as though he had nothing but bones. Yet he had scarcely arrived in a vehicle; now, an old man full of days, he returned home on foot and in good health.

### 3

After these there were Saints Pulcronius, Possessor, and Firminus. We know nothing else about their memory [Note: [Col. 0509] *Nichil* in manuscript 1.] except that from the earliest times their merits were pleasing to God and that they were numbered among the citizens of the saints. It is also read in the Life [Note: [Col. 0509C] See *Acta Sanctorum*, July VII, p. 70.] of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes (450), that Pulcronius, a man of admirable holiness and bishop of the Church of Verdun, shone with such grace of healing that, with his hands bound behind his back, he could command the possessed; and they would recover their senses more quickly than they could fall headlong when their bodies were dashed together.

Certainly, when relics of the aforesaid saints were taken in the time of Lord Bishop Hatto, their monuments too were found beneath the monument of blessed Vitonus, honorably and reverently, as befits saints. Some portions of their bodies, seen by certain people, sufficiently demonstrate that their souls enjoy eternal joy in blessed happiness.

### 4

In the time, therefore, of blessed Firminus (500) [Note: [Col. 0509C] The whole section is taken from the ancient Life of Saint Maximinus of Micy, nos. 5–10, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, I, p. 582.], the inhabitants of this city rebelled against Clovis, king of the Franks, who had been baptized by blessed Remigius. When they were besieged by him, and meanwhile that most holy pontiff had died [Col. 0510A], blessed Euspicius, a priest of this Church, went out and obtained from the king peace and safety for his fellow citizens. Later, when the aforesaid king wished to have him made bishop of this city, and Euspicius refused in every way, the most blessed Father Vitonus, his nephew, was ordained bishop here. Saint Euspicius, together with another nephew of his, namely blessed Maximinus, who was related by blood to the most holy Father Vitonus, went with him to Orléans at the request of that same king and, leading a monastic life there, died in peace. Saint Maximinus afterward became abbot at Orléans and shines with an abundance of miracles.

I have heard many people say that they saw a written Life of the most blessed Vitonus, but until now it has not been seen by us [Note: [Col. 0509C] No earlier Life, so far as I know, has been published.]. The basilica where the aforesaid saints rest was built in ancient times in honor of the apostle Saint Peter [Col. 0510B]. Because of its ancient dignity it also contains many bishops’ tombs and is therefore greatly to be venerated by all the faithful.

### 5

(520) After him there was Bishop Desideratus. In his time, as we read in the “Deeds of the Franks” [Note: [Col. 0509C] Gregory of Tours III, 34, who nevertheless says that King Theudebert gave seven thousand gold pieces.], when famine grew worse, the citizens of this city were in the greatest distress. He went to King Theoderic and borrowed five hundred gold pieces from his treasury [Note: [Col. 0509] *Thessauro* in manuscript 1, and likewise below]. He distributed them among his citizens on the condition that they would trade with them in various places, live from their profits, and, when the crisis had passed, return the said sum to the royal treasury. By doing this, they were rescued from famine and became wealthy.

When the bishop wished to return the aforesaid gold pieces to the king, the king gave thanks to the Lord that his citizens had been rescued from such grievous misery by money from the royal treasury, and ordered him to keep the gold pieces. Through their increase, the citizens have remained merchants to this day [Note: [Col. 0510C] Compare Liudprand VI, 6; Richer III, 103. Verdun merchants returning from Spain are also mentioned in the eleventh-century history of the translation of Saint Sanctinus; compare Calmet I, p. XL.].

### 6 [Note: [Col. 0509] Omitted in manuscript 1.]

(550) After his death, Saint Agericus, one of these citizens, was ordained bishop in this Church. When King Childebert wished to hold an assembly in this city, out of affection for him he kept him at Metz (590), where Egidius, archbishop of the Church of Reims, was deposed [Note: [Col. 0510C] Compare Gregory of Tours X, 19, who says nothing about the city of Verdun and places these events after Agericus’s time.].

A certain very noble man, who ought to have been deprived of life by the king for his crimes, was saved at the request of the aforesaid bishop. Because of this, that man gave the brothers what we possess at Arcus and Mantua. Again, when the aforementioned king was traveling through Verdun, and the holy bishop had only a small quantity of wine in one vessel, Almighty God enlarged it through the bishop’s merits, so that the king and all his companions had enough for their needs from it; indeed, more wine was found in the vessel at the end than at the beginning.

The king, terrified by so great a miracle, learned that this Church had no place from which it could gather wine. Therefore he gave this Church two *amandi* [Note: [Col. 0511C] *Mansi*? I do not know what the word means.] along the Moselle and at Modinum [Note: [Col. 0511C] Moulin near Metz, as Wassebourg and Calmet determined; I have followed them in explaining these names.], and whatever lies between Luceium [Note: [Col. 0511C] Luce and Bage.] and Baia, and everything that we possess below Trier. He also added Marseium [Note: [Col. 0511C] Marcey, Sampigny, Commercy, Marchainville, Harville.], Sampiniacum, Commenias, Mercast, the village of Hairicus, and the adjacent villages of Carniacum [Note: [Col. 0511C] Charny and Neuvilly.] and Novavilla, as well as many other places whose enumeration here would be burdensome. Out of reverence for so great a man, the king and his faithful men handed these over to this Church for possession.

What sort of veneration this man enjoyed at that time is shown by Saint Fortunatus in the verses which he composed *ex* [lacuna] *te* in his praise, which we have thought it useful to insert here. For when Fortunatus was in Italy and suffered severe pain in his eyes, he came to a certain monastery built in honor of Saint Martin. It occurred to him to anoint his eyes with oil from the lamp burning before the altar under the name of Saint Martin. When he did so, he immediately received health through the merits of Saint Martin. Later, burning with the desire to visit Saint Martin’s tomb, he came from Italy to Gaul, and his journey passed through Verdun. Received kindly and charitably by Saint Agericus, he expressed in sacred letters what he saw in him.

### Fortunatus’s Verses [Note: [Col. 0512C] Fortunatus, poems III, 29–30.]

City of Verdun, although enclosed within a small circuit,

you please, enlarged by the merits of your bishop.

Greater glory shines forth within your narrow circumference;

your honor, Agericus, has increased it still more.

You have poured out many seeds of great praise,

which you will reap mature in the fruitfulness of your works.

At the present time you generously give food to the needy;

the coming day will multiply your wealth a hundredfold.

You unlock, pastor, the inner chambers of hidden doctrine;

you feed your flocks not only with food but also with speech.

You renew ancient temples and build new ones more splendidly;

when you serve the Lord, His house is more richly adorned.

You fill the noble fonts of sacred baptism;

thus, filled with the divine spring, you act with piety.

This hall shines white beneath a serene purity,

and, even if the sun should flee, here day remains risen.

From every side eager crowds hasten to the new temples,

and you grant the peoples a greater love of God.

The poor man has found consolation in you, the naked man clothing,

and, alone, you remain drink and food for all.

Happy is he who, by his merits, as a lover of eternal light,

in so short a time prepares things that shall not die!

As Phoebus raises his lofty chariot into the heavens

and scatters his fiery brightness everywhere,

with his outspread rays he claims the whole world for himself,

filling mountains and plains, and holding the lowlands and heights;

so, bishop, you shine with the splendor of your spirit like the sun.

He shines with his own rays, and you with yours,

holy Agericus, whose nurturing speech

makes the fields of the Church rejoice in fruitful abundance.

Sterile in earthly things, fruitful in those above,

scorning human things, rich, you journey toward the heavens.

Rejecting the wanton allurements of the world,

you remain pure, and the bitter love of the flesh has stolen nothing from you.

Slippery guilt perishes, and death does not rejoice in crime,

when you see your members freed from sins.

Dwelling in holy temples, you are held to be so pure

that your hearts, Father, are holy temples of God.

Christ chooses to hide Himself in such a vessel;

He Himself possesses the house He has cleansed for Himself.

There is no deceit upon your lips, nor savage darkness in your mind;

in sincere souls, day blooms upon your mouth.

You pour forth a river of learned speech from a leaping spring,

and refresh barren minds with a voice that waters them.

You open the lofty mysteries of heaven to the earth;

through you one knows, fears, prays to, and loves the Lord more.

You triumph through divine doctrine, eloquent bishop,

giving, as pastor, warnings lest error oppress the sheep.

You refresh them with the delights that heaven, fields, and water provide,

and satisfy the peoples: food from the one, faith from the other.

The poor man receives help, the sorrowful hope, the naked clothing;

whatever you possess, you make available to all.

May lasting health remain with you here, even though the future lies elsewhere,

and for a long time, pastor, may you offer prayers for your flock.

### 7 [Note: [Col. 0511] “VI” in manuscript 1.]

(588) After Saint Agericus, a certain abbot named Buciowaldus sought the bishopric, but, because he was proud, obtained nothing. The royal authority decreed that Caramerus [Note: [Col. 0511] Written in red ink in manuscript 1; “XI” is written above the name, and numerals are likewise added throughout.] the referendary should become bishop with the consent of the citizens [Note: [Col. 0511] *Actoritas* in manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0512C] From Gregory of Tours IX, 23.]. After Caramerus [Note: [Col. 0511] Chapter VII begins in manuscript 1.] came Ermenfridus [Note: [Col. 0512C] Bertarius omitted Godo, who subscribed the Council of Rheims in the year 265: Labbe, *Councils*, V, p. 1689.]. We have no other record of them except that they are found among the bishops in the episcopal succession.

### 8

(360) After Ermenfridus, Saint Paul was summoned from the monastery of Tholey [Note: [Col. 0512C] Tholey, near Saint-Wendel.]. He was a brother of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. 0512C] Mabillon, *Acta*, II, p. 268, pointed out that this is false.], and was consecrated bishop in this Church. His memory is eternal.

For Grimo, a deacon and nephew of King Dagobert, also called Adelgisus, having been reverently educated by Saint Paul from childhood, out of love for that bishop gave, confirmed, and secured by every authority his own property—namely, the monastery of Tholey—to Saint Mary at Verdun, for perpetual possession, by a charter written by himself and by many of the faithful. The same Grimo, out of piety, assigned the village of Frasnidum [Note: [Col. 0513D] Fraisne.] for the sustenance of our brothers. Saint Paul purchased Basonisvillare from his own revenues. He made a privilege for our canons concerning the older villages and confirmed it with his own hand and those of other bishops, under divine attestation.

We also heard this marvelous account of the virtues of our holy Father. While he was still living the monastic life and had obedience in the brothers’ bakehouse, he feared that, when the appointed hour came, the brothers might not have bread. Having removed the fire from the oven, he entered inside, cleaned the oven with his cowl, and arranged the bread there for baking [Note: [Col. 0513] *Quoquendum* in manuscript 1.]. He came out unharmed and distributed the holy bread to the brothers in the refectory at the appointed time.

I have read and seen many miracles depicted that he performed while alive in the bishopric and, after his death, when placed in the basilica of Saint Saturninus, performed through God’s cooperation. For he gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and cured the sick of various illnesses. And why say more? He enlarged this Church in temporal possessions. May Almighty God cause his soul, together with all the saints, to rejoice endlessly in eternal glory.

9. After him there were the bishops Gisloaldus, Gerebertus, Armoinus, [Col. 0513C] and Agrebertus. (648) In his time Saint Crodingus built the monastery of Waslogium [Note: [Col. 0513D] Beaulieu in the Argonne Forest] and placed it under the authority of our Church.

10. After him came Bishop Bertalamius. (710) Through their zeal and industry, Mactigisilus and his wife Hechia gave Tilliacum [Note: [Col. 0513D] Tilly, Estain, and Cassepierre], a royal estate, with its pond and Casa Petria, to our Church, and the village of Frumisiaca [Note: [Col. 0513D] Fromesy] to our brothers, together with very many other things, for the redemption of their souls.

11. (716) After him came Bishop Abbo, and then Bishop Peppo. In his time a considerable rebellion arose between Charles I, who is called Charles Martel, and Rainfridus, prince of the Franks. Because Peppo supported Charles’s party during the rebellion, he obtained, for payment, from Charles and a certain noble vassal of his the village of Calmontem [Note: [Col. 0513D] Clermont in the Argonne Forest?], with all its appurtenances. After God had consolidated the kingdom of the Franks for Charles, he also gave our Church Pontem Petrium [Note: [Col. 0513D] Pierrepont] and confirmed it to us by his written charter. But he retained Merla [Note: [Col. 0514D] Merle] and Casa [Note: [Col. 0513] *casia* in witness 1] Petria, because his retainers had invaded them; and Casa Petria is still retained.

12. (725) After him came Bishops Voschisus and Agroinus. After this the bishopric remained vacant for many days. (735) Then Lord Madelveus became bishop. He belonged to the household of this Church and was a holy and just man. Through his industry and effort, he is said to have obtained by a lease Wasnaum [Note: [Col. 0514D] Vaneau], the court of Warnuncus, Ramisbatium [Note: [Col. 0514D] Rembécourt], and many other properties, as I myself have read in charters confirmed by his own hand.

(750) In his time, too, this Church’s house was burned because of the demands of sin. For this reason he traveled through Gaul and Italy, and then through Greece and Joppa, reaching Jerusalem with great hardship on the roads. From the patriarch of that place he obtained relics of many saints, and brought them to Verdun together with a crystal chalice carved with marvelous workmanship; he reverently placed them in our principal Church. The relics that had been in the older Church he placed on the right side of the altar of Saint Mary, in the underground crypt.

He lived from the time of King Pippin until the time of Charlemagne, and died in the neighboring village called Novavilla. When he was being carried from there to Saint Peter’s or Saint Vitonus’s, it is said that two white doves, as white as snow, came visibly to everyone and settled upon the cross, remaining there until his body had been committed to burial.

He established many good things in this Church. He built the churches in this city very well, honorably ordered the clergy and people of this Church, and proved himself an exemplary father and bishop of this Church. He also frequently visited the properties in Aquitania that had anciently been subject to this Church—namely, the abbey of Saint Amantius, situated at Rodez [Note: [Col. 0514D] Saint-Amand at Rodez], Maderniacum, and Puliniacum—and carried with him the deeds of our aforementioned bishops, so that, through their merits, he might be able to possess those distant properties more freely. On this account, they say that the miracles of Saint Agericus are recorded at Marseille. The Life of Saint Vitonus and the Life of Saint Paul [Note: [Col. 0514D] The Life of Saint Paul was published in *Acta Sanctorum*, February II, p. 173, and in Mabillon, *Acta*, II, p. 268; it is of more recent composition] are said to be found in the neighboring regions beyond the Loire. His body—marvelous to relate—was found intact after forty years, and was reverently buried where it now lies.

13. After him the bishopric of this Church remained vacant for twelve years. (770) But a certain servant of God named Amalbert, made co-bishop according to the custom of that time, governed the Church and led an almost solitary life in a certain oratory dedicated to all the apostles [Note: [Col. 0515] *ducaebat* in witness 1]. At that time this Church lost Waslogium, Tilliacum, the Pond, Merla, Casa Petria, and very many other properties. This occurred during the time of Charlemagne.

14. After him came Peter, an Italian. For when the Frankish army was near Pavia (774) and was besieging it, the city is said to have been handed over by him [Note: [Col. 0515D] Nothing concerning this matter is recorded in the annals of this period.]; for this reason he was honored by Charlemagne with this bishopric. He remained in the bishopric for twenty-five years [Note: [Col. 0515D] These years assigned to the bishops, here and below, do not agree very well with one another, so that it is extremely difficult to establish exact dates], and suffered many adversities there. Indeed, they accused him of disloyalty to the emperor, and for that reason he did not dare to see the emperor for twelve years. But after he had been rightly cleared before the prince by his sons, (794) he later went into his presence [Note: [Col. 0515D] See the *Capitulary of Frankfurt*, 794]. He made many useless leases, and in his days many properties were taken away from this Church.

15. After his death they chose for themselves as bishop Anstrannus, from the king’s palace, the king’s cantor, a vigorous man. Through his industry, the Bracenses [Note: [Col. 0516D] Makers of beer, French *brasseurs*; Dachery understood the term in this way. But *Bracensis centena* occurs in the diploma of Otto II granted to the Church of Saint Vitonus at Verdun] were brought under the authority of this Church. (800) He survived for five years.

16. Then Herilandus took charge of this place, a very simple and exceedingly infirm man. In his time this Church also endured many evils. After twenty-four years of episcopate he died at Aachen and was buried beside Anstrannus in the basilica of Saint Vitonus. (823)

[Col. 0515C] 17. After his death, part of the clergy and people went to the Emperor Louis and asked that Lord Hildinus of Alemannia be given to them, a good and holy man who built many churches in this bishopric and performed many good works. But after the battle fought at Fontenay (841), he was hated by the Emperor Lothar. On the octave of Epiphany (847), amid great sadness and grief, this man, full of all goodness and charity, died in Christ in this city. He had been in the bishopric for twenty-four years. Thereafter I am more freely able to set down in writing what I saw with my own eyes [Note: [Col. 0515] *exequ::::* in witness 1].

18. Lord Hatto was ordained bishop in this Church after him. Because of the aforementioned emperor’s hostility, he found the tunic of Saint Mary—namely, the possessions of this Church—very greatly torn and rent, that is, excessively taken away and alienated. For the sake of recovering those alienated properties and relieving his people, he rose up with all his strength against the enemies of this Church, until, through God’s mercy, he had the tunic of Saint Mary restored and brought back to its proper condition.

Moreover, he obtained from King Lothar the Younger, for the use of the brothers, the royal estate of Marcelliacum, Arbereivilla, and Maureium; also Mercuringas, Brasaida, and Walacras; and, by leases, the villages of Metganis, Commenaria, and Gaugiacum. His intention and immense labor were directed toward raising up this Church and enabling it to enjoy peace, and he accomplished this during the lifetime of Lothar the Younger [Note: [Col. 0515] *lottonii*, corrected to *lottarii* in witness 1]. When Lothar died in August (869), Hatto also died on the Kalends of January (870), and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vitonus, in the crypt beside the body of Lord Hildinus, bishop. He had been in the bishopric for twenty-three years [Note: [Col. 0515] *XXX*, corrected to *XX* in witness 1]. He also began our new church and built a large part of it.

19. After his death, our lord and most holy Father Berhardus became bishop. By the acclamation of the clergy and people, he assumed the government of this Church. His most holy intention and devotion were to bring the basilica already begun to completion; and, by God’s mercy, he did so. In that basilica he installed large and honorable bells [Note: [Col. 0516D] That is, bells], as well as very good smaller ones, made through his own work.

He prepared pontifical vestments and a Gospel book adorned with gold and gems, a golden thurible and a very fine silver one, and a bier where the relics of the saints are now kept, all composed with the most honorable splendor. He gave this Church of his many other ecclesiastical ornaments. He made his canons live according to the canons’ rule, bravely showed the village priests the way of justice, and instructed boys—including me, Bertarius, who was one of them—in human and divine books, personally and through others, with the greatest charity.

He died at the monastery of Teolegius, where his body was also buried, on the day before the Kalends of January (879, December 22).

20. Through Christ’s mercy we now have as our elder Lord Dado, a venerable bishop, who assumed this office in the time of King Louis the German [Note: [Col. 0516D] The Younger, who reigned from 876 to 882]. In the second year of his ordination (881), he also obtained the royal estate of Meinrodum by a royal writ for the use of the Church entrusted to him.

21. After Louis, his brother Charles received the monarchy of the whole empire (882). From him he obtained for his altar the royal estate of Tilliacum, which had formerly belonged to this Church. After Charles, Arnulf, his nephew, received the kingdom (887).

[Col. 0517]

CONTINUATION

[Col. 0517A] 1. After him came Bishop Barnoinus [Note: [Col. 0517] “XXVIIII” is written above the line, and likewise below], whose life is remembered by posterity in name alone because of the negligence of his predecessors.

2. (940) Then Lord Berengarius, a kinsman of the first Emperor Otto, a noble man and a Saxon, became bishop of this city. He restored the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul—in which the body of Saint Vitonus rests, together with those of many of his predecessors and successors—to better condition, enlarged and adorned it (952) [Note: [Col. 0517D] Compare Berengarius’s diploma in Calmet I, p. 541]. He expelled the clerics living there and occupied with many lowly occupations, and established monks there to serve God. Over them he appointed as abbot a man named Humbert, formerly a cleric of that same Church, but at that time, moved by divine love, a monk at Saint Aper’s in Toul, and already made by God the father of that place.

For their sustenance he assigned the village of Scantia with its ban, as well as the abbey of Saint Amantius in Aquitania with many churches of this bishopric. He lived in the time of the aforementioned Otto, king of Germany, of whom it was said [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Otto began to grow toward the triumph and advance of the Church”; and “the age flourished after the empire” are taken from verses on the death of Otto III, although in that poem both verses refer to this emperor]. that Otto began to grow toward the Church’s triumph and to advance toward its prosperity. The second Otto succeeded him in the empire, so that the age might flourish. He died at Rome, was taken away by his own people without the Romans’ knowledge, and lies buried at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0517D] Not Otto II, but Otto III].

This Berengarius, of blessed memory, lived many years in that bishopric and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, on the left side of the choir; an altar has been placed above him and remains there to the present [Note: [Col. 0518D] Hugh of Flavigny, in Labbe I, p. 165, says that the body was transferred there in Richard’s time]. I saw the chasuble in which he had been clothed when he was placed in the tomb (960) [Note: [Col. 0517] *sepulcro*, with *h* written above it (*sepulchro*) in witness 1]. It was later torn away from his body.

I heard from many who reported it that his foot became withered before his death. One day, as he was descending to the church of Blessed Mary, he found a certain cleric lying prostrate on the ground and celebrating the memory of Blessed Mary. He struck him with his foot so that he would rise. The man immediately rose [Note: [Col. 0517] *surexit* in witness 1], and, when he saw him, bore the matter patiently.

The following night, while the bishop lay in bed, still awake and not yet asleep, the Virgin Mary appeared with Blessed Thecla and said: “Strike this man’s foot, Thecla, and avenge the injury done to my cleric.” From that very hour, as a result of this blow, his foot began to burn; and in the place already mentioned he became a monk.

[Col. 0517D] The aforementioned bishop gave Bellamvilla to the brothers of Saint Mary [Col. 0518A]. Also in his time, in the aforesaid church of Blessed Vitonus, the body of Saint Firminus was revealed and found through the most devout woman Eugenia. At the request of the aforementioned Abbot Humbert, to protect the citizens and to increase the renown of its miraculous powers, it was honorably transferred to the village of Flaviniacum, formerly a royal estate.

3. After his death came Lord Bishop Wicfridus [Note: [Col. 0518D] He had been elected while Berengarius was still alive and was already presiding in 962], a German from the regions of Bavaria. He diligently investigated the deeds of his predecessors and wished, by imitating them in every way he could, to embrace their life. When he read much about their virtue and good reputation and carefully investigated by whom this Church had been enriched, he found that among the others Bishop Paul had especially raised it up through the properties given to it and had made it rich from poverty.

Outside the city walls there was a church dedicated to Saint Saturninus, where his body lay buried, situated above the river. In it the Lord granted many benefits through the merit and intercession of his confessor. For oil truly flowed down from his tomb, and by its touch many sick people were restored to health. The inhabitants said that this tomb was weeping because it appeared to be neglected.

Accordingly, Wicfridus vowed zealously to magnify it in honor of so great a bishop, just as his pious devotion demanded. He immediately raised it from its foundations, completed it with God’s will, and, at the request of the citizens, mindful of his vow, placed monks there to serve God and his holy confessor Paul day and night. He consecrated the greater altar in honor of Saint Paul the Apostle.

He took the body of Saint Paul from the tomb [Note: [Col. 0517] *sepulcro*, with *h* written above it in witness 1] and reverently placed it in a silver bier on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. He adorned the church with excellent ornaments and bells, provided food for the monks from the properties of this Church, and gave them the better churches of his villages. He assigned the excellent royal estate of Wasnaum for their support and gave them many other things as he was able.

He made a golden panel before the altar of Saint Mary and adorned the front of the church with ornaments and crowns. He lived in the time of Otto III, who took up the Roman scepter from his cradle and was entrusted to the liberal arts; under his rule there was salvation for the world [Note: [Col. 0518D] Compare *Rhythmi* I: “While Otto III lived, there was salvation for the people”] and glory.

After many years had passed during which he lived in this bishopric, Wicfridus rested in peace on the second day before the Kalends of September and was buried in the monastery that he himself had built in honor of Saint Paul, beside the altar on the right side.

I do not think I should omit what I heard from the abbot of that place. One day, as Lord Bishop Wicfridus was leaving his city on a matter of business, he came to a village of the brothers called Wandersalis [Note: [Col. 0519D] Wandresel, near Sivry on the Meuse]. When night fell and he was detained there, while all his companions had surrendered their limbs to sleep, he was suddenly pursued by Count Sigebert. As happens when a great disaster overtakes the unwary, he was surrounded and captured by the count’s soldiers. While his men rushed to arms, his nephew Richerus was immediately killed, and the bishop was led away captive.

The count was soon excommunicated by all the bishops. At last, moved to repentance and seeking the bishop’s mercy, he first endured bodily pain and then paid a large sum of money to Lord Bishop Wicfridus on the appointed day. From this abundance of metal, among his other achievements, he adorned the church of Saint Mary with crowns so arranged that, if one touched the first with one’s hand, all the others would move as far as the last [Note: [Col. 0519] *ita*, “thus,” is absent in witness 1].

(982 or 983) When such a shepherd had finally been taken away, many adversities and tribulations among the people befell this city. For Lothar, king of the Franks, because the state was less defensible under the aforementioned young Roman prince Otto, besieged this city (984) [Note: [Col. 0519D] Compare Richer III, 101 ff.], but by God’s will he did not capture it. Nevertheless, he devastated everything around the city. When our men went out to fight him, they were defeated by his army; many were captured and carried away. To secure their release, a certain Gobert, a very powerful knight, brought the keys of the city to the king.

4. After this it happened that a certain cleric named Hugh took up the bishopric. When he had entered the city, he summoned the officials and asked how they lived. When they replied that they entirely lacked the revenues that had belonged to the bishop, and pointed out the destruction of the villages from whose revenues he had been accustomed to live, he immediately mounted his horse and turned back.

5. After he had departed, our citizens, without a royal grant, accepted Adalbero [Note: [Col. 0519] *adalboronem* in witness 1], son of Beatrice, the most noble duchess [mother [Note: [Col. 0519] “m. t. d.” written above the line in witness 1; Hugh of Flavigny also has this reading] of Duke Theoderic]. After he had held the bishopric for some time, when the bishop of Metz died (984), he went to that same city, abandoning this bishopric. When our men came to him, he received them honorably and returned the pastoral staff.

[Col. 0520A] 6. Lord Adalbero succeeded him, the son of Count Godefrid, who was the grandfather of Duke Godefrid, who later married the daughter of Prince Boniface and became margrave of the Italians. This Adalbero [Note: [Col. 0519] *His* in witness 1] was honorable and very humble, but extremely infirm. He suffered such bodily weakness that in that same year as his benediction he sought to go to Salerno for the sake of his health, with our men accompanying him.

When he stayed there and could not be cured by the physicians, he returned to Italy. There, as death approached, he summoned all his people and gave the abbey of Saint Germanus [Note: [Col. 0520D] Montfaucon] to a certain Ralph, his nephew [Note: [Col. 0519] *nepote* corrected to *nepoti* in witness 1], who lived until the time of Lord Bishop Richard, full of days. Distributing many other things among his people, he died. (991) [Note: [Col. 0520D] See the Fulda Necrology, 991.]

His body was brought from Italy by his brother, Count Frederick, and placed in his own church, in the choir of Saint Mary before the steps. There it is venerated with the greatest honor and reverence to the present day. He lived in the bishopric for three and a half years [Note: [Col. 0520D] This is not correctly stated, since Adalbero appears to have held the see of Verdun from 984 to 991].

During the time of these bishops, after Lord Humbert, the first abbot of the church of Saint Vitonus, had died, that same Church was governed for nearly sixty years [Note: [Col. 0519] *LXX* corrected to *LX* in witness 1], with every honor, by distinguished men of exceptional ability: the abbots Adelmar, Adelard, Ermenricus, Rohardus [Note: [Col. 0519] *roardo*, with *h* written above it in witness 1], Lambert, and Fingenius. Then, in the time of Lord Bishop Heymo, Lord and venerable Father Richard, newly made a monk there, took over its governance, as we shall relate below. He had been one of the leading canons of the Church of Saint Mary at Rheims and was a man of great religious devotion.

[Col. 0520C] 7. The Church of Verdun, deprived of such shepherds as have just been mentioned, deserved to receive from Germany a shepherd by whom it might truly be pastured and a father by whom it might be kindly nourished and loved: Heymo, most noble both by birth and character, whom we mentioned shortly before. He was of considerable benefit to the place entrusted to him. He greatly enlarged, adorned, and elevated the very small church; acquired Superiacum and many other gifts or leaseholds for the brothers’ prebend; and, through his faithful service and vigorous conduct toward Henry the Peaceful, obtained Jupilia for the table of himself and his successors.

O what concern this man showed for the churches! He transformed the church of Saint John the Baptist, enlarged it after transforming it, and, after enlarging it, had it consecrated by the most holy bishop Maurus. He established a community of nuns there and provided the community’s necessities from the properties of the greater church.

He loved the churches, and his people loved them too. He devoted himself to pious works, and so did his people. For, following his example and desire, the provost Amicus built the church of the Holy Cross, installed twelve canons, and provided them with necessities from his own estates and from properties acquired elsewhere. Finally, at the bishop’s request, he did not refuse to place that site under Saint Maurus.

The provost Dudo also established a church in honor of Saint Lawrence near the castle of Desluwarth [Note: [Col. 0521D] Dieulewart; compare the diploma of King Conrad in Mabillon, *Annales* IV, p. 716], appointed canons, arranged necessities for those appointed, and brought the castle itself to completion through great works, great labor, and marvelous decoration [Note: [Col. 0521] *castrum illud* deleted in witness 1].

After this, Father Ermenfridus, who came from elsewhere, was received paternally by the pious bishop and kindly retained and assisted. He built the church of Saint Mary Magdalene and, after appointing canons, provided their necessities with the greatest zeal for labor. Since he possessed no patrimony, he acquired many things by serving kings, attaching himself to princes, submitting himself to everyone, and invoking God above all with marvelous devotion. His life contributed more than money; his piety before God and human beings more than any possession; and his merit more than any patrimony could have contributed.

8. At the same time, the venerable Father Richard, who, as we said above, was one of the leading men of the Church of Rheims, a man of the greatest religious devotion, renounced the world and became successor to Fingenius, abbot of this Church (1004). Together with the Emperor Henry the Great, he built and completed this Church in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Vitonus.

The life of this remarkable man made the lives of many remarkable. His religious devotion instilled devotion in those who lacked it and increased it in those who possessed it. Indeed, whatever this man was benefited not only those subject to him but also outsiders to no small degree. He watched over the salvation of others as though it were his own, and rejoiced in the correction of others as though it were his own. If anyone converted, his was the conversion; if anyone acted well, his was the action.

Such a life and, I say, such a reputation urged many to live in Christ while he was preparing to die to the world. Noblemen considered themselves ignoble, strong men thought themselves weak, and, so as to conform themselves to such a life, they strove not to be at all what they had been [Note: [Col. 0521] *non erant*, corrected to *erant non* in witness 1].

Following his example and, I say, moved by his desire, the offspring of Duke Godefrid in particular renounced the world. For the venerable Count Frederick entrusted himself to this Father as a son and submitted himself to this lord as a servant. He enriched the Church with estates and freely gave to him not only his possessions but also himself.

Since the occasion has arisen to speak of Count Frederick, I am pleased, for the sake of example, to recount the conversion of the blessed Father at somewhat greater length, especially because we believe that it will please many.

9. These two most distinguished men—namely, the venerable Father Richard and the renowned Count Frederick—by God’s gift jointly resolved to begin their conversion in this Church. At that time the Church was poor in possessions, cramped in buildings, and little distinguished for religious observance. Only seven Scottish monks lived there under their abbot, a man nevertheless of great holiness named Fingenius [Note: [Col. 0521D] “With him he governed the abbey of Saint Felix, founded outside the walls of the city of Metz.” — *Life of Saint Richard*, chapter 4].

Since this new foundation sadly found no opportunity to practice the religious way of life toward which it was piously fervent, it came into their minds to seek with ardent hearts at Cluny, from the holy Father Odilo, what they desired. When they arrived there and explained their intention to that great Father, the wise and industrious man replied that they ought not to remain where nothing was left for them to correct by their example. Rather, they should return to their own place, so that through them a harvest pleasing to the Lord might bear fruit there.

Persuaded by his advice, they returned. But because they grieved inwardly each day that their fellow inhabitants were not corrected as they wished, they again considered migrating elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0522D] “They considered moving to the nearby monastery of Saint Paul, where at that time a new foundation had begun to flourish under Abbot Hervinus and was striving to bear fruit each day.” — *Life of Saint Richard*, chapter 5]. But almighty God, whose ordering no one can oppose, arranged the matter differently from what they wished.

At that time there was a certain religious woman leading a solitary life in seclusion near the church of Blessed Mary, diligently devoting herself day and night to prayers, fasts, and vigils. On the very night when the plan to migrate had been formed, she was divinely commanded to leave the prison in which she had confined herself for many years and to tell the abbot that he must, as the only remaining course, bind the aforementioned men without delay by monastic profession, lest the Church lose them altogether.

Obeying the command, she came out of her cell while all the people wondered, and reported to the abbot what she had seen and heard. He immediately summoned the men and, according to the rule’s command, compelled them to be secured by stability.

After three months, when perhaps his final hour was pressing upon him [Note: [Col. 0521] Or “by chance”], Abbot Fingenius died and was honorably buried in the church of Saint Felix outside the walls of the city of Metz. After his burial, by God’s appointment, this venerable Father was substituted as abbot.

How greatly this Church was increased in honors during his time, how brilliantly it shone in religious observance, and how greatly it grew in its buildings is plain to all who see it. Countess Matilda of Saxony burned with no small benevolence toward this Father and, for the Father’s sake, toward this place. She gave many ornaments and, together with her son Count Hermann, adorned the altar with golden crosses, panels, and a textile. She bestowed many gifts upon the Church, both for the redemption and for the salvation of her soul, by which she is still honored and greatly commended.

This countess, married to Count Godefrid, bore him five sons: namely, Adelbero, who after Wicfridus became bishop of our city; the aforementioned counts Frederick and Hermann; and two men distinguished by the rank of dukes, Godefrid and Gozelo.

The aforementioned Hermann gave to Blessed Vitonus the court of Roger and Felsica, together with the property called Hasluth in the county of Brabant; Munau with half the market of Mouzon; thirty manses with a large household at Harvia; two churches with a chapel of the lord’s estate at Geavia; and many other things.

Their father gave Borracum and Forbacum. Godefrid the duke also bestowed the village of Fontagia upon the aforesaid saint, for the commemoration of his brothers.

The aforementioned Count Frederick, while he was still in lay dress, went to Jerusalem and, for the remedy of his soul, returned to the prebend of the brothers of Saint Mary all the centenae of their jurisdictions by which they had been greatly troubled. He built stone towers for the church of Saint Vitonus at his own expense and gave many other good things to that place, where he now rests buried with his two brothers.

Lietardus, nephew and kinsman of Emperor Conrad, also gave Bailodium [Note: [Col. 0523D] Baileu] and, under the same revered Father, became a monk in that same place.

The pious Father Richard lived until the time of Lord Bishop Richard, whom he had received from the sacred font. He governed the monastery for forty-two years, a venerable man whose way of life made him beloved by all. This Father’s zeal in his religious vocation was marvelous; the whole Church strove to aspire to it and cling to it. All France rejoices in his instruction, and while the Lotharingian land preserves the traces of religious devotion, it triumphs.

What more is there to say? To our city, the greater the benefit this man’s life had been, the greater—not merely the inconvenience but the misfortune—was his death. His sweet memory remains not only in our Church but throughout France and Lotharingia.

These Fathers, who bestowed so many good things upon the Church, lived under Lord Heymo, who remained in the bishopric for thirty-six years.

10. (1024) Raimbert succeeded this pious prelate. He was anxious to defend the Church’s possessions, even if he could not enlarge them; he was of considerable benefit to all his people and a friend to religion and to those who belonged to his order [Note: [Col. 0523] *defendere* is followed by *s.* in witness 1]. He was also exceedingly eager to build an honorable church for the most holy bishop Agericus.

He had scarcely begun the desired work, scarcely installed the monks, and scarcely provided their necessities when he undertook a pilgrimage in his desire for the holy tomb (1038). He died during it and was buried on the road at Bellagrada. At last, through the extraordinary zeal of his canons—namely, Bernerus, son of Constantius, and Bernard—he was brought back, received with eager longing by his fellow citizens, and, in the time of the most pious Bishop Richard and Abbot Baldric, honorably buried in the church of Saint Martin and Saint Agericus, which he himself had begun.

With great devotion he gave Saint Mary two excellent capes, two fans, and other honorable ornaments. He lived happily in the bishopric for fourteen years [Note: [Col. 0523] *XV*, corrected to *XIIII* in witness 1].

11. The grief of the whole city at the death of so great a prelate was relieved by the canonically effected succession of the venerable Bishop Richard. His kindness and, I say, his vigor were the hope of an honored city, the hope of preserving religious observance, and the hope of maintaining the ecclesiastical order.

He took up the country as a duke and the Church as a shepherd, provident toward both. Yet with singular concern for peace he assumed the bishopric in the time of King Henry, son of the Augustus Conrad. He regarded the office as a burden, not an honor; labor, not repose; and toward those entrusted to him he showed exceptional devotion, not relaxation or idleness.

He performed vigorously what belonged to a bishop, adorning the walls of the Church inwardly with life, merit, and character, and outwardly with suitable ornaments. He devoted himself with exceptional fervor to their preparation and expense, placing every vow and every concern after them.

For the Church of Saint Mary, over which he presided, he gave with great devotion two crosses made of gold and precious stones, six silver candelabra, and a three-pound golden thurible. Henry, who had not yet assumed the monarchy of the Roman scepter, ordered it to be made with the most honorable workmanship because of the great love he bore him.

The same venerable bishop gave to the church of Saint Vitonus his own allod, namely the court of Baroncourt [Note: [Col. 0523D] Baroncourt], and what he possessed at Saint Mary, out of love for his foster father, the distinguished Abbot Richard.

The aforementioned Henry also gave this bishop an excellent *acerra* with a precious gem, two pontifical chasubles honorably worked with gold, and seven others without gold. The same bishop acquired seven stoles decorated with gold and seven others, white and without gold, prepared with gold-fringed amices [Note: [Col. 0524D] Embroidered work].

He gave many capes, but fitted out with gold two that had been given by Bishop Raimbert. He gave many pallia, but contributed twelve excellent dorsals together with one very precious curtain. He redeemed one pallium, formerly belonging to the Church, with a gold fringe [Col. 0524D]; two banners; one onyx chalice; and another crystal chalice, which he had entirely fitted with gold and stones. He also gave another silver thurible covered with gold, two smaller silver ones, and three handwashing vessels: one of gold and two crystal ewers.

In his time the religious dean Warmundus gave this Church one cape that the king had given him. This bishop also acquired the allod of Wosophia with all its appurtenances from a certain noble widow, Raingard, in exchange for his leasehold and a large sum of money. He gave it to the brothers of Saint Mary on the condition that they should receive from it the resources for a service on the day of the Annunciation of the Virgin and celebrate her solemnly.

(1044) In his days there was a great quarrel between King Henry and Duke Godefrid. The duke could not make peace with the king until he returned to that bishop and Church a centena of the court of Wandelinus and other rights that he then held by force in this city.

There was peace and truth in this bishopric during his days; both within and without, everyone enjoyed peace. O how prosperous and joyful the city would have been, had it possessed this pontiff continuously! How greatly would the Church have triumphed, had it deserved to retain him! His life, beneficial in every way not only to himself but also to others, brought the greater joy; his death, arriving bitterly and unhappily in the seventh year (1046), brought a correspondingly greater sorrow [Note: [Col. 0525]: “correspondingly greater,” witness 1]. After the death of the venerable abbot Richard, it brought a second grave misfortune in that same year.

All who attended the funeral of the aforementioned abbot testify how eagerly this venerable bishop endured death. For when that venerable Father was oppressed by his final illness, the lord bishop visited him every day, weeping and grieving that he would be left behind. At last, arriving very early on the final day and seeing him already drawing his last breath, at his signal he went to the altar of Saint Lawrence to celebrate a Mass for his release. After celebrating it, he returned to the Father and, bidding his final farewell, fell upon him in tears and kisses. Then, having commended the soul of so great a friend to God, he himself washed his body and clothed him most honorably from his own possessions.

[Note: The *Life of Saint Richard* continues: “He did not allow him to be buried the next day, but after the first vigils of this church, he arranged vigils for him first at Saint Maurus and then at Saint Paul, and he himself attended all the vigils with great devotion. Finally, on the third day, after arranging processions from all the churches, he carried him back with great honor to the church of his see. When the Masses and funeral rites had been celebrated and he was already about to be buried, the same pontiff lifted him by the head, kissed his breast and hands with many tears, and, placing him with due honor in the sarcophagus [Col. 0526D], prayed and entreated him not to remain alive after him for a year. So great was the grief and loving devotion of the living toward the dead, and so great the affection and efficacy of the dead man’s intercession for the living, that in the same year, scarcely four months having passed, the same venerable bishop died, to the greatest grief of the whole country. The venerable Father, our most loving shepherd, departed from the body, heaven applauding and earth mourning, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1046, in the fourteenth indiction, with concurrent 2 and epact 11, and migrated to the Lord.”]

On the third day, when his vigils had been completed and the venerable pontiff was placing him in the mausoleum after the celebration of the Masses, he kissed his breast and prayed that he might intercede for him, so that he would not be left alive after him for a year. That he obtained this request is demonstrated by true evidence: the venerable abbot migrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, and the revered pontiff followed him within half a year, namely on the seventh day before the Ides of November. May his soul rest in peace, and may his memory remain continually among the living and with posterity forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0526A] Bishop Richard of the blessed Mary died in this city of Verdun and was buried on the left side of the principal church of Saint Mary, beside the choir. At his feet stood an altar consecrated in honor of Saints Nicholas and Germanus; before the fire, he himself had consecrated another altar there in honor of Saint Nicholas and all confessors. May he and all the saints intercede with the Lord our God for his sins, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

Now the pontiff himself, the venerable Richard, rests in Christ in the middle of the monastery of Saint Mary. He was transferred there by the lord Theodoric, his successor, who happily ruled as bishop; the translation was celebrated with every honor and with repeated funeral rites, as though he had departed this life on that very day.

The aforementioned Richard, before attaining the consecration of his episcopate, grieved—as though compelled by his sins—that a deplorable calamity had befallen the city: the palaces had been burned, the buildings of his predecessors entirely ruined, and whatever had previously been made glorious reduced to devastation; whatever had been intended for his own honor and that of his fellow bishops had been consigned to miserable destruction. How deeply he grieved is shown by the rebuilding, promptly and fully carried out.

O how provident he was concerning his salvation, and how solicitous for the redemption of his own, when, for the soul of his father, Count Hildrad, surnamed Hecelinus—a military man, vigorous in worldly affairs—he transferred Theon’s estate, with all its appurtenances, by hereditary right to Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus.

[Col. 0526C] [2, omitting the end of the history, adds: “He also legally added to Saint Mary Magdalene, for himself and his own, for the merit, I say, of the devout priest Ermenfridus, his share of Marion’s estate. To show his greater devotion to her, he obtained from his co-heirs that they should make the same transfer of their shares” [Note: [Col. 0525]: “transfers,” witness 2].]

Once consecrated to the episcopate, he began to be more religious in life and conduct [Note: [Col. 0525]: thus]. Having become richer in worldly goods, he began to be more useful to the churches in increasing their benefices [Note: [Col. 0525]: thus]. For he devoutly granted to Saint Mary Magdalene half of the benefice with the ban at Orne, which had long been held by his predecessors and by himself from the Church. He added to the same church an estate of excellent allodial land situated in the city, and obtained the consent and transfer of his co-heirs with no less zeal.

Rambertus, the predecessor of this religious man, was, as has been said, most devoted to the city and to the church. He demolished the very small church of Saint Martin, rebuilt it after its destruction [Note: [Col. 0525]: I have had the words printed in italics; in manuscript 2 they were written by another hand in an erased place], enlarged it in the rebuilding, and devoutly consecrated it to the blessed Bishop Agericus, with monks appointed there, before the work had been completed.

His diligence in advancing this church was so great, and his perseverance in carrying out the work so intense, that he did not neglect or delay to free the very place subject to Saint Paul and destined for the monks’ sustenance [Note: [Col. 0527]: “nor delay” corrected from “and delay” in witness 2]. He had promised to provide compensation for the said church if the hope of a longer life had prolonged his days. But untimely death came upon him, deceived his intention, and interrupted the desire he had held.

This moved the monks of Saint Paul—both with zeal to recover their property and with an even greater desire to subject the place to themselves—to bring lawsuits, pleadings, and complaints. To obtain their object more easily, they brought their case before the Roman curia; no difficulty or harassment deterred them.

Bishop Richard, however, the unique guardian of piety and chief increaser of ecclesiastical honor, joined his desire to the desire of Father Rambertus and his zeal to that man’s zeal, when he returned to them an equally valuable, indeed more valuable, benefice at his estate of Jupilia [Note: [Col. 0527]: “Inpilia,” witness 2]. Once this gift had been confirmed by royal charters and apostolic privileges, and liberty had been acquired for that place [namely, the church of Saint Agericus [Note: [Col. 0527]: these words are superscribed in witness 2]], he ended the whole dispute.

He thereby bestowed upon its proper place the fruit and honor of an episcopate whose hope for his sheep was short-lived. And what if, had life been longer, he had fulfilled their desires? According to the Apostle, “to live was Christ” (Philippians 1:21); according to the same Apostle, he testified by no small execution of works that he had desired the episcopate as a good work (1 Timothy 3:1).

### 12. Bishop Theodoric

The lord Theodoric succeeded him, a German, a canon of the Church of Basel. During his time this Church suffered many adversities. In the second year of his episcopate, the city of Verdun was burned by Duke Godefrid and Count Baldwin (1047), together with the monastery of the blessed Mary, Mother of God. Through this burning the city suffered great loss.

During his time, after the passing of the venerable Father Richard, abbot, this monastery received the lord Walerannus as its ruler.

# In the Year of the Lord 916: Robert, Bishop of Metz

[Col. 0527]

## Historical Notice on Robert

*(From* Gallia Christiana, *the final volume.)*

[Col. 0527C] Robert, also called Ruodpertus or Rupertus, was born of noble Alamannic stock and was the brother of Count Wido, who is honored with that title in Emperor Arnulf’s diploma for the monastery of Saint Maurus. He bound himself to the Rule of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Saint Gall. There he was taught letters by Notker, master of the schools. He addressed several letters to Notker, in which he congratulated himself on his monastic profession, asked his parents for little gifts for his teachers, and informed the then-absent Abbot Burkhard about the discovery of a domestic theft.

Promoted to the episcopal dignity because of his outstanding gifts, he received consecration from Ratbod, metropolitan, in the cathedral church of Saint Stephen at Metz, on 22 April 883. At about that time four hymns in honor of Saint Stephen, sent to him by Notker, a monk of Saint Gall, were composed.

Stephen, bishop of Liège, compiled a little book from many excerpts gathered from the divine books. In it he collected, with useful commentary, short works for the various feasts of the year, together with collects and verses, and sent it to Robert for reading and approval.

The honor of the pallium was conveyed to him from the Apostolic See, as it had been to many of his predecessors. In 884, indiction II, he granted Abbot Lodoine of Gorze permission to make an exchange with Verdinosus, priest of Saint Stephen. At the request of the clerics of Saint Arnulf, who had approached Emperor Charles the Fat asking for confirmation of their possessions and restoration of their offerings, he issued, by the same prince’s command, letters around the year 886. In that year he also granted permission to build an oratory at Bodo’s estate.

He attended the Council of Mainz in 888. In the same year, together with Rathod of Trier, he presided over another provincial council held in the monastery of Saint Arnulf on 1 May.

In the following year he confirmed a donation made at Gorze. When he asked Pope Stephen V whether a certain Flavius, whose left finger had been cut off by the Normans, could be promoted to the orders, he received from the pontiff, in Flavius’s favor, a reply around the year 891.

In the same year, at the request of Deotmar, archbishop of Salzburg and archchaplain, King Arnulf removed from the Church of Metz the monastery of Saint Saviour situated beside Lake Chiemsee, then commonly called Owa, which had formerly been granted to that Church by earlier kings. In its place, the king assigned the abbey of Luxeuil to the Church.

The bishop of Madaura records that, around this time, Robert restored the city walls because of the Normans’ invasion. He attended the Council of Tribur near Mainz in 895, together with the bishops of his province, Dado of Verdun [Col. 0528D] and Ladelmus of Toul, whose consecration by Ratbod of Trier he had attended shortly before. By letter he commended to Ladelmus the cleric Heldrad, whose relatives were harassing him because of possessions transferred to the Church of Metz.

He himself also received a letter of authorization from Ratbod of Trier, dated 15 October 906, concerning the admission into the diocese of Metz of a priest named Gissemarus. He was elected abbot by the monks of Gorze in 910, in which year he is mentioned in a donation of Queen Richildis made for those same monks.

From the aforementioned Emperor Arnulf he acquired the abbey of Saint Servatius, called Maestricht, and from Emperor Louis many castles. He transferred the body of Saint Severus to the monastery of Saint Martin, according to the Trier manuscripts.

After serving in the episcopate for thirty-two years, eight months, and eleven days, he died on the fourth day before the Nones of January 916. He was buried in the chapel of Saint Gall and was later transferred from there to the cathedral crypt.

[Col. 0529]

# Diplomas and Letters of Robert of Metz

## I. Diplomas

*(History of Metz, vol. II, proofs.)*

### I. Privilege by Which Robert Confirms the Exchange between Lodoine, Abbot of the Monastery of Gorze, and the Priest Wuerdingus

[Col. 0529B] The order of reason rightly demands that whenever a sound exchange of worldly goods seeks to obtain a definite course, what generous charity has not refused to grant mutually should be strengthened in every way by written documents, with an inviolable display of charity. Hence what the most prudent antiquity sanctioned, the posterity of a more fragile age also strives to confirm by an unshakable record, so that things reasonably granted may not afterward be disturbed by any change of circumstances.

Therefore it was agreed and settled between Lodoine, abbot, and the brothers of the congregation of the monastery of Gorze of Saint Peter and Saint Gorgonius, on the one hand, and a certain priest named Wuerdingus, of the congregation of the Church of Metz of Saint Stephen or Saint Paul, on the other, that, with the consent and permission of the lord Robert, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Metz, they should exchange certain properties among themselves for the convenience of both parties. This they did.

The aforesaid Abbot Lodoine and the brothers of the aforementioned monastery therefore gave to the already-mentioned Wuerdingus, from the property of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of the gracious Gorgonius, in the district and county of Metz, in the village called Arx, namely:

From one mansus, a parcel measuring seven perches in length, four perches and twelve feet in width along one frontage. Also, in the same boundary, three parcels of vineyard. One of these, adjoining the aforesaid mansus, measures six perches and four feet in length, two perches and ten feet along one frontage, and three perches and five feet along the other. Another vineyard measures ten perches in length and two perches in width along both frontages. The third vineyard measures ten perches on one side and eleven perches on the other, with seven and a half perches along both frontages.

At the upper end of this vineyard, along part of one frontage, there is one perch of uncultivated land.

Also, within the same boundary, one parcel of arable land measuring nine perches in length, six perches in width, and twelve feet along both frontages; within the measurements stated above, everything in its entirety.

In return, the priest Wuerdingus gave from his own property to the Church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the gracious Gorgonius, to Abbot Lodoine and the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, in the district of Scarponne, at Alnaldivilla:

One vineyard measuring eleven and a half perches along one side, fifteen perches along the other, and eight perches and six feet along one frontage.

Also, in the same boundary, two parcels of arable land. One measures thirty-two perches in length, two perches and eleven feet along one frontage, and two perches and eight feet along the other. The second parcel measures fifteen perches in length, four perches and thirteen feet along one frontage, and five perches and fourteen feet along the other; within the measurements stated above, everything in its entirety.

The arrangement was that from the present day onward, whatever either party justly and reasonably granted to the other should pass by hereditary right, and that each party should have full freedom regarding the property transferred—namely, to possess, hold, sell, exchange, and otherwise dispose of it as it decided.

So that this exchange might remain firm and stable forever, we confirmed it with our own hand, supported by a formal stipulation. Done publicly in the monastery of Gorze in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 884, indiction XI, epact XX, concurrent III.

Robert, humble archbishop of the holy Church of Metz, subscribed. Lodoine, abbot, subscribed. Optatus, dean, subscribed. Seguinus subscribed. Gonbertus, archpriest, subscribed. Badicho, abbot, subscribed. Moses, Hildebrand, Scranto, Odelric, Farnulf, Godefrid, Ereugus, Soypertus, Sarouvardus, Harno, Gislebertus, Teudo, Vuichadus, Anuclius, Barnerus, Audinus, Segoldo, Rogembaldus [Col. 0531A], Albricus, Genoz, Ernoldus, Sugerus, Odelricus, Aldricus, Lambertus, Evrardus, Homedeus, Hildoinus, Hominus, Betto, Radouardus, Gisaldus, Attogius, Vuandelmarus, Uncrinus, Ricuvoldus, Rotgerus, Goderonnus.

I, Vuichardus, though an unworthy priest and monk, wrote and subscribed this exchange.

### II. Privilege for the Monastery of Saint Arnulf

In the name of the Lord God eternal and our Savior Jesus Christ.

Radbertus, humble bishop of the holy Church of Metz.

If the shepherd’s care must watch over places dedicated to God with great diligence, lest the sheepfolds of the Lord’s flock entrusted to him suffer loss of their ancestral rights, he must nevertheless labor for his subjects in both spiritual and bodily matters, lest those serving God appear to be dominated by any want.

Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know how the canons of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Arnulf, dwelling in the suburb of Metz, approached the clemency of our most serene lord, the emperor Charles. They carried with them royal precepts confirming the things pertaining to their food and livelihood, which, they said, had been removed through the authority of our predecessor bishops.

The glorious Caesar, moved by love of God and by the brothers’ petition, willingly received their complaint and presented it before his nobles. By the command of his majesty he also ordered us to restore the aforesaid monastery and commanded that everything which his father, the lord King Louis, had once granted for the support of the brothers serving God there, for the remedy of his soul, should be restored in full.

We too, in accordance with the imperial command and with the ancient privilege of his father, the lord King Louis, restored to the aforesaid monastery, by the authority of our pontificate, whatever had been distributed from our demesne through our agents or faithful men for the substance of the brothers dwelling there; namely, the church in honor of Saint Martin situated in the village of Rumiliac, with all its appurtenances, and the estate of Navis at Winuticum, as contained in the royal precept, together with the tithe and the whole integrity of the abbey.

Since they are known to possess the royal precept, it seemed beneficial to us that they should also have a copy of our authority. We therefore ordered this present charter to be written, confirmed it below with our own hand, and caused it to be strengthened by the hands of the canons and noble laymen.

R., unworthy bishop of the Church of Metz, subscribed. Guntbertus, archpriest and archdeacon. Adalinuda, abbot and archdeacon. Herigaudus, abbot. Heininardus, abbot. Cudofridus, abbot. Meinardus, priest. Gundelaio, priest. Garemannus, priest. Otcarius, priest. Ratramnus, priest. Verdinajus, priest. Donatus, priest. Baldingus, deacon. Adelgarius, deacon. Andreas, deacon. Remigius, deacon. Rotlandus, deacon. Ermenaldus, deacon [Col. 0532A]. Viduicus, deacon. Adelardus, subdeacon. Hugo, subdeacon. Tetboldus, subdeacon. Framarus, subdeacon. Tedricus, subdeacon. Ibinus, subdeacon. Gerboldus, subdeacon. Odacher. Hunargus, Winardus, Regimboldus. Albricus. Magimfridus. Liederus. Queldo. Acdricus. Manno. Adoardus. Amalricus. Guntbertus. Gundicho. Waltarius. Erpaldus. Alfarous. Alevingus. Ado. Turingus. Gauzraldus.

I, Rubtlandus, chancellor and notary, wrote and subscribed.

### III. Privilege for the Construction of a Church at Dodo’s Estate

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Robert, humble bishop of the holy Church of Metz.

Let all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know how a certain nobleman named Bivinus sought our favor, so that by our permission he might be allowed to build an oratory in the estate called Dodo’s Estate.

The reason was that the long journey between that estate and Berulfivilla—which lies above the stream Senode, where the tithes from the aforesaid estate were subject—was burdensome for him and his people. He also wished to provide the endowment for it from his own property.

We therefore investigated the will of Abbot Lodoine, who at that time held the abbacy of Gorze and to whom the church situated in Berulfivilla was subject. Since Bivinus was his cousin, Lodoine willingly consented, on the specific condition that the chapel itself, together with its endowment—namely, one mansus with ten journalia at Belciard’s estate, together with the lands attached to it—and the tithes should remain subject forever to the mother church situated in Berulfivilla.

Since we consented to the wishes of both parties, and so that this matter might afterward remain unshaken and stable, we ordered this written record to be made and marked it with the monogram of our name in our own hand, supported by a formal stipulation.

Done publicly at Metz in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 886, indiction IV, concurrent V, epact XII, in the third year of the fortunate reign of King Charles.

Robert, humble bishop of the holy Church of Metz, subscribed. Gambertus, archpriest. Lanfridus, abbot. [Sign] Everus, abbot. [Sign] Notingus, abbot. [Sign] Maintardus, dean.
