[Sign] Geremannus, cantor. [Sign] Vuilerdingus, provost. [Sign] Ermenaldus, priest. [Sign] Segoldus, count. [Sign] Amalricus. [Sign] Ramfridus. [Sign] Fulcherius. [Sign] Lodoine. [Sign] Bolonus. [Sign] Eilulfus. [Sign] Lafridus. [Sign] Leoderius.

I, Adelgarius, wrote this in place of Abbot Haldinus.

### IV. Privilege for a Certain Willermus

*He grants the usufruct of certain properties previously donated to the monastery of Gorze.*

In the name of the Lord.

Robert, humble archbishop of the holy Church of Metz.

Let all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know how a certain Willermus gave us, for the benefit of the church of Saint Peter and Saint Gorgonius of the monastery of Gorze, certain properties of his own; namely, in the district of Scarponne, at Alnaldovilla, two vineyards from which thirty modii of wine can be gathered, and in another place in the same district, at a place called Adsalon’s mansus, eight mansi and portions; meadows yielding eighty-seven cartloads of hay; woodland for fattening three hundred and fifty pigs; and eight bondmen, whose names are these: Lampertus, Adhelradus, Ansaldus, Aginaldus, Agnitrudis, Amalrada, Eugenia, and Leudrada.

Afterward he made a request, and we determined that we should grant as a benefice to him, his wife named Data, and their son Achildu, both the properties he had given and others belonging to Saint Peter and Saint Gorgonius; namely, in the district of Verdun, in the village called Gouderlisia, one church in honor of Saint Martin, to which one mansus and portion belonged; in the same village thirteen other mansi and portions; two hundred modii of demesne arable land for sowing between the two sowings; one hundred and ninety-seven cartloads of meadow hay; woodland for fattening five hundred pigs; and twelve bondmen, namely Audalfus, Rambertus, Hormarus, Bernerus, Tangelrudus, Teutardus, Rodrudus, Adholsirma, Wiredus, Hairedus, Rothoida, and Achilde.

We did this on the condition that, for as long as they lived, they might possess and cultivate all these properties peacefully by precarious tenure, through our benefice and that of our successors, under usufruct, and receive the fruits of the land. They were to have no power to diminish or alienate anything from it, but were to strive to carry out whatever they could add, increase, or improve there.

Each year, on the feast of Saint Gorgonius, which falls on the fifth day before the Ides of September, they were not to fail to pay a rent of two silver solidi to Saint Peter. If they should appear slow or negligent in paying this rent, they were to restore it with the legal penalty, but they were not to lose the precarious tenure itself.

After their death, whenever God should will it, all the properties, both those given and those received, improved and together with every addition, were to return in every way, without anyone’s opposition or judicial assignment, to the church of the aforesaid altar of Saint Peter and Saint Gorgonius.

Done publicly at Gorze, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 903, indiction VII, epact XX, concurrent V, in the third year of the reign of Louis, son of King Arnulf.

Robert, bishop of the holy Church of Metz, subscribed. + Rudolphus, abbot. Seguinus, dean. Furnulfus. Soiperus. Farvavardus. Erengus. Harno. Gislebertus. Teudo. Ancedolius. Agredus. Barnerus. Segerannus. Audinus. Adelmadus. Ardovucus. Johannes. Becio. Astagius. Gisaldus. Vuandelmarus. Teudaldus. Godderannus. Amincus. Agilus. Angelradus. Erloinus. Adelbertus. Giroardus. Girardus. Aginardus. Adovardus. Segeboldus. Rudricus. Anoualdus. Barnerus. Heldouvardus. Girardus again. Rotcherus. Aribardus. Britius. Rotlandus. Ragembertus. Giroinus. Ysembardus.

I, Seguinus, though an unworthy monk, wrote this precarious charter.

## II. Letters

*(In Goldast, *Writers on Alamannic Affairs*, vol. II.)*

### I

To his parents: “The weaned lamb sends a pious bleat.”

Most recently I left you in good health, and I still declare that I am well. I therefore ask that your promise to reward the labors of my teachers may come to fulfillment. Since I am also, as it were, living abroad and unworthy of everything, provide me with the necessities about which you spoke.

### II

“R. sends to T., watered with heavenly dew, whatever good he can.”

Ever since I was brought under the yoke of submission, you have educated me without any reward from my friends, with no less affection than if I had been born from your own body. Since it is written in the Gospel that the laborer is worthy of his wage, I have decided to go to my sisters on the island called Lindouva. There I think I shall receive some little gift with which I may honor your face.

### III

“R. sends certainty of service to one filled with spiritual food.”

I would be ashamed to tell your piety of the pains caused by my nakedness, if it did not know the misery I suffer. Compelled by this circumstance, I implore your compassion: grant me permission to go to my mother, who, as I hope, will not disdain to help me with the necessities of life.

### IV

“To his parents: H., crowned with the clerical habit, sends faithful prayer in Christ.”

You found an excellent plan in sending me to the monastery of Saint Gall for the cultivation of discipline and learning. I confess that there I found both abundantly. This, however, is my request: through your generosity, let a third little gift of your compassion be sent to me more quickly—namely, two shirts and a linen tunic—in which I may walk honorably with my companions, rather than disgracefully in nakedness.

### V

“To the lord R.: T., your least friend, sends faithful prayer and service.”

When I recall how much affection and beneficence I have received from you, I am greatly ashamed that I may perhaps be able to repay nothing fitting. But I ask you not to regret what you have begun merely because we lack the means of repayment. He who will permit no one to be deprived of his reward will repay the debt forever.

As for what you commissioned concerning the instruction of the boy through our Wodalricus: although the very voice and memory of Moerimus, already growing old, are failing, for your sake we gladly devote our efforts. Farewell. May your most sacred prayers not forget me.

### VI

“H. sends abundant greeting, service, and prayer to his dearest niece Ruodep.”

I am sending you, dearest, two men, and I ask you to add a third from your own people, so that under his guidance and with your help they may go around the forest, find some vessel, and bring it for my use. Remember, therefore, your faith and service, and show this mercy with me: help them there and provide your assistance when they return to me.

Farewell, dearest.

### VII

“P. sends greeting and progress in learning to his beloved.”

I have translated into the Theodisc language the words you sent me to explain. They should sound as follows.

**“Because the power of pricking is in the blow of the sting.”**  
The Theodisc text is: “Vuándo des kestirnis chràft fergât unde vir loúfit in sô langero viriste sô man stupf ketûon màg”—“For the power of stinging lies in the stroke of what pricks.”

**Shapeless matter.**  
The Theodisc text is: “That is shapeless timber.”

**Intemperance.**  
The Theodisc form is: “Intrerteda.”

**Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.**  
The Theodisc text is: “Taz chît, kúishéit tére nôh urôugôn”—“That is the certainty of things hoped for.”

**Whomever God loves, he hears. To one with whom God is favorable, he is approachable by prayer.**  
The Theodisc text is: “Temo die héiligen hólt sint, dér mág hórsko gebeton”—“He who is dear to the saints may pray earnestly.”

**In humility his judgment was taken away.**  
The Theodisc text is: “Táz in nióman ze réthe ne liêz táz wárt ze léibe úmbosîna deúmuôti”—“In his humility his judgment was taken away.” [The exact construction of the Theodisc is uncertain.]

**On the previous year’s Easter.**  
That is, on the Easter feast of the preceding year: “the previous Easter day.”

**Ypapanti.**  
That is, the gathering of people of every age.

Noun: *namo*. Pronoun: *fure doz nomen*—“in place of the noun.” Verb: *Vuôrt*. Adverb: *zuoze démo verbo*—“next to the verb.” Participle: *teilnémunga*. Conjunction: *geuugeda*. Preposition: *fúrezeda*. Interjection: *undérvuerf*.

How many accidents belong to a noun?  
“What things happen to the noun?” Six.

Which ones? Quality: *Te wilichi*—“what sort?” What is understood: whether it is common, of substance, or of accident. Comparison: *De widermezùngà*—“the comparison.” Of which? That of the comparative, or that of the superlative, in relation to the positive. Gender: *Tiz chûme*—“the kind.” Whose? Its own, or … [lacuna].

### VIII

You ask me what “the previous year’s Easter” is. It is an admitted gathering of fellow sponsors, observed throughout all the octaves of Holy Week—that is, of baptism—during the year, and according to the order of each person, with a meal shared with the others. What we saw, we testify.

The priest recites the Creed over the infant and participates at the table in the water of wisdom. [lacuna]

### IX

“To our lord and abbot Purkhard, we, your brothers and disciples, offer our due prayers.”

You gladdened us by your letter concerning the matters involving you, because by God’s grace they are proceeding properly. Through your prayers something also happened among us that contributes to more general joy: concerning the ecclesiastical treasure that was stolen, we have recovered no small part of it, and we are holding the thief himself captured in chains.

He is a servant of Kerottus of Pettenhusen, son of Alberic; his name is Gunzo, and his father’s name is Richolf, who is now in the retinue of his lord, who is on military service.

He therefore returned a crown, a golden box without its lid, and approximately one-third of a golden cross. He also returned some fragments of the larger box, although very few of the gems were recovered.

There is still hope concerning the remainder, because it was sold into the hands of a certain merchant from Buchouva named Pero, who had formerly been a mint-worker there, and much of it also into the hands of merchants from Constance, whose names are Eccho, Chomuli, Vuoveli, Albeli, Engezo, and Tegenhart.

God deigned to send us a stranger who secretly asked that an agreement be made with him concerning a payment of two pounds for conveying information, so that he might disclose these matters. After the agreement had been made, he immediately led Brother Anno to Constance, where he had Tegenhart bring before him the worked fragments of gold that he recognized. But Tegenhart testified that he had bought them from Pero of Buchouva.

From there the same brother went to Pero and, through your soldier Hugo, had the thief—who was hiding in Pero’s house—pointed out to him. He was immediately captured and returned whatever remained to him of the treasure hidden underground.

Now you must deal with the king, so that the advocates of both churches may become the enforcers of this matter and restore the goods to their proper place.

You must also be informed that the things which you ordered your stewards to provide for our use are far smaller and fewer than you supposed, and that a mortality of all oxen and livestock is raging throughout our land. You should therefore urge the king to decree relief for us from this, as from an Egyptian plague.

May the Most High grant you, our lord, every prosperity.

# In the Year of the Lord 918: Saint Radbod, Bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine

[Col. 0537]

## Life of Saint Radbod by an Anonymous Contemporary Author

*(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VII, p. 26.)*

## Preliminary Observations

[Col. 0537A] 1. Radbod, also called Radbodo, was the fourteenth bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine after Egilboldus and shone with distinguished piety. An anonymous contemporary writer composed his life from the account of Radbod’s companions, in the form in which Surius found it in a manuscript. Surius would have served our interests better if he had presented the author’s original style to us; from that style one can scarcely depart without errors and loss of the authority properly due to it.

The words of the anonymous author are found in section 5: “We shall recall a few things learned from those who were present at the events.” He speaks in the same sense near the end of section 10.

## 2. Lower Trajectum, called Wiltaburg by its ancient name, was endowed with an episcopal see by our Willibrord, who, associating with himself monks, heralds of the word of God, brought the Frisians to Christ. Various documents from those times [Col. 0537B] prove that the monks first established there in the cathedral church by Willibrord and then by the martyr Boniface remained there at least until the Carolingian period. But whenever the monks there gave way to canons, we infer from the example of Bishop Radbod that for some time afterward the bishops of Trajectum, at least the more devout among them, entered upon this see only after assuming the monastic habit and professing the Rule. Radbod, having been educated at the court of King Charles, went to Guntarius at Cologne; leaving him, he was soon summoned by the people of Trajectum to become their bishop. Without delay, as the author of the *Life* writes in section 4, “he changed his habit, became a perfectly observant monk, and abstained not only from eating meat but from every pleasure of food.” The same writer seems to indicate in section 7 that this was done in imitation of his predecessors Willibrord and Boniface; and writers of English histories show in more than one place that this was consistent with the custom received among the bishops of the Church of Canterbury.

## 3. Before speaking of the deeds of Bishop Radbod, something must be said about his studies at the court of King Charles, about his fellow students Stephen and Mancio, and about [Col. 0537C] Manno, or Nanno, prefect of the palace school. Almost all German writers believe this King Charles to have been the emperor Charles the Fat; but this is refuted by the single fact that the contemporary author of the *Life* assigns to King Charles a son named Louis, who was the son and heir of Charles the Bald, not of Charles the Fat, who left no children.

We have sufficiently demonstrated Charles the Bald’s great zeal in restoring the study of letters, which had been seriously weakened by internal wars and the incursions of the Danes, both in the final preface to the first part of the preceding century [Col. 0538A] and in the *Eulogies* of Paschasius Radbert and Abbot John. But let us hear our author himself, from sections 1 and 2:

> “First Radbod went to the court of Charles, king of the Franks, and afterward to that of Louis, his son—not because he sought palace honors, but because the liberal disciplines were cultivated with distinction within the king’s palace. Manno, a philosopher, presided over that school; the holy boy, ardent and diligent in his desire to learn, attached himself assiduously to him. His fellow students were Stephen and Mancio,” and so forth.

I will not dwell on the modern Belgian or German writers who invent a Nanno, a counselor of Charles the Fat, a Frisian by birth, and the author of several little works which, they say, are widely circulated. That his name was Manno is made convincing by the more accurate reading of Surius; and I readily believe that he was none other than that Manno, provost of the monastery of Saint Augendus in the Jura region, who in 870 claimed a certain church for his monastery at the synod of Vienne. [Col. 0538B] The Petavian codex in which the poems of Florus, published in volume I of the *Analecta*, are copied, bears this title, as do other codices that we have seen in the Boherian library:

> “A BOOK, OFFERED AT THE TOMB OF SAINT AUGENDUS IN FULFILLMENT OF THE VOW OF MANNON OF BLESSED MEMORY.”

Thus Manno, in all likelihood, withdrew from the palace schools to the monastery of Saint Augendus before the year 870, and there consecrated to God a rich collection of books. We shall speak below of Stephen, Radbod’s fellow student and later bishop of Tongeren. Surius wrongly called Mancio bishop of Chalon; he should have called him bishop of Châlons. He is the same Mancio mentioned more than once by Frodoard in Book IV of his *History*, whose letter to Fulco, metropolitan of Reims, concerning a priest who wished to marry, we recently published in a volume of the *Analecta*.

## 4. That Radbod made great progress in the palace schools and, as William of Heda says, was skilled in verse and prose is proved by the catalogue of his works reported by Trithemius in the following form: [Col. 0538C]

> “He wrote several distinguished little works, among which the following are reported: one book of *Praises of Saint Martin*; one book of *Praises of Saint Boniface, Bishop*; one book *On Saint Amalberga*; one book of homilies and sermons; *Flowers concerning Saint Willibrord*; also an entire office for the translation of Saint Martin; and various chants in honor of the saints.”

What Trithemius calls the *Praises* of Saints Martin and Boniface, our anonymous author calls hymns and encomia in section 7, in these words:

> “He composed hymns and encomia about them, to be sung on their solemnities. And lest anyone think that we are saying what is contrary to the truth, the complete Office of blessed Martin, composed by him, still exists.” [Col. 0539A]

The manuscript formerly contained in the Bigotian codex a book about the virgin Amalberga, mentioned by Trithemius, under this title:

> “A Little Book of the Lord Radboud, Bishop of the Holy Church of Trajectum, concerning the Life and Merits of the Extraordinary Virgin Amalberga.”

This little book is nothing other than the homily praised by Trithemius, which we published above from the same Bigotian codex, in the section concerning the virgin Amalberga (below, col. 553). In Part I of the third section of the preceding century, we presented a sermon delivered on the feast of Saint Willibrord [Note: [Col. 0539] The sermon referred to here would be sought in vain at the cited location]; I do not know whether this is the very sermon that Trithemius attributes to our Radbod.

Besides the works that Trithemius assigns to Radbod, William of Heda transcribed several of his poems, which, for their period, display an elegant authorial vein. The same William also transmitted Radbod’s brief *Chronicle*, from which we learn the year in which he began his episcopate and other events of his time. Finally, in volume VI Surius reports an *Eclogue on Saint Lebuin* and attributes it to Radbod. [Col. 0539B] Such, then, are his writings.

## 5. As the year preceding nine hundred was coming to an end, Radbod was summoned to the height of the see of Trajectum. He exchanged the clerical garb for the monastic, and thereafter continually fed the flock entrusted to him by word and example. He also provided for its temporal support, obtaining from Kings Arnulf and his son Zwentibold Deventer, together with the adjoining estates, where he withdrew after Trajectum had been destroyed by the Northmen [Col. 0540A]. Moreover, in the year 914 he received from King Conrad a privilege reported by Heda, by which he secured protection and security for the estates and rights of his church.

At last, after traveling here and there amid the frequent storms of the pagans in order to protect his flock, he died at Homersum, or Othemarshem, and was buried at Deventer. Everyone assigns the day of his death to the third day before the Kalends of December; but the authors differ about the year. Some mark the year 916 or 917, others the following year, while several prefer 919. It seems to us that the year 918 after the birth of Christ was Radbod’s last.

## 6. Our anonymous author praises Radbod’s sanctity exceedingly; but I find no one who bestowed upon him the title “saint” before Adam of Bremen, *History*, chapter 21. Regino in his *Chronicle* calls Radbod a venerable bishop; John of Beka calls him a truly holy man; William [Col. 0540B] of Heda, Trithemius, Wion, Miraeus, Molanus, Cratepolius, and many other later writers say the same of him.

It is preferable to hear our author himself, after briefly noting that those who make our Radbod arch-chancellor of the kingdom are greatly mistaken. That office was conferred upon Radbod, archbishop of Trier, not upon the bishop of Trajectum, as can easily be gathered from various records of his age.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0539]

## 1. The etymology of Radbod’s name; his mother’s lineage; his literary studies. He attaches himself to the palace school.

Blessed Radbod, born of a noble Frankish family, had exceedingly Christian parents, and by his own merits he became a great ornament to the world. For from almost his earliest beginnings he was already directing his mind toward heaven. His name is not without a mystery: in Latin it can be rendered “messenger of counsel.” For he was destined by Christ to be an ambassador of the best counsel to the Frisians, from whom he had received his maternal lineage [Note: [Col. 0539D] Hence most Belgian or German writers call Radbod Frisian by birth. His homeland is said below, in section 3, to have been Lomaganium.], and indeed he gave them the best counsel.

Radbod, duke of the Frisians—whom others call their king—was his mother’s great-great-grandfather; his mother gave him that ancestor’s name. As soon as he seemed capable of learning, he was put to the study of letters. He spent the period of his early youth with Gunther [Note: [Col. 0539D] Also called Guntarius, counselor to King Lothair; Radbod rightly abandoned him when misfortunes befell him—that is, when Pope Nicholas subjected him to anathema because of the king’s incestuous marriage with Waldrada.] [Col. 0539D] archbishop of Cologne, his maternal uncle, applying himself to letters.

But when misfortunes befell that bishop, the boy, of outstanding natural ability, at the urging of his relatives and with the assistance of many others—for the grace of God with which he was endowed made him dear to everyone—went first to the court of Charles [Note: [Col. 0540D] We have shown above in the preliminary observations that this King Charles was not Charles the Fat but Charles the Bald.], king of the Franks, and then to the court of Louis, his son, not because he sought palace honors, but because the liberal disciplines were cultivated with distinction within the king’s palace. [Col. 0540C] The philosopher Manno [al. Nanno] presided over that school, and the holy boy, ardent and diligent in his desire to learn, attached himself assiduously to him.

## 2. Radbod’s companions

His fellow students were Stephen [Note: [Col. 0540D] See also the preliminary observations concerning Manno, Stephen, and Mancio.] and Mancio, older in age but not in zeal. Thus a pious rivalry arose among them, each striving to surpass the other—not through ambition for honor, but through humility and diligence in reading and learning. Their virtue advanced to such a degree that not long afterward both were made bishops: Stephen of the Church of Tongeren, and Mancio of Châlons [Surius: of Chalon, incorrectly].

But Radbod, a venerable young man, sitting like a diligent bee among the flowers of literature, gathered from them a great store of learning until, by everyone’s judgment, he was considered no ordinary scholar. Meanwhile, moved by the strength of his spirit, he restrained the impulses of youth; by frugality he subdued the rebellion of the flesh; he despised the world and all worldly things for love of heavenly things; he longed for spiritual delights; and he firmly resolved to renounce all transient things.

His age was not yet mature, but [Col. 0541A] his character was mature and aged. He rejected every enticement and strove to please God alone. Night and day he devoted himself to spiritual banquets, and already then, in affection and desire, he pursued what he afterward accomplished in deed.

## 3. Radbod’s homeland. He follows Abbot Hugh.

Nor was his virtue hidden from the king. The more earnestly he tried to conceal himself, the more widely his reputation, especially against his own wishes, spread through the mouths of the people. He became dear to the king because of the integrity of his character, venerable to the nobles of the kingdom, and accepted and esteemed by the people, since he plainly appeared pleasing and beloved by God.

After Charles, under whom he had spent the years of his youth, died, he went to visit his relatives in Lomaganium—for so his homeland was commonly called [Col. 0541B]. He also joined himself to Hugh, an abbot of the highest dignity and at that time foremost among abbots. There he surpassed the others in the palm of learning, while continually climbing by the steps of virtue to higher things, so that he shone everywhere brilliantly like a heavenly lamp.

## 4. He is made bishop. He assumes the monastic habit. His abstinence. He changes water into wine.

Meanwhile Egilbertus [Note: [Col. 0541D] He was Conrad’s son, enriched with many monasteries throughout Gaul and also distinguished by his dukedom. He died at Orléans in 887 and was buried at Saint-Germain of Auxerre.] changed life for death as bishop of the Church of Utrecht. The question of appointing a suitable shepherd was discussed, and by the remarkable agreement of clergy and people, not without God’s providence, Radbod was judged the worthiest of all. This was also the judgment of Arnulf, who at that time held the reins of the kingdom, and of the nobles.

Thus, through the zeal and will of the clergy, the king, the nobles, and the people [Col. 0541C], the holy man—at first unaware of the matter, and afterward resisting it for a long time—was made bishop [Note: [Col. 0541D] John of Beka calls him Egilboldus, as do William of Heda and many other authors. Zwentibold writes Eylboldus in his charter preserved by that same William.].

Deeply troubled in spirit by this event, he hesitated for a long time about what to do. At last, while wishing to flee honor, he was dragged, even against his will, to the chair of honor. Having received the blessing, the soldier of the eternal King, about to go forth to battle, girded himself with spiritual weapons in a manly spirit. He changed his habit, added still greater ornaments to his way of life, and, obeying Christ’s teaching, embraced the exceedingly narrow way. He became a perfectly observant monk, abstaining not only from eating meat but from every pleasure of food. By fasts of two or three days he nourished his soul, while sustaining the weakness of his body—scarcely held together by its bones—with the necessities of nature, and those of the humblest kind, [Col. 0541D] yet displaying cheerfulness in his face and conducting himself among his people as though he were eating delicacies.

He wished, as far as possible, to keep his abstinence hidden from everyone, with only a few aware of it. A certain layman [Note: [Col. 0541D] Beka and Heda call him Gummar, but nowhere indicate the authority on which they rely.] who was close to the bishop and frequently visited him wished to test this. On one occasion he sat at table with him and conversed according to custom; finally he asked permission to drink from the cup that had been customarily placed before the bishop. It was made of onyx and suitably adorned with gold, but it was filled with water.

At this point, the event itself does not allow us to remain silent about the wonder that the wondrous God performed through his servant. The bishop would not let him drink from the cup, for he did not want it to become known to others what it contained. Yet when an opportunity presented itself, the other secretly seized the cup. The bishop noticed this, but, since he could not prevent him from drinking, he sighed and groaned to God.

And behold: by the renewal of the ancient miracle, the water was changed into the finest wine [Col. 0542B]. When the investigator perceived this, he fell at the feet of the most holy bishop, asked forgiveness, and promised that he would never again attempt anything of the kind. Although the most holy bishop wished to conceal the matter, God’s work could not rightly remain hidden, in keeping with the saying of the angel Raphael to Tobit:

> “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God.”

## 5. His charity toward the poor. His continence.

His daily conduct, as long as he lived in the body, was so pleasing to God and so welcome and agreeable to human beings, while he continually increased in virtue, that although we cannot describe it adequately, we shall nevertheless recall at least a few things received from those who witnessed his deeds, so that the reader may more readily believe us [Col. 0542C].

Whatever he could possess from the resources of this world, he carefully distributed among the poor. Although he flourished in the practice of every good work, he was second to none in kindness toward the poor. Every day, except on a few solemnities, he washed the feet of the poor with his own hands, provided them with food, clothed the naked, visited the sick, and cared for the lame and the orphans.

He devoted himself to such pursuits and duties of humaneness and mercy day and night, with unbelievable vigilance and solicitude, never wearied by such labors, considering whatever he contributed to the comfort of the wretched a gain. No ornaments or empty worldly pomp were seen in his presence; he did not possess that accursed hunger for gold. He considered it unlawful to take pleasure in such things [Col. 0542D]. Thus, having despised the world and whatever it can offer its friends, he burned with love of heavenly things, living on earth only in body.

## 6. He honors the saints Willibrord and Boniface.

When the Danes had ravaged the Church of Trajectum [Note: [Col. 0541D] Recent historians of that city who have treated the deeds of the bishops of Trajectum assign its destruction to the time of Egilbert. The authority of the author of this *Life* seems preferable to me; he has Adam of Bremen, *History*, chapter 31, supporting him in these words: “Frisia was devastated. The city of Trajectum was destroyed. Saint Radbod, bishop of the city, yielding to the persecution, established his see at Deventer; remaining there, he avenged the pagans with the sword of anathema.” Shortly before this, by the grant of Kings Zwentibold and Charles the Simple, Deventer had come under the jurisdiction of the Church of Trajectum, as Heda notes among other matters.], [Col. 0543A] Radbod often stayed at Deventer, although in spirit he always dwelt at Trajectum. Even when peace had been restored and he frequently went there, he grieved greatly—both for himself and for others—that circumstances and time did not allow him to remain there permanently.

In his mind he set before himself for imitation many holy Fathers, especially those who had first established the foundations of that Church upon Christ, the firm rock—namely, Willibrord and Boniface, outstanding in merits and holiness. He chose them as guides of the arduous path on which they had gone before him and undertook to imitate them. He painted them upon the threshold of his heart and continually contemplated them with concentrated attention.

By the holiness of their character, the excellence of their examples, and the patronage of their merits, they still support the household of the supreme King: one renowned by confessing the faith in peace, the other by the shedding of his blood; both, triumphing over the enemy, enjoy fellowship in the heavenly army. Following in their footsteps, Radbod scattered the seeds of faith among the flock entrusted to him. Each day he offered himself to God as a living sacrifice; with his whole heart he aspired to the heavenly homeland; he died to the world and lived for Christ; he dwelt wholly in heaven.

He was Christ’s lamp, set upon a lampstand, shining upon all who were in the house of God, while remaining humble before God within himself.

## 7. He foretells the future. The succession of his virtues. He composes hymns and the Office of Saint Martin.

Nor was he without the spirit of prophecy. Many things happened quickly just as he had foretold, and many others occurred not long afterward. He always meditated in his heart upon the law of the Lord, and, not content with that, also carried it out in deed. He had become a victor in spirit, a teacher of charity, a practitioner of chastity, a supporter of the poor, a comforter of the sorrowful, an unconquerable hope of consolation for the clergy, an unwearied relief for the people, and a tower of strength against the enemy for all his own. He was so firmly attached to righteousness that neither prosperity nor adversity could induce him to depart from it.

Christ was never absent from his lips; whatever he did, he continually held him fixed in his mind. He was never wearied by the discipline of reading or prayer; he was never satisfied with the duties and works of mercy; he was always devoted to fasts and vigils. Sweetness continually dripped from his lips; they sowed peace and remedies of salvation; his words always sounded forth Christ.

As we have said, he eagerly followed the examples of the preceding Fathers. He used their memory with incredible avidity—by reading, hearing, conversing, or composing something about them. He wove hymns and encomia about them, to be sung on their solemnities. And lest anyone think that we are saying what is contrary to the truth, the complete Office of blessed Martin, composed by him, still exists [Col. 0543D].

He had chosen Martin above all others as his special patron, having no doubt that he would be helped by his patronage. He was never broken by adverse circumstances, never ensnared by the plots of the roaring enemy; fortified on every side by the strongest protection of God, he feared neither hostile weapons nor any harsh misfortunes.

## 8. He strikes the Danes troubling Frisia with an anathema. Hence they are afflicted by a plague.

On one occasion he went to Frisia to visit the flock entrusted to him, so that, if any shoots of the former error should emerge there, he might uproot them with the spiritual plow and water the minds of believers with the teaching of faith. But the Danes encountered him and obstructed his efforts. Nevertheless, deterred by no danger of death, he offered them salutary exhortations, urging them to reject their errors and embrace the way of truth.

But when they hardened their hearts, persisted in wickedness, and even threatened him with death, he pronounced against them the sentence of anathema. Then divine vengeance immediately pursued them. Struck by a dreadful plague as though by a lightning bolt, almost all of them perished; nor did they ever go unpunished whenever they caused him trouble at Trajectum [Col. 0544B]. At once they were chastised by God’s judgment, as the very few among them who rejoiced to have escaped alive often testified.

## 9. He foretells and designates Baldric as his successor. He also foretells the time of his death.

At that time Valdricus [Note: [Col. 0543] Beka and Helda, already frequently cited, give a full account of Baldric’s deeds and assign him Rixfrid, count of Cleves, as his father.], an outstanding young man, son of Count Ricfrid, used sometimes to visit the blessed man. On one occasion, when he was present, Radbod called to him the priest Nitger and the soldier Richard and said to them with prophetic spirit:

> “This young man whom you see will succeed me in the episcopate, and through him God will restore this see, greatly increase the resources of the Church, and repair what has been destroyed and ruined.”

He foretold this about the young man not once or twice, but repeatedly [Col. 0544C]. That he had spoken truly, the event itself declared, with the whole world as witness.

## 10. Once, while the blessed man was celebrating Mass and the Apostle was being read, he summoned to him Eliolf and Rotguit, priests of the monastery of Emmerich, and said:

> “Indeed, I shall not live much longer. Therefore diligently honor this young man Baldric. For after three years and six months I shall depart this life here, and without doubt he will obtain my see.”

When they heard this, they stood astonished, marveling greatly at his prophecy.

Not long afterward, at the time when sacred orders are usually conferred, the same young man brought to the man of God two clerics under his authority, Bennon and Saxon, asking that they receive holy orders from his hands. The holy man, smiling—as he always did with a cheerful face—said to him:

> “Do not, my son, invite me to this matter in vain. It is yours to grant what you ask of me; for they will be ordained not by my hands but by yours, and that after two years and six months.”

But the young Baldric, shaken in spirit, shed tears, fearing everything, even what was secure, and not believing that what the holy man said would come to pass. When the blessed bishop saw that he was suffering greatly, he began gently to console him.

> “Do not fear, Baldric,” he said, “and do not let a noble spirit be broken by cowardice. The resources of the Church, now considered poor and needy, will through you be enriched with countless gifts of God, and the state of things will unexpectedly be changed [Col. 0545A]. You will restore to its former dignity the bishop’s residence at Trajectum, which for many years has lain ruined through the devastation of the Danes.”

The holy man foretold many other things of this kind that would happen. They were afterward fulfilled exactly as he had said, as everyone can now see; indeed, it seems useless for us to ask people to believe his words when each person can prove their truth with his own eyes.

## 11. A bishop ought to be detached from secular offices.

When the king invited him to undertake some office for him, he would courteously reply:

> “No one doubts that it is right to obey higher authorities, but that bishops ought not to become entangled in secular affairs, in whose camps Christ’s soldiers are serving. They, clothed spiritually and armed with ecclesiastical weapons [Col. 0545B], ought to pray to the Lord with their own people for the safety, peace, and stability of the king and the people; by continual prayers they should seek the gain of souls, not pursue earthly things. It is fitting that soldiers girded with the belt of royal service and heaped with benefits should perform such duties.”

Thus, having considered the law of perfect freedom, he could be moved from his judgment neither by flattery nor by any threats, if threats were made, preferring to please God alone rather than human beings.

## 12. He prepares himself for death.

Since he foresaw his death so long beforehand, no one can doubt that, like a burning lamp, he prepared himself for the Lord returning from the wedding feast. He kept watch so that he might immediately open to the one who knocked, and he distributed his Lord’s measure of wheat to the household all the more diligently because he knew with greater certainty that he would soon have to render an account to him.

He did not fear death, for to die was gain to him and to live was Christ. As was his custom, he exhorted his people to pursue peace, concord, and charity; he himself strove, insofar as human weakness permits, to make himself poor in spirit, rich in merits, detached from earthly things, and familiar with heavenly ones. Through fasts, the delights of the Psalms, vigils, and almsgiving, with great exertion of spirit, he took care to fortify himself for death.

## 13. He is refreshed by a vision of the Blessed Virgin and her companions.

We must not pass over that sublime vision which he himself indicated had occurred to him, telling certain members of his household. On one occasion, when he was lying seriously ill and had abandoned all hope of life, the most blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, appeared to him accompanied by the holy virgins Thecla and Agnes. There was a great light, which flooded the entire dwelling with splendor.

But he was so terrified by the vision that through fear he could say nothing, and he was almost lifeless. Then the Gate of salvation, the Lady of the world, applying the medicine of consolation to him and driving away not only all fear but also his illness, said:

> “Do not fear, Radbod; be certain that you behold her to whom you frequently offer suppliant prayers. For I do not disdain to console you by my presence, since in your prayers to God you always remember me. Know, moreover, that no danger from this illness threatens you, but that you will be healed; nevertheless, you will not live long afterward in the flesh. Be secure concerning yourself. Do not cease to keep watch and to work, but continue as you have begun.”

At these words the splendor suddenly disappeared, but a most agreeable fragrance remained for a long time, and the illness was completely removed.

When he had secretly disclosed these things to certain members of his household—for he did not wish them to become known to anyone while he was alive—he also described to them the appearance, clothing, and adornment of the most holy Mother of God, adding that no one could sufficiently admire her beauty. The holy virgins Thecla and Agnes, he said, could be recognized both by their faces and by their clothing.

## 14. He is seized by a fever, applies himself unceasingly to prayer, dies, and is buried at Deventer.

When the three years and six months mentioned above had elapsed, he was seized by a fever in the district of Trent [Note: [Col. 0545D] Drentensis, or Trenta, a district lying between Groningen and Coevorden.]. He immediately ordered his people to depart from there with him, lest, as the fever grew stronger, they should be forced to remain there. For in winter it is not easy for anyone to leave that district.

He himself knew that the time of his departure had arrived. Although everyone was distressed by his illness, they nevertheless complied with his wishes and began the journey to Oetamarsem [Note: [Col. 0545D] This place is now called Otmarsum or Oectmarth [Col. 0546D], in the district of Wente on the river Linchelum, not far from Bentheim; it is the head of the deanery, according to Lindeborn in chapter 8 of his *History of Deventer.]. If his people allowed it, he had chosen that place for his burial. There was then a small oratory, where he often used to stay, situated in a pleasant location.

Having arranged his affairs according to his wish, he was neither wearied by God’s service nor broken by the force of illness. His face was cheerful, he feared death not at all, and, invited as he was to Christ’s banquet, although his body was already half dead, he was increasingly enlivened in spirit.

His lips did not rest even as he drew his final hours. In a wondrous manner he recited the Psalms, drawing floods of tears from those who were present. Like one plainly rejoicing, as long as his tongue could move and breath remained, he repeatedly recited among the Psalms that antiphon, *Ecce laeti*, and so forth, which is the first among the responsories composed by him for blessed Martin, chief of confessors.

Meanwhile, there was no doubt that, surrounded by the most blessed angelic spirits, he feared none of the apparitions of darkness. Nor do we believe that Martin, that outstanding bishop and his special patron, was far away—the man whom he seemed so often to greet in a singing voice.

At last, as the month of November was drawing to its end, he too closed his final day, departing most happily to the Lord. His holy body was soon placed upon a bier [Col. 0546D], and all the clergy and people reverently and honorably carried it to Deventer with hymns and psalmody.

When they had already approached the town, all its inhabitants came out to meet it with sorrowful hearts. Amid the mingled voices of mourners and singers, the sacred body was carried into the church and buried on the side facing the north. His spirit rejoiced and enjoyed the happiness of his Lord, whom he had served in this life—to whom belong honor, power, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0547]

# RADBOD’S BRIEF CHRONICLE

*(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum* of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. VII, p. 267.)*

[Col. 0547A] In the year 900 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a wondrous sign appeared in the heavens. For stars were seen everywhere as though flowing down from above toward the bottom of the horizon around the pole; almost all of them seemed to converge with one another. This prodigy was followed by grievous calamities: an extreme disturbance of the atmosphere, frequent whirlwinds, and rivers overflowing their banks, presenting a terrifying image resembling a cataclysm. And, more pestilential than these, were the dreadful storms of human beings exalting themselves against God [Col. 0548A].

In this same year, but before the epacts changed, Folco, metropolitan bishop of Reims, and King Zwentibold were killed. A few days earlier I, the sinner Radbod, had been counted among the servants of the holy Church of Trajectum. Would that I might be found worthy to attain with them a share in eternal life!

[Col. 0547]

# SERMONS AND HOMILIES OF RADBOD

## SERMON OF SAINT RADBOD ON SAINT SWITBERT

*(From Bollandist, *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, p. 85.)*

[Col. 0547B] 1. As we prepare, dearest brothers, to celebrate the day of our special joy, on which the sacred commemoration of our most blessed patron Switbert must be made, we ought to be prepared for every good work and keep our minds ready: first, to hear the commands of the divine law; afterward, to strive to carry them out in our deeds as far as we can; and finally, in this way, to teach others.

For this is what our Lord Jesus Christ did, of whom it is written: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). Otherwise our teaching will be futile and empty if, by doing nothing, we destroy what we have said. For what benefit is it to someone to hear well but act badly? Or what advantage does it give him to show another the way for his feet while he himself does not cease to go astray in the way of conduct?

Therefore, following the footsteps of our Redeemer, let us gladly hear whatever is good; having heard it, let us complete it by worthy actions; and thus, proceeding in due order to instruct our neighbors, let us advise them through both the teaching and the examples of good things.

To make this possible without delay, we must recall to mind the deeds of our Father, of whom we spoke above: in everything he taught, he first gave an example from himself to his hearers, and he never said that anything should be done in the Church [Col. 0547D] except what he had first done himself.

But so that this too may be clear to those who wish to imitate him, let his deeds pleasing to God and fully necessary for every hearer be recited publicly, so that from them the people of Christ may receive edification and may always rejoice in the glorious prayers of so great a man.

But because some things he did are hidden from us—things that only antiquity, after God, knows—for he is shown to have come from the province of the English, let the writings of the venerable priest Bede be brought forward. In the *Records of the English*, among other things, he leaves the following written about this most holy man.

## 2. In the time of Blessed Willibrord, bishop of Trajectum, the brothers who in Frisia were devoted to the ministry of the word chose from their number a man modest in character and gentle in heart, Switbert, to be ordained their bishop.

They sent him to Britain, where the most reverend Bishop Wilfrid ordained him at their request. At that time Wilfrid happened to be an exile in the regions of Mercia, having been driven from his homeland. For at that time Kent did not have a bishop: Theodore had died, while his successor Berthwald had not yet returned to his episcopal see after going across the sea to be ordained [Col. 0548C].

This Switbert, having received the episcopate and returned from Britain, soon afterward withdrew to the people of the Boructuarians and brought many of them to the way of truth by preaching. But not long afterward, when the Boructuarians were conquered by the ancient Saxons, those who had received the word were scattered in every direction.

The bishop himself, with some companions, went to Pippin. At the request of his wife Blithrude, Pippin gave him a place to live on an island in the Rhine, which in their language is called “in the shore.” There he built a monastery, which his heirs still possess. For some time he led a life of the strictest continence there, and there he closed his final day.

3. We believe that no one can doubt that Bede mentioned the things set forth above concerning this most holy man—unless perhaps someone, being occupied with other affairs, either did not read the book in which these things are written or certainly neglected them while reading. For the rest, we ought in no way to doubt that this man was trained in every pursuit of the Christian religion, since, among those most precious lamps of the Church of God which in those days shone wondrously either among the English or among the peoples of Gaul, he deserved to be ordained shepherd of Christ’s sheep by those very holiest men. For unless he had been thoroughly instructed in pastoral discipline, so great a multitude of Christ’s flock would in no way have been entrusted to his keeping. Moreover, unless he had been in some sense a veteran soldier, strong and undaunted in the contest of martyrdom, he would never have been appointed supreme tribune in Christ’s battle line, never the first-ranking officer of the army of divine law.

But having first touched upon these matters allegorically, we must also explain morally what exercises enabled this distinguished soldier to become, as we do not doubt, unconquerable. This must first be demonstrated in pastoral matters, where either a raging lion or a lurking wolf brings no small harm upon Christ’s sheep. If the ever-watchful shepherd avoids the ambush or bravely drives away the predator by resisting it, he will return with the flock unharmed to the Lord’s folds. But if, standing continually girded, he never lays aside his weapons, and either drives the enemy back from the camp or openly fights in the field and triumphs properly, then afterward he will rule with complete security within the walls of the holy city.

4. We certainly know that blessed Switbert did both of these things. For while exercising the office of bishop in the Church, when he either drew his brothers back from deceptive arguments or recalled them from public disputes, he excluded from the Lord’s flock a most ferocious lion and a most cunning wolf. And when he defended those oppressed by royal power or harassed by whatever cruelty of rulers from tyrannical persecution with the sword of God’s word and the shield of faith, he truly, like an excellent commander, led his soldiers safely back to camp.

Therefore, if you desire to know what weapons this commander of ours used in his daily engagements, understand that they were not forged weapons but wholly spiritual ones. He was not weighed down with iron; rather, he was girded with faith, hope, and charity. He held David’s sling with its stone, struck the terrible Philistine in the forehead, and rescued all Israel from danger of death. Moreover, do not suppose that he was ever accustomed to lay aside such weapons: he was adorned in peace with the same weapons with which he stood armed in war. He was always humble, always gentle and mild, patient in adversity, modest in prosperity.

5. He was also resplendent in chastity, vigorous in abstinence, sober in vigils, and most steadfast in prayer. In judgment he pleaded impartially, not personally; in compassion he pitied humanely, not possessively. He was not covetous of what belonged to others, but a most generous distributor of what was his own. He pursued vice sharply in a person, but embraced the person familiarly.

His speech was sweet as honey; his preaching exceedingly pleasing; his table full of spiritual dishes; his companionship angelic. He rejected all evils as deadly poisons; he loved all good things as the perfumes of paradise. Finally, if you wish to make something like an epilogue: he was wholly perfect, and wholly full of God.

These, brothers, were the weapons of our most blessed patron Switbert in adversity and prosperity. With them he fought in every contest, and always and everywhere he conquered. For his struggle was not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

6. Let us therefore give thanks to almighty God on the feast day of this most holy bishop, praying and beseeching together that, just as we proclaim his glorious life on earth, so we may be worthy to enjoy his patronage in heaven. Amen.

## SERMON OF RADBOD ON THE LIFE OF SAINT AMELBERGA, VIRGIN OF CHRIST

*(From the Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, 10 July, p. 88.)*

[Col. 0549]

[Col. 0549D] 1. Whenever, beloved brothers, we commemorate the saints of God for the praise and glory of his name, so often do we rise from the tombs of our sins. For then our faith in some manner comes back to life, and our voice is renewed with revived sweetness through the service of our lips; and thus there is fulfilled in us what the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man” (Ephesians 4:23). For what else is it to die an evil death, to lie in a tomb and stink there, than to be polluted by the filth of sins? And what else is it to rise from this tomb than to return through confession and repentance to life, which is Christ?

We certainly have many examples of this kind of death in Scripture. It is accustomed to call those dead who are never willing to repent of their sins, as in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke 9:60). For those who buried the bodies were not themselves physically dead; rather, since they were wicked and therefore dead, they buried those whom bodily death had taken away from life. Therefore let us also beware of the harms of this death; indeed, let us hasten by the grace of Christ to rise quickly from the tombs of vices, so that we may be worthy to live with him in eternal blessedness.

[Note: What follows, up to the words “But behold, there presents itself” in the next numbered section, was omitted in Mabillon’s edition [Col. 0550D], replaced by dots as though it did not pertain to the matter.]

2. Therefore let us praise the Lord our God in his saints, and in turn let us praise and honor those same saints in him, since to serve God and his saints truly means to live, and wisely to persevere in this at all times means to avoid the snares of sins.

But behold, today an especially suitable occasion for this matter presents itself to us, on which we recall in an annual festival the memorable life of the extraordinary virgin Amalberga. In this pilgrimage she was most pleasing to God and to human beings, both through the splendor of a twofold beauty and through the merit of virginal chastity. Though she was born of the highest lineage and, because of her extraordinary bodily beauty, was loved by everyone, she chose to adorn herself with the jewels of virtues rather than with costly garments. She resolved to display herself as lowly and contemptible to human eyes, so that she might appear precious and most honorable in the divine sight.

She did not use gold or pearls, because she knew that Christ her bridegroom had not used such things on earth. She did not love purple or fine linen, because she knew that many were plunged into the abyss on account of such things. She did not delight in the murmurs of popular crowds, because she knew that a secluded place was suitable for [or: friendly to] grief.

[Col. 0551C] 3. Having rejected these things, she acted in a very different manner. In place of the relatives and friends of the world, she loved Christ’s poor; in place of gold and pearls, she adorned herself with maxims of spiritual teaching; in place of linen and purple garments, she used ashes and sackcloth. In place of the crowds of the people, which she wholly rejected, she continually remained in the watchings of the Lord’s temples, praying and keeping vigil around the sacred altars.

But how and in what order she reached such a height of heavenly discipline must not be passed over in silence, both for the sake of good example and for the worthy proclamation of her merits. This most chaste maiden lived on the inheritance of her fathers in the days of the Frankish rulers whom, from Charlemagne onward, we may call Carolingians. Because of his many victories and his zeal for undertakings in the Christian religion, he alone among the others earned the name by which he was rightly called “great” and “excellent.”

4. In their days, as has been said, the holy and God-pleasing virgin Amelberga, her parents already dead, lived with her only brother in the possession that had come to her through the succession of her ancestors—a very extensive estate beside the river Scheldt. She served God day and night with fasts and prayers, and gave exceedingly many and generous alms with the greatest cheerfulness, always remembering the apostolic saying: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Since she was extraordinarily beautiful, surpassing all the others in her appearance, she almost suffered the loss of her chastity because of the privilege of her most honorable body. For when her reputation reached the king of the province, Charles—

[Note: Here the name Charles is clearly expressed, whereas it was entirely absent from the manuscript used by Mabillon. Yet, as we said above, the passage may refer no less to Charles Martel than to Charlemagne, since the former as much as the latter belonged to the line of the Carolingians, who derive their origin from Blessed Pippin. Nor is there any difficulty in his being called “king of the province,” since Charles Martel is also called king elsewhere. Henricius renders the name as Charlemagne in his Flemish translation, but I do not remember finding that name in any Latin manuscript.]

—when, namely, this had happened, he was immediately captivated by love for her and began unceasingly to negotiate marriage with her through intermediaries. But after he realized that his desire was being utterly rejected by the blessed virgin, who had vowed herself to a better bridegroom, namely Christ, he secretly attempted by stratagems and certain acts of violence what he had been unable to accomplish by flattery and royal power. But she opposed all these things with the shields of prayer and the swords of heavenly armor.

5. One day, while the most blessed girl was sitting alone within the household walls and singing psalms as usual, a household servant suddenly burst in through the rear entrance, crying out and announcing that the king and his attendants were at the door. Then she, forgetting nothing of herself, entered at a swift pace into the oratory attached to the house. There she immediately prostrated herself in prayer with groans and tears, pleading in a mournful voice that the Lord deliver her from the impending danger.

Then the king, excessively presumptuous, entered the oratory after her and began to flatter her with many blandishments and promise her temporal honors, in order to make her yield, at least to his arguments. But she, unwilling in any way to abandon the bridegroom whom she had chosen, lay motionless, fixed to the ground as though held fast by some roots.

When the king had used every form of flattery—empty talk—and saw that he was accomplishing nothing, he turned royal authority into the fiercest tyranny. Seizing her hand, he tried violently to drag her outside. But when even this produced no result, he finally wrenched the girl’s arm violently and twisted it with all his strength. Having broken the bone of her virginal shoulder, he departed as though he had taken his revenge.

6. Then she, being tender and delicate, wept for a while before the Lord because of the most severe pain of her wound. But she prayed until her bridegroom Christ came to her and restored her to complete health. From that day onward she suffered no secular lover, but remained freely in love with her bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ.

O happy exchange! O exceedingly prudent choice, in which the king of earth is despised for the Creator of heaven and earth; in which God is loved instead of a human being; in which heavenly riches are sought in place of this clay!

O most blessed virgin, if the exaltation of your lineage harmed you greatly, how much more did your voluntary humility and the mortification of your flesh for God benefit you! If the splendor of your beauty encountered danger, contempt for royal majesty crowned you with everlasting glory. If suffering saddened you for an hour, from it you received the fellowship of martyrs and eternal rest.

Behold, now you enjoy all the things you desired in this life, because the King of kings and Lord of lords desired your beauty, and you, O most august queen, stand at his right hand, clothed in a golden garment adorned with varied ornament.

[Note: Mabillon’s edition ends here, suppressing the following two sections, perhaps because they seemed to contribute nothing to the history [Col. 0554B]. We thought that nothing should be removed.]

7. Now, therefore, faith, hope, and charity shine in you; humility reigns; patience triumphs; virginity gleams; chastity glitters; prudence discerns; temperance governs; fortitude prevails; justice judges. And, to make an epilogue, the army of all virtues is contained in you and proceeds from you.

Therefore, in eternal blessedness you not only see ineffable blessings with your most blessed eyes and hold them with your happiest hands, but your remaining senses also enjoy the same happiness. With blessed ears you hear the heavenly organ; with joyful mouth you sing the new song; with venerable nostrils you smell everlasting delights.

Thus nothing further will bring you anxiety or cause you distress. You possess joy without sadness, delight without weariness, security without fear, peace without disagreement, sweetness without bitterness, satisfaction without exhaustion. Light shines for you without darkness; purity gleams without defilement. You possess complete rest; you possess complete life. You suffer neither weariness nor submission to death.

8. What, then, is better? What more delightful? Earthly riches are taken away either by the wheel of fortune or by the condition of mortality; heavenly treasures, however, are made supremely desirable by their very perpetuity.

You, O most blessed virgin, now truly share these treasures with the angels because of your celibate life; with the apostles because of your catholic faith; with the martyrs because of your constancy in suffering; with the confessors because of your holy innocence; with the virgins because of the special chastity of body and soul. Now, returning to your homeland beyond the threshold, you share them by hereditary right and glory in your bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Through him we pray and humbly beseech you not to cease interceding for us with him—the one who strengthened you in this mortal life so that you might overcome an earthly king by the glory of chastity and surpass the devil, prince of hell, by outstanding holiness—with the help of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is glorified as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY OF SAINT RADBOD ON SAINT LEBWINUS

*(From Surius, Supplement to the Lives of the Saints, 12 November.)*

[Col. 0553]

[Col. 0553B] It often happens, dearest brothers, that during a meal a fictional tale is pleasing to those dining, and that the mind, weighed down with bodily food, is pursued by some hunger for fables. While the mind, forgetful of itself, temporarily rejects spiritual nourishment because the body is full, it desires instead images of vanities with which to delight the ears of the flesh, rather than the sweetness of heavenly teaching by which it might restore the nauseated soul with true and perpetual sweetness.

But we rejoice that the opposite is happening to us in the present reading. The more solemnly we receive it through the ears of the flesh, the more eagerly we consume it within him; and we do not doubt that the very thing we take in will create within us, after the venerable hunger, the wealth of satisfaction, and after happy satisfaction, renewed hunger.

Therefore, so that it may shine forth more clearly what delicacy—as it is called—is promised to those hungry for spiritual things by this kind of narrative, let dishes now be set upon the heavenly table more delightful than all the delicacies of this age. As we take from them the sweetest banquets of eternal life, let us return thanks to God, the author of such joyful refreshment, who each year mercifully gladdens us through participation in the sweetest feast, when, at the annual feast of his birth, he presents to us the memory of the most blessed Lebwinus like bread of angels brought forth from the basket of his own mercy.

As we devoutly feed upon this, we hunger healthfully, we are abundantly nourished, and we rejoice cheerfully. To these things are subsequently added a most beautiful disposition of mind, unconquered strength, continual salvation, contempt of the world, desire for heavenly things, and longing for the future. Therefore we ought to consider, brothers, how great are the delights being offered, so that we do not delay to receive them with eager hearts. Filled with them, let us fear no contrivances of the enemy and be terrified by no hailstorm of the tempests of the ages.

And so that by divine mercy we may be able to attain this, we believe that the example of this most holy man can suffice for us. Amid the adversities and prosperities of the world, he repelled the assault of raging fortune, as the tower of Zion and the gate of Jerusalem, defended by angelic protection, repel it; and, with the blows of the engines defeated, he deserved to persevere in the solidity of everlasting faith.

He ascended to such perfection through certain stages of natural goodness. Carried upward by them as though by ladders, he passed beyond earthly things and happily entered the heights of heaven. Finally, in his infancy he was dear to God and to human beings. Since he was teachable in understanding, gentle in spirit, poor in spirit but rich in merits, men of proven virtue eagerly strove to have him assume the religious habit. Once he had done so, he became so devoted to Christ and his Church that he surpassed his contemporaries in literary acuity, obeyed his elders with the greatest dutifulness, and, endowed with true humility, submitted to the commands of the perfect as though they had been given by God.

Moreover, during the years of boyhood he followed the venerable gray hair of the elders in uprightness of conduct and the simplicity of an innocent life, joining these to instruction in heavenly doctrine. During the period of adolescence, he did not weaken himself through the pleasures of a wanton spirit; rather, by the severity of frugality and the continual practice of labor, he subdued the rebellion of youth, chastising his body and bringing it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become disqualified.

He knew that there were many distinguished teachers of this philosophy in the holy Church. Among them he had heard that Willibrod, of blessed memory, and the bishops Boniface had labored especially in cultivating the Lord’s vineyard. Therefore he exercised his mind in works pleasing to God, so that those whom he had had as companions and fathers in Christian progress he might have as companions in eternal happiness.

Indeed, because the sacred memory of such great lights of Christ’s household has entered our account like a ray of venerable light, interrupting for a little while the style we had begun above, let us raise these men, who must be remembered with spiritual joy, to the honor of God with worthy praises, insofar as we can. Thus the glory of our Lebwinus will grow higher in proportion as his life is said to have been more commendable than that of those who preceded him. For he did not turn aside by any bypath from the path of those who, with the greatest efforts, followed the footsteps of such leaders.

Therefore, when the religious devotion of those men is expressed, this man is praised; when their pursuits are set forth beforehand, this man is depicted in his entirety; when their battles against the powers of the air are related, his triumph is clearly displayed. From such considerations it is easily gathered that the lives of those who follow are illumined by the memory of their predecessors, and that honor is increased in sons when the authority of fathers who lived gloriously supports them.

We therefore do not doubt that the men whom we have mentioned were exceedingly holy. One earned admission into the company of the Lamb by confession, the other by martyrdom; and now they possess an inheritance with Christ, since in this life they never allowed themselves to be separated from Christ.

Divine mercy has granted them to us as examples for imitation. Let the man whom the violent hand of an executioner deters from the sword, if he can, make himself equal to the great Willibrod, serving the Lord commendably in the quiet of divine peace. Let the man who considers himself comparable to the combatants not fear to follow Saint Boniface, who shed his blood for the love of Christ.

And if the cruelty of a killer is absent, let each person arm his own hand with the divine sword; let him spiritually become both his own persecutor and his own martyr, provided that he does not neglect to attain either the purity of the one in peace or the victor’s palm of the other in execution.

But after these matters have been recalled in brief, we must return to the history that, as we wrote shortly before, we had omitted. Yet it was not entirely omitted, because the affection of the mind, always clinging to this man, repeatedly arose among the other matters, as though touched by some sweetness, while the preceding material was being composed. though he treated the others with his fingers, he continually pondered Lebwinus in his heart.

Since he had chiefly resolved to write about him, even though he suddenly brought very precious men into the midst of the discussion, the attention of his thought could not be drawn away from this man. For the good things that can be said about him offer themselves freely; and if anyone presumed to set them all forth, he would need the flowers of Ciceronian or Plautine eloquence.

Blessed Lebwinus, therefore, living among the fierce and half-barbarous ways of human beings, retained the innocence of a lamb, remembering the Lord’s saying that he would send the apostles like lambs among wolves. Nor was the holy man lacking in the prudence of the serpent. If anyone attempted to injure his head, that is, Christ, he would without hesitation expose his entire body on Christ’s behalf.

Thus it came about that, through the power of the Most High, he joined the members to the divine head. He inserted himself between them as a kind of bond of charity, joining the lowest to the highest and striving to make human weakness equal to angelic dignity.

He was plainly a wise architect. Building a heavenly house, he placed the rock in its foundation, so that neither raging winds nor swelling storms, nor finally the assaults of every adversity’s engines, might harm the seal of the virtues. The rock was Christ.

Come, then: whoever desires to hear these things, does anything seem to you either healthier than that connection or more solid than this foundation, when what has been joined there is loosened by no dissolution, and what has been founded here is overturned by no storm?

If anyone has time or inclination to lend an ear to monstrous fables, thereby showing himself hostile to true accounts through such vanity, he may devote himself to the ravings of poets. They were so deranged by the deceptive imaginings of their fictions that they did not even recognize as false the things they sometimes asserted were utterly false.

As for us, the Church bears witness that we have lied about none of the things concerning God’s saint Lebwinus. The Church, enriched by his benefits, confesses through the frequent occurrence of healings how great his merit was before the Divinity.

The Church judges that what we say about him will be pleasing, since such a crowd of hearers stands before the reader that even those who seem to be standing in a safe place fear the pressure of the multitude. Scarcely anyone is found departing who does not give thanks to God because he has both heard and experienced the protection of Lebwinus.

Therefore, although we are still going to say only a little, we suppose that no one will be angry with us, especially since the discourse that follows declares that the Spirit of God built a temple in him and made it habitable for himself.

The same thing, I believe, will be sung among the morning praises, but it ought not to have been omitted from the reading, so that through the service of both voices he may receive recognition of how highly this man, beloved in Christ, is esteemed among his own people.

What precedes is as follows:

“The Holy Spirit,” as Scripture says, “dwells in the heart of the righteous man.” His soul, free from every iniquity, is his temple. In it no carnal victim is slaughtered, but spiritual sacrifices are offered; and there is performed there not merely a cleansing of the body, but also the true remission of sin and the perpetual abolition of death.

Blessed Lebwinus deserved to be called and to be such a temple, when, by the Lord’s provision, he became clean from the contagion of crimes, through him who lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0557]

## POEMS OF RADBOD

### I. EPIGRAM TO SAINT MARTIN

*[Sacred Batavia, p. 121.]*

Be gracious to me in speech, Martin, inhabitant of Olympus;  
Be gracious to me in speech, solace for the wretched.

Stretch out your hand, I beg you, lest the deep drag me away;  
The harbor is shipwrecked—stretch out your hand, I beg you.

The shadow of death threatens; now stand near me;  
A matter most grievous—the shadow of death threatens.

Rescue me from darkness and withdraw me from dreadful flames;  
Lover of the light, rescue me from darkness.

Restore me also to heaven, where the kingdom of the Lamb endures;  
You who are in heaven, restore me also to heaven.

### II. EPITAPH, OR ENCOMIUM ON CHRIST AS VIATICUM

*[Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. VII.]*

Hunger and thirst, O Christ God, and the desire to see you  
Now forbid me to partake of bodily food.

Grant me to feed upon you, to drink you as the draught of salvation;  
Be you alone the food of an unknown journey.

The man whom long hunger has consumed as he wanders through the world—  
Satisfy him with your face, O image of the Father.

### III. ALLEGORICAL POEM FOR SAINT SWIBERT

*[In the Bollandists, Martyrdoms, vol. I, p. 86.]*

A new light, Switbert, illumined the Franks and the English,  
So that he might give both peoples the clear light of faith.

He visited the Saxon fields, a memorable cultivator,  
To sow there the seed of Christ’s love.

Nor was the barren and empty field of the Frisians deprived of him;  
He made it fertile with the produce of a new shoot.

Now that the blind night of ancient evils had passed,  
The day of the true sun had begun to appear.

That sun floods the whole world with gentle rays,  
Consuming evils and glorifying good things.

O how great and of what kind is this sun that shines through twice twelve hours,  
The apostolic sun of the sacred people!

How intensely it poured its blazing colors into these men,  
Since it gave them their fiery hearts.

Hence it is that they so despised threatening swords,  
Whether the sweet laws of death were meant for them.

For a powerful fire boiled in their hearts from the altar,  
And had made their limbs equal to baked clay.

Their entire bodies grew rigid against the force of the wounds inflicted,  
And their struck skin rebounded toward the heavens,

Like a strong flint when tender wood is struck against it,  
Or like a diamond when it is lightly tested with a needle.

Kings stood astonished throughout their tents,  
Marveling that the head was harder than the helmet;

And the unarmed, placing their breasts before armored warriors,  
Feared nothing, certainly, from being pressed by the drawn sword.

When wars were prolonged through winding delays, someone said:  
“What is this hardness, or such great desire for cruel death?”

Hear, fierce tiger; hear, lion roaring with open jaws,  
What faith joined with reason says to these things:

The sun whose rays, as we have said, flood the whole world—  
Know that this is Christ, God.

Shining from the light of the Father, burning from the Father,  
Equally aflame, with equal power and measure.

He had kindled their minds perpetually with this fire,  
Burning away whatever was harmful and warming all that was serious.

As though scorched by it, they had become hard, like inflexible baked clay,  
And the enemies and weapons had become like men.

Therefore they could be bent neither by adversity  
Nor terrified by threats pouring from barbarous mouths.

Now they rejoice in rest, and from the lofty citadel of the powerful  
They tread down and bend proud necks beneath them.

Therefore this heat is good, accompanied as it is by  
Riches, virtue, victory, a crown, and heaven.

When Switbert came to our shores,  
He was inwardly aflame and suffused with fire on every side.

Therefore he feared neither dreadful Cyclopes, should they appear,  
Nor savage Harpies, nor any monsters.

As a distinguished standard-bearer, secure, he went wherever he pleased,  
Wearing a laurel wreath by the right of triumph.

O happy soldier, accustomed never to trust in Mars,  
But always to conquer Mars!

What songs shall we return to you for such great merits?  
What praises shall our pipe sing to you?

Does not your ear delight in sweetly measured music  
As it approaches you in the heavenly spheres,

Where the world plunges toward opposing poles  
And the stars roar along parallel courses,

And true music then resounds among the heavenly circles,  
Singing all things and accompanied by its own measures,

Rising so high that it resounds more than three times beyond the highest note,  
Or four times performs the double octave?

That sound passes beyond human senses  
Through its long interval and sings a noble chromatic scale to the blessed above.

Here, holy man, it composes a sweet-sounding melody for you,  
Which two and three sing, four, eight, and nine.

I add another thing that no one beneath the sun can earn,  
Unless perhaps he is your equal in goodness of skill.

Ten times a hundred choirs of angelic companies,  
Thousands to be harmonized with sacred symphonies—

You always hear with blessed ears in heaven  
Those who sing “Holy, Holy, Holy” without end.

You enjoy this hymn, happy bishop, happily;  
You sing it night and day with the others.
