Therefore your praise does not need our mouth,  
From which the dreadful crash of sins resounds.

For the savage mind is carried away by monstrous guilt—  
Alas!—and becomes entangled in the infernal abyss.

Therefore a hoarse voice babbles dreadful cries,  
And with a roar laments its fate in heavy sorrow.

But you, who sing to Christ with symbolic melody  
And surpass all instruments by such modes,

We ask with humbled minds and contrite heart:  
Bend down; in gentleness attend to our humble prayer,

So that, since the integrity of your life has raised you so high,  
You may deserve to hear angelic tones;

And, holy one, make these men, cleansed of the filth of crime,  
Enter fittingly into the melody of praise that belongs to you. Amen.

### IV. ECLOGUE FOR SAINT LEBWINUS

*[From Surius, Lives of the Saints, vol. VI, p. 1070.]*

The renowned Lebwinus, coming from the shores of England,  
With the sacred oars of virtues and Christ as his rower,

Calmed the savage currents of the stormy Rhine,  
Whose mouths were swollen by the heavy force of the wind,

After they had often been stirred by fierce north winds;  
And thus those waters had been impassable to the divine ship.

But after the saint had breathed across the raging waves,  
He obtained once for all from heaven the south wind’s release.

The harsh north wind fell, and soon the peaceful Rhine  
Received the vessels of peace upon a safe sea.

When these had reached the harbor with favorable success,  
Their anchor was fixed in the soil of the ancient city,

And secured by the placement of a stone, lest the dreadful force of a whirlpool  
Should again shake the loosened ships.

Then the land marveled at the distinguished cultivator  
Condemning its harvests with heavenly fire

And burning with divine flames what had been badly born from the soil.

He apportioned these fields by allegorical methods:  
Some he assigned to the furrows of the sincere plow;

Some he cultivated by planting trees of faith,  
Which might illuminate their shoots for the neighboring heaven.

One could see barren grasses shining with flowers,  
And a fertile grove nourishing the fruits of salvation.

Everything useful gave off its fragrance through the whole land,  
After the harvest had clung to the blessed fields through the holy man.

Our Lebwinus accomplished these things figuratively, my friend,  
If you properly consider what the spirit signifies in these poems.

He planted vines when he had built up many people  
With the words of the nourishing book, when he scattered mystical teachings.

He set down a wheat harvest when he made hearts pure  
And joined a chaste company to God.

Moreover, he strove to plant young trees,  
When he established the oaks of faith, when he caused the olive of peace

To grow, and when he made everlasting fruits flourish.

Therefore, with the highest right, we treat him with love;  
With the highest right, reverent honor is offered to him,

Who was a nourisher of goodness and an excellent defender of truth,  
A conqueror of errors, a trampler of greedy vice,

An altar of chastity, and also a prudent dwelling  
For a frugal virgin;

A tower of virtues, and an olive of peace or light.

Finally, he was the guardian, with hope of eternal life, of that virtue  
Which all poems revere,

Which generously strips itself of earthly gold,  
Which is akin to God and desires to die for its brothers.

Therefore, prudent reader, look to yourself, I beg you,  
And with me do not delay to offer sacred vows

To the Lord’s holy man, because everyone loves him  
Who is beloved by Christ.

For he himself loves Christ,  
And Christ loves him; a burning love blazes on both sides.

But more is on Christ’s side and less on his,  
Because everything a mortal does is surpassed by what is divine and perishable.

We also, whom Lebwinus will always have as servants,  
Because he always loves us, let us always love him devoutly.

Let us sing of Christ’s friend in sweet melodies,  
And let his name be sung in the Latin tongue,

As it sounds, separate from the whole world, in British speech.

For there they called the little child’s rattle  
“Liafuvim,” which later baptism approved as sacred,

And determined it to be a sweet and memorable name for God.

For if “Liafuvim,” which the cradle pronounced, is translated,  
It will mean “dear friend”; but a word must be supplied,

Either “of whom” or “to whom.” What better fits here  
Than if, according to the meter, you understand “to Christ” or “of Christ”?

If you join these two, you complete the saint’s name.

And you please in both respects, when Roman and English hearers  
Listen rejoicing, praising the language that teaches them,

Which in its native form praises the armed, and in translation praises the unarmed.

But now distaste warns the poem to restrain itself,  
Lest I injure ears trained by the Muses with rustic verses.

This easily happens when I chatter with my bits of straw,  
Which bleat in the manner of an Arcadian flock,

And scarcely anyone cares to wait for the end of a song  
That seems worthy of not even a small coin at its beginning.

But what matters is what each person sings. We, thinking that we have changed  
Ugly idleness for something better,

Have drawn woodland seaweed from a place destitute of fragrant amomum and palms.

Look upon this, Lebwinus, holy and memorable priest.

I beg you, remembering Christ, who made no use of mighty things, but rather preferred the small coins of the pale widow,  
To receive it graciously,

And by your prayers release my bonds,  
So that after the inns of the flesh

You may make me enjoy true freedom  
With the sacred assemblies of the Lamb.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 920: SALOMON, BISHOP OF CONSTANCE

[Col. 0561]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Canisius, Thesaurus of Monuments, vol. II, part II.)*
[Col. 0561A] Salomon, bishop of Constance, was born of illustrious lineage. He was entrusted by his parents, monks of St Gall, to Grimald, then abbot, and from his earliest years devoted himself to study. Since, under his teacher Iso, he far surpassed his fellow students in progress in learning, the monks—notker and the others—were moved by envy and, unable to bear his being preferred to themselves, pursued him with the utmost hatred. When he wished to enter the monastery of St Gall by night and by day without a cowl, his rivals, “exposing the holy fraud,” attempted to prevent his entrance on the grounds that it was improper for anyone to enter the inner parts of the monastery, especially at night, without monastic dress. Salomon requested permission to put on the monastic cloak while entering the enclosure and to remove it when leaving. The monks, always hostile to him, refused, reproaching him for clothing a wolf in sheep’s fleece.

Embracing what was plainly a divine judgment, the abbot granted his request, so that, if Salomon should one day be made abbot of St Gall, they would be subject not to a canon but to a monk and brother—for at that time monasteries were accustomed to be governed by canons. Thus Grimald, and likewise Hartmut, were abbots of St Gall, although they were canons. So it is read in the *Life of Wirobadus*: after Salomon, the brothers feared that they might be handed over to an outsider, that is, to be governed by secular abbots, as Salomon had been.

Although the hatred of his rivals Notker, Ruotpert, and Tutilo burned against him, he was nevertheless chosen archchaplain of Louis the Pious. Later, while he enjoyed the emperor’s favor, he was appointed provost of the canons at Elwangen and Kempten. When Bernard resigned the abbacy of St Gall, Salomon succeeded him, urged on by Hatto of Mainz, whose praises he inserted into his poems. He had governed the monastery for scarcely eighteen months when he was elevated to the episcopal see of Constance in the year 893.

As bishop he nevertheless governed twelve abbeys, according to the custom then prevailing; Hatto, prelate of Mainz, likewise rejoiced in an equal number of abbeys. Salomon attended and signed the Council of Tribur in 895. He then went to Rome, and from there, it is said, in 919 he transferred the martyr Pelagius, bishop of Constance, in a sarcophagus decorated with gold and jewels.

He published certain poems addressed to his friend Dado. After reading these little verses, there can be no doubt that they are his:

> Distinguished bishop, Dado, receive these greetings of yours,
>
> Written by Salomon in sorrow.

The cause of his sorrow was the untimely death of a brother whom he had loved above all:

> Here was a staff for the weary; here was medicine for the sick:
>
> While he flourished here, nothing was sorrowful for me.

This was the third abbot of St Gall of that name, as is proved by verses perhaps written by Tutilo himself [Col. 0562B] in his praise, on account of the very great gifts he bestowed upon the people of St Gall:

> This third Salomon of the holy place gives gifts to Mary;
>
> This third blessed Salomon gives offerings to Gallus.

He died in the year 919. He was regarded as “a fortunate man, prudent in counsel, eloquent, and exceedingly generous.” (*Life of Notker*, ch. 15.)

[Col. 0561]

# VERSES OF SALOMON, BISHOP OF CONSTANCE, TO DADO, BISHOP

*(In Canisius, as above.)*

## The prologue of the following work begins.

[Col. 0561B]

Simple Triune God, Father, Son, gracious Spirit,

[Col. 0561C] whom the rule of the Trinity shows to be three yet simple, and simple yet three,

and whose order of faith demands that we believe so;

in whom the Persons are tripled, the substance made one,

[Col. 0562B] give devotion to my heart and instruct my tongue with words;

grant cymbals to my lips, so that they may speak rightly;

[Col. 0562C] make me desire what is good and justly fulfill what I desire;

imbue my heart with faith, grant hope, bestow love.

Whoever has received these three from you possesses nothing here that is not upright.

[Col. 0563A] But what the catalogue of these places last,

the Apostle testifies to be greater than the others (1 Corinthians 13);

for without it no one will share

the banquet which the king lavishly prepared for his son (Luke 4);

and by it the offenses of manifold sin are covered (1 Peter 4).

Without it, whether a giver of wealth or one whom suffering renders distinguished,

a person will be cheated of the reward and go without it (1 Corinthians 13).

Christ’s saying agrees with this,

by which, when the scribe first presented the teaching of the commandment,

he said: “If you wish to know the weight of the great commandment,

love the Lord with your whole devotion,

and love him with all your strength and with your entire soul.

Love your neighbor, taking care of him as of yourself” (Matthew 22).

This commandment is recognized as equal to the former.

On these commandments depend the Law and the Prophets.

[Col. 0563B] Behold, by God’s reasoning there is nothing equal to love,

and devout love possesses all the virtues.

What more? The possessor of love possesses every good.

There is no place for merit if love is absent from the heart.

It is now fitting to say what this prologue signifies,

which will now be closed, since more remains to be said.

# VERSES OF BISHOP SALOMON

Dado, renowned Father, mirror, way, light, and orbit,

discerning bishop, venerable vicar of Christ,

sailor, helmsman, nourishment and shepherd of peoples,

who remain for me the cause and occasion of this writing;

through whom the work began, and led by whose sweetness

I marked the forms and threefold names of virtues;

whose love indeed nourishes the love of the preface;

[Col. 0563C] touching on the two too briefly, I discoursed at greater length on love.

Nor was I content to repeat this name only once;

I was pleased to bind it more frequently into the chain of my verses,

so that what suits mortals and joins them to the Thunderer

might unite us to one another in a sincere bond.

Join your heart to mine, holy priest, and your mind as well.

May you yourself wish what I desire, I beg; receive my prayers.

If not yet in body, let us come together in spirit.

Although, if it should happen, if the hour and opportunity should . . . .

and if your face from me . . . the clouds . . . .

I believe—and my faith is not vain—that when we contemplate one another with a companionable face,

when we speak mutual words,

much of the fever that inwardly clouds the heart

is driven away, and dawn rises again in the mind,

as though this parenthesis had suddenly intruded at the beginning.

[Col. 0563D] Believe me: . . . . . . . this was not done through negligence,

but the cause of your separation, brother, has divided the sentence.

For I retrace my steps; what I began to say, I shall say.

If the Almighty should ever summon us together,

what I have often desired I now desire, and certainly shall desire:

it would have been sweeter than all talents of silver and gold,

than purple silk, gems, scarlet, and ivory,

that you might relieve the one whose cause of grief is manifold.

And I, instructed by you, might clearly learn from you

the names of virtues that I have fashioned in little letters:

how great faith can tear mountains apart

and cast them into the middle of the sea and into the depths of the ocean;

what the divine will is, and what the love of a brother means;

with what hope, suspended between heaven and earth, I may always hope for heavenly things;

with what patience amid the accidents of the world I may be strengthened;

[Col. 0564A] what balance may support me if prosperity should perhaps arrive.

Whoever sees his fellow citizen’s house burning

should himself believe that his own can likewise be burned.

It is necessary—indeed, I say, it is necessary—to weigh the matter carefully:

if the painted house of the Lord took its beginning,

the letter Tau (Ezekiel 9) impressing upon us the signs of salvation,

let there also be upon our forehead what may, alas, withdraw us from the enemy.

The line encircles him and passes through the middle of the city,

Jerusalem, marking the one who groans or grieves.

Whoever groans and grieves for the Lord remains marked by him.

Thus the Savior himself, seated on the mountain, had said:

“Blessed are those who now mourn, because the joys

that quickly succeed grief will follow afterward, eternal” (Matthew 5).

If it is believed that laughter must be purchased with tears,

then we have been granted ample opportunity for weeping.

[Col. 0564B] From every side harsh things creep sufficiently upon us.

There is neither a single face of death nor isolated losses,

but, as the Wise Man, observing what follows upon what follows,

confesses that he must fight the world against the senseless (Wisdom 5),

Doctor Gregory began with these words:

“First the hearts of human beings are troubled; afterward, the elements.”

Rightly, therefore, it remains that all things together should strike us,

things which have been wickedly compelled to serve our vices.

Rightly, on the Lord’s behalf, the corrupted world fights,

since human beings first injured it by sinning

and, in vengeance, it itself battles against them.

Heaven, water, earth, and the rest of creation,

departing from their proper order, are violated in their law;

they fight on behalf of the Lord, who scourges us in this way.

Does not a pagan nation,

[Col. 0564C] destroying the mortal things that the world produced, overcome us because of our sins?

Behold, we who were thought to be God’s friends

are handed over as prey to enemies:

the savage beast devours Joseph;

the Philistines slaughter Israel;

a foreign people massacres Jacob;

the accursed Canaanite band triumphs over and defeats the freeborn;

the servile faction cuts down those who were once free.

The ancient Law rejects bringing the price of a dog into the temple (Deuteronomy 23);

now the dog himself, most filthy, enters the house of Christ.

He gives the people over to slaughter, possessions to the crowd, the sanctuary to flames;

the impious hand tears apart the Lord’s sacred table;

a polluted touch handles the holy pledges;

and drives away the flock of the Church, leading it abroad into captivity.

He does not pity the father; there is no compassion for the mother.

Savage violence pierces the son before his parents’ eyes.

Nor does the mother’s lament for the funeral ransom her daughter.

[Col. 0564D] Younger and old, suckling child and girl,

roll about in one another’s slaughter.

The Italian cities, stripped of their citizens, press upon us;

the fields, emptied of their cultivators, lie desolate;

the plains of the slain gleam white with dried bones.

Now, I think, there are not as many living as have been killed by death.

Let us speak words appropriate to that poet’s prophecy (Virgil, *Aeneid* 2):

> It would indeed have been better for the Latins to have decided
>
> the supreme matter beforehand, if they wished,
>
> rather than at such a time to summon a council,
>
> when the enemy was besieging the walls.
>
> Behold where discord has brought the wretched citizens!
>
> Often this evil would have been theirs, if their minds had not been perverse;
>
> the peoples’ internal battles could speak for themselves.

For they say that pigs, accustomed to biting one another,

call forth the teeth of wolves to bite them.

[Col. 0565A] Now the renowned earth scarcely offers pasture to the flocks,

although formerly the poor were accustomed to revel in its rich breast,

while the state stood sound and undisturbed.

We know that Paul, the chosen vessel of Christ, wrote:

“Whether it pleases you to devour one another or to bite one another in turn,

beware lest you consume one another” (Galatians 5).

Look then at the body with bodily sight, and at the mind with the eyes of the mind.

The apostolic utterance of the Laurentine shines amid ruins:

> First raging among themselves in civil strife,
>
> they are handed over to barbarian fury to pay the penalty for their offenses.

Every kingdom divided against itself by schism

is destroyed, and house falls upon house (Matthew 12).

Heaven and earth pass away, but these firm words endure.

Tell me, brother; tell me, bishop; tell me, holy priest:

[Col. 0565B] if a kingdom cannot stand when its parts disagree,

what dangers must we fear when we are divided?

The Psalmist noted that it is good for brothers to dwell together in unity (Psalm 132).

But to you, Sulpitius—may no Gaul hear this—I say:

few among us are those whose minds tend toward unity.

All disagree: prelate, count, and troops;

fellow citizens and fellow tribesmen fight among themselves.

The urban crowd rages, and the towns plot war.

What? Does discord not sting even relatives?

A brother challenges his brother to battle;

one brother roars to engage another,

and the ignoble crowd rages in its hearts.

All mortal things fight with law-breaking blows.

Those who should have been defenders of their homeland and people

make nothing more right for others than for themselves;

to others they become the occasion of strife.

[Col. 0565C] For the descendants of those whose fathers sat amid seditions

sharpen and magnify their anger.

Since such is the division of a single people,

do you now believe that a kingdom so divided can stand?

We render eternal thanks to you, most merciful ruler, Christ,

and consecrate deserved honors to you,

because you did not will to destroy the world as it deserved.

Formerly you ought to have imposed punishment upon the guilty,

but, by bearing with us, you wish us to return to better things

and to repent of the sins each person has committed.

For we lived a long time—if anything among mortals can be called long—

and passed through an age wonderfully granted to us.

Has anything like this ever happened, or has anyone ever heard of it happening?

Does report whisper of anything similar?

That so many peoples, so many nations,

[Col. 0565D] through the passing of so many years and cycles,

[Col. 0566A] should have possessed periods of peace free from a king.

Israel was one tribe, which dark Canopus crushed,

while, with a foot dripping only milk and tender with honey,

it led a trophy from its enemy all around,

killing some and burdening others with taxes.

After it despised the covenant of the divine Law

and provoked God by the deeds of its hands,

it sometimes happened, when the Lord punished its guilt,

that, perhaps through magistrates and tribute,

a king was lacking and it had no leader.

There was no delay: those whom it had previously conquered and subjected

were victorious over it, and it itself served them under tribute.

Then Ammon, Midian, Moab, Amalek, and Philistia,

bold or strong through its guilt and crime,

cut down those who cut down others, and plundered those who plundered.

Moreover, the stock of Judah . . . . . of the right hand . . . . with a wound

[Col. 0566B] flashes forth from here: Judah, Benjamin pressing on bravely,

while, with its brothers cut down, the river of blood flows.

Do not wonder, Father, if we reproach one another with bitter disputes

and fights, if the world boils with unrest;

rather, wonder that all have not been utterly destroyed,

tribes and peoples alike slain in disastrous war,

when they have no one to say, “Do this,” or, “Stop.”

If royal authority had been placed over the troops,

the shifting order would not have flowed about so recklessly,

nor would the rebellious faction have built so much slaughter,

nor would those attempting the same evils and filling themselves with crimes

have been allowed to approach the rewards or throne of the good.

Why should I say more about these things? Wherever rulers are lacking,

discipline collapses; opposition to it rises,

and they say that honor is nothing when there is no fear.

Barbarism, sought at home and imposed by taxation

upon Christian peoples, when no king directs them,

takes the census beneath their roofs and exacts tribute in blood.

For a long time languor has deprived us of a ruler,

[Note: [Col. 0565D] I have now reached the point where I can state clearly what I suspected: these verses of Salomon, in which he laments the kingdom of the Germans’ orphaned condition, refer to Louis, son of Arnulf. Arnulf died in the year 900, “for whom the boy Louis was established in the kingdom,” says our Herman—and indeed he was seven years old, according to Marianus, more truly a shadow of a king than a king. For a kingdom of this kind differs in no respect from an interregnum; this is what the words “he deprived us of a ruler,” and so forth, mean.

Earlier he had said, in column 564, verse 32:

> Behold, we who were thought to be God’s friends
>
> are handed over as prey, and so forth.

He is designating the incursions of the Hungarians, which they carried out with the utmost cruelty in the years 901, 903, 904, and those that followed, as is reported by Regino, Sigebert, and others.

And I do not know whether the following words in the same place may not refer to the story of the Huns, whom most people have thought to be the same as the Hungarians:

> The ancient Law rejects bringing the price of a dog into the temple;
>
> now the dog himself, most filthy, enters the house of Christ, and so forth.

He explicitly laments the disasters of Italy in the following passage:

> The Italian cities, stripped of their citizens, press upon us.

For how incredibly the Hungarians raged there, see the *Annals of Fulda*, F, under the year 900.

At the same time he notes the civil wars of Lambert, Berengar, and the son of Louis of Boso:

> The peoples’ internal battles could speak for themselves, and so forth.

All these circumstances fit the age of Salomon, the third bishop of Constance of that name. CAN.]

still discharging the title of king while he is yet a child.

Neither is his age suited to battle nor fit for laws,

the one to whom God grants kingdoms and possession of the scepter.

But a tender body and strength too late for serious tasks

make him despised by his own people (Ecclesiasticus 10) and bold in the eyes of enemies.

How I fear it; how often I turn over in my mind . . . .

the eulogy of him who, alas, declared that domination by a king

would stand above the nation while the king was still too young—

may the supreme Salvation turn this away from that people,

the people reborn from the saving fountain of him

who is known to be King, Lord, and Priest,

[Col. 0566D] who has received neither beginning nor any end,

[Col. 0567A] whose kingdoms surpass chaos and whose laws surpass the days.

If it were not absurd or perhaps annoying to anyone,

I would like to linger over this fruitful speech,

and, as a new interpreter relieving grief,

bring forth for the reader, concerning myself, something I have nowhere read.

Everyone who believes in the Ancient . . . . . of Days

does not subject such devotion to a young king.

But foolish peoples who worship images,

when they establish for themselves an icon of some image,

submit themselves through empty figures to a young king.

May blessing come to us through the young king,

who thus newly establishes the King . . . . . . .

I have composed these things; I do not detract from sacred writings.

Let the account that the wise man records be authoritative;

the book sets before us an example,

the authentic writing presents it,

[Col. 0567B] showing that one need not grieve excessively over youthful age.

The vigorous king Josiah was eight years old (2 Kings 22)

when he first began to exercise his ancestral kingdom.

But, strengthened in understanding and made firm by age,

having acquired mature strength through full years,

he devoted himself with fervent zeal to serving the Thunderer.

He restored the temple and adorned it with ornaments,

ordered the worship dedicated to God,

admonished the people through the Law and urged them to mourn their guilt,

removed stumbling blocks and ordered the sacred groves to be cut down;

he followed the path of David and steadfastly adhered to the Lord.

Behold how well one who is a mere child succeeds when he takes up a kingdom!

Who, I ask, should now distrust a young king,

provided that the King of kings himself directs everything?

[Col. 0567C] The upright Samuel (1 Samuel 3), and Daniel the prophet (Daniel 13),

were perhaps boys of an even younger age,

yet they pronounced judgment upon elders

and administered justice to the aged.

Some words I placed out of fear, others as consolation,

so that hope might encourage the one whom fear troubles.

Such are the passions that the present page brings forth,

and the whirlwind that mingles them all with various misfortunes:

they dry out my bones and cast a shadow over the mind of one who grieves.

It often happens, when I stupidly deal with such things,

that, as Nonnus wrote—and our blessed priest,

Jerome, our holy and wise teacher,

sometimes my own name becomes forgotten [*oboltum*, for *oblitum*, “forgotten”],

and, with my mind poured outward, it abandons me within.

Then, after a long return to the threshold,

returning . . . . . as a guest of my own new teaching,

[Col. 0567D] what do you do? There is no bread, nor are cups available;

no fire burns there, nor is a bed spread for the sick woman.

She is hungry and thirsty, endures and is naked against the cold.

What can she do? Where can she turn? Who will spread a table for the needy woman?

She weeps, groans, cries, sobs, murmurs, and remains stuck.

While attempting everything, remorse itself comes to her aid,

addressing the healthy one with grief in this kind of exhortation:

“Let friends finally knock at the door in the middle of the night.

If he has gone to sleep, let a swift voice awaken him,

so that the weary traveler may be refreshed with three loaves” (Luke 11).

And, believe me, he does not refuse you,

provided only that earnest prayer asks for it.

Moreover, generous, he offers you water freely,

after drinking which the thirsty person will thirst no more (John 4).

Here you act so that you fear the cold only as much

[Col. 0568A] as a wolf fears the number of sheep, or rivers in spate fear their banks.

He does not ask for money, nor demand any price.

He who teaches giving freely offers what is requested without payment.

This sorrowful mind, weighing the counsels of her sister,

regards such a friend as sweeter than honey and the honeycomb,

and continues knocking at the doors and already seeking entrance,

opening her ears to enjoy his words.

“Come now, break the delays; it is a pleasure to continue,” he says.

But because she has not sufficiently trusted in her own resources,

behold, she openly declares herself needy of a guide,

and confesses that she cannot go anywhere by herself.

Therefore, bishop, support the pupil who does not know the way,

and, I beg, extend a guiding hand to the one who is slipping.

I speak with the Lord as witness, whom no one can deceive.

This is not the game of a painter, nor the manner of poets,

[Col. 0568B] whose law is said to belong solely to the art of deceiving with cosmetics.

One has the right to compose poetry by disguising falsehoods;

but what the words signify, the heart within cries out.

Whatever the hand writes, the mind holds inwardly.

With internal complaints I seek the Father’s support,

revealing how much presses upon me and making known how much assails me,

so that he may raise upright the one whom his own weight,

wearing him down, plunges to the bottom,

the one who stands firm and has abundant strength to stand (Romans 14).

The Apostle, a seeker of heaven, sounded forth with holy mouth:

“I declare concerning myself: truly, ignorant error

clouds the mind and often deceives the one who sees.

Am I not deceived while seeing? Do I not lose sight while looking?

In Paul’s words I speak: I do not clearly understand what I am doing;

unaware, I do what I perform; I do what I do not understand” (Romans 7).

[Col. 0568C] I am tossed about in the fragile world; now I consider useful what . . . (Philippians 1).

As though someone were seeking a seat, which shakes the exhausted world,

it compels me to join my sacred office to the peoples

and to put the care of the brothers before my own care.

Yet often this thought comes upon me and says:

“Leave the world, devote yourself to the Lord, pursue quiet;

learn to dwell with yourself; abandon hostile disputes.

For the world totters, and the deceitful globe slips away.

If you wish to support the world’s ruins,

perhaps its ruinous ruins will envelop you in their rapid collapse.

He strives in vain who carries his effort to the end only to lose it.

If you and the world cannot both be saved,

save at least yourself; for it is better to escape alone

than for two who have suffered the same dangers to perish together.”

[Col. 0568D] Come here, bishop, and intervene as judge in these matters.

This is the whole point of what I began to write long ago:

although I grieved over pontiffs, king, and peoples,

this concern of mine always gnaws at me more sharply.

For I consider myself sicker than any of them;

bearing more wounds, I seek more medicines.

The law that clings to the dwelling of my mind

warns me to pursue leisure and leave behind the world’s uproar.

Against it fights the other law that is fixed in my members (Romans 7).

Alas for me! How harshly this law is accustomed to triumph,

taking captive the wretched man bound by the law of sin.

O patron, be favorable to the weak law.

[Col. 0569A] Through you may the law that struggles, defeated by itself, prevail.

And make certain what is uncertain between the two,

so that the wise Susanna, taking counsel while in doubt,

may escape death, now freed through Daniel (Daniel 13).

You wish, can, and know how to help fellow servants.

The father of the household, setting out for a foreign land,

entrusted you with grain to distribute and did not order you to bury his treasures;

he himself bestowed them abundantly in two talents (Matthew 18).

Tell with what tears Abel’s funeral was mourned.

Divide, distribute, bring forth, give generously, minister

what has descended to you as a divine offering from the heavenly court.

This hero commands it; in giving what has been given, the generous man desires to give:

the more you give, the more you deserve to be given.

The ark becomes famous by giving and is emptied by refusing to give;

whoever diverts his streams to himself alone preserves them for himself.

[Col. 0569B] These words are spoken to exhort you, not to teach you,

for the Spirit has imbued you with theoretical knowledge.

The field, now thirsty, desires rains from you;

rain upon the parched countryside with the rain of your speech.

May you be the discipline of a father to me and the compassion of a mother.

. . . . . . . . . . . OR.

Be present as a faithful teacher to your disciple (*mathētēs*).

May the Almighty grant this, he who supports the axes of heaven

and sustains the heavy earth in the vast abyss.

May I use your equal virtue for a longer time,

and may my life consist in knowing that you live in health.

Pour out prayers to the Lord for me, my brother, I ask this,

and may your prayer be a support of life for the whole people.

While I enjoy this life and feed upon its living breath,

while my senses are sound, while my tongue . . . remain,

[Col. 0569C] I meditate on you always and frequently chew you over in speech.

With continual prayers I beg that you, joined to me,

may dwell in the palaces of light,

and that Jesus may be with you and with me joined to you.

Farewell.

At the end, closing this, I ask with this . . . seal,

that, by the bond of faith with which I know you bind me,

you bind our Hatto and your own with the same bond,

and that, as you wish me to be sound in heart toward you,

so may you be toward him—and even more, because you are worth more.

I ask that those whom you regard as faithful, and whom you have as friends,

may likewise be brought to our faith through you.

We, for our part, will treat you in the same manner,

turning all of ourselves toward you in concord,

while nevertheless observing the law of faith ourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0569D] The title is absent from the manuscript.]

# Poems of Bishop Salomon to Dado, Bishop

[Col. 0569D]

Distinguished bishop, Dado, receive these greetings of yours,

written by Salomon to you in sorrow.

As formerly you were a sharer in my joys,

so now, Father, be a sharer in my sorrow.

“To rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep” (Romans 12):

this is what the writing dictates, and the man of Tarsus commands.

When lamenting the general loss of times gone by,

I wrote certain things to you, beloved bishop.

I grieved that the world was being driven along on a slanting course;

I explained and unfolded various evils in confused order.

Seeking counsel from you, my dear friend, about my troubles,

I discussed one by one the things that had been a burden.

But now one misfortune among many besets me,

[Col. 0570A] and find myself weighed down by the burden of diverse things.

While my brother lived, whatever pressed upon me harshly,

I found lighter by confiding it to him.

He was my harbor; my mind turned back to him

when the sea tossed me and the open waters battered me.

Here was a staff for the weary; here was medicine for the sick.

While he flourished here, nothing was sorrowful for me.

So be it—let it now be past. But when he was present, he subdued it:

while I endured it, I endured nothing.

Who gives water to the head of one who has cause for grief,

to one who wishes to weep and shed many tears?

Tell with what tears Abel’s funeral was mourned,

when the first parents grieved to see him die.

What grief, Adam, or what lament do you utter, Eve,

when he who pleased you more was slain by his brother?

[Col. 0570B] I myself mourn my dead brother even more,

for you receive in his place the offspring of your offspring.

Seth, coming to you, wiped away all your tears (Genesis 4);

but once mine was lost, he did not return.

Jacob himself mourned (Genesis 37) because he thought Joseph had died,

although the father was renowned for his elevenfold stock.

But with what tears must I mourn the loss of my brother,

when I have no other Benjamin left?

Rachel, taught by Scripture (Jeremiah 31; Matthew 21), teach me to weep over the opposite,

you who, in your grief, are accustomed to reject those who console you.

I choose to receive no consolations according to your law,

but to continue the entire day in this wailing.

King David lamented because his handsome son died (2 Samuel 19);

the father weeps for the offspring who pursued him.

[Col. 0570C] He never did anything at all for me except what pleased me,

and although we were two, we remained one person.

What I wanted, he wanted; what I did not want, he himself rejected.

Where will a man like him be found for me?

If you mourned this son, who sought to seize the royal scepter,

although he had often been fierce toward your life,

with what lament and with what worthy mourning should I cry out for this man,

who plainly preferred everything he possessed to be mine?

He was willing to lay down his own life for me voluntarily,

giving himself over to death so that I might survive.

As it is read concerning the blessed living creatures (Ezekiel 1),

if they had eyes before and behind me,

not so many would suffice as I might wish to use for weeping,

even if there were a river of water within me.

The lamentation of the holy Jeremiah in his book

[Col. 0570D] touches me to the heart, as the prophet himself groans.

Behold, let it be permitted me to speak in words of lament,

as your distressed sophist, Christ, said.

“Most holy one, you have taken away from me all my mighty men” (Lamentations 1:15),

and you trample my chosen ones together with my dominion.

Therefore, weeping, I shall draw forth streams of tears,

because the one who had become my comforter is far away from me.

I am indeed the man who now fully sees

my affliction and my poverty.

Here I wish to set down, for my consolation, the verse

which he writes and which the Theologian himself adds:

“O Lord, your holy mercy is sufficiently great,

since we have not been consumed by the reaping scythe” (Revelation 14).

[Col. 0571A] But I shall speak in the voice of the excellent rhetorician Severus:

“I cannot help grieving that I am left to rule.”

The aforesaid writer used these same words

when commemorating the sacred death of Martin.

The disciples are said to have mourned Paul while he was alive (Acts 20),

when he departed from them and sought the sea.

Is one mourned more when separated by the whirlpool of death,

one who sought the sea and . . . did not return?

He who can recall you, Lazarus, weeps for you (John 11).

Does he not rightly grieve who cannot recall you?

The blessed crowd of the Messiah’s disciples

was sorrowful when he foretold that he was going away.

“Because I have said these things,” he says, “I know that you are sorrowful;

but my departure will greatly benefit you” (John 16).

If Jesus’ disciples were saddened in this way,

[Col. 0571B] although his ascent to higher things benefited them,

how is it believed that one whose dear brother has departed,

and who has suffered such a great loss, can keep these cheeks from tears?

Now console me, Father, I beg you, needy and sick,

as the gracious voice commands you to support the weary (Isaiah 50).

The misfortune of the southern climate has fallen to you by lot (1 Samuel 30);

you must feed the fugitive with your bread.

I flee to you; share food with the wretched man,

so that the needy one may not die of hunger.

A cause remains for me which . . . heals my heart from its whirlpool,

by which I shall be relieved from my brother’s funeral.

When I recall that . . . I become more composed,

because, when he departed, the bishops were present,

with whom, often discussing his departure,

he himself arranged the affairs of the one who was going away.

[Col. 0571C] As he came into the world, so he departed almost naked,

sending ahead whatever he possessed here.

And while his limbs were being cooked in the long furnace,

scarcely a thin skin remained clinging to the bone.

Then, laying aside his former mortal man,

the martyr restored to heaven what God had given from it.

I have said that this is a reason to soften the sorrowful lament

which his brother’s death compels me to bear.

Moreover, there is this certainly, which the Fathers established,

those whom the Lord joined together when he blessed them:

finally, moved to consider the dangers of the world,

they began more cautiously to take account of the fate they saw.

Then they decreed that the seventh day of the brother should be observed,

when all had completed the agape with prayer [Note: [Col. 0571D] Perhaps: “when they had completed the agape with prayers.”].

And when the thirtieth day came,

[Col. 0571D] they established that it too should be observed according to a similar rite.

Whenever the annual cycle recalls the same day,

they again perform this work of devotion with prayers.

Bishop, together with the others, remember the brother,

to whom, while he lived, you entrusted yourself, and he trusted in you.

With sincere heart we both loved you,

and we were uniquely united to you.

We, two brothers, ask you to help us both.

You come to my aid if you remember him.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] The title is absent from the manuscript.]

## Quatrain of Bishop Salomon, by which he sends Waldram’s poem to Dado, Bishop

Here I append for you, bishop, a writing to be read,

[Col. 0572A] a certain man sighing over and lamenting my losses [Note: [Col. 0571D] He means Waldram],

who, when a fresh wound brought grief to me,

first grieved with me and made a clamor together with the mourner.

Afterward, setting forth the duties of human life,

he urges me to endure what must be endured.

You too should act in this way; remain my equal in both matters.

After the weeping, I beg you, make me cheerful at last.

[Note: [Col. 0572D] This title belongs here; in the manuscript it was incorrectly attached to the first poem: “Verses of Waldram to Dado, Bishop, sent by Salomon.”]

## Verses of Waldram to Salomon, Bishop, which Salomon sends to Dado

Let the whole people mourn Rachel’s lament with me (Jeremiah 31),

and let Israel itself grieve as over Joseph (Genesis 37).

There was, on the field of Megiddo, a mourning like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon (Zechariah 12).

[Col. 0572B] Josiah departs (2 Chronicles 35); thus now it is fitting to weep.

It is appropriate for me to speak in the voice of someone

who had grief, anxiety, and sorrow within him (Ovid).

I who once completed poems in flourishing devotion

am compelled, alas, in tears to undertake mournful measures.

Behold, the wounded Muses dictate what must be written to me,

and they wet my face with true tears of elegy.

Who, I ask, does not mourn? Who restrains himself from lamentation,

when the one who increased joy is absent?

Who could remember that peaceful face

without pouring out tears and being drenched in sorrow?

Noble, freeborn, foremost, ordinary, poor—

the whole world mourns that he was taken away.

The true things written by the poet’s reed certainly remain,

[Col. 0572C] who, when he perceived the harshness of death, said:

> A harsh condition, and the hour’s irrevocable lot,
>
> which a sorrowful origin brought to the human race.

Because what follows this has been polished with elegant reasoning,

I wish to insert it here for you to read, Lord.

Behold, our parents generated this sorrowful crime for us;

from where it had first begun, the whole race rushes downward.

First, pitiable Abel fell, struck down by a wound,

and by a brotherly . . . . .

Afterward Seth also died, restored in Abel’s place in the same manner;

and although he returned, it was not without an end.

Why should I mention Noah, praised by the voice of the Thunderer,

whom a heavy ark carried, and now a heavy ark presses down?

So too Shem and Japheth, most righteous offspring,

and their holy descendants, ran the same course.

[Col. 0572D] What of the patriarch Abraham, or Isaac, or Jacob, all worthy men?

No one is released from the law of death.

Melchizedek too, the holy priest of the Lord by divine utterance,

and Job as well, or his children, departed in this way.

The lawgiver Moses himself lies dead, and Aaron the priest;

the friend worthy of God’s conversation dies.

His successor, the illustrious leader of the people, Jesus,

and the fathers whom you read of in the books, have perished.

What of Gideon, Samson, or any judge in succession?

No one escaped death under the Lord, the Judge.

The powerful Israelite, King and prophet David,

lies in the tomb with his Solomon.

[Col. 0573A] Isaiah, Daniel, blessed Samuel, and Jonah—

while alive beneath the sea, now he stands pressed beneath the earth.

Peter, the prince with the keys, and Paul, first in teaching—

though their souls were exalted, earth covers their bodies.

Of human seed no one is regarded as greater

than the powerful Baptist, John himself, who died.

Enoch and Elijah each still await this:

everyone born of a human being is destined to die.

The Creator himself, rejoicing, rose quickly from the shadows, Christ;

because he was born a human being, he was buried in the earth in the flesh.

Who, I ask, does not die, when Salvation itself tasted death,

since my Life wished to die in this way for me?

What then do we do here, since we cannot avoid it,

when we can be of no help in the matter?

We weep and groan, but we are unable to help;

there is mourning in our eyes, yet no fruit of assistance.

Our inward parts are tortured, our hearts torn by turmoil;

dear ones have died, and our eyes fall through weeping.

Behold, love calls, but the beloved is not recalled;

nor does he whom the sunken stone covers return to us.

Therefore we shall all go, to be settled in another region;

we shall go to our homeland, we whom foreign lands hold.

Do not, reverend Father, do not by chance . . . be . . . .

It is not fitting to mourn the one whom paradise possesses.

What the Almighty commands, we cannot resist;

perhaps to grieve at that man’s deeds is to act against God.

Behold, we are his creation, and our spirit is from him;

when he commands, we who are his work depart from here.

Receive the consolation (John 16) which you know the Creator promises:

“He who believes in me shall not die” (John 8), he says.

[Col. 0574A] He further promises besides that he will never refuse anyone what the two ask for, knowing that it is to be granted them.

“If two of you,” he says, “agree in their prayers” (Matthew 18) and ask for something, the Father himself will grant it.

If a few can obtain what they ask in prayer, with the Lord’s favor, what might a multitude not accomplish?

A troop of priests, an unarmed company of monks,

Nuns together with widows, a poor and needy phalanx,

Clergy with commoners, the lowly with the highest rich,

The lesser with the greater, the elder with the child?

With lamentations they commend to Jesus the soul itself

Of your brother Germanus, blessed Lord.

A distich of Solomon, with which he sends the following poem to Dado.

[Col. 0574B] Again, holy Father, your affection compels me

To write the skillful words of a learned-speaking man.

Verses of Waldrammus [Note: [Col. 0573C] I suspect that this is Valtrannus, who was bishop of Strasbourg and whom Regino records as having died in the year 905. Bruschius calls him Baldramus; but this conjecture must not be asserted, though neither should it be omitted. I know [Col. 0574C] how readily conjectures of this kind flatter us, and how gently they also deceive; I should like to affirm nothing except what is entirely certain. I have as yet discovered nothing about Dado. CAN.] to Solomon, which Solomon sent to Dado.

Be a man’s noble honor; patiently overcome your grief,

Or at least endure the burden that cannot be avoided.

Such will the people be as they see you to be,

And from your countenance the populace gathers its hopes.

Finally, when Job lost his seven children in one grievous blow,

He returned praises to God with his lips.

Twice-blessed was the devout mother of the Maccabees:

She bore seven sons joyfully in a single funeral.

David the Psalmist, when he lost his beloved son,

Soon placed him in the tomb and gave a festive banquet.

These things, written by hand and also carefully reviewed,

May perhaps lighten your grieving spirit, my lord.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1420. WALDRAMMUS, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG

[Col. 0573]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON WALDRAMMUS.

(Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 787.)

[Col. 0573D] “A man of magnificent holiness,” as Wymphelingus says, obtained from the emperor Arnulf—or, as he is called elsewhere, the duke of the Norici—the abbey of Neuwiller. He soon expelled its abbot Hartmann and appointed the monk Helmerius as his successor. In Helmerius’s favor there is preserved in the charter archive of this monastery a privilege of that same Arnulf, issued in the seventh year of his reign, that is, approximately in the year 894, in which our Waldrammus is mentioned. In the following year he sat in the council of Tribur, and ten years later he died, according to Regino’s Chronicle under the year 905, in these words:

“At that time Waltrammus, prelate of the Church of Strasbourg, and Luidhelmus, prelate of the Church of Toul, departed from this world; they were succeeded in the episcopal chairs by Otbertus in the city of Strasbourg and Drogo in Toul.”

In that same year, as Regino likewise writes, the king visited the city of Strasbourg and restored harmony between the bishop and the people, who were divided against one another. The Saxon chronicler, in Ekkehard, p. 238, says the same, except that he assigns these events to the year 906. [Col. 0576A] Moreover, in this year 906, Reverend Father Laguille records Waldrammus’s death on 13 April, and Wymphelingus on 12 April.

[Col. 0575]

POEMS OF WALDRAMMUS.

See above under SALOMO OF CONSTANCE. We have not wished to separate the poems of the two men because of the close connection between them.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 920. ODILO, MONK OF SAINT MEDARD OF SOISSONS.

[Col. 0575]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(In Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis.)

[Col. 0575B] Odilo, a monk of Saint Medard at Soissons in Gaul, of the Benedictine order, wrote around the year 930 to Ingrannus, dean of his monastery and later, in 932, bishop of Laon, concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Sebastian the martyr and Pope Gregory the Great to Saint Medard at Soissons, carried out in 926. Bollandus published this work without the author’s name in volume II of the January Acta Sanctorum, 20 January, pp. 278–295; Mabillon restored it to its author and enriched it with his preface in volume IV of the Benedictine centuries, p. 383.

However, Papebrochius argues in the Acta Sanctorum, vol. I, 2 June, pp. 206 ff., that the letter to the same Ingrannus concerning the arrival and reception of the bodies of the holy martyrs Tiburtius, Marcellinus, Peter, Marcellianus and Marcus, [Col. 0576B] Probus and Hyacinthus, Marius and Martha, Audifax and Abacuc, Abdon and Sennis, published by the same Mabillon on p. 411, is spurious and entirely untrustworthy.

Besides these writings listed by Fabricius, the Writers of the Literary History of Gaul mention a letter of his published by Father Martène to Hucbald, a monk of Saint-Amand. They also consider three sermons to be attributable to him, which we have read published without the author’s name in the Bibliotheca Floriacensis, vol. II, p. 136. See that History in the same place, vol. VI, p. 175.

[Col. 0575]

ODILO THE MONK’S BOOK ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE RELICS OF SAINT SEBASTIAN THE MARTYR AND POPE GREGORY TO THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MEDARD AT SOISSONS.

(Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. V.)

MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS.

[Col. 0575C] The author of the following little book, which John Bollandus published under the name of an Anonymous author, except for its preface, appears to be Odilo, a monk of Saint Medard, writing to Ingrannus, dean of the monastery, during the reign of Charles the Simple. For in the very old parchment codex of the venerable Claude Joly, canon and cantor of the Church of Paris—formerly a possession of the monastery of Saint Medard—the following inscription is prefixed to this little book:

“LETTER OF ODILO TO INGRANNUS.”

There is also another work by that same Odilo to Ingrannus concerning the translation of the holy martyrs Tiburtius, Marcellinus, [Col. 0576C] and others, which we shall present later.

The inscription of the Resbacensis codex must therefore be corrected: it attributes the following book to Rodoinus as author. The occasion for the error arose from the conclusion of the book, where Rodoinus is said to have left a written account of Sebastian’s miracles.

Ingrannus the dean was still living as the tenth century advanced, as is clear from Frodoard’s Chronicle under the year 932, where it is reported that “Ingrannus, dean of the monastery of Saint Medard, was ordained bishop at Laon.” It should be observed that at that time most monasteries whose abbots were secular were administered by monk-deans, who were sometimes also called pro-abbots and provosts.

2. The translation of Saint Sebastian presently under discussion was celebrated by serious and contemporary authors, especially Einhard in his Annals under the year 826, whose testimony Odilo cites in his preface; and Wandalbert in his Martyrology, both on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February and on the fifth day before the Ides of December, the day on which it took place, in these words:

We celebrate Sebastian, translated from the City on the fifth day (quinis; the reading is uncertain),

By whom the fields of Gaul rejoice as their own patron;

For him a mighty temple rises, together with an altar,

And lofty structures shine, matching the splendor of ancient times.

Ado, bishop of Vienne, writes in his Chronicle, and Baronius and others agree with him, that only part of Saint Sebastian’s relics was translated. Of these relics brought to Gaul, a portion was granted to our community at Fleury, as Adrevald testifies in his book On the Miracles of Saint Benedict, chapter 28: namely, two bones of the hip, preserved to this day. A portion of the sweat-cloth went to Meung-sur-Loire, as is shown in the following chapter, 41. Other portions remained with our community at Saint Medard until the year 1564, when raging Calvinists shamefully violated and trampled the sacred relics on 27 September. Certain pious people gathered them up, together with those of Saint Gregory and Saint Medard, and entrusted them for the time being to the nuns of Sainte-Catherine de Bourbon at Soissons. Later Charles de Roussy, bishop of Soissons, after hearing witnesses, approved them and sealed them in three caskets, as is recorded in the commentary of Alexander Salnove, monk and almoner of Saint Medard, preserved by Bollandus.

3. Odilo also states below, in chapter 15, that the body of Saint Gregory the pope was translated at the same time; Baronius thinks this must be understood as referring only to part of the body. Certainly Charles, surnamed the Bald, “when he was traveling to the city of Soissons in the year 842, was met by the monks of Saint Medard. They begged him to transfer the bodies of the saints Medard, Sebastian, Gregory, Tiburtius, Peter and Marcellinus, Marius, Martha, Audifax and Abacuc, Homesimus, Meresina and Leocadia, Marianus, Pelagius and Maurus, Florianus with his six brothers, Gildardus, Serenus, and the lord Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, to the basilica where they now rest and which was already largely built at that time. He granted their request, remained there, and, as they had asked, transferred the bodies of the blessed saints on his own shoulders with every mark of reverence. In addition, by an edict he added the village called Bernacha to the property of the same church.”

The same matter is confirmed by chapter 20 of book I of the Life of Goswin, abbot of Anchin. While Goswin was ill in the monastery of Saint Medard, “he seemed to see a man emerge from the place of the sanctuary beside the mausoleum believed to contain the bones of blessed Gregory”; through him Goswin was also healed. After this, Gregory “wished what had happened to be made known both to Abbot Geoffrey and to certain members of the cloister, so that, because of the miracle that had occurred and the confusion of the proud who said that Gregory was not in that place, they might be made more joyful through the exaltation of their church.” John of Salisbury also recalls Gregory’s resting in the church of Saint Medard in Letter 159. There he says that the archbishop of Sens, as I think, “having prepared to deliver judgment” against the persecutors of Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, “undertook a journey to the city of Soissons for the sake of prayer, in order to commend his struggle by prayers to the Blessed Virgin, whose memory is celebrated there, to blessed Drausius, to whom those preparing for battle flee, and to blessed Gregory, founder of the English Church, who rests in that same city.”

For the translation of Gregory carried out by Pope Gregory IV, Anastasius and John the Deacon should be read. For the translation of his head to the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens, one should read Clarius, Odorannus, and especially the Bollandist companions in their March volume, where they note [Col. 0578A] that the head of Saint Gregory the pope—whether the first or the second—is believed to be preserved in the church bearing his name at Constance on the Rhine and at Lisbon in Lusitania.

Concerning the other relics of saints translated to the monastery of Saint Medard in the ninth century, see below, after this book. Now, however, we must briefly discuss the origin of this monastery.

4. After Saint Medard died at Noyon on the Oise, in the manner common to human beings, and was buried at Soissons, Clothar began, around the year 560, first to build a cell or oratory of branches and then a basilica. His son Sigibert later completed and furnished it, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, testifies both in his book On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 95, and in book IV, chapter 19, of his History.

An anonymous tenth-century author describes the basilica’s site, eastward in view of the city of Soissons, in a little book On the Miracles of Saint Medard, in volume X of the Spicilegium:

“The countryside where these events took place belonged to the royal fisc and was called Croiacus [Crouy]. From ancient times it had been devoted to the profane worship of idols. Indeed, until the time of the Danes, a two-faced stone image of great breadth stood in the same place before the doors of the sacred building. After the land had been dug up and leveled, a noble mausoleum, worthy of receiving so great a guest, was constructed. The place was consecrated, where a most famous hive of Christ’s sheep throughout the whole world was destined to be established”—that is, a monastery of monks. That monks were first established there by Sigibert is demonstrated by the distinguished Adrian Valesius in chapter 6 of his Dissertation on Basilicas and in chapter 9 of the first part of his Defense.

Hence Paschasius Radbertus, speaking of the city of Soissons, which he more than once calls Vesona, says in book III of his Exposition of Psalm 44:

“To the east it now has the camp of monks, with its holy confessors and martyrs.”

Clothar and Sigibert were buried in this basilica. Pippin, the father of Charlemagne, is said to have been raised to the kingship by the Franks there, according to the short Chronicle of the monastery, which is found in volume II of the Spicilegium.

Because the basilica was too small to contain the crowds of people who flocked to it, Abbot Hilduin, also archchaplain of the sacred palace, with the assistance of Emperor Louis, rebuilt it on a larger scale. Later, around the year 886, King Sigefrid of the Northmen set it on fire, as is recorded in the first Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen in Duchesne. Nevertheless, Duke Henry, whom Emperor Charles had sent with the assistance of the Parisians, was killed by the Northmen and in the following year “was buried in the basilica of Saint Medard,” as Regino testifies in his Chronicle.

The anonymous author already cited writes as follows concerning this rebuilding and fire, in volume VIII of the Spicilegium:

“Let no one suppose that this is the basilica”—namely, the one built by Sigibert—“which, once begun by Emperor Clovis, was recently burned by the Marcomanni. Rather, that earlier basilica, built by King Sigibert, because of the crowds of people who gathered on account of every kind of outstanding virtue at the memorial of the distinguished martyr Sebastian, was utterly demolished by Rodoinus, then provost of the same monastery, by imperial command, with the ever-helpful cooperation of Hilduin of blessed memory, archchaplain and abbot of the aforementioned monastery, and was rebuilt on a grander scale in a more spacious and splendid form.”

Nithardus mentions this rebuilding in section 3. I have no information as to who restored the place after the Northmen’s destruction.

The church, renovated for a fourth time, “was dedicated in the year 1131 by Pope Innocent II on the Ides of October, in honor of the blessed Mary ever-virgin and of the holy apostles and martyrs, and in honor of blessed Medard, bishop and confessor.” After being shamefully profaned by Calvinists in the century just past, it was restored once more in our own century, in which the monastery continues happily as part of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

Distinguished deeds and notable events occurred there; many holy and devout men flourished there. All these matters cannot be included in these observations. For there, besides the events already mentioned, Louis the Emperor was deposed; Pippin, king of Aquitaine, was tonsured by order of Charles the Bald; Charles’s wife, Ermentrude, was crowned by the bishops; and a king named Rudolf was proclaimed, as Frodoard records in his Chronicle. Hincmar held a council there, at which sentence was passed against two monks who had carried Pippin away from the monastery. Pope Innocent II also held a synod there.

5. Archbishop Leidrad of Lyon withdrew there out of desire for a more perfect life, as did Marcus Scotus, a bishop of the ninth century. At that time the holy abbot Rudolf, later archbishop of Bourges, is also said to have governed the place. Hugh, thought to have been a son of Charlemagne, abbot of Novalesa, is added to their number.

Furthermore, the abbots Arnulf and Gerard lived in that monastery in the eleventh century, and Goswin was prior in the twelfth. Here we must make a few observations about Marcus Scotus, the bishop who lived in the ninth century.

6. “Marcus, a bishop of Scottish origin, in the time of Grimald, the canon and abbot, and of Harmutus, his quasi-abbot, visits Saint Gall, as his compatriot, on returning from Rome,” says Ekkehard the Younger in chapter 1. “His sister’s son Moengal accompanies him; later our people called him Marcellus, a diminutive formed from Marcus, his uncle. He was most learned in divine and human matters. The bishop is asked to remain for a time in our place. Winning over his nephew, they deliberated together for a long time and only with difficulty finally consented.”

This occurred during the reign of Charles the Bald. Afterward Marcus withdrew to the monastery of Saint Medard, “since there flourished there a distinguished congregation of monks, whose honorable discipline was celebrated,” as Lisiardus writes in the Life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons.

Hericus, a monk of Auxerre and a contemporary of Marcus, calls Marcus “a holy old man, British by birth but educated in Ireland. After long exercises in episcopal holiness, he imposed voluntary exile upon himself. Thus he was brought into Frankish territory. Attracted by the generosity of the most devout King Charles, he practiced the anchoritic life at the monastery of the blessed Medard and Sebastian, a philosopher of holiness, singular and unparalleled in our time.”

After recounting the miracle of Saint Germanus in Marcus’s own words, Hericus adds:

“The bishop mentioned above assured me on oath that these things were contained in Catholic writings in Britain. Whoever has tested his integrity will in no way doubt that credence must be given to his words.”

From these facts it is clear that Marcus was a holy man, and it has seemed not inappropriate to pause here for a while because of him.

7. It was the opinion of Rothad, the first bishop of Soissons of that name, that the Rule of Saint Benedict had been imposed upon the monks of that place from the beginning. In a certain privilege he says that kings had elevated this monastery so highly “that they set it over all the places under their jurisdiction, so that within Gaul it would be second to none in religion, learning, or abundance of resources, and that they gathered there brothers of noble birth serving God under the regular and monastic Rule of Saint Benedict.”

Certainly, at the already mentioned council of Saint Medard, the Fathers examined the case of two monks of that place “ACCORDING TO THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT” in the year 853. At about the same time Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, wrote to Rothad, bishop of Soissons, “concerning the ordering of the monastery of Saint Medard and the restoration of the Rule in it,” as Frodoard records in book III, chapter 21. He also addressed a letter to the monks of that monastery “concerning Hainoald, a monk who had sought pardon from the king for his offenses”; see also chapter 25.

Finally, how highly the monastery of Saint Medard was esteemed by kings is clear from the fact that they had a palace adjoining the monastery, as will be shown below in chapter 40, and from the fact that they exempted the monks of the place from every burden of exactions and military service—privileges granted to few.

ODILO’S LETTER TO INGRANNUS.

[Col. 0579]

[Col. 0579C] To Ingrannus, worthy of reverence for his magnificent faith and deserving to be extolled in the proclamation of every praise, Odilo, the offscouring of all who live under the rule of monastic discipline.

[Note: [Col. 0579C] In the Resbacensis manuscript, RODOINUS is read here, but this is evidently an error in light of what has been said. In the Jolius manuscript the author’s name is absent [Col. 0580C]; at the beginning it is written ODILONIS. It has therefore seemed appropriate to supply it here.]

Having received your paternal command, which is by no means to be despised, I confess that I remain astonished and perplexed. Although I have professed the monastic girdle in the struggle of spiritual warfare, and the Rule determines that I ought to be ready for everything, however difficult the tasks imposed may be, I nevertheless openly acknowledge that I shall be entirely unfit to carry out what you command.

For you require me to strive swiftly to commit to writing how, and in what order, the powerful body of the most valiant combatant—namely, our lord and most devout protector Sebastian—was brought all the way to us, and what outstanding virtues and great miracles, worthy of the admiration of every age, he performed.

This is indeed a great undertaking, so remarkable in its magnitude that it surpasses the strength of human weakness. Not even Homer himself, if, as they say, he were to arise among the common people, could complete it—how much less could I, so insignificant, unskilled in speech, and entirely devoid of grammatical training, who have not even been able, so to speak, to learn the very “aiones” thoroughly? [The reading “aiones,” also found in the Jolius manuscript, is retained as uncertain.]

If I place so great a burden upon my tearful shoulders, I shall collapse beneath the load before I can take even a single free step. In the end, I ought first to have weighed the magnitude of so great a subject for a long time and examined whether I could conceive anything of the beauty of this material with suitably capable understanding; then, with the Lord’s help, if the examination showed that I possessed the necessary ability, I ought to have undertaken what you commanded.

But since the man who must hasten to carry to Italy what has to be written is already present, and since your insistence requires that the work be brought to completion at once, your holiness must consider that, if I cannot accomplish what you command, you should blame not me, who undertook so great a task, but yourselves, who made me undertake it.

Nor should you look for verbal ornament or eloquence in this work. I have not done what I wished, either in manner or extent, but what I could, in manner and extent. And although I have expressed myself in a rustic fashion, I have nevertheless set down the truth. As the excellent teacher Jerome says: “It is more tolerable to utter truths in a rustic manner than falsehoods eloquently.”

Yet I cannot cease to wonder how so many immense stars, such mighty and age-defying signs of virtue—works which Christ deigned to perform through this martyr, always to be honored, cherished, and venerated by a special privilege—could have remained suppressed in laudable silence until our own age. [Note: Yet at the end of this book the author says that there remains in his cartulary a written account by Rodoinus containing very many miracles of the holy martyr.] This is especially surprising since it is well known that the members of this holy congregation have always been richly endowed with wisdom of mind and refined wit.

Unless, perhaps, we accept the explanation—and it may reasonably be conjectured to be true—that divine miracles became commonplace through their continual occurrence. Since the monks of this place enjoyed an unbroken abundance of signs, and wonderful events constantly followed upon wonderful events, they delighted in the profusion of recent miracles and, thinking it discourteous and of little use to commit to writing the earlier ones, which they said even surpassed counting, they neglected the task through sluggishness.

But Agenardus, surnamed the Wise, who was regarded as eminent in those times, mentioned this most revered citizen of heaven in his Deeds of the Caesars Charles the Great and his son Louis (EINHARD, in the Annals). Among the other matters he dictated in the course of his writing, he thought it no labor to strengthen mortal deeds with immortal testimony, saying:

“While these things were taking place, Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis, sent to Rome and, with Eugene—the then pontiff of the apostolic Holy See—granting his request, received the bones of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Sebastian, and placed them in the basilica of Saint Medard in the city of Soissons. While they lay unburied in the small chest in which they had been brought, beside the tomb of Saint Medard, such a multitude of signs and wonders became manifest, and such power of miracles in every kind of healing shone forth through divine grace in the name of that same most blessed martyr, that no mortal could either comprehend the number of those miracles or explain their variety in words. Some are said to have been so astonishing that they exceeded the faith of human weakness, were it not certain that our Lord Jesus Christ, for whom that most blessed martyr suffered, is known through divine omnipotence to be able to do whatever he wills; and to that omnipotence every creature in heaven and on earth is subject.”

Concerning these matters, Agenardus says the following:

Therefore, most equitable Father, having received the gift of your blessing and fortified by your most blessed merits, I shall strive, as far as divine clemency may favor me with the assistance of that outstanding martyr, to obey your command as a humble executor. Since refusing to obey is judged culpable, and presuming to will what one cannot do is called presumptuous, I would rather be reproached by anyone for incompetence than for contempt of the command of the Rule.

[ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE RELICS.]

A MEMORABLE ACCOUNT, destined to benefit all the peoples of Gaul perpetually, who recall it with solemn devotion: how the venerable body of the most blessed Sebastian, granted by Louis Caesar the emperor and by Eugene, pontiff of the holy Roman See, was finally translated into Gaul, brought to the city of the Soissons people, honorably received and deposited there on the fifth day before the Ides of December.

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0581C]

In the year 814 of the incarnate Word, Louis Caesar Augustus, emperor of divine memory and son of Charlemagne, after the father’s final fate, to be mourned by all ages, had acquired the primacy of the entire monarchy by the prior claim of the Franks, and, with no opposing power set against him, enjoyed the scepters of the consolidated kingdom and was endowed with its royal dignity, he was placed upon his father’s throne amid the applause of all on every side.

Since he surpassed all others in imperial power through the glory of his immeasurable dignity, he took care to adorn himself more magnificently with the immortal insignia of the blessed virtues from which he could never be stripped. Above all, he embraced memory and patience in every action, and was sometimes also prescient of future events.

Among all the leading men of his empire whom he had admitted to his counsel, he loved and exalted Hilduin, the most reverend abbot, a man exceedingly modest in every kind of integrity and endowed with every kind of intelligence and industry, distinguished for justice and renowned for holiness. He loved him so greatly that he entrusted to him whatever had to be handled in greater secrecy and appointed him archchaplain throughout his entire empire.

This venerable abbot, among the many monasteries entrusted to him by imperial benevolence, had under his supervision the noble monastery in view of the city of Soissons. Clothar, once king of the Franks, and his son Sigibert had built it at great expense in honor of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Medard, and had buried his most sacred remains there.

Father Hilduin saw that the brothers of this place excelled in monastic religion and were becoming accustomed to ecclesiastical learning. He rejoiced in their progress and diligently encouraged them with salutary admonitions to strive more and more toward the summit of perfection. Finally, he cultivated, elevated, and enriched the place with such love and care that within Gaul it was considered second to none in religion, learning, or abundance of resources.

[Col. 0582D] At that time Rodoinus was provost of this holy congregation, a shrewd man whose cunning and intelligence I consider no one of our time to have equaled. Because of the merit of his loyalty and the industry divinely bestowed upon him, he gained such favor and intimacy with the same most holy Father Hilduin that Hilduin preferred him to all the provosts of the monasteries subject to his authority.

As a result, when fame spread the news, his name became well known at the royal court. Thus the emperor, beloved of God, having learned of this man’s abilities, began to honor him both privately and publicly. He granted him free permission to bring before the imperial tribunals, without consulting anyone, whatever advantage or benefit he might discover for himself or for the place over which he presided, assuring him that he would obtain it immediately.

Not long afterward, through divine clemency, Rodoinus obtained such favor from the emperor that, both because of his love for the devout Father Hilduin, in whose service he frequently attended the royal court, and because of the shrewd ability in which he was uniquely preeminent, the emperor gladly admitted him among his secretaries whenever matters concerning the welfare of the kingdom were to be discussed.

CHAPTER TWO.

[Col. 0583B] At that time the aforesaid Father Hilduin, as we have already said, held the highest position throughout the entire monarchy of the emperor, above all others of his order. This office, appropriate to his eminent dignity, he administered with a sufficiently suitable diligence, since he was a man of keen intelligence.

Sent by the most devout Caesar to restrain the insolence of certain men who had risen up against Eugene, the supreme pontiff, Hilduin exercised judgment with such prudent discernment that he fulfilled the emperor’s command, satisfied the pontiff, and, after calming the defiance of those who had arrogantly risen against him, restored them to peace and tranquility.

When these matters had been properly completed, the cry of the City was raised in favor of so great a Father; the imperial judgments were approved; the clemency accomplished through this man was praised; love and devotion toward the venerable Father increased abundantly; and the entire senate of the Church implored with supreme devotion that he might live for a long time in the honor of this dignity.

Many kinds of gifts were added to the prayers. He is said to have received from certain people gifts so great and valuable that they seemed to exceed any price. After seeking and obtaining a blessing, and praying that the prince of the apostles would assist him, they received permission to return and, with God’s favor, set out for home.

Meanwhile, those who loved him with a singular affection and greater intimacy deeply regretted his absence, since they saw that he was returning later than they had hoped. Suddenly, uncertain and doubtful, they heard with great joy that he had already reached the regions of Gaul.

Meanwhile Rodoinus and his companions, since he was exceptionally loyal to the Father and the matter particularly concerned him, set out with the most splendid preparations to meet their desired patron. At last they found and saw him again; casting off the grief with which they had been afflicted, they were received in his paternal embrace and restored by immense rejoicing to the long-desired joy.

CHAPTER THREE.

After the paternal embraces and most affectionate kisses, Hilduin gave a lengthy account to those who eagerly questioned him about what had happened to him: how, and with what honor, he had been received by the apostolic lord and by the senate of the holy Roman Church; with what authority and judgment he had restrained the chatter of certain men who had shown themselves defiant against the sacred pontiff; how he had preserved imperial law, obeyed apostolic decrees, and acted as the most equitable judge between both parties; and how he had been treated well and bound by friendship by all the leading men of Rome.

Finally, he explained what was especially pleasing to himself and most welcome to his companions: that, through the favor of the same lord pontiff, he had also been deemed worthy to share a special intimacy and bond of friendship with him.

Whatever had gone well, or whatever had happened unpleasantly through some chance circumstance, he declared that God’s ineffable protection had been present in everything.

After Hilduin had sufficiently recounted to his beloved sons the dangers of his journey and embassy, Rodoinus said:

“We give and render thanks to almighty God, illustrious Father, because all that has been undertaken through him has been granted a successful outcome, and we have been deemed worthy to see you safe and unharmed.
