Indeed, night and day we have asked without interruption that he deign to hear us, although we do not claim this on our own merit, which we judge to be nonexistent. Nevertheless, beloved Father, we rejoice that it has been granted to us from heaven through the goodness of your faith and your sacred merits.

“For the longer our distress lasted during your absence, the more joyful is our happiness in the sight of your return, since the outcome has been prosperous. May we enjoy you as our flourishing patron for as long as the vital breath rules these limbs.””

Moved and greatly delighted by these words, the devout Father Hilduin began to speak about apostolic dignity, ecclesiastical religion, and the veneration of the saints, whose innumerable multitude enriched the city of Rome, recounting the struggles, merits, and names of some of them. The venerable abbot, delighting in these pleasant recollections, prolonged his speech.

CHAPTER FOUR.

Meanwhile Rodoinus, being a man of shrewd mind and, as I believe, divinely inspired, looking ahead with eager vision to the future of the place over which he presided, said:

“A little earlier, my Father and Lord, while you were speaking, I understood you to say that whatever you might at any time find useful or desirable had been granted to you perpetually by the supreme pope, with the inviolable assurance of the apostolic see. We must test whether his promise contains an effective guarantee.

“Certainly, as I think, it may happen that he will not refuse to confer upon you one of the heavenly citizens of outstanding merit among those of whom we have just been speaking. If this should occur, what more salutary gift could he grant you, or what would be more fitting, than that through your agency a companion be given to the holy Medard, your protector in every respect?

“For we enjoy only that one patron. This will be suitable for your salvation, remain forever as a memorial, and benefit the entire homeland perpetually.”

Abbot Hilduin, full of joy, said to Rodoinus:

“You are striving, as far as can be understood, to persuade us greatly to raise and exalt the place of your religious life. I do not disapprove of your desire, nor do I dissent from your request. Rather, insofar as God grants his approval, I promise to employ all my ability, and I appoint you executor of this undertaking.

“Nevertheless, an imperial judgment must be sought in this matter. If it is approved by him, then it will consequently be unalterable.”

Rodoinus replied:

“Your decision, Father, is excellent and worthy of your holiness.”

Companions were again sent out in advance by the most glorious Caesar to conduct the venerable abbot back; they urged that the journey be hastened, affirming that the emperor was filled with a great desire to see him.

Thus they gladly continued their journey and reached the palace at Aachen. Then everyone from every side crowded around him in a throng, rejoicing beyond measure, and led him into the innermost chambers of the emperors.

There, as usual, he was graciously received and unfolded the entire course of the embassy he had completed. When it had ended, the emperor expressed great joy over its successful conduct, returned thanks, and bestowed gifts.

Empress Judith, celebrated and renowned, laying aside the hauteur of imperial majesty, came forth from the dining hall. Receiving the venerable abbot with her customary affection, but even more warmly than usual, she rejoiced greatly and was delighted by his successful return. The entire court also rejoiced at his return as though he were their own father.

CHAPTER FIVE.

After they had been greatly gladdened by joy, Hilduin of good memory—for this epithet belonged to him—did not forget what had been suggested to him by his faithful Rodoinus. Seizing the opportunity, he took care to disclose the matter to the Emperor’s ears. The most benevolent Emperor replied:

“You should not regard as unacceptable what is suggested with ready devotion by your faithful servant and ours. For if the matter achieves its outcome, it will be beneficial not only to us but also to the administration of the whole kingdom. Whom, then, have you chosen as the more suitable person for us to seek?” [Col. 0585C]

Rodoinus was summoned and presented before the king. Questioned by the Emperor on this very matter, he gave a prompt and settled opinion, saying:

“If it pleases your most exalted Majesty, I think that Silvester, once the most holy bishop, should be sought.”

The Emperor accepted his expressed opinion and asked whether all those present approved it. There was unanimous agreement among them on this matter, and together they prayed that it might attain a fortunate outcome. The Emperor willingly assented and promised his full cooperation in carrying it out, insofar as divine grace should favor the undertaking. Then he encouraged and instructed his beloved abbot, together with Rodoinus, concerning the preparations for so great a journey. He fixed for Rodoinus definite stages of travel, commanding him, once they had been completed, to return to his presence. [Col. 0585D]

Rodoinus returned to his homeland and to the place where he had been raised, making no sluggish use of the time granted for the delay. Finally, while procuring the necessities for so great a journey, he took care to furnish his equipment sufficiently and abundantly with everything that the fertile soil of Gaul customarily produces most desirably, and he strove to gather together a very large sum of money.

After this, when the days of the permitted delay had been completed, he returned to the Emperor’s presence. As soon as he had been received with the greatest kindness, the Emperor handed him letters sealed in his name and with the impression of his ring, filled with prayers of every kind for obtaining the holy relics already mentioned. In them he asked the most blessed Pope Eugene to have the aforementioned holy relics conveyed to Rodoinus and his companions at Rome. [Col. 0586A] He also earnestly commended them to devote, according to the capacity of their strength, labor, and intelligence, their efforts to carrying out this task.

## CHAPTER VI

Having been courteously instructed by the Emperor in these matters and embraced individually in arms with kisses sweeter than could be expected from so great a dignity and with sacred embraces, they were graciously dismissed and unknowingly set out upon their journey. At length they continued as far as the city of Langres, where they pitched a most suitable tent in which to refresh their strength for a little while.

Here, before the doors of the mother church, a certain man lay helpless, grievously seized by a very severe illness. On the very night when they arrived there, after long sighs caused by daytime suffering, when he had relaxed his weary limbs in a sleep far too deep, he saw standing before him a figure of indescribable splendor and excessive radiance. Unable to endure the sight of him, he turned his head away; his eyes, struck by no mortal light, could not fix their gaze upon the figure. The apparition then asked him in exceedingly gentle words what he was doing there and by what event he had incurred that affliction. [Col. 0586B]

He explained the cause of his illness and stated how long it had lasted. The figure then asked whether he wished to be restored to his former health. He replied that he had a great desire for this, if he could in any way hope for it.

The figure, pointing with the golden staff that he held in his hand toward the wound and toward the place where they were lodging, said:

“Go into that suburb, and there you will find the men you seek, preparing to travel to Rome. Inform them on my authority that the undertaking they are pursuing is not of divine predestination.” [Col. 0586C]

Trembling and anxious, the man asked him:

“Lord, by what name do you command that you be identified?”

The figure replied:

“I am the martyr Sebastian, who died at Rome, beaten with clubs for confessing Christ, God; there I have lain buried in body until now. Let them know that what has been granted to them by the Lord is mine, not that of the one for whom they are traveling.”

The man answered:

“Not refusing to obey your serene command, I will gladly strive to convey to them what you have ordered me to deliver. Perhaps they will suspect that I intend to deceive them and will accuse me of fraud. If they begin to demand proof of this matter from me, what answer do you command me to give? For, as I think, they will not otherwise be persuaded.”

Then the most blessed martyr stretched out his arm toward him and, as soon as his powerful hand touched him, restored him to health. He continued: [Col. 0586D]

“Be well. And let this be the sign given to you by me, which cannot be rejected with any uncertainty whatever.”

When sleep had been driven away by joy and fear, and he had been restored to perfect health, he recognized that everything he had heard was true. For he appeared completely healthy, as though he had never been afflicted by the fever of any illness.

Then, exultantly exploring the entire city and its suburbs, he began to seek the men whom he had been ordered to find and to make public the healing wrought in him by God through the most sacred martyr. Those who had seen him lying half-dead at the doors of the aforementioned basilica the day before and the day before that came running from every side when they heard what had happened. Struck with amazement at this unknown restoration, they proclaimed their thanks to God everywhere in common songs of praise. [Col. 0587A]

At last he carefully found the men he had sought. He immediately recognized them by the signs that had been indicated, fearlessly recounted what had been commanded him, and openly offered himself as a witness confirming his words.

They received with the greatest reverence the commands delivered by the most blessed martyr. Immensely rejoicing, they did not cease to offer vows of thanksgiving to almighty God and to magnify the saint with joined praises for the favor bestowed upon them.

Thereafter, turning back along their route, they tried gradually to retrace their steps toward home. They sought out the venerable Father Hilduin, the originator of this enterprise, and explained to him in order everything that had been divinely accomplished. They earnestly begged him to deign to report it himself to the Emperor. [Col. 0587B]

They also urgently requested that the imperial letters, by which they had been asking for the relics of the great Bishop Silvester, be altered into a request for the renowned martyr Sebastian. With whatever insistence they dared, they pressed for the matter to be hastened as quickly as possible, lest any misfortune overtake the journey they had begun.

The distinguished Hilduin brought the secret of the divine mission to the pious ruler’s attention and disclosed the salutary revelation concerning the acquisition of the relics of so great a martyr. The Emperor ordered the texts of the letters to be renewed under the patronage of the veteran soldier, filled with repeated prayers. Then, as before, he returned the letters to Rodoinus and his companions, sealed in his name and with the impression of his ring. [Col. 0587C]

They, with the salutary breeze of divine revelation blowing upon them, gladly resumed their journey. No longer hesitating in the least about completing their enterprise, they eagerly made their way to golden Rome.

## CHAPTER VII

In the year 826 of the Incarnate Word, and in the thirteenth year of the reign of the Emperor Louis, Rodoinus entered Rome with a great company and abundant equipment. He prudently discharged the commission entrusted to him, prepared with skillful care, and requested and obtained the life-giving ashes of the martyr Sebastian, renowned for great miracles and healings.

Before approaching the apostolic Majesty, however, he sought out and found certain bishops, abbots, and leading officials of the state whom the venerable Father Hilduin had shown himself to possess there as most faithful friends. [Col. 0587D]

Among these the most ready and most assiduously supportive of the apostolic dignity were Quirinus, Theophylact the *Numenculator*, and the most reverend Abbot Ingoald, who happened at that time to be absent. For, on the Emperor’s command, he had set out among the Beneventans to survey the bishopric of Albocuria. But, pursued by a swift courier and intercepted by a friendly summons, he turned back to the City.

He received the envoys with a cheerful expression and treated them courteously. Above all, he asked whether the aforementioned Father Hilduin was enjoying favorable circumstances. When he learned that Hilduin was in good health, he gave thanks to God for this and prayed from his heart that he might be granted either to see or to hear of his continued prosperity and advancement for many years. Then he asked why they had come so unexpectedly and without warning. [Col. 0588A]

They drew close to his ear in greater familiarity and confidently disclosed the secret of the whole affair. He accepted it calmly and, removing their despair, most kindly encouraged them to proceed. Finally, he fulfilled with tireless purpose what he had promised with his words. For through him the way and every access before the apostolic lord lay open to them.

Then, seeking the most honorable men Quirinus and Theophylact, they handed over the letters and doubled their prayers and gifts concerning the matters contained in them.

Accordingly, struck by the command in the martyr’s name, those men, their faces and hearts covered with pallor, declared that if a third patron were given to the apostles Peter and Paul, they did not know how he could be removed without tumultuous prejudice. They protested that this lay beyond human ability, although they most willingly wished to uphold both the Emperor’s command and the request of their friend. [Col. 0588B]

Rodoinus and his companions, on the other hand, were in no way repelled by this obstacle. They pressed on with greater insistence, repeating the Emperor’s unavoidable desire and the confidence of the Father by whom they had been sent, the confidence he had placed in their eminence.

Moved by such arguments, they declared that, if the permission of God and the martyr’s will allowed it, they would support the undertaking wholeheartedly. They also prudently indicated how it might be begun in the most appropriate manner.

## CHAPTER VIII

At length they were brought into the patriarchal residence before the apostolic lord. Bending their knees to the ground, they reverently clung to and kissed his sacred feet. Then the letters were produced and the documents sent with them were presented.

By the abundance of their words they sought to charm the pious Father’s mind, so that they might perhaps incline him toward their request. They disclosed the Emperor’s authority and explained the loyalty of the named and written-about Father. If the written documents had conveyed anything insufficiently, they supplied it according to their ability and intelligence. [Col. 0588C]

No private persons were present at this conversation except Quirinus and Theophylact. For the apostolic lord was then gravely ill, so that he appeared half-dead; he could hear their embassy only while lying on his bed.

When the letters were read aloud and he heard the martyr’s name,

> He was stunned; his sad mind confounded the organs of speech,  
> Unable to endure the separation of so great a saint.

For the Roman people honored him after the apostles, as though he were a third, with magnificent gifts and praises. What his mind was turning over was revealed by his pale face.

While he remained silent for a long time, they stood in suspense. At last, when he had recovered his breath and given an answer, he removed all hope from the matter and declared that it was beyond his authority. [Col. 0588D]

Yet they continued to press him with every supplication they could offer, and with abundant tears they kissed his knees and feet. He therefore ordered them to wait, so that he might have time to consider the matter and seek counsel from the prudent Roman senate, without whose advice, he said, it would not be right to undertake such a thing.

Rodoinus, considering the matter more attentively than the others because anxiety urged him on more strongly, did not depart at once. Instead, in a corner of the building, he separated the aforementioned men, Quirinus and Theophylact, and earnestly begged them to remain firm in their opinion, saying: [Col. 0589A]

“Deign to have pity on us, who have entrusted our entire hope to your eminence. Remember also the friendship of that man of yours, through which you may both obtain here and now the reward of the finest favors and, with the saint, share in God’s grace in heaven.

“For if what the face reveals is true, we have plainly been allowed to understand his mind: the apostolic lord is not calmly accepting our embassy. Therefore, whatever the matter may be—for you can surely investigate it—we beg you to disclose it without concealment to your faithful servants before we depart and to restore our confidence.”

They, however, as before, gave their word that they would help, if only the will of God and the martyr could be discerned in the matter. Then they were led out of the patriarchal residence and withdrew to their lodging.

## CHAPTER IX

But because a twofold anxiety tormented the sacred bishop—on the one hand, the absence of the saint, and on the other, the friendship of the most excellent abbot, to whom at some time various rights belonging to him had been granted—he summoned a private gathering of priests and of those who served in his confidence. He explained the embassy to them and ordered them to determine its resolution with sound judgment. [Col. 0589B]

Then they were all disturbed and astonished beyond belief. They replied that such a request could come only from a madman or from someone ignorant of the saint’s merit, and they prayed for a more favorable outcome so that the matter might not end badly.

They did not hesitate, in the pope’s presence, to say that if the holy body were given to them, he would be far inferior to the deeds of his predecessors, who had increased the dignity of the Roman Church through ecclesiastical sacraments. What more need be said? They maintained that this ought not to happen and could not justly happen. [Col. 0589C]

The distinguished men Quirinus and Theophylact, on the contrary, said that it both ought to happen and could happen.

When the others withdrew because of the indiscriminate and tiresome confusion of their noise, which seemed to weary the sacred bishop, and only those who served in his more secret counsels remained, he began to converse appropriately with them about the same matter. With God, as we believe, inspiring the counsel of a better judgment, he began to give it his attention and openly demonstrated that his will had become more favorable.

Those who had withdrawn outside because of the nausea caused by their own loquacity nevertheless did not hesitate to investigate with jealous concern what the apostolic lord was reconsidering with Quirinus and Theophylact. They had learned through repeated experience that these men could prevail over them in their master’s favor. Since they were, in fact, arbiters of the whole decision, the others returned to the court, lest the matter should succeed through the counsel of those men without their own advice and they themselves should be regarded as contemptible because they had not been summoned. [Col. 0589D]

Demanding access to the men who had been questioned, they declared that the matter was pleasing. They said:

“We remember, most excellent shepherd and venerable lord, the abundant affection of your son Hilduin toward the majesty of the apostolic see. Nor are we unaware of the Emperor’s supplication in this very matter that has been disclosed to us. Your incomparable blessedness, through divine providence, will arrange both matters in such a way that neither he will accuse you of inhumanity nor we accuse you of cruelty. [Col. 0590A]

“Long ago the supreme pontiff, the lord Adrian, for some purpose unknown to us, undertook the tomb of this martyr, either wishing to transfer him within the walls of the City or to give relics from his body to those who requested them. At his first attempt, however, he was seized by terrifying horror and driven back, and he left the undertaking unfinished. In the end, because he escaped unharmed, he attributed it to the mercy by which the saint had spared him.

“We have also heard that under the blessed Pope Leo the same attempt was made at his command. Then, when a storm suddenly arose with flashes of lightning, it removed the entire temple from its foundations, so that the clergy, fearing that the roof would fall upon them, forgot their chants and cried out. No one thought he could leave alive. [Col. 0590B]

“It is also reported that under the lord Paschal the undertaking had already been begun but was broken off by a similar disturbance. It is therefore clear, from the mystery demonstrated so many times, that he has in no way wished to move from here.

“From this we take confidence both to give him and not to lose him. If, with God’s consent, the matter should turn out in this way, your eminence will see loss suffered by neither side: for them, complete satisfaction; for us, the removal of our grievance. Those who say that they hold devotion toward your eminence will preserve that devotion, and we shall preserve the terms of the faith we have pledged.

“There is also another fact that we know with complete certainty: no Roman can be found who would dare, however much he might be compelled, to lay a hand upon his tomb. Both things will be possible: he can be given and he can be retained.”

When the apostolic lord heard this, he favored it with a tranquil heart and ordered the venerable Bishop John to be summoned. [Col. 0590C] When John arrived, he privately sought with him the most suitable outcome for the matter and, with free authority, sanctioned what was more wisely destined to happen by God’s prompting. But this was not then made known to many.

## CHAPTER X

While these things were being considered, the illustrious Count Ingobert arrived.

[Note: Ingobert is prominently mentioned in the *Deeds of Charles and Louis*.]

Our men thought that he would be hostile to them because they had advanced the matter thus far without his knowledge. For he was exceedingly powerful and influential in every matter with the supreme Bishop, and he was a very close friend of the venerable Abbot Hilduin. They therefore suspected that he would be angry because they had neglected to inform him about these affairs.

Accordingly, they went to him swiftly and, in that man’s name and at his command, disclosed these matters to him, asserting that the task for which they had been sent had been entrusted to him in particular. [Col. 0590D]

He, too, mindful of their ancient friendship, displayed himself as cheerful in this matter with every resource and effort of his shrewdness, insofar as God granted him the strength, and supplied from his own means what was necessary for the undertaking.

Moreover, he spoke with the apostolic lord so that their request might be brought to completion without envious obstruction.

When this had been arranged, they were summoned again and brought before the apostolic lord. As those standing around him pleaded for the fulfillment of their request, while the envoys lay prostrate in the distance with their faces lowered toward the ground, he was at last moved by compassion and, although fearful and trembling, agreed that the saint’s body should be given. [Col. 0591A]

Bishop John was appointed as the most suitable minister of this gift. For, as we have already stated, the pope was suffering from an extreme illness and could not carry this out himself, although he did not deny that he greatly desired it. As later became clear, this was sufficiently advanced by God’s dispensation.

Thus, taking John with them—the venerable pope had appointed him as their willing guide—they all went eagerly to a place that was no longer unknown to them. For they had learned from the account of his passion, splendidly composed by Saint Ambrose, that three miles from the City, at a place called Catacombs because of the station for ships, the most blessed martyr had appeared in a vision and commanded a certain matron named Lucina to bury him at the feet of the apostles Peter and Paul. She carried out what she had been ordered to do with ready devotion, laying him in the tomb with spices.

## CHAPTER XI

On the day after next they devoutly observed the fast imposed upon them, together with the priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy. Among them was Ingoald the archimandrite, with his companions, a most faithful helper to the extent of his strength. [Col. 0591B]

When the observance of the fast had been solemnly completed, as the twilight of night fell, they approached the martyr’s noble tomb to celebrate the vigil in preparation for the translation. They applied themselves to the work with every duty and service required for their undertaking. Spending the night there amid the singing of hymns and the melodies of psalms, amid the continual fragrance of incense and the misty vapors of various spices, they prayed to the Lord that they might be considered worthy to handle the saving relic, and that he would not reject from this task those whom faithful desire and impatient love, through great labor and many dangers, had drawn together there. [Col. 0591C]

Thus they passed the whole night continually in spiritual praises. When the pale dawn restored the day, they asked that the talkative Romans withdraw from the church and permit them the privacy familiar to them.

But when these men withdrew into the choir to perform the litany, our people discovered that they had risen in a hostile and malicious attack upon the undertaking. Those whom our men had thought to be intercessors they recognized as detractors, muttering foolishly against the matter. Moreover, they hurled curses against the supreme bishop, reviling him as more cruel than all his predecessors because, blinded by money, he was not afraid to expel such a great and powerful patron beyond his own borders. [Col. 0591D]

They also begged the holy martyr, with bitterest sobs, not to allow himself to be taken away by ignoble Gauls from his beloved homeland, where he had chosen, by his own direction, to possess both the palm of eternity and the place of his repose.

After those whisperers had been put outside—thus Jol—our countrymen, together with Bishop John and Abbot Ingoald, withdrew into the inner part of the church. Having bolted the doors, they resolutely approached the tomb.

## CHAPTER XII

Meanwhile, John, exhausted by the preceding day’s fasting and by the continuation of the vigils, was sitting on a folding seat [Note: *Cliothetrum* or *cliothedrum*, a folding seat.] when the force of sleep suddenly overcame him and he sank into an incomplete slumber.

As soon as he had lightly relaxed his eyelids into repose, he saw standing before him a man of exceedingly radiant appearance, who addressed him in these very gentle words: [Col. 0592A]

“O John, do not fear to give the body of this martyr Sebastian to the men who have come for it. Know that this is the decree of heavenly predestination and of his own will. Go, therefore, and apply your hand to the tomb in order to lead it to the appointed place.”

When he attempted to carry out what he had been ordered to do, he saw close before his feet stones that were burning and vomiting intolerable heat upon him; they blocked his progress.

When he was now, as it were, halfway along the road, surrounded by the heat of those burning stones and seeing no passage open to him on any side, he was terrified and did not know what to do. But the figure encouraged him, and he was astonished to find that he had suddenly leapt over them without injury. [Col. 0592B]

Then he saw a heap of raging embers lying across his path, and he was forced to stop, unable to advance. Yet, relying on a sign from that same figure, he perceived that he had crossed beyond it.

He wished to continue along the road he had begun, when suddenly a voracious flame had spread enormous fireballs across the way. The sacred bishop was exceedingly afraid of it, especially because there was no place to turn aside. At last, with that same figure giving him its right hand, he was led unharmed beyond it.

Then a brother named Wilharius was sent to summon him. When Wilharius awakened John with a gentle touch, while he was still trembling in terror from the dreadful vision, he announced on behalf of the others that the time had come to perform the sacred task and that it must not be postponed in any way. He told him that they had long been waiting, already prepared, at the martyr’s tomb. [Col. 0592C]

John immediately rose, girded with his priestly vestments, and hurried with the greatest reverence to the place. He excused the delay by disclosing the revelation and encouraged them, setting aside all doubt, to remain confident in hope of receiving the sacrament for which they had sighed so many times.

The *oblationarius* was then summoned, whose duty according to Roman custom it was to open the tomb. He resisted for a long time and with great force, arguing that this was an utterly wrongful act and that no Roman should presume to undertake an unforgivable crime by which the guilt of sacrilege would be marked upon succeeding generations.

John, strengthened by the divine commands, seized an iron tool and, to the extent of his strength, repeatedly struck the sarcophagus until he grew weary, battering and piercing it.

When our men saw him failing from rapid exhaustion [that is, fatigue], at his signal they applied themselves to it with keener spirits and stronger arms. Although they labored greatly to break through the monument—for it was of enormous mass and made of indissoluble bitumen—they finally discovered the most sacred body of the martyr. [Col. 0592D]

## CHAPTER XIII

Meanwhile, all who were standing there inhaled an aromatic fragrance that had previously been unfamiliar and unknown to mortals. They reported that it was of such sweetness and delight that, though they enjoyed it abundantly, no one could be satisfied by it.

From this we clearly establish that it was not a human composition, but the most welcome diffusion of heavenly grace, which had always been fragrant in the most blessed martyr. [Col. 0593A]

As this vapor continued to breathe from the holy place, the whole house was delightfully filled with it. Near its entrance the house had kept a corpse, buried nearly ten days earlier, from whose flowing corruption an execrable stench boiled forth and infected those who entered.

But when the holy fragrance overflowed, the harmful odor was emptied into nothingness and subsided, until everything concerning the saint had been completed with festive celebration.

The most blessed martyr had already appeared secretly in a revelation to a certain archpresbyter, declaring that he wished to leave that church, as I think because he could no longer endure the stench of that corruptible corpse. He seemed to proceed with his face turned away from the apse and to go outside as though in indignation. As he departed, a little boy followed his footsteps, holding a broom in his hands and sweeping away the filth behind him, until the saint had gone away from that place. [Col. 0593B]

The basilica itself was considered equal in size to the basilica of Saint Denis. In it the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul had once been buried, and near their resting places the same venerable martyr had ordered himself to be buried.

Hence it is clear that the church was unworthy of the saint’s most worthy merits and unsuitable for his repose.

Therefore, his ministers and attendants—for our example we have related these things to you—serve him continually with spotless acts of devotion. Consider how much you have obtained through him in time, and recall how much you may hope to obtain without end.

Certainly, since he judged us worthy, though unworthy, to perform his rites here, I dare to say that, if we strive worthily, he will have those whom he has here as servants as his perpetual companions there, through the help of his intercession. [Col. 0593C]

Let none of us shrink from the laborious service of this brief and limited time, since no doubt should break our confidence in the reward of eternal recompense.

## CHAPTER XIV

Thus, amid immense joy and honor, as they wrapped the discovered body, filled with divine fragrance, first in linen and then in richly worked cloths, it miraculously healed a certain cleric who was lying mortally ill from the heat of fever with astonishing speed.

Once the body of the most sacred martyr had been found, breathing forth heavenly fragrance abundantly, as we have said, a messenger was immediately sent to Quirinus and Theophylact so that they might opportunely report this to the apostolic lord. [Col. 0593D]

This was done. Since the apostolic lord could not come there because of his illness, he instructed the venerable Bishop John to deliver the body to them himself.

They received it with complete eagerness and veneration and departed with Bishop John, Abbot Ingoald the archimandrite, and many other clergy and laypeople of the Roman Church.

The reverent choir, singing the sound of sweet melodies, went ahead for a considerable distance and filled the way with its music. Some offered songs of joy; others uttered deep sighs and bitter laments.

In this manner they carried the body to the presence of the apostolic lord, so that it might be sealed with his ring according to custom. After he had carefully completed this, it was carried into the church of Saint Peter and deposited there on that same day. [Col. 0594A]

Thereupon many Romans, stirred by malice and envy, attacked the apostolic lord. They did not hesitate to denounce him as more cruel than all his predecessors because he had permitted such a great and powerful patron to be expelled from his own territory—something no other pope had ever allowed.

They therefore advised that only the arm be given to the envoys and that the remainder be properly reburied there in a fitting place.

This deception could not remain hidden from Ingoald the archimandrite. He immediately revealed it to our men. Acting more cautiously together, they held a council and kept silent that day.

## CHAPTER XV

Moreover, Rodoinus, whom the force of love and impatient desire for obtaining the holy relics had stirred with pious devotion, bribed the attendants in abundance. Their duty at that time was to guard the basilica of Saint Peter. [Col. 0594B]

During that same night he boldly approached the most sacred tomb of Pope Gregory, which stood before the sacristy. His body was lifted with the greatest reverence, properly arranged, carried to the altar of Saint Peter, and deposited beside the venerable body of the aforementioned martyr.

Afterward Rodoinus and his companions gladly accepted the pledge of faith required of them. Over the most sacred limbs of the martyr and the pontiff they willingly swore an oath that they would never reveal or publish to any mortal what had been done, but would bury it in perpetual silence.

Thus our countrymen, praiseworthy for their pious deception, magnanimous in the silent joy they concealed within their breasts, carried the bodies of the saints away without any obstacle and transferred them to the monastery of Ingoald. [Col. 0594C]

[Note: It is not easy to determine which monastery this was; perhaps the monastery of Saint Paul outside the City?]

## CHAPTER XVI

On the following day the apostolic lord ordered them to be brought before him again. For they had not yet obtained permission to return; they had merely received the saint into their possession.

He immediately asked them where they had the saint. They professed that they did not know, except that they had already sent him in the direction of their own country.

“Whatever the truth may be,” he said, “whether you know or do not know, take care to bring him back here at once. Nor can this decision be changed, so that permission for you to return can otherwise be granted from here.”

They, very fearful and sorrowful, confirmed under oath that matters were as they had said and that what he commanded was entirely impossible. [Col. 0594D]

He could scarcely be persuaded of this. But, by God’s mercy, the matter remained as it had begun. For those who had previously favored the envoys changed the situation in the following way.

When they perceived his disturbed state of mind, they drew closer to his ear and said that those who could neither be bent nor turned ought to be treated somewhat more gently and not rebuked so angrily, lest they perhaps depart as ungrateful men and return with the greatest gift unpraised.

In this way, although with great difficulty, they were released and given the blessing. Joining their companions not far from the City, and with great joys arising from the great treasure, they returned home by prosperous roads, accompanied by divine grace.

## CHAPTER XVII

Afterward they reached the city of Piacenza. When the body of the most blessed martyr was being carried into it, a demoniac, tightly bound with ropes, was brought to meet it at the entrance. [Col. 0595A]

The wretched spirit was immediately disturbed and terrified. Indignant that he was being compelled to leave the miserable man whom he had miserably possessed, he began to torment him with extreme violence. Although the man could scarcely be restrained by the hands of many people, he sprang forward, broke the bonds with which he had been tied, and, with disordered movements, now lifting himself upward into the midst of the crowd, now falling headlong to the ground, drove everyone into flight.

But when he came before the saint, he suddenly fell trembling and lay there for a long time, stretched out as though lifeless.

Then, overcome by the powerful arm of the most wicked devil, who could not endure the martyr’s presence, he abandoned the man. Forcefully expelled, defeated, he fled into the darkness and the earth he deserved. [Col. 0595B]

The captive completely recovered the reason he had lost. With his house cleansed by the dew of heavenly power, he aroused many to attend the saint’s rites and kindled everywhere praise of almighty God, whose gift was the deed performed through the martyr.

Along the same stretch of road extending from the City, many suffering from fevers, many lunatics, and many afflicted by various illnesses met the saint. Through his venerable merits they were freed from the forces that tormented them and endowed with the strength of complete health.

## CHAPTER XVIII

They reached Mount Jovis, where the martyr’s fame for distinguished miracles had spread widely.

[Note: This is otherwise called Saint Bernard’s Pass, in the Pennine Alps, not far from Augusta Praetoria.]

Here a cleric named Benedict, the attendant of that place, had been wasting away from a deadly illness for thirty continuous days. As soon as he heard that the saint was turning aside thither by the direct path, he turned aside toward him. [Col. 0595C]

Since he was in no way able to go to meet the saint on his own feet, although he desired to do so, he had himself carried in the arms of others. He was brought to the saint on the public road, not far from that place, so exhausted that he seemed dead. He was set down before him and said, as far as he could make himself heard, that he wished to carry him and humbly begged to be permitted to do so.

Sustained on either side by the arms of others, he received the saint in his own arms with faith rather than presumption. He immediately obtained an increase of his former health and, restored and joyful, carried him as far as Octodurum.

[Note: Octodurum, commonly Martinach, in the district of the Seduni, near Agaunum.]

There, offering to the Savior of all the free sacrifice of praises for his restoration, and kissing the martyr’s *capula* (casket or reliquary; the precise object is uncertain), he returned safely with his companions to his home. [Col. 0595D]

As God glorified his saint through such deeds, no small crowd gathered from every direction.

## CHAPTER XIX

At last they came by a peaceful road to a place called Granant. There, a very small boy who had been deprived of his sight was brought by his parents and placed before the church’s altar, where the most blessed martyr had already been installed.

He spent that night there without sleep, just as he had been cast down before the saint.

When morning dawned, after the completion of the Mass, the saint was being taken onto the road with the company and assistance of the priests. Hearing the tumult of those who were departing, the boy realized that the saint was being lifted from that place. [Col. 0596A]

Immediately stretching out his arm at random, he thrust it into the bier. By that very touch he recovered the light, and with clear vision he saw his illuminator being carried away. He first recognized the form of his own palm.

Calling out the saint’s name, he rendered the proper thanks and displayed himself as an example to others, so that they too might be stirred to do the same.

Joyfully gazing upon the light that he had never before experienced, he declared that he could see. He proclaimed blessed forever by every human being the one who, through an ineffable infusion, had restored to him in an instant the power of sight that nature itself had denied him.

This your seasoned champion, Lord God, has accomplished through your most secret dispensation: he makes your faithful know that he shines in you with everlasting radiance; that he enjoys you, the eternal and inaccessible light; and that, through you, who illuminate every rational creature, he is more and more inflamed and, by being inflamed, made blessed. [Col. 0596B]

Through him we, your insignificant servants, desire to send you, with firm faith and the whole strength of our devotion, the vows and sacrifices of pure praise, so that, by his mediation, they may become pleasing to you and salutary to us. We pray that this may be so.

## CHAPTER XX
The illustrious martyr of the Lord, borne along with an honorific procession, was brought to the cell of Saint Serenus [Note: [Col. 0595D] Commonly called La Celle, now a priory near the abbey of Cantumerula [Col. 0596D], belonging to the Augustinian canons regular in the Briegian district. The matter is mentioned in the manuscript Life of Saint Serenus. There was also an abbey of Saint Serenus at Cahors, concerning which see the *Probationes* to the *Historia Torinensis*, in Justel, p. 5.]. A certain woman, bedridden and always looking toward the ground, never able to raise herself upright, had herself dragged to the church to meet him. As soon as she arrived, she straightened herself fully and, as though she had never suffered from a hunchback, appeared to all who were present restored and healthy through the martyr’s aid. Wonder and astonishment arose, especially among those who had known her before the previous day. Thus freed by wondrous power, she gave thanks to God and the saint and returned to her home.

## CHAPTER XXI

Among the frequent crowds hastening to the saint, a certain deaf, mute, maimed, and lame commoner was brought before the martyr. He had spent three days in this condition before the latter’s life-giving body. On the arrival of the fourth day, while he persevered in votive prayers, he experienced that he had been restored to favor [Col. 0596D] through the saint’s intercession. The deaf man earned back his hearing; the mute produced ready speech; the maimed man’s withered limb was changed into vigor; and the lame man extended his unsteady step into a firm one.

Having received complete health as testimony to his restoration, this man carried God’s most blessed martyr on his shoulders to the village of Calnomus. As he entered it, the renowned martyr restored the light of sight to two blind men, renewed the twisted feet of two lame men of equal number, and, with a speed that seemed invisible, compassionately enabled them to walk before everyone’s eyes, so that they might immediately become companions of his journey.

Thus the blind went ahead, needing no guide, and, cleaving the dense darkness, displayed to the astonished multitude new lights infused from heaven. With their withered nerves softened by divine medicine, and their foundations and soles strengthened, the lame, their strength restored, rejoiced that they were carrying burdens conducive to health.

The fame of these signs, by which the majesty of heaven glorified its saint, brought to him from every direction a devout crowd, eager to offer gifts. For from the whole province, noble and powerful men, distinguished matrons, and common people of every sort came rushing together. Each day they joyfully gazed upon the Lord’s magnificent works, such as they had never seen—and, to say more, had not heard of anywhere at all—and by gazing upon them were profitably nourished.

Thus gladly making their way, they reached the boundaries of the long-desired countryside. They established their station six miles from the city, until the entire army of the heavenly soldier could prepare to go out to meet him and attend upon the most glorious victor. Through him, that army would learn to undertake impregnable battles against the fiercest enemy, shielded itself by the armor of virtues, and, worthily honoring his holy wounds, win a crown and everlasting trophies.

## CHAPTER XXII

At that time the venerable bishop Rothadus the elder governed the church of the Suessiones; at his ecclesiastical summons the whole body of clergy and people advanced in ordered formation. Having discovered the place of repose, he went out to meet the saint. With every kind of sacred song and service [Col. 0597C] he surrounded the wonder-working body, embraced it with all his strength, cherished and venerated it, then solemnly carried it forth and transferred it joyfully into the city amid a vast crowd and festive celebration.

Every sex and age came out beyond the walls to meet him in an admirable spectacle. The joyful crowds enclosed the saint in their ranks, mingled with one another, offered votive gifts, and formed a splendid procession stretching without end. Everyone who could not take part in this most glorious reception considered himself profane.

While choirs sang in gentle melody and the gatherings of the people applauded, he was borne in a triumphal procession into the principal basilica of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Here a man visibly crippled and infirm, known to everyone, stood amid the crowds. He had lived for many years as a resident guest in that same city and, having heard the report of the saint, had happened to enter, unaware that the martyr of the Lord wished there to reveal in him the first signs of his powers.

As he stood amid the crowds pressing forward, he was suddenly shaken by invisible power and trembled all over. His deformed legs were transformed; he cast off his slow and nearly lifeless weakness; and with swift relaxation he extended his useless, bent knees. Without any delay, strength for walking grew firm. He rose nimbly before everyone, walked before the saint, and departed safe and joyful.

From there he was carried to the monastery of the holy Virgin Mary [Note: [Col. 0597D] Up to this point, the distinguished monastery of Benedictine nuns.]. He was magnificently received there. Such a multitude of people gathered that scarcely anyone could turn aside or even move. From there he was carried as far as the river Axona.

## CHAPTER XXIII

The splendid procession had already occupied the nearer banks of the river, as the force of love and the devotion of ineffable longing required. A devout assembly of monks, crowned with ecclesiastical ornaments, stood watching. Animated by unanimous devotion and universal services, they wished to offer fitting homage in receiving him who would remain forever their protector and patron.

As soon as they saw him approaching them to the beat of the rowers’ oars, they fell upon the ground and then rose to receive him with praises born of fervor. Choirs of singers surrounded him on every side, amid hymns and sweet-sounding instruments and the continual vapors of incense and various spices. Some carried glittering banners; others bore the sign of the cross, shining with yellow gold and gleaming with gems of many colors; some carried incense vessels and censers, others candle-bearing standards, increasing the day’s brightness with flashing light.

Borne swiftly in such triumph to the place prepared for him by divine providence and by divine gifts, he was set down beside the tomb of the glorious confessor of Christ, Medardus, while all sang these words in a matching melody:

“O gracious one, voices renowned in praise sound in harmony with your nobility; let us address you in humble supplication. Hail, renowned martyr, companion of the angels, associate of the apostles, fellow citizen of the prophets, and fellow heir with the martyrs, holy Sebastian: intercede for the salvation of us all.”

It was then Sunday (in the year 826) [Note: [Col. 0598D] Namely, the Second Sunday of Advent, on which a verse of this kind is customarily sung at the beginning of Mass.], and the antiphon for the Introit was entitled, with an appropriate melody: “People of Zion, behold, the Lord will come to save the nations.” In fitting song, that singular salvation of the Lord’s Incarnation—which was foretold in this passage as destined to come for all nations—poured salvation and joy upon all the peoples of Gaul through the arrival of this illustrious martyr; and, when sought in faith, through his intercession it grants temporal gifts and eternal rewards.

O day rich in such abundant praises, pregnant with such great joys! On it the imperial champion was carried into the city of the Suessiones; no day more joyful had dawned upon the world, nor had a happier one yet breathed forth.

## CHAPTER XXIV

After he had been set down with glory and fitting reverence, a certain girl, lame in both feet from her earliest childhood and known to nearly everyone [Col. 0598D], was dragged there by her parents and offered to the saint. She obtained restoration with such speed that, without a faltering step, she stood upright on firm feet before everyone, walked away in front of the saint, and returned to her family cheerful and healthy.

After a very short interval, while the bishop and clergy were engaged in the solemn rites of the sacred Masses, a certain weak man with withered knees was brought through the dense ranks before the saint. With his shins collapsed beneath him, he sat upon them; this was his customary seat. But the most merciful martyr, moved by his habitual compassion, also pitied him, loosened the rigidity of his parched nerves, restored him miserably afflicted, and granted him perfect health, while the people who witnessed this magnified the event. He had as many witnesses to his long-standing weakness as citizens from that city were able to press into the spectacle.

Without delay, behold, a woman, wretched and exceedingly pitiable, mentally deranged and deprived of the use of her tongue, was dragged forward bound with ropes. Her entire inner self had been abandoned to a beastlike condition; she knew no concern for what she was doing outwardly and, rushing about here and there in wandering excursions, made lascivious leaps among the crowds. Neither chains could restrain her from her purpose nor threats hold her back.

Her relatives, utterly worn out by their labor, presented such a person to the saint’s sight. The most merciful man of God did not disdain her. He looked upon her when she had been brought to him; by looking, he favored the tearful prayers of her lamenting relatives; he restored to her palate the use of speech that had been entirely removed, and not only reformed her understanding but also greatly increased it.

Joy mingled with fear. Everyone’s eager devotion toward his worship increased, and at last they humbly honored and venerated the majesty of God present there, blessed and praised it, and then returned cheerfully to their homes.

After the sacred rites had been completed, the dense multitude gathered from every direction saw a certain man entering who had been limping ever since his fall. But, to everyone’s astonishment, by the holy martyr’s absolution he immediately departed again on a sound foot.

## CHAPTER XXV

For the saints who, out of love for their Creator, handed over their own bodies to the most savage torments of suffering, no healing of infirmities is difficult. The more fiercely the harshness of torments raged against them, the more greatly the grace of spiritual gifts shone forth in them, so that, in accordance with the truthful promise of the Lord Christ, each person might receive a hundredfold what he had given, and star differ from star according to the quality of its light.

That this is accomplished in the dwellings above through God’s wondrous dispensation is clearly perceived from this: in these intermediate places also, where their mortal remains are preserved, they are glorified by the manifestation of signs, with rewards distributed according to their differing merits.

Among them was this most victorious warrior, more eminent than his fellow martyrs through the most noble trophies of his struggle and, after a first display of his own powers, still more magnificent in the abundance of his miracles. Through divine grace he attained such perfection that it is clear he merited every kind of healing.

Although all these things are wondrous, those are especially worthy of admiration which are more unusual and not granted to many. Therefore I shall recount one such case from among the many.

A certain matron suffering from a flow of blood came on the very day of his reception. She stood at the threshold of the basilica, conscious of her unceasing pollution and presuming herself unworthy to enter. Through the incessant discharge she had been drained of blood. The circuit of eight years had already passed in uninterrupted illness—without remission, recovery, or rest. At last she did not know what to do or where to turn.

Breathing frequent sighs and exhausted by the loss of blood, she could scarcely endure her severe anxieties with her weary limbs. It was exceedingly strange and most wondrous that, after so long a period, the woman’s wound was healed by the holy martyr’s divine medicine within the space of a single hour [Col. 0600A].

For as soon as, filled with hope, she approached him, just as she had been standing before the doors, the stream of corrupted blood that had been flowing continually stopped. The foul ulcer of her belly returned to its former natural state. There was no delay in her recovery once the heavenly physician had deigned to lay his hand upon her. At last not even a scar appeared from the illness; whatever had been painful or harmful vanished. A rosy color suddenly flowed back and covered her livid cheeks, revealing the joys of complete health.

It may be that she had heard from someone ignorant of the sacraments that she ought to observe the rule forbidding her to enter the temple or receive the Eucharist for as long as she remained in the uncleanness of this illness. But it must be understood that the suffering of corrupted nature is not a fault, nor is involuntary pollution punished by ecclesiastical censure with the same blow; it is the tiresome and unavoidable necessity of a natural affliction. The former is endured by a mind enticed through spontaneous consent; the latter was imposed as a penalty upon corrupted nature.

But since many do not know what the decrees of the canons think about this matter, I have judged it not inappropriate to insert here a decree on the same subject by the venerable Pope Gregory, in his response to Augustine. He says:

“Never, when a woman is suffering her monthly flow, should she be forbidden to enter the church, since this excess of nature cannot be counted against her as a fault. Because she suffers it unwillingly, it is not right that she be deprived of entry into the church.

“For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and her illness immediately departed from her. If, therefore, a woman placed in a flow of blood could laudably touch the Lord’s garments, why should a woman suffering her monthly blood not be permitted to enter the Lord’s church?

“But you say: That illness compelled the former woman to seek a remedy for her disease; therefore, the flow of a woman’s monthly blood is an illness. If healing was granted to that woman with the bloody flow, why should it not be granted to all women who are afflicted by a defect of their nature? They should not be forbidden to receive the mystery of holy Communion on those same days.”

After she had recovered complete strength, she cast aside the cloud of shame and first disclosed the matter to the church’s custodians; afterward she did not blush to confess the same thing to all the brothers [Col. 0600D]. Perhaps she had learned that divine teaching which says that it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God (Tobit 12:7).

The people applauded, offering the duties of thanksgiving to God with unanimous devotion and one mind. He had wondrously triumphed in his saint and had deigned to perform through him such great and marvelous deeds of power.

Thus the matron, rejoicing in the renewed health she had obtained, filled with joy the sorrowful home she had left when she returned to it, bringing gladness to her family and admiration to everyone.

## CHAPTER XXVI

As everyone led this day, made exceedingly rich by the restoration of so many, in a festive triumph of wholesome joy and sincere happiness, testimonies of royal authority—which must nowhere be rejected—were not lacking [Col. 0601A].

For the most distinguished Berta, sister of Louis Augustus [Note: [Col. 0601] This Berta had been the wife of Saint Angilbert. It is therefore clear that she survived into the year 826.], attended this remarkable spectacle. She did not cease to marvel at and magnify everything. At the bishop’s command, she approached the altar and stood before the saint for a long time. Making for herself a reliable tally of those who had been healed, she distinguished the circumstances of each, so that at a suitable time she could report them to her brother Augustus and to the leading men of his palace.

## CHAPTER XXVII

On the following day of the splendid station, while the lord bishop ascended the ambo during the sacred offices and poured forth the proclamations of the divine Word to the people who had assembled, teaching them thoroughly to love and desire the true light of the saints, behold, a certain blind woman was intent upon these things.

Through the priest’s ministry she immediately obtained not only illumination of the heart but also, through the martyr’s mercy, the bodily light she had lost. She saw, rejoiced, invoked the saint, adored him, and blessed him. Later, needing no guide, she hurried to his illustrious relics, so that, seeing with her body, she might compel those who were blind in mind, if any were present, to see also. At the same time, she caused them to reflect within themselves how possible it was for him to kindle spiritual lights inwardly who so easily restored them outwardly, and to demonstrate invisibly the invisible medicines by working through them wherever he wished.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Five miles from that monastery there is an estate to which ancient times gave the name Caprea (Chivres) [Col. 0601C]. On it lived a tenant farmer named Gislenteus, oppressed by the heavy burden of a hump. He always walked bent forward with a stooping gait and could scarcely look upon the sky.

By the persistence of agriculture he earned the alms necessary for human subsistence. Thus, on the aforementioned day of the proclaimed station, while everyone in the surrounding area celebrated the day with festive joy, he alone, wishing to carry out his customary tasks, hurried to the field with oxen yoked together, intending to perform the day’s work.

A neighbor met him and repeated that the bishop had proclaimed the day a holiday. He urged and admonished him to return home, celebrate the day with the others in festive observance, and pray through humble intercession that the saint might be his helper.

But the man paid no attention to the salutary advice given by his companion. He refused and, dull and foolish, replied in these words:

“Until now, by carrying out such tasks, I have painfully earned the alms by which I was supported as best I could. As for this saint, on whose observance you earnestly admonish me, I have neither heard anyone mention him nor owe him any acknowledgment of benefits, since I have received no good or evil from him. Therefore, since you advise me about this, I will not listen to you, nor will I desist from the work I have begun.”

When the day had passed, the rest of night came on. Behold, that wretched man, by the just consequence of his insolence, was miserably afflicted: his limbs and joints dried up and his whole body contracted into the shape of a ball, so that his legs clung to his thighs.

On the following night, the mouth with which he had spoken so obstinately was distorted into the shape of the letter X, with the jaws turned away on either side. This pitiable monstrosity became a spectacle for many when the second day dawned.

On the third night, when he was being violently afflicted with intolerable torment and lamented in whatever voice he could produce, he saw standing before him a person of splendid countenance and distinguished appearance. Asked what he was suffering, he gave the reason for so great a calamity and confessed that he had received the punishments he was enduring for his contempt of the saint.

The figure asked whether he wished thereafter to correct himself. The man then bound himself by oath, asserting that from that moment he would in no way remain incorrigible and that throughout his entire life he would perform no work on the feast of the aforementioned martyr.

No sooner had he spoken than he, who—as I said—had been contracted and almost crushed into the form of a little ball, recovered the strength to walk, his legs extending straight before him.

On that day, somewhat stronger, during the watches of the fourth night, the person who had appeared earlier asked whether he was feeling rather better. He replied that anyone could see that he was. The figure then said:

“Recover your health, rise, and hurry to the place where the solemnity of the martyr Sebastian is celebrated with festive joy. Make known to everyone both the punishment and severity with which you were chastised for your contempt of him and the wondrous mercy by which you were freed, so that by your example they may learn that this day must be kept perpetually as a solemn holiday in the recurring cycles of the years.”

Immediately, at the speaker’s command, health followed him. His distorted mouth returned to its proper state; nevertheless, he did not lose his hump until the end of his life.

Without delay he obeyed the command. He hurried to the place where a mixed multitude of people danced for joy and kept watch before the tomb of the holy martyr, and before all the brothers recounted what had happened to him because of his negligence.

After offering God, through the most sacred champion, heartfelt sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise for his restoration, having now been instructed by divine punishment, he returned joyfully to his familiar hut. He proclaimed to everyone who was pouring in from every direction for the saint’s funeral rites that no one could safely neglect to keep the solemn feast of his birth.

## CHAPTER XXIX

A certain letter-carrier of Count Rotfridus, whose name has indeed passed from memory, had lost the freedom to walk because he limped on both feet. He had also lost the ability to write because one hand had been afflicted with withering.

In this weakened condition he was carried by the hands of his relatives and placed before the saint. Without any intervening delay, his withered hand revived, he regained the use of the sense he had lost, and, his foundations strengthened, he immediately stood upright in his proper condition and recovered the power of walking.

O how ineffable and marvelous is the efficacy of divine action! There was no postponement of healing when the martyr’s aid was sought. For him, coming and obtaining health were one and the same thing.

Thus, having gained health throughout his body, he glorified God with praises, magnified the champion of the Lord, and returned on his own feet, whereas he had been carried there on the feet of others.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0603A]

He had not yet left the courtyard when, behold, a little woman followed. She displayed to everyone a withered hand, entirely drained of moisture, with only skin stretched over the bones; she also had a foot similarly shrunken and dry.

When she arrived, she immediately recovered strength, having experienced the martyr’s power. Her hand regained the work of spinning, and her foot the use of walking.

## CHAPTER XXXI

As she went out joyfully because she had obtained strength, a certain limping man was brought inside. After keeping vigil on the ground before the saint for three days, he merited healing through the martyr’s aid.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Gislebertus, count of the Suessiones [Note: [Col. 0603D] Andreas Chesnius did not know this Gislebertus. In Book IV, chapter 3, of the *Historia Castillionensis*, he says that the first count of the Suessiones whose memory survives was Guido, in the time of Lothair and Hugh Capet.], among the signs of virtue by which he excelled in upright character, regularly entrusted the proceeds of his almsgiving to Christ and placed them more securely for safekeeping in the treasuries of heaven.

It was his familiar practice during meals to care for the needy and weak whom he had chosen as the daily guests of his table, and to comfort them piously with what he deliberately withheld from himself.

At last, one of them, a man named Walcherus who had been weak in his feet for fifteen years, lay prostrate before the martyr’s life-giving body. In the very effort of prayer he immediately stood upright and healthy, divine mercy restoring him through the intercession of the illustrious martyr.

More people became praisers of God because of his marvelous recovery than had previously known of his weakness.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Immediately afterward a certain man named Eurulfus followed. His eyes had been condemned to darkness for five years. As soon as he arrived before the Holy of Holies under the direction of the procession, he perfectly regained, through divine illumination, the light he had lost. His sight was restored, and he gazed attentively upon the various colors of worldly things.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

On the following night the appropriate time for the morning assembly arrived. Behold, while we were sitting at the reading, a certain man named Baldegerus was brought in. For a cycle of nine years he had been held in the blind night of deprived pupils.

As was customary, the renowned martyr of the Lord took pity on him. Without any delay, he dispelled the darkness, reopened his eyes, and restored the ancient use of sight. He enabled him to gaze with uninjured eyes upon the sun’s radiance, which prolonged blindness had denied him.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Meanwhile, while the people present were held in astonishment at these miracles, a certain little boy named Tedelgisus was brought and placed before the saint by his parents. He had been lame from his earliest cries, and the venerable bishop Rothadus, already mentioned, was accustomed to care for him during meals.

He was as well known by face to all the townspeople and suburban inhabitants as by his weakness. As he lay beside the saint’s memorial [Col. 0604A], he was immediately raised upright and obtained the perfect health he had never before experienced. What nature had not granted him, he merited to obtain through the power of the Godhead, aided by the prerogatives of the illustrious martyr’s merits.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

It would be exceedingly long, and very difficult for any idle chatterer, to recount individually and personally all that divine power deigned to accomplish through his venerable merits in every kind of suffering and disease that affects the human condition, whether it comes originally through natural susceptibility to suffering or arises by chance.

When an innumerable multitude of people gathered from every region of the world, stirred by the fame of his virtues, such an immense population nonetheless flowed together from every part of Gaul and Germany and even from overseas provinces that it occupied the entire site, which was spread over a sufficiently broad area, like a swarm of locusts.

Among them were such vast numbers of blind, lame, withered, leprous, and possessed people, as well as lunatics and crowds impeded by every kind of weakness, that they seemed to exceed all reckoning.

In all these people, healings were displayed by divine will through the most blessed martyr as frequently as the crowds of those needing treatment were numerous. They were healed not only individually or personally, but also ten and twenty at a time and, so to speak, in herds. Thus, on the vigil of the holy and venerable confessor of Christ, Benedict the abbot, seventy-two people of mixed sex and age, afflicted with various weaknesses, were restored unharmed through the intercession of the wonder-working martyr.

The blind received a light they had never before experienced; the lame obtained a step they had not known.

Among those who came in devotion to experience his benefits, fear was mingled with excessive reverence for his worship. Many openly confessed their crimes; very many were visibly burning with invisible fire. But those whose minds were sounder took greater care not to enter the temple before cleansing their minds within by confession and penance and their bodies with water.

Finally, in the various forms of votive gifts offered by the faithful from different provinces and regions in devotion to the confession of this most distinguished saint, there was such an immense abundance that it seemed almost to exceed every reckoning of weight and number. The heap of silver coinage alone amounted to eighty-five modii, apart from necklaces of men and women, dishes of various weights, and other vessels. The quantity of gold amounted to nine hundred pounds.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

But because envy always accompanies every good thing close at hand, many priests began to burn with the rust of jealousy. They forbade the peoples entrusted to them to hasten to the patronage of the saint, which had been increasingly experienced throughout the world, and to carry their vows to his illustrious relics.

They said that it would be more proper for the churches in which the people had received the gift of baptism and faith to be enriched by these offerings, and for their widows and orphans to be nourished by them. It was not right, they said, that they should be in need while others grew rich; that they should strip themselves while others clothed themselves.

The rust of this resentment grew so great that it infected even the hearts of certain bishops. Among them was Ostroldus, who presided at Lugdunum at that time [Note: [Col. 0605D] That is, Clavus, a city which others call Laudunum, commonly Laon.]. When he had climbed the pulpit to speak to the people about this matter, and after preaching to them at length, he began:

“What,” he said, “are you seeking by wandering throughout Suessionis, as though you would find the martyr Sebastian there? Know for certain that he was buried long ago at Rome after his initial offering and that he still lies there, moved by no one. Here you have the venerable temple of the Mother of God. Frequent it; in it make and fulfill your vows. You have no need to wander elsewhere or seek foreign assistance. Through her, whatever you faithfully ask will all be granted by the Lord.”

After he had addressed the people at length, each returned home. He himself, taking his pleasure in the day and quickly driving away the nearby sorrow that was about to befall him, brought the day to its close. When night came, the bishop, having eaten, went to bed.

When his limbs had relaxed in sleep and the time of silence was already pressing on, behold, a certain youthful man, displaying the elegant form [Note: [Col. 0606D] A Greek name, εὔ and ῥυθμός, here signifying elegant form.] of the lord Sebastian, stood before his bed, with two men beside him, one on his right and one on his left, both shining with similar brilliance and crowned with episcopal ornaments. He himself was wrapped in a military cloak and carried a golden staff in his hand.

After striking the bishop and calling him by name, he addressed him in rebuke:

“I,” he said, “am Sebastian, defender of the Church. Long ago I suffered death at Rome for the love of Christ, where I have lain buried in body until now. But now, by God’s predestination, because of the love of Medardus, bishop of Noviomagus, whom you see standing on the left, I and this man on the right, Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, have been sent to Suessionis, so that we may protect that place and its inhabitants by our patronage and, by protecting them, foster them.

“But yesterday, driven by jealousy, you acted insolently against me, turning away the people entrusted to you so that, going to confess my name, they would not bring their vows in my service to me. Moreover, you falsely declared that my bodily remains were not present there at all.

“But so that every doubt may be driven from your mind, learn through these blows that I lie there, as you now see me, deposited without any diminution of my body beside the tomb of Christ’s confessor Medardus.”

Having said this, he struck him with the staff he held, administering many blows, and commanded:

“Go to Suessionis walking barefoot, and openly display to everyone the marks of the blows I have inflicted upon you, so that all may know that I am present there bodily, that I preside there with spiritual power, and that I benefit not only the inhabitants of that place but all the peoples of Gaul who faithfully cling to my King and my Lord and who render worthy service to me and to my companions, the patrons of that place.”

After these words, he and his companions sought the joys of heaven.

The bishop, sleepless from the pain of the blows and from shame, anxiously awaited the return of daylight, hoping it would come quickly. When daylight was restored to mortals, he summoned his fellow clergy and necessary friends, disclosed the vision, and uncovered the swollen and bruised marks of the blows.

They, greatly anxious and disturbed, urged him to hasten the execution of what had been divinely commanded. The journey was therefore arranged, and gifts to be carried to the illustrious martyr were prepared.

A singing company slowly followed their barefoot leader with hymns until they reached the place where a great crowd of people kept vigil before the martyr’s tomb. Having laid aside all pride and cast their eyes deeply down toward the ground in shame, he fell prostrate on his face with as much humility as the divine severity had seized him.

His prayer continued for a long time; groans and sighs came forth from the depths of his heart. When the prayer had been completed, his supplication was commended by the leading men of the place in a fitting chapter. Then conciliatory vows were offered, and afterward a noble assembly of brothers was summoned.

He confessed his offense, displayed the correction that had followed from the divine judgment, and promised that throughout his entire life his devotion toward the most blessed martyr would remain more fervent.

Thus, now better instructed by divine punishment, the man of God, purer in mind and stronger in body, gratefully returned to the lofty heights of the see of Lugdunum.

The outcome of this affair became all the more widely known because the dignity of the person was all the more famous, and because, having occurred openly in the sun at a place situated on high ground, it could not be hidden under a bushel.

Therefore the venerable man, the aforementioned bishop Ostroldus, made teachable and well instructed by the excellent teacher, began freely to teach both privately and publicly that no one would be immune from divine blows and that no one could safely treat as worthless the practice of honoring the memory of the martyr Sebastian.

Thus the envy of many yielded, defeated by the martyr’s virtues, and through the skin of one body the venom of envy was drawn out from the hearts of many with such malignity.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0606D]

In the province of Aquitaine, in the district of Auvergne, at the village of Tudurnum, there is a monastery consecrated to the merits and name of this most excellent martyr. The circumstances of its original foundation are reported truthfully as follows.

There was in that same region a priest remarkable for the uprightness of his character, Magnus by both action and name. Because of an event that happened to him—not by chance, but by divine command—he gave the place its name, so that it was called and became Magnus-Locus (“Great Place”); for to this day it is considered the most famous and distinguished of all the monasteries of that province.

While he was burning with the fervor of faith and increasing in the devout love of virtue and in spiritual eagerness, he was seized, by the ordering of divine providence—which chastises everyone whom God loves—with a severe fever. As his prolonged illness grew worse, his strength failed and every hope of recovery had deserted him. Then, in a vision, he was instructed to hasten to Rome, confidently seek the most precious mausoleum of the martyr Sebastian, and learned through that truthful vision that he would there be generously healed.

Immediately, having been restored to somewhat better health, he did not hesitate concerning the outcome of the vision. He arranged his modest means in view of the difficulty of a long journey, took what was necessary at the proper time, and, humble and submissive, undertook the arduous labor of so great a journey, his heart breathing with devout dedication.

[Note: [Col. 0607D] In some manuscripts *Opogorico* or *Opporico* is wrongly read for *Hodoeporico*, that is, ὁδειπορικόν, “a travel account” or itinerary.]

Although the journey was completed with difficulty, he at last entered Rome, mistress of the world, according to his long-desired prayer. Climbing the church holier and more famous than any other throughout the world, he entrusted his offenses from the depths of his heart to God through the supreme consuls of the heavenly court, making a very full confession in prayer.

Then, after visiting the tombs of Christ’s martyrs—whose multitude and victories give the Roman city its unique privilege of rejoicing—he came to the catacombs, three miles from the city.
