He entered the church in which the blessed apostles Peter and Paul had once been buried, and at whose feet this most victorious warrior, the subject of our account, had arranged to be buried. There he remained for a long time prostrate in votive prayer.

Then, rising from prayer, he displayed a perfect recovery, restored to such robust health as though he had never been afflicted by the burning of a fever or by the torment of any illness. Afterwards, as I believe, enlightened by divine inspiration, he wiped up the dust that lay around the martyr’s tomb and collected it with the utmost devotion of faith. He placed it with him, intending to carry it home as a great treasure.

After saluting the blessed apostles and all the saints who illumined the Roman city by their merits and presence, he returned joyfully to his native soil of Aquitaine. Once he had entered it, before visiting his familiar home, he came to a certain place made especially delightful by the flowing of its waters and the beauty of its woods. Since the place pleased the eyes, and the growing lateness of the hour, together with the fatigue of slow travel, advised that their bodies be refreshed, they set down their baggage and allowed themselves a meal.

Meanwhile, as the sun declined, the rest of night entered upon them, kindly and inviting with gentle sleep. The priest took the sacred dust that he had carried with him from around his neck, hung it from a branch of the tree beneath whose shade he had reclined, and then went to bed somewhat early, intending to depart earlier the following day.

At first light on the next day, wishing to gather his baggage and return to the road, he laid his hands upon the branch of the tree from which the miraculous dust was hanging. Stretching out his arms with all his strength, he was unable not only to take it, but even to touch it. He tried again and again to loosen it, placing beneath it whatever his feet could reach from the ground; but, his effort frustrated, he stopped.

As the attempts continued, his companions clung to the little tree and labored in vain, sweating from their exertion. News of so great a spectacle flew out and summoned the neighboring villagers. Crowds of every sort gathered from all directions, and, trying the same thing in turn, proved by experience what they had learned by hearsay. They set down their baggage and spent that day hesitating between the desire to remain and the desire to depart. The newcomers, taking turns, exhausted their astonished arms in foolish and futile effort.

From every direction people afflicted with various illnesses gathered. Through the merits of its martyr, divine power performed every kind of miraculous sign: it gave sight to the blind and movement to the lame; it cleansed others possessed by a savage demon; and to some, after removing the harmful impediment, it restored the natural power of hearing and speech.

Meanwhile, the owner of the estate where these things were taking place, seeing such marvelous and astonishing divine sacraments being performed in his own domain, summoned an official notary and, by a legally executed conveyance, assigned the property to the saint, to be possessed perpetually by sacred right.

Thus, as the days passed, both the religious observance and the site itself increased through the generosity of the faithful. At first a small oratory was built there; eventually, as the devotion of the faithful grew, a monastery was established, and by episcopal blessing it was consecrated in honor and under the name of Christ’s most precious martyr, Sebastian. The order of monastic religion was also instituted there under the governance of an abbot.

[Note: This monastery still survives among the Auvergnats. It is described in the Acts of Saint Bonitus, in the first part of the third century.]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

As time advanced and the same place continued to grow in the rigor of monastic discipline, there were in that monastery two pseudo-monks beneath the sheep’s fleece. They disagreed with the sheep of the Lord’s fold, among whom they had been raised, by the obscenity of their character. Often rebuked, admonished, and corrected by the abbot or prior, they turned away the ear of their hearts with insolent restlessness and would not yield in any way to salutary warnings.

Therefore, in accordance with the ordinances of sacred law, lest diseased sheep should infect the whole flock, they were threatened with expulsion from the body of the sacred community through a severe denunciation. When they learned this, they secretly carried away from the monastery whatever they could seize in the dead of night and escaped by flight. Forgetful of the ruin of both their undertakings—their own and, through it, that of their souls—they wandered uncertainly wherever their own desire enticed them.

Finally, seeing Italy as a suitable hiding place for men of their sort, they hastened there, having discarded their clothing lest anyone recognize them. When they had found a respectable place for their pilgrimage and had satisfied the madness of their desires, they remembered the peaceful vows and intimate security they had enjoyed in the monastery. Worn out by the tedium and labor of their disordered exile, they began to consider a return, if there could be hope of being received again, and said to one another that this could become a gain for them.

But the shame of their confusion, proportionate to the nature of their offense, entirely held back their advance. While they were suspended between hope and fear, a plan seemed useful to them: they would conceal their crime, return to their own place with an increase of honor, and, to do so, extend their journey still farther, go to Rome, and purchase some saint whose transportation might win them pardon and favor among their own people.

Animated by this scheme—which they thought had been sent to them from heaven—the wandering Aquitanians, trusting in their wicked deception, arrived to converse with the crafty Romans. They sought out a venerable bishop and senators clothed in the toga, and, in accordance with Solomon’s judgment, carefully looked for men like themselves.

The wicked were quickly joined to the worse, the more depraved to the more depraved. During their alternating and foolish conversations, they were asked about their race and homeland, and they disclosed them. They were then questioned about the reason that had brought them from such distant lands, about why they had chosen to come there, and about the many and great dangers they had endured. The Romans investigated everything with artful sympathy, as though they shared their distress.

The two men revealed their plan and humbly begged that a helping hand be given them in carrying it out. They asserted that they had built a monastery in their region and declared that it was entirely in need of the relics of saints.

The crafty Romans boasted that several important relics were in their custody, entrusted to them by the supreme pontiff himself, and that they could bestow them at will upon anyone they chose. The two men said that they wished to obtain one for money, if the matter could be brought to completion.

The Romans then promised that they would obtain what the two desired, provided that they put faith in their words, and asked which saint they most wanted. They named the martyr Sebastian, swearing that they would bring from their homeland everything they presently possessed for his sake, and much more afterwards, both in greater quantity and of greater value.

Enticed by these promises, the Romans pretended that they necessarily had to determine a suitable time, so that they would not be identified. Once they had found one, they promised to display the relic at the same place in the darkness of night, stipulating that the two men should also be present there.

Meanwhile, while they cunningly devised what fraudulent plan to carry out during the interval, they remembered that in a nearby marketplace there was a sarcophagus belonging to a certain Caesar, filled with a lavish coating of spices. At last the appointed hour arrived.

Before the proper time, the Romans encountered the two men, who were hastening forward, burning impatiently with desire for the object of their vow, while the Romans themselves were eager for profit. They signaled them to be silent and proceeded cautiously to the tomb of that little man who had not experienced Christian rebirth.

If they wanted to see and obtain the martyr they sought, they ordered them to produce and hand over the money they had promised. Then, having removed the lid of the sarcophagus, they showed them the face of a man, fragrant with wondrously powerful amber—commonly called *ambre*.

When the two saw this, they immediately fell upon their knees and tearfully invoked the man for their aid. Having entirely banished every suspicion from their hearts, and believing the Romans completely, as though they were guardians of sacred things, they gave away, with the utmost readiness, whatever they possessed among their belongings, deceived by such a trick.

Then, with as much solemnity as they knew or could provide, they received—not the man whom France boasts of having obtained through a heavenly gift as its excellent defender and unconquerable protector, but a tyrant who was not even worthy, by his own merit, of the mere title of martyr. Exulting with all the fibers of their hearts in an empty hope and heedless of the ruin awaiting them, they returned home at a swift pace. While they imagined that excellent rewards awaited them, they were so disastrously blinded that they could not see the punishments soon to follow.

Before they reached the long-desired borders of their homeland, they prudently sent messengers ahead to announce the arrival of the beloved and ever-honored holy martyr Sebastian and to encourage all the eminent people to take part in welcoming him. They selected a place worthy of so great a spectacle and generously made known the day on which they should hasten to meet him.

The abbot of the venerable place and the pale-faced company of the brothers, having forgotten the crimes of those who had once been their brothers, rejoiced that through them so great a good had been accomplished by that supreme Good. They proclaimed that the two men were happier after their fall and, by unanimous favor, prejudged them to be more eminent within their community.

They unfurled the banners of the cross, brought out trophies and splendid reliquaries—alas, what a grievous exchange they were soon to receive in return! Crowds summoned everywhere by this sweet-sounding report came rushing joyfully to meet them. Commoners and nobles alike, and the powerful of nearly the whole nation, inflamed by religious fervor, went out eagerly, carrying with them the hopes they had formed.

What more need be said? At last they received, not the glorious martyr of Christ, but a savage minion of Antichrist; not that most famous standard-bearer of the first Roman legion, but Satan’s dearest servant, a minister among the pebbles of Cocytus. With great glory of hymns they carried him, alas for the impiety, all the way to the sacred altars.

They celebrated festive rejoicing, soon to be disfigured by mournful lamentation, and marked it for solemn annual commemoration—though it was destined ultimately to come to an end.

After many offices of Masses and hymns, the weary company of brothers proceeded to the inner rooms of the refectory to dine at a more lavish meal. During the meal, every form of hospitality was displayed and multiplied their joy abundantly; but a very near and utterly impious confusion soon overturned it.

For while they indulged too freely in food and wine, those two men who had brought that sacrilegious relic out of Rome, by order of their abbot, sat with the others to guard the church, lest even a small amount of the lamp oil should fail. Then, by divine will, the one who had miserably usurped the worship belonging to that beloved soldier was thrown from the divine holy altar and fell onto the pavement amid a horrible crash and whirlwind.

He fell again and again, colliding with the walls now on this side, now on that; he was tossed sometimes downward and sometimes upward, battered, crushed, and broken into pieces. [Note: [Col. 0609] Thus in ancient writers *josum* or *jusum* means “downward,” as Bollandus proves from Augustine, and Vossius in book II of *On Faults of Speech*.] He lost, amid the mockery and disgrace of the filthy embalmers who had brought him from there, the name and honors of a martyr that he had falsely presumed to claim, and was destroyed from human hearing.

One of the perpetrators of the crime was made savage in spirit, the other empty in mind; nevertheless, both displayed by the gestures of their bodies what they had done. All the others who were present and who had sought the martyr’s intercession and miraculous works were struck by an unexpected and unprecedented terror and hurried away, scarcely alive.

They rushed through the hall where the diners were eating, crying out in frenzied voices for help and assistance:

“Alas, Fathers and lords, rise, hurry, come to our aid! Behold a crime such as the world has nowhere seen!”

“What shame! An everlasting reproach and a blush of confusion that can never be erased! The devil himself has been brought here today in the form of a tyrant!”

Throwing down whatever they had in their hands, the diners leapt from the tables amid a mighty uproar and, arming themselves eagerly with the sign and power of the holy cross, entered the church. The neighboring people who had been held back by affection also came together, running from every direction.

What need is there to recount more? A sudden and unexpected mourning overtook such sudden and unsuspected joy. They saw close at hand the corpse of that most wicked and miserable man, fallen upon the pavement and torn apart piece by piece. They grieved that, in a moment of time, they had lost the joy they had imagined would last forever.

A confused outcry arose, and everyone was stunned with amazement. A great gathering of the crowd roared against the authors of the crime. Some shouted that the sacrilegious men should be stoned; others, that they should be hanged on the gallows; still others, attacking them with abusive speech, proclaimed that they should be burned or punished by some other more terrible death.

But those whose hearts were teachable and whose minds were more sincere declared that men whom they clearly saw to have already been punished by the judgment of divine severity could not properly be condemned by human judgment.

Meanwhile, the fragments of the dismembered corpse of that unfortunate man were collected and thrown into a dung heap, the foulest refuse of the populace. They were buried, trampled underfoot, and cursed with a final and perpetual anathema. The pavements were scraped with rakes, washed with water, and purified by the water of sacred sprinkling.

## CHAPTER XL

It is useful to compare this event with an ancient occurrence of the same kind, which happened among the people of Acharon, whose god was Astaroth, as the history of Kings reports. Unable to tolerate the Ark of God, which had been placed in the entrance of his temple, dwelling in the same house with him, their god was shaken by a certain overwhelming divine power and fell to the ground. His skull and hands were severed on the threshold of the idol, while his headless trunk remained pierced through in its place as it was, leaving his worshipers a perpetual reproach.

Yet the matter is perceived to have happened very differently among those whose faith in God was sincere and whose service, though less instructed and therefore badly deceived, was nevertheless wholehearted. For the Philistines, it was for vengeance and punishment; for these others, it served to strengthen and confirm their faith and religion, so that they would not too easily give assent to uncertain things, nor dare to call any mortal holy before testing him. In accordance with the teachings of the Lord, when people say, “Behold, God is here,” or “Behold, he is there,” they should refuse to believe, lest, by admitting an opportunity for diabolical deception and neglecting the worship of their Creator, they should somehow offend through idolatry.

## CHAPTER XLI

Before a long interval had passed, the most blessed martyr Sebastian, worthy of praise in every respect, was honorably brought to the city of Suessa and received with great rejoicing. As the report of his wonders and signs grew, people even came from the remotest borders of Thule (*Tila*) to seek his fragrant relics.

When the abbot of the aforementioned monastery—the one about whom our account has been speaking—heard this, he was filled with joy. He admonished and encouraged his men to hasten there, offering himself as their leader and guide on the journey, so that, since they could not obtain the whole, they might at least deserve to receive some small part of it in its entirety.

When they arrived, they were received according to custom by the prior Rodoinus and the brothers, who treated them with great kindness. They tearfully explained the reason for their journey and the great burden they had undertaken. They confessed that they were unworthy to obtain the gift they sought; but, because they belonged to the same order and wished to appeal to the brotherly affection that specially blessed them, they asked that their hope and devotion be considered.

“Long ago,” they said, “conscript Fathers, two men from among us went to Rome for the sake of this patron whom, by God’s favor, you now possess. What more need be said? Paying a hidden price, they purchased a certain tyrant whose name we do not know. They brought this miserable man to us, and with him the devil as well.

“He was solemnly received by us, but, to speak as the truth permits, he was cast down in a wondrous manner because God was angered. For, unaware of the sacred Virgin Mary, we placed him upon the altar and adorned him festively. Then, when we had sat down to dine with many who had gathered, he was suddenly lifted from the altar through the air, hurled to the ground, and fell with a terrible shriek. He inspired extreme horror in those who remained in the basilica and drove them, terrified and agitated, from the church.

“When they came to us pale and almost lifeless, they began, in the presence of the whole assembly, to disclose what had happened to them, shouting in the most dreadful voices like madmen. Although we were ignorant of what had happened and signaled them to be silent, they did not yield to our commands. Instead, as they had begun, they irreverently continued to proclaim aloud the public disgrace in loud voices.

“We entered the church at a swift pace and saw him, shaken into pieces, his limbs scattered, precisely as he was—such as he was and however great he was—fitting to our deeds. Because of this report we are marked everywhere, attacked with unbearable reproach, and covered with shame. Therefore, so that we may at last be rid of this disgrace, we flee to your venerable fatherhood. It remains only for your blessedness not to disdain compassion for and assistance to our abandonment.

“For we believe that we shall lay down the burden of our shame if, through your charity, we obtain even a small portion of his relics.”

When he heard this, Rodoinus, moved by brotherly affection, sympathized with and shared their grief. With the permission of Father Hilduin and the agreement of the brothers, he promised to provide assistance. The matter was first reported before the brothers, and they did not reject the request; indeed, they said that they greatly desired the saint’s worship and memorial to increase.

When this had again been reported to the lord abbot, and he too had received the brothers’ petition, he ordered that a linen cloth be given to them through the intercession of the venerable bishop Rothad. The living members of the martyr had been wrapped in this cloth.

[Note: That is, monastic. For the monks did not yet know the distinctive names of the various monastic orders; all of them in those regions were then serving under the Rule of Saint Benedict. The Fathers of the Council of Soissons, held in the monastery of Saint Medard in 853, speak in the same way when, in chapter 5, they order that the two monks who had assisted Pippin in his flight be confined in monasteries of their own order—that is, to exclude the monasteries of clerics or canons.]

When they were assisting with the task and brought out the linen cloth from the reliquary to give it to those who requested it, the visitors became inflamed with anger and said that they had asked for the saint’s relics, not linen cloths, of which they had an abundance in their own region.

The surrounding brothers insisted that it was no other cloth than the one with which his most holy body had been covered from Rome all the way to that place, but there was no way to persuade them to receive it.

“You have heard, Fathers and lords,” they said, “of our disgrace, now known throughout the whole world, which we thought your kindness would wipe away. Why are you trying to renew our dishonor? With your favor, let us return to our homeland unencumbered, without suffering ridicule a second time, just as we came.”

When Rodoinus saw that their spirits had been stirred against him, and was not particularly concerned to offer further explanation, he carefully folded the cloth and put it back into its chest. He said that he would not treat his lord’s garments with such contempt, and added that they ought rather to be given to others whose faith was stronger in their hearts.

The visitors remained there that day. Seeing that they had accomplished nothing by this course of action, they were moved to repentance. They summoned the elders and humbly begged them to act as fathers and intercessors for them before the man, so that they would not be permitted to return from that holy place so sad and empty-handed.

Rodoinus, moved by the prayers of his own people, ordered that not the whole cloth, as before, but a portion cut by priestly hands should be given to them. They received it with much greater gratitude than before, accepting it with devout acts of faith and placing it honorably in a carefully prepared chapel. After Masses had been solemnly celebrated in the martyr’s name, they were escorted home with religious hymns by a company of brothers.

When they arrived, they placed the relics, which had been glorified by the grace of many virtues and healings, in the hall, relying upon the merits and name of that preeminent one. There, to this day, his glorious merits remain active, and the palm of his virtues flourishes in many ways, more abundantly and magnificently than in the place where his wonder-working body is frequented with the proper devotion of faithful peoples.

Therefore, we desire that his beneficial patronage belong both to us and to them, since through the generosity of our fathers we have deserved to share in so great a relic.

## CHAPTER XLII

We have seen men of no contemptible character who declared that they had learned from those who heard it of the future destruction of the city of Suessa, which we fear.

There was in that same city a little tower facing the western regions of the east. Upon it, when dawn had already begun to scatter the dark shadows of night, an ambiguous spirit uttered three repetitions of a terrible sentence, saying:

“Woe, woe, woe to you, Suessa! Like Sodom and Gomorrah of old, you will be burned with powerful flames of fire and reduced to empty ashes of cinders!”

The unseen person, known to no one, having fulfilled the mystery of his office, disappeared with a celebrated gesture into the thin air.

Those who at that time were able to remain awake before daybreak, as we have said, heard this deadly voice resounding terribly—not only the townspeople within the city itself, but also those living in the suburbs in every direction. Its fame flew from region to region and became widely known to everyone.

I heard this account from many people who survived into our own times, and who related it consistently without any suspicion of falsehood. I judged it right to append it to this work as a correction to all who inhabit that city, especially those who are not afraid to defile themselves with the most shameful and unnatural crime.

Our own Fathers and predecessors, who told us these things, attributed this very fact to the merits and intercession of our most devout protector: they observed that it had by no means been fulfilled in their own time.

[Note: Nevertheless, in the Chronicle of Tours, in the account of the deeds of the Northmen at Chesny, it is stated that in the year 855 the Danes or Northmen destroyed and burned Saint Quentin, the city of Soissons, and Paris with the adjacent territory. Was this portent fulfilled later?]

They also added that, before he was brought from Rome, horrible illusions of evil spirits had often been devised against the citizens in the streets and houses. But when he came, the vapor vanished like smoke; everything was quiet and orderly through his benefit and was placed at the service of human well-being by peaceful attendance.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Furthermore, the very generous execution of his plan revealed what sort and degree of devotion the memorable Emperor Chlodovic had toward the saint.

When he learned that miracles were being performed there through the unbounded presence of the divine power by means of Christ’s martyr, he removed his royal purple and threw away his shoes almost three miles from the place. Then, together with his wife, he proceeded barefoot to the monastery where the martyr had already been installed.

The Empress Judith had heard that certain wicked persons, under a force that could not be stifled, had exposed their crimes in a public assembly and that, consumed inwardly by the burning heat of hatred, they had been openly burned outwardly by the terribly fearful ordeal of fire. This had happened because, before they came to the place, they had neglected to restrain the impulses of their sins through the appropriate remedies of confession and penance.

Overwhelmed by storms of great anxiety, and having learned beforehand that the Emperor intended to travel there, she realized that she could not separate herself from him without shame. She therefore turned entirely to the merciful power of the Redeemer. Confessing the burden of her sins through the secret ministry of the venerable priests, she prayed with the Psalmist that she might be cleansed from her hidden faults and absolved from those of others.

Meanwhile, during the interval she had foreseen, she devoted herself without delay to almsgiving and to the performance of other good works. Thus, having become the devout companion of his majesty, she hastened to the shrine of the holy martyr, distinguished by extraordinary merits.

When the most reverend Abbot Hilduin and the richly adorned company of the brothers rose to meet such exalted visitors, came out in festive procession to await their arrival before the doors, and finally led them, once they had been received, to the martyr’s tomb amid the ringing of melodious voices, the emperor and empress, wearing humble clothing, fell prostrate upon the ground before they reached the edge of the altar. With a great company of nobles laying their cloaks beneath them, they poured forth before the universal Lord prayers full of groans and wet with the dew of tears, recalling the merits of the martyr himself and invoking him as their devout intercessor.

Then, rising from prayer, their prayer was commended in a suitable verse, according to the desire of all who were present. After this they entered the hall prepared for such exalted guests, put on imperial and otherwise more splendid garments, and adorned themselves with the diadem.

The emperor then mounted the sanctuary and had the solemn Mass celebrated in honor of the martyr. When the Gospel was reached, he held in his own hands while it was being read a very heavy golden chalice with a paten marked by the monogram of his father, Charles the Great, and dedicated it with the offering to be consecrated.

[Note: A monogram is a sign or name proper to someone, written continuously in a single movement of the letters. Charles the Great appears to have been the first of our kings to use this form of writing.]

After the solemn celebration was completed, he and his wife also approached the martyr’s feet. There, after commending themselves to God through the saint in an extended prayer, they removed their royal adornments one piece at a time, from the crown down to the under-tunic, in an all-embracing act of devotion intended to be remembered throughout every age. Each of them deposited these garments there before the martyr.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] This book is preserved in that monastery to this day, though now covered only with silver plates, which Abbot Ingrannus caused to be made, with this inscription: “This plate was made by Lord Ingrannus, abbot of this place, in the year 1168, the tenth of Alexander III and the twenty-third of the reign of Louis the Younger.” The book itself, however, was offered by Emperor Louis to Blessed Sebastian at the reception of that renowned martyr and of Pope Gregory of the city of Rome.]

Then he offered a copy of the sacred Gospels written in golden letters and enclosed in plates of the same metal, without the admixture of any other material; a thurible weighing forty-eight *sycli* of the same substance; and a large amphora of oil for preparing the lamps, all with the readiest generosity of mind.

He also placed under the saint’s perpetual service the public mint, together with its dies and money-changers, to serve his sacred purposes forever.

[Note: Thus it is clear that the right of striking coinage was granted, a right that was also granted to several monasteries of our order. Claudius Dormay displays some specimens of this coinage at the beginning of the second part of his History of Soissons.]

He also gave, for the construction of the church, the abbey of the protomartyr Stephen at Cauciacum, which is said to contain seven hundred households. By a royal command, strengthened by an oath and the binding of an anathema, he confirmed it with the impression of his ring, so that it might not be seized by any rash person.

[Note: The monastery of Cauciacum, commonly called Choisy, lies somewhat above Compiègne, near the confluence of the Aisne with the Oise, and is distinguished by the burial there of Childebert III. It is now a priory subject to the Abbey of Saint Medard. This monastery and its abbot Bettolenus are mentioned in the Life of Saint Drausius, bishop of Soissons.]

When he visited the monastery repeatedly, he later added such great increase to his original devotion that, one day, as he was going to pray at the chapel of Saint Sophia, which was attached to the palace, he stopped at the threshold. Looking at it from outside, he immediately sang, leaning upon a staff of gleaming gold, the verse of David that he yearned to fulfill in building the Lord’s tabernacle:

“This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it” (Psalm 131:14).

[Note: Some remains of the walls of this chapel still survive, as does the college of canons of Saint Sophia. It is said that the killing of Walter of Ivetot was committed in its oratory; Guaguin was the first to assert that it had been carried out by Chlothar I. A brief chronicle of the monastery says that the church of Saint Sophia at Saint Medard was dedicated by Bishop Arnulf in the year 1142.]

[Note: From this it is clear that the king’s palace was attached to the monastery. The place near the oratory of Saint Sophia still retains its name. It was so called in imitation of the imperial basilica of the same name at Constantinople. Pope Leo IV stayed in that palace for several days in 804, according to the Annals of Metz; in 843 Charles the Bald honorably received the envoys of Pope Nicholas at the monastery itself, and there King Louis celebrated Christmas in 878, according to the Annals of Bertin.]

Wonderful to relate, as though these words had been heard by the martyr standing nearby, that very same evening the splendid trophies of the signs of the great victor appeared. For before he had decided to go to bed, he was granted the privilege of seeing eighteen healings of both sexes, performed during that single night.

The eyes of some, their darkness driven away, shone with the radiance of gleaming light. The hooked hands and withered arms of others were loosened. Their powerless calves and twisted feet were stretched out more straightly, with strength not merely restored but increased. The ears of some, which had flowed with blood and which prolonged deafness had condemned, were shown to be entirely clear by the gentle and faint sound they now perceived. In one person, a most evil malignant spirit was powerfully conquered and expelled. The spots of leprosy were removed, and minds raging in ignorance were properly changed.

After enjoying these gifts according to his desire, and feeling no movement of unbelief in his heart, the emperor carefully vowed that he would preserve for the future his supreme and incomparable love for the holy martyr.

Multiplying his unutterable groans and sighs, sprinkled with showers of tears, he cultivated, venerated, and entreated the martyr as though he saw him present in the flesh. Because he believed without hesitation that the martyr could grant him what he requested, he obtained his desire and received it beneficially.

But what it was that, as we have already said, he asked of him, the following account—or rather, that same account in its most secret part—will reveal.

“Having broken the strength of my once-powerful arm, I, Louis, Caesar, Emperor Augustus, by the dispensation of God’s grace ruling the Roman world, after I had relaxed the reins of authority over the peoples too immoderately, found that certain disorderly men, by attacking our clemency, burst forth into the cruelty of unbelief. This evil grew so fierce [Col. 0617B] that they even compelled my own beloved sons to rage against me and made them deliberate with themselves about the death of their father. By chance we came to a place which, because of the outcome of the broken pledge of peace and the broken oaths, has from that time been called the Field of Lies.

[Note: Theganus, in chapter 42, calls it the Great Field, which lies between Argentaria and Basel and is still called the Field of Lies, because the loyalty of many was extinguished there. On this matter, see the Anonymous author in the book *On the Life of Louis Augustus* under the year 833, and Book II of *The Deeds of Abbot Wala* below.]

Here almost the whole body of my soldiers deserted me; and, as I have reported, that rebellion involved my sons in a dreadful crime and chose them as the authors of the wicked deed, imputing to me, though innocent, many offenses worthy of death. Though I had been repeatedly injured and deceived by those whom I had never injured, and though I did not forget my own wicked deeds, remembering that by God’s most just judgment I deservedly suffered these things, I bore the disaster with equanimity.

Then, surrounded by a hostile troop, I was brought to the city of Soissons and to the monastery of my holy lords. Since they knew that I loved that place very much, they planned that I might perhaps, after despairing, lay down my arms voluntarily there. When they had confined me under public guard in order to complete by action what they had craftily planned, they sent certain men to announce to me that my wife had become a consecrated nun in a monastery of virgins—or, as they had heard more truly, that she was dead.

[Note: Judith, of course, on whose account so many storms were stirred up. In 830 she was first confined in the monastery of Saint Mary at Laon, then at Poitiers in the monastery of Saint Radegund, and in the following third year was exiled to Tortona. Charles, however, was entrusted to Prüm, but was not tonsured, as is related in the *Life of Louis Augustus*.]

They also asserted that my little son Charles, an innocent and promising boy, whom they knew loved me above all others, had been tonsured and had joined the community of monks. When I heard this and could no longer restrain myself—since I had been stripped of the glory of kingship, deprived of my wife, and robbed of my son, and for many days had wailed without enjoying any consolation—I gradually felt myself, through the greatness of my sorrow, burning in the throes of the most violent grief. Since I could have no comforter except God, because access and conversation were denied to everyone, and a path to the church and the brethren was opened only rarely [Col. 0618A], and then under the strictest vigilance of the guards, I resolved to go there.

When I arrived, I threw myself down at everyone’s feet and reported to the wise physicians the wound of the illness with which I was afflicted. I begged them to obtain whatever relief they could from my merciful lords, to celebrate Masses for the repose of my wife, whom I believed to have been removed from this life, and to pray more earnestly. I implored their venerable religious devotion with all insistence.

They wisely pitied my afflictions and miseries and, through the merits and intercession of the saints whom they served, promised—as though foreknowing the future—that healing from the Almighty was near, provided that I applied my mind to the sacraments of faith. Thus, after prayer, they comforted me well and led me back from there to the familiar prison chambers. So at last [Col. 0618B] I was restored.

As the darkness of night followed, I earnestly desired to see the light-bringing star. I entered the prison oratory adjoining the church of the Holy Trinity and, after completing Matins, spent the night there alone. When I directed my gaze outside through the window, I saw one of the guards, unjustly hostile to me beyond measure, lying close by beneath the roof tiles and wishing to preserve his position so that I could not escape even through the smallest opening in the wall.

When I discovered that he was stupefied by sleep and wine, a ridiculous omen, which I interpreted favorably, arose before me amid deep sighs of the heart. Indeed, when I saw that he was stretched out upon the ground and that his sword, which had survived and been exposed to the repeated blows of his pillow, lay entangled near the foundations of the basilica, I quickly climbed the ladder that had been placed in the corner for lighting the lamps and untied from the ceiling a rope lying idle. Then, seeing nearby the poles to which the banners used during the litanies were fastened, I tied the rope with its noose to one of them and threw it through the same window.

By this device I seized and lifted the sword-point and had it thrown into the high, filthy latrines. Then, calling him by name, I said to him: “O ever-watchful guard, the most faithful hope of your charges, are you awake?”

He replied: “I am awake, and very much awake.”

I said to him again: “And what are you building?”

He answered: “What business is that of yours?”

I replied: “If sudden necessity should happen to compel you, perhaps the sword would be absent from your hand.”

As he turned his arms toward his head and searched for it here and there, I said: “If you had guarded me in this way, you would certainly not have had me here today” [Col. 0618D].

He said: “Whatever has been done with the sword-point, I have guarded you sufficiently and more than sufficiently, as I was ordered, and I shall continue to guard you. Go, therefore, and, as a reward for this loyalty and your watchfulness, retrieve in the appropriate armory the sword that you have shamefully lost.”

That very day certain brethren, investigating the truth of my entire affair through Harduinus, who in his daily ministry had been accustomed to chant Masses before me, sent me a written account. When, as was customary, I offered to God offerings to be slain—especially for the absolution of my wife, whom I believed to have been taken from human affairs—he gripped my hand more carefully and said that there was something beside the altar.

[Note: We call it a host. From this it is understood that even then the custom was still practiced among laypeople of offering hosts to be consecrated at Mass, or, as they said, to be slaughtered and sacrificed. The Roman Order says: “While the archdeacon brings the offerings on a paten, none having been sacrificed,” and so forth. They also not infrequently used the word “to consecrate.” This practice of offering hosts continued longer among monks, as is clear from Book II, chapter 30, of the *Customs of Cluny*.

[Note: That is, a little roll or scroll (*rotulus*), namely a slip of paper, by which he might be informed more certainly concerning the safety of his wife and son.]

After the offering had been completed and everyone had gone outside, I remained alone. Picking up from the chapel floor the little scroll, I learned that my wife was alive, that no harm had been done to my son, and that many were already repenting that they had broken faith in this manner and deserted me; with fierce spirits, they were striving together to restore the kingdom. With God’s favor, and as he turned events for the better through the manifestation of his saints [Col. 0619B], they brought this to completion.

Yet although, with the height of the kingdom recovered, I enjoyed more splendidly the glory of my former dignity, I did not forget my vows and prayers by which I had entreated the most excellent martyr Sebastian and which I believed I would unquestionably receive. When rebellion again arose, the tranquillity of the kingdom was everywhere being fought over and the peace of tranquillity was thrown into confusion, I went to the aforesaid place to implore the saint on their behalf. Since I had often experienced his powerful aid in such private or public matters, I earnestly begged him to grant his customary assistance in this matter also.

On the following night, I received in a nocturnal vision what I had asked for some days earlier, apparently granted to me from heaven by him with the clearest indications [Col. 0619C]. Since the collapse of the disasters that were gathering did not allow me in any way to prolong my desired stay there, I departed and tried to devote myself to the danger threatening the peoples entrusted to me by God, and, if circumstances required it, to present myself manfully for the struggle.

As I was departing, Teutherus, provost of this holy community, accompanied me and became my companion on the journey. While he rode beside me and we were being separated from the holy place, I turned my head and, alas, directed my final gaze toward it. Shaken by the grief of my inmost heart, I could no longer restrain the waves of profound sorrow rising over me. Sad and mourning, I poured out bitter tears, fatally enclosed in uncertainty as to what I ought rather to do.

I had vowed a vow to the saint whose appointed day of action I saw approaching. From him I had received the end of my life, and I knew that I was not permitted to transgress the limits he had set for me. Finally, I knew well that the Christian empire entrusted to me by God had to be governed. When I considered that the whole world was being shaken to such an extent and feared the approaching desolation that I had foreseen, I feared that I would be found guilty in this matter and condemned by him to eternal punishments—by him who is the Author and Lord of all and who, as judge, will come to repay each according to his works.

Seeing me thus grieving, Teutherus kept silent for some time, deliberating, for he was faithful in all things. But when he could no longer endure the abundant rain of my tears, he too, moved by this, burst into tears and said:

“What good, excellent Caesar, can these things do for you and for your subjects, who are grievously abandoned? Through you all will be consoled. If your cheerfulness were restored to the sorrowful, it would dispel all their grief. Do not, lord and most glorious emperor, do not openly display to your servants this wound of deadly sadness in yourself, whose face has always been marked by the highest joy and the serenity of your countenance [Col. 0620B]. By this, the hearts and arms of your people will be greatly weakened, while the strength of your enemies will gather power. That alone must remain a secret among your people which could disturb the state of your breast, always so joyful and peaceful. Perhaps, if they faithfully sympathize with you, they will be able to find remedies of consolation; and if this cannot happen otherwise, you will bear it more lightly hereafter, when more people have begun to share in the matter.”

I accepted these words of my comforter, which I knew had been offered in faithful persuasion. I explained the cause to him and immediately revealed with my lips what lay hidden in my heart.

I said that I had loved that holy place very much and that, through the revelation of the holy martyr, I had learned that I would never see it again [Col. 0620C]. I had also made a vow whose fulfillment the instability of the empire entrusted to me would prevent; and unless fear of the enemy were assigned as the reason, or its collapse—which was to be feared beyond measure—were demanded by the Almighty, I had wished to lay down my arms, purple robe, and insignia there with the greatest willingness.

[Note: Here should be related the words of the Anonymous author in his *Life* under the year 811, where he says that Louis wished to imitate the memorable example of his grandfather Carloman, unless his father’s opposition—or rather the command of the divine will—had presented an obstacle. Although Lothair, together with the men of his faction, ordered him to go into a monastery and remain there all the days of his life, he refused and did not consent to their will, since he did not wish at that time to yield to the treachery of his enemies, as Theganus says in chapter 43.]

Then, when I asked him to give me some more salutary counsel, I received this answer:

“Your vow is good, most glorious Caesar, but, as blessed Gregory teaches, nothing is richer before God than good will. It is indeed a great thing that you desire to renounce the world and all that you possess, since by this you could become an imitator of Christ. Yet the salvation of many, through which it is accomplished, promises manifold rewards for each person. The former is counsel for you; the latter is counsel for everyone. The former is great, but the latter is greatest. If the will cannot perform the former, it can be rewarded in the latter.

“Finally, what was more wondrous in God was that he deigned to die for his servants. He himself commended as a greater increase of charity that someone should not hesitate to lay down his life for his brother. He did what he taught: he laid down his life for us [Col. 0621A]. The Lord endured death so that the servant might recover dignity, not succumbing to necessity but ineffably aiding his created being. He displayed in himself the example that we should follow, promised the victor’s palm to the one who labored, and established an enduring reward.

“Since, therefore, he has entrusted his flock to your governance, it will be honorable and praiseworthy for you to fight for it, if necessary, even unto death.”

Instructed eloquently by that man and strongly encouraged to act, I commended myself again and again to his holiness and that of the brethren with the greatest earnestness. Although I was no longer as sad as before, I nevertheless could not depart from there very joyfully, since I knew that I was leaving forever those whom I had loved uniquely.”

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0621B]

When these matters had been reported to the brethren, who were foremost by age and religious merit, they unanimously resolved to beseech the holy martyr that, if it could in any way be done, his revelations might be turned into something else for their salvation. Although this was carefully carried out, they were in no way heard in this matter, since God’s decree of predestination, which is never changed, had been established.

For while he was leading an army by the same route against his legitimate son, who bore the same name, he died bodily on a certain island of the Rhine [Col. 0621C] and, as we suppose, through the merits of the saint whom he had embraced with incomparable love, obtained eternal life with him.

[Note: Near Ingelheim, below Mainz, according to the Fulda and Bertinian Annals.]

His remains were honored at Metz in the basilica of Saint Arnulf, from whom he derived his lineage, and were notably commended both by the abundance of precious treasures and by royal revenues.

[Note: This is known to everyone: Pippin of Herstal, as he was called, descended from Ansegisel, son of Saint Arnulf; from Pippin came Charles, the prince surnamed Martel; from Charles came Pippin, king and father of Charlemagne, and grandfather of Louis.]

And because, as we learned through the saint’s manifestation, he refused to fulfill his vow, he did not deserve to have the long-desired place of burial in the martyr’s estate.

## CHAPTER XLVI

When the ruler of the whole Roman world had been removed from life, an epilogue must at last be added to this subject, compelled by the modesty of the writer [Col. 0622A]. For insofar as the merit of so great a martyr and the dignity of the subject are concerned, everything that human eloquence, however great, can say about him is speechless; human speech is inferior to heavenly praise.

I have treated only a few matters concerning him in unpolished language, and, forgiving tedious readers, I have omitted many more, almost innumerable. Indeed, there remains to this day in our archive a little document sent by Rodoinus to the memorable abbot Hilduinus, in which, in a very extensive series of chapters, the notable signs of his virtues are individually abridged. When their total is reduced to a sum, it rises to four thousand four hundred and seventy.

Thus, overcome by so vast a subject, I place my hand over my mouth and leave all these matters to more learned and scholarly men, and to those who have not yet come into the light, who will follow in successive ages until the end of the world. If any fastidious person desires to be satisfied with richer food, setting aside this bran of ours and seeking the work of the most holy Father Ambrose, which he composed about this celibate martyr’s triumph, he will find there a dish richly filled; after tasting its exceedingly delicious fine flour upon the palate of the mind, he will be able to be delightfully nourished.

Here ends the epitome of the miracles of Sebastian, the most renowned champion, whose name, sounding in Latin as “imperial man” or “imperial,” from the Argive language, is inscribed in splendid characters in the golden volume of that immaculate Lamb. Therefore the earth is full of his praise, and his memorial will not be abandoned [Col. 0622C] forever, because he reigns happily with Christ in eternal glory. Amen.

From the Jolian manuscript.

Memorable martyr, Gondacrus the monk, remember me,

I who have written in this little manuscript the garlands of your virtues.

By your praise, may I be able to ascend to the kingdom of heaven,

Aided by the holy prayers whose help has enabled many

To receive the joyful gifts of body and soul.

## APPENDIX: On the miracles of Saint Gregory and on certain other relics of the monastery of Saint Medard

[Col. 0621]

1. An appendix to volume II of the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum* contains a booklet on the miracles of Saint Gregory, written by an anonymous monk of the monastery of Medard around the year 1150. It relates that Queen Constance, wife of Robert, king of the Franks, was admonished to adorn the tomb of Saint Gregory; that Fulcosius, or Fulco, bishop of Soissons, was rebuked by the same saint in 1025 for having plundered the monastery’s possessions, when Richard was abbot; and that in 1126, under Bishop Joscelin and Abbot Geoffrey—“who afterward became renowned as bishop of Châlons”—the plague was suppressed when the relics of Saint Gregory were carried through the city in solemn procession.

Concerning this plague we possess a book on miracles accomplished through the help of blessed Mary, composed by Hugh Farsitus. Finally, from the *Acts of Saint Goswin, abbot of Aquicinctum*, there is added the account of his cure, effected in that place where he was then prior, through the merits of Gregory the Great. It is sufficient merely to have indicated these matters here.

2. Moreover, the relics of Saints Tiburtius and others were transferred from the city of Rome to the monastery of Saint Medard. I shall append here the history of this matter, described by the monk Odilo, already cited above. I have also read an account by an anonymous author concerning the translation, during the reign of Charles the Bald, of the body of Saint Gildard and the head of Saint Romanus, bishops of Rouen, to that place; I shall refrain from recounting these matters at greater length.

## HERE BEGINS ODILO’S LETTER TO INGRANNUS, ON THE ARRIVAL AND RECEPTION OF THE BODIES OF THE HOLY MARTYRS TIBURTIUS, MARCELLINUS AND PETER, MARCELLIANUS AND MARK, PROTUS AND HYACINTH, MARIUS AND MARTHA, AUDIFAX AND ABACUC, ABDON AND SENNIS, WHICH TOOK PLACE ON THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY

[Col. 0623]

1. Not everything that is said is examined by the authority of certain reason; rather, what is said to have been seen is reported as heard, what is possessed is displayed, and what has been approved by truthful ordinances is believed. Therefore, since many people say many things about the translation of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, Marcellianus, Mark, Protus and Hyacinth, Marius and Martha, Audifax and Abacuc, Abdon and Sennis from the city of Rome to Gaul, and since some pretend not to know the place of their repose while others, by negligently pretending ignorance, maliciously deny it, it was worthwhile that both the truth of the bodily presence of so many soldiers of Christ should be established and the faith of those who doubt should progress for the better through belief and love of the martyrs.

Likewise, the arrival of the blessed martyr Tiburtius and the reception of his body are described with reasoned care, and the glorious deposition of the holy relics of Hermes and Julian is received into the account with no less devotion together with the aforementioned holy martyrs. For it is eminently fitting that, since their will to transfer themselves to Gaul was one and the capacity of a single little receptacle carried them, their arrival and deposition in the monastery of Saints Medard and Sebastian and of Pope Gregory should be marked by one and the same principal solemnity of joy.

## HERE BEGINS THE EPILOGUE OF THE NARRATIVE

2. Our lord and Augustus, namely the ruler of the whole Roman world, the most devout father of the Frankish kingdom, the fortunate and provident emperor of the entire monarchy—Louis, that is, son of the august and venerable memory of Charlemagne, who was raised by the grace of divine dispensation to free the world from tyrannical controls and to restrain domestic evils—after he assumed the governance of his father’s empire, guided all the faithful and children of the holy Church throughout the four regions of the world by devout rule toward the benefits of heavenly happiness.

Among the gifts of virtue and grace bestowed upon him, he gave both examples of honorable faith and multiplied the adornments of ecclesiastical religion in many ways. He also brought many bodies of saints from various parts of Italy into the Frankish realms, where the people, proud above all in nobility, distinguished in military valor, and possessing no small reputation for wisdom, industry, and prudence alike, certainly flourish and prevail.

Through the skill of this people’s intelligence, the bodily remains of the most blessed martyr Sebastian, worthy of praise in every respect, together with the most holy members of Pope Gregory, of blessed memory, were transported to and deposited beside the walls of Soissons in the basilica of Christ’s supreme confessor, Medard, and are visibly and jointly kept there.

3. Since an innumerable succession of miracles was continually taking place at that time in the presence of the saints, the knowledge of their virtues gave off no small fragrance of so great a perfume through the wide spaces of the world. It happened, therefore, that one day, while the aforesaid emperor was wintering at the palace of Aachen [Col. 0624A], he began, in royal fashion, to converse with his nobles during dinner.

Among the many topics of conversation, he suddenly turned to the joy of the translation of the blessed martyr Sebastian and to the greatness of his virtues. The conversation then continued at considerable length concerning the neglected tombs of the martyrs, of whom there was a vast number at Rome.

While these things were taking place, a certain deacon of the holy Roman Church, named Deusdona, came to the king to beg his mercy for his needs. While he remained for a long time at the palace, he earned greater familiarity with Einhard, the abbot and domestic of the royal palace, than with the other courtiers, and received from that abbot every expression of kindness without any reproach.

Meanwhile, when he was preparing to return to Rome after completing the business for which he had come, he received from the same abbot many gifts, in the presence of the king and especially of many others, to facilitate the care of his return.

4. Accordingly, the aforesaid abbot Einhard and the aforementioned deacon of the holy Roman Church set out from the palace of Aachen and reached the city of Soissons. At that time the lord emperor, out of love for the renowned martyr Sebastian, had come to the monastery of Saint Medard with all his retinue and the company of his nobles, intending to celebrate holy Easter with the utmost devotion, as was fitting.

The venerable abbot Hilduinus was present for all these proceedings. He received the aforesaid abbot Einhard and the deacon of the holy Roman Church with distinction and honor, treated them familiarly, and admitted them to knowledge of his secrets. In the course of these intimate services, they were exceedingly delighted and filled with immense joy, and they spent the Easter days in gladness.

Finally, after receiving the blessing for his departure, the aforementioned deacon, lavish in various promises, promised Abbot Hilduinus the venerable body of the blessed martyr Tiburtius. He also faithfully promised Abbot Einhard that, if he sent a trustworthy embassy with him, he would receive many relics of saints in his possession.

Greatly rejoicing at these promises, the lord Abbot Hilduinus and Einhard carefully selected suitable envoys, men distinguished by prudence, industry, and intelligence. Thus, setting out with the aforesaid deacon, they hurried toward Rome with all possible speed.

5. It happened that, when part of the journey had been completed, one of them was seized by the illness of tertian fever. When he had long been grievously tormented by his illness in the silence of the dead of night, a young man of splendid appearance appeared to him in his fever and asked him about the business entrusted to him and the labor of such a journey.

When the man explained to him in order the deacon’s promises concerning relics of the saints to be sent to Abbot Einhard and those that had been made to Abbot Hilduinus of blessed memory, the most beautiful young man replied and said:

“It is entirely clear, and your companions plainly know it, that you have suffered from tertian fever for many days. Rise quickly, hasten on the journey, and proceed without fear. You will obtain the vow promised to you by the Lord. I wish you to receive, as a sign of your faith or belief, the effect of complete health.”

After saying this, he awoke freed from every pain and feverish heat. He carefully reported to his companions everything that he had seen and heard by divine revelation. Thus it came about that they unanimously believed both the vision and the divine words and promises.

6. When they came to Rome, they received lodging beside the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter called “at the Chains,” in the house of the deacon with whom they had come. They remained with him for several days, continually insisting on the fulfillment of his promises.

During this interval of their stay, it was decided that they should go with the deacon to the cemeteries of the saints, so that, if anything worthy could be found there, their desires might be satisfied. Accordingly, having found a guide, one who knew the places, they first reached, in great haste, the basilica of the blessed martyr Tiburtius on the Via Labicana, three miles from the city.

They carefully inspected the martyr’s tomb and cautiously considered whether it could be opened without others knowing. Then they descended with the utmost reverence into the basilica adjoining the same crypt, in which the bodies of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter had been decently buried. After also examining the nature of that monument, they returned together to their familiar lodging, carrying much knowledge with them.

7. But the more secretly they discussed the matter among themselves and decided that their host could remain unaware of what had happened, the sooner knowledge of it reached him. Fearing that the envoys of Abbot Hilduinus might satisfy their master’s will without his consent, the aforesaid deacon preferred to anticipate their plan and act with greater care.

Since that same deacon possessed complete and exact knowledge of the holy places, he addressed them very graciously and earnestly, proposing that, by common counsel, whatever the disposition of heavenly power revealed should be done. They jointly accepted the counsel of the old man, who was the first archdeacon of the Roman see.

The time for undertaking the work was also wisely appointed in haste, and they awaited it with equal resolve and the greatest longing. Then, after completing a three-day fast, they reached the holy places by night, without any Roman citizen noticing.

Entering the basilica of the holy martyr Tiburtius, they prostrated themselves on the ground. They attempted to open the altar beneath which the martyr’s most sacred body was believed to lie. But at the first attempt the strength of the seekers immediately failed, for they were shaken by excessive trembling of mind and body.

The monument, polished from the hardest marble, resisted even harder than iron and easily repelled the hands of those attempting to open it. While they were thus placed in anxiety of heart [Col. 0626A], divine grace immediately came mercifully to their aid.

Indeed, a certain monk named Basil appeared to them at once, like a good angel of God. He had already lived for many days on a mountain in Palestine with his disciples, under the rule of a most approved religious discipline. Encouraged by his salutary counsel and aided by his holy prayers, they finally found, though at the risk of their lives, the most sacred body of the aforementioned martyr.

After the most sacred body had been lifted with every mark of veneration and arranged in costly coverings, it was honorably carried into the crypt of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter amid every expression of jubilation and rejoicing.

8. Soon they descended on bended knees to the tomb of the holy martyrs. The piety of our Lord Jesus Christ was invoked with inward groaning of heart, and whatever had to be done was entrusted through supplicatory prayers to the intercession of the holy martyrs.

Immediately, in the twilight of that very night, the stone covering the top of the tomb was removed from its place. At last they found the most sacred body of Saint Marcellinus, separated and carefully wrapped in the upper part of the same tomb. Near its head they also observed a marble tablet, explicitly inscribed, because the venerable body of the precious martyr had once been buried there and lay honored by the faithful.

At once, lifting the most holy remains with the greatest reverence, wrapped in a clean shroud, they placed them beside the bodily presence of the blessed martyr Tiburtius.

9. When this had been done, their thoughts turned in different directions and no small anxiety arose, because they could not obtain the sacred presence of the blessed Peter, exorcist and martyr, as a companion.

Troubled in mind by this misfortune, they labored with such strength of spirit that they would neither take food nor yield to sleep unless the bodies of the martyrs, companions in their passion, were also carried inseparably joined together on the journey.

Burning continually with these desires, they again approached the crypt of the aforementioned holy martyrs in fear. When the tomb had been opened without any difficulty, they carried away the sacred remains of the blessed Peter, exorcist and martyr, with joy and eagerness, no one preventing them.

Accordingly, they prepared receptacles for the bodies of the saints, making them as light as possible in accordance with the season and the difficulty of undertaking the journey.

10. Amid these services of divine providence and acts of religious devotion, it happened that, while they were circling at night, for prayer, the cemeteries of the holy martyrs Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Abacuc with the aforementioned archdeacon, they received revelations of divine admonition. Clearly instructed by their consolations and signs, they also took up the four bodies of those saints and quickly added them to the receptacles of the saints.

This was accomplished immediately, without any delay or difficulty, with the utmost reverence.

11. Thus the entire distinguished mass of the holy martyrs was entrusted to the care of the industrious archdeacon, and was carried by the envoys of Lord Abbot Hilduinus, who received it with doubled joy [Col. 0627A]. Joined to the relics of the other martyrs, they traveled with exultant hearts and reached Pavia.

There they decided, for the sake of refreshing the pack animals and repairing themselves for the longer road, to grant themselves several days of most welcome rest in that city of the people of Ticinum, namely Pavia.

During this interval of their stay, it happened that envoys of the holy Roman Church, sent by the Roman pontiff, arrived at Ticinum. Fearing that their arrival might bring them some trouble or even an obstacle, the travelers wisely decided to anticipate their presence.

They immediately disclosed to one another the knowledge of their secrets and explained in order what they knew in the depths of their hearts. The Roman pontiff’s embassy announced that it wished to set out as quickly as possible for Gaul and proceed to the emperor, because a considerable necessity of the apostolic see compelled them to hasten.

For this reason, our men became anxious. They made known with clear assurances the loyalty and friendship of Abbot Hilduinus, as well as the authority of the most devout Emperor Louis, and plainly explained the translation of the aforementioned holy martyrs to Gaul.

12. Thus it happened that those whom they had first found to be querulous detractors they afterward discovered to be completely faithful supporters along the entire road.

Everything was therefore arranged, and through the stages of the journey, the dangers, and the winding passes of the Alps, they finally reached Saint Maurice. There they spent a full day and night resting.

Then the bodies of the saints, enclosed in humble receptacles, were more richly and worthily wrapped in silken cloths and decently placed upon a bier, covered above with golden fabrics. From there, accompanied by praises and advanced under the protection of God’s grace, they openly carried the desired treasure, aided by the people who came running from every direction, as far as the boundary of the long-desired countryside.

13. By that time the report of the arrival of the saints had spread far and wide. Therefore, as though from the navel of the earth, an innumerable crowd poured forth from every direction.

At last almost the entire city of Soissons, from nearly two miles away, rushed out to meet them [Col. 0628A], and escorted the sacred remains as far as the crossing of the river Aisne, praising them with joyful cries and songs.

On the other side of the river there was a devout assembly of monks, crowned with ecclesiastical mitres, together with many companies of the faithful. With doubled joy they rejoiced that they were gaining such patrons and were present at the spectacle of the martyrs’ arrival.

Proceeding together from there and brightening the day with lights of many kinds, they advanced with thuribles and crosses skillfully adorned with gold and precious gems, arranged in solemn ranks. Rejoicing, they brought the relics amid hymns and spiritual songs into the inner sanctuaries of the basilica of Saint Medard.”

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 828, on the second day before the Ides of July, the venerable abbot Hilduin received the bodies of the holy martyrs Tiburtius, Marcellinus and Peter, Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Abacuc, and deposited them at Saint Medard’s, in an honored and distinguished place, beside the venerable body of the illustrious martyr Sebastian. At that time it was the third year since Sebastian’s body had arrived and been received. There, especially, they have been venerated by all the people with complete devotion down to the present day, and their bodily remains are preserved with the fitting honor of religion. Just as soldiers are made more glorious by the wounds they have received for their emperor, so God himself—the King of martyrs, our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious emperor of his soldiers—makes those who have been marked by martyrdom for confessing his name glorious in every sign and virtue of miracles.

But since, during that same period, an innumerable multitude from almost the farthest Thule was making its way to that place, because of the many healings and signs that were taking place without distinction in the presence of that same martyr of Christ, Sebastian, all the distinguished miracles that were then manifested cannot be referred individually and properly to the aforementioned holy martyrs. Nevertheless, they may, without compromising faith, be believed and said to be common to them. Indeed, they were truly and beyond all doubt common for this principal reason: just as they are believed to be equal in merit before God, so they may reasonably be thought to work together in performing miracles.

[Col. 0627]

## LETTER OF ODILO THE MONK TO HUCBALD, MONK OF SAINT-AMAND

*(In Martène, Amplissima Collectio, vol. I, p. 266.)*

[Col. 0627D] To the lord Hucbald, conspicuous for the dignity of ancient seriousness and most distinguished in every kind of goodness, supremely experienced in human and divine studies: Odilo, a sinner, bound to him by the bond of true and indissoluble friendship, which is also joined by the glue of Christ.

Ever since I was first deemed worthy to taste the desirable sweetness of your affection, without any prior claim of merit on my part, I have had no doubt that an unfailing fullness of charity dwells in your most faithful paternal heart; and I desire and implore with all the inward depths of my heart that it may remain so until the end.

You sent me a little book on the life of the blessed Lebuin, God’s friend, prudently and elegantly composed and strengthened throughout by every branch of philosophy. I read it, and I could find nothing in it that needed correction, but only what might advance anyone through learning and imitation. As I freely confess, you possess great talent; you have an infinite store of language; nothing in eloquence is more Latin than your speech, nothing more beautiful, and I have never read anything sweeter.

O happy Gaul, illumined by such a teacher! I am amazed that you sent me, an unlearned man of no importance or merit, these flowers of your eloquence to discern. You should not have judged me by the number of my years, nor by gray hair, but by gray hairs of wisdom, as Solomon testifies: “The gray hair of a man is his prudence.”

You have reversed the proper order of things in my case. What I ought to have demanded from you—and what I did demand concerning the virtues of my lord Sebastian—you, whom all Gaul admires as the beacon of all wisdom, have not disdained to request from my littleness. Yet I pardon your condescension. You know how to be exalted, and you know how to be humbled. Scripture commands: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.”

You did this not from necessity but from willingness, and because of the character of our place and your affection for me. I earnestly beg you to remember me when you pray.

“Hucbald the wise man: may wisdom always be his friend;

Hucbald the wise man: always a friend of wisdom.

This I, Odilo the sinner, bowing low, request.”

[Col. 0629]

## THREE SERMONS OF ODILO THE MONK

*(Bibliotheca Floriacensis, vol. II, pp. 136–153.)*

## SERMON ON SAINT MEDARD

[Col. 0629B]

It is worthwhile, dearest brothers, to recall with what excellence of worship and advancement in religion the place of blessed Medard has flourished through successive ages, and with what vengeance his anger has sometimes burned against the enemies of his servants.

For King Chlothar of the Franks, favorably disposed toward the service and reverence of the saints, after the holy man’s death, carried out with effective zeal, insofar as he was able, what he had promised him before his death. Having gathered what was necessary for the expenses required to complete what had been provided either through royal magnificence or through the most willing offerings of the faithful, he began to construct a noble church by the marvelous skill of expert stonecutters. Having founded it with such refined craftsmanship, he would have brought it to completion in a very short time through his sufficiently brilliant and more than adequate intelligence, had the common sentence of death—not, alas and sorrow!—carried him away.

For he had gone to Tours, to Saint Martin, for the sake of prayer. He pleased that saint with devout prayers and gifts, and, visiting the monasteries situated all around with heartfelt devotion, distributed gifts to each as seemed appropriate, under the direction of the Holy Spirit. Having therefore returned to Gaul, he went hunting in the forest of Cotia. There he was seized by a severe fever and began to lose the strength of his body. From there he was carried back to the estate of Compiègne, entered the way of human flesh, and relinquished the reins of the kingdom—he who had subjected foreign nations also to his rule.

His body was brought to the city of Soissons by the services of his people in a funerary triumph, and he was buried with fitting reverence before the holy man of God in the very basilica he had begun but had not yet finished. Such a burial he ought to have, since there he had fixed the stable anchor of his mind, so that not even death could separate him from the one whom in life he had always loved with a single devotion.

At his grievous death all Gaul resounded with the deepest mourning, and that distinguished work, through the exchange of the royal scepter, languished unfinished. But just as evil offspring, imitating the deeds of their evil parents, become heirs of their fathers’ transgression, to their condemnation, so good sons, born of good parents, grow in every virtue, to their parents’ praise.

Sigebert, Chlothar’s son, succeeded his father in the kingship by the unanimous consent of the Franks. He was a zealous founder of divine religion and an indefatigable champion of the Christian profession. Stirred by the innermost zeal of his heart, he burned with the same fire of love for the holy servant of God as his father had, and with devoted zeal successfully brought to the very summit the work that his father’s death had interrupted.

He adorned that monastery, remarkable on both sides for its marvelous structure, with suitable order and religious observance within, among the clergy; and outside he solemnly enlarged, gloriously elevated, and energetically advanced it through the assignment of his estates.

Later, while he was bent on his brother’s death and was preparing ambushes to besiege Chilperic in the city of Tournai, Fredegund, his wife, by her cunning, brought an end both to his rule and to his life. She turned back upon his own entrails the sword he had aimed at his brother, and he immediately perished from the very source through which, in his blind mind, he had continued to plot against blood.

For two young men from Thérouanne, pretending deceitfully to raise him above themselves as king, suddenly pierced his unprepared sides with their spears; as they fell together, they forced his unwilling soul to vomit itself forth. His body, wrapped in precious garments, was carried to Lambres amid the immense grief of his people and was afterward buried with great glory beside his father’s body in the same basilica that he had magnificently built.

This, indeed, was that lofty royal church, distinguished by the nobility of its character and renowned for the refinement of its workmanship, which remained in its solid condition until Louis Augustus assumed his father’s monarchy. When Louis in turn wielded the scepter, that church—which was confined within the narrow limits of the inner court—was demolished from its foundations, so that not one stone was left upon another in the entire structure.

For that glorious Caesar had long before brought the life-giving relics of the blessed martyr Sebastian to that place, and therefore divine power was more readily manifest in healing the weak. Because of the unusual rush and continual crowding of the people, which increased daily on account of the countless wonders performed through the merits of that same martyr, the aforesaid prince razed the former building completely, since it was in no way large enough for the peoples who flocked together from everywhere to witness such marvels.

Therefore, using the expenses of the innumerable offerings, he undertook another church of far greater size, suitable for all who came, whose entire circumference could contain them. Since it possessed every adornment of virtue and displayed the whole form of dignity and glory, it was inferior to none, while its elegance clearly showed it to be superior to all.

This house, I say, once burned by the Marcomanni, has fallen for the most part from the heights of honor on which it stood, and, as though to the disgrace of later generations, only an immense heap of piled stones has been left standing. Even now it remains beyond these times, extending across three dimensions and presenting to all the vast size of its body: rising high in its roof, but excelling greatly in length and breadth.

As time passed, when the same place had already become distinguished, after the death of the venerable Ansbert, who had presided over that monastery, Warimbert subjected the primacy of that place to his tyranny.
