When Drausio, bishop of the city of Soissons, died, Warimbert secured through the king, by the magnitude of his payment and the intervention of his friends, both the administration of the dignity of the episcopate and the retention of his former office as prior.

He was frequently at court and very influential among the king’s household. Thus, although with difficulty, he effectively obtained the fulfillment of his desire. Set over both flocks, he kept a crafty fox beneath his sluggish breast. He treated with the strictness of justice those whom he had previously ruled deceitfully under the guise of a sheep. Although he ought to have protected them from secular obstacles, he continually provoked secular irritations against them, imposing constant complaints which he ought to have defended them from by the authority of justice.

Indeed, by seizing what supplied their livelihood and turning to his own use what was necessary for them, he persistently squandered the goods that ought to have been defended by the shield of a true priest’s virtue. Those against whom the accusation was brought did not endure the damages and insults inflicted upon them with equitable patience; they did not know how to resist one whose most oppressive yoke they had taken upon themselves in their wretched subjection.

There was, then, the extensive estate of the royal property called Matwallis, which is interpreted as “Good Valley,” not from the Latin or British language—although it borders upon the latter—but from its abundance of produce and wealth of complete fertility. For just as it spreads across the territory, so it fills broad purses with the due revenue, since, as it extends its grassy land far and wide, it displays the numerous cultivator of an immense possession.

King Sigebert of the Franks, remarkable among the earlier kings for his piety, had assigned this estate to Saint Medard for perpetual possession, among many other benefits he bestowed. Since its boundary adjoined the county of Le Mans and was separated by a great distance from the borders of Soissons, it seemed very difficult for the officials to transport the countless expenses to the monastery.

Therefore, year after year, its revenues were sold off competitively, and their proceeds were distributed among the monks in various forms. Salt, honey, and other useful commodities that could be transported more easily from there were purchased; thus many loaded barrels were carried by wagon to the monastery.

When Warimbert saw this, he went out arrogantly, seizing the opportunity. Irreverent and slippery, he diverted the loaded wagons to his own property while his men rejoiced. Those who were deprived of the possession granted by heavenly favor were clothed in shame, and amid the sharpest insults they repeatedly drew deep sighs from the bottom of their hearts.

It happened once, while the executioner was intent on his external concerns, that his brothers, having learned of his absence, boldly diverted these same arriving goods into their own storerooms and concealed them there. When he heard this and took the deed exceedingly ill, he immediately burst into anger and threatened that the same presumptuous rashness would be punished with a fitting sentence.

The brothers, on the other hand, troubled, turned unanimously to the protection of prayer. They kept a three-day fast and steadfastly implored heavenly aid with prayers and tears. During that time no voice was heard in the choir; only at the appointed hours did the lips of the singers move, while everything was performed in silence and mourning, as Christian devotion has excellently established for the beauty of the Church.

But this matter became, in the tyrant’s eyes, a great seedbed of envy, hatred, and discord. He found an addition to his grief where an increase of relief ought to have arisen.

Why say more? At last he returned to his seat as though he intended to exact vengeance from those who had violated his wicked custom. Rising at first light, he came to the place with a strong force, agitated in spirit and mind alike. When his companions knocked at the royal doors, no one inside gave an answer, because all alike feared the destruction promised them by the insolent bishop.

He came nearer and struck the same doors repeatedly, battering the gates and violently shaking the bronze valves, full of anger. At this, one of the doorkeepers, imprudently taking up the keys of the church, came out to meet him. When the doors were unlocked, the bloodthirsty man entered with a furious spirit. Immediately raising his right hand high, he struck the head of the doorkeeper with his staff so forcefully that the man was covered in blood and, to his great disgrace, displayed a bruised face and disfigured features.

As he mourned, he cursed from the heart; heavenly clemency immediately made the truth clear by an evident judgment. For the bishop did not go unpunished for having subjected God’s servant to such cruel treatment. Proceeding arrogantly to pray, he had scarcely bent his knee before the Holy of Holies when, by divine action, all his inner organs burst forth through the secret passages of his belly and were poured out upon the pavement. Since he was without piety, he undoubtedly remained empty in his belly as well, and the outcome testified that the priest’s life was far unequal to the dignity of the priesthood.

His body was thrown outside the threshold of the church, and the remaining filth was removed through the service of the faithful. He received burial in the cemetery, in the place he deserved, after his exhausted body had been interred.

From this, let shepherds of souls beware lest a worse punishment one day envelop them, and let them learn to govern their subjects with discernment, lest the subjects, lacking discernment, be deprived of the fruit of salvation. Since it is supremely useful in human life that nothing be done to excess, it is perfectly clear that they ought to moderate discipline with this caution: let fear restrain wickedness, and let love advance justice through its practice.

Thus the success of subjects will prosper, and the progress of those who preside will truly increase; and all things will be in all, so that almighty God may be equally honored by all.

Let the rulers of the Church also remember not to become accustomed to permitting the sins of the people while seizing their substance, for the people’s sake they ought to lay down even their life if necessity demands it. Earthly resources must be distributed entirely for Christ’s sheep, lest, while their possessions are taken away, those bodies by which they are strengthened in the service of God’s apprenticeship be deprived.

Therefore, whoever does not give earthly substance for those entrusted to him will never give his own life for them either, since one proceeds from the first and lesser thing to the final and greater thing, and no one reaches the final greater thing unless he has first practiced the initial lesser thing.

Priests of God ought always to be formed by word and deed, so that even if someone brings forth good things, there may consequently be someone who strives to imitate him. But whoever plunders what belongs to others certainly loses the office of shepherd and, rejected for that reason, strays from the straight path of truth.

Therefore, let neither subjection crush subjects, nor a loftier position exalt prelates. Let the former humbly obey in the place of sons, and let the latter, in the place of fathers, temperately command what ought to be commanded. If the affairs of any prelate should be otherwise, he will undoubtedly be another Guarimbert, who in the matters of his subjects considered the movement of his own spirit rather than the affection of love.

Indeed, a concise discourse of the writer has touched upon some of the principal deeds of blessed Medard and has striven, with measured brevity, to gather into a single account whatever it could find in this and in other sources. His distinguished life had once been confined within narrow limits, and the marks of his virtues, together with the translation of his body, had been set down on humble little pages in a manner almost childlike.

Since Fortunatus’s account was brief and displeasing to readers because it had been treated carelessly, obedience to the command of both authorities made the writer’s little works come together and cohere in harmony. It seemed right that he should discharge the debt of his service at least through the office of his tongue, so that, joined together by a kind of glue and arranged with propriety, the praises of the blessed man might be presented in a somewhat fuller and clearer discourse.

He did not wish in any way to detract from that man who had long ago published the life of the same Father in verse and in extremely compressed prose. Rather, what the former had touched upon as though in passing, this writer thought worthwhile to expand with his pen. What the perfect orator had omitted in his account, this new narrator undertook to transmit to later generations for their knowledge—not extracted from his own inventions, but inserted, however imperfectly, in the old pages of the ancients.

Therefore, brothers, it seems fitting that you should join me in proclaiming with worthy praises the merits of so great a patron. Although he has a house not made by human hands but eternal in heaven, he nevertheless always possessed on earth a temporal dwelling more exalted than the others. Just as he guards his own from the attack of invisible enemies, so he often defends them from the assault of visible enemies through the help of his intercession; and he embraces with himself in the heavenly tabernacle those for whom he exercises pastoral care in the present age.

He himself governs the family of God amid the shipwrecks of the tossing ocean, lest the storm of the tempest carry away our ship or a cruel pirate seize it as eternal prey. He once received this family to govern from the one who said to his disciples—and through them to all the faithful: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matthew 24:45).

Hence the Apostle says: “To each, as God has allotted the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3). What Christ calls the measure of wheat, Paul calls the measure of faith, so that spiritual wheat may be understood to be nothing other than the venerable sacrament of Christian faith.

Therefore, brothers, where our treasure is, there let our heart strive to be, so that we may yearn for love of our heavenly inheritance, to which we trust that our blessed patron has already attained. Joined, then, to the eternal citizens, may he entreat divine mercy for our offenses and make him favorable to us whose everlasting glory he enjoys through continual vision.

But to accomplish these things, may the Only-Begotten Son of God extend the hand of his mercy, whose kingdom and dominion stand firm and endure forever and ever. Amen.

## II. ON THE HOLY MEDARD AND GILDARD

The glory of the holy confessors, dearest brothers, must be exalted through fitting praises, and those who always confessed Christ and bore true witness to him must be advanced to the rank of praise. Since they proclaimed little things about him but great things with steadfast courage, in the one respect they deserved to be called angels, and in the other, archangels.

And since the Apostle says, “You are the temple of the holy God” (1 Corinthians 3:17), they undoubtedly became the temple of the one whose altar and standard they were as priests. For on the table of the eternal King, offering sacrifices of appeasement and expiation through the vows of devout confession, they often presented to God an acceptable sacrifice of human reconciliation.

Thus they obtained, as a gift of virtue, the power to bind and the authority to loose, so that what rested upon their judgment might, through divine authority, be ratified even in heaven. For such privileges of merit, they are rightly advanced to the rank of praise, since the King of justice himself granted them, for confessing his name, the privilege of intimate love.

But those truly love the Lord whose minds are not overcome by sinful pleasure through consent; they grow hot with love for him precisely because they do not know how to yield to the stealthy incursions of impending temptations. Kindled inseparably, they are rightly numbered among the heavenly ranks, between the cherubim and seraphim, and there they receive the lot of their calling, where they fix the anchor of their minds through the practice of continual contemplation.

When the blessed confessors resolved to attain the summit of this perfection, they strove to desire nothing in this world but to burn ardently with longing for their Creator alone. Renouncing earthly desires, they crucified themselves completely to carnal pleasures, so that they might offer their members as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God through rational service (Philippians 4:18).

And because they refused to be conformed to this age but steadfastly persisted in being transformed through the renewal of their minds, walking according to the inner person (Romans 12:2), they were stirred by holy successes from virtue to virtue. For they continually yearned for him to whom they clung everywhere with devoted minds, since they had taken up wings like doves, by which they could fly toward heavenly things and find rest.

They truly loved the Lord, whose commandments and precepts they kept, so that they could not be separated from his love even when the assault of temptations grew fierce. When the Truth says, “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35), how many crosses did those men take upon themselves who were able to tame the flow of lust in their own bodies!

Without iron, they endured a long martyrdom in their limbs, so that what the shedding of blood had not accomplished, the prolonged torment of their members through the scourge might accomplish. At first, food was taken in restraint, and [lacuna] was their drink, since moderation had been prescribed in both, as though, with Ceres and Liber brought to an end, Venus had grown cold.

Their faces became pale from excessive fasting; a bristling habit had brought upon them the squalor of Ethiopian skin; and their spirit remained constant in vigils, lest the mind devoted to God be empty of prayers. They also kept their loins girded, restraining the luxury of the flesh through continence, and held burning lamps in their hands, displaying examples of light through good works to their neighbors.

Since neither great chastity is anything without good work, nor good work anything without chastity, they practiced both with discernment, lest the desire for praise break the intention of a mind directed toward other things. With their loins therefore girded, they held burning lamps in their hands, so that both the purity of chastity might be present in the body and the light of truth might openly shine in their conduct.

Among these men of great veneration, we know the blessed Medard and Gildard to have been outstanding. They imitated the cunning of serpentine prudence and the holy innocence of dove-like simplicity. One suppressed vices, while the other preserved the unimpaired rights of virtues; and the caution of both skillfully knew how to avoid the leaven of malice and wickedness.

Through the former they attacked those who had gone astray, but through the latter they moderated the reins of their attack. For although correction sounded from their mouths, paternal prayer never slept in their hearts. While discipline maintained its severity, gentleness also displayed the meekness of the heart; what one had erased with the file, the other sought to heal and temper through the grace of compassion.

Thus, by the judgment of just examination, they became clearly the thrones of their Creator. Through them the holy Church was governed, and often even the elect were judged for their frail deeds. Therefore, what the vigor of one sharpened, the measured warmth of the other did not cease to moderate in them: the simplicity of the dove inflamed the cunning of the serpent, and the simplicity of the dove tempered the cunning of the serpent.

[Col. 0636C] Supported by good will, they helped all who were caught in the distress of tribulation, and they offered the aid of their consolation with renowned compassion to those afflicted by any calamity. What they attributed to themselves, they undoubtedly attributed to others; and they did not prejudice anyone, since, by an evident judgment of salvation, they had become all things to all people.

They lamented the losses of others as though they were their own misfortunes, although, with God’s approval, the injuries of others had already produced an increase of many virtues in them. They refused to inflict upon others what they themselves wished no one to inflict upon them, nor did they deny another what they prudently saw to be beneficial and advantageous for him.

Since they loved both friend and enemy in God, they flourished, for God’s sake, in love of God and neighbor, on which the fullness of the prophets and the whole sum of the law depend. Nothing richer is ever offered to God than this holocaust, since through what the soul sacrifices to him, it rightly slaughters itself upon the altar of the heart.

Thus, in their devotion to good will, they always took care to please the Most High, the searcher of hearts, while they held humble thoughts about themselves, even when they had at times performed mighty and exalted deeds beyond themselves.

Indeed, the prophetic word says of such men: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isaiah 60:8). These blessed confessors, pure in mouth and hand, were fired by the proclamation of the sacred word and flashed with signs through frequent manifestations and with virtues.

Since their sublime and holy life, and their preaching, had lifted them above earthly contamination, they were flying clouds and also corresponded fittingly to the divine distinctions of the heavenly virtues. When they drove evil spirits from possessed bodies and expelled them by the power of prayer and the force of the authority they had received, they deserved truly to be assigned to the heavenly powers and to be admitted among them through their frequent expulsion of demons.

Having become better by being good, and therefore set over their elect brothers, they rightly occupied both rank and place among the orders, at the seat of eternal dominion. They were found neither in the gall of bitterness nor in the bondage of iniquity. While they lived happily for Christ, through renunciation they were dead to the flesh and to this world.

As they transcended earthly things in mind, the eyes of their hearts were always directed before them; and the things subject to them outwardly served them, so that the transitory things they saw might never obstruct their hearts. Thus they were flying clouds and like doves to their windows: considering perishable things with a simple eye, they were moved or drawn toward them by no desire for plunder.

These two shone forth from one twin birth and with equal progress in one holiness; and just as their births were equal, so the best course of life formed them as one in goodness. Nevertheless, they are read as having been assigned differing lots of life in the maternal womb of the world, although an allegory may underlie the account: the two differed in the quality of merit and grace.

For one was simple, dwelling in tents, while the other practiced worldly warfare with weapons; consequently, the former was chosen, while the latter became wholly apostate and rejected. The blessed Medard and Gildard were indeed brought into the world by one birth; but the same freedom in holiness and magnificence applauded those whom a single birth had given the same beginning.

Born within the space of one hour, they were held together by one confession of faith; and virtue made companions of those whom nature had brought forth as twins within a moment of time. Since they shone forth as such, they displayed themselves like their parents in good works. The world had them as contemporaries, while the bosom of Mother Church nourished them as fellow participants in works of piety.

What is remarkable in them and established as memorable for all ages is that they attained the glory of their consecration together and the same episcopal chair in the governance of the faithful. Just as their bodily birth was equal, so they received equal spiritual consecration; and they proved equal in blessing, although in no kind of justice did they prove unequal.

Both were sanctified under the same condition, both consecrated by an equal lot, and both anointed with divine chrism; they were to receive souls to be cleansed through holy baptism. In one hour, the same day made both true bishops of God; it made both distinguished pontiffs, established them as true lights of the world, brighter than the solar sphere and more splendid than the lunar lamp.

One of them was appointed bishop of Noyon, the other archbishop of Rouen. Thus the former obtained the place of a suffragan, while the latter, as testimony to the higher office, obtained the metropolitan seat. Under their guidance the heavenly kingdom is opened; by their word the heavenly gate stands open to the faithful. “Through them the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it daily through the remedies of repentance” (Matthew 11:12).

Promoted together, therefore, to the office of bishop, they also received together the place of sacred governance, so that those whom one faith had joined together might also be bound together in the same governance by one and the same day.

For the increase of their glory, something occurred which your charity should hear attentively: the blessed confessors were alike taken from the world and alike crowned with glory and honor in heaven. When the course of their life had ended together, they were together snatched from the foul abyss of the world, together drawn from the prison of the flesh, and together consoled by the eternal reward of their labor.

O pious spectacle! O wondrous judgment of piety displayed in these men! Conceived and born together, together married to the first fruits of faith, together they received the sacrament of saving baptism and together undertook the most vigorous apprenticeship of divine warfare.

Together distinguished by apostolic blessing, together crowned with episcopal miters, together sent forth to paternal rule, and together made a mirror and example to their subjects. Together they fulfilled the care of pastoral office, together labored over the Lord’s money, together proved faithful in what had been entrusted to them, and together returned double profit from the talent they had received.

Together they paid the mortal debt of death, together reached the eternal kingdom, together proved themselves most renowned victors, and together were received in triumph into eternal glory. Together, therefore, they were removed from earthly affairs and together inserted into heavenly things; together they escaped all corruptible things and together entered the imperishable joys of eternal life.

Moreover, by joining and doubling their merits, they established a festive day of great solemnity, one ever to be revered by the angelic spirits and likewise to be recalled from the heart by Christ-bearing peoples everywhere. For we must all recall without ceasing and continually bring before the eyes of our minds how exalted was the mind of these men: it found perfect goodness perfectly and, in the end, held it perfectly. For what is more perfect than that to which nothing less is attached and nothing greater; which knows no diminution and admits no increase; which neither comes into being through a beginning nor is confined by any limit of time? God always possesses being, since he possesses his own proper existence; and essentially there belongs to him the fact that he is a good, supreme, ineffable, and uncircumscribed spirit. To possess him fully and perfectly is plainly to live perfectly and without end, because he himself is the life of all: namely, the living bread and eternal food of the angels. Thus, when the blessed confessors reached him in a glorious triumph of perfection, they brought immense joy to the citizens above and supplied solemn gladness to all who commemorate their feasts.

Among these things we too ought to know, so that it may remain continually stored in the depths of our minds, that “the Lord raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap” (Ps. 112:7–8). They became poor in spirit so that they might be enriched forever with unfailing treasures. For there existed in them that poverty which is commended not by lack of possessions but by humility of soul. Hence the pearls that once lay neglected in the dungheap have now been taken up and placed in the adornment of the heavenly King. Now they shine among the citizens above; now they sparkle among those fiery stones of the eternal diadem. For once corruptible on earth, they now exist in heaven as coheirs with the angels; and, carrying off a trophy from the flesh, they enjoy forever the innermost vision of their Creator. By laying aside their bodies, they have also purchased an immortal gain in the kingdom of heaven; and, putting down their earthly burden, they have been clothed in the bright robe of eternal immortality. While their flesh is dissolved into dust, their souls are borne into heavenly rest, where, in those eternal pastures, they are sustained by the glory of eternity together with all the saints. Thus the Lord, rescuing his own who were submerged in the depths from the pit of misery and from the mire of filth, raises the needy from the earth, and divine mercy snatches the blessed poor from the dungheap.

As for the matters we have undertaken: if we now rouse our hopes and spirits, let us consider where they set their feet, so that by the steps of love we may deserve to imitate their footprints. Shall I speak, or shall I remain silent? Supported by the strength of prudence and fortified on every side by the protection of justice, they held fast all that ought prudently to be pursued, and by just examination subdued the crafty arguments of the cunning enemy. Temperate in their conduct, they embraced the restraint of temperance with all their strength; strong in adversity and prosperity alike, against every hostile force they seized the weapons of fortitude. Pursuing the lowest places of humility, they proceeded with steadfast courage along the paths of life. By offering great examples of patience, they stood with unbending constancy on the very path of truth. Finally, strengthened by the virtue of gentleness, they bore meekly Christ’s very light yoke, and in their deeds preserved the modesty that they held in their hearts as something kindred and dear.

Therefore, dearest brothers, it is necessary that we fortify ourselves with such weapons of faith, by which these blessed confessors, friends of God, deserved to become illustrious conquerors. With suppliant devotion let us venerate such men, worthy of every kind of praise and honor, so that through their revered intercession we may obtain, in those heavenly dances, the joys of the paradise of delight. Let us therefore consider where they set their feet, so that we may deserve to follow their footprints, through the grace of our most merciful Redeemer. Amen.

## III. ON SAINT MEDARD

We could not pass over in silence the life of the most blessed bishop Medard, whose virtues are proclaimed throughout the whole world, although we cannot touch upon all his deeds. Since the annual commemoration of his burial invites crowds of every people to seek with evident reverence the day of his solemnity, let devotion increase in every heart through the ardor of faith, while the greatness of its saints is made known. And even if there is someone here who proves to be a rare imitator of his conduct, may his intercession nevertheless make everyone better.

Accordingly, our discourse first indicates his origin so that it may perhaps offend no one who is more blameworthy through the obstacle of despair; for division among peoples does not prevent anyone from loving the Lord with undivided love. Rather, the fullness of united faith prevents anyone from mistakenly judging that divine grace—which is shown to all who desire it in general—is granted only to particular persons.

His father, named Nectardus, was of the powerful Frankish nobility and was not of the lowest rank in freedom. His mother, however, was Roman, named Protagia, and was distinguished by ancestors released from servitude. As we suppose, she bore fruit for Christ’s tabernacles by her childbirth, and benefited more thereby than if, preserving her chastity, she had never submitted herself to marital bonds. Their home and origin are known to have been in the territory of the Veromandui.

When, as a young man, he was attending school in that city, his mother sent the little cloak she had made for him, by his hand, to a craftsman to be repaired. On the way, Saint Medard immediately gave it to a blind man whom he encountered. Likewise, whenever he was tending his parents’ flock and received anything to eat, if he saw a poor person, he handed the food to the needy man, while he himself endured want and spent the day fasting.

Nor should the mysterious significance of this event be left unmentioned. While the holy man was still a small and innocent boy at school, he told a certain boyhood companion named Eleutherus that he would assume a countship in public life, and said that when he reached the age of thirty he would become the highest pontiff of God. He was appointed shepherd of the Church in the city of Tournai. Thus Saint Medard, like a prophet, showed by divine inspiration that what he had foretold came to pass.

Afterward, as he frequently traveled to the shrines of the churches, proclaiming the admonitions of faith, and, weighing his tender years against habits of patience, despising the allurements of the world through the freedom of his own will, he undertook the office of priest. He was transformed in mind and dress alike, surpassed others in the charity of his conduct, and immediately became distinguished before the bishop of the city: eminent in his way of life and sincere in purity of mind before everyone. He never exalted himself excessively through an abundance of joy, nor was he disturbed by the bitterness of sorrow. He was always patient in adversity, gentle in prosperity, preferring everyone to himself through diligent obedience, coming to the aid of the needy with generous compassion, and, having trampled underfoot every source of vice, ascending by the steps of holy conduct along the path of the lofty hill. He shuddered at whatever was hostile and chose whatever was precious. What more need be said? He was seen as a stranger in this world and already as a possessor in heaven.

Then, as each honor of the priesthood increased and, with the proper intervals of time, he advanced through the order of ecclesiastical custom, he was chosen for the office of presbyter and, having been tested, obtained it. Thereafter he began to make himself known through holy virtues to such a degree that he was considered, by the merit of his life, a fosterling of Christ.

It happened that, when the fruits of autumn were ripening and the juice of the clusters was maturing, the abundance of the vintage gave an opportunity for a thief’s boldness to make his grace known. At the dead of night, when rather the burden of gentle, silent sleep rests upon human bodies, withdrawn from the variety of cares, a thief, driven by a dominant desire to seize the fruits, sought out and entered his vineyard. Grasping the prey as his sword cut through it, he himself was more truly seized as prey and confined within the open enclosure. The more violently he wished to flee, the less was he able to escape, being held captive thereafter by his own crime. He did not deserve to taste what he had taken, and, drunk with it, found no way of returning. He could neither relinquish what he had dared to take nor lawfully carry away what he coveted.

At first light, the owner of the vineyard, aware of what had happened, came upon him there. He found the thief whom his own booty had already bound, and each kept the other in servitude, with their rights reversed. Then the saint’s vengeance against the crime became so great that, plucking grapes with his own hand, he increased the thief’s portion by a more lavish offering; and, rebuking the offense, he granted him a way to return.

A similar punishment, or restraint while the ambush continued, befell the man who, anticipating his vessels through a nocturnal theft, had stolen the honey contained in them. By a cunning act of plunder he was able to deceive the keeper, but the reckless man did not escape with the flock he had stolen. The bees left their dwelling in anger, pursuing the thief everywhere—not enriching him through a blameless labor but assailing him with the violence of their stings—until the thief’s exposed shame restored to the saint what he had fraudulently taken, and he found pardon when he prostrated himself. Nor was the priest’s merciful indulgence undeservedly sparing toward the guilty man, since the very booty that avenged itself was tormenting him because of his crime.

A similar mystery occurred under this act of treachery. A traveler was passing near his house with an opportunity to continue his journey. Wishing by cunning fraud to steal a young ox, he removed the bell from its neck and, deceptively closing the opening made in the grass, departed without being detected by anyone. When he already believed that he had escaped the danger of his crime or had gained profit through theft, the stolen object, though secured by no obstacle, began to ring, desiring to return under the Lord’s protection. Although it remained carefully placed in hidden recesses or shut away behind iron-barred locks, it proclaimed the crime by ringing all around, with no one setting it ringing. Opening its wide mouth, it put the author of the crime to shame by redoubling its complaint.

Then the thief, recalling in a confused mind the dangers he had suffered before, terrified, carried back to the owner what he had taken—what he did not even preserve through any desire for profit. Once the right of nature had thus been restored, the inanimate object began to conceal its appearance and reveal itself by sound only when struck. Thus Saint Medard, the athlete of Christ, without personal guilt, was put to shame for another’s offense; and therefore he granted the guilty man recompense on account of his fault, lest he return more sorrowful through his empty ambition.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 920. STEPHEN, BISHOP OF LIÈGE.**

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON STEPHEN

*(Gallia Christiana.)*

Stephen was of noble birth and, as some hold, the son of the count of Salins or Salm, whose sister the count of Namur took in marriage. He was educated in the palace schools with Radbod of Utrecht on the Rhine, and with Mancion, bishop of Châlons, according to Regino. In his youth he was a cleric of Metz; he was also abbot of Lobbes, as Fulcuin testifies in chapter 18 of the *Chronicle of Lobbes*. By virtue of his episcopate, however, the abbey had been united to his see by King Arnulf, as is clear from a diploma of Louis, his son, who confirmed that donation to this Stephen on 28 January 909. He was also abbot of Saint Michael on the Meuse, according to the chronicler of that place and according to a charter concerning the exchange of Hareville and Saponeria, made between Anselm, formerly the son of Count Teuterius, and the monks of Saint Michael, “where lord Stephen, bishop and abbot, presides, and Halevincus is prelate,” that is, provost or dean. Both men subscribe the charter in the third year “of Louis, son of Arnulf,” which corresponds to the year 902 of Christ, in which year Stephen was already bishop of Liège according to Mabillon.

Earlier, “Stephen, venerable abbot,” took part in the synod of Metz in the church of Saint Arnulf in 888. Archbishop Fulco of Reims also wrote to him. Flodoard records in Book IV, chapter 7 of his *History*: “He sends consolatory letters to a certain Stephen, abbot, who appeared to have been elected to the episcopate but was then rejected or disapproved, asserting that he would preserve forever the friendship he had promised him.”

Whether he was secular or regular remains uncertain. Fulcuin, Sigebert in chapter 126 of *Illustrious Men*, Aegidius, and other writers on the affairs of Liège suggest that he was secular; they call him not a monk but a cleric or canon of the Church of Metz. Sigebert calls him in his *Chronicle* “a man distinguished in holiness and knowledge”; Fulcuin calls him “a learned man, and, insofar as concerns the canons, devoted to religion.”

He published the life and passion of Saint Lambert in a more polished style and dedicated it to Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, together with a song on the Trinity. Fulcuin adds that he also composed a certain little book, gathered from numerous flowers of the divine books, in which he collected short works for the individual feasts of the year, together with collects and verses, with useful commentary. In the preface to this little book he shows that he had been educated at Metz from childhood. He sent the book to Robert, “bishop of the same see,” for reading and approval.

The beginnings of his episcopate were distinguished by the restoration of the monastery on the Sambre, which had been destroyed by the fury of the Normans. “In his time,” says Fulcuin in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, “our church was dedicated by him, with Dodilo, bishop of Cambrai, summoned and associated with him for this work; it is easy to see on the bases of the columns which of them dedicated each part.”

In 908, while King Louis was residing at Aachen, at the supplication of our Stephen, with the cooperation of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and other illustrious princes, he confirmed by his authority whatever the generosity of former emperors had granted to the Church of Liège: namely, Lobbes, its roofs and ditches, as well as what he himself had bestowed, namely Heribothesheim and the toll and mint of Maastricht. “Given on 18 January, in the year of the Incarnation 908, indiction 11, and in the eighth year of the reign of Lord Louis.”

Chapeavillus reports this diploma; he also reports another of Charles the Simple, apparently from the year 915, by which Charles granted to the Church of Liège the forest of Test, which Zuentibold had retained for himself when he gave the villa. “Given on 25 August, indiction 3, in the twenty-third year, while the most glorious King Charles was reigning, renewing the eighteenth.” The king asserts that the gift was made at the intervention of Stephen, venerable bishop of Tongeren, “our most beloved kinsman and ally.”

He died in 920, on 19 May, after presiding for eighteen years. He was buried beneath the altar of the Holy Trinity, namely in the crypt of Saint Lambert, during the reign of Conrad, the first Roman emperor of that name.

## LIFE OF SAINT LAMBERT, BISHOP OF MAASTRICHT AND MARTYR, BY STEPHEN, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

*(In Surius, Acts of the Saints, 17 September, from an old manuscript collated with the edition of Chapeavillus.)*

## PROLOGUE

### 1

To the lord Father Hermann, archbishop, Stephen, humble bishop of Tongeren.

[Note: This Hermann is the one called “Hermannus” in Chapeavillus.]

[Note: Stephen was bishop of Liège; but because the episcopal see was first established at Tongeren, then transferred to Maastricht, and finally from Maastricht to Liège, the bishops of Maastricht and Liège were for a long time also called bishops of Tongeren, after the first location of the see.]

Since the deeds of others are daily subjected to scrutiny, and since, if anything blameworthy is found in them, malicious intent does not hesitate to stain them, it is rightly determined that the condemned contagion must be thoroughly cleansed, so that the derisive laughter of blasphemers may at last cease. For certain people who were associated with us, and who appeared to possess literary learning, assailed us with no small insults of contemptuous laughter because the life and passion of the aforementioned Father, composed in no particularly polished language by the ancients, was read among us, while no proper melody of offices was sung.

Thereafter, pressed by the frequent entreaties of our brothers, I was compelled on many occasions to undertake the renewal of all these things by the expenditure of my own judgment, and to drive away from us this kind of infamy. Yet when they argued about this in various ways and supported the undertaking by citing the example of many others, I recalled my mind and resisted, troubled in spirit; and I questioned myself, after prolonged hesitation, whether what they advised would really be good.

### 2

Behold, at last a syllogistic serpent, spreading widely in its twisting coils, swelling its scaly neck with three-forked tongues, and plunging into the depths by pouring itself into the eyes of my heart, stood before me as a messenger of this dialectic and said:

“Everything good is useful, and everything useful is good: useful good; no evil; no evil is useful good; no good is all evil; all evil is no good.”

Therefore what is celebrated in praise of the Creator in his saints, and what is useful to the creature celebrating him in its endeavors, is good. Whatever is shown to be made best by improvement is proved to contain no evil in its existence. Conversely—God forbid, for chance turns all things—what is left neglected contains no good belonging to either.

Then, believing him more truthfully—for truth habitually separates itself from falsehood by an unbroken process—I preferred, eagerly, to derive some useful instruction from what had been advised rather than, through the stubbornness of mute silence, negligently deprive myself of the fruit of labor.

### 3

Thus I considered this plan, examining it with a preference for choosing the better course:

I invoke not the Dryad nymphs, nor do I call upon the Naiads  
to bring forth songs, to furnish verses and adorned words;  
nor do I seek Mercury, proud in tongue and speech,  
who might swiftly scatter winged words;  
but I beseech the true Lord, King of all,  
who bestows everything and suffers no loss,  
who assists all in their need, and whose commands delay nothing at all;  
who sits in the citadel of heaven and governs earth and sea,  
and penetrates all things as though he opened everything with his fist.  
He is Father and Son, and likewise the gracious Spirit,  
three in subsistence, yet believed to be one in substance.  
Subsistence numbers three Persons,  
but substance numbers no separate being.  
Grant light to my feet; grant illumination to my heart;  
may he deign to give help to wretched me, Vernus [variant: Vernae].

[Note: Chapeavillus has *omnia* (“all things”). To avoid accumulating such small matters in the notes, I shall omit them hereafter.]

### 4

Indeed, neither swollen with the arrogance of pride nor holding any of the Fathers in contempt, but willingly obeying the usefulness mentioned above, I hastened to adorn it with the pen of a superior talent. Thereafter, according to the authentic rules of musical art, new responsories are attached together with antiphons, in which the sequence of the tones corresponds to the order of the lessons, so that their number may be extended by being brought into correspondence with one another. Even now it is delightful to dwell in spirit upon the praise of so great a patron.

Therefore songs adorned with the charm of the Muses briefly repeat and recount his deeds.

[Note: Chapeavillus has “Songs stripped of the charm of the Muses.”]

I entrust all these things, Father, to your judgment for correction. You know how never to deceive concerning the knowledge of truth; you strive to overthrow all falsehoods derived from truths, things that ought to be judged by faith greater than by sense.

[Note: I have restored *notitia* from the edition cited above; in our manuscript *notitiam* is read incorrectly. Our manuscript is nevertheless better in the verse immediately following, where it has “falsehoods but from truths,” whereas the other reading there is “falsehoods but from wounds.”]

Therefore let the wavering of my mind, defended by the pastoral crook of your office, now rest upon the firmness of your heart, if it deserves this; but if not, let it be privately chastised [variant: chastise it] by the gentle rod of your fatherhood.

# LIFE OF SAINT LAMBERT

## CHAPTER ONE  
### The saint’s noble birth; his distinguished education; the episcopate of Maastricht and his expulsion from it

### 5

Accordingly, the glorious martyr Lambert, the priest most beloved by the eternal King, was born of a distinguished family in a village of Maastricht. While still a small boy living among most Christian parents and beginning to show a good disposition, he immediately consecrated his earliest years, purified by the wave of sacred baptism, to Christ the Lord; and, insofar as he knew and was able, he devoted himself entirely to the divine will.

For this reason, with heavenly grace leading the way, his relatives unanimously decided that the one whose life of holiness had illuminated him from the years of childhood should be instructed and assisted by literary learning, and thereby brought to the summit of the highest perfection. Once this plan had been established—or rather, once God’s mercy had ordained it—the boy, handsome in appearance and exceedingly receptive in understanding, was entrusted for education to highly skilled men. He became greatly distinguished in ecclesiastical religion and was inwardly inflamed with a fiery love of heavenly mysteries. He drank in the streams of the liberal arts all the more rapidly because he had long since poured his whole self more ardently into the love of God. Nothing obscure escaped him, for where the Holy Spirit is present as teacher, there is no delay in learning.

### 6

At last instructed in divine doctrines and abundantly strengthened by monastic ordinances,

[Note: Concerning monastic ordinances or disciplines, Godeschalcus says nothing in his *Life* of this same Lambert. Sigebert and Nicolaus, however, affirm in the lives they provide that he led a life resembling the monastic under the discipline of Saint Landouldus.]

the boy of good disposition resolved in his heart to return to his father’s house. What he conceived in his discerning mind, he carried through to the completion of the deed. Then his kindly father, lovingly receiving his dearest child, understood with spiritual insight that he had advanced far beyond the years of childhood.

Both rejoiced: Lambert in his father’s honor,  
and the distinguished father in Lambert’s holy deeds.

Indeed, the vigorous boy, striving with all his strength to become a perfect man, went daily “from strength to strength,” according to the Psalmist’s words (Ps. 83), preparing himself to accomplish the works that the unchangeable providence of God had predestined to be done through him before the ages of the world. Although young in age, he was old in the integrity of his conduct. He avoided boastfulness and bravely trampled upon the pomp of the world. Whatever he could possess, he distributed to the poor, storing up treasures in heaven, where he would possess them once, happily freed from transitory things, he began to live more happily among what endures.

[Note: Godeschalcus likewise makes no mention of this generous mercy toward the poor.]

### 7

At the same time, Agius, Bishop Theodardus, the illustrious future martyr of Christ, a man full of priestly reverence and destined to be a blessed priest before the divine presence, was administering episcopal authority in the village mentioned above. The memorable young Lambert, renowned for his nobility and exceptionally handsome in bodily form, was commended to him for education in the royal court, so that, like a precious stone, he might acquire many excellent qualities and become fit for heavenly adornments.

Then Lambert, Christ’s dove without the gall of bitterness, that praiseworthy pupil, diligently adhering to the instruction of the aforementioned bishop, began to venerate him as a lord, to love him as a most dear father, and to serve him in all his actions according to the apostle’s command, as befitted a servant of the Lord (1 Pet. 2). Indeed, from the companionship of so great a Father he was increasingly filled with grace, more richly endowed with wisdom, and daily increased in the abundance of his merits.

The same bishop, observing and investigating this silently with subtle inquiry, understood how great and what sort of person he was; and therefore transferred his entire affection to him, as to a beloved heir and most welcome successor.

[Note: Godeschalcus also relates in his *Life* that Saint Lambert made great progress under Theodardus’s discipline.]

### 8

Having thus obtained the love of the great priest and been thoroughly taught to hold fast the admonitions of Scripture, he fulfilled the twofold commandment of charity: loving God with his whole mind and embracing his neighbor with undivided love as himself. He regarded the present as nothing, as he had vowed in childhood,

[Note: I do not know whether he intended here to indicate strictly a vow made by the holy boy or merely his purpose.]

considering everything worthless except what existed for the sake of eternal salvation. In spirit he thirsted for heavenly things and offered himself as a holocaust to the one who had become his sole desire.

After Theodardus had been killed by the impious and the saint had received the palm of blessedness,

[Note: More probably in the year 669, on 10 September. The martyrdom of Saint Theodardus at Nemetus in Germany appears more probably to have occurred in the year of Christ 669. It is therefore likely that the beginning of Saint Lambert’s episcopate fell near the end of 669 or the beginning of 670.]

the faithful community of Maastricht, deprived of its pious shepherd, began earnestly to seek another man of comparable holiness whom it could place in his stead. After a long search and examination of everyone, no one was found holier than Lambert. Accordingly, the people of Maastricht, assembled together, chose him to become bishop—he who was enriched by the honors of holiness and distinguished by the commerce of frugality—with the mercy of the Holy Spirit leading the way; and they acclaimed him as successor to his teacher.

### 9

When the royal majesty and the multitude of the palace nobles learned of his reputation, they immediately established him and raised him to the episcopal throne. But the gentle man, filled with every goodness and founded by Christ in the degrees of humility, repeatedly declared himself unworthy of priestly mysteries:

“Great, my brothers, is the honor of the episcopate; but heavy is the burden of this honor. I declare myself unworthy; I cannot accept what you desire. I do not possess the strength; the works of holiness are not present in me; I do not know that I have kept the rule of an innocent life. Therefore I hesitate to accept the helm of ecclesiastical governance.”

Against these attempts at excuse, the community of Maastricht replied with these words:

You possess nobility; you shine with the light of your merits;  
you are adorned with character and regarded as radiant in piety;  
you surpass all; therefore you will feed us from every side.

### 10

Then, roaring according to popular custom and rushing upon him amid the clamor of the people, they all said together:

“Lambert is our fellow citizen, renowned for the fullness of his deeds; he ought to become our bishop. This is God’s will; this is what the princes of the kingdom decree. The entire clergy has chosen him; the whole people acclaim him.”

But when the most humble man still did not fully yield to these petitions, they were moved more deeply and inflamed by divine inspiration. From the greatest to the least, they all said to him:

“Do not delay us any longer, Lambert, but know for certain that, whether you wish it or not, you will be our bishop and will be called the shepherd of the people of Maastricht.”

Thus, while all the clergy shouted and both sexes cried out alike, the clamor was raised to heaven, and Lambert’s mind was swayed by such voices. He yielded to their petitions and accepted the care of the episcopate, lest he abandon obedience, which is accustomed to accompany the other virtues. Thus, exalted by God’s right hand and consecrated by the blessing of bishops, the venerable bishop Lambert was installed in the governance of the Church of Maastricht.

### 11

Having finally obtained the summit of religious office, he devoted himself to increasing the works of perpetual piety, now that he had been raised by the episcopal mitre. Every day he sacrificed a holocaust to the Lord, not from another’s flock but from his own body. He was never absent from the solemnities of Mass, celebrating the memory of the saving Passion and offering God a sacrifice for those for whom he knew he would have to render an account.

He was entirely joyful in face, most serene in mind, sweetest in speech, gentlest in conduct, dead to earthly pleasures and living in divine things of the spirit. In his house truth was his glory; in his works equity and justice shone. He devoted himself to constant preaching, reproving sinners with words of truth. He rebuked the sluggish with the utmost moderation, exhorting those who walked rightly with fatherly encouragement. He overflowed with almsgiving, shone with miracles, and instructed those whom he admonished by doctrines and examples.

Neither can the good that the vigorous man, relying on divine grace,  
taught in words and finally displayed in deeds  
be written by the pen or expressed in speech.

### 12

But because a lamp set upon a heavenly lampstand could not remain hidden beneath the shadow of a bushel, he began to be regarded as preeminent among his people. Christ the Lord had ordained that he be made known to the world by such signs.

Meanwhile, the reputation of his holiness, spreading far and wide, reached King Childeric, who at that time held the scepter of the kingdom among the Franks,

[Note: Childeric II, who at that time ruled the kingdom of Austrasia.]

and who learned that Lambert, shepherd of the Church of Maastricht, was regarded as surpassing all mortals in the service of the Creator. As a result, the king honored him with the highest respect, and he obtained the first place in the king’s friendship: a beloved prince in the royal palace and an approachable bishop in the royal council. Through his foresight the deeds of the nobles were directed; through his wisdom the useful affairs of the commonwealth were managed. How magnificent were the king and the army who obeyed the commands of so great a priest!

Although many served God, having conquered crime,  
nevertheless the instigator of wickedness poured his poison  
through the hearts of the evil, rejoicing that every kind of human being  
was moving toward worse, so that it might not be able to reach heaven.

### 13

Therefore he stirred up hatred, aroused quarrels, disturbed the peace of the Church, and made fear the foundation of the kingdom. He inflamed human hearts with such a frenzy of cruelty that they did not see heaven nor remember God’s judgments. When this poison had thus been grievously spread through the members of the devil, the prince of the kingdom, the glorious King Childeric, was killed.

Immediately he stirred up the weight of envy and hatred against God’s servant Lambert. Then, as hostile rage raged ever more fiercely and the devil’s envy wickedly blazed up, Lambert the illustrious priest was deprived of the honors due to him, and the heavenly man was expelled without cause from the episcopal throne.

Alas for the crime! Royal majesty perished; the wickedness of the evil prevailed; priestly holiness was brought to shame; the fairness of justice was profaned.

### 14

Alas! I am compelled to set down in writing the truth of what happened. Then the robber Pharamundus ineptly seized the episcopal throne of the Church of Maastricht. The wretched man seized the care of the episcopate for the miserable pomp of this world, not for the palm of eternal life. He usurped the episcopal residence, invaded its authority, became a robber of souls and the public plunderer of the Church.

He violated the sacraments of the Lord’s body; he defiled the height of canonical rectitude; he violated the sanctuary; he profaned the priesthood; he confused religion; he altered order; he destroyed innocence; he enslaved nature; he battled equity; he detested justice; he scorned receiving blessing; he did not fear acquiring a curse; he abhorred no crime and left no wickedness untouched. By word and deed he showed with what intention of mind he had been introduced into the governance of the Church. I am ashamed to relate more of what the master of deceit had done.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### Retreat to the monastery and life there for seven years; Pharamundus’s expulsion and the saint’s restoration to his see

### 15

But Lambert, the athlete of Christ, bearing everything with gentleness, abandoned the scepter of the episcopate, entrusting the care of the sheep to him who had washed them in baptism and redeemed them with his blood. As the most gentle man departed, subjected to insults of abuse and never shaken into anger, the whole people lamented him, the entire clergy mourned, and, following him with groans, they said:

“To whom are you entrusting us, most watchful shepherd? To whom are you abandoning us, most holy priest? Why are you leaving your devoted flock, and why are you abandoning your suppliant clergy? Who will protect us from the enemy’s snares? Who will pray to God for us? Who will drive away pestilences? Rapacious wolves will attack us; the fiercest enemies will tear us apart. There will be no one to drive them away, no one to resist them. You are the stability of the strong, the restoration of the weak, the defender in adversity, the glory in prosperity, the comforter of the poor, the helper of orphans, the receiver of widows. We shall all follow you; we shall all die with you. If the proud despise you and the sons of Belial persecute you, we, your sheep, love and venerate you.”

### 16

The brothers’ cry and the tears of those who groaned rose to heaven.

Then the Father, overcome, spoke thus as tears sprang forth:

“I shall say a few words concerning the matter:

You will not lack a shepherd, nor care for your salvation.

There is one thing that I command, repeating it, and shall warn you of again:”

O dearest sons, and O sheep of the supreme Shepherd, “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm III). “Turn away from evil and do good” [Col. 0650B] (Psalm XXXVI); the mightiest Helper will be with you, the true Promiser, and Jesus Christ our Lord will not allow those whom he redeemed by his passion to perish; blessed is he forever.

After this, raising his sacred hands and directing his eyes toward heaven, he blessed the clergy and people, marking them with the sign of Christ. Having then sweetly kissed them all, the lord himself, with a few companions,

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Godeschalcus testifies that only two of his companions—whether disciples or servants—accompanied him to the monastery of Stavelot. Moreover, what Stephen here relates concerning the people of Tongeren at the departure of their holy bishop, and concerning the bishop’s address to them, although it is not inconsistent with the truth, nevertheless appears to have been invented or embellished by Stephen himself and set forth according to his own imagination.] went to a certain monastery formerly called Stabulaus,

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Stabuletum, commonly Stavelo, is still famous today as a monastery of the Order of Saint Bernard in the Ardennes. It was founded by Saint Remaclus, whom Nicolaus mistakenly believed was still alive at that time as abbot of that place, in his Life.]

There, in particular, the memorable man, withdrawn from the guardianship of the Lord’s flock, lived among the senators of heaven within the court of paradise.

### 17

A company of monks lived there under regular discipline; the testimony of many virtues showed that their way of life was among heavenly things. Among them came one last in rank, but he proved first in holiness; last in number, he proved foremost in the zeal of his devotion. The fathers of the monastery revered him as their dearest Father; all the brothers rose before him as before their lord and father. He whom God had flooded with grace was lovable to all for every good quality.

Meanwhile, while he remained in the aforesaid monastery, he served God with all his strength, thirsting to please him to whom he had pledged himself to be a temple. He devoted himself to frequent prayers, all the more freely because for a time he had been removed from pastoral care. No one could express in words, nor comprehend with a pen, how much humility he showed toward his superiors and how much kindness he maintained toward everyone. It is unnecessary to praise his frugality, for he practiced it so wonderfully [Col. 0650D] that the very emaciation of his body proved to everyone that he was an acceptable fragrance of sweetness to the Lord.

### 18

Yet what the mercy of the Almighty wished to display for the completion of his perfection must, although briefly, be recalled and not passed over in the present account. One night, then, while he was resting with the brothers in the dormitory, he secretly wished to rise from his bed so that he might devote himself more attentively to extended prayers. As he took one of his boots, the other slipped from his hand and, striking the stone pavement, made a noise that disturbed the brothers’ rest.

The father of the monastery awoke, unaware of this secret matter, and said: “Whoever has just committed this negligence through reprehensible boldness shall fulfill our custom: let him immediately go to the cross and obediently expiate what he has done.”

Then Lantbertus, a most patient priest, most steadfast in hope and most joyful in spirit, willingly fulfilled the superior’s command and hastened to the cross like a sheep to the sacrifice. He took nothing with him to ward off the terrible cold except the single hair shirt in which he was clothed.

### 19

That night indeed was exceedingly harsh with the frost of the most violent cold and frigid with snowy ice. Within, plainly, the flame of the Paraclete Spirit was burning; therefore he despised the torments of the cold without. As the sacrifice of the Holy Trinity stood there and unweariedly implored the aid of his Savior, heaven, as we truly believe, opened to his most pure prayers, and their hearing reached the heights above.

Thus, while he sang David’s words in his heart and uttered them with his mouth—“When shall I come and appear before your face, O Lord?” (Psalm XLI)—it was brought about from heaven that the crowing of the cocks was heard earlier than usual. The devout brothers therefore arose to celebrate the vigils according to the customary rite.

When the service had at last been suitably completed, they all left the sanctuary, eager to kindle a fire at home by which they might remove themselves from the intense cold. As they surrounded it with great eagerness and, as was appropriate, gathered around it on every side, the abbot, looking at those standing there, realized that Lantbertus was absent. He asked the others where the venerable priest was, and the brothers replied that he was the one who had been judged to go to the cross.

### 20

At this the kind abbot was struck with astonishment and, sighing and drawing a voice from the depths of his breast, said: “Alas! What madness has seized you, most unhappy man? It is a crime to condemn the innocent. To send a priest into icy frosts is an abominable deed.”

Mourning, he spoke thus; then he said to those standing by: “Go, brothers, go, I beg you, quickly. Humbly ask our Father to come to us without delay.”

They hurried off and delivered the command. They found the most gentle priest in the cold and nakedness, wonderfully singing psalms to the Lord:

“A contrite and humbled heart, O God, do not despise, but graciously accept the sacrifice of our service, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Psalm L),

to the glory and honor of your name, which is blessed forever.

Moreover, while the most steadfast confessor of the Lord, the acceptable sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, was directing the intention of his heart toward the psalm that followed, the brothers sent to him stood nearby, imploring pardon for the others and announcing that they had come by the abbot’s command.

### 21

“The abbot, your sweetest father, begs that you come to the brothers as quickly as possible.”

He did not refuse their words but hurried with them to the house, where the company of monks had been gathered by an indescribable heat.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] The Greek word καῦμα means *aestus*—heat—in Latin. Stephen therefore must be said to have used it incorrectly, since he intended to indicate that the monks had gathered at the furnace because of the intense cold, unless he wished to say that the place was heated by a violent fire. Chapeavillus reads *medicabili caumate*, “with healing heat,” and thus the sense is complete.]

When he entered the threshold of the house, and his most blessed face shone with indescribable radiance, the abbot and the entire crowd of Christ’s worshipers fell at the feet of holy Lantbertus. They immediately addressed him with these words:

“Forgive us, venerable Father, forgive your brothers. We humbly beg you not to hold against us that we have acted so foolishly toward you. Have mercy on us who plead, and grant pardon to us who ask.”

The hero answered them briefly:

“Do not, I beg you, dearest ones, do not, I beg you, call me ‘Lord.’ Rise, I entreat you, quickly; rather forgive my failings. You have done nothing against me that I could forgive you.”

After they had been lifted up and were exceedingly distressed, the gracious Father said joyfully and cheerfully:

“I beg you, Fathers, do not remain troubled. The force of the cold did not frighten me. The Protector of my life was present, guarding me in the tribulation of necessity and hearing me in his abundant mercy. Therefore give thanks to him and bless his name.”

### 22

Then he lifted his pious hands toward heaven and, blessing the college of the brothers, said:

“O almighty God, filling the heavens with light,

who governs heaven, earth, and sea by your dominion,

so that all things in their time may be subject to your commands,

I ask you: bless these servants of yours forever.

Protect them from snares; preserve them with gracious virtues,

until they see you and seize the kingdoms of heaven,

you granting it, O God, who now and always, throughout eternity,

are blessed in the Trinity of your power.”

When all replied, “Amen. May God do so,” the elders together with the younger men understood that the Lord had exalted holy Lantbertus with immeasurable gifts of reward.

Afterward, desiring to show him the offices of charity and wishing to restore their beloved Father after an unbearable ordeal, they took pains to prepare a bath for him and surrounded him with clean garments. Thus the most courageous worshiper of Christ and most patient athlete of God, honored after obedience, was exalted after his triumph—not as the sincerity of his endurance deserved, but as mortal human ability allowed.

Amid such distinguished miracles [Col. 0652D] Lantbertus lived, Christ’s victim, each day both priest and sacrifice accepted as a fragrance of sweetness; crucified to this world and living for his Redeemer; cast down by pestilential men and summoned by the citizens above; driven from the bishop’s residence and admitted to the fellowship of eternity; driven away from the care of the sheep and invited to the palace of heaven.

### 23

Meanwhile, the unfortunate invader of the Church of Tongeren, namely Pharamundus, the son of iniquity—falsely called a shepherd of sheep, but rightly to be called an angel of darkness—was, because of his own crimes, condemned by the accusations of many

[Note: [Col. 0653D] That is, accusations.]

and expelled from the episcopal chair and from that province. For seven years he presided there only in name, and on no day did his work benefit anyone.

He was rightly persecuted on earth by the faithful, since he was openly opposed to God. But the people, grievously torn apart and mercifully freed by God’s compassion, began with all their strength and by many arguments to determine how they might deserve to receive back the distinguished bishop and modest Father, Lantbertus.

At that time Pippin held the monarchy of the kingdom and the leadership of the people,

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Pippin, surnamed Heristallus, who is designated here, was never king or monarch of the Franks, but mayor of the palace—first of Austrasia, then of the entire monarchy. Nevertheless, apart from the title, nothing of royal power was lacking in him, and therefore some called him king. Here he is said, by prolepsis, to have held the monarchy of the kingdom, although he administered it as mayor of the palace; in fact, he held only the mayoralty of the palace of Austrasia when Saint Lantbertus was restored to his see.]

a man vigorous in arms and an outstanding worshiper of divine religion. Having inquired into the gentleness of blessed Lantbertus and learned fully of his holiness, he sent envoys to the monastery mentioned above,

[Col. 0653B]

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Namely, Stavelot, where he was living the monastic life among the monks.]

to ask for the holy Lantbertus, so that he might deign to come to the king and resume the dignity of his episcopate.

### 24

When those sent by the king arrived, they addressed the priest Lantbertus as follows:

“The king begs you, Father, and the whole people demand that you leave the monastery, receive again the flock which you formerly abandoned unwillingly (or: deserted), and complete the Lord’s work as you began it.”

Then the elder

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Among writers of the Middle Ages, *senior* is a title of honor and means “lord.” Here it is said of Saint Lantbertus.]

spoke through welling tears:

“I confess that I ruled not as I ought; I lived not as I should. I am no longer fit to feed them; I do not desire to preside any longer, since I can benefit no one.”

The men continued, saying to the elder:

“We beg you, noblest of men and holiest of priests, by the love of God and by our love of neighbor, to come with us and graciously resume the governance of your sheep.”

Then the hero replied with a deeper sigh:

“Brothers, I dare not reject what you say; I must not despise the king’s command; I desire to assist the needs of my neighbors. I will not delay going with you. I will begin what you command; God is powerful to complete it and bring it to a sure end.”

### 25

Thus blessed confessor Lantbertus undertook a fortunate exchange, was tested by many trials, and returned to his own see. So the most sacred exile, filled with indescribable patience, received his flock again, protected it magnificently, and watched over it unremittingly.

Who among the most skilled writers could comprehend how great the exultation that arose throughout the entire people was when he returned? The citizens of heaven rejoiced, offering immense praises of proclamation to the indivisible Trinity. All the earth was glad, rejoicing to the Lord with joy. Everyone applauded in the heights and said, not so much with a loud voice as with devout hearts:

“Let us give thanks to the Lord, for he has visited us, the Dawn from on high” (Luke II), because the Lord has restored to us our shepherd, our Father, and our most vigilant guardian.

Thus king and peoples, rich and poor alike,

sang joyfully; praises resounded everywhere. In this way the veteran soldier, the man purified by the greatest tribulation, was fittingly raised up by the voices of his sheep and decently restored to the chair of the people of Tongeren.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] We have already said that this occurred around the year 681 or 682.]

## CHAPTER III  
The saint’s episcopal virtues; the diocese visited by him; the people of Taxandria brought to Christ; his martyrdom; the translation and burial of his body, made renowned by miracles.

[Col. 0654B]

### 26

Having therefore once more been elevated to the episcopal throne, he began to shine with as many holy qualities as are known to have been fitting for a bishop of God. In his heart were sincerity and fullness of the law; in his mouth, truth and the beauty of gentleness; in his counsel, strength and wisdom; in his actions, justice and abundance; in his conduct, innocence and chastity; in his bearing, glory and honor.

He was steadfast in faith, firm in hope, utterly complete in charity, distinguished by prudence, endowed with temperance, strengthened by fortitude, enriched by justice, singular in the display of good works, and admirable in doctrine and virtues. The piety of the eternal Father adorned him both with the merits of his life and with miracles of wonders.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] None of the ancient writers whom I have seen has recorded what miracles Saint Lantbertus the bishop performed.]

He did not look to the persons of the powerful but rather attended to excellence of character. Whoever he knew to live more religiously, he honored more highly. He had become all things to all people, so that he might win all (1 Corinthians IX).

### 27

Within the walls of his house his seats were never adorned.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Mabillon reads: “Nor did he ever adorn himself in private.” I think the reading of our manuscript should be retained, and that Godeschalcus alluded to the episcopal seat, which, while the saint was publicly carrying out his office, he kept adorned according to the custom of bishops, while in private he used the ordinary seat of his home.]

He revolved in his humble mind what he was destined to possess in eternal life. He did not wear garments of especially costly material; his first garment was a sackcloth shirt. He labored to humble his body on earth, so that his soul might deserve to be exalted in heaven.

He visited the villages and towns entrusted to him by Christ, knowing how to find people whom he could make fellow-heirs of an eternal inheritance. Serving these concerns and possessing an unfailing hunger for this justice, he entered Taxandria,

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Taxandria, written by others as Thessandria or Toxandria, is a region of Belgium, situated and bounded from the town of Tongeren toward the north, scarcely three miles away. Hence he earned the title “apostle of the Taxandrians.”]

which was devoted to pagan errors and profaned by the impurities of idols.

When he began to expound the Catholic faith there in eloquent speech, the pagans—that is, the heathen—of the province assembled, wishing to tear the preacher of truth to pieces and, after subjecting him to insulting mockery, consign him to the torments of a shameful death. The confessor of the Lord, Lantbertus, fearless and strong, addressed them as they snarled in anger and raged with demonic spirit:

### 28

“O men and brothers, since you are intelligent and endowed with reason, listen patiently, I beg you, and fix in your rational minds what I shall say to you.

[Note: [Col. 0655D] He here introduces a lengthy speech of the holy bishop, in which Stephen makes him explain Christian teaching according to his own understanding.]

The almighty God, the Father of the Only-begotten, whose servant I am and who ‘alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light’ (1 Timothy VI), himself begot from himself, without time, the Word through whom he made from nothing all things that exist in this world (John I).

We may contemplate with spiritual understanding this birth without beginning and generation without end, but we cannot perceive it with bodily sight. The Father is not earlier, nor is the Son later. From these two Persons, but from one indivisible and incomprehensible essence, proceeds the Holy Spirit, similar to the Father and Son in majesty and consubstantial with them in undivided divinity.

This Trinity in Persons and one, equal divinity in essence, after creating the entire world from nothing, fashioned the first human being from the clay of the earth. While he slept, God took a rib from him and formed a woman from it (Genesis XII), so that from their unblemished offspring the ruins of the fallen angels might be repaired.

### 29

He placed them in the Paradise of Delights and commanded them to eat from every tree, ordering them only to abstain from the tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. Through obedience, without bodily death, they might eventually have passed to the heavenly homeland of the angels, if they had bound themselves by the bond of charity through obedience to their Creator.

But alas! Through the envy of the serpent, the human being was enticed by the allurements of desire, and thus, made subject to death, was expelled from paradise.

Nor did the presumptuous man alone experience the punishment he deserved; he dragged with him the entire offspring of his race and brought it into the bitterness of the deadly crime. From that time the prince of the world subjected all human beings to himself, until the one who made them

[Note: [Col. 0656D] That is, who made or created human beings.]

took flesh from the Virgin, by which he might redeem humanity from the guilt of transgression into which the crafty enemy had led it through the weakness of the flesh.

The one whom I said was born from the Father without time was born in time from an undefiled mother, namely Mary, ever Virgin. Like electrum,

[Col. 0656A]

he was one in both and from both natures: he remained God with the Father, and for our redemption became mortal man from the Virgin Mother. He, true God and man proceeding from the Virgin’s womb, was circumcised according to the custom of mortals and baptized by John in the Jordan. Then he chose disciples, performed many signs of power, and openly declared to the world what he truly was.

### 30

Finally, by the power of his own will he laid down his soul upon the cross, so that he might redeem us by his blood—us whom the devil had held bound in his captivity from the beginning of the world. When the mystery of his passion had been accomplished and the dominion of death destroyed, he rose alive on the third day, restoring to us the privilege of nature that we had lost in our first parent.

After appearing to his disciples for forty days, he appeared to them once more as they reclined at table and commanded them to go into the whole world, so that they might preach the forgiveness of sins and announce to all nations what they had learned. At last, while they watched, he returned to heaven and, victorious over death, sat at the right hand of the Father.
