Refreshed by the gift of the Holy Spirit, they were scattered throughout every region of the world and announced to all this faith, which we unquestionably believe and which we steadfastly preach to you in his name and for his love.

As blessed Lantbertus continued these and similar things and preached the Gospel wondrously, all who had been predestined to eternal life were converted to the Catholic faith. Then the distinguished teacher and most eloquent preacher cast down the idols, sanctified the people through baptism, built churches, ordained priests, consecrated that entire region to Christ the Lord, and committed it forever to the service of God.

### 31

Meanwhile, while the shepherd was occupied with such concerns, fighting the battles of the most victorious King like an unconquered and courageous soldier, he received the triumphant palm of martyrdom in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] This sentence is defective, though it sufficiently reveals the writer’s meaning. Chapeavillus reads: “Christ the Lord bestowed the palm of martyrdom in this manner.”]

Two most wicked brothers, called Gallus and Rioldus, rose up against the blessed servants of Lantbertus, afflicting them with dreadful and manifold calamity. The most patient bishop entreated them with the humblest prayers to repent and reproved them with very frequent warnings. But the more patiently they endured their savagery as the Lord’s sheep, the more stubbornly they tore apart the flock of the Church.

Therefore the bishop’s dependents and relatives, men of exceedingly noble lineage, were provoked by the suffering of their subjects and, without his knowledge, decided by common counsel that they ought to pursue the evildoers. As the insolence of the aforesaid brothers increased and persisted in evil, the men, most distinguished by birth and conspicuous in arms, did not at all withdraw their resolve from the work they had begun.

[Col. 0657A]

### 32

Why say more? They attacked them in battle and inflicted on both the penalty of death. After they had been killed and cast into the abyss of hell, the wretched Dodo, a close relative of those who had been punished, inherited the legacy of their unspeakable crime.

He accepted the succession of the persecution to satisfy the savagery of his rage, not to preserve his own welfare. Inflated with pride, after taking counsel and bristling with weapons,

[Note: [Col. 0657D] I have restored this from Chapeavillus, since our manuscript erroneously reads “with counsel held and cold in weapons.”]

he began in his heart to plot the death of blessed Bishop Lantbertus for the killing of his kinsmen and to lie in wait for him in deed.

Joining to himself bold companions, wicked and exceedingly strong in battle, he went to Liège, where the unmarried man

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Chapeavillus also has this reading. Stephen himself uses it again when speaking of Saint Lantbertus, saying: “The unmarried man is driven from the chair.” Perhaps he wished to signify the saint’s remarkable chastity, or to allude to the etymology of the word, concerning which Festus, in Robert Estienne’s *Thesaurus*, says: “They think that *caelebs* was so called because he lives a life worthy of heaven.”]

was perhaps staying in those days.

That same night the most worthy bishop, destined to be exalted by the crown of martyrdom, left his companions sleeping in the house and went alone to prayer. Prolonging it as long as possible and performing it tirelessly, he continued until the dawn and entrusted all his hope to the Lord.

The fiery sun was already moving toward the starry citadels,

and dawn was driving away the darkness with rose-colored locks,

when the memorable Father returned home, roused his disciples from sleep, and commanded them to sing the morning hymns with him.

### 33

When these had been diligently and, as was fitting, devoutly completed, the lord himself was exceedingly fatigued by fasting and prayers. Because his servants urged him, he was compelled to return to bed, so that he might for a while relieve the weariness of his afflicted body through sleep.

But he sought relief there in vain, since he wished to have no softness. For the body that he tormented throughout the day without respite, he afflicted throughout the night without interruption. Long since cleansed by holy baptism, then exalted through priestly consecration, he was purified by the illumination of the Paraclete Spirit and, at the end, made white by his own blood.

He had not yet fallen asleep but was awaiting a more blessed rest when one of the servants

[Note: [Col. 0658D] This was Baldoveus, according to Godeschalcus in his Life of Blessed Lantbertus.]

went outside the house and saw a hostile band approaching from a distance. He immediately hurried back inside and did not delay in announcing to his companions what he had seen.

Then all of them were suddenly overcome with fearful astonishment and did not dare awaken the lord bishop. They waited silently for a long time, until the approaching enemies came nearer.

[Col. 0657D]

### 34

Nor do I think it should be passed over that, to some who were following the army from behind, the majesty of almighty God displayed itself.

I shall set it down in writing and proclaim it in a loud voice,

so that the whole order of the ages may know it in full.

[Col. 0658A]

They clearly saw a wondrous sign, like the Lord’s cross, shining above the bishop’s house. Because of the splendor of its brightness, it was neither easily seen nor readily described by anyone. Christ the Lord wished to display this to mortals so that through it it might plainly be understood that the man had truly been redeemed by the blood of Christ and crucified to the desires of the world.

When the most savage Dodo, girded with the weapons of wickedness and joined by his impious accomplices, reached the village named above, the minister of evil began to clash his weapons, summon his companions, and search here and there in his frenzy for the holy priest of God. Then his henchmen, obeying the commands of the mad executioner, broke down the doors and tore apart the fences; like wolves among sheep, they entered the enclosure savagely.

### 35

Immediately Lantbertus, the strongest combatant of God, awakened at the clash of weapons.

[Note: [Col. 0658D] Here Stephen differs from Godeschalcus, who says that Saint Lantbertus was awakened not by the noise of weapons but by his servant Baldoveus. Godeschalcus has the greater authority.]

He rose from his bed, seized a sword in his hand, and resolved to fight against the enemies. But without delay he changed the decision of his first impulse, threw the sword to the ground, and said in his heart:

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me; for it is neither my iniquity nor my sin on account of which the strong and wicked have risen against me. Behold, the assembly of the powerful seeks my life; I beg you to receive it in peace, O Lord, who are merciful and compassionate” (Psalm LVIII).

As blessed Lantbertus implored these things with tears, the impious attackers roared insolently, drove their spears into the walls, and attempted to penetrate the house. But his two nephews, namely Peter and Audolecus, bravely resisted them as they sought to enter.

As they roared and acted manfully, the most serene man said to them:

“If you have truly loved me until now, sons, obey my commands in this matter. Confess your sins to Jesus and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

Thus spoke the holy shepherd. But Audoletus replied:

“Dearest Father, they threaten to send fire to burn this house, and we shall all be burned together.”

### 36

At this the venerable man said:

“Do not fear the flames of the fire, sons. Certainly the right hand of God is powerful to rescue us from the danger that threatens. They, as I fear, will be clothed in everlasting shame; over us, as I believe, God’s sanctification will blossom.

“Nevertheless, you who were involved in the crime

[Note: [Col. 0658D] By “crime,” Godeschalcus, as reported by Chapeavillus, and Stephen and Sigebertus understand that Saint Lantbertus induced them to expiate with their own blood the killing of Gallus and Rioldus mentioned above.]

now receive the judgment of vengeance, lest infernal Gehenna torment you, but, purified, may everlasting life receive you.”

Having instructed them all in this way and strengthened them by priestly authority, he ordered his nephews to leave the inner chamber, so that they might deserve to become a holocaust for the eternal King.

When they fearlessly burst out through the chamber door, the enemies immediately struck them down, and they were sacrificed, worthy of martyrdom, before the divine gaze.

Then the distinguished Father and steadfast bishop prostrated himself on the floor in the form of a cross and implored the merciful God with the humblest prayers. But what his blessed soul then said to God, what mortal tongue can reveal? Without doubt, however, he asked for such things as he immediately deserved to obtain.

The raging enemies entered within and killed with the sword everyone they found there.

### 37

Finally, one of the men in that most cruel band, inflamed by the frenzy of savage rage, climbed onto the roof above, saw the blessed bishop lying prostrate on the ground, and, driven at once by a demonic spirit,

struck with a weapon him who was destined to live forever for Christ.

Thus Lantbertus, the precious priest of the Lord and glorious witness, was consecrated by a blessed martyrdom. In this way, living and happily crowned, he entered the kingdom of heaven which he had long desired.

The blessed man’s lifeless body lay there, drenched in a shower of its own blood; but his soul was carried by angels into heaven and placed among the fellowship of the citizens above. There he rejoices and exults in the company of the apostles, the glorification of the prophets, the confession of the martyrs, the joint inheritance of the confessors, and the purity of virgins; he possesses the palm of everlasting glory and the robe of eternal joy.

At last, a few who had escaped the danger of slaughter placed the most sacred body swiftly upon a boat and carried it to Tongeren, where they honorably buried it in the church of the Prince of the Apostles.

The heavenly power did not abandon his lifeless limbs;

it showed the peoples how great his goodness had been,

he whom Dodo, raging in his madness, had killed.

### 38

For when he was being placed in the tomb, an immense fragrance came from heaven, surpassing all spices in the sweetness of its perfume. Nor was the sublimity of the angels absent from his sarcophagus. During the first days they guarded him there and, by the melody of their song, displayed what rewards of gifts his soul possessed in the heavenly court.

“How subtle was the sound of that utterance of the gracious bishop!

Drawn there by profound wonder, the neighboring people

approached repeatedly and sought to learn what it was:

who they were, what they sang, and what gifts the voice possessed.

But when they wished to extend their inward sight

and look farther within, that voice withdrew in a slender breeze,

as it is usually heard when a bronze vessel is struck,

and the rising sound gradually carries itself to the stars.

But when, wisely, they withdrew so that they might be farther away,

the air resounded with voices sweet to hear.”

[Note: [Col. 0659C] He indicates by these words that the voice of Saint Lantbertus was heard amid heavenly melody at his tomb. The verses themselves, as with many others, he drew from an anonymous poet.]

Almost the entire province also gathered, mourning his absence with ineffable grief and sending deep sighs upward to the heavens.

The most sacred bishop and most glorious martyr of Christ, Lantbertus, completed the course of his struggle on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, while the living and true God reigns in the fullness of the Trinity and the majesty of unity. To him belong praise and the rejoicing of the saints, as well as perpetual thanksgiving, now and always, throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

# In the Year of Our Lord 922  
Hervaeus, Archbishop of Reims

[Col. 0659]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX.)

[Col. 0659D]

“That bishop whom Flodoardus calls Herivaeus was raised from the king’s court to the episcopate in the year 900. He was a man of noble birth, namely the sister’s son of Count Hucbald. Although still young, he was advanced to this honor, his ordination being carried out and duly celebrated by Riculfus, bishop of Soissons; Dodilo, bishop of Cambrai; Otgarius, bishop of Amiens; Mancius, bishop of Châlons; Rodulfus, bishop of Laon; Otfridus, bishop of Senlis; and the other diocesan bishops, who gave their consent and confirmed the decree of his ordination.

[Col. 0660D]

“Soon afterward he took pains to show himself so capable of this rank that he was lovable to all good people and even imitable in his very bearing. He was a kindly lover of the poor, a generous comforter of religious persons, exceedingly merciful, and a restorer of grieving wretches. He was especially learned in ecclesiastical chants and distinguished in psalmody, polished by this exercise, cheerful in mind and countenance, gentle and most mild, conspicuous in every goodness, a father to the clergy and a pious patron of the entire people; slow to anger and swift to show mercy; a lover of the churches of God and, by God’s power, a most courageous defender of the fold entrusted to him.

“He recovered the various properties and estates of the Church which his predecessor had distributed to different persons by leases or grants. While he diligently pursued spiritual matters, temporal resources flowed abundantly to him, and he distributed them with honorable prudence, assigning suitable provision to the officers of the episcopal household while remaining constantly devoted to prayer.”

On the day of his consecration, which was the day before the Nones of July, the excommunication of the men of Count Baldwin of Flanders, on account of the murder they had committed against Fulco, was read in the church of Blessed Mary of Reims.

In the year 901, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, he brought the body of Saint Remigius from the cathedral church to his own monastery, with King Charles and Richard, Duke of Burgundy, in attendance.

Flodoard continues:

“This bishop strengthened the fortress of Mosomus with restored walls, and rebuilt from its foundations the church there that had been destroyed; he rededicated it, as it had formerly been, in honor of the holy Mother of God, placing there the bones of Saint Victor, which had been discovered not far from that fortress. He also established and fortified a stronghold at Codiciacum, in a secure location. Likewise, he constructed another fortification at Sparnacum, above the River Marne. He also had several churches restored and consecrated that had been destroyed during the persecution of the Normans. At Vosagus, moreover, within the estate of Saint Remigius, he built a church and, with the consent of the bishop of Mainz, dedicated it to that same saint after depositing relics there. At Reims, too, he consecrated a church built by the city’s canons in honor of Saint Dionysius outside the city wall; there he also deposited, for safekeeping, the remains of the blessed bishop Rigobert and Saint Theodulf the abbot. He also cleansed and adorned the crypt beneath the very seat of the principal church, which had long remained buried under earth, where Saint Remigius is said to have been accustomed secretly to pour out prayers to God; he consecrated it in honor of that holy bishop. He greatly embellished the church of Reims with many gifts and illuminated it with silver crowns and lamps of both gold and silver. He enriched it also with other vessels of these two precious metals, as well as with jeweled vessels. Moreover, he erected and dedicated an altar in the middle of the choir in honor of the Holy Trinity, surrounding it with panels covered in silver. He also covered the larger cross with gold and suitably adorned it with gems and sacred relics. He decorated the venerable church with very many silken ornaments. To me also, and to the others—both clerical canons, monks, nuns, and all who appealed to him concerning their various needs—he granted many good things.”

When the Normans were setting foot in France, while discord was raging among the princes, Hervaeus judged that he ought to devote himself seriously to their conversion, so that the fierceness of the people, mitigated by Christ’s yoke, might put an end to plundering and brigandage. A rescript of Pope John IX to this same prelate is extant. In it, responding around the year 901 to his consultation concerning the Normans recently converted to the faith, he says that they should be treated more mildly and that the severity of the canons should not be extended against them, lest, refusing to bear burdens unfamiliar to them, they should relapse into their former impiety.

He also held two synods in 905 “with the co-bishops of his diocese, at which he wisely and appropriately discussed peace, the religion of God’s holy Church, and the condition of the kingdom of the Franks. At the request also of Witho, then bishop of Rouen, he collected from various authorities of the holy Fathers twenty-three chapters setting out how those Normans ought to be treated, and delegated them to that archbishop.” In 909, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, he held a council at Trosly. Around the year 910, after the death of Anscheric, bishop of Paris, he became chief chancellor of the king.

He made such progress in instructing the Normans that they “after the war which Count Robert of Chartres waged against them, finally accepted the faith of Christ at Rouen, having been granted certain coastal districts together with the city of Rouen, which they had almost destroyed, and other territories subject to it.” When the Hungarians were also plundering the Lotharingian kingdom, while Charles had summoned the nobles of the Franks to his aid against that people, this bishop alone, of all the kingdom’s leading men, came with only his own forces to the king’s defense in 919, bringing with him, as is said, fifteen hundred armed men.

In 920, when nearly all the Frankish nobles had abandoned their king Charles at the city of Soissons because of his counselor Haganon—whom Charles, having chosen him from among men of modest rank, listened to and honored above all the princes—this faithful, pious, and ever steadfast bishop, receiving the king fearlessly at that same place, led him to his camp. From there he brought him with him to the city of Reims and accompanied him for nearly seven months, until he restored his counts to him and restored him to the kingdom itself.

Then he struck Erlebard, count of the district of Château-Thierry, with anathema because of the wrongs he was inflicting upon the bishopric; he also recovered for the Church of Reims the fortresses of Altimont and Macerias, which Erlebard had seized from it. At that time he presided over and subscribed to the synod at Trosly in 921, in the presence of King Charles, at which Count Erlebard, who had been excommunicated, was absolved after his death.

Not long afterward he withdrew from Charles’s service, although up to that time he had been his most faithful and favored servant. Our Mabillon conjectures that this was because, in the preceding year, Charles had entrusted Roger, archbishop of Trier, with the office of chief chancellor that had been enjoined upon Hervaeus. Finally, exhausted by illness, he died on the sixth day before the Nones of July in 922, on the third day after the consecration of King Robert and four days before completing the twenty-second year of his episcopate. He was buried with solemn rites, attended by several bishops who had come to Durocortorum on the day of his death. Andreas Quercetanus, in his *Genealogical History of the House of Châtillon*, where Hervaeus’s eulogy is found, writes that he was the brother of Odo of Châtillon, in whom he placed the entire lineage of that house. On his writings, see our Rivet, *Literary History of France*, vol. VI, p. 185.

[Col. 0661]

# Letter of Hervaeus, Archbishop of Reims, to Witho, Archbishop of Rouen

What penance ought to be imposed on unbaptized pagans, on the baptized, and on those rebaptized who afterward, in pagan fashion, devastated churches and destroyed Christianity. From the opinions of the Fathers, the canons, and the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs.

*(Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, vol. I.)*

[Col. 0661C] To the most reverend and beloved brother and fellow archbishop Witho, Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims, sends abundant greetings in the Savior of all and the happiness of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0663A] Since you asked our humility to seek in the divine oracles how counsel ought to be given concerning those who have been rebaptized and who, just as before baptism, have practiced frivolous pleasures according to pagan custom—like swine returning to their wallow and dogs to their vomit—and concerning those who have not yet been found worthy to receive baptism [Note: See the letter of Pope John IX to Hervaeus concerning converted pagans who live according to pagan custom], we have striven, as far as we could and as the brevity of time permits, to satisfy your request. And so that each chapter might be easier for you to find, we have written it out chapter by chapter in this little document.

And because “the mercy of the Lord fills the earth” (Psalm 32), and to him the Church devoutly says by apostrophe, “You have mercy on all, O Lord, and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking the sins of human beings because of repentance” (Wisdom 11), we have thought it fitting to set forth here, very briefly, the remarkable and most merciful deed of the blessed apostle and evangelist John—or rather, the most gracious work of the Lord himself—just as it is very well known to you and more fully set out in ecclesiastical history.

## I. On Saint John the Evangelist

When John himself, returning to Ephesus, was visiting and enlightening the neighboring provinces, he saw a certain young man of exceedingly fierce character. He commended him to the bishop of that place, who bestowed upon him the grace of baptism. Then, trusting in the grace with which he had been strengthened, John began to treat the young man less strictly. But the young man, having obtained premature liberty, followed the path of corruption. Beginning gradually with theft and other evils, he soon became the leader of robbers.

After some time, when John was visiting the same place, he asked the aforementioned bishop for his charge. When he learned that the young man was absent, he quickly mounted a horse and went in search of him. After finding him, and while the young man was fleeing, the Apostle said to him: “Stop for a moment and believe me, because Christ has sent me.” Hearing this, the young man stopped. Then, trembling, he wept most bitterly and, as the old man approached him, fell at his knees, making amends as best he could by groans and wailings, and was baptized again in the abundant fountains of his tears, hiding only his right hand.

The Apostle, promising under oath that he would obtain pardon for him from the Savior, likewise fell at his knees and kissed that very right hand, by consciousness of whose bloodshed he was tormented, as though it had already been cleansed through innocence. He brought him back to the church, continually pouring out prayers for him and undertaking frequent fasts together with him, seeking from God the forgiveness he had promised him. Nor did he cease until, having corrected him in every respect, he even placed him over the church (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 23).

## II. On Saint Sylvester and the Emperor Constantine

Here it is also helpful to insert the memorable deed of blessed Pope Sylvester toward the emperor Constantine, especially because of the week-long fast he imposed upon him.

“Among other things,” he said, “Saint Sylvester addressed the same Caesar: ‘Require of yourself a fast during this one week. Lay aside your purple, enter your chamber, and there put on sackcloth, prostrate upon the ground. Confess that you have now fallen into error through ignorance by declaring persecution against the Christians. Proclaim Jesus Christ, the Savior of bodies and souls, not only in speech but also by believing, and repent that you have killed many of God’s saints.’”

And shortly afterward: “Command that alms be given throughout the entire week; also provide benefits to those who ask, and appoint suitable persons to carry these things out.”

And after some further remarks: “Saint Sylvester placed his hand upon his head”—that is, upon the head of Augustus Constantine—“blessing him and making him a catechumen. Then, having gathered all the priests and deacons together with the entire clergy, he imposed a fast upon the whole Church, saying: ‘If the inhabitants of Nineveh, at Jonah’s preaching, escaped through a three-day fast the anger and offense of God that he had threatened, how much more shall we escape persecutions at the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ. We gain souls, acquire God’s peace for the churches, and put an end to idolatry. We do these things through fasts and prayers, so that we may obtain them from God.’” And so forth.

## III. Sayings of Blessed Gregory to the People

Blessed Gregory also says in a homily on the Gospel addressed to the people (Homilies 19 and 20 on the Gospel):

“If you were unwilling to live for God in childhood and youth, at least come to your senses in old age, and come, even late, to the ways of life, when you are no longer going to have to labor greatly.”

And after a short interval:

“Such people are often rewarded earlier, because they depart from the body and enter the kingdom before those who seemed to have been called already in childhood. Did not the thief come at the eleventh hour? Although he did not have the opportunity earlier in life, he did have it late, through punishment: he confessed God upon the cross and almost with the voice of the sentence breathed out the spirit of life. The householder began distributing the denarius from the last, because he led the thief into the rest of paradise before Peter.”

Again, the same author:

“The kingdom of heaven wishes to be seized by our tears, although it is not owed to our merits. Therefore, let no quality or quantity of our evils break us from the certainty of hope. That venerable thief offers great confidence in pardon—not venerable because he was a thief, but a thief because of his cruelty and venerable because of his confession. Consider, I beg you, consider how incomprehensible are the bowels of mercy in almighty God. This thief, dragged away from the throat of the road with bloodied hands, was suspended upon the gallows of the cross. There he confessed; there he was healed; there he deserved to hear: ‘Today you will be with me in paradise.’” And so forth.

## IV. The Same Author to Bishop Peter

[Col. 0665A]

Writing again to Peter, bishop of Corsica, he says (book VII, letter 2):

“Your Fraternity should diligently strive, with the Lord’s help, to bring to completion the work it has begun. Whether it concerns those who were once faithful but, through negligence or necessity, have returned to the worship of idols, hasten to bring them back to the faith by imposing penance for a number of days, so that they may be required to mourn their guilt and may hold more firmly to that to which, with the Lord’s help, they are returning, the more completely they have lamented what they are leaving; or whether it concerns those who have not yet been baptized, admonish them, entreat them, terrify them with the coming judgment, and also give an account of why they ought not to worship wood and stones.

“Hasten, therefore, your Fraternity to gather them for the almighty Lord, so that when he comes, when the decisive day of judgment arrives, your holiness may be found among the number of the saints. For what could you do that is more useful and exalted than to think about giving life to souls and gathering them, and to bring immortal profit to your Lord, who has given you a place from which to preach?” And the rest.

## V. The Same Author to Abbot Mellitus

Elsewhere, writing to Abbot Mellitus (book IX, letter 71), he says:

“Because the English people are accustomed to kill many oxen in sacrifice to demons, some solemnity should also be changed in this matter, so that on the day of the dedication or feast of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, they may make tents for themselves from branches of trees around those same churches that have been converted from shrines, and celebrate the solemnity with religious banquets.

“Let them no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, but kill animals for food to the praise of God, and give thanks to the giver of all things for their satisfaction, so that while some outward joys are preserved for them, they may more easily consent to inward joys. For it is undoubtedly impossible to cut away everything at once from hard hearts. One who strives to climb to a lofty place is raised by steps or paces, not by leaps.

“Thus, in Egypt, the Lord indeed made himself known to the Israelite people; yet he retained for his own worship the sacrificial practice that they had been accustomed to offer to the devil, commanding them to sacrifice animals in his own worship. In this way, as they changed their hearts, they would omit one part of the sacrifice and retain another: although the animals they were accustomed to offer remained the same, by sacrificing them to the true God and not to idols, the sacrifices themselves would no longer be the same.”

## VI. Bishop Ambrose

Saint Ambrose adds similar counsel concerning the gentlest reception of penitents in the book entitled *On Penance* (chapter 1):

“He who strives to correct the faults of human weakness must himself endure that weakness and somehow bear it upon his shoulders, not cast it away. For that evangelical shepherd is said to have carried the weary sheep, not to have cast it away. Solomon says: ‘Do not be excessively righteous’ (Ecclesiasticus 17). Moderation must temper righteousness.

“For how can one who regards you with disgust offer himself to be healed by you, when he thinks that he is to be an object of contempt rather than of compassion to his physician? Therefore the Lord Jesus had compassion on us, so that he might call us back to himself, not frighten us away. He came gentle and humble; finally he said: ‘Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11).

“Therefore the Lord Jesus refreshes; he does not exclude or cast away. And rightly he chose such disciples who, as interpreters of the Lord’s will, would gather the people of God rather than reject them. From this it is clear that those are not to be counted among Christ’s disciples who think that harsh things should be followed instead of gentle ones, and proud things instead of humble ones.

“And while they themselves seek the Lord’s mercy, they deny it to others. Such are the teachers of the Novatians, who call themselves pure. What is more arrogant than this, when Scripture says: ‘No one is clean from sin, not even an infant of one day’ (Job 14), and David cries out: ‘Cleanse me from my sin’ (Psalm 50)?”

And shortly afterward:

“No one can do penance well unless he has hoped for forgiveness.”

## VII. Augustine

Blessed Augustine briefly teaches how those in authority ought to deal with wicked people of every kind, saying (Prosper, *Sentences of Saint Augustine*):

“We must not despair of the wicked, but pray for them more earnestly that they may become good, because the number of the saints has always been increased from the number of the ungodly.”

## VIII. On Saint Remigius the Bishop

The following is also read in the appropriate place in the *Life of Blessed Remigius, Apostle of the Franks* (Hincmar, *Life of Saint Remigius*), among the accounts of the conversion of King Louis and his people:

“He”—that is, Saint Remigius—“filled with great joy, instructed the king and the people in clear and brief words concerning how they ought to renounce the devil, his works and pomps, and believe in God. And because the holy day of Easter was approaching, he imposed upon them a fast according to Christian custom.”

## IX. On Saint Vedastus the Bishop

The *Life of the blessed pontiff Vedastus* likewise relates how, on the journey and in the presence of that same king and people, the man of God Vedastus gave sight to a blind man; it also relates how the king came to baptism and, in the city of Reims, entrusted the man of God Vedastus to Saint Remigius.

“The king,” it says, “having been thoroughly instructed by the man of God in evangelical teachings and, through the miracle then present, having been firmly strengthened in faith, delayed nothing on the journey and doubted nothing in faith. With great eagerness of spirit and great haste in travel, he hurried to see the most holy pontiff Remigius, so that, through his sacred ministry and by the working of the Holy Spirit, he might be washed in the living spring of Catholic baptism for the remission of sins and the hope of eternal life.

“He remained with him for several days so that he might satisfy the ecclesiastical decrees and first be cleansed by the tears of penance, according to the apostolic command, when blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, says: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus’ (Acts 2). And thus, in the name of the Holy Trinity, he received the baptism of the heavenly mystery.” [Note: See Surius, *Acts of Saint Vedastus*.]

## X. From the Life of Saint Basil: Concerning a Certain Apostate

A certain apostate is mentioned in the miracles of Blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea. He had denied Christ in writing and handed himself over to the devil as testimony to his denial.

“To him,” the remarkable man Basil said, among other things: ‘Do you wish to return to the Lord our God?’

“The young man replied: ‘Certainly I do, but I cannot.’

“He said to him: ‘Why?’

“The young man answered: ‘I denied Christ in writing and professed myself to the devil.’

“Saint Basil said to him: ‘Do not be troubled. Our God is merciful, and he will receive you when you repent. For he has compassion on our wickedness.’”

After some intervening material:

“That same holy man said to the young man: ‘Do you believe that you will be saved?’

“He replied: ‘I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.’

“Immediately he took him by the hand, made the sign of Christ over him, and, praying, shut him in an inner part of the sacred enclosure. Giving him a rule of life, he labored with him for three days.”

And after some further material:

“On the fortieth day the holy man returned to him and said: ‘How are you, brother?’

“He answered him: ‘I am well, holy man of God. For today I saw you in a vision fighting on my behalf and conquering the devil.’

“Then, when morning came, he summoned the sacred clergy, the monasteries, and all the people who loved Christ, and said to them:

“‘My dearest little children, all of you give thanks to the Lord. Behold, the good shepherd must carry the lost sheep upon his shoulders and offer it to the Church. Therefore it is necessary that we also keep vigil through the night and ask his mercy, lest the destroyer of souls prevail even in this matter.’

“And with the people eagerly gathered together, they asked God throughout the whole night, with the good shepherd, with tears, crying out on his behalf, ‘Kyrie eleison’—‘Lord, have mercy.’ Early in the morning, with the entire multitude of the people, the saint took the young man, held his right hand, and led him into the holy church of God with psalms and hymns.

“And behold, the devil, casting a spell over the eyes of all, came in a mournful form with every destructive power. Seizing the young man invisibly, he tried to snatch him from the saint’s hand. The young man began to cry out: ‘Holy man of God, help me!’

“The saint then turned again toward the devil and said: ‘Most wicked one, corrupter of souls, father of darkness and perdition, is your own perdition not enough, by which you have afflicted yourself and those who are under you, unless you also try to seize the creature of my God?’

“After a very brief interval:

“The holy man of God said to the devil: ‘The Lord rebukes you, devil.’

“He answered him: ‘Basil, you are prejudging me. I did not go to him; he came to me. He denied Christ and professed himself to me. And behold, I have a written document, and on the day of judgment I will bring him before the common Judge.’

“The holy man of God said: ‘Blessed be the Lord my God. This people shall not lower their hands from the height of heaven until you return the written document.’

“Then he turned and said to the people: ‘Raise your hands to heaven and cry out with tears, “Christ, Kyrie eleison.”’

“While the people stood for a long time with their hands extended toward heaven, behold, the young man’s written document was carried through the air and came into view of everyone; it was placed in the hands of our venerable father and shepherd. He received it, gave thanks to God, and rejoiced greatly. Then, before all the people, he said to the young man:

“‘Do you recognize these letters, brother?’

“He answered him: ‘Yes, holy man of God; it is my written document.’

“Saint Basil tore up the document, brought him into the church, and judged him worthy of the sacred ministry and of communion in Christ’s mysteries and gifts.”

## XI. On Saint Lawrence

Among other things, the passion of Blessed Lawrence, archdeacon and martyr of Christ, contains the following:

“There was a pagan who had long been held in prison. Because he had wept over the loss of his eyes, he had become blind. Blessed Lawrence said to him: ‘If you believe in the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, be baptized, and he will give you sight.’

“Immediately after his confession, when he had been baptized, his eyes were opened, and he began to cry out, saying: ‘Blessed is the eternal Lord God, who has given me sight through Blessed Lawrence, because I have always been blind and now I see.’

“After this he also catechized the blessed Hippolytus in the customary manner and, taking water, blessed and baptized him. In the same way he baptized the Roman soldier, who, immediately after being baptized, was crowned with martyrdom.”

## XII. On Saint Sebastian

[Col. 0668C]

The passion of Saint Sebastian contains the following passage:

“When all those who had come to deceive the saints”—namely, Mark and Marcellinus—“unanimously believed in Christ, Nicostratus, together with his wife, kept urging them, saying: ‘I will take neither food nor drink unless the mystery of the Christian religion is given to me.’

“Saint Sebastian said to him: ‘Change your rank and begin to be Christ’s chief secretary rather than the prefect’s. Listen, therefore, to my advice. Gather together all whom the prison has enclosed, whom chains hold, and whom the dungeons wear down. When you have done this, I will bring in a bishop of the sacred law, so that with all who wish to believe you may receive the sacrament of the mystery.

“For if the devil has attempted and still attempts to take Christ’s saints away from Christ, how much more ought we, as an act of piety, to heal those whom the devil has unjustly won and restore them to their Creator?’

“Nicostratus answered him: ‘How can holy things be entrusted to the wicked and criminal?’

“Saint Sebastian said: ‘Our Savior deigned to show us his presence for sinners and revealed the mystery by which every sin and every crime may be taken away from human beings and all the virtues of the Lord bestowed.’

“And after much else:

“Saint Sebastian went to the holy presbyter Polycarp, who was concealed because of the persecution, and told him everything that had happened. When he heard these things, Polycarp gave thanks to God and came with him to the house of Nicostratus. Seeing the crowds of believers, he greeted them with complete joy and said:

“‘Blessed are you all who have heard the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden light”’ (Matthew 11).

“‘You, therefore, our brothers, whom the water of baptism has washed and made most beloved sons by consecrating you to almighty God—for the fact that you tried to call the most blessed soldiers of Christ back from their holy purpose, you needed penance, so that through it you might come to forgiveness.

“‘But now, because you have advanced to such great glory that you even desire and gladly wish to run toward the passion from which you painfully tried to turn others away, this is an ancient device of Christ. For the very man whom the Lord himself deigned to make a vessel of his election and wished to appoint teacher of the nations—who not only turned the minds of the faithful away from their purpose of piety, but also stoned those unwilling to depart from Christ—the Lord himself gave to us as an apostle. From Saul he gave us Paul; from an apostate he made an apostle; and from a persecutor he gave the Church a ruler.

“‘He became a lover of martyrdom, though he had been the author of persecution; and he who had previously rejoiced in the afflictions of others later rejoiced in his own persecutions. The one who then exercised this power in his apostle has now rescued the captivity of your souls from the very prison of hell and from the jaws of dragons, and has opened for you, as you return from darkness to light, the gates of eternal life.

“‘Therefore, since all the demons, who are children of darkness, are saddened, and all the holy angels, who are children of light, rejoice, let each one come forward and give his name, so that, while the fast carries the day through to evening, the appropriate time for the festive sacrament of baptism may be found.’

“And again:

“‘The entire household that was in Nicostratus’s house consisted of thirty-three souls, of both sexes and every age. Then all those who had been bound and brought from the squalor of the prison—sixteen souls—all these forty-nine were baptized by the holy presbyter Polycarp and received by Saint Sebastian.’”

## XIII. Words of the Lord Bede (on John, chapter 3)

“According to the saving and most firm doctrine of the Catholic faith, which is to be observed unanimously and faithfully by all throughout the whole world, what is held concerning bodily generation must also be held concerning spiritual generation: namely, that once it has been completed, it can in no way be repeated.

“Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or a criminal baptizes someone in the confession of the Holy Trinity, the person who has been baptized in this way cannot be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession or bestowal of so great a name appear to be annulled.”

## XIV. Pope Leo

[Col. 0670A]

Those concerning whom it is uncertain whether they have received baptism must be reborn, from the decrees of Pope Leo (letter to Rusticus):

“If there are no indications among relatives or laypeople, and none among clergy or neighbors, by which those about whom inquiry is being made can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they plainly perish; for reason does not permit something to be regarded as repeated when it is not shown to have been done.

“Those who can remember coming to church with their parents may recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if even this is absent from their memory, what is not known to have been bestowed should be conferred upon them, because there is no rash presumption where there is diligent piety.”

## XV. Again, Leo

Penance is to be granted to captives who, compelled by necessity, have eaten sacrificial foods, from the decrees of the same Pope Leo (letter to Nicetas):

“Concerning those Christians who, among the people by whom they had been taken captive, are said to have been polluted by sacrificial foods, we believe that this also should be answered to your charitable inquiry: they should be cleansed by the satisfaction of penance, which is to be measured not so much by length of time as by contrition of heart.

“Whether terror forced this upon them or hunger persuaded them, there should be no doubt that it must be wiped away, since such food was consumed out of fear or necessity, not out of reverence for a religion.”

## XVI. From the Council of Nicaea

[Col. 0670C] Concerning laypeople who denied God, and those who renounced him and afterward returned to the world, from the Council of Nicaea (Council of Nicaea, canon 11):

“Concerning those who transgressed without necessity, whether because their possessions had been taken away, because of danger, or because of something of this kind that occurred under the tyranny of Licinius: although they are proven unworthy of humaneness, the synod has nevertheless decided that benevolence should be extended to them.

“Therefore, all who truly repent shall be counted among the faithful and hearers for three years; for six years they shall humble themselves in complete contrition; and for two years they shall share in prayer with the people, though without the offering.”

## XVII. From the Council of Carthage

(Council of Carthage, year 348, canon 1.)

“Bishop Gratus said: ‘If it pleases you, let us first consider the question of rebaptization. Therefore I ask your holiness to make known the judgment of your minds concerning one who descends into the water, is questioned concerning the Trinity according to the faith of the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, and confesses a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ: whether he may be questioned again in the same faith and immersed again in water.’

“All the bishops said: ‘Far be it, far be it! We decree rebaptizations to be unlawful, and it is entirely foreign to sincere faith and Catholic discipline.’”

## XVIII. From the Council of Ancyra

(Council of Ancyra, canon 1.)

Concerning those who, through fear, performed pagan rites:

“All who went up to the temples in mourning clothing, and, sitting among the others, ate while weeping—if they complete a period of three years of penance, let them be received into communion without the offering; that is, they themselves are not to offer the offering.

“But if, after being brought to the temples, they did not eat, let them remain in penance for two years; in the third year, let them communicate, but without the offering, as stated, so that in the fourth year they may receive the fullness of their restoration.

“The bishop must have the authority to consider the sins of each of them and, according to what he sees in their conduct, assign the standard and rule of their conversion: that is, acting with greater humanity, he may shorten the time for someone according to the manner of his life, or add a longer period if he sees that this is necessary for correction.

“Their earlier and later life must also be examined in all these cases. Thus priestly humanity should moderate its treatment of them.”

## XIX. From the Same Council

(ibid., canon 6.)

Concerning those who frequently sacrificed to idols, from the Council of Ancyra:

“Concerning those who, on the feast days of the pagans, attended banquets in their remote places and nevertheless brought their own food there and ate it: it has been decided that after two years of penance they may be received. However, each bishop must examine their life and, taking into consideration both their past and present conduct, determine whether they should be received with the offering or admitted only to communion.”

## XX. From the Same Council

(ibid., canon 7.)

Concerning those who were compelled to sacrifice to idols, from the same council:

“Those who sacrificed a second or third time under compulsion shall submit themselves to penance for four years; for two further years they shall communicate without the offering, and in the seventh year they shall receive the fullness of communion.”

## XXI. Pope Leo

Concerning those who have taken part in a pagan banquet and eaten sacrificial foods, from the decrees of Pope Leo (letter to Rusticus):

“If they merely attended a pagan banquet and ate sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed by fasts and the laying on of hands, so that afterward, abstaining from food sacrificed to idols, they may share in Christ’s sacraments.

“But if they worshiped idols or were polluted by murder or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.”

## XXII. Again, Pope Leo

[Col. 0671D]

Those who, compelled either by force or fear, inclined their souls toward the repetition of baptism are to be helped by the remedy of penance. Pope Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne:

“Concerning those about whom your Charity has believed that we should be consulted—those who were compelled to repeat baptism, whether driven by fear or led astray by error, and who now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—the following moderation must be established: they are not to be received into our fellowship and the unity of communion except through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

“The periods of penance are to be established by your judgment with the customary moderation, according as you observe the devotion of the converts’ minds; at the same time taking into account the condition of old age and considering the needs arising from every kind of danger or illness.

“If anyone is so severely pressed by these circumstances that, while still doing penance, his salvation is despaired of, he ought to be assisted through priestly care by the grace of communion.”

## XXIII. From the Acts of the Apostles

It is read in the Acts of the Apostles that certain men who had come down from Judea taught the brothers that they ought to be circumcised and observe the law of Moses. The apostles and elders, however, with the whole Church, ordered that no further burden be imposed upon them, except that they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication (Acts 15).

## XXIV. From the Council of Africa
[Col. 0672B] That dealings with the Donatists, who had been condemned by all Catholics, as by the whole world, should be conducted more leniently: from the African council (African Council, year 401, canon 3).

“Having examined and considered everything that seemed conducive to the Church’s welfare, with the Spirit of God approving and directing us, we have chosen to deal gently and peacefully with the men mentioned above, although they have been cut off by their restless dissension from the unity of the Lord’s body, so that throughout all the African provinces it may become thoroughly known, insofar as lies in us, by what pitiable error they are bound, unless perhaps, as the Apostle says, while we correct those who think differently with gentleness, God may grant them repentance for recognition of the truth, [Col. 0672C] and they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they have been taken captive for his will.”

## XXV. From Pope Celestine

That final penance must be denied to no one, from Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul (Letter 2).

“We have learned that penance is being denied to the dying, and that the wishes of those who at the time of their death desire this remedy for their souls are not being granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to despair of God’s mercy, as though he could not at any time come to the aid of one who hastens to him, and redeem a man endangered beneath the burden of sins from which he desires to be released and freed.

“What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul, so that it cannot be absolved? Yet God, ever most ready to help, invites to repentance and promises: ‘On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins shall not be reckoned against him.’ And again: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live.’ Therefore whoever has denied a man repentance at the time of death takes salvation away from him and despairs of God’s clemency, since he has not believed that God can come to the aid of the dying, even in a moment.

“The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would also have lost his reward if the repentance of a single hour had not helped him. While he was in punishment, he repented, and through the confession of a single utterance, with God’s promise, earned a dwelling in paradise. Therefore the true conversion of those placed at the end of life must be judged by the mind rather than by the amount of time, as the prophet declares: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.’

“Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, repentance must not at any time be denied to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things will be revealed.”

## XXVI. From Bede’s Penitential

In the little book entitled *The Penitential of the Venerable Priest Bede* (*On Remedies for Sins*, preface):

“We earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ that, in all the matters noted here, he carefully distinguish the sex, age, condition, status, and person of the penitent, as well as the penitent’s own heart; and according to these considerations let him judge what seems appropriate in each individual case.

“For some, abstinence from foods is required; for others, the giving of alms; for some, the frequent bending of the knee; for this person, standing at the cross; for another, some other action of this kind contributing to the cleansing of sins. For very many, all these things must be performed. It is necessary to correct faults, which, in every examination, must be weighed by a discerning judge.”

May your reverend and most cherished brotherhood always prosper in Christ with happy success and flourish in every good work, remembering us in your prayers, as well as the whole Church.

[Col. 0673]

# COUNCIL OF REIMS UNDER HERVAEUS

In which an anathema was pronounced against those who had killed Archbishop Fulk, on the day before the Nones of July, in the year of Christ 900.

(*In Labbe, Councils*, vol. IX, col. 481.)

[Col. 0673B] In the year 900 of the Lord’s incarnation, on the day before the Nones of July—that is, on the first day on which Hervaeus was ordained archbishop and bishop of Reims—the following excommunication was read in the church of Saint Mary at Reims, in the presence of the bishops listed below.

Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims in name but not in merit, and servant of the people of God; Vito, archbishop of Rouen; Riculfus, bishop of Soissons; Hetlo, bishop of Noyon; Dodilo, bishop of Cambrai; Herinandus, bishop of Thérouanne; Otgarius, bishop of Amiens; Honoratus, bishop of Beauvais; Mancio, bishop of Châlons; Rodulfus, bishop of Laon; Otfridus, bishop of Senlis; Angelrannus, [Col. 0673C] bishop of Meaux.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God everywhere, both clergy and laity, that we and the whole Church entrusted to us are greatly troubled by grief because of an unheard-of crime, after the persecutions of the time of the apostles and their successors—namely, the impious murder, wickedly perpetrated by ungodly men, of our father and pastor Fulk. He labored day and night with all his strength for the welfare of the kingdom and the condition of the whole holy Church, and placed himself as a wall of protection in defense of all the churches existing in this kingdom—for their possessions were being seized, contrary to every divine and human law, by Count Baldwin, son of Baldwin and Judith. Therefore he was most cruelly killed and fell at the hands of Baldwin’s men, Vineemar, Evarard, and Rotfeld [Ratfrid], together with their other accomplices.

Because of his death, the entire order and procession of the Church is rightly saddened and pours forth laments of compassion from the deepest sighs of its heart. Since, therefore, they did not fear to perpetrate in our times such a crime as previously had scarcely been heard of in the Church except, perhaps, among pagans—because it had not otherwise occurred—in the name of the Lord and by the power of the Holy Spirit, and likewise by the authority divinely conferred upon bishops through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we separate them from the bosom of holy Mother Church and condemn them by anathema to perpetual malediction, so that there may never be any restoration of them through human agency, nor any association with Christians.

Let them be accursed in the city and accursed in the field; accursed be their granary and accursed their remains; accursed be the fruit of their womb and the fruit of their land, their herds of cattle and their flocks of sheep. [Col. 0674C] Accursed be those entering and departing; accursed be they in the house, fugitives in the field. Let their entrails pour forth in the privy like those of the treacherous and wretched Arius. Let all the curses that the Lord, through Moses, threatened against the people who transgressed the divine law come upon them. Let them be *anathema maranatha*, and let them perish at the second coming of the Lord.

Moreover, let everything that the sacred canons and the decrees of apostolic men pronounce against murderers and sacrilegious persons come upon them. For we mark them with the name of sacrilegious men, since they dared to lay their hands upon this Christ of the Lord. May complete and everlasting destruction be heaped upon them by the entirely just sentence of divine vengeance.

Therefore let no Christian say “Hail” to them. Let no priest ever dare to celebrate Mass before them, or, if they fall ill, receive their confessions or give them the most holy Communion, unless they repent—even at the very end [Col. 0675A] of their lives. Instead, let them be buried with the burial of an ass, and let them lie as refuse upon the face of the earth, as an example of shame and malediction to present and future generations. And [Col. 0676A] just as these lamps are extinguished today after being thrown down from our hands, so may their lamp be extinguished forever.

# APPENDIX TO HERVAEUS OF REIMS

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675]

# ACTS OF THE COUNCIL OF TROSLÉ

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Troslé is still the name of a village a few miles distant from Soissons. Other councils were subsequently held there in this same century, which Flodoard repeatedly mentions in his *Chronicle*. Whether he remembered this one cannot be determined, because we possess that part of the *Chronicle* in mutilated form. The collectors of canons—Burchard, Ivo, Gratian, and those who came after them—also seem to have been unaware of this council, for they all remain silent about it, except that in our time Antonius Augustinus was the first to use its testimonies in his epitome. JAC. SIRM.]

Held at Troslé in the county of Soissons by Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of Christ 909, in the second year of Pope Sergius III and the seventeenth year of King Charles the Simple.

(*In Labbe, Councils*, vol. IX, col. 520.)

## TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS

[Col. 0675B]

I. On the honor and worship of the churches of God.  
II. On the condition of the kingdom and loyalty to the king.  
III. On the regular order, now almost collapsed.  
IV. On sacrilegious persons and their condemnation.  
V. On the oppression and dishonoring of priests.  
VI. On the endowments and tithes of churches, and on not exacting dues from them.  
VII. On plunder.  
VIII. On abducted women, secret marriages, and incest.  
IX. On the approach to, frequenting, and cohabitation of priests and clerics with women.  
X. On avoiding sexual immorality.  
XI. On restraining perjury.  
XII. On those who are at variance, angry, and quarrelsome.  
XIII. On murderers and liars.  
XIV. On not seizing the property of a church after the death of a bishop.  
XV. Epilogue to the bishops and, generally, to everyone.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0675C]

The holy Council of Nicaea, celebrated generally and without exception by God’s authority, commands (canon 5) that, after all the bishops of a province have assembled together, necessary questions be discussed, and that whatever has been commonly approved by all according to the rule, all should follow—both metropolitans and the other bishops.

Likewise, the Council of Antioch (canons 9 and 14) commands that, whenever something must be done, the provincial bishops should carry it out with the counsel of their metropolitan, and the metropolitan with the counsel of his provincial co-bishops, as is set out there. It commands this not only in the cases of any persons whatsoever, but also—if perhaps, it says, a question should arise among the bishops themselves concerning any matter—the primate of the province ought to appoint bishops as judges.

Roman laws also, and blessed Pope Gregory, repeatedly show that, when the truth has been ascertained through the judgment of such men, disputes among ecclesiastical persons, or between any persons and ecclesiastical persons, ought to receive a beneficial conclusion, provided that in all things what ancient authority teaches is sought.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 909, in the twelfth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, the venerable fathers and teachers of the Church assembled: namely Hervaeus, archbishop of the holy metropolitan see of Reims and servant of the whole people of God, together with the co-bishops of the diocese of Reims, whose names are written below, in the county of Soissons, at the place called Troslé, to deliberate concerning the condition of the holy Church and the welfare of the whole kingdom. After the solemn greeting had been given and all had taken their seats in due order, as is customary, the archbishop began as follows.

## ADDRESS OF HERVAEUS, ARCHBISHOP

Since for several years we have been prevented from assembling according to the decrees of the canons, partly by the attacks of pagans and partly also by the gravest disturbances of the kingdom and the attacks of certain false Christians, now that, with the Lord’s approval, we have been granted the ability to assemble according to the decrees of the canons, and by God’s grace we have come together, he cooperating in whose name we are gathered and who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, it is first and above all necessary for us to preserve “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV), so that we may all think as one and all speak as one in Christ.

In accordance with the saving words of the martyr Cyprian, let us preserve among ourselves love of spirit, honor for the college, the bond of faith, and harmony in the priesthood; and, attending to the regular constitutions of our fathers, let no one be drawn away from the regular custom of his metropolitan see.

Since, according to canonical definition, a synod must be regarded as complete when the metropolitan is present with his suffragans, it is fitting and proper that whatever good we have been able to conceive in our minds and utter with our mouths—by the preceding grace from which comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James I)—we should, with that same grace following after us, strive to bring to perfect completion in action, for without it we can accomplish no good.

It is therefore necessary that you hasten to aid the Christian religion, now already failing and, as it were, inclining toward a precipice, and “the world set in evil” (I John V), through your counsel and episcopal authority. You see how evident is the fury of the Lord and how his hand is extended to strike.

For behold, every year, since we see our land condemned in part to grievous sterility, we see by what disasters the people perish daily. Cities have been depopulated, monasteries destroyed or burned, and fields reduced to desolation, so that we can truly say: “The sword has reached to the soul” (Jer. IV).

The sword has indeed reached to the soul when, by God’s just judgment, external goods have been lost, the body exhausted by scourges and afflictions, and the very strength of the soul seems to fail, wearied, so that almost nothing living remains in it.

These things certainly do not happen by chance or because of some sudden change of times or elements, since it is written: “Nothing on earth happens without cause, and pain does not spring from the earth” (Job V).

Pain does not spring from the earth because, as blessed Gregory says (*Moralia*, book V, chapter 6), “punishment does not at all arise from the creature that strikes, but from the creature that, by sinning, has extorted the force of the blow.

“For behold, we see that, for our correction, the awaited rain is frequently withheld from the parched earth; the darkened air is dried by the burning sun; the sea rages with swelling storms and destroys some whom it has received for crossing, while against others the raised wave, heaped into a mound, obstructs the journey they desire. The earth is not only diminished in the fruitfulness of its growth but also consumes the seeds it has received.

“In all these things it is plainly seen that what a certain wise man testifies concerning the Lord is true: ‘The whole world will fight for him against the senseless’ (Wis. V). Pain does not spring from the earth because the insensible element is stirred up not from its own nature but on account of human deserts, to afflict sinners.”

The prophet also says concerning the Lord: “If there is evil in the city that the Lord has not done?” (Amos III). And the Lord himself says of himself through Isaiah: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLVII)—that is, repose and war. Here “evil” does not signify the opposite of good, but something intermediate, namely affliction. This indeed comes from the Lord, because, by his permission, it is brought down upon a sinful people, so that those who were unwilling to follow God in peace may at least, worn down by blows, fear and turn back, according to what is written: “Affliction alone will give understanding to hearing” (Isa. XXVIII).

These things happen rather because of our sins and those of the whole people whom we ought to govern, since our iniquities have multiplied over our heads and our offenses have grown up to heaven. Fornication and adultery, sacrilege and murder have flooded everywhere, and blood has touched blood.

Blood touches blood when a sinner adds some grave evil to his other evils and sets no limit to his wicked deeds, but, as the Apostle says, advances daily toward worse things.

Indeed, we are almost compelled to groan with the prophet Isaiah, saying to the Lord: “Why, Lord, have you made us err from your ways? Have you hardened our heart so that we would not fear you? We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us, and your name was not invoked over us” (Isa. 63).

When God, by a just judgment, abandons sinful people who not only sin but choose to persist in their sins—when, I say, he abandons such people and permits them to go after the wickedness of their own hearts, he seems to make them err, because he does not mercifully touch them beforehand by a hidden inspiration so that they may turn back.

Just as the first human beings were restrained from doing evil by no law and not even by fear, but freely served the belly, the pleasures of the eyes, and their other vices, so now, having set aside fear of human and divine laws and despised episcopal edicts, each person does what he wishes. The stronger oppresses the weaker, and people are like the fish of the sea, which devour one another indiscriminately. And, with justice trampled underfoot, iniquity increases and grows strong.

This is why we see throughout the world the plundering of the poor and the depredation of ecclesiastical property. This is why there are constant tears and the mourning of orphans, so that now the cry of such people, like that of the people of Sodom, rises to heaven, and what is said by the Psalmist in the voice of the Lord is fulfilled: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. XI).

Almost every order and every condition of the Church is confused and violated. Finally, lest we seem to spare ourselves, who ought to correct the errors of others: we are called bishops, but we do not fulfill the episcopal office. We abandon the ministry of preaching. We see those entrusted to us abandon God and lie in wicked deeds, yet we are silent and do not extend the hand of correction to them.

Even if at times we begin to say things that may displease their carnal minds, they say of us what the Lord said in the Gospel concerning those sitting in Moses’ seat: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger” (Matt. XXIII).

And so it happens that, while we remain silent, the Lord’s flock perishes and, driven headlong over the precipices of vice, lies exposed to the bites of savage wolves. Since there is no one to teach them to enter the paths of life, they freely walk along the byways of error, and what is said through the prophet is fulfilled in them: “Zeal has seized an uninstructed people”; and elsewhere: “Therefore,” he says, “my people have gone into captivity because they had no knowledge” (Isa. V).

Let us consider: who has ever been converted from evil conduct and done penance through the ministry of our tongue? Who has abandoned sexual immorality through our preaching? Who avarice? Who pride?

Therefore upon us, who are counted bishops by name, rests a very great and almost unbearable burden of pastoral office. We must render an account of the business entrusted to us, together with the profit demanded; and the coming of the one who will arrive in terrible majesty is now close at hand. There all shepherds will come with their flocks into the sight of the eternal Shepherd, bringing increase from the flock, profit from their business, and sheaves from their harvest.

What shall we do—we who are called shepherds here but come there without sheep fit to be presented; who here received a talent and were sent to trade, but there return empty to our Lord after the business; who here were sent as laborers into the harvest, but there are presented empty-handed and without sheaves?

We must therefore consider what account we shall render at that great judgment, lest, God forbid, before the entire host of angels and the great multitude of the elect, we be condemned to eternal shame.

Therefore, considering and fearing the danger threatening us through the destruction of so many, gathered together in the name of almighty God, through his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the power of the Holy Spirit, let us take counsel for ourselves and for the flock entrusted to us. Concerning the condition of the holy Church and of the kingdom, the loyalty owed to our king, the condition of the monasteries—whose ancient order and religious observance have almost been erased—concerning plunder and sacrilege, as well as abductions, perjuries, and other crimes, let us pronounce judgment according to the decrees of the sacred canons and episcopal decrees.

By doing these things, let us urge people to repentance and correction either through the episcopal ministry or through pastoral exhortation; but those who remain impenitent and unwilling to be corrected, let us cut down in body and soul with the two-edged sword of God’s word, and punish them with eternal anathema—that is, with alienation from Christ and the Church—both in the present and in the future, unless they even now recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will, and turn to the living and true Lord through some correction and, insofar as possibility allows, suitable amendment.

## CHAPTER I

We have therefore decreed that the worship and honor of God’s churches be religiously preserved in every respect and by everyone, and that due reverence be shown to their immunities and ministers.

It is also fitting for the king and the princes to strengthen the privileges formerly granted to God’s churches and command that they be firmly observed. Just as those churches were honored, enlarged in their possessions, or endowed by preceding kings, so henceforth they should remain in full integrity, with due regard for equity.

Priests, as well as God’s male and female servants, should also enjoy ecclesiastical protection; and royal authority, the strength of illustrious men, and the administrators of the commonwealth should all reasonably and justly cooperate with them in every way, so that they may be able to carry out their ministry worthily.

For if the king and the powers of this world preserve the honor of God and the Church, their honor and power will thereby be increased, strengthened, and established; victories will be granted to them from heaven; and both they and their successors, by God’s favor, will endure in glory and dignity.

But if they act otherwise and despise God, God will despise them, make them contemptible and wretched, and drive them from the throne of the kingdom. They will be cast away like dust from the face of the earth, according to what we read in the Book of Kings concerning Ahab and the other kings who transgressed God’s law, and according to what the Lord says to Eli, the ruler of the Hebrew people: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be without honor” (I Kings II).

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0679B]

Since an account is demanded from us concerning everyone, both rulers and subjects, by him who judges without partiality, and since we shall render an account for the kings themselves to the King of kings, we must address a word of exhortation to your excellence, lord king.

In doing so, we exercise pontifical authority while not forgetting that royal majesty has been established by God, as the Apostle says: “Be subject to the king as to one who is pre-eminent” (I Peter II).

Just as royal power ought devotedly to submit itself to priestly religion, so priestly authority, with every duty of piety, ought to submit itself to royal dignity, as the holy Pope Gelasius showed when writing to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

“There are two things,” he says, “by which this world is principally ruled: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Of these, the burden of priests is all the heavier, since they must render an account for the kings themselves at the divine judgment,” [Col. 0679C] and so forth.

Therefore, since the king needs pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs need royal government for the orderly course of temporal affairs, the king ought to obey pontiffs when they advise what is right, holy, and just; and, in turn, pontiffs ought to obey the king who serves the worship of piety with religion, law, and support.

We therefore exhort your excellence, lord king, to persist in piety and uprightness, and in sacred, truthful, and good conduct, so that you may be found among those of whom it is sung in the psalm (Ps. CI): “When peoples are gathered together as one, and kings, to serve the Lord”—and so that you may know how you ought to serve God as a man and as a king.

For blessed Augustine says this (Letter 50): “A king, because he is a man, serves God by living faithfully; because he is a king, he serves him by enacting with suitable strictness laws that command what is just and prohibit what is contrary.” He develops the rest of this more fully in his letter to Boniface.

It is therefore necessary that a king first interpret his own name and strive to be what the name signifies. A king is so called from *ruling*. Accordingly, the king must first govern his own life with equitable moderation and, as a certain wise man says, restrain lust, despise pleasures, control anger, and drive away from himself the other diseases of the soul.

Only then will he truly be able to be called a king and worthily rule others, when he has ceased to obey the worst masters—dishonor and shame.

After this, he ought to be concerned for the peace of the people and the quiet and security of the whole kingdom. Let him be loved by the good and feared by the wicked; let him raise up the oppressed, console the poor, and defend widows and orphans.

Let him strive to fulfill what Solomon says of a good king: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze” (Prov. XX). A king ought to possess such authority of virtue and justice that, merely by the gaze of his fearful majesty, he disperses those plotting something unjust or evil, so that they do not dare proceed to the crime they have contemplated.

Finally, concerning how a king ought to live justly and faithfully according to the good pleasure of God’s will, we present to you, as is fitting, for your salvation, a few statements collected from the opinions of the holy Fathers, so that you may know and practice them.

On why a king is called by that name and what he ought to be, Isidore writes in the *Book of Sentences*:

“‘King’ is derived from acting rightly. If he rules piously, justly, and mercifully, he is rightly called a king; if he lacks these qualities, he is not a king but a tyrant.”

Although in ancient times all kings were called tyrants, later the name “king” was given to those who ruled piously, justly, and mercifully, while those who ruled impiously, unjustly, and cruelly were given not the name of king but the name of tyrant.

Hence blessed Gregory also says (*Moralia*, book II, chapter 9): “We have learned from the sacred writings that holy men are called kings because they act rightly, govern their own thoughts well, and regulate the impulses resisting them with rational discernment.”

Those, therefore, are rightly called kings who know how to bring both themselves and their subjects to peace by governing well.

The particular duty of kingship is to govern and rule God’s people with equity and justice and to strive that they may have peace and concord.

The king himself ought first to be the defender of churches and God’s servants, of widows, orphans, and all other poor people, as well as of everyone in need.

His terror and zeal ought, insofar as possible, first to ensure that no injustice is committed and then, if one occurs, to permit it to continue in no way. He should leave no one hope of concealment or boldness in doing evil. Let all know that, if anything wicked they have committed comes to his attention, it will by no means remain uncorrected or unpunished, but that the measure of just correction will correspond to the character of the deed.

Therefore he, who is the judge of judges, ought to cause the case of the poor to come before him and investigate it carefully, lest those appointed by him and acting in his place among the people should unjustly or negligently permit the poor to suffer oppression.
