Everyone, whatever his order, ought also to know that, if he must render an account to God for an idle word, much more must he render an account for the ministry divinely entrusted to him.

He should also strive to imitate that model of the wise king which the righteous Job displayed in himself. He says:

“When I sat as a king with the army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful. The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness for me, because I had rescued the poor man who cried out and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the widow’s heart. I put on justice, and clothed myself with it as with a garment and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most carefully the case I did not know. I crushed the jaws of the unjust and snatched the prey from his teeth” (Job XXIX).

When he acts in this way, what Solomon says will be fulfilled in him: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by justice” (Prov. XX).

Thus, becoming an imitator of righteous and elect kings, he will also become a participant in the glory of the heavenly kingdom and a companion of immortal rewards.

Let kings attend to what Wisdom says: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I).

Again, in the same book:

“Listen, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who rule multitudes and take pride in crowds of nations. For power has been given to you by the Lord, and authority by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts.

“For although you were his ministers, you did not judge rightly, nor did you keep the law of justice, nor walk according to his will. He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because the judgment upon those who rule will be severe. The lowly will be granted mercy, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments.

“For the Lord will show partiality to no one, nor will he respect anyone’s greatness, because he himself made the small and the great, and he cares equally for all” (Wis. VI).

There are also many other testimonies of the holy Scriptures appropriate to the name and office of a king. A few passages selected from the sayings of the blessed martyr Cyprian (*On the Abuses of the World*, chapter 9) will demonstrate how much injustice by a king brings adversity upon his kingdom and how greatly his justice benefits it.

After describing how a king ought to conduct himself, he adds:

“Whoever does not administer the kingdom according to this law endures many adversities in his rule. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, disturbances arise even from the kingdom, the fruitfulness of the lands is diminished, and the services of the people are obstructed.

“Many and various sorrows stain the prosperity of the kingdom; the deaths of loved ones and children bring grief; the incursions of enemies lay waste the provinces on every side; wild beasts tear apart herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms in the air and disturbances of the heavens obstruct the services of land and sea; and at times flashes of lightning burn the crops, the blossoms of trees, and the vines.”

He also says:

“Behold how much the justice of a king benefits the world is clearly evident to those who observe it. The peace of peoples is the protection of the fatherland, the security of the common people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, joy for humanity, temperate air, calm seas, the fruitfulness of the earth, consolation for the poor, and an inheritance for children, as well as hope of future blessedness for themselves.

“Nevertheless, let the king know that, just as he has been placed first among human beings on the throne, so also, if he has not practiced justice, he will hold first place in punishment. For all the sinners whom he had beneath him, he will have above him in that future punishment.”

Since, then, according to the testimony of so great and distinguished a man—who could say with the Apostle Paul, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XII)—the justice of a good king brings such great benefits both to him and to his kingdom, while, conversely, the wickedness of a bad king brings such great harms both to him and to his kingdom, with what caution must you live, venerable king, in all your actions!

We therefore ask that you receive these words with a willing ear and that you be pleased to cling to these salutary admonitions, so that, after your conduct has been rightly regulated and, through you, the conduct of others justly ordered, and after you have worthily completed this administration entrusted to you, you may deserve to receive an eternal kingdom from him who gave you a temporal one.

It is also necessary for us and for all who live in your kingdom to preserve just loyalty toward you, show due honor to the king, and, whenever you seek advice concerning the welfare of the kingdom, offer you truthful and useful counsel according to our knowledge and ability.

## CHAPTER III
Concerning monasteries—not their condition, but their decline—we scarcely know what we ought now to say or do. For while the weight of crimes demands it, and judgment begins with the house of God, some monasteries have been burned or destroyed by pagans, others stripped of their possessions and reduced almost to nothing, if indeed any traces of some of them still appear to remain; and in those that survive, no established form of regular discipline is observed. Whether they are monasteries of monks, canons, or nuns, they lack their own rightful superiors; and while, contrary to all ecclesiastical authority, they employ outsiders as prelates, those dwelling in them—partly because of need, partly because of ill will, and especially because of the disorder caused by their incompetent superiors—live in disorderly ways. Those who ought to be devoted to holiness and heavenly religion, as though forgetful of their own vocation, occupy themselves with earthly business.

Some also, compelled by necessity, leave the enclosures of the monasteries and, willingly or unwillingly joined to secular people, engage in secular affairs, although the Apostle says the contrary: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (II Tim. II). Since, therefore, they appear to differ from the common people not only in the merit of their life, but also—because of the base activities they pursue—to be exposed to the mockery of contempt, we are compelled, with the prophet Jeremiah, to lament the losses of our city, namely, the holy Church, and to proclaim publicly: “How the gold has become darkened! The finest color has been changed; the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. IV).

Pope Gregory explains this as follows: The gold has become darkened when the life of priests and spiritual persons, once bright through the glory of virtues, is now shown to be reprobate because of base actions. The finest color has been changed because that appearance of holiness has been brought, through earthly and contemptible works, to the disgrace of dishonor. The stones of the sanctuary, which ought never to have been seen outside, signify those who ought never to be seen engaged in foreign activities. But the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street when those who ought always to have been inward through life and prayer spend their time outside through a rejected way of life; and when, though established in holy dress, they display external things, they lie outside like stones of the sanctuary, and so forth.

Therefore, just as gold cannot be restored to its former and finest color without a goldsmith, so monastic life cannot be restored to its former and best order of living without the care of a regular abbot. Let royal power, therefore—which is so called from acting and ordering rightly—consider how it may administer these matters with sound judgment, according to the will of him to whom it will have to render an account of all its judgments and arrangements, and according to the decrees of the sacred canons and the constitutions of former kings.

For the sacred canons prohibit any layman from presuming in matters of religion. The canonical ordinances likewise prescribe, together with the capitularies of kings that follow them, as is contained in the first book of the Imperial Capitularies, chapter twenty-eight:

“Let clerics and monks, if they have any dispute among themselves, be judged by their own bishop and not by secular persons. For it is not lawful that ministers of the divine office should be subjected to the judgment of temporal powers” [Col. 0682C].

Likewise, chapter 31:

“Let laymen, even if religious, have no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical property.”

Likewise:

“Let places once dedicated to God, whether they are monasteries, remain monasteries perpetually, and let them no longer be made into dwellings for secular persons.”

But now, in monasteries dedicated to God for monks, canons, and nuns, lay abbots dwell with their wives, sons, and daughters, together with soldiers and dogs.

It is also read in the Capitularies (Addit. I, c. 1) that abbots should thoroughly read the Rule of the monks, examining it word by word, and, with the Lord’s help, should strive effectively to fulfill it with their monks. But how will he examine it? How will he read it? How will he understand it? If such a book should perhaps be presented to him, he will answer with the words of Isaiah: “I do not know letters” (Isa. XXIX).

And in the Rule of the monks, the rule of the holy and Spirit-filled Saint Benedict, the most blessed Father, says:

“In his teaching, the abbot must always preserve that apostolic pattern in which he says: ‘Reprove, entreat, rebuke’” (II Tim. IV).

How will one who is ignorant of the Apostle, who knows nothing of the prescriptions of the Rule, or who is wholly unfamiliar even with its alphabetic line, maintain the spiritual measure of discernment? And why say more? At the very beginning of the reading of the holy Rule, we read about the election of an abbot and what kind of person he ought to be.

In the capitulary of Charles the Great, book one, chapter eighty-one, it is written as follows (chapter 86):

“How we have arranged, in part, the affairs of the monks; how we have granted them permission to choose abbots for themselves from among themselves; and how we have ordered that, with God’s help, they might live in peace and guard their vocation without weariness—we have caused all this to be carefully recorded in another document.”

Likewise, in the council held at Tours, after regulations had been made concerning the canonical clergy of the cities who live in bishoprics, the following is added (Council of Tours III, canon 24):

“In the same way, let the abbots of monasteries in which canonical life existed in ancient times, or now appears to exist, carefully provide for their canons, so that they may have cloisters and dormitories, food and clothing, and so forth. Let the abbots,” he says, “be guides and leaders to their subjects by living well, and let them show them the way by which, walking rightly, they may be able to reach a better life.”

Likewise, concerning monasteries of monks, after a few matters that have been stated previously, the following is added:

“It seems good that they should return to their former condition, and that their abbots should strive to walk and live in the habit and manner of life prescribed by the Rule itself,” and so forth.

Finally, it is forbidden that a layman be brought into the refectory merely for the sake of eating and drinking. And how will he be their abbot when he will not even have permission to eat with them?

Likewise, in the second book of the Capitularies, chapter forty (42):

“Women should be placed over nunneries and created abbesses who know how to guard themselves and the flock entrusted to them with great religious devotion and holiness, and who do not cease to benefit those over whom they preside. Let them also watch over themselves and those women in their charge as holy vessels prepared for the service of the Lord. Such a woman ought to present herself to her subjects in dress and in all her conduct in such a way that she may provide them with leadership as they journey toward the heavenly kingdom; and she should know that, for those whom she has received under her governance, she will have to render an account before the Lord” [Col. 0683B].

These arrangements were established and observed after the first ordering of the holy Fathers, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and then, after the canonical authority concerning these matters, were decreed and maintained by earlier emperors and kings. As long as the privileges of the ecclesiastical order were preserved, the condition of the kingdom, preserved by God, advanced and grew. But after these things began to be treated with contempt, that condition of the kingdom—which once flourished and was vigorous—was weakened from day to day and has now almost been reduced to nothing.

The evil that had begun in past years has grown so deeply that the chief authority now thinks it permissible to rush into ecclesiastical matters contrary to what divine authority ordains, and, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, to overturn the order established by the Fathers of the Church [Col. 0683C]. It is our duty to warn about this; and if it cannot at present be corrected in every respect, we must henceforth strive, together with the lord king and his faithful people, until both his good intention, as we believe, and our devotion—which is necessary for us, for him, and for the whole kingdom—may, with God’s cooperation, reach the fullness of perfection.

For we dare not be silent about these matters, lest that prophetic saying be applied to us: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI). Likewise: “You did not go up to the breach, nor build a wall for the house of Israel” (Ezek. XIII).

To those who possess a regard for the fear of God, it is known to be grievous to hear, unlawful to say, and horrifying to witness when, contrary to every [uncertain reading: paratum] and to the authority and custom of the whole Christian religion, laymen sit in regular monasteries in the midst of priests and other religious persons as lords and masters, like abbots, and in a perverse order judge their life, conduct, and Rule—things wholly unknown to them [Col. 0683D].

This is surely that abomination which the Lord foretells in the Gospel when he says: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be, let the reader understand” (Matt. XXIV). This truly is the abomination of desolation—not only of the subjects, or of those who appear to rule over them to their own destruction, but also of the king, the whole kingdom, and all who favor such a detestable arrangement.

We therefore judge that the condition of monasteries be preserved inviolate, according to the ancient tradition of the Rule and the decrees of the canons; that abbots be religious persons who know regular discipline; and that monks and nuns, according to their profession, live soberly, devoutly, and simply. Let them pray for the salvation of kings, the peace of the kingdom, and the tranquility of the Church. Let them not be occupied with secular cares or business; let them not seek worldly displays; let them not disturb ecclesiastical rights [Col. 0684A]; but, in accordance with the proper meaning of their name, let them quietly embrace leisure.

For it is reported that, despising monastic humility and lowliness, they devote themselves to adornments and even to those things that are indecent and shameful for good laymen; and, by no means content with common property, they serve their own possessions and disgraceful profits. This vice, like a most evil cancer, must be torn out by the roots lest it spread further, and must be cut away by the vigilant care of abbots and bishops.

Certainly, lest the monks be given any opportunity to wander about or presume upon such matters, let the abbots or superiors of the monasteries ensure that, according to what the possibilities of time and place permit, everything necessary for them in food and clothing is suitably supplied, as the Rule commands.

# CHAPTER IV.

Against sacrilegious persons, too, it is right that canonical censure should proceed. First, however, it must be said what sacrilege is. Sacrilege is the violation of sacred law [Col. 0684B]. Since it is divided into many kinds of crime, there is also the sacrilege of schism, concerning which the blessed Father Augustine says: “The most manifest sacrilege is schism, if there was no cause for separation.”

Sacrilege also arises from blasphemous speech and from every action undertaken against sacred law. More specifically, however, we now designate as sacrilege that which is committed by plunderers against ecclesiastical property. For it is sacrilege to remove sacred things belonging to the Church; to take, invade, defraud, or seize possessions belonging by right to the Church; or to take anything consecrated or donated to the Church.

Those who do these things are truly sacrilegious and murderers. Of them Saint Anacletus says (Letter I):

“Whoever has taken anything from a father or mother is a participant in murder. Our father is without doubt God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever robs, removes, or defrauds Christ of his money and the Church of hers is a murderer.”

It is likewise said: Whoever robs his neighbor of money commits iniquity; but whoever removes money or property belonging to the Church commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.

And Saint Pope Urban says (single letter):

“The property and resources of the Church are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. If anyone robs them, he will share in the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person ought to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (I Cor. V) [Col. 0684C].

To identify such people briefly, according to what Scripture says about them and what appears pertinent to the matter at hand: all who act against the law, who plunder any ecclesiastical property, or who harass churches and priests contrary to divine ordinances, are called sacrilegious and, unquestionably, infamous sacrilegious persons.

And alas, what a grief! How many know, how many refuse to know, or pretend not to know what sacrilege is, and therefore, through ignorance, have rushed into this most wicked crime [Col. 0684D] and continue to rush into it every day!

Since this anathema exists in the midst of the Christian people, God is not with them, and they cannot stand against their pagan enemies, but flee. Let each person consider whether Israel was unable to stand before its enemies and fled because of the sacrilege committed by Achan, son of Carmi, while the Lord threatened:

“I will not be with you until you destroy the one who is guilty of this crime” (Josh. VII).

If, therefore, when one person sinned, God’s fury raged against the entire people until he and his whole household were destroyed, what do we think will happen to us, who in our time see so many sacrileges committed and so many sacrilegious persons doing evil with impunity—not only fearing nothing, but even rejoicing in their impieties?

We must consider whether, perhaps because of these and similar things, God’s anger has justly been brought upon us, so that when God is secretly entreated, he does not hear. For he has placed a cloud between himself and us, so that prayer cannot pass through.

And just as Joshua was told, “Why do you cry out to me?” so it is also said to us when we pray: “I will not hear you until the sacrilege is removed from among you and the person polluted by this crime is taken away from your midst” [Col. 0685A].

Nevertheless, together with blessed Joshua, let us not cease crying out to him, and let us warn the sacrilegious themselves that, through confession and correction of their guilt, they should give glory to God. And since, as Saint Job says, “God has granted them a place for repentance” (Job XXIV), let them take care not to abuse it through pride.

For this reason divine providence tolerates such people in their wickedness: in order to restrain them from wickedness. But if they turn the time granted for repentance toward guilt, and according to their hardness and impenitent heart store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, the stern Judge at the end will turn the abundant signs of mercy into punishment; and from the clemency granted by the Judge, a heap of curses will increase for them.

Let them therefore by no means flatter themselves because, still sustained by God’s patience, they appear to remain with the good without punishment. Let them consider Judas—not the apostle, but the apostate—like themselves, a sacrilegious thief. Let them hear what the blessed Father Augustine says about him (on John, tractate L):

“Behold, Judas is among the holy ones; behold, Judas is a thief. And lest you dismiss the matter lightly: a thief and a sacrilegious person—not just any thief, but a thief of the money-boxes, and of the Lord’s; of the money-boxes, and of sacred things” [Col. 0685B].

Likewise:

“Theft of private property is not judged in the same way as theft of public property. How much more severely, then, must the sacrilegious thief be judged, who dared to take something not from anywhere else but from the Church? Whoever removes or steals anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas. Such was this Judas, and yet he entered and left with Christ’s holy disciples and approached the Lord’s supper together with them.”

These are the words of Saint Augustine.

But because there are some who pretend not to know in what matters they commit so great a crime, we think it should be briefly recalled that everything offered to the Lord is undoubtedly also consecrated. Not only are the sacrifices consecrated by priests to the Lord upon the altar called the offerings of the faithful, but whatever is offered to him by the faithful—whether it is a person, an animal, a field, or any kind of workmanship, building, garment, or anything movable or immovable among those things that can provide support for the holy Church of God and its ministers, or contribute to its adornment—is unquestionably consecrated to the Lord [Col. 0685C].

And whoever in any way alienates, removes, invades, ravages, diminishes, or plunders any of these things from the Church, because Christ and his Church are one person, and whatever belongs to the Church belongs to Christ, unquestionably commits sacrilege.

Therefore, in the second book of the Capitularies, chapter four hundred and twenty-seven (book VI, chapter 321), it is decreed as follows:

“Correcting ourselves and giving an example to our successors, we generally forbid any layman—whether emperor, king, bishop, or any official or count supported by secular power—to seize by force for himself, or to demand from us, or to presume to invade in any manner, a monastery, its estates, any of its possessions, or anything belonging to the monastery of an abbot or abbess; or to begin to govern in the abbot’s place and hold monks under himself, and to possess money that was purchased by the blood of Christ.

“The ancient Fathers called such a person a plunderer, a sacrilegious person, and a murderer of the poor; a wolf of the devil entering the sheepfold of Christ; and one who must especially be condemned by the bond of anathema before the tribunal of Christ.

“Concerning such people, remember the Scripture of the holy Apostle Paul to Timothy, which says: ‘Command those who are rich in this present age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, who provides all things’ (I Tim. VI).

“If such persons do not accept the correction of the Church, they are like pagans and publicans, with whom the Church of God communicates neither while they are alive nor after they are dead. Against such people, wherever they are found, let us sound the trumpet of God, lest we be condemned for remaining silent and perish together with them.”

If the person who acts impiously is so horrifying to God, then such a person is certainly separated from God and is rightly subjected to anathema. For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God, just as both the Old and the New Testament indicate judgment concerning anathema [Col. 0686A].

No sacrilegious person will possess the kingdom of God except through pure, proven, and public repentance; satisfaction rendered to the holy Church, especially to the one he injured; the laying on of the hands of bishops; and reconciliation.

And so that he may know that in the future he will be alienated from the kingdom of God and from the company of the saints who already reign with Christ and will reign with him forever, he is also alienated in the present from the Church—which itself is the kingdom of God—and from the fellowship of its faithful in God.

Whoever he may be should know this with certainty: unless there is worthy satisfaction, the Church does not communicate with such a person, either living or dead. Rather, as it is said in the book of blessed Job, “He will be buried in destruction”—that is, he will be plunged into eternal punishment—“a burning wind will carry him away” (Job XXVII). This means the evil spirit who kindles the living person toward the crimes of sacrilege and drags the dying person to torments.

And because, according to Jeremiah, “The pot was kindled, and its face was toward the north” (Jerem. I)—that is, because he possessed a heart burning with the heat of plunder and inflamed by the breath of diabolical suggestion—he will be carried away by that burning wind, namely, the devil, and, burning with him, will blaze in the pot of eternal fire [Col. 0686B].

Therefore, gathered together with the Holy Spirit, just as Jeremiah lamented the sinful people with a fourfold alphabetic acrostic, so let us strike the sacrilegious and despisers of God and the Church with a fourfold curse of anathema.

Let the gate of heaven be closed to them and the door of hell opened; let them have no share or fellowship whatsoever with any Christian. Let none of the remains of their food be given to the poor; rather, let it be thrown to the dogs, until through worthy and humble repentance and suitable correction they gladden the Church, which they have provoked through sacrileges and wicked crimes.

But because there are some who fear temporal death more than eternal death, let us review what the laws of this world prescribe concerning such people. In the book mentioned above, chapter four hundred and thirty [Col. 0686C], it is ordered that those who have committed sacrileges, adulteries, depredations, or devastations be punished by capital sentence, and that all their property, movable as well as immovable, be joined to the king’s treasury or handed over to the Church whose possessions they have ravaged, alienated, or removed.

These things have been said concerning sacrilegious plunderers of churches.

# CHAPTER V.

No one of the faithful doubts that the Church of God consists in the bishops and the other priests to whom the Lord’s people are known to have been entrusted, and that it rests upon them as upon certain pillars of its own house. Yet the minds and conduct of certain wicked men, who desire to appear in the house of the Church more by name than by upright conduct, contain such foolish madness that they do not understand that the condition of the Church is weakened when priests—God forbid—are shaken by some force, just as, when the pillars are dislodged, the collapse of the entire structure of a house is threatened. For that reason they not only do not fear the danger of their own fall, but, harassing those same priests of God, they drive and thrust themselves forward so that they may fall together with those who are falling.

Nor do they consider—or rather, they do not revere—the fact that those who inflict injury or insult upon them are injurious and insulting toward our Lord God Jesus Christ, whose representatives they are. And because all who harass churches and priests contrary to divine decrees are regarded as sacrilegious, they are unquestionably called infamous sacrilegious persons.

And lest anyone say that we are inventing these things from our own heart, let him hear the holy judgments of the saints concerning such matters, expressed as follows.

Clement, instructed by the most holy mouth of the apostle Peter, says concerning all who sin against fathers, in his second letter to James, the brother of the Lord:

“What condemnation, and what curse, threatens those who sin against fathers, divine Scripture teaches us. For when Ham, the son of Noah, saw his father naked, he did not cover his father’s bodily nakedness but went out and reported it to his brothers, and they covered it with a garment. Ham himself, and those who were born from him, were placed under a curse; but those who covered him merited a great blessing. Much more, then, are those worthy of a greater and more extensive condemnation who attempt to oppose fathers or rise up against them, because whoever resists them resists God, and whoever inflicts injury or insult upon them does so against God, whose embassy they perform.” (Epistle 1)

Likewise, in the third letter, the same Clement speaks concerning the honor of bishops:

“If, therefore, all the presbyters, deacons, or subdeacons, and all the remaining clergy, and all rulers, both of higher and lower rank, and the rest of the peoples, tribes, and languages do not obey you bishops, they shall be not only infamous, but exiles from the kingdom of God and from the fellowship of the faithful, and strangers to the thresholds of the holy Church of God. For it is your duty to instruct them; theirs, however, is to obey you as God, whose embassy you perform, says the Lord: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me’; and: ‘Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me’ (Luke 10).

“For nothing is more unjust or dishonorable than for sons to rebel against fathers, or for clergy or laity to be disobedient or rebellious toward teachers, or for disciples to be disobedient or insolent toward masters. For we know that the first man fell through disobedience. Therefore we earnestly warn all to avoid this vice, and because ‘the Lord resists the proud but gives grace to the humble’ (1 Peter 5), our Lord commands us—sending us in his place, in the place of the apostles, to preach—to teach everyone, and commands everyone who faithfully obeys us to obey as they would him.” [The printed text has *existere*, “to exist”; the sense appears to require a verb such as “to be.”]

Likewise, from the decrees of Pope Anacletus, that bishops are to be judged by God, not by human or wicked men:

“It is clear that the highest priests, that is, bishops, are to be judged by God, not torn apart by human beings or by men of wicked life, but rather supported by all the faithful. The Lord himself gave the example when, by himself and not through another, he ‘drove the sellers and buyers out of the temple, and overturned with his own whip the tables of the money-changers and the seats of sellers, and expelled them from the temple’ (Matthew 21). And as he says elsewhere: ‘God has taken his stand in the assembly of gods; in the midst of the gods he judges’ (Psalm 81). And elsewhere: ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’ (ibid.).

“For, as I think, no one among us is found who would wish his servant to be judged by anyone other than himself. If this were presumed, he would either grow angry with great indignation or, rather, seek vengeance against the offender. If this is done among human beings, what do you think the God of gods and Lord of lords will do, who promised not to delay vengeance upon his servants?

“Thus he himself speaks through the Prophet: ‘God of vengeance, the Lord, the God who acts freely in vengeance,’ and what follows (Psalm 93). And the Apostle says: ‘Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master’ (Romans 14). And he himself says: ‘Do not judge one another, but judge rather that you do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother’ (ibid.). And the Lord says through the Prophet: ‘Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye’ (Zechariah 2).

“For if someone now begins to harm the eyes of some ruler, he is openly judged guilty of treason and becomes infamous, or rather is subjected to capital punishment. These things, brothers, must be greatly avoided; and what human beings do not wish done to themselves, they ought not to inflict upon the God of gods, lest the Lord perhaps grow angry and exact vengeance even upon those who have not sinned, since very often the just man perishes for the wicked.”

Likewise, in the same decree, that no one should easily dare to accuse a bishop:

“The apostles and the successors of the apostles, considering the matter, decreed that the pillars of the holy Church of God—not without reason called apostles and their successors—should not easily be disturbed, torn apart, or accused. But if anyone has become angry with them or their churches, or has some grievance against them, let him first hasten to them in a spirit of charity, so that, having been admonished in a familiar conversation, they may heal what ought to be healed and correct charitably what they recognize must justly be corrected.

“But if anyone should presume to tear them apart, accuse them, or harass them before doing these things, let him be excommunicated and by no means absolved before he has performed, through satisfaction, fitting penance, as has already been said, because the injury done to them concerns Christ, whose embassy they perform.

“Nor is this surprising. If any one of us were to assign an embassy to one of his own people, and the envoy were hindered by someone or despised by one of his subjects, he would immediately become indignant and angry, or would avenge such things as he could, considering the deed an injury and insult to himself; and if he could not repay it in the offender’s presence, he would repay it in the future. If such things occur in human affairs, what do you think God will do concerning his own, when he has said that not even one hair of their head shall perish?”

Therefore the Lord speaks through the prophet Nahum:

“God is jealous and avenging; the Lord is avenging, and possesses wrath; the Lord is avenging against his enemies and is angry with his foes” (Nahum 1).

From the decrees of Pope Evaristus, concerning the honor of bishops (Epistle 2):

“A bishop ought, opportunely and inopportunely, and without interruption, to teach his Church, and wisely govern and love it, so that it may abstain from vices and be able to attain eternal salvation. And the Church ought to receive his teaching with such reverence, and love and cherish him, as God’s ambassador and herald of truth, because, as Truth testifies: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16).

“This sentence, brothers, is to be feared greatly, and you must take care not to offend those who have received such power from the Lord. Therefore they are rather to be obeyed, loved, and venerated with the utmost devotion—not disparaged, torn apart, or expelled, but supported and loved—the Lord himself saying: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke 10).

“Therefore we write to you and to all the faithful, brothers, so that you may guard yourselves against these things and leave to your successors not a bad but a good example, because injury to bishops concerns Christ, whose place they occupy.”

From the decrees of Pope Alexander, concerning the harassment of priests (Epistle 1):

“It has come to the awareness of the apostolic see that there are some so foolish that they do not at all observe the Lord’s commands or the statutes of the apostles and their successors, and that they do not hesitate merely to touch those of whom the Lord says, ‘Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye’ (Zechariah 2), but even do not fear to persecute them.

“And although they persecute us—for they cannot persecute either us without them or them without us, since we are disciples of him who ‘commanded us to lay down our lives for our brothers’ (1 John 3)—nevertheless we have not dared to conceal their dangers and destructions, lest, God forbid, we be condemned by the prophetic sentence which says: ‘If you announce his wickedness to the wicked man, you have saved your soul; but if you do not announce it to him, I shall require his blood at your hand’ (Ezekiel 3).

“Those, therefore, who persecute bishops through sacrilegious persuasion and attempt to tear them apart, or those who rightly offer sacrifice to the Lord, unquestionably persecute and lacerate the Lord, whose place they occupy. Hence the Lord says through the prophet Joel: ‘Will you repay me with vengeance? And if you take revenge against me, I shall quickly repay your retaliation upon your own head’ (Joel 3).”

Considering these acts of piety and avoiding the dangers to souls, together with all the priests of God who have gathered with us in this sacred city, and with all the members of this body, just as we received from the blessed apostles, the other holy Fathers, and their successors, we establish and decree that all who persecute the holy Fathers or openly attempt to remove or tear them apart shall be infamous and shall be made strangers to the thresholds of the Church until satisfaction is given. For God hates those who arm themselves against fathers in such a way that invaders or destroyers of fathers become infamous because they persecute fathers.

Likewise, from the same source:

“No one, brothers, doubts that the good are always persecuted and afflicted by the wicked. Therefore we must humble ourselves under the mighty hand, so that he may free us in the time of tribulation. For just as ‘a roaring lion goes about seeking someone to devour’ (1 Peter 5), so the devil does not cease to go around and seek whom among the faithful he may destroy, especially those whom he finds more fervent in the service of the Savior and more closely attached to him.

“I call those ‘close to him’ whom he wished to be consecrated to himself and established in the order of the apostles. They intercede for the people and consume the people’s sins, because by their prayers and offerings they wipe them away and destroy them. The more worthy they are, the more readily they are heard concerning the needs of those for whom they cry out. ‘For,’ as the apostle James says, ‘the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful’ (James 5).

“Whoever persecutes you persecutes the one whose embassy you perform. For just as the Son of God himself was mediator between God and human beings, so you have been appointed in his place in the Church to perform an embassy between God and human beings. If anyone hinders your embassy, he turns aside the progress of not one person but many; and just as he harms many, so he must be reproved by many and excluded from the fellowship of the good. And because he hinders God’s cause and disturbs the condition of the Church, let him therefore be kept from its thresholds.

“Everyone must also beware of such a person, and he must not be received into the communion of the faithful until satisfaction has been given. For it was established long ago that whoever disturbs the condition of the Church should be kept from its thresholds and should not communicate with the faithful—whoever turns away their good.”

From the decrees of Pope Telesphorus, concerning bishops not being reproved or accused (Epistle 1):

“It is right that all teachers of the law throughout the world should know the things that belong to the law, and not stain the priests of the Lord with their lips or by any sort of contrivance. For while they intend or desire to stain them, they stain and wound themselves instead. Therefore whoever accuses a priest, or desires to condemn him, accuses God’s ordinance; and all the faithful ought to beware of such persons, because not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those who do them are guilty.”

From the decrees of Pope Pontianus, concerning the honor of bishops and the fact that they should not be harassed but venerated (Epistle 1):

“Priests are not to be harassed but honored. In them also the Lord is honored, whose embassy they perform. Therefore, if they should perhaps fall, they are to be raised up and supported by the faithful. They are not, however, to be accused by infamous, criminal, hostile, or sectarian persons, or by people of another religion. But if they have sinned, they are to be reproved by the other priests and restrained by the highest pontiffs; they are not to be reproved or excluded by secular persons or by people of wicked life.”

These, then, are the decrees of the apostles—or rather, the words of Christ himself. Whoever attempts to oppose or contradict them proves himself not a Christian but an Antichrist.

Therefore, if the priests of God are not to be harassed, saddened, accused, reproved by secular persons, criticized, condemned, excluded, stained or torn apart by any sort of contrivance, disparaged, subjected to any injury or insult, and still less persecuted, blinded, or killed, then concerning injury or dishonor done to priests the following is written in the sixth book of the aforementioned capitulary, chapter 91 (98):

“If anyone inflicts any injury or unjust dishonor upon a bishop, let him make composition for his life; and let all that he is seen to possess be assigned in full to the church over which the bishop is known to preside, and let our fine—that is, sixty solidi—be paid to us threefold; or let him himself be permanently assigned to the service of our fisc, until he redeems himself threefold according to his wergild, if he is able.”

“Now the holy Church consists in its priests. Therefore those who inflict injury or insult upon bishops or other priests are to be punished with a severe penalty. For the disparagement of priests concerns Christ, whose embassy they perform in the Church.”

Likewise, from the same book, chapter 297 (304):

“If anyone should break out into this kind of sacrilege, attacking churches and their property and inflicting any injury upon priests and ministers, or upon worship itself and the place, or doing anything to the injury of divine worship, let him know that those convicted or confessed as guilty are to be judged by capital sentence. Nor should it be awaited that the bishop demand vengeance for his own injury, since the holiness of forgiveness has been left to him alone as a glory. Let it be not only permitted but even praiseworthy for everyone to pursue as a public crime the atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers, and to merit vengeance against such guilty persons.”

Concerning those who have injured the clergy, from the capitulary of Emperor Charles (Book 5, chapter 121):

“Whoever, whether a judge or a secular person, presumes to inflict injury upon a presbyter, deacon, or one of the younger clergy without the hearing of the bishop, archdeacon, or archpresbyter shall be regarded as excommunicated from the entire fellowship of Christians.”

## CHAPTER VI

And since there are some inflamed by such a fire of greed that they not only fail to use properly what has been granted to them by God, but also pursue what has not been granted as though it were lawful, and demand from priests exactions and rents from what has been handed over and offered for divine worship—what, according to the law of the Lord, is holy of holies and belongs to the right of priests—and afflict presbyters with gifts, feasts, post-horses, or the fattening of horses, although from whatever has been given to each church, whether as an endowment or through whatever devotion of the faithful, they ought to demand no other service than the spiritual one, it seems necessary to us to restrain such presumptions in every possible way, because they are committed against canonical authority.

From ancient times, finally, it was established by the holy Fathers and by our ancestors that, just as a bishop has in his ordination the whole diocese in general, together with all rural parishes that he has possessed securely for thirty years, so also each presbyter, in his ordination and in the care of his administration, should have his own parish with its endowment and the tithes of the church—namely, with the counsel and arrangement of his bishop—according to the rules established anciently and divinely.

Saint Basil demonstrates that this was once foretold by the Holy Spirit through the prophet, before Christ’s incarnation, and decreed by the same Holy Spirit through the holy men of God after Christ’s ascension into heaven, when he explains the verse of the psalm: “I shall measure out the valley of tents” (Psalm 59):

“‘He shall measure out the valley of tents,’ that is, the whole globe of the earth, which is called the valley of tents because of the dwellings of bodies. It is divided and measured out, as though by lot, among the individual places, being divided into the parishes and habitations of the churches of God,” and so forth.

Again it is written: “Distribute its houses” (Psalm 47), namely, those of the universal Church, by preaching among the parishes entrusted to your care, “so that you may declare it to the next generation,” and what follows.

But because the administration of properties and endowments belonging to churches, according to the ancient constitution of the canons, belongs solely to the arrangement of bishops and to the administration of presbyters, the Council of Toledo makes this clear, saying (Third Council of Toledo, canon 19):

“Many, contrary to the decrees of the canons, demand that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they consider the endowment they have bestowed upon those same churches not to belong to the bishop’s administration. This action was displeasing in the past and is prohibited in the future; but everything, according to the ancient constitution, shall belong to the administration and authority of the bishop.”

If it is asked what “everything” means, there is no doubt that it includes tithes, the firstfruits of crops, and their offerings, together with whatever the faithful offer to parishes in lands, vineyards, slaves, money, or any other things. All these things ought to remain undisturbed, free from fiscal taxes and every exaction by lords, under the authority and administration of bishops, as we have said, and under the governance and stewardship of presbyters.

The lord Emperor Louis also established this concerning a mansus given to a church and the other things belonging to it, in his capitulary (Book 1, chapter 61):

“It has been decreed,” he says, “that one whole mansus shall be assigned to each church without any service, and that the presbyters established in them shall perform no service from the tithes, the offerings of the faithful, the houses, the courtyards, or the gardens situated beside the church, or from the aforesaid mansus, except the ecclesiastical service; and if they possess anything more, they shall render from it the service owed to their lords.”

Yet, on the contrary, some presume to constrain, injure, or even expel presbyters from the churches entrusted to them, or to strip them of tithes or possessions, not fearing to scorn the decrees of so many holy Fathers. For the Council of Carthage says (First Council of Carthage, canon 14):

“If anyone transgresses and violates the decrees, or considers them to be of no account, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his rank.”

And in the often-mentioned seventh book of the Capitularies, chapter 139 (154):

“No judge shall, without the knowledge of the bishop, constrain or presume to condemn a presbyter, deacon, cleric, or younger member of the Church on his own authority. If he does so, let him be separated from the church to which he is known to have done the injury, until he acknowledges and corrects his offense.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 165:

“It has been decreed that without the authority or consent of the bishops, presbyters may neither be appointed nor expelled from any churches; and if anyone thereafter attempts to do this, let him be struck down strictly by synodal judgment.”

And in Book 2, chapter 47 (36), that churches established in ancient times are to be deprived neither of tithes nor of any possession.

In bringing these matters forward, we by no means remove from them the lordship of the lords, as though those lords ought not or could not hold lordship over things granted to them by God. Rather, we indicate that the churches ought to belong to the bishops; that is, we designate the bishop’s governance and do not claim the lord’s authority for ourselves.

And because we are disciples of the gentle and humble Master, we ought to give our presbyters examples and admonitions of humility—namely, that they should render suitable honor and due obedience, spiritual and ecclesiastical, to those in whose jurisdiction their churches stand, and do so without any arrogance, contention, or rebellion.

While preserving the right of their ministry, they ought to show themselves agreeable to their lords and parishioners, from whose offerings they live, and with due humility administer spiritual services to them. Indeed, they ought to perform these services freely even if they received no temporal support from them.

Let presbyters therefore know, according to the Apostle, that they must render to all what is owed: “Honor to whom honor is owed; fear to whom fear is owed.” Let what follows also be applied to them: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13).

But since there are some who, ignorant of—or rather despising—God’s justice, seek to establish the injustice of their own obstinacy, and with sacrilegious boldness steal and defraud God of the portion of tithes owed to him, saying, to their own destruction, that they ought not to give tithes from military service, trade, craftsmanship, the shearing of wool, or any other commerce granted to them by God, let them hear—not our commands, but God’s commands concerning such matters through the holy Scriptures, and the sacred examples of the holy Fathers. Let them recognize that we are not, as they claim, now demanding something new, but rather recalling what was established by God’s laws and granted through the devotion of the ancient Fathers.

First of all, let them consider that, for God’s sake alone, they ought to give their offerings and tithes to priests [a folio is missing in the source], to God himself; and that by giving them faithfully they contribute nothing to God, who has no need of the good things he himself has bestowed upon us, but return to him what is his. In exchange for small things in the present, they acquire great things that will benefit them in the future.

It is written in Leviticus:

“All the tithes of the land, whether of grain or of the fruits of trees, belong to the Lord, and they are consecrated to him” (Leviticus 27).

Likewise, in the same book:

“All the tithes of cattle and sheep, and everything that passes under the rod, every tenth one that comes shall be consecrated to the Lord. You shall not exchange good for bad, or bad for good” (Leviticus 32).

In Deuteronomy:

“In the place which the Lord your God shall choose, so that his name may be there, you shall bring there everything that I command you: burnt offerings and sacrifices, tithes and firstfruits of your hands, and whatever is most excellent among the gifts that you have vowed to the Lord” (Deuteronomy 12).

Likewise, in the same book:

“You shall set aside a tenth part of all your crops that are born in the land each year: a tenth of grain, wine, and oil, and the firstborn of your herds and sheep, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 14).

In the Book of Numbers:

“I have given all the abundance of oil, wine, and grain, and whatever they offer as firstfruits to the Lord”—that is, to Aaron—“all the firstfruits of the crops that the earth produces and that are brought to the Lord shall fall to your use. Everything that the children of Israel return from a vow shall be yours” (Numbers 18).

Likewise, in the same book:

“To the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession, in return for the ministry with which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant” (ibid.).

There you have heard whose the tithes are, to whom they are sacrificed, and to whom they ought to be given—namely, to God. But you have also heard what he commands to be given to himself: not only all the tithes of everything that grows from the earth, but also all the firstfruits of the crops that the soil produces, as well as the tithes of cattle, sheep, and all herds, together with their firstborn; also the tithes and firstfruits of your hands, and, in addition, vows and gifts. All these things he commands you to offer at the place of his temple, so that they may be used by the priests in return for the ministry by which they serve in the tabernacle of the Lord.

Perhaps someone will say: “I am not a farmer; I have no means by which I can give tithes of earthly fruits or of herds.”

Let whoever he is—whether a soldier, merchant, or craftsman—listen: the skill by which you are nourished belongs to God, and therefore from it you ought to give him tithes.

Concerning military service, hear what is said in the Book of Genesis about the patriarch Abraham after he returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him:

“When Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, had blessed him,” Scripture says, “Abraham gave him tithes of everything” (Genesis 14).

Likewise, in the same book it is read that blessed Jacob, going to Mesopotamia of Syria to Laban, for whom he served twenty years in return for wages, spoke as follows:

“If the Lord,” he said, “is with me on the journey on which I am walking, and guards me, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and I return safely to my father’s house, the Lord shall be my God, and this stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be called the house of God; and of everything that you give me I shall offer tithes to you” (Genesis 28).

It is also read concerning the holy Tobias that he went to Jerusalem, to the temple of the Lord, and there worshiped the Lord God of Israel, faithfully offering all his firstfruits and tithes (Tobit 1).

There you have examples of the holy Fathers to imitate: they faithfully offered tithes to God from everything they possessed.

And why do we propose this concerning the praiseworthy patriarchs, when we hear the Pharisee, rejected by God for the swelling of his self-display, saying in the Gospel: “I give tithes of everything I possess” (Luke 18); and when we hear God himself reproaching the scribes and Pharisees because, while neglecting God’s commandments, “they tithed even mint and dill and every herb” (Matthew 23)?

At least let us Christians be ashamed either to be unwilling or unable to imitate the Pharisees in this respect, when we hear Christ himself threaten us in this way:

“Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

And yet they gave tithes of everything they possessed.

But perhaps you will still say, after so many things have been enumerated, that no divine command concerning the shearing of wool has yet been explicitly cited. Should not what is said—“from everything”—be sufficient for you? But because, shamefully, some also make excuses concerning this form of tithing, let them hear the Lord saying in Deuteronomy:

“This shall be the judgment of the priests from the people and from those who offer sacrifices: whether they sacrifice an ox or a sheep, they shall give the priest the shoulder and the stomach, the firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, and a portion of the wool from the shearing of the sheep. For the Lord your God chose him from all its tribes, so that he might stand and minister in the name of the Lord” (Deuteronomy 18).

Moreover, we make known to those who do not know, and recall to the memory of those who do know, something further and greater: to use the words of the blessed Pope Gregory, we ought to give God not only tithes of our possessions but also tithes of our days, which all the faithful endeavor to do each year during Lent.

And lest anything appear to have been omitted in paying to God the debts of tithes or firstfruits, let everyone know what the law also establishes concerning food. It is written in Deuteronomy:

“When you enter the land which I shall give you, and eat of the bread of that region, you shall separate firstfruits from your food for the Lord. Just as you shall separate firstfruits from your threshing floors, so also you shall give the first portion of your cooked foods to the Lord” (Numbers 15).

And lest anyone dare, in any way—not to say to withhold or defraud—the things that must be offered, or rather returned, to God, the giver of all good things, or even to delay them, let him hear God saying to him in Exodus:

“You shall not delay in offering your tithes and firstfruits to me” (Exodus 22).

If, therefore, delaying to give is a transgression of the law, how much worse is it not to have given these things?

Therefore, if you determine to fulfill the devout commands according to the Lord’s authority, you will rejoice to receive from him the rewards promised through the prophet Malachi:

“Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this, says the Lord, whether I shall not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing for you in abundance; and I shall rebuke the devourer for your sake, and he shall not destroy the fruit of your land, nor shall your vine be barren in the field, says the Lord of hosts, and all nations shall call you blessed” (Malachi 3).

Again Scripture says:

“Honor the Lord from your substance and from the firstfruits of your crops, so that your barns may be filled with grain and your winepresses may overflow with wine” (Proverbs 3).

There you see how your tithes benefit you more than God, since you very quickly receive them back a hundredfold as interest.

Scripture also says:

“Each shall give a ransom for his soul, and there shall be no disease or calamity among them” (Exodus 30).

Behold, together with abundant fruits, you also obtain bodily health.

We add further that, by fulfilling the divine commands, you earn heavenly rewards, while by violating them you acquire infernal torments for yourself, as a transgressor, unless you satisfy God and the Church through suitable penance and correction.

Indeed, because we deny God the firstfruits of our possessions, by his just judgment we are turned upside down in our own firstfruits, and we are brought back to a tenth: after withholding nine parts, we scarcely receive a tenth part. Therefore our harvest, deprived of the blessing of rain, fails in barren weakness; hail strikes the vintage or frost destroys it. And because we are unwilling to give to God and his priest what is owed, we give what is not owed to the pagan and impious soldier.

Having carefully considered these matters, and following the admonition of Scripture, let us devoutly honor God by giving the firstfruits and tithes of everything we possess, so that we may deserve to receive from him both the necessary good benefits of temporal life and the rewards of eternal happiness.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0694A]

Now we must deal with those who, addicted to plunder in various ways, lay ambushes for the innocent or inflict losses and deaths upon them, and fill their houses with such spoils. They eat the bread of impiety and drink the wine of wickedness; their feet run continually toward evil, and they hasten to shed blood or, after taking away all their property, to kill the innocent by hunger. And while they lie in wait for another’s blood or think that they must live by fraud, as Solomon says, “they themselves lie in wait for their own blood, and plot deceit against their own lives” (Prov. 1).

They act against their own blood because, as though there were a judge who would execute just judgment against them, they are punished with temporal death; but they act against their own lives because they will be condemned to eternal destruction. Those who, out of love of money, keep watch for the plunder and slaughter of the innocent thereby destroy themselves. The Lord rebukes them through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “You have devoured my vineyard” [Col. 0694B]—that is, the Christian people—“the plunder of the poor is in your house” (Isa. 3), namely, in the house of your dwelling and in the house of your body, since from it you fill not only yourselves to surfeiting but also your treasuries.

But the Lord does not conceal through the same prophet what awaits such people. “Woe,” he says, “to the wicked man unto evil; the recompense of his hands shall be made to him” (ibid.). And again: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field, and so forth” (Isa. 5).

Their number—something grievous to say—is great, and they have drunk in such a love of plunder as though it were lawful and honorable to live by what one has seized. Yet these wretched and pitiable people do not consider how many thousands of innocent human beings they kill every day—not by the sword, which would certainly be lighter, but by the hardest and most atrocious death from hunger. Can these wretches, guilty of so many murders, be secure even for a single hour? Certainly, it is damnable not to give bread to the hungry, since the Lord himself will say at the final judgment: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food, and so forth” (Matt. 25), to whom he added: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

From this, therefore, one must infer with what condemnation those who seize what belongs to others will be punished, if those who indiscriminately and mercilessly retained their own are struck by such a sentence. Job briefly enumerates how manifold plunder is and in how many ways it is practiced, saying:

“Others have moved boundary markers, they have plundered flocks, they have driven away the orphan’s ass, they have taken the widow’s ox as a pledge, they have overthrown the way of the poor, they have oppressed together the meek of the earth, they reap a field that is not theirs and harvest the vineyard of the one whom they have oppressed by force, they leave men naked, taking away the clothing of those who have no covering in the cold; they have used violence, plundering orphans, and have stripped the poor populace. From the naked and those who walk without clothing, and from the hungry, they have taken the ears of grain. From the cities they have made men groan, and the soul of the wounded cries out, and the Lord will not permit this to go unpunished” (Job 24).

Of such people the prophet says: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own—how long?—and loads himself with thick mud” (Hab. 2). To load thick mud upon oneself is to heap up earthly profits together with the weight of sin.

And in the Gospel the Lord says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 15)—that is, what does it profit him if he gathers everything outside himself, if he condemns what he himself is? For the things they seize they leave behind in this world; but they carry with them to judgment the charges arising from their plunder and their own condemnation.

Let robbers hear what Paul, the chosen vessel, who was caught up to the third heaven, said about them: “Neither will robbers,” he says, “possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore no robber and no plunderer of the poor will possess the kingdom of God unless he has performed complete penance and restored what he unjustly took.

There are some who indeed wish to repent, but do not wish to restore what they have seized—a certainly most evil kind of people, for whom the medicine of repentance is entirely useless. For if a stolen possession, when it can be restored, is not restored, repentance is not being performed but feigned. These people, as Saint Augustine says (Epistle 54, to Macedonius), desire that their crime be forgiven them while they retain the thing on account of which the crime was committed.

The sin of plunder, therefore, will not be forgiven unless what was taken is restored—when it can be restored. Often, however, the person who takes something loses it, either by suffering harm from others or by living wickedly himself, and has no means by which to restore it. Let every robber know, then, that the sin of plunder is not forgiven him unless, when he can, he restores what he has stolen.

For Zacchaeus the tax collector, who had received the Lord as his guest and was suddenly transformed into a holy life, said: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19).

Thus, then, let every robber act: let him first restore what he unjustly took, if he desires to perform true repentance and obtain the true mercy of God. But if he has no means by which to repay, we cannot say to him, “Restore what you took.” Nevertheless, even if he undergoes certain torments while he is believed to possess what he could restore, there is no injustice in this; for although he has no means of returning the money he took, he nevertheless deservedly pays the penalty for the sin by which he wickedly took it, being compelled to make restitution through bodily afflictions.

Therefore, because countless acts of plunder and pillage were once committed in this kingdom without regard for the fear of God, and are still being committed, and because they stand before the eyes and ears of the Lord of hosts, we now suffer devastation and barrenness—the punishment that the Lord once threatened against the Israelite people, saying: “Unless the deserted houses, great and beautiful, are without inhabitants, ten acres of vineyard will produce one small jar, and so forth” (Isa. 5).

And because, by the just judgment of God, as the penalty for our sin demanded, we have fallen into such madness that we neither perceive the blows by which we are chastised nor wish to understand the correction [Col. 0695C], we rightly experience a twofold captivity: namely, barbarian captivity and, what is more grievous, demonic captivity. As the Lord testifies through the prophet Isaiah: “Therefore,” he says, “my people have been led away captive, because they had no knowledge” (ibid.)—namely, knowledge by which to understand the divine judgment, their own correction, or the practice of good.

And again: “Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without limit” (ibid.), namely, so that with insatiable greed it may devour forever those who are destined to be punished. “And the strong men of the earth, and the people, and its lofty and glorious ones shall descend to it” (ibid.).

Let them therefore at last awaken to such a great thunderclap. Let them hear the Lord terrifyingly threaten through the same prophet: “Every violent plunder with tumult, and every garment mixed with blood, shall be for burning and fuel for fire” (Isa. 9). For every violent plunder of the wicked, and the tumult and disturbances by which they have oppressed the poor and all those beneath them, mixing blood with blood, shall be for the burning of Gehenna and fuel for eternal fire.

Again he speaks through the Psalmist: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. 2)—that is, I will exercise vengeance very soon.

And again the prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord will not despise the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow when she pours out her lament. Do not the widow’s tears descend upon her cheek, and her cry against the one who causes them to flow? For from her cheek they rise up to heaven, and the Lord, who hears, will not take pleasure in them” (Ecclus. 35).

But since this impiety now rages not only against outsiders but, so to speak, against its own entrails, and each person devours the flesh of his own arm, we must fear that the Apostle’s words may apply to such people: “See,” he says, “that while you bite and devour one another, you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5). Whoever eats himself soon perishes.

For the Psalmist says: “To you, Lord, the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 10). “He will rescue the needy from the hand of his mighty oppressors, the poor and afflicted from those who plunder them” (Ps. 34).

Certainly, the statutes of the ancient Church prescribe that the gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by priests (Council of Carthage IV, canon 94), and rightly so, since such gifts are abominable before the Lord, as Scripture testifies: “Whoever offers,” it says, “a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slaughters a son in the presence of his father” (Ecclus. 34).

Concerning the rich and powerful who oppress the poor, Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 418 (31), contains the following: “Let judges or powerful men who oppress the poor, if they do not amend after being admonished by their bishop, be excommunicated.”

And unless they perform worthy penance for such acts, they themselves, as blessed Paul testifies concerning the rapacious, “will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

Moreover, royal power ought to punish such people according to the sanctions issued by the ancient kings concerning those who commit plunder within the kingdom (Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 288), or in whatever place the crime is recognized and a portion of the plunder is found, as well as those who are discovered to have indicated persons or property for plunder.

Among these provisions, concerning one who grants the opportunity for plunder or one who distributes what has been carried out, Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 384 (289), prescribes that he be burned alive. Likewise, whoever is found to have committed violence shall suffer capital punishment.

## CHAPTER VIII

There is, moreover, a certain execrable kind of plunder, or rather sacrilege, which country people, from the act itself, call *raptus*—abduction. We shall show in a few words, for the caution of all the Christians entrusted to us, how great an evil this is and how it has been condemned not only by divine but also by human authority.

First, concerning girls who have been abducted and are not yet betrothed, we have considered it necessary to set out again what the sacred canons prescribe. In the Council of Chalcedon, where six hundred and thirty Fathers were present, chapter 27 contains the following:

“The holy synod has decreed that those who abduct girls under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors, if they are clerics, shall be deposed from their own rank; but if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

These words make it plainly understood how the authors of this evil must be condemned, since those who participate in it or connive at it are struck by so great an anathema. They also show that, according to canonical authority, abducted women can in no way be claimed by their abductors as lawful wives.

Concerning betrothed girls who have subsequently been abducted by others, the Council of Ancyra, chapter 10, reads as follows:

“It has pleased us that betrothed girls who are afterwards abducted by others be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by their abductors.”

Accordingly, the holy assembly decreed that the abductor should be punished with public penance. But if the bride’s fiancé refuses to receive her, and she herself did not consent to the same crime, permission to marry another man is not to be denied her. If she also consented, however, she shall be subject to the same sentence. If after this he presumes to join himself to her, both shall be anathematized.

Whoever wishes to know what the law of the emperors commands concerning such abductors will find it in Book V, chapter 239.

Likewise, in Book VII, chapter 247, concerning abductors of widows or virgins, it is decreed: “It is enacted that abductors of widows or virgins be expelled from communion with the Church.”

Again, concerning those who abduct women so that they may not have them as wives, and concerning what is to be done with the abducted women, Book VII, chapter 395, states:

“It has pleased us that those who abduct, steal, or seduce women, so that they may in no way have them as wives, shall not have them as wives, even if they subsequently come to an agreement with them, endow them, or receive them in marriage with the consent of their parents. If anyone wishes to have a woman as his wife, let him receive her canonically and legally, and not abduct her. But whoever abducts, steals, or seduces her shall never have her as his wife; rather, he shall restore her by law to her relatives and pay the lord’s fine threefold, and in addition perform public penance canonically.”

At this all cried out with one voice, saying: “We all wish firmly to uphold these provisions, and we desire that they be preserved by everyone forever.”

Therefore we too decree, according to the ancient constitution, that no one shall arrange a secret marriage or commit abduction, nor shall he take as wife a woman whom a relative has had. Rather, whoever wishes to have a wife shall receive one who has been endowed and given by her parents, through the blessing of priests, as is urged in the book mentioned above, chapter 179 (127), in these words:

“It is enacted that public marriages be conducted by those who desire to marry, because serious sins often increase or accumulate in marriages performed secretly—whether involving the betrothed of others, relatives, adulterous unions, or, what is worse to say, unions between blood relatives. From such unions the blind, lame, hunchbacked, squinting, and others marked by disgraceful blemishes are often born, and everyone must take care that this not happen thereafter.

“But first the priest in whose parish the marriage is to take place must be consulted. In the church, before all the people, the priest himself must inquire together with the people whether she is his relative or not, or another man’s wife, betrothed, or adulteress. And when they have found everything to be lawful and honorable, then, with the counsel and blessing of the priest and after consulting other good men, he ought to betroth her and endow her lawfully.

“For blessed Augustine writes concerning a legitimate marriage as follows:

“‘The woman who is to be taken as a wife must be such that, according to the law, she is chaste in virginity, lawfully endowed, given by her parents to her fiancé, received by the bridesmen, and thus, according to the law and the Gospel, honored by a public marriage; she is to be lawfully taken in marriage and, throughout all the days of her life, is never to be separated because of a man, unless by mutual consent and for the purpose of serving God. If she commits fornication and her husband wishes it, she is to be dismissed; but while she lives, another woman is not to be taken, because “adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). Penance is to be imposed upon her.

“‘Men, do not take wives whose former husbands are alive, for such marriages are adulterous. And, as we have said, this must be guarded against entirely: that she not be his relative, because it is written: “No man shall approach his near relative to uncover her nakedness” (Lev. 18). Likewise it is written: “You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife, nor defile yourself by the mingling of his seed” (ibid.).

“And in the decretals of Pope Gregory it is read (Gregory II, in the First Roman Synod):

“‘If anyone takes as wife a deaconess, a nun, a spiritual godmother, his brother’s wife, his niece, his stepmother, his daughter-in-law, his cousin, a woman from his own kindred, or one whom his relative has had, let him be anathema.’ And they all answered three times: ‘Let him be anathema.’

“Again: ‘If anyone abducts a widow, or steals another man’s wife, or consents to him doing so, let him be anathema.’

“And: ‘If anyone abducts or steals a virgin unless he has betrothed her, or consents to him doing so, let him be anathema.’ And they all answered three times: ‘Let him be anathema.’

“Elsewhere in the canons it is commanded that no one marry within the line of affinity or the nearness of his own blood, nor presume to marry virgins without the blessing of a priest. These things must be avoided with the greatest care.

“But after all these matters have been examined and nothing has stood in the way, then, if she is a virgin, she is to be taken as a wife with the blessing of the priest, as is contained in the sacramentary, and with the counsel of many good men, publicly and not secretly, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, good children may be born from them, and not those of the kind mentioned above.”

Likewise, in Book VI, chapter 419 (306):

“If anyone joins himself, not in an equal rank but in an incestuous relationship, to those persons with whom the divine rules forbid union, both shall be deprived of communion until they demonstrate their penance through separation after [delete *post*]. Nor shall they have permission either to hold military office in the palace or to conduct lawsuits in the courts.

“For if in any way they have joined themselves in the incest described above, the bishops or priests in whose diocese or district the act occurred shall notify the king or the judges that the crime has been committed, so that, once it has been reported to them, the offenders may be separated from their communion or cohabitation.

“Their possessions shall pass to their first parents until the separation has taken place, on the condition that, before they are separated, they may not by any means—neither through their parents, nor through purchase, nor through royal authority—obtain their own property, unless they confess the aforementioned crime by separation and penance.”

Likewise, from Book III of Theodosius’s laws, chapter 12 (Theodosian Code, Book III, title 12): “That those guilty of incest are not legitimate heirs, but that both persons are marked with infamy.”
