Therefore, again and again, by ecclesiastical authority we forbid anyone henceforth, as the ecclesiastical canons prohibit, to take in an illicit marriage, by force or consent, as his wife any virgin devoted to God; anyone living under a religious habit; anyone who has professed continence as a widow; any woman related to him; or any woman through whose illicit union he could incur the stigma of infamy.

For a marriage cannot be true if it is drawn from a better purpose into a worse one and is carried out under the guilt of a false name, through incestuous pollution and the impurity of fornication.

If from now on people of either sex from any nation attempt to commit this abomination, they shall be separated from one another in every way and sent into perpetual exile.

Likewise, in Book VI, chapter 412 (309): “You should know that the person who defiles himself with one consecrated to God or with a veiled woman inflicts blasphemy upon God.”

Likewise, chapter 413 (310): “If a cleric defiles himself with a veiled woman or with one consecrated to God, he shall be deprived of his own dignity.”

Likewise, chapter 414 (311): “Everyone must know that the bodies of women consecrated to God are proved by the testimonies of Scripture to be temples, consecrated to God through the vow of their own pledged commitment and through the words of the priest. Therefore those who violate them are sacrilegious and are known, according to the Apostle, to be sons of perdition” (1 Cor. 3).

## CHAPTER IX

Since this plague attacks not only any ordinary people, whether of higher or lower rank, but also—something we confess not without shame and with the greatest sorrow—defiles ecclesiastical dignities, to such an extent that even the priests themselves, who ought to cut away this corruption of the disease from others, rot in the filth of lust; and since, not content with their own shameful destruction, they also injure the lives of good priests by the infamy of their reputation, while secular people say, “Such are the priests of the Church”; and since by giving offense to others they disgrace the holy ministry and also violate the canonical statutes of the holy Fathers, which forbid clerics access to, association with, and cohabitation with women, we are compelled to recall certain decrees of the earlier Fathers and, against the ever-renewed forms of this disease, seek new remedies.

Therefore we shall now set out again what our predecessor of blessed memory, Bishop Hincmar, delivered in speech and writing concerning such matters at an assembly of priests held in the metropolitan city of Rheims in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 852 (Hincmar, *To the Priests*, chapter 21. From here through chapter X, Hincmar):

“Concerning the access, association, and cohabitation of clerics with women, which according to the sacred canons we expressly and specifically forbid in every synod, we must make firm, explicit, and careful inquiry, both ourselves and our fellow ministers.

“For just as the sacraments given to those who preceded the Lord’s coming in the flesh and to those who followed it are different in accordance with the times, yet converge upon the religion of one and the same faith and salvation, and, as it is written, ‘Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied’ [Col. 0699A] (Dan. 12), so, as the ages have advanced, the dignity and multiplication of commandments have increased—both through the Lord himself and through angels in the Old Testament, and likewise in the New Testament through himself and through Catholic teachers and masters of the Church, who, as the prophet testifies, are also called angels (Mal. 2).

“The Lord himself gave commandments in paradise to Adam, after the flood to Noah, and to Abraham the command concerning circumcision. But he gave the law through angels to Moses, the mediator between himself and the people, as the Apostle shows.

“In the New Testament, having become incarnate, he himself said: ‘You have heard that it was said, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” But I say to you, love your enemies’ (Matt. 5); and, ‘Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven’ (ibid.); and, ‘It was said to the ancients, “Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment”’ (ibid.), and so forth.

“And he spoke through his saints, of whom it was said: ‘It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matt. 10).

“He taught that the virtue of chastity should increase with the passage of time, especially among the ministers of the Church, establishing this through the mystical Council of Nicaea in the following manner (canon 3):

“‘The great synod absolutely forbids a bishop, a priest, a deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion.’

“From this, Christian emperors promulgated the following law (Theodosian Code, *Concerning Bishops, the Church, and the Clergy*, book 44):

“‘All who exercise the office of the clergy are forbidden to maintain the familiarity of foreign women. Let them know that only the assistance of mothers, sisters, or daughters is granted to them within their house.’

“But because, under the pretext of these persons, other women began to be introduced, the holy African canons decreed (African Council, canon 3) that bishops and priests themselves should not visit widows, virgins, or any women alone, but only where clerics or other serious Christians are present.

“Thus, as blessed Gregory wrote to the ministers of the Roman Church (Book VII, indiction 2, Epistle 39), blessed Augustine did not agree even to live with his sister, saying: ‘Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.’

“From this Saint Gregory says:

“‘The caution of learned men ought therefore to be a great instruction for us. For it is presumptuous and heedless that what the strong man fears, the weaker does not fear. He wisely avoids what is unlawful who has learned not even to make use of what is permitted.’

“And because at that time, when the faith was still new, clerics were made from men who were lawfully married and had turned from marriage to continence, the Apostle therefore prescribed, when the matter concerned married men, that a man of one wife be chosen for the highest priesthood (1 Tim. 3; Tit. 1).

“From this Christian emperors enacted a law, saying (Justinian’s Novella 123, chapter 29):

“‘To priests, deacons, subdeacons, and others enrolled in the clergy who do not have wives, we too, in accordance with the divine rules, forbid having a woman in their house, except a mother, daughter, sister, or other persons who avoid every ground for complaint.

“‘But if anyone, contrary to this rule, keeps in his house a woman who can give rise to suspicion of disgrace, and his fellow clerics tell him that he ought not to live with such a woman, but he refuses to drive her from his house, or is proved, when an accuser appears, to have behaved dishonorably with such a woman, then the bishop shall remove him from the clergy according to the ecclesiastical canons and hand him over to the city council of the city whose cleric he is.’

“And as Saint Innocent and his predecessor Siricius write (Innocent, Epistle 2, to Victricius), if in ancient times the priests of God did not leave the temple during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, nor touch their own house at all—although the use of wives had been permitted to them for the sake of producing offspring, since no one from another tribe and outside the seed of Aaron had been commanded to approach the priesthood—how much more ought those priests or Levites to preserve chastity whose priesthood or ministry exists without succession and who do not pass a day without being occupied either with divine sacrifices or with the office of baptism?

“For if Paul also writes to laymen, saying: ‘Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’ (1 Cor. 7), much more ought priests, whose constant duty is to pray and sacrifice, always to abstain from such association.

“If one of them has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he perhaps presume to sacrifice? Or with what conscience, or by what merit, does he believe that he will be heard, when it is said: ‘All things are pure to the pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure’ (Tit. 1)?

“And lest anyone say, ‘If I live with women, my conscience is sufficient for me,’ quoting the Apostle: ‘This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience’ (2 Cor. 1), let him attend to what the same Apostle also says—through whom, as he himself acknowledges, Christ speaks truthfully: ‘Providing what is good not only before God but also before men’ (Rom. 12).

“For, as Augustine teaches, the conduct of the saints to whom the Lord says, ‘Be holy,’ ought to be not only holy but also cautious, lest, although it is not evil through wantonness, it become evil through negligence.

“And again the Apostle commands: ‘Let us be without offense to all’ (1 Cor. 10), ‘giving no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed’ (2 Cor. 6).

“And: ‘Let no brother perish because of our conscience, for whom Christ died.’ Thus, he says, ‘When you sin against your brothers in this way and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ’ (1 Cor. 8).

“Therefore, filled with the Holy Spirit, our holy Fathers decreed that ministers of the altar should not live with women nor introduce women into their households, lest they either burn with desire or defile themselves by the worst kind of consent, and lest they stain the consciences of the weak through evil suspicion.

“Accordingly, we do not trouble ourselves to inquire, through parishioners or neighbors of any priest, about priests’ intercourse with women. For the ancient heresy called Cynic—that is, doglike, on account of its shamelessness—has been abolished. It said that intercourse was natural and therefore ought to be practiced publicly without shame, although we read that the first human beings, after the sin of disobedience, became conscious of desire in their genital members and covered themselves from one another’s sight.

“For although the blindness of the human mind in the performance of disgraceful acts cannot be hidden from the divine and angelic eyes, nor from the eyes of the saints who are in heaven, nevertheless even any countryman who has intercourse, including with his own wife, avoids the sight of many people as best he can. How much more will a priest, if he possesses human understanding, take care to conceal an evil deed, since he knows that, once exposed, it will cause him not only to lose his ecclesiastical rank [Col. 0700D] but also to forfeit whatever he possesses in the world?

“We do not therefore inquire immodestly about what the Apostle himself, speaking to those lawfully married, decided to call not by a naked but by a veiled name, saying: ‘Return again to the same thing’ (1 Cor. 7). And: ‘Let no one defraud his brother in the matter’ (1 Thess. 4).

“Only concerning priests’ access to, association with, and cohabitation with women contrary to the canonical prohibition shall we inquire through such men as the holy African canons command (African Council, canons 96, 98)—that is, those whom public laws admit as accusers or witnesses, whether in the public court or in the hearing.

“These witnesses shall be examined after the example of Daniel and as the laws prescribe. And if any priest, not only in our parish but in our diocese, confesses or is convicted in a lawful and regular judgment of cohabitation, association, or access with women contrary to the canons, then, as the Apostle says, ‘If anyone does not obey our word, whether by word or by letter, take note of that person and have nothing to do with him’ (2 Thess. 3), he shall in every way, according to the decrees of blessed Gregory, be deposed without restoration to his rank, in accordance with the chapter of the great Pope Leo in which he says (Epistle 1, to the bishops throughout Campania):

“‘Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act contrary to these constitutions and dares to admit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion, since he refused to be a companion in discipline.

“‘But lest anything should perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by your affection that, if anyone transgresses them, he should know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.’”

“For blessed Augustine also wrote as follows to his archbishop concerning Abundantius, a presbyter of his parish [Col. 0701B] (Epistle 216):

> ‘Since he did not walk in the ways of the servants of God, he began to have a bad reputation. Alarmed by this, yet not rashly believing anything, but becoming decidedly more concerned, I took pains to discover whether I could somehow obtain reliable indications of his misconduct. First I learned that he had diverted a certain peasant’s money, which had been entrusted to him in payment for wine, so that he could give no plausible account of it. Then, having been convicted, he also confessed that, when he had no cleric with him, he had eaten lunch and dinner at the house of a certain woman of ill repute, and had stayed in the vicinity and in the same house. For what he denied, I left him to God; what he was not permitted to conceal, I judged.’

Therefore, as Gregory decreed, the presbyter of ill repute shall be examined under oath by suitable witnesses, as we have stated above; and those who swear on the matter shall swear in this form:

“Concerning what you ask me about this presbyter—what I know about it—as far as I know, I shall neither tell you a lie nor conceal the truth [Col. 0701C]; so may God and these saints of God help me.”

After this oath, he should be questioned in the following manner:

“Holy canons prescribe that a presbyter must not have such intercourse, association, or cohabitation with women as could give rise to evil suspicion and an unsuitable reputation for a priest. Therefore tell me whether you have seen, or know for certain, that such intercourse, association, or cohabitation exists between women and this presbyter, from which evil suspicion and bad reputation could arise, in accordance with the oath you have just sworn, so that you neither conceal the truth about it nor tell a lie about it.”

Apart from the accusers, there shall be seven suitable witnesses who shall state the truth about the matter under oath. Six of them shall swear, and the seventh, if the condition or status of the person permits it, shall come forward for judgment, declaring that the six stated the truth about the matter under oath. For many have already been found among us to have perjured themselves after being hired for a price.

And if by this procedure the presbyter has been convicted [Col. 0701D] of unsuitable cohabitation with women, he shall be deposed, as Pope Zosimus decreed, saying (Epistle to Hesychius, chapter 2):

> “Let anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the Apostolic See, has neglected this know that it will be punished by us with the greatest severity, so that he may have no doubt that he cannot retain his office if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this may be attempted with impunity. For whatever is repeatedly practiced despite prohibition is done in a spirit of insult.”

It is established in the Law, and confirmed in the Gospel, that “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew XVIII). The Apostle also commands Timothy (I Timothy V)—in whose person, as Leo says, he instructed the entire number of Christ’s priests—that an accusation against a presbyter should not be received except under two or three witnesses. And the holy Council of Nicaea commands that a newly ordained bishop who has been reproved by two or three witnesses be kept apart from the clergy (Canon II).

But because in the account of Susanna (Daniel XIII) we read of two witnesses who [Col. 0702A] seemed suitable; and in the account of Naboth (III Kings XXI), as well as in the account of the Lord’s Passion (Matthew XXVI), we read that two witnesses gave false testimony; and because Christ, the power and wisdom of God, says, “Through me lawgivers decree what is just” (Proverbs IX), and so forth; and because Saint Gregory frequently commands in his letters that the case of ecclesiastical ministers be settled legally and according to rule; and because Saint Augustine, explaining the Apostle’s statement (in the book *On Penance*), “If anyone is named as a fornicator among the brothers” (II Corinthians V), says:

> “The Apostle did not wish a person to be judged by another person according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion, or even by an extraordinary judgment usurped without authority, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church—whether the person had confessed voluntarily, or had been accused and convicted. He wished that ‘naming’ to be understood as that which takes place when a sentence is pronounced against someone in judicial order and with integrity. For if mere naming were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since a crime is often falsely alleged against someone.”

In accusations against presbyters [Col. 0702B], we have seen that the authority of the laws concerning the number of suitable witnesses must be followed: namely, that seven suitable witnesses, as we said above, are required; and, if reason or the case demands it, fourteen or twenty-one witnesses should be sought, so that the truth may be brought to light and displayed. (HINCMAR, same work, chapter 23.)

But if a bad reputation concerning a presbyter has spread throughout the parish on the basis of probability, while legal accusers and witnesses are lacking, then—so that the hearts of the weak may not be troubled by the presbyter’s bad reputation, so that our ministry may not be criticized, and so that presbyters, feeling more secure, may not fall more freely into sin—according to the decree of the younger Gregory (Epistle 9), an oath shall be placed between the parties, and the presbyter of ill repute shall have as his witness in the oath of his purification the one whom he will also have as judge. (HINCMAR, same work, chapter 24.)

And since we often read in the letters of blessed Gregory that a priest who had been defamed offered only an oath in purification of his reputation, while legal, apostolic, and canonical authority accepts the testimony of three witnesses [Col. 0702C] for condemnation, it does not seem unreasonable that it should be accepted for purification as well. In sacred history and in the letter of blessed Gregory we also read that blessed Peter, first of the apostles, when believers reproached him for entering among the Gentiles, appeased them with a humble explanation and even produced witnesses in the case of his reproach, saying: “These six brothers came with me” (Acts II). And the Carthaginian canons decree (Council of Carthage, chapter 20) that if presbyters or deacons have been accused, their case should be examined by their own bishop, joined by a lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places—namely, six besides himself in the case of a presbyter, and three besides himself in the case of a deacon.

We say that it is consistent with authority that, if a presbyter has been defamed and suitable accusers or witnesses are lacking, he should, according to the quality and gravity of the case and of the person, and according to the benefit and protection of weak consciences, clear himself by oath either alone, or with two other witnesses, or with six other witnesses [Col. 0702D], from the evil opinion held against him. And the decree of the younger Gregory is not contradicted if more witnesses are required for the purification of a defamed presbyter. For when the same pontiff wrote to Boniface, bishop of Mainz, through the presbyter Denuald, he said that if the defamed presbyter could not be convicted by suitable witnesses, an oath should be placed between the parties; but he did not determine whether the presbyter should swear alone or with others. (HINCMAR, same work, chapter 25.)

And since, as it is written (Job IV), wickedness was found even among the angels; and since, according to the testimony of the prophet Malachi (Malachi II) and the evangelist John (Revelation I), priests are called angels; and since we have learned by experience that certain men have conspired with one another, so that they might assist one another in their purifications but in fact harm one another, just as presbyters full of wicked thoughts conspired against Susanna (Daniel XV), it does not seem inappropriate that, when there is a trustworthy envoy of the bishop, those presbyters who have offered themselves to take an oath together with the defamed priest in his purification [Col. 0703A] should undergo the following examination through the advocate of the defamed presbyter, so that they may not destroy themselves before God by their oath, as we have already found certain men here to have been refuted. (HINCMAR, same work, chapter 26.)

Since, as Saint Augustine says, new kinds of illnesses compel us to seek new experiments, instructed by the authorities cited above and without prejudging any matters that may be understood more soundly by wiser judgments, we have determined that these procedures should be followed. In this way we may recall presbyters from the precipice of lust, vindicate by whatever means we can the canonical prohibition so often repeated against its violators, and avoid being judged negligent in correction, as the priest Eli was condemned because he corrected his sons less strictly and less vigorously than he ought to have done; and both he and his sons perished (I Kings II).

For, as Leo says (Epistle 3 to Januarius):

> “The faults of those in lower orders should be attributed to no one more than to lazy and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while they fail to apply the necessary medicine.”

And Saint Gregory [Col. 0703B] says:

> “Whoever does not correct what must be cut away commits it.”

Again, Leo, writing to Bishop Januarius, says to each of us:

> “Let your Love have no doubt that, if—as we do not believe—what we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith should be neglected, we shall be moved to vehement action.”

For, as Pope Hilary says, the sanctions of sacred traditions are violated no less by wrongdoing than the Lord himself is assailed by an insult.

But how those who, through contempt, violate the sanctions of sacred traditions, or assail the Lord himself, are to be treated, Saint Leo determines in his letter to Bishop Rusticus, saying:

> “For those who have fallen, private withdrawal should be sought in order to obtain God’s mercy, so that, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful. We are not permitted to depart from this rule of discernment, promulgated by the Holy Spirit, through any kind of misplaced pity. For although compassion is owed to our neighbors, uprightness is owed toward vices.”

[Col. 0703C] Therefore Holy Scripture always joins uprightness to simplicity, because simplicity without uprightness is foolishness. Thus simplicity toward vices, as Catholic teachers say, is lax and foolish; while uprightness toward one’s neighbors, without the simplicity of compassion, becomes austere and harsh.”

## CHAPTER X

We proclaim to every order of the faithful that the heats of lust must be avoided with the utmost care, as the Lord commands through the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII). Although we ought to resist the remaining vices with every virtue, against lust it is not so much useful to fight as to flee. Hence the Apostle Paul also commands, saying: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body” (I Corinthians VI); and again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews XIII). And when the Apostle says in the same place, “You are the holy temple of God” [Col. 0703D] (I Corinthians III), and likewise, “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Corinthians VI), far be it from us that, for the sake of a brief pleasure of miserable flesh, we should take away Christ’s members and make them members of a prostitute.

For the lust of the flesh, since it is hateful to God, is therefore conspicuous to all good people, because it is immediately disgraceful in itself. Its first weapons are the eyes, its second its words. But whoever is not carried away by the eyes can resist words; and whoever restrains the pleasure of lustful suggestion does not proceed to consent to lust.

Lust grows strong through rich foods, blazes up through excessive fullness of the belly, and pierces the soul with the goad of drunkenness. For chastity is difficult to preserve amid luxuries. In the end, fullness of food and drink moves the mind toward play and the flesh toward debauchery. Nor, because these are the luxuries of the powerful, should the poor exercise less caution: for lust exerts its authority both in silk and in rags. It fears neither the purple of kings nor [Col. 0704A] despises the squalor of beggars.

Since lust kills the life of the soul and robs it of its heart, it also inflicts blindness upon the mind; it quickly weakens the body itself, hurls it, broken, into miserable old age, and, unless the merciful kindness of God alone stretches out the hand of his most gracious clemency, lifts up the one lying prostrate, and brings him to repentance before death comes, it plunges the man into hell and drags him into the punishments of Tartarus.

Woe, then, to the one whose lust ends only when his life ends. Therefore it is altogether necessary for us to obey the salutary counsel of Scripture, which warns: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII); and again: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, and evil desire” (Colossians III), and so forth.

We exhort every rank, every order, and both sexes to flee utterly from this rotten lust and, with loins girded, to hold fast the virtue of chastity. For we know with certainty that the Apostle’s most truthful word [Col. 0704B] cries out terribly among other things: “Neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males will possess the kingdom of God” (I Corinthians VI).

## CHAPTER XI

Among the other duties of our admonition, it seems to us sufficiently necessary to restrain the abominable practice of perjury—not only perjuries contrived as part of some faction or undertaken in the desire to deceive and mislead others, but also those which, arising from a corrupt habit already deeply ingrained, are admitted in almost every word by people for whom it is equally customary to swear falsely and truly.

If, perhaps because of those who are slow to believe and are not moved to accept a statement—who also commit a serious offense in forcing those who speak to swear—it should become necessary to produce an oath, then the oath must have truth, judgment, and justice as its companions, as the Lord says [Col. 0704C] through the prophet Jeremiah: “You shall swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’ in truth, in judgment, and in justice” (Jeremiah IV).

For if these are absent, it will not be an oath but perjury. The Old Law indeed permitted swearing but prohibited perjury: “You shall not take,” it says, “the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold him innocent who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain” (Exodus X).

When this command is understood more deeply, we know that it instructs us not to think that Christ, the Son of God the Father, is a creature—calling him merely a human being and depriving him of the honor of divinity. Yet in the simple sense, the person who takes the name of his God in vain is one who, in any frivolous matter, and while deceiving his neighbor under oath, does not fear to invoke his holy name in such vanity, sometimes in an unnecessary matter or an idle word.

In the New Testament the Lord himself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit perjury.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matthew V), and so forth. Therefore evangelical truth does not accept an oath [Col. 0704D], since every faithful word should serve in place of an oath.

There are also many who constantly make others swear, yet do not fear to swear falsely by God and all the saints. Some swear by the bodies of the saints, by their own soul, or by the soul of their mother, father, or some loved one, making light of their own soul and the salvation of their family. Others swear by the whole world, despising the Lord’s command: “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth” (ibid.), and so forth. For whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits upon it.

Whoever therefore wishes to avoid the crime of perjury should not cultivate the habit of swearing. Scripture says: “Do not accustom your mouth to swearing” (Ecclesiasticus XXIX); and again: “A person who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house” (ibid.).

Hence Bishop Isidore says (*Sentences*, book II, chapter 31):

> “Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot commit perjury. Let the person who fears sin never [Col. 0705A] swear.”

But what should be said about those who lie in order to deceive others, or who commit perjury by some verbal artifice, deceiving themselves rather than another? The Lord, who is the witness of the conscience, receives the matter as the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it.

Hence Saint Augustine says:

> “Those are not perjurers who, without keeping to the words, have fulfilled what was expected of them when they swore; and those are perjurers who, even while keeping the words, deceive the expectation of those to whom they swore.”

Alas, how many crimes these wretched people are held guilty of: exposed as transgressors of the whole sacred Law, old and new, because they speak falsehood, because they take the name of their God in vain, because they catch their neighbor through deceit, and moreover commit perjury.

Unless they perform worthy penance, such people seem, while still carrying living bodies, to bear dead and miserable souls. For this reason the Christian kings also enacted the following concerning oaths not to be sworn lightly, in book V, chapter 349 (197) [Col. 0705B]:

> “We wish oaths not to be taken hastily; rather, let every judge first investigate the case truthfully, so that the truth cannot remain hidden from him and so that they may not readily proceed to an oath.”

Likewise, concerning the avoidance of perjury, from book V, chapter 276:

> “We command that perjury be avoided and that witnesses not be admitted to an oath before they have been examined.”

And below:

> “If anyone is convicted of perjury, let him lose his hand or redeem it.”

Therefore, although, in order to avoid perjury, it may sometimes be necessary to keep an oath once it has been made, we nevertheless wish everyone to know that there is a certain oath which Christians must in no way observe: namely, one by which some evil is rashly or even knowingly promised under oath. This would be the case if someone promised an adulterous woman perpetual fidelity to remain with her, or if someone bound himself by oath either not to return to peace or to commit some disgraceful act.

It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to persist in what one has wrongly promised or to carry out the disgraceful act one has resolved to commit.

And lest anyone say that we are encouraging perjury [Col. 0705C], or suppose that this is something insignificant or trivial, let what the Council of Lérida established in chapter 74 be recalled:

> “Whoever has bound himself by oath never to return to peace with anyone with whom he is litigating shall, for this one perjury, be separated from communion of the Lord’s body and blood for one year. Let him absolve his guilt through almsgiving and tears, and through as many fasts as he can undertake. Let him hasten quickly to the charity that covers a multitude of sins.”

## CHAPTER XII

Since our subject is those who are discordant, angry, and quarrelsome, we have thought it necessary to demonstrate in a few words how harmful these vices are to the soul and how carefully all Christians must avoid them.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to the world because of scandals! For it is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the scandal comes” (Matthew XVIII).

Since, as blessed Jerome says [Col. 0705D], it is necessary that scandals occur in this world, and each person is exposed to scandals through his own vice, nevertheless woe to the person who, though it is necessary that such things occur in the world, causes them to occur through his own vice.

Hence Solomon says: “A perverse person stirs up quarrels, and a talkative person separates rulers” (Proverbs XVI). Again: “The wicked person always seeks quarrels, but a cruel angel will be sent against him” (Proverbs XVII).

The cruel angel is an unclean spirit sent by the Lord against those who sin and seek quarrels, so that it may afflict them in the present life or even carry them away to destruction after death.

Again Solomon says: “An angry person provokes strife, but the patient person calms what has been stirred up” (Proverbs XV). Again: “Whoever meditates on discord loves quarrels” (Proverbs XVII).

Certainly God is not with such people, since, as the Apostle Paul testifies, “God is not a God of dissension but of peace” (I Corinthians XIV). God has called us to peace.

Here the gentle teacher of the Church, Gregory, says: God is in unity, and those deserve to have his grace [Col. 0706A] who do not divide themselves from one another through the scandals of factions.

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go; first be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew V).

Hence the aforementioned teacher, showing how serious the fault of discord is, says: A gift is not accepted by God unless discord is first expelled from the heart.

The Lord also says of angry people: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (ibid.). Hence James says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James I). And the Apostle Paul admonishes us, saying: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians IV). Solomon likewise says: “Do not be quick to become angry, because anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclesiastes VII). Again: “Who can endure a spirit easily provoked to anger?” (Proverbs XVIII). And likewise: “Anger has no mercy, nor does an outburst of fury; who can withstand the force of an enraged person?” (Proverbs XVII).

[Col. 0706B] Anger must therefore be restrained, discord driven away, and quarrels curbed, so that we may not only refrain from provoking anyone through our own fault, but also, when provoked and gravely injured, may—as Paul says—be patient, bearing with one another and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another. As God forgave us in Christ, so let us also forgive one another what is owed to us, so that what is owed by us may be forgiven (Colossians III).

For we make such a covenant with God in prayer when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke II).

All of us must therefore take the greatest care. For whoever does not forgive the person who wrongs him does not pray for himself when he makes this petition; rather, he brings a curse upon himself. He seeks in vain to make God favorable toward him if he neglects to make peace with his neighbor.

And because such people have been separated from him who is peace, they are rightly also separated from the Church unless they lay aside their enmities. The Council of Agde decreed this in chapter 31 (3):

> “It has also seemed good that, as frequently happens [Col. 0706C], whenever people have been divided from one another by hatred or a prolonged lawsuit and cannot be recalled to peace despite sustained efforts, they should first be rebuked by the bishops of the cities. If, with a destructive determination, they refuse to lay aside their enmities, they shall be expelled from the assembly of the Church by the most just excommunication.”

And the Council of Carthage (IV) decreed in chapter 93:

> “The offerings of brothers who are at odds with one another shall not be received into the treasury.”

Therefore, since the offering of such people is not received into the sanctuary of the present Church, there is no doubt that their souls are excluded from fellowship with the heavenly sanctuary—that is, the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER XIII
Therefore we strongly urge that discord, together with anger and quarrelling, be restrained, because we know that from them is begotten offspring hateful to God and to those who love him—namely, that unspeakable crime, murder. How grave this crime is, and how many evils are committed through it, is evident to every sound-minded person. [Col. 0706D] For this reason we wish to trace its wretched origin more deeply and disclose it to all, so that, once everyone has recognized its deadly root, they may either in no way touch it, if that can be done, or, if it should happen to intrude—as it commonly does—may at its first contact immediately remove its most bitter poison from their lips before they are infected.

Accordingly, when the first-formed humans, who had been created with that condition of nature by which they were capable both of immortality and of death, had been condemned to death after the guilt of their first transgression—having lost by their own will the condition of not dying, while retaining no longer voluntarily the ability to die, or, so to speak, having acquired for themselves the inability not to die—so that whatever arose from their stock was likewise held subject to the same penalty, and what had succeeded them punitively on account of sin followed naturally in those born from them, the ancient enemy’s serpentine envy did not nevertheless rest. The envy that had poured itself into the forbidden fruit so that it might taste sweet in the mouths of our parents, once transferred into the succeeding offspring, passed into the innermost hearts of their children. [Col. 0707A] And although death had entered the world in this way through the agency of that very envy, it nevertheless seemed to itself to have accomplished little if it merely allowed mortals to await the due end of death.

Thus—grievous though it is to say—it spread and poured itself forth to such an extent, pursuing the innocence of the first creation, that even those who were first born on earth could not maintain peace and harmony between themselves. Although they were still, together with their parents, the sole lords of the whole world, one of them, moved by envy, killed the other and, having anticipated for him the appointed moment of death, forced him to return to his own earth before the final limits of a mature life.

When God had condemned him under a curse to sevenfold punishment for so great a crime, so that he himself might suffer the penalties of his fratricide and envy as a wandering exile down to the seventh generation, and his offspring likewise be subject to the curse in the seventh generation; and when, finally, the second murderer, Lamech, had struck seventy times seven, according to the interpretation of his name, with the crime of the forbidden and accursed deed now added and multiplied vengeance accordingly added—[Col. 0707B] the human sense, once corrupted, and the thought of the human heart infected with ancestral poison, could not be restrained from the impiety it had begun, even by fear of punishment, since, as the Lord himself says, “the inclination of the human heart is toward evil from its youth” (Gen. VIII).

Rather, the more the human race increased in number, the more the enormity grew—not only of cruel murders but of every crime as well—having taken its beginning from the devil’s envy, while those who belong to his side imitate him. Therefore what could not be restrained by divine fear had necessarily to be prohibited by the law—both the old and the new, both ecclesiastical and secular—and, once prohibited, had rightly to be punished by judicial correction.

Let us therefore recount in part what was anciently decreed concerning the deranged perpetrators of murder. In the Decalogue of the Old Law, the Lord commands through Moses: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). [Col. 0707C] Likewise: “Whoever strikes a man and kills him shall be put to death” (Exod. XXI).

In the Gospel, however, the Lord himself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V). When anger is entirely removed, what place is left for murder? For when we are commanded to offer the other cheek to one who strikes us, to love our enemies, and to pray for those who persecute us, every occasion not only of murder but also of the anger from which murder arises is taken away.

The Lord reveals who murderers are, what sort of people they are, whose children they are, and whose works they perform, when he says to the Jews: “You seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you” (John VIII). It is as though he were saying: “Your heart does not contain it, because it is not received by your heart.” For if it were received, it would receive it; but it would receive it for salvation, not for destruction.

Likewise: “You do the things that you have seen with your father” (ibid.). What, finally, are the things they had seen with their father? He discloses this in what follows, plainly showing who their father is: the one whom they imitate, not the one by whom they were created. [Col. 0707D]

Again: “You do the works of your father” (ibid.). And when they—as do certain wretched people even now, Christian in name but diabolical in conduct—boasted of the fatherhood of the one God, saying, “We were not born of fornication; we have one father, God” (ibid.), they heard: “If God were your father, you would certainly love me” (ibid.).

It is as though he were saying: “You call God your father; acknowledge me at least as your brother.” Would that we Christians might hear what the Jews refused to hear: that, if we truly wish to glory in the grace of the heavenly Father’s fatherhood and to be his adopted children, we should love with all our heart our brother, the Lord Jesus Christ, the true and proper Son of God. Let us also love our neighbors, according to his commandment, as ourselves. Let us recognize the sound of his speech, like his own sheep, lest he reproach us with what he said to the Jews: “Why do you not recognize my speech? Because you cannot hear my word” (ibid.). [Col. 0708A]

And why is this? “You,” he says, “are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (ibid.). And as though he were asked what that father’s desires are, he says: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth.”

“He was a murderer from the beginning”—certainly in the first human. He became a murderer from the time murder could come to be; for he envied the first human and killed him. Therefore those who imitate him in doing or desiring such things are certainly his children. And with such a father, unless they quickly repent, they will inherit the punishment of eternal fire, which has been prepared for him, his angels, and his children.

And since an opportunity has now presented itself to speak about liars, let us hear the Lord himself showing us who is regarded as the father of lies and of human falsehood. For when he had said of the devil, “He was a murderer from the beginning,” he added the reason: “And he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and its father”—that is, the father of his own lie, which he himself generated, because he heard it from no one. [Col. 0708B]

For any human being who receives a lie from another and repeats it is a liar, but is not its father. Liars, therefore, see and hear in their father the devil what he speaks—that is, the lie—which, because it has arisen from him, he teaches to be uttered by human mouths so that, through the lie uttered by them, he may kill their souls. Scripture plainly attests this: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I). The portion of all liars will be in the lake of burning fire and sulfur.

For this reason the apostle Paul admonishes everyone: “Do not lie to one another” (Col. III). Likewise: “Putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one to his neighbor” (Eph. IV). And Solomon says: “A lying tongue is an abomination to the Lord, but those who act faithfully are pleasing to him” (Prov. XII). Again: “A faithful witness delivers souls, but a deceitful person utters lies” (Prov. XIV). Likewise: “Whoever speaks what he knows is a judge of justice, but whoever lies is a fraudulent witness” (Prov. XII).

Here Jesus, son of Sirach, says: “Do not wish to utter every kind of lie” (Sir. VII). For, as blessed Father Augustine says, there are eight kinds of lies, and a perfect man must not lie in any of them.

Hence Isidore says: “Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care”; and again: “Flee every kind of lie with the greatest care. For everything that disagrees with the truth is iniquity. Be truthful in speech; deceive no one by lying; do not say one thing and do another; do not say one thing while holding another in your heart.” [Col. 0708C]

And in a letter of Pope Callistus: “No one who is faithful desires evil. If anyone is faithful, let him see to it that he does not speak falsely or lay snares for anyone.”

The Psalm says: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V). If you ask why, it is because a lie is contrary to the truth, which is Christ. It belongs to what is not, not to what is. For if what is is said, it is said truthfully; but if what is not is said, it is a lie.

Therefore, he says, “You will destroy those who speak lies,” because, abandoning what is, they have turned aside toward what is not. Although some wish this to be understood not of every lie but only of heretics, we, fleeing from the father of lies, should hasten to the Father of truth and speak truth from heart and mouth with our neighbors, so that we may deserve to be found participants in eternal truth and coeternal with the Father, reigning with him forever.

But let us return to the murderers, who are said to have the same father as liars, namely, the devil. Let them heed what the Lord said to his servant Noah after the flood: “I will require the blood of your souls from the hand of man; from the hand of a man and of his brother I will require his soul. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed in return; for man was made in the image of God” (Gen. IX). [Col. 0709A]

Although this sentence prohibits murder under threat of punishment, no foolish person should therefore suppose that the human soul, which is immortal, consists in blood. The soul is called *anima* as though from *anaema*—that is, something far removed from blood. Let him understand that “the blood of souls” is to be taken figuratively as life itself, by which human beings in the flesh are animated, sustained, and live through the soul.

Human blood is not believed to belong to the substance of the soul, although elsewhere the lawgiver seems to say: “The soul of every creature is in its blood” (Lev. XVII). This was not said because blood is the soul, which is properly a spiritual substance, but because, as we have said, the soul is figuratively signified by blood—an invisible reality through a visible one—just as it is said: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X), not because the rock actually was Christ, but because it signified Christ.

In this sense we must also understand what follows: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall likewise be shed” (Gen. IX). Many have shed blood, yet their blood has not been shed. Very many are killed by poison, hanging, or some other means, and their blood is not shed. [Col. 0709B]

Since, then, the one who kills may not have shed blood, how will the Lord shed his blood? Unless, as we have said, “the blood of man” is understood as his vital force, by which he exists. Whoever sheds it—that is, whoever kills a human being by any kind of death—will have his blood shed; that is, his vital portion will be destroyed. For just as he took temporal life from the one he killed, so by sinning he took eternal life from himself.

“For the soul that sins, it shall die.” To this corresponds what was said to Peter: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI). It is as though it were said: “All who unjustly kill a human being perish themselves in soul through the same killing.”

And because God made human beings in his own image, in that which he willed to remain unto eternity, he therefore requires the souls of human beings from those by whom they are driven from their bodies. [Col. 0709C]

Let deceitful people and false witnesses therefore hear the Psalmist say: “The Lord will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” (Ps. V). Again: “Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days” (Ps. LIV). And because the Lord abhors such people, the Church also will abhor them.

Accordingly, the following was decreed concerning them in the Council of Agde, chapter thirty-five:

“We have therefore judged that murderers and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion, unless they wipe away the crimes they have committed by the satisfaction of penance.”

And in the Council of Ancyra, chapter twenty-one:

“Those who have voluntarily committed murder shall indeed submit themselves continually to penance, but they shall attain perfection toward the end of their life.”

Concerning those who commit murder involuntarily, the same council says in chapter twenty-two:

“Concerning involuntary homicides: the earlier ruling prescribed that perfection be attained after seven years of penance; the second prescribed the completion of a period of five years.” [Col. 0709D]

And concerning murderous sorcerers, the Council of Elvira says in chapter six:

“If anyone kills another by sorcery—for he could not complete such a crime without idolatry—communion is not to be granted to him even at the end of his life.”

Since this crime of murder is now being committed with increasing frequency among our people, and not only the blood of Christians of every kind but even that of the ministers of Christ themselves, and moreover that of the highest priests, is being recklessly shed; since the fear of God, observance of the sacred old and new law, priestly reverence, and the decrees of the canons are being trampled underfoot; since the entire ecclesiastical order is being thrown into confusion and treated as a laughingstock by such people, and “those who are darkened are filled with houses of iniquities”—what are we to do when holy religion is being destroyed and right and justice are confused?

It remains only to cry out to the Lord with the Psalmist and say: “Arise, O God, judge your cause; remember the reproaches directed against you all day long by the foolish” (Ps. LXIII). [Col. 0710A]

Nevertheless, let human fear restrain those whom divine fear does not restrain. Let the emperors’ edicts be placed before them. In Book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 90, it is decreed:

“Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay down his weapons and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life, never to return to the world, and shall perform public penance for seven years.”

From the same book, chapter twenty-eight (97):

“If anyone kills or maims a priest, deacon, or monk, let him pay compensation according to the statutes of the earlier capitularies that were added to the Salic Law, and in addition pay us our ban, that is, sixty solidi. Let him lay down his weapons and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life under severe penance, never afterward serving the world or worldly affairs, nor marrying a wife.”

Likewise, in Book VII, chapter 225 (18):

“Concerning murderers, we have commanded that this be observed: whoever, in reckless daring, kills another without cause shall be struck with the penalty of death and shall never be permitted to redeem himself by payment. And if it should be agreed that someone may descend to a settlement, let none of his relatives or friends assist him in anything; if anyone does so, let him pay his entire *wergild*.”

Since such a strict judgment is pronounced concerning these matters, what will be decreed concerning the killing of bishops? Perhaps this appears to have been omitted here because, after the persecution of Christians exercised by the pagans had been quieted, such a monstrous crime was either exceedingly rare among Christians or had not been committed at all; and therefore no law was established here concerning how one should repent of it or how it should be punished.

Only this is found among the other writings of the *Capitularies*, in Book V, chapter 261: whoever kills a bishop is to be judged liable for nine hundred solidi.

Certainly, how vengeance is to be exacted in such cases—since it is not human vengeance that is sought but God’s, lest so great a crime appear, from the human point of view, to remain unpunished, and lest his just judgment come upon those who ought to have been God’s avengers, while they avenge their own injuries more severely but those of God either lightly or not at all—let the king see to it that, by judging such matters rightly, he fulfills his name by his deeds. [Col. 0710C]

Let his dukes and counts, who bear the sword of God for the punishment of evildoers, take heed. The Apostle says of them:

“Rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it, for it is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword without reason. He is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (Rom. XIII).

Let them also provide for themselves and for their subjects, following the example of Moses, God’s servant. To execute God’s vengeance, Moses gathered, armed, and encouraged the sons of Levi; although he was exceedingly gentle, he raged, as it were, against certain idolaters while punishing them, commanding his men:

“Let each man place his sword upon his thigh” (Exod. XXXII).

And again:

“Go and return from gate to gate, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor,” lest God’s anger rage against the whole people. [Col. 0710D]

If the king himself and his men, who are charged with carrying out this task, should in any way disregard God’s judgment, let them look to themselves.

For the Apostle Paul’s sentence stands firm—the sentence in which Truth itself, Christ, was speaking:

“The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and wickedness of human beings, who suppress the truth of God in wickedness” (Rom. I).

And shortly afterward:

“Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand”—that is, they did not wish to understand—“that those who do such things deserve death; and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

And again:

“We know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things” (Rom. II).

As for such people, if perhaps at last, even at the end of their lives, they should repent and ask forgiveness from the depths of their hearts for such grave offenses, we say that penance must by no means be denied them. We do not wish to appear to close the door of God’s mercy—a door that cannot be shut—or, God forbid, to drive anyone to despair of his mercy, and thus, so to speak, add death to the dead. [Col. 0711A]

For we believe that God is merciful and most ready to help the wretched who flee to the refuge of his kindness. He invites everyone to penance and cries out through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII).

Nevertheless, we say that the forms and periods of penance are to be determined according to the character of the sin, as is established in the African Council, chapter ten:

“For penitents, the periods of penance are to be determined by the judgment of the bishop according to the differences among sins.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 74:

“Let the priest impose the laws of penance upon one who seeks penance, without respect of persons.”

We have indeed done concerning these matters what belonged to us.

Finally, following the judgment of blessed Paul the Apostle (1 Cor. V), so that those who have done this might be removed from the midst of Christians, we have already judged that, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with us assembled and his Spirit present, and with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, those who have acted in this way are to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ—provided, however, that they are willing to do penance. [Col. 0711B]

For the same Apostle testifies that he acted in this way toward those who had suffered shipwreck concerning the faith—that is, who had gone astray by living wickedly in the faith—when he wrote to Timothy:

“Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. V).

But if they persist in their wickedness as they began, and despise the riches of God’s goodness, patience, and long-suffering, storing up wrath for themselves according to their hardness and impenitent heart on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will render to each according to his works, then we do not hand them over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh so that their spirit may be saved. Rather, they have handed themselves over entirely to Satan, so that they may perish with him on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore we too, together with the whole Church of Christ, because we neither ought nor can communicate with them, whether living or dead, will have no communion with them. Moreover, according to the power bestowed upon us in blessed Peter and the other apostles, to whom it was said, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII), we will continue to bind them with the bond of that anathema. [Col. 0711C]

Thus, according to Paul’s words, because they do not love our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. XVI)—indeed, because they hate and persecute him, and have killed the Lord’s Christ, the one who bore his name with the sacred anointing and acted as his representative—let each one of them who perpetrated this most unspeakable crime in deed, and everyone who in any way favors them and consents by associating with them, be *anathema maranatha*—that is, condemned until the Lord returns; or destruction; or, as has been said, condemned on the day of judgment, when the Lord will come.

May the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ be with us and with his entire Church. Amen.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0711D]

Although a discussion of sacrilegious persons among us has already taken place above, where we showed in part how grave that crime is and by what punishment a sacrilegious person is rightly chastised, nevertheless, because this most wicked custom has become established among our people—that, when a bishop of a church has died, the ecclesiastical possessions are immediately seized by various powerful persons, as though they had belonged to the bishops personally, even though, if they had been his, such an action would still be contrary to every law—we grieve, knowing that this monstrous crime of sacrilege has already often been committed.

So that no one may presume to do this again, we prohibit it by the authority of God and of his saints, who reign with him in heaven, and also by our episcopal ministry, to which the Lord, although we are unworthy, has given authority in his apostles, saying:

“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

Among the other canonical constitutions on this matter, the following is written in the Council of Valence, chapter 2:

“It has also pleased us that, when a bishop is summoned from this world at the Lord’s command, the clergy must entirely abstain from greedy hands reaching for any furnishings or whatever may be in the house of the church or of the bishop—books, valuable objects, utensils, vessels, crops, flocks, animals, or absolutely any other possession—and must seize nothing in the manner of thieves.

“Unless they are restrained by the authority of the canons, they shall be compelled, by the strict judgment of the metropolitan or of all the priests of the province, to restore to its former condition everything they have seized, so that under this just constitution nothing necessary may be lost to the bishop or to the future administrator.

“And so that this may be preserved with greater confidence while justice remains intact, according to the decrees of the Council of Riez (chapter 5), when a bishop departs from the body, the bishop who is nearest to him shall come to him. After the customary funeral rites have been celebrated, he shall immediately take the strictest care of that church, so that, before the future pontiff is ordained, nothing may be permitted to the remaining clergy for subversion or plunder.

“Thus, an inspection of everything found and a most faithful inventory shall, if possible, be carried out under the supervision of the present bishop within the octave of the deceased. [Col. 0712A] Thereafter, the inventory, having been properly prepared, shall be brought to the metropolitan’s attention, so that, by his choice, a person may be appointed to administer the ecclesiastical household who will distribute the customary stipends to the clergy and, if there should perhaps be delay in ordaining the bishop, be able at suitable times to render an account to the metropolitan of the property entrusted to him.

“Under this salutary constitution, therefore, let the clergy remain entirely content with their stipends; let them not plunder the possessions of the bishop who has died; and let the future pontiff not enter the vacant house of the church with sorrow, but rather let him himself be able to rejoice in what his predecessor has left behind and to distribute it to others.”

Likewise, chapter 3:

“In the same manner, let notice also be given to the parents and relatives of the deceased bishop, if he died intestate, so that, without the knowledge of the metropolitan or of the priests of the province, they may not attempt to seize anything belonging to the deceased. Otherwise they might perhaps appropriate among hereditary possessions something that belonged to the church or had been mixed with ecclesiastical property.

“Let them wait until the future bishop is ordained, or, if the matter should take a long time, let them have recourse, as has been said, to the metropolitan’s admonition.

“If any cleric or layman, forgetful of divine fear, should wickedly attempt to act against these holy synodal decrees, let him be deprived both of communion and of fellowship with the Church, since it is a serious matter for him to come to the Church whom he did not fear to strip—unless, perhaps, corrected by a better spirit, he should cease from his presumption and recover forgiveness.

“If, however, anyone reasonably and modestly seeks what is legally owed to him, let neither the property nor his lawful claim be denied him without any penalty by the metropolitan or by whomever he appoints.

“These canons also bind all those who, whether in the past or in the future, seize and plunder the property of the church or of the bishop.”

Likewise, chapter 4:

“Since it often happens through the absence of the bishop responsible for commendation that the funerals of holy bishops are delayed, so that the venerable members of the pontiff, while burial is postponed, are wholly exposed to indignity, we decree with prudent counsel that the bishop who, after the death of his brother, is customarily invited to come for his burial should, when warned, not delay visiting him while he is ill and still in the body.

“Thus he may either rejoice more fully at the priest’s recovery or, at least, admonish his brother concerning the ordering of his household and put his worthy wishes into effect. After offering the sacrifice to God for his commendation, he should immediately and diligently commit the one departing from this world to burial, and should not delay fulfilling what has been established above by canonical authority.

“If, however, as commonly happens, the bishop should depart through sudden death, and the neighboring priests cannot arrive from a distance, let the lifeless body of the priest remain for only one day and its accompanying night. It must not be kept without the attendance of brothers and religious persons or the vigil of those singing psalms. It should be carefully placed by priests in a coffin and set apart, but not immediately buried; rather, it should be honorably commended until a bishop, invited from wherever necessary, can come without delay and solemnly bury it as is fitting. [Col. 0712B]

“In this way both the occasion for indignity will be removed and the ancient custom in the burial of priests will be observed.”

In the synodal decree enacted in the city of Toledo (Council of Toledo VII, canon 3), we likewise read:

“Things required by propriety often fail to be carried out because of the negligence of certain persons. Therefore, since it is known from the canons what dignity is to be preserved in the funeral of a dying bishop, we add only this to the tradition of ancient custom: if any priest, having been summoned according to the statutes of the Council of Valence to come to the human remains of a bishop who has died, should delay through sluggishness, then, if the clergy of the deceased bishop appeal against him before the synod or the metropolitan bishop, he shall have absolutely no license for the space of one year either to celebrate Mass or to receive communion.

“Presbyters, however, or other clergy who hold a place of greater honor in that same church whose bishop has died, if they are found slow to summon assistance for the funeral either of the bishop already dead or of one who is immediately dying, or if they are proved to have neglected this through any disturbance of mind, shall be assigned to penance in monasteries for the entire period of one year.” [Col. 0713A]

Since, then, the fathers have established such regulations concerning the funeral of a deceased bishop, we nevertheless consider it useful now to make this known to everyone, so that no one may dare to commit so great a sacrilegious crime. What it is unlawful and contrary to the laws for any individual to do, let no one presume in any way to do to holy Mother Church.

And since in certain places circumstances make it possible for two or three bishops to assemble for the death or funeral of one of us, and it is recognized that this is pleasing to your beloved brotherhood in Christ, it is fitting that holy charity should display itself at the funerals of the dead—the charity that burned in the hearts of the living.

Indeed, it has become known to us that in the eastern regions the errors and blasphemies of a certain Photius concerning the Holy Spirit still persist: he blasphemously claims that the Spirit proceeds not from the Son but from the Father alone. [Col. 0713C] We therefore exhort your brotherhood, together with myself, that, according to the admonition of the Roman See, each of us, having examined the judgments of the catholic Fathers, should draw the sharp arrows of the Mighty One from the quivers of divine Scripture, to pierce the beast of the monster reborn and crush the head of the most wicked serpent.

## CHAPTER XV

Having thus prefaced these matters, let us now address all generally who wish to live justly and piously in communion with the holy catholic Church, which is the one body of Christ, having one Lord, one faith, and one baptism.

Although this Church, generally speaking, was built by Christ himself, its head, upon the rock—that is, upon Peter’s confession—it is nevertheless evident that throughout all Italy, Gaul, and Spain no one established churches except those whom the venerable Peter or his successors appointed as priests. [Col. 0713D]

And because the Church in our regions also, as has been said, was not only founded upon this solidity of the rock but was also taught by him and his successors, it has endeavored, with God’s grace and through the merits of blessed Peter assisting it, to preserve unshaken to this day the firmness of the faith it first received, and it has admitted no fellowship with the faithless.

But since many are Christians in faith alone while in conduct they dissent from Christian teaching, and since, as the apostle James testifies, we have learned that faith without works is not merely idle but dead, for he says:

“What benefit is it, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” (Jas. II).

And blessed Jerome says:

“What benefit is it if, while acting impiously, you invoke God with your voice, whom you deny by your works?”

The holy Pope Gregory likewise says:

“What benefit is it if we are joined to our Redeemer through faith but separated from him in conduct? Therefore the one truly believes who practices in works what he believes.”

Great care must be taken so that those who are called faithful, if they desire to be blessed with faithful Abraham—who merited justification not only from faith but also from works—may strive to live blessedly.

For, as Saint Jerome says, blessed is the one who both lives rightly by believing correctly and preserves right faith by living well.

But alas, what grief! Through the carelessness as well as the ignorance of us, our fellow ministers—both those who have already departed and those who still remain—many, almost countless, people ruined by vices are still found among the ecclesiastical people, of every sex, age, and condition alike, who, even into their old age, have not yet acquired, as they ought to have done, knowledge of the simple faith. [Col. 0714A]

They do not even know the words of the saving Creed, or at least the prayer of the Lord’s Prayer.

How, then, even if such people appear to possess some good conduct, will they build the edifice of good works without the foundation of faith? And what excuse can we offer for this, when such people depart from the body and are carried away not to the life they did not know but to eternal death, which they could in no way escape without faith, by which the just person is believed to live?

We therefore, as blessed Gregory says, are authors of death when the people perish, although we ought to have been guides to life. For through our sin the multitude of the people has been struck down, because through our negligence it was not instructed for life.

Let us strive by every means to escape this exceedingly terrible condemnation, which threatens both us and them, through ourselves and through our fellow priests of the second order. Let us continually instruct those entrusted to us both in the words of faith and by examples of good works, so that in everything we may present ourselves as God’s ministers, lest our ministry be reviled, and lest it be said of us:

“The priests did not know knowledge.”

And again:

“The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ Those who held the law did not know me” (Jer. II). [Col. 0714C]

Let us also avoid incurring the offense that the priest Eli is known to have incurred, because he did not properly rebuke his sons when they acted shamefully (1 Sam. IV).

## In General for All

Therefore, first of all, let every Christian establish for himself the foundation of the Christian religion—without which no one can rightly be called or be a Christian—namely, the catholic faith: that he believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one true God, three in persons and one in substance. Let him likewise believe that the person of the Son alone assumed flesh for our salvation, in which he suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, and with which he will also come for judgment. Let him believe also in the Holy Spirit, and that through him, in baptism, the remission of all sins is granted; and that by his gift, in the Church of Christ, through repentance and the priestly ministry, forgiveness of sins is unfailingly bestowed.

Let him also truly believe that at Christ’s coming there will be a resurrection of all in true flesh. This foundation of true faith must necessarily be adorned with good works; for just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so faith cannot be perfect unless it works through love. Moreover, if it has no works, it is dead in itself.

Let holy faith therefore be adorned, so that it may be true and fruitful, with hope, charity, humility, chastity, self-restraint, sobriety, unanimity, concord, justice, mercy, innocence, simplicity, and other such virtues that consist in love of God and of one’s neighbor. Let each person beware lest he stain its beauty with various crimes. Among these, we perceive that the following must especially be avoided, and we know for certain that the more hidden they are, the more dangerous they are: pride, which knows how to turn an angel into a devil and cast him down from heaven; envy, invented by the devil in order to expel mankind from paradise and introduce death throughout the world; hatred and discord, followers of the crimes mentioned above, but no less destructive, because they drive out charity, the mother of all virtues, and when she has been banished, they corrupt all good works together, if any are present.

These things, therefore, must above all be uprooted from the hearts of the faithful; and along with them, those matters which we have partially indicated above must be utterly abhorred. Likewise, those practices that are almost naturally customary must be avoided, such as drunkenness, feasting, quarrels, detraction, enmities, and things of this kind, which, according to the Apostle, exclude people from the kingdom of God: “For,” he says, “those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5).

In the same way, those actions must be restrained by every means which are contrary to the law of human society, such as thefts and the execrable acts of plunder mentioned above, calumnies, oppressions, and invasions. These must first be repaid and then corrected through the remedy of repentance.

We also prohibit in every way, with an emphatic protest, the most evil frenzy for profit—namely, the invention of usury—which clerics pursue no less than laypeople, forgetful of the Lord’s commandment: “You shall not lend your money at interest.” And again: “You shall not take usury from your brother, nor receive more than you gave” (Leviticus 25).

There are also other evils of various crimes, which divine law rejects and condemns, on account of which the people are afflicted by devastation and the sword, by famine and pestilence, and the condition of the Church is weakened and the kingdom endangered. Among these are the most abominable pollutions with males or animals, on account of which our sweet and gracious God is provoked to the bitterness of wrath all the more severely because they are demonstrably contrary to nature. There are also those practices that still appear to survive from pagan ritual, namely magic, lots, amulets, sorcery, divinations, and interpretations of dreams. Divine law commands that all these be punished, because in such practices there is most plainly slavery to the devil.

Concerning these matters, the following is written in canon 23 of the Council of Ancyra:

> Those who seek divinations and follow the custom of the pagans, or who introduce such people into their houses to inquire into something by magical art, or for the purpose of purification, shall remain under the rule of five years, according to the established degrees of penance.

Likewise, every Christian must beware of things that may indeed seem trivial but are contrary to the divine commandments: scurrility and foolish talk, idle stories, and shameful and obscene conversations. Many not only speak and willingly listen to these things in their homes and at their banquets, but also, to provoke God to anger, do not cease to occupy themselves irreverently with them in basilicas consecrated to him and to his saints, without any regard for fear.

Let the worship, honor, and reverence due to the Lord’s day and to the holy solemnities be maintained. Let the appointed fast and also the fast of the four seasons be observed. Let dangerous and harmful lies cease—lies that are practiced far too constantly—as well as oaths, curses, shameful songs, and other similar things, which would indeed take too long to enumerate but which must be corrected with all speed.

Considering, therefore, that we shall render an account of all our works and words, and even of our thoughts, to him who will come in terrible majesty to repay each person according to what he has done, whether good or evil, and that sins, whether small or great, cannot remain unpunished; and considering also the scourges that for these same sins we already justly suffer—indeed grievous, but lesser than we deserve—let us not be insensitive, incorrigible, or murmuring beneath his hand extended to strike, a hand whose blow we neglected to forestall while we were still being chastised as sons by paternal kindness. At least, let us hasten by swift conversion and worthy satisfaction to temper his hand, lest he strike us even unto destruction, even unto the soul; lest, like wicked servants, we be struck by stern correction in the present and dragged toward harsher punishments in the future.

While there is still opportunity, while he who has been offended is still, for the sake of our repentance, overlooking our sins, and while, wishing us to turn from his severity to his goodness, he cries out with encouragements and threats, let us not harden our hearts as our fathers and we ourselves have done until now. “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity.” Now, therefore, having returned to our consciences and judging the evils we have committed, let us confess them to the Lord in a pure and true confession, for he is good and his mercy is forever.
