Let us fall down and weep before the Lord who made us, for he is our Lord, gracious and merciful, patient toward evil, who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. If, therefore, turning to God with our whole heart, we perform true repentance and works worthy of repentance—persisting in frequent and holy fasts, chaste vigils pleasing to him, and prayers not drenched in a false shower of tears, together with rightful almsgiving and the other works of mercy and charity—and if we profess that, with his help, without whom we can do nothing, we shall never return to the former crimes of our impiety; if we persevere in these things, making satisfaction to God and the Church for past sins through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart, we shall quickly obtain the mercy of him who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart and whose proper work is always to show mercy and pardon.

We say “quickly” because, with the gracious God, the measure of time does not count as much as the measure of sorrow. For he himself speaks through the prophet, saying: “When you have turned and groaned, you shall be saved.” And again: “The impiety of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his impiety” (Ezekiel 33).

Since, therefore, the kindness of the Lord our God is so great, let us not neglect, postpone, or delay turning to him. Rather, as the holy apostle Paul exhorts us, “let us approach with confidence the throne of his grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help” (Hebrews 4), through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong power and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Subscriptions of the Bishops

Hervaeus, archbishop of Rheims, assenting to these decrees, subscribed. Wito, bishop of Rouen, subscribed. Rodulfus, bishop of Laon, subscribed. Erluinus, bishop of Beauvais, subscribed. [Col. 0716D] Raubettus, bishop of Noyon, subscribed. Letoldus, bishop of Châlons, subscribed. Abbo, bishop of Soissons, subscribed. Stephanus, bishop of Cambrai, subscribed. Hucbertus, bishop of the church of Meaux, subscribed. Otfridus, bishop of Senlis, subscribed. Stephanus, bishop of Thérouanne, subscribed. Otgarius, bishop of Amiens, subscribed.

## Council at Trosly, in the Year 921

In which Erlebald, excommunicated by Hervaeus, was absolved after his death.

*(In Labbé, Councils, vol. IX, col. 579.)*

Concerning this synod and the causes on account of which excommunication had been inflicted upon Erlebald, Flodoard writes in book 4, chapter 16, of his *History*, as follows:

> “Hervaeus,” he says, “the bishop, had excommunicated Erlebald, count of the Castricensian district, because he had seized land belonging to the bishopric of Rheims and had built there a certain fortification on the Onosa, from which he repeatedly inflicted harm upon the ecclesiastical household. Moreover, he had secretly attacked the castle of Altmont. But when he still did not desist from the evils he had begun, the archbishop proceeded with his men to seize the fortification that he had built and called Maceriae. After besieging it for almost four weeks, he captured it while Erlebald was at last defending it; and, having stationed guards there, returned to Rheims.
>
> “Erlebald, however, went to the king, who was then staying in the Warmacensian district against Henry, prince beyond the Rhine. There he was killed when enemies of the king came upon him. Nevertheless, later, at the synod that the same lord archbishop held at Trosly with his diocesan bishops, at the king’s intervention and urgent request, he absolved him from the bond of excommunication.”

The same Flodoard says in his *Chronicle*:

> “In the year 921 a synod was held at Trosly, presided over by Hervaeus the archbishop, with King Charles also present; through his intervention Erlebald the Castricensian was absolved there.”

This is what he records for that year; the rest he had explained in the preceding year.

## In the Year of the Lord 823: Walter, Bishop of Sens

### Historical Notice Concerning Walter

*(From Gallia Christiana, vol. XII, p. 223.)*

Walter, nephew of Walter, bishop of Orléans, and a canon of the major church, highly distinguished for learning and nobility, succeeded Evrard in March and was ordained on 2 April 887. He consecrated Herifred, bishop of Auxerre, in the monastery of Nigelles in the diocese of Troyes on 29 August, and installed him in his see on 8 September of the same year.

In the following year he joined with the Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanians in choosing as king of the Franks Odo, son of Robert the Strong and Adelaide; he anointed him in January 888. At the synod held at Meung on the Loire in 891, at Walter’s urging, it was decreed that thereafter no one should be ordained or appointed father or rector of the monastery of Saint Peter unless the monks themselves had chosen him from among themselves, according to their own decision and free will.

The constitutions attributed to Walter, however, belong to more recent times; in them, conventual priories, regular canons, and black nuns are mentioned—terms unfamiliar in the ninth century.

At the royal assembly held at Verberie in 892, together with other judges of the district of Atuyer, he adjudicated the cell of Alfa to the monastery of Adremar against the monk Agnius. About that time, with Fulco, archbishop of Rheims, he established certain judgments concerning the case of Hildegard, an abbess of his diocese. When Walter was unable to carry them out, Fulco ordered that they be executed as quickly as possible, asking Walter to ensure that he appear at the appointed meeting and present the aforesaid abbess. Otherwise, Fulco himself, by his authority, would accomplish the matter—something he had until then delayed out of affection for Walter.

In 896, Sens was surrounded and captured by Richard, duke of Burgundy, against Walter the archbishop and Garnerius the count, as reported by Odorannus and Flodoard. Because of certain disputes between them, Walter the bishop was captured by Richard in the ninth year of his episcopate, on 8 June, and placed in custody for nine months, while King Odo was still alive. After nine months, he returned from custody to Sens in peace on 22 February, having given hostages to Duke Richard under oath, as Clarius says.

From that time Richard held lordship over the city of Sens. After his death, his son Rodulf succeeded him; Walter anointed Rodulf, who had been elected king, in the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons on 13 July 923. Walter himself died that same year, on 19 November, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, in the chapel of Saint Petronilla.

## Statutes of Walter

*(In Labbé, Councils, vol. IX, col. 577.)*

### I

We decree that abbots and conventual priors who neither come [apparently, “to the synod” is missing] nor excuse themselves by alleging a canonical impediment shall be suspended from entering the church for eight days and shall be subjected to the penalty established for this matter by the councils, under threat of a greater penalty if they are found guilty of such offenses in subsequent years [apparently, “let them be fined” is missing].

### II

Because serious scandals arise from the conduct of nuns, we decree concerning black nuns that they are not to receive in their houses any deposit [the text reads *dispositum*; perhaps *depositum*] from any persons except with the permission of their bishop. Above all, they must by no means allow the chests of clerics or laypeople to be deposited with them for safekeeping.

### III

Likewise, all are to eat together in the refectory and sleep in the dormitory, unless, for a just and necessary reason, the abbess specially permits otherwise.

### IV

Likewise, all the private chambers of the nuns are to be destroyed, except any that must necessarily be retained for receiving the bishop, for establishing an infirmary, or for another reason that seems just and necessary to the bishop.

### V

Likewise, nuns are under no circumstances to be permitted to go out or to spend the night outside, except for a serious reason and rarely. Abbesses are to be instructed not to permit them to leave in any other way; and if an abbess at any time permits one of them to leave for a just reason, she must instruct her to return without delay.

### VI

Suspicious and superfluous doors are to be blocked. In this matter the bishops must exercise diligence and care, both personally and through their ministers, and they must restrict the women’s ways of life and conduct, so that through their diligence the scandals presently arising from their life may be silenced.

### VII

We decree that all judges, both ordinary and delegated, restrain and control themselves from general excommunications. They are not to excommunicate persons jointly under a general sentence, unless a very grave and outrageous offense occurs.

### VIII

The chapters of secular persons, especially cathedral chapters, are to be admonished to assemble, arrange, and deliberate so that in their churches, day and night, by themselves and through the clerics of the churches, divine service may be celebrated continually and suitably, according to the number of institutions and the resources of the churches. They must apply effective diligence and care to divine service, so that the manner of conducting themselves in church, both in the choir and outside it, may be clearly and adequately corrected wherever correction is needed, within one year.

### IX

The canons and secular clerics are likewise to be admonished to observe faithfully and obediently, in their dress and in other matters, the precepts laid down in the general council.

### X

We decree that in places or priories where a conventual community customarily exists, the community is to be restored there if the resources of that church are sufficient.

### XI

Likewise, in houses or places where priories formerly existed, if the resources of the places are sufficient, monks or regular canons are to be restored there to celebrate divine service.

### XII

We admonish abbots and conventual priors to establish in the abbeys and priories subject to them as many servants, if the resources of the places suffice for this, as were accustomed to serve there. They must not demand from them a pension or rent that was not customarily demanded from them in former times, unless perhaps the bishop allows it to someone for a just reason.

### XIII

We decree that ribald clerics, especially those commonly called “of the household of Goliath,” are to be ordered by bishops, archdeacons, officials, and Christian-deans to have their hair cut or even shaved, so that no clerical tonsure remains to them—provided, however, that this is done without danger or scandal.

### XIV

Likewise, renewing once more an ancient statute of the provincial council, we order that when any land has been placed under interdict on account of the offense of the lord of the land or of the bailiffs, the interdict is not to be lifted in any way until the parish priests have been fully compensated, or security has been provided for their compensation, at the discretion and under the regulation of the person lifting the interdict, for the damages and losses inflicted upon them on account of the interdict.

## In the Year of the Lord 923: Radbod of Dol

### Letter of Radbod to King Æthelstan

*(Warthon, Anglia Sacra, vol. II, under Saint Aldhelm.)*

To the glorious and munificent king Æthelstan, in honor of the most high and indivisible Trinity and through the most excellent intercession of all the saints, I, Radbod, provost of this age, [wish] the glory of this world and the blessedness of eternity.

Let your piety, excellent King Æthelstan, whose kindness, majesty, and most devout and universally renowned praise surpass those of all the earthly kings of this age, know that, while the stability of our region still endures, your father Edward commended himself by letter to the fellowship of Saint Samson, the supreme confessor, and of Jovinian, the senior archbishop, my cousin, and his clerics. From that time until today we have poured forth unceasing prayers to Christ the King for his soul and for your salvation.

Seeing day and night that your great mercy is manifested toward us, in our psalms, Masses, and prayers, as though I and my twelve canons had fallen on our knees before you, we promise to pray to merciful God for you. And now I send you relics which we know to be dearer to you than all earthly substance: namely, the bones of Saint Senator and Saint Paternus, and of Saint Soubilion, the teacher of that same Saint Paternus, who likewise departed to Christ on the same day and at the same hour as the aforesaid Paternus.

These two saints most certainly lay in the tomb with Saint Paternus, one on his right and the other on his left; their feasts, like Paternus’s, are celebrated on 23 September. Therefore, glorious king, exalter of the holy Church, humbler of wicked heathendom, mirror of your kingdom, example of all goodness, destroyer of enemies, father of clerics, helper of the needy, lover of all saints, invoker of angels, we beseech and humbly implore you—we who, through our merits and sins, are dwelling in France amid exultation [or lamentation] and captivity—not to let the great mercy of your most fortunate generosity forget us; and from now on, whatever you deign to entrust to me, you may obtain without any delay.

## In the Year of the Lord 923: Abbo, Monk of Saint-Germain

### Abbo’s Three Books on the Parisian War

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, vol. II, p. 776.)*

### Preliminary Notice

Abbo, a Neustrasian by birth, priest [Note: The obituary of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Bouq[uet]: his deposition was on 9 March.] and monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, flourished under the kings Charles and Odo. He wrote five sermons, published by D’Achery in volume 9 of the *Spicilegium*, and the work we are now about to publish: a poem on the wars of the city of Paris against the Normans. He took part in these events not merely as a spectator but as one who, holding up the cross, encouraged the combatants amid the flames [Note: Preface; Book I, lines 25–26 and 593–597; Book II, lines 300–302].

He therefore attempted not to sing as a poet but to transmit in verse the history of the siege and the miracles performed by Saint Germain [Note: Preface]. He dedicated the book, continued to the year 896, to Gozlin the monk and to Aimoin, another monk of Saint-Germain and author of the prose edition of the *Miracles of Saint Germain*. As he himself admits, he added to it—for the sake of the Trinity—a third book on clerics, here published for the first time, and despised no more by the ancients than by more recent people.

For I found in London, in the Harleian manuscript no. 3271, not only an expanded copy of its preface, but also an Anglo-Saxon translation written on parchment in the eleventh century, a specimen of which I append [Note: Harleian manuscript 3271, parchment, eleventh century, fol. 114:

> “Here begins Abbo’s book translated into English. O cleric—O you cleric—do not remove, do not ever diminish, the double tablets, the wax boards, from your side; flee—avoid—the little hearts, the life of the slipping game; do not rejoice—do not be glad—you at the fetid, splendid sand-bier [the exact phrase is uncertain], nor at the district, nor at the lord of hell,” etc.

Fol. 117:

> “Here begins the noble prologue of the most eloquent teacher Abbo. ‘You may discover, reader,’” etc.

Fol. 117:

> “Here ends Abbo’s prologue. Here begins the book of the same teacher: ‘Cleric, never remove double wax-boards from your side,’” etc.

Fol. 119:

> “With which, cleric, you may likewise hold me with you, ask.”]

The work was written in a convoluted and at times very obscure style and required explanation in many places. Conscious of this, the author added glosses [Note: Preface], which contribute greatly both to understanding the text and to observing the customs of his age. For this reason, I have decided to retain here the much larger part of them that has until now remained unpublished, as well as the individual words that the poet wrote in the margin. For who, capable of understanding the history of that period, would omit such words as *HYRONIA* in Book II, verse 466?

Pithoeus prepared the first edition of Books I and II with the aid of a single manuscript, in *Scriptores coætanei*, volume 12. Chesnius reprinted it in *Scriptores Francici*, volume II, p. 499, and in *Scriptores Normannici*, p. 35; Jacobus Breulius at the end of Aimoin, Paris 1603, folio, p. 400; and Joannes de Bouchet in *Origins of the First and Second Lines of the Kings of the Franks*, Paris 1642, folio. Most recently, Bouquet reprinted the Pithoean edition in *Scriptores Francici*, volume VIII, p. 1 ff., although he himself complained that many words were certainly corrupted and could not be amended or restored because the manuscript witnesses were lacking.

Nevertheless, Abbo’s sole and authentic manuscript was preserved in the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, of whose congregation we know Bouquet himself to have been a member; it was later transferred to the royal library of Paris. When I therefore undertook a new edition, I resolved first of all to investigate the fate of that manuscript and examine it again with the greatest care; and, with the favor of the distinguished Guérard, I soon achieved my wish.

Pithoeus himself had indeed offered the book to the library of Saint-Germain, where it had formerly been marked with the number 535 and later with 1633. It is a small quarto parchment manuscript, written at the end of the ninth century, and consists of forty-three leaves, each normally containing twice eighteen lines.

Our work was therefore chiefly devoted to presenting the text with the greatest possible accuracy, after the model of the manuscript, publishing all glosses of any importance, and adding the third book, previously omitted, to the others. We introduced divisions that are almost never found in the manuscript and judged it appropriate to add only a very few notes necessary for illuminating the text.

## A Singular, Humble Sheet of Abbo to His Dear Brother Gozlin

*[Note: “Humble” is a gloss.]*

Abbo, the least of all God’s creatures [Note: “Forms” is a gloss.] and an unworthy fellow Levite, to his brother Gozlin, whom he embraces with the pure [Note: “Pure” is a gloss.] fire of a love surpassing [Note: “Transcending” is a gloss.] every earthly [Note: “That is, love” is a gloss.] love, sends whatever joy in Christ remains of both lives.

The affection of your exceedingly dear brotherhood has repeatedly and earnestly requested that the little book, born of my labor, concerning the wars of the Parisian city and the kingdom of the most excellent prince Odo from its origin [Note: “Origin” is a gloss], should be sent to you, eager as you are for the study of so near a little intellect [Note: “Neighboring” is a gloss.] and, moreover, mindful of a brotherly goad [Note: “Love” is a gloss.].

For that same reason, dearest brother, know with good fortune that this little page is directed to you: first, so that such a rare request may not be frustrated while it is with me [Note: The manuscript reads *peticio*, corrected to *petitio*]; and second, so that, as a consolation to every reader who is a most friendly companion, it may serve in the place of the one who sends it until the end; and, further, that it may be lifted from its deviations [Note: “Errors” is a gloss.] by your wise hand [Note: “Your” is a gloss.].

For I have never had leisure to restore it because of the multitude of schools, whose advantage I have attended to everywhere. But how [Note: “In what manner” is a gloss.] it was first brought forth is still evident on the following page, after the parchment has been altered only once [Note: The manuscript reads *simel*, corrected to *semel*]; afterward, like another Phoebus, may it be illuminated by your discerning judgment.

Finally, since the purpose of this transmission has been removed [Note: “Set forth” is a gloss.], it is considered right to disclose also the two reasons [Note: “Reasons” is a gloss.] for beginning the little work. The first reason was exercise. For at that time, still a novice in the literary [Note: “Grammatical” is a gloss.] discipline, I was cutting through [Note: “Reading for the first time” is a gloss.] the eclogues of Maro. The second [Note: “That is, reason for beginning” is a gloss.] was to provide an example for the guardians of other cities who would remain.

Furthermore, I strive to make known to your nourishing charity and that of the other readers that I have not undertaken this metrical volume in order that I may be called a poet [Note: “Named” is a gloss.]. For this work contains none of the fictions found among the greatest poets. Nowhere have I gathered Fauns or wild beasts into the play of song in the manner of Silenus [Note: The manuscript reads *silene*, corrected to *sileni*.], nor forced the rigid tops of oaks to move; forests, birds, and even walls have never accompanied my footsteps because of the sweetness of song; nor, by any melody, have I in the manner of Orpheus snatched souls from Tartarean darkness by Orcus or other shades.

Even if the desire had sometimes been present, ability nevertheless never favored such actions. Therefore I am called neither a poet [Note: “Poet” is a gloss.] nor are fictions found here; rather, let the resources of my ability be present. [Note: The manuscript reads *quidaem*, corrected to *quidem*; *mollior*, corrected to *molior*.]

Moreover, I entrusted my three books [Note: The manuscript reads *bilos*, corrected to *biblos*. Gloss: “books.”] to the Trinity, adorned only [Note: “Only” is a gloss.] for sight and hearing [Note: “Adorned” is a gloss.]. Of these, two shine with miracles—not only of the battles of the city of Paris and of King Odo, but also, and especially, of my gracious and heroic lord [Note: “Lord” is a gloss.], Germain, formerly the distinguished bishop of that same see, miracles otherwise unheard of.

The third, which completes the Trinity, is ignorant of these matters. For it most appropriately adorns the *cleronomoi* [Note: “Clerics” is a gloss.], although its setting remains narrow [Note: “Strict,” or “confined,” is a gloss.]; it also eagerly pleases schoolmen seeking glosses in its commentaries, while its allegory shines somewhat for anyone who wishes to investigate it.

Because it clings to obscure words [Note: “Obscure” is a gloss.] by itself, I have placed glosses [Note: “Glosses” is a gloss.] upon its language with my own hand. I have chosen the feet in all the verses of the little work so carefully that perhaps only very rarely, through ignorance or forgetfulness, have I left any crippled verses; but I ask that they be restored to their proper strength by the reader’s painstaking skill [Note: “Skill” is a gloss.].

The penthemimeral caesuras, or those together with the third trochee, and the hepthemimeral caesuras proceed everywhere with an accepted likeness [Note: “Example” is a gloss.], although there are very few bucolic diaereses. Moreover, I have not made frequent use of syllables excluded from ordinary patterns [Note: “Syllables” is a gloss.], together with diaeresis [Note: “Separation” is a gloss.] and episynaloepha [Note: “Conjunction” is a gloss.]; I have not used them densely [Note: “Frequently” is a gloss.].

Therefore, by divine gift, this ability has been suggested to me. What more? Every verse is catalectic. Many other serious matters [Note: “Useful” is a gloss.] will also appear inserted for the reader. Yet let no one think this was done for any other reason than to draw material either from your wisdom, sweetest brother, or from that of some other eloquent man [Note: The manuscript reads *disserti*, corrected to *diserti*.], when the metrical work comes into his hands.

The dactylic trimeter verses placed at the beginning explain [Note: “Reveal” is a gloss.] the reason for their own existence, but they have not been heard. What has not been gained from a teacher may at least deserve to be received from a brother.

> May joys and honors, like Phoebus’s rays, be yours,  
> From end to end, secretly also, with God beyond the end.

### Here Ends the Letter

## Dactylic Verses to the Teacher

> O sacred teacher, radiant  
> In pious merits, Aimoin,  
> Worthy in your starry beauty:  
> Your bowed Abbo, your pupil [Note: “Disciple” is a gloss.],  
> Wiping your feet and toes with his mouth,  
> Asks you repeatedly:  
> Receive the clusters which your vine  
> Still bears for you, green; let them redden  
> Through your rain and your rays.  
> You continually sow and dig [Note: “Teach and correct” is a gloss.];  
> You, worthy of praise, think of it,  
> And now you desire that it shine  
> Through the rains of another  
> And the light of another?  
> I beg you to grant me sweet honey.  
> For the branch and the grape remain yours.  
> These things flowered for me at Paris,  
> A noble and exceedingly venerable city,  
> Asking you to bear its wars.  
> Once its renown is recognized  
> Throughout the wandering world,  
> May its flying palm enclose the heavens [Note: “Fill” is a gloss.],  
> And may its fame reign everywhere, shining  
> As it advances above through your mouth.

## Here Begins Book One of the Wars of the City of Paris

> Tell, lively Lutetia, saved by the supreme God—  
> Thus once called, now you bear the name of a city—  
> Isia, set amid the broad region of the Danaans,  
> Which shines through a harbor more venerable than all others.  
> This exceedingly greedy Argive thirst for riches  
> Celebrates you, because, by a novel transformation of form,  
> The name of another shape [*metaplasm*] now honorably marks you,  
> O companion Lutetia, by your name;  
> And you, Paris, are called by a new name throughout the world,  
> As though Isia’s equal companion, possessing the same merit.  
> For lying in the midst of the Seine,  
> And of the cultivated kingdom of the Frankish people,  
> You establish yourself in lofty places by singing:  
> “I am the city, shining like a queen above all cities!”  
> You shine from your harbor [Note: “From the port” is a gloss.]  
> More venerably than all harbors [Note: “Harbors” is a gloss.].  
> Everyone who desires the wealth of the Franks venerates you.  
> The island rejoices in you; the river offers its circuit to you,  
> Its arms embracing the walls and soothing them all around.  
> On your right, the waters inhabit tents beside the bridges,  
> And on your left they close them [Note: “That is, the bridges” is a gloss.].  
> On either side, before the city, watchtowers [Note: “Towers” is a gloss.] look out,  
> And likewise beyond the river [Note: “On the far side” is a gloss.].
>
> Tell us, therefore, most beautiful city, what gift  
> The friendly offspring of Pluto, the Danish [Note: “That is, Danish, Norman” is a gloss.] people,  
> Offered you at the time when the bishop of the Lord,  
> The sweetest hero Gozlin, both shepherd and kind protector,  
> Nourished you.
>
> “Can anyone,” someone may say, “recount these things?  
> Did you not see them with your own eyes? Then tell them!”
>
> “Indeed I saw it,” [Note: The poet’s voice.] “and I shall gladly obey your commands.  
> These offerings the savage men sacrificed to you:  
> Seven hundred airy ships, besides many more  
> Whose number cannot be counted;  
> The common people call them *barcas* [Note: “To call, name” is a gloss.].  
> So swollen was the deep channel of the Seine  
> As they fled for more than two leagues and a little beyond,  
> That you would marvel into what cavern the river might withdraw,  
> Leaving nothing behind. For firs had covered it,  
> And oak and elm together, as well as wet alders  
> [Note: For the ships were constructed from these trees.]
>
> “When on the second day [Note: “Day” is a gloss.] they reached the city  
> (885), the excellent Sigefredus approached the hall  
> Of the shepherd. Though a king only in word [Note: Since he lacked a kingdom, he was king only in name.],  
> He commanded his companions. With bowed head  
> He addressed the bishop and began:
>
> “‘O Gozlin, have pity on yourself and your flocks.  
> We beg you: lest you perish, favor our words.  
> Grant us merely that we may cross  
> This city. We shall never touch it,  
> But we shall strive to preserve your honors,  
> And all those of Odo.’
>
> “This count [Note: “That is, count.”], revered as a future king,  
> Was the city’s protector and the coming nourisher of the kingdom.”
>
> In reply, the bishop of the Lord uttered these most faithful words:

“The city was entrusted by us to Charles, the basileus [Note: that is, king],

by whose authority almost the whole cosmos [Note: that is, world] is governed,

after the Lord, the king and ruler of the powerful—

not so that the kingdom might suffer destruction through it,

but so that through it it might be saved and remain secure.

If, perchance, the walls had been entrusted to you

as they have now been entrusted to us,

and you had done what you say is right for you,

what would you decree should happen?”

Sigemfredus replied: “My head, honored by the sword,

and finally worthy even of the dogs.

But if you do not yield to these appeals,

our strongholds will furnish you with poisoned weapons

when the appointed day comes,

when the plague of hunger departs [Note: specifically, the twentieth day],

and each year they will accomplish this.”

He said this, and then departed and gathered his companions.

Thus Dawn snatched away the head as the combat was lost.

All rush toward the tower in boats,

which they strike fiercely with slings and fill with arrows.

The city resounds, the citizens tremble, and the bridges shake;

everyone runs together and increases the assistance given to the tower.

Here the counts Odo, his brother Rotbert,

and likewise Count Ragenarius shone;

there stood Ebolus, the pontiff’s nephew [Note: Gozlin’s nephew on his sister’s side], a most courageous abbot.

Here the bishop was lightly touched by a sharp spear [Note: that is, wounded];

there his young soldier Fredericus,

a soldier, was struck by a similar sword [Note: namely, as the gloss specifies].

The soldier died, while the elder

[Col. 0727C] recovered, God’s medicine healing him.

Here many were deprived of life, but they inflict wounds

on still more, and at last withdraw,

bringing many lifeless Danes with them.

Already the sun, having followed Apollo of the southern climate

to the farthest limits of Thule [Note: that is, Thule],

was inclining toward the world’s western extremity.

As yet the tower showed nothing of its completed form;

only its foundations had been solidly built,

its walls raised a little, and its windows made.

But on that same night, after the battle,

it grew higher with boards laid around it;

for an additional wooden structure, half again as large,

was placed upon the fortress.

Thus the sun and the Danes together salute the tower again.

They hurl enormous weapons against the faithful [Note: that is, the Christians];

javelins fly here and there, and blood falls through the air.

Slings and battered ballistae are mingled with them;

[Col. 0728A] nothing else flew between earth and heaven.

But at night the tower groans, pierced by darts—

for night was its mother, as I sang above—

the city trembles, the citizens shout, and trumpets [Note: horns] call,

without delay, for everyone to come to the trembling tower.

The Christians fight and strive to withstand the battle.

Among all the warriors two shone,

stronger than the rest: one a count, the other an abbot.

The one was victorious Odo, unconquered in every battle;

by encouraging the weary he restored their strength,

and continually patrolled the tower, killing the enemy.

But for those who wished to cut down the wall with “mice” [Note: iron tools; a musculus is an instrument with which walls are pierced, and hence it is called, as it were, a little wall; it is made like a tunnel],

he supplied oil, wax, and pitch,

mixed together, melted, and made very hot over the fire.

These burned and tore the Danes’ hair from their heads.

[Col. 0728B] Some they killed, while others they persuaded

to approach the river’s fords. Our men shouted this together:

“Burned men of the Seine, run to the sea,

where, by giving back your manes, you may restore them more neatly!”

The mighty Odo struck down countless men. But who was the other?

His companion was Ebolus, equal to him and matching him.

With a single arrow he could pierce seven men,

while, laughing, he ordered the others to be supplied for the kitchen [Note: that is, *coquinae*].

Of these two, neither was first, middle, or anywhere behind the other [Note: namely, the two glosses refer to these two];

but the others fought bravely, scorning death [Note: *spraeta* corrected to *spreta*].

Yet what is a single drop beside a thousand conflagrations?

A double P [Note: if the Greek letter P is doubled, it signifies CC, since a single one signifies C] sustained the faithful [Note: the faithful],

though they were few [Note: it sustained and encouraged them];

and afterward the fierce M [Note: likewise, the Greek M signifies XL; *chile* signifies a thousand; there were so many Normans, namely forty thousand],

the thousand—forty thousand [Note: XL]—

the thousand [Note: I, that is, one thousand]—that is what it amounts to [Note: that is, “it stands for”]—

These men now come in relays to the tower;

they renew the foul [Note: ugly] battle continuously [Note: continuously].

[Col. 0728C] The clamor and uproar grow loud,

and the enormous voices of those rushing from every side

fill the air; stones resound as they strike painted shields,

shields groan, and helmets ring as arrows pass through them.

Here the mounted men return with booty and crowd the fighting.

They approach the tower unharmed and well-fed,

and before many longboats [Note: ships] return,

they hurl stones and burden the tower with their stoning.

They say that Danish women spoke thus to men still drawing sweet breath [Note: soul], each tearing her hair and weeping for her husband:

“From where do you come? Are you fleeing from the furnace [Note: they called the tower a furnace]? I know you, son of the devil.

No victory of yours will be able to overcome this?

Have I not now sacrificed Ceres, boars, and Bacchus to you?

[Col. 0728D] Why do you return so quickly to the shelter of your bed?

Are these things to be set before you again? When you return,

[Col. 0729A] shall I pour them out, as others do? May they deserve a similar honor!”

Because of the tower’s low height [Note: its size],

the furnace, bent [Note: curved, or spreading] around it,

poured out its savage fire through the openings, though the name was lowly.

Then they began to split open its base with saws [Note: that is, *sciri*, “to know”; the reading is obscure]:

behold, a huge gaping opening, even greater than words can express!

Inside, the nobles suddenly appear, already summoned by name,

and they see them all crested [Note: helmeted];

they look upon each man individually, though none enters.

For horror prevented what courage did not undertake.

Soon a smooth wheel [Note: wheel] is hurled from the tower against them.

It sent six times two souls to Avernus [Note: so the gloss reads],

and those dragged away by the feet complete the number of the dead.

Then they placed a hearth [Note: fire] at the doors, with Vulcan’s care [Note: namely, the fire that is Vulcan’s].

[Col. 0729B] From there they sought to punish the men who hoped [Note: *rentes*, “hoping”]

and to destroy the tower.

A dreadful pyre is made, and from it a most horrible smoke

mingles clouds with the soldiers and advances with the shadows,

like pitch-black arches [Note: so the text reads], as though the hour were prolonged.

For the tower could not at all endure for long those whom it already knew,

but our Lord, taking pity, ordered it to change

into the blind lot of a people generating fog.

That furious Mars strove to reign more powerfully [Note: he endeavored to do so].

Behold, a double standard-bearer comes from the kindly city [Note: Paris],

carrying two lances; he climbs the tower,

and the yellow garment of terror to the Danes is visible

from his enormous ears.

Then he struck down a hundred, whose life he drove out

with a hundred arrows [Note: *catapulta*, “arrow”], exceedingly swift from the body,

and the boats led by their hair [Note: so the gloss indicates] return to their shelter.

[Col. 0729C] Here the Lemnian dies crippled,

while great Neptune prevails;

the waters poured out moisten the fires.

A soldier of the pestilential race is struck by a bitter blow.

The fortunate Rotbert breathed his last there from a spear,

and a few others perished, with God commonly giving assistance.

Yet afterward, like a bold wolf,

they blushed at having taken no booty.

He indeed returns to the deep forest,

and they carried back with them a very subtle little flight [the reading is uncertain].

Three hundred lifeless men, weeping, received by Charon,

with night accompanying them [Note: following them],

the tower strove to heal its wound.

These two battles, with its chariot resting at the boundary [Note: end],

occurred before November came,

cold, to complete December,

three days before it cut off [Note: gave] the end of the year.

[Col. 0729D] While the sun pours its golden rays beneath the sky,

on Dionysius’ day [Note: that is, the heathens],

they indeed survey the resting places

of Macharius [Note: holy], on the banks of the Seine,

and strive to construct a camp around blessed Germanus

in the rounded valley [Note: Saint-Germain d’Auxerre; “rounded” in shape],

working with a mixed heap of stones and clods.

After the mountains and fields, the forests [Note: woods],

the open plains, and the villages,

the mounted men [Note: Normans] and bloodstained foot soldiers roam through them,

killing infants, children, young men, and gray-haired old age,

fathers and sons, and mothers as well.

Before a wife’s eyes they gave her husband the slaughter;

before a husband’s eyes the woman tasted carnage;

before the face of parents, offspring, and before mothers, their children!

The free man is made a slave, and the slave likewise a free man;

the household servant [Note: servant] becomes a master,

and conversely the master becomes a servant.

The vine-dresser and the farmers, together with all the vines,

[Col. 0730B] and the earth itself, bear the cruel reins of death.

France, now left both to masters and to servants, grieves;

it rejoiced under no hero [Note: Lord] and is drenched in tears.

No stable household is governed by a living ruler.

The rich land is stripped of its abundant treasures

by blood-gushing, torn, black, devouring [Note: consuming],

equal [Note: equally distributed] wounds, plunder, slaughter, flames, and mutilation.

The dreadful cohort, the deadly phalanx, and the grim host

overthrow, strip, kill, burn, and ravage.

Power favored them at once, and they carried themselves

as though everything had been seen before them, already bloodied.

The humble valleys flee far away; then the proud men [Note: proud people] flee the Alps,

and at the same time they love weapons [Note: they love them greatly],

along with the groves, with fearful hearts.

No one is visible; everyone flees—alas! no one resists.

[Col. 0730C] Thus, as far as their power allowed, they carried away

the beauty of the handsome kingdom;

thus they bear away in their ships the ornament [Note: glory] of the famous region!

Yet amid the terrible battle-lines, an undertaking stood firm:

Paris, laughing, unafraid, stood in the midst of such things.

Therefore they make sixteen [Note: sixteen carts with sixty wheels, capable of carrying sixty men]—

a marvelous sight [Note: work]—

monsters unknown to wheels, joined in a triad of measurements [Note: a measure joined to the Trinity],

of enormous oak [Note: oak], and upon each a ram [Note: that is, a battering ram] lying

beneath a lofty, covered roof.

For the enclosed spaces, the secret recesses of that ram’s womb [Note: namely, of the ram],

held sixty helmeted men, so rumor says.

They had one form, sufficiently ample in size.

When two had been completed and the third was in progress [Note: that is, while the third was under construction],

a *falarica* [Note: ballista] was artfully dispatched [Note: through an artful device]

to strike [Note: strike] the tower [Note: tower],

[Col. 0730D] having shot two craftsmen [Note: masters] with one bowstring apiece.

Thus they earned for us a prepared death [Note: that is, death];

then, with the monad [Note: unity of the blow] killed,

the most savage duality [Note: the Norman pair] perished.

[Col. 0731A] They also construct a thousand tents on high supports,

made from hides stripped from the necks and backs of young cattle.

They could shelter [Note: cover] two, four, or three men [Note: three],

and these tents [Note: tents] the Latin calls *plutei*

[Note: *plutei* are barriers woven from raw hide, set before the enemy],

or leather-covered hurdles [Note: leather-covered].

Night receives neither rest nor sleep.

They sharpen, repair, and forge arrows;

they prepare shields, and make new ones from old.

When the light of old Phoebus already climbs

into his swift, life-giving chariot,

and the rising sun lowers its eyes upon the city,

behold, Satan’s offspring suddenly burst from their raging camp,

overloaded with weapons for the terrified.

They hurry to the tower, as slender bees approach their own kingdoms,

laden on their outspread shoulders with cassia and thyme

[Col. 0731B] and, together, with the flowers of pleasant fields.

So likewise the wretched people press toward the fortress,

their shoulders beneath bent arches [Note: bows],

and iron trembling in their hands.

They cover the fields with swords, the Seine with shields,

and a thousand leaden projectiles fly thickly into the city;

with powerful catapults they sow the bridges and the tower.

Mars rages, rising on every side, and reigns proudly.

The curved [Note: bent] metal of the whole church [Note: bells]

roars, and fills the empty air with mournful clangs.

The fortress sways, the citizens tremble, and the great sound of trumpets

resounds; fear enters everyone, together with the towers.

Here many nobles and strong men resisted.

Bishop Gozlinus was foremost above them all;

with him was his nephew Ebolus, a martial abbot;

here were Rothbertus, Oddo, Ragenarius, Utto, and Erilangus.

[Col. 0731C] All these were counts, but Odo was nobler,

for he killed as many Danes as he sent arrows [Note: arrows].

The unhappy people fight, and the kindly people battle.

The fierce man armed three wedges, which he brought against the fortress:

the larger one against the painted bridge [Note: with a painted bridge],

and two paired wedges [Note: wedges] against the ship [Note: vessel],

thinking that they could overcome this [Note: the tower], if they could overcome that [Note: the arrows].

The tower suffers this warfare, but that man suffers much greater things.

The former groans, reddened beneath wounds of many colors;

the latter mourns the men, their strength, and their flowing deaths.

No road through the city remains untouched by the blood of men.

Looking out from the tower, he sees nothing beneath him

except painted shields; the earth was hidden beneath them.

Then, looking above, he saw harsh stones

and dreadful, dense as bees, swimming arrows [Note: this line was later deleted].

[Col. 0731D] [Jupiter, looking down, saw sharp darts.] [Note: “son,” according to the gloss.]

The air measures nothing between them and the tower but itself.

The voice is immense, the fear greater still, and the uproar grows loud.

These fight, those battle; with weapons resounding,

the Normans sharpen their truly cruel warfare.

No one born upon earth could have enough life

[Col. 0732A] to look upon so many infantrymen clothed in swords gathered together,

and to marvel at such a painted tortoise-formation.

With this formation they fashioned for themselves the sky that nourished life

[Note: that is, protected them],

which none of their heads wished to surpass,

while beneath it they often receive the weapons of dreadful death.

A thousand fought together, standing in the struggle;

a thousand at once, since they could not all reach the tower

at the same time, strove to fight in companies.

Watching the fortress, because the enemy was bare-armed [Note: bare-armed],

the people renew the contest with open mouths

and turn their raised yew bows [Note: the reading has *inos*] into hooks

[Note: that is, they stretched bows that were not strung];

from one side an arrow is sent into an open mouth.

Another, suddenly trying to cover [Note: shield] the one moving,

indeed tastes the food which the first had drawn into his mouth [Note: pulled in].

But as another arrives to complete the blessed number [Note: the Trinity],

[Col. 0732B] he tries secretly to remove these two,

and, struck by a quiver, also asks pardon from the tower.

Others hide them beneath a shield and drag them away,

whereupon, growing extremely fierce, they renewed the battle.

Shields raise laments when struck by stones;

the helmets that receive them vomit bloodstained cries into the air;

the cruel sword pierces the corselet.

The Almighty, looking back upon his own limbs and structures that the Danes were beginning somewhat to overcome,

and displayed to our men strength and courageous spirits,

while he imparted to them a sense of trembling.

Then the wretched men perish, and more are carried away to the heights,

placing their souls in the arms [Note: ships] that torment them.

Now Titan hastens to send his swift steeds on ahead to Ocean, that he may provide them with beds and grant them rest [Note: rest].

[Col. 0732C] The grim crowd, whose tents I have already sung,

brought woven cloth from the woods, with slaughtered young cattle.

Some passed the night in battle, others in sleep,

while they made paths around them [Note: arranged them];

they brandished feathered battle-lines [Note: arrows]

dripping with gall [Note: to be brandished],

while the soldiers watched the excellent fortress by night [Note: guarded it].

In the morning, with the light burning, they renew the battles,

with full weapons fixed in a circle around the savage earth, forming a tortoise.

Many others were striving to work at the ditches

that lie around that tower [Note: tower] and to fill the furrows.

From here they brought clods from the earth and leafy branches of the woods,

and also crops deprived of their own yield,

as well as meadows, shrubs, and vines without buds.

From here they brought old bulls, beautiful oxen, and calves,

and finally killed the young deer [Note: the reading is uncertain]

which they had kept captive, carrying all these things

through hollow furrows, and spent the entire day standing in the struggle.

Seeing this, the devout bishop, weeping, calls out

in a clear voice to the mother of the Lord and Savior:

“Blessed mother of the Redeemer and salvation of the world,

shining Star of the Sea, brighter than all the splendid stars,

[Col. 0733A] mercifully incline your ears to the prayers of those who plead with you.

If you should ever be pleased to celebrate Masses for me,

may the impious, fierce, savage, and cruel man,

who kills captives, be caught in the snare of death!”

The bishop Gozlinus, suddenly casting a weapon down from the fortress,

strove to bring upon that man what he prayed for in tears

[Note: the Norman],

who had delivered captives, themselves bound, to the reins of death,

and, wretched, extended his shield and foot toward his companions.

He opened his mouth, fell by his own strength,

and filled the furrows, measuring the earth,

breathing out his ill-born soul,

beside the captives whom his sword had brutally mutilated.

The city shines in honor, consecrated to exalted Mary,

through whose aid we now enjoy life in safety.

Therefore, if we are able, let us render her unutterable thanks

and echo peaceful hymns;

let a lofty voice resound and sing praises, because she is worthy:

“Hail, beautiful mother of the Lord, queen of the heavens;

our radiant nurse, you stand as ruler of the world.

You deemed it worthy to free the people of Paris

from the savage hands of the Dane and his threatening sword,

and you were fully able to bring salvation to Paris,

you who bore the Savior in the unstable cosmos.

The heavenly host, virtues and dominions,

principalities, powers, and thrones of heaven,

O mother worthy to be celebrated, mother of the offspring of the highest King,

rejoice in you, remember you, praise you, venerate you, and adore you.

O blessed mother, who were able to enclose in the chamber of your womb

him whom neither the heavens, nor the earth, nor the vast sea can contain;

and, chosen, you bore your own Father for us.

You poured forth upon the earth a shining Moon, far more resplendent than the sun,

and, remaining full of him,

by illuminating it you restored our fallen race.

Therefore, O queen of heaven, to whom can I compare you?

You are holier than all and more blessed than every woman.

Have pity on your worshiper, child now born of the Mighty One.

Glory, praise, honor, and radiant splendor be yours forever;

blessed be the Mother of God, bearing the scepter in Jesus.”

(At the edge of the codex is written: “DIAERESIS.”)

Phoebus departs, and the calm darkness of night returns.

The tower is surrounded by abundant [Note: plentiful] and wicked watchmen [Note: the Normans].

As dawn revolves around the poles, the fortresses too revolve.

Since deadly weapons are striking them,

they assemble battering rams [Note: move them],

placing one from the east against the tower;

the high north watches another at the gates.

Opposite its side it held another, seated in a threefold arrangement [the text is obscure].

[Col. 0733D] With great weight our men prepare beams,

whose dense upper surface a cable passes through,

so that the machine might pierce the Dane more quickly.

They construct, likewise, with long doubled timbers,

the machines commonly called *mangana*,

with which they hurl enormous stones;

or, by hurling them,

they strike the low structures [Note: sheds] of the savage people.

Often indeed they drag the clever neck [Note: the reading is uncertain] of young deer,

[Col. 0734A] alas! and crush many Danes, as well as more shields [Note: shields].

No shield was immune [Note: unharmed] to a blow that shattered it,

and no miserable man whom such a blow touched

was free from death [Note: the gloss says that the shield was immune].

But the unfortunate phalanxes strive in vain to fill the pits,

and were unable to fill even one.

For they were trying to overthrow the tower with battering rams.

Since they could not bring them down across level ground,

they seized three boats [Note: ships], sufficiently high,

and strove to load them with leafy woods blazing with fire;

at last Vulcan, burning, was placed upon them.

The rising sun slowly sends them forth,

and they themselves were dragged by ropes [Note: cords] along the banks

to the bridge, or to burn the conspicuous tower.

The forest vomits flames, the waters and the sea-waves dry up,

[Col. 0734B] the earth groans, and the green grasses die from the fire.

Lemnius, powerful over Neptune, stands with a worn-out foot [Note: a crushed foot];

the dark one penetrates the realms of heaven and passes through the clouds.

From here earth, field, waters, and sky are set ablaze.

The city grieves, the towers fear, and the walls mourn.

Alas, how great the tearful rivers pour forth

before blessed eyes!

Beautiful young men give them, as does white-haired old age,

lamenting groans;

mothers, tearing their hair, beat their dry backs

and roll their hair across the fields—

these women, stripped of their garments, now beat their breasts.

Others have cut their cheeks, wet with tears.

Then the citizens tremble, and all call upon the celebrated Germanus:

“Germanus, have pity on your wretched people!”

Once the most holy bishop of Paris had been

he whose venerable body illumined it—

[Col. 0734C] the walls repeat the name of Germanus,

and every soldier in the tower cries out, together with the foremost men:

“O Germanus, learn to come to the aid of your servants!”

The shore of the liquid water [Note: that is, of the Seine] calls the deep sea;

the heavenly thrones, on which he shines like nourishing light,

are struck by innumerable cries, with echo accompanying the uproar.

The city answers Germanus and calls upon him.

Mothers, young men, and girls alike

run to the tomb of the saint to seek his gracious intercession.

Because of this, the unhappy people experienced immense joy,

mocking the citizens and the company of the Lord.

They struck their shields with blows,

filled with wicked laughter;

their throats swelled and widened with shrill uproar,

and while the townspeople lamented,

the air was filled with a great sound,

with a cry no less immense.

A voice is heard in the heights, and grief in the heavens!

[Col. 0734D] But almighty God, restorer of all creation,

the world’s repairer, comes when summoned by the saint’s prayers;

and you yourself, O Germanus, come to aid the humble people.

By leaping upon the high heap of stones,

you forced the fire-breathing ships

to avoid striking the bridge;

you yourself compelled them, and that embankment supports the bridge.

At once the Lord’s people descend into the fires,

[Col. 0735A] and, plunging them into the waters, seize the ships as victors.

From this the blessed company of God gained joyful celebration,

whereas before it had uttered great groans and pains.

Thus it goes for our people, and the day of battle withdraws;

night entrusts the tower itself to foolish [Note: inept, stupid] guards.

Before the sun enters its still-unbright chariot,

under the light they secretly return their hurdles to their own camp,

and the battering rams, commonly called *carcamusae*,

but they left two behind; the removal of the *pallos* was forbidden.

Our men seize these and joyfully strip them.

And Sigenfredus, king over all the Danes,

withdrew the Danes whom the tower feared

would tear out its own eyes [Note: doors].

Thus, with God’s help, harsh Mars came to rest.

(At the edge of the codex: “EPISINALIFFA.”)

[Col. 0735B] The final day of January established a three-day period,

and the following month strove to bring these contests to an end.

The third day of that month was the holy Purification

of the revered Mother of Christ,

which granted our people joy in triumph.

(Year 886.) Moreover, the unfortunate band mounts horses slower than birds,

returning toward the eastern regions,

which grieving France still possessed, not yet ravaged.

After killing everything previously spared,

they seek the huts [Note: houses] belonging to Rotbertus,

famous by the surname “Farettratus.”

He was now the only soldier in attendance,

and a single house held them.

The soldier said to his elder:

“I see the Normans coming swiftly!”

Rotbertus, wishing to take up his shield [Note: receive it],

saw nothing, because his own people had carried it away.

He nevertheless went to meet them in the open place with drawn sword.

Of them he killed two, and he himself, as the third,

fell into death, with no one coming to his aid.

Therefore his nephew Adalaelmus, grieving greatly,

stood among the count’s [Note: earl’s] people and said to them:

“Come, brave men, take up shields and weapons,

and let us hasten to avenge my uncle!”

Having said this, he went to the village;

there, in fierce encounters, he immediately defeated and slaughtered the wicked men,

filling the village with dead Normans as victor.

Because flight prevented them, they carried nothing remaining

back to the ship [Note: vessel].

Rotbertus had been striving to do the same thing.

After resting beside the plain [Note: meadow], near the blessed white [Note: beautiful] hall,

[Col. 0735D] they frequently attempt to climb to Germanus,

who is repeatedly invoked,

where his tomb is known to shine in its appearance.

Here his venerable body continually lay,

and that monastery was nobler than all others,

which Neustria was learning to cherish in its broad bosom.

[Col. 0736A] From there he would be carried into the city by his own servants.

He himself [Note: the saint], whenever the Danes left their tracks in the meadow,

while the soldiers watched the tower [Note: guarded it] of the city

standing in his countryside,

immediately delivered them to be captured.

When one of them entered his church [Note: the saint’s church]

to tear apart the windows,

striking the glass with a wooden weapon,

he was immediately confused by mad fury,

bound to the black chariots of the Furies [Note: joined to them]

by the blessed one [Note: Saint Germanus];

and death, following the wretched man, destroyed him,

with mercy removed.

Exhausted by these punishments, he went to the underworld.

Holy Germanus, take care that my spirit

does not one day enter that place whose miracles I sing.

I beg you, blessed one, favor me also

so that I may complete these things.

At the Father’s and the Son’s bidding, may the dove [Note: the Holy Spirit]

sit upon my lips and fill my mind,

[Col. 0736B] O gracious Lord,

and adorn it with sacred acts and flowers of virtues,

driving far away dark vices by means of the sacred *sestrice* [Note: an obscure word; it appears to be a feminine form—because of “sacred dove”—expressing the third person of the Godhead, that is, the Holy Spirit].

Another man, climbing to the lofty summit of the little tower,

changes the path by which he ascended

and turns his steps across the exceedingly steep heights

of the lofty temple.

The sacred roof’s summit broke his bones,

compelled by the merits of Germanus.

Standing above the city’s walls [Note: walls],

the future king [Note: future king] Odo revealed this to all the crowd

gathered around him, pointing it out with his finger.

He himself reported that he had seen the Dane falling.

A third man, arriving, turned his eyes toward the broad

mausoleum of the saint,

unwilling to leave those whom he had left there.

[Col. 0736C] When a fourth entered it,

he was taken away from the upper air

and soon fell silent, sunk in sleep beneath his fate.

The fortunate fifth hastens, Germanus,

to open the bed of your parent;

but, when the first had been removed,

he then strikes his own chest with a stone,

forcing the suffering soul to depart from the body,

the disease unwillingly touching the thresholds

of the dark abyss.

The right hand preserves the illustrious father of holy offspring;

the left holds the sacred mother of offspring.

The father is Eleutherius; the mother is Eusebia.

Alas! Behold, the middle of the bridge fell in the silent night,

covered with alluvial mud, while swollen waters raged [Note: ran].

For the Seine, spreading widely, poured its realm around,

and with its waters [Note: waters] covered the fields and open spaces.

The southern height supported it [Note: the bridge],

and also the fortress

[Col. 0736D] founded on the earth of the holy one who was loudly invoked [Note: the text is so distinctly marked in the codex; perhaps it means “of the invoked saint”; Pithou conjectures that *beati* should be read].

The bridge and the tower clung to the city’s right side [Note: the gloss says “bridge and tower”],

one [Note: the bridge] to the other [Note: the tower].

In the morning, as it rose, the Danes likewise rise fiercely,

board their ships, and load them with weapons and shields.

[Col. 0737A] They swim across the Seine, surround the wretched tower,

and launch many battles against it with dense weapons.

The city trembles, horns [Note: trumpets] roar,

the walls are drenched with tears,

the whole countryside groans, and the sea roars back.

Stones and arrows circle through the air in confusion.

Our men cry out, and all the Danes shout at the same time.

The earth trembles; our men mourn, while those others rejoice.

Although they wish to help the tower,

the citizens are unable to come to its aid

or bring assistance to the men gasping in battle,

whom the Dane’s sword or fear of the weapon never terrified,

though they fought in a number below twelve.

It is difficult to tell the battle, but the names [Note: of the combatants] are given:

Ermemfredus, Eriveus, Erilandus, Odaucer,

[Col. 0737B] Ervic, Arnoldus, Solius, Gozbertus, Uvido,

Ardradus, and likewise Eimardus and Gozsuinus.

Several joined themselves to death among the enemy

[Note: because they killed thirty].

These men [Note: twelve], since their grim spirits could not be bent,

set before the fortress doors a cart filled with dry grass,

before the doors of the wretched fools [Note: stupid Normans].

And just as fields are confused by lightning-bearing storms beneath Phoebus,

the high night, empty of the sky’s beauty [Note: splendor],

is thrown into confusion.

It is permitted for no one to scorn his own house [Note: home] with a smiling face [Note: in lawful fashion]—

the text is difficult here—

and likewise smoke concealed the tower from the catapults,

which were for a while plunged into roaring heat [Note: fire].

Each of the twelve [Note: one of the twelve] released its own fiery breath,

like hawks set free from loosened thongs,

lest they perish in the disaster.

When they now all wish to extinguish the pyre [Note: fire],

they lack vessels with which to draw the flowing water.

For they feared that no Dane would dare

to touch the waters with his foot

of the Confessor, whose miracles had already been revealed [Note: the wording is corrupt; “for this reason,” according to the gloss].

They retain only a flask that was by no means small,

which, when thrown to the clear fires high above the Seine,

slips from the fingers of the servants and falls beneath the fires [Note: the gloss refers to the fires].

Neptune perished, weaponless, beside the lame Vulcan.

The hearth [Note: fire] leapt over the tower and crushed everything.

The timbers groan together, oppressed beneath the fire,

the pyre dominating the battle even more.

The tower is abandoned to the soldiers,

who enter the remaining extremity of the bridge.

They establish new and savage battles there,

until Phoebus bent his head toward the deep waters of Ocean.

[Col. 0737D] The enemy people, who were about to dine

in Pluto’s urn [Note: pot],

hurled javelins, stones, and swift arrows.

But because they could not overcome such a conflict

[Note: the twelve who were in the tower],

they cried out to the soldiers [Note: twelve]:

“Your faith has been accepted, though it is empty;

men, hurry to our side; do not be afraid!”

Alas! They foolishly trusted these falsely fashioned speeches,

hoping that they could be redeemed for a large price.

Otherwise they would not have been captured in that daylight.

Alas! Unarmed, they meet the sword of the savage people

and send their souls to heaven with flowing blood [Note: blood].

They receive the palm of martyrdom and the precious crown.

Soon, when Erveus appeared to the remaining men [Note: his equals],

he was believed to be a king,

because he shone in face and was handsome in form [Note: “for he was,” according to the gloss],

and, as the plunderer raged, he protected his own men with gifts [the text is uncertain].

Immediately, when he saw his beloved companions

being struck down [Note: beheaded],

he himself raged like a lion at the sight of blood,

and, attempting to escape the hands of those holding him,”

Source preparation: One embedded Greek reading was recovered from the supplied local archive and translated as part of this section.

Pressed on every side, as though compelled, he wished to take up arms and avenge his own wound and the wound of his allies [Col. 0737: *ad ulciscendum*, “for avenging”]. Lacking even this pretext, he nevertheless thundered into their ears in an unconquered voice:

“Release me with neck outstretched; [Col. 0738B] let no money at all purchase my life while these men are dying!

Why do you allow me to live? Your desire is frustrated!

The light was not his; rather, the following day shone by his breath.”

What voice, what tongue, what mouth could recount so many wars undertaken in the field by these outstanding men [Col. 0737: *ab his*, “by these men”; German gloss of the sixteenth century], or tell how many Normans they killed here, and how many living men they led away with them? Then none of them dared climb the broad field of the Saint.

I bring forth the battles of those men who, amid terror, surrendered their lifeless bodies to the cruel Seine. Their praise and name will continually fly through the mouths of men, and their distinguished deaths and wars will likewise be celebrated until the sun learns to parade the darkness of night with its rays [Col. 0737: “learn”], and the moon and stars alike learn to arrange the day.

[Col. 0738C] Then they overthrow the watchtower, grieving for the death of its guards. The Danish standard-bearer fell beneath the striking weapon; he sent his limbs and breath to Charon.

Let no one rise up against my words to wage war on this matter; for no one can produce anything more truthful, since I drank it in with my own eyes. Thus also the man who himself was present reported it to us—he had been able to escape the savage swords by swimming.

Then they leap across the Seine, make for the Loire and their homeland, and travel between these two rivers, seizing booty that the region itself will disclose at my command as its ruler.

Meanwhile Ebolus, the strongest abbot, hoping that all the pagans had entered this place, almost alone rushed upon the fortress [Col. 0737: “he fell by a leap”], carrying a spear, and attacked their fortifications, hurling his lance at them. No horse carried this weapon back to us, nor brought it there.

[Col. 0738D] Immediately, relying on the protection of his companion, he attacks the savage camp and strikes the walls. He orders Lemnius himself to come there. Our men fight, and fight the more resolutely. An exceedingly loud din [Col. 0737: “a resonant sound”] already rises from them; they leap outside and drive away the common people without touching them, since there had been more of them than of us. [Col. 0739A] Yet Ebolus, together with his companions, stood there as a hero to meet them.

They had not dared touch him with iron. Even if he had then been supported by five hundred men, he would have thrown himself into the camp and driven all their lives from their proper dwelling. But because he lacked soldiers, he ceased this sport.

O Neustria, nobler than all the regions of the world, you who had once been the mother of mighty ruling nobles, do not hesitate, I beg you, to bring forth from the captured tower how many palms, and of what kind, the Danes took from you; nor how many udders of cattle they milked as they traversed your once-expanded tract, still swollen with varied riches [Col. 0739: “which once was full of wealth”].

*(At the margin of the manuscript: VOX NUSTRIAE, “Voice of Neustria.”)*

Can anyone reckon my offspring [Col. 0739: “For this poet was a native of Neustria”]? [Col. 0739B] Even if all the birds were present, they could not utter as many voices as there were men, horses, sheep, and cattle whose sons and daughters, and their own young, they stole from me [Col. 0739: “they robbed”].

My rivers resound with the bleating of lambs; my joyful meadows and fields echo with the dense lowing of young cattle [Col. 0739: “they were echoing”]; the woodland of the deer answers with a hoarse cry; and the grunting of my boars split the forests.

These savage men took them from me—if you recognize and hear me! I beheld these things with my own eyes, standing above the city walls; neither sight nor number [Col. 0739: “number”] could encompass them.

But since they cannot be enclosed within meadows or kept away from the fields, the courtyard of the German bishop is made into a cattle-yard. [Col. 0740A] It is filled with bulls, calves [Col. 0739: “young cattle”], and deformed goats.

There they draw out long sighs and open their mouths [Col. 0739: “they gape”]; their bodies breathe sweet winds [Col. 0739: “breaths”] amid agonizing pain.

The stablemen [Col. 0739: “Norman”] arrive to carry them to the kitchen, while the banquets already remain swarming with countless worms and the church is filled with their stench. They carry them out [Col. 0739: “outside the church”] and convey those animals to the Seine [Col. 0739: “those animals”], not to the kitchen; they cleanse the church of cattle, and no further slaughter takes place.

*(At the margin of the manuscript: VOX NUSTRIAE, “Voice of Neustria.”)*

You have read of the plunder; learn also of the trophies! The supreme will resisted the capture of every town; but weak power, though granted by the Lord, proved an obstacle [Col. 0739: “This verse is absent from the printed editions”].

The Allophili brought countless battles to Chartres [Col. 0739: “Chartres”], but they left behind a thousand corpses—here five hundred at once—while the red conflict ravaged them.

[Col. 0740B] One day wished to play this game in such a manner, under these leaders, Godefred and Odo. Both had been warriors of Count Odo.

That same Odo also opposed them repeatedly, and repeatedly conquered as victor. Alas, his right hand had once left him in battle; iron enclosed the place, though scarcely was it less powerful than the hand itself!

Nor did these men gain anything better among the Cenomanni; indeed, the remaining cities did not yield more pleasantly.

Now, since Apollo [Col. 0739: “the sun”] calls, let the pen earn its rest.

**THE FIRST BOOK ENDS; THE SECOND LITTLE BOOK OF THE WARS OF THE CITY OF PARIS BEGINS.**

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739C] Rise quickly, Muse; the lamp has lit the eastern regions [Col. 0739: “eastern”]. Hurry to overtake the light-bearing foot.

Ainricus, a strong and mighty Saxon, came to the aid of Gozlin, bishop of the city. Having inflicted defeat upon them, he gave joy; with bloodshed—alas—of only a few, he preserved our men and carried off abundant booty from the enemy.

Therefore, on a certain night, he entered the Danish camp and captured many horses there for himself. As the butcher’s army withdrew before Ainricus, an exceedingly loud cry and din arose. Thus rest abandoned our men, and they surrounded the walls [Col. 0739: “of the city”].

The dying Danes poured forth excessive cries; the citizens resounded with immense uproar, terrified that they would suffer from these men the accustomed labor as before. [Col. 0739D] Ainricus too finally left the camp, but without delay was carried back to the fortress.

They exchanged missiles and sharp greetings [Col. 0739: “sharp”]. The gate was opened to the soldiers; close combat pressed hard, shields slipped, and swords flashed.

[Col. 0740C] Life loves my right hands and hates the left; death loves the hostile, while life guides the friendly.

Then sleep again overtook the citizens, and wretched flight overtook them.

While King Sigemfredus [Col. 0739: “so the manuscript”] was speaking with Odo, they ran at once from the watchtower in a large troop and attempted by force to lead the savage Odo away with them. He, striking first, leapt over the ditch of the palisade in rapid flight, carrying a shield and a javelin [Col. 0739: “spear”].

Having performed his customary service in battle, the hero stood facing them. The men leapt out, giving their lord support, and everyone of noble rank marvelled at his deeds.

Seeing that our men were fierce in the struggle, Sigemfredus said to his companions: “Leave this place; it is not destined that our men remain here long, but that they depart from here!”

[Col. 0740D] Thus, when Ainricus withdrew to his halls, they scorned the shores of the polished Saint Germanus and chose those of a namesake, upon whose deeds I gladly feed [the syntax of *Germani … aequivocique* is difficult].

They surround the camp across the open ground [Col. 0739: “meadow”], and he is enclosed on every side by a rampart, like a thief in prison, while my lord himself is guilty of nothing. A wall surrounded his church, exalted because of our guilt.

[Col. 0741A] At last the king, taking ten times six pounds of shining silver as the price of our return, and accompanied by all the Normans, wished to pour the sweet honey of the river’s waters into the sea, where the mouth of the strait seizes the white tail of the Seine, and the sea’s head, shaken by wings, wishes to display itself [Col. 0741: “wishes”] to the Seine’s waters.

But when these pagans [Col. 0741: “pagans”] refused, he began:

“Come, Danes, capable of circling the city walls; men, dress the citadel on every side with strength, and load your shoulders with the bow and mighty arrows! Let each man carry stones, and let him supply missiles from every side! I myself shall also attempt to see this battle!”

At these words, as he sat in repose, they all rise together. They enter the islands, the city’s districts on which it stands [Col. 0741: “that is, the islands”], and surround the walls, laden with savage swords [Col. 0741: the manuscript has *honorati*, “honoured”; corrected to *onerati*, “laden”].

[Col. 0741B] Our men descend outside and surround the towers. They kill twin kings and many others, and they greatly love deceptive flight [Col. 0741: “they greatly love it”], but they love true triumph.

The deep Seine River was our aid: swallowing some of them utterly, it submerged them and sent them across to Avernus.

Sigemfredus, rejoicing and laughing at the dying men, said:

“Now fortify the battlements, men; seize the city! Measure out the houses in which you are to dwell here!”

Then he said to his men: “Let us depart; behold, the time has come when it will be pleasing for us to have gone away from here!”

Soon he happily left the Seine after receiving the gift. Others would have done the same, had they then deserved the same gifts [Col. 0741: “gifts”].

Who can understand what is whispered beneath the open ear? Let earth groan, and the sea, the sky, and the world’s side as well:

[Col. 0741C] Gozlin, the Lord’s bishop, the gentlest of heroes, seeks the stars, departing to the Lord and shining like the stars themselves [Col. 0741: “the stars”]. He remained our tower, our shield, and also our double-edged sword [Col. 0741: “sword”]; he was a strong bow and a strong arrow!

Alas! Fountains of tears pierce the eyes of all, and grief, crushing their inward parts with terror, rends them.

In this storm Hugo, the prince and abbot, died; Senones was widowed of its learned bishop Evrard. Then the enemies joyfully gained their pleasures.

They claim that, keeping watch through the dark silence of the damp night, they saw Germanus, radiant in a shining form, moving around the limits [Col. 0741: “boundaries”] of his little place, carrying a lamp that often gleamed with light, perhaps where the holy limbs had been buried.

The solemn festival of his day was approaching. The castellans rebuke them because they do not celebrate the sacred rites; then they burst into loud laughter in high spirits.

[Col. 0741D] They move a wagon loaded with sheaves [Col. 0741: “bundles of grain”] through the fields, driving its oxen forward by repeatedly pressing the point of the goad into their backs.

At once they yoke other oxen to these, whose lameness was through no fault of their own, then still more and more. The wretched men [Col. 0741: “wretched”] and the unvanquished oxen strained with shoulders and horns; already they were washing their own sides in red blood.

[Col. 0742A] They could not separate the axle fixed in the earth, and, astonished, they marvelled at the miracles of our lord.

The bulls were released, and the fierce goad rested. The crop sprang up again and freed the wheels of their burdens, restoring the axle to its movement from the clod.

One of these men [Col. 0741: “Normans”], ordered to be slaughtered, escaped and entered the church of the Saint; he also seized the tomb [Col. 0741: “sepulchre”]. From there the wretch was driven out, to be killed as an exile through piety.

Woe to the wretched! They punish the wretched men, and they themselves are punished. The gift they had given to their companion, they all deserved to receive with similar piety, having obtained it through the merits of Germanus [Col. 0741: “having received it”], afflicted from heaven because of such deeds.

Therefore the priests established a place in which they would celebrate Masses and the sacred offices [Col. 0739: “canonical hours”] for them.

[Col. 0742B] Then they forbid everyone [Col. 0741: “that is, the savage men”] to remove anything from this place. One man violated the prohibition and attempted to carry a church covering to his own bed. Beneath it, visibly, his image was reproduced as a child [Col. 0741: “His image was reproduced—namely, a diminished image of a child; the event occurred only once”], reduced in a manner resembling no other event.

He had previously been known to those people, yet no one could recognize him in any town. I marvel where his veins and sinews had lain hidden; his bones likewise fled as his marrow departed, and his entrails entered the hollow of a slender cavern.

He had been regarded as greater among the great—O wondrous deed!—but the man who had until then been greater now appeared, at death, to be smaller than children; and his life [Col. 0741: “his life”], groaning, fled indignantly beneath the shadows.

[Col. 0742C] The same most holy servant of the Lord appeared in a vision to someone. As he sought rest in his breast through the clouds of night, he received clear water in his hands to bless, through the holy prayers of Marcellus and Clodoald. Then, sprinkling the city, he walked around its walls.

To this man he disclosed his own name and, promising hope to the city, left himself visible to the beholder.

There was also in this city a nobleman whose flesh was melting away. He was wasting away and, fearing death, scarcely had breath left; at that very time he also feared that the fortress would be captured by the Normans.

In a dream the citizens appeared to him wishing to abandon the city, since it remained deserted of all arms. Then a cleric of wondrous beauty stood before him, speaking with a peaceful mouth and shining with a serene face:

“What do you fear? Rise, lay aside your trembling fears, and, forgetting flight, see how many are prepared for battle!”

He rose joyfully and saw all the walls fortified with wedges of young men, heavily burdened with helmets.

[Col. 0742D] A voice thundered: “This city is defended by these protectors. But I am Germanus,” he said, “and I am also its bishop. Take courage; you will fear nothing, for now this city will not be ravaged by the mouths of criminals!”

The saint spoke, and the man’s flesh answered the blessed breath. The blessed one spoke, and the evil disease fled from the man. The Saint addressed him, and the sick man rose from his bed.

[Col. 0743A] The sick man came forth restored by blessed remedies and explained what he himself had learned through the night’s vision.
