Then, on a certain day, while the blessed body was being carried around the walls by its own soldiers, with seven townsmen following the Almighty and repeatedly addressing God in vows with melodious voice, one of the bearers, named Gozbertus, was struck by a pagan [Col. 0743: “by a pagan”] with a stone [Col. 0743: “stone”]. The striker fled dying into the Tartarean shadows, while the monk who had been struck [Col. 0743: “the struck monk”] suffered nothing from the stone’s blow, with the Saint’s aid.

Meanwhile the city endured the sword from without, battered by violent storms of slaughter; and, alas, the disease of the noblemen’s people was utterly tearing it apart within [Col. 0743: “inwardly”].

[Col. 0743B] Within, we had no ground capable of providing burial for the bodies of the dead. Close at hand [Col. 0743: “near, that is, hand to hand”], there was no day that did not produce savage wars among the townsmen [Col. 0743: “citizens”] and the suburban inhabitants; nor did any day pass without carrying the pestilential dead with it to the caverns of hell.

King Odo, then about to come [Col. 0743: “future”], was sent from there to the aforesaid Charles, emperor of the Franks, so that he might quickly bring aid to the city.

Afterward none of the nobles remained except Abbot Marcius [Col. 0743: “Ebolus”], whose memory is often brightly recorded above.

He himself compelled six horsemen to clothe themselves in the Danish manner. One day, at the return of daylight, they flew over the fields and traversed the plains beyond the Seine.

They killed as many Normans, filled with various arms and savage sleep, as there had been horsemen themselves.

[Col. 0743C] From this a tumult arose in the camp. When their voice resounded, the savage men seized their shields, while our men took to the boat.

They were cutting down the cattle of our shores of Saint Denis, which they had repeatedly led away for themselves after spying them [Col. 0743: “Normans”]. But Abbot Ebolus was continually there to meet them; on one occasion he struck down the companion of one of them with a weapon. Therefore the Danes left the bank and carried away the corpse.

Soon Ebolus sent six horsemen from the fortress; four of them killed three men in a dreadful battle.

At night the citizens more frequently approached the cattle-guards beneath the darkness, drove some away, and consigned others to slaughter; they did this often.

By this sign they brought the Danes into the city without breath and alive at the same time, so that they might have been believed to be such.

On another occasion they entered the island in the customary manner, where three hundred savage men occupied the city walls.

[Col. 0743D] Immediately two of our men struck down nine of them with the sword [Col. 0743: “namely, two of our men”], inflicted wounds upon thirty [Col. 0743: “they commended them”], and none was granted to see the light of a fourth day.

Two of our men joined the battle, men who, rejoicing in an illustrious death, carried holy feet above the stars. The elder was Segebertus, the younger Segevertus.

Then, by chance, Odo, mighty in arms, shone above the summit of the Mount of Mars [Col. 0743: “Montmartre”], surrounded by three wedges of helmets.

[Col. 0744A] The new sun shone upon his shields, having spurned the saffron chamber of Ocean with its vast foot. He, loving the sun—*ἥλιος*, “sun”—greets the fields before them; the citizens are captivated by his appearance and by their deep love for him.

But the enemies, wishing to prevent the doors of the tower from being reached, leap across the Seine and surround the shore.

Nevertheless Odo returned to the castellans on horseback, amid the savage men, while Ebolus opened the gates for him [Col. 0743: “the tower”]. Everyone marvelled at this noble deed.

From there, as his companions immediately returned, the iron enemy pursued them, following behind. The named Count Adalelmus was more than two leagues away from them.

“Come,” he said to his men, “let us proceed against them; it is better for us to go against them here than for them to find us here!”

[Col. 0744B] Adalaelmus said this. The pestilential men took flight, and our men gained a trophy.

Shields thundered, javelins flew, and the Danes’ bodies covered the consul’s fields, while Adalelmus’ sword ruled.

He did not release them until he forced them to retreat to the river; then he returned in triumph as victor.

Behold also Ainricus, frequently called among the blessed [Col. 0743: “among those above”]; he was killed while wishing to surround them with a siege.

King Sinric, striving to cross the Seine to his own men, entered it with his companions—three times fifty men—after rejecting two boats. He suffered shipwreck in mid-river and went to the bottom; the damaged verse then makes the riverbed the place where he and his companions “fixed their tents for death.”

There, where the Seine rises and flows forth, he said that his camp would first touch the river’s bottom before he would leave the realm of the Franks; and, by the Lord’s granting, what he said came to pass.

[Col. 0744C] At last, when the middle of the world is kindled by the sun [Col. 0743: “by the sun”], when the earth thirsts and shade is more pleasing to cattle, and the welcome west wind whistles through pleasant woods, the city’s fortress is surrounded by deadly enemies.

The city endured battle everywhere; the walls, watchtowers, bridges—all fought as one. The sea fought, while the land was even broader.

The trumpets [Col. 0743: “horns”] thunder loudly, and the citizens leave their tables [Col. 0743: “that is, from the tables”]. “Away!” cry the trumpets [Col. 0743: “horns”]; “let everyone abandon the feasts!”

The whole city, and the citizens together, were invaded by terror. There was no place in the city that did not conceal warfare.

Missiles battered the towers [Col. 0743: “towers”], while many shattered catapults covered the fields like rain. Heavy leaden missiles and great stones gave groans to the shields, like fruit; these were the rewards they always granted us.

[Col. 0744D] In reply, our men likewise directed swift stones and ballistae at the savage enemy, as well as rapid arrows.

The air was sown broadly in every direction with these flying missiles. Nothing else passed between the heavens and the fields.

Mars rules more and more, and in fear exults.

The head of the virgin of God, Genovefa, is carried through the city; immediately, by her merits, our men overcame them. From there they drove them far away as though on wings.

[Col. 0745A] Gerboldus, abundant in strength but small in body, accomplished this, a soldier accompanied by five armed men [Col. 0745: “armed men”]. No catapult’s bloody beak struck dry earth [Col. 0745: “the earth”] without making a river-wave of blood; the compressed syntax is uncertain, but the image links the missile’s beak, earth, and a stream of blood.

From other parts of the city fiercer battles arose far away; lamentations, shields, helmets, and shrill sounds [Col. 0745: “so the manuscript”] were raised. Our men fought, but the enemy fought more strongly.

The right hands grew weak, exhausted by war.

Alas! Weeping excessively, they drew out lofty laments. Gray old age groaned greatly, and flourishing youth likewise.

The monks wept; every cleric lamented. The bronze instruments thundered with their voices, but grief also filled the sky [Col. 0745: “fills”].

These sad men revealed the city’s fear that it would be captured by the enemy; the stern men, rejoicing in heaven, twisted their resonant laughter and mocked the walls.

[Col. 0745B] The womanly sex, lamenting and tearing at itself, swept the ground with its loosened hair.

Alas! They struck their naked breasts with their own fists, and with their nails cut their sorrowful faces and mouths [the manuscript has *ac*; another hand in different ink has *et*].

With tearful voice all cried out:

“Blessed Germanus, help your people, or else we shall now die!

“O pious one, hasten to help us now; help us, we are dying!”

The earth and the river echoed Germanus; the shores and every surrounding grove resounded together:

“O holy Germanus, have mercy on us, we beg!”

The bells of the temples [Col. 0745: “bells”] boomed and cried out in mourning. At these voices the earth trembled and the river roared.

The city, fearing the omens of its approaching last day, wept and poured forth bitter laments [Col. 0745: “filled”].

[Col. 0745C] Behold, Germanus was present to all, worthy of remembrance throughout the world, delaying neither his body nor his aid for the prayers.

The greater the battles of Mars became, the more he forced the Danish standard-bearers to gain death, and then many others besides, driving them far from the city [Col. 0745: “far from the city”] and from the bridge at the same time. The greatest tower, watching its lord before its own eyes, rejoiced.

Therefore the exhausted men recovered their strong powers and strove to resist the insolent enemy in battle. The insolent men [Col. 0745: “the insolent ones”] returned to the tower, or abandoned the bridge and walls.

A thousand watchtowers stood together, since the one place could not prevent all the battles, with such a great number opposing it.

The entrails pierced by various blades slid down upon the ground, just as rain is carried from the sky and to the ships [Col. 0745: “that is, the Normans”].

Now, as the radiance was being received and Tethys, departing beneath the marble Ocean, was closing her doors, a very high fire was set beneath the tower [Col. 0745: “by the pagans”]. [Col. 0745D] The flames surrounded the lofty summits of the tower; they fought with weapons and with the hostile fire.

The fortress is abandoned to the right hands, and they order the gates to be opened, preferring to climb to a precious death rather than entrust themselves entirely to treacherous faith.

[Col. 0746A] No one stood above the watchtower except, as often before, the servant of the aforementioned Saint [Col. 0745: “that is, the poet himself”], holding the holy wood of the Cross in the flames. He saw these things with his eyes and spoke, for dense smoke had covered the tower too heavily.

Then, once the gates had been opened, “dry Vulcan,” the fire, died unarmed; the intervening words *ense / portu ni madido* are corrupt and do not yield a secure agent or means. Many grim men sought a stealthy escape, carrying many corpses away with them, and Mars rested.

By the power of the holy Cross and the merits of the blessed bishop Germanus this victory was achieved [Col. 0745: the manuscript has *Caeditur*, corrected from *Ceditur*]. The rejoicing people return to the basilica of Saint Stephen the martyr [Col. 0745: “martyr”], echoing in lofty voice:

“We praise you as God, and we confess you as Lord!”

He was the city’s illustrious bishop, the city’s protection, which had obtained grief and joy in turn.

[Col. 0746B] The king, utterly changed in spirit [Col. 0745: “that is, Charles”], as though observing the sea stirred by the wind [Col. 0745: “wind”], said to the Franks:

“Prepare beneath the city a position suitable for six hundred of our men, on our platforms [Col. 0745: “seats”].”

“Would thieves dare such things in my presence?” [Col. 0745: “that is, servants dared to act thus.”] They add obedience to the commands [Col. 0745: “the Franks”].

While the path leads these men [Col. 0745: “six hundred Franks”] back to the court of the prelate, the wicked men [Col. 0745: “the pagans”] pursue them and mass their ranks behind them [Col. 0745: “behind them”]. They join battle [Col. 0745: “that is, the Normans”], conquer [Col. 0745: “the Franks”], yield, flee [Col. 0745: “the Normans”], and die.

The fleeing band [Col. 0745: “pagan”] enters the precincts of the temples within the walls of the victors. Two men break into a certain church—wondrous is what I relate—and leave it filled with death [Col. 0745: “pagan”].

[Col. 0746C] Afterward the two remount their horses by a leap [Col. 0745: “that is, those two”] and cling together as equals.

Thus, with three men laid low at the Seine and at the summit of Mars, six hundred are joined from the thousands, and from there they return.

For the fame of the two brothers proclaimed that they had been Theoderic and Aledramnus, nobles.

Behold the prince of whom song is made, surrounded by weapons of every kind, like the sky with starry splendors: the emperor Charles is present, accompanied by a rich multitude of different speech, pitching his tents beneath the feet of Mount Mars and beside the watchtower.

The noble and distinguished Anschericus, adorned with the honor of the sacred office and renowned for every root of virtue, is restored to the church, which had long been widowed of its shepherd.

[Col. 0746D] Permission is granted to the savage men to approach Senones; seven hundred pounds of silver are given in the month of Mars as the price of returning to their impious kingdoms.

Then the age of torpid November was freezing [Col. 0745: “was growing cold”]. Thus Charles returned, soon destined to die.

[Col. 0747A]

You were unwilling, O sluggish Burgundy, to name beforehand the men whose swords you endured in war, unless Neustria adorned her marriage-bed with lofty nobles [Col. 0747: “with well-nurtured daughters”]. Now, easily guided by counsel, you know them at last [Col. 0747: “that is, you know the names of the Normans”].

*(Year 887.)* From there they return and set up their camp in their own field, now worshiping the temple of the Saint as before.

Here my lord Germanus restored four men, whose limbs had been excessively contracted, to their former use. By his movements he brought the organs [Col. 0747: “sinews”] close to their own fibers; he restored to their knees and feet the feet that had long been drawn up [Col. 0747: “repaired”], according to their proper function. He also restored the rays of the sun to one man whose eyes had been extinguished, so that he could see them shining again.

[Col. 0747B] A woman, Beisino, came here amid a savage company. Nothing harmed her, but through the merits of the Blessed One she was safe. Later, being blind, she also obtained sight.

Beside the resting-place of the saint there is a well [Col. 0747: “This well still exists: BOUQ.”]. Whoever drinks its waters, suffering from fever, will immediately receive healing, trusting in the Saint’s aid.

A certain woman, wishing to prepare bread with these waters [Col. 0747: “waters”], ordered a Danish woman to be brought to her by force. The text reads *scotta*; perhaps it should be read *scorta*, equivalent to *scortum*. Certainly here *scotta* meant a certain Danish woman. For the priest who guarded the church was selling the well-water to the sick at a high price.

When the bread was placed [Col. 0747: “entrusted”] in the flame, it immediately took on the red appearance of blood. Later another woman, a Dane [Col. 0747: “Danish woman”], attempting to draw the liquid [Col. 0747: “to scoop it up”], was discovered to have drawn blood.

Who could traverse all the miracles of so great a saint? If I had a thousand mouths and just as many tongues, filling the air and sky with their voices and din, I could not recount the deeds of my father or number them.

[Col. 0747C] This is Germanus, this is the man who, though still suffering, continued to shine forth and accomplished deeds exceedingly wondrous to the whole world.

In his mother’s womb, before he saw the light, he first learned to pour forth signs of lofty power.

Who, reader, ever accomplished such things among the saints? Name one, holy man, if you dare: John the Baptist.

Therefore let my Germanus be considered like him.

He restored life to three corpses, returning the fallen souls to their proper dwellings.

Now speak, O city of Paris: under which princes were you defended?

*(At the margin of the manuscript: VOX URBIS, “Voice of the City.”)*

“Who could defend me, except this foremost man, Germanus, who is all my power and love?

“[Col. 0747D] After the King of Kings and his holy mother, he himself was my king, my shepherd, and also my strong companion.

“This is my double-edged sword; this is my catapult, my shield and open wall, and also my swift bow.”

Since the forests [Col. 0747: “the peoples”] resound sufficiently with these things [Col. 0747: “that is, about the miracles”], let the nightingale be silent.

[Col. 0748A] Let us turn back the plectra of our voice after the wonders [Col. 0747: “miracles”], and speak of the fragile treaty by which they had been deceived.

The bands of Normans, unwilling to descend from the lands of the Franks into their own caves, but rather desiring to approach the waters of the Seine and return again to you—waters that display fields while retaining silver for themselves—O Burgundy, they did not desire this [Col. 0747: “that is, they did not desire it”]; a feigned desire lay hidden. The desire that followed had been present in their hearts, but this was nevertheless upon their lips.

Therefore they conceive a plan to cross the bridges, Tethys exerting itself to draw its chariots onward, secretly through a gift [Col. 0747: “without a gloss”] pleasing to the just.

At once word is carried to Bishop Anschericus while he is at table. But, while Ebalus was at his dishes [Col. 0747: “tables”], and the sun was marking the light-bearing figure of the sky with its gnomon [Col. 0747: “clock”], Paris cries out that the pagans are beating the waters with many oars [Col. 0747: “channels”] and ascending by the eastern stream.

[Col. 0748B] Paris cries out. Both rise, unconcerned for their food; they take up arms, choose the banks, and man the battlements [Col. 0747: “fill the walls”].

Here Ebalus drags the rope and brandishes the arrow. The boatman ahead received it in his armpit through the opening of the ship; it had been bored through slightly with a drill.

Thus the charioteer of death and the little sea-vessel suffer their fate [Col. 0747: “certainly”]. The remaining men [Col. 0747: “Normans”] therefore stay and kill beneath the fortress.

They are called headless [Col. 0747: “why are they called headless?”] because they lose Christ, the head itself [Col. 0747: “that is, they lose him”].

Then they ask pardon [Col. 0747: “peace”] and prepare oaths by hostages: they will touch no other shore except that of the Seine, and will quickly retrace their steps as before.

[Col. 0748C] For the Marne River had given us everything that sustains life, ordinarily calling it safe [Col. 0747: “that is, tranquil”].

It was a great horror for the Danes to violate this safety [Col. 0747: “that is, security”] of our people. Hence a common treaty was established between them: one house, bread, drink, dwelling, road, and bed.

They marvel that the two peoples were mixed together. The men of Senones had first established this pact on migrating and preserved it until they were granted, despite unwilling opposition, the right to gain the upper waters and drag their boats through the rivers [Col. 0747: “that is, a permitted entry”].

Alas, along the shores of life they bound two dozen Catholics to themselves, whether by slaughter or by bonds [the syntax is uncertain].

Soon they bring to their own camp, without eating, “life encircled by two” and embers that are “death without the twofold covering” [Col. 0747: the two coverings are wood and ashes]. The verse is syntactically damaged; its gloss explains the controlling image: a coal protected by flame and ash lives continually, but without them it dies.

Our men hoped to hold these camps safe through prayers.

[Col. 0748D] They break the security, despise Senones, and plow the Marne in their sea-going chariot. The news is brought to the city.

Thousands of throats crackle, and there is also lamentation and uproar [Col. 0747: “sounds”].

[Col. 0749A] The common peace [Col. 0749: “the peace that existed between Christians and Normans”] departs; every treaty is destroyed.

Immediately everyone runs through the city and marketplace, searching for the savage men [Col. 0749: “cruel”], in case any might be found.

“Hurrah!” [Col. 0749: an exclamation of rejoicing] They discover five hundred and slaughter them with blows.

The outstanding warlike Abbot Ebolus joined them—if only he had not been excessively greedy [Col. 0749: “if he were greedy”], wanton, and ready for every course.

For he shone beautifully in the studies that the grammar-master Bishop Anschericus had permitted to depart on account of the treaty, though he ought rather to have caused them to fall.

From there the savage men strike the men of Meaux and also surround the city.

*(Year 888.)* Meanwhile Charles, stripped both of kingdom and of life, sadly embraces the hidden entrails of the goddess Ops [Col. 0749: “earth goddess”].

The joyful Odo embraces the name of king and the power of the kingdom [Col. 0749: “that is, he embraces them”], while the people of the Franks rejoice and give abundant support.

[Col. 0749B] At once his hand [Col. 0749: “Odo’s hand”] takes up the scepter, and his head the diadem [Col. 0749: “that is, he embraces them”].

France rejoices, although he was a native of Neustria; for it could not find anyone of equal birth. Nor, because Burgundy lacked a leader, did Neustria fail to come forward for the honor of her distinguished son.

Thus the kingdom rejoices in a threefold celebration under one ruler.

Moreover, he hastily attacked the crafty Aquitanians. After subjecting them to himself, he revisited the kingdoms of the Franks, while the walls of Meaux were still crowded by the Danes.

The surviving text breaks off in a nominal sequence: “whose resident bishop was Segemundus; Tetbertus, Bishop Anschericus’ warrior hero; Germanus, count” [Col. 0749: “that is, he was a count”]; “in no way Delian, nor Phoebean” [Col. 0749: “Phoebe”]. The antecedents and syntax of this terminal fragment are incomplete.

did he destroy the grim [foes] on this side of the walls? I cannot say  
how many blasts he had endured from weapons—[Note: [Col. 0749] gloss: speak].  
Alas! The mighty warrior is absent from mortal affairs,  
falling amid arms, with no prince—[Note: gloss: king] ever coming to his aid;  
and thereafter the city—[Note: gloss: city]—suffered and paid the price  
of destruction, with its bishop captured. Hence a happy omen shines for King Odo!

*(At the edge of the manuscript: HYRONIA.)*

### (Year 889)

At last they fly back to the secure heights of Lutetia.  
He summons here all his own men dwelling throughout the realm.

[Col. 0749D] Behold, Odo, already surpassing number itself, gathers an army.  
The French hasten, proud with heads held high;  
Aquitaine, you came with cunning, with your battle-line, and with your tongue,  
and after deliberation and a feigned flight they reached Brugundiones.  
The engagement is brief enough, and victory is frustrated.

[Col. 0750A] I know not who deceived the allies and struck down the Danes—  
not a few, though, as the report was, only a small populace—  
Ademarus by name, coming like the wind [the syntax is uncertain].  
Then Sclademarus gave two men—[Note: gloss: Normans]—to the sword,  
and he himself was the first to be given over; first he paid  
his due to the shades of gloomy Lutetia, after the first signs appeared.  
He held the beginning of the sword and received its end:  
this [Note: gloss: the beginning of the sword] against the treacherous men, that [Note: gloss: the end] against the body of his opponent.  
Sclademarus had been the warlike man of Count Rotbert.

Terror had scattered the helmets and, beneath the city itself,  
three hundred crescent-shaped shields, as many as the stadiums allowed.  
Moreover, with four hundred withdrawn from a thousand,  
he laid low the headless foot-soldiers upon the ground:  
three hundred in the host, led by the shepherd,  
the noble Anscherichus, powerful through the Virgin’s word.

[Col. 0750B] Thus the joyful men bring back much booty to the walls of the city,  
with God, who reigns on high, granting success.

From this point let us recount Odo’s worthy triumphs.

They call it Falcon, where he defeated nineteen thousand horsemen,  
and thereafter at Montfaucon—[Note: Montfaucon, a town between the Meuse and the Aisne]—a profane multitude of infantry.  
In turn this won for him a natal trophy on the festival-day of John,  
the Lord’s forerunner—[Note: gloss: one, singular].

For, adorned on both sides with shield-bearing men,  
a thousand in number, he was making his way, when, from the mouth of the young hunter,  
the news spread through the wooded fields that hares were approaching,  
and that savage horsemen were advancing by the thousand.  
He received that report together with his shield, which hung from his neck,  
and with his companions drew his weapons, entering unexpectedly  
into battle. He seeks heavenly consolation and seizes the entrails;  
others lay down their shields and their lives;  
the rest prepare their backs, beneath the royal arms,  
in which it pleased three boys to rest beside Odo.

Then he [Note: gloss: Odo] said to his own men: “Perhaps others are following these;  
therefore gather together in formation as one.  
If anyone has a report of this, let no one delay!”

He added: “I myself will climb the hill—[Note: gloss: mountain]—to keep watch;  
if the trumpet-blast strikes you, let no delay overcome anyone!”

Calling for his horn and climbing the rocky height, he sees—behold!—  
the armor-clad infantry moving with slow step.  
Then the trumpet, whose mouth roared, immediately awakens everything far and wide;  
its echoes flew through the stars and across the fields,  
and it stirred all things in every manner, both solid and broken—[Note: gloss: in a solid manner].

Every grove gave answers to the voice—[Note: gloss: of the king]—by serving it,

[Col. 0750D] and the trumpet travels with swift reverberation through all the elements.  
“Nothing strange,” I say, “for a royal head is thundering.”

Then his men rein in their chariots—[Note: gloss: horses]—and climb them with a leap;  
they move into the midst of the Allofili, and one—[Note: gloss: a Norman]—  
with a blow of his axe struck the cone—[Note: gloss: helmet]—from the king’s head,  
which fell upon his shoulders. Because he had presumed to strike the true Christ—[Note: gloss: the anointed one]—of the Lord,  
the prince’s javelin immediately cast the wind—[Note: gloss: soul]—from his breast.

The battle grows fierce; they lay down their lives with the blood of the foolish—[Note: gloss: senseless].  
The infamous men take flight, and the first trophy—  
so many thousands—[Note: gloss: nineteen]—Phoebus laid low beneath a single gaze,  
with the perpetual sword, until he pursued them  
from the borders of the Franks and drove them out.  
(Year 892.) Yet that brought no rest to him [Note: gloss: Odo],  
for he soon learned that the Aquitanians were abandoning him  
and setting aside his authority.

Therefore, raging, he attacks them, devastating and laying waste  
the fields and the populace—[Note: gloss: he was devastating]—though he tried to shut them up  
against the cities; nevertheless, his capacity was very slightly increased—[Note: gloss: increased for him].

But by chance Ademarus rose up against them, the sun being placed  
beneath the wandering vault of the sea of heaven,  
the consul Ademarus, joined to the king by descent,  
of whom I have spoken—[Note: gloss: Ademarus]. Long ago  
Proserpina yielded to him, while he routed Odo’s wedges.  
The shadow puts the stars to flight; Ademarus saves himself from Odo’s host—[Note: gloss: Odo’s].  
Odo sleeps; his kinsman—[Note: gloss: Ademarus]—tramples his own arms.

The stars shine; the king—[Note: gloss: king]—keeps the first watch, but his royal kinsman himself,  
joyful in his fertile blood—[Note: gloss: fruitful]—quickly takes flight.

Why, then, should I recount such things, since once, when he was in power,  
the king was pleased to give the strongholds to his brother  
Rotbert of Poitiers, whereas he was not so pleased with Ademarus—[Note: gloss: he was pleased]?  
Indeed, Robert took Poitiers for himself—[Note: gloss: Poitiers]—because he loved himself more than Ademarus—[Note: gloss: “Rotbert”; correction: *Rotberto* for *Rotbertus*].

From there, approaching Limoges and the Auvergnian fields,  
he [Note: gloss: the king] sees the very powerful forces of William, the enemy, with him—[Note: gloss: with the king],  
unless the river in their midst had prevented them  
from engaging one another.

Therefore William lost there the honors  
given to Hugo, who, while the king reigned—[Note: gloss: while he was king]—  
had been consul and prince of the Bituriges. Thus a monstrous duel  
was fought between these two counts.

The illustrious William of Clermont mourned more than a thousand and a hundred  
men killed by Hugo—[Note: gloss: that is, killed, not “denied”].  
The latter—[Note: gloss: Hugo]—mourned fewer in number,  
but fewer by a greater thousand—[Note: gloss: that is, by one thousand].  
The note explains that William lost eleven hundred in that battle,  
while Hugo lost one hundred, including himself.

At last, when this Hugo is captured by William’s sword,  
he begs that William’s mercy come to his aid.  
William replied that mercy had come to him only so late—  
that is, that he had spoken to him too late—  
and more swiftly than the word itself, a spear passed through his breast.

Among Hugo’s ranks were Rotgarius and the very brave man Stefanus,  
bringing great joy to William’s own men; one, Rotgarius—[Note: gloss: Rotgarius]—was Count Hugh’s nephew,  
[Col. 0751D] and the other was the exceedingly bold soldier Stefanus.

Alas, Hugh, you mourn your death; William, you begin your trophy—[Note: gloss: you began].

### (Year 893)

Meanwhile a messenger shakes the royal ear,  
carrying on his lips the news that Gaul has proved false to him:  
the neck of Louis, Charles’s son, is pressed beneath the yoke—[Note: gloss: “by the letter c”]—  
Louis who was called Balbus—[Note: gloss: “with the heavenly surname”].

### (Year 893)

Then Odo sets out, rashly going to seek  
how he might skillfully obtain the German kingdoms for himself.  
The illustrious Odo attacks the castles and defeats the rebels—[Note: gloss: rebels].

### (Year 894)

From there he drives away Charles, in person—[Note: gloss: by his presence, not by the sword]—and all his followers,  
as Apollo drives away darkness, as Lucina drives away atoms.  
Odo admits those who had long been proud in neck and bearing, now humbled.

### (Year 895)

What speech could tell how often the sword of Odo,  
thundering behind him, drove into flight Cendebald,  
the son of the exalted emperor Arnulf?

Here was Charles’s support, strength, and hope against Odo;  
yet his boldness never came near Odo’s gaze.  
But that brought him [Note: gloss: Odo] no rest.

### (Year 896)

Behold, once again I speak with miserable groaning:  
the savage Allofili—[Note: gloss: pagans]—are coming. They devastate the land  
and slaughter the peoples; they go about the cities on foot,  
and the houses of the ruler—[Note: gloss: Odo]—as well.  
They seize the country people, bind them, and send them across the sea.

The king hears, but Odo does not care; he replied in words:

“Oh, what a crime—that you did not give such an answer  
with your own mouth! Surely a demon of your own has favored you.  
Does your mind not care for the sheep entrusted to you by Christ?  
Perhaps that man does not care for your honor any longer.”

When they received these words—[Note: gloss: statements]—spoken while probity was neglected—[Note: gloss: despised]—,

[Col. 0752C] they exult joyfully and drive their boats through all  
the rivers with which Gaul is blessed; they hold land and sea  
under their authority, their guardian bearing up the whole realm!

France, why do you hide your ancient strength? Tell me, I ask.  
With what greater triumphs have you triumphed,  
and what kingdoms have you subjected to yourself?  
Because of a threefold vice and threefold offense—[Note: gloss: that is, you are hiding].

For Venus’s proud brow and foul beauty—[Note: gloss: shameful beauty]—  
and the ostentation of precious clothing lift you up in your own eyes.

You are so wholly Aphrodite—[Note: gloss: to such an extent]—that at least—[Note: gloss: or]—  
you cannot keep your parents away from the bed,  
nor the nuns consecrated to the Lord.  
Or why, if you have women enough,  
do you despise nature when they present themselves?  
We stir up both what is lawful—[Note: gloss: what must be admonished]—and what is unlawful—[Note: gloss: what must be done].

[Col. 0752D] A golden brooch bites into your splendid garment;  
you make your warm flesh precious with Tyrian purple—[Note: gloss: purple].  
You desire to be clothed in nothing but a golden cloak—[Note: gloss: to be dressed]—  
[Col. 0753A] and no belt adorned with gems warms your loins,  
nor anything but rods of gold your feet.  
Neither humble dress nor clothing can conceal you.

You do these things; no other peoples do so.  
Unless you abandon these three things, you will abandon—[Note: gloss: that is, you will abandon]—  
all your strength and your father’s kingdom.  
Every crime comes from these—[Note: gloss: the three vices]. The books testify that Christ was born;  
flee from these things, France!

I am not weary of singing—[Note: gloss: “I” is understood]; yet Odo’s deeds are lacking—[Note: gloss: are deficient],  
although he, a noble man, still delights the upper air.  
I pray that, placed—[Note: gloss: an alternative reading: “poet”]—amid the pleasant regions of heaven, I may be able,  
with the enemy—[Note: gloss: the devil]—conquered, to rejoice, reader,  
in the welcome halls—[Note: gloss: be glad].

[Col. 0753] **Here ends the second little book of the wars of the city of Paris and of the miracles of Bishop Germanus.**

**Here begins the third: namely, the ornament of clerics and the benefit of novices.**  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the words they follow.]

Cleric, never remove the diptychs—[Note: tablets]—from your side.  
Flee the court of the sliding game—[Note: the leader of a game]—lest  
the foul—[Note: obscene]—bier—[Note: baccaulus]—or the toparch—[Note: ruler of one place, that is, the devil of Erebus]—rejoice in you.  
Let battle—[Note: conflict]—be yours, so that the sacred principate—[Note: or “may the sacred principate of Tartarus be festive for you”]—  
may not be a sewer.

[5] Let neither money—[Note: enteca]—nor a banquet—[Note: alogia]—be with you; rather, let a shining sanctuary—[Note: absida]—  
remain with you, since sharpness of mind—[Note: vigor of mind or bodily industry]—does not bite.  
Let your champion—[Note: combatant]—be your belly—[Note: ambasilla]; let your mind  
read nothing heavenly—[Note: uranium]—beyond color—[Note: chroma], since it often  
wishes to be God; pursue twin medicines—[Note: anodiam].

[10] Fear to stand as a slanderer—[Note: calumniator]; nevertheless be vigorous and robust—[Note: boba].  
Let writing—[Note: gripphia; corrected from Gripphia to Gripphia]—touch you, together with pastoral vessels—[Note: carchesia]—and frequently the poet’s garment—[Note: toga].  
Let a composition of letters—[Note: grammaton sinteca]—often remain before you at a distance;  
but let eye-clouding—[Note: glauconia]—and the mass of crime—[Note: offa]—stand apart.

Then let a purple gold-leaf—[Note: brathea blatta, “gold leaf, purple”—]—and humility—[Note: enclitiva, “inclining downward”]—  
and the lineage of Christ’s warfare never be absent from you.

[15] Let a shaggy covering of lay peoples—[Note: amphytappa laon]—be present, and also a traveling bed—[Note: badanola].  
Let a splendid garment—[Note: effipiam; the gloss describes a finely ornamented garment or a bright drink filtered through linen]—shine like a diamond,  
and likewise a striped covering and a ceremonial robe—[Note: propoma].  
Let the unmarried Agagula—[Note: seduction]—drive away the sheep—[Note: aginat, “drives away”]—and not an open vessel—[Note: ablundam].

Let the effipia and striped cloth be a bordered court garment—[Note: a courtly garment].  
[20] A woman uses the anabola—[Note: a woman’s adornment]—but she herself abuses it.  
Apozema—[Note: water boiled with various condiments]—is suitable for the weak, as is a cake—[Note: porridge].  
May you remain a noble rhetorician or poet—[Note: Codrus]—and eloquent.  
With your purse—[Note: literally, the scrotal sac]—hold horses—[Note: yppos]; do not be a keeper of a wife—[Note: uxorius].  
May you lack the name of a madman—[Note: lymphaticus]—and be golden-mouthed—[Note: chrysostomus].

[25] Be present as a minister of secrets—[Note: aposicrarus]; let brief sermons—[Note: aphorisms]—guard your mouth.  
Stand as a king—[Note: basileus]—, sober—[Note: abstemius]—, and as a copyist or chancellor—[Note: antigraphus].  
Be a describer of the world—[Note: cosmographus]—, and be solely your own scout—[Note: catasscopus].  
Be naked—[Note: gimnus]—from unlawful things, and do not be a worldly secular agent—[Note: biotticus].  
Celebrate lightly fermented bread—[Note: acrizimum]—frequently; be an observer of the hours—[Note: oroscopus]—and a teacher—[Note: didasclus].

[30] In bed have a shaggy covering—[Note: amphyballum]—and let the beardless man—[Note: effebus]—be absent.  
Let a gelding—[Note: canterus]—be available to you in abundance, but let a lover—[Note: one loved for shameful reasons]—be absent.  
Take care not to be smoky and irritable—[Note: cerritus]—and circumlocutory—[Note: perifrasticus].  
Let a dining-board—[Note: abbachus]—be in your hand, and let the theologian—[Note: divine speech]—shine upon your lips.  
May you happily see yourself carrying a bier—[Note: baccaulum]—to the ditch—[Note: cloaca].

[35] Do not be prodigal, crooked—[Note: obliquus, distorted]—, one-eyed—[Note: monotaimus]—, or suborned.  
Avoid mockery and the abyss—[Note: barathrum, hell]; pursue the trophy—[Note: the praise of victory].  
Let amphitheaters—[Note: places of spectacle where gladiators fight]—stand far from you, and eye-diseases—[Note: egilopia]—likewise;  
for they produce a scruple in ΨΙΧΗ [*psychē*, “soul”] and trouble the pupils.  
Climb the reading desk; let gold—[Note: crisis]—shine from the teacher’s mouth.

[40] Turn away from the two-wheeled chariot—[Note: birotum]—; seize the prize and the folding chair—[Note: cliotedrum].  
Have the pitch-coated sack—[Note: culleum]—; know diameters—[Note: half the sphere; also a clock]—  
and do not know the workhouses—[Note: ergastula, places of exile].  
[Note: According to Roman law, the parricide’s sack is the container in which the parricide, a cock, and a serpent are placed.]  
Add a half-verse—[Note: emistichium]—when you write couplets—[Note: two verses].  
Accustom yourself to loosen urine—[Note: lotium]—in a wine vessel—[Note: enoforo liba].  
Love the hospice—[Note: xenodochium, a house where the poor are gathered]—[Note: corrected from xenodoxium to xenodochium],  
and hate jealous zeal—[Note: zelotipia].

[45] From there, tame your vinegar vessel—[Note: acitabula]—or let a measure—[Note: congia]—restrain your household.  
[Col. 0757] Let the pomerium—[Note: an empty or open place]—be short; let orchards—[Note: pomaria, green spaces or places planted with fruit trees]—be suitable for apples.  
Let purple shine in the churches, and let foul odor—[Note: human excrement]—be far away.  
Let basket-like estates—[Note: quala]—be established for you; let the winds stir the garden plots—[Note: flogra, winds, rods, or green spaces].  
So that the gorgon—[Note: something proper to a serpent]—may flee from afar, drink diamoron—[Note: a bitter medicinal drink].

[50] Spurn the total mud—[Note: platon olon]—and the drinking parties, so that a road—[Note: odon]—may cleanse you.  
May you flourish as the middle son—[Note: temeson]—, if you cannot be innocent.  
Let there be for you a household shrine—[Note: lar, provisions]—where nectar may give off fragrance, and let money from the woods—[Note: lucarque]—not be absent.  
Remember your hired laborer—[Note: gallonis], and fear Ambro when summoned by the dissipated man—[Note: cieri, “I summon,” according to the gloss].  
Let your muleteer—[Note: mulio]—not be cross-eyed—[Note: strabo; gloss: “uuekus”]—, nor your unarmed horse-provider—[Note: agoson].

[55] Let the weak house—[Note: abaso; corrected from Abbaso]—where he may be be accompanied by a frequent leech—[Note: hirudo, a bloodsucker].  
Let a separation—[Note: intercapedo]—quickly divide the strong—[Note: “an interval, agilely”].  
If some strong-minded woman—[Note: virago]—enters you—[Note: penetrates], remember the roof—[Note: doma].  
Let counsel—[Note: bule]—cover Christ’s mind for you, and a cloth—[Note: gausape]—the table.  
Let command—[Note: entole]—adorn you, and let kings and nobles wear golden necklaces—[Note: baben].

[60] Let your belly by no means exceed your body, but rather let command—[Note: teche]—do so for you.  
Do not be heavenly yet new—[Note: uranei neotericus]—, nor newly converted—[Note: neofitus]—  
in doctrine and faith; rather be ancient from of old.  
May these four things accompany you throughout the age:  
the command of God, the sacred—[Note: ieron]—, the prince—[Note: archon]—, and the repeated and doubled praise—[Note: palinodia].

[65] Live circumcised—[Note: ancisus]—, and do not die afflicted with heart-pain—[Note: cardiacus, suffering from a pulsation of the heart].  
If you wear dark—[Note: ceruleas, “black”]—clothes, ask for a laundry—[Note: colimbus].  
A corded edge—[Note: anguina]—is drawn around the ship—[Note: limbus], and an arch—[Note: arcippio]—as well.  
The horse—[Note: canterius]—is ridden with front-pieces—[Note: antelis]—and rear-pieces—[Note: postelis].  
[Note: “Here it is written and erased.”]

May you suffer anxiety—[Note: aporia]—and also bodily wasting—[Note: atrophia], so that your pleasantness—[Note: aca]—

[70] may gather its everlasting companion—[Note: aterva appodix]—for itself.  
Such things truly seek out—[Note: anquirunt, seek very earnestly]—the pain of the mind—[Note: algema],  
but they drive away insensibility—[Note: aphatia]—and also establish a generous meal—[Note: antecenia].  
Love bears alien labor—[Note: agape]—; love is exceedingly fitting.

[Col. 0759] Follow the goat—[Note: aegidia]—in circles with sharp efforts.

[75] Keep your kinsmen—[Note: agnati]—; speak also of rain—[Note: aregidia].  
Pant, but do not be the enemy’s—[Note: the demon’s]—mourner—[Note: atratus, dark or sorrowful]—for the spoil—[Note: aslum].  
Let curtains—[Note: aulea]—not constrict the soul with crime, but rather warmth—[Note: aprilax].  
Let the heavenly one wash over you; do not become an apostate—[Note: transgressor]—through wrongdoing.  
Carry a shield—[Note: ancile]—in your left hand, and in your right confidence and eagerness—[Note: agonia]—of faith.

[80] Remain outside by auspice—[Note: auspicio a, “from the beginning”]—; enlarge some deep underground structure—[Note: apogeum, a building beneath the earth, a cave, or a granary].  
Lift a veil—[Note: armenum]—from your heart; add a monastery—[Note: arcisterium, a monastery, that is, dedication to God’s service].  
The master of the house—[Note: architriclinus]—cultivates an amical—[Note: suited to friendship]—white ornament—[Note: amineum],  
and autumn loads him with vessels suitable for carrying fruit—[Note: apofereta].  
Let a man—[Note: antropus]—live as a celibate—[Note: agamus, without a spouse; celibacy or chastity], and thus

[85] behold the silver city—[Note: argiripa]—, his ancestral homeland and blessed citizens.  
For him there is no concern about sudden death—[Note: apoplexia], nor does cunning—[Note: astu]—  
constrict anyone; he is accustomed to make wretched men—[Note: amartetes]—ancient—[Note: antiquare, restore to an earlier condition or drive away].  
He drives away Venus and wears a linen cloak—[Note: anaboladia].  
For him, his fruit-bearing vessels—[Note: apofereta]—shine white with pale fruit—[Note: albuneis].

[90] All virtues accompany him in friendship;  
the left-hand forces—[Note: the devils, according to the gloss]—do not strike him by shaking him to and fro.  
Since wine-born children—[Note: bibiones, gnats born from wine]—go forth from Bacchus,  
he speaks foolishly—[Note: platterat]—if they have stood in white wine—[Note: amineus],  
and, bringing something unworthy to his throat—[Note: branchus], he becomes utterly brutish.

[95] That woman does not go there—[Note: bittit, “goes there”]—where every person is honored twice—[Note: bimetur].  
I confess that the red-black—[Note: burra]—good—[Note: probum]—young man—[Note: buteo]—is one who digs the fields with a two-pronged tool—[Note: bidentat].  
He is also freeborn and retains a similar parentage.  
The eunuch—[Note: buggeus]—adorns and constructs dwellings or camps—[Note: burgos], but, being bilious—[Note: sad]—,  
he also prepares flesh—[Note: boson]—and a tomb—[Note: taphium]—sorrowful—[Note: sibiliosum]—for himself.

[100] Thus the body composes a bitter—[Note: mournful]—life for the soul—[Note: “is given”].  
But the Almighty prepares the stars for the joyful person, if the mind is happy.  
As a servant-soldier, admonish all these men courteously.  
Moreover, when someone secretly hides wrongdoing in a cave—[Note: hell],  
and virtue stumbles and binds together—[Note: constrains]—crimes,

[105] [Col. 0761] it fortifies the mind, growing—[Note: coalescens, increasing]—courteously,  
for the secret thing flourishes—[Note: shines and is strong]—in the harbor of his breast,  
and yet that hidden virtue will not be able to remain established for long,  
as the Thunderer bears witness, consecrated through the mouths—[Note: through the evangelists]—above.

When you see cunning—[Note: astus]—overthrow the wicked ages,  
remain here as the Lord’s heir, guardian—[Note: protector]—of his household—[Note: clientela, familiar association],  
so that you may climb the gentle slopes—[Note: ascents or hills]—of virtues,  
and may sound forth for God—ΘΗΟ [theō, “to God”; printed form uncertain]—  
your briefly and elegantly composed praises—[Note: concinnas].  
May you be able, in the name of the One who exists in three persons,  
to say “Hail” to the One alone,  
yet in everlasting majesty, authority—[Note: nutus, power]—and glory—[Note: doxa].

[115] May I possess this together with you; ask for it, cleric.

**The little work of Cernuus: of the outstanding catechist and confessor Germanus, and of the account of the Parisian battle, by the most humble deacon Abbo, is finished.**

[Col. 0761]

# Five Selected Sermons of Abbo

## Acherius’s Notice to the Reader

*(Spicilegium, vol. I, p. 336.)*

[Col. 0761A] The sermons of Abbo, a coenobite and priest of the monastery of Pratum, were supplied by a written codex of that same abbey. Among several works not unworthy of the light, we judged these worthy of publication. We have therefore transcribed five, which above all display the ecclesiastical discipline observed at that time and teach, more clearly than the others, the manner of reconciling public penitents to the Church and the time for imparting the Eucharist to them. We set the rest aside for the present, perhaps to publish them on another occasion when a suitable opportunity is given.

[Col. 0762A] But why Abbo composed and published these sermons, he explains in the argument, or brief preface, placed before the sermons, in these words addressed to the reader: “I strip this little work bare for you,” and so forth. Abbo also composed two books in verse about the siege of Paris by the Normans in the years 886 and 887, at which time he was alive. He was a man acquainted with Sacred Scripture, the councils, and the holy Fathers, and, for the age in which he lived, sufficiently eloquent.

# Here Begins the Argument of the Following Book

[Col. 0761]

Know, reader or hearer, whoever you are—rich in moderate eloquence but lacking Latin—that I strip this little work bare for you, made wholly plain, so that, since you do not understand the Gospels through the obscure commentaries and homilies of learned men, you may at least turn your attention to this little book borrowed from them, whether by reading or by hearing it.

For in this little volume you will find disclosed, for your salvation and for that of other people to whom it will be revealed, everything you read here: namely, explanations of the Gospels, together with little sermons most suitable to their subjects and occasions.

The bishops compelled me, Abbo the monk, more miserable than all mortals, namely Froterius of the see of Poitiers and especially Fulradus of the see of Paris, to fashion this task in a slender style for the benefit of simple clerics, so that from it at all times they may take courage—[Note: “may take courage.” Baluzius suggests that *haustum*, “a draught,” may have been intended. To me the matter seems quite different: in the word *ausum*, “courage,” I see nothing that ought to displease anyone; but the word *potum*, “drink,” which follows, is, unless I am mistaken, defective, and I have little doubt that *potestatem*, “authority,” or some similar word should be restored in its place]—and draw a drink for preaching to those subject to them.

Therefore remember, readers, Abbo in your sacred rites: the native-born guardian of blessed Germanus, Paris, in the face of hostile siege. It is right that I, who had fulfilled the commands of the bishops with almost unspeakable toil, should feel some assistance in my mind through your prayers.

# Sermon I: On the Lord’s Supper

[Col. 0763A]

This day, then, dearest brothers, is spent by Christ’s faithful, dispersed far and wide throughout the world, with fitting devotion in the praise of this most celebrated solemnity.

Today the most worthy Passover is celebrated by the Lord and by the disciples; by him, as an example of the humility to be imitated, their feet are washed, and the holy mysteries of his body and blood are given. Today the holy chrism is prepared by the bishops for the gathering of new peoples; the floors and altars of the temple, and also the sacred vessels, are purified.

Today the devout mother Church rejoices over her adopted sons, whom she bore in faith and whom she once sent out to be corrected for certain expiations of their errors—[Note: The printed *amisit* means “lost”; as above in the case of Baluzius, so here I am compelled to refute Acherius’s conjecture. His suggestion that *admisit*, “she admitted,” should be read is pointless; nor should anyone doubt that *emisit*, “she sent out,” is much more appropriate. Below, in my view, *quoniam imprudenter arripuimus*, “because we rashly took up,” must be restored.]—when she sees them return to her again through reconciliation.

On this day, then, we recognize that all of you are hastening to the same reconciliation, so that you may be absolved from your offenses. With the abundant grace of heavenly mercy granting our request, just as we ask with devoted hearts, we who are debtors and will render an account for you wish to administer this reconciliation to you, relying with all the effort of our inmost hearts on the confidence of him who said: “Whatever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

But when we find that we, wearied by the burden of our sins, are undeservedly subject to the burden of pastoral care—because we rashly took up what we ought not to have taken up—we fear to rise to this task, lest that prophetic saying seem to be turned against us, which is spoken of reprobate shepherds: “They were putting to death souls that do not die, and they were giving life to souls that do not live” (Ezekiel 13:19).

Therefore it is so necessary that we first cleanse our own stains of crime with continual tears, and then admonish each one of you with pastoral concern, that whoever desires to obtain this absolution should return inwardly, turn the eyes of his heart back toward his conscience, and, if he has committed any unlawful acts—acts from which no one is free—should, by remembering his sincere confession and with a contrite spirit, sacrifice an offering to the Lord on the altar of his heart, and strive to correct himself in all things.

For no one can perceive the intentions of our thoughts except he who “searches all hearts and understands all the thoughts of minds” (1 Chronicles 28:9). All indeed come to obtain the effect of absolution, but not with equal disposition. Some, having slipped into the filth of sins, persist with hardened minds; others, when they have at some time acted unjustly, not only are ashamed to commit such acts again, but also earnestly seek to punish them with the bitterest tears.

Of the latter it is written: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14); of the former it immediately follows: “But whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (ibid.).

Therefore, by paternal admonition, we command that no one delay turning to God, since he says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live” (Ezekiel 18:23). And: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, all his sins will be delivered over to oblivion” (Ezekiel 33:12–15).

For this reason he himself also says in the Gospel: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine just persons who do not need penance” (Luke 15:7).

But when, dearest brothers, so many examples from the holy Scriptures, and many others besides, bring such consolation to our minds in understanding, and we do not wish to turn to God, how do we seek forgiveness for our sins?

For the Lord says through the prophet: “I will rain upon one city, but upon another I will not rain” (Amos IV, 17). The Lord rains upon one city when he pours the life-giving shower of the Holy Spirit upon the hearts of certain faithful people who turn to him. But he does not rain upon another city when he withdraws the grace of his visitation from many whose minds are hardened.

Thus it may be feared in this Church that the grace of absolution may be granted to some according to the quality of their merits, while from others, God forbid, it may be withdrawn. For you have heard what the Lord commanded his disciples when he sent them to preach, saying: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there” (Luke 9:4); and: “If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke 10:6).

Therefore, brothers, take every care that the grace may not be unequal, but that, just as the grace of baptism is common to all, so also the grace of absolution may be present for all. For today, as has been said, he celebrated the Passover with his disciples, and tomorrow underwent a glorious death; and by rising from the dead he rescued us from the enemy, Jesus Christ our Lord.

# Sermon II: On the Lord’s Supper and on the Many Sacraments of That Day

Dearest brothers, today, on this day, all Christ’s faithful who are throughout the whole world rejoice and are glad. You ought to know for what reason all Christians should be happier today than on any other day.

You ought therefore to be glad, because on this day the Lord celebrated the Passover with his disciples; on this day the Lord washed the feet of his disciples and showed all people an example of humility, so that all people might humble themselves and wash the feet of the poor.

On this day the Lord held supper with his disciples—that is, he ate and drank with his disciples. On this day the Lord consecrated, for the first time, his body from bread and his blood from wine. On this day the Old Testament ceased, and the law of the Jews reached its end. On this day the New Testament began, that is, the Gospel. Today the religion of Christians began at the Lord’s Supper itself.

Today, on this day, all bishops ought to consecrate—that is, bless—the chrism from which we make new Christians. Today the churches, the altars, and those holy vessels that are in the church ought to be washed. Today holy mother Church rejoices to receive and reconcile to herself her sons, that is, Christians, whom she sent outside because of their faults.

And on this day, brothers, we see that you have come to this mother Church for this reason: so that you may obtain the reconciliation that you lost because of your sins, and by which you may be absolved from all your sins.

Truly, dearest brothers, you ought to know where this practice began, by which bishops cast sinful people out of the church at the beginning of Lent and, after they had completed a worthy penance, received those sinners back into the church.

For when our Lord, who is Almighty God, first made the man Adam, he made him wholly holy, just, and immortal. Holiness, justice, and immortality caused Adam to possess the image and likeness of God.

Therefore God said before creating Adam: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26)—that is, let us make man holy, just, and immortal.

The Lord commends us to possess this image of his when he says in the Gospel: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). And elsewhere he says: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

Therefore, because God made Adam so good and so holy, we read “that he sent him into paradise to work it and guard it” (Genesis 7:15). In that paradise the Lord gave him every glory. There he saw the angels and spoke with them; and he would never have died if he had not sinned.

There he heard the Lord speaking with him and commending to him such obedience that he should never eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

But at the very hour in which Adam sinned, the Lord, who is the Bishop of bishops, drove him out of paradise and said to him: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 3:19).

And after Adam had been driven out of paradise, what did he do? Certainly he performed a long penance for six hundred years and more. Finally, after his death, he was sent into the infernal prison, where for a long time he wept and grieved because through his sin he had lost paradise. For a very long time he remained there grieving and doing penance, until our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the High Priest of high priests, absolved him through his Passion, freed him from the punishments of darkness, and restored paradise to him.

Therefore, brothers, we bishops are the vicars of our Lord Jesus Christ in this world; we have been sent and ordained in his place. For this reason, after the apostles, the Lord gave us the power to bind souls and to loose them, and commanded us to build up and plant good people in the house of the Lord, and to uproot [from it], that is, from the Church. Thus the Lord says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, and to build and to plant in the house of the Lord (Jer. I, 10).” Pay attention, brothers, with a good disposition, to what we wish to say to you. For this reason the Lord sent Adam into paradise, so that in that paradise all the elect might be born, might carry out God’s will until the fullness of old age, and from there might pass into the heavenly homeland. And indeed they would have done so if Adam had not sinned.

Brothers, we bishops hold this example of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Church, while sinners hold the example of Adam. For example, just as the Son of God sent holy and righteous Adam into paradise, so we and all priests send people sanctified and justified in baptism into the Church. Why do we send into the Church people who have already been made holy through baptism? For the very reason for which the Lord sent Adam into paradise—that is, so that he might work in and guard that paradise. Likewise, we priests send baptized people into the Church so that at all times they may carry out God’s will in it and guard that Church, that is, Christendom.

Almighty God gave Adam a law which he had to observe through obedience. What law? That he should not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Likewise, through us the Lord gives you a law which you must keep in the Church. What law does the Lord give you through us, that is, through our admonition? “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery (*moechaberis*); you shall not adulterate (*adulterabis*); you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not swear falsely; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Exod. XX, 13).” Brothers, the Lord gives you all these commandments through us, so that you may guard them and carry them out in obedience.

But what did the Lord do to Adam because he did not preserve obedience? Certainly, he expelled him from paradise, weeping, mourning, and suffering great anguish. Likewise, because you did not preserve obedience to God’s commandments, which we named above, we bishops expelled you from the Church and sang after you what the Lord sang after Adam when he drove him from paradise: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread (Gen. III, 19),” and the rest.

But what did Adam do after he had been expelled from paradise? Certainly, Adam performed great and worthy penance, so that he might be worthy for God to receive him again into paradise. Likewise, you have performed worthy penance during this Lent, so that you might be worthy to enter the Church and communicate in the body and blood of the Lord. Therefore holy Mother Church joyfully receives you among her children, who are God’s adopted children, that is, the elect. Yet you must know this: as blessed Ambrose said, no bishop can absolve penitents unless their penance itself has been worthy of absolution.

Penance takes its name from *poena*, “punishment,” so that the sinful person may undergo punishment in the body by fasting and afflicting his flesh through abstinence, and by keeping vigils in prayer. Hence blessed Jerome says: “Great fasts drive powerful vices from a person, and prolonged moderation in food and drink kills lust.” Therefore we tell you this: if you have not yet performed the kind of penance that pleases God, complete it of your own will. And if you cannot fast or give alms, which free your souls from hell, you must not suppose that you should never do more penance than has been prescribed for you. Rather, you ought to do more of your own will, as the saints did: they wore haircloth, abstained from meat and wine, and fasted until evening out of desire for eternal life. Such penance was never prescribed to those holy people by priests.

Brothers, Adam has now been received into the heavenly paradise; through his very arduous penance he merited fellowship with God’s faithful, redeemed by Christ’s blood. And you, thanks be to God, have today been received into the Church, as into paradise, because of your penance. Since you have gathered on this day to receive fellowship with holy Church and absolution from your sins, and since you have come with the fullest desire to receive such great joy from the solemnity of Easter and to communicate in the Lord’s body and blood, pride must not remain in you—the pride through which the angel Lucifer fell from heavenly glory into hell. Of this pride it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives his grace to the humble (James IV, 6).” If that angel Lucifer lost eternal glory through pride, we who are human can never possess that glory except through humility.

All anger must cease among you. Of anger the apostle John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John III, 13).” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins (Matt. VI, 14).” You must also forgive, so that you do not deceive other people through your vicious lies and your most artful oaths. Truly, the whole Church curses people of this kind who do such things, praying with the Prophet: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips (Ps. XI, 4).” And: “Those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts: give them, O God, according to their works (Ps. XXVII, 3).”

The Lord admonishes you to restrain the gluttony of the belly, saying: “Take care lest your hearts be weighed down with feasting and drunkenness (Luke XXI, 34).” Feasting and drunkenness mean eating too much and drinking too much. You know well that because of gluttony of the belly the rich man is tormented in hell. Those people who always eat and drink to satiety and intoxication make a god of their belly. Hence the Apostle says: “Whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. III, 19),” that is, their shame will belong to those whose minds are set on earthly things. And again the Apostle says: “‘Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods (1 Cor. VI, 13),’” that is, for nourishment. But God will destroy both this belly and these foods at the end of the world.

This also admonishes us to flee the foulness of lust and every kind of fornication. Hence the Apostle says: “Neither fornicators nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. VI, 9).” And blessed Jerome says: “The person who lives in luxury is dead while living.”

Moreover, it is a great goodness to abandon greed, of which the Apostle says: “Greed is the service of idols (Eph. V, 5),” that is, the greedy person worships idols and serves demons. And again the Apostle says: Those people “who wish to be rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare (1 Tim. VI, 9),” that is, into the devil’s chain, and they fall “into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction (ibid.).” Hence the apostle James says to such rich people: “Your riches have rotted; your garments are eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted; and their rust will be a testimony against you, and the rust itself will devour your flesh like fire (James V, 2).”

Everyone who has riches, possesses sufficient clothing, and owns gold or silver, yet sees poor people dying of hunger or cold before him, is a murderer. Regarding discord, we must admonish you that discord should never exist among you, because under heaven there is no plague that so devastates kingdoms, cities, villages, and the people themselves as discord does, as the Savior testifies in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself,” that is, in conflict with itself, “will be laid waste (Luke XI, 17),” that is, it will become a wilderness.

For all these sins mentioned above, you ought to beseech God to grant you the performance of such penance and such amendment as may please God and profit you for eternal life, with the help of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. At the church door, for penitents who have not yet obtained reconciliation

[Col. 0769A]

You also, brothers, whom Mother Church does not now receive because the time of your completed penance has not yet arrived—you, I say, need exhortation and consolation, namely, so that you may not be saddened because Mother Church does not yet receive you. For we dare not, nor ought we, deceive your souls, which have been entrusted to us so that we may lead them to eternal life. Certainly no bishop can grant absolution except after penance has been performed and worthy satisfaction has been made.

Therefore we wish you to be strengthened, consoled, and exhorted, so that you may not be sorrowful, but may observe your penance with every care. For your penance, if it has been properly performed, is great joy for the angels in heaven. As the Savior himself says: “There is joy before the angels of God in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need penance (Luke XV, 7).” Therefore repent with all humility and purity of heart, without anger and without causing any scandal, and beseech the merciful God to look upon you and graciously receive your humility.

Take care also that, by repenting and fasting, you do not fall into any criminal sin, because the person who fasts and sins is like the devil, who is always fasting and always sinning. You must also observe this in your penance: perform a fast that is sanctified for two reasons, namely, through prayers and almsgiving. Hence the Prophet admonishes us: “Sanctify a fast (Joel I, 14).” May the Almighty grant that we and you may perform such a fast at all times, one that may open paradise to us.

As for drunkenness, I rebuke you, brothers and fellow citizens: turn away from it and do not make it your habitual practice. For drunkenness excuses no vice, but generates every sin, and it is a great and criminal sin. This drunkenness, which you maintain from morning until deep night, is the destruction of your souls. Truly, you will never have eternal life except through abstinence from feasting and drunkenness, that is, from excessive eating and drinking.

You also do not observe the fast by which you ought to conquer the devil; instead, you break every fast, both that commended by God and that commanded by our authority. You do not consider that the person who breaks one day during Lent breaks the whole of Lent. Therefore the holy canons prescribe that whoever breaks one day of Lent should repay his God, the author of the fast, forty days for that one day.

Because of gluttony and greed for food, Adam was expelled from paradise. And if we wish to receive our inheritance, that is, paradise, it is necessary for us to return to paradise by another way—that is, through fasting and abstinence. May he deign to grant this, who, perfect in Trinity and unity, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Lord’s Supper, for reconciled penitents

Today, brothers, is the Lord’s Supper, at which our Lord ate with his disciples and washed their feet, giving us an example so that we likewise might do this for our servants and the poor. Today the chrism is consecrated, through which all become Christians. On this day penitents receive fellowship with the Church, and the holy angels rejoice over the reconciliation of those people who truly repented that they had sinned and patiently endured tribulation in their bodies by fasting, keeping vigils, and going around to places of prayer, so that they might obtain God’s favor.

To you, therefore, brothers, whom holy Church receives today, I speak this admonition and exhortation. This warning is especially appropriate for you: remember at all times what sort of people you were before confession, penance, and the forgiveness that, by God’s inspiration, you have now obtained. For God himself said: “Without me you can do nothing (John XV, 5).”

Therefore, before the confession and penance for your sins, you were children of the devil and slaves of sin, because “the one who commits sin is a slave of sin (John VIII, 34).” But now, because you have fled the devil and come through penance to merciful Christ, you have been freed from sin and made servants of God.

It is therefore necessary for you, with all diligence and care, to labor in every good work: not to eat too much, not to drink to intoxication, neither before the hour nor after it; and to strive to live by your own justice, not by plunder, because, as the Apostle says, “Plunderers will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. VI, 10).”

You must also remember the Apostle’s terrible sentence: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all (James II, 10),” that is, whoever commits one sin offends God, who forbade us to commit all sins. Therefore I tell you these things so that, if you do not commit again the sins for which you repented, you may not commit others either. For repentance is of no benefit if, after penance, a person returns to sin. Such a person is like a dog returning to its vomit.

Of people who repeat sins they have already committed, the Holy Spirit says through the prophet David: “For they did not seek the Lord’s ordinances (Ps. CXVIII, 155),” that is, they did not remain faithful to the promises they made in baptism and in the confession of their iniquities. May God grant that you avoid such conduct at all times—God who receives you today into fellowship with his people.

## SERMON V. On the foundation and growth of Christendom

Consider, dearest brothers, and reflect with all your heart and all your soul, how great a name “Christendom” is, and how it has grown and spread among all the nations inhabiting the whole world. Certainly, no cause, no kingdom, and no construction of cities ever built with complete labor was as great as Christendom, which our wicked life daily destroys.

Although Christendom grew, and its sacred religion was established amid hardships impossible to describe, it nevertheless gloriously conquered every superstition and the deadly idolatry of paganism, and cast it down to the dust. Holy Christendom, which is the city of God, finally led its observers to perfection. Nor is it surprising if a perfect work makes perfect people.

From what, then, did the Christian religion proceed? From an immovable foundation, plainly, the firmest of all founded things. Concerning this foundation the Apostle speaks with truthful assertion, saying: “No one can lay another foundation besides that” foundation of Christendom “which has already been laid (1 Cor. III, 11).” The prophet David also calls it a pavement, saying: “My soul has clung to the pavement (Ps. CXVIII, 25).”

This foundation, or pavement, is therefore Jesus Christ our Lord, upon whose death the Christian religion was founded. O what labor was involved in building Christendom! Observe, you worshipers of God, with what indescribable torment of death our Lord established the Church of Christendom, which those who hate justice wickedly destroy. In order to found it and also establish it throughout the various regions of the world, the Lord Jesus endured the devil’s temptations, human reproaches, spitting, the crown of thorns, and finally the dreadful death of the cross, with nails of fearful weight in his hands and feet. At the same time, holy Christ, himself holy, willingly received the spear in his side.

Apart from that sacrament of Catholic worship, however, he fully created and governs without any hardship all things that divine activity created and rules. At the very beginning of the world’s formation, he created heaven and earth, angels, air, and water from nothing, without any burden. On the first day of the world he made light from nothing; on the second day he established the firmament in the midst of the waters without any labor; on the third he brought forth the kinds of sea and land, with shoots rooted firmly in the earth; on the fourth, the lights of heaven from the light that had appeared as made on the first day, without any burden at all; on the fifth he created swimming and flying creatures from the waters without any pain; and on the sixth day he formed the remaining living creatures, and the human being partly from earth and partly from nothing.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, accomplished all these things gently and without any bitterness, while always remaining with the Father and the Holy Spirit—personally a Trinity, substantially a Unity. Yet it did not please the Almighty, who was dead and behold is alive for ever and ever, holding the keys of death and Hades, to allow the worship of orthodox religion to flourish so easily. How, then, did it please him? Brothers, be intensely attentive, so that you may perceive this with the hearing of your hearts. He undertook the altar of the cross, where he also cast himself as the foundation of Christendom, and set before his followers an example for perfecting that same religious life.

Mindful of this pavement and example, blessed Peter the apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. II, 21).” Christ the Lord therefore surrendered his fleshly life in order to establish the Church of Christendom, which unjust judges ceaselessly overthrow in blind greed. Christ God for this reason handed over his saving body to burial, so that every sacrilegious greed might lie buried forever and thus remain continually silent and at rest. Christ God by the death of the flesh killed the death of the soul, so that the appetite of human flesh might always remain dead in a human being made like God.

Moreover, Christ, the Almighty and Life, rose from the dead, strengthened the apostles, and sent them into the vast world against wolves as sheep. He clothed those first apostles in the armor of true Christendom and, with his blessing, commanded them to fight their battles bravely.

Consider, therefore, brothers, with how much labor and how many tribulations the apostles—those trees of paradise and pillars—spread Christendom, the kingdom of heaven, through the earth, and built the seat of God in spite of the world’s rulers, who are called wolves and are brands of hell.

Thus the apostles each chose provinces for themselves, some larger than others, in which to build the sheepfolds of Christendom. Andrew built Christendom in Achaia, purchased by the gallows of the cross, with Aegeas made a brand of hell as proconsul. Thomas, pierced by four spears in four parts of his body in Nearer India, established the hall of Christendom, while King Misdaeus resisted and was for that reason turned into fuel for Hades. Bartholomew likewise courageously founded the enclosures of Christ-loving faith in Further India through decapitation, under the conquerable King Astyages. Matthew also brought Christ to Ethiopia’s King Hyrcanus and strengthened him there through martyrdom.

The apostles Simon and Judas, likewise imitators of Christ, their sole foundation, poured the teachings of the worship of God into countless hearts of pagans in the kingdom of Persia. For this most precious deed they were killed by the priests of idols, and they obtained heaven for themselves and for the Church of the entire kingdom of Persia, while those same priests were reduced to firewood for the flames of Avernus.

In this way Christendom, which is the city of God, was propagated—founded upon the savage deaths of its propagators. James, the brother of the most blessed evangelist John, and likewise his namesake James, the brother of our Lord Jesus Christ, also died in order to establish the holy faith in Samaria and Judaea: the one by Herod’s sword, the other by the deadly blow of a certain fuller and by being swiftly buried beneath the stones of the Jews.

John, nevertheless, the dearest to Christ among his fellow disciples, offered Asia the streams of wisdom drawn from his master’s breast, and established Christ’s Christendom there most honorably as a bride. Philip likewise, teaching the heavenly life—that is, Christendom—fixed the chief enclosures of that religion in Illicinae.

[Note: “Fixed the chief enclosures of that religion in Illicinae.” Let others determine whether there is any city or region of this name; I myself know of none, and I suspect that the manuscript used by Acherius is no more accurate here than in the passages that follow.]

Thus it was not the pleasures of the flesh, nor luxuries, nor the riches of this age, nor honors that planted Christendom throughout the world, but the grievous deaths of the apostles and of those who obeyed their teachings. Yet first came the saving religion, and Christ, ever multiplying its offspring, caused the whole most holy religion, shining more brightly than the sun, to reign everywhere among the kingdoms.
