The most blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, began to preach Christ in Judaea and, amid many tribulations, to plant Christendom through various cities and their regions. At last they reached Rome, where the head of the world was located, where the leading men of the world remained, and where, consequently, gatherings of all nations converged.

Pay attention, brothers, to Rome, where Nero was emperor of only the lower world—for there is another, higher and starry one—and where Simon Magus, infinitely skilled in wickedness, was also present. The apostolic princes, appointed by God over the whole earth, came there in order to take worldly rule away from the devil and his members, Nero and Simon, and restore it to the heavenly King, to whom it rightfully belongs. And so, thanks be to God, it happened.

For the heavenly envoys planted such a great and expansive Christendom there that it almost filled the whole world and even shattered every idol in it. But the ancient enemy, the possessor of Nero and the Magus Simon, saw this work of divine religion flourishing and growing, worthy of all praise, and, grieving over it, persuaded those who were brands of Avernus to kill Christ’s envoys, who were trees of paradise, because by words and miracles they were striving with all their strength to plant Christ and his worship. Simon and Nero, on the other hand, vied with each other in striving to uproot it as far as they could.

Such a struggle to build what was good and to uproot it burned among the athletes of God and the kindling of Avernus. But so that this contest would not last long, and so that Nero would believe Simon Magus to be God, unclean spirits began to carry Simon through the air. Paul prayed; Peter commanded Satan; and Simon, flying, was hurled down. In revenge for the Magus’s ruin, Nero therefore returned the citizens of God to the stars: Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the loss of his head.

Thus Christendom was planted and established through the precious deaths of the apostles and of all the saints, especially the martyrs, who died in various ways; and it was increased throughout the world upon Christ, its foundation. Thereafter it was illumined by the sound examples and teachings of the blessed confessors. Then pious kings and their religious nobles founded monasteries and religious houses of Christendom everywhere and enriched them with their possessions and gifts.

Moreover, rulers who were illustrious possessors of cities abandoned those cities and built halls of Christ in them, establishing episcopal sees there, by which the hearts and souls of the faithful who believe might be ceaselessly strengthened in God. They handed themselves and all they possessed—their villages and estates—to these sees and to the monasteries, and contributed generously to those canons and monks who served Christ there day and night. For those foremost rulers knew with certainty that in no other way could the Christendom established from heaven stand securely and endure to the end of the world.

Therefore, alas, those who are now the rulers of the world daily dissipate this religion, so dear to God and so salutary to human souls: kings, counts, viscounts, consuls, proconsuls, their deputies, the lord’s vassals, their retainers, and all wicked judges.

By perverse cunning they take away from urban churches and monasteries the property and estates by which bishops, monks, and canons ought to live. Through various tricks and frauds, these invaders destroy the defenses of Christendom—that is, episcopal sees and monasteries—by plunder, robbery, false leases, and unjust grants of immunity. Since they possess these properties, they disdain to return the revenues entered in the records. Thus sacrilegious possessors transfer Christ’s property to themselves as a holding and hereditary estate; sometimes they violently seize the same ecclesiastical property and possess it unlawfully.

For this reason we already know and see many monasteries abandoned by clerics because the property from which they ought to live has been taken away from them. What else, then, are such sacrilegious people, plunderers, and violent robbers except brands of hell, the devil’s food, and uprooters of paradise, which is the Church of Christ?

In hell the devils consume no other food than the souls of those who devour the property of God’s churches, laying it waste or possessing it unjustly. Certainly, after the end of the present life, demons consume their souls every hour, and they will devour them forever. Woe to you, plunderers and robbers of churches and of their poor! Truly, those poor people come daily to the tombs of the saints, crying out that they are being killed by plunderers through hunger and nakedness.

But what will happen to those who inflict such evils upon the churches, their ministers of God, and their servants? True and everlasting punishment. And what will come to the ministers of God and their poor servants who suffer countless such evils? Truly, eternal glory—provided that they patiently endure adversity.

Therefore, brothers who are truly Christians, do not greatly fear the false Christians who oppress you daily. Indeed, if they devastate you, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, whose name you bear, honors you himself and daily enriches you with his resources, so that you become poor not so much through your enemies as rich through God himself.

Thus Scripture exhorts us: “Those who fear God will never lack good things (Ps. XXXIII, 11).” And again the Prophet says: “I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread (Ps. XXXVI, 25).” And: “Hope in the Lord, do good, and you will be fed by his riches (Ps. XXXVI, 3).”

Know therefore, brothers, that God has never shown himself to love anything as much as Christendom. For in the Scriptures he calls it his city, in which he is continually pleased to dwell. Concerning this city the Prophet says: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God (Ps. LXXXVI, 3).”

This same city, that is, Christendom, is plainly called the bride of the Lamb, that is, of the Son of God. Blessed John therefore bears witness to it in the Apocalypse, saying: “One of the seven angels said to me: ‘Come, I will show you the new bride, the wife of the Lamb (Apoc. XXI, 9).’” Let all the Christian people rejoice, therefore, because they have been called and made the bride of the Lamb, that is, the bride of the Son of God.

Christendom is likewise called the heavenly Jerusalem, as the same John proves in the same Apocalypse: “I saw Jerusalem,” he says, “coming down from heaven, adorned with pure gold and woven with precious stones (ibid., 10).”

Let all Christendom spread throughout the whole world rejoice, therefore, because it has merited being called the bride of Christ and the city of God, which the evangelist of the Apocalypse asserts descended from heaven.

Truly, whatever begins from the earth is earthly; everything earthly is transitory; and whatever is transitory is worthless. Therefore Christendom, which is the city of God and the seat of God—of which it is written, “God sits upon his holy seat (Ps. XLVI, 9)”—did not begin from earth, but descended from heaven in its most glorious author, Christ.

Consequently, the Christian name is not earthly, and the Catholic religion is not transitory but everlasting. Nor is it worthless, but most dear to Christ, like his own flesh, like his own soul, which he delivered to death for Christendom. Christendom is his throne; the Church is his temple: “The temple,” says the Apostle, “is holy, which you are (1 Cor. III, 17),” you Christians.

The door, entrance, and gate of this city and temple is Christ the Lord and our God. I think that the patriarch Jacob said of this place: “Truly, this place is holy, and it is nothing other than the house of God (Gen. XXVIII, 16),” which is Christendom, and “the gate of heaven,” which is Christ. He himself confirms this, saying: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved (John X, 9).”

Therefore, brothers, let us strive with every effort and with exalted desires, finally praying without ceasing, as we are taught by the apostolic voice, so that through God’s immense mercy we may be made worthy to enter more and more through that door, to become daily capable fellow workers of Christ’s city, and to grow in this valley of tears from virtue to virtue, until we see the God of gods in heavenly Zion.

Already a great part of Christendom rejoices there with its author Christ and exults with its foundation: the chief apostles, the holy martyrs, the venerable confessors, and the consecrated virgins. May we, who are the remaining forms of that same religion and are still afflicted and burdened by the weight of an earthly body, be joined to them through unceasing love, perpetual contemplation, and inexpressible joy.

Therefore, brothers, just as we bear the name of Christ and the name of citizens who are already heavenly, so let us pray that we may follow and imitate their sacred footsteps and examples, so that in both name and life we may be deemed worthy of their fellowship.

Indeed, our brotherhood, which is the city of God and Christendom having Christ as its foundation, encompasses and embraces all the earth where their sound went forth and all the regions of the world to which their words reached (Ps. XVIII). In this way we are all Christian brothers; living throughout the kingdoms of the world, we are also fellow citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Among us, many already possess spiritually, beyond the stars, halls gleaming with the various splendor of their merits; the rest, still remaining in earthly flesh, inhabit earthly monasteries. All these hosts—those rejoicing above and those wandering below—are the city of God, which the evangelist John saw descending from heaven, adorned and arranged with every beauty.

For the prosperity of this city we pray daily as we sing the psalm: “Save your people, O Lord,” that is, all Christendom, “and bless your inheritance,” namely, that same Christendom, “and rule them,” the Christians, “and exalt them forever (Ps. XXVII, 9).”

Without doubt, this Christendom is the holy Catholic Church of God—that is, universal and orthodox—spread throughout the entire world. This is the house of God, the temple of the Lord, and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, this is the vineyard into which the Lord brought us to work his will. To the laborers he promised one denarius, namely, one eternal life. This is that house and city of God concerning which the following words of the Holy Spirit shone forth through the Prophet: “Unless the Lord builds the house and guards the city,” that is, Christendom, “those who wish to build and guard it labor and keep watch in vain (Ps. CXXVI, 1).”

Concerning this very city, that is, concerning Christendom, the aforementioned Evangelist testifies: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, prepared by God. And I heard a voice from the throne saying: ‘Behold, the dwelling place of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them (Apoc. XXI, 2).’”

That city of God, to be sure, the unjust and sacrilegious lovers of this age strive every day utterly to destroy, by plundering it and afflicting it with every kind of scourge. Who are these rapacious wolves who, pursuing Christianity without respite, devour and tear it apart? In the eastern and southern regions of the world there are the Idumeans and Ishmaelites, Moabites and Hagarenes, Ammonites and Amalekites, together with the pseudo-Christians who are worse than they. In the northern and western climate there are the Norman people, likewise the Danes, and also the utterly impious nation of the Tungri; and our own people, more cruel than all these nations, who are Christians only in name. They do not cease at any hour to kill Christ’s people [Col. 0777A] with hunger and cold—namely, by eating the food and drinking the clothing of the poor. Why do they do this? Because they are more friends of the world than of God: they love fields more than the stars; they cherish their horses and dogs more than the poor whom Christ purchased with his blood.

Such plunderers and ravagers plainly destroy and abandon Christianity of their own accord, scorning to dwell in the city of the divine Emperor. Consequently they become less and less citizens and members of God’s household, but instead become members of the devil’s household and firebrands of hell. Therefore, O Church of God! O city of God! Patiently endure these wolves, who devour you, Christ’s lambs. For the evil which our adversaries suppose that they are doing to you, they inflict much more heavily upon themselves. No one can harm another before harming himself. [Col. 0777B] Concerning these wolves, grieving for you, the Lord says through the Prophet:

> “All who work [Col. 0778A] iniquity thus devour the people as though they were eating bread” (Psalm 52:5).

Therefore that same merciful shepherd of ours, Christ the Lord, strengthens us with kindly consolation, saying:

> “Do not be afraid, little flock, because it has pleased our Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

Therefore, brothers, let us be patient toward everyone with one accord, both toward guests and toward enemies. For a person who possesses patience can easily overcome every vice, as Scripture testifies. Thus, truly, with the help of the same Lord Jesus Christ, who is the beginning and the end of all things and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever, we shall at all times be able to cultivate the city of God that is within us—that is, Christianity, founded upon the blood of our Redeemer—and to guard it with sacred vigils and adorn it with devout conduct. [Col. 0778B] Amen.

# In the Year of Our Lord 923. Dado, Bishop of Verdun.

[Col. 0777]

## Historical Notice

*(From Gallia Christiana, volume XIV, old edition.)*

[Col. 0777C] Dado, the nephew and disciple of Berhard, is mentioned in the Life of John, abbot of Gorze, whose associate he was, as a man of the highest intelligence and of the most renowned holiness. He too was abbot of Saint-Viton, and was raised to episcopal dignity through the favor of Louis, king of Germany, in the year 881. Bertolf, archbishop of Trier, although requested by a letter from Pope John VIII to approve his election, could not be induced to do so. Nevertheless, Dado was ordained without his consent, and with the greatest prudence administered for a long time both the abbey of Saint-Viton, which he retained, and the church of Verdun, for which he acquired extensive possessions.

Together with Archbishop Ratbod of Trier and the other bishops of the province, he attended the councils of Mainz and Metz in 888. Wasburg reports that he composed a poem in elegiac verse, later destroyed, concerning the calamities inflicted upon the church of Verdun in his own time and that of his predecessors, especially during the invasion of Lorraine by the Northmen in 889, when the cities of Toul and Verdun were burned and many priests and clerics, both of the cathedral and of Saint-Viton, were slaughtered.

He appears to be the same Dado, bishop of Verdun, to whom Remigius, a monk of Auxerre, wrote a letter around the year 890. There is also another letter to him from Solomon, bishop of Constance. In 893 he composed an abridged Life of his predecessors Atto and Berhard, in which he lists the properties they had bestowed upon the church, as well as the abbey of Mont-Falcon, which, by a gift of King Arnulf, was to be held in perpetuity.

He divided the property of the church of Verdun between himself and the chapter [Col. 0778C] in obedience to the thirteenth canon of the Council of Tribur, which he had attended in 895. In 906 he sent a letter to Ratbod of Trier, asking him to admit Arduinus, a priest of the church of Verdun, into the parish or diocese of Trier. He subscribed the charter of Charles the Simple assigning the abbey of Suestrensis to the monastery of Prüm, on 19 January 916.

Because of his loyalty to the kings of Germany, he was hated by that same King Charles and by Boso Guntrannus, who blamed him for the killing of King Zwentibold. Not long afterward, Boso gathered troops and began devastating the lands of the bishopric, bringing slaughter everywhere. To make Verdun secure from the enemy, Dado summoned soldiers to the city; but he could not prevent the cathedral and the greater part of the town from being treacherously burned in 917. In that fire the records, books, and memories of the bishops of the church of Verdun were destroyed.

To prevent these things from being entirely consigned to oblivion, Bertarius, a priest of Verdun, composed a short history of the bishops [Col. 0778D], which he dedicated to Dado in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate. With Uncrimnus, a monk of Saint Michael on the Meuse, he entered into an exchange concerning two meadows situated at Rofiedicourt, at Castella, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, in the eighth year of the reign of King Charles in the kingdom of Lothair—that is, in the year 919.

He is said to have attended the consecration of Gauzelin, bishop of Toul, in 922. Around the same time he was also present at the election of Libo, bishop of Lausanne, according to a charter in which he is called Tatto. He died in 923, according to Hugh of Flavigny and Flodoard, and was buried in the basilica of Saint-Viton.

[Col. 0779]

## Dado’s Historical Fragment on the Life of Hatto and Berhard, His Predecessors

*(In D. Calmet, History of Lorraine, volume I, proofs, p. 540.)*

[Col. 0779A] In the year 893 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, while the most glorious lord Arnulf reigned as king in his fifth year, and in the thirteenth year of my own ordination, in the ninth indiction, I, DADO, bishop of the church of Verdun, began to consider in my mind the various events of the present age, to recall the deeds of former pontiffs to memory, and diligently and profitably to investigate them from the faithful of our church. For this reason I recorded in writing the deeds of orthodox prelates, so that the memory of those whose names we believe to have been written eternally in heaven might remain eternal with us.

Lord Hatto, therefore, our predecessor, lived in the time of Emperor Lothair and likewise of his son Lothair, and continued until the first year of King Charles. That venerable pontiff bestowed many things upon the Church worthy of remembrance; we have thought it useful to commend a few of them in writing. For he obtained from King Lothair possessions lying in many places, namely, in the county of Verdun, Alberevilla, and so forth.

That same venerable bishop also began this new basilica; but it was honorably completed by his successor, namely our uncle, Lord Berhard, bishop. He too assumed the governance of this church in the time of Charles and governed it successfully until the time of Louis, King of Germany. For—to recall briefly a few of his successful deeds—this renowned shepherd, our uncle Lord Berhard, was extraordinarily zealous in ecclesiastical discipline, beyond what could be believed or accomplished, [Col. 0779C] and, being most devoted to the episcopal ministry and the religious life, bestowed very many things upon this church, which now bear eternal witness to his zeal. He also gave other things.

In the basilica of Saint Peter and Saint Viton he also established eight canons, and gave them the properties belonging to that church, just as he then held them under his authority; also a tithe of the rams which are received for our use from the hundred of Brasensis at the appropriate times. He also gave to that altar a priestly vestment ornamented with gold, namely a *platena*, that is, one made of *dirotanum*, with drops, and so forth. He also placed a pallium over the tomb of that holy patron, and so forth.

We too, who by divine disposition succeeded him and, after our uncle, assumed the governance of this church from Lord Louis the king, and after his death assumed the emperor Lord Charles, his brother, and have now reached the time of the most glorious King Arnulf, their nephew, have judged it most salutary to add to this work whatever I have been able, with the Lord’s help, to add to the church entrusted to me—in properties and dependents, and in all ecclesiastical ornaments. He gave, and so forth.

All these things the emperor Lord Charles assigned to the aforesaid church according to solemn custom and granted it to possess perpetually. The most glorious King Arnulf likewise gave as its own, by a charter of his authority, to the aforesaid church the abbey called Mont-Falcon, built in honor of Saint Germanus and situated in the county of Dol, together with everything belonging to it, and so forth. [Col. 0780C]

# In the Year of Our Lord 927. Agio, Archbishop of Narbonne.

[Col. 0779]

## Historical Notice

*(From Gallia Christiana, volume VI, p. 25.)*

[Col. 0779C] After the killing of Arnust, the clergy and people of Narbonne assembled to determine how they might avenge it and elect another archbishop. They thought it best to summon their neighbor Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles, for consultation. He went to Agde before the day appointed for the election and before the bishops of the province of Narbonne had gathered together. Together with Amelius, bishop of Uzès, he raised to the metropolitan see Gerard, Amelius’s nephew, who, as Saxius says, had been “a priest” to Hugh, son of Bertha, “the senatrix and administrator of the Roman Church”—that is, he lived on alms.

Thus Rostagnus crossed over to the opposing party. He went to Narbonne to expel Agio, abbot of Vabres, who had been elected by the suffragan bishops assembled in the legitimate interim procedure, and to substitute Gerard for him. Saxius further adds that Pope John X sent a letter to Rostagnus concerning the deposition of Agio. Catellus, however, reports the contrary: he cites a letter of that same Pope John, published by the Sammarthani in the four-part *Gallia Christiana*, which we too reprint. From it it is plainly evident that Gerard went to Rome to have his election approved by the supreme pontiff, suffered rejection, and, after returning, devastated the bishopric of Narbonne by armed force under forged papal letters, capturing Agio by treachery so that he could not travel to Rome.

After hearing these things, the supreme pontiff instructed the bishops of the province of Narbonne not to recognize Gerard as bishop, and sent Agio the pallium, as he had requested, around the year 914. Gerard nevertheless did not become quiet. For he continued to conduct himself as archbishop and was excommunicated by the same pontiff somewhat later, as we learn from the latter’s letter to the archbishops of Narbonne and Lyon, preserved in Catellus, *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 83 and following.

Meanwhile, in 915, Agio attended, together with the archbishops of Lyon and Besançon, the council held at Saint-Marcel of Chalon. Around the year 922 he wrote this brief letter to the bishops Agambert and Elefons, published by Catellus in book [I] of the *History of the Counts of Toulouse* and corrected by Baluzius on the basis of an old exemplar:

[Col. 0781C]

> “Agio, bishop of the see of Narbonne, sends manifold prayers to the venerable bishops Agambert and Elefons.
>
> “We have heard that you must travel to the court in these days. For this reason we went to beseech our counts Ermengaud and Raimund, in order that we might entreat you not to disdain to obtain a royal charter for us. Thus we pray and entreat you: do not be reluctant to obtain from the king the matter reported above, as it has been written. Fare well.”

**Note:** [Col. 0781] These are Ragemundus and Ermengaud, princes of Gothia, whom Flodoard, under the year 932, reports as having commended themselves to King Ralph.

This letter had a favorable outcome, for the desired charter of Charles was issued in the same year—namely, in the thirtieth year of the reign of Lord Charles, on 9 July, in the tenth indiction—“at the estate of Turnus,” according to Catellus, *Commentaries on Occitania*, p. 776, who explains this as the city of Tours. In the authentic document, however, it is expressly written “at the estate of Ternis,” as Baluzius informs us in book IV of *Maria of Spain*, p. 375; he also writes that this place was in Belgica Secunda.

Indeed, Turnus seems to Mabillon in *Supplement to the Diplomas*, p. 49, to be an estate in the district of Reims near the Aisne. In any case, this charter contains no mention of the bishops named above, but only of Wigo of Girona, whom they may perhaps have employed as mediator because of his greater authority, or whom Agio himself may have summoned as patron. See Mabillon under the year 922, no. 51.

Elefons, who is mentioned in Agio’s letter, is the same person who, in the charter of Charles the Simple preserved in Catellus, p. 777, is called “Bishop Erifons, residing at Narbonne.” These words persuaded some that he had been archbishop of Narbonne, which is not true; Baluzius instead counts him among the prelates of Venasque or Carpentras.

In the year 924—or in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Charles the Simple in Aquitaine—on 17 December, with the consent of Agio the archbishop, the viscount Odo and his wife Richildis transferred an allodial holding [reading uncertain: *alolium*] near Sallelas to Alfonso, abbot of Mont-Olivier.

Agio is mentioned in a charter of donation made to the church of Narbonne by a certain Teuderic and his wife Sposia, concerning everything they possessed in the estate of Sejanus in the territory of Narbonne, in the twenty-ninth year of King Charles, on 28 September. In the following year, a woman named Gildrica showed herself generous toward the same Agio, or Aigo, while Charles reigned in his thirtieth year, according to the cartulary of Saint Paul.

Not long afterward he passed to the better life—namely, at the end of 926 or the beginning of 927. He may perhaps be the same as the archbishop Aidagius recorded in the Crassense necrology on 11 March.

[Col. 0781]

## History of the Abbey of Vabres, by Agio

*(History of Languedoc, volume I, appendix, p. 308.)*

[Col. 0781D] At the time when, from the regions of Europe and the northern quarter, the most savage and more than barbarous people of the Marcomanni spread forth and, entering Gaul, afflicted the holy Church with their fiercest blows—for no one could withstand the madness of the barbarians—there was no small tribulation. For churches were scattered through nearly all the districts along the Gallic Ocean, cities were depopulated, and monasteries cast down.

The rage of the persecutors had been so great that any Christians whom they could seize they either killed with the sword or, if fear of the slaughter of the innocent had taken hold of them, attempted to preserve in exchange for a ransom. Some Christians, having experienced the harshest persecution, abandoned their estates and cast aside their ancestral lands, giving themselves to inhabit the eastern regions. Many had resolved that it was better to fall beneath spears than to leave their ancestral homes unharmed.

Still others—and they were more numerous—whose hearts had scarcely taken root in the faith, neglected the bath of holy regeneration but loved the hidden cunning of the pagans, and gave themselves over to their alliance and vices [lacuna]. They were more savage and cruel than the barbarians. Since they were Christians, they first sought to investigate the hiding places of their fellow Christians; and, so that their favor and cruelty might be strengthened among the barbarians, they rejoiced to pour out the blood of their neighbors with murderous hands.

The rest awaited true peace, not at all recognizing their own sins, although divine vengeance had been exercised against none [reading uncertain: *cum nullis*]. For before this storm of destruction occurred, one person gnawed away at another’s life, and the rich craftily desired to take from the poor what he possessed. Therefore a dreadful and prolonged tribulation was given to him. For the savagery and extreme cruelty of the Marcomanni had truly continued so long that churches raised by noble construction were reduced to wilderness, and a dense grove covered the highest peaks of their walls.

Most especially near the sea, the land remained uncultivated and human access there was rare, except in the safest and most strongly fortified castles. For, as we stated above, when disaster struck, the inhabitants had either been transported to other regions, or nearly all those who remained had been killed, or else had been mingled with the barbarians. The others who had escaped lived in various strongholds.

At that time, therefore, there was a monastery in the province of Gaul, in the district of Périgueux, called Palmatus. There the servants of God continually served Christ, possessing nothing of their own except what the rule of Saint Benedict allowed. There were also many other monasteries in the same province, considerably richer; but when the aforesaid pestilence struck, and the danger of famine arose, many of the monks began to neglect the rule of Saint Benedict and began to possess private property contrary to its practice.

The monks of Palmatus avoided them, judging this wicked and unlawful, while recalling in their hearts the teachings of Paul, that excellent preacher:

> “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8:35).

They themselves also said that no one could truly be a monk who sought private property on earth—nor, evidently, his own will—unless it were his own fault and his own place. They were poor in possessions but rich in faith. Their abbot was named Adalgasius, a man of venerable gray hair, upright conduct, cheerful appearance, born of noble lineage, and most eloquent in speech.

Seeing that there could in no way be [lacuna] on account of the present slaughter, he began, like a good shepherd, to travel through all the regions, in case he might find somewhere to preserve his poor little sheep from the mouths of the raging men. For it was by no means suitable for him to remain in his own land, where he saw frequent and pitiable slaughter among his beloved pupils.

Word therefore reached the ears of the distinguished marquis Regimund, who at that time held the office of governing the Toulouse monarchy: the venerable abbot Adalgasius had been driven from his native land together with his dependents by the incursion of the pagans.

The marquis, considering the matter in his mind under divine inspiration, found a saving plan: that the man of God, whose fame was celebrated throughout the entire province, should establish a monastery on the marquis’s ancestral lands in which to live together with his disciples, so that through their intercession the sins of the marquis and of his parents might be wiped away.

Finally, he repeatedly sent urgently to the aforesaid abbot and had him asked not to be reluctant to come to Toulouse to speak with him. But the abbot could not go to him immediately, since he was nearly sixty miles from the city of Toulouse and did not wish to travel to him for an uncertain matter. He therefore sent two disciples to him, asking that through them he reveal the reason for which he had been ordered to cross so great a distance. They hurried there and fulfilled the commands of their Father.

When the aforesaid marquis discovered that the venerable abbot’s presence would in no way be available for the appointment he had arranged, but also learned that the monks sent by him were present, he took care not to disclose the reason for the abbot’s arrival—indeed, lest the abbot should be able to come promptly to Toulouse and do almost anything he wished. Nevertheless, he did not fail to reveal to the men of God whom he had sent what he desired to provide for the abbot and his monks.

He preferred, however, to appoint a time and day when the venerable abbot could travel to Toulouse, fearing that, just as storm clouds often arise for a marquis from many directions, so during the venerable Father’s overly delayed journey many adversities might arise and prevent him from accomplishing the useful undertaking. Therefore he thought it best to set a nearby and convenient appointment, so that, freed from other business, he might discuss with him in exact detail the means for carrying out so useful a work.

After hearing these words, the disciples departed. When they had returned to their own place, they reported everything to the revered Father. When he had learned from his disciples what had been conveyed by the marquis, he consulted the Almighty Lord and set out for Toulouse.

At that time the distinguished Helisachar was exercising the episcopal ministry in that city. When the illustrious marquis learned that Abbot Adalgasius was present, he ordered him to be summoned and had the abbots of his district assemble. Then the glorious marquis went to the emperor Charles on behalf of the monastery’s welfare. Moved by pious concern that his parents should not suffer hardships after his death, he handed the monastery over to him by charter to possess under the terms of a grant, and soon received from him a document containing its provisions.

## Charter of Charles the Bald for the Abbey of Vabres

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.
>
> “We believe that we increase the protection of our kingdom in the greatest way if, with devoted goodwill, we grant suitable benefits to the places of the churches. With the Lord’s protection, we commit these things to writing so that they may endure securely.
>
> “Therefore let all bishops, abbots, counts, viscounts, vicars, centenarii, judges, and all the faithful, present and future, know how the venerable Count Raimund, from the monastery which he himself built as a new work, by proprietary right from its foundations, in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and of holy Mary ever-virgin, and of the most excellent martyr Saint Dionysius, and of the other saints, at the place called Vabres, in the district of Quercy, on this side of the Dordogne, approached our clemency. With fullest deliberation he appeared to have transferred the aforesaid monastery, together with all the possessions and ornaments of its church and its appurtenances and dependencies, into our hands; and he appeared to have handed over that holy place to us to govern under our protection and authority.
>
> “Therefore, at his request, we have appeared to grant this benefit to that holy place for eternal reward: in the churches, places, fields, and other possessions of the monastery which it now appears justly to possess, whether through our donation and confirmation or through those of other faithful persons, in whatever places anything has been bestowed there for the love of God, and whatever divine goodness may hereafter wish to increase in the right of that holy place, whether through us or through others, we command and order—and anathematize—that no count, bishop, abbot, or any person invested with judicial authority ever dare enter or presume to exact anything there for hearing cases, demanding fines, providing lodging or provisions, taking sureties, or distraining the people of this monastery, whether free or servile, who appear to reside upon the land of the aforesaid monastery; nor may anyone seek any exactions or unlawful pretexts, or demand any rent whatsoever, at any time.
>
> “Rather, the abbot himself, or his successors, or the monks of the aforesaid place, present and future, may rule that place under the name of complete immunity, for the sake of the Lord’s name, without disturbance or opposition from anyone; and they shall never dare to pay any rent whatsoever to any person for any matter. We wish that the holy place itself remain under our protection and authority.
>
> “Therefore we establish and order that neither you nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, ever presume to act in the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery, or concerning anything written above. Rather, what we have granted to the aforesaid monastery for the sake of the Lord’s name and eternal reward shall prosper as an increase for all time.
>
> “And whenever, by divine summons, the aforesaid venerable Abbot Adalgasius [Col. 0786A] or his successors have departed from this light to the Lord, let that holy congregation have the right, through this authority of ours and the aforesaid grant, to choose as abbot whichever better and in every respect more faithful man they wish, whether from the aforesaid monastery or from any place, provided he is able to govern that holy congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Wherever they wish to be ordained, whether they themselves or their monks, let them have authority to do so through any bishop by our command and consent, so that those servants of God who appear to serve God there may gladly entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and children, and the stability of the entire kingdom entrusted to us by God and to be preserved by him.
>
> “Sign of Charles the king. Adalguarius the notary wrote this in the place of Gissenus.
>
> “Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth indiction, in the twenty-first year, while Charles the most glorious king reigned. Done at the city of Paris, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

The most glorious King Charles granted these things to the venerable marquis by charter, and also received from him by an imperial charter places all around that were useful for livestock and suitable for cultivation. Having been honored with a great gift by the emperor—namely, two pounds of silver—he returned in peace to his monastery.

Let anyone who wishes to read or hear this life know that this is the head of all monasteries—not only those that appear to have been built in the regions of Gothia, but also those in other regions that were built at that time and afterward by its example and enriched from its treasures, as was related earlier.

It is worthwhile to consider carefully with what [reading uncertain] humility and reverence that place, which appears to have been fortified by so many princes, ought to be regarded. For Christ the Lord is the Prince of all princes, King of kings, and Lord of lords. The blessed mother of God, Mary, is believed to be queen of all virgins. Michael is placed above all the ranks of angels. Peter and Andrew are the heads of the apostles. Stephen the protomartyr holds primacy in the choir of witnesses. Martial shines like a jewel among the prelates, while Benedict is the Father of all monks.

# Appendix

[Col. 0785]

## Charter of Raimund, Count of Toulouse, for the Foundation of the Abbey of Vabres

[Col. 0785D] The authority of ancient laws and of emperors and consuls decreed that if any person born of noble lineage wished to transfer his property into the right of another, whether to churches or to other persons, he should have permission to do so by charters, codicils, and lawful transfers.

For this reason, I, Raimund, by God’s favor count and marquis, and my wife Berteyz, in God’s name, considered the condition of our human frailty, fearing the final day lest sudden and unexpected death should come and deliver us into the snare of its death. And so that the Lord may deign to grant us forgiveness, for the salvation of our souls, and for the salvation of the soul of my father Fulguald, and for my mother Senegund, and for my brother Fredelo, now deceased—so that those who shared a common love may also share a common almsgiving—we cede, and wish to be ceded in perpetuity, our property situated in the district of Rouergue, in the vicariate called Quercy: the estate called Vaber, in its entirety, and likewise Vedetium, likewise Biarcium, likewise Nogareda; and in Tarnesca, in the estate called Betianus, our vineyards which Leotgarius established there.

For these things mentioned above, together with two chapels and four manses belonging there, we hand over to Abbot Adalgasius and his monks, and wish them to be ceded in perpetuity, for the construction of a monastery in honor of Saint Savior and Saint Mary, mother of God, and Saint Dionysius, the most excellent martyr of our Almighty God, so that they may gather in that place a single community of monks who will serve there according to the rule of Saint Benedict, receive guests, refresh the poor, and faithfully pray for us.

Of the bondservants we cede to that holy place the following persons: Trudinare and his wife with their children, except Franco; Aribert and his wife with their children; Elizabeth with her children, except Elianus; Harfred with his children, except Ragranfred; Ostrenus and his wife with their children; Eldradus with his wife and children; Elianus with his children; Lambert and his wife with their children; Februus and his wife with their children; Stabilis and his wife with their children; Ingibald and his wife with their children, except Raganfredonus and Mudricus; Ingilsindonus with his children, except Vandalberganus, and the cleric whom we have left free; Ebradus’s wife with her children; Grimald and his wife with their children.

All these persons named above, together with houses, chapels, farmyards, vineyards, meadows, woods, mills, and appurtenances—rural and suburban places, what has been acquired and what is to be acquired—we hand over to Almighty God and all the saints, and to Abbot Adalgasius and his monks, and to all who will be there after them.

We transfer them from our power and from the authority of my dominion on the condition that no king or other power shall have permission to grant these properties as benefices, exchange them, or give them away, except that they shall remain perpetually under the protection and immunity of the king. As long as I live, I shall be guardian and defender of that holy place.

After my departure, we appoint our son Bernard not as lord or heir but as defender, so that in my place he may defend the sacred place, nourish the monks, and protect the household. After his death, if our son Fulguald survives, we likewise entrust that place to him for the doing of good. But if the Lord permits our son Odo to survive, we leave him in the same guardianship and defense, while the monks themselves shall remain in their own right and under their own authority.

Let them have as abbot whomever they elect according to the rule of Saint Benedict when the previous abbot has died. Concerning repudiation, we declare that if we ourselves, having changed our mind, or any of our heirs, or any person acting with evil intent, should produce an earlier or later testament as though made by me—although I neither made nor decreed it—it shall have no effect, and the presenter shall be held liable as guilty of forgery.

Let the person who wishes to destroy our almsgiving first incur the wrath of Almighty God, receive eternal damnation with Dathan and Abiram, have no share with the elect at the final resurrection, and be condemned forever with Judas, who sold the sacred body of the Lord; moreover, let him not obtain what he attempts to accomplish.

Whoever presumes to act against this cession or to bring any claim shall not obtain what he seeks; furthermore, under compulsion of the fisc, let him pay thirty pounds of gold and one hundred weights of silver. But let this present cession, supported by stipulation, retain inviolable validity for all time.

This cession was made on the third day before the Nones of November, in the twenty-third year of the reign of King Charles. Sign of Raimund, count and marquis; sign of Berteyz, his wife, who requested that this cession be made and confirmed. Sign of Bernard, their son and count; sign of Fulguald, their son; sign of Odo; I, Elisachar, bishop of Rouergue, have subscribed; sign of Bergantz; sign of Bergon, viscount; sign of Gerald; sign of Rustagnus; sign of Gislamar; sign of Jorius Buca; sign likewise of Gerald; sign of Tiodric; sign of Amard; [Col. 0788C] sign of Brumalus; sign of Robert; sign of Hislo; sign of Gerald; sign of Rudger. Ermenric, deacon, wrote this.

# In the Year of Our Lord 928. Cyprian, Archpriest of the Church of Córdoba.

[Col. 0787]

## Historical Notice

*(In Antonius, Old Hispanic Library, volume I, p. 469.)*

[Col. 0787D] 1. Cyprian, archpriest of the church of Córdoba, was a poet of some reputation in his own time. Some genuine works of his still survive—epigrams, epitaphs, hymns, and other poems—while others are attributed to him by those who, assuming the mask of antiquity, love nothing more than deception and playing games with history.

A man distinguished in learning and integrity, and a close personal acquaintance of mine, whom I recently mentioned, the lord Joannes Lucas Cortesius of Seville, now a royal judge in Madrid in the criminal court, possesses a certain codex. It may perhaps be the same one that once belonged to Michael Ruiz de Azagra. Ambrosius Morales saw it [Col. 0788D], and in it only the following poems of Cyprian are read, under this heading:

2. The epigrams of Lord Cyprian, archpriest of the see of Córdoba, begin.

**Note:** [Col. 0787D] In our copy transcribed from the Toledo codex, the heading is somewhat fuller, namely: “The epigrams of Lord Cyprian, archpriest of the see of Córdoba, published at the request of Adolphus begin.” Cardinal de Aguirre.

I. On the sacred books deposited by Count Adolphus at Córdoba in the church of Saint Acisclus.

II. Likewise, another by the same author, at the request of his son Zoilus, placed at the end of the library that he had written for Saturninus the archdeacon.

III. Another epigram without a title.

IV. An epigram to Count Guifred and his wife Guisinda.

[Col. 0789A] V. Also another poem by the same author on the fan of the same Countess Guisinda.

VI. An epitaph which the same author composed in heroic meter for the tomb of Lord Samson. It was published by Ambrosius Morales in Book XV of his *History of Spain*, chapter 21.

VII. Also an epitaph, published by the same author, over the tomb of Hermildis, a servant of Christ.

VIII. Also one over the tomb of Saint John the Confessor. In Morales there is only a single couplet to be read [Note: [Col. 0789C] In the notes to Book I of the *Memorials of Saint Eulogius*, preface, no. 6.].

IX. Two hymns by the same author for the feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, citizen and patroness of the city of Toledo. Cortesius added, however, that these are absent from his own codex [Note: [Col. 0789C] They exist, in the same order and under the same [Col. 0789D] titles, in the Toledan codex of Ruiz Azagra, from which Flórez seems to have transcribed them in Volume XI, p. 524. In our copy, too, as in his, the two hymns for the feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, citizen and patroness of Toledo, are missing. In another Gothic codex of the same Toledan church, immediately after the verses of Cyprian just mentioned, there follow other verses, as though they belonged to the same author, under these titles: “Epitaph of Paula”; “Inscription of the Tomb”; “The Same Author’s Hexameter”:

> Paula, whom Scipio begot, had as her ancestors  
> The offspring of the Gracchi, the illustrious seed of Agamemnon.  
> She lies in this tomb; those before us called her Paula.  
> Mother of Eustochium, foremost of the Roman senate,  
> She followed Christ’s poverty and the countryside of Bethlehem.

Also: “At the Entrance of the Cave.” It begins: “You look upon the narrow…” Moreover: “Another.” It begins: “Believe my words…” and others, whose attribution to Cyprian is uncertain.].

3. These are Cyprian’s poems [Note: [Col. 0789D] All of them are preserved by us from the Toledan codex [Col. 0790C] (although, through the copyist’s ignorance, they are disfigured by several errors), except for the hymns, of which our exemplar contains no mention. Cardinal de Aguirre.] which ought to be regarded as genuinely his, unless other poems, entirely free from suspicion, are produced from elsewhere. Nearly all the rest are of the following sort, except those which are scattered through the *Spanish Martyrology* of John Tamayo. We give here a list of them, taken from a certain manuscript codex of the poems of Aulus Halus and others, from which, as he says, he drew material for almost all his pages.

### Volume III

June 3: He produces a certain poem concerning Saint Isaac, monk and martyr of Córdoba, which, on conjecture alone, he attributes either to Cyprian or to Alvarus, p. 430.

XV: On the tomb of Saint Benildis, martyr of Córdoba, p. 533. The epitaph of Blasius, bishop of Toledo, p. 534.

XXV: For Saint Gallicanus Ovinus, a consular man and martyr, p. 604.

XXVI: On Saints John and Paul, Spanish martyrs, p. 620.

### Volume IV

July 16: On Saint Sisenandus, martyr of Córdoba, p. 144.

XX: On Saint Paul, deacon and martyr of Córdoba, p. 182.

XXV: On Saint Theodemirus, abbot and martyr of Córdoba, p. 254.

[Col. 0789C] August 2: On Saint Flavius Rutilius, African martyr, p. 340.

XXI: Epitaph of Saint Samson, abbot, p. 536.

This is the genuine poem of the sacred poet praised by others, and therefore it must be removed from the category of suspect works.

XXV: To Saint Genesius, martyr of Córdoba, p. 570.

### Volume V

September 3: For Saint Sandalius, martyr of Córdoba, p. 39. For Saints Habundus, Marcus, and their fellow martyrs of Córdoba, p. 43. He says that this was taken from a codex of the hymns of the Cordoban saints, rather than, as we stated, from the codex of the poems of Aulus Halus and others.

[Col. 0790A] XV: On Saints Emila and Jeremiah, martyrs of Córdoba, p. 190.

XVI: On Saints Rogelius and Leovigildus, martyrs of Córdoba, p. 204.

XVII: On the tomb of Saint Columba, virgin and martyr of Córdoba, p. 223.

XIX: On Saint Pomposa, virgin and martyr of Córdoba, p. 272.

XXVII: For Saints Adulphus and John, brothers and martyrs of Córdoba, p. 342.

October 14: On Lupus and Aurelia, his wife, martyrs of Córdoba, p. 525.

XIX: On Saint Laura, widow and martyr of Córdoba, p. 585.

### Volume VI

December 9: Two hymns in the ancient office of Saint Leocadia of the Church of Toledo are attributed to Cyprian, p. 430 [Note: [Col. 0790D] Perhaps these were the two hymns “For the feast of Saint Leocadia” which, shortly before, we said were missing from the Toledan codex of Ruiz Azagra. Or were they rather fabricated wholesale by John Tamayo? Here is a sample of each:

**At Matins**

> Rejoice, Toledo,  
> On this sacred feast;  
> To her, wholly joyful,  
> Be present with prayers, etc.

**At Vespers**

> On Leocadia’s feast,  
> Which is celebrated today,  
> Let us sing a hymn  
> To the King of the heavenly court, etc.].

XX: On Saint Gregory of Eliberis, bishop, p. 491.

XXI: On Saint Amasindus, abbot, p. 524. Ambrosius Morales published part of this poem [Col. 0790B] or epitaph on the last page of the third volume.

4. John Tamayo admits that, through the kindness of Don Martín de Ximena Jurado, he obtained all those poems contained in a certain codex of the Church of Toledo which Morales had seen. “Although,” he says in Volume III, on June 15, p. 534, “these eulogies are missing from it, they are listed in another manuscript codex of mine, among the epigrams of Aulus Halus and others, with the title written above. For not all Cyprian’s poems are included in that Toledan codex, but only eight epigrams written on different occasions, although he wrote many others, as will plainly appear in the proper places from the tables of this work.” Yet when he needed to prove this, he adds—as is clear from the account of Julian, archpriest of Toledo, certainly a competent witness in the matter—that Julian, in the cited no. 284 of the *Adversaria*, lists this Cyprian of Córdoba as the author of a hymn beginning, “Rejoice, Toledo.” This hymn, however, is not found at all in the Toledan codex.

[Col. 0790C] 5. I had thought that Julian required highly trustworthy witnesses in order for his credibility to be established, rather than that his testimony alone could provide even a degree of confidence concerning anything. But when the two genuine poems of Cyprian already published are compared with the others drawn from Tamayo’s storehouse, it will not be difficult to see that the two poems which we append bear the features of their own age and author, while all those attributed by Tamayo continue to display the marks of novelty.

### Epitaph which the same author, Cyprian, composed for the tomb of Lord Samson in heroic meter

> Who and how great was Samson, the most illustrious abbot,  
> Whose sacred limbs remain in this holy chamber beneath this roof?  
> His fame, nourished in the West, resounds.  
> Bend God by your prayers, reader—bend Him now, I entreat you—  
> So that he may ascend to heaven with his sins cleansed.  
> He departed, long renowned and full of days:  
> For on the twenty-first day of the month of Sextilis,  
> On the twenty-first sun of the sixth month.

[Note: [Col. 0790D] In our exemplar it reads otherwise: “Whose sacred limbs remain in an urn, yet in a church.” Cardinal de Aguirre.]

Era 928.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] In Morales, in the notes to Book I of the *Memorial of the Martyr Saint Eulogius*, preface, no. 9.]

Also, on the tomb of Saint John the Confessor:

> John endured prisons and harsh iron chains  
> For the love of Christ. Having completed his course, he rests in this chamber.

6. In these two poems you recognize the characteristic diction of one man and of his age. In both, *chamber* is used for a tomb, or for the sacred building in which the tomb is located. In the latter poem, *having completed his course* means “dead.” For Alvarus, his contemporary, uses the verb in this way—in his letter to John of Seville: “or I shall return the dead man to the earth for burial.” Therefore the remaining poems falsely attributed to Cyprian must be examined with the greatest precision.

Whether they were composed about the Cordoban martyrs during the time of captivity, or about others whose genuinely Spanish deeds have remained obscure, or finally about others whose origins are unjustly assigned to Spain by that troop of historians whom we have so often overturned, they are, to use Lucretius’ expression, separated and segregated from every path of truth. You will find none of these poems—apart from the celebrated eulogies of the Cordobans’ martyrdom under the Muslims—modeled on the acts of the martyrs or other saints whom we formerly knew as genuine and whom we have always defended, whose history is clear and consistent. They belong only to those whom the backward, indeed wholly condemnable, contrivance of the Toledan potter has thrust upon us through its agents Dextrus and his followers, in order to support Dextrus’ fabrications. This is the surest mark of forgery, deeply impressed upon all these authors who sprang from that workshop, and from every other workshop subsequently opened in imitation of it. The inventors and vendors of such wares seem to have foreseen that deeds otherwise famous required no, so to speak, substructures of testimony, whereas only deeds that are invented require them.

7. In celebrating the struggles of the Cordoban martyrs, the purpose of Pseudo-Cyprian was likewise to make Saint Eulogius’ entirely truthful account appear richer by adding other, false events. For example, Eulogius had said only a little about the martyr Benildis (*Memorials*, Book III, chapter 9):

> Finally, Benildis, following these men—Anastasius and his fellow martyrs, whom we mentioned shortly before—a woman already advanced in age and, as they say, not moderately fearful [for “moderately”], fell under the profession of the others on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the same year as above [891]. Their bodies, after some days, were burned in a great fire and finally thrown into the river and scattered.

These obscure and meager facts became the material of Pseudo-Cyprian’s drivel. Filled, indeed, with that god who inspires mad frenzy rather than sound poetry, he preferred to bray rather than sing this poem about Benildis, which our martyrologist published under June 15. Here is the first couplet, so that you may recognize the lion by its claw:

> Córdoba gave me birth; Córdoba, while I lived,  
> Taught me the sacred doctrines and faith of Christ.

I venture to affirm that not even the license of the most wretched Latin could have allowed *nascens* to be used for *nascentem*, or *vivens* for *viventem*. Yet this practice—which equally provokes every form of crudity and ignorance of grammatical art—is not foreign to the grammar of the *Martyrology*.

8. A second example. In speaking of Saint Sisenandus, martyr of Córdoba, Saint Eulogius had said that he was born in the town of Pacensis (*Book II*, chapter 5). More sensible writers rightly interpret this as Pax Julia, a city of Lusitania [Note: [Col. 0791D] Ambrosius Morales, Book XIV, chapter 9, and in the notes to this passage of Eulogius. Marieta, Book II, chapter 71; Roa, *On the Cordoban Saints*, fol. 117.]. But when Tamayo decided to assign everything connected with Pax—today the town of Beja in Portugal—to Pax Augusta of the Castilians and of his own province of Extremadura—today Badajoz—he acted here, as usual, by assuming the role of Cyprian, in a poem which we have partly given and which may otherwise be sought in Tamayo himself [Volume IV, July 16, p. 144]:

> Sisenandus, your sacred limbs, O Levite,  
> The reliquary guards at the holy threshold of Acisclus;  
> Them the pious courage of the female sex joined  
> To you, whom provident Pax Augusta, by God’s will,  
> Granted to us, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0792D] We said elsewhere, namely in Book IV, chapter 2, no. 23, while discussing Apringius of Beja, that both names—Pax Julia and Pax Augusta—apply to the colony of Pacensis, that is, to the modern city of Beja in Transmontane Lusitania. See Resende, *On the Colony of Pacensis*; Flórez, Volume XIV, treatise 51, chapter 1.]

9. A third example. Eulogius had discussed Saint Paul the martyr (*Book II*, chapter 6). Certain Benedictines—Uvion and Menard—claimed that he was a monk of their order, while others contradicted them [*Annals of the Benedictines*, centuria 4, under the year 851]. Tamayo wished to silence the Benedictines by means of a poem by Pseudo-Cyprian, in which that Paul is asserted to have been a cleric, not a monk.

10. A fourth example. Eulogius writes that the corpse of this Paul was buried with the body of Blessed Theodemirus, a monk of Carmona, at the shrine of the martyr Zoilus; the latter himself died as a young man six days after Saint Paul, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, a Friday, in the same year as above. Eulogius reports nothing further about him (*Book II*, chapter 6). But Antonio Quintanadueñas, a historian of the saints of the diocese of Seville, believing Pseudo-Julian (*Chronicle*, no. 418), had written that this man had once been bishop of Calahorra, and was precisely the person whom Claudius of Turin, when he admonished him concerning the veneration of sacred images, answered in a most impious *Apology*. Since this rightly displeased Tamayo, he ran to the arsenal of his Pseudo-Cyprian, from which he could draw a weapon to strike the throat of the opposing view: namely, a poem [Volume IV, July 25, p. 254] in which there is no mention of episcopal office, but only of the palm of martyrdom.

11. A fifth example. Eulogius mentions Adulphus and John, martyrs, only in passing (*Book II*, chapter 8). They therefore had an absolute need of that poem by Pseudo-Cyprian which we read under October 27.

12. A sixth. Eulogius had written about Emila and Jeremiah (*Book II*, chapter 12). The former was called Emila by some and Emilianus by others. Tamayo did not wish to settle on either form; instead he invented the new name *Emilias*, belonging to no language, with which he called the saint a martyr in the first verse of the poem that he wanted us to believe Cyprian’s:

> Emilias follows, first a Levite by blood,  
> A Cordoban. But “follows,” as grammarians may now learn to speak correctly from this example:

> … Jeremiah also, who together with the nations  
> And with the noble exalt the wondrous name of Christ  
> As holy.

This misuse of the adverb *together* with the conjunction *and*, which is otherwise badly placed, together with an intolerable hyperbaton and the mere babbling contained in the preceding words—as though he meant to say that Jeremiah too, like Emila, was born at Córdoba of noble lineage—all these features are as like one another as an egg is like an egg, and resemble the compositions of those writers whose twin versifiers Tamayo frequently employs from his manuscript codex of various poems. This will conveniently become clear from some of their passages reproduced here; and from them it will be evident that nearly everything produced under so many headings is a single hydra belonging to one brain.

13. Reader, you will marvel at how much this foolish man delighted in using the adverb *quoque*—“also”—barbarously, again and again. Julian’s poem on Saints Socrates and Stephen, martyrs, under September 17:

> Through every scourge also, Christ.

Another by the same author, October 15, on Saint Carithina, virgin and martyr:

> Whom the virgin also favors.

Another, November 4, on Saint Clarus, martyr:

> While also he presses the steep path with his voice.

Another, December 1, on Saint Evasius, bishop and martyr:

> Whom also he takes up by the cross.

Aulus Halus speaks no differently, November 8, on Saints Castorius and his companions:

> Claudius clings to him, and the following crowd also.

Likewise, September 1, on Vincent and Laetus, martyrs:

> Toledo, the royal seat, honors them as its own;  
> Aquensis too loves them as her children by the same mother.

The diction is no different in some unknown author, or authors, who fill almost every page of the *Martyrology*. September 24, on Saint Firminus:

> While he lives as a citizen, while he also serves as bishop.

October 4, on Julianus Urbanus, bishop of Toledo:

> By which also he flies to the stars.

October 13, on Saint Peter, bishop of Braga:

> Whom also you nourish with a gift.

December 3, on Saint Anthemius, bishop and martyr:

> Who also cuts the limbs.

Finally, Tamayo is no more elegant when he speaks in his own name, November 3, on the image of Saint Dominic:

> … But you shine everywhere  
> With signs, whether living, or whether also you go painted.

And the same may be said of the epitaph of Saint Columba, on September 17 in Tamayo, a martyr whom Eulogius mentions in Book III, chapter 10, and of that of Saint Pomposa, October 19, likewise mentioned by Eulogius in Book III, chapter 11. In it, more than one mark of Tamayo’s eloquence stands out.

14. There are also other poems of Pseudo-Cyprian, devised to clothe the naked histories of genuinely Spanish saints. Let the first example of this be the following.

Saint Sandalius, whom tradition commonly reports to have been celebrated as a martyr at Córdoba, while his acts have been lost [Note: [Col. 0793D] Baronius’ *Martyrology*, September 3, and several others cited by Tamayo on the same day]. Pseudo-Cyprian was therefore ready to supply this lack of acts in the poem whose heading is: “For Saint Sandalius, martyr of Córdoba, September 3.”

15. A second. Lupus and Aurelia are praised in the martyrologies of Bede and Ado on October 14 as martyrs in Córdoba, Spain; later writers agree, adding nothing further about them. This open field invited Tamayo to wander freely under Cyprian’s name and to include their status, the time of their martyrdom, and—what was most valuable—the martyrs’ place of residence, in the city of Illipa, Tamayo’s native city, in these verses:

> Córdoba, provident, venerates your sacred limbs,  
> O Lupus, and those of Aurelia, your wife, together.  
> Fleeing the snares of treacherous Nero,  
> You both leave Italy and seek homes in the city.  
> Illipa, in Baetica, receives you as her children; but later  
> Happy Córdoba carries you away through martyrdom.  
> From then on each city will be counted as great:  
> The one because it was your cradle, the other because it was your tomb.

Born in the town of Zalamea—which John Tamayo believed had once been Illipa [Note: [Col. 0793D] See Volume V, September 14, p. 183], although in fact it was Julipa, as we have shown elsewhere—Tamayo somehow summoned Lupus and Aurelia there, built his own edifice upon them, and wished to foist it upon his fellow citizens.

16. A third. Saints Habundus, Marcus, and their companions, long celebrated as martyrs at Córdoba, are mentioned by Ferrarius in the tables of this Church under July 11. Pseudo-Cyprian likewise clothed their otherwise naked memory in a poem found in Tamayo under September 3.

17. The cause and origin of the remaining poems attributed to Cyprian was the same as that common to many others: Tamayo’s credulity and the confidence he placed in the pseudo-histories of the Toledan workshop. To lend them greater authority, those men of leaden hearts, born only for this purpose, did not hesitate to strive by frauds and inventions—so that, as the cuttlefish does, according to Pliny (*Natural History*, Book IX, chapter 29), by pouring out ink to prevent the truth from being detected, they might muddy the waters of history. Let us come to the matter itself.

18. First, the Roman martyrs John and Paul are exceedingly well known; their feast day is June 26. So too is Gallicanus, a consular man and commander of the Roman army against the Persians and Scythians, who suffered at Alexandria in Egypt on the twenty-fifth of the same month under Julian the Apostate, as did the aforementioned John and Paul, who converted him to the faith. A certain Terentianus, who ordered John and Paul to be beheaded, committed the acts of their martyrdom to writing, and to this day we read them in Surius and others under June 26.

A mad desire to claim all three seized the lightest-minded of all bipeds, the craftsman Julianus. His words, in no. 8 of the *Adversaria*, induced him to make the following offering to falsehood:

> “Saints John and Paul,” he says, “and Ovinus Gallicanus, a consular man—this one suffering at Alexandria, those at Rome—were Spaniards, Saguntines, and for a long time lived at the emperors’ court.”

Again, in no. 399:

> “At the same time”—when he had come to Braga with Bernard, archbishop of Toledo—“I learned that Saint Ovinus Gallicanus, a consular man and martyr, and John and Paul, his relatives, born at Bragantium, not very far from Braga, were most renowned martyrs, having been taken to Rome.”

19. This is a mere fable, contradicting itself and charging falsehood against itself through the very author by whom it was born. It is plainly impossible for them to have been both Saguntines and Bragantines by birth. Therefore a reconciliation was immediately sought for the chatterer’s rash statements [Note: [Col. 0793D] So it appears in Tamayo, June 25, p. 602. Father Higuera, in the manuscript *Spanish Martyrology*.]: the martyrs, though born at Bragantium, were said to have traced their origin to the city of Saguntum.

Since neither Terentianus, the writer of the acts, nor anyone else after Ado and Usuard had expressed anything concerning their Spanish origin, it was necessary, so to speak, to support the Julian fabrication with Cyprian’s following structure:

> In this tomb lies the noble Gallicanus Ovinus,  
> Who was a Spaniard, once of great Saguntine origin,  
> Whose famous city witnessed his deeds  
> And his illustrious triumphs at Rome, where he was consul twice.

[Note: [Col. 0794D] *Ovinius Gallicanus* appears in an inscription in Gruter, p. 284, and in Onuphrius’ *Fasti* under the year 1067.]

> It also learned that his thresholds afterward endured  
> The trophies of the faith, etc.

[Col. 0795A] Likewise, on Saints John and Paul, June 26:

> Paul, the glory of our people, and venerable John,  
> Spanish nobles, blessed Roman martyrs,  
> Both born at Saguntum and, by origin, brothers,  
> Illustrious in wealth and both unconquerable in faith.  
> Your Spain always longs for your fellowship,  
> And although Rome holds your bones, here in our hearts you lie.

[Note: [Col. 0795D] He ought to have said “our glory.” Today the people of Saguntum venerate the holy martyr Gallicanus Ovinus as their fellow citizen; in the principal church of that town a special altar was recently erected to him under this name, at which his memory is solemnly renewed each year with an eulogy of the holy martyr. One of its chief claims is that he was born there. Yet this belief scarcely prevails even in the town itself—which is one of the chief and noblest cities of the kingdom of Valencia—except among the uneducated populace.]

20. Another of Cyprian’s poems, among those in which he conspires with the pseudo-historians, concerns Rutilius, an African martyr, whom only Tertullian mentions in Book 5 of *On Flight in Persecution*:

> “Rutilius, a most holy martyr,” he says, “having fled persecution so often from place to place, and even, as he thought, having bought off danger with money, after all the security he had provided for himself was unexpectedly seized and brought before the governor, was torn apart by tortures—I believe as punishment for his flight—and then handed over to the flames. He returned to the mercy of God the passion which he had avoided.”

Tertullian does not even say a word about the places to which the martyr fled [Col. 0795B]. There remained, therefore, an opportunity for clever speculation—or rather dreaming—about these matters. The architect of the fiction supplied it through four testimonies from Pseudo-Dextrus (under the years 110, no. 5, and 116, no. 5) and Pseudo-Maximus (under the year 612, no. 22), which assert that Rutilius came to Córdoba as an exile.

Pseudo-Cyprian did not wish to be lacking here either. He piled fiction upon fiction, asserting that Rutilius was Italian by birth in the poem read by Tamayo under August 2, which begins:

> Behold, the Italian Rutilius, in body, visits our homes,  
> Fleeing the fear of Trajan, etc.

21. We also have a poem on Saint Genesius, martyr of Córdoba, whom the same crowd of pseudo-historians tried to persuade us was a martyr, lest the church of that city—famous in Eulogius and others under the title of Saint Genesius—be deprived and empty of a citizen martyr. They therefore joined together, as though with one head and one mouth [Note: [Col. 0796D] Luitprand, under the year 668; Julian, no. 376 at the beginning, and *Adversaria* 149, 389, 481. Bivarius should be consulted in his letter to Ramírez in the edition of Luitprand’s works, p. 345. Tamayo, August 25.], to invent a new martyr of Córdoba under Nero, whose name had never been mentioned elsewhere—as though it were unlawful for churches to be dedicated to martyrs who were not citizens, or to foreign martyrs. In truth, not only at Córdoba but also at Toledo, Madrid, Seville, Salamanca, and perhaps elsewhere, sacred churches were formerly built to the martyr Genesius—of Arles, as we believe, because of the greater proximity and the ancient unity of Gaul Gothica and Spain under the same dominion.

Pseudo-Cyprian therefore did not hesitate to lend his support to this invention of a new martyr in the poem whose opening is:

> Córdoba gave you birth, Genesius; afterward a martyr,  
> It also knew you taken away through martyrdom, etc.

22. We also have a poem by Cyprian on Saint Laura, likewise a martyr of Córdoba, under October 19, so that Luitprand might not be the only witness for assigning a new protectress—if only a certain one!—to this most noble city. Read Luitprand, *Adversaria* 281 [Note: [Col. 0796D] In Ramírez’s edition: for in the other edition, that of Thomas Tamayo, many things are missing, among them this passage], concerning the discovery of Laura’s body in this very city.

23. Tamayo also attributes to Cyprian two hymns that were sung in some ancient office of the Church of Toledo for Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, in order to support Julian’s testimony. Julian had previously recorded this in *Adversaria* 284, where Cyprian is also said to have composed one of them, beginning “Rejoice, Toledo,” at the request of Count Adulphus, Abbot Athanagildus, and the presbyter Valentinianus, all natives of Toledo, in the year 1120. Certainly, in the list of this poet’s poems transmitted to us, which we mentioned above, these two hymns are praised [Note: [Col. 0796D] I would not buy either hymn even for a hollow nut. Moreover, they are absent from the Toledan codex of Ruiz Azagra.]. For the present, therefore, we do not regard them as his.

24. And indeed Count Adulphus is mentioned in the heading of the first poem in the series of genuine works, unless the opportunity for deception was taken from that fact. But if any credence ought to be given to Julian, we would not have assigned a poet of the twelfth century, at the proper place, to the writers of the ninth century, since immediately after the words from his *Adversaria* cited above he adds:

> “The count himself, Adulphus, died in 1104; Cyprian in 1060; [Col. 0796B] they lie at Córdoba.”

But we would rather depart from the road with Morales than follow the straight path with these potter’s phantoms. The former would be attributed to error, the latter to stupidity and foolishness.

23. Concerning Gregory of Eliberis, bishop, whom another poem by Cyprian celebrates in Tamayo under December 20, enough has already been said when we discussed this Gregory; those remarks may be brought here to overturn the credibility of this poem.

26. Outside the regular order of this final class of poems—those in which the recklessness of the author conspired with that of the pseudo-historians—we place the last poem falsely attributed to Cyprian, composed in praise of Amasindus, abbot. John Tamayo authenticated it with his seal so that it might be received as genuine, under December 21, p. 524.

This is that Amansvindus the monk whose epitaph, found in the mountains of Málaga, was first published in the previous century by Ambrosius Morales on the appended leaf of the final book of his *History of Spain*, and subsequently by Bernard Alderetus, Book III of *On the Origin of the Castilian Language*, chapter 18, and Martin de Roa, *History of Málaga*, chapter 14. The author of the poem, which begins:

> In this urn, too, lies the noble bodily form of Amasindus,

gave what is practically a paraphrase of it, and ends:

> I, Cyprian, set this poem upon the marble for him,  
> That my heavenly friend might now obtain pardon for me.

If it were genuinely by our Cyprian, and the stone shows that Amansvindus departed to heaven in the year 1020—that is, in 982—we would thereby know that Cyprian was not a contemporary of this age but at least of the eleventh century, and that he lived after Amansvindus. But this is plainly one of Tamayo’s wares, as its own facility demonstrates: the barbarous ease with which he pours whatever comes into his mind into verse. But enough has now been said about Cyprian, the poet of Córdoba, and the poems which John Tamayo falsely attributed to him.

[Col. 0797]

# EPIGRAMS OF CYPRIAN OF CÓRDOBA

(See *Patrologia*, Volume CXXI, column 567, in the appendix to the works of Alvarus of Córdoba.)

# POPE JOHN X

[Col. 0797]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From Mansi, *The Most Extensive Collection of the Councils*, Volume XVIII, second part, p. 315.)

[Col. 0797A] John, formerly archbishop of Ravenna, became pope—or rather pseudo-pope—in the year of Our Lord 912, during the reign of Constantine, emperor of the East. Theodora, an utterly shameless prostitute, passionately inflamed by the beauty of his appearance, arranged for him to replace Pope Lando; Lando himself had ordained him archbishop of Ravenna after he had been bishop of Bologna. Theodora did this, says Luitprand, so that, despite the two hundred miles separating Rome from Ravenna, she might enjoy intercourse with her lover more frequently. Thus a shameless man, powerful at Rome through the influence of a prostitute, became a pseudo-pope and criminal usurper of the see.

To make this seem possible, reader, remember that Theodora, as Luitprand testifies, had two daughters: one named Marozia, whom she prostituted to the pseudo-pontiff Sergius; the other, Theodora, who by adultery with Adalbert, marquis of Tuscany, bore Alberic, who at that time usurped the rule of the city of Rome and almost alone dominated it. Moreover, after Sergius’ death, Marozia married Wido, the son of Alberic and the legitimate ruler of Tuscany, whose power was so great that he seemed more worthy to be called king than marquis. In these storms Peter’s little boat was tossed about. Yet Christ, sleeping within it, allowed it to be covered and submerged by those tempests, but not wholly swallowed up. For after freeing it from countless heresies, he made it so secure against the gravest scandals that, for the very reason on account of which heretical innovators impiously blaspheme the Church, the sons of that same Church, grateful to God, praise and bless Him.

It is certainly established by sound reasoning that John’s pontificate began in the year of Christ 912 [Note: [Col. 0797] Rather 913; for the Saracens were defeated in August 915, and John began his pontificate in 913, toward the end of January. Here is the third year.]. This follows from the *Chronicle of Cassino* by Leo of Ostia, Book I, chapter 55, where he says that a great victory over the Saracens occurred in the year 915 of our Redeemer, in the third indiction, and in the third year of John’s invasion. If this is correct, it is necessary to assert that he intruded himself into the apostolic see in 912.

From the events that occurred under this pontificate it may be inferred as probable that the man who had entered as usurper, thief, [Col. 0797C] and robber began to be regarded as the legitimate Roman pontiff when, with his forces joined to those of Alberic, son of Adalbert, marquis of Tuscany, he went into battle with that same man against the Saracens, with the consent of the clergy. For after the Saracens had been defeated, various embassies from different parts of the world are recorded as having been sent to him to request pallia and other matters.

To repay Berengarius for the assistance he had given against the Saracens, John crowned him emperor in September 915. Wounded in conscience by many earlier crimes and languishing with grief of heart, he sent an envoy to Compostela to venerate the body of Saint James the Apostle, and gave him letters to Saint Sisenandus, bishop of that same church, asking that continual prayers be offered to God for him before Saint James, so that in this life and at the hour of his death he might have God favorable to him.

When Sisenandus, wholly occupied with investigating the rites of the Roman Church, found them plainly different in many respects from those contained in the Missal of the Spaniards called the Mozarabic Missal, as the papal envoys were leaving Spain he added his own envoy, through whom he obtained from Pope John permission to amend the rites of his missal wherever they appeared to be of greater importance. (Ambrosius Morales, *History of Spain*, Book XV, chapter 47.)
