The same pontiff rejected Hilduin, bishop of Tongeren, whom the clergy and people had elected, and ordained Richarius, whom the king had proposed; he assigned to him the cause and dispute that had lasted two years. He sent a pallium to Seulfus, archbishop of Reims, after the death of Heriveus.

Heribert, the most powerful count of Aquitaine, had made an agreement with this Heriveus that his own son should be placed over the Church of Reims. His intention was plainly that, since the power of anointing kings lay with the archbishop of Reims, whichever king he chose might be anointed king of Gaul. When, therefore, the count’s servants, impatient of delay, removed Archbishop Seulfus by administering poison, the son of Count Heribert, a boy not yet five years old—oh, unheard-of crime!—was elected archbishop of Reims.

This monstrous act, never previously seen or heard of in the Christian world, indeed, I think, never even conceived in the mind, Pope John not only failed to condemn but rather wished to have the election confirmed; he entrusted and delegated the episcopal functions to Abbo, bishop of Soissons. By this action the infamous pontiff offered posterity an example, so that many princes, not only in that age but also in subsequent centuries, would, to the great harm of the Churches, arrange for boys related to them by blood to be promoted to the highest sees. It was truly a deed worthy of such a pontiff, whom an infamous woman had thrust into Peter’s throne by an infamous act. (Flodoard, Book IV, chapter 19.)

[Col. 0798C] During his time the Church of Constantinople, divided by a schism between the supporters of the patriarchs Euthymius and Nicholas, was reunited, and the controversy over trigamy was removed—the controversy that had arisen at Constantinople because Leo the Wise had married for a fourth time. (The *Curopalates*.)

After Conrad’s death, Henry became king of Germany. He married the veiled widow, the daughter of the elder Erwin; then, overcome by concern for sacrilege, he abandoned her, went on foot to Rome, and performed penance. Setting out to subjugate the Lotharingians, through an envoy of Charles the Simple he received the hand of Saint Denis, enclosed in gold, as a gift.

The emperor Berengarius, having entered into an alliance with the Saracens out of hatred for King Rudolf, was killed by his own men. (Luitprand.)

[Col. 0799A] And when John had held the papal see for sixteen years, Wido, marquis of Tuscany, at the urging of his wife Marozia—who had formerly prostituted herself to Pope Sergius—removed him from the see and threw him into prison because of Peter, the pope’s brother, whom they persecuted with the utmost hatred. Not long afterward, he himself died in that same prison, or was most wickedly suffocated after a cushion had been placed over his mouth, and the invader and unjust detainer of the apostolic see met an end worthy of his crimes: he who had violently seized the most holy see through his shameless mother Theodora, by the just vengeance of God was expelled and cast into prison by a son equally shameless, and there lost both that see and his life. (LUITPRAND and FLODOARD.)

[Col. 0799]

# Letters and Privileges of Pope John X

## I. Letter of John X to the Bishops of the First Province of Narbonne (914)

He confirms the ordination of Agius as metropolitan, condemns Gerald as an intruder, and sends the pallium to Agius.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII.]

[Col. 0799B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Reginald, bishop of Béziers; Armand, bishop of Toulouse; Riculf, bishop of Elne; Gimar, bishop of Carcassonne; Wigo, bishop of Girona; Gerard, bishop of Agde; Theuderic, bishop of Lodève; Reubert, bishop of Nîmes; likewise Theuderic, bishop of Barcelona; George, bishop of Ausona; and Rudolph, bishop of Urgell: the most reverend and most holy bishops of the churches of Christ.

Having received the letters of your Holiness concerning the metropolitan Agius [Col. 0799C], and learning of the snares and frauds inflicted upon him by the most wicked Gerald, we grieved deeply and, as though receiving them in our own body, were brought to exhaustion. Therefore we wish your Holiness to know that the aforesaid Gerald, a deceiver, coming to this holy Roman and apostolic Church, which by God’s authority I serve, tried to steal from us, as though innocent, the episcopate. Although we did not yet fully recognize the cunning of his iniquity, we nevertheless refused to grant it to him without canonical judgment.

But he, as we have learned from the truthful report of many, carrying certain false letters to you by subterfuge, as though issued in our name, is on this pretext plundering the bishopric of Narbonne by armed force. The venerable Agius, ensnared by his plots, is being prevented from coming to the holy apostolic see [Col. 0799D]; and we have learned many other things about him, even before hearing them through your letters. Therefore, through the archbishop Eyminus [of Besançon], we sent you our apostolic letters, instructing you not to count the often-mentioned Gerald, who is entirely a deceiver, among the bishops.

Now, because we have fully learned from your brotherhood of his malice, iniquity, and frauds, we wish and command by apostolic authority that, as we have already written to you and as the sacred canons testify, you not count him among the bishops. For he was neither sought by the clergy or the people nor ordained by you, his comprovincials, according to the customary practice.

We have sent the privilege and the pallium, together with the use of the pallium, to your metropolitan Agius, as your affection requested, because we deny no church what justly belongs to it [Col. 0800B]. We wish you, now and always, good health in Christ.

## II. Privilege Granted by John X to Abbot Haicho (917)

He confirms the privileges of the monastery of the Savior at Fulda.

[Dronke, *Diplomatic Code of Fulda*, no. 308.]

[Col. 0800C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Haicho, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through him to his successors, the abbots of that venerable monastery, forever.

Since we bear the greatest concern for all venerable places, we strive, insofar as possibility is granted by divine assistance, to labor for their stability. For by this diligence divine mercy is appeased and praise is secured for the Church of Christ. Indeed, with greater confidence we dare to implore eternal mercy for the obtaining of pardon for our sins.

And therefore your Reverence requested of us that the aforesaid venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, built by Archbishop Saint Boniface at the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the protection of a privilege of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

Favoring this pious desire, by this our apostolic authority we commit to effect what is requested, according to the text of the privilege which you took care to show us as having been permanently granted there by our predecessor, Marino of blessed memory, bishop of this life-giving see [Col. 0800D]. Therefore, apart from the apostolic see and the bishop in whose diocese the same venerable monastery is known to have been built—to whom we grant permission only when the consecration of an altar is required—we prohibit every priest of any church from claiming any authority or jurisdiction in the aforesaid venerable monastery.

We likewise prohibit anyone from presuming to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless invited by the monastery’s abbot, so that, in accordance with what is established under the apostolic see by the firmness of this privilege, it may remain endowed immovably and may enjoy perpetual security, without anyone’s opposition, in its places and possessions—both those which it now holds or possesses and those which divine mercy may in future increase within the right of that monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful [Col. 0801A].

Moreover, after deliberation, we decree that at appropriate times it be reported to our ecclesiastical concern how the monastic community is directed by regular observance and committed to concord in accordance with ecclesiastical rite, lest—God forbid—under cover of this privilege the mind and conduct of your rectitude should in any way be turned aside from the rule of justice.

Nor shall it be lawful for a king, bishop, count, or any other person, great or small, to inflict any force or raise any dispute concerning the possessions or dependants of the same aforesaid venerable monastery [Col. 0801B]. By our authority we also prohibit any woman ever from presuming to enter it. No one shall hold a judicial assembly in this venerable monastery or in any of its other properties. No one shall compel its servants or tenants to perform any service, except those persons to whom the abbot grants consent for the useful fulfillment of his needs. The brothers shall have full power, when necessary, to choose and appoint an abbot from among themselves, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, without opposition from anyone.

And to you, beloved son Haicho, since we know you to be a well-educated and eloquent man, we both grant and command, by the authority of Saint Peter, that you preach the word of God.

Therefore, establishing and decreeing with apostolic care through this document of our decree, we declare that whoever—whether a bishop of any church or a person invested with any dignity—presumes to violate the authority of this privilege, which we confirm by the prerogative of the prince of the apostles, shall, unless he promptly repents, be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, he shall be excluded from the assembly of all the saints; and nevertheless the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, strengthened by apostolic authority. But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege shall obtain blessing and grace from God.

Written by the hand of John, chief secretary of the holy apostolic see, in the month of May, in the fifth indiction. Farewell. Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [May 19], by the hand of Stephen, deputy secretary of the holy apostolic see, in the fourth year—by God’s favor—of the pontificate of Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the tenth of that name, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter; in the second year of the reign of the most pious lord patrician Augustus Berengar, crowned by God as great emperor, and in his second year as patrician, in the fifth indiction.

## III. Privilege of John X for the Church of Autun (919)

At the request of Bishop Heriveus, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Autun.

[In Gallia Christiana, vol. IV, documents, p. 70.]

[Col. 0802A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy bishop of the holy Church of Autun, and through you to that Church forever.

It is fitting that we, who by the support of divine mercy have received the office of ecclesiastical leadership, should, in the defense of ecclesiastical property, sympathize with the injuries of our confrères and bishops and assist them with the weapons of ecclesiastical authority; and that, in restoring the faithful, we should rejoice with those who rejoice by offering the aid of confirmation with assured devotion.

Since, therefore, your filial devotion requested our fatherhood to confirm, by the privilege of our authority, the properties and estates assigned for the use of your Church—namely, those consecrated in honor of the blessed martyr Nazarius—we decree as follows: the estate of Tilignac with its appurtenances, which your predecessor and uncle, with the consent and authority of Count Richard and his sons, had assigned for their use; likewise the mint of your city, which that same predecessor had obtained through a charter of our son, the most glorious King Charles; and, from your grant, the tithes of the revenues of all the churches of your diocese, payable every third year from that time onward, both from what is owed to you and from what falls to your officials; and also three chapels: one in honor of Saint John, another in honor of Saint Leodegarius, and the third in honor of Saint Eptadius.

By the authority of our privilege we decree that the above-named estate, together with all the things mentioned above, shall remain forever, without ambiguity or delay, for the use of the canons. Not that estate alone, but also all their other properties: namely, Ruiliac, which the munificence of your mother, with the consent of Count Richard, bestowed upon them; likewise Bilignac; and also Sussiac, Mariasol, Simpignac, and Marignac, with all their entirety and all their appurtenances, we confirm for their use by the privilege of apostolic authority [Col. 0802C]. Under penalty of excommunication, we prohibit by pontifical governance and by every means that anyone dare violate this.

If any presumptuous person, with reckless boldness, should attempt to oppose, infringe, contradict, withdraw, or diminish in any respect what our apostolic generosity has strengthened and confirmed by the authority of this privilege at the petition of your humility, for the alms of kings and princes, and for the soul of your predecessor [Col. 0802D], let him know that he is eternally bound by the chain of anathema by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that, together with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the sacrilegious thief who, having a money box, stole what was to be distributed to the poor, he is to be burned in the fire of eternal punishment, assigned to the abyss with the demons, and plunged there without hope of recovery.

May blessing and the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ graciously preserve the guardians and observers of this decree throughout the ages.

Written by the hands of Adrian, secretary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of November, indiction 8. Farewell.

## IV. Privilege of John X for the Monastery of Saint Gall (919)

He again confirms to Solomon, bishop of Constance and abbot of Saint Gall, the privilege of immunity and free election granted to the same monastery by emperors and kings and confirmed by Pope Sergius III.

[In Neugart, *Diplomatic Code of Alemannia*, vol. II, p. 11.]

[Col. 0803A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God.

We wish your religious community to know that a certain venerable man named Solomon, from the regions of Germany, bishop of the Church of Constance and abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, informed us through his legates that, with the permission of his lord, King Conrad, he wished to visit the threshold of Saint Peter for the sake of prayer and also to visit us, but that he could not come because of the attacks of turbulent peoples raging in those regions [Col. 0803B].

[Note: [Col. 0803D] Thus, already at the beginning of 919, the disputes of Burchard, duke of Alemannia, and Rudolph II, king of Burgundy, brought disaster upon Swiss territory. Hepidannus and Hermannus Contractus mention, under that year, a battle fought between the two armies at Vitodurum.]

The same legates also informed us that he had already come to Rome under our predecessor, Pope Sergius of blessed memory. Having been kindly received by him and granted the familiarity of his authority, among other things he requested an apostolic confirmation concerning the privilege of the aforesaid monastery. From ancient times until the reign of King Arnulf, it had been subject only to kings, so that the brothers dwelling there would have the power to elect and appoint an abbot from among themselves; this privilege had been violated because of him.

For he had acquired that monastery as a benefice from King Arnulf and, through petitions to his son Louis, obtained from them an order that it should be restored anew; and, having obtained permission from them, he requested that it be renewed and confirmed by apostolic authority [Col. 0803C].

[Note: [Col. 0803D] The notary was more devoted to brevity than to clarity in reporting the substance of Sergius’s bull.]

Just as the bishop himself, when present, requested this from our predecessor, so through his legates, after receiving permission from his lord King Conrad, he obtained it from us. We, recognizing his religious devotion, willingly granted his petition and, by the authority of our apostolate, had a formal document written, by which we firmly confirmed the privileges and statutes granted to the aforesaid monastery in ancient times.

Thus, now and henceforth, no bishop, abbot of another monastery, count, or any other person whatsoever shall dare to disturb the brothers of the aforesaid monastery. Rather, what has been sanctioned and established by apostolic authority shall remain firm and inviolable for all time, forever.

If anyone—which we do not wish and indeed prohibit—should presume to act against this privilege of our authority and attempt to violate it, let him know that, unless he repents, he shall be subjected to the bonds of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God. Whoever presumes to do so and does not repent shall be anathema, shall depart alienated from the kingdom of God, and shall be plunged into hell, there to remain forever with the devil.

The religious bishop also made this request, while his venerable legates earnestly petitioned that, contrary to our custom, this document should be written on the parchment they had brought with them, in exchange for the Roman paper [Col. 0804A]. We granted this, and, so that there might be no doubt about the contents written here, we ordered them sealed below with our ring [Note: [Col. 0803D] By “Roman paper” I believe Egyptian papyrus is meant, either because it was manufactured at Rome or because, even in the tenth century, papal bulls were still written upon it. Compare Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book I, chapter 8.].

May those who prove to be the true executors and observers of what has been written by our authority deserve eternal blessing and grace from the Lord God. Amen. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Epiphanius, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February. Given by the hand of Peter, bishop of Orte [Note: [Col. 0803D] Peter of Orte, as John X’s legate, presided over the council of Altheim in Rhaetian Swabia, held on September 20, 916, as Hermannus Contractus mentions under that year. Orte, or Hortanum, the see of Peter, is a town on the borders of Umbria near the Tiber, beside it, contrary to the view of Antonio Pagi, *Critical Notes on Baronius* under the year 916, who understood it as Ortona, a city of the Abruzzo Citeriore on the Adriatic coast. He was refuted by Justus Fontanini in *Antiquities of the Colony of Horta in Etruria*, book II, chapter, no. 13. The episcopal see of Orte, or Horta, was united in 1437 with the bishopric of the city of Civita Castellana. On the bishops of Ortona in Abruzzo, see Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. VI, pp. 966–976.], on March 8, indiction 8 [Note: [Col. 0804D] The indiction should be 7.], while Lord Berengar was reigning in his fourth year [Note: [Col. 0804D] Berengar’s fourth imperial year was still running before March 24, on which day, joined to the solemnity of Easter, John X placed the imperial crown upon him at Rome, according to an anonymous poet who wrote before the middle of the tenth century, in H. Valesius, Paris, 1663; Leibniz, *Writers on Brunswick Affairs*, vol. I; and Muratori, *Writers on Italian Affairs*, vol. I, part II.], after Caesar had been happily consecrated in the name of God. Amen.

## V. Privilege Granted by John X to Paul, Bishop of Adria (920)

[In Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, II, 401.]

[Col. 0804C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend Paul [Note: [Col. 0804D] This is the man who built the town of Rovigo and established his residence there, after Adria had driven out its inhabitants because of its unhealthy air and climate. John X ratifies that migration by this privilege.], bishop of the holy Church of Adria.

Because you requested us to grant to you, and through you to your already established Church, the estate of Boneuno, which is called Rovigo, and the forest called Grumpi, or Piscarium, which is called Longole; also the estate called Romiliac, situated at Caneglada; and the holding of Crispo, with all their appurtenances and adjoining properties, so that you might be permitted to build a fortress at the aforesaid place of Rovigo for the protection of the people of your holy Church, and so forth.

Moreover, we grant the aid of the resident population from the boundary of Rovigo as far as the city of Adria, for the restoration of your ruined and utterly destroyed Church, decreeing that no one shall be permitted to act from the territory of Rovigo onward, and so forth.

## VI. Privilege Granted by John X to Honestus, Archbishop of Ravenna (921)

[In Mittarelli, *Camaldolese Annals*, I, appendix 34.]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. To our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the seventh year of his apostolate; while our lord Berengar, most serene emperor, was reigning, in the [lacuna] tenth year of his imperial rule, in the month of March, indiction 9, at Rome, in the Lateran.

Because you requested from us, Lord John, supreme and universal [Col. 0805B] pope, from the apostolic and most sacred see of the blessed Peter, on behalf of Honestus, by divine favor archbishop of our holy Church of Ravenna of Saint Apollinaris, that we should grant the following for him and his successors to possess forever.

Therefore, by our apostolate of the blessed apostle Peter, the patron Father, [lacuna] the way of obtaining [lacuna] whenever you request benefits from our holy Roman Church that do not harm its rights, but by which Rome may rather increase than diminish. Therefore, just as [lacuna] from the apostolate of this holy universal Church of ours, as we recognize to be worthy and just, [lacuna] to receive blessing [lacuna] we grant and give and hand over, or [lacuna] of this holy Roman Church of ours, to you, Honestus, our beloved confrère of our holy [lacuna], and through the hands of [lacuna], the aforesaid holy Ravennate [lacuna] Church, daughter of this holy Roman Church of ours, [lacuna] for you and your successors to possess forever by your own right.

That is, we grant, alienate from ourselves, hand over into your hands, and emancipate for you, just as our other holy Fathers handed over and emancipated them: so we likewise, through this document of our decree, in the manner both of emancipation and of confirmation, emancipate the entire estate called Campilio, together with all its lands, all its legal appurtenances, its fisheries and hunting rights, and everything subject or pertaining to it, situated in the territory of Gavello between the river Adige and the river Po.

Likewise, we bestow, confirm, and hand over, and permanently transfer from the right of our holy Roman and universal Church to the aforesaid holy Church of Ravenna, namely, the entire and undivided estate called Fiscalia, together likewise with its lands and all its legal appurtenances, and also with all the villages and parishes established in that estate, its fisheries and hunting rights, likewise with every tribute, rent, and [lacuna] temporal and annual payment or exaction, and with everything belonging from the aforesaid estate to the holy Roman Church, situated in the territory of Ferrara.

In this manner we hand over and emancipate both estates from ourselves to you, Honestus, archbishop, and to your successors, to have, hold, administer, dispose of, [Col. 0806A] and judge them forever, with your successors, for the rights of the holy Church of Ravenna of Saint Apollinaris. As we have said above, we have freely and absolutely, without any condition, remitted and emancipated them to you and your successors forever.

If anyone from the whole clergy, or any person adorned with a dignity, or any private person, should bring any lawsuit against this title of our privilege and emancipation, let him pay and give one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our Lateran treasury and half to the holy Church of Ravenna of Saint Apollinaris. Let him also be excommunicated by our most exalted apostolic see and placed under anathema and [lacuna], and under the [lacuna] of the holy councils of Nicaea and Constantinople [Col. 0806B], [lacuna] and whatever [lacuna] honor he appears to possess, from that [lacuna] census [lacuna].

## VII. Letter of John X to Herimann, Archbishop of Cologne (921)

He orders him to come to Rome together with Hilduin and Richer, who were disputing the bishopric of Tongeren.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy confrère Herimann, archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne.

Since by heavenly mercy we are rulers of the Lord’s people, it is especially fitting that we should continually consider God’s protection for the salvation of our subjects, lest—God forbid—when souls have been frustrated by the snares of the ancient enemy, we should be compelled to render a strict account before the shepherd of all. For the faithful and prudent servant is known to have been appointed over the household of the Lord for this reason: that he may give them their food at the proper time.

At the proper time, priests appointed to office give fruit to God when they offer what is expedient for the salvation of all entrusted to them. And because your brotherhood rejected in practice the Apostle’s judgment (1 Tim. 5), which urges that hands be laid lightly upon no one, we are astonished that you did not refuse to adorn Hilduin with the episcopal dignity, although the canons opposed him, without the election of the clergy and the acclamation of the laity, through fear of Gislebertus.

An ancient custom prevails, according to which no one is to confer a bishopric upon a cleric except the king, to whom the scepter has been divinely bestowed. As for the manner in which Gislebertus did not fear to undertake what had not been granted to him, I judge that, since he presumed unlawfully, he will reasonably remain weak.

Yet because Richer, as King Charles’s testimony declares and the letters of our beloved son, the most glorious Emperor Berengar, attest, was first elected by the clergy and sought by the people, we are utterly astonished that you did not hesitate to impose upon him the gift of the Holy Spirit—as though it were a temporal advantage—when you had no right to do so, since it is written: “The intelligent person shall possess the helm of government” (Prov. 1).

In the Old Testament also, divine law decreed that priests should take the breast from the Lord’s sacrifice (Lev. 7), surely for no other reason than that through the sacrifice they might learn what they themselves owe to offer to their Creator. And since we ought diligently to offer ourselves to God, why do we not refuse to follow others who are in error, when it is written: “If you separate what is precious from what is vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15)?

Therefore, because you feared human beings more than God, we earnestly admonish you, instructed by our warning, to take pleasure in correcting as quickly as possible what has been uselessly done. We have not hesitated to express our great astonishment that you attempted to act contrary to reason without the king’s command, although you should remember that this must in no way be done: no bishop may be consecrated in any diocese without a royal order.

Nevertheless, make every effort to come to the threshold of the apostles by mid-October, together with Hilduin and Richer [Note: [Col. 0807D] Richer was abbot of the monastery of Prüm. Gislebertus, whom the Lotharingians had adopted as their duke, is called by some the count of Chèvremont. [Col. 0808D] Jacques Sirmond.], so that, assembled before us and our bishops, it may not be refused to explain what canonical authority commands in this matter.

And if perhaps you cannot come then because of fear of the pagans, come to us as quickly as possible on the Kalends of April [April 1], setting aside every excuse, as has been established above. Then, after every error has been uprooted from the foundation, let the one found worthy enter the sheepfold through the door, and not from elsewhere, lest he be considered a thief.

For we in no way wish to take away the honor of King Charles. Rather, out of regard for the strength, affection, and kinship of our beloved son, the most glorious Emperor Berengar, we are pleased that Charles should retain an unblemished and unshaken rule, as was the earlier custom of his royal predecessors. And just as it has been laudably established by the authority of our predecessors that his earlier predecessors should appoint a bishop in each diocese, so we order King Charles to do this by confirming it.

Until that time, however, as established above, let the bishopric of Liège remain in your power, so that Hilduin may in no way dare to exercise any priestly ministry there.

## VIII. Letter of John X to King Charles III (921)

He states that he has written to Herimann ordering him to come to Rome with Hilduin and Richer; he also states that he has excommunicated Hubert for plundering the Roman Church.

[In Mansi, same work.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king.

Because sincere charity and perfect gentleness shine forth in you, we give immense thanks to our Creator, God, since this is accomplished through divine dispensation. Therefore, exhorting your filial devotion, we admonish you to remain always vigilant and not permit those entrusted to you to continue traveling along precipitous paths for long.

For in this your kingdom’s lofty scepter remains secure, when, through the dispensation of the Holy Spirit, you do not neglect to correct what has been uselessly done. Our beloved son, the most glorious Emperor Berengar, sent to our apostolate a letter concerning Richer, elected by you at Liège and by the entire clergy and people, and concerning how your faithless Gislebertus did not fear to order Hilduin to be consecrated there [Col. 0808A].

Moved by the request of our beloved son, we took care to send an apostolic letter to Archbishop Herimann, so that, by mid-October, he should not delay coming to the threshold of the apostles together with them. There, by credible evidence, the one who is worthy may be canonically approved, while the one who merely supposes himself worthy may then be shown to be rejected.

Until that time, we command by warning that Hilduin dare neither retain any governance nor exercise priestly office in the aforesaid church called Liège. Since, however, the affection of our son abundantly flows forth in you, it is fitting that your sincerity [Col. 0808B] and kinship should appear more readily in him, and that he should remain so faithful through your affection that you may recognize this at present through his assistance.

We have grieved deeply over what Gislebertus has uselessly done against your scepter, because ancient custom and the dignity of the kingdom have judged that no one should ordain a bishop without the king’s command. And because Archbishop Herimann, fearing human beings more than God, did not delay consecrating Hilduin at Gislebertus’s command, for this reason we sent him a summons, so that by mid-October—or, if he cannot come then through fear of the pagans, on the Kalends of April, with every excuse removed—he should in no way delay coming with Hilduin and Richer.

Then, once assembled there and having carefully discussed the honor of your kingdom, we shall not fail to uproot from the foundation what has happened to you through Gislebertus, so that afterward neither he, who acted as the author of this iniquity against your scepter, nor anyone else may dare to inflict any injury upon your kingdom.

We also inform your filial devotion that, together with our beloved son, the most glorious Emperor Berengar, we sent a warning to Hubert, urging him to correct the plunderings and burnings which he had not feared to commit against the holy Roman Church. He resisted and, rejecting this in a haughty voice, refused to make amends.

We, however, in accordance with the effect of our ministry, placed him under excommunication and bound him, together with all his followers, by the chain of anathema [Col. 0808D]. We disclose this to your Highness so that no one in your kingdom may follow him or offer him assistance, since we have bound not only those who follow him but also those who take pleasure in offering him assistance.

## IX. Letter of John X to John, Archbishop of Salona (Spoleto), and His Suffragans (914–928)

[Note: [Col. 0808D] We give only summaries of this letter and the two following ones from Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, since of the work cited by him (*Illyricum Sacrum*) only the first two volumes—covering the fourth through seventh centuries—can be found in our libraries [Col. 0810D]. EDITOR.]

He rebukes John and his suffragans for having so long neglected the Roman see and laments that they follow the teaching of Methodius. He urges them, using the counsel of John, bishop of Ancona, and Leo, bishop of Palestrina, to correct their vices and take particular care that the ministry of sacrifice be performed according to the customs of the Roman Church, namely in the Latin language and not in a foreign one.

[In Farlati, *Illyricum Sacrum*, p. 93.]

[Col. 0809A]

“Since religion, etc.”

## X. Letter of John X to Tamislaus, King of the Croats; Michael, Duke of the Chulmians; and Others (914–928)

He exhorts Tamislaus, king of the Croats; Michael, duke of the Chulmians; John and his suffragans; all the župans; all the priests; and the entire people of Slavonia and Dalmatia to offer the tenderest children to God from their cradles through the study of letters, and not permit sacrifice to God to be offered in the barbarian, that is, Slavonic, language.

He proposes the example of the Saxons, who received from Pope Gregory both doctrine and the study of letters in the language in which the apostolic Church remained vested. He advises them to follow the instructions of John, bishop of Ancona, and Leo, bishop of Palestrina.

[In Farlati, same work.]

[Col. 0809B]

“Divine, etc.”

## XI. To John, Archbishop of Split (914–928)

He orders John to come to him together with Gregory, bishop of Nin, in order to settle a dispute that had arisen in the presence of his legates.

[In Farlati, same work.]

[Col. 0809C]

“Because in you, etc.”

## XII. Bull of John X for the Monks of Saint Launomarus among the Arverni (928)

[Note: [Col. 0810D] This bull is incorrectly attributed to John VIII.]

He confirms the possessions donated by Count William of Auvergne to the monks of Saint Launomarus, who had been driven out by the pagans.

[In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fourth century, part II, p. 254.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops and lords of Gaul, and to all the other faithful of the holy Church of God, greetings.

[Col. 0809D]

Since by the piety of the apostles’ successors we are universally bound to provide for everyone in such a way that we must also investigate the circumstances of each individual without weariness, we must strive no less to wish to be useful than to preside. Know, therefore, that the illustrious and most dear Willelm, governor of the Auvergnats, and his wife Ingelberga, through their faithful envoys—namely, the most reverend bishop Adalelm and the distinguished men Ocbert and Calseus—have made known to us that, for the love of God, they have received the monks of Saint Launomarus, confessor of Christ, together with the body of that saint, driven from their place by the prolonged persecution of the pagans. They have given them, as a refuge, some of their possessions at present, and, should the opportunity arise, intend thereafter to give them more in the region of Auvergne: namely, the estate of Magenciacum, with the church consecrated under the name of Saint Peter; the demesne vineyard of the same estate; another estate near Magenciacum; and, near those estates, the estate called Blavignacus; also a portion in the estate called Espidincus (Espezin), consisting of two manses; in the estate of Regniacum (Regnac), a demesne vineyard; and in the estate of Malamorte, the entire inheritance of a certain Asterius, which they acquired from Gerald and Lucretia, his wife; at Barennis, a demesne vineyard; and in that same county, the estate of Bornicum (Bort), which they acquired from . . .; and, upon the river Dore in the county of Clermont, the estates called Piscatoria, with male and female servants, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, and a mansus, which they obtained in exchange from Fulcher; likewise Prisciniacum (Precignac) in its entirety, together with three other manses situated nearby, namely Vallecinga, Floriacum, and Montjocundum.

Concerning this matter they earnestly addressed our apostolate, which we exercise in the place of blessed Peter, through the religious and venerable bishop Adalelm and the aforementioned noblemen Ocbert and Calseus, who were devoutly visiting the Roman See according to custom, asking that we confirm their donation, according to the custom of our predecessors of the holy apostolic see, by the privilege of the apostolic See, so that in the future no one’s covetousness or disturbance might threaten it. Thus, for all time thereafter, without anyone’s violence or secret seizure, the monks, together with their abbot, and their successors may remain there and observe the rule of their profession with complete fidelity.

Rejoicing in their pious deeds and assenting to their just petitions, we decree by this privilege of apostolic authority, and by that power which we received from God in the blessed apostle Peter, that both the possessions named above and any others which either that God-loving governor and his wife Ingelberga, or perhaps other lovers of God, may thereafter give to the same monks or their successors, shall serve our Lord and Savior, holy Peter, and blessed Launomarus for the monks’ uses and various needs; and, at the coming of Christians [lacuna], they shall on no occasion suffer any legal harassment. Rather, the servants of God who inhabit that place shall be permitted, with the counsel and consent of their abbot, to hold and administer those possessions with secure stability, as may be expedient for them.

But if anyone, led by covetousness or any wickedness, should attempt for any reason to violate their testament and this privilege of our authority, and should bring any accusation or trouble concerning the aforesaid possessions against the servants of God [*ingerere*, “to bring”] . . . or impose upon them any abbot except the one whom the entire community, in agreement, shall have chosen from among itself, one capable of benefiting and governing them according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, then, by the authority of the Holy Spirit and the holy apostles, we separate and exclude him from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and from the fellowship of all Christians, binding him with the bond of anathema. Unless he quickly repents and corrects everything he has corrupted, he shall be struck with perpetual damnation and excluded, together with the rapacious, from the kingdom of God.

## XIII. Letter of John X to Aimeric, Archbishop of Narbonne (Year 928)

He confirms the possessions of the Church of Narbonne.

*[Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, Instruments, p. 16.]

[Col. 0811B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Aimeric, archbishop of the holy Church of God of Narbonne, beloved son and our fellow-bishop.

We received with apostolic patience the letter which your unanimity sent to our apostolate, and, accepting what you reported, we grieved that you had endured so many hardships and have sympathized with you. For if one member suffers, all ought to suffer with it, since, according to the Apostle and distinguished preacher of the nations, we carry such concern within us; for, to confess it in apostolic words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Corinthians 11:29; the supplied text prints II Cor. II, 29). Especially since I humbled myself in order to win them . . . we, who in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, have resolved to establish you, do not wish to be set by the Lord Himself in a watchtower.

Accordingly, your fraternal Reverence requested that we confirm by a privilege of our holy apostolic authority all the immovable possessions of that holy first-ranking church of Narbonne, built in honor of Saints Justus and Pastor, where the body of blessed Paul, confessor of Christ, rests. These possessions are all its houses, cells, churches, estates, farms, parishes, lands, meadows, and woods, as well as half of the saltworks and of the tolls, and the *rafica* and shipwreck-right; the monastery of Saint Lawrence and its cells, with everything belonging to them; together with their household of both sexes; and whatever has been granted to and remains in that church of Narbonne by pious lords, emperors, margraves, or other God-fearing men, both in the county of Narbonne itself and in the counties of Redès, Minerve, Ausona, Béziers, and Nîmes; and, in the county of Besalú, the monastery of Bagnola, which is a church founded in honor of Saint Stephen the martyr.

Therefore, moved by your salutary petitions, we have decreed, and from the present first indiction we confirm and strengthen by this privilege of our apostolic confirmation, and by apostolic authority confirm in perpetuity, for the use and support of that holy first-ranking church of Narbonne over which you are recognized as presiding, all the houses, cells, churches, estates, farms, parishes, lands, vineyards, meadows, and woods, as well as half of the saltworks and tolls, and the *rafica* and shipwreck-right; the monastery of Saint Lawrence and its cells, with all their appurtenances; together with their household of both sexes; and everything that has been granted or will be granted by pious lords, emperors, margraves, or other God-fearing persons to that church of Narbonne, whether in the county of Narbonne itself or in the counties of Redès, Minerve, Ausona, and Béziers. We further wish that all these possessions be held and governed by you and your successors under the firmest legal right.

## XIV. Letter of John X to King Rodulf of the Franks, Wido, Archbishop of Lyons, etc. (Year 928)

He commends the monastery of Cluny, to which he wishes the property of the monastery of Gigniacum, donated by Abbot Berno and taken away by Abbot Wido, to be restored.

*[Bullarium Cluniacense*, 2.]

[Col. 0812C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Rodulf, glorious king of the Franks; and to our most reverend and most holy fellow-bishop Wido, archbishop of the holy Church of Lyons; and to the most reverend bishops Stateo and Berno, and to the counts Hugo and Gislebert.

[Note: This rescript lacks chronological annotations; but Mabillon infers from Wido’s letter that it was written before the sixth year of King Rodulf, that is, in the year of Christ 928, shortly after Berno’s death.]

We have heard with our apostolic ears that Abbot Guido violently took from Cluny what Abbot Berno had bequeathed from the property of the monastery of Gigniacum, to be held under a census.

[Note: Commonly Gigny, in the territory of Lyons.]

Therefore we admonish Your Affection to restore all those possessions to the monks of Cluny. But since the aforesaid Wido complains that Abbot Berno did not do this lawfully, because he did not specify in his testament the limit of time or the persons concerned, we, to whose jurisdiction both places belong, order and decree that, as long as any of those monks who made profession at Gigny or were offered at Cluny remains alive, the Cluniac monks shall hold those possessions under our authority, unless those monks should of their own accord relinquish them.

[Note: Wido accepted this compromise by issuing a document whose clause reads: “I, Rotgarius the priest, having been asked, wrote, subscribed, and endowed this document, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of King Rodulf’s reign.”]

For the rest, we commend to you, O son Rodulf, and to your faithful supporters who may be especially able to benefit the monastery of Cluny, both the abbot and the community, so that that place, which has been entrusted to our holy See, may rejoice in having chosen well, through love of the apostles, that is, of the judges of the world, and through paternal affection.

## XV. Letter of John X to Wenni, Archbishop of Hamburg (Years 914–928)

He sends him the pallium and confirms the privileges of Hamburg.

*[Apud Lappenberg, Hamburg Documents* I, 39.]

+ John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved fellow-bishop Wenni, venerable archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, and to your successors forever.

[Col. 0813B]

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the minds of petitioners their assent with eager devotion. For we shall undoubtedly earn the chief reward of profit with God when venerable places, suitably ordered, have through us been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, because you asked us to confirm in its entirety the archbishopric of Hamburg to you and your successors, as it was decreed by blessed Gregory, Nicholas, and our other predecessors, moved by your prayers, we send you the pallium according to custom. Whatever was given by them to your Church and to your predecessors and confirmed by privileges, we grant to you by apostolic authority and confirm by our privilege—namely, everything that generally and specifically belongs to the aforesaid archbishopric, and whatever your predecessors . . . to Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0814B]

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Leo, chancellor of the holy Roman See. In the first year of the lord Pope John, indiction 9.

## In the year of the Lord 939. Pope Leo VI.

[Col. 0813]

## Historical Notice

Leo, son of Christophorus the primicerius, the sixth of this name, became pope near the end of the year 928, during the reign of the emperor Constantine. In the following year he was thrown into prison, and after six months and five days [according to another reading, fifteen] he died, as the verses of Frodoard on the Roman Pontiffs testify, in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, third century, part II, p. 607:

> In place of John, Leo the Sixth assumes  
> The lofty rule of Peter,  
> And preserves it for seven months and five days,  
> Then seeks the company of his prophetic predecessors.

[Col. 0813]

## Letter of Pope Leo VI to the Bishops of Dalmatia (Years 928, 929)

He exhorts Forminus of Zadar, Gregory of Nin, and the other bishops of Dalmatia to obey John, archbishop of Split, who has received the pallium. He orders each bishop to remain content within his own boundaries, specifically the bishops of Osor, Rab, and Dubrovnik, and commands Gregory, bishop of the Croats, to be satisfied with administering the Church of Skradin.

*[Apud Ughelli, Italia sacra*, vol. V, p. 1421.]

[Col. 0813C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Forminus, bishop of the holy Church of Zadar; to Gregory, bishop of the holy Church of Nin; and to all the bishops dwelling throughout Dalmatia, etc.

Because the gracious mercy of almighty God has placed you in the episcopal dignity, it is fitting that you should gladly show the highest reverence to your metropolitan, the archbishop of the holy Church of Split, so that, walking according to the order and norm of justice, you may advance securely and fearlessly toward divine contemplation.

For what is seen to be worse than for a bishop to be disobedient to his own metropolitan, when it is written in the African Council that no bishop ought to do anything without the knowledge of his own metropolitan? And if this is so—and we know that it is so, namely, that no bishop ought to disregard his own metropolitan—why do you, bishops of Dalmatia, as despisers and, as it were, plunderers by stealth of other men’s parishes, usurp for yourselves a profane title which is evidently seen to have been taken away from you by the ancient Fathers?

Therefore we admonish all the bishops to remain content within their own boundaries. We admonish Forminus to retain his own parish as it remained in ancient times. Likewise, we wish the bishop of the Church of Osor, the bishop of Rab, the bishop of Dubrovnik, and the archbishop of Split in the land of the Croats to retain their own parishes, just as the Church of Salona retained them in antiquity.

For a parish cannot be confined within the walls of a city, but lies across distant stretches of land among rural communities, from villages, estates, and churches, as was anciently determined among the people.

As for Gregory, who was made bishop in the land of the Croats by the probity of the time (*probitate temporis*; the wording is uncertain), we order him to minister only in the Church of Skradin. We command him in no way to usurp other parishes any longer; for if he does so, he shall undoubtedly remain excommunicated by our pontifical authority.

We have entrusted the pallium and the use of the pallium to John, archbishop of the holy Church of Split, as was the ancient custom. We wish you to obey him with your whole heart and to love him as a true father, because now, by the grace of God, it has dawned upon his subjects, together with their superiors, that they should gladly render the care of obedience.

## In the year of the Lord 830. Hucbald, monk of Saint-Amand.

[Col. 0815]

## Historical and Bibliographical Notice

Translated and arranged in French in the *Literary History of France*, volume VI.

### § I. History of Hucbald’s Life

[Col. 0815C]

Hucbald or Hucbold is regarded, after Remigius of Auxerre, as the most celebrated teacher France possessed at the end of the ninth century and during the first years of the following century. On his mother’s side he was the nephew of Milo, whose history we have given, and, like him, he embraced the monastic profession at the abbey of Elnone, or Saint-Amand, in the diocese of Tournai (Trithemius, *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, vol. I, p. 33; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXVII, no. 35).

Some writers (Bollandists, 16 June, p. 34) have asserted that he first became a monk at Saint-Bertin before becoming one at Saint-Amand; but this opinion is supported by no evidence and cannot be maintained. With a rich natural talent, and a taste and ardor for the sciences, Hucbald studied them under Milo, director of the monastery school; and it later happened that the nephew surpassed the uncle in every kind of liberal learning (Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 266; Mabillon, ibid.).

[Col. 0815D]

It is claimed, without proof (Bollandists, ibid.; Mabillon, ibid., book XXXIX, no. 81), that Hucbald, having quarreled with his teacher over an office in honor of Saint Andrew, was forced to leave Saint-Amand and withdrew to Nevers; that there he opened a school; and that the bishop of the place, having taken a liking to him, gave him great marks of esteem and confidence. Finally, it is said that at the bishop’s death Hucbald was permitted to take away the body of Saint Cyr, the martyr, and transport it to his monastery.

What is certain is that Hucbald went from Saint-Amand to Saint-Germain of Auxerre, where he perfected his studies under the pious and learned Heiric, together with the learned Remigius and other distinguished fellow students. Elsewhere we have seen how famous these two schools then were. With such assistance, Hucbald became one of the greatest men of letters of his time. He acquired not only a rich treasury of Latin learning but also all the knowledge of philosophy and the other liberal arts: “His mastery of the liberal arts was so distinguished,” says Sigebert of Gembloux, “that he could be compared with philosophers.” Ademar of Chabannes, earlier than Sigebert, indeed assures us that Hucbald and Remigius inherited all the learning admired in their teacher Heiric.

Hucbald distinguished himself especially by his skill in music, but he made no less progress in theology than in secular letters. Almost all those who praise his profane learning likewise emphasize his great store of sacred learning (Mabillon, *Acts of the Blessed*, vol. VII, p. 325, no. 3; Martène, ibid., pp. 265–266; Sigebert, *On Writers*, chap. 107; Trithemius, ibid., *On Writers*, chap. 284).

To all these great qualities Hucbald added others, highly suited to uphold worthily the character of the priesthood with which he was invested (Mabillon, ibid., vol. II, pp. 938–939). Those who knew him best (Martène, ibid.) observed in him all the gravity of the ancients, the most perfect integrity, and consummate prudence and wisdom. These qualities made him an object of admiration throughout all the provinces of Gaul, where he shone like a bright lamp, and caused France to be considered fortunate in being illuminated by so eminent a teacher. Finally, he possessed a modesty and humility equal to his profound wisdom and extensive learning.

Such was Hucbald (Bollandists, ibid., p. 36; Mabillon, ibid., vol. V, preface, no. 196, and *Annals*, book XXXVII, no. 35) when he succeeded his uncle in directing the school of Saint-Amand, perhaps even before Milo’s death, which occurred in 872. The school was then no less flourishing than it had previously been. After forming disciples capable of replacing him there (Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. III, pp. 530, 532; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXVIII, no. 68; book XXXIX, no. 60), Hucbald went to Saint-Bertin to hold the same position.

Rodulf, abbot of the house, who possessed only a moderate acquaintance with the sciences, was pleased to have so skilled a man near him from whom he might learn them more thoroughly. He therefore requested Hucbald and obtained him in 883. Although already advanced in age, Rodulf took lessons from Hucbald and, out of gratitude, gave him a considerable tract of land in Vermandois. But Hucbald, who valued the love of poverty no less than the other virtues, accepted his disciple’s generosity only so that he himself might have the opportunity to make another gift, by transferring the land to the monks of Saint-Bertin. The practice of such gifts from disciples to masters, and the freedom masters possessed to dispose of them in favor of whomever they wished, were then fairly common among monks (Mabillon, *Acts of the Blessed*, vol. II, p. 710, no. 5).

When Fulk, archbishop of Reims, conceived the plan of restoring the two ancient schools of his church, he also turned his eyes toward Hucbald to help him carry it out (Flodoard, book IV, chap. 9; Mabillon, ibid., vol. VII, pp. 325, 327; *Annals*, book XXXIX, no. 81). He called him to Reims with Remigius of Auxerre around 893, and thus these two great men became colleagues after having been fellow students.

The renewal of learning effected through their ministry in these schools maintained the love of letters there and multiplied scholars throughout the whole course of the tenth century. Elsewhere we have said how flourishing these schools then were. The glory they acquired was originally due to our two professors. Hucbald in particular enjoyed a standing equal to his reputation. We learn this from a diploma which Archbishop Fulk, chancellor of the kingdom, obtained from King Charles the Simple. At the end of this diploma, dated at Reims in the year 899, we read that it was granted at Hucbald’s request: “Obtained through the agency of the monk Hucbald” (Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 250).

It seems very likely that after the death of this prelate, which occurred in June of the following year, Hucbald returned to withdraw into the solitude of Saint-Amand. In the cartulary of that abbey there are indeed two charters from the year 905 subscribed by a Hucbald in the capacity of notary—that is, doubtless, chancellor of the house—and there is no reason to distinguish this Hucbald from the one who is the subject of this article (Mabillon, *Annals*, book XLI, no. 29).

The life of Saint Rictrude, which he composed there in 907 amid the almost continual disturbances into which fear of the barbarians threw him, together with other works that followed it, suggests that Hucbald’s principal occupation was study and writing for posterity (Acts, vol. II, pp. 938–939). He lived to about ninety years of age and died on 20 June, which was a Sunday (Bollandists, ibid., p. 35, no. 6).

Ancient and modern writers, however, disagree about the year of his death. A chronicler of Saint-Amand (Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 1395; Alberic’s *Chronicle*, p. 268) places it as early as 929. Sigebert, followed by Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, places it two years later, in 931. John of Ypres (Martène, ibid., p. 547; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XLIII, no. 32), whom Dom Mabillon seems to have preferred to the others, postpones it another year, to 932. Nevertheless, most authors who have written about him assign it to the year 930, and their opinion must be acknowledged as the best founded, since in that year 20 June actually fell on a Sunday (Bollandists, ibid., p. 36).

Hucbald was buried at Saint-Amand, in the church of Saint Peter, and placed in the same tomb as his uncle Milo.

Hucbald was acquainted with most of the men of letters of his time. We have seen that Odilo of Saint-Médard chose him as a critic of his writings, just as Hucbald himself acted toward Odilo (Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, ibid., pp. 265–266). We possess two letters, one by Odilo and the other by Peter, archdeacon of the church of Cambrai, both filled with praise of our author.

Frodoard, who had studied under his disciples, praises his profound learning, especially in the most difficult branches of philosophy (Flodoard, book IV, chap. 9). We have already reported several other expressions of praise given him by Ademar of Chabannes and Sigebert of Gembloux. Trithemius and the other modern writers who came after them esteem his merit and learning no less. These later writers particularly recognize in him an author who possessed the talent of writing judiciously and with a certain polish uncommon in his century.

It is important, moreover, not to confuse Hucbald of Saint-Amand either with Hucbald, monk of Orbais, who was celebrated like him in the writings of Frodoard, or with Hucbold, cleric of the church of Liège, who was still teaching in Paris at the end of this century, as has been shown elsewhere (*Chronicle of Anjou*, year 937).

### § II. Hucbald’s Writings

Few authors worked longer than Hucbald to enrich the republic of letters. It appears that he devoted more than sixty-five years to this work, something rare in every age. The first evidence of this is found in the length of his life; the rest will appear in what follows.

Among the writings of his own composition that he left to posterity are counted:

#### 1. A poem in praise of bald men

This poem, in heroic verse, is mentioned by Sigebert and highly praised by Trithemius (Sigebert, *On Writers*, chap. 107; Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, vol. I, p. 33; *On Writers*, chap. 284).

The text of the first of these two bibliographers misled a great many writers, who supposed from it that the poem contained three hundred verses. It contains only one hundred and thirty-six, divided into twelve short chapters, not counting the exordium and conclusion.

Elsewhere attention has been drawn to the singularity of this composition: the poet deliberately allowed it to contain only words beginning with the letter *c*. This affectation cost him labor whose usefulness remains difficult to recognize. The first verse of the preface is phrased as follows, and is repeated at the head of every chapter and of the conclusion:

> Sing songs for the bald, O clear-sounding Muses.

[Col. 0818D]

This poem bears the title *Eclogue* both in the manuscripts and in printed editions. Hucbald undertook it for Charles the Bald, to whom he addresses it under the title of emperor. He therefore completed it in 876 (Angl. *Bib. ms.*, vol. II, p. 189; Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XLVI, chap. 22).

Ademar of Chabannes and an ancient poet of Saint-Amand took occasion from it to give the author the surname “the Bald” (Mabillon, *Acts of the Blessed*, vol. VII, p. 325, no. 3). It is easy to foresee that a composition of this kind, governed by perpetual constraint, can possess neither charm nor beauty and is notable only for its unprecedented singularity.

Nevertheless, it was often printed. Two editions were produced at Basel, in 1516 and 1546. But the poet’s text is not complete in them. Valerius Andreas records another edition from Louvain, printed by Jerome Wallaeus, without giving its date.

In 1619 Hucbald’s poem was included in the *Amphitheatrum sapientiae Socraticae*, which appeared at Hanau in two folio volumes (Andr., *Bib. Belg.*, p. 395; Wion, *Lig. Vit.*, part I, vol. II, p. 427; *Bib. barb.*, vol. I, pp. 37, 553).

Gaspard Barthius later inserted it into his *Adversaria*, where it is accompanied by a few brief notes (Barthius, ibid., pp. 2175–2173). This critic speaks of another edition of the same poem that had preceded his own by one hundred and sixty years. It must therefore have been from the year 1463, since he mentioned it before 1624, the date of the edition of his *Adversaria*.

#### 2. A short elegiac poem to the emperor Charles the Bald

Hucbald also composed another short poem in elegiac verse, again addressed to the emperor Charles the Bald, asking him to accept the poem on sobriety which Milo had left at his death and intended to dedicate to that prince.

Since Milo had been unable to send it to him, although he had completed it and adorned it with a dedicatory letter, Hucbald carried out the task in the same year in which he presented to the same emperor his poem on bald men (Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. I, pp. 45–46).

#### 3. Milo’s epitaph

The short epitaph of Milo, consisting of five heroic verses and reported in its proper place, is believed to have been composed by Hucbald (Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXVII, no. 35).

#### 4. Lives of saints, hymns, and offices

The work that most regularly occupied our author in his literary labors was writing the histories of several saints and composing hymns and offices in their honor.

If his journey to Nevers is as real as is supposed, among his earliest writings of this kind must be placed what he composed about Saint Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims. His work is in verse, but the hagiographers do not otherwise agree about its character.

Meyer, in his *Annals of Flanders* under the year 930, calls it a poem. The successors of Bollandus simply say that, while Hucbald was at Nevers—where he is thought to have been shortly after the year 860—he composed songs, apparently hymns or responsories, about Saint Cilinia, at the urging of the bishop of the place (Bollandists, 16 June, p. 34, no. 2).

Dom Mabillon says more and maintains that, having found her life there, Hucbald put it into verse (Mabillon, ibid., book XXXIX, no. 81). M. Baillet seems to go still further and supposes that Hucbald was the actual author of this verse life, which, in his view, is inferior to what the history of her son Saint Remigius tells us about the saint (Baillet, 21 October, *Critical Tables*, no. 4).

There is reason to hope that the learned Bollandists, who have mentioned the matter only incidentally, will provide all necessary clarification when they reach the twenty-first day of October in their calendar.

#### 5. The martyrdom of Saint Cyr and Saint Julitta

The history of the martyrdom of Saint Cyr and Saint Julitta followed the preceding work soon afterward, since it was on account of their relics—which Hucbald, as is again supposed, brought from Nevers to Saint-Amand—that he undertook to write it.

For lack of other sources, the author drew his material from the apocryphal acts of these holy martyrs. For this reason his work is regarded as a composition of no authority, although he took care to exclude the fables found in his source (Bollandists, ibid., pp. 18–19, nos. 8–10).

Defective as his work is, it nevertheless served as a model for Philip Harveng, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, who essentially copied it and altered its style in what he wrote about the same holy martyrs. Mombrice (p. 21, no. 18) is thus far the only person to have printed our author’s text.

#### 6. The office of Saint Thierri

When Hucbald was teaching at Reims, he composed, at the request of the monks of Saint-Thierri, a night office in honor of that saint and notated it to be sung at the solemnity of his feast (Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXIX, no. 81).

The responsories were matched to the antiphons, and everything was drawn from the saint’s Life. Two hymns belonging to this office have been preserved, together with the letter Hucbald wrote on that occasion.

Dom Mabillon had already published these three pieces (pp. 691–692; Bollandists, 1 July, pp. 81–82) when the continuators of Bollandus printed them in turn on the first day of July.

Nothing worthy of special notice is found in them except substantial expressions of piety. Since the author had requested prayers in return for his work, he took care to indicate at the end of his letter the prayers he wished to be offered for him during his life and after his death.

#### 7. The Life of Saint Rictrude

The Life of Saint Rictrude, first abbess of Marchiennes, having perished amid the ravages of the Normans, the nuns of that monastery persuaded Hucbald to write a new one (Mabillon, *Acts of the Blessed*, vol. II, pp. 938–939).

For this purpose they supplied him with everything they could unearth from their records concerning the saint’s history. Hucbald, for his part, approached learned and trustworthy people in order to collect what was known about her by tradition.

With these resources he set to work, and as soon as the composition was finished he sent it to Stephen, bishop of Liège, asking him to review it and make corrections. This led the chronicler of Marchiennes to believe that Hucbald had undertaken it at the prelate’s insistence (Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 1395).

Stephen found nothing to correct. He merely wanted the author to put his name to the work, which he had not done out of modesty, and to indicate the year in which he had worked on it (Mabillon, ibid.). This was a wise precaution, one that it would be desirable for all writers to have adopted. It would have freed us from many difficulties and better enabled us to assess their works.

Hucbald, responsive to Stephen’s advice, informed us that he completed his work in 907. At that time Saint Rictrude had not been in the world for two hundred and nineteen years, as M. Baillet and Father Le Long calculate, but for only two hundred and ten years (Baillet, 12 May, *Critical Tables*, no. 5; Le Long, *French Library*, p. 286, col. 1).

The author nevertheless succeeded in giving us a history that has deserved the praise of Baronius and later critics, both for its sincerity and fidelity and for the natural manner in which its events are related. It is not without defects, especially with regard to chronology. These errors, however, may have originated with the copyists just as easily as with the original author.

Some editors indeed observe that most of the dates marked in the printed editions are not found in all the manuscripts (Bollandists, 12 May, p. 79, no. 1). In his work Hucbald adopts the common opinion of our eighth- and ninth-century historians concerning the origin of the Franks, whom they derive from the Trojans (Mabillon, ibid., p. 939, chap. 1).

Surius appears to have been the first to publish it widely, but he did the author the injustice of changing its style on the false pretext that it was obscure and too simple (Surius, 12 May, pp. 230–238).

Dom Mabillon, who published it after Surius, restored its original integrity with the help of an ancient manuscript from the abbey of Marchiennes (Mabillon, ibid., pp. 937–950).

The successors of Bollandus (Bollandists, ibid., pp. 79, 89) produced yet another edition, revised against the preceding one and collated with several other manuscripts. Both editions are highly estimable, both for the accuracy of the text and for the learned observations with which it is furnished.

John, a monk of Saint-Amand in the eleventh century, judged this work sufficiently interesting to take the trouble to put it into verse (Mabillon, ibid., p. 937, no. 1).

### 8. We have already announced on page 638 of our third volume that Hucbald had worked on the history of Saint Aldegund, abbess of Maubeuge, who died in 684. This is what he appears to have undertaken at about the same time, or shortly after he had finished the Life of Saint Rictrude. He did not have the same reason for undertaking the work now in question, since there were already two legends of this saint: one by a contemporary author, the other composed a century, or a century and a half, later. The most plausible conjecture that can be made on this subject is that Hucbald’s great reputation [Col. 0821A] led the nuns of Maubeuge to hope (Sur. 13 Nov., p. 300) that he would succeed better than the two earlier writers in composing the history of their holy foundress. With this hope, they persuaded him to undertake it.

Nevertheless, what is best in Hucbald’s work is drawn from that of the first author. Properly speaking, he merely gave a new form, and sometimes a new arrangement, to what he borrowed from him, without, however, naming or indicating the source from which he had taken the facts he reports. At the beginning there is a dedicatory epistle to the nuns who had appealed to his pen. In it he strongly recommends observing the division of chapters that he established, should copies of his work be multiplied. He did not put his name to it, as he did to the history of Saint Rictrude; but the editors have no doubt that it belongs to him. (Ibid.; Boll. 30 Jan., p. 1035, n. 5.)

Since Surius had not yet unearthed it when he printed his January volume, where it should have found its [Col. 0821B] place—Saint Aldegund having died on the thirtieth of that month—he placed it on 13 November, the day on which one of her translations is celebrated (Sur. ibid., pp. 300–309). In later editions, however, care was taken to place it on the day of her death. Bollandus reprinted it on that same day (Boll. ibid., pp. 1040–1047), following the works composed on the same subject by the saint’s first two historians. Dom Mabillon did not think it necessary to accord it the same honor, and limited himself to reporting several passages in his notes on the earliest writer, whom he alone chose to publish. Bollandus (pp. 1047–1050) appended to Hucbald’s work that of a monk of Saint-Ghislain on the same holy abbess. But this writing, which dates only from the eleventh century, teaches us nothing that is not found in the other three works, which had treated the same subject before it. The notice given here of this piece should suffice; it will not be mentioned again below.

### 9. The writing of Hucbald that has received the most praise, and that deserves the most, is the Life of Saint Lebuin, or Libwin, an English priest and apostle of the region of the Upper IJssel, who died in 776. M. Baillet supposes (Bail. 12 Nov., tab. crit., n. 8) that the author wrote it on the occasion of the translation of the saint’s relics carried out by Baldric, bishop of Utrecht. Hucbald, however, says not a word about this, and speaks of no translation other than the one carried out by Saint Ludger, more than a century before Baldric (Sur. 12 Nov., pp. 285–286). He ends his work with that event. Nevertheless, we know from other sources that he dedicated it to the latter prelate (p. 277), who succeeded Saint Rodbod in 918. Thus at least 142 years had elapsed since Saint Lebuin’s death when Hucbald undertook to compose his Life. He does not tell us where he obtained the events that he incorporated into it. But the manner in which they are reported, together with their circumstances, makes one judge that good records had been supplied to him.

[Col. 0821D] As soon as he had put the finishing touches to his work, he communicated it to Peter, archdeacon of the church of Cambrai, and to Odilo, a monk of Saint-Médard at Soissons (Mart. am. Coll., vol. I, pp. 265–266). Both men, who occupied themselves with literature, wrote him a letter on the subject, each vying with the other in praising the author’s merit and the value of his work. We know nothing else about this archdeacon; but as for Odilo, it has been seen in his article that he left various other writings of his own. A man named Judion (pp. 267–268), who calls himself a disciple of Hucbald, having come upon his history of Saint Lebuin, also praised it in a poem of thirty-six elegiac verses addressed to Bishop Baldric. At the end he added a prayer to God in a kind of iambic dimeter verse, which shows, as do the preceding verses, that Judion was anything but a good poet. Trithemius thought so highly of Hucbald’s Life of Saint Libwin that he named it before all the other works of this kind that he attributes to the writer (Trit. Scri., c. 284; Chr. Hir., vol. I, p. 33).

Modern critics have formed no less favorable judgment of it. According to M. Abbé Le Beuf, one discovers in it a superior style and a sufficiently pure and flowing Latin (Le Beuf, vol. II, p. 62). In constructing his sentences, Hucbald avoided falling into rhymes or consonances, a defect into which some poor authors of his time fell. He even knew how to place a great number of passages from Scripture with such art that, far from weakening his diction, they adorn it. As soon as the work left its author’s hands (Mart. ibid., p. 266), Odilo noticed the same beauties in it: a Latin uncommon at that time, judgment accompanied by the graces of expression, and a method and arrangement showing that Hucbald possessed every branch of philosophy. “Prudently and elegantly composed, strengthened everywhere by all the branches of philosophy.” [Col. 0822B] This Life is printed in Surius’s collection, which respected its style (Sur. ibid., pp. 277–286).

### 10. The industrious continuators of Bollandus (Boll. 1 Aug., pp. 73–74), having unearthed a writing under Hucbald’s name and bearing the title *Exhortation*, published part of it to serve the history of Saint Jonat, or Jonas, first abbot of Marchiennes, who is mentioned there. Following this exhortation (pp. 74–75) comes the history of the elevation of this saint’s body by the same author, who divided it into nine short lessons. The editors retained the same division when printing this piece together with the preceding one.

### 11. Several bibliographers also count among Hucbald’s writings a Life of Saint Madelberta, abbess of Maubeuge, which was preserved in manuscript in the library of Saint-Ghislain in Valère André’s time (Andr. *Bib. belg.*, p. 395; Oud. *Scri.*, vol. II, p. 418).

[Col. 0822C] ### 12. He is also credited with a Life of Saint Brigida, which Sanderus had seen in manuscript at the Abbey of Saint-Amand (Ibid.; Cave, p. 495, n. 2).

### 13. Dom Martène (Mart. *in reg. S. B. pr.*) assures us that a commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, belonging to our author, exists in manuscript in the same library. Dom Calmet attests the same thing and gives the title of the work, which indicates that it is a fabric of sentences selected from the holy Fathers: “A book extracted from the sayings of the holy Fathers on the Rule of Saint Benedict” (*Liber ex dictis sanctorum Patrum defloratus super regulam sancti Benedicti*) (Cal. *in reg. S. B.*, vol. I, p. 74).

### 14. Hucbald also wrote on music, which he had studied particularly. In giving us a notice of his work on this subject (Sigeb. ibid.), Sigebert says that he placed the letters of the alphabet on the different keys of the monochord with such skill that anyone could thereby learn, without the assistance of any teacher, a melody previously unknown to him [Col. 0822D].

### 15. There exists another short treatise by our writer on the same branch of literature, preserved among the manuscripts of the royal library under this title: *Enchiridion Uchubaldi Francigenae*—“Handbook of Hucbald the Frank” (Le Beuf, vol. II, pp. 98–99). The handwriting of this manual is from the tenth century. It shows that the author invented signs independent of lines and letters to mark each of the sounds of the octave. He gives a table of their values, applied to the hymn of the martyrs, *Sanctorum meritis*. This table, which may very well be by the author’s own hand, is accompanied by a learned explanation of the structure of song, representing it as a grave counterpoint that was scarcely made perceptible except at the points of distinction, as they were then called—that is, at the pauses in the chant.

### 16. Sigebert and Trithemius attest that Hucbald also made use of his knowledge of music to compose and notate offices in honor of several saints (Sigeb. ibid.; Trit. *Chr. Hir.*, ibid.). The one he composed for Saint Theodoric has already been mentioned. Trithemius specifically names another, in honor of the holy King David. Molanus claims that he undertook and completed the same work for Saint Cilinia (Andr. ibid.); and what the continuators of Bollandus say appears to confirm this (Boll. 16 June, p. 34, n. 2). Thus our author would have put the life of this saint into verse and composed an office for the day of her feast.

For a time it was believed (Mart. *am. Coll.*, vol. IV, p. 858) that the office of the Holy Trinity, which we mentioned in the article on Stephen, bishop of Liège, was also Hucbald’s work. It was later established, however, that it belongs to that prelate, through the discovery of the testament of Riquier, his successor, in which it is expressly attributed to him [Col. 0824A].

### 17. Trithemius also counts among Hucbald’s works a collection of letters to various persons (Trit. *Scri.*, ibid.). But since he does not indicate that he had seen it, and since we have no other guarantor of the fact, it may legitimately be doubted.

### 18. Rosweide wished to transfer to Hucbald the honor of having written the legend of Saint Eusebia, abbess of Amay, which exists in both verse and prose. But his fellow Bollandists did not judge his opinion sufficiently well founded to adopt it (Boll. 16 Mar., pp. 450, nn. 1–2). Indeed, it seems to rest only on the fact that almost the same things are read there as in the history of Saint Rictrude. That, on the contrary, should lead one to conclude that this legend is not Hucbald’s work, since he does not copy himself in this manner.

[Col. 0823]

## A SECOND NOTICE CONCERNING HUCBALD

*(In Fabricius, Medieval and Later Latin Library.)*
