[Col. 0823B] Hucbald—also Hugbald, Hubald, or Huabald—was a monk of Saint-Amand of Elnone in Hainaut, on the river Elnon, in the diocese of Tournai, of the Benedictine order [Note: [Col. 0823C] Trithemius, ch. 284, *On Ecclesiastical Writers and Illustrious Benedictines*, II, 49], a man nobly trained in the philosophical disciplines. Archbishop Fulco of Rheims summoned him to Rheims and through him enlightened the Church of Rheims with distinguished teachings, as Flodoard testifies in Book IV, chapter 9, of his *History of the Church of Rheims*. According to Sigebert, chapter 107, he wrote Lives of many saints; this is also confirmed by his epitaph.

He wrote the Life of Saint Aldegund, virgin, abbess, and foundress of Maubeuge in Hainaut, which, after Surius’s edition of 30 January, is presented in a more corrected form by Mabillon, *Benedictine Centuries*, century II, p. 710, and in the *Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. II, pp. 1040–1047.

He wrote the Life of Saint Lebuin, patron of Deventer, addressed to Albric, or Baldric, bishop of Utrecht, in Surius, 12 November; and the Life of Saint Rictrude, abbess of Marchiennes in French Flanders, addressed to Stephen, bishop of Cambrai—not York, as Vossius says on p. 324—in Surius, 12 May, and in the *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. III, pp. 81–89, as well as in Mabillon, *Benedictine Centuries*, century II, p. 937.

The same writer composed the Life of Saint Madelberta, abbess of Maubeuge, which is read in manuscript at the monastery of Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut, according to Valère André, p. 395, and Aubert Miraeus in his notes on Sigebert; and the History of Saint Cilinia, mother of Blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks, together with an office and chant concerning her.

He also wrote the Life of Saint Brigida, preserved in manuscript at the Elnone monastery of Saint-Amand, according to the same Valère and Sanderus in the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum Belgii*, p. 55.

His verses, in which he sent to the Emperor Charles the Bald the poems of his uncle and teacher Milo in praise of frugality, were published by Edmund Martène, vol. I of the *Anecdota*, pp. 45 ff.

According to Sigebert, he also wrote for the same emperor [Col. 0824B] a book of three hundred verses—not “poems,” as Cave mistakenly wrote under the year 916—in praise of the Balds, every word of which begins with the letter C, beginning as follows:

> *Carmina clarisonae calvis cantate Camoenae.*  
> “Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound to the Balds.”

In the Basel editions of 1516 and 1546, and the Louvain edition of 1561, there are no more than 136 verses, just as there are none more in Caspar Dornavius’s *Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Socraticae*, where the same poem is read in vol. I, pp. 290 ff. But Caspar Barthius, who presents it in Book XLVI, chapter 22, of his *Adversaria*, added fifteen further verses from some document or other.

With similar ingenuity, a more recent writer named Christian Pierius published at Frankfurt in 1576, in octavo, a poem on Christ crucified in which the first letter of every word is C.

Sigebert adds: “And because he excelled in the art of music, he composed the chants of many saints with sweet and regular melody” [Note: [Col. 0824C] “With sweet and regular modulation.” The same Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 879]. He wrote a book on the art of music, tuning the strings of the monochord with letters of the alphabet, so that anyone might learn through them, without another’s instruction, a chant unknown to him [Col. 0824C].

Finally, Trithemius mentions letters of Hucbald to various persons.

The writings of this author’s *Acts of the Martyrdom of Saints Cyriacus and Julitta his mother*, which are read in Mombricius, should also be mentioned, as should the ecclesiastical office of Saint Theodoric for the monastery of Rheims. From this work Mabillon published in the *Annals*, vol. III, p. 641, in the appendix to the Lucca edition, the letter prefixed by Hucbald and two hymns.

Finally, Martène asserts that a commentary by this author on the Rule of Saint Benedict survives in manuscript codices, and the authors of the *History of French Literature* report the same from him, vol. VI, p. 220. The book is entitled:

> *Liber ex dictis SS. Patrum defloratus super Regulam S. Benedicti.*  
> “A book extracted from the sayings of the holy Fathers on the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

# PART ONE OF THE WORKS OF HUCBALD THE MONK—HAGIOGRAPHICAL

[Col. 0825]

## LETTER ON SAINT THEODERIC

*(In Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. III, p. 691.)*

[Col. 0825A] To the beloved fathers and brothers of the congregation of the gracious confessor of Christ, Theodoric:

Hucbald, humble though unworthy priest in office and monk in habit, wishes every joy of the blessed life.

Your devout religion, your most ardent devotion to God and to his saint Theodoric, and your simultaneous zeal for what is good have approached my lowliness, requesting that, in imitation of our predecessors, who with most willing minds composed melodious songs suited to each occasion in praise of God and his saints, I too should adapt to you nocturnal responsories, sweetened with the melodies of chants and fitted with antiphons, to be sung at the sacred feast of the aforesaid worshiper of God and your special patron, Lord Theodoric, recounting his memorable deeds.

I undertook this task with as much eagerness as your devotion demanded that it be done. And behold, by divine grace, what your charity suggested has been obediently completed by the humility of my littleness.

But because, as the evangelical voice bears witness, “the laborer is worthy of his wage” (Luke VII), when I humbly requested it and your goodness graciously assented, you promised me, in compensation for my very small service, and with the pledge of your word, that after this nocturnal office had been completed you would annually commemorate me in your sacred prayers—not only while I seem to enjoy the revolving sun in the course of this present age, but even more when, by God’s appointment, I should have died from this present life.

You also added that, through the succession of ages, you would leave this expression of goodwill toward me to the affection of posterity, as a law of good custom [Col. 0826A].

Therefore, may the firmness of this promise between us and the truth of your faith remain ever unshaken and open before God, who promises that the one who speaks truth in his heart and has not acted deceitfully with his tongue shall dwell in his tabernacle and rest upon his holy mountain.

And lest I seem to you to ask great things in return for small ones, let your affection know that you will receive from him the rewards of the charity you have lavished upon me, for he habitually repays the greatest things for the smallest deeds faithfully performed.

Thus, having received your gracious pledge and command, may this aforementioned remembrance of us, by God’s mercy, remain among you as you persevere in this, just as the following items are recorded on this page:

For the living: the psalm *De profundis*; the Lord’s Prayer; the chapters *Save your servant*; *Turn, O Lord, how long?*; *Send him, O Lord, help from the sanctuary*; *May the enemy profit nothing against him*; *Be to him, O Lord, a tower of strength*; *O Lord, hear my prayer*; *O God, who justify the ungodly and do not desire the death of the sinner.*

For the dead: the psalm *De profundis*; the Lord’s Prayer; *Grant him eternal rest, O Lord*; *Do not deliver the soul that confesses you to the beasts*; *May his soul dwell among good things*; *From the gate of hell*; *Grant us, O Lord, that the soul of your servant Hucbald may deserve to receive the remission of sins which he has always desired.* Through the Lord, etc.

[Col. 0825]

## HYMN ON SAINT THEODERIC

[Col. 0825C]

Let the company of brothers now sing

Festive songs to Christ,

Who is ever wondrous and worthy of praise

In his saints,

And who made Theodoric despise

Earthly things and the delights of the flesh

In his heart,

And fix his mind upon himself.

[Col. 0826C]

Thus, despising the world

And giving his bride to Christ,

He asks Remigius

To be his guide to the heavenly court.

Having been excellently instructed by him

In celebrated doctrine,

He is given as father to the monastery,

Which he establishes through the announcement of heaven.

[Col. 0827A]

Distinguished in doctrine

And still more exalted in deeds,

He prepared for many

The narrow path to the realms above.

Divine mercy soon

Shines upon him with miracles,

So that, sowing the words of life,

He may also grant healing.

For he raised up

The only daughter of Theodoric,

And afterward restored

The king’s clouded sight.

Let us therefore humbly pray

That through this man’s prayers

Christ may lift us from our vices

[Col. 0827B]

And enlighten us with virtues.

Let praise, glory, virtue, and honor

Be to the Father, the Son, and the Comforter;

Let glory be to the Trinity,

To the one God throughout the ages. Amen.

Let our assembly rejoice in the Lord

With tranquil heart,

Offering praises and jubilations

At the holy and venerable feasts

[Col. 0828A]

Of the eminent Theodoric.

Touched by the rays of the gracious Spirit,

When he saw the joys of the world pass away,

He despised them, fixing the clear eyes

Of his mind upon the place where Christ’s sure gifts call us.

For he followed the teaching

Of the master Remigius,

And afterward set aside the harmful things of the age.

To him the governance of the monastery

Was soon entrusted,

Whom he worthily honored

With brilliant doctrine.

In him heavenly virtue shone wondrously,

And he relieved the sick from varied affliction;

By a wondrous ordinance,

Through prayer he recalled the king’s offspring

From the cavern of death.

Therefore, Christ our Redeemer,

[Col. 0828B]

We beseech you, set us free

From all sins through this man’s merits,

And join us to the blessed hosts

In the light of the kingdom.

Let praise and glory be to the unbegotten Father;

Let power and honor be to the Begotten;

Let equal majesty be to the Comforter;

One God, who is through all ages. Amen.

[Col. 0827]

# LIFE OF SAINT RICTRUDE, ABBESS OF MARCHIENNES, BY HUCBALD

*(Published by Surius, but restored from the Marchiennes codex by the work of the Reverend Father Simon Guillemot, subprior of Saint-Ghislain; in Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, century II, p. 937.)*

## MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0827C] 1. Hucbald, a monk of Elnone, known for various writings, restored the Acts of Saint Rictrude, which had been destroyed by the devastation of the Northmen, partly from the accounts of the elders and partly from various documents gathered more or less accurately. On this subject, the Marchiennes chronicler says the following in manuscript Book I, chapter 17:

“Stephen, bishop of Liège, a very old man and of remarkable holiness, ordered Hucbald, a monk of Saint-Amand, to compose her Life. This is the bishop who composed the chant of the Trinity and the Life of Blessed Lambert the martyr with as much devotion as elegance, and who, inspired by God, uttered many other things that Mother Church has preserved in her memory and authority. For this reason he chose Hucbald to compose her Life: he was a learned man, and among the monks there was a sound opinion of his conduct. Faith in his statements is established by his long labors and the blameless course of his life.”

Hucbald set his hand to this work in 907, as he himself expressly states in the prologue. Shortly afterward, John, likewise a monk of Elnone, rendered the same Life in verse for Stephen, a monk of Ghent, at the request—or rather the command—of the bishop of the Church of Cambrai, “Erluin.” Erluin held that dignity from 996 to 1011. Nevertheless, Hucbald should stand for all the others: although he fell into error in some matters, he surpasses the rest in authority and antiquity.

2. The name of Saint Rictrude, widow and abbess of the monastery of Marchiennes, is absent from the ancient Martyrologies [Col. 0828C]. A few things must be said about her origin. Marchiennes, or Marcenna, commonly Marchiennes, a town formerly in Flanders on the Scarpe River, between Douai and Saint-Omer, in the diocese of Arras, gave its name and location to the monastery of Marchiennes—or, as it is written, Marchianense—constructed by Saint Amand and solemnly dedicated by him together with Saint Aubert, bishop, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul. Saint Jonatus was placed in charge of this monastery as its first abbot.

From the beginning, there was a double community in that place, of monks and of holy women; Jonatus governed the monks, and Rictrude the women. The Marchiennes chronicler relates that monks were first placed there, and then shortly afterward—that is, about the year 647—virgins consecrated to God were installed in honor of Saint Rictrude, the benefactress.

After the monastery was devastated by the Northmen in 869, the nuns gradually declined into worse conditions, until Count Baldwin, surnamed the Bearded, expelled the women and substituted monks for them in 1028, according to Meier. He summoned Lietwin, the distinguished abbot of the monastery of Saint-Vaast, who governed the place for nine years and then entrusted the government of Marchiennes to his disciple Alberic. When Alberic died in 1048, Saint Poppo, abbot of Stavelot, succeeded him; after a month, Poppo was succeeded by Wido.

These details are summarized from the Chronicle of Marchiennes, whose author we shall also discuss below in the notes on the Translations of Saint Rictrude. This monastery, now devoted to Benedictine monks, continues to flourish. Among its distinguished men were Saints Jonatus and Poppo, as well as the venerable Amandus and Blessed Hugh, its abbots; among its women were Saint Rictrude and her daughter, Saint Clotsendis, who became abbess after her. We may omit Saint Maurontus and Saint Eusebia, who also lived for some time in that place.

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

[Col. 0829]

[Col. 0829A] To the excellent lord Stephen, bishop, in the structure of Christ’s members, as superior and therefore deservedly more honorable; crowned by men according to the sign of his name with apostolic reverence, but ultimately to be crowned by God, because of the distinction of his merits, together with those whose offices he performs:

Hucbald, least of all priests and monks of the same community, wishes joy in the crown that blooms unfadingly with the flowers of virtue.

I was asked by the clerics and holy women of the congregation of God’s beloved servant, Blessed Rictrude, to apply a new pen to writing the deeds of herself and her children. For a long time I resisted, both because I knew my small measure of knowledge to be unequal to so great a subject, and because, after so long an interval, I had neither seen nor heard any written account based on reliable testimony concerning these matters, fearing that I might assert uncertainties as certainties or falsehoods as truths.

When I continued to resist, they showed me certain copies of histories agreeing with their statements. Thereafter, persons whose standing seemed not unworthy of respect assured me that the things they related had once been committed to writing but had perished in the Northmen’s destructive invasion. Finally, adjured by the fearful name of the divine majesty, I yielded. And although I did not persist as I ought, I did persist as I was able, wishing not to serve verbal embellishment but to promote the edification of readers and hearers.

When the little work had been completed and was being handed over to be read, or rather to be examined by your excellence, your prudence judged that certain matters normally required by scholars to establish the authority of every book were missing: namely, the person, place, and time.

It seemed to me, however, that it was more than sufficient [Col. 0829D] if, in written speech, the names and deeds of such distinguished men were retained while the place and person of the writer were suppressed, lest through the writer, as through a dark cloud, the stars of such brilliance should appear obscured.

But as it has pleased your holiness, whose famous name shines like a lamp, our darkness too, though foul, will be illumined; and while the preface of this little book speaks of Stephen, the renowned bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0829D] Surius rendered it as follows: “While the preface of this little book speaks of Stephen, the illustrious bishop,” removing the expression “of Liège”; and he supposed that Stephen, to whom this Life is dedicated, was bishop of Cambrai], mention will also be made of my insignificant person.

As for the place, you know that I do not now possess one of those cities once so famous [Col. 0830B], since I would rather gladly glory in being the least monk of the monastery of Saint-Amand, the distinguished confessor of Christ and formerly also your predecessor, were it not that, because of my sins, I am so often driven from there by fear of barbarian persecution.

What shall I say about the time, which, if I may put it so, seems to be a second and worst matter? I wish only to cry out to God with the Psalmist:

> “We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us,  
> for the years in which we saw evil.  
> Look upon your servants, O Lord, and upon your works”  
> (Psalm LXXXIX).

Finally, we are compelled to heed the Apostle’s admonition:

> “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil”  
> (Ephesians V).

Nevertheless, lest I appear to pass beyond the authority of your command, omitting the names of our kings, let it be known that the time was the nine hundred and seventh year from the birth of Christ the supreme King, this writing having been produced after the cycle had completed its tenth year of the indiction. For the advancement of the Catholic Church, I wish you prosperity in accordance with our common prayers.

May your discerning prudence favor our prayers,

You who everywhere spread the sweet fragrance of fame;

May it also uncover the clouds of falsehood

As a worshiper of truth;

And may it not disdain to regard this work

With a peaceful countenance,

Correcting its faults, if any evil error has introduced them,

And weighing it with a just examination.

But if the scale, once set in motion, tips to neither side,

And no deceit joins me to either unequal portion,

You know, illustrious father, that it is just to rejoice

With a pious labor,

And to render worthy thanks to the Lord

That we are, think, and move in this life;

Since rather we behold [perhaps: hope for] the joys of the true life,

Which Christ the Lord may grant us together to enjoy,

Through the prayers of the saints

Whose deeds we have recorded.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 0829]

## CHAPTER ONE. The Franks Brought to the Faith through Saint Remigius

[Col. 0829D]

When divine grace had once wished to bring the nation of the Franks, which had sprung in ancient times from its leading men from lesser Phrygia and had descended from the royal line of the Trojans, and which had long been deceived by the fanatical madness of idols, to the recognition of truth [Col. 0830D], it determined to accomplish, almost at the end of the world’s ages, what it had predestined before secular time: namely, through the devoted zeal of the most blessed bishop Remigius, when the energetic King Chlodoveus was ruling the scepter of that nation.

That most holy pontiff, powerful both in the sacred integrity of his conduct and in the astonishing power of his signs, imbued the aforesaid king, together with the greater part of his army, with the teaching of the Catholic faith and—as is related—with the chrism received from heaven. In a single day, he baptized approximately three thousand people with the chrism of Christ’s baptism.

From that time onward, both holy religion among the Franks and their dominion over the kingdoms bordering them, and even over certain more distant regions, grew stronger and stronger, partly through the efforts of their leading men. They did not gain this dominion through the wildness of their character, from which some suppose that the Franks received their name, because a kind of natural ferocity of spirit is thought to exist in them and their manners are uncultivated.

Rather, they advanced everywhere to greater heights because divine grace went before them and followed them, and because they were supported by two great columns upon which the whole condition of the entire Church appears to rest: namely, the authority of holy bishops, in the excellence of the honor which they exercise in Christ’s place, and the strength of powerful kings, prudent in every matter concerning the administration of the commonwealth.

Finally, “where sin had once abounded, the grace of God abounded far more” (Romans V, 20), so that, just as the heavens are adorned by the varied beauty of the stars, so the land of the Franks was illumined by the glory of numerous perfect saints, both natives and those arriving from foreign regions, of both sexes and every order, from the Father of lights, “from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes down” (James I, 17).

## CHAPTER TWO. Rictrude’s Noble Parents

From this most holy company Rictrude shone forth like a star of exceedingly beautiful brightness: a devoted servant of Christ, acceptable to God himself and beloved by good people, and praiseworthy for her justice and holiness.

She was born from a sufficiently distinguished stock, the daughter of Ernold, a noble father, and of Lichia, her mother, from the active and warlike people of the Gascons. The ancestors of this people were first called *Vaccei* [Note: [Col. 0831D] See what we noted on this subject in the Life of Saint Amand under the year 679], taking the name from a town situated near the Pyrenees. Later, having changed the name from *Vaccei* to *Wascones*, with the letter c altered to s, they were called Gascons; and their region, previously called Vacceia, was named Gascony.

Although at that time almost all the inhabitants were devoted to demonic worship, Rictrude, chosen by God, came forth from these impious and godless people like a rose accustomed to bloom from thorny briars. From her earliest infancy, as her tender age advanced, she was brought up and instructed in honorable conduct [Col. 0832A].

She lived in the time of the great King Chlothar, who, as previously stated, was the fourth of the Frankish kings after Chlodoveus, the first to be converted to the faith of Christ, and also in the time of his son, the illustrious King Dagobert. Dagobert had been raised by the most blessed Arnulf, bishop of Metz, so that he might reign together with and succeed his father; and, as it is written of him, he was worthy both in ability and in strength.

After the death of his father Chlothar, Dagobert assumed the royal scepters and the duty of governing. He was pleased, as a wise measure, to grant his brother Charibert—who was not his uterine brother—the counties and cities on this side of the Loire and of the frontier extending toward Gascony and the Pyrenees, establishing such a firm agreement that his brother would never again demand anything from him of their paternal kingdom.

Charibert, therefore, holding his seat at Toulouse, and also reigning in the region of Aquitaine, soon afterward brought all Gascony under his authority.

## CHAPTER THREE. Instructed in the Faith by Saint Amand, Who Was Ordered into Exile

The aforementioned King Dagobert governed the royal rights very well in many matters, but he was excessively devoted to the love of women. Because the woman whom he had taken in marriage appeared to be barren, he left her, took another in marriage, and wished her to be queen.

When he was reproved for this crime by the bishops, and especially by the most holy man and miraculous worker, Bishop Amand, he was moved by royal indignation and arrogance, and expelled that venerable bishop from his entire kingdom, not without injury.

Amand endured with the greatest patience the persecution inflicted upon him for the sake of the truth, which is Christ. Since he very gladly desired to pour out his own blood for Christ, he sowed the seed of the divine word in various places. At last, among other regions, he entered the native land of Blessed Rictrude, namely Gascony, so that there he might illumine with the light poured into him from heaven both many people and this beautiful star, and also believing that, because of the ferocity of that people, he might obtain there the palm of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Amand Recalled by the Womanizing Dagobert; He Declines the Care of the Royal Child and Baptizes Him
Meanwhile, the aforementioned prince and King Dagobert, since he had no son whose succession he could rejoice to see, was exceedingly distressed about this and took a third wife to his bed [Note: [Col. 0831D] Namely, Ragnetrudis, concerning whom Fredegarius Scholasticus reports in *Chronicle*, chapter 59, that this occurred in the eighth year of Dagobert’s reign, that is, in the year of Christ 630]. At last he turned to the Lord and sought the intercession of many men; and, by God’s gift, that same year he had a son by her, obtained through many prayers and generous almsgiving. Finally, anxious about whom he should entrust him to be washed in the sacred font and instructed in divine law—so that, just as he himself had had the blessed Arnulf as tutor, he might likewise have his own boy educated by one of God’s greatest servants according to the practice of the Christian religion—he remembered and regretted his former deed, that he had committed so great an outrage against a man of such great holiness. After his ministers had searched most diligently throughout the surrounding regions and had scarcely found him, he asked that the most reverend Bishop Amandus be recalled to him. What more need be said? The true preacher and practitioner of the Gospel, the venerable bishop, was brought back from exile, like the Evangelist John returning as a new man from Patmos. There was common joy for the king and the nobles alike, and the whole people held a solemn celebration at his return. The king therefore fell at his feet and asked forgiveness, which he obtained very readily; he offered a prayer for his son, but his request was frustrated. For that thrice-blessed man replied to him in the words of our Paul [Col. 0833B]—Paul—that one who serves God ought not to become entangled in secular affairs. After saying this, he immediately withdrew from the king’s presence; but the royal ardor did not withdraw from its desire. Finally, what he could not accomplish personally, he eagerly sought to achieve through the suggestions of good men. Accordingly, the king sent to him Audoenus and Eligius, men outstanding in holiness and prudence, and therefore deservedly most beloved and intimate with Amandus, as reliable executors of his wish. Since it was not right to oppose the holy man’s petition, he yielded to their holy request, although compelled by the king’s command.

The royal infant was therefore brought—he was said to be not more than about forty days old from his birth—to receive through the blessed priest the holy grace of blessing, but already to lose [Col. 0833C] the etymology of his natural name. For while he was being made a catechumen by him, and when the prayer had ended no one in that great multitude answered “Amen,” the Lord, who opens the mouth of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent, opened a mouth—not, so to speak, that of an infant but of a boy—and he answered “Amen” in a clear voice, so that all could hear. The event was exceedingly astonishing: those standing around were silent contrary to custom, while he spoke contrary to nature. Immediately the holy bishop regenerated him through life-giving baptism and ordered that he be called Sigebert [Note: [Col. 0833D] “Charibert,” says Fredegarius, chapter 62, “coming from Orléans, received Sigibert from the holy font” [Col. 0834D]. Read the *Life of Saint Amandus* under the year 679], whom King Haribert, the king’s brother, received from the sacred font. Thus, while the Lord glorified his saint and magnified him in the sight of kings, he filled both kings and both armies with great joy and wonder at such a sign [Col. 0833D]. In the year following this, King Haribert died, and shortly afterward his little son also died; and King Dagobert brought his entire kingdom, together with Wasconia, back under his own authority. I have inserted all this both because of certain preceding matters and especially because of what follows, so that readers and hearers may know what occasion the blessed Rictrudis had for coming to Francia.

## CHAPTER V. Rictrudis Marries Adalbald.

In the aforementioned times, when Wasconia was frequently made accessible to the Franks, the girl Rictrudis, already of good character and now apparently marriageable, was loved and chosen by a certain Frank named Adalbald, born of distinguished and upright parents. His mother, moreover, had been Gerberta, the daughter of Saint Gertrudis, who now rests in the monastery she herself built at Hamaticum. He too, instructed from childhood in the finest disciplines, possessed abundant estates and wealth and was highly esteemed and honored at the king’s court—a man plainly worthy to become the husband of the worthy Rictrudis. He was betrothed to her according to custom, endowed with a dowry, and, although some of the girl’s relatives were unwilling, received into the marital union. The reason for taking a wife was not lack of self-control but the desire to have beloved offspring. Yet the qualities ordinarily sought in choosing a husband or wife were present in both. In the man there were virtue, birth, beauty, and wisdom—the last of these the chief quality for producing the affection of love. In the woman there were beauty, birth, wealth, and character, qualities that should be sought more than the others. In short, according to the Apostle, their marriage was honorable and their bed undefiled (Hebrews 13). They had not heard with deaf ears the words of that same Apostle: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6). Thus, clinging to one another through the bond of faith and charity so that they were two in one flesh, and no longer two because they were one flesh, with one mind, one voice, and harmonious action they honored God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, serving the Lord all their days in holiness and righteousness before him, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house.

## CHAPTER VI. She Bears Children.

Children were also born to them according to the blessing that the Lord first gave to humanity: “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). Their firstborn was named Maurontus, afterward a holy abbot and levite; and they had three daughters, sacred virgins: Clotsendis, who after her mother’s death became ruler of that monastery; Eusebia, a good worshiper of God, in accordance with the interpretation of her name [Col. 0834D]; and after these, Adalsendis. Since their parents were righteous, they raised and instructed them in the fear of the Lord, both personally and through servants of God who were close to them, causing them to grow from infancy in heavenly blessing. The venerable and God-worthy priest Richarius became Maurontus’s spiritual father and regenerated him for God through holy baptism. The distinguished Bishop Amandus received Clotsendis from the saving font with sacred and worthy hands and made her worthy of God in all things. Queen Nanthildis, Dagobert’s wife, received Eusebia from the sacred font. Truly a blessed offspring, pleasing to God. Of them it is rightly said: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with glory!” (Wisdom 4). For indeed, although the righteous are often enriched with spiritual gifts, they are also endowed with temporal goods, as the Psalmist sings: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord” (Psalm 127:1), and so forth. Although the meaning of these words is spiritual, temporal advancement is nevertheless sometimes granted to the righteous in accordance with them.

## CHAPTER VII. She Mourns Her Slain Husband.

Afterward, Adalbald, a man of good and praiseworthy memory, husband of the devoted servant of Christ Rictrudis, from the district of Austrebatum [Note: [Col. 0835D] The district of Austrebatum, Ostrewant in Belgium, lay enclosed by the rivers Scarpe, Sensée, and Scheldt. It was so called, as is rightly conjectured, because it was a boundary of Austrasia; for *bant* means “boundary” among the Belgians. Concerning the reason for Adalbald’s journey and the place of his murder, opinions vary widely [Col. 0836D]. He was buried in the monastery of Elnon; some of his relics were transferred to Douai in 1221. He is commemorated on the fourth day before the Nones of February. Consult Bollandus], undertook a journey to Wasconia, exceedingly sorrowful to his own people, although he was also enriched with numerous possessions there. The noble matron Rictrudis accompanied him for a short distance, but as soon as possible she sorrowfully returned home, as she had been ordered. Her mind, in a certain way prescient of future grief, already foretold what she did not yet know; and what she had not yet suffered she was already, as it were, lamenting. What more need be said? During the journey, the righteous man was attacked, wounded, and killed by the ambushes of wicked men—and, as is reported, by those who had disliked the holy marriage. Then, buried with the honorable rites that were fitting, he died to the world but lives to God. He lives, I say; his blessed soul lives, clinging to him who is the true life. The signs that are frequently displayed at his dead bones, in order to make his merits known, bear witness to this. Nor was there much delay in reporting these things to Rictrudis, the servant of God. Struck by so grievous a report, she was afflicted with no small sorrow of heart. The pain of her grieving children increased her grief, and the mourning of her grieving household increased her lamentation. At length, after some time had passed in such great weeping, she took counsel with her familiar friends who loved Christ, especially with Amandus, the most holy bishop of God, and began a salutary course. That true counselor of souls set before her the words of the Apostle Paul: “A woman is bound to her husband as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice” (1 Corinthians 7). At this she raised her ear and also raised her mind. From him she also heard—or rather, deeply received—that sweet evangelical voice beloved by those who love Christ: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24); and, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

## CHAPTER VIII. She Rejects a Second Marriage. She Takes the Veil before the King.

Fixing the anchor of her mind in these sacred and life-giving words, Rictrudis, who had been left by Adalbald but loved by God and loved God, set aside every wavering delay in deliberation and promised to rest in the bishop’s salutary counsels. But behold, the devil’s envy attempted to obstruct both the salutary advice of the bishop and the pious resolve of the holy matron through a covert plot. In disturbing these things, he did not move only the lowest or middling people but the highest nobles of the world. Finally, through the king himself, he tried to persuade her to join herself in a second marriage to one of his nobles. When she utterly rejected this, many blandishments and exhortations were poured out in vain. Since her position, firmly fixed in God, was not moved by these things, the terror of royal threats was also brought before her, though fruitlessly. But she despised the king raging just as she had despised him flattering.

Because among the three branches of philosophy she had chiefly grasped that which consists in action and concerns right conduct—which in Greek is called *ethics* and in Latin *moralis*, and is known as the teacher of good living—and because this is divided into the four principal virtues, namely prudence, justice, courage, and temperance, she rendered to each of them what was due. Through justice she had resolved to obey God rather than human beings; through courage she could neither be softened by enticements nor broken by adversity; through prudence she carefully sought to avert the king’s anger from herself; and through temperance she strove to preserve the rule and measure of humility in every word and deed.

Finally, following the counsel of her fellow initiate—namely, the God-bearing Amandus—and for a time concealing her firm resolve concerning the service of God, she promised the king that, with his counsel or permission, she would undertake whatever he judged would be more advantageous for her. What more need be said? Having thus made the king suspect that she wished to obey his will, she prepared in her estate, that is, in the villa of Baireio (Boiry, near the city of Arras), a sumptuous banquet worthy of royal magnificence. She invited the king with his nobles and, while they dined, delighted everyone with the pleasantness of her witty conversation. When hunger had been removed and the desire for eating had been satisfied, then, after the banquets had been greatly enlivened by bright wine, she rose and—neither timidly but steadfastly, nor lukewarmly but fervently, nor sluggishly but shrewdly, nor womanishly but manfully—carried out in deed what she had conceived in her mind.

First she asked the king whether he would grant her permission to do freely in her own house whatever she wished in his presence. He readily agreed, supposing that, after taking a drink, she would, as is customary with many, cheer him or his companions by compelling them to drink. But she, following the salutary advice of her counselor, the illustrious Bishop Amandus, brought from her bosom a veil, invoked the name and aid of the terrible God, and placed it upon her head before the king and all the astonished company [Col. 0837A]. The bishop had already blessed it.

When this was done, the king, moved to anger, left the unwelcome banquet and departed from the feast. But she, casting her resolve upon the Lord, entrusted herself and all that belonged to her entirely to his judgment, so that they might be nourished and comforted by his ever-merciful consolation. First, after prudently distributing the resources and possessions left to her, and completely uprooting from the soil of her heart the thorny cares of this world, she who had previously borne thirtyfold fruit in married life began afterward, in widowhood, to bear fruit sixtyfold through a doubled growth. And she who had formerly been Martha, while striving to minister to Christ in her members, now, sitting beside his feet, listening to and guarding his word, became Mary. Since, as he himself testified, she “chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42), she deserved to receive the excellent reward of that beloved and chosen portion in recompense.

## CHAPTER IX. As She Changes the Disposition of Her Mind, So She Changes That of Her Body.

Indeed, so that what the human being carried within might also be shown outwardly, just as she had changed the disposition of her mind, so she changed that of her body. She cast off the splendid garments in which she had been adorned as a married woman, formerly thinking about the things of the world and how she might please her husband; and together with them she stripped herself of every impediment of this world, so that although she appeared to be a widow—that is, separated from her husband—she was no longer separated in spirit, but was always concerned with the things of the Lord and solely with how she might please God.

She put on the garments of widowhood, whose very appearance displayed contempt for this world. For just as white garments suit exaltation and solemn joy, so black garments suit humility and mournful sorrow. Therefore the head, which is the principal part of the body, was also covered with a gloomy veil, so that the chief part of the soul—that is, the mind—might be signified as veiled by the grief of sorrow and repentance. Although this is brief and, so to speak, momentary, it produces the consolation of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

And in order to overcome bodily pleasures once experienced and the troublesome suggestions of demons, she undertook frequent fasts with excessive vigils and continual prayers. She clothed herself in an elephant-hair cilicium, whose constant prickings would tame the prickings of lust; and, as the poet said, “without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.” Truthfully she sang with the Psalmist: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth, and humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Psalm 34).

## CHAPTER X. She Chooses the Monastery of Marcianas, Where She Might Devote Herself to Spiritual Exercises.

As the place where she could devote herself to spiritual exercises, with the counsel and assistance of the aforementioned bishop, who served as her confidant, she chose a very suitable one: the monastery called Marcianas, which the same bishop had built on the river Scarpe. To complete and organize it, that bishop had appointed his disciple, the holy abbot Jonatus, a venerable man, whose sacred body is still buried in the same monastery. In it the blessed Amandus had wished an order of monks to be maintained, but the aforementioned abbot had gathered nuns there, as seemed best to him.

The servant of God Rictrudis therefore sought this place, suitably remote. With the consent of Blessed Amandus, who acted as mediator of reconciliation between the king and herself, she received it with the privilege of royal authority, so that there, although placed in fragile flesh, she might bravely overcome bodily desires. And not this alone: by wrestling against the rulers of this world’s darkness and against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places, and by conquering them together with the world, she might await and receive from the heavenly spectator the triumph of victory and the fitting rewards of her struggle [Col. 0838B].

## CHAPTER XI. She Consecrates Her Daughters to God.

So that she might be sufficient for carrying these things to a successful conclusion, and so that it might be clear to all, by way of example, from how great a perfection she had begun her way of life—according to the Gospel saying, “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5)—after casting off the burdensome loads of estates and riches, after professing before God the continence of widowhood, and after putting on the holy garment of the religious life, she was not content merely to present herself as a living, holy, and pleasing offering to God. She also offered to the Holy and Undivided Trinity the sacred and excellent firstfruits of the earth—that is, of her womb—namely, her three aforementioned daughters, white as doves, as most acceptable sacrifices to him.

Thus, pure in heart and body and preserving perpetual virginity, they might “follow the Lamb, the son of the virgin mother, wherever he goes” (Revelation 14:4), blooming in body with the freshness of an undefiled virginity and shining in heart with the purity of inviolate truth, so that they might always be without blemish before God’s throne, singing to him a new song—that is, rejoicing with him forever in the incorruption of the flesh. Although others may be able to hear this song, none of the saints will be able to sing it except that radiant company of the undefiled.

Since these things are most truly so, hear, I beg you, and receive them with your ears, all you who have ears to hear, for whom it is still permitted to rise to the privilege of angelic chastity, to acquire fellowship in so noble a society, and to resound with them in the melody of the new song. Hasten, run, make haste; remembering Lot’s wife, do not look back. Flee foul lust; trample down carnal desires. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.” Let these exhortations penetrate the innermost parts of your hearts. They are not my own compositions but are borrowed from the words of Father Augustine, that distinguished teacher, with which he exhorts virgins (Augustine, *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 27):

“Proceed,” he says, “holy boys and girls of God, men and women, celibate and unmarried; proceed perseveringly to the end. Praise the Lord more sweetly than you think and more abundantly; hope more joyfully in the one whom you serve more earnestly; love more ardently the one whom you please more attentively. With your loins girded and your lamps burning, await the Lord when he comes to the wedding. You will bring to the wedding of the Lamb a new song, which you will sing on your harps—a song of such a kind that no one will be able to sing it except you.” And shortly afterward:

“Follow him, because the flesh of the Lamb is also virgin. Follow him in virginity of heart and flesh wherever he goes. For what is it to follow except to imitate? ‘Because Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps’” (1 Peter 2:21).

## CHAPTER XII. She Encloses Herself at Marcianis.

Rictrudis, the faithful woman of God, who had devoted herself entirely to him in holy continence, also betrothed her three daughters, while they were still young, to one husband, Christ, so that they might always follow the Lamb’s footsteps; and, since she herself could not yet sing the song by her own efforts, she caused it to resound for him through the harps of her daughters. After arranging everything so wisely and stripping herself of all the cares of the world, she entered the monastic gymnasium, where she would run the course of this present life in struggle and contend by wrestling against the devil. Like athletes in the arena, she entered naked, so that she might not be held by the wicked adversary in any respect, and anointed with the oil of heavenly grace. According to the Apostle, striving in the contest, she abstained from everything, and by her example taught her daughters to live.

Her firstborn, Maurontus, still wearing secular clothing and occupied with royal services and military affairs, was detained by his body rather than by his mind in the affairs of the court; concerning him an appropriate account will be given below.

## CHAPTER XIII. She Bears Equanimously the Death of Her Daughter Adalsindis.

In those days Adalsendis, the last of her daughters, died; she who had been the last to enter the gate of the present life was the first to enter the gate of death. But why do we say that she died, when, at the annual revolution of the cycle, on the very solemnity of the Lord’s holy Nativity—when the remedy by which death is driven away with its prince came into this world, dead in sins—she was not dead but rather brought forth into light and eternal life [Note: [Col. 0839] Saint Adalsindis is commemorated in the Benedictine Martyrology and others on the eighth day before the Kalends of January]?

But the good Rictrudis, strong and patient amid adversity, what was she to do then, when two very contrary emotions confronted her—joy and sorrow? On the one hand she heard the angel proclaiming throughout the world: “Behold, I bring you good news of great joy which shall be for all the people” (Luke 2); on the other she saw her daughter dead before her eyes, and nature itself compelled her to grieve for her. Yet the strength of the manly spirit within her overcame womanly feeling. She did not allow the mourning for her daughter’s death to dominate her, nor did she permit there to be a place for sadness where the birthday of Life was being celebrated.

To summarize briefly what is worthy of remembrance: the duty of burial was completed according to the custom of the faithful, while the practice of mourning for her loved one was set aside. Thus the first day of the succeeding solemnities passed, then the second, then the third. On the fourth day, when the holy Church commemorates the slaughter by Herod of the little children for Christ and the pitiable grief of their mothers, prudent Rictrudis, knowing what duty she owed to each occasion, and knowing that there is a time and season for everything under heaven, distinguished between a time for rejoicing and a time for weeping. After the sacred mysteries had been completed—mysteries in which honor, not grief, is offered to those holy martyrs for the praise of God, and vows of ceremonies, not tears, are made—and when a bodily refreshment had already been prepared for herself and the other nuns, she summoned them all and said:

“Now let your communal charity, beloved sisters, go forth and rejoice, sharing with thanksgiving in the gifts of God. But let me, following the example of my mistresses, namely, the mothers of the holy innocent children, whose loud weeping and wailing have been heard today, be permitted also to mourn my innocent little one, in a somewhat similar manner, snatched away by premature death.”

Having said this, she sought a secluded place suitable for grief and satisfied the demands of nature. O praiseworthy and imitable woman in prudence, patience, and endurance, whose works praise her at the gates! O strong woman, who girded her loins with strength in chastity and strengthened her arm in perseverance in good work, and therefore did not allow her lamp to be extinguished in the night!

## CHAPTER XIV. The Deeds of Her Son Maurontus.

Since the deeds of the blessed man Maurontus have been mentioned above, it seems appropriate to narrate something about him briefly. He was the spiritual son in baptism of the distinguished priest of Christ, Richarius. It happened on one occasion that the same venerable priest, both because of Rictrudis’s holiness and because of his friendship with her, visited the blessed woman while riding a horse. After they had taken together the sweet nourishment of heavenly life in sacred conversation, and the man of God, mounting his horse, wished to return home, the same servant of God went a short distance from the house out of affection. She carried in her arms her own son by natural generation, but his spiritual godson by spiritual generation, and followed his steps so that the child might be fortified by his fatherly blessing.

When the man of God, already seated on his horse, had taken the infant into his arms either to bless or to kiss him, the enemy of all good, the envious devil, suddenly infused an extraordinary ferocity into the horse. Raging like one possessed, gnashing its teeth, kicking with its feet, and rushing violently here and there, it struck both of them with a double but common fear [Col. 0841A]. The priest feared for himself and the boy; the mother feared for the priest and her son. In her anxiety, almost lifeless, as though she saw death impending before her eyes, she turned her face away, obscured by tears, lest she should behold the miserable end of both at once. The sorrowful household too, grieving and crying out, gathered around the sad spectacle with loud lamentation.

But the servant of God, holding the boy lest he should fall from his hands, poured out a prayer to the Lord. When it was completed, the boy was lowered to the ground unharmed, as though he were a light little bird taking flight, and the horse was restored to its former gentleness, like a peaceful sheep. At last the mother, recovering her breath, recovered her son safe and lifted him up in her arms, laughing. Thus the enormous sorrow of all who were present was turned into great joy. No one ought to doubt that this was granted through the merits of both.

And since the mercy of almighty God is so great that, from the very point at which the wicked enemy attempts to crush the righteous, he makes them progress more and more, this temptation also advanced the holy man in virtue. For reflecting that, when the Lord and his God went toward the redemption of the human race, he rode—not in a proud display, not on a caparisoned horse, but on a donkey spread with the garments of the apostles—in order to present an example of humility, he too afterward, whenever necessity required him to travel somewhere, used a similar conveyance in imitation of that example.

## CHAPTER XV. Maurontus Flees Marriage and Is Tonsured. The Meaning of the Clerical Crown.

When the same venerable Maurontus had reached manhood, he remained attached to the king’s side, as his nobility required, devoted—as has been said—to his continual service; and he was also bound by the ties of betrothal [Note: [Col. 0841D] Surius rendered the meaning of this passage as though Maurontus had not even accepted a betrothal, but had rejected the bride offered to him. This Maurontus must be distinguished from the Maurontus mentioned in the *Life of Saint Richarius*, chapter 12, as overseer of the royal forests. This is clear from the fact that Maurontus, overseer of the royal forests, was already flourishing at a mature age in Dagobert’s court, whereas Morontus, the son of Rictrudis, abbess of Marcianas, was born during Dagobert’s reign. Furthermore, Maurontus praised in the *Life of Saint Richarius* does not seem different from the Maurontus who in the *Acts of Saint Walaricus*, chapter 23, is called the highest among the palace nobles while Walaricus was still alive. Yet Walaricus did not live beyond the year of Christ 622 [Col. 0842D], by which time that palace Maurontus was already married, whereas this Maurontus had not yet been born. Finally, Maurontus, guardian of Dagobert’s forests, became a monk under Richarius’s discipline in the cell of Crisciacum, or Foresticella; but this Maurontus came under the rule of Saint Amandus, first in the monastery of Marcianas and afterward in Brolles, of which he was also abbot. In fact, the Marcianas Maurontus seems to have been the same as Richarius’s spiritual son, whose mother was Rictrudis, a woman devoted to God, praised by Alcuin in the *Acts of Saint Richarius*.]

But, prompted by Bishop Amandus, the gainer of souls, who set before him the sweetness of spiritual love and the delights of eternal joy, he quickly loosened the pleasurable fetters of carnal love in which he had, as it were, set his foot. When he reported to his holy mother the resolve of his mind—that he by no means wished to live with his betrothed—she feared that perhaps, through the precipitous courses of wantonness, as is customary among certain young men, he might decide to follow the broad road that leads to hell. She was therefore struck by the greatest sorrow of heart and again asked Amandus, the physician of diseased minds, to come to her aid. He came to Marcianas and soothed her with gentle words and consolations familiar to him; thus he restored her former joy in God [Col. 0842A].

After the bishop had celebrated the solemnity of Mass, while Maurontus himself was present, the aforementioned bishop saw a bee circle three times around the man’s head. The man, full of God, immediately understood what the omen of this sign indicated. He summoned Maurontus and urged him to carry out as quickly as possible in deed what he had long ago begun in his heart and recognized, by God’s initiative, had been revealed to him. Maurontus did not delay in doing so.

Then the most holy Bishop Amandus, blessing him according to ecclesiastical custom, cut off the hair of his head and tonsured him as a cleric, making him bear the sign of the crown. Through these outward actions he indicated what was to be preserved inwardly by their symbolism: namely, that the uncovered top of the head signifies that all the secrets of the heart are naked and open to God, and that whatever is thought or done in secret lies open to the eyes of him who sees all. The frequent cutting of the hair teaches that the excesses of evil thoughts must frequently be cut away.

The beauty of the crown also expressed both the tiara of the supreme priest and the diadem of royal dignity. Through these things he might know that he belonged to the royal priesthood and that, after completing the endurance of various temptations and proving himself through patience in them, he would deservedly receive from God the crown of eternal life promised to those who love him.

The holy man Maurontus not only received this from the salutary tradition of the bishop but also took it from the sacred teaching of Holy Scripture, committing it to memory through reading and admonition. He strove most devotedly always to fulfill it through continual practice. Later he became a levite and took care to conduct himself in a manner and life worthy of that name and office.

Born of a distinguished family, he also shone prominently at the king’s court and was honored with a royal seal, being a prudent notary who wrote out the edicts of royal commands. For the purpose of increasing and completing the benefit of his holy way of life, God also added to him the companionship of the holy Bishop Amatus. This blessed man, elected and elevated to the episcopate of the city of Sidon [Note: [Col. 0842D] Read “Sens,” as is established from the *Life of Saint Amatus* itself and other authors], was falsely accused before King Theodoric, who was exercising an unjust tyranny, as though he were guilty of disloyalty. He was ordered to undergo exile in the monastery of Perona, situated in the town of the Vermandois, where the holy abbot Ultanus presided [Col. 0842D].

Afterward, following the death of Blessed Ultanus, he was handed over to the aforementioned servant of God, Abbot Maurontus, so that he might commit him to custody in the monastery called Broilus [Note: [Col. 0843C] The monastery of Broilus, situated on the river Leye, was destroyed in the year 870, when, with the Danish persecution impending, the brothers serving God and Saint Amatus transported Blessed Amatus’s body to Menrivilla—this is what they call Broilus, as though it meant “Maurontus’s villa,” according to the *Life of Saint Eusebia*, number 2 below—and placed it in their own church of Blessed Mary. This church of the Mother of God is now a collegiate church called Saint Amatus. From the archives of that church Colvenerius transcribed this and other material in his notes on the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book 1, chapter 22], recently built by him in the territory called Letium.

When he had received him and experienced his religious way of life, Maurontus devoted all the diligence of his life to serving him, as though preserving a heavenly treasure. In him he possessed a most beautiful mirror of his own life and holiness and of that of his fellow brothers [Note: [Col. 0843D] We have read the *Life of Saint Amatus* excerpted from the Marcianas and Compiegne manuscripts. It contains almost nothing worthy of note, but rather a tedious adaptation of commonplaces; therefore we have omitted it. Read Balderic, bishop, in *Chronicle*, book 1, chapter 22. Amatus was led by Maurontus from Perona to Cambrai. For the sake of prayer, he used a ray of sunlight as his servant, placing his cloak upon it. Both proceeded to Hamaticum, where they stayed for a very long time and made considerable progress. Finally, after leaving the monastery of Hamaticum, the holy bishop was led to Broilus. Beside the basilica he ordered a cell to be built for himself, in which, whenever suitable, he confined himself and constantly wearied his body with vigils, prayers, and fasts, until the Lord summoned so distinguished a soldier from earth to heaven, around the year 690, as recorded in the silver book of the collegiate church of Saint Amatus at Douai, where his relics are preserved. They had been brought there from Menrivilla, the burial place of Broilus in ancient times, in the year 870. Colvenerius demonstrates this from the same copy in his notes on Balderic’s *Chronicle*. Read the notes below on chapter 20.]

## CHAPTER XVI. Eusebia, Twelve Years Old, Succeeds the Dead Abbess Gertrudis of Hamaticum, but Is Recalled to Marcianas at Her Mother’s Command. She Withdraws to Hamaticum by Night with Amatus.

Meanwhile, God’s servant Gertrude, who had been the grandmother of the venerable man Adalbald, lengthening her life through good works, entered upon the way of all flesh in the monastery at Hamaticum, which she herself had built, where the holy virgin Eusebia, her great-granddaughter, was also being raised. Eusebia succeeded her, as though to the office of government: a girl indeed of good disposition, but still of very tender age, being only twelve years old.

Her mother Rictrudis, however, a true worshipper of Christ, employing deeper counsel and prudence, well aware that the craft of the malignant enemy deceives many even at a mature age after they have been exercised in many virtues, was afraid for her daughter, lest, if she obtained premature freedom, she might be tempted by the serpent’s deceit. Therefore she wished Eusebia to come to her and live with her. When Eusebia refused and wished to remain at Hamaticum, her mother was compelled to appeal to the ears of the king, so that by his authority she might recover her own daughter. When he granted this and sent a letter ordering her return, Eusebia, sorrowful, returned to her holy mother at Marcianas, together with the body of her holy great-grandmother Gertrude, with the relics of the saints that had been buried there, and with her entire community.

When her mother had thus obtained what she desired, she frequently exhorted her daughter to serve God with her in spiritual warfare. Eusebia most willingly obeyed her words, continually devoting herself to divine services; but her intention could not be turned away from her love of the place that was, so to speak, her native home. This happened very frequently, almost every night: after the completion of the evening office, when she was thought to be taking bodily rest with the others, she would leave her sandals beside her bed as a pretext for concealment and travel silently to Hamaticum in the dead of night, together with the most holy bishop and monk mentioned above, Amatus by name and religious way of life [Note: [Col. 0844D] These things absolutely cannot fit together. Amatus was exiled no earlier than the year 678, at which time Eusebia was no longer twelve but forty, since she had been received from the sacred font by King Dagobert and Queen Nanthild. Certainly Gertrude, abbess of Hamaticum, whom Eusebia is said to have succeeded as great-granddaughter, did not live beyond the year 650; she died on the eighth day before the Ides of December, on which day she is customarily commemorated. The monastery of Hamaticum, or Hamatgium, not far from Marcianas, was reduced to a priory subject to Marcianas and called Hamay.], who was for a time living in exile there under the care of the holy abbot Maurontus, and with her foster-sister and other trusted companions in her secret, as she supposed. After celebrating the vigils and the offices of all the hours there, she returned to the monastery at Marcianas, having committed a faithful theft, though not altogether cheerful, lest she should seem to be absent there also during the nocturnal or matutinal hours.

## CHAPTER XVII. She is injured when beaten with rods by her mother on this account; after consultation with the bishops, she is permitted to return to Hamaticum.

[Col. 0844C]

Someone did not fail to report these things to her mother. Calling her daughter to her, Rictrudis addressed her now with gentle persuasion and flattering words, now with harsh speeches intended to frighten her, so that she might recall her from the purpose of her own will, knowing for certain that Eusebia was held to her more by bodily proximity than by any closeness of mind.

When she could achieve nothing in this matter either by herself or through her friends and household, she took counsel with her son Maurontus, a levite and venerable abbot. It seemed to both of them that, for this disobedience and a certain obstinacy of spirit, Eusebia ought to be corrected with blows. When her mother had decided that this should be done by her brother, Maurontus ordered it, and the girl was handed over to correction, held tightly between the arms of servants assigned to the task [Col. 0844C]. Since the boy who held her was girded with a sword, while the virgin bent this way and that amid the confinement of the blows, the sword’s hilt injured her tender side, as is reported, to such an extent that for many years afterward she survived by expelling saliva mixed with pus and blood from her mouth.

When not even this caused the intention of the holy virgin to cease from what she had begun, they summoned bishops, abbots, and distinguished men from the vicinity. All of them dealt with her in different ways, seeking to turn her away from such a desire. She, however, resisted all their addresses with great steadfastness. When they saw that her spirit was inflexible, they advised her mother to permit her to return to the place she desired. Her mother consented, though unwillingly, strengthening her religious way of life with her counsels and commending her to God in sacred prayers.

Having obtained the long-desired fulfillment of her wishes, Eusebia, filled with joy, returned to the monastery at Hamaticum with her entire little community, having once again received the holy body of her great-grandmother together with the venerable relics of the saints. There she lived an angelic life on earth and, in the very midst of her youthful years, was carried away to the chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom, lest, as Scripture says, wickedness should change her understanding or deceit should mislead her soul; and, having been perfected in a short time, she fulfilled many years (Wis. 4), for her soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to lead her out from the midst of iniquity.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The author answers an objection.

Indeed, because of the foolish chatter of certain people, I am willing to lengthen my style for a little while, sharpening it so that the tongues of those who speak wickedness against the just in pride and abuse may be pierced (Ps. 30:19)—those who set their mouths in heaven, since they do not hesitate to slander those whom they believe, now removed from earthly things, to reign with God in the heavens.

For they invent and repeat arguments of this sort: “See what sort of saints these people are said to be! The mother persecutes an innocent daughter who wishes to serve God; the daughter curses and avoids her own mother as though she were an enemy; the son, in agreement with his mother, brings away his fugitive sister, betrayed by a secret sign, and subjects her, as though guilty of theft, to the most savage beatings, almost to the point of death. Even if he does not kill her at once, he nevertheless makes her waste away through prolonged torment. Do such actions make people saints and pleasing to God? What holiness, what peace, what charity is there in these people?”

What, then, shall we answer people of such insane mind? O foolish arrogance of a deranged spirit! O rabid barking, not of men but of dogs, belonging to fools! What can be given or added to a deceitful tongue except the sharp arrows of the mighty (Ps. 119:3)—that is, the darts of almighty God’s words, brought forth from the quiver of the sacred Scriptures? They are so effective that they pierce not only loquacious mouths but also swollen hearts themselves.

First, such people are struck by the thunder of the Gospel: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Matt. 7:1), and so forth. Listen, if you can, and take heed.

Holy mother Rictrudis does not persecute an innocent daughter; rather, she considers her immature age, knowing that “everything has its time,” and that there is a time for every matter, and that, as the most wise Solomon says, “A child left to his own will brings shame upon his mother” (Prov. 29). She also hears Scripture saying: “You have daughters; preserve their bodies” (Sir. 7). Indeed, she desires her daughter to remain with her chiefly so that, by her exhortations and example, she may advance her toward greater perfection.

Her daughter Eusebia, although betrothed to the heavenly King, does not therefore proudly reject or despise her blessed mother, knowing that her Bridegroom had issued this command: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20). But, in the sight of the grace of him who had betrothed her with his ring, and burning solely with love for him, she did not wish the affection of any other love, not even that of her mother, to be shown toward her, lest she be separated even slightly from the love of the fervor implanted within her.

Nor does her brother Maurontus, minister of Christ, torture his sister with blows out of hatred or cruelty. Rather, in fraternal charity, he corrects the young girl as though she were insolent and—as one might put it—disobedient to a parent, as her age required, knowing what is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13:24), and because “the rod and correction give wisdom” (Prov. 29:15).

And what is surprising if mother and son, judging by human standards, make a mistake in correcting the holy virgin, being still unaware of the divine grace that was within her, when holy prophets themselves have sometimes uttered a human judgment as though it came from the Spirit of God? Let foolish speeches of fools cease, then—let them cease! For works of iniquity cannot be assigned to deeds that proceed from the root of charity, as Truth itself bears witness when it says: “If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6).

## CHAPTER XIX. Another objection.

As for the claim that, because of this event, the blessed virgin is said to have been subject to bodily illness during her life, who does not see that this contributed to the increase of the grace already bestowed upon her, so that when she grew weak in body she might be strengthened in spirit, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12)?

Therefore let the mouth of those who speak wickedness be stopped, since the divine voice thunders concerning such people through the prophet Isaiah:

“I will deal with their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them, and their offspring and their descendants shall be known among the nations and among the peoples. For all who see them shall recognize them, that they are the offspring whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. 61:8–9).

The truly good cultivator of God, Eusebia, departed this life full of virtues on the sixteenth day of March, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 689, at the age of forty-six [Note: [Col. 0845D] Thus reads the Marcianas exemplar; the chronological figures are absent from Surius and seem to have been inserted, as do the statements below concerning the age and length of office of Saint Rictrudis. Concerning Saint Eusebia, see below.].

## CHAPTER XX. Amatus dies; Maurontus also dies.

After the Lord had taken the holy bishop who was dear to him, the monk Amatus, from the weariness of this burdensome pilgrimage to the heavenly homeland on the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 0846D] The Marcianas codex agrees, presenting the Life of Saint Amatus, at whose end it is read that the passing of Blessed Amatus on the Ides of September had been determined by his predecessors, but had rashly been assigned by a certain Stephen to the third day before the Kalends of May, as was evident from ancient books found at Saint-Medard, in the Marcianas archive, and in the libraries of many monasteries.], the holy Maurontus honorably buried his sacred body in his own possession and transferred to him, by written documents, all the estates of his inheritance.

The venerable abbot Maurontus himself, a levite worthy of God, although he outlived his holy mother in this life, after completing the duties of his pious administration and being released from his office, was carried up to the palaces of heaven on the third day before the Nones of May [Note: [Col. 0848D] Saint Maurontus the levite died in the year 701, as Colvenerius reports from the silver manuscript codex of the church of Saint Amatus at Douai. Concerning his relics, see below.], to receive the rewards worthy of his labors; living forever with Christ, he rejoices with him in perpetual glory.

## CHAPTER XXI. Rictrudis dies after renouncing the office of governance.

But, to return to the matters whose explanation we began, Rictrudis, God’s most devoted servant, devoted to good works with the whole effort of her mind and the whole service of her body, walking from virtue to virtue, ran untiringly with an enlarged heart along the path of God’s commandments, in the arena of faith and righteousness, drinking eagerly with open ear: “Run while you have the light.” Thus she might be found worthy to receive the heavenly prize and might show herself perfect in all things, imitating him who said: “I have not come to do my own will” (John 6:38).

She submitted herself to another’s rule and obeyed her commands with the greatest obedience. Serving the others as a maidservant, she always kept before her eyes the saying: “I have not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20). Never and nowhere leaving the enclosure of the monastery, she offered herself to all as an example of good works: in humility, obedience, patience, chastity, fasts, vigils, continual prayers, long-suffering, gentleness, modesty, and kindness.

And why say more? As a daughter of God she always walked in the light, whose “fruit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth” (Eph. 5:9). Persevering in this purpose of holy virtues, after completing seventy-four years of her earthly sojourn, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, having attained the joy of her long-desired hopes, she gave her little body to the earth but her holy soul to heaven, in the year 687, at the age of seventy-four and after forty years of governance.

## CHAPTER XXII. Her burial.

She was honorably buried in the same place [Note: [Col. 0848D] The Marcianas chronicler specifies the place more precisely: before the altar of John the Baptist and the Apostle Andrew, on the right-hand side of the church.] by priests of God and others serving with her in the order of ecclesiastical dignity, while very many men of the Christian religion streamed from every direction to the funeral rites of so great a mother. They mourned her temporal absence but rejoiced in the eternal glory that she enjoys with Christ.

And now, with the hope of ineffable rejoicing, she awaits the great day of her greater glorification, when “what is sown in corruption shall rise in incorruption; what is sown in dishonor shall rise in glory; and what is sown in weakness shall rise in power” (1 Cor. 15:42–43). Then, in that blessed resurrection, she will be glorified with a double glorification, rising in blessed glory with all the saints and being happily crowned on the right according to the merits of her deeds.

## CHAPTER XXIII. She shines forth through miracles.

[Col. 0848B]

So that no one may doubt the efficacy of the living merits of this servant of God, numerous truthful proofs provide us with conspicuous signs of the powers displayed at the tested members of her body. There, the blind have frequently received sight, the deaf hearing, the mute the use of speech, the lame the ability to walk, and those suffering from fevers and various illnesses have received—and continue to receive, when they ask in faith—the health they desire.

Many witnesses of this fact still remain: both those who have obtained the gifts of the desired health and those who, seeing these things and praising God as wonderful in his saints, have rejoiced in his benefits.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The author’s invocation.

[Col. 0848C]

Therefore, holy and beloved servant of God, Rictrudis, we ask you with the whole affection of our hearts that, through your sacred intercession and merits, by which you loosen the bonds of various illnesses, you may also release us from the chains of our sins, so that, freed by the grace of kindly Jesus on the dreadful day of his judgment, when the heavens and earth are burning, he himself may snatch us, rescued from the flames of Gehenna, with you into the joys of eternal blessedness. His mercy and compassion have no end; to him, with God the Father, coeternal with him, and the Holy Spirit, belong kingdom, power, honor, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0847]

# ON THE TRANSLATIONS AND MIRACLES OF SAINT RICTRUDIS

[Col. 0847D]

The Marcianas Chronicle, which we received in manuscript through the kindness of the Reverend Father Simon Guillemot, subprior of Ghislenghien, is divided into two books under the following heading:

“Two books by an anonymous author concerning the Life and Miracles of Saint Rictrudis.”

That author wrote after the middle of the twelfth century, while Gosvinus, abbot of Aquicinctum, was still alive, as appears from Book II, chapter 20, where, speaking of the resignation of Lietbert, abbot of Marcianas, he says: “The lord Gosvinus, abbot of the church of Aquicinctum, who still survives, a religious man . . . did not approve the restoration of that abbot.” Saint Gosvinus died in 1196.

The same author testifies in Book II, chapter 40, that he had been a monk under John, abbot of Marcianas—namely, the John who succeeded Blessed Hugh around 1158. From this we infer that this author was none other than Andrew Silvius, prior of Marcianas, who died in 1196 and composed three books on French affairs.

Whoever this chronicler may ultimately have been, he reports the various fortunes of the monastery of Marcianas with sufficiently mature judgment, and frequently inserts numerous miracles of Saint Rictrudis and mentions translations of her relics. A few matters concerning these must be discussed.

### 2.

In Book I, chapter 18, he mentions a diploma of the Roman Emperor Charles, by which he “ordered that everything belonging by right to the people of Marcianas should be possessed in perpetuity, free from every secular exaction, by the brothers serving God.”

The author adds: “In the archives of the church there is an imperial subscription, confirmed by the impression of his ring. In the final line of this privilege, royal munificence, out of love for the aforesaid noblewoman [Col. 0849B] Rictrudis, established that, if any of the brothers or sisters serving her should lack anything, it should be supplied from the royal domain.”

From this it is evident that even in the ninth century monks lived at Marcianas together with the nuns.

### 3.

After the account of the Norman devastation given in Book I, chapter 20, the author adds:
