“When the monasteries situated along the Scarpe River had also been destroyed—including the monastery of Marcianas, where the body of Blessed Rictrudis rested—and the inhabitants of the land had been driven away or killed, it too was obliterated. The bodies of the saints that had been buried in the churches destined for destruction were transported safely, by divine providence, to safer places.

“In that destruction all the adornment of the church of Marcianas perished: documents, privileges, books, the acts of the saints, and the other things belonging to the beauty and use of the place.

“If someone should perhaps ask where the body of the aforementioned woman was transferred because of the pagans’ attacks, let him know that it was still resting quite decently in a stone tomb before the altar of Blessed John the Baptist. When it was raised from there, or by what persons, is not sufficiently clear to us.

“Nevertheless, in an investigation concerning the elevation of Saint Jonatus, abbot and disciple of the illustrious confessor Amandus, we found it written that, in the time of Abbess Judith, who governed the monastery of Marcianas during the reign of Lothar, the bodies of the saints were still resting in stone tombs placed before the altars: namely, those of Blessed Rictrudis, a noble matron, and of the good confessors Maurontus and the aforesaid Jonatus.”

And in chapter 21:

“When, through divine revelation, the relics of the aforesaid confessor had been raised and honorably placed in the crypt, the same narrator who records these things adds: ‘There too, afterward, the relics of Blessed Rictrudis, the noble matron, and of Maurontus, her beautiful offspring, were placed, and they are venerated with religious devotion by the peoples who come afterward.

“‘As for us, we have celebrated the day of the elevation of that most blessed woman, the seventh day before the Ides of February, according to the custom handed down by our predecessors, with the greatest devotion for sixty years’” [Col. 0849D]—that is, six times twenty.

### 4.

In Book II, chapter 16, the translation of Saint Maurontus is described in these words:

“The relics of Saint Maurontus, resting for a long time with the relics of his mother in the monastery of Marcianas, were later secretly taken away—whether God permitted or desired this, I do not know—and were transferred to Douai. There, in the church of the holy Mother of God, now called Saint Amatus, they placed them fittingly and joyfully in a gilded vessel beside the body of that same bishop, who at that time served God there.”

And below:

“Accordingly, since most of the relics of Blessed Maurontus had been taken to Douai with the connivance of the clergy and people, it was established that on the third day before the Nones of May, which is the day of his burial, his memory should be solemnly commemorated each year by all who lived there.”

### 5.

In chapter 20 of the same book, the second translation of the relics of Saint Rictrudis is related as follows:

“The devotion of the ancients had adorned the reliquary of that same saint quite suitably with gold, silver, and precious stones. But their descendants, who lived a long time before us, did not fear to spend the entire exterior ornament, shining with its bright appearance, in order to gratify carnal desires.”

With the agreement of the abbot and brothers, “expenses were prepared, and a new vessel of gold and silver, containing a considerable quantity of these metals, was restored.”

The people of Ypres and other inhabitants of the surrounding area, “approaching the abbot [Lietbert], devoutly asked that the body of the holy woman be solemnly carried and transferred to Reninga, formerly her estate. They promised to restore the tithe and other revenues that the church had lost through the negligence of their predecessors” [Col. 0850B].

“The abbot agreed to their devout request, and the matter, with the appointed day, was announced to the bishop of Thérouanne, Milo. When he heard that the ceremony was to be celebrated in his diocese, he rejoiced and replied that he would attend in person, setting aside every excuse.

“Alvisus, the revered bishop of Arras, likewise, when asked by the church, decided that he would come there with his clergy. Then, after two small reliquaries had been taken, the most sacred body was conducted to Reninga with the greatest devotion of all, although the aforesaid Bishop Milo excused his physical presence because of illness.

“On the fourth day of Pentecost, with the clergy, the nobles of the land, and an immeasurable multitude of people standing by, the most sacred body was enclosed in a new reliquary by the sacred hands of the Bishop of Arras, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1140.

“After that same bishop had delivered a sermon to the people and completed the solemnities of the Mass, they returned to their own places, bringing the sacred body back to Marcianas with equal honor.”

[Col. 0850C]

### 6.

Finally, when the reliquary of Blessed Rictrudis had once again been stripped, the monks of Marcianas restored it anew, with “Brother Hugh secretly supplying forty marks of silver.”

“When the vessel had been completed with a great display of gold and silver, the venerable Lord Henry, archbishop of Reims, came to Flanders. On the third day before the Nones of August in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1164, in the third year of his archbishopric, he visited us.

“Granting the prayers of Abbot John and the whole church, on that same day he took the relics of Blessed Rictrudis from the old vessel with his own hands and placed them in the new one. Andrew, bishop of Arras, was present with his clergy and the neighboring abbots.

“Anyone who, by virtue of his own authority, was able to obtain anything from the abbot out of those relics rejoiced that he had received something of great value. The archbishop himself, reserving a portion for himself as a solemn memorial, carried it with due honor back with him to France.”

### 7.

From these things it is clear that Raphael Beauchamp, a monk of Marcianas, does not correctly interpret this final translation in his appendix to the Merovingian Synopsis, as though it had been the transfer of the relics of Saint Rictrudis from the monastery of Andernes in the diocese of Morini. The monks of that monastery gloried in possessing the body of Saint Rictrudis, whom they call Rotrudis.

See the Chronicle of the Monastery of Andernes by William, its abbot, in volume IX of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. Whatever right the monks of Andernes may have had to the relics of Saint Rictrudis, it is certain that they are now preserved in the church at Marcianas.

[Col. 0851]

# THE PASSION OF THE HOLY MARTYRS QUIRICUS AND JULITTA, BY HUCBALD

*(In Monbritius, Acts of the Saints, part II, no. 18.)*

[Col. 0851A]

Recalling with due veneration the holy struggles of Christ’s martyrs, let us praise the Lord, wonderful in his saints. He strengthened the blessed infant Quiricus from the very day of his birth, before three full years had passed, and his holy mother Julitta, noble by birth and upright in conduct, by the grace of a heavenly gift. Through that grace, the weak in age and sex conquered for the love of his name, and to them he granted the glorious palm of martyrdom in heaven.

To us, however, he grants very many benefits through their intercession, as we believe. Therefore, just as he urges us through his bishops and through holy Mother Church, by daily exhortation, to act in this way, it is fitting and just that we too should glorify God our Lord by praising him beneficially at all times and in every place, and should always praise and bless him with thanksgiving, so that we may fulfill the Psalmist’s words: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:1).

This is the sacrifice by which God is devoutly worshipped by all ranks of those who live well, when they render him, as far as possible, fitting thanksgiving for his deeds. He himself also admonishes us through blessed David, saying: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49:14).

Finally, this is a worthy response to his immeasurable benefits and a just offering of our service. On that very day, by the equity of such reasoning, it is also salutary for our souls and bodies. For sacred Scripture clearly reveals how much this benefits us. After saying, “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High,” it immediately adds: “And call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15). Again, elsewhere it says: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. 17:4).

Finally, because these holy men of God, whose memory we now celebrate, and the other divine martyrs strove most devoutly and steadfastly to fulfill this, praising and calling upon him in their tribulation, he rescued them from the immediate affliction of their enemies and saved them in his heavenly kingdom. There, rejoicing in perpetual happiness granted by him, they rightly honor him with everlasting praise.

Let us too, placed in the exile of our earthly dwelling amid the many hardships of the present life, praise and call upon the Father of all consolation, believing that here also he will console us in all our tribulation, since we hope in his mercy; and that there he will grant us the joys of that consolation which no sorrow follows, through the merits of these saints, whose solemn feast we now venerate and whose wondrous struggles we have undertaken to recount briefly.

We reject—or rather, spurn as filthy things—the frivolous dung that a certain ignorant, lying mimographer published about them in an exceedingly coarse style. For this reason it has rightly been rejected as apocryphal by faithful worshippers of Christ, and especially by Blessed Pope Blaise, among many other works.

We, however, recall with admiration, for the honor of your holy name, Lord, the marvelous trophy of Quiricus, a small child and a great martyr. Before he was able, because of his bodily age, to know you, “you went before him with blessings of sweetness, and from the mouth of infants and nursing children you perfected praise” (Ps. 26:4) of your marvelous name. Through him you wondrously destroyed the enemies who resisted you, and, through you, having joyfully completed his martyrdom, you filled him with gladness in your presence (Ps. 20:7).

Therefore, as in all things, may the magnificence of your power be blessed, since through Quiricus, beloved by you, it so wondrously conquered the ancient enemy. Through his intercession, we ask you to grant us victory over the snares of that same malignant enemy. Let us now proceed to set these things forth faithfully.

At the beginning of the sixth age now being lived, when the Lord Jesus Christ, true God and man, deigned to consecrate his coming—namely, in the forty-second year of the reign of Octavian Caesar Augustus, who held power for fifty-six years according to the will of true Peace, then appearing in the flesh, and afterward ruled the whole circuit of the ocean in peace, after all nations had been united in a single peace, possessing the monarchy of the entire world and leaving that imperial power—

among his successors, Aurelius Alexander became the twentieth emperor after him, approximately two hundred and twenty-six years, more or less, after the Lord’s birth. During his reign, when the churches were suffering the greatest persecution, glorious struggles of martyrdom were undertaken by Christ’s soldiers for the sake of piety; through endurance of punishments they were granted by God the crown of immortality.

Among them was Blessed Father Callistus, pope of Rome in the dignity of the priesthood, sixteenth in succession from the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. While he stood firmly in the house of the Lord, persevering in his commandments and in holy charity, and, like a chosen ram, as leader of the whole flock, in the pious sheepfold of the Lord, he was suddenly seized by order of Alexander himself, committed to prison, tortured by prolonged hunger, beaten daily with clubs, and finally thrown from a window of the house. With a stone tied around his neck, he was plunged into a well, and rubble was heaped over him from above, so that he was buried there. Thus God adorned him with the crown of martyrdom.

His successor was Saint Urban, bishop of the same holy Roman see. By salutary teaching he summoned many to martyrdom, and he too drank the cup that he had offered to others.

After this persecution of Christians under the emperor Alexander had begun, as we have said, and the savage determination to persecute them had flared up everywhere beyond measure, it reached the borders of the eastern provinces as well. In those regions a governor named Alexander was in charge, equal in ferocity to his emperor, just as he was equal to him in name.

Among the countless people whom he had afflicted with various tortures and devised punishments, he ordered that Julitta, a noblewoman who meditated day and night upon the law of the Lord and was renowned for the good fragrance of her reputation, should be brought before his tribunal by his officials.

Julitta served the Lord in chaste fear and was raising her little son Quiricus. Together with her milk she transmitted to him the discipline of divine law. Amid the dear embraces and kisses of his mother’s affection, so that he might recognize, honor, and love his true Parent, while he was nourished on sweet milk from her breasts, he was for the time being instructed by her mouth in the doctrines of pure faith.

When persecutors rose up against her, she cried out to the Lord for her own safety and that of her child. Finally brought before the governor and asked by him from what province or city she came, or what her proper name was, she replied:

“I am from the province of Isauria, born among the leading families of the city of Hybonia. To avoid your persecutions I migrated to the regions of Cilicia, and I stayed at Tarsus. Since I am truly a Christian, my name is Julitta.”

The governor said to her: “I urge you: take thought for yourself, carry out the emperor’s commands, and offer the required libations to our gods.”

Blessed Julitta replied: “I do not sacrifice to unclean demons, because I am a true worshipper of the one living and true God.”

The governor said: “Sacrifice to the gods before you are led to torture.”

She replied: “I will neither sacrifice to your vain gods nor fear torture.”

Meanwhile, while these words were being exchanged between them, Quiricus’ noble mother was distressed by no small anguish of spirit because, standing in the battle-line for the confession of faith, she was deprived of the consolation of her little son. At her suggestion, however, and by order of the governor, the tender child Quiricus was sought out—as though his mother had betrayed him—and found by the governor’s soldiers. He was brought before the governor himself.

At first, as befitted an infant, he was soothed with gentle flatteries; then he was provoked by threats. But he, regarding the one no more than the other, steadfastly professed with a mature mind and most eloquent speech that he was a Christian, and firmly declared that he could in no way be separated from his profession.

Our eternal King, our God, who, appearing in the flesh, armed himself to battle the strong man (Luke 11), and girded himself with the strength of his majesty against the world lying in wickedness (1 John 5; Ps. 17), and who established the world, namely, the holy Church spread throughout the whole earth (Ps. 93), so that it would not be moved from the stability of its faith and so that the gates of hell might not prevail against it (Matt. 16)—he himself, through the Holy Spirit, gave the firm steadfastness of his power to the heart of his beloved infant Quiricus and placed eloquence of speech in his mouth, “who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. 10).

Thus, while the infant boy stood before the governor, naturally still without speech, it was not he who spoke, but the Holy Spirit spoke in him and through him. His soul and heart were filled with the Spirit’s richness and abundance.

Alexander said to him: “I want you to tell me truthfully who was the teacher of this holy doctrine, and at the same time to abandon this obstinacy as quickly as possible, lest you be severely punished for contempt of the gods and the emperor.”

The child replied: “Governor, I marvel at your ignorance. Seeing in me such a tiny child, you ask who taught me divine wisdom, even though, with the course of three years not yet completed, I am scarcely capable of learning ordinary knowledge.”

Having heard such words, the governor was seized with fury and ordered the child to be beaten with the utmost violence. But while he was being beaten, with his eyes raised to heaven and his little hands spread out like a strong athlete, he blessed the Lord on high:

“I give thanks to you, Lord God; my soul blesses you, and all that is within me. Praise belongs to you, Lord of powers, because you perfect strength in my weakness” (1 Cor. XII).

Then, as though taunting the executioners, he repeatedly cried out in a loud voice, as loudly as his strength allowed: “Indeed, I am a Christian!” And whenever he uttered this pious confession, new bodily strength was restored to him, so that both the governor and all who were present marveled at such endurance in one so young and weak. For the God of justice, who had justified him by his grace in the earliest years of infancy, mercifully heard him when he cried out to him in tribulation and wondrously glorified him before everyone.

When his glorious mother saw him placed in such a contest, she rejoiced with all her heart and, stretching her hands toward heaven, glorified the Lord with a voice of exultation and confession; she encouraged her son to persevere steadfastly in the faith. She feared, indeed, that because of the tenderness of his body he might perhaps yield to the scourging. But when the hands of those beating him were already almost exhausted and collapsing, he himself, strengthened by the Spirit of God dwelling within him, maintained a steadfast spirit and was renewed with fresh strength to endure.

Again the governor ordered the mother and son to be brought before him. Since he could in no way turn them back from their resolve in the true faith, he had them tortured by various kinds of punishment and finally confined in dreadful prisons. But the holy martyrs of God, shut up in a most restricted dungeon, joyfully sang these words to God:

“Grant us, Lord, a sign for good, so that those who hate us may see it and be put to shame, because you, Lord, have helped us and comforted us” (Ps. LXXXV).

They remained steadfast in prayer and praised God, asking that by the power of his strength they might be snatched from the snares of the devil’s wickedness [Col. 0855A] and from the tyranny of his henchman Alexander. But they did not allow the respite granted them for this one purpose—that the bitterness of many punishments might be prepared for them—to make their suffering useless to those nearby. By their courage of spirit, steadfastness of faith, and endurance in suffering, they summoned the weaker to imitate them.

In that same custody, approximately four hundred and forty-four men were held in chains. These holy servants of God urged them to turn to the faith of Christ, bearing witness that there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which anyone can be saved (Acts IV). And when they proved by both words and examples that these things were true, through the grace of him who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. [Col. 0855B] II), those men renounced all the works and pomp of Satan. They confessed that they believed in the one true God, the almighty Father; in Jesus Christ, his only Son and Lord; and in the Holy Spirit. They confessed that these three are not three gods but one God, who alone is powerful enough to rescue his faithful from every tribulation and bring them safely into his heavenly kingdom. Thus, established more firmly in the solidity of this confession, they were made fit for the kingdom of God.

When Alexander learned that this newly converted multitude had been enrolled in the service of Christ through the efforts of the devout mother Julitta and her son Quiricus, he was overcome by an excess of raging madness and ordered that whole praiseworthy phalanx to be brought before his tribunal. When they stood there, without any change of mind, they declared with one harmonious voice that they were nothing other than Christians. Then the governor pronounced sentence and ordered them to be punished at once with capital execution.

But with joyful minds, signing themselves with the sign of Christ, they eagerly extended their necks to the executioner. Thus taken away from the afflictions of this world, they received life through him, with him, and in him—eternal life—for whose love they did not hesitate to undergo temporal death.

When this exchange of so happy a bargain had been completed, these holy merchants of God—four hundred and forty-four men—died on the day before the Nones of June, like the merchant seeking fine pearls. For when they found one precious pearl, they gave not only all they possessed but also themselves, and purchased it. Now possessing it by hereditary right, and beholding its beauty with the eye of a pure heart, they rejoice over it with complete and perfect joy. But after the blood of Christ’s holy martyrs had been shed, the bloodthirsty governor ordered their precious limbs to be cut apart and their bones and entrails scattered, so that no one might bury them. Thus the Psalmist’s sentence was fulfilled:

“They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Ps. LXXVIII).

After these martyrs had been brought to completion, the governor Alexander immediately, like a roaring lion, ordered new instruments of punishment to be brought before him—the instruments he had earlier ordered prepared for the combatant Julitta [Col. 0856A] and her little recruit—and applied each of them individually. He eagerly desired to inflict particular tortures upon each of their limbs.

But after they had repeatedly glorified God through their sufferings and torments, as they were taken from their chains to the tribunal and from the tribunal back to their chains, they were delivered from every tribulation amid terrifying and exquisitely devised forms of torture succeeding one another in turn. While the precious limbs of Christ’s martyrs were stretched by various torments, they were always rescued by heavenly consolation, because, as the Psalmist says:

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII).

And again:

“The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them and delivered them from all their tribulations” (ibid.).

When the tyrant perceived that the saints of God were joyful in endurance and unconquerable in combat, he pronounced sentence: their heads were to be severed from their necks.

Thus, after they had sweated through so many contests of martyrdom, their blessed souls, released from bodily bonds and clothed in white, were joined to the choirs of the holy martyrs. From their gracious teacher and rewarder, Jesus, they received their individual robes of immortality. Resting beneath God’s golden altar and behind the inner veil, they offer him incense of praise. And because in the former tabernacle they offered him not the blood of goats or calves but their own bodies—a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—they now offer a most pleasing sacrifice of exultation, awaiting with great devotion [Col. 0856C] and desire the day when they may rejoice in twofold robes, when “this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality” (1 Cor. XV), and when “in their land they shall possess double,” according to the prophetic promise of Isaiah (ch. LXI).

Clothed, therefore, in robes of eternal glory and holding the palms of victory in their hands because they conquered the devil and the world in Christ, they sing—not with the service of the mouth but with the supreme sweetness of charity:

“Alleluia. Praise and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just” (Rev. XIX).

And again and again the word is repeated: “Amen.”

Considering these splendid rewards of thanksgiving and these delightful gifts of joy, the Psalmist sings to you, Lord of powers, with a devout heart:

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Your heavenly house, desirable to all the blessed, Lord, your beloved Quiricus entered—not trusting in his own strength but in the abundance of your mercy. And because, by your gracious gift, he was innocent and without blemish, since he knew no evil and practiced no deceit with his tongue, he shall not be moved from it forever. There, rejoicing eternally where there is day without night, joy without sorrow, and praise without weariness, he is glorified with those who love your name.

But we, placed in this valley of tears amid various temptations, ask you, Lord, for help in overcoming them, so that you who gave us the law of justice [Col. 0857A] may grant us the blessing of your grace. May we, by the intercession of these saints, advance by a happy ascent from virtue to virtue and be worthy to see you and praise you with them in the heavenly Zion.

Certainly, while we remain in this corruptible body and are exiles from you, we must meditate along the way on what must be done in our homeland. Yet here, as far as we are able, we must partly do what will always have to be completed there, so that we may bless you at all times and your praise may always be in our mouth (Ps. XIII). Although praise is not seemly in the mouth of sinners (Eccli. XV), it is truly beautiful in the Church of the saints, which always sings a new song to you. There the holy child Quiricus and his devout mother Julitta, joined to the choir of the holy martyrs, rejoice in praising you forever.

Now, recalling their glorious solemnity and proclaiming the mighty deeds your grace bestowed upon them, we bless you and glorify you, O blessed and glorious Trinity, one God! O how great you are, Lord, and greatly worthy of praise, performing wonders in heaven and on earth! How wonderful you are in your saints—you who gave the holy child Quiricus, not yet three years old, such virtue and strength that, by your power, he naturally surpassed the law you assigned to each person. Though a child of such tender age, he displayed such steadfastness in the wisdom of his mind, the eloquence of his tongue, and the endurance with which he bore his torments, persevering to the end for faith in and love of your name!

May your name, God, be blessed forever!

[Col. 0857C] You also, all holy and humble witnesses of Christ, faithful even to the shedding of your blood, bless the Lord with us. He has adorned the company of the martyrs with the praiseworthy number of the innocent Quiricus. We humbly ask, moreover, that your fellow citizen, Quiricus—small in age, great and renowned in martyrdom, to whom the wondrous gift of divine grace was granted—may intercede for us all with his Glorifier in heaven, who is God over all [Col. 0858A] forever and ever. By his grace cooperating with them, these saints completed the blessed martyrdom of their contest on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, during the reign of the emperor Alexander, who began in the year of the Lord 224 and ruled for thirteen years.

Having completed, as far as we have been enabled to know through a faithful and fitting account, the story of your admirable passion, O gracious martyr of Christ Quiricus, intercede for us with the merciful Lord, so that for this work of ours, though small, we may receive the recompense of a great reward and may be in the fellowship of Julitta, your noble mother, and of all the holy martyrs clothed in white; and so that he may always make us participants both in his grace and in your glory. To him, with God the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor, power, and dominion through infinite ages of ages.

Since the venerable passion of the martyrs Quiricus and Julitta is known among the Christian people in various accounts, though with the same true martyrdom, I have undertaken to offer, as it were, a small draught from the immeasurable depth of their miracles, by which, through God’s ordering, they shone in this world, and I have endeavored to investigate them in sacred pages for the honor of the Church.

After many years had passed since they received the crown of martyrdom, Saint Amator, bishop of Auxerre, while traveling through the territories of Antioch with the illustrious count Savinus, found their most sacred bodies by the grace of Christ. With great reverence he brought them into Gaul [Col. 0858C]. When they had been conveyed to the city of Autrica, and only the boy’s arm had been granted in answer to Saint Savinus’s prayers, he honorably buried them again in his own house, since that prelate, illustrious for the glory of his merits, was venerated there by the faithful. Thus that city, adorned with the titles of many saints, deserved to receive this incomparable treasure from God, so that the salvation of bodies and souls might come to its people.

[Col. 0857]

## LIFE OF SAINT ALDEGUNDIS, VIRGIN, BY HUCBALD

(From Bollandus, 30 January, based on ancient manuscripts and Surius.) (G)*

## THE AUTHOR’S DEDICATION

[Col. 0857D] 1. Not forgetful of you, and not ungrateful for your remarkably diligent services toward me, I complied with your wishes. If I have done so later than you wanted, or less suitably than was fitting, attribute it not to a careless spirit in me but rather to the difficulty of the task. An unworked mass cannot easily be purified by a small fire.

If anyone mocks the inelegance of the composition, blame it on you. Certainly I preferred to be ridiculed by some rather than fail to obey you. If anyone is displeased with me because I have not sewn on broad, brilliantly shining purple cloths, but have even removed them, let that person know that I did not wish, in the manner of young girls, to dress dolls without the outlines of limbs, or to paint lifeless figures on walls. Rather, I wished to display plainly for all to imitate a woman’s solid breast—indeed, a manly spirit—full of virtues, like a lamp lit by God.

If you wish to transcribe the work, please preserve carefully the divisions of the chapters. As for the preface, which treats generally of the deeds of the saints, intends to exhort everyone to imitate them, especially reproves the negligence of the slothful, demonstrates that no one can be excused on the ground of ignorance, and shows that the Lord working in the saints is to be loved and glorified, take care to place it before the chapters, as it has been prefixed [Col. 0860A].

[Note: [Col. 0859D] We have nowhere found this list of chapters prefixed to the Life, nor is the division of chapters everywhere the same. Therefore we have divided it according to our own practice, as seemed appropriate.]

But if this too should not please you, or the teachers to whose hearing you may perhaps bring it, let the hateful and inept parchment perish in your hands, or be erased, or be committed to the fire. Whatever happens, I ask you as a friend not to let our name be recognized in this work.

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859B] 2. The mercy of divine goodness has always cared for human salvation in many ways. After humanity’s fall, through both the sayings and examples of the righteous, it led the erring back to the way of truth. Before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, it mercifully set before beginners of both sexes a pattern of virtue to imitate.

The Scripture of both Testaments is full, like a shining heaven, not only with great lights—namely, the sun and moon—but also with smaller stars. That is, it is filled not only with the brightness of the true light, which illuminates rational creation, and with the beauty of the universal Church, which brightens the whole world, but also with the radiance of the individual saints, who console us in the night of this age like shining stars.

Whoever, therefore, by God’s gift, has healthy eyes should walk toward the light of the sun and follow the footsteps of the Lord and Savior. Whoever, however, is less able to look upon so great a radiance because of weak eyes should turn his gaze toward the mountains, already glowing with the light of the true sun—namely, the holy apostles and their successors, who illuminate the whole world alike by their teaching and their examples. Let him follow the leaders of the faith, like rams going before the flock to the pastures of life.

But if some slower person despises evangelical and apostolic teaching—which is extremely dangerous—or if, because of the weakness of his faith, he negligently attends to the mighty deeds of the great fathers or their teachings—which is a sign of a badly diseased soul—then at least, by reading or hearing the Lives of the saints who lived in more recent times, let him recognize the grace of the Creator always working in the saints; and, recognizing it, let him grow warm with love for him.

If some delicate person, because of the tenderness of the flesh, is afraid to imitate men, let him consider women and tender girls who, through love of their Redeemer, conquered the world, and let him blush with shame. Ignorance will excuse no one who can read or hear someone reading. Where do the words of Scripture not resound? In churches they are read daily by lectors, sung delightfully by singers, and expounded profitably by preachers.

What homeland, what city, what village has not been adorned by the special patronage of some saint through the providence of the Creator? Everywhere the Savior flashes forth through his members. “His name is oil poured out”; everywhere he thunders, everywhere he rains through the Gospel, through the apostles, through teachers, and through the examples of the saints.

And, to come from many to one, who else is indicated in the life of the blessed virgin Aldegundis as worthy of love, following, and embracing, except Christ? The virgin girl loved him, and because of her chastity she rightly follows the Lamb wherever he goes. Therefore, if we say something in praise of him who, though the same in all, works great and small things and various things without being various, and dissimilar things without being dissimilar, let no one reject the discourse undertaken concerning the life of this virgin; rather, let him attend to what we strive to express.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 0859]

## CHAPTER ONE: The Birth, Formation, and Visions of Saint Aldegundis

[Col. 0859C]

[Col. 0859D] 3. Around the year 630 of the Lord’s Incarnation, during approximately the period when the following pontiffs successively presided over the apostolic See of Rome—Honorius, Severinus, John, Theodore, and Martin [Note: [Col. 0859D] Honorius succeeded Boniface V, who died on 25 October 625; the others mentioned here followed him in order. Saint Martin died in exile in 655.]—and when Heraclius ruled at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0859D] Heraclius ruled from 610 until 11 March 641. Dagobert began to reign in Austrasia in 612, with the approval of his father, Clotaire II; after his father’s death, he also ruled in Westria, or Neustria, in 628, after granting part of Aquitaine to his brother Charibert. He died in 644.], and Dagobert, son of Clotaire, who was fourth from Clovis, whom Saint Remigius baptized, was reigning in Francia, the virgin Aldegundis was born in the territory of Hainaut [Note: [Col. 0860D] Manuscript of Malboden: Hainon, from the river Haina, which flows beside the mountains and joins the Scheldt at Condé; the territory or district was called Hainaut and was later greatly enlarged. It is now commonly called Hainonia.] of royal lineage, to Walbert as her father and Bertilia as her mother.

Her elder sister Waldetrudis had been lawfully married to a highly distinguished man named Maldegarius, also called Vincentius [Col. 0860C]. Later, inspired by God and encouraged by religious men, he rejected the world and followed the Savior Jesus Christ with all his heart.

At that time many religious men, most devoted cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard, were illuminating the western regions of the world like bright lights in the sky and were leading many into the way of salvation both by preaching and by the example of their lives: Amandus, bishop of Tongeren, moving everywhere like a rain-bearing cloud and raining all around; Arnulfus, bishop of Metz; Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai; Eligius, bishop of Noyon; Audoenus, bishop of Rouen; Gislenus, who came as a pilgrim from Athens to Gaul; and many others in the Church [Note: [Col. 0860D] These saints are commemorated as follows: Arnulfus, 18 July; Eligius, 1 December; Audoenus, 24 August; Gislenus, 9 October.] like bright heavenly luminaries.

4. The girl Aldegundis, carefully brought up under the care of her parents, was instructed in the sacred writings by divine providence. Advancing greatly in their knowledge and embracing the doctrines of the Christian religion in her mind, she began already in her girlhood to burn intensely with love for her heavenly Bridegroom.

Her parents, although proud and elevated by the arrogance of their blood [Note: [Col. 0861D] Manuscript of Laetium and one of Malboden: “exalted.”], nevertheless remembered the Christian name they bore [Col. 0861B] and raised their daughter according to the fear of God, so that already in tender age she desired to please the Lord Christ more than the world.

5. While she was still in her parents’ house, frequently lifted up in heavenly contemplation, sometimes while awake and sometimes in sleep, divine grace began to reveal many kinds of visions to her. She committed these visions, which she herself described [Note: [Col. 0861D] Manuscript of Malboden: “to a man.”], to a certain religious abbot named Sobinus of the monastery of Nivelles.

Although some people, weighing what they read or hear less worthily, think such things superfluous or unworthy of belief, no wise person considers it strange or incredible that a girl serving God with her whole heart should, awake or asleep, be nourished by frequent visions of holy angels. On the contrary, any soul carelessly devoted to the impurities of lust is sometimes deceived by demonic illusions.

To summarize briefly what she saw: one night she heard in a vision that immeasurable riches were promised to her. At first she thought them earthly, but immediately in spirit she recognized that heavenly riches were being promised to her. Then, carried aloft in a vision, she heard someone advising her to put aside what passes away so that she might more easily obtain heavenly things.

At another time she heard a voice: “Seek no other bridegroom than the Son of God.” At another time she saw Christ in the form of a most beautiful boy, bringing her a white robe and the palm of victory. Again she was raised up in hope of heavenly things when she heard in a vision that she would be in the company of the saints.

Amid these visions she saw the devil, burning with the torches of envy and sorrowful over her election. Then she saw an angel of God encouraging her to persevere in virginity and to keep far from the vanity of the world.

Greatly refreshed by visions of this kind, she advanced from day to day in the love of virtue, and so that she might make greater progress by persevering, she saw greater things every day. Indeed, a girl appeared to her as though coming from a journey and declared that she had been sent by the Mother of God so that Aldegundis might ask for whatever she wished.

She immediately replied cheerfully that she desired what the Lord wished and preferred that Christ’s will be done in her. She frequently saw angels encouraging her. She saw blessed Peter admonishing her concerning the kingdom of God. She also beheld the Lord Christ, appearing to her in the form of the sun and the moon, as an image of the kingdom of God.

In all such revelations the prudent virgin humbled herself more and more, drew nearer to the kingdom of God, and yearned ever more fervently to cling to her heavenly Bridegroom.

6. If anyone wishes to know these visions more fully, let him read her Life. From it we have extracted only a few things, attempting merely to indicate briefly the events to those who desire to know how great was the merit of this virgin, who was so often refreshed by angelic consolations according to the perfectly ordered dispensation of the Creator, who knows how to apply the fitting measure of his sweetness to each person.

And, to bring this sequence of revelations to an end, the blessed virgin Aldegundis, advancing from virtue to virtue, deserved to be raised by the Lord to such a height of holiness that not only did an angel frequently appear to her in the highest states or in ecstasy, but he also appeared openly to her while she was awake and offered familiar conversation concerning her resolve to preserve virginity. The holy virgin confidently asked his name and heard from him that his name was glorious and wondrous.

## CHAPTER TWO: Her Resolve to Preserve Virginity Opposed by Her Mother

7. When the virgin’s parents were preparing to give her in marriage, her mother summoned her daughter and urged her with exceedingly sweet words not to conceal her wishes from her. She disclosed her own and the father’s desire that, according to the dignity of her lineage, she should not refuse to accept a noble bridegroom.

She pointed out the size of the household, the extent of the estates, the farms, the abundance of possessions, and the treasures filled with wealth. Flattering her, she set before her the wealth, nobility, and beauty of a certain young man. With such blandishments the mother persisted, trying to bend her daughter’s mind to her own will.

Aldegundis, however, upright in conduct, sweet in speech, devoted to divine reading, and diligent in meditating on holy Scripture, could no longer conceal the Bridegroom she had chosen and carried in the love of her heart—namely, the Lord Christ, whom she had come to know through reading and to whom she had already wholly devoted herself. Taking this opportunity, she said:

“What are you doing, my lady mother, dearest mother? Why do you flatter me? Why do you burden my mind with so many persuasive words? I shall no longer conceal my will from you; I shall reveal the desire conceived in my heart long ago.

“You speak to me of some poor bridegroom; but I desire such a rich and mighty bridegroom whose estates are heaven, earth, and sea, whose fields shall never fail, and whose riches continually increase and never diminish. If you can, mother, obtain such a bridegroom for me [Note: [Col. 0863D] Another reading: ‘seek one for me’], not a sinful, wanton man who will soon die.”

When the mother heard this, although she could not move the virgin’s mind from its constancy, she nevertheless, with feminine persistence, repeatedly returned to the subject, reminding her daughter of the marriage arrangement.

But what happened? She poured out her words in vain. She struck uselessly at the girl’s mind, founded upon Christ like a tower that would not fall. Christ the Lord, beautiful beyond the sons of men, was the one she loved; him she hungered for and thirsted after, and him, thirsting, she hungered for. She possessed a merciful spirit toward the poor and continually nourished her mind with divine readings. In her replies she was extremely cautious, gentle toward all, humble among the noble [Col. 0863B] [Note: [Col. 0863D] Manuscripts of Laetium and Malboden: “humble toward the lesser.”], and toward those of lower rank like an equal. In the moderation of food and drink she was so devoted to abstinence that none of her companions could equal her.

8. But while the mind of the tender virgin was constantly wearied by her mother’s blandishments, urging her to satisfy her parents’ will by accepting a bridegroom—since refusing to obey them seemed improper, while obeying them by loving them more than the Lord Christ seemed most dangerous—the mercy of divine providence freed her from this temptation in the following way.

Her sister, the blessed Waldetrudis mentioned above, had already separated from her husband by mutual agreement for the love of holy religion. While he was living religiously in the monastery called Hautmont, she herself had built a monastery of nuns, on the hill called Castrum-Locus, with the counsel of the venerable Gislenus. There, together with other maidservants of God, she sweetly nourished her mind in heavenly contemplation.

She had received the sacred veil, that is, the religious habit, from the hand of blessed Autbertus, bishop of the church of Arras and Cambrai, who at that time, among the other priests of God then flourishing, watched diligently over the Lord’s fold.

Therefore, by divine inspiration, God’s servant Waldetrudis, remembering her dearest sister Aldegundis and greatly fearing that she might be bound by the chain of carnal love, and desiring with all her heart to have her as a companion in the habit of holy conduct [alternative reading: *carnis illigaretur amans et exoptans*, “might be bound by the flesh, loving and desiring”], sent a letter to their mother. She earnestly requested that her sister be sent to her, saying that she wished Aldegundis to stay with her for a while; she seemed to herself to receive no little consolation from her presence; and whenever it pleased their mother, she would immediately send her back [Note: [Col. 0863D] Another reading: “send her back.”].

The mother agreed and sent her daughter. For those whose minds were intent on serving the Lord, a single household thus became a fitting place for them to dwell together. Who could adequately express how much spiritual edification they gained from their mutual conversation, and how great an example of good works they offered to the other sisters through their way of life?

You might have seen those sisters from the Gospel, Martha and Mary, eagerly ministering to the Lord and Savior. Yet you could not easily discern which of them more desired to sit at his feet, since each strove to do so, while each unwillingly attended to external concerns (Luke X).

9. Not much time had passed when, behold, their mother, suspicious with feminine anxiety that her daughter’s virgin mind might be alienated from the world by her sister and persuaded to receive the sacred veil, sent to the monastery and summoned her virgin daughter back to herself.

Blessed Waldetrudis reluctantly sent her sister back, lest she offend their mother, but earnestly begged and encouraged her to make herself entirely separate from the world, to prepare herself for an immortal Bridegroom, and to return to the monastery as soon as she could.

Sorrowful, she took leave of her sister [Col. 0864B] and returned to her mother, who was then staying at her estate called Curtissolra. Yet, mindful according to Scripture that parents must be honored, the well-disposed girl showed her mother the reverence due to her. She humbled herself at her feet and begged her with tears to permit her to live in the dwelling that stood beside the church, saying that it was not suitable for her to associate among secular men and women.

She also reminded her mother how holyly and religiously her sister Waldetrudis conducted herself in the monastery; how she instructed the servants of Christ who had withdrawn from the world; and how, admonishing them daily, she taught them lofty truths concerning the kingdom of heaven.

As the virgin reported these things to her mother, though the virgin considered them quite pleasing to her, the latter showed that they were not only displeasing to her but also extremely burdensome. In anger she threatened to beat her if she dared speak to her any longer about such matters.

The wise virgin not only endured her threats patiently but, prepared even to endure blows, prudently remained silent.

The mother then brought out fine linen, handed it to her daughter, and ordered her to prepare from it garments for her betrothal, intending to marry her shortly to a noble young man according to the law of marriage.

The virgin received the linen and entered the little house beside the oratory that she had obtained from her mother. Through a pious deception, she made garments from it for those baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity. Afflicting her body severely, she prayed to the Lord day and night with tears that she might not be separated from the company of holy virgins and might be joined to no bridegroom other than the Lord Christ.

The virgin’s prayers were heard. The marriage that her mother was preparing within fifteen days was postponed, and the young man to whom she intended to betroth her was prevented from coming for many days.

## CHAPTER THREE: Her Resolve Finally Approved by Her Parents

10. [Note: [Col. 0864D] This chapter was absent from Surius; it has been supplied from a manuscript.]

Meanwhile, the most blessed virgin, whose mind had already become fixed upon hope of heavenly things and rejection of all things destined to perish with the world, remembered that conversation with the wicked sometimes brings corruption even to those of good character. She therefore decided secretly to withdraw for a time from her mother’s company, trusting in the guidance and fellowship of the one whom she had chosen as her bridegroom and father [Note: [Col. 0864D] Another reading: “as her patron and father.”]

O happy and greatly praiseworthy separation of mother and daughter! In it the young soldier of Christ revealed what merit she possessed before God, and it was shown that the Savior’s presence is never absent from his faithful, just as he himself had promised.

The virgin of Christ fled and came to the bank of a certain river called the Sambre. Seeing nowhere a boat by which she might be carried across, she stood at the farthest edge of the river.

What should she do? Where should she turn? Nowhere did she see any means open for crossing the river, except the unfailing refuge of the Savior, with whom the petition of the faithful is never void.

Remembering, therefore, that the Lord had promised his faithful that those who believed in him would do the works he did and even greater works (John XIV, 12), and that he had made the sea passable beneath the feet of the chief of the apostles (John XXI, 7; Matt. XIV, 19), and that the Apostle Paul, immersed night and day in the waves of the sea, had suffered no loss of life (2 Cor. XI, 25), she knew that nothing is impossible to perfect faith.

She armed her body on every side with the sign of the Lord’s cross and, thus piously trusting in the Lord, mounted the river’s waves as though they were a solid road. She walked upon the waters, while angelic spirits supported her on the right and left, and the edges of her garments did not even touch the river’s flood.

Let no one think it foreign to the rule of Catholic religion that holy angels should have rendered service to the virgin, since it is written that heavenly spirits are sent to minister to the saints and that angels are made servants (Ps. XC, 11); and holy men who imitate angelic life are called angels (Mal. III, 1). Thus John the Baptist, than whom no greater had arisen among those born of women, deserved to be and to be called an angel (Matt. XI, 10–11).

When the holy virgin had reached the farther bank of the river, she gave thanks to the Lord, by whose grace what is contrary to nature both could and did happen.

11. Then she humbly entreated the Lord to direct her resolve toward the good and came to a place overgrown with many kinds of shrubs, which her parents possessed by hereditary right against the most holy Gertrude, their niece.

There she built a very small church, after uprooting a considerable quantity of thornbushes [Col. 0865D].

Immediately the event became known throughout the surrounding region: a virgin of such distinction had abandoned her home and her father’s possessions, sought the solitude of the wilderness, and followed the Lord while carrying his cross.

Then the father learns what has happened, and the celebrated mother,

and together each laments their blessed daughter,

that she had rejected them and thus sought the wilderness;

and the whole company of servants laments the same.

But the devout father, reflecting in his heart that this was in his daughter a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Ps. LXXVI, 11), divine grace being at work, experienced no small alleviation of his grief, commending to the Lord both the beginning and the end of his daughter’s purpose.

## 12. [Col. 0866A]

But her mother, mourning for her daughter as though she were dead, was afflicted with such grief that she was in danger of the separation of body and soul—that is, death (Heb. IV, 12). When the clemency of heavenly goodness saw that the kindly mother was bearing her daughter’s absence with excessive anguish, it implanted in her breast a longing to see her daughter, whose absence she could not endure without distress. Taking several companions with her, she hastened to visit her daughter; it is beyond our ability to express how greatly the daughter rejoiced at her arrival. Receiving her mother, and after offering greetings and affectionate kisses, the daughter admonished and encouraged her devout mother to despise earthly things utterly, seek heavenly things, and make friends for herself from the mammon of iniquity, by whom she might be received into eternal dwellings (Luke XVI, 9). Among other things she added:

> It is no small praise, mother, if you obey Christ,  
> Despising the world’s harmful things and following the Lord;  
> For, as I think, it is not right to pursue what must perish.

When the blessed mother saw that her daughter had chosen the better way, she hastened to grant for the glory of incorruption what, by hereditary right, she had intended to bestow upon her for the loss of her virginity, expecting to receive a hundredfold from Christ and, in addition, eternal life in everlasting blessedness (Matt. XIX, 29). Accordingly, without delay, the devout mother transferred to her daughter the household of both sexes, together with estates [Note: [Col. 0865D] Ms. Laetien: “the mother of the household.”], and handed over a considerable possession of woods. This act was confirmed before everyone by a written testament. The daughter rejoiced that her mother had given herself to the Lord; the mother rejoiced that her daughter had not obeyed her in entering a marital union. Thus the mother rejoiced in her daughter, and the daughter in her mother.

## CHAPTER IV. The Veil Received. The Monastery Founded.

### 13.

When her mother fell ill and had already despaired of life, she called her virgin daughter and gave her gold and silver, costly clothing, estates, villages, male and female servants, and everything she possessed, except what she distributed at that time to the poor for the remedy of her soul, and what she assigned for the use of the servants and handmaids of God serving the Lord in monasteries. When her mother had died and had been buried beside her husband in the aforesaid village of Curtissolra, in the church of the holy Mother of God, by the priests of God and others of ecclesiastical rank, the young Eudo—whom the aforementioned mother had intended to give her daughter in marriage—heard of her death. Nevertheless, he persisted in seeking to take the virgin as his wife and ordered his retainers to prepare the wedding arrangements.

When the virgin heard this, she was greatly afraid. Fleeing by night to a wooded place called Melbodius, she hid there for several days. But when she heard that the holy bishops Amandus and the venerable Autbertus had arrived at the monastery of Altimont, she hastened there barefoot, with great humility of heart. She prostrated herself at their feet, disclosed the desire of her heart, and explained the contrary assaults of temptation that had attacked her through the devil’s snares.

Then blessed Amandus—already almost known throughout the world through the most celebrated fame of his virtues, who, like a vigorous laborer in God’s harvest, had led many surrounding nations to the Catholic faith and had built many monasteries for men and for the handmaids of God—opened his mouth, eloquent with the rain of heavenly teaching, and so strengthened the girl’s wearied spirit that she not only rejected the world itself but became ready, if occasion arose, to undergo martyrdom for Christ the Savior.

Why say more? The holy bishops led her into a certain oratory of that same monastery, dedicated in honor and memory of Saint Vedastus. There, having been worthily consecrated by them with priestly blessing and betrothed to her bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, she received the veil and habit of sacred religion.

### 14. [Col. 0867B]

[Note: [Col. 0867D] The material from here through no. 15 is absent from Surius.]

After this work had been begun by Christ’s priests with the appropriate blessing, it pleased divine Goodness to show that it is not absent wherever any assembly of the righteous is formed in his name. For the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove to the holy bishops while they were singing the appointed hymns at the consecration of the virgin. Gradually descending, he lifted the veil that was being consecrated from the ground with his feet and mouth. So that there might be no ambiguity concerning the display of so great a miracle, he raised the veil high above the ground before the eyes of all who were present and placed it upon the head of the most blessed virgin. Once this had been accomplished, the dove, sent from heaven, immediately disappeared from the sight of those who saw it. The holy virgin, however, attributing what had occurred not to herself but to the merits of the blessed priests of Christ, rendered countless thanks to God, whose unmerited benefits toward her she proclaimed to be so great.

### 15.

The blessed Aldegund, then, returned from Altimont to the place where she had previously hidden, which she herself had called Melbodius. Since the place was still deserted, she began with great skill to cultivate it, uprooting thorns and shrubs from the roots, constructing dwellings, and gathering servants and handmaids of God there. Finally, she built there a church in honor and memory of holy Mary, the Mother of God, in which she daily performed divine praises and the duties of prayer.

Then, considering the riches of this world as nothing, she legally distributed her estates, possessions, and all the ornaments her parents had left her among holy places and gave them to the poor, so that she might attain that perfection of which the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, come, and follow me” (Matt. XVIII, 21). She also restored for the better the place where her mother and father had been buried, and established twelve nuns there to serve Christ the Lord.

In the aforementioned place of Melbodius, with the counsel of blessed Bishop Amandus and the assistance of King Dagobert, she surrendered herself together with the two daughters of her sister, the blessed Waldetrudis. After many others had also gathered there with her in the habit of holy religion, she remained in a holy way of life and left before the eyes of all an example of good works worthy of imitation. She was a faithful servant of God, serving her Bridegroom in humility, obedience, and patience; weakening her body by fasts; spending nights in vigils and prayers; patient in hope; gentle toward her household; modest in speech and in preserving the church’s property; and kind in distributing it.

### 16. [Col. 0868A]

She carefully instructed the two nieces, the daughters of her sister, according to the rule in the monastery, and diligently taught them from the earliest beginnings of childhood to choose the Lord Christ as their bridegroom. One of them was called Madelberta, the other Aldetrudis.

Aldetrudis, a girl of good character, strove to imitate the conduct and life of her maternal aunt. She constantly sat at her feet and thirsted to be instructed in the teaching of life. Although she flourished in many virtues, she was especially devoted to humility and obedience.

On one occasion the blessed virgin Aldegund had ordered her to gather together fragments of wax, taking care that not even the smallest objects belonging to the monastery should be lost. She obeyed immediately, collected the scattered pieces of wax, lit a fire, and placed above it a bronze vessel—that is, a basin—filled with wax.

But when the pile of wood, consumed by the prevailing flame, had fallen, and the boiling pan, surrounded by the heat of the fire, tilted to the other side, causing the fire to blaze up more fiercely there, the young girl feared that some harm might occur. Armed with faith, she stretched out her bare hands and extended arms, quickly lifted the boiling [Col. 0868C] *luter* from the midst of the flames [Note: [Col. 0867D] *Luter* is a type of vessel, or a basin.], and set it down on the floor, suffering absolutely no injury to the skin of her flesh. Without doubt, she thereby obtained before God both the merit of the one who commanded and the virtue of the obedient one [Note: [Col. 0868D] Another manuscript reads: “of obedience.”].

## CHAPTER V. The Virtues and Miracles of Aldegund.

### 17. [Col. 0868D]

The blessed Aldegund did not abandon her purpose. Rather, advancing from virtue to virtue, as she had begun in childhood, she persevered daily in holy works and abounded in them. While she was still in her parents’ house, tender in age but mature in heart, she mercifully gave to the poor whatever belonged to her by right.

Although the virgin sometimes lacked the means, her willingness to give never diminished. Her mother Bertilia, however, had amassed a considerable treasure of money. Although her daughter was not unaware of it, because her mother concealed its location she took nothing from it before her mother’s death. After she had survived both her parents, she immediately began distributing her mother’s treasure to the poor.

As time passed, when she had become mistress of the household together with her sister, she called a trusted servant, brought out silver to purchase clothing for the use of Christ’s servants and the poor, and ordered him to report to her whatever money remained. The servant fulfilled his mistress’s command: he bought a large quantity of clothing and returned what money was left. The amount of silver was found to be as though nothing had been spent. Who could explain how many thanks they gave to God, astonished at the Creator’s immense generosity?

### 18.

One night, while the two sisters devoted to Christ the Lord were keeping vigilant watch and thoughtfully meditating on their love for the heavenly Bridegroom, their regular way of life, and the salvation of the sisters entrusted to them by the supreme Shepherd, a candle placed before them suddenly fell and was extinguished.

When they waited for someone who might arrive and relight it, and some delay occurred, the virgin, a lover of light, stretched out her hand and took the lamp. At once, in her hand, the lamp received light by divine power. Through this miracle our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true light (John I, 9), revealed that he was present to his handmaids, whom he had gathered in his name, and did not permit them to endure darkness even for a moment.

### 19.

Not long afterward, while the same sisters, beloved of the heavenly Bridegroom, were caring for the flock entrusted to them, they were walking through the monastery and came to the basilica of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, at the sixth hour, the hour of prayer, to carry out some task. They knocked at the door.

The church’s doorkeeper was absent, but the doorkeeper of heaven was not absent. He immediately opened the church doors, though they were shut, for his handmaids, lest they be deprived of the grace of prayer and their spirit, stretched like a bow for divine service, be relaxed from its concentration on heavenly contemplation.

Entering then the “house of prayer” (Matt. XXI, 13), they performed their appointed office with greater devotion than usual and deeper compunction, and returned to their own place with joyful hearts.

### 20.

But, to recall briefly what came before: after the wise virgin Aldegund, estranged from worldly pomp, had been clothed in the garments of a nun and had again been strengthened by angelic admonitions and gladdened by a wondrous vision in which she was permitted to see the Lord Jesus, shining like the sun and surrounded by angels, she also remembered the discourse of Amandus, the man of God, concerning complete contempt for temporal things and the summit of perfection.

What she had earlier begun to fulfill in part, she now resolved to complete entirely: to renounce everything she possessed, possessing nothing on earth and desiring to store up treasure in heaven. She therefore had an inventory made of the total treasure and of all the money she possessed in gold, silver, gems, and royal ornaments—things that had been given to her by the king and queen, princes, relatives, and parents after she had received the veil, and after the generous gifts she had distributed to Christ’s poor on the advice of the blessed bishops Amandus and Autbertus.

All these things the most prudent virgin, who also loved the outward adornment of God’s house, devoutly donated for the adornment of the churches. She granted her estates and innumerable possessions by public donation for the use of those who served the King Christ there. She assigned all the rest for the expenses of the poor, reserving nothing for herself except a cheap garment suitable to holy religion and the daily food by which she lived in common with the other handmaids of God.

But the kindness of the Lord Savior, in order to strengthen the faith of his handmaids, did not delay in showing how pleasing to him was the contempt of passing possessions undertaken for love of his name. On the very day when the handmaid of God had completed this glorious act of generosity, as evening was falling, she ordered her ministers to bring her water to drink from the spring that had supplied wine from water to those celebrating the wedding at Cana of Galilee (John II, 9). He himself changed the spring water into the taste of marvelous wine to refresh his bride.

When this deed became known to all the handmaids of God in the monastery, such love for the Lord Christ inflamed their minds that, out of regard for his love, none of them afterward cared to possess anything earthly.

### 21. [Col. 0870B]

On one occasion one of the handmaids filled a little pitcher with water, with which the holy virgin was to wash her hands. During an intervening delay, the pitcher was emptied for other uses, without the knowledge of the woman who had filled it. When she was about to pour the water over the virgin’s hands and found the pitcher empty, she tremblingly wished to hurry back to the spring. Suddenly she felt that the pitcher was filled with water. When this sign was made known to everyone in the monastery, they admired the virgin’s merit, and all offered praises to the Lord Jesus.

### 22.

One day the virgin’s fisherman brought her a fish that was still alive. Reserving it out of charity more for the use of the servants of God who might arrive than for her own, she ordered it to be thrown into the nearest spring. While it was swimming near the bank, it leapt into the air, landed on dry ground, and began to struggle on the parched earth.

> Ravens flew in from nearby, croaking,  
> Wanting to tear the fish apart with claws and beaks.

Wonderful to relate and extraordinary to see! A lamb was grazing nearby. Smaller than the other sheep, it quickly ran up, seized the fish from those who were devouring it, and fought against them with its horns, feet, and the exertion of its whole body, driving the ravens away.

The sisters, who had seen the strange battle from the monastery, hurried over. They found the fish unharmed and, greatly astonished, carried it back to God’s handmaid Aldegund. But the same lamb, the fish’s defender, followed those carrying it until the fish had been presented to the virgin abbess.

### 23. [Col. 0870D]

At a certain time the sisters of the monastery had lit a fire and, as was their custom, hung a cauldron filled with water over it for washing clothes. One of them, wearing the tunic of the blessed virgin Aldegund, was standing beside the embers when, behold, the ancient serpent, envying the humble service of Christ’s handmaids, pushed her, as she stood close to the fire, into the flames and poured the boiling water over her.

As she fell, she invoked the name of the Holy Trinity. The handmaids of God hurried to her, pulled her from the midst of the flames, and found her unharmed, although they had feared that the heat of the fire had dissolved her limbs one by one. The prayers and merits of blessed Mary had come to her aid.

## CHAPTER VI. Visions. Prophecy. Illness.

### 24. [Col. 0871A]

Among the other benefits of divine consolation that the grace of the Lord Savior bestowed upon this virgin, this is especially worthy of admiration: by often comforting her familiarly through angelic visitation, it did not permit her to remain afflicted by any sadness for long.

This may easily be inferred even from small matters. She had once heard a word of slander spoken about her by certain wicked people who devoted themselves to idleness and whose very bad habit was always to disparage their betters. When the virgin’s spirit, as human weakness makes possible, was somewhat distressed by this, an angel appeared and consoled her as usual, caressing her with sweet words.

“What,” he said, “O sweetest virgin, bride of the Lord Jesus Christ, why are you saddened by the words of idle and envious people, when a seat in the heavenly kingdom has been prepared for you, while eternal punishment and infernal torment are reserved for them unless they repent?” Refreshed by such words, the virgin thereafter paid no attention to the vanities of her detractors.

### 25. [Col. 0871B]

After this, as is found more fully in the Life of blessed Gislenus, blessed Amandus, full of days, departed on the Lord’s Day night, like ripe grain to be stored in the heavenly granary, laying aside the chaff of the flesh.

At that very hour the blessed Aldegund was devoutly engaged in vigils and hymns in the church of the monastery of Melbodius, before the altar of the glorious Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, Mary. Since she had loved him greatly in this life—for by his teaching she had learned to ascend the heights of virtue—the grace of the Lord Savior revealed to her both the merit of the man whose exhortation she had received and that she herself would soon follow where that leader was going before her.

While she prayed, lifted up in an ecstasy of mind, she contemplated an old man, venerable with gray hair, dressed in priestly and splendid garments and holding a staff in his hand, passing toward the heights. A great crowd of those clothed in white traveled before and behind him. The holy virgin herself rejoiced that she was hastening along in the same company.

When she was asked who that leader of so glorious a multitude was, she replied that she did not know. Then the angel said:

“Amandus, beloved of God, has departed from this world. Since in his life he took care by God’s grace to preserve himself without blemish and, by faithfully distributing the talents entrusted to him, doubled them, he has now ascended in glory with the holy souls whom he acquired for the Lord by word and example, to the joys of his Lord.”

The most prudent virgin revealed this vision to none of those living with her that day. She sent word to blessed Gislenus, asking him to come to her with her sister, the blessed Waldetrudis, for the sake of the vision. When they came to the place called Meruius [Note: [Col. 0871D] In the Life of Saint Gislenus, by the monk Reinerus, this place is called Meinrivus.], she hurried out to meet them.

After she had disclosed her vision to blessed Gislenus amid other conversation concerning their salvation, the man of God understood what the vision signified and sighed deeply:

“O dearest sister,” he said, “beloved and devout bride of the eternal King, our Lord Jesus Christ, give unceasing thanks to the divine condescension, which has shown you beforehand both the most sweet shepherd’s passage to the heavenly realms, already accomplished, and your own, which will soon occur. Since, by the Lord’s revelation, you have already tasted in advance the sweetness and flavor of the heavenly homeland, it is necessary that you persevere with all diligence in his service until you deserve to obtain what he promised to those who love him.”

### 26. [Col. 0872A]

On another occasion the blessed Aldegund saw in a vision, by the Lord’s revelation, the enemy of the human race in great sadness. She earnestly questioned him, asking why he persisted so greatly against the human race and what profit he hoped to gain by continuing to drive so many thousands of people into hell.

The malign one replied that he was tortured by no small grief of envy against the sons of Adam, who daily ascended to the place from which wretched he and his followers were exiled.

### 27. [Col. 0872B]

Most devoted to divine law, constantly hungering to be nourished by the heavenly word, and desiring to imitate the life of holy and religious men, the prudent virgin had visited Humbert [Note: [Col. 0871D–0872D] The Life of Saint Humbert, which Simon Posquierus, abbot of the same place, had arranged to have copied for us many years earlier from ancient codices of the most noble monastery of Maroilles.], who lived at Maricolas, a man remarkable for holiness and renowned for his knowledge of Holy Scripture, bearing on his crown the sign of the cross impressed by an angel.

Having feasted for several days on the abundant nourishment of the divine word flowing from his mouth, she was once walking with him in the vicinity of the monastery. But when the heat of the day grew intense and she was almost fainting from thirst, the man of God prayed with the virgin, and immediately a new, sweet spring flowed from the earth. The virgin was refreshed, and the spring has continued without failing to the present day.

Blessed Humbert, knowing in advance the day of his death, asked the virgin for linen garments for his funeral. While she was sending someone to deliver them, another messenger sent by the virgin, who foresaw the future, met the blessed man’s messenger halfway along the road with the requested garments.

### 28. [Col. 0872D]

The blessed Aldegund, who had chosen the Lord Savior as her bridegroom, was frequently strengthened by visions of angels. They often addressed her familiarly, recognizing her as their fellow servant and fellow citizen in many respects. Foreknowing through a revelation of the Holy Spirit that the day of her falling asleep was approaching, she begged the Lord—who still sanctifies the holy and still justifies the righteous (Rev. XXI, 11), and who scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. XII, 6)—to deign to purify his handmaid in the present life by thus chastising her flesh, so that after this life her soul might enter without blemish into the rest of her Lord.

She knew that no one in this life is so perfect that he can be entirely free from every contamination of sin. Divine goodness did not delay mercifully to grant what she had humbly requested. Not long afterward a disease called cancer arose in her right breast. Torturing her flesh, it consumed her until the last day of her life. But the prudent virgin, following the example of blessed Job and other saints, endured patiently and, rejoicing as though she had received a gift from God, wisely gave thanks to the heavenly condescension.

### 29. [Col. 0873A]

When an angel had warned her that the time of her dissolution was near, and on the appointed day no bodily suffering was troubling her, an angel appeared to her again. She began to complain to him that she was being delayed from the kingdom prepared for her.

He said to her: “Know that the holy angels have obtained from the Lord for you this additional span of temporal life, so that you may still have time to attain perfection in the virtues.”

On another occasion, when she was suffering from tertian fever, after a week had passed, the devil caused such a burning thirst to invade her around midnight that, unless she drank immediately, she seemed about to die. Since she resisted bravely and wished to abstain from drinking, regarding the force of the fever rather than the enemy’s temptation, she fled to prayer.

And behold, before dawn she saw the ancient enemy standing before her with a hideous and dreadful face. He was forced to confess that he had inflicted such burning thirst upon her. The blasphemer added, saying to the blessed virgin that a hard and narrow road still lay before her and that it was uncertain whether she would persevere in God’s service.

The virgin replied steadfastly: “The Lord is my helper; I do not care about your threats.”

Immediately Satan fled in confusion, and the thirst departed from her. After the devil’s temptation, divine consolation appeared in many forms. In a vision she saw herself as though asking the Lord for perseverance in his love, and she saw what seemed to be a priest—the Lord himself—kindly granting her request.

She also saw blessed Peter the apostle bringing her white bread, and she received it from his hand with immense joy. Her sister likewise heard from heaven during sleep that her penance had been accepted by the Lord and that her virgin sister Aldegund had won Christ as her bridegroom.

## CHAPTER VII. Her Death and the Miracles Connected with It.

### 30. [Col. 0873D]

Meanwhile, while the virgin’s spirit was continually nourished by visions of this kind and lifted up to contemplate heavenly things, a little child was brought to her whose family had already despaired of his life. She immediately ordered him to be placed before the horn of the altar. When this had been done, he was at once restored to health.

When the virgin was informed of the child’s sudden recovery, she remembered her vision and perceived that this had happened because he had touched the place through which she had seen the Lord pass a few days earlier. What could she do but give thanks to God?

Not long before, she had seen herself as though standing in a street, with what seemed to be a fiery globe descending upon her from heaven. On the fourth day after this, at midnight on the Lord’s Day, when she was entering the church for vigils, one of the sisters came out and saw the street in which the vision had earlier appeared shining with extraordinary light, while at that same hour darkness covered the whole earth.
