When morning came, the sisters spoke about it and wondered. The blessed virgin understood the reason for so great a brightness, but at that time she disclosed it to none of them. Soon another witness to these visions came forward, affirming that he had seen our Lord Jesus Christ with an army of angels speaking with the virgin herself before the horn of the altar.

When she asked the man at what hour he had seen the vision, she recognized that it was the very hour at which she had seen the Lord in her own vision. On the fourth day afterward, the child was healed, as has been said above.

### 31. [Col. 0874A]

At that time a priest of good reputation, living blamelessly (Phil. III, 6) in the monastery from childhood to mature age, was accustomed to report that he had seen at night a fiery globe descend from heaven upon the dwelling where Christ’s handmaid lay ill.

After the night hymns, one of the more mature handmaids of God, having tasted a little sleep, saw the blessed Aldegund standing before the altar in the priest’s place. She had broken the Lord’s body in a chalice and said to her:

“Go, please, tell the priest to celebrate the mysteries of the Lord Christ in this chalice. Since yesterday, because of bodily illness, I could not receive Communion, today I shall become a partaker of the Lord’s body and blood.”

When day came, the priest went forth and celebrated Mass. During the celebration he saw the chalice lifted into the air and immediately settle back into its place. Then the aforementioned handmaid of God reported to Christ’s bride the vision she had seen, and the priest reported what he had seen concerning the chalice suspended in the air. Both understood that these visions foretold her death.

### 32. [Col. 0874C]

Among the other signs of virtue that the Savior’s power worked through his beloved handmaid, a certain man, either because his sins demanded it or so that the virgin’s faith might be revealed, was brought almost to the point of death through madness of mind. When his parents despaired of his life, they brought him to the monastery of the nuns and, groaning, told the blessed virgin what misery he was suffering.

Moved by compassion in her inmost heart, she had him brought to her in the evening. She prayed for him, made the sign of the cross over him, and ordered him to return home. He soon recovered and was restored to health.

On the fifth day before the blessed virgin’s death, her sister, the handmaid of our Lord Jesus Christ, Waldetrudis, lifted up in contemplation of heavenly things, saw in a vision the glorious Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ coming with companies of saints and taking her sister, the virgin Aldegund, with her to the heights.

### 33. [Col. 0874D]

In the monastery of Nivelles, where the body of Saint Gertrudis rests, a certain nun of extraordinary simplicity and obedience, who had been perfectly converted from love of the world to love of our Lord Jesus Christ before his tribunal, saw in a vision, on the Friday before the Sabbath and the falling-asleep of God’s handmaid Aldegund, around midnight, a tremendous brightness of light enter the church of blessed Peter, where the aforementioned blessed Gertrudis had been buried.

The light illuminated the entire building from the floor to the beams, as though by the midday sun. While she was overcome with fear and astonishment at the sight of such brilliance, she heard choirs singing psalms, so that she could distinguish the voices of men and women, girls and boys, singing antiphonally in turn.

### 34. [Col. 0875A]

On the third night before she departed from the body, while many religious people and the blessed Waldetrudis, the virgin’s sister, had gathered through the grace of the visitation, behold, an immense radiance, shining with extraordinary brightness, appeared above the house in which the Virgin, the bride of the Lord Christ, fearlessly awaited his arrival.

While those present marveled at the unusual vision, and the blessed Waldetrudis, uncertain between hope and fear, trembled as she awaited the outcome and wondered what it might foretell, that holy soul—which had loved the true Light, the Lord Christ, and thirsted for his presence—was released from the flesh and departed from this world together with that light.

She was buried in a village once under her authority, called Solra [Note: [Col. 0875D] It is called Curtis Solra, perhaps to distinguish it from Castrum Solra, a town three leagues from Melbodius in the direction of Laetia.], where both her parents and afterward her sister Waldetrudis were buried. She remained there for a long time, until, by Christ’s gift, her body was transferred to the town of Melbodius [Note: [Col. 0875D] Her body was later transferred to Montes Sanctae Waldetrudis.], which she herself had built from the foundations. There her memory now shines, and, through the aid of her merits, divine clemency deigns to bestow abundant benefits upon those who ask.

### 35. [Col. 0876A]

Behold, among the other deeds of the saints, whoever you are who read or hear this piously, here too you have something to imitate.

While still a girl, she despised earthly things and desired heavenly ones. She subdued the desire of the flesh through love of virginity. She restrained the desire of the eyes—that is, curiosity—through meditation on divine reading. She trampled down ambition in life, that is, pride, through humility. She despised a mortal bridegroom and chose an immortal one. Though she possessed riches, she did not place her hope in treasures of money (Ecclus. XXXI, 8). Rather, wisely distributing everything to those in need, she embraced poverty.

She found a hidden treasure in a field and, selling everything for joy over it, bought it (Matt. XIII, 44). She sought fine pearls; the devout merchant found one precious pearl, bought it, and possessed it (ibid., 45–46). She shuddered at darkness, loved the light, departed with the light, and will possess the light of everlasting life.

Therefore imitate what you read; live as she lived; walk where she walked. Without doubt you will arrive where she arrived, with the help of the grace of the Creator, who mercifully works in his saints, who gives virtue and strength to his people. Blessed be God forever (Ps. LXVII, 36). Amen.

---

# THE LIFE OF SAINT LEBWINUS, PRIEST AND CONFESSOR, WRITTEN BY HUCBALD TO BALDRIC, BISHOP OF UTRECHT

*(In Surius, Acts of the Saints, 2 November.)*

[Prefaced from volume I of Martène’s extensive collection are a letter from Peter, archdeacon of Cambrai, to Hucbald, and verses by Judion to the same man in commendation of this book.]

## [EPISTLES AND VERSES]

### LETTER OF PETER, ARCHDEACON OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF CAMBRAI, TO HUCBALD, MONK AND PRIEST OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT AMANDUS, CONFESSOR OF CHRIST, AUTHOR OF THE DEEDS OF THE BLESSED PRIEST OF CHRIST, LIBUINUS

*(Around the year 910.) He praises his book on the Life of Saint Libuinus.*

[Col. 0875C]

To Hucbald, monk of the most holy monastery of Amandus, my lord and teacher, adorned with sacred apostolic doctrine and with the jewels of all philosophy, Peter, a sinner serving as archdeacon of the holy Church of Cambrai, offers fitting assistance in present needs and perpetual happiness in Christ in the future.

Since the lamp of your wisdom is recognized in these times as shining uniquely in Gaul through heavenly grace, it seems worthy of wonder why your discerning prudence and prudent discernment should have sent for remarkably careful examination and approval the work of your pen composed concerning the memorable Life of blessed Lebwinus.

Indeed, however small my knowledge may be, it lies prostrate beneath the feet of your wisdom and does not approach even one of your students in scholastic discipline. But he who filled you with wondrous knowledge also strengthened you with wondrous humility, since the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge is likewise the Spirit of fear of the Lord, from whom true humility flows.

Moreover, the splendid arrangement of your writing, in the manner of a gnomon, portrayed the heavenly character of a thoughtful and excellent man and commended with probability his origin, life, and blessed end. In carrying this out, it represented practical and theoretical life alike, physics also in a twofold series of description, and ethics in the sacred formation of conduct.

It refined logic in the eminence of heavenly and sublime arguments, so that, while striving to disclose the astonishing integrity of one man, it might educate the unlearned ignorance of many. Truly, then, we know that the sacred Scripture is fulfilled in you which says: “Give the wise man an opportunity, and wisdom will be added to him.”

I read, therefore, the shining flower of your speech and found something that I would altogether admire, not something that I would in any way correct. May the protection of divine guardianship preserve forever unharmed the lightning-bright lamp of your wisdom, for the advancement of the holy Church. Amen.

### LETTER OF ODILO, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MEDARDUS THE BISHOP, SENT TO HUCBALD

*(Around the year 940.) He approves with praise the little book on the Life of Saint Libuinus, which Hucbald had sent him for examination.*

[Col. 0877B]

“Distinct in the conspicuous strength of ancient dignity,” and so forth. For the remainder, see above under ODILO.

## VERSES OF JUDION, SENT TO BALDRIC, THE BISHOP, IN CONFIRMATION OF THE WORKS OF HIS TEACHER HUCBALD

At the beginning [Note: [Col. 0877] This Baldricus was bishop of Utrecht, to whom Hucbald dedicated the Life of Saint Libuinus.]:

> First of all, Baldric, farewell, most illustrious bishop,  
> An ornament in name and deed, a work of nobility.  
>   
> This is the work of the deeds of the beloved father Lebwinus,  
> Which the teacher Hucbald adorns with his pen.  
>   
> Hence he is held worthy of heaven and memorable on earth;  
> But you, more worthy than he of praise, surpass him.

For whose auspicious undertaking he did that very thing,

[Col. 0877C] Therefore you are raised up by praise for your share in the work.

Therefore, henceforth, may it be permitted me to say before you

to your reader what I desire.

Your reader will be Nitgerus, your dear brother,

who worked so diligently that the work might be read.

While he repeatedly coaxed your friendly scribe,

at last he obtained what he had earnestly desired.

After reading it, at my teacher’s command,

I sign this poem, and then rejoice together in it.

I confess, dear reader, that I have read nothing better

than what Hucbald wrote and taught.

[Col. 0878A] You can discover what I have said in the little book of the Life

of Liaffirin, that holy and magnanimous Father.

If you read it carefully, you will encounter many serious matters

which the rhetorician and grammarian alike have sown here.

And if you possess the judgment to discern wisely,

both evangelical and historical discourse proceeds.

For throughout the whole work the rule of art so guides the way

that no one is deceived by the path or misled by the road.

There is also a learned construction like that of Cicero,

and you will find Augustine here as well, as he teaches.

Provided that a thoughtful person, neither envious nor defamatory,

turns this over while reciting it and reads it again,

whoever reads these things, therefore, not with a hostile heart,

pray earnestly with Judion:

“May God grant that this Hucbald endure for many years.

[Col. 0878B] After the death of the flesh, may He join him thereafter to the heavenly ones,

so that he may praise you with the saints throughout all ages,

you who are one God, present and remaining threefold in yourself.”

Amen.

Thanks be to God.

God, judge of the ancients,

we ask with our voices

that you may graciously assent

to what the faithful alike offer.

Through the merits of Libuin,

by which you may loosen our sins,

with which, as though bound by fetters,

we are seen to be entangled.

But what we cannot obtain,

wounded by great guilt,

grant it to Libuin,

to whom you deny nothing among your saints.

May he be our guide and forerunner

in every danger;

at his prayer, may the terrified

hostile enemy withdraw.

May he restore us, cleansed of our filth,

to the heavenly places,

where, in happy joy,

we may enjoy an endless age.

Amen.

# THE LIFE OF SAINT LEBWIN BEGINS

[Col. 0877]

[Col. 0877D] 1. Our Lord Jesus Christ, because of his immeasurable love with which he loved us throughout the ages of ages, became human not only for us but also from among us, while remaining the same true and perfect God, our King before all ages. Having wrought our salvation through the passion of the cross and the resurrection from the dead, according to his name, in the midst of the earth (Ps. LXXIII), and having completed the work of the divine mystery that had been hidden from the ages and generations but has now been manifested to his saints (I Tim. III), to whom he wished to make known the riches of this mystery (Col. I), he ascended on high and led captivity captive (Ps. LXVII). As the Apostle says, “He gave grace to each of the faithful of the Church according to the measure of his gift,” appointing some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers [Col. 0879A] (Eph. IV).

Among the countless benefits that this generous giver spread throughout the wide spaces of the earth, he also looked down from heaven upon the lands of the Franks and Saxons. For their salvation, instruction in his law, and confirmation in perseverance in good works, after many distinguished lights of teachers—which the same Sun of justice had illuminated with his own radiance so that they might dispel the darkness of the West and themselves also be the light of this world—he graciously brought forth for their illumination, as the day of this age was already nearly setting, one outstanding star, abundantly suffused with the grace of his brightness: namely, Lebwin, his beloved friend, in accordance with the meaning most suitably conveyed by his name.

For it is reported by those skilled in his native language that he was called *Liefvuyn* in his homeland, which in Roman speech means “dear to friends.” When certain letters were removed or altered into Latin, he was called *Lebvinus*. But see how full of dignity was the foretelling contained in this name, since what he was destined to be in his conduct was already marked out in his name.

For if one asks whose friend this man was, certainly not the friend of worldly people or of this world, to which he was not merely an enemy but also crucified, as the Apostle teaches: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (Jas. IV). Rather, he was a most faithful servant of the Creator of the world. Among those who deserved to hear, “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV), he is rightly counted because of his service.

Nor should anyone consider it unreasonable that we diligently inquire into the interpretation of this name. We know that certain Fathers received names even before conception, while others later had their names changed; and it is clear that these names corresponded to their own causes, whether preceding or future. Sacred Scripture therefore marks such things out for us so carefully in order to show plainly that this applies not only to these persons but also to certain other names of the saints that deserve our attention. Their deeds or words sufficiently indicate what their names prefigured.

Thus it may be understood that this holy man also received such a name as a portent of future things, so that in his native tongue he was called “dear friend of God.” Enough has now been said about his name. Let us proceed to his deeds, pleasing to God and to good people, although our foolish style moves onward.

[Col. 0879D] II. Britain is an island situated in the ocean, conspicuous for its ancient dignity yet widely known, separated from the whole world by the intervening sea, lying between the north and the west, and named from the designation of its people. It contains many great rivers, hot springs, and a rich and varied abundance of metals; agate is found there in great quantity, as are pearls. Scotland, or Ireland, lies adjacent to it. There are many peoples there: Britons, Saxons, Picts, and Angles.

Abundant in animals and crops and blessed with fertile soil, it had long been devoted to the worship of idols. But after the time predestined by God for having mercy on it had come (Ps. X), as we read in the praiseworthy deeds of the most eloquent man, Pope Gregory, God inspired his heart by providing him with an opportunity. Since he was called an apostolic man and had been entrusted with responsibility for all things, God caused him to become especially the apostle of this particular people. We shall refrain from recounting in detail how diligently he administered and fulfilled this pastoral duty, with the grace of God cooperating from heaven, since we remember that it has been sufficiently revealed in the book of the life of that thrice-blessed pontiff Gregory.

It is enough to recall this much: strong and faithful farmers sent by him cultivated the soil of the best heart, vigorously working it with the well-polished ploughshare of their tongue, and scattered abroad the seed of the divine word. They carefully guarded it, lest it perish through a double injury: both along the worn path of evil thoughts and through the devouring wickedness of spiritual birds. Moreover, lest the seed that had quickly sprung up should wither because of the hardness of the rock—that is, of the unconquered mind—or because of the heat of temptations (Luke VIII), they irrigated it with the unfailing moisture of holy charity.

Finally, wherever necessary, after the thorns—that is, riches, which are accompanied now by anxiety, now by pleasure—had been uprooted, they rejoiced that the good soil had answered their labor and produced abundant fruits: the thirtieth in the chaste bond of marriage, the sixtieth through the considerable labor of continence endured, and the hundredfold (Matt. XIII) in the attainment of the virginal crown.

The harvest of this seed grew to such a mass that it not only satisfied the inhabitants of that homeland but also fed the hungry of foreign regions. For who could explain how many lights of teachers, perfected in word and example, came forth from there? Our France rejoices that it gratefully received them as true apostles of Christ as guests, abundantly sustained them with provisions, honorably endowed them with possessions and resources, gladly listened to their preaching, and obeyed their admonitions to her own salvation. It also rejoices that to this day it reverently guards the blessed relics of the saints’ bodies for the protection of its people, hoping through all these things to share with them in eternal blessedness.

From that most holy company shone Saint Lebwin, born in the aforementioned land of the Angles and devoted from the very beginnings of childhood to exercises in the worship of God. Even then, through his efforts in good conduct, he displayed what he would become through pious deeds, so that it might plainly be understood that he would be a true worshiper of God, meditating on his law day and night (Ps. I), just as Solomon promises in the Proverbs in a general statement concerning such people: “From his pursuits it is understood whether a boy’s works are upright and pure” (Prov. XX).

[Col. 0880D] III. From there he was handed over to liberal, or rather sacred, literary studies, longing, as Scripture says, to know wisdom, to understand words of prudence, and to receive instruction in doctrine, justice, judgment, and equity (Prov. I), so that astuteness might be given to the child and knowledge and understanding to the young man. He watched daily at the doors of wisdom, keeping watch at the posts of her entrance (Wis. IX).

As he practiced these things continually, he desired that the spirit of wisdom might come into him. From the depths of his heart he prayed to God and said: “Give me, Lord, the wisdom that sits beside your thrones; send her from your holy heavens and from the seat of your greatness, so that she may be with me and labor with me, that I may know what is acceptable before you” (Wis. VI).

While he prayed for these things repeatedly, wisdom herself came to meet him—she who travels about seeking those worthy of her. She showed herself to him cheerfully and came to meet him like an honored mother, standing upon the highest and lofty heights, in the middle of the paths beside the gates of the city, at the very entrances.

As someone who loved her had previously described her for us, she had an exceedingly venerable appearance, blazing eyes surpassingly keen beyond ordinary human power, a vivid complexion, and inexhaustible vigor. She was so full of age that she could in no way be thought to belong to our time, and her stature was of indeterminate proportion. For now she restrained herself to the ordinary measure of human beings; but at other times she seemed to strike heaven with the crown of her highest head. When she raised her head higher, she even pierced heaven and eluded the gaze of those who looked upon her.

She had built herself a house, hewn out seven columns for herself, sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table. She sent her maidservants to summon people to the citadel and the walls of the city, saying: “If anyone is a little one, let him come to me”; and likewise to the foolish: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you. Leave childishness and come, and walk in the ways of prudence” (Prov. IX).

Then, looking with a peaceful face among the numerous hearers of the abundant crowd, she addressed humble Lebwin, whom before the ages she had foreknown and predestined to be her dear friend, in a friendly voice: “I love those who love me,” she said, “and those who rise early to seek me will find me” (Prov. VIII). “The beginning of attaining me is the fear of the Lord; good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ps. CX).

Hearing these words with a hearing ear, Saint Lebwin rejoiced in the Lord in his heart and said: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXV). “Direct my steps according to your word, so that no iniquity may rule over me. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it. Behold, I have longed for your commandments; in your equity give me life” (Ps. CXVIII).

From then on, suffused by her with the oil of gladness (Ps. XLIV), he advanced from day to day through the grace of her friendship.

And lest anyone perhaps think that, setting aside the sequence of actual events, we have invented certain fabulous and frivolous tales about this blessed man’s striving to learn the paths of wisdom and attain knowledge of her, we wish a sober reader or hearer to know with certainty that no one can walk rightly by any other way if he wishes to behold her desirable form. For it is most firmly established that whoever neglects to investigate the aforesaid steps of progress by which one ascends while advancing toward her cannot philosophize at all.

[Col. 0881D] IV. Therefore, because this blessed man pursued these paths of prudence with all his strength from early youth, he earned the greatest distinction of divine grace. Through this grace he possessed such effective cautious circumspection that, like an animal with eyes before and behind, he advanced in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame (Luke I).

He was a man of great abstinence, sparing toward himself and generous to the needy; serene in speech, chaste in body, unceasingly devoted to sacred reading, vigils, and prayers; pleasant in conversation, sober in the quality of his conduct, and endowed with every goodness.

By shining with these and similar virtues, he attained the dignity of the clergy. Believing that this dignity of rank and title had been divinely bestowed, he diligently watched over himself so that his conduct might not disagree with his name. For *klēros* (Κλῆρος) is called “lot” or “inheritance” in Latin. Hence they are called clerics because they belong to the Lord’s lot and, as it were, to his special inheritance, just as in the Old Testament he took the Levites from among the children of Israel as his own. Or else they are called so because those who are truly clerics desire no inheritance in this mortal region except God, awaiting with living hope that incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance kept in heaven (I Pet. I), which they can attain through him, with him, and in him (Rom. II), just as he himself promises them, saying: “I am their inheritance” (Ezek. XLIV). They continually meditate and say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me. The measuring lines have fallen for me among splendid things; indeed, my inheritance is splendid for me” (Ps. XV).

Devoted to these things, and diligently recalling what the holy Fathers had established in almost these words concerning the conduct of clerics, Saint Lebwin abstained from common life and worldly association, from the pleasures and spectacles of the world, from the pageants of the age, from public banquets, from usury and the pursuit of shameful profits, from frauds, and from avarice itself, the mother of every crime. He did not pursue secular offices or affairs, nor ranks of honor through ambition, nor solicit gifts in return for the remedies of God. He fled deceit and conspiracies, hatred, rivalry, disparagement, and envy. He did not walk with wandering eyes, an unbridled or wanton tongue, or a swollen bearing; instead, he displayed modesty and restraint of mind in his simple dress and manner of walking, utterly abhorring obscenity both in words and in deeds. He never sought visits to widows and virgins or companionship with unrelated women, but constantly strove to preserve the chastity of an undefiled heart and body.

Amid these things he showed due obedience to his elders and did not exalt himself through any fault of vainglory. And what more need be said? He devoted himself continually to reading, instruction, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, knowing well that clerics ought to be those who strive to offer themselves as devoted to divine worship.

Thus, presenting himself to God in this way, after such a life of continence, with his head shorn and shaved, he did not place his hair to be burned by the fire of the ancient sacrifice (Num. VI). Rather, as a true Nazirite, consecrating the perfection of his devotion, he offered his whole self as a living and holy sacrifice, pleasing to God (Rom. XXI), to be continually burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that his service might become reasonable worship (Rom. XII). The sign of the tonsure, which was represented upon the body, was enacted in him, in whom Christ dwells in the inner person: outwardly his hair was cut off, while inwardly all sins were cut away, and he shone anew with renewed senses, like fresh-growing locks.

Moreover, wearing, as it were, the tiara of the true priesthood on the shorn upper part of his head, and expressing the dignity of a royal crown on the lower part, he rejoiced that this typological likeness was fulfilled in him—the likeness of the gift with which blessed Peter rejoices that the universal Church has been endowed: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II).

V. Thus Lebwin, the man of the Lord, mature both in age and in the advancement of his virtues, a cleric truly irreproachable in every respect, having gradually ascended the ranks of ecclesiastical dignity according to canonical institutions, was chosen for the office of presbyter, so that he who was perfect in knowledge and conduct might instruct others through teaching and encourage them to do good by his example.

A generous executor of his own name and entrusted office, he carefully strove to be and to appear a presbyter—that is, an elder—not greater in number of days, nor more honored because of gray hair, but more advanced through the increase and excellence of his virtues, so that he might belong to the number of those whom Moses chose at the Lord’s command. “Gather for me,” he says, “seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and their teachers,” and so forth (Num. XI).

Such presbyters are not appointed to the priesthood through popular favor. They are chosen by Moses, the leader of the Christian people, who knows them—that is, the one who has granted them such grace that through the merit of wisdom and holiness they are elders of the people. And because they stand before him with an unbending posture of justice, they deserve to be rewarded with a share in his spirit. In them is fulfilled what the Almighty says to Eli: “Those who glorify me will be glorified” (I Sam. II).

The glory of these elders, as it is said in Proverbs, chapter XX, is their gray hair—undoubtedly that of which it is read elsewhere: “For understanding is gray hair” (Wis. IV), that is, men of wisdom, and the age of old age is an unblemished life.

Endowed, therefore, with these spiritual gifts, Lebwin became, in a worthy manner, a worthy priest, fulfilling in word and deed the name and office of sacred leadership. With a pure mind and clean hands, he acted, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, as priests must act, confecting and giving life-giving sacraments to the faithful, teaching each person with suitable exhortations according to the character of his profession and conduct.

VI. He who works in all things according to his good will, both the willing and the accomplishing (Phil. II), by his freely given gift worked in his faithful servant Lebwin a will that could in no way differ from his own will: namely, a constant longing to win souls for salvation and an unceasing devotion to that desire.

Thus, just as Paul bears witness concerning the special grace of the apostleship of blessed Peter and himself, saying: “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised worked also in me among the nations” (Gal. II), so we may confidently say of this apostle of ours that he too worked through Lebwin among the Franks and Saxons.

Since he was sent by God to teach these same peoples, he may appropriately be called an apostle, which in Latin means “one who is sent.” For just as he himself commanded his disciples, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII), so he addressed this disciple of his and, as though by the same command, ordered him to teach the aforesaid peoples the sacraments of the catholic faith, bathe them in saving baptism, and thereafter command them to observe all the commandments given to him.

And just as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Paul and Barnabas, that the Holy Spirit commanded, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have taken them” (Acts XXV), and they departed to teach the nations in a similar manner—that is, by the command of the same Holy Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills and works all things in all people (I Cor. XII)—so that faithful servant and strong worker, Lebwin, was set apart and taken up for the work assigned to him by the Lord.

VII. Moreover, so that his fellowship in the work might be worthy not only of the apostles but also of the patriarchs, the imitation of Abraham, the supreme priest, was set before him. For just as God commanded Abraham, “Go out from your land and your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you” (Gen. XII), and he immediately obeyed that command, so this venerable man, hearing it and as though it had been specially assigned to him, held fast to this decree without wavering, following the example of the blessed patriarch.

Thus, departing energetically from his land and kindred, he left behind the island of the Angles and traveled by ship to Trajectum, the fortress anciently called Wiltenburg and now called Trajectum. There he found a venerable man named Gregory, born of noble Frankish blood, formerly nourished from childhood by the blessed Archbishop Boniface, and a presbyter in ecclesiastical rank, though at that time serving as vicar of the episcopal office in that fortress and its parish. Lebwin explained to him the whole course of his pilgrimage and of the preaching entrusted to him.

VIII. Since mention of the good disciple Gregory has brought to mind the excellent teacher Boniface, it does not seem unworthy to give, even if briefly, a worthy account of so great a prelate for the memory of all.

This man, born in the aforesaid homeland of the Angles and dedicated to God from childhood, increased day by day in wisdom and every kind of holiness as he advanced in age. He entered voluntarily upon the path of holy poverty and pilgrimage and, with the grace of God cooperating with him, undertook the task of evangelizing many peoples.

Under the Frankish rulers Carlomannus and Pippin, he served as a Germanic envoy at the apostolic see. With the aforesaid rulers consenting to the judgment of the clergy and the favor of the peoples, he was ordained archbishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory himself, a man sufficiently learned in Greek and Latin. This pope was the twenty-sixth in the order of pontiffs after that other Gregory, the blessed apostle of the Angles, that marvelous teacher of the Church.

The man previously called Winfrid, by the grace and merit of his good works, was, as some maintain, called Boniface. As is read concerning him, by his preaching he converted the Thuringians, Hessians, and Austrasians to the true faith and Christian religion, from which they had long strayed. He was also the first to build monasteries of monks and virgins in the regions of Austrasia.

Among the distinguished signs of his good works, so that the Catholic Church might be propagated, enlarged, and strengthened not only through his vigilance but also through that of other bishops, he established, with Carlomannus’s consent and supported by apostolic authority, that the fortress of Wittenburg, now called Trajectum, should be an episcopal see.

When the same glorious Carlomannus had rejected an earthly and temporal kingdom through a most blessed exchange, so that he might deserve to attain the heavenly kingdom, which is eternal, he traveled to Rome to the thresholds of the blessed apostles. There he assumed the clerical habit, and not long afterward, when a monastery had been built on Mount Soracte, he ascended to the height of perfect attainment. Having professed himself a monk in the monastery of blessed Benedict, he appeared to have chosen the better part with Mary, the beloved and loving one of the Lord; according to the Lord’s promise, it shall never be taken away from any of the elect who steadfastly desire it (Luke X).

The dignity of the kingdom and principate that they had formerly divided passed to his brother Pippin. But after Pippin had gained possession of the entire realm, on the advice of Pope Zacharias and with the unanimous consent of the Franks, at an assembly held in the city of Soissons, he was called king and given the royal throne through the anointing of the most holy Archbishop Boniface. Childeric, who had previously been called king under a useless title, was rejected and tonsured.

But when blessed Pontiff Boniface, preaching the word of God to the Frisians together with his fellow ministers, was, as they say, crowned with martyrdom along with fifty-two others, the aforementioned Gregory, once his disciple, remained in the aforesaid fortress. A good imitator of his teacher, he diligently carried out and practiced what he had learned from him.

IX. When Saint Lebwin, as we have already said, had reported to him what he intended to undertake according to the will of God, Gregory rejoiced in the Lord. He encouraged him with counsel, strengthened him with assistance, and sent him to a place divinely shown to him beside the river Isela, so that he might become a most certain and powerful boundary in the frontier between the Franks and Saxons. Like a boundary stone placed in place of that living, supreme, and cornerstone, he was to receive into one faith two peoples coming from different directions (I Pet. II).

God, who examines hearts, looked upon the devoted humility of his beloved Lebwin and did great things for him, because he is powerful (Luke I), so that he might preach to Franks and Saxons his holy and terrible name (Ps. CX).

Abbot Gregory also provided him with a companion, a venerable man named Marcellinus, one of the disciples of the holy bishop Willibrord.

But how wonderfully our spirit is stirred when mention is made of such men! It cannot bear to pass over, even briefly, what its own style may express about so great a bishop, Willibrord.

This man too, filled with God and proceeding from Britain, the land of the Angles, became a pilgrim for the sake of his eternal homeland. He came to Rome in the time of Pope Sergius, who was the twentieth after the blessed teacher Pope Gregory. Warned by an angelic visitation, Sergius honorably received this holy man and ordained him bishop of the Frisian people, giving him the surname Clement.

Entrusted with an office no less important, he did not, like a wise architect, place his work upon another’s foundation. Instead, after first uprooting the dense thicket of thorns, he dug deeply and laid a firm foundation of faith upon the rock that is Christ. Then, gathering stones of different qualities and sizes from various places and joining them together into the same structure, he endeavored to cleanse with pure water those that were rough and filthy.

That strong laborer strove to make them, once circumcised on every side, squared and polished, fitted together at their joints for the construction of his work. And because those stones were not material but living and rational, he exhorted them in the words of blessed Peter: “Putting aside all malice and all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and slanders, like newborn infants, long for rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet. Approaching him, the living stone, you too, like living stones, are built upon him into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II).

By these and other holy preachings he subdued the savage hearts of the pagans and brought countless losses to the devil’s party and no small increase to the Christian community. And because he had faithfully distributed the talents entrusted to him by his Lord, he rightly deserved, as a good and faithful servant, to enter into his joys.

Having briefly summarized these few things in memory of Willibrord, our beloved blessed bishop, let us turn to the deeds of our dear Lebwin.

X. The man of God therefore came with his companion Marcellinus to the place shown to him by God. For some time he made use of the hospitality of a certain widow named Abachilda. Fearing nothing, he labored daily at evangelical preaching, showing ever more insistently that, having neglected the living and true God, they served the worship of idols, which were empty and entirely useless.

Why delay over many details? All who had been predestined to eternal life, instructed by his saving admonitions, believed. At their expense a first small oratory was built in a place called Wilpa, toward the western bank of the river Isela.

Not long afterward, as the number of the faithful gradually increased, they built another, larger oratory for him on the eastern side of the same river, and beside it a house suitable for his habitation. There the saint of the Lord fulfilled daily vows of vigils and Masses to the Lord, nourished those who flocked to him with the bread of the divine word, and showed himself gracious in face, words, and conduct to all who saw him. For this reason he was especially dear to many of them, including some of the more distinguished.

Meanwhile the ancient enemy, always envious of every good, saw that those who were clearly being joined to Christ through blessed Lebwin were being taken away from him. Through the agents of his wickedness he therefore worked to stir up a great murmur of furious complaint about him among the people.

They said: “What is this wandering phantom that, by its tricks, [Col. 0887B] alienates minds, befuddles understanding, and perverts the conduct of our people? Do you not see that he has already corrupted many, removing them from the condition proper to their nature and making them almost delirious? Therefore, before he deceives us all in the future by the frauds of his enchantment, let him be sought out quickly, driven away, or rather destroyed, or else, together with that magic stage [magicali, “magical”] of his, let him be handed over alive to the flames.””

After repeating these things, they rushed upon the place, set fire to it, burned the church-house, and drove away from the area all the Christians they found there, pursuing them farther afield.

But the Lord, who guards all who love him (Ps. CXLIV), rescued his servant from their persecution and preserved him unharmed for the salvation of many. Nor was the blessed man frightened by their savagery into ceasing his persistence in evangelizing. Rather, as a strong athlete, taking up the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation (Eph. VI), he prepared himself for dangers renewed and more severe.

XI. In the Saxon people, in ancient times, there was neither knowledge of the supreme and heavenly king, so that fitting reverence might be offered to his worship, nor the dignity and honor of any earthly king whose governance might direct them, whose judgment might correct them, or whose diligence might defend them. Rather, that people, as it still exists to this day, was divided into three orders.

There are among them those called *Edlingi* in their language; there are those called *Frilingi*; and there are those called *lassi*, which in Latin means nobles [freeborn], free men, and servants.

According to their own inclination and, as it seemed to them, prudent counsel, individual leaders presided over the individual districts. At a fixed time once each year, twelve men were chosen individually from each district and from each of the same three orders. Gathered together in the middle of Saxony beside the river Weser, at a place called Marklo, they held a general council, discussing, establishing, and making public matters of common utility according to the law they had established by their own decision.

If the danger of war happened to threaten, or if the joy of peace smiled upon them, they also deliberated about what they ought to do in these circumstances.

Knowing that this assembly was approaching, Lebwin, the soldier of Christ, resolved to go there, intending either to gain for his king a large number of a faithful army or, fighting bravely against his enemies, to carry away the glorious triumph of victory.

Meanwhile, it happened that he turned aside to the house of a certain illustrious and powerful man named Folebert, in whose household he enjoyed familiar companionship among many whom Folebert held dear and who held Folebert dear.

Receiving him with the greatest joy, Folebert said: “I congratulate you, my beloved friend, on having arrived at this opportune moment. Indeed, since I have been anxious for you, your presence is a welcome gift to me. But please tell me where you are heading.”

The holy man replied: “With the help of heavenly grace, I intend to visit the assembly of the Saxons.”

Folebert answered: “I do not fail to recognize that, because of the merit of your holiness, you are accepted by very many of our people. Yet I also know that some are hostile to you and gladly plot against your life. Therefore I ask you, listen to me: turn aside elsewhere for the moment, return home, or go to your familiar friend Davo, until, once the assembly has ended, you can safely visit us again.”

When he tried by such words to dissuade Christ’s athlete, Lebwin, inspired by the Holy Spirit under whose influence he acted, replied firmly: “I can in no way pass over, nor do I dare to pass over, what Christ Jesus, my own King, God and Lord, has appointed me to do. I consider it wicked to transgress his command.”

Folebert said: “I fear for your life.”

The man of God replied: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. CXVII).

Seeing that his face was firmly set, Folebert at last, grieving, gave his consent.

## XII

[Cols. 0888C–0889D]

When, therefore, the appointed moment arrived at which the assembly of the council was to convene, those whose business required it appeared, with a gathering assembled from every direction. The good soldier Lebwinus was also present—not as a coward or sluggard, but as a vigorous and dutiful man, with the loins of his mind girded in truth, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, his feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace, protected by the shield of faith, wearing the helmet of salvation, taking up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and surrounded on the right and left with the weapons of righteousness and of his power (Ephesians 6). Although he was inwardly fortified with all these things, the fitting outward ornaments of conduct were not lacking.

Marked out by his clerical form, adorned also with the priestly headgear, and as though signifying something divine by the radiance of his countenance, he carried the sign of the cross in his hands, as the standard-bearer of his king. He also bore on his arm the Gospel of Christ, which he continually recalled in his mind, preached with his mouth, and practiced in his deeds.

The whole multitude of that assembly, gathered from different regions, first sought to preserve the institutions of their forefathers, offering vows and sacrifices to their deities. When Lebwinus, the strong athlete of Christ, saw these sacrileges being committed, burning with zeal for the Lord, like the prophet Elijah of old (3 Kings 18), he burst into the midst of their ranks and, crying out unexpectedly, raised his voice like a trumpet, publicly announcing and rebuking their crimes.

“Listen,” he said, “all of you; listen to me—and not so much to me as to him who speaks to you through me. I proclaim to you the commands of him to whose authority and judgment all things are subject.”

When they looked at him in astonishment and, marveling at the man’s appearance and clothing, fell silent, he continued:

“Listen, pay attention, and know that the Lord, creator of heaven and earth, of the sea and of all that is in them, is himself alone the one and true God. He made us, and not we ourselves (Psalm 99); nor is there any other besides him.

“The images that you believe to be gods, and that you, deceived by the devil, worship with reverence, are gold or silver, bronze, stone, or wood. They do not live, move, or feel. They are works of human beings, and they cannot help anyone else—or even themselves.

“Therefore God alone is good, God alone is just. His mercy and truth endure forever. Pitying you, miserably seduced by the error of demons, he has commanded me to undertake this embassy, so that, repenting of your ancient error, you may turn to him with upright and sincere faith, by whose goodness you were created.

“In him, finally, we and all of you live, move, and exist (Acts 17). If, faithfully acknowledging him, you repent, are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and obediently keep his commandments, he will preserve you from all evils. Granting you the tranquility of peace, he will allow you here to enjoy temporal goods and in the future life to possess all good things eternally.

“But if you do nothing about his most salutary commands—or nullify them—and refuse to correct the error of your wicked hearts, know that you will suffer the judgment of a heavier punishment for having despised the warning of his kindness. For I proclaim to you, by the sentence of his mouth, which is unchangeable, that unless you obey these admonitions, the evil of unforeseen tribulation will come upon you with the utmost speed.

“For the King of heaven, ruler of all ages, has foreordained a strong, prudent, and most fierce king, not from far away but from nearby, hastening like a swiftest torrent to soften the ferocity of your hardened hearts and restrain the obstinacy of your stiff necks.

“He—namely, Charles the Great—will attack your region with violent force and lay waste to everything with sword, devastation, fire, and destruction. As the avenger of the wrath of God, whom you have always provoked, he will kill some of you by the sword; others he will cause to waste away through hunger; and others he will consume with the sorrow of perpetual exile.

“He will distribute your wives and children everywhere for servitude, and if any remain, he will subject them in disgrace to his dominion, so that what was long ago spoken of you may now rightly seem to have been foretold: ‘They became few, and were afflicted by the tribulation and distress of evils’ (Psalm 106).”

## XIII

[Cols. 0890A–B]

While the blessed man proclaimed such things in a prophetic spirit, those men, raging with a demonic spirit and filled with fury and madness, raised a confused uproar everywhere:

“Look! There is that seducer, the enemy of our sacred rites and of our entire homeland. It is right that he should pay the deserved penalty with his blood.”

Then they seized stakes from the nearby hedges, cut and sharpened them, intending to kill him with those poles, just as is customarily done with stones. But while the fury of the wicked against the holy man was thus inflamed, God, protector of his faithful, sheltered him beneath the covering of his wings.

Indeed, just as the Lord Jesus himself was once led by the perfidious Jews to the brow of the mountain to be thrown down, yet by the power of his might passed unharmed through their midst (Luke 4), so this servant of his, surrounded by the protection of the same Lord, passed unharmed through the midst of those who wished to kill him.

Among them, however, were certain men of sound mind whose hearts God had touched and who did everything possible to prevent these things from being done against the holy man of God. One of them, more honored than the others, named Bruto, standing in a more elevated place, protested as follows:

“O men, whoever among you are sensible, receive with your ears the words of my mouth. Often envoys from various peoples—the Northmen, Slavs, and Frisians—have come to us. As is customary, we received them in peace, carefully considered the words of their embassy, and sent them honorably back to their own people, enriched with gifts.

“And now behold: the envoy of the highest God, bringing us commands of life and of our salvation, has not merely been rejected and despised by us; he has also been pursued with insults and has nearly suffered the danger of death.

“How powerful must he be who sent him, since he has so powerfully and miraculously rescued him from our hands! Therefore, what he prophetically threatened you would happen, you will without doubt experience as exceedingly true, when these things have been inflicted upon us by the judgment of his God, who is so powerful.”

Struck somewhat by such words of rebuke—or rather of terror—their savage spirit was subdued. By common agreement they decreed that no one should attack that messenger of God, but that wherever he wished to go, he should proceed safely and without any injury.

## XIV

[Cols. 0890C–0891A]

Thus the holy and humble-hearted Lebwinus, protected by divine power from the attacks of the wicked, blessed the Lord, because he is praiseworthy and glorious forever.

When he saw that he could not attain the martyrdom he ardently desired—laying down his life for his brothers—he nevertheless carried out a long martyrdom by denying himself, taking up his cross after Christ, crucifying his flesh with its vices and desires, and enduring hunger and thirst, vigils and fasts, and very many labors. All these things he bore willingly and patiently.

Yet, retaining within himself an unfailing spirit full of the fervor of charity, he effectively administered the apostolic office entrusted to him by God. For who could worthily and adequately recount the graces of his teaching and words, by which he converted many from iniquity?

Of this man it was rightly foretold through the prophet: “The law of truth was in his mouth” (Malachi 2). Likewise: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (ibid.).

As he proclaimed the word of truth, a dwelling-place for God was prepared in the heart of the people who believed him, and his testimonies became exceedingly trustworthy (Psalm 92). All who heard his speech were built up in faith and in works, and he kindled within them the fervor of holy charity. What especially reinforced the teaching of his words was that whatever he urged with his mouth, he practiced in his deeds.

After he had produced countless proofs and examples of holy virtues, and scarcely any interval of time passed in which he did not seek the advancement and benefit either of himself or of others, the most holy man, made exemplary in every form of sacred and God-pleasing conduct, was now being summoned by the heavenly hosts as a fellow citizen belonging to them by divine predestination and by a manner of life worthy of them.

## XV

[Cols. 0891A–D]

Lebwinus’s beloved vows were also presented to God through the ministry of angels. In intention, deed, and speech they harmonized and continually cried out to him:

“How beloved are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for them” (Psalm 83).

Likewise:

“My soul thirsted for you. How greatly my flesh longs for you, that I may see your power and your glory” (Psalm 62).

And again:

“My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Psalm 41).

But since the burden of bodily matter held back this unquenchable desire of his mind, and he could not otherwise obtain the building from God, the eternal house not made with hands in heaven (Hebrews 1), unless the house of his earthly and worldly dwelling were dissolved, he who is the fiery fountain of souls—who, by forming the human being and sustaining the elements, made discordant things harmonious—determined that this should take place in the blessed man. Once dissolved, the elements were to be recalled separately to their proper origins: the flesh was to be returned to its source, and the spirit was to go to him who had sent it.

Therefore, having sent fellow-workers to carry out the purposes of his dispensation—those who are “ministering spirits sent forth for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1)—he commanded that the bonds of the breast be severed. The limbs were loosened, the hidden passages opened, and the difficult delays of the soul were removed.

At last, when the doors of its prison had been opened, the soul sprang forth joyfully and, to the amazement of those who beheld it, more brightly than light, joined the ranks of the inhabitants of heaven. With them it entered, singing hymns, the hall of the heavenly kingdom on the day before the Ides of November, and received from its kind benefactor the incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance (1 Peter 1), preserved for it with all the saints.

This was the inheritance “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” which God in his mercy prepared from eternity for him and for all who love him (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2). Having prepared it for this man, dear to him according to the omen of his name, he graciously bestowed it upon his beloved friend, addressing him in friendly speech:

“Well done, my dear one; well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

Then that holy soul of the holy man entered the secret chamber of eternal praise. Clothed in the first robe of blessed immortality and filled with ineffable joy, living in everlasting glory, it sang alleluia in melody with all the holy spirits and continually praised God throughout the eternal ages.

## XVI

[Col. 0892A]

The pure and clean vessel of his body, in which the blessed soul had been placed—the soul that had nourished many like heavenly manna—was buried with due honor in the church of the port of Deventer.

It is established that this place received its name from a certain Davo, an honorable and powerful man who, while Saint Lebwinus was still alive, was his closest companion. The church itself had been built by the same holy man and certain faithful people, as we have already said, but was burned by unbelievers and rebuilt once more.

This occurred at the time when the most radiant dawn, Christ the sun of righteousness, first visited the formerly unbelieving Saxons through the blessed teacher Lebwinus, in order to give them the knowledge of salvation (Luke 1), to illuminate those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, and to direct their feet into the way of peace—blessed forever (ibid.).

Having now completed, as best we could, the course of our narrative concerning the deeds of the blessed confessor of Christ, Lebwinus, we wish to append a few remarks concerning the discovery of his body.

## XVII

[Col. 0892B]

After his blessed passage to the heavenly realms, it happened, through the prompting of the evil enemy, that the Saxons—most of whom still persisted in unbelief—again set fire to the basilica in which his sacred body lay buried and devastated everything around it.

Although they searched for his tomb for three days, by God’s providence they were unable to find it. As a result, the same place remained desolate for a long time.

## XVIII

[Cols. 0892B–0894A]

Meanwhile, when the venerable abbot Gregory, whom we mentioned above, migrated from this unstable dwelling to the house of eternity, his kinsman Albricus assumed the dignity of the see of Utrecht.

He had a certain man worthy of God, bound to him by special affection, named Ludgerus, who was later elevated to episcopal dignity. He addressed him as follows:

“My dearest brother Ludgerus, since I know that you diligently seek out matters pertaining to divine religion, I urge and ask you to devote your care to the place where the sacred body of Lebwinus, priest of Christ, was buried, and to labor with all your might so that, with God’s revelation, it may be found by you, and that a church may be built there over it for the composition of praises to God.

“For you know very well what sort of man and how great he was.”

The excellent Ludgerus accepted these instructions. Applying every care, he cultivated, to the best of his ability, the field in which that treasure was hidden, like a man diligently seeking a good pearl.

Although he was quite unable to find what he desired, he nevertheless, deeply saddened, began to build a basilica within the area where the body was thought to be contained. But the manifestation of the Lord’s goodness did not fail the good man who sought good things.

At last, in a dream, he seemed to see the most holy priest of Christ, Lebwinus, speaking with him and revealing the location of his tomb. He addressed him in these words:

“I approve your praiseworthy and God-pleasing zeal, most loving brother Ludgerus, by which you are striving to rebuild, for the honor of God’s name, the temple that was destroyed long ago. You will find the members of my little body after removing this southern wall that you are erecting.”

The servant of God, Ludgerus, had no doubt about the vision. He assembled a great multitude of Christ’s people, demolished the wall he was building, and rejoiced that he had found what he desired in the place shown to him.

Having therefore offered to God, as was fitting, thanksgiving in hymns and psalms, he enlarged the space of that building so that the treasure he had found through the Lord’s revelation might there be praised.

How precious it is has been demonstrated from that time to the present by the signs and virtues that the ineffable power of the kindly Jesus, our God and Lord, continually deigns to work through his merits among his faithful.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

# HISTORICAL COMMENTARY

## NOTICE ON THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS

[Col. 0893]

The Bollandists published a historical commentary on Saint Jonatus for 1 August. In it are interwoven fragments of Hucbald’s sermon on the same saint, and at the end is read the history of the elevation of Saint Jonatus’s body, written by Hucbald.

We present here this most learned investigation; the passages that are Hucbald’s are distinguished by italic type.

## HISTORICAL COMMENTARY ON SAINT JONATUS, CONFESSOR AND ABBOT OF MARCHIENNES IN BELGIUM

*(In the Bollandists, under 1 August.)*

### § I. Information about the place and the saint, together with his deeds and age

#### 1

We have already had occasion to speak many times in our Acts about this celebrated monastery, founded by the true apostle of Belgium, Saint Amandus, along with so many others. This was especially the case when we discussed its first founder on 6 February, its benefactor Adalbold on 2 February, and its benefactress Saint Rictrudis on 12 May, in an extensive and learned manner; likewise when we discussed her daughter Eusebia on 16 March.

I say, we have had to deal with it so often that we could pass over the matter here at greater length, unless at least a few points had to be prefaced—points connected by a certain singular bond with the first abbot of the place.

Its chronicler describes the location of the monastery quite briefly, and in this respect is by no means suspect, when he says:

“The place of Marchiennes is surrounded by flowing waters and marsh reeds. Toward the north it has a great forest; on the southern side, the river Scarpe, which flows eastward. On both sides of it lie meadows covered with marsh grasses.”

It lies between Douai and Elnone, or Amandopoli—not Audomaropoli, as Mabillon incorrectly writes along with others—about three leagues distant from each on either side. Concerning the early straitened circumstances of the monastery and the very extensive possessions with which Saint Rictrudis later endowed it, its Life, chapter 2, should be consulted.

#### 2

A manuscript chronicle in our possession explains the matter as follows:

“In that same place, Jonas, a most vigilant shepherd and a faithful and simple administrator, inwardly and outwardly, was first given to those male persons who had been assigned to serve there. He was one of the disciples of the blessed bishop Amandus and, thoroughly instructed by his sacred teaching, was found suitable for this office.

“But not long afterward, after more careful consideration, it was decided that, since the glorious mother Rictrudis, founder of the place and mistress of all that had been entrusted there, appeared to be serving God in that holy community among the servants of God, it would be more fitting to bring faithful women there also and to establish the order of nuns as the governing body of that holy habitation.

“Accordingly, after the small community of men had been set aside—peace be with them—noble matrons streamed there eagerly from every direction. Religious widows, women who truly were widows, hastened together joyfully. The chaste youth of maidenly modesty was also introduced. All together they undertook the training-ground of the spiritual gymnasium.

“Meanwhile the place became a dwelling of chastity, a school of virtues, and a sheepfold of the Lord’s sheep. At all this the soul of the thrice-blessed Rictrudis rejoiced greatly in the Lord of lords.”

#### 3

Mabillon brings these matters into some sort of sequence, though in his preliminary observations to the second century, page 938, he gives a text not entirely corresponding to what has just been quoted. There, briefly recalling the lamentable vicissitudes of the renowned monastery, he says that it was solemnly dedicated by Saints Amandus and Autbertus, bishops, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul:

“Saint Jonatus,” he says, “was placed as the first abbot over this monastery. A double congregation was founded there at the beginning, one of monks and one of nuns; Jonatus presided over the former, Rictrudis over the latter.”

The chronicler of Marchiennes reports that monks were first placed there, and shortly afterward—that is, around the year 647—virgins consecrated to God were established there for the benefit of Saint Rictrudis, the benefactress.

After the monastery was devastated by the Normans in the year 879, the nuns gradually fell into worse conditions, until Baldwin, surnamed the Bearded, expelled the women and substituted monks, bringing in Lietuinus, the celebrated abbot of the monastery of Saint-Vaast. After governing the place for nine years, he appointed his disciple Albericus to the administration of Marchiennes.

When Albericus died in 1048, Saint Poppo of Stavelot succeeded him; after a month, Wido succeeded Poppo. From this point the succession of the abbots of Marchiennes follows quite correctly in the *Gallia Christiana*. Between Saint Jonatus and Lietuinus, however, you will find no one.

#### 4

Saint Jonatus, with whom we are chiefly concerned here, was sent by Saint Amandus from the monastery of Elnone to govern Marchiennes. He was not placed over that monastery alone, but also over Elnone itself, as Cointius demonstrates from the chronicle of that monastery under the year 643, number 2.

The words of the chronicle are:

“Amandus, concerned for the flock entrusted to him, resolved to visit his diocese of Utrecht. Before doing so, however, he appointed his disciple Ursus to exercise his functions at Elnone and to govern it as abbot. Ursus ruled commendably for several years and at last rested in a blessed death.

“Saint Jonatus, a most modest man and a monk of that same monastery, was ordained by the blessed Amandus as his successor. The same blessed Amandus had previously established him at Marchiennes as its first abbot.”

The chroniclers cited above would have deserved great praise if, as was their task, they had connected each deed with its proper year, just as we find in the passage that Cointius reports from them under the year 653:

“When Amandus, after visiting the thresholds of the apostles, returned to Elnone, we find that Jonatus returned to Marchiennes. There, living according to the rule for several lustrums after the death of the blessed Amandus, he brought various people of both sexes into religious life and chastity.”

It will become clearer below that those “several lustrums” can be explained with reasonable precision.

#### 5

As for the virtues and deeds already mentioned, and the unquestionably illustrious and sublime achievements of Saint Jonatus, I would certainly have no doubt about them. Yet no one has hitherto undertaken to extract them from our chroniclers, whether the Elnonian or the Marchiennian, so that I cannot at all understand what Silvius’s editor, Bellecampius—or, as Bollandus calls him, Beauchampius—intends when, after making many grand promises in his *Antiquity of Marchiennes*, he writes emphatically on page 505:

“But we intend to furnish much more concerning our most holy prelate Jonatus of Marchiennes when he is treated in our Marchiennian Hagiology.”

This, I suppose, was the prospect of a work that was never completed and never saw the light. One may infer this from the fact that neither our predecessors nor Mabillon ever mention such a *Hagiology*.

Perhaps Bellecampius undertook this project but, prevented by death, was unable to finish or print it. Thus the attempt may have remained among the Marchiennian papers, which I wish that Dom Synonymus, our holy man’s namesake and the present prior of the aforementioned monastery, had consulted. Through friends I repeatedly pressed him without success; he rejected and refused their repeated requests as well as mine in a manner certainly neither courteous nor honorable, and not customary in such matters, although I was asking only for documents that might contribute to the glory of Saint Jonatus, his patron.

I shall say no more about the rest.

#### 6

As for the saint’s age, our chroniclers have left it equally doubtful and obscure. Nowhere, not even remotely, do they indicate approximately in what year he was born, when he became a monk, when he was appointed abbot, how long he ruled alone, how long with Saint Rictrudis, how long he governed both monasteries, Elnone and Marchiennes, or in what year he finally received from the Lord the reward for his labors.

Bellecampius struggles, contends, and exerts himself remarkably to defend a verse of Blandinium, composed, I do not know by whom:

> In the six hundred and tenth year Amandus founded  
> Blandinium, giving Peter as its patron.

Since he assigns his monastery of Marchiennes to exactly the same period as the Blandinian monastery, he thinks that by an unavoidable consequence he has proved that his Marchiennian monastery already existed in the year 610, and that in that same year, if heaven so willed, Saint Jonatus was already presiding over it—although perhaps he had not yet been born.

He repeats and emphasizes this so often against all opponents that it becomes wholly nauseating to readers. He had learned from his own chronicler, no doubt, that Saint Amandus died in 651 and was therefore born in 571. This opinion had long entangled many people, but it was long ago overthrown by Henschenius in section 11 and following of his commentary. The lustrums also collapse—the lustrums by which that chronicler, and Bellecampius after him, ineptly assert that Saint Jonatus survived Saint Amandus.

#### 7

Consider, I beg you, the paradox. This man’s thesis is that Saint Jonatus was abbot of Marchiennes from the year already mentioned, 610 or 611. He defends this epoch of his with the utmost ferocity, as if fighting for hearth and altar, relying on his preconceived Achilles—that Saint Amandus died as a nonagenarian in the year 661—whereas, as we have already demonstrated, he died in 684.

Saint Jonatus is then said to have survived him by several lustrums. Several lustrums indicate at least three or four, from which it necessarily follows that this saint lived beyond the end of the seventh century and was therefore abbot of Marchiennes for a full ninety years or more, so that the final dates correspond to the beginning.

Before I admit this, I would like Bellecampius or his associates to demonstrate it by some authority other than that of this chronicler.

It is agreed that Saint Amandus died at the age of ninety. But if you place his death in the year 661, he must have been born in 571. Since he is assumed to have been about forty when he built both monasteries, Blandinium and Marchiennes, the year 610 fits perfectly.

But if everything is moved back twenty-seven years—as Henschenius demonstrates that everything must plainly be moved back—you will clearly see all the Bellecampian contrivances collapse, so that his lengthy treatise goes up in smoke.

#### 8

Here now is a more suitable chronological arrangement of Saint Jonatus’s life, taken from Henschenius. In the passage cited, he establishes and clearly proves that the monasteries begun at Ghent—both the Bavo monastery and Blandinium—were founded in 636; Elnone was built in 638; and Marchiennes only in 645. At that time the same prelate Amandus placed his disciple Jonatus, a venerable man, over it, prescribing the establishment of a community of monks.

As for what we said above, namely that the monastery of Elnone was also entrusted to the aforementioned Jonatus of Marchiennes, this happened when Amandus resigned his episcopal care and visited the thresholds of the apostles for the third time, namely in the year 650.

Two years later, after Saint Adalbaldo had been murdered, he persuaded Saint Rictrudis to embrace chastity. Not long afterward she went to Marchiennes, for the reason stated above, and under Saint Jonatus’s direction presided over the nuns until the year 688.

Jonatus, full of labors and merits, is believed to have followed that holy woman around the year 690, as Cointius plausibly deduces under that year, number 25, by the following argument.

Since the administration of this monastery remained in the hands of nuns for approximately 333 years, if one counts backward from the year 1024, when they were expelled—or, according to others, from 1028—it does not seem possible to assign Saint Jonatus a longer life. Certainly, so far as I know, his age has never yet been elucidated to that extent.

Let us now proceed to his cult and eulogies.

### § II. Sacred cult and scattered eulogies

#### 9

I shall here briefly gather everything I can find that pertains to the saint’s ancient cult, setting aside those writings which, with lengthy digressions, report nothing more or more certain about the saint’s life and deeds than what Molanus and Miraeus faithfully drew from whatever Marchiennian records they could find. I shall soon quote their texts, as well as those of a few martyrologies.

To the chronicle’s statement about the several lustrums by which Saint Jonatus survived Saint Amandus, the following is expressly added:

“His feast is celebrated on the Kalends of August.”

Cointius testifies that the following verses were read at his tomb in the church of Marchiennes, in the place cited above:

> Here lies the most holy body of Saint Jonatus,  
> who first ruled this house.

The remaining verses do not concern this matter.

Cointius adds only the following:

“After the death of Saint Jonatus, the monks whom he had governed departed from Marchiennes, and the entire monastery passed to the nuns, over whom Clossendis had presided as abbess for three years.”

This is precisely the most widely accepted opinion of Molanus and others, and, if I am not mistaken, it should be understood in such a way that the monks remained to govern the virgins. Thus the diploma of the emperor Charles, cited by Mabillon, is preserved, since it shows that in the ninth century mention was made equally of brothers and sisters.

But this matter has already been discussed so often that I do not wish to begin the whole thread again. Let us continue with the saint’s cult.

#### 10

It is sufficiently remarkable that in the older sacred calendars no mention of him is found anywhere, not even in the more recent ecclesiastical lists, except those of Belgium—if Ghinius is excluded, for he rather generously enrolled Saint Jonatus among his own canonical saints.

We have discussed elsewhere the date of Usuard of Anchin, where we judged that he should be assigned approximately to the thirteenth century. He is the first and oldest writer who mentions Saint Jonatus, in these exact words:

“At Marchiennes, the deposition of Saint Jonatus, abbot.”

Molanus is somewhat clearer, and Canisius follows him:

“On the same day, the birthday of Saint Jonatus the confessor, disciple of Saint Amandus.”

He repeats this somewhat more briefly in later editions.

Wion also mentions him, together with the other monastic writers. Among them Meinardus elegantly announces him in this form:

“At Marchiennes, Saint Jonatus, abbot and disciple of Saint Amandus, and spiritual father of Saint Rictrudis.”

With these words he has nearly gathered together everything that has been handed down in memory concerning Saint Jonatus, since otherwise either no one undertook to recount his deeds expressly, or they perished through the devastations.

For what circulates under Hucbald’s name is not a history of his Life, but merely a discourse composed in the saint’s honor. There is also another extremely verbose work under the name of Gualbertus, from which one can finally extract only that the saint’s body was transferred to Saliacum and then brought back to Marchiennes, and that during some procession extinguished candles were rekindled by fire sent down from heaven, as you will see in the following section.

#### 11

Saussayus adorns Jonatus with a proper eulogy in his customary manner:

“At Marchiennes, near Douai in Flanders, in the diocese of Arras, the deposition of Saint Jonatus, abbot and confessor. He was a disciple of Saint Amandus and shone adorned with every excellence of virtue; by his examples and prayers he led many to Christ.

“He was the religious instructor of blessed Rictrudis and, because of his excellence in faith, teaching, and morals, was appointed director of the brothers and nuns of the same place. He set before both groups the precepts of each way of life by his deeds and conduct, so that by an unstained path he showed them the way to heaven.

“Finally, enriched with the merits of holy conduct, he cast off the flesh and happily sent his spirit to the Lord, to be joined in glory to the citizens above.”

Let the aforementioned Ghinius have a place here as well, although he is mistaken about the year of the saint’s death. He almost condenses Molanus as follows:

“At Marchiennes, the deposition of Saint Jonatus, abbot and disciple of Saint Amandus, who, adorned with every excellence of virtue, led many to Christ by his examples and prayers. He rested there in the diocese of Arras around the year of the Lord 670.”

Ghinius undoubtedly followed the opinion of those who think that Saint Amandus died in the year 661.

#### 12

Molanus himself, however, has presented the entire matter more solidly and elegantly in his catalogue of the saints of Belgium, so that there is no need to seek eulogies elsewhere. He writes:

“Saint Jonatus the confessor, disciple of Saint Amandus, was the first abbot at Marchiennes, or Marcennes, and was raised there and rests there. He was adorned with every excellence of virtue and led many to Christ by his examples and prayers.

“After him, that place was a monastery of virgins for approximately 333 years, the most holy Rictrudis being their first superior.

“The place is renowned for piety and pleasantness, not far from Douai in Flanders, in the diocese of Arras.

“His feast falls on the Kalends of August; his elevation on the sixth day before the Ides of April, as you will find noted on that day among the entries omitted from the main lists.”

Nearly the same words of Molanus, with only a slight alteration of phrasing, are also explained in the *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*. In all these texts Molanus’s opinion is plainly evident: after the death of Saint Jonatus the monks withdrew, and after 333 years, under Baldwin the Bearded, the nuns were expelled and the monks returned to the monastery.

It will not be irrelevant to add here what Miraeus reports in his *Belgian Fasti*, so that it may supplement the deficiencies of the others for a while. His words are as follows:

#### 13

“Amandus of Utrecht and Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai, dedicated the monastery of Marchiennes, built by Saint Rictrudis, widow of Adalbaldo, duke of Douai, in honor of Saints Peter and Paul on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

“In that monastery, after monks had first been established to serve God, Jonatus, a most vigilant shepherd and disciple of the blessed Amandus, was appointed.
