“But afterward it seemed consistent with reason—for blessed Rictrudis had consecrated her possessions to this place and had determined to serve God there—that nuns should also be placed there.

“They governed the church of Marchiennes for approximately 333 years.

“After the Norman devastation, Leduinus, abbot of Saint-Vaast, at the request of Baldwin, count of Flanders, placed Benedictine monks in that place, as is narrated more fully in the manuscript chronicle of Marchiennes, which also exists at Rubravalle (Rougeval).

“These are the commonly printed eulogies concerning Saint Jonatus that we have judged worth transcribing.”

Miraeus goes on to report verses read around the choir of Marchiennes, in which various bodies of saints buried there are enumerated, including the two whom we quoted above from Cointius. Anyone who wishes to know the others should consult the source itself.

14. From this it is altogether clear that no Life or Legend of Saint Jonatus exists anywhere, since in the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum* he is treated so briefly that, from the Acts of Saint Rictrudis herself, vol. II, p. 937 onward, only a few details are supplied—details so closely corresponding to those already reported that they do not deserve to be transcribed. In the preliminary observations the editor praises Jonatus among the other saints because he flourished in the monastery of Marchiennes. On page 944 [Col. 0899D] there is reported what we have already stated: namely, that Saint Amand appointed his disciple Saint Jonatus, a venerable man, over the completion and organization of the monastery; his sacred body is still preserved buried in that same monastery. Saint Amand also wished the order of monks to be maintained there, but the abbot just mentioned incorporated nuns into it, as he had thought appropriate. How, and for how long, they remained there can be understood without difficulty from the foregoing account. Those lamentable times followed in which discipline among the nuns completely collapsed, and whatever remained in that place became prey to the barbarians; consequently both the monastery itself and the writings concerning the deeds of the Marchiennes saints perished together. Here we may cite what is additionally mentioned in passing about Saint Jonatus in the *Chronicle*, as reported by Mabillon, p. 951.

15. “When the monasteries situated along the Scarpe River were likewise destroyed, including the monastery of Marchiennes . . . , after the inhabitants of the land had been driven away and killed, it too was obliterated. The bodies of the saints, however, which had been buried in the churches destined for destruction, were transported safely, by divine providence, to more secure places. In that destruction all the ornamentation of the church of Marchiennes was lost—namely, charters, privileges, books, accounts of the saints’ deeds, and the other things pertaining to the dignity and use of the place . . . . Yet, while investigating the elevation of Saint Jonatus, the abbot who had been a disciple of the excellent confessor Amandus, we found it written that, in the time of Abbess Judith, who governed the monastery of Marchiennes during the reign of Lothair, king of the Franks, the bodies of the saints still lay in stone tombs, with altars placed before them: namely, those of the blessed Rictrudis, a noble matron, and of the good confessors Maurontus and the aforesaid Jonatus.”

The monuments of Marchiennes offer nothing further relevant here to the glorification of the saint, except for a few eulogies corresponding to those already mentioned, which may be extracted from Hucbald’s little exhortations—or apology for his boldness—distributed, as it were, among the lessons. The history of the elevation of the sacred body and of the candles that were kindled will, as I said above, be the subject of the following section.

16. Thus Hucbald, in lesson 3, after citing the scriptural passage “If you wish to be perfect,” and so forth, speaks of our saint [Col. 0900C]:

“Saint Jonatus, not slow to obey and fulfilling this commandment, humbly approached the holy bishop Amandus, the truthful teacher whom God had appointed for the peoples; and, desiring to be instructed by his wonderful teaching, he imitated with complete obedience the holy works that illustrious man performed. The same bishop received him devoutly and taught him all the observances of Christian doctrine, wisely entrusting to him the commandments of service to the Lord. Obeying the precepts of so great a teacher, he showed himself a faithful servant and, by his exemplary conduct, stirred many to divine service.”

Then he continues in lesson 4:

“Accordingly, these holy men, Amandus and Jonatus, shining like bright lamps in the house of God, dispelling the thickest darkness of unbelief and sin, sprinkled all people with the light of heavenly glory [Col. 0900D]; and by their examples and prayers they happily led many into the kingdom promised in heaven.”

The remaining eulogies collected there clearly follow the same vein and express entirely the same meaning; they are shared equally by Saint Amandus and Saint Jonatus. Then, in lessons 8 and 9, Hucbald praises several qualities that apply somewhat more particularly to the latter, as follows:

17. “For the monastery of Marchiennes he appointed the holy and in every respect praiseworthy man Jonatus to complete what was lacking and to preserve the rule of holiness in all things, commanding him always to enlarge, day by day, whatever was holy, so that it might increase. This holy man, Jonatus, appointed abbot for that purpose [Col. 0901A], obeyed and fulfilled the commands; and, in recompense for this, received the crown of eternal glory.

“Saint Amandus had indeed planned to gather monks at Marchiennes for the service of the Lord; but Jonatus, authority having been granted to him by Amandus himself, cherishing virginal purity of mind and body, established nuns there. Perhaps he did this after receiving heavenly inspiration, so that the place might later be suitable for the blessed Rictrudis and her daughters, all holy virgins, and might be suitably withdrawn from secular society.

“Thus the fervor of divine love in the holy Jonatus—praiseworthy and manifold—had accumulated a considerable harvest of holy virtues and spread the fame of his goodness far and wide. For he was chaste in heart, humble in mind, serene in countenance, approachable to all, and loved by everyone.”

[Col. 0901B] 18. “Finally, Saint Rictrudis and all who lived with her had in him a certain mirror and exemplar. The same saint delighted them with his words, encouraged them with exhortations, and by his most holy works urged them toward the highest summits of sanctity. What more need be said? Such singular grace shone forth in him that, just as a precious gem, skillfully and appropriately set in a golden ornament, displays the charm of its beauty and draws those who see it to love it, so this blessed man, adorned with every beauty of virtue, appeared gracious to God and to good people.

“Since, then, this blessed and most holy Father of ours, Jonatus, was such and so great, when the end of his calling drew near, he was withdrawn from the world and, by divine grace, placed in heaven. There, together with all the saints, blessing the name of the Lord, he is comforted by the joy of blessed happiness [Col. 0901C] and rejoices without end.

“He was buried at Marchiennes in a prominent place, and there he is venerated by all the people, to the praise of Christ. Through his merits and prayers, fitting remedies are granted to the needy, so that it may be evident to all that God is omnipotent and wondrous in his saints.”

§ III. The Elevation, Translation, and Return of the Sacred Body

19. After the little exhortation just discussed, Hucbald adds the following title: “How the body of Saint Jonatus, confessor of Christ, was elevated”; and he proceeds to narrate the entire event in another nine, shorter lessons, which we transcribe here faithfully in their proper order, observing three barbarous words whose meanings we have not neglected to explain.

FROM LESSON I [Col. 0901D]:

“Marchiennes is the site of a monastery consecrated by blessed Amandus in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. The church is sufficiently adorned with an honorable design and appropriate beauty; but it shines far more becomingly and attractively for spiritual people because it preserves there the pledges of the saints who rest within it. Through their intercessions the devout people strive onward, and an abundant and fruitful supply of the grace of heavenly dew is granted.

“There the order of monks, in honor of the saints, joins in singing with the divine Majesty through psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. The holy place is frequently visited by the ministry of angels, and the prayer of those who devoutly petition hastens, flying toward the ears of divine hearing.”

20. LESSON II. In this church, therefore, the body of blessed Jonatus [Col. 0902A] was buried, in the proper manner of the faithful, in a prominent and, as it were, more sacred place. It was nevertheless entrusted to the innermost recesses of the earth in such a way that, above it, beams placed twice over and crosswise, together with a great construction of stones and a mass of cement, were fitted together, entirely denying the ability to find it to anyone who did not seek it piously.

The places and tombs of the saints there were venerated without any inscription placed above them, only by the altars set before them—as is still done in Italy and in Rome itself, which is glorious for the bones and dust of Saint Peter and innumerable saints.

But whenever, by the secret impulse of the divine counsel, the relics of saints are raised into human sight, the mind is surely stirred to a more fervent and eager devotion toward them. This happened at the elevation of the aforesaid Father Jonatus, when he ordered himself to be elevated through a warning repeated frequently, and gladdened the minds and hearts of the inhabitants of his own place and of the whole people. So that the manner of this elevation may become known to all who wish to read it, let it be set forth more plainly in humble writing and rustic language.

21. III. Since, as was said above, Saint Jonatus, Saint Rictrudis, and blessed Maurontus had long lain buried in the innermost recesses of the earth, with no title placed above their tombs, nevertheless, at some time by God’s permission and will, during a vigil observed on Sunday, blessed Jonatus—tall in body, handsome in appearance, with a swanlike head, and venerable in the clothing of his garments—appeared to a certain priest of his congregation named Malgerus, gentle and cheerful, and said:

“Go,” he said, “on my behalf; and command Abbess Judith [Col. 0902C]—for at that time the place was governed by nuns—to have the relics of my bones elevated and brought forth into the sight of everyone.”

22. IV. But when the priest said that he was not sufficiently capable of making this known and that no one would believe him, the saint, gentle again after repeating his warning, added:

“See that, by becoming disobedient to my command, you do not appear worthy of unheard-of blows.”

This occurred through a threefold warning in an apparition; but because of the priest’s negligence and disobedience, the commanded elevation did not take place. Nevertheless, Malgerus, greatly astonished at the saint’s command and fearing that, because of the apparition made to him, he would be thought a liar and a false speaker, undertook frequent fasts and, through prayers and almsgiving, sought and disclosed the instructions of this *oromatis* [vision or dream] [Col. 0902D]. Then, behold, during another vigil observed on Sunday, Saint Jonatus appeared to the same priest in the form described above, holding a staff in his hands. He struck the same priest across the shoulders and said:

“Because you have become disobedient to my voice and have in no way ordered my relics to be elevated, from now on you shall receive no food of bread until the time appointed for you.”

23. V. When Malgerus awoke, he immediately began to tremble in his bones and throughout his whole body. At the same time, although unwillingly and with disgust for the food of bread, he confessed to Abbess Judith, who governed the monastery, what he had long concealed. He declared it and, with many entreaties and tears, urgently begged that the elevation of so great a Father be carried out as quickly as possible.

The priest himself, being disgusted by bread as food for almost an entire year and content with small and very moderate portions of other foods [Col. 0903A], was greatly distressed, yet rejoiced that the day of the elevation was approaching. But because unavoidable circumstances of worldly business intervened, and negligence also crept in, the undertaking was delayed for some time.

24. VI. When somewhat less than a full year had passed, Abbess Judith summoned from the see of Cambrai ministers and faithful men devoted to her bishop, and took due care to bring forth the body of Saint Jonatus. Removing the joining of the beams that, as we said above, had been fitted together over his burial, and lifting away a considerable mass of stones and cement, she at last found, exactly as she had most earnestly desired, the immeasurable treasure of her vow: that honorable body lying in the tomb. She had its bones and ashes received by the hands of clerics [Col. 0903B] in silken garments.

25. VII. Afterwards she replaced these relics in the title set above his tomb—that is, in the *appario*, which in common usage they call a *repa* [a bier, used as a cover]. There, too, the precious relics of the saints—the mother and son, namely Rictrudis and Maurontus, her fair offspring—were likewise placed, and are there venerated with the fullest devotion by the people who come.

After this Saint Jonatus deigned to appear to Abbess Judith and told her that his command had been fulfilled. Moreover, he promised that he would arrange the affairs of the whole congregation over which she presided.

26. VIII. Now, therefore, dearest brothers, as we celebrate today with spiritual joy the great deeds of the Lord toward his saints, it is fitting that, with corresponding vows, we should humbly venerate and adore him, and faithfully proclaim his name, which is wondrous throughout the whole earth. His immense and immeasurable mercy is clearly proved by his chosen ones, to whom he grants the rewards of his promise eternally.

You, therefore, saints of God, placed in the confession of the Lord’s praise above the heavens, and joined on earth by the bond of a blessed fellowship through your patronage—namely, most blessed confessors Jonatus and Maurontus, and the blessed and venerable matron Rictrudis, who have honored this place with our relics [or rather, “with yours”?]—deign to accept the devotion of our praise. Come to the aid of every people who ask in accordance with a holy petition, so that the most merciful clemency of almighty Christ may kindly forgive our sins, consign them to perpetual oblivion [Col. 0903D], and, through the intercession of your prayer, deign to open for us the gate of eternal life and lead us into it. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

27. Let this, then, suffice concerning the miraculous elevation of the sacred body, according to the faith of the writer. It remains for us to extract a few details about its translation and return from the large folio manuscript, p. 24, said to be attached to the work of Gualbert, the monk, *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Rictrudis*. Its discourse is tedious; you will find its entire substance presented more clearly under 12 May, beginning on page 104, where the title of chapter 3 indicates the subject itself: “Various Evildoers Punished by God; Candles Kindled of Their Own Accord.” Here, however, only a few matters are related—matters that the author of this writing adorned and enlarged with countless figures and excessive flourishes, so that it is often impossible to understand where he is going or what he intends.

Here is the title: “Prologue on the Miracle by Which the Lord Glorified His Most Holy Confessor Jonatus, the Abbot.” These are bombastic, inflated, and sesquipedalian words, followed by the account of the miracle itself: candles that had been extinguished but were rekindled by heavenly light. All this is reported in a sufficiently clear abridgment at the place already cited.

In brief: after the death of the excellent Charles, count of Flanders, the wars that broke out everywhere and the resulting plundering of the possessions of the people of Marchiennes persuaded the abbot to transfer his sacred relics—and among them those of Saint Jonatus—to Saliacum, for the protection of the place, as a heavenly fortification. It is said that many things turned out favorably for the inhabitants [Col. 0904B] through this measure.

28. While the sacred relics had been deposited in that place and were often carried around in procession, it happened that torches or candles were extinguished and, in what they describe as an obvious miracle, rekindled by heavenly fire. This is the core of the entire lengthy composition, although many other matters are inappropriately mixed into it.

Among these, in what more closely concerns the saint, the orator Gualbert notes the negligence of his own people in honoring Saint Jonatus, in these exact words:

“Nevertheless, not without divine prompting have I often reflected in my heart that the confessor of the Lord, namely Saint Jonatus, about whom there is now much talk in our region, has just cause to complain about us up to the present time, and especially about the ancients, because of such lukewarm service—neither cold nor hot, as it is said in the Apocalypse—particularly on the anniversary of his sacred burial, a service lacking the proper lessons and the frequent occurrence of his miracles, as well as the resounding celebration.

“Therefore, it is greatly to be feared that at some time he may withdraw his favor from the protection of this place, which his sacred presence inhabited for so long. But what devotion the people of Marchiennes afterward showed, or now show, toward their holy patron, I have so far sought in vain for someone who might inform me.”

29. Several confused proofs of veneration follow there, to such an extent that the people of Marchiennes took care to bring the sacred bodies of the saints back to their original seat. Hear Gualbert again:

“At last the same brothers of Marchiennes [Col. 0904D] came to know and experience in reality that the presence of the saints beneficially presides over places deprived of human assistance, is of no small advantage, inspires terror in enemies, and daily increases in some measure the prosperity of the good.

“For when the time of harvest was approaching, the minister worthy of God and a worthy successor—Amandus, both in reality and in name, the father of the monastery—foreseeing that, because of the necessary work imposed by the crops, there would be less care for the holy confessor of the Lord, Jonatus, while he was in the countryside, ordered that the worthy burden of the holy relics be returned to the well-deserved and, as it were, native dwelling-place of the Marchiennes community, secretly and without any worldly commotion.

“Accordingly, in accordance with the command of the aforesaid spiritual father, Saint Jonatus was returned to the habitation that was proper and suited to his former way of life. With due honor, and accompanied by the favor of a great multitude—especially the people of Saliacum, whom he had long protected by his defense—he was received as he revisited his own home, greeted by the joyful, white-clad procession of the entire congregation.” [Col. 0905A]

Here we withdraw our hand from the tablet, since nothing more could be obtained.

HUCbALD THE MONK’S WORKS, PART TWO—MISCELLANEOUS

SHORT WORKS ON MUSIC

(D. Gerbert, *Writers on Music*, vol. I)

[Col. 0905]

NOTICE

Hucbaldus is perhaps the first among all the ancients, both Greeks and Latins, to have written anything about polyphonic music, which we call harmonic music because it consists of the concert of several voices and different consonances. Hucbald’s immediate rules on this subject are indeed based on the succession of the consonances of the fourth, fifth, and octave. Our music theorists entirely exclude such a succession from harmonic concert, whereas Hucbald places the whole art of his *diaphony*, as he calls it, or *organum*, in nothing other than the succession of consonances of this kind.

On the authority of manuscripts, we publish various works of his which either bear his name somewhere, agree with his distinctive method, or, because they occur continuously in the codices without an inscription and their true authors could not be discovered, we have not thought it appropriate to separate from them.

First we place his book *On Harmonic Instruction*, based on a paper manuscript of the Civic Library of Strasbourg, collated with manuscripts of the Library of Cesena belonging to the Conventual Franciscans. Immediately following it in the Strasbourg codex is Boethius’s *On Harmonic Consideration*, and so forth, as in the manuscript of Saint Emmeram under the title *Another Music*, up to the words: “Seek the eighth tone as above.”

Then, in the Strasbourg codex, there follows *Music* beginning with ἀπὸ τοῦ μῶσαι [“from *mōsai*”], which has been excerpted piecemeal from Aurelianus. Then come *On the Measurements of Organ Pipes*, *On the Weights of Cymbals*, *On Musical Modes*, and *On Five Symphonies or Consonances*. At the end of all these is read: “Here ends the music of Ubaldo.”

We publish his *Enchiridial Music* on the authority of the manuscripts of Einsiedeln, Tegernsee, Salem, Saint Blasien, Monte Cassino, and Strasbourg, with scholia divided into three parts. These scholia are nevertheless absent from the codices of Calinensis, Salem, Saint Blasien, and Strasbourg, as well as from the Royal Paris manuscript, which, like the Florentine Magliabechian manuscript, is filled with interpolations from beginning to end.

In some manuscripts there follows a brief *Memorandum on the Tones and the Melodic Setting of Psalms*. At the end of this little work, the following couplet is read in the manuscript of Saint Blasien:

> Reader, you see the remarkable words of the younger Cato:  
> Cultivate these virtues; may kindly faith remain safe.

This little work was written out with the musical signs peculiar to Hucbald. In the Saint-Emmeram codex there follows, without an inscription, an incomplete short treatise, in which the author, after prefacing a description of the monochord, chose to describe the harmonic rule of the *Enchiriadis*.

[Col. 0905]

HERE BEGINS HUCbALD’S, THE MOST SKILLED MUSICIAN’S, BOOK ON HARMONIC INSTRUCTION

[Col. 0905B] Anyone entering upon the foundations of music who seeks, even in some measure, to gain an understanding of songs must carefully observe the quality or position of every kind of voice.

[Col. 0906B] First, what voices are equal and uniformly alike; then, which are unequal and differ from one another by certain intervals; finally, what distinctions there are among these intervals and by how many variations they can be regulated. We must also consider afterward by how many and by what sounds—sounds that serve as elements—the entire song is governed.

Now, once someone has been accustomed through exercises of no little duration to these matters, as though at the outer doors, he may perhaps finally be granted admission to the inner sanctuary of the discipline itself. The dullness of his vision will gradually be removed, as it were, and radiance will be admitted: namely, an understanding of how all these things, or any of the matters treated by them, are arranged with the greatest appropriateness according to the rational structure of consonances and how everything is composed and fitted together in accordance with their patterns.

Concerning equal voices, since they are self-evident, nothing need be said except that [Note: [Col. 0907D] The Cesena codex has “continuously.”] they are produced by the force of a common voice in the manner of a reader reciting prose; and that, however often they are repeated, there is only one voice—just as if you repeatedly wrote or pronounced a single letter, for example, “a, a, a.” There is no consonance between them, for they are *aequisonae*, “equal-sounding,” not consonant. For in consonance two voices, entirely distinct from one another, sound together harmoniously.

In these voices, even if the same sounds are produced by several people, they are nevertheless not separated from one another by any interval, as in this antiphon [Note: [Col. 0907D] We have decided not to add the musical notes placed above the text, since they are now unknown. Those skilled in these matters may consult the modern antiphonaries of the Roman Church, expressed with common musical notation, which are almost the same as the ancient ones.]:

> A. “The kings of the earth stood together.”  
> A. “When I shall have been sanctified.”

And in Sebastianus’s [antiphon] to Nicostratus, up to the words: “He deigned to present his own.”

In passages of this kind, where so many syllables are joined continuously under one voice, with no higher or lower pitch intervening—as though a straight line had been drawn directly onward—equality can easily be perceived.

But in a song of varied sound, if one asks which voice is similar or equal to another in the same melody, this becomes apparent only to someone more thoroughly accustomed to it. Nevertheless, it will in no way hinder an earnest student, as in this antiphon: “A child is born for us.” If you ask which voice of the same introit corresponds to the first, it appears in the first and third syllables of this phrase: “He was given for us, whose, and Angel.”

This is called *Cirus* or *Circulus* (“circle”), because it returns to the same point from which it began. Again, if I ask about this word, “Puer” (“Child”), these are the corresponding syllables: “Na—Nobis” (“born—for us”). And “Fi—hic ca—N.” [Note: [Col. 0907D] In the entire antiphon these syllables are equal in pitch: “A child is born for us, and a son is given to us; whose government is upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called the Angel of the great council.” Psalm: “Sing to the Lord,” etc.]

The same applies to other examples. There is also very frequent use of this observation at the endings of sections or neumes, as in: “Hail, Mary, full of grace.” Likewise: “Blessed Agnes in the midst, with her arms extended.”

The unequal sounds, which are called disjunct, offer various species. These are called unequal voices when two voices joined to one another are produced, one with a sharper and the other with a lower sound, at some interval; but the intervals themselves are smaller in some cases and larger in others. Beginning from a certain very small interval and gradually increasing by additions one by one, they rise to nine kinds of enlargement.

They can never be perfectly recognized, however, until the entire series of all fifteen sounds, which will be discussed later, has been learned. For the present, though, I shall briefly indicate them, showing each by two examples, one for the higher and one for the lower pitch.

The first kind occurs when two voices are joined by the division of an extremely small interval, so that scarcely any distinction can be perceived between them, as in the antiphon “Gabriel was sent,” at the words “to Mary.” Likewise, “Virgin.”

The second is somewhat more perceptible [Note: [Col. 0908D] That is, the interval or space.], as in “Gabriel was sent.” Likewise, “to Mary the Virgin.” Likewise, “Angel.”

The third is separated by a still slightly larger interval [Note: [Col. 0908D] That is, by a somewhat larger interval or space.], as in: “Gabriel was sent to Mary the Virgin.”

The fourth is still more extended, as in the antiphon: “Blessed are those who walk.”

The fifth is wider still, as in: “Do not be afraid, Mary.” And: “On that day rivers shall flow.”

The sixth is broader yet, as in this responsory: “Now his body.” “Whose father a woman.” Likewise, the responsory: “These are the days which you must observe in their seasons.”

The seventh surpasses these by an interval of its own, as in the antiphon: “Blessed Agnes in the midst of the flames’ threats.”

The eighth you will find in: “You, man Symphorianus, hang upon the tortures.”

The ninth, stretched by a more extensive interval than all the others, reaches the limit of these divisions. For you will never find a division of voices wider than this one or narrower than the first. It occurs in this antiphon:

> “To you I have lifted up my soul.”  
> “My God, in you.”  
> Responsory: “Among those born of women, not . . .”

In these kinds of intervals, anyone attentive can observe how, with equality serving as a kind of source and the proposed material, this entire principle of inequality flows from it. First there is a departure from equality by the smallest possible interval; then, by gradual increase, it grows until it reaches the point at which the human breath naturally imposes a limit.

Beyond this final division, if you seek voices containing still greater distances, you will find neither such a thing in any rational song nor the capacity of human execution suited to it. With voices so far apart, it would not be possible to move so easily, in a single stroke, from the highest to the lowest; rather, the change would almost be into a new voice. These intervals can be shown by the following lines, provided that the copyist carefully observes the spaces between them.

[Col. 0909]

[Col. 0909A] In these spaces, attention must be paid to how the things that follow always arise from those that precede, and how later elements are constituted from earlier ones. The first interval, because it is contiguous with the equality from which it derives [Note: [Col. 0909C] The Cesena codex has “second.”], always seems to produce something twice as great; but this is not entirely true, as will be discussed later. Hence the second is thought to contain only a little more than the first.

The third consists of the first and second; that is, it possesses alone as much space as both of them contain together. The fourth consists of two seconds. The fifth consists of the first and two seconds. The sixth consists of three seconds. The seventh consists of the first and three seconds. The eighth consists of four seconds. The ninth consists of the first and four seconds.

To a more subtle observer it also becomes apparent how the quantity of the first interval is added to each of the several kinds in an orderly progression. Thus, add the first to itself and you make the second, although in this there appears to be some difficulty, as stated above. Then the first is added to the second and the third is produced; likewise, the fourth is produced by adding the first to the third. In the fifth and the remaining intervals the same increase is maintained.

According to the discipline of music, the first two intervals are called the following: the first, a semitone; the other, a tone. From these two the structure of all the remaining intervals is completed.

The third consists of a semitone and a tone. The fourth embraces two tones. The fifth joins a semitone to two tones. The sixth likewise consists of three tones. The seventh consists of three tones and a semitone. [Col. 0909C] If you add a tone and a semitone, it will leap to the ninth voice [Note: [Col. 0910C] The Cesena codex has “new.”].

It must not, however, be thought that these differences among voices are counted as consonances, which musical authority discusses. Consonance is one thing, interval another. Consonance is a measured and harmonious mixture of two sounds, and it exists only when two separately produced sounds come together in a single modulation, as happens [Col. 0910A] when a male and a child’s voice sound together, or in what is commonly called *organum*.

There are six consonances: three simple and three compound, which are called by their proper names: diapason, diapente, diatessaron, diapente diapason, diapason diatessaron, and bis diapason.

Among the intervals described above, only two of these consonances can be found: diatessaron and diapente—namely, in the fifth and seventh species—and if the two little voices are uttered together, they produce a consonance. Otherwise, neither among these intervals nor among the remaining ones is there any consonance; there are only certain differences among the voices, confined within intervals of such definite limits [Col. 0910B].

For the moment, however, these matters should be left unmentioned, especially since their practical benefit can scarcely be obtained before the arrangement of the sounds has been demonstrated in order. Once these matters have been brought within perception, it will be possible to discern all of this and also certain other things that contribute considerably to usefulness and even to delight.

One further point should be added concerning these nine kinds: they are contained in only seven voices. You have an example of them in this authentic tetrardus antiphon:

> “The eleven disciples, seeing the Lord in Galilee, adored him.”

Up to the syllable *ve-* there are seven voices. For the final syllable, which is placed eighth from the first, will sound in the same way when compared with that first syllable, although one is sung with a man’s voice and the other with a child’s. This is the consonance diapason, and is therefore excluded from the reckoning of intervals.

Let these same voices be arranged according to their steps, with the intervals between them marked according to their proper quantities, indicating where they contain a tone and where a semitone; and let the same kinds be marked by linear extension between them. These examples have now been demonstrated from the middle series of sounds, to which the authentic tetrardus and its corresponding plagal modes appear to belong. Nevertheless, in other orders, or even tones, it will also be possible to find these same kinds with exactly the same intervals. Their demonstration must be postponed for the moment; we must now turn to the series of sounds.

The sounds by which the ancients judged that one should enter music through certain elements, as it were, they wished to call by the Greek name *phthongi*—that is, not just any sounds, such as those of arbitrary insensible things or the voices of irrational animals, but only those which, distinguished and determined by a rational quantity and suitable for melody, they established as the most certain foundations of the entire song.

Thus they also called them elements, or *phthongi*: just as the whole variety of speech is confined by the elements of letters and everything that can be said is arranged through them, so they carefully ensured that the immensity of songs should possess certain beginnings and, being contained within a definite measure, should proceed through them without any error in whatever had to be sung, with nothing in them that did not possess complete rational order.

They are called *phthongi* ἀπὸ τοῦ φθέγγεσθαι, “from *phthengesthai*,” as though by a likeness to speaking: just as intelligible words are produced through speech, so sounds fall under these, implicitly understood [Note: [Col. 0911D] Or, “with these sounds implicitly understood.”]; and practiced discernment sometimes distinguishes even irrational sounds by them [Note: [Col. 0911D] The Cesena codex has “divides.”].

For this reason they wished to define a sound of this kind—not a general sound—as follows:

“Sound is the fall of a voice that is *emmelos*, that is, suited to melody, produced in a single measure”—for example, when it is uttered with any voice, such as “A,” or when a single-stretched string has sounded.

When, therefore, there were initially only a few such rational *phthongi*—for at first only four had been discovered—these alone remained in use among singers for a long time. Later, for various non-irrational reasons, the number of *phthongi* gradually increased: first to seven or eight, then to nine or eleven, and finally, for the time being, it reached the limit of fifteen.

They more commonly called these *phthongi* by the name “strings,” because they could be displayed more readily on the instruments to which they were attached. Concerning their mention, order, and the names of the individual strings, many other writers on the same discipline, both Greek and Latin, and especially the remarkable teacher Boethius, the wisest investigator of all the liberal arts, explain sufficiently in the first book of his *Harmonic Instruction*.

Among these *phthongi*, or strings, one must not suppose that any is similar to another. Rather, they proceed like the steps of a ladder from the lowest to the highest, or from the highest to the lowest, each separated from the next by the quantity of its own interval.

The entire series is not separated by one uniform interval. Instead, it always proceeds through the two types placed first in the formulas of the higher intervals [Note: [Col. 0911D] The Cesena codex has “second.”]—namely, the tone and the semitone—with each of them occurring only in its own definite position.

First, it must be said what a tone and what a semitone are. Once these have been learned in advance, since they serve almost as the elements of the subject, everything that follows will readily be understood.

A tone, then, occurs when a voice deviates or rises from another voice, whether lower or higher, by a moderate interval—so to speak, by the removal of a single point—in such a way that the ear can readily perceive the division between them. A tone is therefore the interval between two voices joined together in this manner; not the voices themselves, which are nothing other than sounds, but the interval that lies between them. In every musical instrument an example of this is found between the first two properly arranged strings, or simultaneously between the first two pipes of a water-organ [hydraulia].

[Note: Cicero calls it hydraulis, Pliny hydraulus: an organ or musical instrument in which water is used to produce sounds; the term comes from the Greek ὕδραυλις, “water-pipe.”]

In this connection you can prove the matter in the antiphon “Ite dicite” (“Go, tell”): the tone descends in “Ite dicite”; the tone ascends in “Ite dicite Joanni” (“Go, tell John”).

A semitone appears to have been so called because it contains half a tone. But if that were so, a tone could be divided into two equal parts; and the more careful investigators have made it plausible that this cannot happen at all. A tone is indeed divided into two parts, but in such a way that either part exceeds half, or remains less than half. Both divisions are called semitones: one is the greater, the other the lesser—just as when you divide this [division].

When these two parts are brought together, they make a complete tone. But if two greater semitones are joined, they exceed a tone; if two lesser semitones are joined, they do not reach its measure at all. A semitone was therefore named not because it is half a tone, but because *semum* is said of either part of a thing divided into two unequal parts, as when three is divided into one and two.

A semitone occurs when two voices are joined by an extremely small interval, so that at times scarcely any distinction between them can be perceived. Sometimes, however, the term is used of the lesser semitone: although the greater semitone likewise has voices very close to one another, the interval between them is perceived somewhat more distinctly. Here too observe that it is not the voices themselves, but the interval between them, that is the semitone.

Thus there are two semitones, but only one tone. However high or low the sound may be produced, it will contain neither more nor less of the interval, and therefore it will always be one and the same tone.

You may notice an example of a semitone on a six-stringed lyre, between the third and fourth strings, whether ascending or descending. In ascending, its arrangement is shown in the antiphon “Cum audisset populus. Acceperunt ramos” (“When the people heard. They took branches”). In descending, it is shown in the antiphon “Hodie completi sunt dies Pentecostes” (“Today the days of Pentecost were completed”); the same arrangement occurs in the water-organ at the corresponding place. Examples of both tones and semitones should likewise be marked in every chant containing a progression through six strings, the strings taking the place of lines; the place where a semitone occurs should always be noted between the strings.

Wherever, therefore, in any melody you find an interval of this kind, such as the interval here between the syllables *ec* and *ce*, or *ra* and *he*, or *do* and *o*, or *no* and *on*, do not doubt that it is a semitone. Where, however, you find voices differing in the manner of *li* and *ta*, or *lus* and *no*, or *ce* and *ve*, or the final *non* and *est*, it will unquestionably be a tone. Between *re* and *is*, and *he* and *li*, and *quo* and *do*, there is an interval of both semitone and tone. The remaining pairs are said to be equal and direct, as *vere* and *Isra*, and *in quo*.

According to these two qualities, once they have been established in their proper places and order, the entire structure of what follows is distributed in due proportion.

The union of fifteen *phthongi*—that is, notes or pitches—one above another is arranged as follows. If one is to ascend, beginning with the first sound, which is placed outside the series and separated from the next by a tone, one then ascends by a semitone, tone, and tone, up to seven voices. After these, another tone is admitted as a separation, and the upper seven voices proceed throughout in the same manner. In descending, if one begins at the highest point, one proceeds by tone, tone, and semitone through seven voices; after these have been lowered and separated from the following voice by a tone, one arranges the lower seven in the same pattern. The last voice, which in ascending had occupied the first position, is placed outside the series, distinguished from it by a tone. Let the whole series be marked by these signs of points: [Col. 0913].

It is nevertheless no cause for perplexity if, when examining a water-organ or any other musical instrument, you do not find the voices arranged according to this diagram, or if the number of strings appears to exceed the number indicated. This distribution was established according to the arrangement of the most eloquent Boethius, who examines all these matters with careful attention to the commensurable harmony of numbers.

Nor should the instruments in question for that reason be thought alien to any intellectual system, since their long-standing use, handed down through so many generations to wise men, shows them to have been devised and tested by the greatest of intellects. They also contain, without question, the pattern of the arrangement described above. For they are correctly governed throughout by the same two qualities and should be thought to differ from the others only in that they measure their beginnings in a different order: they begin, so to speak, from the third position of that arrangement.

The number of strings or pipes—twenty-one or more—is not supplied because the sounds extend beyond fifteen or perhaps sixteen. Rather, the same sounds that are lower are repeated. This is done for the sake of the variety of the modes, which are now called tones, such as *autentus protus* and the others. Since not all modes can begin from the same lowest places, whichever starting point is chosen must provide a sufficient range for proceeding.

Their arrangement is finally such that one ascends by tone, tone, and semitone, then by three continuous tones and a semitone, through eight voices; beginning again from that eighth voice, the upper series is measured in the same degrees in the following manner. An example is supplied by the offertory “Angelus Domini descendit” (“The angel of the Lord descended”). This place is intended for all the voices placed one above another.

In this arrangement, as also in the preceding one, it must be observed that the upper eight voices are the same as the lower voices, except that the former are, as it were, childish voices, while the latter are, as it were, manly voices. Therefore, after producing the seventh sound, one immediately leaps to the eighth and ninth voice.

Thus the first voice will consonate with the eighth, the second with the ninth, the third with the tenth, and so on in order, each lower voice struck together with its corresponding upper voice, with complete sweetness and harmonious agreement, as though there were one simple sound. This kind of agreement is called the consonance of the diapason.

Boethius divides the upper arrangement into four tetrachords and organizes it in this way: he joins two tetrachords to one another by a single string, and separates them from two further tetrachords similarly joined to each other.

A tetrachord is a union of four strings. We call these strings voices, and likewise use the terms voices and strings interchangeably. The four strings that make up every tetrachord are arranged so that they cling very closely to one another in interval; no other sound can properly be inserted between them. They are separated by a sound, a tone, or a semitone, placed in its appropriate position. No equality of sound is maintained among them; rather, according to the law of ascending, they will all surpass one another in pitch, or else descend from one another in depth.

The arrangement of the remaining tetrachords proceeds according to the model of one. Boethius, beginning with the highest voices and placing them beneath one another in turn, adds at the lowest a single string, as if from outside, in the fifteenth position. Dividing it by tone, tone, and semitone, he arranges it so that the two upper tetrachords, joined to one another by a single voice, are separated by a tone from the other two upper tetrachords, which are likewise joined to one another by a voice.

There will therefore be only fourteen voices. But in order to complete the perfection of the consonances, a fifteenth voice, as stated, is inserted at the lowest part outside the series of the tetrachords. The first four little vocal phrases of the melody of *autentus protus* will show an example of each tetrachord; these will subsequently follow this pattern.

If you wish to begin this same series from within, leaving the first voice outside in the same manner, you proceed through the remaining voices, in the reverse of the upper arrangement, by semitone, tone, and tone, carefully preserving the places of conjunction and separation in the same way. Four examples of the first voices are supplied from the responsory “Redimet Dominus populum suum” (“The Lord will redeem his people”), with the first syllable—or the following syllable in the same phrase, “Et liberabit eos” (“And he will free them”)—placed beneath; these are marked as follows: *Re. Et.* These voices surpass one another in due order through the four tetrachords.

If, however, you wish to gather the tetrachords beginning entirely from the first series, take the example from the invitatory “Christus natus est nobis” (“Christ is born for us”), at the phrase “Venite” (“Come”). You will lead the progression by tone, semitone, and tone up to the seventh voice. There, with the separation of the upper voice already described, you will direct two tetrachords in the same tenor, adding a single voice at the highest according to the following pattern.

If you seek likewise to descend from the highest to the lowest, leaving the highest voice outside, you will produce the descending path by tone, semitone, and tone. An example of this is supplied by the beginning of the neume marked in the sequence “Stans a longe” (“Standing afar”).

With matters standing thus, a certain tetrachord is sometimes inserted in the middle of these, which writers on the art call *sineugmenon* [*synezeugmenon* or *synemmenon*], that is, “joined.”

[Note: *Synezeugmenon* or *synemmenon*, a term that must likewise be noted in what follows.]

Thus there will be five tetrachords. When the water-organ or organ instruments do not admit this arrangement, however, they frequently lack the facility for performing many chants.

[Note: Alternatively, “capacity.”]

The tetrachord is placed after the seventh string of the upper order, so that that seventh is itself the first of this tetrachord. In this arrangement three tetrachords will be joined to one another, and therefore after the eighth voice there will be a semitone where, in the upper series, a tone would have been added. The three are arranged as follows.

If this tetrachord is not inserted, the tetrachord that is placed third in the upper arrangements after the seventh voice is called *diezeugmenon*, that is, “separated.” In the various modes of different chants you will find them proceeding now in one melody, now in another: sometimes one of them completes the melody by itself, sometimes the melody turns back and forth from one to the other.

For example, when the *synemmenon* is present here, the melody may descend back into it. The responsory “Nativitas gloriosae Virginis Mariae” (“The Nativity of the glorious Virgin Mary”) provides an example: up to the phrase “ex stirpe” (“from the stock”) it proceeds entirely through the *diezeugmenon*. But at the third point of the syllable *pe*, which is marked as follows—

[Note: The marks are found in the manuscript.]

—it descends into the lower *synemmenon*. The entire neume on the name “David” is sung through the *synemmenon*.

Likewise, in the introit “Statuit ei Dominus” (“The Lord established for him”), the second point on the syllable *sta*, which is five positions distant from the first point, is joined upward at the third point through the *synemmenon*. There is a semitone between the second and third points.

When the syllable *Do* rises in the *diezeugmenon*, the syllable *mi* again descends into the *synemmenon*. Likewise, *tes* and *fe* belong to the *synemmenon*, while *fa* belongs to the *diezeugmenon*; again *mi* alternately claims its place in the *synemmenon*.

Although examples of this tetrachord frequently occur in all the modes or tones, they are especially apparent everywhere in *autentus tritus* and its plagal modes. It is scarcely possible to find a melody in them without a mixture of these tetrachords, namely the *synemmenon* and the *diezeugmenon*. Anyone attentive will be able to observe this in the melody of *autentus tritus*, which is marked as follows:

“NO EANE”—*synemmenon*; *diezeugmenon*.

Likewise, in the antiphon “Ecce jam venit” (“Behold, now comes”):

*diezeugmenon*: “plenitudo” (“fullness”);  
*synemmenon*: “R. Paganorum multitudo” (“R. A multitude of pagans”).

Here, only at the beginning, up to the syllable *tu*, does the *diezeugmenon* enter; the rest, to the end, is governed by turns through the *synemmenon*.

These, then, are the five tetrachords. To each they assigned its own technical name. The first, which is also the lowest or deepest, they called *hypaton*; the second, *meson*; the third, *synemmenon*; the fourth, *diezeugmenon*; and the fifth, *hyperbolaeon*.

[Note: I. *Hypaton*: C D E. II. *Meson*: E F G a. III. *Synemmenon*: a b c d. IV. *Diezeugmenon*: c d e. V. *Hyperbolaeon*: e f g a [a].]

The first takes its name from the principal string of the tetrachord itself, which is called *hypate*; the second from *mese*, the middle string of the whole series; the third, fourth, and fifth derive their names from the meaning of the terms. For *synemmenon* means “of joined strings,” *diezeugmenon* means “of separated strings,” and *hyperbolaeon* means “of higher or surpassing strings.”

To make the complete series of these names easier to understand, the names of all the strings must now be set out in order. Their sounds are certainly shown to return exactly to the points already distinctly placed in the preceding arrangements. The first order, which proceeds by semitone, tone, and tone, will be specifically fitted to this arrangement. For Boethius sets out their ordered melody in this manner.

These, then, are the names of the fifteen sounds, excluding the *synemmenon* tetrachord. When that is counted, the total becomes eighteen.

[Note: At this point the manuscript continues with the customary table of all eight differences, using the familiar vowels of “saeculorum amen” (“of the ages, amen”), preceded by the beginning of each antiphon or responsory. We omit this table, since, owing to the lack of musical signs, it would otherwise be of no use.]

Each authentic tone ascends from its final up to the ninth sound. It descends to the sound next to it, and sometimes to the semitone or to the third. A plagal tone descends as far as the fourth and ascends as far as the fifth.

If the *synemmenon* tetrachord is inserted, its place being between *mese* and *paramese*, the following three will be placed after *mese* in this order:

*Mese. Trite synemmenon. Paranete synemmenon. Nete synemmenon.*

Among these, only one—*trite synemmenon*—has a sound different from those above. For *paranete synemmenon* will sound with the same voice as *trite diezeugmenon*; they differ only in name. They are nevertheless assigned different names because, whenever a melody is composed so that after *mese* a semitone is followed upward by a tone and a tone, and the return to *mese* is made by tone, tone, and semitone, it is necessary to say that the passage proceeds through the tetrachord called *synemmenon*, that is, “joined,” because it is joined to *mese* by a semitone.

Whenever, on the other hand, after *mese* the tetrachord proceeds by a tone’s interval of separation from *paramese* up to *nete diezeugmenon*, that tetrachord must be called by another name, namely *diezeugmenon*, “separated,” because the distance between *mese* and *paramese* is a tone.

Beginning from the upper end, one tetrachord extends from *nete hyperbolaeon* to *nete diezeugmenon*. Another extends from *nete diezeugmenon* itself to *paramese*. These two are joined to each other, because *nete diezeugmenon*, the last and lowest note of the upper tetrachord, is at the same time the first and highest note of the lower one and binds the two together.

Each consists of tone, tone, and semitone, in the following order:

| Sound | Name | Interval |
|---|---|---|
| a or d | *Nete hyperbolaeon* | Tone |
| g or c | *Paranete hyperbolaeon* | Tone |
| f or [uncertain] | *Trite hyperbolaeon* | Semitone |
| e or a | *Nete diezeugmenon* | Common to both |
| d or g | *Paranete diezeugmenon* | Tone |
| c or f | *Trite diezeugmenon* | Tone |
| [uncertain] or e | *Paramese* | Semitone |

The two lower tetrachords, separated from these, are likewise divided by the same intervals of tones and semitones. One, the third, extends from *mese* to *hypate meson*; the other, the fourth, extends again from *hypate meson* to *hypate hypaton*. These are joined to one another as follows:

| Sound | Name | Interval |
|---|---|---|
|  | *Mese* | Tone |
| f | *Lichanos meson* | Tone |
| e | *Parypate meson* | Semitone |
| d | *Lichanos hypaton* | Tone |
| c | [uncertain in the source: *hypaton*; perhaps *hypate meson*] | Common to both / tone |
|  | *Parypate hypaton* | Semitone |
| a | *Hypate hypaton* | Tone |

There remains *proslambanomenos*, which Boethius declares to have been added in accordance with the ratio of the double-octave consonance.

If we wish to have three joined tetrachords, the *synemmenon* is placed between *mese* and *paramese*, as was discussed at length above. The sounds of these same strings have already been distributed sufficiently above, where we gave the example of the first four voices from the melody of *autentus protus*, namely: “No. Ne. no. y.”

Boethius gives a brief interpretation of these names, while Martianus explains them more fully.

*Proslambanomenos*: “acquired,” because this string was added after all the others.

*Hypate*: “low” or “principal.”

*Parypate hypaton*: [the name is incomplete in the text.]

[Note: There appears to be a lacuna; it may perhaps be supplemented as “*Parypate*, next to *hypate*, or the principal [string].”]

*Lichanos*: because in Greek this is the name of the index finger. On a lyre, if you touch the first string, *proslambanomenos*, with the little finger, the index finger comes to that string; for this reason it too acquired the name *lichanos*.

*Mese* means “middle.” It is placed in the middle of the entire order and is the eighth string of both regions.

*Paramese*: “next to *mese*.”

*Trite*: “third,” either from *mese* or from *nete.”

*Nete*: “high” or “sharp.”

*Paranete*: “next to *nete*.”

At first there were only eight strings with these names: *hypate, parypate, lichanos, mese, paramese, trite, paranete,* and *nete*. Later, as the number of strings increased, the names of the strings mentioned above were substituted. Anyone wishing to know more fully about their invention or addition may be carefully instructed by the first book of Boethius on harmonic theory.

Now let the discussion turn to the musical signs assigned to each of the strings, which provide no small benefit to students of melody. These signs were discovered for the following purpose: just as the voices and divisions of words are recognized in writing through letters, so that they do not mislead the reader’s judgment, so every melody that has been marked with these signs can, once they have been learned, be sung even without a teacher.

The signs now handed down by use, although they are useful for certain purposes and are nevertheless deformed into different shapes according to the variety of places, cannot provide sufficient assistance for accurate recall. For they always lead the person who sees them along an uncertain path, as is evident if you consider the following pattern:

“AEVIA.”

When you look at the first sign, which appears to be higher, you can easily produce it at whatever pitch of the voice you choose. But when you wish to join to it the second sign, which you observe to be lower, you cannot possibly know how to do so—whether it ought to be separated from the first by one, two, or perhaps three points—unless you learn it by hearing it from someone else. You cannot discover that it was fixed in this way by the composer. The same is true of the remaining signs.

If, however, you see the same pattern written with the string-signs that will be described below, you will immediately understand without doubt how it proceeds, as follows:

“Alle [IM] lu [pm] ia [cf].”

Here *I* is *mese*, and *M* is *lichanos meson*: between them lies the interval of a tone. *p* is *parypate meson*, which is likewise a tone distant from *lichanos meson*. *m* is likewise *lichanos meson*, sloping down above *parypate meson*. *C* is *hypate meson*, a semitone distant from *parypate meson*. *f*, the final sign, preserves *lichanos hypaton*, a tone from *hypate meson*.

In this familiar melody of *autentus protus*, above which we write the corresponding signs, it will become clearer which are the higher tones:

“No [Im] Ne [m] NO [p] e [im] A [pc] NE [f].”

Whatever sign or letter from among these you see in the preceding formula, do not hesitate to produce it in the same way.

These customary signs are not entirely unnecessary. They are indeed considered highly useful for indicating the slowness of a chant, where a sound contains a trembling voice, how sounds are joined together or distinguished from one another, and where they are closed below or above according to the arrangement of certain letters. The artificial signs cannot show any of these things at all.

Therefore, if the same little letters that we regard as musical signs are placed above or around these signs for each *phthongus*, it will be possible to discern the exact truth perfectly and without error. The former signs indicate how much higher or lower each voice is carried; the latter fix more securely in the mind the variations mentioned above, without which a proper chant cannot be constructed.

There are therefore many string-signs that have been used from great antiquity. Boethius assigns two of them to each string in each of the eight modes, producing 288 signs. Expressed also in some cases by straight Greek letters and in others by letters variously altered, they appear to occupy a very large amount of space on the page. For the present we adopt only those belonging to the Lydian mode, some placed above and some below. We have set them out as compactly as possible, since they can be attached more briefly and concisely, and we think them sufficient for present use.

Having brought the discussion this far, so that everything from the beginning may now be surveyed, it must henceforth be explained more clearly what is produced by these matters and what fruit arises from the scattered seeds.

Once the intervals of the voices have first been arranged by the distinction of points, then by the names of the strings themselves, and finally by the signs of those strings, the way in which these elements are combined with one another and proceed into different modes must now be disclosed.

Four of the first strings—namely, *lichanos hypaton, hypate meson, parypate meson,* and *lichanos meson*—are adapted to the four modes or tropes now called tones: *protus, deuterus, tritus,* and *tetrardus*. Each of these four strings governs two modes subject to it: the principal mode, called authentic, and the lateral mode, called plagal.

Thus *lichanos hypaton* governs *autentus protus* and its plagal mode, that is, the first and second tones; *hypate meson* governs *autentus deuterus* and its plagal mode, that is, the third and fourth; *parypate meson* governs *autentus tritus* and its plagal mode, that is, the fifth and sixth; and *lichanos meson* governs *autentus tetrardus* and its plagal mode, that is, the seventh and eighth.

Consequently, however variously any melody may turn above or below any one of these four strings, every chant whatsoever must necessarily be brought back to one of them. Hence they are called finals, because everything that is sung receives its ending in them.

We mark them with the signs placed here:

In the lower register: c m p c f.  
Likewise in the higher register: f c p m.

The remaining tetrachords, one of which rises below and three above, likewise derive their intervals and the qualities of their sounds from the same model. The addition of the examples above has shown all this sufficiently.

Nothing need be made of the fact that, when the *synemmenon* tetrachord is removed, the fifth positions are always joined to these four upper positions by a kind of connecting union. Indeed, many melodies appear to end in them as though according to a regular rule, and for that reason they neither contradict reason or hearing nor fail to proceed correctly within the same mode or trope.

This association therefore joins *lichanos hypaton* with *mese*; *hypate meson* with *paramese*; and *parypate meson* with *trite diezeugmenon*. Each pair is separated from the other by five positions.

*Lichanos meson* and *paranete diezeugmenon*, together with the lower fourth positions and in some cases the fifth positions, have an equivalent relation of a kind, although they are assigned not to endings but to beginnings. The following are the limits to which they descend when a melody begins: *proslambanomenos* to *lichanos hypaton*; *hypate hypaton* to *hypate meson*, though rarely; *parypate hypaton* to *parypate meson*; and *lichanos hypaton* to *lichanos meson*. In the last case the descent sometimes reaches as far as *parypate hypaton*, that is, the fifth position; in the others, only very rarely.

No tone whatsoever will ever have the power to begin from its final above the fifth upper position or below the fifth lower position. Rather, within these nine voices—or sometimes eight—the principal and lateral modes will contain their endings or beginnings.

Let this be explained through examples for each tone. In *autentus protus* and its plagal mode, the following eight positions are assigned; from them you will see in this order how melodies may begin.

In this mode alone the melody turns as far as the ninth position from the first upper position, and from the final, *lichanos meson*, it extends into the fifth *phthongus* in either direction. In this mode alone it reaches as far as “Spiritus Domini replevit” (“The Spirit of the Lord has filled”).

In the first diapason:

- E contains the whole of F and its octave, that is, the ratio 9:8.
- D contains the whole of E and its octave, that is, the *epogdous*.
- C contains the whole of F and its third, which is *sesquitertia* or *epitrita*, that is, a diatessaron.
- B contains the whole of C and its octave, which is a tone; or the whole of E and its third, which is a diatessaron; or the whole of F and its half, which is a diapente.
- A contains the whole of B and its octave, that is, a tone; or the whole of D and its third, which is a diatessaron; or the whole of E and its half, which is a diapente.
- G contains the whole of E and its third, which is a diatessaron.

G, which is *trite synemmenon*, contains the whole of D in the first diapason and its half, which is a diapente.

In the second diapason:

- F contains the whole of G and its octave, which is a tone; or the whole of B and its third, which is a diatessaron; or the whole of C and its half, which is a diapente; or another F doubled, which is a diapason.
- E contains the whole of F and its octave, that is, a tone; or the whole of A and its third, which is a diatessaron; or the whole of B and its half, which is a diapente; or another E doubled, which is a diapason.
- D contains the whole of E and its octave, that is, a tone; or the whole of A and its half, which is a diapente; or another D doubled, which is a diapason.
- C contains the whole of F and its third, which is a diatessaron; or the whole of G and its half, which is a diapente; or another C doubled, which is a diapason; or the first F doubled and two-thirds of it, which is a diapason together with a diatessaron.
- B contains the whole of C and its octave, that is, a tone; or the whole of E and its third, that is, a diatessaron; or the whole of F and its half, that is, a diapente; or another B doubled, that is, a diapason; or another F tripled, that is, a diapason together with a diapente.
- A contains the whole of B and its octave, which is a tone; or the whole of D and its third, which is a diatessaron; or the whole of C and its half, which is a diapente; or another A doubled, that is, a diapason.
- G contains the whole of C and its third, that is, a diatessaron; or another G doubled, that is, a diapason.
- F contains the whole of G and its octave, that is, a tone; or the whole of B and its third, that is, a diatessaron; or the whole of C and its half, that is, a diapente; or another F doubled, that is, a diapason; or a third F quadrupled, that is, a double diapason.

## Rapid and true division of the monochord in the diatonic genus

Half of *proslambanomenos* is *mese*. Half of this is *nete hyperbolaeon*, to which one-third of itself is added to obtain *nete diezeugmenon*. Likewise, half of *nete hyperbolaeon* is added to it to obtain *paranete diezeugmenon*, from which one-quarter is subtracted to obtain *paranete hyperbolaeon*. Half of this is added to obtain *trite diezeugmenon*. One-quarter of this is subtracted to obtain *trite hyperbolaeon*. One-third of *nete diezeugmenon* is added to it to obtain *paramese*.

You now have eight divisions. Give each of them its diapason, that is, up to *proslambanomenos*, and you have fifteen sounds established within these diapasons.

The first species of the diatessaron consists of tone, semitone, tone. The second consists of two tones and a semitone. The third consists of a semitone and two tones. The fourth consists of the first species of diatessaron with a tone added below.

The first species of diapente consists of the first species of diatessaron with a tone added above. The second consists of the second diatessaron with a tone added above. The third consists of the third diatessaron with a tone added below.

*Protus* consists of the first species of diapente and the first species of diatessaron above. Its subordinate or plagal mode consists of the same diapente and the same species of diatessaron below.

*Tritus* consists of the third species of diapente and the third species of diatessaron above. Its subordinate mode consists of the same species of diapente and the same species of diatessaron below.

*Tetrardus* consists of the fourth species of diapente and the first species of diatessaron above. Its subordinate mode consists of the same diapente and the same diatessaron below.

If the second contains the whole of the first and one-eighth of it, it will be separated from it by a tone. If the second contains one-third and one-fourteenth of the first, the two produce the consonance of a tone. If the fourth contains one-third, one-eighth, and one-eighth of that eighth, it produces the consonance of a semitone. If the fourth contains the fifth and one-fifth of it, and one-fifth of the fifth, it will be a diapente in relation to the first. If the seventh resounds with the sixth and one-seventh of itself, it produces the semitone called *synemmenon*.

## Measurement of the monochord

First, I judge that the entire monochord should be divided lengthwise by four lines. The first, together with its interval, is to be assigned to the diatonic genus; the second to the chromatic; the third to the enharmonic. These three genera are constituted by different measurements in the arrangement of the monochord.

But so that the measure of the others may more easily be determined, the measurement of the diatonic genus should first be written down. Through its regular division we shall then be better able to establish the proportions of the others artificially.

First divide it into four equal parts. In the first, write the final letter F, *proslambanomenos*, with the number 9,216. In the second, B, *lichanos hypaton*, 6,412. In the third, F, *mese*, 4,108. In the fourth, F, *nete hyperbolaeon*, 2,304.

From this F, that is, *nete hyperbolaeon*, draw a line into the chromatic and enharmonic genera, and establish F in both of them as in the diatonic. Divide the part assigned to F, *nete hyperbolaeon*, into eight, and take a ninth part inward. Mark E, which is *paranete hyperbolaeon*, with the number 2,492.

Again, from E, *paranete hyperbolaeon*, take an eighth part up to the end, with a ninth part measured inward. Assign D, which is *trite hyperbolaeon*, the number 2,416.

Between E, that is, *paranete hyperbolaeon*, and D, *trite hyperbolaeon*, draw the line of the chromatic genus in the upper division. In the chromatic genus, the interval between E and F is a tone, and that between D and E is a semitone. Whereas in the diatonic genus there are two complete tones, between D and E and between E and F, in the enharmonic genus there is a complete tone between E and F.

Again, in the diatonic genus, taking three parts from F, *nete hyperbolaeon*, toward the end, the fourth inward gives C, that is, *nete diezeugmenon*, with the number 3,072. Lines are then drawn to D, E, and C in the diatonic genus; to C and D in the enharmonic; and to C, D, and E in the chromatic.

Thus what is a semitone between C and D in the diatonic genus is likewise a semitone in the corresponding upper part of the chromatic genus between C and D. In the enharmonic genus that same semitone is divided between C and D.

Again, in the diatonic genus, measuring three parts from *paranete hyperbolaeon* [E] to the end, the fourth interval in the lower part gives B, that is, *nete synemmenon* and *paranete diezeugmenon*, with the number 3,456.

Again, in the diatonic genus, taking three parts from *trite hyperbolaeon* [D] to the end, the fourth lower part gives A, that is, *paranete synemmenon* and *trite diezeugmenon*.

Between these—that is, between A and D—divide the diatonic line in the upper chromatic division. There the interval between A and B is a semitone, and that between B and C is a tone.

In the enharmonic genus, since there is a tone between B and C, draw the line that divides the whole interval from A in the diatonic genus into the enharmonic genus.

Again, measuring three parts from *nete diezeugmenon* to the end, the fourth gives G, that is, *paramese*, with the number 4,096. From this point—that is, from the diatonic *paramese*—draw the line into the enharmonic genus.

In the diatonic genus, the interval between G and A is a semitone; the same is true between G and A in the chromatic genus, although in the enharmonic genus this semitone is divided. Thus between G, A, B, and C the pattern appears to be semitone, tone, tone; while in the chromatic genus it is, conversely, semitone, semitone, tone. Likewise, in the enharmonic genus, between G, A, B, and C, it is semitone, semitone, tone.

Again, from paranete [A] synemmenon, with Trite diezeugmenon VIII units given, the ninth will be lower at the extremity. G, that is, trite synemmenon, with IIIJ CCCLXXIIII, from which a line is drawn into the chromatic genus; and the chromatic G is marked in like manner. When these have been taken in this order, two of the other parts that we placed at the beginning have been wholly used up. We shall describe the order of the following parts by the ratio of this single measure. Where, in the division of four parts, we ordered mese to be placed with IIIJ d. CVIII, there let the order of the two parts begin afterward—but in such a way that what is established as the single measure in the smaller division should appear as the double measure in the generation of the following one. For example, the interval that is reduced to the single measure between nete hyperbolaeon and paranete hyperbolaeon is doubled between mese and lichanos meson. [E] Lichanos meson, with [F] V CLXXXIIIJ in number, is a complete tone from mese. Thus, by the necessary consequence of this order, the same conclusion will inevitably prove true in the remaining cases.

Nor is this doubled only in the diatonic genus; it is also doubled through the same letters, though not in the same position, in the chromatic and enharmonic genera. Therefore, since it would be tedious to treat again in sufficient detail each of the matters already discussed, the names alone of the preceding tones, together with the numbers of the remaining tones that are to be doubled with them, shall be set down, with the explanatory reasoning omitted. After lichanos meson D, [E] which is parypate meson, with the number V. d. CCCXXXII, comes hypate meson, with VI. CXLIII. After it comes lichanos hypaton B, with the number already mentioned. This is followed by A, parypate hypaton, with the number VII. d. CCLXXVI. Behind it comes G, hypate hypaton, with VIII. CXCII. After that, at the very beginning of the monochord, F, proslambanomenos, is assigned the number stated above. This ratio is to be preserved in all three genera: whatever is treated as the single measure in the higher strings must always be doubled at the appropriate place in the lower strings. When these arrangements have been made, if the measurer is careful, the measure will never deceive him.

The third [tropus] begins with a diatessaron that has a semitone at its end: [Note: [Col. 0927] Here the beginning is missing, concerning the first tone; some matters are explained on the following page.] it is harsher, though gentler in the middle; for this mode scarcely proceeds through the synemmenon. The second mode has two tetrachords, meson and hypaton. Its proper divisions are parypate hypaton and lichanos hypaton; sometimes mese and lichanos mese are treated as proper, and occasionally parypate meson as well. It never proceeds through the synemmena.

The third mode has three tetrachords: paramese, mese, and hypaton. It has six, or rather five, divisions, from trite diezeugmenon down to hypate meson—namely, trite diezeugmenon, paramese, mese, lichanos meson, and hypate meson. Of these, only mese and lichanos meson are certain; this mode legitimately proceeds through the synemmena.

The fourth has two tetrachords, meson and hypaton. It has five divisions: lichanos hypaton, hypate meson, lichanos meson, and parypate meson; frequently it extends as far as parypate hypaton, up to paramese, or trite diezeugmenon and paranete diezeugmenon. This mode too legitimately proceeds through the synemmena.

The fifth mode has three tetrachords, hypate meson and, frequently, hyperbolaeon. It has six divisions, of which the more certain are trite diezeugmenon and paranete diezeugmenon; the others are unstable, from paranete diezeugmenon down to parypate meson. The remaining notes proceed through the enharmonic divisions; this mode also legitimately proceeds through the synemmena.

The sixth has five tetrachords, hypaton and meson, retaining one most firmly established division, namely parypate hypaton, and three others of less firmness: lichanos meson, lichanos hypaton, and hypate hypaton. It legitimately passes through the synemmena.

The seventh mode has three tetrachords: diezeugmenon, meson, and synemmenon. It has five divisions: hyperbolaeon, paranete hyperbolaeon, nete diezeugmenon, trite diezeugmenon, mese, and lichanos mese. The synemmena are rarely allowed to this mode.

The eighth has four tetrachords: hypaton, meson, diezeugmenon, and hyperbolaeon. It has three divisions: meson, perfect lichanos hypaton, and rare and imperfect parypate meson. Care must be taken that the diapente is not rendered from the diatessaron toward the lower part and toward the higher part [the text appears corrupt here]. Every species of diapente or diatessaron is performed either continuously or discontinuously, with the melody raised or lowered.

In the first whole he says [Note: [Col. 0929] Note the expositor; but the matters that he expounds concerning the first whole, as we said, are missing.] that there are three tetrachords, of which the one beginning toward the lower part from paramese exceeds the diatessaron consonance, since three tones follow one another continuously there. Again, as he says, in this same mode there are five divisions in themselves, because the melody is divided in the same manner as a sentence: for the course of the human breath, moving through cola and commata, comes to rest. But the body of a melody is completed by arsis and thesis—that is, by the raising of the tones and their settling—until it ends in a period, that is, a clause or circuit distinguished by its members.

For example, “Alleluia, which is ‘The just man shall sprout like the lily’,” has a division at lichanos hypaton; “And he shall flower forever” has a similar one. Concerning the consonances, and how there are eight in this mode, let whoever has the capacity for understanding examine the matter.

## ANOTHER MUSICAL TREATISE

Boethius discussed harmonic consideration as follows: proportion is not found in the terms alone, nor in the differences alone, but commonly in both.
