He asks that, just as the extreme terms stand in relation to one another, so the difference of the greater term from the middle should contain the difference of the middle from the last term. You will also frequently find the proportions of the musical consonances, which they call symphonies, in almost this single kind of mean. For the diatessaron symphony, which is the first and in a certain way possesses the force of an element, is found in means of this harmonic kind. Thus, let the terms of such a mean be VI and VIII, whose extremes are in double proportion; and let there be others whose extremes are in triple proportion:

| VI | VIII | XII |
|---|---|---|
| IIII | VI | XII |

The duodenary is therefore double the senary; and in the other arrangement XII is triple IIII. If we collect their differences and compare them with one another, the epitrite proportion—that is, the diatessaron symphony—is obtained. For the difference between VI and XII is six, while that between IIII and XII is eight, since eight makes a sesquitertian proportion with six.

In the same mean the diapente symphony is also formed. In the double arrangement, XII to VIII, and in the triple arrangement, VI to IIII, are sesquialteral. After this comes the diapason consonance, as VI to XII. In the triple arrangement the diapente and diapason symphonies are combined together, as in VI, VIIII, XVIII. Since the triple contains two consonances, namely diapente and diapason, we shall find the same triple relation in its differences. For the difference between VI and VIIII is ternary, and that between VIIII and XVIII is novenary, which is triple the ternary.

In the double arrangement, the greater term is triple the difference between the middle terms taken in relation to one another. Again, the lesser term is triple the difference between itself and the middle term. For the difference between VIII and XII is quaternary, which is triple in relation to the same duodenary; and the difference between VI and VIII is binary, which again is triple in relation to the same senary.

That greatest symphony, which is called bisdiapason, as though twice double, is derived from a double proportion. For the middle term is found to be quadruple the difference between the lesser term and itself, as the difference between VI and VIII is binary, which is quadruple in relation to the same octonary. In triple extremes, likewise, the greater difference is quadruple the lesser difference. For the difference between VI and XVIII is duodenary, the difference of the extremes; and the difference between IIII and VI is ternary, which is quadruple in relation to the duodenary.

In the double arrangement also, in which the middle term sounds a diatessaron against the lesser and a diapente against the greater, if the extremes are brought together and multiplied by the mean, the result will be double the number produced by multiplying the extremes alone, as in VI, VIII, XII. The joined extremes, VI and XII, produce X. VIII, which, multiplied by octonary, increases to CXLIIII. Half of this total is LXXII, which is produced by multiplying VI and XII by one another.

This arrangement also has the following property: the middle term exceeds the lesser by one part of itself and is exceeded by the greater by another part; and it surpasses the lesser by the same part by which it is surpassed by the greater. But if the double arrangement is such that the middle term sounds a diapente against the lesser and a diatessaron against the greater, as in VI, VIIII, XII, then, since the differences are the same but the proportions are not, it should be called an arithmetical rather than a harmonic mean.

For that is truly a harmonic mean which is obtained by the determination of a cube. Every cube has twelve edges, eight angles, and six surfaces, arranged thus:

| VI | VIII | XII |
|---|---|---|

Having prefaced these matters, let us come to the arrangement of the eight tropes, which the Latins call modes. First it must be understood that *tropus* is called a conversion from Greek into Latin, because, apart from its own property, one is converted into another. Tones are so called because, with the exception of the semitones, they themselves are the common measure of all the tropes. They are also called modes because each trope retains its own mode and does not exceed its measure. Once a single constitution has been made, woven together from doubles, triples, quadruples, sesquialters, and sesquitertians, with the voices of fifteen strings interposed, these eight tropes or modes must necessarily be distinguished.

The first mode, therefore, the gravest of all, is the hypodorian, formed from the first species of diapason and ending at the string called mese, the middle string. The second mode, hypophrygian, is formed by the second species of diapason, which ends at paramese. The third mode, hypolydian, is determined by the third species of diapason, ending at the string called trite diezeugmenon. The fourth mode, Dorian, is produced by the fourth species of diapason, which ends at paranete diezeugmenon. The fifth mode, Phrygian, ends with the fifth species of diapason, whose last string is nete diezeugmenon. The sixth mode, Lydian, is likewise brought forth by the sixth species of diapason, whose end is trite hyperbolaeon. The seventh mode, mixolydian, is shaped by the seventh species of diapason; paranete hyperbolaeon determines it.

But because one double—that is, one diapason possessing eight voices—does not admit more species, since every symphony admits one voice and several species, Ptolemy added the eighth mode, hypermixolydian, which he formed from the properties of the second and third modes. For a diatessaron consists of IIII strings and three species; a diapente of V strings and four species. Therefore a diapason consists of VIII strings and seven species.

Finally, the first species of diatessaron has its semitone in the third place, the second species in the second place, and the third species in the first place. Whether through a disjunct or conjunct tetrachord, the same species always returns in the fourth places at the fifth places; yet diapentes do not always follow one another in succession. Hence it is clear that the three species of diatessaron constitute the first three species of diapente when one tone is added. The fourth species ends with a semitone, and the first begins from nete diezeugmenon.

It remains to investigate the properties of the species of diapason. The first species therefore uses the semitone in the third and sixth places; the second in the fourth and seventh; the third in the first and fifth; the fourth in the second and sixth; the fifth in the third and seventh; the sixth in the first and fourth; the seventh in the second and fifth; and the eighth, like the first, in the third and sixth.

But, to return to the species of diapason themselves: since lichanos hypaton belongs to the hypodorian, while proslambanomenos and mese belong to the Dorian, and since mese—which is paranete diezeugmenon of the hypodorian—is a complete diatessaron consonance higher than the mese of that same hypodorian, there is likewise a difference between Phrygian and hypophrygian, and between Lydian and hypolydian. For mixolydian differs from hypermixolydian by only one tone.

Now something must be said about the cubic numbers that suggest harmonic consideration and show how the aforesaid eight species of the modes differ. First, however, it should be stated that the diatessaron is measured in the harmonic rule by VII, that is, by III and IIII, while the diapente is measured by V, that is, by II and III. For we recognize both greater numbers from lesser numbers and lesser numbers from greater numbers in the same proportion.

This is what Boethius says in Book 2, chapter 9: if the difference of two numbers has been measured exactly, the numbers measured by that difference are in the same proportion in which are the numbers according to which their difference has been measured. Thus, between VI and VIII there is a binary difference, which measures the senary three times and the octonary four times. Likewise, between VIIII and XII there is a ternary difference, which measures the novenary three times and the duodenary four times.

Thus, however great the numbers may be, whenever a sesquitertian proportion occurs, the ternary and quaternary do not abandon it, since they are the first numbers and, as it were, the roots of the sesquitertian proportion. In the same way, in a sesquialteral proportion, the difference between VI and VIIII is ternary, which measures the senary twice and the novenary three times.

All these matters become clearer in the harmonic rule with a compass, since by that instrument every double is divided into equal parts. Given any numbers for producing a double, the middle is always found, separated from both extremes by equal differences. Thus, between II and IIII is III, which differs from each extreme by one unit. Between IIII and VIII, VI is likewise the middle; between VI and XII, VIIII; and between XII and XXIIII, XVIII. Each of the two doubles differs from the middle, the one by ternary and the other by senary.

The numbers mentioned are in some way incommensurable with one another, because novenary rejects the binary by which VI, VIII, and XII are measured, while, conversely, octonary does not admit the ternary by which VI, VIIII, and XII are measured. Quaternary is the common measure of octonary and duodenary; and for this reason, according to some, the triple of the hypodorian begins from quaternary and ends at duodenary.

Thus the melody of the first mode, which is NONANOEANE, appears to be enclosed by VIII and XII. But to the same clausula, which consists of a diapente, some add a tone, so that the first species of diatessaron may first sound in the same melody, then the second, and afterward the third may be raised; finally, in order, the first species of diapente may be lowered from VIII to XII.

Here begins the melody of the second mode, which is NOEAGIS, and it reaches not VIII but VIIII, as do all the songs of this same mode. For they are closed by two diatessaron consonances. For the remainder, the senary, which is single in the Dorian, is tripled in the hypodorian and Phrygian; it is quadrupled in the Phrygian and Lydian. Where the senary is tripled in relation to the Dorian, the octonary is found twice in relation to the same. Again, where the senary is quadrupled, the octonary is repeated threefold.

Finally, the novenary, which is single in the Dorian, is double in the others, except in the Lydian, which rejoices in its quadrupling and in the tripling of the duodenary. In opposition to this repetition of the hypolydian, the senary answers sixfold, the octonary threefold, and the novenary fourfold. Mixolydian repeats the duodenary and novenary once, in a single progression, and strives to triple the senary and octonary. In another progression it triples the duodenary and octonary, quadruples the senary and novenary, and in its own consonance presents the duodenary four times, the senary eight times, and the octonary six times.

Finally, hypermixolydian, in one series, repeats the duodenary and novenary once and presents the senary and octonary tripled. In another series it triples the duodenary and octonary and quadruples the senary and novenary.

Finally, it must be understood that, after the symphonies proposed at the musician’s discretion—diapason, diapente, and diatessaron—one tone is sometimes added toward the lower or higher part. This is called *emmeles* (ἐμμελής), that is, suitable to the melody.

In that constitution in which we say that fifteen strings are arranged proportionally—diapason, that is, twice six, or twice VIII, or twice XII—[Note: [Col. 0933D] Something is missing here, so that the sense may be completed.]

Let us finally come to an exposition by someone concerning the tropes or modes mentioned above, so that, with God’s help, we may shed some light upon that exposition.

“Every first tone,” he says, “which we call Dorian, will have either three times six in a double proportion, that is, a diapason—as in ‘Drop dew, you heavens, from above’—or four times V, which is XX, that is, II of VIII and III of XII, producing a diapente in a sesquialteral proportion—as in ‘And let the clouds rain the Just One; let it be opened’—or three times VII, which is XXI, that is, III of VIIII in relation to IIII of XII, which produce a diatessaron in a sesquitertian proportion—as in ‘earth, and let it bring forth the Savior.’”

We explain this gradual antiphon, assigning each symphony to each incision, as follows. Between VI and XII, which together make XVIII, the senary is the difference, because the melody of the first incision proceeds upward through the whole range, namely from lichanos hypaton to paranete diezeugmenon, with a tone first added toward the lower part, which is called *emmeles*, that is, suitable to the melody. Finally, the ternary divides this same difference equally, and thus, from the senary to the novenary, the diapente is completed.

Since this symphony consists of a diatessaron and a tone, it proceeds through the second incision of the antiphon as a whole, so that there are II of VIII and III of XII, because the octonary exceeds the senary by binary, and therefore a sesquitertian proportion can exist. The novenary, however, surpasses the senary by ternary, which is half of that same senary and therefore the fourth part of the duodenary. Thus III of VIIII is equal to IIII of XII, since the former is a third part of the latter’s number and the latter a fourth; and in this way a diatessaron consonance is produced, which closes from the novenary into the duodenary. The third little incision of the antiphon follows.

Those gradual antiphons proceed in the same way: “Rejoice in the Lord,” “And incline, Lord,” and “You are just, Lord.” Likewise the nocturnal antiphons: “They placed upon the head,” “But Jesus, when he had fasted,” and “But the betrayer.”

It must also be observed that it often happens that twice, or three times, or even the whole of an antiphon, or of any chant, belongs to the first tone: either it proceeds through VI and XII, which is a diapason; or through V and X, which is a diapente; or entirely through VI and VIII, which is a diatessaron. This is what he says: “It concerns a double diapente.” [Note: [Col. 0933] Read: “What he says, ‘through V and X,’ refers to a double diapente.]

For when any two numbers compared with one another in a sesquialteral ratio have one term—the lesser—never lacking a half, it is certain that the lesser is divided into two equal parts, by one of which it is exceeded by the greater. Hence, just as the lesser is always divided by binary, so the greater is divided by ternary. This is what he means by saying that the diapente is made through five and ten, because II and III produce V, and, when doubled, X. For IIII and VI complete X.

He also commands every sesquitertian proportion to be divided through VII, which consists of III and IIII, because in any two numbers of the same proportion one term—the lesser—is distributed into III equal parts, while the other—the greater—is distributed into IIII. Hence, since the whole consonance of the hypophrygian is said to be explained by a diatessaron, it is believed to have been measured through the septenary.

In the hypodorian or Lydian there is a measurement by the denary. The Dorian, however, proceeds from XII to VI through a diapason in the Alleluia, ‘The just shall shine.’ The same Alleluia, ‘The just shall shine, and, like sparks in a reed-bed, they shall run forever,’ proceeds by diapente from XII to VIII, and from VIII—or rather from VIIII—to VI. Nor is the gradual responsory belonging to this mode absent, namely ‘You have placed, Lord.’”

## ANOTHER NEW EXPOSITION BY SOMEONE ON THE SAME SUBJECT

The first mode begins from the first species of diapason, which is mese, that is, O; and it ends in the lowered diapente, which is E. This is the form NOANNOEANE. For it has V differences and VIIII places in the nocturnal chants.

The first difference is in O, and has two places: the first in itself, “The Lord will come”; the second in I, lowered in the enharmonic genus, “with his treasures opened.” The second difference is in M, lichanos meson, and has three places in itself: “Sound the trumpet.” A lowered diatessaron in E: “Behold the name of the Lord.” A lowered diapente in C: “In the dead of night.”

The third difference is in I, and has one place in itself, namely a lowered diatessaron in C: “O blessed pontiff.” The fourth difference is in H, and has one place in itself: “Jesus, bending down.” The fifth difference is in C, and has two places in itself: “Well done, good servant”; and a lowered sesquioctave in E: “Let your loins be girded.”

The form of this mode is enclosed within a complete diapente. Each string has one difference, and the first difference has two places, the second three, the third one, the fourth one, and the fifth two. Hence it is established that this mode has five differences and nine places in the nocturnal chants.

In the diurnal chants this mode has three differences: the first in I, with one place in C, as in “Incline”; the second in H, with a place in P, “He established”; the third in C, with a place in itself, “Rejoice.” Thus it is apparent that in the diurnal chants each difference has one place.

Because of the remarkable nature of the differences of this mode, some do not add C to its consonance, because no difference is marked by it. Its verse in the nocturnal chants proceeds as follows: [Note: [Col. 0935D] We omit the old musical notations placed above the text.] “Glory to the Father,” and so forth. In the diurnal chants the verse proceeds as follows: “Glory,” and so forth.

## CONCERNING THE SECOND TONE

In the same exposition of the modes, the second mode follows. Three times VI, that is XVIII, in relation to XII, which together make XXX, produce a diapente through a sesquialteral proportion. In relation to VI of the first tone, these three times VI of the second tone form a triple proportion, because the latter, when tripled, surpasses it.

Likewise, twice VIII in relation to XII makes XXVIII, that is, four times VII, and produces a diatessaron through a sesquitertian proportion. This proportion of the number—twice VIII in relation to VIII of the first tone—is double, and therefore falls within the diapason: XXIIII, that is, four times VI and twice XII. Likewise, twice VIIII, which is XVIII, in relation to XII produces a diapente, as above.

You will count the whole melody of the second tone either by the denary through the diapente, as in the antiphon “Behold, he comes,” in which there are V or X; or entirely through the diatessaron, that is, through VII, as in the antiphon “Come and show.” Likewise, the diapentic antiphon “Your almighty word,” and the diatessaron antiphon “The Lord God is my helper.”

But if the proportion of the second tone enters the diapason—that is, XII to VI, twice VIIII to VIIII, and twice VIII to VIII—it produces the first tone, since each mode has its own constitution. The two modes always look toward one another from the side, so that sometimes, in fraternal harmony, one may lean away into the other, and one may rise into the other by ascending.

For the hypodorian passes into the Dorian if it exceeds its diapason. This is what he means by saying, “if XII reaches VI,” since, compared with it, the hypodorian exists three times lower. If VI are assigned to nete hyperbolaeon in this range, it will have XII as mese, XVIII as lichanos hypaton, and XXIIII as proslambanomenos; and XII will be the difference between XII and XXIIII.

The melody of this range in the antiphons scarcely exceeds this difference toward the higher part; but below, you will count either a diatessaron through VII or a diapente through X. There is a complete diatessaron consonance between the two modes, since lichanos hypaton belongs to the hypodorian and proslambanomenos to the Dorian.

Boethius says that this consonance is generated from the double and triple as follows. Let the terms of one mean be such that its extremes are double, and the terms of another such that its extremes are triple:

| VI | VIII | XII |
|---|---|---|
| IIII | VI | XII |

The duodenary is therefore double the senary, and in the other arrangement XII is triple IIII. If we collect their differences and compare them with one another, the epitrite proportion—that is, the diatessaron symphony—is obtained, and so forth.

Since this is so, it is certain that paranete diezeugmenon of the hypodorian, to which six are assigned, is mese of the Dorian. If the chant of the second mode reaches this Dorian mese, it will now be called Dorian rather than hypodorian, as in the gradual responsory “All who await you.”

This responsory ranges throughout the difference XII, which exists between twice XII and XII. Its verse, having an intensified diapente at its beginning, proceeds from XVIII to XII through VIIII, which are the difference between twice VIIII and VIIII. The nocturnal responsory “They surrounded me,” with its verse, completes its course by sharpening one tone beyond the difference that we said exists between XXIIII and XII.

## ANOTHER NEW EXPOSITION BY SOMEONE ON THE SECOND TONE

The second mode begins from the fourth species of diapason, which is in C, where the first mode ends; and there it also ends, where it begins. Its form is enclosed within the diapente, which extends from M to C. This is its form, NOEAGIS.

This mode has one difference in e, with three places: a lowered diatessaron in A, “that the heavens may rejoice”; a lowered sesquioctave in C, “justly and piously.” Hence it is established that this mode has one difference and three places in the nocturnal chants.

In the diurnal chants this mode has the same difference and the same places: a lowered diatessaron in A, “Behold, he comes”; a lowered tone in C, “those who thirst”; “Serve”; “from necessities.”

The verse of this mode in the nocturnal chants proceeds thus: “Glory to the Father,” and so forth. In the diurnal chants the verse proceeds thus: “Glory to the Father,” and so forth.

## CONCERNING THE THIRD TONE

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Codex S. Em. continues: “The expositor of the tones follows.”]

The third tone has two A’s, one on account of the measure of the authentic deuterus, the other on account of its plagal form, in whose diapason it explains its own semitone, [Note: [Col. 0936D] Namely, the plagal form; as must also be read in the preceding passages.] and another semitone in the diapason of the second mode, on account of the triple proportion, as has been said, and the quadruple proportion, on account of four times VI in relation to one III of the first.

For four times VI in relation to four times III of XII gives four times IX, which are XXXVI—a diapason, that is, six times six, or three times XII. Likewise, three times VIII in relation to XII, because these are double proportions. Twice VIIII in relation to XII is a sesquialteral proportion, that is, a diapente in XXX.

Therefore this third tone will be either a diapason or a diapente, as in the gradual antiphons “Confession and beauty,” “He distributed, he gave,” and “I have known, Lord.” The nocturnal antiphons are “He who is of the earth,” “When you were born,” and “He will destroy the evil men.”

“The tone,” he says [Note: [Col. 0937D] This is again another exposition.], “the third, has two O’s,” that is, twice XII, for O is taken for XII. “One,” he says, “on account of the measure of the authentic deuterus,” that is, the Phrygian, “and the other on account of its plagal form,” that is, the hypophrygian.

For the mese of the Phrygian, that is, XII, is the nete diezeugmenon of the hypodorian, where the fifth species of diapason begins. Therefore the hypate meson of the former is the proslambanomenos of the latter. Moreover, the hypate meson of the Phrygian is the mese of the hypophrygian. Hence he says, “in whose diapason it explains its own semitone,” because the mese completes the diapason of each constitution, and from the same hypate meson the melody of the fourth mode always begins, whether here or there.

For this is the beginning of the melody of the third mode and its ending, since it imitates the softness of the chromatic genus, in which the diapente is more frequently received throughout the whole diapason. For paramese, beginning in the fourth place, explains its own diapason and its own semitone. But for the sake of euphony it adds a tone to that diapason, as in the melody of the first mode, so that, lowered a diatessaron from mese together with the tone, it may be a diapente.

As for what he says, “its own semitone,” it is certain that each species of diapason is distinguished by its own semitones in the second place; if these are moved from their position, they transform the whole quality of the mode, while, if preserved in their place, they preserve it. The tones called protus and deuterus, and the rest, also contribute greatly to this.

Regarding the triple and quadruple proportion, which he mentions, it should be understood that the second mode consumes three times VI in lichanos hypaton, while the third mode determines four times VI in proslambanomenos, which is one sesquioctave shorter than the higher string.

He adds that four times VI in relation to four times III of XII is a diapason, because the first duodenary, that is, twice six, reaches its mese, whose fourth part [Note: [Col. 0937D] Or third part.]—that is, III—the melodies of this mode traverse more frequently; and they descend through the fourth part of twice XII, so that the diapason may be completed.

You will also perceive this by singing AIANEOANE. For, after completing the fourth species of diapente from paramese, it descends to lichanos hypaton, then ascends by each string, intensifying the diapente, to lichanos meson; again, lowering it, it descends to trite diezeugmenon; finally it ends at its final note, hypate meson.

The gradual antiphon “Confession and beauty” first touches this final note and then ascends as far as III of XII, after which it returns to its own final note. The antiphon “I have known, Lord,” and “When I cried to the Lord,” likewise begin with an intensified semitone. The nocturnal antiphons or responsories proceed in the same way: “He will destroy the evil men,” “I have sinned beyond number,” “Alleluia,” “The Spirit of the Lord,” and the offertory “God, you will turn.”

Thus, in this same mode, one sings not only through the diapason XXXVI or through the diapente below XXX, but also frequently through the diatessaron, either intensified or lowered.

## CONCERNING THE FOURTH TONE

The musician Aristoxenus, measuring not the voices themselves, as Pythagoras did, but collecting the measures of the differences between voices, distinguished each tetrachord by three numbers, which neither exceeded LX nor fell below it. For in four tetrachords he placed the same number between the first and second strings and between the second and third; between the third and fourth he added what remained of LX, as follows:

| VI | VI | XLVIII |
|---|---|---|
| VIII | VIII | XLIII |
| VIII | VIIII | XLII |
| XII | XII | XXXVI |

Two tetrachords remain, one of which has:

| XII | XVIII | XXX |

and the other:

| XII | XXIV | XXIV |

The ratio of these same numbers is as follows: he assigned XXIV to the tone, XII to the semitone, VIII to the third part of a tone, VI to the fourth part, which is the diesis; and from the fourth part of a tone, VI, together with the eighth part, III, he constituted VIIII.

He called the first tetrachord enharmonic, the second soft chromatic, the third hemiolic chromatic, [Note: [Col. 0937D] Read “hemiolic, or sesquialteral.” See Aristoxenus, Book II of the *Harmonics*, p. 50, Meibom edition.] the fourth tonic chromatic, [Note: [Col. 0938D] Or *toniaean*, Greek τονιαίου.] the fifth soft diatonic, and the sixth intense diatonic. [Note: [Col. 0938D] Meibom, cited above, renders the Greek term of Aristoxenus συντόμου as “compressed.”]

In all the tetrachords the greater extreme number is larger than the other two, except in the final two, which are of the diatonic genus. Therefore the measurement of the symphonies of the tetrachords is according to the greater extreme, since XLVIII is twice XXIIII—that is, twice diapason [Note: [Col. 0938D] Codex Em.: “that is, diapason, which is four times XII, six times VIII, and eight times VI.”], which is indeed four times VI, three times VIII, and eight times VI.

Likewise, twice XII, that is, twice diapason, is XXIIII, which is four times VI and three times VIII. Twice VIII in relation to four times VI, which is a diatessaron, gives XLII; and twice VI in relation to twice VIIII, which is a diapente, gives XXX. Finally, twice VI in relation to four times VI, which is a diapason, gives XXXVI.

Therefore the expositor mentioned above added: “The fourth tone, which we call hypophrygian, has twice XII in relation to twice VIIII and three times VIII in relation to three times VI in one consonance of numbers; for it is a double diatessaron. In the diapason, however, VI in relation to XII, that is, XVIII, agrees with it.”

For this reason three times VI is not compared with twice XII, since it is not divisible by three; rather, as has been said, three times VIII is compared with three times VI, and twice XII with twice VIIII, in a sesquitertian proportion, which together make XLII. For this entire tone will always be through a diatessaron.

The diapason consonance, however—that is, VI in relation to XII—is produced by three times VI, twice VIIII, three times VIII, and twice XII. Their proportion, that is, the comparison of the greater to the lesser and of the lesser to the greater, having a diatessaron, will always be measured by the septenary, as in the gradual antiphons “I have risen,” “The mercies of the Lord,” and “In your will, Lord.” Likewise, in the nocturnal chants: “The bush that he had seen,” “A great crowd,” and “Three are the gifts.”

[Col. 0939B] In this exposition, only the following point seems to require investigation: he says that “three times six is not compared with twice twelve, because it is not divisible by three”—as though it were impossible to measure twice twelve, that is, twenty-four, by a third part. But since twenty-four can be measured both by two and by three, it is clear that he intended two to correspond to two and three to three in the same consonance, although he denied that three corresponds to two.

As for what he added, namely that six compared with twelve produces the diapason, although he had already mentioned twice twelve, it should be recalled that the measure of differences must be gathered not only within the sounds themselves but also between the sounds. For when he said “twice twelve,” he made six compared with twice twelve a fourfold proportion; consequently, between six and twelve there is a difference of six. Again, between twelve and twice twelve there is a difference of twelve. No one is unaware that these differences, compared with one another, produce the diapason.

This, then, is what he means when he says that the diapason consonance—namely, six compared with twelve—is produced by three sixes and the rest. This difference, which is twelve, retains both consonances, that is, twice the diatessaron, and does not exceed it in the smaller antiphons. If it should exceed it, it will already possess the force of the Phrygian mode.

Moreover, its melody, which is **NOEAGIS**, begins from the *hypatē mesōn*, that is, from the sharpened semitone, and, after passing through the final at the same pitch, ends with a diapente. How every diatessaron is measured by seven, through four and three, has been explained above. Here, however, in twice twelve and three times eight there are four times six, while in twice nine there are three times six.

The gradual antiphons follow. The first is **Resurrexi**. Its beginning is on *lichanos hypatōn*, its middle and end on *hypatē mesōn*, and the summit of its ascent on *mese*. The gradual responsory **Haec dies** likewise belongs here. The nocturnal responsory **Rex noster** also belongs here, passing beyond *paramese* by its ascent. The **Alleluia Pascha nostrum** likewise remains within this mode, almost reaching its diapason.

## A New Exposition of the Third and Fourth Modes

From the first species of the diapason, where the first mode begins because of a certain natural property, the third mode also begins and ends in the diatessaron. Its form is enclosed, namely, within the diapente from O to e and the diatessaron from O [Col. 0940A] to cc.

The form of this mode is **NOEOEANE**. In the nocturnal chants this mode has three differentiae: one on M., which has one place, namely **Qui odit animam**; another on O., which has one place, with a lowered diatessaron in **Qui de terra est**; and a third on X., which has an enharmonic lowering in M., in **Et respicientes**.

In the diurnal chants this mode has the same differentiae and the same places: M., as in **Ego autem**, with the O. differentia; and this place, **Dum sanctificatus**. In the nocturnal chants the verse runs as follows: **Gloria Patri, etc.**  
[Note: [Col. 0939D] The whole passage, with the musical notation.]  
In the diurnal chants the verse likewise runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.**

## The Fourth Mode

From the fifth species of the diapason, where the third mode ends, the fourth begins—namely, from H.—and ends on the same H. Its form is enclosed within the diapente from O to e, with the addition of a lowered sesquioctave proportion from c to e.

The form of this mode is **NOEAGIS**. In the nocturnal chants it has two differentiae. The first is on h and has four places:

- **O quam clarus est**, that is, **Jerusalem**;
- the lowered sesquioctave in C., **Rubum quem viderat**.

The second differentia is on c and has one place, in C.: **Bethlehem, non es minima**.

Thus it is clear that this mode has two differentiae and their assigned places in the nocturnal chants. In the diurnal chants this mode has one differentia on M., as in **Resurrexi**. In the nocturnal chants its verse runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.**  
[Note: [Col. 0939D] The whole passage, with the musical notation.]  
In the diurnal chants: **Gloria Patri, etc.**

## Also Concerning the Fifth Mode

[Col. 0940C] The fifth mode, which we call Lydian, is everywhere measured by ten and is always based on the diapente. For three times eight compared with three times twelve, and four times six compared with four times nine, fall into the diapente through a sesquialterous proportion; their consonance is the diapason at twelve. For four times nine and three times twelve, compared with four times six and three times eight, produce sixty.  
[Note: [Col. 0940D] F. reads “three times eight compared with three times twelve,” as the following context requires.]  
[Note: [Col. 0940D] That is, four times nine compared with four times six, and three times twelve compared with three times eight.]

Among these are the gradual antiphons **Domine refugium**, **Circumdederunt me**, and **Domine, in tua misericordia**; and the nocturnal antiphons **Solvite templum hoc**, **Salve crux**, and **Exultet spiritus meus**.

Here I see nothing else requiring investigation except his statement that the numbers proposed for making twice the diapente produce the diapason consonance at twelve. For only two of them—four times six and three times eight—produce the diapason with that same number. Who, indeed, could understand four times nine and three times twelve as belonging to the stated proportion?

It should therefore be understood that the diapason arises from twelve in relation to twice twelve, which, in relation to forty-eight, completes another diapason. Between these two lies the proper character of this mode, since the consonance formed by three times twelve compared with three times eight looks from one side to twelve and from the other to forty-eight; and each of these numbers makes a diapason with three times eight.

Moreover, three times twelve, on the lower side, observes the limits of this mode. Beginning from *tritē diezeugmenōn*, under the third species of the diatessaron, its melody, **NOEOEANE**, carries out the third species of the diapente downward as far as *parypatē mesōn*, which is its final.

The gradual antiphon **Domine refugium** returns twice to the same chord. Just as **Circumdederunt** begins, so does the offertory **Immittet angelus**. The nocturnal responsory **Obsecro, Domine** begins from the lowered enharmonic *mese*, so that a sharpened chromatic interval immediately follows.

The second species of the diapason, which begins from *paramese*, is distinctive in that it proceeds directly through three descending tones without a semitone in a single sequence. Nor does the octave itself contain an octonary interval between six and twelve; for this reason the *synemmenon* tetrachord is of considerable assistance there.

The **Alleluia Beatus vir** likewise traverses the entire fifth species of the diapason, ascending from the final chord of this mode toward the octave.

In the numbers mentioned above, the diapente consonance falls under a fivefold measure, since three times eight and four times six are reduced to twice twelve. But four times nine compared with three times twelve preserves the diapente of the binary and ternary numbers, which together make five.

## A New Exposition of the Fifth Mode

The fifth mode begins from the third species of the diapason, which is Y., and ends in the diapente, which is l. Its form is enclosed within the diapente from l. [Col. 0941D] to DD.  
[Note: [Col. 0941D] C. Em. reads “from y to i, with the addition of the enharmonic, namely y to DD,” which is preferable. For the diapente is contained from i to y, and from y to DD is the enharmonic interval, that is, two tones. The words added by C. Em. were accidentally omitted from the text here.]

The form of this mode is **NOEOEANE**. In the nocturnal chants it has two differentiae: one on O., which has two places, namely the antiphon **Obsecro, Domine**, with the lowered enharmonic in I., **Vox clamantis**; and another differentia on Y., which has one place, namely **Hodie nobis**.

In the diurnal chants this mode has four differentiae and three places: **Exaudi, Deus**; another on M., which has one place in I., **Circumdederunt me**; and a third on Y., **Justus Dominus**.

In the nocturnal chants the verse of this mode runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.** In the diurnal chants it runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.**

## Also Concerning the Sixth Mode

[Note: [Col. 0941D] C. Em.: “The same expositor continues concerning the sixth mode.”]

The sixth mode is the species formed by six times six compared with six times four, from twice twelve, and by four times nine compared with four times six, from twice twelve, since the sesquialterous proportion falls into the diapente. Six times four compared with three times eight, just as six times four compared with twice twelve, arrives at the diapason consonance—namely, at twelve—through twice twelve and three times eight, which are forty-eight, just as six times six and four times nine are seventy-two.  
[Note: [Col. 0942D] C. Em. reads “three times.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0942D] C. Em. reads “they arrive at six compared with twelve.”]

This entire mode is measured either by the diapason consonance, that is, six compared with twelve, or by the diapente, namely by ten, as in the gradual antiphons **Os justi**, **Omnes gentes**, and **Quasi modo geniti**. Likewise in the nocturnal antiphons **O admirabile**, **Vade, Satana**, **Virgo hodie fidelis**, and **O quam gloriosum est**.

Since there are eight modes, four are called authentic or principal, while the others are plagal or subordinate. It should be understood that each mode does not differ from its corresponding principal or subordinate mode either in the character of its numbers or in the nature of its symphonies.

Consequently, such measures and numbers belong more properly to the principal Lydian mode than to its subordinate counterpart. The former more frequently traverses the sixth part of twice twelve, namely four, and the fourth part, namely six; the latter in certain antiphons scarcely reaches twice twelve, after the manner of the subordinate modes.

When he instructed that twice twelve, that is, twenty-four, be measured by its sixth or fourth part, this is what he later means when he says that the consonance of this mode, namely the diapente, is measured by ten, since six and four belong to the measure of ten.

When he wished six times six to be compared with six times four, which is sixty, the same thing is meant as if he had said that thirty-six should be compared with twenty-four through the diapente consonance.

Next, he said that three times eight and twice twelve form the diapason consonance through six compared with twelve. This means nothing other than that three times eight and twice twelve have the same relation to twelve as the aforementioned diapason in the smaller numbers, namely six to twelve.

For from its final, *parypatē mesōn*, the melody proceeds upward through the diapente and downward through the diatessaron. From both consonances together the diapason always arises, as you can observe in the antiphon **Omnes gentes**. For it descends to *parypatē hypatōn* and, as stated, reaches *tritē diezeugmenōn*, producing the diapason.

The offertory **Stetit angelus** likewise ascends and descends in the same manner. The nocturnal responsory with its verse, **Aspiciebam** and **Esto nobis**, seems to ascend to *netē hyperbolaiōn*. The melody of the **Alleluia Omnes gentes**, which is **AANNES**, retains this mode through its intonation. Indeed, the melody touches *mese* while ascending and then descends, in a lowered form, through the third species of the diatessaron.

## A New Exposition of the Sixth Mode

From the sixth species of the diapason, where the fifth mode ends, the sixth begins, namely from I. Its form is nevertheless enclosed within the diapente from O to E, with the addition of a sesquioctave proportion on the lower side, from E to C.

The form of this mode is **NOEAGIS**. In the nocturnal chants it has one differentia with three places: **Aspiciebam**; the sharpened enharmonic in O., **Modo veniet**; and the lowered diatessaron in C., **Per memetipsum**. Thus this mode is marked by one differentia with three places.

In the diurnal chants the same differentia has two places: **Os justi**; and the lowered diatessaron in C., **Qui manducat**. In the nocturnal chants the verse runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.** In the diurnal chants: **Gloria Patri, etc.**

## The Seventh Mode

[Note: [Col. 0942D] C. Em.: “The Expositor continues concerning the seventh mode.”]

The seventh mode, which we call Mixolydian, contains the entire diatessaron in the proportion of the fourth mode, the entire diapente in the proportion of the fifth mode, and, in its own proportion, four times twelve, which is the diapason.

When he says that the Mixolydian is made from the proportions of the fourth and fifth modes—for this reason it is called Mixolydian, because it is mixed from the Lydian—it should be understood that in the fourth mode twice nine compared with twice twelve, and three times six compared with three times eight, produce the diatessaron through forty-two.

In the fifth mode, however, six times six compared with six times four, from twice twelve, and four times nine compared with four times six, from twice twelve, produce the diapente through sixty.

In its own proportion it contains the diapason, namely four times six compared with four times twelve, and six times four from twice twelve compared with six times eight. These numbers together make forty-eight.

The melody of this mode, beginning from *paranētē diezeugmenōn*, ends on *lichanos mesōn*, its final, through a diatessaron and a tone, first producing a lowered diapente; then the third species of that diapente appears to lie within this consonance. Since, upward from its final, this seventh mode carries out the seventh species of the diapason, it will be measured by seven, like the fourth mode, which is measured by the diatessaron, and by ten, like the fifth mode, which is measured by the diapente.

The end of this species on the higher side is *paranētē hyperbolaiōn*. Where the melody of this mode, **NOEOEANE**, ends, the melody of the eighth mode, **NOEAGIS**, begins with a sharpened diatessaron. It immediately lowers this interval, yet does not differ from its principal on account of this difference; it is designated by its name as *hypermixolydian*. It is properly called Hypermixolydian because it transcends the Mixolydian, which, according to Ptolemy, traverses the eighth species of the diapason, the highest of all the others, while consisting, like the Mixolydian, of the properties of the fourth and fifth modes.

The Mixolydian is sung in the gradual antiphons **Puer natus est nobis** and **Audivit Dominus**. The nocturnal responsories likewise begin in the same manner: **Iste est frater vester** and **Dixit Judas fratribus suis**.

Moreover, the first antiphon, **Puer natus est**, raises the diapente to *paranētē diezeugmenōn*. The melody of this mode has there an opening like that of the responsories **Ecce dies veniunt** and **Nascetur nobis**, which likewise begin in this mode.

The melodies of the eighth mode, however, run below the fourth species of the diapason in the manner of subordinate modes. For above *mese* there are four chords nearest to the *synemmena* and most inwardly adjacent to them, which, from the higher side, provide the beginnings of the first four species of the diapason and of the melodies of the four modes.

These modes, or sounds, are called in Greek: the first **Protus**, the second **Deuterus**, the third **Tritus**, and the fourth **Tetrardus**. Each differs downward from its final by a pentachord, which is the diapente. Above, however, they require a tetrachord, which is the diatessaron, so that each may retain its own species of the diapason and freely travel upward and downward through it.

An interval is often added externally to this diapason; it is called *emmelis*, that is, “suitable for melody.”

It should also be known that the Dorian mode is governed chiefly by the Protus, the Phrygian similarly by the Deuterus, the Lydian by the Tritus, and the Mixolydian by the Tetrardus. In certain melodies these sounds lightly touch and taste their own plagal—or oblique—forms, so that the plagal Protus touches the Protus, the plagal Deuterus the Deuterus, the plagal Tritus the Tritus, and the plagal Tetrardus the Tetrardus. This can be tested in the gradual antiphons.

In nocturnal or diurnal responsories, and in any ecclesiastical melodies, the plagal forms themselves pleasantly exceed the limits of their sounds and traverse, as they please, the species of the diapason that they had begun from the lower side. For each final chord attacks one of the species.

The limits of these species, observed above and below by the principal modes, are respectively those of the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian modes. All the species of the diapason can be begun both above and below. For example:

- the first, from O to A or from A to O;
- the second, from x to b or from b to x;
- the third, from y to c or from c to y;
- the fourth, from cc to e or from e to cc;
- the fifth, from dd to h or from h to dd;
- the sixth, from ff to i or from i to ff;
- the seventh, from nn to m or from m to nn.  
  [Note: [Col. 0943D] It seems that hh should be read instead of nn, as also below.]

There are therefore four upper notes, O., X., y., and cc., and three lower notes, H., i., and M.  
[Note: [Col. 0944D] C. Em. reads: “four lower notes, namely e., n., i., and m.”]

The upper notes, from the higher side, produce the Hypodorian, Hypophrygian, Hypolydian, and Hypermixolydian modes. The lower notes, from the lower side, produce the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian modes; hence they are called finals.

Consequently, a melody running below the species of the Hypodorian belongs to itself, but when it ascends above it, it belongs to the Dorian. Similarly, a melody below the species of the Hypophrygian belongs to itself, but when it ascends above it, it belongs to the Phrygian. The same is true of a melody below the Hypolydian: when it ascends above it, it belongs to the Lydian. The same must be understood of the Hypermixolydian.

Thus the Dorian melody ends on the higher side at CC.; the Phrygian melody ends at dd.; the Lydian melody at ff.; and the Mixolydian melody at nn. Hence the Dorian either descends from o to e or ascends to cc. Likewise, the Phrygian either descends from X to h or ascends to dd. In the same way, the Lydian either descends from y to I or ascends to ff. The Mixolydian likewise either descends from cc to M or ascends to nn.

Each principal mode always has a diapente below its middle chord and a diatessaron above it, as though there were eight between six and twelve. Each subordinate mode, however, has a diapente above its final chord and a diatessaron below it, as though there were nine between six and twelve.

If a tone should extend above or below any mode beyond the octave species, it is not improper to place an *emmelis*, so that wherever it touches on either side there may be a diapente and a tone, or a diatessaron and a tone.

It remains to speak of the three direct modes, whose course the *synemmenon* tetrachord cuts off, when between O. and X. there intervenes the *tritē synemmenon*, namely q. Yet reason scarcely ever permits a sound after *paramese*; it is found either after O. or after T.

It occurs after O., for example, in the third sound of the antiphon **Justus es, Domine**.

Finally, the eighth mode retains the same species of the diapason as the first, but differs from it in that the first has m. as the middle chord guarding its quality, whereas the latter has O. under the name of Protus. Whoever does not know this distinction falls faultily now into one mode and now into the other.

This occurs in the antiphon **Urbs fortitudinis**, which begins in the first mode and ends in the eighth because of the semitone that an unwary singer added to the chord m. in the wrong place, namely where he introduced **Aperite portas**.

In the gradual antiphons, however, the eighth mode includes **Ad te levavi** and **Domine, ne longe**. In the nocturnal antiphons: **Repleti sunt omnes** and **Lux de luce**. The nocturnal responsories are **Montes Gelboe** and **Dixit Ruben**; the diurnal responsories, **Dilexisti** and **Qui sedes**; and the offertory, **Si ambulavero**.

## A New Exposition of the Seventh and Eighth Modes

The seventh mode begins from the fourth species of the diapason, which is above *mese*, namely cc., and ends in the diapente at m. Its form is enclosed within the diapente from cc to m, with the addition of a sesquioctave proportion from m to i.

The form of this mode is **NOEOEAGIS**. In the nocturnal chants it has three differentiae:

1. one on cc., which has one place, with the lowered diapente in m., as in **Summae Trinitati**;
2. another on y., which has two places in itself, as in **Dixit Judas**, with the sharpened tone in cc., as in **Aspiciens**;
3. a third on O., which has two places in itself: **Attende, Domine, ad me**, with the lowered tone in m., as in **Missus est Gabriel**.

All the antiphons that, because of an erroneous ending, we assign to the fourth mode belong to this differentia, such as **Benedicta tu**.

In the diurnal chants this mode has one differentia on m., with one place in itself, namely **Puer natus est**. In the nocturnal chants the verse runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.** In the diurnal chants: **Gloria Patri, etc.**

## The Eighth Mode

The eighth mode begins from the seventh species of the diapason, which is M., where the seventh mode ends. It ends where it begins. Its form is enclosed within the sharpened diapente from m. to cc., with the addition of the lowered sesquioctave proportion from m. to i.

The form of this mode is **NOEAGIS**. In the nocturnal chants it has one differentia containing five places:

- **Ecce dies veniunt**;
- the lowered sesquioctave in I., **Doceam iniquos**;
- the sharpened sesquioctave in O., **Quodcumque**;
- the lowered diatessaron in y., **Ecce ancilla Domini**.

Thus it is evident that in the nocturnal chants this mode is marked by one differentia with five places.

In the diurnal chants this mode has one differentia with two places: **In virtute tua**, with the lowered diatessaron, and **Domine, ne longe**.

In the nocturnal chants the verse runs: **Gloria Patri, etc.** In the diurnal chants it runs as follows: **Gloria Patri, etc.**

## The Preceding Expositor Continues

[Col. 0946A]

As Vitruvius said in his book *On Architecture*, according to the physicists there are no more than eight winds: four principal winds and four subordinate ones. The four added to make twelve are related as four semitones are to eight tones.

For in the waves of the sea and of rivers the first wave always sounds more strongly than the seven that follow. The ninth wave, however, resembles the eighth.

Similarly, there are eight distinctions in thunder. From these the philosopher Pythagoras discovered the eight aforementioned consonances of the tones, in accordance with the harmony of heaven, on Mount Atlas, which is close to heaven. He completed their proportions in the likeness of the five zones of heaven, whose balance governs this world.

Every consonance in music has either two in a double proportion, three in a triple proportion, four in a quadruple proportion, five in a sesquialterous proportion, or seven in a sesquitertian proportion.

Finally, as stated above, the diapason—the first tone—is completed from five tones and two semitones. It is represented by six and twelve, to which every musical consonance is referred.

Any number that can be compared with twelve in such a way that it can be divided by three and four, or by four and three, in relation to that same twelve, is musical, since it remains within the proportions mentioned above. Pythagoras accordingly set the double proportion at six, the sesquialterous at eight, and the sesquitertian at nine, in relation to twelve.

Thus, from five simple tones—namely, the diapente, the diatessaron, and the diapason—and from compound tones, such as the diapason together with the diapente, as in the third and sixth modes, and the diapason together with the diatessaron in the same fifth mode, and the double diapason in the eighth mode, together with the double and triple proportions, the whole system is formed.  
[Note: [Col. 0945D] Something seems to be omitted here.]

That he compared the tones with winds was done for a fitting reason. For it is clear that either a plectrum or a fixed support is necessary to produce a sound.

As for his claim that four semitones are contained in these same tones, it should be understood that, apart from the one joined to *mese*, there are only four direct tetrachords, each marked at its lower end by a semitone.

The physicists investigate how the waves of the sea and rivers return. Hyginus likewise discusses, in his treatment of the agreement of years, days, and months, how recurrence occurs sometimes after seven years—that is, in the eighth recurring year—and sometimes after seven days, in astrology, because of the excellence of the number eight, by which the celestial sphere is divided above and below in the equinoctial circle.

At that time also, four parts of the same sphere are visible above and four lie hidden below. As for his addition that the ninth wave resembles the eighth, there is nothing surprising in this, since the ninth string is so similar to the eighth that it produces the same sound when one is struck in place of the other.

For example, in each species of the diapason the first and eighth strings have the same sound, though not the same position or the same interval of length or shortness. Indeed, in a heptachord, without any confusing error, the first answers for the eighth, the second for the ninth, and the third for the tenth. Consequently, in an octachord the first answers for the ninth, so that the eighth is almost similar to it and likewise produces the same sound; for this reason it is superfluous except on account of the higher pitch.  
[Note: [Col. 0947D] C. Em. reads “almost.”]

I have refrained from inserting a discussion of human philosophy concerning thunder, just as concerning waves. The comparison of the five symphonies with the five zones should not be despised, since in the former there is a contemplation of the whole of music, whereas in the latter there is the revolution of the celestial sphere.  
[Note: [Col. 0947D] C. Em. reads “revolution.” “Fifth” should be read shortly afterward.]

Let us therefore take six as the unit. In relation to it, two sixes give the double proportion below eighteen and eight. In relation to the same number, three sixes give the triple proportion below twenty-four. Four sixes in relation to it produce the quadruple proportion below thirty. Compared with two sixes, three sixes give, below thirty, the sesquialterous proportion. Similarly, three sixes compared proportionally with four sixes answer below forty-two to the epitritic proportion.

Consequently, the first mode is in the double proportion, the second in the triple, the third in the quadruple, the fourth in the epitritic, the fifth in the sesquialterous, and the sixth, like the third, in the diapason together with the diapente. The seventh contains the diapason together with the diatessaron; the eighth contains the double diapason together with the double and triple proportions. I have set out the reasoning for all these above, mode by mode.

Now I must not pass over the power of the duodenary number, to which every number divisible by three and four is adapted in musical consonances. The members or parts of twelve are six.  
[Note: [Col. 0948D] C. Em. has five, and consequently proceeds as though the sixth were present.]

The first is unity, the second six, the third four, the fourth three, and the sixth two. It also has this distinctive property: because it arises from the first odd number, its half—namely six—consists of three members and is the first perfect number.

If twelve is doubled, and is unquestionably taken as the double in relation to six, the result of this doubling is that numbers doubled by successive odd numbers receive their members, that is, their parts.

For example, from three are doubled the numbers six, twelve, twenty-four, and forty-eight. The first of these is marked by three members, the second by five, the third by seven, and the fourth by nine.

If twelve takes its beginning from four, the doubled numbers increase by four. For in twenty-four there are eight, produced by doubled four; and in forty-eight another eight are added to the same eight, giving four times twelve in forty-eight.

This is what he means when he says that numbers compared with the same twelve are musical if they are divisible by three and four. For eight, which is divisible by four, and nine, which is divisible by three, compared with the same number, yield either the epitritic or the hemiolic proportion.

Finally, since he said that some tones are compound and others simple, it should be understood that their composition is like that found among grammarians, where two complete parts are joined, as in **magister equitum**, “master of the cavalry.”

Since the first tone is distinguished by the diapason consonance, while the fifth is uniquely formed by the diapente, the second is composed of both consonances when it is extended through the triple proportion.

For, as stated, the gradual responsory **Universi, qui te exspectant**, with its verse, traverses the entire species of the Hypodorian diapason and, in addition, the diapente, so that the fifth may be completed through the triple proportion. The triple proportion occurs when the larger number is compared with the smaller; the subtriple when the smaller is compared with the larger.

Consequently, twenty-four compared with eight, and eighteen compared with six, must be triple proportions. One of these is completed, together with its verse, by the melody of the aforementioned responsory.

The simple modes, however, are those content with a single symphony, such as the fourth and fifth. The fourth proceeds through seven—that is, through three and four, which constitute the diatessaron. The fifth proceeds through ten—that is, through four and six, which constitute the diapente.

Boethius says of this: “This is the simpler and principal mode, which we now call Lydian.” Hence Plato ordered that children should by no means be trained in every mode, but rather in the strong and simple ones.

## Exposition of the Same Tones

Again, VIII compared with XII makes XX. This proportion is called sesquialterous in relation to XII because XII contains VIII and another part of it, namely IIII; and it produces the diapente.

Again, VIIII compared with XII makes XXI. This proportion is called sesquitertian because XII contains VIIII and a third part of it, namely III; and the diatessaron is produced, that is, three times seven, which are XXI.

Every first tone, therefore, will contain either three times VI in a double proportion, that is, the diapason, as in **Rorate caeli desuper**; or four times V, that is, three [Note: [Col. 0951D] St. Emeram has II. This should be read, since the sesquialterous proportion contains not III and III but II and III.] of VIII and three of XII, which in a sesquialterous proportion produce the diapente, namely XX., as in **Et nubes pluant justum. Aperiatur**; or three times VII, that is, three of VIIII, compared with four of XII in a sesquitertian proportion, which produce the diatessaron, as in **Terra, et germinet Salvatorem**.

Likewise, the introit **Gaudete in Domino**, etc.; **Inclina, Domine**; and **Justus es, Domine**. The antiphons **Urbs fortitudinis**, **Jesus autem**, and **Traditor autem**.

It should also be observed that it often happens that either twice, or three times, or even the whole of an antiphon or any chant belonging to the first tone proceeds either through VI and XII, which is the diapason; or through V and X, which is the diapente; or entirely through VII, which is the diatessaron, as in **Urbs fortitudinis** and **Joannes autem**.

The second tone, by three times VI, that is, XVIII, compared with XII, yields XXX according to the sesquialterate proportion and produces the diapente. Compared with VI of the first tone, three times VI of the second tone gives a triple proportion, because the latter, being tripled, exceeds it. Likewise, twice VIII compared with XII, according to the sesquitertian proportion, yields XXVIII, that is, four times VII, which is the diatessaron. Let this, then, be the proportion of the number: twice VIII compared with VIII of the first tone is double, and therefore falls into the diapason, XXIIII, which is four times VI and twice XII. Likewise, twice IX, which are three times VI, that is, XVIII, according to the sesquialterate proportion yields XXX, as above, [Col. 0951D] the diapente. For every melody of the second tone will either count the whole through the diapente by ten, as in the antiphon *Ecce advenit* (“Behold, he has come”), in which there are LXV. [Note: [Col. 0951D] I do not know why LXV is written here; from what precedes I conclude that LX would be the better reading.] Or it will proceed entirely through the diatessaron, or through three times VII, as in *Veni et ostende* (“Come and show”). Likewise, the antiphon *Omnipotens sermo tuus, Domine* (“Your almighty word, O Lord”) is diapentic, and *Dominus Deus auxiliator meus* (“The Lord God [is] my helper”) is diatessaronic. But if the proportion of the second tone reaches the diapason, whether VI compared with XII in relation to the first, as three times VI compared with VI of the first [Col. 0952A] tone, or twice VIII compared with VIII of the first tone, it produces this result. [Note: [Col. 0952D] Saint-Emmeram adds: “and twice VIIII compared with VIIII.”]

The third tone is that which has two A’s, one because of the first measure of the authentic *deuterus*, and the second A because of the plagal form of the authentic *deuterus*, in whose diapason it unfolds its semitone, and that of the second tone, both of which are semitones, because of the triple proportion, as was said, and the quadruple proportion, because of four times VI compared with one VI of the first. For four times VI compared with four times III of XII gives four times VIII, which are XXXVI, the diapason—that is, six times VI and three times XII. [Note: [Col. 0952D] Saint-Emmeram has VIIII, and this is better; for four times VI and four times III are XXXVI, or four times VIIII.] Similarly, VI compared with XII, because these are double proportions, and twice VIIII compared with XII, because this is a sesquialterate proportion, yield XXX, the diapente. Hence this third tone will be either the diapason, through VI compared with XII, or the diapente, that is, XXX, as in the introits *Confessio et pulchritudo* (“Majesty and beauty”) [Col. 0952B], *Dispersit, dedit* (“He scattered; he gave”), and *Cognovi, Domine* (“I have known, O Lord”), and in the antiphons *Qui de terra est* (“He who is of the earth”), *Quando natus es* (“When you were born”), *Malos male perdet* (“He will miserably destroy the wicked”), and *Homo quidam fecit* (“A certain man made”).

The fourth tone has twice XII compared with three times VIII, and with three times VI and twice VIII: one consonance of numbers in the diapason. VI compared with XII, that is, XXIIII, agrees with them. Therefore three times VI is not compared with twice XII, since it is not divided by three; rather, three times VIII is compared with three times VI, and twice VIIII with twice XII according to the sesquitertian proportion. This entire tone will always be the diatessaron, while the consonance will be the diapason: that is, six times VI compared with XII, three times VI and twice VIIII and three times VIII and twice XII produce it. Their proportion—that is, the comparison of the greater with the lesser, and of the lesser with the greater—will always be measured as a diatessaron, that is, by the number seven. Thus in the introits *Resurrexi* (“I have risen”) [Col. 0952C], *Misericordia Domini* (“The mercy of the Lord”), and *In voluntate tua* (“By your will”), and in the antiphons *Rubum quem viderat* (“The bush which he had seen”), *Turba multa* (“A great multitude”), and *Tria sunt munera* (“There are three gifts”). [Note: [Col. 0952D] Saint-Emmeram has VIIII, more correctly, as is clear from what follows.]

The fifth tone is always entirely diapentic, through ten, because three times VIIII compared with three times XII and four times VI compared with four times VIII fall into the diapente according to the sesquialterate proportion. Their consonance is the diapason, that is, in the duodenary relation, four times VIIII and three times XII, and four times VI and three times VIII, as in the introits *Domine refugium* (“O Lord, [you are] a refuge”), *Circumdederunt me* (“They surrounded me”), and *Domine, in tua misericordia* (“O Lord, in your mercy”). And in the antiphons *Solvite templum hoc* (“Destroy this temple”), *Salve Crux* (“Hail, Cross”), *Exultet spiritus meus* (“Let my spirit exult”), and similar pieces.

The sixth tone is six times VI compared with six times IIII of twice XII, and four times VIIII compared with four times VI of twice XII, because the sesquialterate proportion falls into the diapente; and six times [Col. 0952D] IIII of three times VIII and six times IIII of twice XII come into the diapason consonance, that is, VI and XII, through VIII, which are XLVIII, just as six times VI and four times VIIII amount to LXXII. For this entire tone will be measured either through the diapason consonance, that is, VI and XII, or through the diapente, that is, by ten. Thus in the introits *Os justi* (“The mouth of the just man”), *Omnes gentes* (“All nations”), and *Quasi modo geniti* (“As newborn [children]”), and in the antiphons *O Admirabile* (“O wonderful [thing]”) and *Virgo hodie fidelis* (“The faithful Virgin today”).

[Col. 0953A] The seventh tone, in the proportion of the fourth tone, contains the whole diatessaron; in the proportion of the fifth tone, the whole diapente; and in its own proportion it has twelve times XII, the diapason, which are CXLIIII. Seek the eighth tone above. [Note: [Col. 0953D] Up to this point the Saint-Emmeram manuscript; in the Strasbourg manuscript there follows an exposition of a certain musical work.]

## On the Measurements of Organ Pipes

The first shall have eight times its diameter. The second shall contain the first, an eighth of it, and an eighth of its diameter. The third shall contain the second, an eighth of it, and an eighth of its diameter. The fourth shall contain the first, its third, and a third of its diameter. The fifth shall contain the first, its half, and half its diameter; or the fourth, an eighth of it, and an eighth of its diameter. The sixth shall contain the fifth, an eighth of it, and an eighth of its diameter. The eighth shall contain the first doubled.

[Col. 0953B] Another account, differing from the foregoing.

The first is measured by an eighth: E T. [Note: [Col. 0954D] The letter T added to another marks a whole tone, just as S marks a semitone.] The second is sesquioctave to the first: D T. The third is sesquioctave to the second: C S. The fourth is sesquitertian to the first: B T. The fifth is either sesquialterate to the first, or sesquitertian to the second, or sesquioctave to the fourth: A T. The sixth is sesquioctave to the fifth, or sesquitertian to the third, or sesquialterate to the second: G S. The seventh is sesquioctave to the sixth, or sesquitertian to the fourth, or sesquialterate to the third: F. The eighth is sesquioctave to the seventh, or sesquitertian to the fifth, or sesquialterate to the fourth, or double to the first: E. The ninth is sesquioctave to the eighth, or sesquitertian to the sixth, or sesquialterate to the fifth, or double to the second.

Another account.

[Col. 0953C] The first may be of any size whatever. The second is sesquioctave to the first. The third is sesquioctave to the second. The fourth is sesquioctave to the third. The fifth is sesquitertian to the second. The sixth is sesquioctave to the fifth. The seventh is sesquioctave to the sixth. Once these have been arranged, a single one must be introduced in second place, which is sesquitertian to the one that was previously fourth.

Another account.

Given any length for the first or smaller pipe—and it seems better if the diameter, that is, the width of the opening, is given eight times in the length—wherever a tone is to be made thereafter, the larger pipe shall contain the entire smaller pipe, its diameter, and an eighth of its diameter. In the diatessaron, the larger shall contain the smaller, its third, and in addition a third of its diameter. In the diapente, the larger shall contain the smaller, its half, and in addition half its diameter. In the diapason, the larger shall contain the smaller doubled, and in addition the whole diameter. The remaining intervals will easily be obtained through numbers. The diameter is either the half of the part that is wider at the opening, or the transverse width of the opening at the broader side through which the pipe is blown, beneath which lies the passage of the opening.

Alternatively:

If you seek a tone, let the larger pipe contain the smaller, an eighth of it, and an eighth of that eighth. If a diatessaron, [Col. 0954A] let the larger contain the smaller, its third, an eleventh of the third, and a sixth of the eleventh. If a diapente, let the larger contain the smaller, its half, an eighth of the half, and an eighth of that eighth. If a diapason, let the larger contain the smaller doubled, and in addition one eighth of it and an eighth of that eighth. If a diapason and diapente, let the larger contain the smaller tripled and its two eighths, that is, its fourth. If a double diapason, let the larger contain the smaller quadrupled and in addition its three eighths.

Another account.

If the pipes are of equal thickness, and the larger contains twice the length of the smaller, with in addition the diameter of its hollow, they will sound the diapason consonance with one another.

If the larger pipe contains four times the length of the smaller within itself, and in addition contains three times the measure of the diameter of the hollow, they will sound the double diapason consonance.

If the larger pipe contains the entire smaller pipe and in addition its third part, together with a third of the diameter of the hollow, they will sound the diatessaron consonance.

If the larger pipe contains the smaller and in addition half its length, together with half the diameter of the hollow, they will sound the diapente consonance.

If the larger pipe contains the entire smaller pipe and in addition the sixteenth part of its length, together with a sixteenth of the diameter, this consonance will be a semitone. [Col. 0954C] But it is better to derive the semitone through the diatessaron.

## On the Weights of Cymbals

The first may have any weight whatever. The second is sesquioctave to the first. The third is sesquioctave to the second. The fourth is sesquitertian to the first. The fifth is sesquioctave to the fourth. The sixth is sesquioctave to the fifth. The seventh is sesquitertian to the fourth.

## On the Modes

*Authentus* means authoritative and full of authority. *Protus* means first; *deuterus*, second; *tritus*, third; *tetrardus*, fourth. To these, in due order, are subordinated four lateral modes, which they call the plagal mode of the *protus*, the plagal mode of the *deuterus*, the plagal mode of the *tritus*, and the plagal mode of the *tetrardus*. Likewise, in Greek:

ANNANEANE.  
NANANEAGIES.  
AGIANNEAGIES.  
NENOTEANES.  
NOEAGIS.

Likewise, the *parapteres*: NENOTENEAGIS.

Antiphon: *mea nox* (“my night”).  
Antiphon: *o mors* (“O death”).  
Antiphon: *miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”).

ANAIETANENAGIS  
AIANNEAGIES.

Antiphon: *Nos qui vivimus*.

Likewise, it is necessary to retain the *parapteres* written above, which are confirmed in the shorter antiphons, especially those taken from the psalms, which do not end in the same way in which they begin. They are called *parapteres* because they prepare the way for descending in the verses of the antiphons.

NENOTENARSIS. The first *parapter* touches the second tone and enters into the verse as the second tone, but ends like the first tone, as in *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”), *A delicto* (“From sin”), and many others.

ANOS. The second *parapter* touches the fourth tone and ends there. These are the antiphons *Quia mirabilia* (“Because [he has done] wonderful things”), *Sede a dextris* (“Sit at [my] right hand”), *Speret Israel* (“Let Israel hope”), *Omnis terra* (“All the earth”), and many others.

ANAGETANENAGIS. The third *parapter* touches the seventh tone and ends in the fourth tone. There are many antiphons that descend there, whose enumeration would be lengthy. Let us mention a few: the antiphons *Benedicta* (“Blessed”), *Rorate* (“Drop down [dew]”). There is also AIANNEAGIES.

The fourth *parapter* touches the eighth tone, but does not ascend into another voice; it ends in a moderate register, and such examples are found only occasionally—perhaps four or five antiphons: *Nos qui vivimus* (“We who live”), *In ecclesiis* (“In the churches”), *Martyres Domini* (“Martyrs of the Lord”), *Angeli Domini* (“Angels of the Lord”), [Col. 0955B] *Virgines Domini* (“Virgins of the Lord”).
