Blessed Augustine declares that the person who takes more pleasure in the height of the voice than in the meaning of the words commits a punishable sin in sacred songs, because one must sing not with the voice but with the heart. For this purpose the use of psalmody was established: just as David, by playing the lyre, restrained the evil spirit in Saul, so singers, by modulating or jubilating, should drive every diabolical desire from the hearts of those who hear them and persuade them to participate in heavenly harmonies. Therefore we must take care not to abandon the practice of singing, and not to sin through the exaltation of the voice. Hence David says: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation.”

Anyone who desires to possess knowledge of music ought to know that all musical consonances consist either [Col. 0957A] in a double proportion, as II to IIII; or in a triple proportion, as II to VI; or in a quadruple proportion, as II to VIII; or in a sesquialterate proportion, as III to II; or in a sesquitertian proportion, as IIII to III. What is called sesquitertian in arithmetic is called the diatessaron in music; what is called sesquialterate in numbers is called the diapente in melody. What is double in proportions is the diapason among consonances. The triple is the diapente together with the diapason; the quadruple is the double diapason. The consonance that governs every musical modulation cannot be produced without sound. Sound, however, is not produced without a certain pulsation and striking; pulsation and striking cannot exist unless motion has preceded; and this species is called the *climax*.

We read that music was simple at the beginning, [Col. 0957B] so much so that it consisted entirely of four strings, and that this remained so up to Orpheus. The first and fourth strings produced the diapason consonance; the middle strings, both with one another and with the outer strings, produced the diapente and diatessaron, so that there was nothing discordant in them, corresponding to the transformation of the cosmic music, which consists of four elements. Mercury is said to have invented this four-stringed instrument.

Some say that at a certain time the Nile overflowed to an extraordinary extent, so that the lands around its banks were covered. After the waters receded, countless fish died across the fields that had been left without water. At that time Mercury is said to have found a *cochlea*—a shell—and, taking it up, found nothing except the four strings of the fish that had been inside it. Touching them one by one, he is said to have been the first to discover this tetrachord.

But the whole essence of this art, as it seems to us, is revealed in the regular division of the monochord. In that division, the greater length of string and the greater quantity of number produce lower sounds. But if the length of the string is shorter, or marked by fewer numbers, the sound is correspondingly lower or higher; when we measure the spaces and sounds of the strings, we must follow the nature of things, assigning greater extensions to the greater length of strings, but shorter ones to the lesser length from which the sharpness of the voice arises. The *proslambanomenos* [Col. 0958B] compared with G. B., which is the *hypatemeson*, makes the diapente consonance. Again, A. B., the *proslambanomenos*, compared with C. B., the *hychanos hypaton*, has a diatonic diatessaron consonance. Thus the skilled reader of music will rejoice to find legitimate tones in the rationally arranged numbers of the strings. So difficult a work cannot be explained in a way that becomes clear to those less skilled, even through an extended treatment. Hence it is evident why some have not unreasonably maintained that music, with Boethius, has truly ascended to heaven.

[Col. 0957C] Just as letters are the elementary and indivisible parts of articulated speech, from which composed syllables in turn combine words and names, and these form the text of complete discourse, so the *phthongi* of singing voice—which in Latin are called sounds—are the origins of song, and the whole content of music ends in their ultimate resolution. From the combination of sounds arise intervals, and from intervals systems are formed. Sounds are the first foundations of song. Not every sound is called a *phthongos*, but only those sounds of the singing voice that are arranged at legitimate intervals from one another and are suited to melody. Their order is naturally continued by ascending and descending in such a way that four and four of the same kind always follow one another. Yet each of these four differs from the others by a suitable distinction, [Col. 0957D] so that they differ not only in sharpness and gravity, but each possesses, through its own sharpness and gravity, the qualities proper to its nature. A fixed and differentiated interval of greater sharpness or relaxation again forms these qualities among the individual sounds. For example, these notes in order: D E F G.

The first, which is also the gravest, is called in Greek *protus*, or *archoos*. The second is *deuteros*, separated by a tone from the *protus*. The third is *tritos*, separated by a semitone from the *deuteros*. [Col. 0958C] The fourth is *tetrardus*, separated by a tone from the *tritos*. Through their continuous multiplication an infinite sequence of sounds is woven, and four by four of the same kind continue to follow one another until, by ascending or descending, they run out, as follows: for, as this little diagram shows, whether one leads the sounds upward or downward in order, this succession, as it were, of tetrachords will not cease until the voice is exhausted. The power of these four sounds also creates the authority of eight modes, as will later be said in its proper place. Through their mutual diversity the whole harmony is unified.

But because, as has been said, their multiplication [Col. 0958D] proceeds without limit, the reason of the discipline chose a definite number from this boundless confusion and established its study in eighteen sounds, in which four groups of four are contained, with two additional sounds. In these, first is the lowest tetrachord, that of the graves; next to it is the tetrachord of the finals; after these comes the tetrachord of the superiores; then that of the excellentes. Two final sounds remain, whose arrangement is as follows. [Note: [Col. 0957] Note, reader, that here and hereafter B. b. is to be understood as what was formerly called square B; after the distinction between soft and hard B began to be made, this will become clear in its proper place.]

## CHAPTER III. Why the Tetrachord of the Finals and the Others Are So Called

They are called terminal or final sounds because every melody must end in one of these four. The melody of the first tone, together with its subordinate tone, is governed and brought to an end by the sound *archoos*. The second tone, with its subordinate, is governed and brought to an end by the sound *deuteros*. The third tone and its subordinate are governed and brought to an end by the sound / *tritos*. The fourth tone, with its subordinate, is governed and brought to an end by the sound *tetrardus*. An authentic tone is called the major form of any tone, and the plagal form—the *plagis* or *plagius*—the minor.

## CHAPTER IV. Why There Is One Tetrachord Below the Finals and Two Above

The final or terminal sounds have beneath them one tetrachord, called the tetrachord of the graves. Above them they have two, those of the superiores and excellentes, together with the two remaining sounds. This is because simple and legitimate chant does not descend lower than the fifth sound from its final. In [Col. 0959D] the first and second modes, it descends from the final *archoos* or *protus* to that same grave sound . In [Col. 0960A] the third and fourth modes, from the final *deuteros* to that same grave sound . In the fifth and sixth, from the final / *tritos* to that same grave sound N. In the seventh and eighth, from the final *tetrardus* to that same grave sound . In ascending, however, the voice can be carried from any final up to the third sound of the same name, that is, as far as the Excellentes.

## CHAPTER V. The Difference between Authentic and Minor Tones

Moreover, although each authentic tone and the tone subordinate to it are governed and ended by the same sound, and therefore are counted as one tone, they nevertheless differ in this respect: the minor tones have smaller intervals in their ascent, and every lower tone ascends only as far as the fifth sound from its final. [Col. 0960B] Even this occurs rarely.

Every musical sound has, on either side of itself, at the fifth place, a sound of its own quality. [Note: [Col. 0959] In the margin of the Einsiedeln manuscript: “False rule. ## CHAPTER IX. What Is the Difference between *Phthongi* and Sounds, between Tones and *Epogdooi*; Also between Tone and Mode or Trope; What Are the Sections? What Are an Interval and a System?

But once these matters have been understood as preliminary exercises, or as somewhat humble beginnings, we shall proceed by an easier path to the principles of harmony.

Harmony is the suitable joining together of different voices. Since in these voices we generally use “sounds” and “*phthongi*” indifferently, it is necessary to explain what belongs properly to sounds, *phthongi*, and *epogdooi*. [Note: [Col. 0966C] Saint Blaise: “we understand sounds, and also tones, tones and *epogdooi*, concerning which…”] Sound is the general name for any voice; but we call the sounds of the singing voice *phthongi*. A tone is the legitimate size of the interval [Note: [Col. 0966C] Saint Blaise: “legitimate distinction.”] from one sound to another. Because this interval of musical sounds is in the sesquioctave proportion, it is called by the Greek name *epogdoos*. For just as a proportion is called sesquialterate, or *hemiolia*, when the greater exceeds the lesser by half of the latter; sesquitertian when the greater exceeds the lesser by a third of the lesser; sesquiquartan [Note: [Col. 0966C] Saint Blaise: “sesquiquartan when by a fourth; sesquiquintan when by a fifth; sesquisextan when by a sixth; sesquiseptiman when by a seventh of itself the greater surpasses the lesser; likewise sesquioctave…”] when the lesser is exceeded by the greater by a fourth part of itself; sesquiquintan when one is greater than the other by a fifth part; sesquisextan when by a sixth; sesquiseptiman when by a seventh; so, in the sesquioctave comparison, one sound stands in relation to another when the higher sound contains within itself the quantity of the lower and, in addition, an eighth of it. A semitone is an incomplete interval of a tone, and is sometimes also called a *limma* or *diesis*. Modes or tropes are kinds of modulations, about which we spoke above: authentic or plagal *protus*, authentic or plagal *deuterus*, and so on; or the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and other modes, which received their names from the names of peoples. Sections are the cola or phrases of a song, which divide the song by their endings. Cola are formed by the suitable joining of two or more phrases, although sometimes a phrase or a colon may be named indiscriminately. The phrases themselves are formed through *arsis* and *thesis*, that is, elevation and lowering. Sometimes the voice rises and falls once in a phrase through a simple *arsis* and *thesis*; sometimes more often. [Col. 0966B] The difference between the highest and lowest voice of a phrase is called an interval. These intervals may now be smaller, as in what we call a tone; or larger, containing the interval of two, three, or several tones in succession. Further, just as cola consist of phrases, so we call the spaces of phrases intervals; but the spaces within cola, or within any complete melody, we call systems.

## CHAPTER X. On Consonances

The voices mentioned above do not all mingle equally sweetly, nor do voices joined in every possible way produce harmonious effects in song; just as letters, if joined together indiscriminately, often do not combine into suitable words or syllables. [Col. 0966C] So in music there are certain fixed intervals capable of producing consonances. A consonance is the sweet concord of unequal voices joined together.

[Col. 0967A] The simple and primary consonances are three, from which the others are composed: one is called the diatessaron, another the diapente, and the third the diapason.

*Diatessaron* means “from four,” either because it makes four voices sound in relation to one another, or because it is a composition of four sounds in order—for example, if in the following diagram one either descends to any fourth sound or counts four sounds in order, as follows:

In it, accordingly, the voices may be called not so much consonant as equal-sounding, and in it the voice is renewed anew. The double proportion brings these consonant sounds to you.”]

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0971A] Certainly, consonance is not produced only from one particular sound to the fourth, fifth, or eighth; rather, almost every sound, both toward the lower and toward the higher side, answers to sounds four degrees away in diatessaron, and each answers to sounds five degrees away in diapente, while every sound on both sides of itself resounds at the diapason with the sound an octave away. Again, just as each sound answers to the middle diapason at the eighth interval on either side, so, as has been said, the sounds at the fifteenth interval answer one another in disdiapason. Thus the space of the diapason is always completed by diatessaron and diapente. For the two middle sounds in this interval, while answering on either side to diatessaron and diapente, produce the result that whichever of them is diapente on one side is diatessaron on the other, and whichever is diatessaron to the one is diapente to the other side. Thus the greatest symphony is completed by two lesser ones.

Moreover, the greatest symphony is called diapason because in it a more perfect consonance than in the others is produced [Note: [Col. 0972D] Read: “than the others.” Below: “Consider how, at the extremes, the voice is rendered one. / Attend, that Ptolemy’s saying may rule in your mouth. / And all the melodies of these are unfolded in order. / While one voice is added to the pair, as one to the fair sun. / Beneath these equal-sounding ones are seven dissonant signs.”]: whether one begins from the higher or the lower sound, when one changes the voice at the eighth degree to a higher or lower one, it is regarded as unison with the first voice, as one sings [Col. 0971C].

Thus the succession of sounds advances without limit, so that from each sound, at intervals of eight, a new order emerges with a voice reborn, so to speak; and, as with the days, the eighth is the first and the first the eighth. Hence Virgil too says, in connection with Orpheus in Elysium, “He strikes out seven distinctions of voices in his measures”—that is, the order of sounds is continued through seven unequal voices, but at the eighth it changes into a new one.

For just as, in the decimal number, whatever is added to it remains within it, whole and undiminished, while this does not happen in the other numbers, so it is also in this consonance. If you add two to three, you immediately produce five, and the form of the number is changed. But if you add the same numbers to ten, you make twelve, and the binary number joined to ten remains preserved. The ternary likewise, and the others in the same way. Thus the diapason symphony preserves whatever other consonance it receives: it neither changes it nor turns a consonance into a dissonance.

From this it follows that, just as fifteen—which consists of two eighths—are mixed together consonantly, so every pitch sounds through diapason at the twelfth just as it does at the fifth in diapente; and just as it sounds at the fourth, so it sounds at the eleventh in diatessaron. A remarkable relation must also be observed here: although, whether one sings freely or examines the sounds in sequence, the same sounds are found to be ninths to ninths, not eighths to eighths, nevertheless in the symphony [Col. 0972B] not only in diapason, which proceeds at the eighth interval, but also in the marvelous transformation of bisdiapason, eighths and eighths are identical.

## CHAPTER XII. Likewise, concerning the same symphonies

There are four modes in which the first symphony, called diatessaron, is found. Although each differs from the others by a concordant diversity of character, and although harmony is woven from their tetrachord as from an element, it is nevertheless necessary that, through successive groups of four and four, sounds of the same condition should always emerge at the fifth; and that, through the comparison of fifths, a symphony of the same condition or quality, as has been shown, should answer to it. This is called diapente.

Although something has already been said about its force [Col. 0972C], as also about the others, nevertheless, so that what follows may be explained more clearly, let its principle be examined again through the following representation of the strings. As before, let the progression of the strings be arranged opposite the signs of the sounds, with the diapente symphony placed between the strings, as follows: [Col. 0972D]

Therefore, when one thing after another is sung at the fifth interval according to the principle of this diagram, you will perceive that they sound consonantly with one another by the diapente symphony, as belonging to the same kind of quality.

But among those four sounds, each distinguished from the others by natural law through the fourfold arrangement of tones and semitones, it cannot happen that a melody of the same condition or mode [Col. 0973A] can remain unchanged if it is transposed from some sounds to others. We touched on this somewhat above, and it must now be repeated more fully with renewed examples.

Let the series of tetrachords be spread out as before, as if arranged in order, and let the same melody, which has now been set out in the diapente symphony [Col. 0974A], be expressed through four or five descriptions of the tones. You will see that the same melodic form cannot remain unchanged in its transposition, but that, through the distance of an epogdoic interval or of a semitone, each mode is transformed into another, as follows: [Col. 0973]

[Col. 0973B] If you make the first diagram, which begins and ends on the sound and is assigned to the first mode, higher by one whole degree or interval throughout—as the small line inserted between the strings indicates—it is immediately changed into the deuteros mode, which begins on a sound and ends on the same sound. Make it two degrees higher, beginning from the sound /, and it will be the tritos mode; if three, the fourth mode will arise. If it is raised still one interval higher, it will again be the first at the fifth position; and similarly in the other cases, the original order returns after the fifth.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the character of the symphonies

[Note: [Col. 0973C] From this point the Paris manuscript, Royal Library, differs substantially and gives other rules, more concise [Col. 0974C] but exceedingly obscure, concerning diaphonia or organum. We have placed the more important matters in our work on chant and music for the reader to infer, Book II, Part II, chapter I.]

It has now been shown how each sound in the tetrachord differs from another by its own distinctive condition, and how, from their concordant diversity, different species of modes or tones [Col. 0973C] arise. It has also been stated at which intervals voices separated from one another successively produce individual symphonies. Let us now pursue what symphonies properly are and how they are constituted—that is, how the same voices relate to one another when sung together.

This is what we call a diaphonic chant, or, in the customary term, organum. It is called diaphonia because it does not consist of uniform singing, but of a concordant dissonance in combination. Although this is common to all symphonies, the name has especially come to be used of diatessaron and diapente.

First, let an example of an organum melody in diatessaron be supplied: according to the following diagram, when two sounds have been inserted between them, let one voice answer another by singing together at the fourth interval, as follows:

For when two or more sing together with only a restrained and concordant slowness, you will see that, from this mixture of sounds, a sweet combination arises, which is the proper character of this melody.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the higher diaphonia by diatessaron, and its diagram

A simple voice is not joined only to a simple voice in this arrangement. A simple organum may also answer a double voice, or a double voice a simple organum; and if both are doubled through the diapason, you will perceive that voices in such proportions sound sweetly with one another, according to the following diagram.

[Col. 0973]

[Col. 0975A] Explanation of the same diagram

Whether you add a double organum to a simple chant—which can be represented by the first and third verses, which serve as organum for the second verse—or refer a simple organum to a double chant—which is represented by the second and fourth verses, containing the organum in their middle—or double both the organum and the chant, or even make both triple, they are consonant with one another according to the arrangement shown.

Human voices, and also voices in certain musical instruments, can be joined in this way not only two and two but also three and three, provided that, whether one voice or three voices are uttered together in a single impulse, an equal number of voices answer as organum.

Here one must observe that the middle voice does not stand at an equal distance from the two others, since in the number eight there is no half of unity. Rather, if from the lower side it answers the chant at the interval of a diatessaron, from the upper side it answers at the interval of a diapente.

[Col. 0976A] To make this clearer for those who do not know it, without tediousness to those who do: if a man’s voice is organized together with a child’s voice, these two voices are consonant with one another by the diapason. But with respect to the voice which they contain between them—the voice to which both answer as organum—the higher voice, which is the child’s, stands five degrees above it, while the man’s voice is four degrees lower.

Thus the symphonies bind one another by a related connection: whatever sound on this side stands in a fourth relation to another, on the other side looks back to that same sound at the fifth interval through the diapason.

## CHAPTER XV. A diagram of the higher diaphonia by diapente

Again, when diaphonia is sung by diapente with three or four voices, the voice which stands at the fifth degree on the lower side must answer the middle voice from the higher side at the fourth degree through the diplasion, in this manner: [Col. 0975]

[Col. 0975C] Explanation of the same diagram

The four-part series of this diagram, arranged in the same order as the preceding one, has organum answering the middle voice in both the first and the third verse, to the middle voice in the second and fourth. The third verse, which is in the middle, joins in diapason consonance with the simple organum, or at least indicates a double organum together with a double chant.

Here too you see that, from below, the third verse is compared with the second at the fifth interval; and again the third with the fourth, while the first is consonant with the second at the interval of a fourth. By these arrangements the two symphonies mingle various sweet melodies.

## CHAPTER XVI. What Boethius reports Ptolemy to have thought about these matters: namely, concerning the consonance of diapason and diatessaron

[Col. 0975D]

Here we can judge Ptolemy’s assertion to appear the more truthful—an assertion which Boethius records him as having held against the Pythagoreans, who say that diapason and diatessaron are not consonances. Certainly, whether you sing either of these diagrams with a double voice and organum, a double voice is joined to a double voice as though a simple voice were added to a simple one.

Likewise, if we join those singing together—the second and fourth verses of the preceding diagram—and add the fifth, only four degrees toward the lower side, then diatessaron is consonant with diapason in the proper way. Let us sing according to the following diagram, joining the fourth and second and adding the first; similarly, this consonance agrees with diapason.

The aforementioned distinguished teacher continues the same matter, according to Ptolemy’s view, in the fifth book of his musical theory, placing the higher sounds on the nearer side and the lower ones on the farther side, as follows: [Col. 0977A]

“For,” he says, “the diapason consonance produces such a joining of voices that it seems to be one and the same string; and the Pythagoreans too agree with this. Therefore, if any consonance is added to it, it remains whole and undiminished.

“Thus diatessaron is added to the diapason consonance as though to a single string. Let the diapason consonance, then, be contained between hypate meson and nete diezeugmenon. These two agree and are joined to one another in sound so completely that one voice, as though struck from a single string rather than mixed from two, reaches the ear.

“Whatever consonance, therefore, we join to this diapason consonance is preserved intact, because it is joined as though to a single little voice and string. If, then, hypate meson and nete diezeugmenon have been joined by a diatessaron toward the higher register, nete diezeugmenon is joined to nete hyperbolaeon, while hypate meson is joined to mese. Each will be consonant with each: mese with nete diezeugmenon, and the same mese with hypate meson; likewise nete hyperbolaeon with nete diezeugmenon and with hypate meson.

“Again, if both diatessaron consonances are extended toward the lower side, then to mese—which is hypaton—there will be hypate hypaton, retaining the consonance of diatessaron; while to nete diezeugmenon there will be paramese. Hypate hypaton and hypate meson will also be consonant with nete diezeugmenon.

“Paramese, moreover, will have nete diezeugmenon and hypate meson, but in such a way that the lower note, which retains a diatessaron consonance with the one nearest to it, has with the farther note [Col. 0978A] a diatessaron and diapason. Thus hypate hypaton has with hypate meson a diatessaron, but with nete diezeugmenon a diatessaron and diapason.

“Likewise nete hyperbolaeon, which is the higher note, has with the nete diezeugmenon nearest to it the consonance of diatessaron; with hypate meson, a diatessaron and diapason; and so forth.”

This is what Boethius says.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the order of consonances, consonance and dissonance

Furthermore, with regard to diapason and disdiapason, no further diagram is needed. They occur so naturally in singing at every age that they require no instruction in the art. It has been sufficiently stated in the discussion of disdiapason that the middle voice is compared with both at the eighth interval, while the extreme voices answer one another at the fifteenth.

Nevertheless, the measure proper to each symphony must be stated. The diatessaron symphony consists of two tones and a semitone, and the diapason symphony consists of two such units. Therefore, in the diapason symphony, voices of different kinds resound with one another with greater perfection than in the others.

The second after this is the diapente symphony. But in diatessaron, since pitches four degrees apart do not agree sweetly throughout the entire series of sounds, a melody is not produced there with the same completeness as in the other symphonies.

Accordingly, in this kind of song, voices are divinely accommodated to one another by a certain rule of their own. Throughout the whole series of sounds, the tritus subquartus [Note: [Col. 0977D] Bl. reads “tritus quartus subquartus,” etc.] is consonant; only the deuteros falls short of the symphony and becomes dissonant with it, because alone among them it exceeds the measure of the diatessaron symphony and is separated from the aforesaid sound, to which it is subquartus, by three whole tones.

Therefore the voice called organal ordinarily accompanies the other voice, called principal, in such a way that in every tetrachord and in every division it neither descends in position below the tetrardus sound nor rises in its beginning, because of the dissonance of the tritus sound, which is immediately below the tetrardus. To make this clearer, let it be set out in a diagram as it can be displayed to the eye.

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977D] By singing according to this diagram, one easily perceives how, in the two parts shown, just as the organal voice cannot begin its answer below the tetrardus sound, so it cannot proceed in position below that same sound. For this reason it is occupied by the principal voice at the finality of the positions, so that both may meet together, while the organum seeks places now higher, now lower. [Col. 0978D]

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the organum seeks places now higher, now lower

Since, then, it is confined within a narrow interval by the opposition of the aforesaid limit [Col. 0979A], and the organal voice has room only in three or four sounds, it consequently changes according to the position and location of the divisions. For as the divisions wander—while the chant now rises upward and now descends to the depths, and while each division at one time occupies a position around the higher sounds, at another around the final sounds, and sometimes around the lower ones—the organal voice always follows the finality of the positions by this rule: below the tetrardus sound at which the finality of the division has arrived, or which is nearest to that finality, it can neither begin a rise nor properly bring the begun chant to its final resting place. [Col. 0979]

[Col. 0979B] Thus, in the first two preceding divisions—“King of heaven,” “Lord of the sea resounding with waves,” and “and of radiant Titan”—the first three syllables, which sound tetrardus, archous, and deuteros, have no organal answer below the tetrardus, namely because of the dissonance of the deuteros sound with the tritus sound, which is immediately below the tetrardus.

The same applies in the following phrases, “You, humble servants,” and “they beg that you command them,” when they stand at a higher rise and position: at a higher place the organum is likewise confined by the same rule. For in the three principal sounds—tetrardus, archous, deuteros—the organal voice cannot properly answer below the tetrardus; rather, it remains on the same sound until it finds its established answer immediately below it.

[Col. 0979C] So that it may be clearly discerned how greatly the dissonance of the two aforesaid sounds dominates in the diatessaron symphony, let us sing something through a fourfold transposition, so that it may appear how, in different transpositions, the voice accompanies the other voice in a different manner but not according to a different rule.

Let this therefore be the first diagram, which was also arranged above, beginning from a sound and ending on the same sound, where the organal voice accompanies the principal voice.

[Col. 0979D]

By singing in this way you will perceive that, despite the dissonance of the deuteros and tritus [Col. 0980B] sounds, the rise of the organal voice is imposed consonantly at the sub-fourth interval; but, because the same dissonance obstructs it, its position does not pass beyond the tetrardus sound.

Let us take the second transposition, which begins from a sound and ends on the same sound.

By singing in this way you will perceive that, both in rising and in position, the organal answer fails at the deuteros sound, and therefore does not descend beyond the tetrardus. [Col. 0980C]

Let us take the third transposition, which begins and ends on the tritus sound:

This transposition, since it proceeds chiefly through the deuteros sound, does not properly receive an organal answer.

Let us take the fourth transposition, which begins from the tetrardus sound and ends on the same sound.

[Col. 0980D]

By singing in this way you will perceive how the organal voice begins from the tetrardus sound and ends on it, and cannot proceed below it, because of the tritus [Col. 0981A] sound, which, as has often already been said, is dissonant with the deuteros.

Something of the outward surface of musical art has thus been indicated for the adornment of ecclesiastical songs. Yet it also contains, inwardly, a no less venerable object of contemplation. Why certain sounds agree with one another in so sweet a mixture, while other sounds, unwilling to blend with one another, disagree unpleasantly, belongs to a deeper and divine reason; and in certain matters it lies among the most hidden secrets of concealed nature.

Many works of the ancients have been written on this subject. Into their labors, in this respect also, the Lord has permitted us to enter. There it is established by thoroughly tested arguments that the same principle of proportion which governs the concords of voices also modulates the natures of mortals; and that by the same numerical parts through which unequal sounds, when compared with one another, agree, life with bodies, the strife of the elements, and the whole world have come together in eternal harmony.

## CHAPTER XIX. That in some matters the depth of this principle is less penetrable

The ancients invented the story that Aristaeus fell in love with Eurydice, the wife of Orpheus, and that while she fled from him she was killed by a serpent. By Orpheus—whose name, “Oreophone,” means “excellent voice”—we understand a skilled singer or one whose song is sweet. His Eurydice—that is, “deep discernment”—if a good man, which is what Aristaeus signifies, follows lovingly, so that it cannot be held completely, divine wisdom is intercepted, as if by a serpent.

But when it is summoned again from its secrets, as if from the underworld, through Orpheus—that is, through the excellent sound of song—it is imaginatively brought as far as the air of this life; and while it seems to be seen, it is lost. This is because, among the other things which we still see only partly and in an enigma, this discipline too does not possess a rationale fully penetrable in the present life.

We can indeed judge whether the construction of a melody is sound, recognize the qualities of sounds and modes, and understand the other features of this art. We can also reduce the intervals of musical sounds and the symphonies of voices to numerical proportion and give certain accounts of consonance and disagreement.

But how music has so great an exchange and fellowship with our souls—even though we know that we are joined to it by a certain likeness—we cannot explain clearly. Nor are we able to judge melody solely from the natural character of sounds, but also from that of things. For the emotions of the things being sung ought to be imitated by the emotions of the song: in calm matters, the neumes should be calm; in joyful matters, they should be joyful; in sad matters, mournful; what is harshly said or done should be expressed by harsh neumes, shaped according to sudden, clamorous, agitated, and other qualities of events and emotions. The divisions of neumes and words should likewise end together.

Although our judgment can operate in such matters, many things nevertheless remain hidden from us under more secret causes.

There are sometimes things that can be received equally fittingly in this mode or that mode, so that they can be sung. There are sometimes things that by no means assign their meaning equally to this mode and that, so that, if transposed, they either do not retain their former sweetness or become unfitting in relation to their meaning.

It is said that wild animals and birds take greater pleasure in certain modes than in others; but why or how this or that should be so is not easily investigated. Therefore, let us use only for the praises of God what, by God’s gift, we understand in this art; and let us employ in jubilation, celebration, and singing those things which the laborious inquiry of the ancients discovered for us—things that were not known to the sons of men in earlier generations but have now been revealed to his saints.

The outstanding author Boethius discloses many marvels of the musical art, demonstrating everything in detail through the mastery of numbers. If God permits, the following little work will contain some excerpt from him. Here, then, let us bring this brief discourse to an end.

[Col. 0981]

## ON THE ART OF MUSIC

[Col. 0981D] **Student.** What is music?

**Teacher.** The science of singing well.

**Teacher.** To regulate a melody with a pleasing sound. But as to how far this belongs to the art—

**Student.** What does it mean to sing well?

I do not see that one sings well if one abuses the sweetness of the art in vain things; nor does the person himself know how to use the art properly when it is required, although anyone can sing sweetly to the Lord with a devoted heart.

**Student.** I think so.

[Col. 0982D] **Teacher.** You think correctly: melodies become good only through good use; nor is it good to use sacred melodies if they are delivered unpleasantly without discipline. Since this discipline is especially necessary for ecclesiastical songs, so that they are not disfigured by negligence or incompetence, let us see what is required for the ability to sing well.

**Student.** I see that there are many things which a singer ought to observe; if he does not know them, he cannot be an expert. But it is your task to explain them more reliably.

[Col. 0983A] **Teacher.** Some things are demanded by the proper character of sounds; others by the principle of numerical proportion; others again by those external circumstances which arise and to which the discipline of singing suitably conforms itself.

**Student.** What are these sounds?

**Teacher.** Here we call sounds *phthongi*, that is, little voices concordant in song; they are the elements of harmony. For just as speech consists of letters, so harmony consists of phthongi.

**Student.** What is demanded by the proper character of the sounds?

**Teacher.** That nothing in them should become dissonant through a corrupted natural quality.

**Student.** How does this dissonance occur in the phthongi?

**Teacher.** If they are pronounced either too sluggishly or more sharply than they ought to be. This defect first damages both the quality of the sounds in human voices and the whole song. It occurs when what is sung becomes too low through a slack relaxation, or is not properly driven upward.

This defect cannot occur in musical instruments, because, once the order of the phthongi has been arranged, each sound retains its own pitch. Another dissonance occurs when one sound is measured falsely against another—that is, when one is used in place of another. A third dissonance occurs when one sound does not answer another at the degree at which it ought to do so.

These last two defects arise from the same cause, but they differ in this: the former occurs within the same neume, while the latter occurs in leading and responding.

**Student.** Explain how these two defects arise.

**Teacher.** Since harmony consists of four sounds suitably distinct from one another, each retains its own quality only in its own order and does not give another a place in its own position. I think you already know their sequence.

**Student.** I entrust everything rather to your instruction; I shall hear these sounds as you sing them.

**Teacher.** Behold, I shall sing:

Thus they are arranged downward.

[Col. 0983D] Thus they are arranged upward.

In ancient times names were assigned to them. The first, that is, the gravest, is called *Protos* or *archous*. The second is *Deuteros*, which is separated from the Protos by a tone. The third is *Tritos*, which is separated from the Deuteros by a semitone. The fourth is *Tetrardos*, which is again distinguished from the Tritos by a tone.

They are also marked by signs of the following kind. The first is the sign F, *dasian*, inclined toward the head, thus: . The second is c, turned toward the head, thus: . The third is a simple and inclined iota, thus: /. The fourth is c, reversed toward the head, thus: .

**Student.** How can harmony consist of only these four, rather than of a multitude of sounds?

[Col. 0984A] **Teacher.** There are obviously innumerable sounds in songs. But the plurality of sounds increases as groups of four and four of the same condition follow one another in rising and falling. Prove this also as I sing:

Thus, in every concordant series of sounds, the song proceeds upward and downward through these tetrachords, as it were; and four little voices, differing from one another in a social succession, remain joined to one another in a fitting sequence until they either fail through becoming too attenuated or fall silent through being lowered.

Furthermore, each of the individual sounds from the four tetrachords mentioned above presides over its own pentachords.

They belong to tetrachords when four sounds are successively lowered through each one, as follows: [Col. 0984B]

[Col. 0984C] They belong to pentachords when one is added toward the higher side, so that the same sound becomes both first and last, as follows: [Col. 0984D]

The pentachord that begins and ends with the archous sound we call the first pentachord. It consists of two tones, a semitone, and a tone.

The pentachord that begins with the deuteros sound is the second pentachord; it consists of three tones and a semitone.

The pentachord that begins with the tritus sound is the third pentachord; it consists of a semitone and three tones.

The pentachord that begins with the tetrardus sound is the fourth pentachord; it consists of a tone and a semitone, and two tones.

**Student.** What, then, is a semitone?

[Col. 0985A] **Teacher.** We call semitones, or *limmata*, intervals that are not complete sound-spaces. Nevertheless, when placed in their proper position, they both assign their proper character to the sounds and contain the song within the sweetness of concordance. When they are not placed in their proper position, they make the melodies disagree.

For one must understand that the natural quality is ordered in the series of sounds when the sounds are measured against one another by their natural interval. But if one sound is measured falsely against another, it immediately moves into a different quality and overturns the order that was begun. This is the first of the two kinds of dissonance mentioned above.

**Student.** I detect this dissonance too.

**Teacher.** Observe also a fourth form of dissonance in this category, contrary to the second: if, on the following side, /, from the tritus, another tritus is measured as if from the tetrardus. Let there be a pentachord from the protus: [Col. 0987C]

**Student.** I recognize that too, because, instead of the deuteros being measured from the tritus sound /, a tritus is abusively measured from the tritus / as though from the tetrardus, at an interval longer than it should be.

**Teacher.** And if we add a pentachord of such a kind that it is damaged on both sides by these defects, the dissonance will be of this form. Let there be a pentachord of the tetrardus:

**Student.** Certainly dissonant; there is nothing pleasant in what you sound.

[Col. 0988A] **Teacher.** Having understood, then, how one sound is measured falsely against another, let us see how it also happens that, when sounds do not answer sounds at the degrees where they ought, melodies do not resound concordantly with one another.

**Student.** I ask for that as well.

**Teacher.** Come here, then, and observe how the order of the fourfold variety is arranged in tetrachords or pentachords, so that you may clearly contemplate at what interval one sound is constituted from any other.

For just as, if colors are placed four and four in order and arranged in a line—for example, red, green, yellow, black—it is necessary that each color should be found at the fifth place after three other colors have intervened, so it also happens with sounds: as they continually follow one another in a new repetition, each is answered on both sides by its counterpart at the fifth place. [Col. 0988B]

**Student.** How, you ask, can they be counterparts when they differ in height and depth?

**Teacher.** They differ in height and depth, certainly, but by a certain natural association they are nevertheless concordant with one another. Moreover, each sound which it has as the second on one side has as the fourth on the other; and the one which it has as the third on this side it has as the third on the other.

But I have said this according to the way in which the order of the fourfold variety is arranged in the continuation of the tetrachords.

**Student.** To distinguish which sound is this one or that one, I wish to know the particular quality belonging to each of them.

[Col. 0988C] M. You rightly ask this. For when the distinct qualities of the sounds are first clearly understood, there is less error in the other matters. But you will easily acquire the ability to distinguish these through practice. Therefore, take a melody to sing that ends, for example, on the sound *archus*. Immediately add another that begins from the same sound, or from its higher or lower counterpart; or let it begin from the fourth sound, or from the second sound.

Thus, unless what is to be added begins on the sound *archus*, you should place it either at the same pitch as the final sound of the preceding melody, or exactly five places above or five places below it. But what begins from the sound *tetrardus* should be placed either two places below or three places above. Again, what begins from the sound *tritus* should be placed either three places below or three places above. But what begins from the sound *deuterus* should be placed either two places above or four places below. Otherwise, according to the following description of the sounds, what follows cannot agree with what precedes.

The same occurs with all sounds: what follows cannot be brought into one body of concord with what precedes if they are mutually joined above or below, when the proper measure determines the ending of the one and the beginning of the other. Therefore, wherever this concord must be observed, the ending and beginning sounds must measure one another according to their natural order. But where this is neglected, or where there is no need to observe it, the sounds of the things sung can indeed proceed concordantly within themselves; yet, when one is joined to another, they cannot be united concordantly. It must therefore be left to the singer’s skill to know where one thing may suitably follow another in concord and where this is unnecessary.

Enough has also been said about this discrepancy. It should nevertheless be understood that the first concordance is that which is produced in the manner mentioned above, according to the course of the melody. The second is a somewhat lesser concordance, when, wishing either to ease the difficulty of a higher elevation or to raise a more subdued gravity, we join one passage to another by transposing it upward or downward by five places. There is also a third concordance, which is made in the eighth region of the sounds—that is, when we change the melody into a new, sharper voice. By these comparisons of melodies a certain unanimity can be preserved; otherwise it cannot, unless the entire melody is altered by transposing it into another form. If you transpose any melody within the same series of sounds by the interval of one, two, or three sounds, either higher or lower, the form of the mode also changes into another species.

D. Give an example of this change.

M. For example, if I sing five tetrachords or pentachords in succession in this manner: [Col. 0989C]

Just as, by singing in this way, the pentachord of the first mode, made one interval higher, is changed into the pentachord of the second; from the second it passes into the third, from the third into the fourth, and from the fourth returns again to the first—so whatever you transpose entirely by one, two, or three tones, higher or lower, will likewise be transformed into another mode.

For example, the customary regular neume for the first tone is this:

Therefore, if I make the entire structure of this regular neume one interval higher, it will immediately become the second tone instead of the first. Similarly, when transposed from the second, it will arrive at the third mode. Again, if the third tone is raised by one interval, the fourth follows. If it receives the sharpness of one further interval, the first is born again. What if these same examples were also represented by little diagrams? Would not everything become clearer, as though set before the eyes?

D. Certainly.

M. Let us therefore arrange five little diagrams in lines, expressing these successive transpositions of the tones as they are connected to one another, in this manner: [Col. 0990B]

[Col. 0990D] The first little diagram is of the first mode, the second of the second, the third of the third, the fourth of the fourth, and the fifth again of the same mode as the first. In this way, as has been said, whatever melody you transpose will immediately be changed into another species of mode. And if the change of the mode is greater, the mode into which it has been transformed will also be greater.

The *tropi*, or modes, are those which people improperly call tones. I think you have by now learned the distinction and number of each of them.

D. I have indeed learned them.

M. Sing some melodies in the first mode, in the second also, and in the remaining modes.

D. Here is the first mode. Here is the second. Here is the third. Here also is the fourth.

M. Now tell me how they are judged by the ears to differ from one another in a certain diversity, and what is the cause of their diversity.

D. They are perceived as differing from one another by a certain distinguishable quality proper to each. But I wonder what causes this.

M. To begin making this somewhat clear, give me a first tetrachord, or at least a pentachord.

D. Here—I have sung it.

M. Apply to it whatever modes of the first mode you wish, and you will see that everything sung in the first mode ends on the first sound.

D. I see that this is so.

M. Now give me another pentachord, one interval higher, beginning from the second sound and ending on it. [Col. 0991B]

D. It is sung in this way.

M. Sing melodies of the second mode, and compare them with the second sound, to see whether they happen to end on it.

D. They do indeed.

M. Now give me a third pentachord, two intervals higher, beginning, of course, from the third sound and ending on that same sound.

D. It is as follows.

M. Apply the modes of the third tone to it, and you will find that they end on the third sound.

D. Certainly.

M. Now give me a fourth pentachord, three intervals higher—that is, beginning from the fourth sound. [Col. 0991C]

D. It is made in this way.

M. Now examine the modes of the fourth tone, to see whether you perceive them to rest on the fourth sound.

D. I perceive this most clearly.

M. Now give me a fifth pentachord, and again, with a new tetrachord, the same order of sounds and modes returns.

D. This too is certainly astonishing.

M. The power of each sound therefore gives form to the melodies. Accordingly, note now in those four *phthongi* the remarkable power of variation and the distinctive character proper to each, by which they differ from one another and, according to themselves, produce the distinctions among the modes.

D. I seem to see this to some extent. But I wonder: since it is customary to count eight modes, why do you say that no more than four are generated by these sounds?

M. We customarily count eight modes, but in such a way that two modes—a greater and a lesser—are governed by each of the sounds in a tetrachord, and for that reason are assigned to one mode, since they are governed by the same sound: by *archus* or *first*, the authentic first and the plagal; by the second, the authentic second and the plagal; by the third, the authentic third and the plagal; by the fourth, the authentic fourth and the plagal. We properly call the authentic mode “authoritative,” and the plagal “subordinate” or “lateral.” Thus each is recognizable both by the quality proper to it and by the tetrachords and pentachords over which it presides; and, as has been said, they distinguish the tones or modes.

D. Does the power of the final sound alone therefore produce any mode, so that a mode or tone is called the mode or tone of this or that sound simply because the melody ends on it?

M. The power of any mode does seem chiefly to reside in whatever final sound it has, because the mode rests there when it ends. Yet it must also be added that this same final sound and its more frequent associates occur at the ends of *commata* or *cola*. Each sound has its associates not only five regions away, but also seeks other counterparts four places away, which is the position of the third concord. Thus, in the small divisions that are members of a song, the *cola* or *commata* almost always seek these associations of sounds in raising or lowering; either the rising movement or the falling movement strives to reach them. Proper melodies provide sufficiently valid examples. To avoid searching farther, look at the regular neume, or the small phrase, which we have at hand and which is completed by two *commata*.

Observe how the placement of both *commata* tends toward the fourth sounds, and how the phrase begins from one sound and lowers itself at the end onto that same sound. We call larger phrases *cola*: they contain two, three, or more *commata* and also provide certain appropriate divisions of their own. *Commata*, joined to one another in their rises and falls, complete a *colon*; nevertheless, there are occasions when the same unit may indifferently be called either a *colon* or a *comma*.

D. How do the greater and lesser tones differ from one another if they end on the same sound and are governed by the same sound?

M. We shall explain what must be said about this more conveniently after first describing the proper signs of the sounds. We assign signs to eighteen sounds, namely, four tetrachords and a half-tetrachord. The first, which is the lowest, we call the grave tetrachord; the second, the final tetrachord; the third, the higher; and the fourth, the excellent. We designate the little sounds that we call “final” with the signs described above, thus: ; the grave sounds with nearly the same signs, but facing backward, thus: ; the higher sounds with the final signs turned downward, thus: ; and the excellent sounds with the grave signs turned downward, thus: . The third sound is exceptional: in the grave sounds it has an inclined N, N; in the higher sounds an inverted and inclined N; and in the excellent sounds an iota pierced through, X. We express the remaining two voices with reclining signs, arranged in order as follows: [Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991D] D. How can I distinguish which are the final sounds, which are the higher sounds, and which belong to this or that order?

M. It is established that everything musical is relative to something. For no sound can be musical without the addition of another sound, in relation to which it sounds musically at its natural interval. Therefore, just as what is relative to something cannot be understood by itself, so when several sounds are listed absolutely, they cannot properly be called higher, final, or of any other order. But since whatever is sung correctly must end higher or lower on one of those four sounds, whichever of them is the final point becomes, together with the other sounds of its tetrachord, the final sound. From this the other tetrachords take their order. From the same sound it also takes its measure, whether the tone is greater or lesser.

For since we cannot place every lower tone five places higher, nor every higher tone five places lower, as was shown above, a sound is not called higher or lower because one is sung higher or lower than another, but according to the relation that the two tones have to the final sound. They have it in this way. From the final sound, the lesser tone has equal power to reach upward and downward—that is, on either side, as far as sounds five places away. This does not mean that it always does so, but that such is the extent of its interval. If, however, it passes through the system to the fifth sound on the higher side, it is usually assigned to the greater tone. The greater tone has twice the interval of the system on the higher side, that is, as far as the ninth sound.

D. What is a system?

M. In *cola* or *commata* we call the intervals *diastemata*; in more complete phrases, or in an entire period, we call them systems. A *diastema* is any interval of sounds embraced by a phrase—that is, the span within which the higher and lower voice are contained. A system is the interval of the entire melody. Systems are also the species of tetrachords, pentachords, and octachords, which give each mode its particular species [Note: [Col. 0993D] Teg. C. adds: “For whenever a song begins higher by a tone or semitone in tetrachords, pentachords, or double intervals, another species is immediately produced.”].

D. Why is one tetrachord established among the final sounds, but two above the final sounds?

M. Because, whether any simple and legitimate melody is sung in a higher or a lower voice, it descends no farther than the fifth sound from its final sound, and ascends no farther than the ninth.

Thus the preceding discussion concerning the kinds of discrepancies to be avoided has reached its conclusion. We shall now proceed to what, with God’s gift, must be said for the adornment of melody. First of all, we must see that every melody is delivered rhythmically.

D. What does it mean to sing rhythmically?

M. It means attending to where longer and where shorter pauses should be used. Just as one observes which syllables are short and which are long, so one must observe which sounds should be prolonged and which shortened, so that what lasts longer may properly correspond with what does not last as long, and so that the song may be measured as though by metrical feet. Come, let us sing as an exercise: I shall beat the feet while leading, and you will imitate by following.

[Note: [Col. 0993] To view the following two lines as printed in Migne, double-click the ornament icon that follows.]

“I am the way, the truth, and the life. Alleluia, alleluia.”

[Col. 0994A] Only the final notes in the three members are long; the rest are short. Thus to sing rhythmically is to measure fixed pauses with long and short sounds, neither prolonging nor shortening them in places more than is appropriate, but keeping the voice within the rule of scansion, so that the melody may end with the same pause with which it began. If, however, on occasion you wish to alter the pause for the sake of variation—that is, to make the movement more extended or more rapid around the beginning or the end—you should do so by doubling it: turn a prolonged pause into one twice as short, or a shortened pause into one twice as long.

D. I think it is useful to try each of these things and turn them into practice.

M. You think rightly. For this reason, let us take whatever melody you wish to sing, sometimes more briefly and sometimes more fully, so that the pauses that are now prolonged may then become short in relation to their own shortened forms, and those that are now short may likewise become prolonged in relation to those that are more extended. Let us sing as follows: the first pause is made shorter; a prolonged pause follows; then a short pause again.

[Note: [Col. 0994] To view the following two lines as printed in Migne, double-click the ornament icon that follows.]

“I am the way, the truth, and the life. Alleluia, alleluia.” [Note: [Col. 0994D] In the codex the same text is placed three times beneath the same signs, without any variation; yet according to the rule proposed, this ought to be done differently.]

This principle of rhythm therefore suits every learned song and adorns it with the greatest distinction, whether it is sung slowly or quickly, by one person or by several. It also happens that, when singing rhythmically, one person prolongs or shortens no more and no less than another, so that the voice of the multitude seems to be heard as though from a single mouth. Likewise, in alternating or responding, the concord of pauses must be preserved by the same rhythmic measure no less than the concord of sounds.

D. How must songs agree with one another through their pauses?

M. The manner in which the concordant joining of songs occurs through the proper position of their several sounds has been shown above. Concord of pauses, however, is achieved if what is to follow responds either with an equal pause, or, for an appropriate reason, with a pause twice as long or twice as short.

D. It is clear that everything mentioned above belongs to a skilled song. Continue, if anything further is necessary for good modulation.

[Col. 0994D] M. I also say that the principle of divisions must be observed: that is, you must know what ought to remain joined and what ought to be separated. You must also see what pause suits this or that melody. For one melody is appropriately sung more quickly, while another becomes sweeter when delivered more slowly. This can immediately be recognized from the very construction of the melody, whether it is composed of light or heavy neumes. Therefore, you will provide each melody with the pause suited to it, according only to the circumstances of time, place, and whatever external cause may arise; and likewise with the pitch suited to the pause and to clear and pleasant neumes. By such observations you will govern music that is dignified and well ordered. [Col. 0996A] Moreover, the fitting mixture of concords will add the greatest sweetness to songs.

[Col. 0995] The first part ends.

THE SECOND PART BEGINS: ON CONCORDS.

[Col. 0995]

[Col. 0995A] D. What is a concord?

M. A sweet mixture of certain voices. There are three simple concords: the diapason, the diapente, and the diatessaron. There are three composite concords: the disdiapason, the diapason with the diapente, and the diapason with the diatessaron.

[Col. 0995B] D. What is the diapason concord?

M. It is sung with six sounds interposed, across the eighth position.

D. What are the diapente and the diatessaron?

M. The diapente is made across the fifth positions, the diatessaron across the fourth, just as the outermost sounds of pentachords and tetrachords correspond to one another.

D. Why is it called diapason?

M. *Diapason* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “from all,” because the ancient cithara contained only eight strings.

D. Why is it called diapente or diatessaron?

M. *Diapente* means “from five,” because it contains five voices. *Diatessaron* means “from four,” because it embraces four voices.

[Col. 0996A] D. How is the diapason sung?

M. When one voice is changed into another either downward or upward, so that the higher and lower voices are not merely consonant but equal-sounding, agreeing in this correspondence, they sing a diapason. For example, if one descends from H to A, or rises from H to P, according to the following diagram: [Col. 0996B]

Whether one voice is taken after another across the eighth positions, or two equal-sounding voices are sung together, a simple diapason song is made in this way. But let us sing three voices together according to the three written parts, and a double diapason song is made in this manner. If, with the middle voice removed, it is sung across the fifteenth positions, it will nevertheless be a disdiapason. Let us sing everything according to the method written above:

On the diapason and disdiapason.

[Col. 0995]

[Col. 0995B] This concord, because it is easier and clearer, is called the greatest and the first.

ON THE DIAPENTE.

The diapente concord follows. It occurs when voices are taken across the fifth regions, one after another, or when both are brought together according to the following method. [Col. 0996B]

[Col. 0997A] To make a diapente simply is therefore done in this way. The first composition is a diapente when the organal voice is doubled by the diapason in such a way that the principal voice is in the middle, like the fifth between the first and the eighth. By “principal voice” I mean the complete song; by “organal voice,” the voice added to it according to the rule of concord. Let us sing according to the method written below: [Col. 0997]

[Col. 0097A] Its second composition is made when the voice that we called principal is doubled by the diapason in such a way that the organal voice is in the middle, like the eighth between the fourth and the eleventh. Let us sing according to the method written below: [Col. 0997]

[Col. 0997A] The third composition of the diapente is made when the organal voice is doubled downward by the diapason, so that the principal voice is the highest, like the twelfth against the eighth and the first. This concord also agrees across the twelfth positions, with the middle voice removed. The fourth composition is likewise a diapente when the principal voice is doubled upward by the diapason, so that the organal voice is the lowest, like the first against the fifth and the twelfth. This likewise has concord when the middle voice is removed.

The fifth composition of the diapente is made when both voices, doubled by the diapason, are sung with four different voices, so that the first and eighth answer the organ at the fifth and twelfth. Let everything be sung according to the method written below.

[Col. 0997]

[Col. 0999A] The sixth composition of the diapente is made when the organal voice is the highest, like the fifteenth against the twelfth and the fifth, according to the method written below. [Col. 1000A]

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 0999B] Either one voice or both may also be tripled by the disdiapason, and the same concord may thereby be varied in many forms.

ON THE DIATESSARON CONCORD.

The diatessaron concord follows. It occurs when voices are joined together across four positions. It should be understood, however, that it is not made as simply as the other, greater concords; rather, the organal voice is derived from it according to another natural law, which will be explained later. Nevertheless, when delivered with measured slowness, which is especially proper to it, and produced with careful concord, it will be a most dignified sweetness of song.

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 0999C] The diatessaron concord is also composed in the same ways as the diapente. Its first composition is made when the organal voice is doubled by the diapason [Col. 1000C] so that the principal voice is in the middle, like the fourth between the first and the eighth, according to the method written below.

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 0999D] Its second composition is made, conversely, when the principal voice is doubled by the diapason so that the organal voice is in the middle, [Col. 1000D] like the eighth between the fourth and the eleventh.

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 1001A] The third composition of the diatessaron is made when the organal voice is doubled downward by the diapason, so that the principal voice is the highest, like the eleventh against the eighth and the first.

The fourth composition of the diatessaron is made when the principal voice is doubled upward by the diapason, so that the organal voice is the lowest, like the first against the fourth and the eleventh. The fifth composition of the diatessaron is made when both voices—the principal and the organal—are doubled by the diapason, so that the first and eighth answer the organ at the fourth and the eleventh.

[Col. 1001] [Col. 1001B] The sixth composition of the diatessaron is made when the organal voice is the highest, like the fifteenth against the eleventh [Col. 1002B] and the fourth. It is sung according to the method written below.

[Col. 1001]

[Col. 1001C] It should also be noted that whenever the principal voice, the organal voice, or both are doubled by the diapason, the voice of a boy can always supply the place of the higher voice.

D. What, I ask, is the difference between the first composition of the diapente and the second composition of the diatessaron, since in both cases the extreme voices are separated from the middle voice by an equal interval? Likewise, what is the difference between the second composition of the diapente and the first composition of the diatessaron?

M. You ask why, in the first composition of the diapente, the middle voice is rather the principal than the organal voice, while in the second composition of the diatessaron the middle voice is rather the organal than the principal voice, although in both cases the middle voice stands at the same intervals from the extremes. Again, you ask why, in the second composition of the diapente, the middle voice is called organal, whereas in the first composition of the diatessaron the middle voice is called principal.

Know that the reason is this: in the diatessaron concord the organal voice does not accompany the principal voice as simply and absolutely as it does in the diapente. Rather, according to its own natural law, it comes to rest at particular positions and cannot proceed farther in concord, as the diagrams mentioned above also show: it does not descend below the fourth sound. It should also be understood that the diatessaron and diapente differ in another respect in the compositions mentioned above. Since the return of modes or tones always occurs at the fifth and eighth positions, when the lower voice responds to the higher voice in the same mode by a diapente, both voices must again be answered from their octave in the same mode. Thus, when the organal voice is doubled by the diapason and the principal voice is in the middle, the lower organal voice is separated from the middle one by fifths and the higher by fourths. This is the first composite diapente.

But when the principal voice is doubled by the diapason and the organal voice is in the middle, the lower principal voice is distinguished from the middle voice by fourths and the higher by fifths. This is the second composite diapente.

Conversely, in the diatessaron, since the lower voice does not answer the higher voice by fourths in the same mode, the principal and organal voices must be answered not in the same mode but each in the mode proper to its own octave. Thus, when the organal voice is doubled by the diapason and the principal voice is in the middle, the lower organal voice is four positions from the middle voice and the higher five positions away. This is the first composite diatessaron.

But when the principal voice is doubled by the diapason and the organal voice is in the middle, the lower principal voice is separated from the middle voice by five positions and the higher by four. This is the second composite diatessaron. All this is shown by the diagrams given above.

D. But what follows from this? You said that the diapente concord sings the same modes, whereas the diatessaron does not sing the same modes; and therefore, in the compositions of the two concords mentioned above, although the middle voice is separated from the extremes by a similar interval, because it is not the same mode in both cases, it is principal in one and organal in the other. I ask what difference there is between the principal and organal voice in the diapente concord, since their modes are not different.

M. Recall what has just been said. If, when the organal voice is doubled in the diapente, the middle voice—that is, the principal voice—had the same interval from the extremes, there would seem to be no difference between the principal and organal voices. But now, since the organal voice is lower than the principal voice by five positions while being higher by four positions through the diapason—and conversely, in the diatessaron, the organal voice is lower than the principal voice by four positions while being higher by five positions through the diapason—you can similarly understand clearly that, when the principal voice is doubled by the diapason, the intervals of the middle voice from the extreme voices are not the same. The power of the diapason, which multiplies both voices, thereby arranges at definite intervals which voices are principal and which are organal.

D. Why, in the diatessaron concord, can the organal voice not agree with the principal voice as absolutely as it does in the other concords?

M. Because, as has been said, the same modes are not found across the fourth regions, and the modes of different tones cannot proceed together through the whole range. Therefore, in the diatessaron concord, the principal and organal voices do not agree throughout the entire fourth region.

D. I would also like to know how the kind of the modes is different across the fourth positions.

M. You will easily perceive it. For whether the melody is transposed one tone higher or four positions lower, the mode of the different tone becomes clearly distinguishable to the ear. Let it be sung according to the method written below:

[Col. 1004A]

D. I plainly distinguish that the authentic first tone passes by this transposition into the authentic second. But now give me the reason why voices are so consonant across some regions, while across others they are either discordant or not so fully in agreement.

M. We may attempt to discover, insofar as the Lord grants the means, the causes of voices that agree sweetly and of those that disagree, and also to apprehend somewhat the nature of the different modes, why they migrate into other species when transposed, or return again to their own. For just as, when counted absolutely, the series of numbers is simple and, by its own ease, evident even to children—one, two, three, four, and so forth—whereas when one thing is compared unequally with another, it falls into various species of inequality, so the *phthongi* in music, whose mother is Arithmetic, that is, numerical science, are indeed listed in an easy order. But when produced in relation to something else, they yield not only species of sweet concords but also the sweetest ratios of those concords.

D. How is harmony generated from Arithmetic as its mother? And is the same harmony also music?

M. Harmony is understood to be a concordant mixture of unequal voices. Music is the principle of their concord. Just as it is joined in every respect to the principle of numbers, and to the other mathematical disciplines, so it must be understood through numbers.

D. What are the mathematical disciplines?

M. Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.

D. What is mathematics?

[Col. 1004D] M. A doctrinal science.

D. Why is it called a doctrinal science?

M. Because it considers abstract quantities.

D. What are abstract quantities?

M. Those which are treated by the intellect alone, without matter—that is, without bodily admixture. In quantities there are multitudes, magnitudes, fewnesses, smallnesses, forms, equalities, relations, and other such things which, to speak in Boethius’s words, are by nature incorporeal and immutable substances, existing through reason, but are changed through participation in body and pass, through contact with changeable matter, into mutable instability.

These quantities are considered one way in Arithmetic, another way in Geometry, and another way in Astronomy. [Col. 1005A] These four disciplines are not arts invented by human beings, but investigations to some degree of divine works. They lead well-born minds, through the understanding of the world’s creation, to the most marvelous principles, so that those who, through these things, know God and his eternal divinity are without excuse if they do not glorify him as God and give thanks.

D. What is Arithmetic?

M. The discipline of numerable quantity considered in itself.

D. What is Music?

M. The rational discipline of consonant and dissonant voices according to numbers that are related to the numbers found in sounds.

D. What is Geometry?

[Col. 1005B] M. The discipline of immovable magnitude and of forms.

D. What is Astronomy?

M. The discipline of movable magnitude. It contemplates the courses and all the figures of the heavenly bodies and investigates, by reasoned inquiry, the relations of the stars to one another and to the earth.

D. How do the other three disciplines depend on the science of number?

M. Because everything comprehended through these disciplines is formed according to the principle of numbers, and cannot be understood or expressed without numbers. For how can one explain what a triangle or quadrilateral is, or anything else belonging to Geometry, unless one first knows what three or four are?

[Col. 1005C] D. In no way.

M. What can be known in astronomical reasoning without number? From what do we learn the risings and settings, the slowness and speed of wandering stars? From what do we recognize the age of the moon and its manifold changes, or what part of the zodiac the sun, moon, or any other planet occupies? Are not all things governed by definite laws of number, and therefore unknown without number?

D. Certainly.

M. What makes voices equal-sounding at the eighth positions, consonant at the fifth and fourth? Likewise, what makes them respond equally across the fifteenth regions, and consonantly across the twelfth and eleventh? What are these measures that join voices so fittingly to one another that, if one voice is slightly sharper or flatter than another, they cannot agree with one another?

D. It is certainly astonishing what kinds of commensurability there are among voices, by which the concords themselves agree with one another so sweetly and the remaining sounds are joined together in such a fitting order. But it is your task to explain what you have proposed.

M. I say that voices are equal-sounding across the eighth positions—that is, in the diapason—because they are compared according to a double ratio: six to twelve, and twelve to twenty-four. Likewise, there is equality of sound across the fifteenth positions, which is called the disdiapason, because it is established in a quadruple proportion, as six to twenty-four.

They respond consonantly across the fifth regions, which is the diapente, because they stand in the sesquialter ratio. The sesquialter ratio is where the lesser contains two parts and the greater three, as six against nine, or eight against twelve.

The voices across the fourth positions are consonant, which is the diatessaron, because they stand in the epitrite ratio. The epitrite, or sesquitertian, ratio is where the lesser has three parts and the greater four, as six against eight, or nine against twelve.

They therefore agree in the twelfth comparison because the diapason responds to the diapente—that is, the sesquialter ratio to the double ratio—as eighteen against twelve and six, and as eight against twelve and twenty-four.
