Or it is because triples are made across the twelfth positions: eighteen against six, and twenty-four against eight.

They are also consonant in the eleventh region because the diatessaron resonates with the diapason—that is, the epitrite ratio with the double ratio—as sixteen against twelve and six, and as nine against twelve and twenty-four.

Likewise, the voices that complete the concords mentioned above—four voices making the diatessaron and five making the diapente—agree by this ratio because the diatessaron and diapente are joined to one another by the epogdous ratio, that is, the sesquioctave ratio. For the difference between the sesquialter and sesquitertian ratios is always epogdous. In whatever proportion eight is to nine, so sixteen is to eighteen, and thirty-two to thirty-six, and so indefinitely.

A diagram of these matters is given below.

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005D] Moreover, the concords in the diapason and disdiapason are more perfect than those in the diatessaron and diapente, because the former belong to multiple inequality, whereas the latter belong to superparticular inequality. Multiple inequality is more perfect than superparticular inequality.

The voices of the proportions mentioned above—double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter, sesquitertian, and sesquioctave—are therefore consonant or equal-sounding because these relative numbers alone, in all the disciplines, are commensurate and numbered together. For this reason they are assigned to concords and to the other musical voices; indeed, melodically modulated voices are produced from these numbers. You understand, then, that music can be explained only by arithmetical ratios?

D. I understand clearly that Arithmetic is necessary for knowledge of music.

M. Entirely necessary, since music has been wholly fashioned according to the pattern of numbers. For if you make one string twice as long as another of equal thickness, or one pipe twice as long as another, so that XII is to VI as XXIIII is to XII, they sound an octave (*diapason*) against one another. If you make a string, or a pipe of equal bore, longer by a third than the other, so that VIII is to VI as XVI is to XII—or make the longer one shorter by a fourth, so that VIIII is to XII as XVIII is to XXIIII—there will indeed be the consonance of a fourth (*diatessaron*), VIII to VI and XVI to XII. Likewise, VIIII to XII and XVIII to XXIIII. Furthermore, VIIII to VI and VIII to XII, and similarly XVIII to XII and XVI to XXIIII, will be a fifth (*diapente*).

This occurs in the following way: just as, within the double proportion, the sesquialter and sesquitertian proportions are contained—for example, between VI and XII there are, alternately, XVI and XVIII—so that what is sesquialter to the smaller number, as VIIII is to VI and XVIII to XII, becomes subsesquitertian to the larger, as VIIII is to XII and XVIII to XXIIII; and again what is sesquitertian to the smaller, as VIII is to VI and XVI to XII, is subsesquialter to the larger, as VIII is to XII and XVI to XXIIII.

Thus, between two sounds that resonate an octave against one another, nature has always arranged the consonances in the fourth and fifth positions, so that the consonance which is a fourth (*diatessaron*) for one side in the fourth position is a fifth (*diapente*) for the other side in the fifth position; and the consonance which sounds as a fourth for that side sounds as a fifth for this one.

Moreover, just as, in the sesquioctave proportion, VIIII exceeds VIII, and XVIII exceeds XVI, and XXXVI exceeds XXXII, so, if a larger pipe or string exceeds a smaller one by an eighth, they sound a tone against one another. Therefore, whatever is pleasing in melody is produced by number through the fixed measurements of sounds; and whatever delight rhythm provides, whether in melodies or in any rhythmic movements, is wholly brought about by number. Sounds pass away swiftly, but numbers—which are discolored by the bodily matter of sounds and movements—remain.

Therefore, as Saint Augustine says, reason, which in rhythms—called *numeri* in Latin—or in melody itself, understood that numbers reign and accomplish everything, examined the matter most diligently and found them divine and everlasting. Then this same reason, surveying heaven and earth, perceived that nothing else pleased it except beauty, and in beauty figures, in figures dimensions, and in dimensions numbers. These, too, it distinguished and arranged into a discipline, and called that discipline Geometry. The movement of heaven greatly stirred it and urged it to consider attentively; there too, through the most constant alternations of time, the fixed and determined courses of the stars, and the measured intervals of their spaces, it understood that nothing else ruled but that same dimension and numbers. Linking these matters into an ordered discipline by defining and separating them in the same way, he brought forth Astrology. Thus, in the mathematical disciplines, everything numerical presents itself; and the numbers that are sensed are rather shadows and images of the immortal numbers apprehended by thought and contemplation.

Who, then, would call the rationale of numbers mutable, or say that any art exists except through it?

D. It now seems sufficiently indicated that not music alone, but also the other three disciplines, depend in their teaching upon numbers. But I ask you to begin treating the nature of numbers more fully, and to review each of the matters already set forth, so that, under the guidance of numbers, I may in some measure reach the inner sanctuaries of musical reasoning.

[Col. 1007] Here ends the second part.

## THE THIRD PART BEGINS

[Col. 1007D]

Disc. I ask you first of all to state what quantity is.

M. We speak of quantity both in numbers and in movable things. Quantity in numbers is properly called multitude, which is assembled from units. The particular kind of quantity that exists in movable things is called magnitude, which is divided into units. For multitude increases through infinite plurality, whereas magnitude is diminished through infinite division. That is, multitude, tending from plurality toward one, increases in extent; magnitude, tending from one toward a plurality of units, diminishes through divisions of extent.

For example, the smaller the number into which a stone or a tree is divided, the greater the intervals of the divisions become; but the more parts into which it is divided, the smaller those intervals themselves become. Thus, of twenty-four, one-half is twelve, one-third is eight, and one-fourth is six; likewise, of twelve, one-half is six, one-third is four, and one-fourth is three.

By the likeness of these two kinds of quantity, therefore, arithmetic draws music forth from itself and, in a marvelous way, arranges melodic sounds in sweet concord through the contrary affections of both. For when one sound increases in relation to another by a double, triple, or quadruple proportion—producing an octave, an octave with a fifth, or a double octave—it preserves the nature of numerical quantity. But when one sound exceeds another by a half, a third, a fourth, or an eighth—producing a fifth, a fourth, or a tone—it bears the image of continuous quantity. Since, therefore, variations of sounds consist in quantity in this way, they agree with one another through a sweet mixture according to the contrary natures of twofold quantity.

[Col. 1009A]

If these matters are now clear, let us continue with what remains.

D. It is indeed clear that this kind belongs to numerical quantity because its increases grow according to the order of numbers. But this belongs to continuous quantity because it decreases by diminution according to the same order of numbers. For just as the former exceeds by a double, so the latter surpasses by a half of one; just as the former becomes three or four times greater, so the latter, correspondingly, becomes a third or a fourth part greater. It remains for you to explain how, and in what order, concord among sounds is arranged through these twofold quantities.

M. To explain this, with the Lord’s help, let us first set forth a few matters about the nature of numbers, as we proposed. We said that there are two species of quantity: multitude and magnitude. Again, of multitude and magnitude, some are immovable and others movable; some exist in themselves, such as a people, a chorus, a mountain, one thousand, two thousand, or three thousand; others do not exist in themselves but are referred to something else, such as double, triple, and quadruple.

Geometry treats of immovable quantity, while Astronomy contemplates movable quantity. Let us therefore contemplate that which exists in itself through arithmetic, and that which is relative to something else because through it divine harmonic sweetness is regulated.

Every number, and everything that is said according to number, is either said in itself or with some relation. A number in itself is one that is stated without relation, such as I, II, III, IIII, and so forth. Whatever is stated relatively, however, is either equal or unequal.

That is equal which, when compared with something else, is neither below it by a smaller total nor exceeds it by a larger one: for example, ten to ten, three to three, a cubit to a cubit, or a foot to a foot, and similar cases. This part of relative quantity—that is, equality—is naturally indivisible. No one can say that one instance of equality is of one kind and another of another kind.

[Col. 1009D]

D. That is certain. For where one thing is of the same kind as another, what other species could exist there?

M. Now observe what the divisions of unequal relation are. First, it is divided into greater and lesser; then the greater has five species. One is called multiple, another superparticular, the third superpartient, the fourth multiple-superparticular, and the fifth multiple-superpartient.

Opposed individually to these five parts of greater inequality are five other parts of lesser inequality, distinguished by the prefix *sub-* while otherwise bearing the same names. They are called submultiple, subsuperparticular, subsuperpartient, multiple-subsuperparticular, and multiple-subsuperpartient. Let us now examine what each of these species of both kinds of inequality is.

## On Multiple Inequality

Multiple inequality exists when the greater number contains the lesser two, three, four, or any number of times. Thus, when two is compared with one, it is double; three to one is triple; four to one is quadruple; and so forth.

The corresponding submultiple is that which is contained below the multiple two, three, four, or any number of times. For example, one is contained twice in two and is called subdouble; in three, three times, and is called subtriple; in four, four times, and is called subquadruple; and so forth in the same manner. Hence, as you recognize, this is what we discussed a little earlier.

D. I recognize that this inequality belongs to that kind of quantity whose greater part was said above to be capable of increasing indefinitely.

## On Superparticular Inequality

M. Attend also to another inequality belonging to that kind of quantity whose greater part, conversely, is known to decrease indefinitely. This is called superparticular inequality, in which one number, compared with another, contains the whole of the smaller and some part of it.

If it contains one-half of the smaller, it is called sesquialter; if one-third, sesquitertian; if one-fourth, sesquiquartan; and if one-fifth, sesquiquintan. Thus, as the form of superparticular relationships proceeds indefinitely, their names will likewise continue indefinitely.

The lesser numbers that accompany them, and that are contained within the greater together with some part of themselves, are called respectively subsesquialter, subsesquitertian, subsesquiquartan, and subsesquiquintan; and the sequence proceeds according to the rule and number of the greater relationships. You can now see clearly enough that this kind differs from the preceding one.

D. I certainly see it, because in the first kind the smaller number measures the greater by its whole quantity; but here it does so by one of its parts—by a half, as in two and three, or as VI and VIIII, or XII and XVIII; by a third, as VI and VIII, VIIII and XII, or XII and XVI; or by a fourth, as IIII and V, VIII and X, or XII and XV.

The half-part, however, by which the greater exceeds the smaller is larger than the third part, the third larger than the fourth, the fourth larger than the fifth, and so on indefinitely: the part named from the greater number itself decreases.

## On Superpartient Inequality

M. Attend also to the third form of inequality, called superpartient. It occurs when one number, compared with another, contains the whole of the lower number and, in addition, two, three, four, five, or any number of its other parts.

For example, III is contained in V together with two of its parts, and this is called superbipartient. IIII is contained in VII together with three of its parts, and is called supertripartient. V is contained in VIIII together with four of its parts, and is called superquadripartient; and so forth.

The lesser number enclosed by the greater is called subsuperpartient. Of this form of inequality, too, let these examples suffice, if you agree.

D. I think they suffice.

## On Multiple-Superparticular Inequality

M. After the three simple relationships there follow two compounded from those above. The first is called multiple-superparticular inequality, which consists of both kinds, as in II to V, III to VII, IIII to VIIII, and V to XI. For the fact that the compared number contains the lesser more than once makes the relation multiple; the fact that it exceeds the lesser by a part makes it superparticular.

When one number contains another twice and also one-half of it, the relation is called double-sesquialter; when it contains it twice and one-third, double-sesquitertian; when twice and one-fourth, double-sesquiquartan; and so forth.

If it contains it three times and also one-half, one-third, or one-fourth of it, it is called triple-sesquialter, triple-sesquitertian, triple-sesquiquartan, and so forth. Let this also suffice concerning this inequality.

D. Certainly, it suffices.

## On Multiple-Superpartient Inequality

[Col. 1011B]

M. The fifth is the inequality called multiple-superpartient. It occurs whenever one number, compared with another, contains the other whole more than once, together with two, three, or any number of its smaller parts. According to the form of the superpartient number, these relations are called, in terms of their proper parts, double-superbipartient, as when VIII is compared with III: for it contains two threes together with two of their parts. The same applies when XVI is compared with VII.

Likewise, there are double-supertripartient and double-superquadripartient; and again triple-superbipartient, triple-supertripartient, and triple-superquadripartient.

Thus, whatever is unequally compared with something else in the world, and whatever quantity is unequally compared with another quantity, relates to it according to one of these inequalities. Multiple inequality, as has been said, belongs to numerical quantity; quantity in spatial dimensions belongs to the other four inequalities.

Musical sounds—that is, those that agree in harmonious sweetness—are expressed conjointly according to the multiple and superparticular kinds; discordant sounds imitate the remaining inequalities. Since the confusion of such inequalities is innumerable and infinite, an infinity of discrepancies likewise follows from infinitely confused inequality. Only two, I say, belong to music, as we stated at the outset; the remaining three are excluded.

D. How, then, do only these two belong to music?

[Col. 1011D]

M. Because every agreement of tones (*phthongoi*) is formed according to these numbers: they are either multiple or superparticular. Sounds that are not consonant, however, arise according to the remaining inequalities.

D. By what reasoning do consonant and nonconsonant sounds imitate these numbers or those?

M. Because by that arrangement different sounds agree with one another, and differ according to those inequalities.

D. In what does this difference consist?

M. In sharpness and heaviness, in raising and lowering.

D. How do they differ from and agree with one another according to the numbers mentioned above?

M. All tones—that is, little sounds that agree with one another—are separated either by a double, triple, or quadruple interval, which are species of multiple inequality; or by a sesquialter, sesquitertian, or sesquioctave interval, which are species of superparticular inequality. An interval is not a silence between tones, but the spatial extent by which one surpasses another.

D. Which tones are separated by a double interval?

M. Those that are always separated through octave regions, which is called an octave (*diapason*).

D. Which are separated by a triple interval?

M. Those that are always separated through twelfth regions, which is called an octave with a fifth (*diapason et diapente*).

D. Which are separated by a quadruple interval?

M. Those that are always separated through fifteenth regions, which is called a double octave (*disdiapason*).

D. Which tones are sesquialter?

M. Those that are always separated by fifth positions; this is called a fifth (*diapente*).

D. Which are sesquitertian?

M. Those that are separated by a fourth position; this is called a fourth (*diatessaron*).

D. Which tones have a sesquioctave interval?

M. Each one in relation to another, as a string to a string; this is called a tone. A semitone is also added to these intervals; it is an interval that does not complete a full tone.

By these arrangements of intervals, therefore, divinity has ordered the concordant diversity of sounds, and by them harmonic sweetness is regulated. Whatever sounds above or below what the measures of these proportions require falls into one or another of the remaining forms of inequality and becomes discordant and unsuitable for song.

D. How are we to know that musical tones possess the measures mentioned above, when they are subject neither to sight nor to touch?

M. It is known first from the fact that these relationships alone—that is, the multiple and the superparticular—are counted and measured against one another, and are in a certain way kin through their mutual commensurability. Nor are there any movable things or powers in the world that are joined together harmoniously unless this kindred relationship of proportions connects them.

These are also the only proportions by which meters run harmoniously through their various feet. So great is the power of their capacity to join things together that even the contrary powers of the four elements are united by the fellowship of these proportions, as is revealed in the *Timaeus* and by other philosophers.

Hence also the following lines:

> You bind the elements with numbers, so that cold things may agree with flames,  
> and dry things with liquids.

Therefore musical sounds would not come together in one melody so sweetly if the commensurability of the aforesaid proportions did not join them through suitable and consonant intervals.

D. What is commensurate or connumerate?

M. It exists wherever there is some common measure of the greater and the lesser, as in II to IIII, II to VI, and II to VIII. Does not two measure four twice, six three times, and eight four times?

D. Yes.

M. Thus, in multiple relationships, whenever you multiply the simple number by any number, that same simple number measures the greater total as many times. For three doubled gives six, tripled gives nine, quadrupled gives twelve, and so forth.

What happens in superparticular relationships, such as IIII to VI? Does not two measure the smaller twice and the greater three times, which is sesquialter? Likewise, in VI to VIII, two measures the smaller three times and the greater four times, which is epitritus. Likewise, in VIII to X, two measures the smaller four times and the greater five times, which is sesquiquartan.

Thus, indefinitely, by whatever part the greater number surpasses the other, by that same part the two numbers measure one another: for example, VIII is surpassed by VIIII by an eighth of itself—that is, by one—and that same unit, by which they differ from one another, measures both.

You now understand that these inequalities receive both their increase and their resolution through any common dimension.

D. I understand why these are called commensurate or connumerate. But explain how the other inequalities lack this same connumeration or commensurability.

M. Let us consider this also, as you request. Take III to V, which is a superbipartient comparison, and observe by what part of three five exceeds it.

D. I cannot find how to say that it exceeds it by the whole or by a whole part.

[Col. 1013C]

M. It certainly cannot be found. In this kind or quantity, the lesser does not measure the greater by its whole quantity, as in multiple relationships, nor by some part that is the difference between the two, as in superparticular relationships.

For in the sesquialter proportion, as in IIII to VI, the two that constitute their difference measure both; and in the sesquitertian proportion, as in VI to VIII, the two that constitute their difference likewise measure both. But in the superpartient proportion, as in III to V, the two that constitute the difference measure neither.

The same occurs in multiple-superparticular relationships, as in II to V, which is double-sesquialter; II to VII, which is triple-sesquialter; and III to X, which is triple-sesquitertian. The same occurs in multiple-superpartient relationships: III to VIII, which is double-superbipartient; III to XI, which is triple-superbipartient; and IIII to XI, which is double-supertripartient.

You see, therefore, that such proportions are measured neither by their simple quantity nor by their differences; they are neither increased by the parts in which they differ nor resolved into those parts. For this reason they are rightly called incommensurate and inconnumberate.

Moreover, just as we distinguish crooked and straight things with our eyes, and everything else that lies before the sight, so, since our nature is composed together with the aforesaid parts, sounds that agree in commensurable intervals delight the hearing, while the others are discordant. But do you wish to learn more about this commensurability?

D. It is yours to judge concerning that.

[Col. 1014A]

M. We have said how multiples are measured by their own quantity, and how superparticulars are measured by their difference. Let us now examine what kinship multiples themselves have with superparticulars.

Set out an ordered sequence of multiples, and at the same time construct a sequence of superparticulars. They may be the primary numbers, whose difference is one and which are the roots of multiple and superparticular numbers; or they may be the greater numbers derived from this combination.

The primary numbers are I, II, III, IIII. For the number four perfectly completes all the consonances. Two to one is double, which is the octave; three to one is triple, which is the octave with a fifth; four to one is quadruple, which is the double octave; three to two is sesquialter, which is the fifth; and four to three is sesquitertian, which is the fourth.

Derived numbers are VI, XII, XVIII, XXIIII, and so forth. For XII to VI is double, XVIII triple, and XXIIII quadruple. Triple to double is sesquialter; quadruple to triple is sesquitertian. Likewise, fivefold to fourfold is sesquiquartan; sixfold to fivefold is sesquiquintan; sevenfold to sixfold is sesquisextan; and so forth indefinitely.

Superparticulars accompany multiples, so that it is not without reason that music is said to be produced from both together.

D. The connumeration and kinship of such numbers are undoubtedly apparent.

M. Since it has therefore become clear how multiples, arranged in order, relate to the superparticulars, may it likewise become clear to you how multiples—double or quadruple—are composed from superparticulars, namely from sesquialters and sesquitertians.

Let us begin with six. To the number VI let a sesquialter be added, and it becomes VIIII. To nine let a sesquitertian be added, and it becomes XII. Thus twelve, in relation to six, is double and is completed by a sesquialter and a sesquitertian.

Likewise, let a sesquialter be added to XII, and it becomes XVIII. Let a sesquitertian be added to XVIII, and it becomes XXIIII. Thus XXIIII in relation to XII is double and is completed by a sesquialter and a sesquitertian.

Conversely, let a sesquitertian be added to VI, producing VIII. Let a sesquialter be added to VIII, producing XII. Thus twelve in relation to six is double and is completed by a sesquitertian and a sesquialter. Similarly, let a sesquitertian be added to XII, producing XVIII; let a sesquialter be added to XVIII, producing XXIIII. Thus twenty-four in relation to twelve is double and is completed by a sesquitertian and a sesquialter.

And so forth: one double is always completed by an increase of a sesquialter and a sesquitertian.

Moreover, the sesquialter and the sesquitertian are joined by a common epogdoic measure in such a way that if you subtract an epogdoos from a sesquialter, a sesquitertian results; and if an epogdoos is added again to a sesquitertian, a sesquialter is restored. It is therefore established that sounds agreeing with one another derive their concord from numbers agreeing with one another.

D. That is plainly demonstrated by reason.

M. Observe, however, that sounds agree not merely in any relation to one another, but in the following way. For example, the number XXIIII is double in relation to XII, triple in relation to VIII, quadruple in relation to VI, sesquialter in relation to XVI, epitritus in relation to XVIII, subdouble in relation to XLVIII, subepitritus in relation to XXXII, and subsesquialter in relation to XXXVI.

So every tone sounds as an octave in relation to one, as an octave and a fifth in relation to another, as a double octave in relation to another, as a fifth in relation to another, as a fourth in relation to another, as a sub-octave in relation to another, as a sub-fourth in relation to another, and as a sub-fifth in relation to another. This would not happen unless, through their commensurability, they were kin according to the relationship of multiple and superparticular proportions; from this it can be known according to which proportion each consonance is formed.

D. Since it has been sufficiently demonstrated that the principle of commensurability joins musical sounds to one another, how can it nevertheless be known to which proportion each consonance should be assigned? For by what is it known that the octave belongs to the double relationship, the fifth to the sesquialter, the fourth to the epitritus, the octave with a fifth to the triple, and the double octave to the quadruple?

M. The first proof of this is that, just as one double is always completed by a sesquialter and a sesquitertian, as was just said, so one octave—which contains eight little sounds—is completed by the two lesser consonances, namely the fifth and the fourth.

Whether you measure a fourth tone from the lower or from the higher side, beginning with the fourth tone you measure the fifth, or the fifth measures together with the fourth: in either case, one is always completed by two consonances.

This would not happen if there were other consonances that completed them, or other ones that were completed by them.

Boethius also speaks of these matters: “Among all the consonances that we have mentioned, judgment must be made both by the ear and by reason as to which should be considered the better.” For the ear is affected by sounds, and the eye by appearances, in the same way that the mind is affected by number or continuous quantity.

When a number or line is set before us, nothing is easier than to perceive its double with the eye or the mind: for example, XII in relation to VI. After the judgment of the double comes that of the half; after the half, that of the triple; and after the triple, that of the third part. Since the representation of the double is easier, the consonance that is easier and more clearly grasped by the senses is rightly assigned to it.

The first and sweetest consonance, therefore, is that which is formed at the eighth position and is called the octave (*diapason*). After the double stands, I say, what exceeds it by half of the subdouble—that is, the sesquialter, as VIIII in relation to VI—and what exceeds it by twice its quantity, that is, the triple, as XVIII in relation to VI.

Since these two proportions follow immediately after the double, although by contrary division, the consonances that we perceive by the ear to come second after the octave are rightly assigned to them: namely the fifth, and likewise the octave with a fifth.

Since consonant sounds are least distant when they occupy the interval of a fourth (*diatessaron*), we rightly assign this consonance to the proportion in which the greater number exceeds the smaller by a third, namely the epitritus, as VIII in relation to VI.

Since the sounds that produce the consonance of the double octave are the farthest apart, we rightly assign it to the proportion that departs by a quadruple measurement of interval, as XXIIII in relation to VI. The order of consonances then comes to an end: it can extend neither beyond the quadruple nor contract below the third part.

Thus consonance has taken the order given in numbers by the increases of multiplication and, conversely, by the decreases of superparticularity. There is also another suitable proof, which confirms the foregoing reasoning not only through hearing but also through sight.

Strings or pipes, if they are of equal thickness and the longer contains the shorter twice in its length, will sound an octave in consonance, as stated above; if it contains it three times, they produce an octave with a fifth; if four times, they produce the consonance of a double octave.

If the greater exceeds the smaller by half of the smaller, the consonance is a fifth. If it exceeds it by a third of the smaller, it is a fourth. If it exceeds it by an eighth of the smaller, they agree in a tone.

D. It has now been amply proved why no more than three species of multiplication and no more than three species of superparticularity belong to music—not only so that music may arise from counted or commensurable numbers, but also so that each consonance may be attached to the particular species of counted numbers appropriate to it.

But it is surprising why no more than three forms of multiplication and no more than three forms of superparticularity are admitted into music, and why only the double, triple, and quadruple relationships, and only the sesquialter, sesquitertian, and sesquioctave, produce consonances.

[Col. 1016C]

M. The interval does not extend beyond the double octave—that is, beyond the quadruple—because nature has assigned this limit to sounds. If individual double-octave consonances are arranged at each sevenfold interval in the octave scale, the double consonances cannot proceed any farther.

The intervals are not contracted below the third part—that is, below the epitritus—because, since a third part is smaller than a half, a fourth smaller than a third, a fifth smaller than a fourth, a sixth smaller than a fifth, and so forth; and since the sesquialter, which is the interval of a half, contains three tones with a semitone, while the epitritus, which is the interval of a third part, contains two tones with a semitone; it follows that the smaller intervals thereafter can contain neither two tones and a semitone nor an interval commensurable with two tones or with one and a half tones. Only the sesquioctave interval is admitted, because it measures a tone.

D. Why does the entire measure fall into this one proportion alone?

M. Because this proportion is produced solely by the comparison of the sesquialter and the sesquitertian.

D. How does it arise from the comparison of the sesquialters and sesquitertians?

M. Is it not easy to understand that the number six, by its half, grows into its sesquialter—that is, into nine—and by its third part grows into its epitritus—that is, into eight? But just as nine is sesquialter to six, so it is sesquioctave to eight.

Likewise, the number twelve, by its half, measures its sesquialter, which is eighteen; and by its third part, its epitritus, which is sixteen. But just as XVIII is sesquialter in relation to XII, so it is sesquioctave in relation to the epitritus.

D. I understand.

M. Therefore understand this also: between one sound and another there can be no interval of a whole tone either smaller or greater than that which has once been measured by the difference between the sesquialter and the sesquitertian.

Thus only sesquioctave intervals are commensurable with sesquialters and sesquitertians; their intervals, as was said, are completed commensurably by tones with semitones.

Again, only sesquialter and sesquitertian intervals are commensurable with doubles and quadruples, by which their intervals are similarly completed.

But the sesquiquartan, sesquiquintan, and the remaining decreasing intervals have no commensurability whatever with the double, triple, quadruple, or sesquialter. For this reason they are excluded from music.

If you also wish to confirm, through the dimensions of strings and pipes, the kindred commensurability of the proportions admitted into music, make one string longer than another by a sesquialter, or one pipe longer than another by a sesquialter; add an epitritus to the sesquialter, and you have produced a double. For the one that is an epitritus in relation to the second is twice as long as the first.

Conversely, measure one string against another, or one pipe against another, as an epitritus; add a sesquialter to the epitritus, and the double is produced. Arrange these in order as VI, VIII, VIIII, XII, and you will find between the two middle terms an epogdoos properly measured: that is, the longer string or pipe exceeds the smaller by an eighth.

Again, in another way: measure one pipe against another twice as long. To the short pipe apply an epitritus; to the long pipe apply a subepitritus; and arrange in order the subdouble epitritus and the subepitritus double.

Thus an epogdoos naturally falls between the two middle terms. By its interval, each of them is sesquialter in relation to the more distant side, and each is epitritus in relation to the nearer side. Furthermore, if you double the epitritus, the sesquialter, and the double, you produce together another octave interval in the same order as before.

D. How is it that the other superparticular relationships have no commensurability with the double and the quadruple?

M. To make this clear to you, let us begin with twelve, the smallest number by which the matter can be exemplified. This number measures XXIIII by its own quantity, XVIII by its half, XVI by its third part, and XV by its fourth part.

But XVIII, which is sesquialter in relation to XII, is commensurable with XXIIII by the epitritus relationship. Again, XVI, which is epitritus in relation to XII, is commensurable with XXIIII by the sesquialter relationship. But XV, which is sesquiquartan in relation to XII, is not commensurable with XXIIII; it is dissonant according to a supertripartient form.

Likewise, the number XXIIII measures XLVIII by its own quantity, XXXVI by its half, XXXII by its third part, and XXX by its fourth part. But XXXVI, which is sesquialter in relation to XXIIII, is commensurable with XLVIII by the epitritus relationship. Again, XXXII, which is epitritus in relation to XXIIII, is commensurable with XLVIII by the sesquialter relationship. But XXX, which is sesquiquartan in relation to XXIIII, cannot be commensurated with XLVIII.

You see, therefore, that as soon as the intervals begin to contract within the sesquitertian, the superparticulars have no connumeration with the doubles, and consequently no consonant mixture.

D. By what reasoning does it happen that, in the series of sounds, tones in the fourth positions are epitritian, those in the fifth are sesquialter, those in the eighth are double, and the others have their own relationships in their own positions?

M. Since it is established that a double is completed either by an epitritus, by a sesquialter, or by two epitrituses with an epogdoic interval between them, the intervals of the epitrituses themselves are again completed by epogdooi.

The two middle little sounds in an octave interval—that is, the fourth and the fifth—while each sounds as a fourth toward one side and as a fifth toward the other, are both separated from their respective side by an epitritian interval.

But each of these epitritian intervals is in turn enclosed by epogdooi in such a way that the intervals are divided into three intervals containing four little sounds: specifically, two individual intervals contain one epogdoos each—that is, one tone each—and the third is completed by the *limma*, which is a semitone.

Thus it comes about that in the fourth positions the sounds are sesquitertian, in the fifth positions they are sesquialter, in the eighth positions they are double, in the fifteenth positions they contain two doubles, and in the twelfth positions they are triple.

D. I ask by what reasoning or order tones are woven together with semitones in the series of sounds.

M. You will be able to observe this more clearly if I first explain what the arithmetic mean, the geometric mean, and the harmonic mean are.

D. Please explain.

Master. After proportions, proportional relationships are considered. For a proportion is the relation of two terms, whereas a proportional relationship involves no fewer than three. Therefore, a proportional relationship is joined either by arithmetic mean, geometric mean, or harmonic mean. We call it a mean [Col. 1018D] when two extremes of two or fewer limits are bound together in concord by a connecting relation. We call the limits, or terms, the sums of numbers. Thus arithmetic mean exists where the distances between the terms are equal, but the terms themselves are not in the same proportion, as you see: I, II, III.

Disciple. I certainly see it: I to II is double, II to III is sesquialteral.

Master. Likewise, geometric mean exists where not equal differences but equal proportions are considered, as you see: I, II, IV.

Disciple. I see indeed: just as I is to II, so II is to IV.

[Col. 1019A] Master. But harmonic mean exists where neither the same proportions nor the same differences are sought, but where the extremes stand to one another in the same relation as the differences of those same limits, as you see: III, IV, VI.

Disciple. I see, namely, that the extreme limits and their differences are separated by a factor of two.

Master. These matters, then, had to be prefaced in order to see according to which mean the measurements of the tones are related. For although each individual mean belongs to its own category, music appears to be woven from all of them. The geometric mean links all terms to one another in doubles, so that just as XII is related to VI, so XXIV is related to XII; and again, just as XXIV is related to XII, so XLVIII is related to XXIV. Then, when these double intervals are completed by two terms, one of them joins its two extremes by arithmetic mean, the other by harmonic mean. For by the number by which the limit IX exceeds the limit VI, it is exceeded by the limit XII. Likewise, by the number by which the limit XVIII exceeds the limit XII, it is exceeded by the limit XXIV—by arithmetic mean alone. Again, by whatever fraction the limit VIII exceeds the limit VI, it is exceeded by the limit XII in the same fraction. For you see that VIII is greater than VI by one third, and XII is greater than VIII by one third of itself. XII likewise relates to XVI, and XVI again to XXIV, by harmonic mean.

Disciple. I see that too: since VIII differs from VI by whatever fraction, XII differs from VIII by the same fraction, so it follows that the differences are in the proportion in which the extreme terms themselves stand to one another. For as VI is to XII, so II is to IV. The difference between VI and VIII is two; between VIII and XII it is four.

Master. You understand perfectly. But now observe how the tones themselves, which complete the intervals of the terms mentioned above, are not diminished and increased by arithmetic mean, like days in equal portions one after another; nor are they, by harmonic mean, in dissimilar proportions. Rather, measured by geometric mean, they complete epitrite and [Note: [Col. 1019D] Salemit., sescupla.] sesquialteral intervals. For just as the second sesquioctave is related to the first, so the third stands in relation to the second. Just as the number LXXII is sesquioctave in relation to LXIV, so LXXXI is sesquioctave in relation to LXXII.

Disciple. I now understand how tones are measured from tones according to the manner of these numbers. But tell me why you chose these numbers as an example.

Master. Because it could not be shown with a smaller number than eight multiplied by eight. That produces LXIV. Since this is the second multiple of eight, it produces two sesquioctaves from itself. For when an eighth of LXIV is added to it, the number LXXII results. Then, when an eighth of LXXII is added to it, LXXXI results. Thus there are two sesquioctaves: LXIV, LXXII, LXXXI. But since my purpose was to explain more fully how two tones with a semitone are arranged within an epitrite interval, and how semitones are arranged with tones throughout the entire series of sounds, a fourth limit ought to be added which would be epitrite to the first. A semitone would be placed between it and the third limit. But since the number LXIV cannot be divided into three equal parts, an epitrite cannot be added to it. Let it therefore be multiplied by three, and immediately an epitrite is added to it. So, three times LXIV—what number does that produce?

Disciple. CXCII.

Master. Quite so. Let us therefore take this number as the starting point for explaining what we have begun. You will therefore give me its double.

Disciple. Twice CXCII makes CCCLXXXIV.

Master. Certainly. Here, then, you have these two numbers in a double interval: CXCII and CCCLXXXIV. We must now fill this double interval with two epitrites. [Col. 1020B] Give me, then, the epitrite of CXCII.

Disciple. A third of CXCII, namely LXIV, added to it produces CCLVI. Since this number is epitrite in relation to the subdouble term, it is sesquialteral in relation to the double.

Master. Give me the sescupla of CXCII.

Disciple. Half of CXCII, namely XCVI, added to it makes CCLXXXVIII. Since this number is sescupla in relation to the subdouble term, it is epitrite in relation to the double.

Master. That is certainly so. Let these four terms now be set out in order: CXCII, CCLVI, CCLXXXVIII, CCCLXXXIV. Since, then, the interval between the first and second terms is epitrite, and likewise the interval between the third and fourth terms is epitrite, let us now fill these epitrite intervals with tones and semitones. I shall take an eighth of CXCII, which is XXIIII; by adding this tone, the number CCXVI results as the second tone. I shall take an eighth of CCXVI, which is XXVII; by adding this tone, the number CCXLIII results as the third sound. I cannot take an eighth of CCXLIII, because between it and the fourth term, CCLVI—which is epitrite to the first—there are only thirteen units, and this distance is in the relation of a semitone. Thus the diatessaron modulation is complete, reckoned as two tones and a semitone.

Again, since the sescupla is greater than the epogdoan relation, I shall take from the fourth sound, that is, from the number CCLVI, its eighth, which is XXXII; by adding this tone, the number CCLXXXVIII results as the fifth sound. From the fifth sound I shall remove its eighth, which is XXXVI; by this addition the number CCCXXIIII results as the sixth sound. From the sixth sound I shall remove its eighth, which is XL and a half; by adding this tone the number CCCLXXXIIII results as the seventh sound. But from the seventh sound to the number CCCLXXXIIII and a half, which is the eighth sound, there remain eighteen units in the relation of a semitone; and the diapente modulation is complete, reckoned as three tones and a semitone.

Description of these matters.

[Col. 1021A] But if you also desire a demonstration by measurement, make one string longer than another string—or one pipe longer than another—by an epitrite, the one that is to be placed fourth. Make another longer by a sesquialter, to be placed fifth. Make another twice as long, which you will place eighth. Likewise, take an eighth of the first string or pipe and add it to the second. Take an eighth of the second and add it to the third. You will not be able to take an eighth of the third in order to measure the fourth, which has already received its measure from the first, in relation to which it was made epitrite. Similarly, there is no need to measure the fifth again through the fourth, because, since it is sescupla to the first, it becomes sesquioctave to the epitrite. Taking an eighth from the fifth, you will measure the sixth; taking an eighth from the sixth, you will measure the seventh. You will not be able to measure the eighth through the seventh, because, since the eighth has been made epitrite in relation to the fifth, the distance between the seventh and eighth will be a semitone. In this manner of intervals, different sounds come together in a pleasant joining.

Disciple. It is certainly remarkable that sounds cannot harmonize in any other way unless the intervals of semitones are now compressed within an epitrite, now within a sesquialteral space, so that they do not even reach half the preceding tone.

Master. Truly, this happens by a wondrous and divine arrangement. But so that you may recognize everything clearly, let us also attempt to undertake the division of the monochord according to the same rules. First understand this: longer strings or pipes produce lower sounds, and the shorter they are, the higher the sounds; so, conversely, a half sounds double, and a quarter quadruple. Let there be a stretched string, as it were, from a to z. I shall remove half of this space, as it were from h to z; when the half is struck, it sounds the diapason in relation to the whole. I shall remove half of the half, as it were from h to p; and it sounds the disdiapason. Likewise, let the lesser consonances be arranged within each diapason space: that is, from a–z, in a–h, and again from h–z, in h–p. I shall remove a quarter of the space a–z, and d–z gives the diatessaron. I shall remove a third of a–z, and e–z gives the diapente. Likewise, in the space h–p, when a quarter has been removed, the diatessaron sounds; when a third has been removed, it will be the diapente.

Now let us arrange the diatessaron and diapente spaces by epogdoan intervals. For when a ninth is removed from the space a–z, b–z will be a tone. When a ninth is removed from the space b–z, c–z will be a tone, and d–z a semitone. Since the difference between the diatessaron and diapente is a tone, d–z to e–z will likewise be a tone. When a ninth is removed from the space e–z, f–z will be a tone; when a ninth is removed from the space f–z, g–z will be a tone, and h–z a semitone, and the diapason interval is complete. In the same way, in the other diapason—that is, in the space from h–z to h–p—you will arrange tones with semitones according to the intervals of the diatessaron and diapente, in the manner of diatonic modulation.

[Col. 1022B]

Disciple. Since there are four kinds of tetrachords following one another, how can each of them consist of the same placement of tones and semitones?

Master. They cannot at all. For there is one tetrachord consisting of two tones and a semitone; the next, being one tone higher, consequently consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone. The one that follows this in the third place, being a semitone higher, necessarily consists of a semitone and two tones. Then [Col. 1022C] the one that follows in the fourth place, being one tone distant from the preceding one, happens to consist of three tones. Again, the one in the fifth place, with the first arrangement returning, consists of two tones and a semitone.

Disciple. Are these several arrangements peculiar to the several kinds of tetrachords?

Master. Certainly. For this is why the same quality of song returns at the fifth positions: because the order of the same arrangement revolves back.

Disciple. In what way, then, does the semitone fall between the sounds?

Master. Give the upper one the form of the tritus, the lower one the form of the deuteros, and the others according to how far each tone is removed from the semitone. For when a sound has one tone toward the upper side as far as the semitone, but two tones toward the lower side, that is the sound we call archous or protus. But when it has two tones toward the upper side and one tone toward the lower side, it becomes the one we call tetrardus.

Now you can easily distinguish the tetrachords, because the one arranged upward by two tones and a semitone consists of these sounds: tetrardus, protus, deuteros, tritus. The one arranged by a tone, a semitone, and a tone consists of the sounds protus, deuteros, tritus, tetrardus. The one arranged by a semitone and two tones consists of deuteros, tritus, tetrardus, protus. The one arranged by three tones consists of tritus, tetrardus, protus, deuteros. And so that this may become clearer, let the description of each be set out in this manner.

[Col. 1023B]

[Col. 1023C] In this description of the four tetrachords, since the distances of the tones are marked by the intervening little lines, while the lines inserted between the sounds indicate that they differ by semitones, the distinctive character of each is evident.

Disciple. Certainly, it is plainly evident. But why does one tetrachord consist of three tones?

Master. This too can be understood from what has been said. Since two tetrachords complete one diapason, while each individual tetrachord is completed by two tones and a semitone, and a whole middle tone divides the two tetrachords, it follows that the form of the fourth tetrachord, when the space of the diatessaron—that is, two tones with a semitone—has already been exceeded, is completed by three whole tones. This also appears clearly in the present description.

Disciple. I now understand it plainly, both from the description and from the reasoning; and, as I see, the very transposition of the semitone is a change of modes.

Master. There is no doubt about it. For from this each phthong has its own distinguishable quality, the tetrachords and pentachords have their own kinds, and, as you will admit, all the forms of the modes; and the same semitone itself becomes, in a certain way, the heart and soul of the song. The power of the semitone is so great in altering the character of the phthongs that, if beneath the same two phthongs, which differ by an epitrite, you place a different order of semitones, the phthongs themselves together pass into a different form.

For example: make one string longer than another by an epitrite, so that they sound a diatessaron in relation to one another. Since this consonance contains two tones between its other two sounds, let a tone be placed between the first and second, beginning from the lower side—that is, from the longer string or pipe—and likewise between the second and third. Let us separate the third from the fourth by a semitone; then the tetrachord will be arranged in these sounds: tetrardus, protus, deuteros, tritus.

Again, if we begin from the higher side, and a tone likewise distinguishes the first from the second and the second from the third, while the interval between the third and fourth is measured by a semitone, there will then be another kind of tetrachord. Just as the placement of the tones differs, so also does the character of the sounds: the first, which is higher, becomes protus, then tetrardus, then tritus, and in fourth place deuteros, as this description shows:

Moreover, it must be understood that the tritus and deuteros have a distinguishable quality between them, since they alone differ by a semitone; but among the other sounds, which are separated by a tone, the distinction of quality is not so directly perceptible, but is gathered rather from the order. For from the surrounding context it can easily be recognized which one or the other it is. Hence, as an introduction to the art, the Greek names of the phthongs themselves are sung, rising and falling as far as the third, so that the character of the sounds may be recognized from their order, in the following manner.

[Col. 1025A] Disciple. Everything has been set out abundantly: both the causes and the number of ways in which the arrangements of the tetrachords vary, and how the kinds of modes or tropes arise from the several variations of arrangement. Yet one point still remains open to inquiry. You said that the same mode of a trope returns through the fifth regions because the same order of arrangement returns.

Master. I said so plainly; and I also said that, because of the sesquialteral relation, the consonance harmonizes through the fifth regions, and that the same mode of the trope returns because of the same order of arrangement. Therefore, when something is taken in a foreign place, it either differs from what precedes it while retaining the quality of the trope, because it does not find the arrangement of its own order; or, yielding to a foreign order, it changes the quality of the trope through transposition. But explain what you wish to investigate.

Disciple. I ask this: since the mode of the same trope appears to be nothing other than the same order of tones with semitones in the same melody, and since the arrangement of the same order does not return in the octave regions, why do sounds separated by an octave agree in the same trope?

Master. It is true that, just as in the fifth region, so rather in the ninth than in the eighth region, the same arrangement is reproduced in the same constitution of sounds: just as the first and second are distinguished by a tone, so there is a tone between [Note: [Col. 1025C] S. the eighth and ninth:] the ninth and tenth sounds; just as between the second and third, so between [Note: [Col. 1025C] S. the ninth and tenth.] the tenth and eleventh; but just as the third and fourth are divided by a semitone, so [Note: [Col. 1026C] S. the tenth divides the eleventh and twelfth.] the eleventh [Col. 1026A] is divided from the twelfth.

But it must be understood that in this greatest consonance, the sound which has approached the higher and lower sound at octave intervals does not follow the order of its own position, but that of the sound to which it responds consonantly. For there would be no consonance if either a tone should confront a semitone, or a semitone, in turn, should confront a tone.

Disciple. How would tones confront semitones?

Master. If, among phthongs separated by an octave region, some were distinguished by a semitone and others by a tone—for example, if there were a tone between the first and second, and correspondingly a tone between the eighth and ninth; a tone between the second and third, and correspondingly a tone between the ninth and tenth; but if there were a semitone between the third and fourth, and, conversely, a tone between the tenth and eleventh; likewise a tone between the fourth and fifth, and, conversely, a semitone between the eleventh and twelfth sounds—then, with semitones disagreeing with tones in opposition, there could be neither a double relation nor consonance nor the same trope between the fourth and eleventh sounds, or between the fifth and twelfth.

But now, since there is a tone between the eighth and ninth sounds corresponding to the first and second, a tone between the ninth and tenth corresponding to the second and third, and a semitone between the tenth and eleventh just as between the third and fourth, this correspondence in opposition between tones and semitones preserves the double proportion and the consonance, and retains the mode of the trope.

[Col. 1026C] The *Scholica Enchiriadis* ends. [Note: [Col. 1026C] Codex Tegernsee: “The book of the musical art ends.”]

[Col. 1025]

## HERE BEGINS A BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE MODULATION OF TONES AND PSALMS

The duty of our service, since we have been appointed to the ministry of praise, ought not only to be complete and full, but also pleasant and agreeable through becoming harmony and sweetness. Therefore it is fitting that we be skilled in our office, so that we may confess his holy Name knowingly and artistically, and glory in his songs; so that praise pleasing and beautiful to our God may be offered, and those who hear may be kindled to praise and reverence for the works of God. For although God is more pleased by one who sings with the heart than by one who sings with the voice, both nevertheless come from him; and it is doubly beneficial if both are done—if one sings sweetly in spirit before God, and the sweetness of a melodious voice moves human beings with holy devotion. Although the devotion of many is also very pleasing to God, even when in psalmody they cannot properly pronounce the words themselves, nevertheless that devotion is not wholly complete if one does not offer to God what one ought to offer, as well and reverently as one can.

Harpists and flute players, and the others who carry musical instruments, as well as secular male and female singers, strive with every effort to regulate by the principles of their art whatever is sung or played on the harp, so as to delight their hearers. But we, who have deserved to take the words of Majesty upon our lips—are we to utter the songs of holiness without art and carelessly, and not rather assume in sacred things the beauty of art which they abuse in trifles? Therefore accept from me this small piece of instruction intended for your practice, so that through knowledge of small matters you may become more capable of greater ones.

[Col. 1027] Accordingly, we divide the melody into eight tones, which we name as follows. It is blameworthy for an ecclesiastical singer to be ignorant of their differences and properties, unless impeded by slowness of intellect. Four of these are principal, while the other four are joined laterally to the individual principal tones.

The first principal tone is therefore called by singers *autentus protus*, that is, the first authentic or authoritative tone; joined to it is the one called *plagis protus*, that is, the first lateral or oblique tone. The second principal tone is called *autentus deuterus*, that is, the second authentic or authoritative tone; accompanying it is *plagis deuterus*, that is, the second lateral tone.

The third principal tone is *autentus tritus*, that is, the third authentic or authoritative tone; with it is *plagis tritus*, that is, the third lateral tone. The fourth principal tone is *autentus tetrardus*, whose subordinate is *plagis tetrardus*, that is, the fourth lateral tone.

According to the properties of these eight tones, our singers use particular modulations for responsories, and likewise their own modulations for the greater antiphons, which are sung at the Introit of Masses or at Communion at the end of the celebration. I shall set out in this little work, as best I can, those modes by which the psalms are modulated to the antiphons, omitting the other earlier matters because of their length. For clearer understanding, I have taken care to note them below either by signs of the sounds or by the individual strings of the sounds.

Let the regular neume of the first tone be taken, which among us is as follows:

The psalm modulation follows, ascending as far as the upper deuteros of the tetrachord and consisting of six sounds.

## SECOND TONE, THE SUBORDINATE OF THE FIRST

The psalm modulation follows, rising to the terminal tetrardus and descending, supported by five sounds, to the lower tetrardus.

## THIRD TONE, THAT IS, THE SECOND AUTHENTIC TONE

The psalm modulation follows, raised to the upper tetrardus and comprising seven sounds.

## FOURTH TONE FOLLOWS, THE SUBORDINATE OF THE THIRD

The psalm modulation follows, raised to the upper deuteros.

## FIFTH TONE FOLLOWS, THAT IS, THE THIRD AUTHENTIC TONE

The psalm modulation follows, rising as far as the upper tetrardus and ending with six sounds.

## SIXTH TONE, THE SUBORDINATE OF THE FIFTH

The psalm modulation follows, consisting of four sounds.

## SEVENTH TONE FOLLOWS, THAT IS, THE FOURTH AUTHENTIC TONE

The psalm modulation follows, raised as far as the highest deuteros.

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to receive.” “Under the throne.”

## EIGHTH TONE FOLLOWS, WHICH IS THE SUBORDINATE OF THE SEVENTH

The psalm modulation follows, reaching the fourth of the upper tetrachord.

“Through the mercies of our God.”

These are the modulations which we use for antiphons in the eight tones, which have taken their order from the order of the sounds counted upward. Nevertheless, when a slower song is required, as for the songs of the Gospels, we customarily use these same modulations when occasion permits, according to what was expressed above. For singing the ordinary course, however, we use the same melodies in a more rapid form; I have nevertheless indicated them in the notation below. The *noane* are not words signifying anything, but syllables suited to investigating the melody. [Note: [Col. 1029] To view the following list as it is printed in Migne, double-click on the ornament icon that follows.]

1. TONE. “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.”  
2. TONE. “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him.”  
3. TONE. “For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways.”  
4. TONE. “You commanded that your commandments be diligently kept.”  
5. TONE. “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your justifications.”  
6. TONE. “Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments.”  
7. TONE. “I shall confess to you, Lord, in the direction of my heart, for I have learned your judgments.” [Col. 1031]  
8. TONE. “I shall keep your justifications; do not utterly forsake me.”

Besides these, other psalm modulations are also fitted to many of the tones mentioned above, for example to these antiphons: “Blessed are you among women,” and “From Egypt I called my son,” and others like them. These can be sung alternately between the choirs in two different modes, so that one choir pronounces its verse in its own mode and the other answers in another mode.

“Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

[Note: [Col. 1031] To view the following text as it is printed in Migne, double-click on the ornament icon.]

“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people. And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant.”

Likewise, in the sixth tone, psalms are modulated to antiphons in the following manner:

[Note: [Col. 1031] To view the following text as it is printed in Migne, double-click on the ornament icon.]

“The Lord has made his salvation known, alleluia. Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done marvelous things. His right hand and his holy arm have saved him. The Lord has made his salvation known; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness,” and so forth.
