[Col. 1039] These examples, then, have been assembled for the benefit of the slower brothers, perhaps in greater abundance than was appropriate. Yet they are not without purpose, if someone takes care over them and does not censure such diligence as superfluous. This, however, must be pointed out: certain antiphons of different tones have an undifferentiated similarity at their beginnings, so that in the sequences it may be seen which melody is to be fitted to each; and especially the ending of each chant must be observed, in which the characteristic quality of each tone is more clearly evident. For example:

[Note: [Col. 1039] To view the text that follows as it is printed in Migne, double-click the ornament icon.]

From the age of two years and younger Herod killed many boys for the Lord’s sake. They will walk with me in white garments, because they are worthy, and I shall not erase their names from the book of life.

These antiphons indeed begin with a similar opening, but soon diverge as they proceed, and it becomes apparent that one is to be assigned to the melody of the second tone and the other to that of the fourth. The same occurs in many cases. There are also antiphons to which the psalms are to be sung according to the principal melody, although they have a subordinate ending; or they are to be modulated according to the subordinate melody and end in the principal one. Some do not end on the final sound, but on the lower sound beneath it. The final neume, however, repeats the sound in which the chant properly rests and ends, as in:

[Note: [Col. 1039] To view the text that follows as it is printed in Migne, double-click the ornament icon.]

We know that for those who love God all things work together for good—for those who are called saints according to his purpose.

There are certain musical signs to which psalms are not fitted in their proper manner; these can be communicated more effectively by comparison. In all other respects, above all, one must carefully observe that the chant be delivered with equality. If it lacks this, it is deprived of its chief right and robbed of its legitimate perfection. Without it, the choir is confused by discordant singing; no one can sing concordantly with the others, nor can anyone sing alone with skill. God, the author of all things, plainly established that every beauty should consist in proportion—not less in what is perceived by hearing than in what is perceived by sight—because he arranged all things according to measure, weight, and number.

Therefore, inequality must not corrupt sacred song. No neume or sound should be indecorously prolonged or shortened by individual moments; nor, through negligence in a single chant—for example, a responsory or another piece—should one begin to prolong it more sluggishly than before. Likewise, short notes should not be more impeded than is appropriate to short notes. Rather, all long notes should be equally long, and the brevity of the short notes should be equal, except for the divisions, which must be observed in the chant with similar care. Everything that lasts long must correspond rhythmically, through legitimate intervals, with what does not last long, and every chant must be carried through from beginning to end with the same rate of speed.

Nevertheless, once this principle has been observed, when a chant is sung rapidly, the melody may toward the end—or sometimes toward the beginning—need to be extended by a longer pause; or a chant sung slowly may need to be brought to an end by quicker measures, so that, according to the degree of brevity, its length is extended, and according to the pauses of length, brief moments are formed. Thus neither a greater nor a lesser proportion should occur, but one should always exceed the other by twice its duration. When one singer responds to another more slowly, both must preserve the measure; neither should sing more hesitantly or more quickly than the other. Equal care must likewise be taken that the voices of both come together as one, and that the one who sings after the leader does not respond lower or higher than the one who leads, but, as far as possible, this discordance must be avoided. Whether both voices belong to the same mode, or one must be changed for the sake of suitability or necessity, both should nevertheless be, insofar as possible, in unison. By “the same mode of the voice,” I mean its remaining so until it passes into another and is changed into a new one.

Moreover, just as psalms and every other melody must be sung higher or lower according to the nature of the occasion or season, and according to the smaller or greater number of singers—for one ought not to perform the chant of every season at an indifferent pitch: for example, the joy of morning should be celebrated with a higher voice than the nocturnal assembly, whereas the nocturnal service should be performed watchfully but with restraint—so too the psalms that are sung continuously with their antiphons should be sung only five or four at Vespers, and six or three at the nocturnal offices. Those assigned to the morning office should either all be begun at an equal elevation, or certainly the melody ought gradually and moderately to rise from the first to the last.

The Gospel canticles should be sung higher and more slowly than the others. Just as, in singing the psalms, reason dictates the proper measure in raising and lowering the voice, so also it dictates how extended or abbreviated the words should be. Whether they are sung more slowly or more quickly, one must always take care that they be pronounced with a suitable pace in noble and full neumes, so that the hearer is not wearied by excessive prolongation and the mouth singing them does not pour them forth ignobly with irreverent haste.

In the recitation of psalms with antiphons, the beginnings of the verses should always be prolonged by one long syllable—long, however, according to the degree of shortening—so that the whole choir may take up the beginnings of the verses together and carry them forward in concord. Similarly, the ends of the verses should contain one or two prolonged syllables of the same length, so that the following verse is neither snatched up before the preceding one has ended nor, conversely, a greater interval occurs between one verse and the next than the legitimate length of the final syllables.

The repetition of the antiphons, which takes place during singing at the ends of the verses, should proceed at the same speed as the psalm. Once the psalm has ended, however, the antiphon should be prolonged by the proper length—only twice as long—except when the Gospel canticles are sung so slowly that the antiphon ought to follow with the same slowness rather than with a longer duration.

I have collected and written down these observations, whatever their worth, concerning the melodies of the psalms and equality in singing, from various sources, as I was able. I do not thereby prejudice those who possess the same melodies in another form, yet no less correctly, and perhaps better. This equality in singing is called *rhythm* in Greek and *numerus* in Latin, because the whole melody must carefully be measured according to the manner of meter. Schoolmasters ought diligently to impress this upon their pupils and, from the beginning, train children in the same discipline of equality or rhythmic proportion, teaching the measure during singing by striking the feet, hands, or by any other beating. Thus, from their earliest practice, they may learn the distinction between equal and unequal durations and become familiar with the discipline of praising God, so that they may serve God knowingly with humble devotion.

It should carefully be noted that what follows—immediately appended in the manuscript to the brief commemoration—is a diagram of the eight ecclesiastical tones expressed in the musical signs of the *Enchiridial Music*, which, as far as we have understood, were used by Hucbald. The signs placed above these were uncertain and wandering before Guido of Arezzo added the lines that we still use today, in order to determine a fixed position and tone for each sign. In this diagram, that function is performed by Hucbald’s signs, that is, by the signs of the *Enchiridial Music*, which are placed below and designate a fixed and certain tone, unlike those signs placed above, from which the use of chant was named, because accurate modulation was learned only after long practice. We have made this clear in our work *On Chant and Music*, Book II, Part II, chapters 1 and 2, where we presented the form and method of musical notation before and after Guido. The matter will become still clearer from the works of Guido of Arezzo themselves, which will be cited later.

Reader, you see the marvelous words of the younger Cato. Cherish these virtues; may the life-giving faith remain safe.

[Col. 1041]

# Hucbald the Monk’s Eclogue on the Praises of Baldness

(Apud C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, vol. I, book LX.)

[Col. 1041]

Here begins the eclogue of Hucbald, monk of Elnone, of the Order of Saint Benedict, addressed to the emperor Charles the Bald.

He who was frantic, attempting to attack the bald,  
sang verses of abuse: let the bald be celebrated  
in conspicuous and brilliant song; let everyone learn the poem.

## Prologue.—The Muses are summoned to praise the bald

[Col. 1042]

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

[Col. 1043A]

I shall endeavor to compose a fitting poem for the bald,  
to confound the curled locks around the neck.  
Let the skillful Muses celebrate bright songs together;  
let them praise the bald, let them bark against those  
who, with gnashing laughter, attempt to attack the bald.  
Let the cause of the bald ascend to the summit of heaven;  
let all the long-haired be silent, their hair gathered together.  
Let all the bald, those who make others bald, sing together  
concordant poems for the bald.

## Chapter I.—That baldness appears to come to each person as a sign of future things

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Three verses are missing here; they occur in fragments of the same *Eclogue* edited by Cardinal Mai (*Classici Auctores*, vol. V):

“Most costly celestial camps gather many bald men, competing in celebrating songs to Christ, etc.

“They compose pages and fashion bright poems, etc.” — Editor.]

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

When the bald crown of the head grows around the neck,  
it marks a bald man of strong support for the clergy,  
who, with Christ granting it, is destined to receive  
a radiant crown.

[Col. 1043B]

As though tearing out the hair of his head, the bald man tears out the sins of his heart;  
with his heart he beholds the Creator and heaven with his body,  
desiring to touch the citizens of heaven in devotion.  
Let him despise all sins together with fleeting cares,  
eagerly desiring the ascent of heaven and the harmony of the heavenly citizens;  
he praises the Creator of all things.

## Chapter II.—That the bald are singers, abbots, teachers, and also bishops and priests

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

The bald rejoice together with a clear, melodious shout,  
and keep up their choirs to sing chaste dances.  
All alike in head and concordant in body,  
they strive to establish the pleasing enclosures of the clergy.  
When the horn has been seized, they sound heavenly trumpets;  
they prepare the bright chrism in Christ’s name,  
and join together companies sprinkled with chrism.

[Col. 1043C]

In agreement and prudence they celebrate the banquets of the supper;  
they fill Christ’s guests with flesh and blood.

## Chapter III.—That the bald are kings and emperors, as well as consuls, legislators, and judges

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

The bald reign together; the conspicuous ascend to the summits,  
resplendent, adorned, with golden crowns upon their necks.  
Merciful in wealth, they yield to the requests of their clients.  
With elegance—beware!—the bald condemn crimes.  
It is established that a bald censor exercises censorship;  
believe that the bold bald man, full of judgment, must be feared.  
The blind believes that the one making others bald is blind in body;  
you who are blinded, cease to attack baldness.  
Cease, cease to gnaw at the bald pate; cease!

## Chapter IV.—That the bald are leaders of armies, themselves warriors, learned and strong

[Col. 1043D]

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

The bald lead companies renowned in battle.  
The helmeted bald fight together in crested helmets;  
the swift men twist and ruffle the troops amid slaughter.  
They seize the curls and trample down the long-haired with their heels;  
they pierce them with the spear, their bodies torn apart by the flashing sword.  
Necks fall, and the bald celebrate with a shout of triumph.  
The bald man, stirred and skilled to fight in battle,  
tramples and strikes, forcing the long-haired to give way.

[Col. 1044A]

He captures captives and constrains the captured by the neck.

## Chapter V.—Praise of the bald in their knowledge of medical art, both pharmacy and surgery

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

You will find that the bald provide support for the brain;  
you will find that the bald cure catarrhs of the head;  
you will find that the bald cure blind cavities.  
Chronical illness yields to the bald, and cachexia likewise.  
The heart-piercing cardia is stopped; colic ceases.  
Handling the steel, he restrains the torn flesh  
and the corrupted blood of the head, with the neck cauterized.  
Why do I sing so many things? In his perishing body  
he secretly dispels all things corrupt and cures collapsed bodies.

## Chapter VI.—An attack by one rebuking a mocker who insults the bald

[Col. 1044B]

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

Beware of contending with the bald, you curly-haired man,  
and cease to heap insults upon a creature.  
The all-powerful Creator of all things established  
all things and, taking care to bestow solicitude upon creatures,  
arranged for a distinguished company of the bald to arise.  
He grants the summit to him before whom he compelled all things to yield.  
Why does the madman bark with a dog’s voice?  
A collapsed pumpkin had buried the bald man in mud:  
let the muddy slander of that man fall silent more quickly.

## Chapter VII.—Likewise against the same man, and praise of the bald for humility, charity, and chastity

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

Why do you think that the bald man tears away the hide of executioners?  
The bald man tears away the sins of the heart.  
Why do you think that the bald sprinkle ashes upon his head?  
The bald man knows that the body grows together with ashes.  
Why do you think that the flesh of the bald is burned with hot charcoal?  
The bald burn their hearts, cooked by the heat of Christ.  
Why do you think that the chaste bald man is castrated in body?  
In his heart the company of the bald is castrated from all faults.  
You who slaughter the bald man in song, restrain your mockery.

## Chapter VIII.—Reproach of his poem, and an example concerning the prophet Elisha and the boys who insulted him

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

I beware of joining blind things to brilliant poems;  
let the summits be trampled by the heel, trodden down in mud.  
Let the muddy man, singing muddy things, shut up his pipe.  
It is certainly established, by the book of censors, that the clear-sounding bald man—  
whose conscience is stirred by what is to follow—  
was condemned amid the mocking laughter of a circling puppy,  
who shouted: “Climb up quickly; climb up, bald man!”  
The blind men were immediately condemned for their offense,  
and their bodies, gnawed by reproach, fell apart piece by piece.

## Chapter IX.—On the eminent bald man, the apostle Paul, who, called by Christ, was blinded and carried up into the third heaven

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

Let the songs of the bald be heaped up in the poem of the bald,  
the conspicuous one whose cruel purpose of slaughter  
had been to put Christ’s worshipers to death.  
Let all rejoice around the bald man, resplendent with charisms,  
the blinded man: summoned by Christ’s cry,  
he fell suddenly, as though pierced by the point of a spear,  
and at once received an ascent to the summit of heaven,  
beholding the Almighty with clear vision,  
whose heart shines as a heavenly vessel.

## Chapter X.—That he became a preacher from a persecutor, and that he forbade growing the hair and uttering shameful speech

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

Gather the choirs; sing of the bald in dances.  
We have learned that the renowned bald man was adorned  
as one worthy of honor; the counselor of heaven,  
with vigilant intelligence, refutes the faults of speech  
and restrains everything belonging to muddy conversation;  
he regards common benefits as belonging to all.  
He cuts off the curls and establishes civic communities.  
By reconciliation, he stirs the hearts of Christ’s fellow worshipers,  
striving to join the body to the head.  
Let the madman cease despising the renowned bald.

## Chapter XII.—The poet addresses the Muses about the mocker who suggests that the bald king’s judgment blinded him

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

Restrain with reproach the man who, with futile effort,  
attempts to attack all the bald, caught in his crime;  
shut up in blind prisons the convicted man  
who composes the inventions of transient slander.  
The bald fool thinks that the man caught in his crime is blinded by condemnation.  
Blind dog, cease despising the bald man;  
whine, dog, inventing accusations against the bald;  
whine, dog, barking against the bald in your offense;  
whine, dog, and cease gnawing at the bald.

## Chapter XII.—A summary of the praise of the bald from the position and beauty of the body, and that the bald man is a microcosm

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

Gather a distinguished assembly, a company of the bald.  
When you see a bald man, understand that he is encircled by heaven.  
Recognize the crown of baldness as the center of heaven;  
the remaining bald features commend the circuit of the cosmos.  
Join the bald together; gather together the shining bald.  
Cynthia will cease to compare golden colors;  
darkening her horns, she will yield to the growing baldness.  
The bald shine; the helmet of the bald gleams;  
flashing, the bright abundance of heaven glitters like lightning.

### Conclusion of the poem

Sing, Muses, songs of clear sound for the bald.

It will be fitting to set bright reeds together in the enclosures;  
the singable poem is completed with brilliant bald men.

[Col. 1045] (Here ends the poem of Hucbald the monk to Charles on the praise of the bald.)

[Col. 1045]

## Notes

Many things in this poem require restoration if anyone wishes to avoid mere nonsense. In the prologue, read:

“Let them bark against the one clear in crime.”

Chapter 1. I think it should be read:

“With his heart he beholds the Creator, and with his heart heaven.”

Chapter 3:

“Cease, bald-pate; cease, cease to gnaw vainly.”

Chapter 4:

“The crested bald men fight together in helmets.” That is, by terrifying their common enemy.

Chapter 5, write:

“The corrupted blood of the head, hip, and neck.” [The transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain.]

Chapter 7, I read:

“Cocio is castrated in his heart from all faults.”

*Cocio*, a soothsayer in Plautus and other authors, denotes a prophet for this monk. And indeed we must admit that the man possessed no little learning. For he clearly imitates and expresses Virgil, Persius, Terence, Plautus, Lucretius, and several other excellent authors, without completely suppressing the rays of his ingenuity despite such severe constraints.

I had written this when I received from Bohemia a written sheet by this same author; and behold, it was enriched by several verses of equal value. These verses, namely, report a vow for Caesar Charles the Bald not expressed elsewhere. Since I consider it so relevant to the rest, I think I should explain the occasion that moved the author to write.

Muse, beware of making bald men bald in a bright poem;  
let curled, tailed slander fall against the curl [reading uncertain].  
Sing the graces of the bald in a bright poem.  
Let them fall silent amid a swiftly sounding blast.  
Let Caesar’s chains fall together with heaven’s heights in Christ’s worship;  
let the prudent Cato’s *cata cista* [uncertain reading] close the clergy’s poems that seize upon faults.  
Muse, bring to a close the poem of the bald, adornment of the bald.

Charles, sing with the bald, most illustrious Caesar,  
the efforts of the clergy made glorious by the crucified Christ.  
The closed Muse embraces fitting care together with Caesar.

[Col. 1047]

Beware of the adorned crown; the Charoleans adorn, with Caesar the Bald,  
poems celebrating the bald.

Christ, look upon the bald head with its adornment,  
whose cross forgives sins to all the bald.

And with this addition may the reader be enriched, lest he be able to say that we have uselessly spent and consumed so much tedium and so much paper, both for ourselves and for him.

[Col. 1047]

# Metric Epistle of Hucbald the Monk to the Emperor Charles the Bald

He sends him the poems of his teacher Milo on the praise of frugality.

[Note: [Col. 1047B] The preface to this book, now lost and omitted by us under MILO, is presented here from Martène. — Editor, *Patrologia*.]

[Col. 1047B] Preface of Milo, monk of Elnone, to King Charles, for a metrical book on the praise of frugality.

To the glorious King Charles, Milo, suppliant.

We know that the Muses pleased ancient rulers,  
and that honours were received in return for such a gift.  
Virgil did not regret wearing down his pen’s nib,  
because he preserved his lost little fields.

And Naso, a foreign exile on the shores of Tomi,  
soothed the prince’s ears with manifold song.  
They may suppose that Porphyry, who painted verses on varied tablets,  
was released from exile by a *biathanaton* utterance [reading uncertain];  
because that impious man vomited very many insults against Christians,  
I complain that you, Muses, supplied him with aid.

When Tarquinius Priscus wished to purchase the Sibyl’s writings,  
he complained that the price was excessive  
and refused to give what the greedy prophet demanded.  
But after three books had been burned at great cost,  
the remaining six were valued at the same price, though late.

When a little Greek brought Augustus a gift of verse  
and received no gift from so great a prince,  
he did not first restrain his bold Muses,  
until, by eliciting verses from Augustus himself,

[Col. 1048B]

he returned to him two coins offered for the poem,  
receiving a distich and repaying a small sum in poverty;  
he declares himself generous and condemns the king as miserly.

After a raven had been offered to him and was rejected  
while greeting him with its voice,  
he poured forth these complaints from his mouth, lamenting,  
remembering that his labor had been wasted and that he could offer  
no consolation in return to the needy bearer;  
and thus he brought back many exchanges previously denied.

Milo, your poet, most illustrious king of kings,  
I am a croaking raven who greet you in a humble voice—  
not that treacherous raven of Noah who fled the holy enclosure,  
but the one who fed the holy man in the morning and the prophet in the evening.  
Because my heart burns with manifold love for you,  
I send this very small theme and pray  
that safe health and perpetual glory may be yours  
throughout the whole time of your life, until, transferred to the stars,  
you remain with Christ, flourish with blessed kings,  
and a happy succession of the kingdom proceed from your descendants.

Poems lack worth if they deserve no rewards.

Here follows the title of the book:

**USEFUL WEAPONS OF SACRED FRUGALITY** against the cook of Babylon, drawn from the quivers of divine Scripture through the labor of Milo, coenobite of Saint Amandus, the holy and blessed bishop of Christ.

.

(Apud Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 45.)

## To the Emperor Augustus Charles, Hucbald

[Col. 1047A]

Golden light of the world, glory of the Frankish kingdom,  
illustrious Caesar, hail, hope and honor of your fatherland.  
Retaining the name of your forefathers and likewise their divine dignity,  
you, Charles, are dear to Christian peoples.  
To you God himself has entrusted the world he created  
and has given a pious seat of empire.  
Since you nobly guide the reins of the kingdom,  
all strive to bend their necks to you.  
Under your covenant the whole world gathers,  
seeking to have its laws established under your rule.  
Indeed, rejoicing at the omen of so great a prince,  
Rome herself, head of the world, has bowed her head.

More could be said, but the page concludes it in a few words:  
you burn with love for him; in his honor you possess power.

Moreover, since you fittingly administer the laws  
of the kingdom entrusted to you according to God’s law,  
while wisdom shines inwardly in your understanding  
and your house gleams outwardly with wealth,

[Col. 1048A]

powerful like Solomon and strong in prudent understanding,  
you fill the earth with praise and hold heaven in your mind.  
And because you search out the sayings of exalted wisdom,  
and your mind often rejoices in attending to it,  
receive these great gifts, though small in weight,  
which this *Pandect*—the “all-containing” work—gathers together for you.  
Here shine the sayings, gathered together, of the ancient law,  
which Milo, your poet and likewise our teacher,  
wrote in this small book. This work aptly displays his talent.  
He once described the Life of Amandus in verse,  
and brought it to you.

While he desired to celebrate his vow  
in this little book, written in your honor,  
he died, paying the debt owed by human life,  
and thus took the heavenly road above the stars.

[Col. 1048B]

But before life left his chilled limbs,  
he had ordered these dear pledges to be given to me.  
Thus I began in eagerness, but soon was consumed by grief,  
wondering what I should put on the title page of this book,  
not thinking it right to remove it from the illustrious name,  
since it belonged to a distinguished Ausonian prince.

Yet a firm anchor steadied my doubtful mind,  
lest the silent page mourn its title.  
Rather, fulfilling his duties as a suppliant in place of the deceased,  
I myself would happily give these things into Caesar’s hands.

Here is the work; here is the poem begun under so great a name;  
it awaits your kindly examination.  
Come here, Augustus, in your clemency toward all,  
you who are powerful in virtue and flourish in goodness.  
Here you have praises of sobriety, wars, and triumphs,  
poems written briefly with watchful ingenuity.

[Col. 1050A]

If these should perhaps be granted your favor,  
you bear pious gifts to the honor of the holy Church.  
Here shine the way, the life, and salvation; here, rich in divine treasures,  
the renowned gifts of God shine, calling you above the stars.  
May the Almighty, after this life has run its course,  
place you happily in the blessed realms, where you will hold the kingdom.

Therefore, pious king, although these poems may be rough  
and obscure in verse, do not despise them, but read them again.  
Caesar, live powerful; live happily; farewell without end.  
I ask, I entreat, I beg you: remember Hucbald.

[Col. 1049]

# Epitaph of Milo, Monk of Saint Amandus of Elnone, Hucbald’s Teacher, by Hucbald

(Apud Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.)

Milo, poet and wise man, lies enclosed beneath this marble,  
sweet-speaking in verse, who published the book of Sobriety  
and beautifully depicted holy Amandus,  
adorning him with flowers and embellishing him in meter and prose—  
the palm, head, and crown of so great a bishop.

[Col. 1049]

# Hucbald’s Twofold Epitaph

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VI.)

## I

[Col. 1049B]

In this tomb sleeps a simple dove without bitterness,  
a teacher, the flower and honor of both clergy and monks,  
Hucbald, whose fame throughout the regions of the world  
is proclaimed by the published melodies and deeds of the saints.  
Here he brought to our shores the precious relics of Cyricus,  
discovered at Nevers, and wrote his triumph.

## II

Most illustrious orator, sweating balsam over the world,  
honey-sweet rhetorician, known above the heavens,  
Hail, Father Hucbald, with reverence throughout the ages.

[Col. 1050B]

You are a lamp to monks, a flower and glory to the learned;  
the people, mourning forever, lament that you have been taken from them.  
Flourish always, wise man; farewell, dear lover of God.

You had published, in a polished style and with honorable skill,  
the contest of the mother Julitta and of Cyricus, her beautiful offspring,  
like a renowned and energetic teacher, a master in all things.  
May what I ask be praised, flourish, be read, and be loved.

Whoever you are who read these words, may God grant him rest;  
may he carry the palm with the blessed in dances above the stars.  
Glory to the poor man who completed these verses as a client.

In the year of the Lord 930. Pope Stephen VII, or VIII.

[Col. 1049]

# Historical Notice

(Apud Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. XVIII, col. 381.)

[Col. 1049C] Stephen, a German by nationality, was elected by the Romans in the year of Christ our Redeemer 939 through the influence of King Otto, with the votes of the cardinals set aside, during the reign of Constantine VIII and Romanus, the Eastern emperors. [Col. 1050C] He was disfigured in the face by frequent sacrilegious blows from the tyrants whose hatred he had aroused against himself because of his election. Alberic, who at that time held power in the City, believed that he could not securely possess dominion over the world unless some kinsman well known to him held the pontificate of the Roman city. For this reason, being little favorable toward Stephen himself, he allowed him to be so grievously lacerated by the hands of the impious and disfigured in the face. Although these marks, inflicted by Satan’s ministers for the sake of justice, were not a disgrace but an ornament, he nevertheless for this reason generally abstained from public gatherings of men. This act aroused Otto’s determination to avenge the crime of the Romans and restrain the tyrannical power that they had hitherto exercised in the promotion of pontiffs. But when he accomplished this, it will be related below in its proper place.

[Col. 1052A] When the Frankish nobles rebelled against King Louis and refused to receive him, Stephen sent word through a certain Damasus, acting as an envoy, that they should receive their king; if they refused, they should know that they would incur the sentence of excommunication. In Italy, the war between Hugh and Alberic, previously settled once by Odo, abbot of Cluny, broke out again after the peace had been shattered. On this account Odo was once more summoned to Rome by Stephen; but before peace was restored, he died there. Shortly afterward Pope Stephen also died, having, according to the Vatican lists, occupied the see for three years, four months, and five days.

[Col. 1051]

# Letters and Privileges of Pope Stephen VII

## I. Bull of Stephen VII for the Monastery of Saint Vincent of Volturno

[Note: [Col. 1051D] Whether this mutilated bull is genuine is difficult to determine amid such a scarcity of documents; nevertheless, it cannot escape suspicion, since we know that the monastery of Volturno was not without forgers. — Jaffé.]

(Year 930)

He confirms to the monastery of Saint Vincent of Volturno and to its abbot Raimbald all its rights and possessions.

[Muratori, *Writers of Italian History*, I, II, 422.]

[Col. 1051B]

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Raimbald, venerable man and abbot of the monastery of Christ’s martyr Vincent, situated in the region of Samnium, in the territory of Benevento, above the source of the Volturno River, and through you to all your successors who are regularly to be promoted in that same venerable monastery, forever.

[Col. 1051C] Exercising pious concern for the holy Churches of God, for the salvation of the sheep entrusted to us by God, and especially for monks serving God, we strive to assist those who devote themselves to divine contemplation, so that together with them we may obtain the grace of divine reward. Since you have therefore asked us to fortify, by the authority of our privilege, the monastery of blessed Vincent, martyr of Christ, with all that belongs to it—cells, chapels, castles, and lands—under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, we grant that it be held by you and your legitimate successors, the abbots, so that it may be subject to no other Church’s authority. Rather, together with all its dependencies and cells, including the monastery of blessed Peter beside the river in the territory of Sabbati, Benevento; the monastery of the Lord Savior at Alise; the cell of Saint Mary at the Two Basilicas; the cell of Saint Mary beside the Trinius River; the cell of Saint Mary at Castanieto; the cell of Saint Mary at Palene; the cell of Saint Mary at Apinianici; the cell of Saint Peter at Vipera; and the cell of Saint Vincent at Taccu, together with all the monasteries and cells,

[Col. 1052B]

let them remain under the protection of the apostolic see.

Moreover, whatever has been granted to that monastery by kings, dukes, princes, or other faithful persons, or may happen to be granted in the future, and whatever is known to have been confirmed for your predecessors by the privileges of our predecessors, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We decree also that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with contrary vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit those for whose support and governance it was granted.

When the abbot of that place, or one of his successors, dies, no one shall be placed there by any trickery or violence except one whom the brothers have chosen by common consent or by wiser counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or basilicas, and the ordinations of monks or clerics belonging to the monastery from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer.

We also forbid any bishop to dare summon or excommunicate the abbot or a monk of this monastery to his synod. Nor do we permit any priest of any Church, apart from the apostolic see, to exercise authority there, so that no one may presume to celebrate the solemn Mass there unless invited by the abbot.

Priests and clerics from any church who come to live among the congregation of the brothers, or to receive the monastic habit, shall be received immediately, and no one may prevent this.

No one may presume to lay violent hands upon the monastery, its cells, possessions, or property, or to inflict any loss through malice. Rather, at all times the same place, together with its dependencies, shall be preserved freely and peacefully under the protection of the apostolic see.

If anyone should presume to violate the constitution of this apostolic privilege, unless he makes worthy amends, let him lose the dignity of his honor, be separated from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be condemned with the devil and his ministers to eternal fire. But whoever observes these provisions justly and piously shall receive from the Lord the fullness of the grace of blessing and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen the *primicerius* in the year of the pontificate of our lord Stephen, supreme pontiff, the seventh . . . . . .

## II. PRIVILEGE OF STEPHEN VII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY OF BRONNE  
*(Year 920–931.)* He confirms the foundation of the abbey of Bronne, in the county of Namur, while residing in Rome, at the request and in the presence of Saint Gerard, abbot and founder of Bronne.

*[In Mansi, Councils, vol. XVIII.]*

[Col. 1053B]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, and of holy Mary, ever virgin, Stephen, supreme bishop of the apostolic see, servant of the servants of God, to our brothers and sons living in the Catholic faith throughout the whole world.

We wish it to be known to all, present and future, how our son and brother Gerard, abbot, by the favor of divine mercy, informed us concerning the monastery of Bronne, which he reformed and restored for the better [Col. 1053C] in honor of holy Mary, ever virgin, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saint John the Baptist.

Afterward, in addition to the relics of many saints, he also gathered there the body of Saint Eugene, martyr, archbishop of the see of Toledo, a disciple of and ordained by Saint Dionysius the archbishop, and brought it there with great reverence and honor. He also devotedly and voluntarily gave to the aforesaid monastery his own inheritance, both in lands and in slaves, and in everything attached to it by hereditary right.

After he had informed us of these matters, he fell at our feet and asked that, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, everyone who should attempt to remove anything from their monastery—whether from the relics [Col. 1053D] of the saints, or from the vestments and books, or from the territories, or from the slaves, or from any other things that it now possesses as gifts or that by God’s mercy it may subsequently obtain—should be cursed.

He also earnestly requested that all who should in any way presume to violate the privilege concerning that place and monastery, which royal magnificence and imperial authority had already established, should be bound by the same anathema.

Specifically, no bishop, no count, no advocate, no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority in the Church, should presume in our times or in times to come to enter the church, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery, whether to hear legal cases or to make demands, or to exact fines, tributes, or any provisions, or to impose lodgings, make enclosures or forest clearings, take sureties, or unjustly distrain the people of that monastery—both free persons and slaves—who dwell upon its land; nor should anyone enter upon any other restitutions or unlawful pretexts [Col. 1054A].

Rather, the aforesaid servant of God Gerard and his successors, together with their monks, shall be permitted to possess and administer the aforesaid monastery’s property peacefully under the protection of our immunity, without the participation of any external authority, unless the abbot himself and his monks reasonably request that such a thing be done.

He likewise earnestly requested that anyone who should presume in any way to devastate or violate that place and its inhabitants within their boundaries by hostile fire, slaughter, or any unjust oppression should be condemned by the same curse [Col. 1054B].

Therefore, with the bishops and brothers of this holy Roman see standing by and consenting, we have decreed that the petition of God’s servant Gerard be confirmed by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, by the authority of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; of holy Mary, ever virgin, Mother of God; of all the heavenly powers; of Saint John the Baptist; of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; of Saint Eugene, martyr, patron and protector of that place; of the saints whose relics are there; and likewise of all the saints whose names are written in the book of life, we excommunicate, anathematize, and condemn all who invalidate or violate any of these provisions concerning the immunity and liberty of the Church and place of Bronne mentioned above—unless they repent, do penance, obtain pardon from the abbot and his brothers, and thereafter make amends [Col. 1054C].

But whoever proves to be an observer of this our command and of the royal decree may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

I, Castorius, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, acting with apostolic authority and at the direction of holy Pope Stephen, have authenticated this document [Col. 1054D].

Sign of the glorious Lord Pope Stephen.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord . . . .

Executed at Rome, successfully. Amen.

I, Leo, archpriest of the holy Roman Church, at the request of our lord Stephen, have subscribed. Amen.

I, Valentianus, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

I, Agapitus, bishop, at his command have subscribed. Amen.

I, Emerentianus, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

I, Simphorianus, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

I, Liberius, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

I, Laurentius, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

[Col. 1055A] I, Florentius, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

I, Gregorius, bishop, have subscribed. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 936. POPE JOHN XI

[Col. 1055]

### HISTORICAL NOTICE

*[In Cocquelines, Collection of the Bulls and Privileges of the Roman Pontiffs.]*

John XI, successor of Sergius III, born of Marozia, a prostitute, was appointed pope through the power of Wido, marquis of Tuscany [Note: [Col. 1055B] If one believes Liutprand, book II, chapter 13.] after the death of Stephen VIII. He sat for four years and ten months [Note: [Col. 1055B] According to Vignoli’s catalogues, in the first of which four months and ten days are mistakenly recorded; and according to seven others prefixed to the critical edition of Baronius [Col. 1056B], as well as nearly all chroniclers and chronologists.]. He lived during the reigns of the emperors Constantine Porphyrogenitus in the East and Henry the Fowler in the West. Held in custody by his brother Alberic, he died at the beginning of January 936; the ten months added to his four years are to be understood as a rounded calculation.

[Col. 1055]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE JOHN XI

## I. PRIVILEGE OF JOHN XI FOR THE MONASTERY OF CLUNY  
*(Year 931.)* He confirms Saint Odo as abbot in the administration of the monastery of Cluny, as well as the monastery’s exemption from every form of domination. He establishes that, after Odo’s death, the abbot’s election shall be free and conducted without consultation with anyone. He also confirms the Roman monastery granted to Cluny by Rudolf, king of Burgundy. He further grants permission to receive monasteries offered for reform. He restores the tithes of the Cluniac chapels that had been taken away by bishops. He likewise confirms Cluny’s own mint, as granted by Rudolf, king of the Franks. He also grants permission to receive temporarily brothers who, for the improvement of their lives, wish to transfer from other monasteries to Cluny. Finally, he declares that the monastery of Cluny belongs to the holy apostolic see for protection and support, and orders that, as a sign of this protection, ten solidi be paid at Rome for five years.

*[Cluniac Bulls, p. 1.]*

[Col. 1055C]

[Col. 1055D] John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo [Col. 1056C], venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the territory of Mâcon, and through you to that monastery and your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance, with benevolent compassion, to come to the aid of the pious requests of those who ask, and with eager devotion to grant assent to their desires; for by this we shall especially earn a reward from the Creator of all things, God. Therefore, since you have asked us to decree by our apostolic authority that the aforesaid monastery should remain perpetually in the condition in which Duke William determined by his testament that it should remain, it is subject to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve. Moved by your prayers, we grant it to you to govern.

Accordingly, let that monastery, with all its possessions—both those it now has and those that shall thereafter be bestowed upon it—be free from the domination of every king, bishop, count, or any of William’s relatives. No one [Col. 1057A] shall presume, against the will of the monks, to appoint a superior over them after your death. Rather, without consultation with any prince, let them have the free power to appoint for themselves whomever they wish according to the Rule of Saint Benedict—unless, God forbid, they should prefer to choose someone who consents to their vices; whoever wishes, in zeal for God, must prevent this.

The monastery called Romanum, which the mother of our son King Rudolf donated to the aforesaid Cluny, shall remain subject to it, together with the estate of Vaning, just as she determined in the deed of donation. If, however, you agree to receive into your jurisdiction any monastery that those to whose disposition it appears to belong voluntarily offer for improvement, you shall have our permission for this [Col. 1057B].

The tithes that formerly belonged to your chapels and that have been taken away by some bishop under a supposed authority or permission, we restore to you in full. As for the chapels, whether some have already been built or are yet to be built there, we permit them to remain in such a way that nothing is diminished from the tithes belonging to your churches. We decree that what our beloved son Bishop Berno granted to you from the aforesaid chapels shall remain permanently valid.

Moreover, whatever from vineyards or cultivated lands belongs to your religious community, and also a portion of the tithes belonging to your hospice, we decree to be yours; likewise with regard to those possessions that you are to receive. We also confirm by our apostolic authority what Leobaldus, at his death, returned and left to the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1057C]. Similarly, we confirm and restore to you what is at Agiona, or elsewhere among the possessions that ought to belong to that monastery, and the chapel of Saint Martin situated in the estate of Maceio.

You shall also have your own mint, just as our son Rudolf, king of the Franks, granted it. And since, as is all too evident, nearly all monasteries are now deviating from their purpose, we grant that if any monk from any monastery wishes to transfer to your way of life solely for the purpose of improving his life—provided that his own abbot has neglected to provide him with the regular means of overcoming the desire to possess property—you may receive him until the manner of life in his monastery has been reformed [Col. 1057D].

We grant you immunity in the manner owed everywhere to holy places, so that no one may in any way presume, without consulting you, to distrain or invade your slaves or any of your possessions.

Indeed, in acknowledgment that the aforesaid monastery belongs to the holy apostolic see for protection and support, ten solidi shall be paid for five years. But if anyone attempts to resist this most salutary constitution of ours, or tries to violate any of its provisions, and does not observe everything that we have established in this privilege, let him know that, under the solemn warning of divine judgment, he is eternally bound by the bond of anathema [Col. 1058A], unless he repents; that he is to be excluded from the kingdom of God and tortured without end with the devil.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this most salutary decree of ours may deserve to receive from Christ the Lord a blessing, and from the holy apostles, judges of the world, absolution both here and in the age to come.

Written by the hand of Andrew, archivist, in the month of March, in the fourth indiction.

## II. PRIVILEGE OF JOHN XI FOR THE SAME MONASTERY  
*(Year 932.)* At the request of Saint Odo and through the intervention of Hugh, king of Italy, he confirms the monastery of Cluny with all its possessions and properties, both those it has and those it will acquire in the future. Among other things, he wishes the monastery called Carus Locus, in the territory of Mâcon, to remain perpetually subject to the Cluniac monastery.

*[In Cocquelines, Collection of the Bulls and Privileges of the Roman Pontiffs.]*

[Col. 1058B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, called Cluny, and through you to your successors who shall serve in that venerable monastery forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance, with benevolent compassion, to assist those endowed with pious religion and to grant the requests of those who ask with eager devotion. For then the greatest reward is stored up for us with God, the Creator of all, when venerable [Col. 1058C] places, suitably ordered, have unquestionably been brought into a better condition.

Therefore, since your religious community and the intervention of Hugh, our beloved son and most glorious king, have entreated our apostolate to confirm by our apostolic authority the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, with all its possessions and properties, both those it now appears to possess and whatever shall thereafter be offered or donated to that monastery, we confirm it.

Indeed, we also confirm to that holy place another monastery belonging to the Roman Church, called Carus Locus, in the territory of Mâcon, so that it may remain there in perpetuity, under this arrangement: no one, whether of the ecclesiastical order or a layperson, shall inflict any disturbance upon that monastery or upon the possessions belonging to it.

But if any person, whether clerical or lay, should use force against those possessions that shall thereafter be given or donated there, or should wish to withdraw them from its jurisdiction, those possessions shall return to their donors and their heirs [Col. 1058D]. Nevertheless, if they remain with those possessions within the monastic order, whether during the time of this abbot or of his successors, this privilege shall remain unshaken, subject, of course, to the payment owed to the holy Roman Church.

By the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose viceregency we exercise, though unequal to his merits, with the support of divine grace, and under the prohibition of anathema and the solemn warning of divine judgment, we establish that no one may in any way tear down what has been decreed by us, but that it shall remain firm, stable, and unshaken throughout perpetual ages [Col. 1059A].

If anyone, however, should attempt or undertake to act against the provisions of this apostolic privilege of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the anathema of our Lord’s chief apostle Peter, and that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most atrocious pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Let him likewise be plunged into the abyss and Tartarean chaos and perish with the impious.

But may those who, with pious regard, prove to be guardians, obedient persons, and observers of this salutary decree of ours deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly recompense from our Lord, the just judge [Col. 1059B].

Written by the hand of Theodore, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the fifth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Urso, first archivist of the holy apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the eleventh, in the most sacred second year of Saint Peter’s see, in the month of June, in the aforementioned fifth indiction.

## III. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XI FOR THE MONASTERY OF VÉZELAY  
*(Year 933.)*

*[In Acher, Spicilegium, vol. II, p. 504.]*

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Aymo [Col. 1059C], venerable abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and to the entire community of that monastery, forever.

Whenever we are asked to grant things that unquestionably accord with reason, we ought to concede them with a willing mind and provide the petitions of those who ask with appropriate assistance. Therefore, since you asked us to make an apostolic-see privilege for the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are recognized as presiding—a monastery formerly built by Gerard, a most noble and Christian man, and by his wife Berta, in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, mother of that same Lord Jesus Christ; situated, namely, in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the territory of Avalois; and bestowed by the aforesaid founders upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through pious devotion and the text of their testament—we have willingly decreed, moved by your prayers, that this should be done.

By this apostolic privilege, therefore, we confirm and establish that no king, no prelate, no count, nor anyone else may disturb that monastery, diminish, remove, or appropriate for personal use the things given there by the aforesaid founders or by other faithful persons, or whatever may in the future be offered there under any pretext or guise [Col. 1059D]. Rather, we wish and command that these possessions be held without disturbance for the support of that monastery and for the use of the abbots and monks serving God there under the rule of the holy Father Benedict.

This is subject to the following condition: none of our successors, pontiffs of this holy see which we serve by God’s authority, shall ever or anywhere in future times permit any of these possessions to be granted as a benefice to anyone, exchanged, or conceded under any form of rent. Instead, receiving only the rent assigned in the testamentary deed of transfer by the founders who made the Roman Church the holy heir of that monastery—namely, one pound of silver each year—our successors shall diligently strive, through paternal support, to provide pastoral protection to that monastery against all who attack it [Col. 1060A].

We further establish that, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery dies, no one else shall be appointed there through any stratagem of improper influence, except one whom the monks’ consensus, in the fear of God and according to the institution of the Rule of Saint Benedict, has chosen and whom the pontiff of this apostolic see has judged should be appointed, or whose appointment he has approved at the monks’ request [Col. 1060B].

We add the following provision to this present chapter in order to exclude avarice: no king, bishop, priest, or any other faithful person may, either personally or through an appointed representative, dare to accept anything under any pretext as a gift in connection with the appointment of that abbot, clerics, or priests; the giving of chrism; the consecration of a basilica; or any matters belonging to that monastery. Nor may the abbot himself presume to give anything for his appointment, lest on this account the offerings that the faithful present to a pious place be consumed [Col. 1060C].

Nor may the bishop of that city or diocese celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, nor announce stations in that monastery, lest the peace of God’s servants be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering. Nor may he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it.

We do not merely refuse to allow the reception of the faithful and of religious men, and the charitable hospitality that the Apostle commands to be offered to all according to the resources and capacities of the place; rather, we encourage it. But the proper number of the community must also be maintained, so that neither an excessive number may produce scarcity nor a small number of inhabitants lead to the abandonment of the place.

We also confirm by our authority the privilege granted to that monastery by our predecessor, Pope Nicholas, of pious memory, except for the fact that he assigned it under the title of “handmaids of God,” who, because of the frequent attacks of the world, cannot now remain there in an orderly manner. For the sake of greater usefulness, we decree that they should instead appropriately live under the monastic habit [Col. 1060D].

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person attempts to act against this charter of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power or office, acknowledge himself guilty before divine judgment, and—unless he bewails the wrongs he has committed—be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1061A] and subjected to the strict judgment of eternal vengeance.

But may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who rightly observe what is due to that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Andrew, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the sixth indiction.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January, by the hand of Gregory, beloved of God, treasurer of the holy apostolic see, in the third year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the eleventh, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostles.

## IV. LETTER OF JOHN XI TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF AUTUN  
*(Year 933.)* He asserts for the Church of Autun the right to elect its bishop freely.

*[In Baluze, Capitularies, vol. II, p. 1495.]*

[Col. 1061B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church of Autun, and through you to your successors forever.

It has been heard by our apostolic ears, and frequently reported, that violence is being inflicted upon the Churches of Gaul, contrary to the decrees of the canons, in the election of their bishops. We, to whom the care of all the churches has been entrusted, although unworthy, grieve over this from the depths of our heart. Desiring by the authority of God and blessed Peter to cut away this violence from all the churches [Col. 1061C], we have determined to write this privilege of our decree especially for you, the holy Church of Autun, first entreating the kings of the Franks to observe it.

In it we decree and regularly establish that henceforth no king, prince, or any other person may presume to impose or appoint over you or your successors anyone other than a son of that Church, according to the written canons: one whom the clergy has elected and the people acclaimed, if a worthy person can be found within it. But if, as we do not believe will happen, no such person should be found there, then, by the unanimous counsel of both clergy and people, the most worthy person from elsewhere shall be sought.

Finally, with regard to the dignity you have obtained from your lord, your houses, your canonries, the common cause of the brothers, and all your property, we grant you by apostolic authority permission, without the impediment of any contrary dispute, to arrange the establishment and election of lawful successors from that household [Col. 1061D].

If anyone, great or small, should in any way rise against this decree and grant of ours, or presume to violate or weaken our apostolic authority [Col. 1062A], let that person know that, by invocation of the holy Trinity, by the power of the blessed apostle Peter, and by our authority, he is eternally struck down and condemned with the enemies of God and those who oppose him, until satisfaction is made, and is condemned forever.

But may those who preserve this decree of ours obtain peace, joy, and blessing from God, the giver of all good things, and deserve to possess eternal life.

Written by the hand of Theodore, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March and in the sixth indiction. Given . . . . Farewell.

## V. [Note: [Col. 1061] This bull is not free from suspicion. Jaffé.] PRIVILEGE OF JOHN XI FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY AND SAINT MARTIN AT POITIERS  
*(Year 931–936.)*

*[In D. Bouquet, Collection of the Historians.]*

[Col. 1062B]

In the name of God the Father, I, Pope John, make known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that our brother Frotharius, bishop, sent his legates to us and [entreated us] that we might confirm and strengthen the written privilege of his monastery, which is built outside the walls of the city of Poitiers on the river Clain.

With God’s permission, we have willingly fulfilled his request in our benevolence. This monastery is dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Virgin and Mother of God, and also of Saint Martin.

We wish that from this day forward that place be safe from every adversity, and that the monks who remain in it may joyfully and without any opposition fulfill the service of God. No one shall demand any debt from that place, hold a legal assembly there, or demand any subjection, except that on ordinary days they shall say one private Mass and one psalm at every hour for the community of Saint Peter.

We excommunicate, moreover, in the name of almighty God, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, all God’s saints, all bishops, and all our successors, so that whoever violates this written privilege shall be accursed forever from the body and blood of the Lord [variant: Christ], unless he comes to make amendment and give satisfaction [Col. 1062D].

And so that this privilege, most willingly made by us, might possess firmer force, we have confirmed it with our own hands and caused it to be strengthened, in the word of God, by religious men and the consuls at Rome.

Sign of Pope John, who ordered this privilege to be made.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 928. SEULF, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 1063]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*[In Flodoard, History of the Church of Rheims, book IV, chapter 18.]*

[Col. 1063A] Seulf succeeded Heriveus. At that time he was serving the city of Rheims as archdeacon: a man sufficiently trained both in ecclesiastical and secular disciplines, who had studied the liberal arts under Remigius, his teacher at Auxerre.

After he had been ordained bishop through the consent and command of King Robert by Abbo of Soissons and the other prelates of the province of Rheims, Odo, formerly the brother of Archbishop Heriveus, and Heriveus, his nephew, brought a complaint against him before the same prelate, alleging that they had not at all kept the fidelity they had promised him. Because they refused either to come before that pontiff to give an account or to settle the matter by single combat with their accusers, the Church possessions, many of which they held from that bishopric, were taken from them; Count Heribert then brought them to King Robert. They were held in custody until King Robert’s death: Odo with Heribert himself, and Heriveus at Paris.

It is said that at that time this archbishop and his counselors made an agreement with Count Heribert concerning the election of his son to this see in exchange for the expulsion of the aforesaid men [Col. 1063B]. Finally, this prelate sent legates of the Church to Rome to obtain Pope John’s consent to his ordination, and received from him the pallium sent to him together with the letter of privilege of this see [Col. 1064A].

He also held a synod at the estate of Trosleius with the bishops of the diocese of Rheims, where several counts were also present. At that synod Count Isaac came to make satisfaction for the wrongs he had committed against the Church of Cambrai, having burned, through a deceitful seizure and invasion, a certain castle belonging to Stephen, the prelate of that city.

For this crime, after being bound over at this synod, he made peace with the aforesaid bishop for one hundred pounds of silver, with Heribert and the other counts of France who were present taking care of the matter.

This prelate surrounded the monastery of Saint Remigius, together with the adjacent churches and houses, with a wall, and established a castle there. He repaired the episcopal residence with chambers and embellished it with paintings. He also made a large golden chalice, weighing ten pounds, with gems, in honor of the Mother of God. He prepared certain other ornaments for the church as well.

He began to cover with silver the ciborium over the altar of Saint Mary, but, overtaken by death, he was unable to complete the work. It is said that he ended his life after being given poison by the household servants or retainers of Count Heribert [Col. 1064B].

[Col. 1063]

# COUNCIL OF RHEIMS UNDER SEULF

At this council, penance was imposed on those who had taken part in the war at Soissons between Kings Robert and Charles in the year 923 [variant: 924].

*[In Labbe, Councils, vol. IX, col. 381.]*

[Col. 1063C] In the year 923 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the episcopate of Lord Seulf, the holy Fathers assembled—namely Seulf, archbishop of Rheims; Abbo, bishop of Soissons; Adelelmus of Laon; Stephen of Cambrai; also Adelelmus of Senlis; and Airardus, then ordained bishop of Noyon—together with the legates of the other bishops of the same diocese of Rheims.

They decreed that the following penance should be imposed upon those who had taken part in the battle fought at Soissons between Robert and Charles: namely, that for three years they should perform penance during three Lents, so that during the first Lent they should remain outside the church and be reconciled on Holy Thursday [Col. 1064C].

During all three of these Lents, on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, they were to fast on bread, salt, and water, or redeem the obligation. Likewise, they were to fast for fifteen days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist and for fifteen days before the Nativity of the Lord and Savior, and also every Friday throughout the year, unless they made compensation, or a major feast happened to fall on that day, or they happened to be detained by illness or military service.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 913. POPE LEO VII

[Col. 1065]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*[In Mansi, Expanded Collection of the Councils, vol. XVIII, p. 375.]*

Leo VII of this name obtained the pontificate in the year 936 of the Redeemer, during the time of the eastern emperors Constantine and Romanus. Concerning him, Flodoard writes the following in his Chronicle under that year:

“After Pope John, the brother of Alberic, had died, a certain Leo, a servant of God, was appointed pope at Rome. He summoned Odo, abbot of Cluny, a man renowned for holiness, to Rome, so that he might act as mediator in arranging peace between Hugh, king of Italy, who had begun to besiege Rome, and Alberic, ruler of Rome. The most holy abbot came, and through his intervention he obtained from both men that Alberic should take Hugh’s daughter as his wife and that Hugh should lift the siege.”

During his pontificate, Henry, king of Germany, the glory of the Christian religion, died. After subduing many other peoples mentioned above, he converted Cnut, king of Denmark, to the faith of Christ and turned the Danes away from human sacrifice. He left as heir of the kingdom his son Otto, not unlike himself in piety and military courage.

At this same time, to the affliction and disturbance of the Church, Manasses, bishop of Arles, added a new misery. An ambitious man, by no means content with his own see, through the efforts of Hugh, king of Italy, he seized not only the Churches of Verona, Trent, and Mantua, but also that of Milan, claiming that he was acting on the example of the prince of the apostles, who had likewise possessed the Churches of Rome, Antioch, and Alexandria simultaneously. This is reported by Liutprand, who assails the despiser of God and the laws with very sharp invective.

After Leo had sat for three years and six months, he died [Note: [Col. 1065B] The Vatican Great Bullarium differs somewhat in its chronological notices. It reads as follows: “Leo VII, an Italian, a Roman by origin, ordained before the ninth day of January in the year 936. He sat for three years and ten days” (as agree, besides other authors, four catalogues edited by Vignoli [Col. 1066B]), “while Constantine Porphyrogenitus ruled in the East and Otto the Great, son of Henry, in the West. He died around 18 July 939 and was buried at Saint Peter.”].

[Col. 1065]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE LEO VII

## I. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF FULDA  
*(Year 926.)* He confirms the privileges of the monastery of the Savior at Fulda, at the request of Abbot Hadamar:

*[Dronke, Diplomatic Code of Fulda, p. 315.]*

[Col. 1065A]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hadamar, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through you to your successors, the abbots of that venerable monastery, forever.

We bear the concern of all venerable places and, insofar as possibility is granted by divine assistance, strive to care for their stability. Through this concern divine clemency is appeased and praise for the Church of Christ is advanced. For this reason, with greater confidence, we dare to implore eternal mercy for the obtaining of pardon for our sins.

And therefore your Reverence requested from us that the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, built by Saint Boniface the bishop in a place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the protection of a privilege of the Apostolic See, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church. Favoring this pious desire, by this our apostolic authority we commit what is requested to effect, according to the text of the privilege which you have taken pains to show us as having been permanently established there by our predecessor, Marino of blessed memory, bishop of this venerable see.

Therefore, we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any authority in the aforesaid venerable monastery, except the Apostolic See and the bishop in whose diocese that venerable monastery is known to have been built; to the latter we grant permission only when the occasion arises for consecrating an altar. No one shall presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, so that, according to what is established below by the firmness of the privilege subject to the Apostolic See, it may remain endowed without disturbance and may perpetually enjoy security—without contradiction from any person—in the places and possessions which it now holds or possesses, as well as those which divine mercy may in future wish to increase within the right of that monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

Moreover, after deliberation, we decree that at suitable times a report be made to our ecclesiastical care concerning the manner in which monastic religion is directed according to the rule and entrusted to suitable concord in ecclesiastical observance, lest—God forbid—under the pretext of this privilege the mind and conduct of your rectitude be in any way turned aside from the norm of justice.

Nor shall it be lawful for a king, bishop, count, or any other person, great or small, to inflict any force or raise any dispute concerning the possessions or dependents of the same aforementioned venerable monastery. By our authority we also prohibit any woman from ever presuming to enter it. No one shall hold a court of justice in that venerable monastery or in any of its other places. No one shall compel servants or tenant-farmers to perform any service, except those persons to whom the abbot has given his consent for the useful fulfillment of his needs.

When necessary, the brothers shall have full power among themselves to choose their own abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, without contradiction from any person. And to you, beloved son Hadamar, because we know you to be a well-educated and eloquent man, we both grant and command that you preach the word of God by the authority of Saint Peter.

Accordingly, acting with apostolic care, we decree through the text of this our decree that if any bishop of any Church, or any person endowed with whatever dignity, should presume to violate this authority of our privilege, which we confirm by the prerogative of the prince of the apostles, and does not quickly repent, let him be anathema; let him incur the wrath of God and be excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, strengthened by apostolic authority. Whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this our privilege shall obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Leo, scriniarius (archival officer) of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the ninth indiction. Given on the third Ides of May by the hand of Nicholas, first secretary of the supreme Apostolic See, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Leo, supreme pontiff and universal sixth pope, in the most holy see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the month [of May] and the ninth indiction.

## II. Bull for the Monastery of Subiaco (936)

He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Subiaco, devastated by the Saracens, at the request of “Alberic, most glorious prince and senator of all the Romans.”

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, VI, 201.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Leo, priest and monk and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Benedict, situated at Subiaco, and to your successors forever, etc.

For those who devoutly and diligently offer praise to God day and night without interruption, we hope to receive reward or recompense from God, because for the restoration of their pious places [lacuna] especially those which, whether by fire, or by some other devastation, or by ruin [lacuna] for this reason we have taken care, with the Lord’s protection, to restore to its former condition and preserve forever the monastery of our most blessed Father Benedict, where our venerable and beloved son Leo appears to preside, and where also the love of our magnificent man and most beloved faithful Alberic burns with the ardor of charity. We have done this both in response to his petition and through the watchful concern of our clemency.

For God permitted us to be foremost in this work so that those who are known to be subject to us may learn from our pastoral example and concern, and may clearly understand what they ought to do when circumstances arise. Therefore, amid the sins and iniquities that increase in this world, the ancient enemy seeks, through his destructive device, to inflict various and manifold losses.

And because, at a certain time, the monastery of the teacher and confessor of Christ, blessed Benedict, in the place called Subiaco, was consumed by fire and ravaged by the Agarene peoples, they burned not only the things that we had brought for use or benefit, but also all the written documents which, in that venerable monastery, had been freely offered both by Roman pontiffs and by certain Christian people for the remission of sins; everything was burned together with the monks’ supplies.

When we heard of this unforeseen deed, we were greatly terrified. Nevertheless, for the reward and remedy of our soul, and of that of our most beloved son, namely Alberic, most glorious prince and senator of all the Romans, and for the restoration of yourselves after the losses of the aforesaid monastery, its possessions and charters having been consumed, etc., through this apostolic privilege, just as by our predecessors, the former pontiffs Nicholas and John, or by others, etc.

Written by the hand of Leo, scriniarius (archival officer) of the holy Roman Church, in the month of July, in the ninth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fifth Ides of July by the hand of Nicholas, first secretary of the supreme Apostolic See, in the first year of Lord Leo the sixth pope.

## III. Bull for the Monastery of Cluny (937)

He asserts the possession of the estate of Escutiola for Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, and his successors.

[*Cluniac Bullary*, 3.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors forever.

A desire which is shown to pertain to religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without delay. And whenever our consent is sought in matters relating to their usefulness or advantage, together with the customary protection of apostolic authority, it is fitting that we willingly come to their aid out of a regard for benevolence, and establish what is requested with sound reason for complete security, so that both the safety and freedom from harm of that venerable place may thereby be secured, and that for us also the richest reward of gain may be assigned by the Creator of all things, God, in the heavenly courts.

Therefore, because your Reverence requested us to confirm to you and to your monastery the estate called Escutiola, with its churches, houses, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow-groves, fruit-bearing trees, whether fruitful or barren and of various kinds, wells, springs, streams of perpetual water, and all its adjacent cultivated and uncultivated lands, together with the male and female servants residing there or elsewhere, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to that estate—which is situated in the county of Mâcon or Autun and which the good man Count Gaufred, both for the redemption of his own soul and that of his parents, gave to the aforesaid monastery by the text of a charter—we, moved by your prayers, who retain the apostolic office and are entrusted with care of all the Churches, especially of this monastery, confirm it in the same manner in which the aforesaid Count Gaufred gave it to the aforesaid monastery by the text of his charter.

Thus no person, small or great, or of whatever dignity, shall dare or presume to make any invasion, annoyance, or disturbance against this our privilege in the aforesaid estate or in any other possessions belonging to that estate. Rather, from this present tenth indiction onward, by our apostolic authority these possessions shall remain securely and peacefully in the same monastery forever.

Therefore, invoking the divine judgment, we further decree that no one may dare to take them away by any device or pretext. Rather, in perpetual right they shall increase in the same venerable monastery, as stated above, and shall remain to be administered and possessed under the power and jurisdiction of Abbot Odo, or of all his successors in the abbacy and of the monks serving God there.

But if anyone should attempt, with reckless boldness, to act or proceed against the text of this our apostolic command promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema of our Lord’s prince of the apostles, Peter, and that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most savage pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Let him likewise sink into the abyss and Tartarean chaos and perish with the impious.
