But may those who, out of pious regard, prove to be guardians, obedient, and observers of this our saving command deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly recompense from the just Judge, our Lord God.

## IV. Privilege for the Same Monastery (937)

He asserts the estate of Savinias for Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, and his successors.

[*Cluniac Bullary*, 3.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors forever.

A desire which is shown to pertain to religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without delay. And whenever our consent is sought in matters relating to their usefulness or advantage, together with the customary protection of apostolic authority, it is fitting that we willingly come to their aid out of a regard for benevolence, and establish what is requested with sound reason for complete security, so that both the safety and freedom from harm of that venerable place may thereby be secured, and that for us also the richest reward of gain may be assigned by the Creator of all things, God, in the heavenly courts.

Therefore, because your Reverence requested us to confirm to you and to your monastery the estate called Caviniae, with its houses and vineyards, lands and woods, fields, meadows, pastures, willow-groves, fruit-bearing trees, whether fruitful or barren and of various kinds, wells, springs, streams of perpetual water, and all its adjacent cultivated and uncultivated lands, together with the male and female servants residing there or elsewhere, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid estate—which is situated in the county of Mâcon and which Rodulf, of blessed memory, gave to the aforesaid monastery by the text of a charter for the redemption of his own soul, and of those of his parents and his brother Hugh—we, moved by your prayers, who retain the apostolic office and are entrusted with care of all the Churches, especially of this monastery, which is subject to the right of the holy Roman and Apostolic Church and to us, confirm it in the same manner in which the aforesaid Rodulf gave it by charter to the aforesaid monastery.

Thus no person, small or great, or of whatever dignity, shall dare or presume to make any invasion, annoyance, or disturbance against this our apostolic privilege in the aforesaid estate or in any other possessions belonging to that estate. Rather, from this tenth indiction onward, by our apostolic authority these possessions shall remain securely and peacefully in the same monastery forever.

Therefore, invoking the divine judgment, we further decree that no one may dare to take them away by any device or pretext. Rather, in perpetual right they shall increase in the same venerable monastery, as stated above, and shall remain to be administered and possessed under the power and jurisdiction of Abbot Odo, or of all his successors in the abbacy and of the monks serving God there.

But if anyone should attempt, with reckless boldness, to act or proceed against the text of this our apostolic command promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema of our Lord’s prince of the apostles, Peter, and that, together with the devil and his most savage pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, he is to be plunged into eternal fire and Tartarean chaos and perish with the impious.

But may those who, out of pious regard, prove to be guardians, obedient, and observers of this our saving command deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly recompense from the just Judge, our Lord God. Amen.

## V. Letter of Leo VII to Gerhard, Archbishop of Lauriacum (937)

He sends him the pallium.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII, 376.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Gerhard, archbishop of the holy Church of Lauriacum, for all the days of your life from this time onward.

[Note: [Col. 1071] Compare below, in its proper place, the letter of John XII to Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury. HARD.]

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure heat and frost day and night for the protection of their flock, and with ever-watchful eyes look about them lest any of the sheep should perish by wandering or be carried off, torn by the bites of wild beasts, let us consider with how much labor and care we ought to remain vigilant, we who are called shepherds of souls, and let us not cease to discharge the office we have undertaken toward the guardianship of the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the guilt of negligence torture us before the supreme Shepherd because of our sloth.

Therefore, because of the greater dignity of honor, we now judge [are judged, HARD.] you to be exalted among the others. We grant the pallium to your Fraternity for the celebration of the solemnities of Mass, allowing you to use it—not otherwise, while the privileges of your Church remain in their proper state—not only on the day of the consecration of the chrism, and on the holy and venerable Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and on the feasts of the holy apostles and of blessed John the Baptist, and on the festivals of holy Mary, Mother of God, and likewise on the day of our Lord’s Nativity, and on the solemnity of your Church, and on your own birthday, but also at the consecration of bishops and priests, and whenever a synod is held by you, if perhaps a gathering of neophytes should be present there who are to be led to the faith through your exhortation, and also on the feast of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and of Saint Lawrence, and of those saints who rest bodily in your parish—on the day of their feast—as was established by our predecessor Lord Gregory, bishop of this venerable see.

Your Fraternity must put on the pallium in the sacristy (*secretarium*) and then proceed to the solemnity of Mass, claiming nothing for yourself through rash presumption, lest, while something is seized disorderly in outward dress, even those things which might lawfully be permitted should be lost in due order. Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by modest vitality of action, we exhort you to ensure that the adornments of your conduct correspond to it, so that, with God as your author, you may rightly be conspicuous in both respects.

Therefore, let your life be a rule for your sons. If any crookedness has been introduced into them, let them be set straight by it; in it let them see what they should imitate; by constantly considering it, let them make progress, so that, after God, their having lived may appear to be your benefit.

Let not prosperity, which temporally flatters, lift up your heart, nor adversity cast it down; whatever it may be, let it be conquered by the virtue of patience. Let hatred find no place with you, nor indiscriminate favor. Let the good experience you as kind, and let the wicked recognize you as strict. Let no evil suggestion make an innocent person guilty before you; let favor not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest by failing to punish what you should punish you permit it to be committed.

Let there be in you both the sweetness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of judgment: one quality to cherish those who live innocently, the other to restrain the restless from wickedness by striking them. But since correction sometimes passes into cruelty when strictness seeks to punish the crime of the wicked, restrain anger by judgment, and use the discipline of censure in such a way that you strike at faults without withdrawing affection from the persons whom you correct.

Show yourself merciful to the poor insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let modest correction oppose the oppressors. Do not accept anyone’s face against justice; do not despise anyone seeking justice. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither the rich, emboldened by their power, may dare anything beyond the path of reason among you, nor the poor, because of their lowliness, be made to despair. Thus, with God’s mercy, you may become such as sacred reading commands when it says: “A bishop must be blameless” (1 Tim. 3).

You will be able to use all these things beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows charity never departs from the right path. Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood, these are the duties of the pallium. If you carefully observe them, you possess inwardly what you have received outwardly.

As for the faith which you briefly set out in your letters—although you ought to have explained it more fully—we nevertheless give thanks to our Redeemer because we have recognized it as sound in that very brevity. May the Holy Trinity surround your Fraternity with the protection of its grace and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to reach eternal sweetness. Amen.

## VI. Letter of Leo VII to Hugh, King of the Franks and Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Martin of Tours (938)

He forbids women access to the monastery of Saint Martin.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the glorious prince of the Franks, our son, Hugh, namely abbot of the most blessed Martin, and to his successors forever.

Christ the Lord, Creator and disposer of the universe, through the most holy mystery of his Incarnation, graciously joined the universal Church to himself. Within that same Church he arranged various saints as different members in one body, and, according to what pleased his inward counsel, wondrously ordered each one in the body of that Church, of which he graciously became the head.

He adorned some more excellently, so that, just as in the body certain members are more honorable and suited to their functions, so in the Church each person, whether more excellent or lower, might fittingly fulfill his own office, with Christ as disposer, so that, according to the Apostle, “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15).

Among those whom divine dispensation has raised to greater eminence, the most blessed Martin, archbishop of the see of Tours, shines with no ordinary brilliance. The whole of Christendom bears witness to his glory, for, moved in some way by divine inspiration, it commonly loves him with special affection, so that nowhere else after the thresholds of the holy apostles do pilgrims from such distant and diverse nations gather as they do at his venerable tomb.

The sacred place where he rests has also, from ancient times, been held in great reverence, not only by ordinary people but also by the most distinguished kings and princes, as some of you know from having seen it. For, as we have heard, no woman was ever permitted access within the bounds of the monastery, even in pagan times.

But when it became necessary, because of the incursions of those peoples, to establish it within the city, its guardians lamented because they could no longer venerate it with the same great reverence as formerly or prevent the gathering of women. For this reason you also undertook to build a wall beside its basilica, so that the place might either be protected from fire or preserved in its former dignity.

But the matter has turned out otherwise, because under the pretext of the fortress women now enjoy an immodest and unrestricted association there, although this is caused by nothing other than the negligence and sluggishness of its servants. For the day of judgment will come, and each person will rise in his own order, and it will be made clear through whom religion was upheld and through whom it was neglected.

We must grieve that perilous times have come and that charity appears to have grown cold among many, while iniquity has greatly abounded. But because the holy Church was specially entrusted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through him to his successors, each of us must, insofar as God grants the ability, support the usefulness of that Church through some authority for as long as it needs such support. Therefore it seems right to us to admonish, through our prohibition, your negligence regarding the veneration of that most holy place.

Accordingly, first of all we enjoin in the Lord that you, the most excellent abbot Hugh, and the superiors of that monastery, take the greatest care that throughout the entire circuit of the old wall, as far as the road which runs beside the northern side of the basilica, no woman, after seeing this letter, be permitted to reside there, nor even to enter except for the sole purpose of prayer.

If any of the ministers should neglect this apostolic prohibition, or if any woman should presume to enter, let that person remain excommunicated until, having promised amendment, he or she may deserve to be absolved. But if anyone, through audacity and contempt, should persist in transgressing this command, we excommunicate him or her outright. May grace and the peace of Christ, through his apostles and through the prayers of Saint Martin, be multiplied upon those who observe these provisions.

Written by the hand of Theodore, notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, and in the eleventh indiction, “with Louis king of the Franks” [Note: [Col. 1073] The words “with Louis king of the Franks” are plainly extraneous.]

## VII. Privilege of Leo VII for the Monastery of Cluny

At the request of Abbot Odo, he confirms the monastery of Cluny, with all its possessions, free from the dominion of every person; he forbids it ever to be entrusted to any canon, layman, or even monk who is abbot unless he lives according to the rule. He also asserts the freedom to elect the abbot himself.

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo, religious abbot of the monastery of Cluny, consecrated in honor of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, built by William, duke of Aquitaine, and through you to your successors forever.

As is clear to the piety of the faithful, the care of the universal Church was specially entrusted to blessed Peter and, through him, to his successors. Therefore it is fitting for our administration that we, who by God’s authority preside over the holy Roman See, should eagerly strive to assist with pious benevolence all faithful persons who live or conduct themselves according to religion, wherever they need or seek our support.

For this reason we have decided, through our apostolic authority, to exalt and strengthen the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, first out of love for the blessed apostles in whose honor it was consecrated and for the religious observance maintained there, and then also out of affection for our sons, namely Kings Hugh and his son Lothar, who, as we have heard, greatly favor that place.

Therefore, as is contained in the privileges of our predecessor, Pope John, we decree that the aforesaid monastery and all possessions belonging to it, whether those which the monks now hold or those which they will justly acquire, shall be free and absolved from the dominion of every person. It shall be subject only to the Roman See, as is contained in the testament of William, of blessed memory, so that it may never be entrusted to a canon, layman, or even a monk who is abbot unless he lives according to the rule.

As for the estates which King Rodulf, of pious memory, bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery, we confirm them entirely to that monastery because, although they are said to have belonged to the Church of Lyon or Mâcon, no one of such advanced age exists who has ever seen any investiture of those estates held in the aforesaid churches. Since the legal period prescribed for recovering such claims has elapsed, let every further claim cease.

Moreover, concerning the appointment of the abbot and the immunity of the possessions of that monastery, let what is contained in the aforesaid privileges be observed forever.

But if anyone should presume to usurp or retain those estates which the aforesaid kings, our sons, bestowed upon that place, or anything else belonging to the possessions, or anything from the monastery called Carilocus, which our predecessor gave to Cluny by the authority of a privilege, we excommunicate him.

Furthermore, all who have been helpers of that monastery or brotherhood in good works, insofar as the power granted to us by God through blessed Peter permits, we absolve, as faithful of the holy Church, from their past sins if they wish to amend. Those who in any way have proved hostile we bind, as stated above, under the bond of anathema until the day of the Lord, unless they repent. May the peace and grace of Christ be multiplied upon those who observe these provisions.

Written by the hands of Leo, notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the eleventh indiction. As for the chapel of Petronnano, which is opposed to the church of Saint Peter of Lango, we excommunicate it utterly, as was enacted in the council of bishops at Chalon, and we command all priests, by the authority of God and Saint Peter and by our own authority, that no one presume to perform divine service there.

## VIII. Privilege of Leo VII for the Monastery of Saint Benedict of Fleury (938)

He confirms the discipline of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Fleury, restored by Abbot Odo and Hugh, duke of the Franks, together with its possessions and privileges.

[In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, V, 907.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Benedict, also called Fleury, in which he himself rests bodily, and through you to that venerable monastery and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid, with kindly compassion, of those who excel in pious religion and to grant with eager devotion the assent sought by their minds. Through this we trust to obtain the richest reward from the Creator of all things, God, when venerable places have been restored through our assistance. We must devote every effort to this, because, since the order of things has been greatly disturbed by reason of our sins, we must take care to support it insofar as God grants us the ability.

Therefore we have greatly rejoiced because we hear that the monastery of the most blessed Benedict, who is the father and leader of monks, is flourishing again according to the norm of monastic religion. Since the monastic order has everywhere been greatly diminished, we have hope that if religious observance flourishes again in that monastery, which is like its head and beginning, the other monasteries situated around it, like members, may recover strength.

For, as the Apostle says, when one member rejoices, the other members rejoice with it; conversely, every head is sick and every heart sorrowful [lacuna]. “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” [lacuna]. Therefore, so that [lacuna] of conduct [lacuna], as we have learned from a certain and most trustworthy report, our son Odo, the venerable abbot, and the venerable man Hugh, namely duke of the Franks, have recently established in this monastery, may progress more eagerly and securely in regular discipline, we have decided, by our apostolic admonition and authority, to favor and assist that place in every way.

Therefore, by that authority and power which Christ our Lord granted to the rulers of the holy Church in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and also by the [decree] of our apostolic authority, we establish and ordain that neither that place nor any possession belonging to it shall ever be subjected to the power of anyone except the king alone. Nor shall the king himself or any prince ever hand over that place to a bishop, canon, abbot, layman, or any other person for domination.

Rather, as the aforesaid Father Benedict established, after the departure of the aforesaid Abbot Odo the monks shall have as abbot the person whom the entire community, or its smaller part acting on the sounder counsel according to God, chooses—whether he comes from that community or from any other monastic brotherhood.

But if—which God forbid—they should prefer to choose a person who wishes to preside through bribery or ambition for empty glory, we prohibit this in every way in the name of the Lord and of his holy Mother, in whose honor that place is dedicated, and also in the name of blessed Peter, prince of all the Churches.

Whoever, whether one of those monks or any person of whatever order, should prove hostile either in the appointment of an abbot, or in harming the possessions, or in disparaging or impeding the manner of life which the new brothers appear to have adopted, we bind under the bond of anathema until he is humbled and repents.

As for the estates which are known to have been assigned for the work of the brothers by the authority of an ancient testament—namely the entire valley itself, Caput-Cervium, Evera, Arminicourt, Diacum, Toriacum, Sarmaciola, whatever it appears to possess at Étampes, Vinolium, and all the other possessions contained in the aforesaid testament—let the brothers hold them in common, so that neither the abbot himself nor any other person may transfer anything into another’s power.

In appointing the abbot, the king, the bishops, good princes, and laymen shall have this power, in accordance with the precept of blessed Benedict: they must not allow the consent of the wicked to prevail, but must appoint a person who strives to preside according to the Rule and the religious customs of the aforementioned Fathers.

Since the aforesaid order had almost everywhere been gravely violated, and certain brothers in some monasteries lament that they are unable either to live without private property or to correct others who wish to do so, it has seemed right to us to grant them this permission: those who wish, out of a desire to improve their way of life, to flee to that leader of monks must not be denied permission by their own abbots. Let them remain there according to the custom they find among the brothers of the aforesaid monastery for as long as the regular order appears to flourish in their own monasteries.

Conversely, we permit that if [lacuna] should have become burdensome to someone, let him rather depart to his own detriment [lacuna], so that he may not disturb others.

Moreover, the immunity [lacuna] established by our authority shall remain inviolate in all places, so that no person in a position of power may presume to oppress the dependents or usurp or disturb the possessions themselves.

But so that all these provisions may be held more firmly, all who have been helpers of that monastery’s brotherhood in good works, insofar as the power granted to us by God through blessed Peter permits, we absolve, as faithful of the holy Church, if they wish to amend. Those who in any way have proved hostile we bind, as stated above, under the bond of anathema until the day of the Lord, unless they repent. May the peace and grace of Christ be multiplied upon those who observe these provisions.

Written by the hand of Theodore, notary and subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell. Given on the fifth Ides of January by the hand of Nicholas, first secretary of the supreme Apostolic See, in the third year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Leo, pontiff and universal seventh pope, in the most holy see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the month and indiction stated above.

## IX. Letter of Leo VII to Guido of Lyon, Tutelo of Tours, etc. (938)

He laments the deplorable condition of the Church and speaks of the regular discipline restored into the monastery of Fleury by Abbot Odo.

[In Mabillon, cited above.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the brothers and sons—namely, the archbishops and their suffragans—GUIDO of the Church of Lyon, TUTELON of Tours, GERUNCUS of Bourges, GERLAUNUS of Sens, ARTALDUS of Reims, and their successors forever.

As your faith and piety well know, Christ our Lord loved the holy Church so greatly that he purchased her with his own blood. He entrusted her also to the other apostles and their successors, but he determined that she should be governed chiefly through their princes, the most blessed Peter and Paul. Their successors, both in this holy see and throughout the world, whoever has lived by faith, have each in his own time endeavored to govern her according to the form of apostolic institution.

But, as is plain to those who consider the matter, perilous times have come in our days, and, as charity grows cold, iniquity abounds exceedingly. Thus the whole order of things has been almost entirely disturbed, and no place seems now to remain for religion. We, however—and this is greatly to be lamented—neither strive to rise up against the evil nor to restrain impiety; rather, whatever else opposes religion, we negligently pass over with the eyes of our minds closed. Moreover, although we are sluggish and idle and do not greatly fear our negligence, we cannot fail to know that we shall render an account to God for our stewardship. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us strive, as far as we can through divine grace, not to be found altogether empty of the care of religion or of pious deeds.

But, to come to the matter on account of which we have begun to say these things, it has been reported to us—and we have learned it through a certain and most truthful account—that our son Odo, the venerable abbot, seems to maintain, to some degree, with his brothers serving God there, the regular way of life handed down by his predecessors in the very venerable monastery called Floriacum, constructed in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Peter, where rests our outstanding father, the most blessed lord Benedict, the glory and jewel of monks. This order, then, in the aforesaid place, with God’s favor, to some extent, as we have heard . . . . . Thus ends the Floriacum copy; would that we possessed it complete.

## X. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SUBIACO

To Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Subiaco, and to his successors, “through the intervention of his beloved spiritual son Alberic, the glorious prince and senator,” he entrusts the monastery of Saint Erasmus on the Caelian Hill for governance.

[Cocquelines, I, 246.]

[Col. 1078C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LEO, monk and priest, and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Benedict at Subiaco, and to your holy congregation and the successors of your monastery forever.

The care of the stewardship entrusted to us impels us, and the ardor of the Christian religion moves us, to be concerned for the stability of venerable places and the security of those who serve God, so that, through this pious labor, those devoted to Christ—who have determined to serve him day and night—may persevere undisturbed, and so that those foundations which Christians have built to the praise of God may also remain secure.

Since, therefore, it is established that the monastery of Saint Erasmus, the holy martyr of Christ, constructed in this Roman city on the Caelian Hill, has for some time been entirely stripped of a congregation of servants of God, and since we have seen that it is deserted, with neither a superior nor a monk dwelling in it, we have decided, through the intervention of our beloved spiritual son Alberic, the glorious prince and senator, to entrust the aforesaid monastery of Saint Erasmus to you and to unite it with your monastery at Subiaco, for refuge and for the benefit of the congregation of brothers who in that venerable place offer praises to the Lord our God.

[Col. 1079A]

We decree in perpetuity—lest, God forbid, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict be destroyed by the persecution of pagans or by wicked men—that the said monastery of Saint Erasmus, with its cells, houses, and other buildings, its surrounding walls, together with its gardens, lands, seed-fields, olive groves, fruit-bearing trees, and all its appurtenances, situated in Rome in the second region, before the venerable church of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr of Christ, on the aforesaid Caelian Hill, shall have these boundaries:

On the first side are the entire court of Gregory, the public road, the little house of Peter John, the little house of several persons, and other buildings with a crypt, together with the seed-land commonly called “of a Hundred Shields.”

On the second side are the seed-land of Leo, the devout priest, and the public road that leads to the decennias.

On the third side are the seed-land of the heirs of Adrian, formerly of the Neapolitan Bath, and the vine-planted garden of Sergia, a noble woman.

On the fourth side is the little house of the oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

There is also the public road and part of the boundaries of the monastery of Saint Erasmus, with everything belonging to it, both within and outside it and around it, or wherever it may have been situated, together with the estate called Quintum and all its appurtenances.

In its entirety, from the present eleventh indiction, we grant and confirm it to you and to your successors, the abbots of that monastery, forever, to be governed and held in the fear of God for the use and benefit of the aforesaid monastery of Subiaco.

[Col. 1079C]

Therefore, invoking the divine judgment, we promulgate and decree that no one ever—whether one of our successors in the pontificate, or a person of whatever rank or condition—may dare to take it away from your jurisdiction or inflict any injury upon it by any device or pretext. Rather, it shall remain securely possessed under the jurisdiction of your monastery.

But if anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God. Unless he repents, let him know that he will be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most terrible punishments, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and that, together with the impious, he will be plunged into the abyss and Tartarean chaos.

But those who, from pious regard, prove themselves guardians, obedient servants, and faithful observers of this saving command of ours, may they deserve from the just Judge the grace of blessing and the reward of heavenly recompense.

[Col. 1079D]

Written by the hand of Leo, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the aforesaid eleventh indiction. Farewell. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of February, through the hand of Nicholas, primicerius, in the third year of the pontificate.

## XI. LETTER OF LEO VII TO WIDO OF LYON, TEOTOLON OF TOURS, ETC. (Year 938)

He entrusts to them the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter at Ripoll, and orders that whoever invades its possessions be anathematized.

[In Marca, Appendix to Marca Hispanica, p. 851.]

[Col. 1080A]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brothers and sons, namely, the archbishops and bishops and their successors: WIDO of the Church of Lyon, TEOTOLON of Tours, GERUNCUS of Bourges, GERLAUNUS of Sens, ARTALDUS of Reims, AIMERICUS of Narbonne, RICULFUS of Elne, GODMARUS of Girona, WILLARANUS of Barcelona, WADAMIRUS of Ausona, WISADUS of Urgell, and their successors forever.

As your piety well knows, Christ our Lord loved the Church so greatly that he purchased her with his own blood. He entrusted her also to the other apostles and their successors, but chiefly determined that she should be governed through their princes, the most blessed Peter and Paul. Their successors, both in this see and throughout the world, whoever has lived by faith, have each in his own time endeavored to govern her according to the form of apostolic institution.

But, as is plain to those who consider the matter, perilous times have come in our days, and, as charity grows cold, it has come about that no place now seems to remain for religion. We, however—and this is greatly to be lamented—neither strive to rise up against the evil nor to restrain impiety; rather, whatever it is that opposes religion, we negligently pass over with the eyes of our minds closed. Moreover, although we are sluggish and idle and do not greatly fear our negligence, we cannot fail to know that we shall render an account to God for our stewardship. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us strive, as far as we can through divine grace, not to be found altogether empty of the care of religion or of pious deeds.

[Col. 1080C]

But, to come to the matter on account of which we began to say these things, it has been reported to us, and we have now learned through a certain and most truthful account, that our son Arnulfus, the venerable abbot, seems to maintain, to some degree, with his brothers serving God there, the regular tradition of our lord, the most blessed Benedict, who is the glory and jewel of monks, in the very venerable monastery called Ripoll, constructed between the two rivers Tezer and Freber in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Peter, where the order of the most blessed Benedict seems to be observed. He appears to preserve this regular tradition with his brothers serving God there, by the authority of his predecessors.

Therefore, with God’s consent, we have resolved to foster with all our strength this order, which, as we have heard, is in some measure flourishing again in the aforesaid place, in matters that concern us. For this reason, in the place of the prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, whose office we are seen to hold, although unworthy, we send this letter of apostolic authority to your kindness concerning our son Arnulfus, the abbot, his successors, and the monks of that monastery. We beseech and command you—as we trust in your common obedience and solicitude—not to neglect to assist their needs in matters pertaining to pastoral care.

[Col. 1081A]

Wherever this unanimous brotherhood, in the service of God, and that place itself, with God’s favor, has spread and grown both in religion and in estates and villages, and likewise wherever the adjoining or distant places of the saints serving the almighty Lord have been established, together with holy religion, we decree as follows:

If any violent or rapacious person attempts or presumes to disturb those possessions, plunder them, or violate the villages with all their appurtenances and dependencies, and everything belonging to the monks of that holy monastery of Ripoll and to the members of that holy congregation living according to the rule, we command Bishop Guadamirus of the see of Ausona, in whose diocese the monastery is situated, and all his successors, to summon the offender in our place, by means of a copy of this document, whoever he may be, with our admonition, and, if possible, to correct and reform him.

If he does make amends, we permit him to receive grace and communion within the bosom of holy Mother Church. But if, after my admonition and yours, he refuses, as a rebellious and wicked man, to correct his sins, then, in the place of blessed Peter, we command all the archbishops and bishops named above, together with your successors, to bind that thief and violator of the holy Church of God with the chain of anathema [or: “to bind him”]. Let his portion be with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive because of their pride.

Let his children be orphans and his wife a widow; let his children, still young, be driven away and wander about, and let them beg; let them be expelled from their dwellings. Let the moneylender search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labors. Let there be no helper for him, nor anyone to show mercy to his orphans (Psalm 108:9).

And again: “All who have said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as our inheritance’: my God, make them like a wheel and like straw before the face of the wind. As fire burns the forest and as a flame consumes the mountains, so may God pursue them, and fill their faces with disgrace, so that they may be ashamed, disturbed, confounded, and perish” (Psalm 82:13).

Let those curses also be upon him which the Lord proclaimed through blessed Moses against the children of Israel if they refused to heed him. Let him be cursed in the city, cursed in the field; cursed be his granary, cursed the fruit of his womb, cursed the fruit of his land, cursed the herds of his oxen and the flocks of his sheep; cursed be he when he goes out and when he returns.

May the Lord quickly destroy him from the earth. May the Lord strike him with hunger and thirst, poverty, fever, and cold, until he perishes. May he deliver him, as he falls, before his enemies; may his corpse become food for all the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth. May the Lord strike him with a most grievous ulcer, with scabies and itching, madness, blindness, and fury of mind; and at midday may he grope as a blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness.

And just as the Lord gave blessed Peter and his successors—whose office we hold, although unworthy—the power that whatever they bound on earth would be bound in heaven, and whatever they loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven, so, if they refuse to amend, we close heaven against them, deny them the earth for burial, and let them be plunged into the depths of hell, where they shall pay to the last farthing for what they have done.

[Col. 1082A]

We send this letter not only to the bishops but also to the abbots, near and far, who live according to the rule which the Lord established through blessed Benedict, so that they may join us in tightening the bond of this excommunication. Thus, if that fool should think the excommunication of a few bishops can be disregarded, at least his impiety may be broken by the agreement of many, and the members who are concerned for one another may be held more peacefully and firmly in the body of Christ.

We mark this letter, through which we speak to you, with the seal of apostolic dignity and authority, and deliver it to be preserved forever both in the monastery of the blessed Virgin Mary and in the other holy places. Farewell in the love of Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

## XII. PRIVILEGE OF LEO VII FOR THE MONASTERY OF CLUNY (Years 936–939)

He confirms Savigny and Ambariac to Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors, at the request of “Hugh, the glorious king, together with his son, King Lothair.”

[Bullar. Cluniac., 2.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the lord ODO, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors forever.

[Col. 1082C]

A desire shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without delay. Whenever our assent and the customary protection of apostolic authority are sought for certain benefits of such places, it befits us, of our own accord and from a kindly regard, to assist and to establish the matter firmly on reasonable grounds for its complete security. Thus the safety and security of the venerable place may be secured, and for us also the highest reward of profit may be prepared by the Creator of all things in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, because our beloved son Hugh, the glorious king, together with his son King Lothair, has petitioned our apostolate that we confirm by our apostolic privilege the gift of two estates called Savigny and Ambariac, which King Hugh himself, by the document of his command, gave to the aforesaid venerable monastery—built in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul—for the salvation of his own soul and those of his parents, together with their churches, lands, vineyards, houses, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, fruit-bearing and other productive trees, non-fruit-bearing trees, wells, springs, streams of perennial water, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances and adjacent lands, together with the male and female dependants residing there or elsewhere, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid estates, except for three persons whom the aforesaid king retained for himself in his own charter, situated in the county of Lyon—

[Col. 1083A]

we, moved by their prayers, in whose person we hold the apostolic office and to whom the care of all the churches has been entrusted, especially of this monastery, which is subject to the right of the holy Roman and apostolic Church and to us, confirm all these things exactly as our aforesaid son gave them by his charter to the monastery. No one, great or small, or of whatever rank, may dare or presume, contrary to the authority of this apostolic privilege of ours, to invade or seize them; rather, they shall remain securely and peacefully in that monastery forever.

Therefore, invoking the divine judgment, we promulgate and decree that no one may take them away by any device or pretext. Instead, as established above, they shall remain permanently in the same venerable monastery and under the authority and jurisdiction of Abbot Odo, all his successors in the abbacy, and the monks serving God there, to be administered and possessed by them.

But if anyone should attempt, with reckless audacity, to act or proceed against the terms of this apostolic command of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the anathema of our Lord’s prince of the apostles, Peter, and that, together with the devil and his most terrible pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, he will be burned in eternal fire and, together with the impious, sink into the abyss and Tartarean chaos and perish.

But those who, from pious regard, prove themselves guardians, obedient servants, and faithful observers of our saving command, may they deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly reward.

## XIII. LETTER OF LEO VII TO ADALDAGUS, BISHOP OF HAMBURG (Years 937–939)

He sends him the pallium.

[In Lappenberg, Hamburg Documents, p. 42.]

Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy ADALDAGUS, bishop of the holy Church of Hamburg, which is situated beyond the river called the Elbe, for the days of your life only.

“If shepherds of sheep,” etc., as in the bull of Nicholas I and Stephen V for the same Church, up to “the Assumption of holy Mary, Mother of God” . . . The rest is lacking in the original document.

## XIV. LETTER OF LEO VII TO FRIDURICUS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ (Years 937–939)

He declares Friduricus “his vicar and envoy in all the regions of the whole of Germany.” He permits him to expel Jews from the cities unless they accept the Christian faith, but forbids baptizing them against their will.

[In Wurdtwein, Letters of Saint Boniface, 373.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother FRIDURICUS, archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz.

[Col. 1084A]

For the days of your life only . . . we are bound by the love of brotherhood and summoned by the governance of the apostolic see, so that, after consulting our brothers, we may respond as the Lord grants, and instruct them by the authority of the apostolic see. Since your affection requires the counsel of the apostolic see—which we neither ought nor can deny you, because it is clear that our predecessors did this for the bishops of many regions—fraternal charity compels us, who by the Lord’s generosity have been placed in the same see, to do likewise.

Accordingly, since you wished to consult this holy Catholic and apostolic Church—namely, the Roman Church, head of all the churches—which always follows the sincere and profound authorities of the holy Fathers in all its actions, that is, our apostolic see, we take care without hesitation to direct what you ought to do.

Since, therefore, you wished to ask our apostolate that, by our authority, we grant you to be the vicar and envoy of our apostolic see throughout all Germany, and since you assert that the ancient metropolitans of the see of Mainz deserved, by the authority of our apostolic see and of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to be made vicars and apostolic envoys of all Germany, know that we carefully examined in the archives of our holy Church the documents of privileges which, as you assert, were granted by our two predecessors, Gregory, Zachary, and Stephen, with apostolic confirmation, to Boniface, the bishop of your see. We examined them with attentive care and intense concern, and were able to find only one document with that authority . . . [The reading of the source is corrupt here.]

[Col. 1084C]

Therefore, because you earnestly and humbly implore us to let our clemency grant you, by our apostolic authority, a command and permission by which, in our place, you may have the power to rebuke wicked and depraved persons and call them back to the way of truth by your exhortations, we grant you permission in our place. Since you promise from this point forward to show submission and complete fidelity to the holy see, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we give you the power to be our vicar and envoy in all the regions of the whole of Germany.

Wherever you find bishops, priests, deacons, or monks to have transgressed against the canons and the constitutions of the holy Fathers, or against ecclesiastical discipline, do not fail, by apostolic authority and according to the canons and the constitutions of the holy Fathers, to correct them and bring them back to the way of truth.

Regarding the Jews, concerning whom your fraternity has sought our authority—whether it is better to subject them to the sacred religion or to expel them from your cities—we command you as follows: preach to them without ceasing, with all prudence and wise counsel, the faith of the holy Trinity and the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, with reverence toward God. If they wish with all their heart to believe and be baptized, we give immense thanks to the almighty Lord. But if they refuse to believe, expel them from your cities with our authority, since we ought not to have fellowship with the enemies of the Lord, as the Apostle says: “For what fellowship has light with darkness, or what portion has the believer with the unbeliever?”

But do not baptize them by force, without their will and request, because it is written: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet.”

For the rest, believe and hold the faith of the holy Trinity—which you preach to Jews and Gentiles and which you have sent to the holy Roman Church, your mother, for approval—whole and undefiled, just as the apostles and their successors handed it down to us and as the holy Roman Church preaches it to all peoples everywhere.

## XV. LETTER OF LEO VII TO THE GAULS AND GERMANS (Years 937–939)

He orders the correction of many matters relating to discipline.

[In Mansi, XVIII, 378.]

[Col. 1085B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to kings, dukes, bishops, abbots, counts, and likewise to EGILOLPHUS of Chur, ISINGRIMUS of Regensburg, LANTBERTUS of Freising, WISUNDUS of Säben, venerable bishops of the churches, and to the others dwelling throughout Gaul, Germany, Bavaria, and Alemannia.

If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, there would be no diversity in those orders and consecrations. But since each person considers that he must uphold not what was handed down but what seems right to him, different practices appear to be observed or celebrated in different places and churches. This causes scandal among the people, since many things seem to be usurped in your province contrary to the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of the elders.

These matters could easily be cut away if the bishops did not appear to be their authors. Occupied with secular affairs and seeking human favor, they violate religion and corrupt the orders.

We are indeed urged by divine commands and apostolic admonitions to keep watch over the condition of all the churches with untiring vigilance. Therefore we make known to your fraternity that Gerard, archbishop of the holy Church of Lauriacum, came to the threshold of the apostles for the sake of prayer and earnestly sought to visit our apostolic presence and receive from us the grace of blessing. In tearful words he reported to our ears many things worthy of reproof, seeking with all the intention of his heart the counsel of our apostolic authority concerning what is being done in your provinces contrary to the rule of the canons and the decrees of the elders.

[Col. 1085D]

For you know that the care of all the churches was entrusted by the Lord himself to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—and to his vicars—as the voice of Truth says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 26). He also entrusted his own sheep to him, saying: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21). Therefore we are concerned for all the churches, and, placed as though on a watchtower, we diligently keep watch over what is being done throughout the provinces of the whole world.

We therefore take care to inform you through these letters of ours what he asked the apostolic see about and what answers we gave him. His questions were arranged as follows.

Concerning augurs, female diviners, and sorcerers who have been put to death by the people in various ways: whether any penance ought to be required for this.

What the page of the Old and New Testaments teaches concerning such persons is clear. For in the Mosaic Law it is written: “You shall not permit sorcerers to live” (Exodus 22). Likewise, in the Book of Samuel we read that Saul exterminated all the pythonesses from the land, along with other matters too lengthy to enumerate.

Nevertheless, we ought also to draw such persons to penance through our exhortations, so that they may live by repenting under ecclesiastical judgment rather than be punished by the avenging sword, as the blessed apostle Paul says: “For God has not appointed us for wrath but for the acquisition of salvation” (1 Thessalonians 5). But if they despise ecclesiastical judgments, let them be subject to human laws. They must remember that powers have been granted by God, that the sword has been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that God’s minister has been appointed for such punishment. When the authority of the laws is exercised against such wicked persons, as blessed Innocent says, the legislator will be free from blame.

It was also asked whether bishops ought to pronounce “Peace be with you” or “The Lord be with you.” Throughout your province the practice must be the same as in the holy Roman Church. On Sundays, on the principal festivals, and on the feasts of the saints, we pronounce “Glory to God in the highest” and “Peace be with you.” On the days of Lent, on the Ember Days, at the vigils of the saints, and on the other days of fasting, we say only “The Lord be with you.”

[Col. 1086D]

After this he asked whether the Lord’s Prayer ought to be used in the blessing of food. This ought not to be done, because the holy apostles sang this prayer alone in the sanctification of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and in the Gospel we read that, after the Lord had celebrated the supper, they went out to the Mount of Olives after singing a hymn.

After this he asked about a man who takes as his wife a spiritual mother and daughter. The sacred canons absolutely forbid this from being done. In the canons of Zachary it is written:

“No one shall have relations with a priest’s wife, a deaconess, a nun, or even with a spiritual mother or a spiritual daughter. For whoever has committed such an act must know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, condemned by the judgment of God, and excluded from the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. And any priest who presumes to communicate with him, being condemned by their judgment, shall be deprived of the honor of his priesthood.”

Next he introduced a matter lamentable and exceedingly grievous: that priests of the Lord publicly take wives, and that their sons might even be promoted. Since all sacred Scripture contradicts this crime, and since the holy Council of Nicaea forbids priests to presume to live with women—much more, therefore, to be joined or united with women—we prohibit it in every way according to the sacred canons.

For in the Council of Neocaesarea it is written as follows (canon 1):

“If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order. And those who are found in such a crime shall, by the authority of our apostolate, be deprived of every honor.”

Their sons, however, are free from their sin, as the prophet says: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18), and in holy baptism all sins are forgiven.

Next he asked whether churches ought to be consecrated by a chorepiscopus, whether priests ought to be ordained by him, or whether confirmation with chrism and the imposition of hands ought to be performed by him.

We forbid all these things to be done by chorepiscopi, according to the decrees of the canons. In the Council of Antioch, chapter ten, it is written:

“Although those who are called chorepiscopi in villages and estates have received the imposition of hands from bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decided that they should recognize their proper limits and govern the churches subject to them. They may also ordain lectors, subdeacons, and exorcists; these promotions are sufficient for them. They may not presume to ordain either a priest or a deacon. But if anyone attempts to transgress the statutes, let him be deposed and deprived of the honor he held.”

He also asked whether a man and woman joined by consanguinity in the third or fourth degree, who marry without knowing this, may afterward, moved by regard for God, confess their sins secretly to a priest and be cleansed by the giving of alms and the performance of good works.

Many examples concerning such persons are found in the Old and New Testaments, especially in the councils of Gregory and Zachary. These contain the rule that no one may presume to join in marriage with a female cousin, stepmother, niece, brother’s wife, daughter-in-law, a woman from his own kinship, or one whom a kinsman has had.

If anyone has entered such a wicked marriage and remains in it, let him know that, by apostolic authority, he is bound by the chain of anathema, and no priest may give him communion. But if he has been persuaded and separated from the unlawful union, let him be subjected to penance, as the priest of the place shall judge.

Concerning the destroyers of churches, about whom he inquired, we write nothing other than what the apostle Paul says in writing to Timothy: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all authority” (2 Timothy 4).

[Col. 1088B]

Having set forth all these matters, we admonish your fraternity through this apostolic command of ours to be obedient and helpful to this Gerard, the archbishop, to whom we have entrusted our place throughout all your regions, in everything that pertains to ecclesiastical order. Thus, remaining in one accord, you may ensure that ecclesiastical rights and the religion of Christianity in your regions—which appear to have been corrupted and deformed by the incursions of pagans and the persecution of evil Christians—may, by the Lord’s generosity and through the cooperation of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, be restored to the standard of righteousness.

Then, at the future judgment, you may securely hear the voice of the Lord saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

[Col. 1088C]

In addition to this, by our authority we enjoin Eberard, duke of the Bavarians, to provide the aforesaid archbishop Gerard with assistance in everything, so that, through his aid, the condition, rectitude, and proper vigor of his Church may reach its full height and ancient dignity—if, through God’s mercy and that of Saint Peter, he wishes to receive from us remission of his own sins.

## In the Year of the Lord 942. Pope Stephen VIII, otherwise IX

[Col. 1087]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

[In Cocquelines, *Collection of the Bulls and Privileges of the Roman Pontiffs*.]

Stephen VIII, otherwise IX, whom almost everyone says was German by nationality, was immediately substituted for Leo VII and ordained in July of the year 939. For in the fourth catalogue of Vignoli there appears the following: “In his time, namely in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 939, the sun was darkened from the second hour until the third hour in the month of July, on the nineteenth day, in the twelfth indiction.”

He therefore sat in the pontificate for three years, four months, and fifteen days. Accordingly, Stephen must be said to have died on the second or third day of December in the year 942. His body was buried in the basilica of the prince of the apostles.

[Col. 1089]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE STEPHEN VIII

## I. PRIVILEGE OF STEPHEN VIII FOR THE MONASTERY OF TOLLENSE (Year 939)

The monastery of Tollense, in the diocese of Piacenza, is received under the protection of the apostolic see and is declared to be wholly subject to the abbot alone.

[Cocquelines, *Expanded Collection of the Roman Pontifical Bulls*.]

[Col. 1089A]

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ARIBERTUS, reverend abbot of the monastery of Tollense, which blessed Tobias appears to have built in honor of the Lord Savior and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so long as through you . . . and to your successors forever: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although the example of devout Fathers teaches us that we ought, out of love for Christ—who willed that all the Churches spread throughout the whole world should be subject to the ministry of our office—to assist them, necessity nevertheless compels us to come to the aid of certain monasteries of ours, established in honor of the Lord Savior or of blessed Peter the Apostle. Through the negligence of certain rulers, these monasteries once unjustly fell under the domination of secular men; and certain bishops, contrary to the decrees, laws, and rights of our predecessors, have wholly violated their lawful rights. Therefore, as you request of us, venerable Abbot Aribert, by this privilege of apostolic authority we decree that both the aforesaid Tollense monastery and all its possessions everywhere, as is just, removed from the power of all margraves, counts, secular men, and bishops, shall henceforth remain perpetually under your authority as long as you live, and afterward under the lawful authority of your successors or the monks.

Nothing whatsoever of the things granted by our predecessors or by the kings of the Italian kingdom, whether in the property or in the liberty of the place itself, is to be diminished in any way, on any pretext or by the title of any document. By the authority of the holy Roman Church, we therefore forbid the bishops—namely, those of the Churches of Pavia, Piacenza, Parma, and Reggio, in whose dioceses the monastery or its possessions appear to lie—and all others, whether near or far away, ever to presume to take anything from it as though by their own right, or to claim for themselves the baptismal churches or their tithes, which you formerly held.

[Col. 1089D] Let the consecrations of churches, or whatever pertains to the sacred ministries, be performed by whichever bishop you or your successors may wish to request [lacuna] and may you never cease to pray to the Lord for our safety, for that of the most excellent emperor, and for that of the whole Church.

But if—which we do not desire—the monks established in that monastery should be found lukewarm in the love of God or transgressors of your rule, we decree that they are to be corrected by you and your successors. If, however, you or your successors should be discovered guilty of some offense arising from an evil reputation, we decree that you are to be heard and legally corrected before the Apostolic See, under whose authority your monastery stands.

If anyone should presume to diminish or alter this precept of our authority, or the laws or decrees of our ancient prelates, let his attempt utterly fail. First, let him be deprived of the rank of his order and punished by the vengeance of anathema; at the final judgment let him share the portion of Judas the traitor; and, by the authority which blessed Peter merited in heaven and on earth for binding and loosing, let him be deprived of power and participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and excluded from our fellowship unless he repent [lacuna] so that these statutes may remain in force by perpetual definition and the violators of this present decree may suffer manifold punishments for their presumption.

Written by the hand of Peter, arch-scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the thirteenth indiction.

## II. Privilege of Stephen VIII for the Convent of Saint Mary at Buxerias (A.D. 941)

He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Buxerias monastery, founded by Gauzlin, abbot of Toul.

[At D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, Documents, col. 350.]

[Col. 1090C]

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved daughter Rothilda, abbess of the monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God, which is situated in the bishopric of the Leuci, on the mountain above the village called Buxerias.

Since almighty God has specially decreed to gather together, unite, and order his Church through the glorious princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, it is fitting that all their successors, upon whom the same responsibility has been imposed, should provide the protection of apostolic authority wherever circumstances require it. Although unworthy of so great an office, we nevertheless desire, with concern for the salvation of all the faithful, to fulfill this to the best of our ability, so that when we come to render an account, we may behold the Judge with confidence.

Having therefore learned through the venerable Abbot Archembald with what zeal our sweetest brother Gauzlin, bishop of the Leuci, labors to establish and exalt his Church in every form of religious order, we rejoice with maternal affection and beseech the Lord’s mercy that his work may prosper. Accordingly, just as he himself requested, we have most willingly decreed, by the authority of the holy Apostle Peter and by our own, that whatever he judged should be observed thereafter concerning his monasteries be confirmed.

Therefore we entrust to you, daughter Rothilda, and to your successors, the community of maidens which our aforesaid dearest brother the bishop built in its entirety, together with its appropriate buildings, on the slope of the mountain above the village called Buxerias. It is dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and is an alms of all Christians, to be protected, governed, and administered according to the rule of Saint Benedict and the institutions of the holy Fathers. Thus, by living religiously, may you acquire there the gain of souls for God and fulfill the appointed hours by day and by night.

But so that you may carry this out with cheerful minds, with the consent of all the faithful of the holy Roman See we grant you whatever that same bishop gave: namely, the church of Saint Martin with all its appurtenances, and whatever Saint Stephen is known to possess in that village. We also grant you the church of Sasiriac with all its dependencies, and the allod of Hersendis.

We further grant you the church which Bernard the primicerius, in the village of Giruni, in the county of Bedensis, on the River Meuse, bestowed upon the aforesaid place, together with everything belonging to it; and a certain vineyard which he likewise gave on Mount Barrisno, in the county of Toul. Whatever else has been given by that bishop in other places, or may in any way be given by others to the same place, you shall possess perpetually without any contradiction.

Finally, we beseech the glorious piety of the aforesaid prelate, since he does not know what will happen after him, not to grow cold in his mercy toward that place. We also solemnly charge all [lacuna], counts, abbots, and citizens of that region, both present and future, by the ineffable charity of God, to support the same place for the love of God, increase it by their donations, and preserve this our institution forever inviolate.

But all persons, whatever their order or rank, whoever they may be, who attempt to act against this privilege of apostolic institution, or oppress the monastery by their presence, injure its possessions, or prevent it from remaining at peace, we excommunicate until the day of judgment. Whoever may be its helpers, however, we decree to be absolved insofar as apostolic authority permits.

Each year, on the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, a candle weighing two pounds shall be paid to the bishop of the Leuci. In order that the provisions written in this privilege may meanwhile be preserved inviolate, we have ordered it to be confirmed below with our seal. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Stephen, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction. Given by the hand of Nicholas, primicerius of the Apostolic See, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Stephen, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter, first of the apostles, in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction.
